units.la: DEcretum Synodi sic se habet, vertente è Gallico in Latinum Sermonem D. Garissolio, in Ecclesia & Academia Montalbanensi Verbi Dei Ministro & SS. Theologiæ Professore.
units.tr: The Decree of the Synod reads as follows, translated from French into Latin by D. Garissolius, minister of the Word and professor of sacred theology in the Church and Academy of Montauban.

units.la: CVM relatum fuisset ad Synodum, scripta quædam, alia typis evulgata, alia manu exarata prodijsse, quæ totam rationem peccati originalis sola corruptione hæreditaria in omnibus hominibus inhærente definiunt, & primi peccati Adæ imputationem negant: Damnauit Synodus doctrinam ejusmodi, quatenus peccati Originalis naturam ad corruptionem hæreditaria tariam posterorum Adæ ita restringit, ut imputationem excludat primi illius peccati, quo lapsus est Adam: Adeoque censuris omnibus subijciendos censuit Pastores, Professores, & quoscumque alios, qui in hujus quæstionis disceptatione à communi sententia recesserint Ecclesiarum Protestantium, quæ omnes hactenus & Corruptionem illam, & Imputationem hanc in omnes Adami posteros descendentem agnouerunt. Sed & illud eadem Synodus omnibus Colloquijs & Synodis Prouincialibus iniungit, ut quos Theologiæ candidatos ad sacrum ministerium euehendos curauerint, ij iubeantur huic Decreto Chirographum suum subscribere.
units.tr: When it had been reported to the Synod that certain writings had appeared, some printed and others handwritten, which define the whole account of original sin solely as the hereditary corruption inhering in all men, and deny the imputation of Adam's first sin, the Synod condemned such doctrine insofar as it restricts the nature of original sin to the hereditary corruption of Adam's posterity in such a way as to exclude the imputation of that first sin by which Adam fell. Accordingly it decided that all ministers, professors, and any others who in the debate over this question depart from the common opinion of the Protestant Churches, which until now have all acknowledged both that corruption and this imputation descending upon all Adam's posterity, are to be subject to censures. The same Synod also enjoins on all colloquies and provincial synods that those whom they have seen to be advanced to the sacred ministry as candidates in theology be ordered to sign this Decree with their own hand.

units.la: HOC Decretum, etiam ab ipsis Synodis Prouincialibus, varie acceptum est. Quibusdam enim placuit illud executioni mandari: Alijs vero visum est judicium suum suspendere, illiusque Decreti executionem vsque ad alteram Synodum Nationalem suspendere. Fuere ex pastoribus & priuatis hominibus, qui illud vt necessarium, vt æquissimum, vt verissimum exscularentur: Non defuere contrà, qui illud, vt nouum, vt non necessarium, vt nimis festinanter, re haud satis pensitata, Synodisque Prouincialibus inconsultis factum, immo vt minus Dei verbo confentaneum reijcere auderent. Interim disseminatus est rumor per totam Galliam, isque etiam ad exteras nationes permanauit, eo Decreto damnatam fuisse Placci de imputatione primi
units.tr: This Decree was received in various ways, even by the provincial synods themselves. Some were pleased to have it put into execution; others thought fit to suspend their judgment and to defer the execution of the Decree until the next National Synod. There were pastors and private persons who welcomed it as necessary, most equitable, and most true. On the other hand, there were not lacking those who dared to reject it as new, unnecessary, made too hastily without sufficient weighing of the matter and without consulting the provincial synods, and even as less in accord with the Word of God. Meanwhile a rumour spread through the whole of France, and it also flowed out to foreign nations, that by this Decree the opinion of Placaeus on the imputation of Adam's first sin had been condemned.

units.tr: This Decree: the sentence beginning "Alijs vero" is printed as such; the initial H is a large woodcut-style initial.

units.la: Adæ peccati sententiam, quem illi, qui animo erant Academiæ Salmuriensi minùs beneuolo, auidè arripuerunt, famamque Placei tanquam ἱπεξαιρέσεως à Synodo Nationali conuicti & damnati, varijs cum sermonibus tum scriptis, imò libris typis excusis, expresseque etiam in quibusdam ejus nomine, dilacerarunt. Vnde natum est apud multos infirmos graue scandalum, & studiosorum SS. Theologiæ ingens perturbatio, magnum vulnus. Academiæ Salmuriensi illatura, nisi Synodi quædam Prouinciales medicinam adhibuissent in tempore. Placeus enim sibi in hac causa fere defuit, nihilquæ præter manuscriptum illud compositum, quod D. Garissolius Manuscriptum posterius appellauit. Nimirum bonâ conscientiâ & veritate, cujus Deus opportuno tempore vindex est, fretus, rem totam ejus prouidentiæ, & Synodo Nationali proximæ committendam putauit; hortantibusque amicis sese potius ad consutandos Socinianos, & diuinam Domini nostri Iesu Christi essentiam demonstrandam conuertit. Sed potuit mea quidem sententia vtrumque facere, & pro diuina Domini nostri natura propugnare, & famæ suæ Academiæque Salmuriensi, præsertim apud exteras gentes, libello aliquo edito consulere; Ac, nisi fallor, debuit: potuit enim explicatione sententiæ suæ omnem ab ea reprehensionis maculam abstergere, conseruata Decreti Synodici autoritate illibata: reuera enim cum eo non pugnat, immò congruit magis quàm eorum opinio, qui eam oppugnant; ac propterea vt videri posset & à Synodo damnata, & ab ipsis confutata, eam quia vel non intellexerunt vel intelligere noluerunt, adeò immutarunt, vt in oppositam transformauerint. Id quod nisi faciam luce meridiana clarius, non recufo quin pro mendace & calumniatore habear.
units.tr: which those who were less well disposed towards the Academy of Saumur eagerly seized upon, and they tore apart the reputation of Placaeus with various speeches, both spoken and written, and indeed with printed books, and expressly in some of them in his name, as one convicted and condemned of heresy [ἱπεξαιρέσεως] by the National Synod. From this there arose a grave scandal among many weak people, and a great disturbance and a great wound among students of sacred theology, which was about to inflict harm on the Academy of Saumur unless some provincial synods had applied a remedy in time. For Placaeus in this matter almost failed himself, and had nothing but that manuscript which he had composed, which D. Garissolius called the later manuscript. Trusting in a good conscience and in the truth, whose God is avenger at the opportune time, he thought the whole matter should be committed to God's providence and to the next National Synod; and, urged by friends, he turned himself rather to refuting the Socinians and demonstrating the divine essence of our Lord Jesus Christ. But in my opinion he could have done both: he could have defended the divine nature of our Lord, and by publishing some little book he could have consulted his own reputation and that of the Academy of Saumur, especially among foreign peoples. Unless I am mistaken, he ought to have done so. For by explaining his opinion he could have wiped away every stain of censure from it, while the authority of the Synod's Decree remained unimpaired. Indeed it does not conflict with that Decree; rather it agrees with it more than the opinion of those who oppose it. Therefore, so that it might appear both condemned by the Synod and refuted by them, they have so altered it, because they either did not understand it or were unwilling to, that they have transformed it into its opposite. Unless I make this clearer than the noonday light, I do not object to being held a liar and a slanderer.

units.la: Cùm igitur videam & Synodum Nationalem deanno in annum differri, cupientesque quasi fugere, ciuili bello quòminùs conuocari possit jam ab aliquot annis obstante, & interim quibusdam in locis seuerius cum SS. Theologiæ studiosis agi, & exteras gentes à libris Placei, tanquam ab hæretico autoritate Synodi nationalis damnato conscriptis, abhorrere, & permultos cognoscere quæ sit Placei sententia vehementer cupere: putaui me consulturum veritati & gloriæ Dei, ædificationi & paci Ecclesiæ, honori Synodi Nationalis, famæ Academiæ Salmurienfis & Placæi, consolationi studiosorum Theologiæ, necnon operis quod pro diuinitate Domini nostri Placeus inchoauit, continuationi, si ostendero, nec damnatam esse à Synodo Placei de imputatione primi Adæ peccati sententiam, nec eam talem esse, qualem hactenus plerique omnes sunt opinati. Ita, nisi vehementer fallor omnis ista de imputatione peccati Adamici controuersia, etiam antequam conueniat Synodus Nationalis, extinguetur, id quod à Domino nostro Iesu Christo, cujus ope fretus hoc opus aggredior, vehementer opto & spero.
units.tr: Since I see that the National Synod is being deferred from year to year, and, as if trying to escape, cannot be convened because civil war has for some years now stood in the way; and meanwhile in some places the students of sacred theology are treated more harshly, and foreign peoples shrink from the books of Placaeus as written by one condemned as a heretic by the authority of the National Synod, while very many earnestly desire to know what Placaeus's opinion is: I thought I would be serving the truth and the glory of God, the edification and peace of the Church, the honour of the National Synod, the reputation of the Academy of Saumur and of Placaeus, the consolation of the students of theology, and the continuation of the work which Placaeus began in defence of the divinity of our Lord, if I showed that Placaeus's opinion on the imputation of Adam's first sin was neither condemned by the Synod nor such as most people have hitherto supposed. Thus, unless I am gravely mistaken, this whole controversy about the imputation of Adam's sin will be extinguished even before the National Synod meets. This I earnestly wish and hope from our Lord Jesus Christ, by whose help I undertake this work.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Eo Decreto non esse damnatam Placei sententiam septem argumentis probabilibus ostenditur.
units.tr: By seven probable arguments it is shown that Placeus's opinion was not condemned by that Decree.

units.la: EO Decreto damnatam non esse Placei sententiam multis argumentis partim valde probabilibus, partim plane necessariis probare possum.
units.tr: BY that Decree I can prove that Placeus's opinion was not condemned, by many arguments, some highly probable and some plainly necessary.

units.la: Primum
units.tr: First.

units.la: Primùm enim de primi peccati, quo Adam lapsus est imputatione nullum ante Synodum illam Nationalem scriptum à Placeo prodierat, præter Theses de statu hominis lapsi ante gratiam disputatas publicè mense febr. An. 1640. quinquennio ante quàm illud Decretum fieret, eodemque anno ad eos omnes Pastores missas, qui in finitimis Prouincijs librorum edendorum examini præfecti erant: Atque etiam ipsi Synodo Pictonum, quæ eodem anno Castro eraldi habita est, oblatas Placei nomine à Clariss. ejus Collega D. Amyraldo ad eam Synodum ab Andum Prouincia delegato. De illis autem Thesibus toto illo quinquennio nemo litem Placeo mouerat, nemo eum accusauerat, neque causa ista vllo modo vel in Senatu Academiæ, vel in presbyterio Ecclesiæ, vel in Andum Synodo, cui ipse subest, vel (quantum ante Synodum illam Nationalem rescire potuit) in vlla alia Synodo agitata fuerat. Itaque sub Clypeo Art. xxxi. Cap. V. Disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ quam viginti septem Synodi nationales comprobauerant, necnon Decreti Synodi Nationalis Alençonij conuocatæ An. 1637. prohibentis ejusmodi de doctrina accusationes ad Nationalem immediatè deferri, ac jubentis ante & admoneri eum qui accusandus videretur, & causam in ea Synodo Prouinciali cui subijcitur cognosci & disceptari, securus dormiebat. Accusari enim se in Synodo Nationali non posse intelligebat, nisi violatis illis Decretis, quæ apud omnes Pastores & Synodos Prouinciales putabat sacro-sancta & inuiolata esse debere. Cùm igitur verisimile non sit tanta quemquam, præsertim Pastorem, cupiditate, ne dicam pruritu, Placeum, à quo nullo modo læsus fuerat, accusandi, vt maluerit iciens prudens, tam veneranda Decreta violare, quàm ab accusando sibi temperare, veriffimile etiam non est, Placeum fuisse à quoquam accusatum, qui fi non est accusatus, profecto damnatus non est.
units.tr: For, first, no writing by Placeus on the imputation of the first sin, by which Adam fell, had been published before that National Synod, except the Theses on the state of fallen man before grace, publicly disputed in February 1640, five years before that Decree was made. In that same year they were sent to all the ministers who were appointed to examine books for publication in the neighbouring provinces. They were also offered in Placeus's name to the Synod of Poitou, which was held at Châtellerault that year, by his distinguished colleague Mr. Amyraut, who had been sent to that Synod by the province of Anjou. Yet during all that five years no one had raised a complaint against Placeus over those Theses, no one had accused him, and the matter had not been discussed in any way, either in the Academic Senate, or in the consistory of the church, or in the Synod of Anjou to which he is subject, or (so far as he could learn before that National Synod) in any other Synod. Therefore, sheltered under Article xxxi, Chapter V, of the Discipline of the Church, which twenty-seven National Synods had approved, and under the Decree of the National Synod convened at Alençon in 1637, which forbade such accusations about doctrine to be brought directly before a National Synod, and ordered that the person who seemed liable to accusation be warned beforehand and that the case be examined and debated in the Provincial Synod to which he is subject, he slept securely. For he understood that he could not be accused in a National Synod unless those Decrees were violated, and he thought that these were to be regarded as sacred and inviolable by all ministers and Provincial Synods. Since, then, it is not likely that anyone, especially a minister, would be so eager, not to say itchy, to accuse Placeus, from whom he had suffered no harm whatever, that he would knowingly and deliberately prefer to violate such venerable Decrees rather than refrain from accusing him, it is also very unlikely that Placeus was accused by anyone. And if he was not accused, he has certainly not been condemned.

units.la: Frustra quis reponat, Aliquando contingere, vt necesfarijs de causis ab ordine smel constituto discedere debeant, qui ordinem posuerunt. Quinam enim ordinem illum posuerant? quinam Decreta illa condiderant? Synodi Nationales. Fuitne ergo Synodus Nationalis Placei accusatrix? Annon fi accusatus est, aut ab aliqua Synodo Prouinciali, aut ab aliquo Synodi Prouincialis delegato accusatus est, neutro ordinis illius autore, vtroque Synodi Nationalis autoritati & Decretis subjecto? Deinde qui ordinem posuerunt ab ordine semel prudenter constituto non discedunt nisi necessarijs de causis. Quænam igitur causæ necessariæ discedendi ab ordine tam sapienter instituto, & violandi Decreta tam æqua tamque necessaria fuerunt? frustra eas requiro. Nullæ apparent. Forte Succrescenti malo ita occurrendum fuit. Cui malo? Placei sententiæ? In ea duo: id quod credit, & id quod non credit. Quicquid credit, idipsum quicunque non sunt Pelagiani aut Semipelagiani crediderunt semper. Quod non credit, id neque vlla publica autoritate firmatum est vnquam, neque ab eo reijcitur, nisi quia nouum est, & à Dei verbo, à Doctrina Ecclesiarum protestantium, à recta ratione alienum. Itaque ab ea rejectione nihil fuit metuendum mali.
units.tr: Someone may vainly object: "It sometimes happens that, for necessary reasons, those who set up an order must depart from an order once established." But who had set up that order? Who had drawn up those Decrees? The National Synods. Was then the National Synod Placeus's accuser? Or, if he was accused, was he not accused either by some Provincial Synod or by some delegate of a Provincial Synod, neither of which was the author of that order, while both were subject to the authority and Decrees of the National Synod? Further, those who set up an order do not depart from an order once wisely established, except for necessary reasons. What, then, were the necessary reasons for departing from an order so wisely instituted, and for violating Decrees so fair and so necessary? I seek them in vain. None appear. Perhaps: "the growing evil had to be met in this way." What evil? The evil of Placeus's opinion? Two things are in it: what he believes, and what he does not believe. Whatever he believes, all who are not Pelagians or Semi-Pelagians have always believed. What he does not believe has never been confirmed by any public authority, and he rejects it only because it is new and foreign to God's Word, to the doctrine of the Protestant churches, and to sound reason. Therefore no evil was to be feared from that rejection.

units.la: Sed fac malum fuisse cui esset occurrendum. Num ei fuit ita occurrendum, vt violarentur illæ leges, illa decreta, quibus Synodi Nationales sapientissimè præscripserant, quomodo tali malo, si quando oriretur, esset occurrendum? Quid, quòd præpostera illa occurrendi ratio magis ad malum illud augendum, quàm ad tollendum, accommodata fuisset? Cum enim Deus fit Deus ordinis, & velit omnia fieri in Ecclesia fecundum ordinem & decenter, accusatio fratris à fratre ordinem in Ecclesia Dei recte constitutum violans probabilius perturbationi alicui humanae quàm Dei spiritui ascribi potuisset, & quantas Placeo opportunitates quaerendi, ac sententiam suam defendendi & propagandi attuliffet li vti occasione voluisset?
units.tr: But suppose there was an evil to be met. Was it to be met in such a way that those laws and decrees, by which the National Synods had most wisely prescribed how such an evil, should it arise, is to be met, were violated? And what of the fact that this perverse way of meeting it was better suited to increasing the evil than to removing it? For since God is a God of order, and wills all things to be done in the Church according to order and decently, an accusation of a brother by a brother, which violates an order rightly established in the Church of God, could more probably be ascribed to some human disturbance than to the Spirit of God. And how many opportunities would it have given Placeus to seek, defend and spread his opinion, if he had chosen to use the occasion!

units.la: Quaenam igitur tandem necessaria causa fuisset violandi ordinem tanta autoritate & sapientia politum? Respondebit forte aliquis, Exclusos fuisse per angustias temporis qui rem ad Synodum nationalem detulerunt, quominus postea constitutioni obtemperare possent. Scilicet per angustias quatuor aut quinque annorum non licuit accusatoribus expoltulationes suas ad Synodum Andum deferre. Sed enim Septembri demum mense habita est in Occitania superiori ea Synodus, in qua primum expositum est hoc negotium & vero proximo Decembri convocandus erat Carentonij nationalis conuentus: Esto. At primò cur expectata est illa Synodus Prouincialis Nationali proxima? Cur in praecedente aliqua expofitum non est hoc negotium? Excusari non potest thesium Placei in ea prouincia ignoratio. Nam & quinquennio ante, vt dixi, vulgatae fuerant, & missae ab ipso Placeo ad D. Delonum Ecclesiae Montalbanenfis Pastorem. Cur igitur tandiu dilata est Thesium illarum accusatio, siquidem sunt accusatae? Deinde cur saltem toto illo trimestri, quod inter Prouincialem illam Synodum & Nationalem interfluxit, fcriptum non est ad Placeum, vt saltem aliqua ex parte ordini fatisfieret. Cur non est admonitus de errore? Cur abeo petita non est clarior opinionis explicatio? Cur saltem de futura illa accusatione non est aliquid vel ad ipsum, vel ad Senatum Academicum,vel ad Ecclesiam Salmurienfem perscriptum aut aliqua alia ratione significatum? Potest enim sanctè iurare se nihil quicquam de futura illa accusatione inaudiuisse, nisi nescio quid ex incerto rumore, & quidem cum ferebatur Synodus nationalis aut jam soluta, aut mox soluenda. Nam neque antequam coiret, neque illa durante verbum vllum de futura illa accusatione à Synodi superioris Occitaniæ delegatis aut ad ipsum Placeum, aut ad ejus Collegas qui tum Salmurij erant, scriptum est. Quod quo pertinere potuisset, nisi vt Placeus absens, incautus, inscius accusaretur & opprimeretur? Id autem de Synodo illa Prouinciali, deque ejus legatis suspicari, nedum credere, nonne tibi, pie lector, religio est?
units.tr: What, then, could have been the necessary cause for violating an order so well founded in such great authority and wisdom? Perhaps someone will answer: "Those who brought the matter before the National Synod were prevented, by the shortness of time, from afterwards complying with the regulation." Certainly, by the shortness of four or five years they could not bring their complaints before the Synod of Anjou! But indeed the Synod of Upper Occitania was held in September, and it was there that this business was first set out, and the National Assembly at Charenton was to be convened the following December. Granted. But first, why was that Provincial Synod awaited, when it was next to the National one? Why was this business not set out in some earlier Synod? The ignorance of Placeus's Theses in that province cannot be excused. For they had been published five years before, as I said, and sent by Placeus himself to Mr. Delon, minister of the church of Montauban. Why, then, was the accusation of those Theses so long delayed, if indeed they were accused? Further, why at least during that three-month interval which lay between that Provincial Synod and the National one, was nothing written to Placeus, so that at least some part of the order might be satisfied? Why was he not warned of the error? Why was no clearer explanation of his opinion asked of him? Why was nothing at least written, or otherwise signified, about the future accusation, either to him, or to the Academic Senate, or to the church of Saumur? For one can truly swear that he had heard nothing of that future accusation, except some uncertain rumour about a something, and indeed when it was reported that the National Synod had either already dissolved or was about to dissolve. For neither before it met, nor while it was sitting, was any word about that future accusation written by the delegates of the Synod of Upper Occitania either to Placeus himself or to his colleagues who were then at Saumur. To what could this have led, except that Placeus, absent, unwary and unaware, should be accused and overwhelmed? But to suspect that of that Provincial Synod, and of its delegates, let alone to believe it, is it not a scruple to you, pious reader?

units.la: Huic argumento aliud non minus probabile subnectam. Si Placeus apud Synodum nationalem accusatus fuisset, nonne Synodus eum ad se vocari & citari curauisset? Quis enim eam voluisse credat, pastorem, profesforem Theologiæ, integræ eousque famæ, viuentem, absentem, inauditum, nec prius citatum, aut saltem de accusatione admonitum κακοδοξίας damnare, cum magno multorum infirmorum scandalo, ac misterij ipsius, necnon Academiæ cui inseruit damno? Atqui eum Synodus illa nullo modo, neque directè, neque indirectè citauit aut citari curauit, cùm tamen id per ordinarium tabellarium qualibet septimana bis terue fieri facillime posset.
units.tr: To this argument I add another, no less probable. If Placeus had been accused before the National Synod, would the Synod not have taken care to have him summoned and cited before it? For who would believe that the Synod wished to condemn for heterodoxy [κακοδοξίας] a minister and professor of theology, of unimpaired reputation until then, living, absent, not heard, and not previously cited or at least warned of the accusation, to the great scandal of many weak people and to the harm of his office itself and of the Academy to which he belongs? Yet that Synod in no way cited him, neither directly nor indirectly, nor took care to have him cited, although this could very easily have been done every week, twice or three times, by the ordinary courier.

units.la: Reponet forte aliquis, nihil opus citatione fuisse, quoniam in illo judicio non persona in discrimen, sed doctrina duntaxat ad examen vocabantur. Quid audio? Non vocabatur in discrimen pastoris & profefforis Theologiæ fama, quæ ipsi debet esse ipsa vita carior? Non vocabatur in discrimen ejus ministerium, cujus efficacitati obesse nihil magis potest, quàm si erroris momentofi in causa religionis damnatus à Synodo Nationali existimetur? Non subijciebatur ejus persona censuris omnibus, si quidem eo decreto ejus doctrina damnabatur? Non judicabatur pastoris & professoris Theologiæ munere priuandus, si quidem eo decreto studiosi Theologiæ ob eius errorem à sacro verbi Dei ministerio excludebantur?
units.tr: Someone may perhaps reply that there was no need for a citation, since "in that judgment it was not persons who were brought into danger, but only doctrine was called to examination." What is this I hear? Was not the reputation of a minister and professor of theology, which ought to be dearer to him than life itself, brought into danger? Was not his ministry brought into danger, a ministry whose effectiveness nothing can hinder more than if he is judged by a National Synod to hold an error of weight in a matter of religion? Was his person not subjected to all censures, since by that decree his doctrine was condemned? Was he not judged to be deprived of the office of minister and professor of theology, since by that decree students of theology were excluded from the sacred ministry of God's Word on account of his error?

units.la: Dicet forte etiam aliquis, ad fuisse inter omnes eximium, doctrina percelebrem & eloquentia, Placei Collegam, qui eius, quàm ipse, sententiam multò melius & eloquentius apud Synodum defenderet. Aderat is quidem, eiusque dotes Placeus & admiratur & colit, & in parte fœlicitatis suæ ponit talem habere Collegam. Sed neque cum eo de quæstione illa contulerat vnquam, neque aliam ab eo in Synodo defensionem sperabat, nisi vt, si accusaretur, intercederet, quominus absens & inauditus condemnaretur. Quare si Placei causam suscepit apud Synodum orandam, id præter Placei mentem euenit, eiusque in collegam beneuolentiæ ascribendum est, neque Synodum impedire debuit, quominus ipsum Placeum, si quidem nominatim accusabatur, citaret. Is enim, cùm ejusmodi accusationem ordini in Ecclesia constituto repugnantem diuinare, à nemine admonitus, non posset, neque sibi in Synodum veniendum putauerat, neque alium rogandum, vt pro se respondere, causamque suam apud Synodum tueri vellet. Porrò si eius causam Clarissimus Collega suscepit, cur coactus est defensor accufatoris loco, hoc est, primo verba facere? Cur deinde postquam accusator dixit, respondere objectaque argumenta & testimonia diluere defensori permissum non est? Quis vnquam audiuit rei accusati aduocatum (fi tamen aduocatus dicendus est qui, reo inscio & accusationis prorsus ignaro, causam eius suscipit) priorem orare debere, postquam autem accusator orauit, respondere non debere?
units.tr: Someone may perhaps also say that Placaeus had as colleague a man outstanding among all, highly renowned for learning and eloquence, who would have defended Placaeus's opinion before the Synod far better and more eloquently than he himself could. That colleague was present, and Placaeus both admires and honours his gifts and counts it part of his good fortune to have such a colleague. But he had never discussed that question with him, nor did he hope for any defence from him in the Synod, except that, if Placaeus were accused, the colleague would intercede so that he would not be condemned in his absence and unheard. So if the colleague did take up Placaeus's cause to plead before the Synod, this happened against Placaeus's intention and must be ascribed to the colleague's goodwill toward him. Nor ought the Synod to have been prevented from summoning Placaeus himself, if he was indeed accused by name. For Placaeus, who could not foresee, and no one had warned him of, an accusation so contrary to the order established in the Church, did not think he ought to come before the Synod, nor that he should ask someone else to answer for him and defend his cause before the Synod. Furthermore, if his most distinguished colleague took up his cause, why was he compelled to speak first, in the role of the accuser's advocate, that is, to open the proceedings? Then, after the accuser had spoken, why was the defender not permitted to answer and to refute the objections and testimonies brought against him? Who has ever heard that the advocate of an accused person (if indeed one may call an advocate someone who takes up the cause of a man without his knowledge and entirely ignorant of the accusation) must speak first, but once the accuser has spoken, must not reply?

units.la: Attamen ille solutâ subtilitate, solitoque sermonis fplendore coram venerando Consessu suam & ὁμοθνήσων caufampublicè per bihorium egit. Suamne egerit necne, ipse viderit. Placei certè causa tantillo spatio agi non potuit. Potest enim pro sua causa tot argumenta, tot teftimonia afferre, vt eis leuiter attingendis, nedum explicandis & ab exceptionibus vindicandis bihorium vix poffit sufficere. Immò nescit an vel unum argumentum possit tam breui tempore, vti par est, expendi acdiudicari. Solet enim ipse in vno argumento examinando non raro plures horas, immò dies ponere, sua ipsius experientia edoctus quod primo aspectu, aut leui adhibito examine verum apparet, nonnunquam tandem accuratius inspectum falsum esse cognosci. Sed pergamus, tertiumque addamus argumentum.
units.tr: Yet that man, with his accustomed subtlety and his usual brilliance of speech, pleaded his own cause, and the cause of the consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον], publicly for two hours before the venerable assembly. Whether he pleaded his own cause or not, let him judge for himself. Placaeus's cause certainly could not be handled in so small a space of time. For he can bring forward so many arguments and so many testimonies for his cause that merely touching on them lightly, let alone explaining them and vindicating them from objections, could scarcely be sufficient in two hours. Indeed, he does not know whether even one argument can be weighed and judged properly in so short a time. For in examining a single argument he himself often spends several hours, indeed days, taught by his own experience that what at first sight, or after a slight examination, appears true, is sometimes at last recognised as false when inspected more carefully. But let us proceed and add a third argument.

units.la: Nonne Theses Placei, fi accusatæ apud Synodum Nationalem fuissent, ei Synodo exhiberi, eaque audiente legi, & rationes omnes quibus opinionem suam Placeus breuissimè quidem, sed tamen, ut ipse putat, inuictè probauit, sigillatim & diligenter expendi debuiffent? Atqui id in ea Synodo factum non esse certiffimum est. Non fit igitur verisimile, fuisse, aut accusatas illas theses, aut saltem ita accusatas vt sint damnatæ. Enimuero cur damnatæ fuissent Theses
units.tr: Would not Placaeus's Theses, if they had been accused before the National Synod, have had to be presented to that Synod, read out in its hearing, and all the reasons by which Placaeus proved his opinion, very briefly but yet, as he himself thinks, invincibly, have had to be weighed one by one and carefully examined? But it is most certain that this was not done in that Synod. It is therefore not probable that either those Theses were accused, or at least that they were accused in such a way that they were condemned.

units.la: quæ fortiter communes aduersarios oppugnabant, vel expugnabant potius, Socinum, Pelagium, Pighium, cum separatim thesibus primis quindecim, tum coniunctim sequentibus?
units.tr: For why should Theses have been condemned which vigorously attacked, or rather overthrew, the common adversaries, Socinus, Pelagius and Pighius, both separately in the first fifteen theses and together in those that follow?

units.la: Succurrit etiam argumentum quartum. Nam si Synodus damnare Placei opinionem suo illo Decreto voluisset, num illa, qua erat prudentia, locis Scripturæ & argumentis, seu numerum, seu robur spectes haud quaquam contemnendis, quibus ille suam opinionem confirmauerat, contenta fuisset nudum Protestantium consensum, quasi oblita Art. V. Confessionis fidei, quam suo calculo ipsa recens comprobauerat, opponere, & tanquam regulam fidei ac fundamentum suo illi Decreto substernere? Hoc mihi quidem certè non fit verisimile.
units.tr: A fourth argument also comes to mind. For if the Synod had wished to condemn Placaeus's opinion by that Decree, would it have been content with the bare consensus of the Protestants, as if it had forgotten Article V of the Confession of Faith, which it had itself recently approved with its own vote, and had laid down that Confession as the rule of faith and foundation for that Decree? Surely this, at least, is not probable to me.

units.la: Sed neque mihi etiam verisimile videtur, Synodum prudentissimam, inconsultis Synodis Prouincialibus una sessione definire voluisse controuersiam momentosam, in nulla vnquam alia Synodo antea agitatam, aut decisam. Id enim cum experientia periculosum esse docuit, tum abhorret à consuetudine Synodorum nationolium, quæ de rebus longè minoris momenti pronunciare tutum sæpè non censuerunt, nisi confultis prius omnibus prouincijs: adeò vereri solent, ne vel potestate sua abutantur, vel eâ cum cuiusquam infirmi scandalo minùs circumspectè vtantur. Attamen id fecit, si Placei sententiam suo illo decreto damnauit. Nam neque prouincias consuluit, & vna Sessione res confecta est, & ea peccati Adamici imputatio, quam Placeus thesibus suis rejecerat (non enim omnem rejecerat) nulla vnquam Synodo, nulla vnquam publica autoritate fuerat confirmata. Quis igi-
units.tr: But nor does it seem probable to me that the most prudent Synod, without consulting the Provincial Synods, would have wished to settle in a single session a controversy of such weight, never before debated or decided in any other Synod. For experience has taught that this is dangerous, and it is contrary to the custom of National Synods, which have often judged it unsafe to pronounce even on matters of far less importance without first consulting all the provinces; so careful are they lest they abuse their power or use it too carelessly to the scandal of some weak person. Yet the Synod did this, if it condemned Placaeus's opinion by that decree. For it neither consulted the provinces, and the matter was finished in one session, and that imputation of Adam's sin, which Placaeus rejected in his Theses (though not every imputation), had never been confirmed by any Synod, by any public authority. Who then

units.la: [no footnote] tur credat sapientissimam Synodum talem imputationem tanta cum festinatione definire voluisse, atque ad eam credendam & docendam omnes Synodos Prouinciales, omnia colloquia, omnes Pastores & Professores, omnes sacri Ministerij candidatos, omnium censurarum metu incusso obligare?
units.tr: would believe that the most wise Synod wished to settle such an imputation with such haste, and by inspiring the fear of every kind of censure, to bind all the Provincial Synods, all the colloquies, all the ministers and teachers, and all the candidates for the sacred ministry, to believe and teach it?

units.la: An etiam ille ipse qui Placeum accusasset, accusatoris partes strenuè egisset oratione praemeditata, magno apparatu, multa eloquentia, magna vehementia, calens adhuc ab illa accusatione, ac sanguine commoto, nulla responsione, nulla mora interposita, Iudex inilla causa sedisset, praesesque sententias rogasset? Num id passura fuisset æquissima Synodus, si in eo judicio de doctrina, de fama Pastoris & professoris Theologiæ actum fuisset, praesertim absentis, nec citati, nec ulla unquam censura notati? id certè non est verisimile.
units.tr: Or would that very man who had accused Placaeus have played the part of accuser so vigorously, with a prepared speech, with great display, much eloquence and great vehemence, still glowing from that accusation and with his blood stirred, while no answer was given and no delay interposed, and would the judge in such a case have sat and asked the judges for their sentences? Would the most equitable Synod have permitted this, if the judgment concerned the doctrine and reputation of a minister and professor of theology, especially of one absent, not summoned, and never marked by any censure? This is certainly not probable.

units.la: Multum abest Placeus ut probet, vel imitari velit morositatem Remonstrantium coram Synodo Nationali respondere detrectantium, magnamque ex ea parte delegatorum submoueri postulantium. Nam si etiam apud infensissimos iudices ratio fidei nostrae reddi potest & debet, & ab ipso Christo, eiusque Apostolis & martyribus reddita est, quanto magis apud Synodum ex fratribus constantem ac legitima magistratus autoritate convocatam reddi potest & debet? Si qui Remonstrantes ante accusauerant, aut sententiam suam declarauerant, illi censendi erant sumpta delegatorum ad Synodum Nationalem persona, atque religione iurisiurandi interposita, affectus & praeiudicia posuisse. Illud unum vrget Placeus, quod est ab illa ipsa Synodo Dordrachtena fandè affirmatum, Neminem posse in judicio eodem, ejusdemque causa defenso-rem
units.tr: Placaeus is far from proving, or wishing to imitate, the obstinacy of the Remonstrants, who refused to answer before the National Synod and demanded that a large part of the delegates be removed. For if the reason of our faith can and must be given even before the most hostile judges, and was given by Christ himself, his Apostles and martyrs, how much more can and must it be given before a Synod, made up of brethren and convened by the lawful authority of the magistrate? If any Remonstrants had previously accused or declared their opinion, they were to be regarded as having, in the role of delegates to the National Synod and under the bond of an oath, set aside their feelings and prejudices. Placaeus presses only this one point, which was asserted by that very Synod of Dort, that no one can be, in the same trial, both judge and defender of the same cause.

units.la: Num etiam Synodus illa prudentissima Placeum, si quidem eum erroris momento damnatum voluisset, fuisset, vt antea, & SS. Ministerio in Ecclesia, & S. Theologiæ professione in Academia Salmuriensi fungi, nulla adhibita vel ob præteritum censura, vel in futurum cautione? Non curauissēt eum ab aliquo Pastore de errore priuatim aut publice admoneri, vt ab eo, si fieri posset, reuocaretur? Non iussisset saltem Andum Synodum cum eo agere, ne pergeret turbare Ecclesiam Dei? An etiam putasset Synodus sua vnius autoritate metienda esse Religionis dogmata, & adducta à Placeo Scripturæ loca & argumenta præponderari? Absit vt de ea id credamus, quod in Ecclesia Romana, vt tyrannicum, ab omnibus Protestantibus tantopere damnatur. Ipse sibi Placeus indignus videretur qui pro reformato haberetur; si pluris faceret vnius Synodi nudam autoritatem quàm Scripturam & deprompta ex Scriptura argumenta, quamdiu ei apparent insolubilia. Dedisset igitur certè operam Synodus, vt ab aliquo, cum argumenta Placei soluerentur, tum ea, quibus mota Synodus Placei sententiam damnauisset, exponerentur, vt & iudicii sui æquitas pateret & conscientias patefactione veritatis potius persuadere quàm fidei dominari videretur. Quandoquidem igitur nemo eorum qui Synodo illi interfuerunt, ne-mo eorum iussu vel hortatu vllum cum Placeo verbum siue viua voce, siue scripto habuit, quo eum à sententia dimouēret, aut eius argumenta diluerēt, aut con-trariā proponeret, annon eo satis aperte significatum est, non esse Decreto illo Synodali Placeum damna-tum?
units.tr: Again, if that most prudent Synod had wished to condemn Placaeus as holding an error of weight, would it have allowed him, as before, to exercise both the sacred ministry in the Church and the professorship of theology in the Academy of Saumur, without any censure, either for the past or any caution for the future? Would it not have taken care that he be admonished of his error by some minister, privately or publicly, so that, if possible, he might be brought to retract it? Would it not at least have bidden the Synod to deal with him, so that he would not go on disturbing the Church of God? Or would the Synod have thought that the doctrines of religion must be measured by its own authority alone, and that the Scripture passages and arguments brought forward by Placaeus must be outweighed? God forbid that we should believe of it what is so widely condemned by all Protestants as tyrannical in the Roman Church. Placaeus himself would seem unworthy to be regarded as a reformed man, if he set more store by the bare authority of one Synod than by Scripture and the arguments drawn from Scripture, so long as these appear to him insoluble. The Synod would therefore certainly have taken pains that someone should resolve Placaeus's arguments, and then set out those on which the Synod, moved by them, had condemned Placaeus's opinion, so that both the equity of its judgment might be plain and it might seem to persuade consciences by the manifestation of truth rather than to rule over faith. Since, then, none of those who were present at that Synod, none of them by order or exhortation, ever spoke a single word with Placaeus, either face to face or in writing, to turn him from his opinion, or to refute his arguments, or to propose the contrary, is it not sufficiently clear from this that Placaeus was not condemned by that Synodal Decree?

units.la: C
units.tr: C

units.la: Huc accedit quod Placei nomen abest à Decreto, cur, fi Placei nominatim accusati doctrina damnabatur? Aut enim damnasse Placei sententiam Synodus videri voluit, aut noluit. Si voluit: cur eius nomen non expressit? Si noluit, à Synodi mente illi abeunt, quibus eam damnasse videtur.
units.tr: To this is added that Placaeus's name is absent from the Decree. Why, if the doctrine of Placaeus, accused by name, was being condemned? For either the Synod wished to be seen as condemning Placaeus's opinion, or it did not wish this. If it wished it, why did it not express his name? If it did not wish it, then those things by which it seems to have condemned it depart from the Synod's intention.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Idem probatur argumentis necessarijs.
units.tr: The same is proved by necessary arguments.

units.la: SVperiora argumenta, vt ego arbitror, valde probabilia fuerunt sequuntur necessaria. Primùm enim qui damnari sententia Placei in ea Synodo potuit, in qua non est proposita vel exposita? Atqui non est in illa Synodo nationali exposita quae fecit illud decretum. A quo enim fuisset exposita, nisi ab eo, à quo fuisset accusata? Si quis autem eam accusauit apud Synodum, is fuit D. Gariffolius Synodi illius praeses. Is autem quomodo eam vti est exponere tunc potuisset, qui, ne quidem quadriennio post, eam qualis est proponere potuit? Certè in sua Decreti Synodici explicatione & defensione is Placeo sententiam tribuit, quam Placeus non agnoscit, quaeque cum illis verbis aperte pugnat quibus mentem suam Placeus exposuerat cum datis ad eum literis, tum in eo manuscripto quod ei posterius appellare placuit, vt suo loco faciam sole meridiano clarius.
units.tr: The preceding arguments, as I judge, were very probable; the following are necessary. For first, how could anyone have been condemned by that Synod on the basis of Placeus' opinion, when it was not set out or explained in it? Yet it was not explained in that national Synod which made the decree. For by whom would it have been explained, unless by him by whom it was accused? If anyone accused it before the Synod, that was Mr. Gariffolius, president of that Synod. But how could he then have explained it as it really is, when not even four years later he has been able to set it forth as it is? Certainly, in his explanation and defence of the Synodal Decree, he attributes to Placeus an opinion which Placeus does not acknowledge, and which openly contradicts the words in which Placeus had set out his mind, both in the letters sent to him and in that manuscript which he afterwards chose to publish, as I shall make clearer than the midday sun in its place.

units.la: Ad hoc argumentum aliud accedat ex eo ductum quod ad fe relatum fuisse Synodus ipsa testatur. Cum relatum, inquit, fuisset ad Synodum scripta quaedam, alia typis euulgata, alia manu exarata prodiisse, qua totam rationem peccati originalis sola corruptione hereditaria in omnibus hominibus inhaerente definiunt, & primi peccati Adae imputationem negant. Illis enim verbis aut expositá non est Placei sententia, aut male exposita est. Is enim primi peccati Adae imputationem nunquam simpliciter negauit, nunquam negatam voluit. Negauit tantum certam quandam peccati illius imputationem. Cum igitur imputationem primi illius peccati quandam affirmet, quandam neget non exponitur eius sententia, si dicitur simpliciter & nulla distinctione adhibita primi peccati Adae imputationem negare.
units.tr: To this argument another may be added, drawn from what the Synod itself testifies was referred to it. "When," it says, "certain writings had been referred to the Synod, some published in print, others having appeared in handwritten form, which define the whole account of original sin by hereditary corruption alone inhering in all men, and deny the imputation of Adam's first sin." For by these words either Placeus' opinion was not set out, or it was set out badly. For he never simply denied the imputation of Adam's first sin, nor ever wished it denied. He denied only a certain particular imputation of that sin. Since therefore he affirms one imputation of that first sin and denies another, his opinion is not set out if it is said simply, and without any distinction, that he denies the imputation of Adam's first sin.

units.la: Tertium argumentum nobis suppeditat Synodi sententia damnatoria, Damnat Synodus doctrinam eiusmodi, quatenus peccati originalis naturam ad corruptionem hereditariam posterorum Adae ita restringit, vt imputationem excludat primi illius peccati quo lapsus est Adam. Illis enim verbis non damnat Synodus simpliciter eos, qui peccati originalis naturam ad corruptionem hæreditariam restringunt, sed qui ita restringunt vt excludat imputationem primi illius peccati quo lapsus est Adam. Atqui Placeus nunquam peccati originalis naturam ad illam corruptionem ita restrinxit, vt imputationem excluderet primi illius peccati quo lapsus est Adam. Placeus igitur non est Synodi sententia damnatus.
units.tr: The third argument is supplied by the Synod's condemnatory sentence: "The Synod condemns a doctrine of this kind, insofar as it restricts the nature of original sin to the hereditary corruption of Adam's posterity in such a way as to exclude the imputation of that first sin by which Adam fell." For by these words the Synod does not simply condemn those who restrict the nature of original sin to hereditary corruption, but those who so restrict it as to exclude the imputation of that first sin by which Adam fell. But Placeus never restricted the nature of original sin to that corruption in such a way as to exclude the imputation of that first sin by which Adam fell. Therefore Placeus has not been condemned by the Synod's sentence.

units.la: Hoc confirmant verba quibus Clar. D. Gariffolius in Epistola sua dedicatoria ad Ecclesiarum & Academiarum Tigurinae, Bernensis, Basileensis, Scaphusianae praesides sententiam Synodi expressit pag. 13, ait enim Synodi consultum factum esse, quo eorum sententia condemnatur, qui rationem originalis peccati in sola natiua corruptione ita constituunt, vt nulla ipsius Adami inobedientia, imputationem agnoscant. Atqui Placeus rationem originalis peccati in sola natiua corruptione non ita constituit, vt nullam primæ Adami inobedientiæ imputationem agnoscat: agnoscit enim aliquam. Cum igitur nullam agnoscere, & aliquam agnoscere, contradictorie opponantur, perspicuum est eo Synodi confulto Placei sententiam non esse damnatam.
units.tr: The words of Mr. Gariffolius in his dedicatory epistle, addressed to the presidents of the Churches and Academies of Zurich, Bern, Basel and Schaffhausen, confirm this, where at page 13 he expresses the Synod's sentence. For he says that a consultation was made by the Synod, by which the opinion is condemned of those who so constitute the account of original sin in native corruption alone that they acknowledge no imputation of Adam's own disobedience. But Placeus does not so constitute the account of original sin in native corruption alone as to acknowledge no imputation of Adam's first disobedience: for he acknowledges some. Since therefore to acknowledge none and to acknowledge some are contradictory opposites, it is clear that by that consultation of the Synod Placeus' opinion was not condemned.

units.la: Idem etiam sonant verba Exscripti ex actis Synodi Montalbani habitæ Octobri mense Ann. 1645. quod D. Gariffolius libro suo præmisit. Perlectum est Decretum Synodi Nationalis Carentonensis, quo eorum doctrina damnatur, qui primum Adæ peccatum docent posteris nequaquam imputari. Atqui Placeus non docet primum Adæ peccatum posteris nequaquam imputari. Immo contrà docet imputari, imputatione nimirum mediata seu consequente, quam ipse Dominus Gariffolius fatetur se agnoscere. Doctrina igitur Placei non est eo Decreto damnata.
units.tr: The words of the extract from the acts of the Synod of Montauban, held in October 1645, which Mr. Gariffolius prefixed to his book, say the same: "The decree of the National Synod of Charenton was read, by which the doctrine of those is condemned who teach that the first sin of Adam is in no way imputed to his posterity." But Placeus does not teach that the first sin of Adam is in no way imputed to posterity. On the contrary, he teaches that it is imputed, namely by mediate or consequent imputation, which Mr. Gariffolius himself confesses he acknowledges. Therefore Placeus' doctrine is not condemned by that decree.

units.la: Hoc ipsum ex Synodi Nationalis testimonio colligi potest. Testatur enim omnes Ecclesias Protestantes & corruptionem illam, & imputationem hanc in omnes Adami posteros descendentem agnouisse. Id quod de illa imputatione primæ Adami inobedientiæ quam Placeus credit & docet, vere dicitur: de illa vero quam negat, non item. Vnde enim sciri potest Ecclesiarum Protestantium sententia, nisi aut ex fidei confessionibus, aut ex decretis Synodicis, aut ex eorum libris quorum opera Deus vsus est ad reformandam Ecclesiam suam? Atqui ex ejusmodi Confessionibus, Decretis, & libris nulla imputatio vniuersaliter agnita colligi potest, præterea vnam, quam Placeus agnoscit. Hanc igitur vnam qui negant, eos, non autem Placeum, Synodus damnat.
units.tr: This very thing can be gathered from the testimony of the National Synod. For it testifies that "all the Protestant Churches have acknowledged both that corruption and this imputation descending upon all of Adam's posterity." This is truly said of that imputation of Adam's first disobedience which Placeus believes and teaches, but not likewise of that which he denies. For whence can the opinion of the Protestant Churches be known, except from their confessions of faith, their synodal decrees, or the books of those through whose labour God was pleased to reform his Church? But from such confessions, decrees and books no imputation universally acknowledged can be gathered, except the one which Placeus acknowledges. Therefore it is those who deny this one, and not Placeus, whom the Synod condemns.

units.la: Praeterea Synodus omnes Pastores & Professores Imputationem hanc de qua loquitur negantes omnibus censuris subijciendos censet, quo significat se talem imputationem intelligere, quae sit dogma religionis momento sum, & creditu necessarium. Id quod de imputatione quam placeus negat vere dici non potest sed de ea tantum quam ille probat, & confitetur.
units.tr: Moreover, the Synod judges that all ministers and teachers who deny this imputation of which it speaks are to be subjected to all censures, which signifies that it understands such an imputation as is a dogma of religion of the greatest moment and necessary to be believed. This cannot truly be said of the imputation which Placeus denies, but only of that which he proves and confesses.

units.la: Denique Synodus non obscure innuit, illam imputatione primi Adae peccati, quam vult agnosci, tam aperte veram esse, vt probatione non egeat. Eo enim pertinere arbitror, quod eam nullo Scripturae testimonio, nulla ratione firmandam sibi censuit. Id autem in illam imputationem, quam Placeus agnoscit, competit, in eam vero quam negat, nullo modo. Quam enim illa necessario & evidenter vera videtur, tam ista diligenter inspicienti ne probabilis quidem apparet.
units.tr: Finally, the Synod not obscurely hints that the imputation of Adam's first sin which it wishes to be acknowledged is so plainly true that it needs no proof. For I judge this is what it means by judging that it was not to be confirmed by any testimony of Scripture or by any reasoning. Now this applies to the imputation which Placeus acknowledges, but in no way to that which he denies. For what seems necessarily and evidently true, that latter imputation does not even appear probable when examined carefully.

units.la: CAPVT IV. Decretum Synodi atque adeo Placei sententia, exponitur.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV. The decree of the Synod, and Placeus's opinion, is set out.

units.la: SED vt res fiat clarior, nullusque in animo lectoris scrupulus haereat, Decretum paucis exponendum est, quidque revera Placeus sentiat aperiendum. Pendet autem id totum ex duabus distinctionibus, vna primi Adae peccati, altera imputationis illius. Et primum quidem Adae peccatum distingui potest in primum peccatum actuale, & primum peccatum habituale. Illud fuit actio inobedientiae Adami quae transfijt, hoc fuit ab illa actione productum vitium; quod instar habitus in Adamo permansit, & ab eo vna cum natura humana propagatum est in omnes eius posteros, vno Christo excepto. Hoc vitium vere peccatum esse omnes, quicunque Pelagiani non sunt, agnoscunt. Imputari etiam Adae posteris, & damnandi vim habere, nisi condonetur, omnes Ecclesiae Protestantes hactenus summo consensu crediderunt, vt ex eorum patet Confessionibus. Itaque si de huius primi Adae peccati imputatione Decretum Synodi accipitur, id pro verissimo aequissimoque habet Placeus, meritoque damnatam eorum doctrinam censet, qui hoc quidem peccatum se agnoscere profitentur, nulli tamen imputari, quantumuis infideli, contendunt. Esse enim hoc seculo qui id doceant, & quidem editis libris, testis est Doctiff. V. Valaeus Theologiae Lugduni Batauorum dum viueret Profeffor, Epist. antep. ad Henricum Flokenium Bremam scripta.
units.tr: But so that the matter may become clearer and no doubt may remain in the reader's mind, the Decree must be explained briefly, and what Placeus actually holds must be made plain. The whole question depends on two distinctions, one concerning the first sin of Adam and the other concerning the imputation of that sin. First, Adam's first sin may be distinguished into the first actual sin and the first habitual sin. The former was the act of Adam's disobedience, which passed away; the latter was the corruption produced by that act, which remained in Adam as a kind of habit and was propagated from him, together with human nature, to all his posterity, except Christ alone. All who are not Pelagians acknowledge that this corruption is truly sin. All the Protestant Churches have hitherto agreed, as their Confessions show, that this sin is imputed to Adam's posterity and has the power to condemn them unless it is forgiven. Therefore, if the Decree of the Synod is understood of the imputation of this first habitual sin, Placeus holds it to be wholly true and just, and he rightly judges condemned the doctrine of those who profess that they acknowledge this sin but contend that it is imputed to no one, however unbelieving. That there are people in this age who teach this, and in print, is attested by the most learned V. Valaeus, while he lived as Professor of Theology at Leiden, in his penultimate letter written to Henricus Flokenius at Bremen.

units.la: Sin vero per primum Adae peccatum, primum eius peccatum actuale intelligitur, (id quod mihi verisimilius videtur: nam & illud omnium absolute primum fuit, & eo magis proprie lapsus esse Adam dicitur, quam primo suo peccato habituali) distinguenda est imputatio in Imputationem immediatam seu antecedentem, & imputationem mediatam seu consequentem. Illa fit immediate; hoc est, non mediante corruptione, haec fit mediate, hoc est, mediante corruptione haereditaria. Illa ordine naturae corruptionem antecedit; haec sequitur. Illa corruptionis causa censetur esse, haec effectum. Illam Placeus reijcit; hanc admittit.
units.tr: But if by Adam's first sin is understood his first actual sin (which seems to me more probable, for that was absolutely the first of all his sins, and Adam is said to have fallen more properly by it than by his first habitual sin), then the imputation must be distinguished into immediate or antecedent imputation and mediate or consequent imputation. The former takes place immediately, that is, without the mediation of corruption; the latter takes place mediately, that is, through the mediation of hereditary corruption. The former precedes corruption in the order of nature; the latter follows it. The former is held to be the cause of corruption, the latter its effect. Placeus rejects the former and admits the latter.

units.la: Quaeritur nunc an fuerit eius sententia Synodi Decreto damnata? Si damnata est, ideo damnata est vel quia vtramque illam imputationem confundtim non admittit, vel quia imputationem immediatam seu antecedentem reijcit. Primum dici non potest. Coniunctim enim admitti non possunt absque contradictionis implicatione. Nam qui dicit primum peccatum actuale Adami eius posteris imputari immediate, is negat imputari mediate: idem enim immediate significat ac non mediate. Imputari igitur immediate, & imputari non mediante corruptione idem plane sunt. Qui igitur affirmaret simul imputari primum illud peccatum immediate & mediate, is simul & negaret mediante corruptione imputari & affirmaret, seqeque adeo contradictione implicaret. Id quod sine dubio à nobis exigere Synodus noluit. Taceo non esse æquitati consentaneum, vt idem numero peccatum eidem bis imputetur, semel ante corruptionem hæreditariam, & iterum post illam corruptionem. Vna certè imputatio sufficit.
units.tr: It is now asked whether his opinion was condemned by the Decree of the Synod. If it was condemned, it was condemned either because it refuses to admit both of those imputations together, or because it rejects the immediate or antecedent imputation. The first cannot be said. For they cannot be admitted together without involving a contradiction. For whoever says that Adam's first actual sin is imputed to his posterity immediately, denies that it is imputed mediately, since "immediately" means the same as "not mediately". Therefore to be imputed immediately and to be imputed without the mediation of corruption are plainly the same. Whoever therefore affirmed that this first sin is imputed at once immediately and mediately would at once deny that it is imputed through the mediation of corruption and affirm it, and so would involve himself in contradiction. This the Synod undoubtedly did not wish to demand of us. I say nothing of the fact that it is not consistent with fairness that the same sin, numerically one, should be imputed twice to the same person, once before hereditary corruption and again after that corruption. At any rate one imputation is enough.

units.la: Quandoquidem igitur ambæ illæ imputationes simul retineri nequeunt, alteraque eligenda est repudiata altera, vel Synodus in dubio reliquit quam intellexerit, mediatam an immediatam; vel id non reliquit in dubio. Si prius, etiam in dubio reliquit, vtrum Placei sententiam Decreto suo condemnauerit, necne. Quare decet illius Lectores suum de Placeo iudicium suspendere, neque eum magis damnatum, quàm indemnatum existimare.
units.tr: Since, then, both those imputations cannot be retained together, and one of them must be chosen while the other is rejected, either the Synod left in doubt which of the two it meant, the mediate or the immediate; or it did not leave this in doubt. If the former, then it also left in doubt whether it condemned Placeus's opinion by its Decree or not. Therefore the readers of Placeus ought to suspend their judgment about him, and to regard him neither as more condemned nor as uncondemned.

units.la: Sin est aliquid in Decreto quod imputationem determinet. Si damnatur eorum doctrina qui negant imputationem mediatam, non damnatur Placei doctrina. Is enim imputationem mediatam agnoscit. Si damnatur eorum doctrina qui negant imputationem immediatam, damnatur quidem Placei sententia; sed absit vt damnetur, Damnaretur enim cum ea ipsius Apostoli Pauli doctrina, testibus magnis viris.
units.tr: But if there is something in the Decree that determines the imputation, then: if the doctrine of those who deny mediate imputation is condemned, Placeus's doctrine is not condemned, for he acknowledges mediate imputation. If the doctrine of those who deny immediate imputation is condemned, then indeed Placeus's opinion is condemned; but far be it that it should be condemned, for the doctrine of the Apostle Paul himself would then be condemned along with it, as great men bear witness.

units.la: Videbiturne tibi lector testis idoneus Ægidius Hunnius Augustanæ Confessionis Theologus celebris? En eius testimonium Art. de peccat. Ostendit ergo (Apostolus Paulus) lapsum Adami NON IMMEDIATE & per se, sed MEDIATE & propter aliud nobis eius posteris IMPVTARI, quia videlicet per lapsum illum polluta est natura primorum parentum, vt non nisi peccato corruptos & vitiatos liberos procreare possent, sicut scriptum est, Genuit Adam filium ad imaginem suam Gen. 5. Alias sifieri potuisset vt in posteros non vitium proprium deriuaretur a primis parentibus, tum lapsus ille, tanquam peccatum alienum, eis plane non imputaretur. Palam igitur ostendit Paulus vnum illud delictum nobis ad condemnationem cedere TANTVM MEDIATE, quatenus per delictum illud actuale introducta est in naturam horribilis corruptio, quam per carnalem generationem propagauit in ipsos posteros. Ita vt a lapsu corruptio naturæ, a corruptione naturæ in nos deriuata mors & damnatio peruenit, quatenus omnes peccauimus, inquit, id est, quatenus ipsi in possessionem illius hereditariam deuenimus.
units.tr: Will the learned Aegidius Hunnius, the celebrated theologian of the Augsburg Confession, seem to you a fit witness? Here is his testimony in the article on sin: Therefore the Apostle Paul shows that the fall of Adam is imputed to us, his posterity, NOT IMMEDIATELY and of itself, but MEDIATELY and on account of something else, because, namely, through that fall the nature of our first parents was so polluted that they could beget children only corrupted and vitiated by sin, as it is written, "Adam begat a son in his own image" (Gen. 5). Otherwise it could have happened that no proper vice was derived from the first parents into their posterity, and then that fall, as another's sin, would not be imputed to them at all. Paul therefore plainly shows that this one offence falls to our condemnation ONLY MEDIATELY, insofar as through that actual offence a horrible corruption was introduced into nature, which it propagated by carnal generation into the posterity itself. So that from the fall comes the corruption of nature, and from the corruption of nature derived into us comes death and condemnation, insofar as, he says, "all have sinned", that is, insofar as we ourselves have come into the hereditary possession of that corruption.

units.la: Potuitne clarius vel difertius testimonium desiderari? habes in eo distinctionem imputationis primi peccati actualis Adæ in mediatam & immediatam, illam assertam, hanc reiectam, eamque doctrinam Apostolum Paulum palam docuisse.
units.tr: Could a clearer or more explicit testimony be desired? In it you have the distinction of the imputation of Adam's first actual sin into mediate and immediate, the former affirmed, the latter rejected, and the Apostle Paul openly teaching this doctrine.

units.la: Sed fortasse aliter sentiebant reliqui Protestantes. Audi igitur etiam Caluinum Commentarium in Rom. cap. 5. verf. 12. Quod vnius delicto periisse nos, tradit, sic accipe: quia ex ipso in nos corruptio transfusa fuit. Neque enim sic perimus eius culpa, quasi extra culpam ipsi simus: sed quia eius peccatum peccati nostri causa est, exitium nostrum illi Paulus adscribit. Peccatum nostrum voco, quod nobis ingenitum est & cum quo nascimur. Alia Caluini loca hic non proferam; Quid enim ille senserit testem habeo locupletem D. Garissolium, De Imp. primi pecc. cap. 1 x. §. x 1. pag. 299. Quantumuis, inquit, lapsus primi reatus ad nos NON peruenit NISI MEDIANTE CORRVPTIONE, QVOD CVM-CALVINO AGNOSCIMVS; & superius expositum est, illud tamen obstare non potest, quominus reatus ille sit non tantum corruptionis nostrae, sed & primi actualis Adae peccati reatus, nempe illius, est immediate, huius mediate. Hæc est ipsissima Placei sententia; quæ si damnata est, etiam Apostoli Pauli, etiam Ægidij Hunnij & Caluini, immo ipsius D. Garissolij (li suam ipse sententiam verbis illis fideliter expressit) doctrina damnata est.
units.tr: But perhaps the other Protestants thought otherwise. Hear then also Calvin, in his Commentary on Romans 5, verse 12: Take it thus, what he says, that we perished by the offence of one: because corruption was poured into us from him. For we do not perish by his fault as if we were outside the fault ourselves; but because his sin is the cause of our sin, Paul ascribes our ruin to him. I call it our sin, which is innate in us and with which we are born. I will not produce other passages of Calvin here; for I have a sufficient witness of what he thought in the venerable Garissolius, On the Imputation of the First Sin, chapter 10, §11, page 299: However, he says, the guilt of the first fall does NOT reach us EXCEPT THROUGH THE MEDIATION OF CORRUPTION, WHICH WE ACKNOWLEDGE ALONG WITH CALVIN; and it has been set out above; yet that cannot prevent that guilt from being not only the guilt of our corruption but also the guilt of Adam's first actual sin, namely, that of the former immediately and that of the latter mediately. This is the very opinion of Placeus; and if it has been condemned, then the doctrine of the Apostle Paul, of Aegidius Hunnius, and of Calvin has been condemned, and indeed that of the venerable Garissolius himself, who expressed his own opinion faithfully in those words.

units.la: Idem D. Garissolius eodem lib. cap. v iii. §. iii. pag. 206. testatur imputationem de qua agitur Rom.5. Necessario cum corruptione natiua coniungi, imo EAM SEQVI. Si eam sequitur, imputatio est consequens seu mediata, quam cum Apostolo Placeus docet. Si eam sequitur, igitur eam non præcedit: Si corruptione natiua posterior est, igitur eadem corruptione prior non est. Idem etiam eodem libro cap. 27. §. 30. ait actuali imputationi peccati Adæ præcurrere feminis corruptionem, adeoque vitiositatem inhærentem, tanquam conditionem & causam sine qua non. Potuitne clarius imputationem consequentem seu mediatam docere?
units.tr: The same Garissolius, in the same book, chapter 8, §3, page 206, testifies that the imputation spoken of in Romans 5 must necessarily be joined with native corruption, nay, FOLLOWS IT. If it follows it, the imputation is consequent or mediate, which Placeus teaches along with the Apostle. If it follows it, then it does not precede it; if it is later than native corruption, then it is not earlier than the same corruption. In the same book, chapter 27, §30, he also says that the corruption of the women precedes the actual imputation of Adam's sin, and therefore inherent viciousness, as a condition and a cause without which it does not happen. Could he have taught consequent or mediate imputation more clearly?

units.la: Addam hic quoque testimonium Petri Martyris, Loc. Com. De pec. orig. §. 34. Vt res, inquit, difficilius expediatur, dico in vnoquoque nostrum, quoties punimur, causam esse eur puniri debeamus: itaque in omnibus, non
units.tr: I will add here also the testimony of Peter Martyr, Loci Communes, On Original Sin, §34: That the matter may be more easily explained, I say that in each one of us, whenever we are punished, there is a cause why we ought to be punished; thus it is not another's fault but each one's own fault that is condemned, in all, not

units.la: · Si eam sequitur, igitur eam non præcedit. alienam, sed propriam cuiusque culpam damnari. Quod si legimus, Deum in nobis vlcisci peccatum Adami, id ita intelligendum est, quod vitium nostrum ab illo habuit originem. Vt si quis pesse laborans, alios inficiat & illi moriantur, dicetur illorum quisque, non alienà, sed propria, & sua pesse esse mortuus. Atsi quis eos dicat ex eius pesse, unde contagium contraxerunt, perijsse: id ita intelligendum est, quod is primus pestem inuexit, & illis affricuit.
units.tr: If it follows it, then it does not precede it. another's, but his own fault that is condemned. And if we read that God takes vengeance on us for the sin of Adam, this must be understood to mean that our vice took its origin from him. As when someone who is suffering from the plague infects others, and they die of it, each of them will be said to have died not of another's plague but of his own; but if someone says that they perished from his plague, from which they caught the contagion, this must be understood to mean that he first brought the pestilence in and passed it on to them.

units.la: Sufficiunt, opinor, hoc loco hi teltes: libenter tamen ijs adiungam doctissimum VValæum, Refp. ad Cenf. Coru. cap. viii. pag. 238. Reatus, inquit, primi peccati ad condemnationem, & vt Apostolus loquitur, Rom. 5.16. ΧΡΙΣΤΑ ΕΙΣ ΚΑΤΑΚΡΙΜΑ NON POTEST posteris IMPVTARI NISI MEDIANTE illa peccati inhærentis vitiositate; quum Dei justitia non permittat, vt posteris nullum in se peccatum habentibus primum peccatum imputetur in condemnationem.
units.tr: Those witnesses, I think, are enough here. Yet I gladly add the most learned Walaeus, in his Response to the Censure of Corvinus, chap. 8, p. 238: The guilt of the first sin, he says, leading to condemnation, and as the Apostle speaks in Rom. 5.16, [ΕΙΣ ΚΑΤΑΚΡΙΜΑ] CANNOT BE IMPUTED TO POSTERITY EXCEPT BY MEANS OF that indwelling viciousness of sin, since the justice of God does not permit the first sin to be imputed to posterity, who have no sin of their own, unto condemnation.

units.la: Si igitur damnasset Synodus Placei doctrinam, haberet ille quidem solatium miserorum, confortes huius condemnationis viros maximos, sed profecto eam vti iam multis argumentis probaui, non condemnauit. Id quod etiam hoc argumento potest confirmari. Si suo illo Decreto eorum doctrinam Synodus damnasset, qui negant imputationem immediatam seu antecedentem, eadem utique damnasset absolute eorum doctrinam, qui peccati Originalis naturam ad corruptionem hæreditariam posterorum Adæ restringunt. Qui enim illam imputationem immediatam docent, illi nullo modo peccati originalis naturam ad illam corruptionem restringunt, sed vel duo peccata originalia faciunt, vnum imputatum, alterum inhærens; vel duas peccati originalis partes, quarum præcipuam ac primariam in illa imputatione, minus vero praecipuam in illa corruptione collocant. Atqui Synodus non (implicite) damnauit doctrinam, quae peccati originalis naturam ad corruptionem hereditariam restringit, Sed quae ita restringit, vt imputationem excludat primi illius peccati quo lapsus est Adam. Non enim frustrà limitationem illam adhibuit, quatenus ita restringit vt, &c. Ergo Synodus eorum doctrinam non damnauit, qui negant imputationem immediatam seu antecedentem primi illius peccati quo lapsus est Adam. Quorsum enim illam limitationem adhibere voluit, nisi vt innueret, se imputationem primi peccati, quo lapsus est Adam, intelligere, quae cum restrictione naturae peccati originalis ad corruptionem hereditariam potest consistere? Atqui sola imputatio Mediata seu consequens est ejusmodi: eam igitur solam Synodus intellexit.
units.tr: If therefore the Synod had condemned Placeus's doctrine, he would indeed have the consolation of the wretched, since great men share this condemnation with him. But he has certainly not been condemned, as I have already shown by many arguments. This can also be confirmed by the following argument. If the Synod had by that Decree condemned the doctrine of those who deny immediate or antecedent imputation, it would certainly have condemned absolutely the doctrine of those who restrict the nature of original sin to the hereditary corruption of Adam's posterity. For those who teach immediate imputation do not restrict the nature of original sin to that corruption at all. Rather, they either make two original sins, one imputed and the other inherent, or two parts of original sin, placing the chief and primary part in that imputation and the less principal part in that corruption. But the Synod did not condemn (implicitly) the doctrine that restricts the nature of original sin to hereditary corruption; it condemned the doctrine that so restricts it as to exclude the imputation of that first sin by which Adam fell. For it did not use that limitation in vain: insofar as it restricts it so that, etc. Therefore the Synod did not condemn those who deny the immediate or antecedent imputation of that first sin by which Adam fell. For why would it wish to add that limitation, except to indicate that it understood the imputation of the first sin by which Adam fell, which can stand together with the restriction of the nature of original sin to hereditary corruption? But only mediate or consequent imputation is of this kind. So the Synod understood that alone.

units.la: Itaque ea prudentia Decretum suum contexuit, vt cum ter corruptionis ac imputationis meminerit, perpetuo prius corruptionem quam imputationem nominauerit. Quorsum, nisi vt insinuaret, intelligendam esse imputationem, non quae antecederet, sed quae sequeretur corruptionem illam hereditariam? Hoc certe postremum argumentum ab ordine verborum deductum, refelli à D. Gariffolio non potuit, vtitur enim argumento simili libri sui de Imp. primi peccati cap. 17. pag. 617. sed multo debiliore, planeque infirmo; ac propterea responsionis Placei, quam in Manuscripto posteriore legerat, cum refutari non posset, ne meminit quidem.
units.tr: Therefore the Decree was framed with such prudence that, although it mentions corruption and imputation three times, it always names corruption before imputation. Why, except to insinuate that the imputation to be understood is not the one that precedes, but the one that follows that hereditary corruption? Gariffolius certainly could not refute this last argument, drawn from the order of the words. He uses a similar argument in his book on the imputation of the first sin, chap. 17, p. 617, but it is much weaker and plainly feeble. Therefore, since he could not refute Placeus's reply, which he had read in the later manuscript, he does not even mention it.

units.la: Omitto verba illa Decreti; & corruptionem illam, & imputationem hanc, in omnes Adami posteros descendentem, melius imputationi consequenti seu mediatæ conuenire, quàm antecedenti seu immediatæ. Intelligitur enim descensus ab Adamo, per propagationem naturalem: sic enim descendit corruptio. Potest autem imputatio consequens, dici ab Adamo in eius posteros descendisse mediante corruptione, quæ illius est causa proxima & fundamentum, & in nos vere descendit. At minus proprie id dici potest de imputatione antecedente: nam & hæc propagationem naturalem diu antecessisse putatur, & pendere non ab aliqua re quæ nobis insit, sed à Dei voluntate, cui sic placuisse dicitur, primum illud Adami peccatum toti generi humano imputare. Vno verbo nullus imputationis in homines descensus, qui corruptionem antecesserit, animo concipi potest.
units.tr: I pass over those words of the Decree, and the fact that this corruption and this imputation, descending upon all Adam's posterity, agree better with consequent or mediate imputation than with antecedent or immediate. For descent from Adam is understood through natural propagation; thus corruption descends. But consequent imputation can be said to have descended from Adam to his posterity through corruption, which is its proximate cause and foundation, and truly descends upon us. Yet this can be said less properly of antecedent imputation. For this is thought to have preceded natural propagation by a long time, and depends not on anything inherent in us but on the will of God, to whom it is said to have pleased to impute that first sin of Adam to the whole human race. In a word, no descent of imputation upon men that preceded corruption can be conceived in the mind.

units.la: Denique Decretum Synodi, aut congruit cum S. Scriptura, aut non congruit. Si non congruit, quominus recipi debeat obstat Art. V. Conf. Fid. quem illa ipsa Synodus comprobauit. Si congruit, vtique non damnat eorum doctrinam, qui retenta imputatione primi Adæ peccati mediatâ, solam illius imputationem immediatam seu antecedentem negant. Hæc enim imputatio immediata ex sacris Literis exsculpi nequit. Quæcunque pro imputatione primi peccati quo Adam lapsus est afferuntur, ea, aut nullam vim probandi habent, aut mediatam duntaxat imputationem probant. Suppeditat autem Scriptura aduersus imputationem immediatam argumenta multa, eaque inuicta, cum nihil habeat imputationi mediatæ repugnans. Ex negata imputatione immediatâ, nihil prorsus absurdi sequitur, cum eâ posita multa consequantur absurda. Decet autem nos Decretum Synodi potius in meliorem partem, quàm in sequiorem accipere.
units.tr: Finally, the Synod's Decree either agrees with Holy Scripture or it does not. If it does not agree, what prevents its reception is Article V of the Confession of Faith, which that very Synod approved. If it agrees, it certainly does not condemn those who, while retaining the mediate imputation of Adam's first sin, deny only its immediate or antecedent imputation. For this immediate imputation cannot be drawn out of the Sacred Scriptures. Whatever is advanced for the imputation of the first sin by which Adam fell either has no force of proof or proves only mediate imputation. Scripture, however, supplies many arguments against immediate imputation, and unconquered ones, since it contains nothing opposed to mediate imputation. From the denial of immediate imputation nothing absurd follows; but with it posited, many absurdities follow. Moreover, we ought to take the Synod's Decree in the better part rather than the worse.

units.la: Vt sit finis, ipse D. Garifolius, quo nemo mi us æquus Placeo fuit, hanc imputationis distinctionem probauit, eaque bene intellecta controuersiam istam finiri posse putauit. cap. 2. §. 16. pag. 43.
