De attributo, inquit, Deinde cum agitur, distinguitur imputatio peccati in Priorem, sive Antecedentem, aut immediatam; & Posteriorem, sive consequentem, aut Mediatam: Haud incommode sane; nec dubito, si modo recta explicatio adhibeatur consensum hic facile stabiliri posse: si nempe utraque imputatio eodem referretur, id est, si intelligeretur de peccato Adami eadem significatione accepto, sive de actione illa, qua primum Adamus reum se fecit Legis Diuinae Majestatis. Atqui distinctione illa sic intellecta consensus nullo modo stabiliri posset, si quidem Decreto illo Synodico damnata esset doctrina, quæ admissa imputatione mediata actionis illius, negat immediatam. Maneret enim perfecta inter Decretum illud & Placei sententiam dissensio. Non est igitur existimandum eo Decreto doctrinam illam esse damnatam. Cæterum Placeus utramque imputationem eodem retulit, id est, de actione illa qua primum Adamus reum se fecit intellexit.
units.tr: To put an end to it: Gariffolius himself, than whom no one was less fair to Placeus, approved this distinction of imputation, and thought that the controversy could be settled if it were rightly understood. Chap. 2, §16, p. 43: On the attribute, he says, then when the matter is treated, the imputation of sin is distinguished into the Prior, or Antecedent, or immediate, and the Posterior, or consequent, or Mediate. Not unreasonably indeed; nor do I doubt that, if only a correct explanation is applied, agreement can easily be established here: namely, if both imputations were referred to the same thing, that is, if they were understood of Adam's sin taken in the same sense, namely of that action by which Adam first made himself guilty before the Majesty of the divine Law. But with that distinction understood in this way, agreement could in no way be established, if indeed the doctrine that, while admitting the mediate imputation of that action, denies the immediate, had been condemned by that Synodical Decree. For a complete disagreement would remain between that Decree and Placeus's opinion. It is therefore not to be thought that this doctrine was condemned by that Decree. Moreover, Placeus referred both imputations to the same thing; that is, he understood them of that action by which Adam first made himself guilty.

units.la: Præcesserant enim in Manuscripto illo, quod D. Garifolius Posterius appellat, hæc verba. Est igitur quæstio inter nos instituta duntaxat de primo peccato Adami sumpto primo modo, hoc est de actuali ejus inobedientia, de actione illa interna & externa, qua Dei legem transgressus est actu, præcisa ab habituali corruptione, quæ actionem illam sequuta est, num ea nobis nascentibus imputetur? cui quæstioni nondum negatione simplici, sed distinctione rursus satisfaciendum videtur. Est enim eius distinguendum attributum. Itaque enim animo concipi duplex imputatio, immediata & mediata, vel (vt idem aliis verbis dicam) Antecedens & Consequens. Potuitne Placeus apertius significare, se distinctionem illam imputationis de actione illa, qua primum Adamus reum se fecit, intelligere? Deinde subijciebatur, Imputationem immediatam esse eam, quaputatur actio illa Adami, hoc est, vetiti fructus manducatio, eius posteris omnibus (Christo excepto) proxime, immediate, hoc ipso quod filij sunt Adami, imputari ad duas poenas proprie dictas, privationem iustitiae originalis, & mortem aeternam. Iam autem de quo vnum distinctionis membrum intelligitur, de eodem intelligi debet alterum; alioqui non esset distinctio: non enim vnum quid distingueretur. Denique subjungebat Placeus, Imputationem mediatam esse eam, quae fit mediante corruptione hereditaria. Cujus autem, quaeso, peccati imputatio fieri potest mediante illa corruptione, nisi peccati actualis Adami, quod corruptionem illam peperit? Addebat etiam hanc rationem, Hujus enim corruptionis participatione communicamus peccato Adami, eique, vt ita loquar, habitualiter consentimus. Quibus verbis aperte distinguebat peccatum Adami ab illa corruptione. Itaque non ipsam corruptionem intelligebat per peccatum Adami, sed actualem inobedientiam, unde illa fluxit.
units.tr: For in that manuscript which Gariffolius calls the Later, the following words had come before: The question instituted between us is therefore only about the first sin of Adam, taken in the first way, that is, about his actual disobedience, about that inner and outer action by which he actually transgressed God's law, set apart from the habitual corruption which followed that action: whether that is imputed to us at birth? To this question a simple denial, but rather a distinction, seems to need to be given. For its attribute must be distinguished. Thus a twofold imputation is conceived in the mind, immediate and mediate, or (to say the same in other words) antecedent and consequent. Could Placeus have signified more openly that he understood that distinction of imputation to concern that action by which Adam first made himself guilty? Next it was added that immediate imputation is that by which that action of Adam, that is, the eating of the forbidden fruit, is imputed to all his posterity (Christ excepted) proximately and immediately, by the very fact that they are sons of Adam, to two punishments properly so called, the privation of original justice and eternal death. Now whatever one member of the distinction is understood to be, the other must be understood to be the same; otherwise it would not be a distinction, for one thing would not be distinguished from another. Finally Placeus added that mediate imputation is that which is made by means of hereditary corruption. But of what sin, I ask, can imputation be made by means of that corruption, except the actual sin of Adam, which produced that corruption? He also added this reason: For by participation in this corruption we are communicated with Adam's sin and, so to speak, we consent to it habitually. By these words he plainly distinguished Adam's sin from that corruption. Therefore by the sin of Adam he did not mean the corruption itself, but the actual disobedience from which it flowed.

units.la: Hanc autem Placei rationem D. Garissolius approbauit & commendauit, ac etiam retorsit. Sed in quem? nescio; in Placeum enim non potuit, vt jam patet. Si quis autem alius Placeo notus imputationem actualis peccati Adae negauit & refutauit, id de imputatione immediata seu antecedente sola accipi debet, non de mediata seu consequente, quam neque vult negatam, neque etiam ejus argumenta oppugnant.
units.tr: Gariffolius approved and commended this reasoning of Placeus, and even turned it back. But against whom? I do not know; for it cannot have been against Placeus, as is now clear. If indeed some other man known to Placeus denied and refuted the imputation of Adam's actual sin, that must be understood of immediate or antecedent imputation alone, not of mediate or consequent imputation, which he neither wishes to be denied nor attacks with his arguments.

units.la: Idem D. Gariffolius sententiam Placei tacitè probat, cum aliquoties affirmat & inculcat reatus ex peccato Adæ, & ex vitio nobis inhærente, non esse duos reatus distinctos, sed unum eundemque reatum ex utroque consurgentemCap. ix. §. vii. pag. 190. & § xv. p. 306. & cap. xxvii. § xxx. p. 809. &c. Posità enim imputatione peccati Adæ immediatâ, ponuntur necessariò duo reatus distincti, quorum unus ex peccato Adæ, alter ex vitio nobis inhærente consurgit: Ille antecedit corruptionem hæreditariam, hic sequitur: Ille prior est vitio inhærente, hic posterior: Ille causa est corruptionis, hic potiùs effectum: Illius pœna est vitium inhærens, huius non item: Ille est peccati alieni ac extra nos siti, hic est peccati nostri, nobis inhærentis: Ille est omnium hominum communis identitate numerica peccati, hic est multorum numero peccatorum, & suus cuique homini proprius: Ille pendet à sola Dei voluntate, hic ab ipsa corruptionis nobis innatæ natura & naturali demerito. Ille prius fuit quàm ij essent quibus imputatur, hic contrà non fuit nisi posterius. Qui possunt igitur non duo esse distincti reatus, inter quos tot tantaque possunt notari discrimina?
units.tr: The same Mr. Garissolius tacitly approves Placeus's opinion when he repeatedly affirms and insists that "the guilt arising from Adam's sin and from the vice inherent in us are not two distinct guilts, but one and the same guilt arising from both" (Ch. 9, §7, p. 190; §15, p. 306; and Ch. 27, §30, p. 809, etc.). For once the immediate imputation of Adam's sin is posited, two distinct guilts must necessarily be posited: one arising from Adam's sin, the other from the vice inherent in us. The first precedes hereditary corruption, the second follows it. The first is prior to the inherent vice, the second posterior. The first is the cause of corruption, the second rather its effect. The punishment of the first is the inherent vice, but not so of the second. The first is the sin of another, existing outside us; the second is our own sin, inherent in us. The first is one sin numerically identical in all human beings; the second is one of many sins, each proper to each person. The first depends on the will of God alone; the second on the very nature of the corruption born in us and on its natural demerit. The first existed before those to whom it is imputed existed; the second, by contrast, could only come after. How, then, can they not be two distinct guilts, when so many and such great differences can be noted between them?

units.la: Hinc patet sententiam Placei cum Decreto, quatuor apud Helvetios civitatum Evangelicarum, quod Carentonien si D. Gariffolius subiungit, minimè pugnare. Nam vel Decretum Synodi Carentonianæ laudant, cum quo Placei sententia, ut iam probaui, concordat; vel cur laudent rationem reddunt his paucissimis verbis, In Adamo enim & cum Adamo qui peccarunt, Adami illis peccatum merito imputatur, quam propositionem Placeus verissimam esse agnoscit. Æquum enim profecto est vt qui in & cum Adamo peccauerunt, his peccatum imputetur quod in eo & cum eo commiserunt. Communis peccati communem esse imputationem iustum est. Sed quid est nos in & cum Adamo peccasse? Peccatum Adami nobis imputari? ita accipit D. Gariffolius cap. viii. §. xxii. Quomodo enim, inquit, qui multis post facul sext terunt, d cip ffunt iam antea in alio peccasse, nisi q ia ille cum actum exercuit, qui posterorum ita reputatur, ac si ipsi ill m commisissent? Et subijcit Theologos, cum docent nos in Christo satisfecisse, non aliud sibi velle, quam Christi satisfactionem nobis imputari. Congruit hæc eius interpretatio cum eo quod sæpe inculcat, peccatum Adami non nisi per imputationem nostrum esse. Hinc enim sequitur nos in & cum Adamo non peccasse nisi imputatiue. Sed sic doctissimorum Theologorum ratio evaderet nugatoria. Idem enim probarent per idem, Imputationem peccati Adami per imputationem peccati Adami: quam nugationem, præsertim in tam grani Decreto, illis tribuere nefas est. Quid ergo sibi vult illa phrasis? id poterit ex simili intelligi. Si quis enim diceret, nos in & cum Adamo fuisse, sensus esset, non Esse Adami nobis imputari; sed Esse Adami nobis cum per propagationem naturalem esse communicatum. Sic cum dicimur in & cum Adamo peccasse, sensus est, non peccatum Adami nobis imputari (id enim esset; ut dixi, nugationem in præstantissimorum virorum Decretum importare) sed peccatum Adami nobis cum per propagationem naturalem esse communicatum. Ex quo sequitur illud merito nobis imputari; sed imputatione mediata seu consequente, quam Placeus constanter agnoscit & tenet.
units.tr: From this it is plain that the opinion of Placeus is in no way at odds with the Decree of the four Evangelical cities of the Swiss, which Mr. Garissolius appends to the Carentonian Synod. For either they praise the decree of the Carentonian Synod, with which Placeus's opinion, as I have already shown, agrees; or, in praising it, they give their reason in these very few words: "For in Adam and with Adam those who sinned have Adam's sin imputed to them as their desert," a proposition which Placeus acknowledges to be entirely true. For it is surely fair that those who sinned in and with Adam should have imputed to them the sin they committed in him and with him. It is just that the imputation of a common sin should be common. But what does it mean that we sinned in and with Adam? That Adam's sin is imputed to us? So Mr. Garissolius understands it in Ch. 8, §22: "For how," he says, "could those who sin many ages later be said to have already sinned in another, unless because he performed the act which is so reckoned to his posterity as if they themselves had committed it?" And he adds that "theologians, when they teach that we have satisfied in Christ, mean nothing else than that Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us." This interpretation of his agrees with what he often insists upon, that Adam's sin is ours only by imputation. For from this it follows that we did not sin in and with Adam except imputatively. But in that case the reasoning of the most learned theologians would be trifling. They would be proving the same thing by the same thing, the imputation of Adam's sin by the imputation of Adam's sin; and it is wrong to ascribe such triviality to them, especially in so grave a decree. What, then, does that phrase mean? This can be understood from an analogy. If someone said that we were in and with Adam, the sense would not be that Adam's essence is imputed to us, but that Adam's essence was communicated to us through natural propagation. So when we are said to have sinned in and with Adam, the sense is not that Adam's sin is imputed to us (for that, as I said, would import triviality into the decree of such outstanding men), but that Adam's sin was communicated to us through natural propagation. It follows that it is rightly imputed to us; but by mediate or consequent imputation, which Placeus constantly acknowledges and maintains.

units.la: Vt fit finis, illi ipsi, qui Decretum Synodi Nationalis fecerunt, sententiæ meæ astipulantur, suoque testimonio Placeum a condemnatione liberant, in primis Clarissimus & piissimus vir D. Drelincourtius, fidelissimus Ecclesiæ Parisiensis Pastor. Cùm enim hucusque in hoc scripto progressus essem, id, antequam prodiret in lucem, cum quibusdam amicis suis viris doctissimis & prudentissimis communicatum Placeus voluit, præcipuè verò cum dicto D. Drelincourtio, cujus in conficiendo illo Decreto plurimùm valuisse authoritatem non ignorabat. Is autem eo perlecto pro suo insigni candore & pacis Ecclesiæ studio humanissimas scripsit ad Placeum literas Lutetia, An. 1653. die 10. Decemb. quas, cum bona ejus venia, huc transcribere non grauabor: interest enim & veritatis, & pacis, & causæ quam ago, ut in vulgus emanent. Erant autem Gallico sermone ita conceptæ.
units.tr: To make an end: those very men who drew up the decree of the National Synod side with my view, and by their testimony free Placeus from condemnation. Foremost among them is the most distinguished and most pious man, Mr. Drelincourt, most faithful minister of the Church of Paris. For when I had progressed thus far in this writing, Placeus wished it to be shared, before it appeared in print, with some of his friends, men most learned and most prudent, and especially with the said Mr. Drelincourt, whose authority he knew had counted for very much in the making of that decree. Having read it through, Drelincourt, out of his notable candour and zeal for the peace of the Church, wrote a most kindly letter to Placeus from Paris, in the year 1653, on 10 December. With his good permission I will not hesitate to transcribe it here, since it is in the interest both of truth and of peace, and of the cause I am pursuing, that it should be made public. It was written in the French language, and was couched as follows.

units.la: Monsieur & tres-honoré Frere.
units.tr: Sir and most honoured brother.

units.la: I'ay leu auec vne satisfaction tres-particuliere l'écrit qu'il vous a pleu me communiquer; Et je loüe Dieu de tout mon cœur de voir par là heureusement terminé ce dont j'apprehendoit du trouble & de la diuision en nos Eglises. Car, Monsieur, je vous puis bien asseurer, & tous ceux qui en peuuent douter, que l'intention du dernier Synode National de Charenton n'a nullement esté de condamner ny vostre personne, ny la doctrine que vous proposez. I'en puis parler auec certitude: veu que non seulement j'ay eu l'honneur de me trouuer en cette celebre compagnie, mais aussi d'estre du nombre des commissaires qui dresserent l'acte dont il s'agit. Nous n'auons jamais pensé à poser cette imputation du peché d'Adam que vous appellez antecedente & immediate : Mais seulement celle que vous nommez consequente & mediate. Et de moy ie l'ay toujours ainsi conçeu & enseigné. De sorte que ce m'est une grande joye & consolation de voir sur cet important article l'uniformité de nos sentimens. Si l'occasion se presente de vous justifier envers ceux qui ne sont point informez de ces choses, ou qui ont des préjugez à l'encontre, je vous asseure, Monsieur, que ie ne m'y oublieray pas. Il y va de la gloire de Dieu, & de l'edification publique, que cette verité soit connuë, afin qu'il n'y ait rien qui empesche, que les graces eminentes dont Dieu vous a enrichy ne produisent leur fruit par tout. Je vous embrasse de tout mon cœur, & suis
units.tr: I have read with particular satisfaction the writing which you were pleased to communicate to me, and I thank God with all my heart that by it there is happily ended what I feared would bring trouble and division into our Churches. For, Sir, I can assure you, and all who might doubt it, that the intention of the last National Synod of Charenton was in no way to condemn either your person or the doctrine you propose. I can speak with certainty, since I not only had the honour of being present in that celebrated assembly, but was also one of the commissioners who drew up the act in question. We never thought of laying down that imputation of Adam's sin which you call antecedent and immediate: but only that which you name consequent and mediate. And as for me, I have always conceived and taught it thus. So it is a great joy and consolation to me to see that our sentiments agree on this important article. If the occasion arises to justify you before those who are not informed of these matters, or who hold prejudices against you, I assure you, Sir, that I will not neglect to do so. The glory of God and the public edification require that this truth be known, so that nothing hinders the eminent gifts with which God has enriched you from bearing their fruit everywhere. I embrace you with all my heart, and am

units.la: Monsieur,
units.tr: Sir,

units.la: Vostre tres-humble & tresobeïssant serviteur
units.tr: Your most humble and most obedient servant

units.la: DRELINCOURT.
units.tr: DRELINCOURT.

units.la: In gratiam eorum qui Gallicè nescsiunt vertam Latinè.
units.tr: Translated into Latin for the sake of those who do not know French.

units.la: Domine & honorande Frater.
units.tr: Sir and honoured brother.

units.la: Scriptum, quod mecum communicatum voluisti, singulari cum voluptate legi; quòdque eo finitum id videam, unde Ecclesiis nostris perturbationem aliquam & diuisionem metuebam, Deo ex toto corde gratias ago. Possum enim tibi, Domine, aliisque omnibus, si qui dubitant, confirmare, consilium ultimæ Synodi nat. Carent. nullo modo fuisse te, tuamue, quam proponis, doctrinam condemnare. Id pro certo testari possum. Quippe, cum dignus habitus fuerim, qui, non modo celebri illi confessui interessem, sed etiam vnus essem ex delegatis illis, qui Decretum, de quo agitur, conscripserunt. Nunquam nobis in mentem venit eam imputationem peccati Adamici constabilire, quam tu antecedentem & immediatam appellas, sed eam duntaxat, quam tu consequentem & mediatam vocas. Ego quidem ita perpetuo sensi & docui. Quocirca magno gaudio, & consolatione afficior, quod videam de hoc momentoso dogmate te mecum idem sentire. Si tui apud eos justificandi, qui hæc, aut non satis intelligunt, aut adversis præjudiciis laborant, sese mihi dederit occasio, confirmo tibi me causæ tuæ non defuturum. Interest gloriæ Dei & publicæ ædificationis, ut hæc veritas omnibus innotescat, nihil ut sit, quod obstet, quominus quibus te ditauit Deus dotes insignes vbique fructum ferant. Ego te toto pectore complector, & sum, &c.
units.tr: I read with singular pleasure the writing you wished to be communicated to me, and I give thanks to God with my whole heart that it brings to an end what I feared would cause some disturbance and division in our Churches. For I can confirm to you, Sir, and to all others who doubt it, that the mind of the last National Synod of Charenton was in no way to condemn you, or the doctrine you propose. I can testify this for certain, since I was thought worthy not only to attend that celebrated assembly but also to be one of those delegates who drew up the decree in question. It never entered our minds to establish that imputation of Adam's sin which you call antecedent and immediate, but only that which you call consequent and mediate. I have always thought and taught this myself. Therefore I am greatly delighted and comforted to see that you and I think alike on this weighty doctrine. If the opportunity should arise to vindicate you before those who either do not understand these matters sufficiently or labour under hostile prejudices, I assure you I will not be wanting to your cause. It is for the glory of God and the public edification that this truth be made known to all, so that nothing may hinder the outstanding gifts with which God has endowed you from bearing fruit everywhere. I embrace you with my whole heart, and am, &c.

units.la: Quid potes amplius ad plenam Placei justificationem, Lector pie, desiderare?
units.tr: What more can you, pious reader, desire for Place's full justification?

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Distributio dicendorum.
units.tr: The division of the matters to be discussed.

units.la: Reconciliato cum Synodo Placeo, nihil superesset, nisi vt stantes vtrinque argumentorum acies, alteram pro imputatione, alteram contra imputationem primi Adæ peccati conciliemus inter se, vt positis odiis, sublata dissensione, conjunctis viribus ad Decretum Synodi tuendum & confirmandum quicquid habent roboris concorditer conferant. Id autem fiet, si demonstrauerimus, neque argumenta, quæ pro imputatione primæ Adæ inobedientiæ afferuntur, quicquam valere ad probandam imputationem antecedentem seu immediatam, neque argumenta, quæ contra peccati illius imputationem proferuntur, vllam vim habere aduersus imputationem consequentem seu mediatam. Vbi enim patuerit, nec illa probare imputationem quam ista improbant, nec ista eam improbare quam illa probant, nonne manifestum euadet, in speciem tantum inter se argumenta illa pugnare, re autem vera conspirare aßnicè ad imputationem mediatam, repudiatâ immediatâ, firmandam, Decretumque Synodi, vt à me expositum est, defendendum? Nisi hoc vtrumque præstitero, species illa repugnantiæ terrorem perpetuò incutiet, & bellum veluti intentabit, nec, intercedentibus præjudiciis, nonnullisque fortasse perturbationibus, firmæ pacis constabiliendæ spes certa exorietur. In id igitur mihi totis viribus incumbendum est, vt vtrumque illud demonstrem. Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum supplex rogo, vt mihi id facere indulgeat ita clarè & efficaciter, vt omnis in posterum de hac re dubitandi dissentiendique ansa prorsus tollatur, omnesque virtute & vnitate ejusdem Spiritus sancti in eandem sententiam conueniamus, in eaque constanter perseueremus. Amen.
units.tr: Now that Placaeus has been reconciled with the Synod, nothing remains but that we bring into agreement the opposing lines of argument on each side, one for and one against the imputation of the first Adam's sin. Laying aside hatreds and removing the dispute, they should unite their strength and together contribute whatever force they have to defending and confirming the decree of the Synod. This will happen if we show, first, that the arguments brought forward for the imputation of the first Adam's disobedience have no value in proving an antecedent or immediate imputation, and, second, that the arguments brought forward against the imputation of that sin have no force against a consequent or mediate imputation. For once it is clear that those arguments do not prove the imputation which these others reject, and these do not reject the imputation which those prove, will it not plainly turn out that the arguments only seem to fight against each other, while in truth they agree closely in confirming the mediate imputation, with the immediate one rejected, and in defending the decree of the Synod as I have set it out? Unless I accomplish both of these, that appearance of conflict will constantly strike fear and as it were threaten war, and, with prejudices standing in the way and perhaps some disturbances, no sure hope of establishing a firm peace will arise. Therefore I must apply myself with all my strength to demonstrate both points. I humbly beg our Lord Jesus Christ to grant me to do this so clearly and effectively that every future occasion for doubting and dissenting on this matter is entirely removed, and that all of us, by the virtue and unity of the same Holy Spirit, agree in the same opinion and persevere in it steadfastly. Amen.

units.la: Hoc autem ordine procedemus. Primùm argumenta quæ pro imputatione primi Adæ peccati afferuntur, ad examen revocabimus, & planum faciemus, si quam peccati illius imputationem probant, eam nonnisi consequentem seu Mediatam esse. Deinde argumenta quæ contra imputationem primi illius peccati militare videntur, similiter ponderabimus, nullamque vim habere ostendemus, nisi aduersus imputationem antecedentem seu immediatam. Ita hæ duæ erunt partes eorum quæ nobis dicenda restant.
units.tr: We shall proceed in this order. First, we shall bring to examination the arguments which are put forward for the imputation of the first Adam's sin, and make it plain that, if they prove any imputation of that sin, it is only a consequent or mediate one. Then we shall similarly weigh the arguments which seem to militate against the imputation of that first sin, and show that they have no force except against an antecedent or immediate imputation. In this way there will be two parts of what remains for us to say.

units.la: CAPVT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Non aliam Imputationem primi Adæ peccati, quam consequentem seu mediatam Argumenta Clariss. D. Marefij probare.
units.tr: That the arguments of the most distinguished Mr. Marefius prove no imputation of the first Adam's sin other than the consequent or mediate one.

units.la: POst vltimam Synodum Nationalem pro imputatione primi Adæ peccati scripserunt libris typis excusis, quos quidem viderim, Clarissimi viri, Andreas Riuetus, Samuel Marefius, Ant. Garissolius, Carolus Daubuz, & Steph. Blancus, manuscriptis vero alij complures. Sed primus illorum celeberrimus Riuetus non autoritate Scripturæ, nec rationibus, sed corrasis vndecunque potuit virorum doctorum testimonijs, etiam adhuc viuentium, eorumque nonnullorum, quorum nomen nobis antea inauditum fuerat, pugnandum sibi censuit, itaque nunc quidem omittatur. Decet enim prius audiri eos qui testimonia Scripturæ, & argumenta afferunt. Non enim quærimus quid homines sentiant, sed quid nobis sentiendum sit, quid Deus nos sentire voluerit. Regula fidei nostræ est Dei verbum, non hominum opiniones. His ergo in vltimum locum rejectis, deprompta è Scripturis argumenta inspiciamus. Prodiit Groningæ apud Ioan. Nicolaum Anno Domini M. DC. XLVI. Theologiæ Elenchticæ nova Synopsis, sive Index controversiarum fidei ex sacris Scripturis a Iacobo Tirino Iesuita concinnatus, & Censura perpetua auctus, emendatus, refutatus, per Samuelem Marefium S. Theol. D. eiusdemque Facultatis Professorem ordinarium in Academia Provinciali Groningæ & Omlandiæ, in quo, Controversia xi. de statu primorum parentum & de peccato originali. Num. 4. occasione quorundam Tirini verborum, digreditur vir clarissimus in Controversiam de imputatione primæ Adami inobedientiæ, ac cum Socini, Curcellæi, aliorumque omnem imputationem illius peccati negantium, nec-non Decreti Synodi Nationalis Ecclesiarum Galliæ, libellique a Cl. Riueto editi meminisset, subjecit, Nec solum οι ἐξ ἐναντίας illam imputationem impugnant, sed etiam (quae fuit occasio illius Decreti Synodici) Reu. doctissimus ac celeberrimus vir, meus quondam Commilito in studiis suavissimus D. Iosue Placeus Disput. Salmur. parte 1. p. 206. & seqq. illam omnino reicit praeter ius & fas, dum bene & orthodoxe studet propugnare hereditariam, quae omnibus inest, corruptionem: cum & illa debeat admitti, & hac fit agnoscenda, utpote quae pari passu ambulent; sic tamen ut ordine naturae, & in signo rationis traducem innatae corruptionis, primi peccati praecedat imputatio.
units.tr: After the last National Synod, the following distinguished men published books in print, which I have seen: Andreas Rivetus, Samuel Marefius, Antonius Garissolius, Carolus Daubuz and Stephanus Blancus. Several others wrote manuscripts. But the first of these, the most celebrated Rivetus, judged that he had to contend not with the authority of Scripture or with arguments, but with the testimonies of learned men, gathered from wherever he could get them, including men still living and some whose names had previously been unknown to us. So let him be set aside for now. For it is right first to hear those who bring forward the testimonies of Scripture and arguments. We are not asking what men think, but what we ought to think, and what God wished us to think. The rule of our faith is the Word of God, not the opinions of men. Therefore, with these put last, let us examine the arguments drawn from the Scriptures. There appeared at Groningen, from the press of Johannes Nicolaus, in the year of the Lord 1646, Theologiae Elencticae nova Synopsis, sive Index controversiarum fidei ex sacris Scripturis a Iacobo Tirino Iesuita concinnatus, & Censura perpetua auctus, emendatus, refutatus, per Samuelem Marefium S. Theol. D. eiusdemque Facultatis Professorem ordinarium in Academia Provinciali Groningæ & Omlandiæ, in which, in Controversy 11, on the state of the first parents and on original sin, number 4, the distinguished man, on the occasion of some words of Tirinus, digresses into the controversy on the imputation of the first Adam's disobedience. After mentioning Socinus, Curcellaeus and others who deny every imputation of that sin, as well as the decree of the National Synod of the churches of France and the booklet published by the Reverend Rivetus, he adds: "Not only do those on the opposite side [οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας] attack that imputation, but also (which was the occasion of that synodal decree) the most learned and celebrated man, the Reverend Josue Placeus, my former fellow-student, most pleasant in our studies, in Disput. Salmur. part 1, p. 206 and following, rejects it altogether, against right and law, while he zealously and orthodoxly strives to defend the hereditary corruption which is in all. For both must be admitted, and the latter acknowledged, since they walk side by side; yet in such a way that, in the order of nature and in the reasoning of the mind, the imputation of the first sin precedes the transmission of innate corruption."

units.la: Ejus se Commilitonem in studiis non sine voluptate Placeus reminiscitur, veterisque amicitiae reliquias in elogiis illis agnoscit, quibus se minime dignum ab eo ornari videt: optasset tamen clarissimum virum aduersus Iesuitam scribentem, hujus, si quam inter nos esse putat, controversiae non meminisse, nolletque se ab amico in eundem quasi fasciculum cum Curcellio, a quo vehementer dissentit, compactum esse. In posterum, uti spero, vir doctissimus Placeum neque condemnatum à Synodo Nationali fuisse, neque imputationem primi Adæ peccati omnino rejicere, sibi affirmandum putabit. Non enim opinor, existimabit, Dei gloriam Ecclesiæque ædificationem flagitare, vt pro condemnato ab omnibus habeatur. Quod autem ait, imputationem & corruptionem pari passu ambulare, fi imputationem intelligeret consequentem, non me haberet repugnantem, sed cùm antecedentem intelligere videatur, ei assentiri non possum. Illa enim imputatio nullo modo, nec Scriptură, nec ratione, Scripturæ & rationi repugnans; hæc verò corruptio multis Scripturæ testimonijs, multis rationibus, ipsaque adeò experientiâ certissimè probari potest.
units.tr: Placeus recalls with pleasure that he was a fellow-student of that man, and he recognises in those praises the remnants of an old friendship, though he sees that he does not deserve such honours from him. Still, he would have wished that the most distinguished man, when writing against the Jesuit, had not mentioned this controversy, if he thinks there is one between them. He would not want to be bound by a friend, as if in one bundle, to Curcellaeus, from whom he strongly dissents. In future, as I hope, the most learned man will not think it must be affirmed of Placeus that he was neither condemned by the National Synod nor entirely rejects the imputation of the first Adam's sin. For I do not think, he will judge, that the glory of God and the edification of the Church require that Placeus be regarded by everyone as condemned. As for his saying that imputation and corruption walk side by side: if he understood imputation as consequent, he would not find me opposed. But since he seems to understand it as antecedent, I cannot agree with him. For that imputation is in no way opposed either to Scripture or to reason, whereas that corruption can be most certainly proved by many testimonies of Scripture, by many reasons, and indeed by experience itself.

units.la: Talia præfatus vir Clariff. subjungit hæc pauca argumenta verbis breuissimis, quibus etiam breuissimè respondebimus.
units.tr: After this preface, the most distinguished man adds the following few arguments in very brief words, and we will also reply very briefly.

units.la: I. Eam culpam censeri illis imputari, qui eius reatui & pœnæ subiacent est certissimum. Omnes autem Adami posteros subjci reatui & pœnæ culpæ, quam Adam commisit, tota clamat Scriptura, ac præsertim Rom. v. 12. 1. Cor. xv. 21. 22. Distinguo, clamat subjici subjectione, quæ antecedat ordine naturæ vitium hæreditarium, Nego, subjectione, quæ sequatur illud vitium, Concedo, testemque laudo ipsum D. Gariff. cap. 8. § 3. p. 206.
units.tr: I. "It is certain that those are counted as having that guilt imputed to them who are subject to its guilt and punishment. But all the posterity of Adam are subject to the guilt and punishment of the sin which Adam committed, as all Scripture proclaims, and especially Rom. 5:12 and 1 Cor. 15:21-22." I distinguish: that Scripture proclaims they are subjected by a subjection which precedes, in the order of nature, the hereditary vice, I deny; by a subjection which follows that vice, I concede. And I cite Garissolius himself, chapter 8, § 3, p. 206.

units.la: II. Addit, Nec potest fieri, quin illis imputetur Adami transgressio, qui incurrunt pœnam, mortem scilicet, illi transgressioni diuinitus denunciatam. Nam vt bene dicuntur imputata Christo nostra peccata, quòd pœnam illis debitam sustinuerit, & rectè nobis imputari censetur eius iustitia, quòd eius meritum & præmium æternum consequamur, ita Adami peccatum ÿs imputari dicendum, qui eius reatum & poenam sustinent. Respondeo, fieri quidem non posse, quin illis imputetur Adami transgressio, qui incurrunt poenam illi transgressioni denunciatam; sed manet integra quaestio, utrum eam immediatè, ac ordine Naturæ priusquam corrumpantur, incurrant, an verò tantùm consequenter & mediante illa corruptione? Prius nego, nec probat D. Marefius, posterius affirmo. Ad Christum quod spectat, imputata sunt illi peccata nostra, non tanquam autori, sed tanquam innocentissimo peccatorum vadi: itaque propterea peccator dici non potuit. Nobis autem peccatum Adami imputatur, non tanquam illius vadibus, sed tanquam illius auctoribus, ac verè peccatoribus. Itaque plurimum distant illæ imputationes. Adde quod non sunt imputata peccata nostra Christo, imputatione antecedente, sed consequente tantùm ejus consensum, sine quo non potuissent ei imputari. Similiter discrimen magnum est inter iustitiæ Christi & peccati Adamici imputationem. Illa enim ex gratia, hoc ex iustitia nobis imputatur: & tamen ipsa iustitiæ imputatio non est immediata seu antecedens, sed consensum nostrum & fidem consequitur, absque quo nulla esset. Tantummodò est memorabilis differentia. Nam fides non est iustitia, nec meretur vitam æternam, cùm vitium hæreditarium sit verè peccatum generi humano damnando sufficiens. Nimirum, ut dixi, imputatio iustitiæ est ex gratia, peccati ex merito.
units.tr: II. He adds: "Nor can it be that the transgression of Adam is not imputed to those who incur the punishment, namely death, which was announced by God for that transgression. For just as our sins are rightly said to be imputed to Christ, because he underwent the punishment owed to them, and his righteousness is rightly considered to be imputed to us, because we obtain his merit and eternal reward, so Adam's sin must be said to be imputed to those who sustain his guilt and punishment." I answer: it is indeed certain that Adam's transgression must be imputed to those who incur the punishment announced for that transgression. But the question remains entire: whether they incur it immediately, and in the order of nature before they are corrupted, or only consequently and through that corruption? The former I deny, and Marefius does not prove it; the latter I affirm. As far as Christ is concerned, our sins were imputed to him not as to their author, but as to the most innocent surety for sins, and therefore he could not be called a sinner. But Adam's sin is imputed to us not as to a surety, but as to its authors, and truly sinners. So those imputations differ greatly. Add that our sins were not imputed to Christ by antecedent imputation, but only by consequent imputation, which followed his consent, without which they could not have been imputed to him. Likewise there is a great difference between the imputation of Christ's righteousness and the imputation of Adam's sin. For the former is imputed to us from grace, the latter from justice. Yet even the imputation of righteousness is not immediate or antecedent, but follows our consent and faith, without which it would not exist. There is only one memorable difference: faith is not righteousness, nor does it merit eternal life, since hereditary vice is truly sin, sufficient to damn the human race. Namely, as I said, the imputation of righteousness is from grace, and the imputation of sin is from desert.

units.la: III. Atque hæc imputatio, inquit, non nititur solo Dei iure in creaturas, ac Domino absoluto (ut quidam volunt) sed eius iustitia æquissima, ac valde iusto iudicio.
units.tr: III. This imputation, he says, rests not only on God's right over creatures and the Lord's absolute dominion (as some hold), but on his most equitable justice and a very just judgment.

units.la: Fateor, si imputatio intelligitur Mediata: Immediata enim, (vt suo loco, Deo dante, manifestum faciam) cum diuina iustitia non parum pugnat. Pergit, Nam saepe etiam hoc fit in foro humano absque vlla iniquitatis specie, sed iustissime, vt vnius culpa peccatum & vitium vniuersam communitatem aut posteritatem quoad poenae extensionem implicet, quod dum fit illa culpa toti vel communitati vel posteritati imputatur. Primum hoc in Lege sua damnat Deus diuertis verbis Deut. 24. 16. etiam cum de crimine laesae Maiestatis agitur 2. Reg. 14. 6. vetatque ne tale quid de ipsius iustitia dicatur Ezech. 18. 3. &c. Ierem. 31. 29. 30. Deinde, si vnius culpa vniuersam communitatem implicat, id fit, quia supponitur vniuersa communitas in eam culpam consensisse: alioquin id iuste fieri nequit. Saepe, addit vir Clarissimus, vsuenit, vt quicquid delirent Reges, plectuntur Achiui, nimirum illi non minus quam sui Reges delirabant.
units.tr: I grant this if imputation is understood as mediate. For immediate imputation (as I will show in its place, God willing) fights not a little with divine justice. He goes on: For this also often happens in human courts, without any appearance of injustice but most justly, so that the guilt of one person and its fault involve the whole community or posterity as far as the extent of punishment goes; and while this happens, that guilt is imputed to the whole community or to posterity. First, God condemns this in his Law in different words, Deut. 24. 16, even where the crime of treason is in question, 2 Kings 14. 6, and he forbids that anything of this kind be said of his justice, Ezek. 18. 3, etc.; Jer. 31. 29, 30. Second, if one person's guilt involves the whole community, this happens because the whole community is supposed to have consented to that guilt; otherwise it cannot be done justly. Often, the distinguished man adds, it happens that whatever the kings go mad about, the Achaeans are punished, namely, those people were going mad no less than their kings.

units.la: Qua Procurator aut Mandatarius peccat, ijs peccat, quorum nomina fuerint. Nempe quia hi consenserant vt is eorum esset ea in re Procurator aut Mandatarius. Sequitur ergo imputatio, si qua est, eorum consensum, non antecedit. Quis autem nostrum, tanto antequam esset, suum vnquam Procuratorem aut Mandatarium constituit Adamum? Multis in locis obtinet, vt si Vassallus infidelis fuerit suo Domino, peccet non solum sibi, sed suis posteris, qui sic feudo excidunt, aliās ad se peruenturo. Eatenus certe posteris peccat, quia feudum quod amisit, cum amplius non habeat, tradere liberis suis non poterit. Id quod etiam euenit Adamo, qui, cum iustitiam originalem amisisset, eam in posteros propagare non potuit: quis enim dare possit, id quod non habet? Nec tamen sequitur propterea infidelitate posteris imputari. Nam si feudum vendidisset, aut potentioris vel vi, vel fraude amisisset, eo pariter,absque vllius culpæ imputatione, priuarentur posteri. "Et apud Macedonas, addit vir doctus, crimen maiestatis ab aliquo commissum in vniuersam eius cognationem vindicabatur. Quid? An homi-num crudelitatem ab ipsa Dei Lege damnatam putat vir clariss. Deum imitari? aut ex hominum injustitia, quid Dei justitiam deceat,debere colligi? Aliam ei mentem & opto, & esse puto.
units.tr: Whoever a proxy or agent sins against, sins against those whose names were given. Clearly, because these people had consented that he should be their proxy or agent in that matter. Therefore imputation, if there is any, follows their consent; it does not precede it. But which of us, long before we existed, ever appointed Adam as our proxy or agent? In many places it holds that if a vassal is unfaithful to his lord, he sins not only against himself but against his posterity, who thus lose the fief that would otherwise have come to them. To that extent he certainly sins against posterity, because a man who has lost a fief, no longer having it, cannot hand it down to his children. This also happened to Adam, who, having lost original righteousness, could not propagate it to his posterity: for who can give what he does not have? Yet it does not follow that for that reason his unfaithfulness is imputed to posterity. For if he had sold the fief, or lost it through the power or fraud of a stronger man, his descendants would equally have been deprived of it, without any imputation of guilt. And among the Macedonians, the learned man adds, a crime of treason committed by someone was avenged upon his whole family. What then? Does this distinguished man think that God imitates the cruelty of men, a cruelty condemned by God's own Law? Or should we infer from human injustice what befits God's justice? I both hope and think he has a different mind.

units.la: Sequuntur in ejus libro, Et quamuis major sit ἵσότης Legum quæ obtinent inter Christianos, sæpe tamen euenit, vt læsæ Majestatis aliudue grauius crimen sic imputetur liberis & posteris ejus qui illud commiserit, vt bonis suis in siscum redactis, etiam nobilitatis gradu excidant. Nempe liberi opum & nobilitatis patris sunt hæredes, si quas habet, si vero nullas habuit, aut habuit quidem, sed aut sua, aut nulla culpa amisit, qui earum possent esse hæredes? Hoc vero quid ad imputationem antecedentem primæ hominis inobedientiæ probandam facere potest? Pestem contrahit aliquis sæpenumero non soli sibi, sed domesticis etiam & vicinis suis. Num vlla fit eis propterea illius viri vel actionis, aut passionis, qua pestem contraxit, vel pestis ipsius imputatio?
units.tr: The book continues: And although the equality of the laws that hold among Christians is greater, it often happens that treason or another more serious crime is so imputed to the children and posterity of the one who committed it, that when his goods have been confiscated to the treasury, they also lose their rank of nobility. Clearly, children are heirs to their father's wealth and nobility, if he had any; but if he had none, or had some and lost them through his own fault or through no fault, who could be heirs to them? But what does this have to do with proving the antecedent imputation of the first man's disobedience? Someone often catches the plague, and not only he but his household and neighbours as well. Does the imputation of that man's act or suffering, by which he caught the plague, or of the plague itself, therefore fall on them?

units.la: Præclare Chamierus Panst. tom. 3. lib. 1. de hom. corrupto. cap. 8. § 10. Atqui totam naturam (peccatum Adami) læsit, inquit Salmero: itaque factum est commune omnium. Nego consequentiam. Læsio ipsa facta est communis, at non causa læsionis. Sic si domus vna conflagret, vt sæpe fit, ob segnitiem Domini, indeque vicinæ domus: erit quidem incendium commune: at segnities tota illius Domini, non reliquorum : non est enim segnities ipsa incendium; sed tantùm caussa incendij, quod ad reliquos peruenit. Sic qui miles excubias agit negligenter, nocet ille quidem toti exercitui: sed non fuit tamen totus exercitus segnis. Sic Neronis crudelitas Romanis nocuit: nec Romani tamen crudeles. Sexcenta sunt hujusmodi.
units.tr: Chamier rightly says, in his Panstratia, vol. 3, book 1, On Corrupt Man, ch. 8, §10: But Salmeron says that it injured the whole nature (the sin of Adam), and so it became common to all. I deny the consequence. The injury itself became common, but not the cause of the injury. So if one house burns, as often happens through the negligence of its master, and the neighbouring houses with it: the fire is indeed common, but the negligence belongs wholly to that master and not to the rest; for the negligence itself is not the fire, but only the cause of the fire that reached the others. Likewise, a soldier who keeps watch carelessly harms the whole army, yet the whole army was not negligent. Likewise Nero's cruelty harmed the Romans, yet the Romans were not cruel. There are six hundred such examples.

units.la: IV. Superioribus alia quædam Cl. Marefius adjungit argumenta. Ecquis vero, inquit, neget quod nos peccauimus, nobis merito jureque imputari? Iam autem nestrum esse quoque illud peccatum, clare docet Apostolus, qui omnes in Adamo peccasse scripsit. Rom. s. 12. Omnino quod nos peccauimus, nobis merito imputatur. Sed illud peccare nostrum prius est, saltem ordine naturæ, ipsa illius imputatione. Præscinde ergo cogitatione imputationem, nolsque si potes, demcnstra peccasse ipsum primum actuale peccatum primi hominis. Qui antecedentem imputationem tenent, aiunt peccatum illud nostrum non esse nisi per imputationem. Si nostrum non est nisi imputatione, nostrum est quia nobis imputatur, non contrà nobis imputatur quia nostrum est. Ad locum Apostoli quod attinet, nec verbo peccauimus primum actuale Adæ peccatum significatur, nec Apostolus nobis videtur dicere in quo sed eo quod potius, nec si vertas in quo propterea elici vlla poterit imputatio, nisi forte consequens seu mediata, vt suo loco, Deo dante, de-monstraturus sum.
units.tr: IV. Marefius adds some other arguments to the above. Who, indeed, he says, would deny that we sinned, and that it is rightly and justly imputed to us? But that this sin is also ours, the Apostle clearly teaches, who wrote that all sinned in Adam. Rom. 5. 12. Certainly, that we sinned is rightly imputed to us. But that sinning is ours comes before the imputation itself, at least in the order of nature. So set imputation aside in your thought, and if you can, show that the first man's first actual sin was itself a sin. Those who hold the antecedent imputation say that this sin is ours only through imputation. If it is ours only by imputation, it is ours because it is imputed to us; it is not imputed to us because it is ours. As for the Apostle's text, the word sinned does not signify Adam's first actual sin, and the Apostle does not seem to us to say in whom but rather because. Nor, even if you translate in whom, can any imputation be drawn from it, unless perhaps a consequent or mediate one, which I shall show in its place, God willing.

units.la: V. Addit, Si enim in Abrahæ lumbis decimatus est Leui, Heb. vii. 9. quanto magis in lumbis Adami nos omnes peccasse censebimur, vtpote qui in illo essemus, vt rami in radice, massa in primitiys, membra in capite, Rom.
units.tr: V. He adds: For if Levi was tithed in the loins of Abraham, Heb. 7. 9, how much more shall we all be counted as having sinned in the loins of Adam, since we were in him, as branches in the root, the mass in the firstfruits, the members in the head, Rom.

units.la: xi. 16. 1. Cor. xv. 22. Si quis similiter argumentaretur: Si in Abrahæ lumbis decimatus est Leui, quanto magis in lumbis Sethi, vel Enofchi, vel alterius alicuius Patriarcharum qui ante diluuium vixerunt, nos omnes peccauimus? Probaretne consequentiam vir doctus? aut quid posset respondere, quod ei reponi similiter non possit? Nulla igitur est confequentia. Qua enim arte inde elicietur imputatio primi peccati actualis potius quàm sequentium, & Adami potius quàm Sethi aut Noachi; & antecedens potius quàm consequens? Sed, vt liberaliter agam, fateor nos in lumbis Adami peccaffe: num inde sequitur, nobis ejus primum actuale peccatum imputari imputatione quæ corruptionem hæreditariam antecedat? sequitur contrarium potius. Peccauimus enim in Adamo, quia in eo fuimus. Fuimus autem in eo vt rami in radice. Ita autem sunt rami in radice, vt nihil radicis ramis imputetur proprie, sed trahant rami à radice naturam suam & succum vitalem, qualis est in radice, bonum vel malum. Sic nos ab Adamo currupto naturam corruptam traximus. Cæterum nec massa in primitijs proprie fuit, sed in massa primitiæ, nec alia membra in capite. Itaque hæ comparationes ab eo quod agimus alienæ videntur, nec vllam imputationem inducunt, nedum immediatam aut antecedentem.
units.tr: xi. 16; 1 Cor. 15. 22. If someone argued in the same way: If Levi was tithed in the loins of Abraham, how much more did we all sin in the loins of Seth, or Enoch, or some other of the patriarchs who lived before the flood? Would the learned man accept that inference? Or what could he answer that could not equally be turned back on him? So there is no valid inference. For by what art would an actual imputation of the first sin be drawn from it rather than of the later sins, and of Adam rather than of Seth or Noah, and an antecedent imputation rather than a consequent one? But, to be generous, I grant that we sinned in the loins of Adam. Does it follow that his first actual sin is imputed to us by an imputation that precedes hereditary corruption? The opposite follows rather. For we sinned in Adam because we were in him. We were in him as branches in the root. But branches are in the root in such a way that nothing of the root is properly imputed to the branches; rather, the branches draw from the root their own nature and vital sap, whatever it is in the root, good or bad. So we, from the corrupted Adam, drew a corrupt nature. Moreover, the mass was not properly in the firstfruits, but the mass was in the firstfruits as their first portion; nor are the other members in the head. Therefore these comparisons seem foreign to what we are discussing, and they bring in no imputation at all, much less an immediate or antecedent one.

units.la: VI. Sed nescio quid subjicit probationis.
units.tr: VI. But I do not know what proof he adds.

units.la: Erat quippe is persona publica & totum genus humanum repræsentabat longè efficacius quàm summus Sacerdos in sanctuario totam gentem Israeliticam. Primum, nonne id æque facile negari a me potest, ac affirmatur à viro docto? Deinde, fac ita esse, an igitur vna aliqua, eaque prima, summi Sacerdotis actio genti Israelitica imputabatur? Si ais, da locum Scripturæ qui id doceat. Si negas, quid hoc facit ad probandam imputationem solius primi peccati actualis Adami, & quidem antecedentem? Repræsentabat populum Israeliticum summus sacerdos ex munere, vt vas fœderis legalis, eumque super humeris & corde, quodammodo gestabat. Diciturne tale quid de Adamo?
units.tr: For he was a public person and represented the whole human race far more effectively than the high priest in the sanctuary represented the whole Israelite nation. First, can I not deny this just as easily as the learned man affirms it? Next, suppose it is so: was some one action of the high priest, and that the first, imputed to the Israelite nation? If you say so, produce a passage of Scripture that teaches it. If you deny it, what does this do to prove the imputation of Adam's actual sin alone, and indeed an antecedent imputation? The high priest represented the Israelite people by virtue of his office, bearing them as it were upon his shoulders and in his heart, as the vessel of the legal covenant. Is anything like this said of Adam?

units.la: VII. Nec minus, inquit, verum est, nos in Adamo peccasse, adeoque iuste nobis omnibus eius peccatum ad pœnam imputari, quàm postea nos concrucifixos Christo in ipso satisfecisse iustitiæ diuinæ, adeoque merito eius satisfactionem & obedientiam nobis imputari apud Deum ad Iustitiam. Fateor nos in Adamo peccasse, & iuste nobis omnibus eius peccatum ad pœnam imputari. Sed id nunc quidem inter nos non versatur in quæstione. Quæritur tantum de imputationis modo, seu, vt ita loquar, specie, vtrum antecedenter seu immediate imputetur, an mediante corruptione? Hoc affirmo, illud vir Clar. probare, nec conatur quidem. Aberrat igitur à statu quæstionis, quæ inter ipsum & Placeum esse debebat. Cæterum in Christo satisfecisse iustitiæ diuinæ dicimur, tanquam in vade nostro, qui loco nostro satisfecit, cum is pro se satisfacere nullo modo deberet. Dicemurne similiter peccasse nos in Adamo tanquam in vade nostro, qui loco nostro peccasset? Scilicet nos tunc tenebamur Deo parere, Adamus non item. Ille autem in locum nostrum venit, vt nostro loco legem violaret. Hoccine placet viro celeberrimo? non arbitror. Iam autem obseruaui satisfactionem Christi nobis imputari mediante consensu nostro seu fide: itaque nihil ex illa comparatione effici posse, nisi ad summum peccatum Adami nobis imputari mediante consensu nostro, qui habitualiter in vitio hæreditario includitur: quæ ipsissima Placei sententia est.
units.tr: VII. "Nor is it less true, he says, that we sinned in Adam, and so his sin is justly imputed to all of us for punishment, than that afterward, being crucified with Christ in him, we satisfied divine justice in him, and so his satisfaction and obedience are imputed to us before God for righteousness." I grant that we sinned in Adam, and that his sin is justly imputed to all of us for punishment. But this is not now the matter in dispute between us. The question is only about the mode of imputation, or, as I may put it, its kind: whether it is imputed antecedently or immediately, or through corruption? I affirm the latter; the illustrious man has to prove the former, and does not even attempt it. He therefore strays from the state of the question, which ought to lie between him and Placeus. Moreover, we are said to have satisfied divine justice in Christ, as in our surety, who satisfied in our place, although he by no means ought to have satisfied for himself. Shall we likewise be said to have sinned in Adam as in our surety, who sinned in our place? Surely then we were bound to obey God, whereas Adam was not likewise bound. But he came into our place so as to violate the law in our place. Does this please that most celebrated man? I do not think so. Now I have observed that Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us through our consent or faith. So nothing can be drawn from that comparison except that Adam's greatest sin is imputed to us through our consent, which is included habitually in hereditary vice; and this is precisely Placeus's own opinion.

units.la: VIII. Vltimo loco hoc pugnat argumento.
units.tr: VIII. Lastly, he contends with this argument.

units.la: Atque hæc peccati Adamici imputatio eo æquior est, quod sicut vitæ conditionem & promissionem non sibi tantum, sed etiam suis posteris acceperat, si staret, ita debuit mortis reatum suo lapsu non sibi tantum, sed etiam suis omnibus contraxisse: nam ad quem pertinent commoda, ad illum quoque onera & incommoda pertinere æquissimum est. Quomodo intelligit, Adamum vitæ conditionem & promissionem non sibi tantum, sed etiam suis posteris accepisse si staret? An sic, posteros Adami futuros fuisse sub eadem conditione & promissione vitæ, sub qua erat Adamus, hoc est, perpetuò victuros, si Dei legem non violassent? Hoc verissimum est. Nam sub quo fœdere sunt patres, sub eodem etiam eorum liberi sunt. An Adamum communicaturum cum posteris justitiam suam originalem, quam conferuasset, fuisse? Nihil verius; sed quid ista ad imputationem peccati Adamici, præsertim antecedentem? Peccato suo se priuauit justitia originali, & corruptionem contraxit, eamque priuationem & corruptionem propagauit in posteros, & per eam suum mortis reatum. Quare, vt fuit sub lege peccati & mortis, sic liberos genuit similiter sub lege peccati & mortis. Communicauit enim cum illis suum peccatum, & per peccatum, mortem. An denique intelligit, justitiam Adami, si stetisset, omnibus ejus posteris ad vitam æternam imputandam fuisse? Primùm hoc negat, & aliquot argumentis refellit D. Gariffolius lib. de Imput. primi peccati cap. xv. §. 14. pag. 510. 511. Deinde, vnde id sciri potest? Denique, oportuisset Adamum gignere liberos sibi dissimiles,hoc est, immutabiles seu impeccabiles. Ponamus enim eos peccaffe, fuissent simul & justi imputatione paternæ justitiæ, & injusti proprio peccato, atque adeo simul & vita & morte digni. Si dixeris, peccando ab illa imputatione excidisse, reponam igitur illam imputationem superfluam ac inutilem fuisse, quippe quæ, fi peccaffent, eis nullo fuisset vsui; vtpote non minus propria justitia justis, quàm ipse fuerat Adamus. Valet igitur hoc argumentum ad euertendam potius quàm ad stabiliendam imputationem antecedentem Adamici peccati. Quis enim credat, Deum æquissimum eam legem posuisse Adamo, vt fi obediret, quantumuis constanter & perpetuò, non imputaretur ejus obedientia posteris, imputaretur tamen ejus inobedientia, fi contingeret eum vel semel non obedire; atque ita (quod ad imputationem attinet) contrario modo sese obedientia & inobedientia haberent?
units.tr: And this imputation of Adam's sin is the more equitable, because just as he had received the condition of life and the promise not only for himself but also for his posterity, had he stood, so he ought by his fall to have contracted the guilt of death not only for himself but for all his descendants: for it is most equitable that the burdens and disadvantages pertain to the one to whom the benefits pertain. How does he understand that Adam received the condition of life and the promise not only for himself but also for his posterity, had he stood? Does he mean that Adam's posterity would have been under the same condition and promise of life under which Adam was, that is, would have lived forever, had they not violated God's law? This is most true: for under whatever covenant the fathers are, under the same their children also are. Or does he mean that Adam would have shared with his posterity the original righteousness which he had preserved? Nothing is truer; but what has this to do with the imputation of Adam's sin, especially an antecedent one? By his sin he deprived himself of original righteousness and contracted corruption, and he propagated that deprivation and corruption into his posterity, and through it his guilt of death. Wherefore, as he was under the law of sin and death, so he begat children under the same law of sin and death. For he communicated to them his sin, and through sin, death. Or finally, does he mean that Adam's righteousness, had he stood, would have been imputed to all his posterity for eternal life? First, D. Gariffolius denies this and refutes it with several arguments, in his book on the imputation of the first sin, chap. 15, §14, pp. 510–511. Second, whence can this be known? Finally, Adam would have had to beget children unlike himself, that is, unchangeable or unable to sin. For let us suppose they sinned: they would at once have been righteous through the imputation of their father's righteousness, and unrighteous through their own sin, and so at the same time worthy both of life and of death. If you say that by sinning they would have fallen from that imputation, I will reply that the imputation would then have been superfluous and useless, since, if they had sinned, it would have been of no use to them, being just no less by their own righteousness than Adam himself had been. This argument therefore serves rather to overthrow than to establish the antecedent imputation of Adam's sin. For who would believe that God, most equitable, laid down such a law for Adam that, if he obeyed, however constantly and perpetually, his obedience would not be imputed to his posterity, yet his disobedience would be imputed if he happened to disobey even once; so that (as far as imputation is concerned) obedience and disobedience would stand in opposite relation?

units.la: CAPVT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Si quam imputationem primi Adæ peccati probant Argumenta D. Garissolij, eam nonnisi mediatam seu consequentem esse.
units.tr: If the arguments of Garissolius prove any imputation of Adam's first sin, it is only mediate or consequent.

units.la: I. SIc se habuerunt argumenta D. Marefij. Edita Oeft Montalbani Anno M. DC. XLVIII. Decreti Synodici Carentonienfis De Imputatione primi peccati Adæ explicatio & defensio , autore Ant. Gariffolio in Ecclesia & Academia Montalbanenfi Verbi Dei ministro, & SS. Theologiæ Profefsfore ; Amplissimis Ecclesiarum & Academiarum Tigurinæ , Bernenfis , Bafileenfis , Schaphufianæ Præfidibus , supremisque Scholarchis &c. dicata , apud quos de quibusdam, quos non nominat, spargit multa, & queritur, veritatis & pacis, fuique adeo ipsius honoris causa , fi quid intelligo, potius tacenda. Qui apud tantos viros tam publicè accusati, sibi, nisi paci & tranquillitati Ecclesiæ, quàm famæ suæ, consu!tum maluissent , haudquaquam defuissent. Sed quia ( quod mihi vehementer dolet ) præmatura morte magnus ille vir ereptus Ecclesiæ est, parcitum ejus memoriæ,quantum possum , cupió.
units.tr: I. Such were the arguments of Maresius. Garissolius published at Montauban in 1648 his Explanation and Defence of the Decree of the Synod of Charenton concerning the Imputation of Adam's First Sin, written by Antoine Garissolius, minister of the Word of God and professor of sacred theology in the church and academy of Montauban. He dedicated it to the most distinguished presidents of the churches and academies of Zurich, Bern, Basel and Schaffhausen, and to the supreme scholarchs. In it he scatters many charges against certain persons whom he does not name, and he complains about them. As far as I understand, these matters should rather be passed over in silence, for the sake of truth and peace, and for his own honour. Those who were so publicly accused before such men would not have been lacking, had they preferred to look to the peace and tranquillity of the Church rather than to their own reputation. But because that great man, to my great sorrow, was snatched from the Church by an untimely death, I wish to spare his memory as far as I can.

units.la: II. Missa igitur Epistola dedicatoria, is toto fere libro duo quædam manuscripta, Placeique theses refellere studuit. Eorum Manuscriptorum alterum prius, alterum posterius appellat, credo quia alterum ante Synodum nationalem , alterum post scriptum fuit. Prius illud paucis ante Synodum nationalem mensibus suus auctor ab amico pastore fatis grandæuo rogatus ex tempore quasi fuderat, autographumque suum , quia tabellarius vrgebat , nullo retento exemplo , nec cum vllo vel collega, vel amico communicatum, nec postea à fe vllo modo visum, adeum miserat. Itaque fi qua illius disseminata sunt exemplaria, id, aut ab eo, ad quem missum fuerat, aut ab ipso D. Gariffolio, cum quo ille id communicauerat, factum fuisse oportuit. Illud certè nec suus autor habet, neque Placeus, & quis illius aliquod habeat exemplar , nunc quidem me prorsus fugit. Itaque non possum illud cum D. Gariffolij refutatione vllo modo conferre.
units.tr: II. Having sent his dedicatory letter, he set himself, throughout almost the whole of his book, to refute two manuscripts and the theses of Placeus. He calls one of these manuscripts the former and the other the latter, I suppose because one was written before the national Synod and the other after it. The former was thrown off hastily by its author a few months before the national Synod, at the request of an old friend who was a minister. Since the courier was pressing, the author sent his autograph to that friend without keeping a copy, and without sharing it with any colleague or friend, and he never looked at it again. So if any copies of it have circulated, they must have been made either by the man to whom it was sent or by Garissolius himself, with whom that man had shared it. Neither its author nor Placeus has it, and at present I have no idea who may possess a copy. So I cannot in any way set it against Garissolius's refutation.

units.la: Ad posterius manuscriptum quod spectat, scriptum fuit à Placco festinanti calamo ineunte anno 1647. nihilque est nisi responsio ad aliud manuscriptum ipsius Thesibus oppositum, ab amico quodam ipsi ob ætatem, & doctrinam & munus venerandum, compositum, & ad ipsum, vt ei, si minus acquiesceret, celeriter responderet, missum. Paruit ei Placeus, & respondit. Peruenit ad manus D. Gariffolij ea responsio. Putauit eam manuscriptam & priuatam vnà cum priore illo manuscripto publice, libro typis excusa, & apud Reuerendos Heluetios, qui fortasse ne fando quidem quicquam de ea acceperant, sibi esse refutandam: quam, si vna cum refutatione sua vulgasset, virisque amplissimis legendam exhibuisset, facillimum fuisset eis de tota hac causa iudicium ferre. Sed placuit viro docto Aduersarium suum, (si tamen Aduersarius appellandus est is, qui, ne verbo quidem, eum offendere cuperet) intra priuatos parietes conclusum tenere, ac velut immisso lupatho coercere, dum foris, omnibus audientibus, apud illustrissimos viros, eum grauissimè accusaret, causamque ipsam totam aduersus eum disceptaret.
units.tr: As for the latter manuscript, Placeus wrote it with a hurried pen at the beginning of the year 1647. It is nothing but a reply to another manuscript, written against his theses by a certain friend who was to be honoured for his age, his learning and his office. That friend sent it to Placeus so that, if he was not satisfied, he might answer it quickly. Placeus obeyed and replied. Garissolius came into possession of this reply. He thought that it was a private manuscript, and that he had to refute it together with the former manuscript, which was not published in print. He believed that the Reformed of Switzerland, who perhaps had not even heard a rumour of it, had to be answered. If he had published it along with his own refutation and put it in the hands of those most distinguished men to read, it would have been very easy for them to form a judgement on this whole matter. But the learned man chose to keep his opponent, if indeed he is to be called an opponent (one who did not wish to offend him even by a word), shut up within private walls and, as it were, held in check with a bridle, while outside, before all listeners and before those most illustrious men, he accused him most severely and argued the whole cause against him.

units.la: Ita autem duo illa manuscripta citat, quasi ab eodem autore conscripta essent, cùm tamen non ignoraret solius posterioris Placeum' esse autorem; id quod etiam vno aut altero loco non obscurè innuit: Et cùm posterius hoc manuscriptum in capita xiv. esset distributum, extractas ex eo particulas vbique fere disseminat, capite nunquam notato; vt nescias ex quo manuscripto, vel manuscripti capite excerptum fit id quod citat & refutat : quæ res mihi manuscriptum posterius ( illud enim prius, vt dixi, nec habeo, nec vnde habere possim scio) cum eius refutatione conferenti, plurimum dedit negotij.
units.tr: He cites those two manuscripts as though they were written by the same author, although he did not fail to know that Placeus was the author of the latter alone, a fact which he also hints at openly in one or two places. And although this latter manuscript had been divided into fourteen chapters, he scatters extracts from it almost everywhere, never noting the chapter. So one cannot tell from which manuscript, or which chapter of it, the passage he cites and refutes was taken. This has given me, in comparing the later manuscript (for I do not have the former, as I said, and I know of no way to get it) with his refutation, a great deal of trouble.

units.la: Quoniam autem in eo manuscripto Placeus primum statum quæstionis constituerat perquam accurate, deinde argumenta eius pro imputatione immediata peccati Adamici quicum disputabat, à Scriptura, à ratione, à Patrum & Reformatorum testimonijs ducta dissoluerat, suamque refponsionem varijs contra illam imputationem, vt ferebat occasio, rationibus consperserat, exagitauit D. Gariffolius vehementer illam status quæstionis constitutionem atque expositionem, eaque neglecta sententiam Placeo, quam non agnoscit, vbique attribuit, eamque argumentis ita oppugnauit, vt passim aliquas vel responsiones vel rationes Placei inseruerit, & refellere studuerit. Argumenta autem illius, cui Placeus respondebat, quam vim habeant, non aliunde melius cognosci poteft quàm ex manuscripto illo posteriore, in quo diligenter & summa cum fide ad rationis examen sunt reuocata. Argumenta vero D. Gar. vel eadem sunt cum illis, vel, si ab illis aliquo modo differunt verbis & modo proponendi, idem tamen fere est pondus, vt vix à Manuscripti illius cum libro D. Gar. collatione & contentione eximi possint. Eximam tamen quoad potero, & hoc in loco lectori meo sistam, vt videat ea nihil antecedentem imputationem iuuare.
units.tr: Since in that manuscript Placeus had set out the state of the question very precisely, and then had refuted his arguments for immediate imputation of Adam's sin, which he was debating, drawn from Scripture, from reason, and from the testimonies of the Fathers and the Reformers, and since he had scattered his response to those arguments with various reasons against that imputation, as the occasion arose, Garissolius attacked vehemently that statement and explanation of the state of the question. Neglecting it, he attributed to Placeus everywhere an opinion which Placeus does not hold. He assailed the arguments in such a way that here and there he inserted some of Placeus's answers or reasons and tried to refute them. How strong the arguments were to which Placeus was replying can best be learned from that later manuscript, where they were carefully and faithfully recalled for examination by reason. As for the arguments of Garissolius himself, they are either the same as those, or, if they differ from them in wording and manner of proposing, they have almost the same weight, so that they can hardly be separated from one another except by collating and contending with that manuscript against Garissolius's book. Nevertheless I shall separate them as far as I can, and at this point I shall set them before my reader, so that he may see that they help the antecedent imputation not at all.

units.la: Ille igitur constituto, non vt voluit Placeus, sed vt ipse contra verba & mentem Placei voluit, statu quæstionis absque vlla imputationis distinctione, quoniam satis intelligebat, imputationem antecedentem seu immediatam per se ipsam probari nullo modo posse, statim digressus est totis quatuor capitibus iv. v. vi. vii. ut probaret in genere, imputationem alieni peccati injustam non esse. Id quod primum non tam argumentari est quàm respondere Argumento, quo imputatio antecedens primi Adæ peccati impugnatur, ex eo ducto, quod illa videatur cum justitia pugnare. Deinde id probat quod Placeus non negat. Qui enim imputationem agnoscit peccati alieni mediatam seu consequentem, is certè fatetur aliquam imputationem alieni peccati injustam non esse. Non igitur in genere probandum id erat de alieni peccati imputatione; constat enim & iustam & iniustam esse aliquam posse; sed in specie de tali imputatione, qualis ponitur esse imputatio peccati Adami antecedens seu immediata. Id quod prosecto probatu prorsus impossibile est. Sed quicquid fit, nunc enim mihi non libet cum viro docto excurrere, hæc nulla est consequentia: Aliqua imputatio alieni peccati non est injusta, Ergo primum peccatum actuale Adami omnibus ejus posteris imputatur, & quidem imputatione corruptionem hæreditariam antecedente. Non enim ex illo antecedente consequitur magis talis peccati, nempe primi actualis Adami, talis imputatio, nimirum antecedens, quàm cujusfuis alius peccati alieni, sive ipsius Adami, sive aliorum Patriarcharum quælibet imputatio.
units.tr: Having laid down, then, a state of the question not as Placeus meant it but as Garissolius himself wished it to be, against the words and mind of Placeus, and without any distinction of imputation, since he understood well enough that antecedent or immediate imputation could in no way be proved by itself, he at once turned aside through the whole of chapters iv, v, vi and vii, in order to prove in general that the imputation of another's sin is not unjust. This, first, is less an argument than a reply to the argument by which antecedent imputation of Adam's first sin is attacked, on the ground that it seems to conflict with justice. Then he proves what Placeus does not deny. For whoever acknowledges an imputation of another's sin as mediate or consequent certainly admits that some imputation of another's sin is not unjust. So the point to be proved was not the general one, that imputation of another's sin is not unjust, for it is clear that some imputation may be just and some unjust. The point to be proved was the particular one, concerning that kind of imputation which is posited as the antecedent or immediate imputation of Adam's sin. This is, assuredly, altogether impossible to prove. But whatever the case, for I do not now wish to digress with a learned man, this is not a valid inference: Some imputation of another's sin is not unjust; therefore the actual first sin of Adam is imputed to all his posterity, and indeed by an imputation that precedes hereditary corruption. For from that premise it does not follow that this kind of imputation of the first actual sin of Adam, namely the antecedent kind, is any more valid than any imputation of any other sin of another, whether of Adam himself or of any other patriarch.

units.la: Missa igitur illa digressione cap. viii. Argumenta quædam profert ex cap. v. Ep. ad Rom. ˈf. 12. & seqq. Sed ea argumenta non probare nisi imputationem, quæ corruptionem hæreditariam consequitur, Primum ipsemet fatetur, cap. 8. §. 3. p. 206. & alibi, vt est a nobis obseruatum supra cap. 4. p. 21. & cap. proximo p. 35.
units.tr: Having set aside that digression, in chapter viii he puts forward some arguments drawn from chapter v of the Epistle to the Romans, verse 12 and following. But first he himself admits, in chapter 8, section 3, page 206, and elsewhere, as we have noted above in chapter 4, page 21, and in the preceding chapter, page 35, that those arguments prove only the imputation which follows hereditary corruption.

units.la: Deinde cum sint duc̈ta a comparatione, quam instituit Apostolus inter Christum & Adamum, posset iis omnibus vna responsio opponi, nimirum similitudinem in re tantum esse non in rei modo. Quam responsionem Placeus non didicit à Socino, sed ab Apostolo Rom. 5. 15. 16. à Caluino Com. in Rom. 5. 17. &, vt alios omittam, à Clariss. Theologo Andreæ Riueto, cujus hæc sunt verba in Catholico Orthodoxo Tract. iv. Quæst. 2. §. 18. Nihil tamen est in hoc argumento quod nos adigat vt agnoscamus necessitatem qualitatum inhærentium. Id enim probari tantum potest, nos in Christo justitiam habere, quemadmodum in Adamo iniustitiam. Erit autem comparatio causarum, non modi quo nobis res communicatur. Nam peccatum Adami nobis communicatur per generationem, iustitia autem Christi per imputationem. Itaque non comparat Apostolus modos quibus iustitia recipitur, sed causas, effectus & subiecta vtriusque. Causa salutis est obedientia secundi Adami, vt causa condemnationis sit inobedientia primi. Effecta sunt quod vna nos iniustos constituit, altera iustos. Subiecta sunt multi, per vnum iusti, per alium iniusti redditi. Ideo Episcopus Bipontinus eiusdem cap. hæc verba explicans. Sed non sicut delictum, ita & donum, Ex tota præcedenti similitudine concludit, Similitudo igitur est quoad rem inter hæc, sed non quoad modum. Hoc cum ita sit, aduersariorum claudicat argumentum quia a re ad modum rei non bene argumentantur. In edit. Gall. §. 8. hæc vltima verba efferuntur plenius, Cela estant, l'argument des Aduersaires ne vaut rien ; pource qu'ils concluent en iceluy, que nous sommes instifiez en Christ, de mesme façon que nous sommes rendus pecheurs en Adam, ce que l'Apostre ne dit pas. Quid pro ista nostra responsione, & contra argumenta D. Gar. dici potuit difertius? Ea tamen expendamus breuiter. Non referam omnia eius verba: sunt enim nimis prolixa; sed ea tantùm, in quibus neruus & vis argumenti consistit.
units.tr: Then, since they are drawn from the comparison which the Apostle makes between Christ and Adam, one single answer could be opposed to all of them: namely, that the likeness is in the thing itself and not merely in the manner of the thing. Placeus did not learn this answer from Socinus, but from the Apostle in Romans 5:15–16, from Calvin in his commentary on Romans 5:17, and, to omit others, from the distinguished theologian Andreas Rivetus, whose words in his Catholic Orthodox, tractate iv, question 2, section 18, are these: Yet there is nothing in this argument that compels us to acknowledge the necessity of inherent qualities. For it can only be proved that we have righteousness in Christ, just as we have unrighteousness in Adam. The comparison will be of causes, not of the mode by which the thing is communicated to us. For Adam's sin is communicated to us by generation, but Christ's righteousness by imputation. Therefore the Apostle does not compare the modes by which righteousness is received, but the causes, effects and subjects of each.
