The cause of salvation is the obedience of the second Adam, just as the cause of condemnation is the disobedience of the first. The effects are that the one makes us unrighteous, the other righteous. The subjects are many, made righteous through one and unrighteous through the other. For this reason the Bishop of Zweibrücken, explaining these words of the same chapter, [says]: But not as the offence, so also the gift. From the whole preceding comparison he concludes: The likeness, then, is in the thing between these, but not in the mode. Since this is so, the argument of our opponents limps, because they do not argue well from the thing to the mode of the thing. In the French edition, section 8, these last words are expressed more fully: Cela estant, l'argument des Aduersaires ne vaut rien, that is, since this is so, the argument of our opponents is worth nothing, because they conclude from it that we are justified in Christ in the same way as we are made sinners in Adam, which the Apostle does not say. What could have been said more clearly for this answer of ours, and against the arguments of Garissolius? Still, let us briefly weigh them. I shall not report all his words, for they are too long, but only those in which the sinew and force of the argument consist.

units.la: Arg. 1. Apostolus id sibi propositum habet posteriori capitis 5. parte, quæ a verf. 12. vsque ad finem pertingit, vt, quæ de justificatione docuit, ea nobilis typi expositione confirmet. &c. Docuit autem cap. 4. justificationis nostræ rationem in eo consistere, quòd per imputationem justitiæ Christi fide perceptæ, justificemur, id est, justi habeamur & absoluamur apud Deum &c. Itaque hoc vult Apostolus ex ista Christi cum Adamo collatione concludere, justificationem nobis obtingere ex imputatione iustitiæ Christi. Atqui hoc nulla legitima ratione concludi posset, nisi poneretur imputatio peccati Adæ. &c. Quæ enim est eiusmodi consequentia vis aut ratio? Peccatum naturaliter ex Adamo in nos propagatur, sine omni imputatione. Ergo iustitia secundi Adami, qui Christus est, non propagatione, sed imputatione ad nos descendit. Resp. 1. Primam illam Majorem propositionem, Apostolus quæ de iustificatione cap. 4. docuit, ea nobilis typi expositione confirmat, vel vniuersaliter accipi, vel particulariter, hoc est, Apostolum vel omnia quæ docuit confirmare, vel quædam. Si prius, falsa est propositio. Docuerat enim, fidem imputari ad iustitiam, non iustificari hominem ex operibus legis, promissionem non esse per legem, quænam sit fides per quam justificamur &c. Quæ tamen proprie non confirmat ductis ab isto typo argumentis: quippe quorum in illa comparatione ne meminit quidem. Si posterius, vitiosum est argumentum, nec vllam concludendi vim habet: est enim in prima syllogismorum figura. Quod si concipiatur in tertia figura subjuncta minore vniuersali; ea minor sine dubio falsa erit aperte.
units.tr: Arg. 1. The Apostle has this purpose in the latter part of chapter 5, which runs from verse 12 to the end: to confirm by the noble exposition of the type what he taught about justification. For he taught in chapter 4 that our justification consists in this, that by the imputation of Christ's righteousness, received by faith, we are justified, that is, held and absolved as righteous before God, etc. So the Apostle wants to conclude from this comparison of Christ with Adam that justification comes to us by the imputation of Christ's righteousness. But this could not be concluded by any lawful reasoning unless the imputation of Adam's sin were laid down, etc. For what force or logic is there in such an inference? Sin is propagated from Adam to us naturally, without any imputation. Therefore the righteousness of the second Adam, who is Christ, comes down to us not by propagation but by imputation. Reply 1. That first major premise, the Apostle confirms by the noble exposition of the type what he taught about justification in chapter 4, may be taken either universally or particularly, that is, either as the Apostle confirming all that he taught, or some of it. If the former, the proposition is false. For he had taught that faith is imputed for righteousness, that man is not justified by the works of the law, that the promise is not by the law, what faith is by which we are justified, and so on. Yet he does not properly confirm these by arguments drawn from that type, since in that comparison he does not even mention them. If the latter, the argument is faulty and has no force of inference: it is in the first figure of the syllogism. But if it is conceived in the third figure with a universal minor premise, that minor will clearly be plainly false.

units.la: Resp. 2. Vt ponamus vitio carere Syllogismum, ejus conclusionem non obesse Placeo. Concedit enim vltrò primi Adæ peccati imputationem, modò consequens seu mediata intelligatur, quam intelligi, non autem antecedentem seu immediatam, illa ipsa Christum inter & Adamum comparatio flagitat. Nam imputatio justitiæ Christi fide perceptæ, nostrum consensum, nostram fidem consequitur, eaque mediante fit. Consentaneum est igitur, vt imputatio primi Adæ peccati ei respondens, aliquem nostrum, si non actum, saltem habitum, si non actualem, saltem habitualem consensum sequatur, eoque mediante fiat.
units.tr: Reply 2. Even if we grant that the syllogism is free from fault, Placeus says its conclusion does no harm. For he freely concedes the imputation of the sin of the first Adam, provided it is understood as consequent or mediate, and not as antecedent or immediate. That is what the comparison between Christ and Adam itself requires. For the imputation of Christ's righteousness received by faith follows our consent and our faith, and comes about through them. It is consistent, therefore, that the imputation of the first Adam's sin, corresponding to it, should follow some consent of ours, if not an act, at least a habit, if not an actual consent, at least a habitual one, and should come about through that.

units.la: Resp. 3. eam D. Gar. conclusionem adscribere Apostolo, quæ ex illa comparatione deduci non potest, nisi euersa constante omnium Patrum, omniumque Ecclesiarum Orthodoxarum doctrina. Vult enim hanc esse conclusionem Apostoli. Ergo iustitia secundi Adami, qui Christus est, non propagatione, sed imputatione ad nos descendit. Quæ conclusio sequi non potest nisi ex hoc antecedente, Peccatum Adami non propagatione, sed imputatione ad nos descendit. Nam si ponas peccatum Adami partim propagatione, partim imputatione ad nos descendere, qua consequentia inde conficies, iustitiam Christi non propagatione, sed imputatione descendere? Oportet certè similiter in antecedente propagationem peccati Adæ negare, quam omnes & Patres & Protestantes constanter docuerunt. Quid, quod etiam posito isto falso & erroneo antecedente, consequi non potest illa conclusio, nisi vi majoris istius propositionis quam subticuit, Quomodo peccatum Adami ad nos descendit, eodem, & non alio, descendit ad nos Christi justitia. Iam autem ista propositio si ita universaliter intelligitur, aperte falsa est. Descendit enim in nos peccatum Adami non ex gratia, sed ex justitia; naturaliter, non supernaturaliter; nobis actu non consentientibus &c; Eodemne modo descendit ad nos Christi justitia? Sin autem intelligitur particulariter, ut sit similitudo in quodam modo, non in omni, vitiosa erit consequentia, ut pote ex majore particulari in prima figura. It ergo & contra Ecclesiæ doctrinam hæc argumentatio, & Apostolum facit male ratiocinantem. Quæ omnia viro docto excidisse, & quidem in ipso primo ejus argumento, dolendum profecto est, ut & illud quod sequitur.
units.tr: Reply 3. D. Gar. ascribes to the Apostle a conclusion which cannot be deduced from that comparison, unless the constant doctrine of all the Fathers and of all the orthodox Churches is overturned. For he wants this to be the Apostle's conclusion: Therefore the righteousness of the second Adam, who is Christ, comes down to us not by propagation but by imputation. This conclusion cannot follow except from this antecedent: the sin of Adam comes down to us not by propagation but by imputation. For if you say that Adam's sin comes down to us partly by propagation and partly by imputation, by what inference will you conclude that Christ's righteousness comes down not by propagation but by imputation? Certainly one must likewise deny in the antecedent the propagation of Adam's sin, which all the Fathers and Protestants have constantly taught. Moreover, even if this false and erroneous antecedent is posited, that conclusion cannot follow, except by virtue of that major premise which he left unstated: in the way that Adam's sin came down to us, in that same way and no other, Christ's righteousness comes down to us. Now if that proposition is understood universally in this way, it is plainly false. For Adam's sin came down upon us not from grace but from justice; naturally, not supernaturally; without our actual consent, etc. Does Christ's righteousness come down to us in the same way? But if it is understood particularly, so that there is a likeness in a certain respect and not in every respect, the inference will be faulty, as it is from a particular major premise in the first figure. Therefore this argument is both contrary to the doctrine of the Church and makes the Apostle reason badly. It is truly to be regretted that a learned man should have overlooked all these things, and indeed in his very first argument, as well as what follows.

units.la: Alterum hoc, inquit, rectissime & evidentissime concluditur: Adamus est typus Christi, & sunt Adamus & Christus capita generis humani in contrariis effectis. Atqui Adamici peccati imputatione omnes sumus peccatores & rei. Ergo & justitia Christi imputatione omnes justificamur, seu justi constituimur apud Deum. Quomodo enim id rectissime & evidentissime concluditur, cùm sint in argumento sex aut septem termini? Et quomodo hoc voluit concludere Apostolus, qui neque imputationis peccati Adamici, neque imputationis justitiæ Christi in toto hoc capite meminit? Et quomodo si hoc Apostolus voluit, Caluinus, Martyr, & alij in suis commentariis, eius mentem & verba exposuerunt, nulla, neque imputationis peccati Adami, neque eiusmodi argumentationis, facta mentione? Quid, quod istud argumentum, adeo non rectissime & euidentissime concludit, vt etiam pofsit retorqueri. Nam quae est consequentia, Adamus & Christus sunt capita generis humani in contrariis effectis. Ergo contraria istae effecta ab iis eodem prorsus modo procedunt? Annon potius sequitur, contraria cum sint effecta, illa ab iis contrario modo procedere? id quod etiam res ipsa confirmat. Nam ab Adamo nascimur peccatores naturaliter, a Christo fimus iusti supernaturaliter, ab illo ex iustitia, ab hoc ex gratia, ab illo sine actuali nostro consensu, ab hoc per actualem nostrum consensum, ab illo per propagationem naturalem, (id enim ex quo nata est haeresis Pelagiana perpetuo ab orthodoxis creditum fuit.) ab hoc nullo modo per eiusmodi propagationem. Mitto caetera discrimina, quorum quaedam, vt dixi, ipse Apostolus obseruauit, quaedam Caluinus ad Vf. 17. iis, quae Apostolus obseruauerat, adjunxit. Sed fac argumentum illud D. Gar. recte concludere, concedet Placeus nos omnes Adamici peccati imputatione consequente seu mediata esse peccatores & reos, negabit antecedente seu immediata. Quid facilius quam ita respondere?
units.tr: The second, he says, is most rightly and most evidently concluded: Adam is a type of Christ, and Adam and Christ are the heads of the human race with contrary effects. But by the imputation of Adam's sin we are all sinners and guilty. Therefore also by the imputation of Christ's righteousness we are all justified, or constituted righteous before God. For how is this most rightly and most evidently concluded, when there are six or seven terms in the argument? And how did the Apostle, who mentions neither the imputation of Adam's sin nor the imputation of Christ's righteousness anywhere in this whole chapter, want to conclude this? And if the Apostle meant this, how is it that Calvin, Martyr and others in their commentaries explained his mind and words without mentioning either the imputation of Adam's sin or any such argument? Moreover, this argument does not conclude so rightly and evidently that it cannot even be turned back. For what is the inference: Adam and Christ are the heads of the human race with contrary effects; therefore these contrary effects proceed from them in exactly the same way? Does it not rather follow that, since the effects are contrary, they proceed from them in contrary ways? The thing itself confirms this. For we are born sinners from Adam naturally; we are made righteous from Christ supernaturally; from the one by justice, from the other by grace; from the one without our actual consent, from the other through our actual consent; from the one by natural propagation (for this is what gave rise to the Pelagian heresy, and what has always been believed by the orthodox), from the other in no way by such propagation. I pass over the other differences, some of which, as I said, the Apostle himself noted, and some of which Calvin added on verse 17 to those the Apostle had noted. But grant that D. Gar.'s argument concludes rightly: Placeus will concede that we are all sinners and guilty by the consequent or mediate imputation of Adam's sin, and will deny the antecedent or immediate imputation. What could be easier than to answer in this way?

units.la: Hic D. G. Laudato loco ex Clar. Amyraldi lib. de Iustif. in Millet. c. 3. ex eo sic colligit. Audis, inquit, ex inobedientia Adami, quae fuerit vnica actio, in nos descendentem condemnationem, quae non sit aliquid inhaerens, sed obligatio ad poenam (addiderat Cl. Amyr. vel obligationis gationis illius declaratio à potestate superiori. ) Qui autem propter inobedientiam alterius obligatur ad pœnam, reatum sustinet illius inobedientiæ, adeóque imputatur ei illa inobedientia.
units.tr: Here D. G., after quoting a passage from the most famous Amyraut's book on justification, in Millet, chapter 3, draws this inference from it: You hear, he says, that from the disobedience of Adam, which was a single act, there descends upon us a condemnation which is not something inherent, but an obligation to punishment (the most famous Amyraut had added: or a declaration of that obligation by a superior power). But whoever is obliged to punishment because of another's disobedience sustains the guilt of that disobedience, and so that disobedience is imputed to him.

units.la: Audio quidem ex illa inobedientia descendere in nos condemnationem, sed non audio descendere immediatè & ante corruptionem hæreditariam. id quod tamen vnum inter nos controuertitur. Dixit vir Clar. Adamum inobedientia sua condemnationem & mortem inuexisse, nimirum quia inuexit peccatum in omnes homines, causam condemnationis & mortis, vt patet ex Rom. 5. 12. Dixit eos qui cum Adamo communionem habent, eius condemnationem participare, & vna cum eo mortï esse subiectos. Intelligit autem communionem cum Adamo, non quatenus fuit homo (hanc enim etiam ipse Christus habuit) sed quatenus fuit peccator. Habemus autem communionem cum Adamo quatenus fuit homo, quia traximus ab eo naturam nostram, & quatenus fuit peccator, quia traximus ab eo peccatum nostrum. Sustinemus itaque reatum illius inobedientiæ, sed mediante corruptione ab eo in nos deriuata.
units.tr: I indeed hear that condemnation descends upon us from that disobedience, but I do not hear that it descends immediately and before hereditary corruption; and this is the one point that is disputed between us. The learned man said that Adam by his disobedience brought in condemnation and death, namely because he brought sin into all men, the cause of condemnation and death, as is clear from Rom. 5. 12. He said that those who have communion with Adam share his condemnation, and are subject to death together with him. But he understands communion with Adam not as far as he was a man (for Christ himself had this too), but as far as he was a sinner. Now we have communion with Adam as far as he was a man, because we have drawn our nature from him, and as far as he was a sinner, because we have drawn our sin from him. Therefore we sustain the guilt of that disobedience, but through the corruption derived from him into us.

units.la: Hinc ansam arripit D. Gar. inuehendi in eos qui Rom. 5. Vf. 12. 13. peccati nomine, non ipsum Adami peccatum actuale intelligendum contendunt, sed potius & solum corruptionem internam, & nobis propagatione carnis ex Adamo inhærentem. Voluit fine dubio taxare Placeum, immemor ante hoc vltimum seculum, & superioris finem hanc fuisse omnium aut saltemferè omnium quotquot non fuerunt pelagiani aut Pighiani, communem expositionem. Interim non diffiteor, quin nomine lapsus & inobedientiæ etiam actuale
units.tr: Hence D. Gar. seizes the opportunity to attack those who contend that by the name of sin in Rom. 5:12, 13 is meant not Adam's actual sin itself, but rather, and only, the internal corruption that is inherent in us through the propagation of the flesh from Adam. Without doubt he wished to rebuke Place, forgetting that before this last age the common interpretation of all, or at least nearly all, who were not Pelagians or Pighians was the reverse. Meanwhile I do not deny that by the name of lapse and disobedience, that first sin of Adam ought to be understood, including also the actual sin.

units.la: L
units.tr: L

units.la: illud primum Adami peccatum intelligi debeat.
units.tr: That first sin of Adam ought to be understood.

units.la: Sed nescio quid argumenti D. Gar. subjungit. Quomodo, inquit, de justitia Christi loquitur Apostolus, ita etiam de peccato Adami. At proprie nonnisi de illa justitia loquitur, quæ est ipsius Christi formaliter & subjectiue, nostra vero relatiue & per imputationem. Ergo & proprie nonnisi de illo peccato Adami loquitur, quod in Adamo inhæsit, sed imputatione nostrum fit. Taceo duplex hujus syllogismi in forma vitium, unum, quòd majori affirmanti negantem subsumit in prima figura: alterum, quòd in Majore de modo loquendi agitur, in minore verò de de re ipsa, hoc est, de quadam justitia: posset enim utrumque facile corrigi. Taceo etiam Apostolum non meminisse justitiæ, τῆς δικαιοσύνης Christi, sed ἑνὸς δικαιώματος, τῆς ὑπακοῆς τε ἑνός. Illud obiceruo: In suum autorem recidere hoc argumentum, & quidem duplicato ictu. Nam primò justitia quæ fuit in Christo formaliter & subjectiue, justitia fuit habitualis, actiones enim non sunt formaliter & subjectiue in agente, sed ab agente. Unde sequitur similiter Apostolum de Adami peccato habituali loqui: quod tamen hoc ipso loco D. Gar. negat. Deinde per justitiam Christi D. Gar. justitiam intelligit, quæ vniuersam totius vitæ Christi obedientiam complectitur. Oportet igitur etiam per peccatum Adami omnem totius vitæ ejus inobedientiam intelligere. Id quod falsum esse & omnes fatentur, & ipse D. G. clamat. Quod si per iustitiam Christi, vnam tantum singularem Christi obedientiam intelligi voluit, oppositam vni tantum singulari peccato Adami, agnoscet quidem Plac. ita accipi ab Apostolo παράπτωμα, & παρακοῆς nomina ᴥ 1.
units.tr: But I do not know what argument D. Gar. adds here. How, he says, the Apostle speaks of the righteousness of Christ, so also he speaks of the sin of Adam. But properly he speaks only of that righteousness which is in Christ himself formally and subjectively, and ours relatively and by imputation. Therefore he also properly speaks only of that sin of Adam which inhered in Adam but becomes ours by imputation. I pass over the double fault in the form of this syllogism: first, that in the major premise he takes an affirmative and in the minor a negative, in the first figure; second, that the major concerns a mode of speaking, while the minor concerns the thing itself, namely a certain righteousness. Both could easily be corrected. I also pass over the fact that the Apostle does not mention the righteousness [τῆς δικαιοσύνης] of Christ, but one righteousness [ἑνὸς δικαιώματος] and the obedience of one [τῆς ὑπακοῆς τε ἑνός]. This is my objection: the argument recoils on its own author, and with a double blow. For first, the righteousness which was in Christ formally and subjectively was habitual righteousness, since actions are not formally and subjectively in the agent but come from the agent. It follows that the Apostle speaks similarly of Adam's habitual sin, which D. Gar. in this very place denies. Next, by the righteousness of Christ D. Gar. understands that which embraces the whole obedience of Christ's life. It is necessary, then, to understand by the sin of Adam all the disobedience of his whole life as well. This everyone admits to be false, and D. G. himself cries out against it. But if by the righteousness of Christ he meant only one singular obedience of Christ, opposed to only one singular sin of Adam, Placaeus will certainly agree that the Apostle uses the words παράπτωμα and παρακοή in this sense, as in Rom. 5.

units.la: 18. & 19. Sed negabit inde sequi, aut imputationem immediatam inobedientiae actualis Adami, aut Apostolum per τὸ ἁμάρτιαν Vf. 12.13. non designasse vitium inhaerens: ac nihilominus hujus D. Gar. argumentationis vanitatem sic ostendet: Subsumet enim, Atqui Apostolus proprie non loquitur de prima Christi iustitia seu obedientia, sed de vltima. Ergo & proprie non loquitur de primo Adami peccato, sed de vltimo. Quid salsius ista conclusione? Quid tamen obstat, quominus aeque recte & evidenter colligi videatur ac illa D. Gariffolij? Quod porro ait justitiam Christi nostram fieri per imputationem, id si verum est, ideo est verum, quoniam illa imputatio gratuita eius donatio est. Fit enim nostra proprie loquendo Christi justitia, Dei & Christi dono, & nostra per fidem acceptione; quo modo certe peccatum Adami fieri nostrum non potest. Quod discrimen passim Apostolus inculcat τῷ παραπτώματι & χάρι- ματι opponens τὸ χάρισμα, τὸ δώρημα, τῷ δωρεᾷ ἐν χάριτι, τῇ δωρεᾷ τῆς χάριτος ἐξ τῆς δικαιοσύνης. Quod subjungit, peccatum quod in Adamo inhaesit imputatione nostrum fieri, mihi vehementer absurdum videtur. Inde enim sequitur, peccatum illud non imputari nobis, quia nostrum sit; sed contra nostrum esse, quia nobis imputetur; atque adeo illam imputationem causam esse cur peccatores & rei sumus, sicut donatio & imputatio justitiae Christi causa est cur sumus justi. Id quod quam sit a Dei judicis (nam imputatio est actio judiciaria) aequitate alienum, nemo pius non videt. Caeterum lege si placet comm. Caluini in Vf. 17. Hic etiam D.G. confitetur, imputationem sequi corruptionem natiuam, quo confesso, quam imputationem probare potest,nisi consequentem ? Imputatio, inquit, necessario cum corruptione natiua coniungitur, imo eam sequitur.
units.tr: 18 and 19. But he will deny that it follows from this either an immediate imputation of Adam's actual disobedience, or that the Apostle, by τὸ ἁμαρτίαν in verses 12 and 13, did not mean inherent vice. Nevertheless he will show the emptiness of D. Gar.'s argument in this way: he will assume, "But the Apostle does not properly speak of the first righteousness or obedience of Christ, but of the last. Therefore neither does he properly speak of the first sin of Adam, but of the last." What is more absurd than this conclusion? Yet what prevents it from seeming to be drawn as correctly and evidently as that of D. Gariffolius? As for his further claim that the righteousness of Christ becomes ours by imputation, if that is true, it is true because that imputation is a gratuitous gift of Christ. For properly speaking, Christ's righteousness becomes ours by the gift of God and Christ and by our acceptance through faith. In that way the sin of Adam certainly cannot become ours. The Apostle constantly insists on this difference, setting τῷ παραπτώματι against χαρίσματι, τὸ χάρισμα, τὸ δώρημα, τῷ δωρεᾷ ἐν χάριτι, τῇ δωρεᾷ τῆς χάριτος, and ἐξ τῆς δικαιοσύνης. As for his addition that the sin which inhered in Adam becomes ours by imputation, this seems to me utterly absurd. For it follows that the sin is not imputed to us because it is ours, but on the contrary is ours because it is imputed to us. Then that imputation would be the cause of our being sinners and guilty, just as the gift and imputation of Christ's righteousness is the cause of our being righteous. How far this is from the equity of God as judge (for imputation is a judicial act), no godly person fails to see. Moreover, if you like, read Calvin's commentary on verse 17. Here too D. G. confesses that imputation follows native corruption. Since he confesses this, what imputation can he prove except a consequent one? Imputation, he says, is necessarily joined to native corruption, nay it follows it.

units.la: Videtur §.6.aliud quoddam argumentum afferre, Sed reuera idem est cum superiori, fi vim & pondus spectes, vt nihil fit opus alia refponfione. Id tamen quale fit videamus. Sed & illud, inquit, ad scopum huius loci pertinet, quod causæ contrariorum effectuum comparantur, vt scilicet Adamus & Christus, tanquam causæ ejusdem generis producant effectus suos in suis. Itaque quemodo Christus est causa iustificationis, ita est Adamus causa condemnationis. Nempe Christus iustificationis & reconciliationis nostræ causa meritoria: Adamus itidem causa meritoria condemnationis & abdicationis nostræ &c. Hinc colligit; Qui peccato suo nobis reatum & pœnam meruit, illius peccatum nobis imputatur. Sicut qui iustitia sua nobis reconciliationem meretur & vitam, illius iustitia imputatur. Atqui Adamus peccato suo nobis meruit, vt reii fimus & pœnis obnoxij. Itaque dubitari non potest, quin illius peccatum nobis imputetur. Singula expendamus: Fateor Christum & Adamum esse causas contrariorum effectuum in suis, illum iustificationis, hunc condemnationis, nego inde sequi, Quomodo Christus est causa iustificationis, ita esse Adamum causam condemnationis, nisi quomodo accipiatur pro quam vere. Contrarium enim potius, vt jam monui, inde sequitur. Causæ enim contrariorum effectuum non agunt eodem modo, nisi forte generali, sed potius contrario. Non enim quod calefacit, eodem modo speciali agit ac quod frigefacit, sed opposito potius; illud enim agit calefaciendo, hoc frigefaciendo. Christus fuit causa iustificationis obediendo;
units.tr: In §6 he seems to bring forward another argument, but in reality it is the same as the previous one, if you look at its force and weight, so that no other answer is needed. Let us see what it is. But that also, he says, belongs to the purpose of this place, that the causes of contrary effects are compared, namely that Adam and Christ, as causes of the same kind, produce their effects in their own people. Thus just as Christ is the cause of justification, so Adam is the cause of condemnation. Namely, Christ is the meritorious cause of our justification and reconciliation; Adam likewise is the meritorious cause of our condemnation and rejection, etc. From this he infers: whoever by his sin has merited guilt and punishment for us, his sin is imputed to us. Just as whoever by his righteousness has merited reconciliation and life for us, his righteousness is imputed. But Adam by his sin has merited for us that we are liable to guilt and punishments. Therefore it cannot be doubted that his sin is imputed to us. Let us weigh each point. I grant that Christ and Adam are causes of contrary effects in their own people, the one of justification, the other of condemnation. I deny that it follows that, as Christ is the cause of justification, so Adam is the cause of condemnation, unless as is taken to mean how truly. For, as I have already said, the opposite follows from this. Causes of contrary effects do not act in the same way, except perhaps in a general sense, but rather in an opposite way. That which heats does not act in the same specific manner as that which cools, but rather in the opposite; the one acts by heating, the other by cooling. Christ was the cause of justification by obeying;

units.la: Adamus condemnationis inobediendo ; Ille edendo de fructu vetito, hic moriendo ; Ille soluendo quod debebamus vt vas noster, hic alio plane modo: nam, nec vas noster erat, nec fecit aut soluit quod debebamus, tantum fecit id quod non facere tenebatur. Quare egregie ad object. Bellarm. ex Rom. 5. sicut regnauit peccatum in mortem, ita & gratia regnet per iustitiam ad vitam aeternam, respondet Clarissimus vir, cuius quondam auditor fuit Placeus, Chamierus, his verbis ( transcribam enim totam eius responsionem, quia lectu dignissima est. ) Respondeo, iustitiam hoc loco, intelligi internam renouationem nostram, concedi non posse: sed iustitiam illam Christi, cuius imputatione iusti: Neque concedimus vllam in Antithesi vim esse, quae illud inferat. Peccatum fatemur intelligi id, quod regnabat per opera mortifera: sive melius ipsam illam corruptionem nobis inhaerentem unde opera mortifera: sed propterea iustitiam intelligendam nobis inhaerentem prorsus negamus. Non enim omnino eadem ratio cadendi, quae resurgendi. Sed vicissim, qui per proprium peccatum cecidit, non potuit resurgere, nisi per alienam iustitiam. Quomodo non potest decoctor in servo esse nisi per propriam indigentiam: sed servo soli idem non potest, nisi per alienam opulentiam; nimirum eius, qui pro eo pecunias numerat. Itaque comparatur peccatum iustitiae, non tanquam inhaerens inhaerenti, quo scipsum decipit Bellarminus: sed tanquam causa causae, illinc mortis, hinc vitae. Hactenus Chamierus. Cum igitur propositio, Quomodo Christus est causa iustificationis, ita est Adamus causa condemnationis, non fit uniuersaliter vera, non potest ex ea deduci haec conclusio;
units.tr: Adam the cause of condemnation by disobeying; the one by eating of the forbidden fruit, the other by dying; the one by paying what we owed as our surety, the other in a quite different way: for neither was he our surety, nor did he perform or pay what we owed; he only did what he was not bound to do. Therefore the most distinguished man, under whom Place was once a student, Chamier, answers excellently to the objection of Bellarmine from Rom. 5: as sin reigned unto death, so also grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life. I shall transcribe his whole reply, for it is most worthy of reading: I answer that by righteousness in this place the internal renewal of ourselves cannot be meant: but that righteousness of Christ, by whose imputation we are righteous. Nor do we concede that there is any force in the antithesis which would imply that. We grant that by sin is meant that which reigned through deadly works; or better, that very corruption inhering in us, from which come the deadly works. But we absolutely deny that by righteousness is meant what inheres in us. For the manner of falling is not wholly the same as that of rising. Rather, conversely, he who fell through his own sin could not rise again except through another's righteousness. As a bankrupt cannot be in a servant's position except through his own want, but the servant alone cannot be in the same position except through another's wealth, namely of him who counts out the money for him. Thus sin is compared with righteousness not as one inherent thing to another inherent thing, by which Bellarmine deceives himself; but as cause to cause, the one of death, the other of life. So far Chamier. Since therefore the proposition, "as Christ is the cause of justification, so Adam is the cause of condemnation," is not universally true, the following conclusion cannot be deduced from it:

units.la: Ergo vt Christus est causa meritoria iustificationis, sic Adamus est causa meritoria condemnationis.Quocunque enim modo ex ea formetur syllogismus, eius, fi fit in prima figura, vitiosa erit forma; fi in tertia, minor erit aperte falsa. Demus tamen, Adamum esse causam meritoriam condemnationis: num inde consequetur peccati Adamici imputatio immediata ? nullo modo. Est enim causa meritoria, noftrae condemnationis, non immediate, aut merito antecedente corruptionem hæreditariam, sed mediante illa corruptione quam nobiscum communicauit. meruit enim nobis condemnationem, quia meruit sibi condemnationem, & suum meritum seu peccatum in nos propagauit, ac per peccatum seu meritum condemnationem. Constat enim nos omnes ex Adamo reatum & condemnationem mediante corruptione hæreditaria ab eo in nos propagata trahere. Id quod similiter de Christo dici non potest, nos iustificationem ab eo, mediante inhærente iustitia in nos propagata, trahere: non enim, vt corruptio hæreditaria vere peccatum est nobis condemnandis sufficiens, sic iustitia nobis inhærens meretur vitam æternam aut ad nos iustificandos sufficit. Hoc discrimen qui nos oppugnant, fi agnoscunt, vident sua huiusmodi argumenta ruere; fi non agnoscunt, discedunt a fidei confessione, quam 28. Synodi Nat. confirmauerunt. vtrumuis eligunt?
units.tr: Therefore, just as Christ is the meritorious cause of justification, so Adam is the meritorious cause of condemnation. However the syllogism is framed, if it is in the first figure its form will be faulty, and if in the third its minor premise will be plainly false. Yet grant that Adam is the meritorious cause of condemnation: does it follow that the imputation of Adam's sin is immediate? By no means. He is the meritorious cause of our condemnation not immediately, nor by a merit preceding hereditary corruption, but through that corruption which he shared with us. He merited condemnation for us because he merited it for himself, and he propagated his merit or sin into us, and through sin or merit, condemnation. For it is agreed that we all draw guilt and condemnation from Adam through hereditary corruption propagated from him into us. The same cannot be said of Christ, that we draw justification from him through inherent righteousness propagated into us. For just as hereditary corruption is truly sin sufficient to condemn us, so the righteousness inherent in us does not merit eternal life, nor is it sufficient to justify us. If those who oppose us acknowledge this distinction, they see that their arguments of this kind collapse; if they do not acknowledge it, they depart from the confession of faith which the National Synod (28th article) confirmed. Which of the two do they choose?

units.la: Quid superioribus argumentis pro imputatione peccati Adæ, præsertim immediata, debilius? Laudat tamen ea suus auctor, &c, vt fine Lectoris fastidio repeti possint, in breue compendium redigit. Comparantur, inquit, causæ, comparantur causarum effecta, comparantur effectorum modi. Causae, scilicet Christus & Adamus, comparantur, quod vtraque eundem respectum & χαρ habeat ad illa, quae in hominibus producunt, effecta, nempe respectum meriti; quod vtraque non tantum per quamcunque efficientiam, aut quomodolibet dictam, sed per meritoriam efficientiam producant, altera iustificationem, altera condemnationem. Causas & causarum effecta comparari fateor; nego effectorum modos; Nego vtramque causam eundem respectum habere ad illa, quae in hominibus producunt, effecta: habent enim diuersum potius: Altera enim per naturam, altera per gratiam producit effectum suum; Illa per generationem carnalem, haec per gratuitam donationem; Illa propagando in nos peccatum inhaerens quod meretur condemnationem, haec remittendo nobis illud peccatum inhaerens; Illa χαρ habet ad vnum tantum peccatum & reatum, haec ad omnes reatus omnium peccatorum nostrorum. Quomodo ergo demonstrabitur, eundem esse vtriusque respectum, & quidem meriti? Meruit nobis Christus remissionem peccatorum. Is enim debita nostra exsoluit. Is Iustitiae Diuinae loco nostro satisfecit. Is mortem, quam eramus commeriti, passus est, &, vt loquitur Apostolus, factus est pro nobis peccatum, vt efficemus iustitia Dei in ipso. Is suum nobis vltro meritum dedit: nos id per fidem oblatum accipimus. Haec Patris, haec Filii mens, haec voluntas, hoc consilium, hic fcopus fuit. Id Scriptura passim inculcat. Dicit-ne de Adamo tale quid? Voluit-ne is nobis sua illa inobedientia mortem mereri? Peccauit-ne loco nostro? Dedit-ne nobis suum illud meritum? Illud-ne accipimus per aliquem mentis voluntatis-ve actum nostrum? Quomodo ergo dicitur vtriusque idem esse respectus, eadem χρονς? An si vitium inhærens nobis damnandis sufficiens in nos ab Adamo propagatum est, consequens est, iustitiam inhærentem nobis iustificandis sufficientem in nos à Christo propagatam fuisse? Videant tamen, quæso, qui nobis in hac causa aduersantur, annon hoc æquè ac imputatio antecedens Adamici peccati Argumentis D. Garissolij colligi possit? Quantacunq; igitur inter vtramq; causam, non jam identitas, sed similitudo meriti dicatur esse, arctè tenendum est, in modo communicandi meriti haud exiguam dissimilitudinem obseruari debere.
units.tr: What could be weaker than the earlier arguments for the imputation of Adam's sin, especially immediate imputation? Yet their author praises them, and, so that they may be repeated without weariness for the reader, he reduces them to a brief summary. Compared, he says, are the causes; compared are the effects of the causes; compared are the modes of the effects. The causes, namely Christ and Adam, are compared, in that each has the same relation [χρῆσιν] and respect to those effects which they produce in men, namely the respect of merit; and in that each produces by meritorious efficiency, not merely by any efficiency or by whatever name it is called, but the one justification, the other condemnation. I grant that causes and the effects of causes are compared; I deny that the modes of the effects are. I deny that each cause has the same respect to those effects which they produce in men; they rather have different ones. For the one produces its effect by nature, the other by grace; the one by carnal generation, the other by free gift; the one by propagating into us inherent sin which merits condemnation, the other by remitting to us that inherent sin; the one has its relation [χρῆσιν] to one sin and guilt only, the other to the guilts of all our sins. How then will it be shown that the respect of each is the same, and indeed a respect of merit? Christ merited for us the remission of sins. He paid our debts. He satisfied divine justice in our place. He suffered the death which we had deserved, and, as the Apostle says, he was made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. He freely gave us his merit; we receive it, offered to us, through faith. This was the mind, the will, the counsel and the purpose of the Father and of the Son. Scripture everywhere impresses this. Does it say anything like this of Adam? Did he will to merit death for us by that disobedience of his? Did he sin in our place? Did he give us that merit of his? Do we receive it by any act of our mind or will? How then is it said that the relation [χρῆσις] and the use [χρῆσις] of both are the same? Or if the inherent vice propagated from Adam into us is sufficient to condemn us, does it follow that the inherent righteousness propagated from Christ into us is sufficient to justify us? Yet let those who oppose us in this matter, I beg, consider whether this cannot be deduced from the arguments of Garissolius just as well as the antecedent imputation of Adam's sin. Therefore, however great a likeness of merit is said to exist between the two causes, it must be firmly held that there is no small dissimilarity in the manner in which merit is communicated.

units.la: Subnectit D. G. Syllogismum. Illud cuius consideratione & merito, vel condemnamur, vel iustificamur, imputatur nobis, vel ad culpam & reatum, vel ad iustitiam & absolutionem. Atqui consideratione & merito peccati Adæ condemnamur; consideratione & merito iustitiæ Christi absoluimur & iustificamur. Ergo & peccatum Adæ & iustitia Christi nobis imputantur.
units.tr: Garissolius adds a syllogism: That by whose consideration and merit we are either condemned or justified is imputed to us, either for guilt and liability, or for righteousness and absolution. But by the consideration and merit of Adam's sin we are condemned; by the consideration and merit of Christ's righteousness we are absolved and justified. Therefore both Adam's sin and Christ's righteousness are imputed to us.

units.la: Concedi potest conclusio. Probat enim imputari quod Pl. non negat: non probat imputari immediate seu ante corruptionem inhærentem. Id quod vnum Pl. negat: Concedit enim vltrò & peccatum Adami mediante corruptione nostra, & iustitiam Christi mediante fide nostra, nobis imputari. Distinguenda est itaque minor. Nam si consideratio & meritum intelligitur antecedens corruptionem hæreditariam, negatur minor; sin consequens, conceditur. Vel distinguitur peccatum Adæ: condemnamur enim consideratione & merito peccati Adæ in nos propagati, peccati verò Adæ præcisi à propagato vitio, & ante illud immediate spectati, non item.
units.tr: The conclusion may be granted. For it proves that what Placaeus does not deny is imputed; it does not prove that it is imputed immediately, or before inherent corruption. This alone Placaeus denies. For he willingly concedes that both Adam's sin is imputed to us through our corruption, and Christ's righteousness through our faith. The minor premise must therefore be distinguished. If "consideration and merit" is understood as preceding hereditary corruption, the minor is denied; if as following it, it is granted. Or the sin of Adam may be distinguished: for we are condemned by the consideration and merit of Adam's sin as propagated into us; but of Adam's sin taken apart from the propagated vice, and regarded immediately before it, not so.

units.la: Deinde,
units.tr: Next,

units.la: Vt enim justitia Christi fit nostra per fidem, sic peccatum Adami fit nostrum per communicatum inhærens vitium.
units.tr: For just as Christ's righteousness becomes ours through faith, so Adam's sin becomes ours through the inherent vice communicated to us.

units.la: Deinde, inquit, comparantur effecta illarum causarum, nimirum peccatum & justitia. Quod à Christo ad nos pertingit, non est tantum iustitia inhærens & nostra subjectiue, sed etiam iustitia extra nos, & aliena, & nostra nonnisi imputatiuè. Ergo quod ab Adamo ad nos pertingit, non est tantum corruptio inhærens, & habitualis, sed etiam peccatum & inobedientia extra nos, & aliena, & nostra nonnisi per imputationem. Primùm nulla est hæc consequentia: nititur enim omissa propositione majore, quæ quocunque modo concipiatur, erit, si vniuersalis, falsa; si particularis, inepta ad hanc efficiendam conclusionem. Deinde fateor nos à Christo non tantum morale͞m, sed etiam forensem justitiam habere, quarum illa corruptioni inhærenti, hæc reatui, qui corruptionem sequitur, opponitur; itaque ab Adamo ad nos pertigisse non tantum morale͞m, sed etiam formam injustitiam, nempe corruptionem & reatum. Eatenus est similitudo. Sed admisceat D. G. falsa quædam. Primò falsum est iustitiam Christi non esse nostram nisi imputatiuè. Est enim nostra Dei & Christi dono, nec-non acceptione nostra per fidem. Itaque donum, donatio per gratiam, redundantia gratiæ, donum iustitiæ vocatur ab Apostolo. Quæ nomina quis non videt discrimen ponere inter justitiam quæ à Christo, & peccatum quod ab Adamo ad nos pertingit, in modo quo sunt nostra? Offertur nobis hoc donum prædicatione Euangelij & accipitur per fidem. Itaque fide justificamur. Melius igitur loquitur Pareus, Vt donum fit nostrum; cum manu accipitur: f. vi 17.
units.tr: Next, he says, the effects of those causes are compared, namely sin and righteousness. What reaches us from Christ is not only righteousness inherent and ours subjectively, but also righteousness outside us, and alien, and ours only imputatively. Therefore what reaches us from Adam is not only inherent and habitual corruption, but also sin and disobedience outside us, and alien, and ours only through imputation. First, this inference is no good: it rests on an omitted major premise, which, however it is conceived, will be false if universal, and if particular, unfit to yield this conclusion. Next, I grant that from Christ we have not only moral but also forensic righteousness; the former is opposed to inherent corruption, the latter to guilt, which follows corruption. So from Adam there has reached us not only moral but also forensic unrighteousness, namely corruption and guilt. Thus far there is likeness. But Garissolius mixes in certain falsehoods. First, it is false that Christ's righteousness is ours only imputatively. For it is ours by the gift of God and of Christ, and by our acceptance through faith. Hence the Apostle calls it gift, gracious donation, abundance of grace, gift of righteousness. Who does not see that these names make a difference between the righteousness which comes from Christ and the sin which reaches us from Adam, in the manner in which they are ours? This gift is offered to us by the preaching of the Gospel and received through faith. Therefore we are justified by faith. Pareus speaks better: That the gift may be ours, it is received by the hand: f. vi 17.

units.la: Comm. in Rom. ita donum justitia nostrum fit, quando fide id nobis applicamus. Deinde quam Christi justitiam intelligit? habitualem? habitualis igitur Adami injustitia intelligenda erit, non autem ejus peccatum actuale. Actualem totius vitæ? Erit ergo similiter intelligenda actualis injustitia totius vitæ Adami, quod nemo tamen dixerit. Passiuam quam vocant, quæ morali quidem sensu iustitia non est, sed forensi? Hæc proprie foli reatui opponitur. Nascitur autem ex corruptione reatus. Ab Adamo igitur ad nos pertingit reatus corruptionem sequens, qui per illam corruptionem nostrer est, non autem per imputationem tantum. Hoc qui negauerit, is à Scriptura & omnium Ecclesiarum protestantium doctrinâ, fidei confessionibus, & aduersus Pelagium & Pighium disputationibus declarata discedet. Si quis autem eo non contentus alium dicat ab Adamo ad nos pertingere reatum, qui corruptionem antecedat, & nostrer non fit nisi per imputationem, is & duos reatus ponet, alterum priorem, alterum posteriorem corruptione, contradicente D. Gariffolio locis jam à me notatis pag. hujus lib. 27. & Deum faciet autorem peccati nostri: quippe qui judiciaria sua imputatione peccatores nos facit, alioqui non peccatores: &, ut reliqua taceam, inuehet nouum dogma in Ecclesiam præter Scripturam, & fidem antiquam. Sed pergamus.
units.tr: Commentary on Romans: So the gift of righteousness becomes ours when we apply it to ourselves by faith. Next, what righteousness of Christ does he mean? Habitual righteousness? Then the habitual unrighteousness of Adam must be meant, and not his actual sin. Actual righteousness of the whole life? Then likewise the actual unrighteousness of Adam's whole life must be meant, which nobody would say. Passive righteousness, as they call it, which is indeed not righteousness in the moral sense, but forensic? This is properly opposed only to guilt. But guilt arises from corruption. Therefore there reaches us from Adam guilt following corruption, which is ours through that corruption, and not through imputation alone. Whoever denies this will depart from Scripture, from the doctrine of all the Protestant Churches, from the confessions of faith, and from the disputations against Pelagius and Pighius. If anyone, not content with this, says that another guilt reaches us from Adam, one preceding corruption, which becomes ours only through imputation, he will posit two guilts, one prior to corruption and one posterior to it, contrary to Garissolius in the passages I have already noted, page 27 of this book; and he will make God the author of our sin, for by his judicial imputation he makes us sinners, otherwise we would not be sinners; and, to pass over the rest, he will introduce a new dogma into the Church, contrary to Scripture and the ancient faith. But let us proceed.

units.la: Denique, inquit, comparatur modus effectorum, quæ ab illis causis ad nos pertinent. Iusti constituimur per Christum: peccatores per Adamum. Quomodo iusti per Christum? imputatione iustitiæ ipsius. Quomodo peccatores per Adamum? imputatione inobedientiæ ipsius. Iam ego & Clarik. Riuetus negauimus comparari modos, & rectè quidem: nam quærenti, Quomodo iusti per Christum ? Si quis autore Apostolo respondeat, donatione iustitiæ per gratiam, poterit-ne quærenti, Quomodo peccatores per Adamum? similiter respondere, donatione iustitiæ ? Et quidem per gratiam ?
units.tr: Finally, he says, the mode of the effects is compared, which come to us from those causes. We are made righteous through Christ, and sinners through Adam. How are we made righteous through Christ? By the imputation of his righteousness. How are we made sinners through Adam? By the imputation of his disobedience. Now I and Clarik. Riuetus have denied that the modes are compared, and rightly so. For if someone, following the Apostle, answers the question How are we righteous through Christ? with by the gift of righteousness through grace, can he answer the question How are we sinners through Adam? in the same way, by the gift of righteousness? And indeed through grace?

units.la: Superiora argumenta ducta fuerunt à scripto Apostoli, sequuntur ea, quæ ducuntur ex ejus verbis. Missa breuitatis studio Vf. 12. explicatione, quid inde concludat videamus. Certè, inquit, oppositorum eadem est ratio, & ex vnius intelligentia in alterius cognitionem facile deuenitur. Si norimus quid sit iustitia per Christum allata, intelligemus & quid sit peccatum per Adamum introductum. Atqui iustitia per Christum introducta duplex est, imputata & inhærens, ita tamen, vt ex ratione materiæ & argumenti, quod disceptatur à Paulo, imputata hic proprie intelligenda veniat, cum de iustificatione agatur, inhærens autem, nonnisi ex consequentia rerum, quatenus scilicet nullus imputatâ iustitiâ donatur, cui non Deus etiam inhærentem largiatur. Ergo similiter, peccatum per Adamum introductum, est illud quidem duplex, imputatum & inhærens in nobis, ita tamen vt ex ratione negotij, quod hic agitur, imputatum proprie intelligatur; inhærens autem nonnisi ex consequenti, propter arctissimam & indissolubilem coniunctionem imputationis & corruptionis originalis. Hæc expendamus. Certè, inquit, oppositorum eadem est ratio: omnium ne, inquam, & omnis, an quorundam tantùm & quædam? Si hoc, vitiosa est argumentatio; Si illud, falsa est propositio. Opponuntur auaritia & prodigalitas, est-ne eadem prorsus vtriusque ratio? Si est eadem, est-ne etiam eadem prorsus liberalitatis, quæ vtrique opponitur?
units.tr: The arguments above were drawn from the writing of the Apostle; what follows are those drawn from his words. Passing over, for the sake of brevity, the explanation of verse 12, let us see what he concludes from it. Certainly, he says, the reasoning of opposites is the same, and from the understanding of one we easily come to the knowledge of the other. If we know what righteousness is brought in through Christ, we shall understand also what sin is introduced through Adam. But the righteousness introduced through Christ is twofold, imputed and inherent; yet in such a way that, from the nature of the subject and of the matter which Paul is treating, the imputed righteousness is here properly to be understood, since it is a question of justification, whereas the inherent righteousness is understood only from the consequence of things, namely, that no one is given imputed righteousness to whom God does not also bestow inherent righteousness. Therefore, similarly, the sin introduced through Adam is likewise twofold, imputed and inherent in us; yet in such a way that, from the nature of the business which is here at issue, the imputed sin is properly understood, whereas the inherent sin is understood only as a consequence, on account of the very close and indissoluble connection of imputation and original corruption. Let us weigh these things. Certainly, he says, the reasoning of opposites is the same. Of all, I ask, and of every kind, or of only some and certain ones? If the former, the argument is faulty; if the latter, the proposition is false. Avarice and prodigality are opposed: is the reasoning of each entirely the same? If it is the same, is it also entirely the same for liberality, which is opposed to each?

units.la: Sed fac ita esse, annon erit intelligenda propositio de iis, quæ formaliter & adæquatè & in genere opponuntur, non autem de certis quibusdam eorum indiuiduis ? In genere enim obedientia & inobedientia, justitia & injustitia opponuntur, itaque altera cognita, altera facile cognoscitur. Sed in specie, vel indiuiduo, potest certa quædam vnius obedientia cognosci, ignorata certa quadam alterius inobedientia & vice versa, hæc cognosci, illa ignorata: ac ne discedamus a subjecta huic disputationi materia, potuit olim cognosci inobedientia Adami non cognita, quæ ei medetur. Christi obedientia, & hæc potuit quibusdam è gentibus nota fieri antequam quicquam de Adami inobedientia edocerentur. Nimirum cùm & subjectis, & objectis, & lege, & tempore, & omnibus aliis circunstantiis differât, sunt quidem oppositorum generum duo quædam indiuidua, sed ipsæ per se non opponuntur proprie, nisi ratione effectorum, vt morbus & remedium. Formaliter enim & Logicè loquendo inobedientia Adami opposita fuit debitæ ab eo obedientiæ, & obedientia Christi inobedientiæ quam ex eodem subjecto exclusit. Sed missis illis Philosophicis propositionibus veniamus ad Theologicas. Atqui, inquit, justitia per Christum introducta duplex est, imputata & inhærens. Agnosco: nam illa reatui, hæc vitiofitati medetur; illa sensu forensi; hæc morali justitia est. Probo etiam quod addit, imputatam hic proprie intelligendam venire, cum de justificatione agatur. Nimirum inhærens non justificat. itaque non est hujus loci. Ergo similiter, inquit, peccatum per Adamum introductum est duplex, imputatum & inhærens in nobis. Non sequitur: nam inhærens vtrique iustitiæ opponitur, inhærenti per suam inhærentiam & vitiositatem, imputatæ per suum, quem fundit, reatum. Peccatum enim inhærens simul est inhærens & imputatum: nam & inhæret nobis, & merito, nisi remittatur, nobis imputatur. Dispar est iustitiæ inhærentis in nos a Christo deriuatæ ratio: hæc enim inhæret tantum, non autem ad iustificationem imputatur. Itaque alia opus est iustitia imputata, hoc est, remissione peccatorum, quæ peccati inhærentis reatum tollat, qui nisi tollatur, iustitia inhærens in corruptionis locum non introducitur. Non igitur sicut iustitia inhærens non fuit huius loci, in quo de iustificatione agitur, sic non est huius loci peccatum seu corruptio inhærens. Non enim si illa non iustificat, consequitur hanc non condemnare. Nam illa quidem non iustificat, sed hæc reuera condemnat, facitque in foro diuino reos, & iustitiæ imputatæ ea de causa opponitur. Vides iam, opinor, candide lector, saltem respectu iustificationis & condemnationis, valde diuersam esse iustitiæ inhærentis à Christo, & corruptionis inhærentis ab Adamo introductæ rationem. Illa non meretur vitam, hæc meretur mortem. Hic, igitur, vt verba vsurpem præstantis Theologi Tigurini, Probè tenere nos decet discrimen, quod inter Adamum & Christum nuper annotauimus. Ille enim peccatum ita in omnem posterita-tem propagauit, vt natura omnes nascamur peccatores, & in nobis hæreat peccatum proprium, quod nos æterni supplicij reos facit: Christus autem suam iustitiam sic nobis communicat, non vt in nobis illa infit essentialiter, aut vt propria iustitia in Dei iudicio defendamur, sed quod nostra dicatur per imputationem gratuitam, idque propter solam fidem, quæ nos illi conjungit, vt eius fratres, imo corporis fui membra efficiamur. Patere me quaeso, quisquis haec legis, tanto viro monente, hoc discrimen probe tenere, quod suis istis argumentis nequicquam tollere conatus est D. Gariffolius. Sic se habuit primum eius argumentum. Accedamus iam, inquit, secundo loco ad verba illustria ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον, qua vel sola potuerunt ad doctrinam de imputatione stabiliendam sufficere. (Hoc quàm sit falsum mox clarum fiet.) Nam ita significat Apostolus, omnes omnino homines, qui fuerunt, sunt, aut futuri sunt usque ad finem saeculi, in Adamo peccante peccavisse. (An id significet mox videbimus.) Itaque quicunque veterum aut Recentiorum de imputatione hac egerunt, illi omnes hoc praesertim loco doctrinam illam confirmarunt. Prudenter addidit limitationem quicunque de imputatione hac egerunt. Nam & Caluinus, & Martyr, & alij maximi viri doctrinam illam hoc loco non confirmarunt, confirmaturi sine dubio, si imputationem illam verbis illis doceri credidissent. Nubem illam testium, qua lucem veritatis obscurare nititur, Deo dante, suo loco dissipabimus. Nunc cum eo rem ipsam consideremus. Nimirum, inquit, opponit haec duo Apostolus, in Adamo omnes peccaverunt, in Christo omnes justificantur. Itane, inquam, illis verbis ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον? Sed pergat. Sive oppositione sive verba speciales, quibus oppositio explicatur, imputationem habes ex eo consurgentem. Ex oppositione. Nam ut in Christo justificantur homines, ita in Adamo peccasse intelliguntur. Atqui in Christo justificantur per imputationem justitiae illius. Ergo & in Adamo peccasse intelligendi sunt, per imputationem peccati Adae. Primum nego in illis verbis ejusmodi oppositionem fieri. Id erat non supponendum, sed probandum. Deinde, ut jam aliquoties inculcaui, ( nihil enim differt hoc argumentum a superioribus ) vniuersaliter vera non est propositio, & similitudo potius est in veritate rei, quàm in modo. Nimirum tam verè in Christo iustificantur homines, quàm verè peccauerunt in Adamo; Sed non iustificantur eodem prorsus modo quo peccauerunt: id enim res ipsa pati non poterat; sed diuerso. Subsumam enim, Atqui in Christo iustificantur homines per suam quisque fidem. Ergo & in Adamo peccasse intelligendi sunt per suam quisque fidem ne dicam, an incredulitatem? Nonne hæc minor propositio vera est, Apostoli & omnium Christianorum calculis confirmata? Aut igitur major falsa est, aut admittenda est conclusio conclusioni D. Gar. non obscurè opposita. Quid horum pie lectOr eligis?
units.tr: But grant that it is so: will the proposition not have to be understood of those things which are formally, adequately and generically opposed, and not of certain individual instances of them? For obedience and disobedience, righteousness and unrighteousness, are opposed in kind, so that when one is known the other is easily known. But in species, or in the individual, a certain obedience of one may be known while a certain disobedience of another is unknown, and vice versa: the one known, the other unknown. And, not to depart from the matter under discussion here, Adam's disobedience, which Christ's obedience heals, could once be known without being known, and this could have become known to some of the Gentiles before they were taught anything about Adam's disobedience. Indeed, since they differ in subjects, objects, law, time and all other circumstances, these are indeed two individuals of opposed genera, yet they are not properly opposed in themselves, except by reason of their effects, as disease and remedy. For, speaking formally and logically, Adam's disobedience was opposed to the obedience due from him, and Christ's obedience to the disobedience which it excluded from the same subject. But, setting aside those philosophical propositions, let us come to the theological ones. But, he says, the righteousness introduced through Christ is twofold, imputed and inherent. I agree: for the former heals guilt, the latter heals vitiosity; the former is forensic righteousness, the latter moral righteousness. I also approve what he adds, that the imputed righteousness is here properly to be understood, since it is a question of justification. Clearly the inherent righteousness does not justify, and so it does not belong to this place. Therefore, similarly, he says, the sin introduced through Adam is twofold, imputed and inherent in us. It does not follow: for inherent sin is opposed to both kinds of righteousness, to inherent righteousness by its inherence and vitiosity, and to imputed righteousness by the guilt which it pours out. For inherent sin is at once inherent and imputed: it clings to us and, unless it is forgiven, is imputed to us as deserved. The manner of inherent righteousness derived from Christ into us is different, for this only inheres, and is not imputed for justification. Therefore an imputed righteousness is needed, that is, the remission of sins, which removes the guilt of inherent sin; unless this is removed, inherent righteousness is not introduced in the place of corruption. Therefore, just as inherent righteousness was not in place in this passage, where justification is treated, so inherent sin or corruption is not in place here either. For it does not follow, because the former does not justify, that the latter does not condemn. For the former indeed does not justify, but the latter truly condemns, and makes us guilty in the divine court, and for this reason it is set against imputed righteousness. You now see, I think, candid reader, that at least with respect to justification and condemnation, the manner of inherent righteousness from Christ and of inherent corruption introduced by Adam is very different. The former does not merit life, the latter merits death. Here, therefore, to use the words of that eminent Zurich theologian: It behoves us to hold well the distinction which we lately noted between Adam and Christ. For he so propagated sin into all posterity that by nature we are all born sinners, and our own sin clings to us, which makes us liable to eternal punishment; but Christ communicates his righteousness to us, not so that it inheres in us essentially, nor so that we are defended in God's judgment by our own righteousness, but so that it is called ours by free imputation, and this solely on account of faith, which joins us to him, so that we become his brothers, indeed members of his body. Allow me, I beg, whoever you are who read these things, with so great a man admonishing you, to hold well this distinction, which Dr. Gariffolius has in vain tried to remove with his arguments. Thus stood his first argument. Let us now come, he says, in the second place, to the famous words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον [in whom all sinned], which alone could have been sufficient to establish the doctrine of imputation. (How false this is will soon become clear.) For the Apostle thus signifies that all men absolutely, who have been, are, or will be until the end of the age, sinned in Adam sinning. (Whether this is what it signifies we shall soon see.) Therefore whoever among the ancients or the more recent writers have treated of this imputation confirmed that doctrine especially in this passage. He wisely added the restriction, whoever have treated of this imputation. For both Calvin and Martyr, and other very great men, did not confirm that doctrine in this passage, though undoubtedly they would have confirmed it had they believed that imputation to be taught in those words. That cloud of witnesses, which seeks to darken the light of truth, by God's grace we shall dispel in its place. Now let us consider the matter itself with him. Clearly, he says, the Apostle sets these two against each other: in Adam all sinned, in Christ all are justified. Is that so, I ask, from those words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον? But let him go on. Whether from the opposition or from the special words by which the opposition is expressed, you have imputation arising from it. From the opposition. For as men are justified in Christ, so they are understood to have sinned in Adam. But they are justified in Christ through the imputation of his righteousness. Therefore they are also to be understood as having sinned in Adam, through the imputation of Adam's sin. First, I deny that such an opposition is made in those words. That was not to be assumed but proved. Next, as I have already often insisted (for this argument differs nothing from the earlier ones), the proposition is not universally true, and the resemblance lies rather in the truth of the thing than in the manner. Men are indeed as truly justified in Christ as they sinned in Adam; but they are not justified in exactly the same manner in which they sinned, for the thing itself could not admit that, but in a different manner. For I shall argue: But men are justified in Christ, each through his own faith. Therefore they are also to be understood as having sinned in Adam, each through his own — shall I say faith, or unbelief? Is not this minor proposition true, confirmed by the reckoning of the Apostle and of all Christians? Either therefore the major is false, or the conclusion must be admitted, which is not obscurely opposed to the conclusion of Dr. Gariffolius. Which of these do you, pious reader, choose?

units.la: Ex verbis addit. Nam vis Aoristi ἀ῾ρίστου hic perpendenda. Etenim tempus hoc, in vsu Scripturæ, aliquando absolutum est à speciali significatione temporis, vt cùm dicitur, Omnes deflexerunt, inutiles facti sunt, peccauerunt. Rom. 3, 12. 23. Hoc enim omnia tempora præteritum, præsens, & futurum continet; vt significetur peccasse, qui fuerunt, peccare qui sunt, peccaturos qui erunt. Hic ta-men vbi multiplicat Apostolus Aoristos, vis eorum singulariter spectari debet peccatum intrasse, mortem introiisse, omnes peccauisse. Intrauit autem peccatum, vt primùm Adam peccauit, & mortis reatus vna cum illo peccato introiit. Ergo & vt primùm peccauit Adam, nos omnes peccauisse intelligimur; quod sanè melius exponi non potest, quàm si dicamus peccatum Adæ omnibus imputari. Non dicam peccare hoc argumentum ignoratione elenchi; nec id concludere quod erat inter suum autorem & Placeum controuersum: Hoc enim peccant omnia D. Gar. argumenta : Nam neid quidem quod concludit probandi vim vllam habet. Etenim si Aoristi, omnes deflexerunt, inutiles facti sunt, peccauerunt, Rom. 3. absoluti sunt a speciali significatione temporis, quid est, quamobrem similiter non sint ab ea significatione absoluti Aoristi, peccatum intrauit, mors introiit, omnes peccauerunt, Rom. 5 ? Obstat, inquies, eorum hoc loco multiplicatio. At nonne æquè illic atque hic tres numerauit Aoristos ? ac tribus illis quos laudauit ex Rom. 3. addere potuit alios duos ex Ψf. 13. & 17. linguis suis ad dolum vsi sunt, viam veritatis non cognouerunt. Quanquam non video cur si duo aut tres Aoristi ita accipi debeant, non possint eodem modo quatuor, vel quinque, vel sex accipi. Non enim multiplicatio Aoristorum mutat eorum significationem. Affirmanti igitur, nec probanti negationem oppono: possem & magnorum, qui ante nos vixerunt, Theologorum autoritatem opponere, sed studio breuitatis mihi tempero, & in alium locum reseruo. Illud obseruo, mortem introiisse in omnes homines non vnam numero omnibus imputatam, sed suam cuique homini propriam. Hoc non potest negari. Constat etiam per vnum hominem peccatum reuera intrasse in omnes homines non vnum numero, sed suum cuique propriam & inhærens. Nonne? Hæc si agnoscis, cur iis non acquiescis? Si negas, qui publicæ fidei confessioni subscribere te profiteris? Renocabo-ne ad examen etiam verba sequentia? Quid-ni? interest enim veritatis quicquid rectum non est corrigi. Intrauit autem, inquit, peccatum, vt primum Adam peccauit. Certè quidem in Adamum, sed per Adamum in alios omnes homines, qui tunc nulli erant, quomodo tunc intrare potuit? Non dicit autem Apostolus, peccatum intrasse in vnum hominem, sed per vnum hominem in mundum, id est, in omnes homines. Constat autem per vnum hominem intrasse in omnes homines, vno Christo excepto, peccatum inhærens nos in foro diuino reos mortis constituens. Cur ergo illud in Pauli verbis non agnoscamus? Quis etiam credat, Apostolum per mortem reatum mortis, potius quàm per peccatum, intelligere? Da enim locum, si potes, vbi mors non mortem, sed tantùm reatum mortis significet, præsertim cùm spectatur, vt fit hic, tanquam peccati effectum & stipendium, ab eoque distinguitur? An aliter peccatum actuale Adami in omnes homines introiit, quàm quatenus ejus vel praui-tas propagatione, vel reatus imputatione in eos introit? Si ergo reatum D. Gar. intellexit cùm dicitur peccatum introiisse, qui eundem reatum intelligere potuit, cùm additur, per peccatum quod introiit in omnes homines, in eosdem mortem etiam introiisse? Cæterum vt primùm peccauit Adam, nos omnes peccauisse intelligimur, nimirum quomodo, vt primùm fuit vel creatum est, nos omnes fuisse vel creati fuisse intelligimur. An igitur ferendus esset, qui simpliciter diceret, nos omnes ab initio mundi fuisse?
units.tr: On the words added. For the force of the aorist [ἀορίστου] must be weighed here. For this tense, in the usage of Scripture, is sometimes detached from the specific meaning of time, as when it is said, All have turned aside, they have become unprofitable, they have sinned. Rom. 3, 12. 23. For this covers all tenses, past, present and future, so that it signifies that they who were have sinned, they who are sin, and they who will be will sin. Here, however, where the Apostle multiplies the aorists, their force must be regarded singly: sin entered, death came in, all sinned. Sin entered, indeed, as soon as Adam sinned, and the guilt of death entered together with that sin. Therefore we are understood to have sinned when Adam first sinned, which can certainly be explained in no better way than by saying that the sin of Adam is imputed to all. I will not say that this argument commits the fallacy of ignoratio elenchi, nor that it concludes what was in dispute between its author and Place, for all of D. Gar.'s arguments commit this error, and not even what he concludes has any force of proof. For if the aorists, all have turned aside, they have become unprofitable, they have sinned, Rom. 3, are detached from the specific meaning of time, why is it that the aorists sin entered, death came in, all have sinned, Rom. 5, are not likewise detached from that meaning? You will object, he says, their multiplication here. But did he not count three aorists there just as here, and could he not, besides the three he cited from Rom. 3, add two others from Ps. 13. and 17., with their tongues they have used deceit, they have not known the way of truth? Yet I do not see why, if two or three aorists must be taken in this way, four, or five, or six cannot be taken in the same way. For the multiplication of aorists does not change their meaning. So I set against one who affirms, not a proof of the negation. I could also set against him the authority of great theologians who lived before us, but for the sake of brevity I restrain myself and reserve that for another place. This I observe: that death entered into all men, not one death imputed to all in number, but each man's own death. This cannot be denied. It is also established that through one man sin really entered into all men, not one sin in number, but each one's own and inhering. Is that not so? If you acknowledge these things, why do you not assent to them? If you deny them, to what public confession of faith do you profess to subscribe? Shall I also call the following words to examination? Why not? For it matters to the truth that whatever is not right be corrected. Sin entered, he says, as soon as Adam sinned. Certainly it entered into Adam, but through Adam into all other men, who then did not exist; how could it enter them then? The Apostle does not say that sin entered into one man, but through one man into the world, that is, into all men. It is established that through one man sin entered into all men, Christ alone excepted, inhering and making us guilty of death in the divine court. Why then should we not acknowledge this in Paul's words? Who would also believe that the Apostle by death understands the guilt of death rather than sin? For show me, if you can, a place where death signifies not death but only the guilt of death, especially when it is viewed, as it is here, as the effect and wages of sin, and is distinguished from it. Or did the actual sin of Adam enter into all men in any way other than insofar as it enters them either by its depravity through propagation or by the imputation of guilt? If then D. Gar. understood guilt when it is said that sin entered, who could fail to understand the same guilt when it is added that through the sin which entered into all men, death also entered into the same men? Moreover, as soon as Adam sinned, we are understood to have sinned, namely in the same way as, as soon as he was or was created, we are understood to have been or to have been created. Would one be tolerated who simply said that we all existed from the beginning of the world?

units.la: Audio virum doctum alio argumento hoc confirmantem, id attendamus. Quod idem, inquit, conficiunt vocula illa in quo. Nam qui, cùm nondum essent in rerum natura, dicuntur in alio peccasse, censentur procul dubio eo committente peccatum, & ipsi etiam commisisse, quod euidenter ad imputationem pertinet. Atqui homines omnes cùm nondum essent, dicuntur in Adamo. peccasse. Ergo censentur eo committente peccatum, & ipsi etiam commisisse, quod euidenter ad imputationem pertinet. Atqui homines omnes cum nondum essent, dicuntur in Adamo peccasse. Ergo censentur eo committente peccatum, & ipsi commisisse, quod ad imputationem peccati Adæ manifestè pertinet. Primum nititur hæc argumentatio hypothesi, voculas εφ' ᾧ hoc loco significare in quo. Id quod non concedimus. Negari enim non potest, quin verti possint eo quod, propterea quod, quatenus &c. Si sic verti possunt, non est necesse ut vertantur in quo; si non est necesse ut vertantur in quo, nulla est argumentationis, quæ nititur illa versione, necessitas. Quomodo ergo probat D. Gariff. debere hoc loco reddi in quo, potius quàm eo quod &c? Affert indicem magnorum virorum antiquorum & recentium qui reddiderunt in quo, sed eorum autoritas non impediuit, quominus alij, & ipsi magni viri, versioni in quo prætulerint versionem eo quod, quatenus &c, Theodoretus, Syrus interpres, Caluinus, Martyr, Bucerus, Aretius, Pisçator, Paræus, Erasmus, Leoluda, Vatablus, Autores versionis Gallicanæ, quâ vtuntur Ecclesiæ nostræ, nec-non Anglicanæ, &c. nam longum esset omnes enumerare. Fauerunt-ne propterea isti maximi viri Pelagianæ hæresi? Quid est quare Placeus non debeat eorum exemplum sequi, & receptâ versione respondens niti? Nihil-ne præterea D. Gariffolius? Addit etiam vim vocularum illarum ex vsu Scripturæ: nam, inquit, frequentissimum est vt ἐν accipiatur pro ἐν, quod vt probet multa laudat exempla. Nempe id probat quod non negatur, quod vero negatur id non probat. Nemo enim ei negauit ἐν aliquando accipi pro ἐν. Sed an inde sequitur, esse illam prεpositione per enallagen vsurpatam hoc loco, & positam ἐπί pro ἐν? Immo li dixisset Apostolus ἐν ᾧ, nihil prohiberet quominus etiam illæ voces eo quod vel quoniam &c. redderentur, vt factum est ab omnibus fere interpretibus Rom. 8. 3. Extant autem ἐφ' ᾧ eo sensu 2. Cor. 5. 4. nec aliter accipi solent quoties nullu est antecedes, ad quod ᾧ commodè referri possit. Cæterum quod ait, verlionis in quo, nos autorem facere Bezam, vnde habeat nescio. Id certè Placeus neque dixit, neque scripsit, neque cogitauit vnquam. Rationes quas nobis tribuit, non sunt Placei, nec eis opus est respondenti secundum verlionem ab Ecclesiis nostris probatam. Quam si flagitas à me, Lector, vt probem, Primum duas Placei rationes afferam, deinde quinque illas, quas sibi D. G. objecit, ab ejus exceptionibus breuiter vindicabo. Primum igitur si vertas in quo, relatiuum quo, quia referri non poterit ad nomen masculinum proximum, vel propinquum, sed ad remotius, trajectio admittenda erit, eaque insolens & dura admodum. Iam autem ejusmodi trajectio admitti non debet absque necessitate, quæ hic nulla apparet, cum voculæ ἐφ' ᾧ non minus & proprie & commodè reddi possint eo quod, vel quoniam, vel quatenus. Deinde verba omnes peccauerunt, cum causam contineant ejus quod immediatè præcessit, cum eo jungi flagitant: quis enim negare potest, quin mors in omnes inuaserit, quia omnes peccauerunt? Cur ergo à se inuicem separaremus ea orationis Apostolicæ membra, quæ non modò situ & collocatione ab Apostolo juncta sunt, sed etiam sensu & rerum significatarum indissolubili nexu cohærent?
units.tr: I hear a learned man confirming this by another argument; let us attend to it. The same thing, he says, these little words accomplish in quo. For those who, when they did not yet exist in the nature of things, are said to have sinned in another, are without doubt judged to have sinned by that one's committing the sin, and to have committed it themselves too, which clearly pertains to imputation. But all men, when they did not yet exist, are said to have sinned in Adam. Therefore they are judged to have sinned by his committing the sin, and to have committed it themselves too, which clearly pertains to imputation. But all men, when they did not yet exist, are said to have sinned in Adam. Therefore they are judged to have sinned by his committing the sin, and to have committed it themselves, which clearly pertains to the imputation of Adam's sin. First, this argument rests on the hypothesis that the little words [ἐφ' ᾧ] mean here "in which." This we do not concede. For it cannot be denied that they can be rendered "because," "for the reason that," "insofar as," and so on. If they can be so rendered, it is not necessary that they be rendered "in which"; and if it is not necessary, the argument that rests on that rendering has no necessity. How then does D. Gariffolius prove that here it must be rendered "in which" rather than "because" and so on? He brings a list of great men, ancient and recent, who rendered it "in which," but their authority did not prevent others, and great men themselves, from preferring "because," "insofar as," and so on to the version "in which": Theodoret, the Syriac interpreter, Calvin, Martyr, Bucer, Aretius, Piscator, Paraeus, Erasmus, Leoluda, Vatablus, the authors of the French version which our Churches use, and likewise the English, and so on, for it would be long to list them all. Did these very great men therefore favour the Pelagian heresy? Why should Place not follow their example and, adhering to the accepted version, rest his answer on it? Does D. Gariffolius have nothing further? He also adds the force of those little words from the usage of Scripture: for, he says, it is most frequent that [ἐν] is taken for [ἐν], and to prove this he cites many examples. Indeed he proves what is not denied, but what is denied he does not prove. For no one denied that [ἐν] is sometimes taken for [ἐν]. But does it follow from this that the preposition is here used by enallage and put for [ἐπί] instead of [ἐν]? Indeed, if the Apostle had written [ἐν ᾧ], nothing would prevent those words from being rendered "because" or "since," as was done by almost all translators at Rom. 8. 3. Moreover [ἐφ' ᾧ] occurs in that sense at 2 Cor. 5. 4., and it is not otherwise understood whenever there is no antecedent to which [ᾧ] can conveniently refer. As for his claim that we make Beza the author of the version "in which," I do not know where he got that. Place certainly neither said nor wrote nor ever thought it. The reasons he attributes to us are not Place's, nor is there any need for them in answering according to the version approved by our Churches. If you, reader, demand that I prove this, I will first set out two of Place's reasons, and then briefly defend against D. G.'s objections the five reasons he raised against him.
