First, then: if you translate "in which," the relative "which" cannot be referred to the nearest masculine noun but must be referred to a more remote one, and a transposition must be admitted, and an unusual and quite harsh one. Now such a transposition should not be admitted without necessity, and here no necessity appears, since the words [ἐφ' ᾧ] can be rendered no less properly and conveniently as "because," "since," or "insofar as." Next, the words "all sinned," since they contain the cause of what immediately precedes, demand to be joined with it. For who can deny that death came upon all because all sinned? Why then should we separate from one another those members of the Apostle's sentence which are joined not only in position and arrangement but also cohere in sense by an indissoluble bond of the things signified?

units.la: Ad alias rationes quod spectat, vtinam eas suus
units.tr: As for the other arguments, I wish that their own author had taken them up to defend,

units.la: autor suscepisset tuendas, qua mihi videtur esse & sapientia & eloquentia, præstitisset id, quàm ego, multò melius. Prima sic fe habet, referente D. Gariffolio; Manuscriptum enim ex quo sunt desumptæ non habeo. Fidem esse penes eum oportet. Nemo nescit illud, εφ' ῳ, apud bonos autores, vel denotare finem rei, ἐ χάειν, vel causam antecedentem, vt apud Synefium, ἐφ' ῳ γεννάδιον ἐγκάλεσ. Cum igitur finis hoc loco denotari non possit, sequitur vt causa antecedens designetur, & vertatur eo quod, vel propterea quod. Quid respondet D. Gar? Hoc vnum, εἰ' junctum cum relatiuo ὅς, ἥ, ὅ, quanquam aliquando finem, aliquando causam antecedentem notet, tamen frequentissime vim habere præpositionis ὑπ. Marc. 2. 4. ἐφ' ῳ κατέκειτο in quo jacebat &c. Sed quid hoc est, nihil aberratio ab argumento? Nam in argumento agebatur de vocibus ἐφ' ῳ absolute positis, hoc est, absque expresso antecedente ad quod pronomen ῳ referatur. Cum enim est in proximo antecedens ad quod refertur, quis vnquam eas vertendas putauit eo quod vel propterea quod? Hic autem ponuntur absolute, quod enim proximè antecedit est nomen θάνατῳ bis vsurpatum, ac ante illud ἀμφῆ; ad neutrum referri constat. Præcedit quidem Genitiuus ἀνθρώπου hominem; Sed quominus ad eum referri possit, obstant interjecta nomina, immò commata.
units.tr: The author ought to have taken up the other arguments, which seem to me to have both wisdom and eloquence, and he would have done it far better than I can. The first runs as follows, as reported by Dr Gariffolius, since I do not have the manuscript from which it was taken. Trust must be placed in him. Nobody is unaware that εφ' ῳ in good authors either denotes the purpose of a thing, ἕνεκα, or an antecedent cause, as in Synesius, ἐφ' ᾧ γενναδίῳ ἐγκαλεῖς. Since, then, purpose cannot be denoted here, it follows that an antecedent cause is indicated, and it should be rendered "because" (eo quod) or "for which reason" (propterea quod). What does Dr Gar reply? Only this: that ἐπί joined with the relative ὅς, ἥ, ὅ, although sometimes it denotes purpose and sometimes an antecedent cause, very often has the force of the preposition ὑπ. Mark 2. 4. ἐφ' ᾧ κατέκειτο, "in which he lay," etc. But what is this, except a wandering away from the subject? For the question was about the words ἐφ' ᾧ used absolutely, that is, without an expressed antecedent to which the pronoun ᾧ refers. When there is a nearby antecedent to which it refers, who has ever thought such words should be rendered "because" or "for which reason"? Here, however, they stand absolutely: the word that immediately precedes is θανάτῳ, used twice, and before it ἀμφῆ; it is clear that the phrase refers to neither. The genitive ἀνθρώπου, "of man," does indeed come before, but the intervening nouns, and indeed the commas, stand in the way of its being referred to that word.

units.la: Secunda ratio. Si Apostolus de imputatione cogitaffet, locus hic vnice flagitabat, vt eam diserte commemoraret: & debuit dicere ἵνα ῳ, non ἐφ' ῳ, quia res ardua est, & à communi sensu abhorrens, itaque oportuit eam clare exprimere, ne quis de ea dubitaret.
units.tr: Second reason. If the Apostle had been thinking of imputation, this passage above all required that he mention it plainly. He ought to have said ἐν ᾧ [in which], not ἐφ' ᾧ, because the matter is difficult and abhorrent to common sense, so it was necessary to state it clearly, lest anyone doubt it.

units.la: Respondet primò, an imputari aliena peccata a communi sensu abhorreat, jam supra disputatum est. Immo abhorret, vt imputentur aliqui prorsus innocentibus, vt ob aliena imputata hi puniantur ea poena quæ sit verè peccatum, eosque faciat inhærenter peccatores, vt hac imputationè fiant rei mortis æternæ, alioqui non rei. Hoc, inquam, à sensu communi, à Scriptura, & ratione, ab ipsoque conscientiæ sensu mihi videtur vehementer abhorrere. Quid? nonne si quis diceret, alia Adami, aut aliorum Patriarcharum peccata nobis omnibus imputari, is videretur à communi sensu abhorrentia dicere? Sit aliqua alieni peccati non injusta imputatio, an id probatum est de omni, ac nominatim de ista tali, primi peccati actualis imputatione immediata, qua nulla mihi singi posse videtur injustior?
units.tr: I reply first that whether the sins of others can be imputed to us is abhorrent to common sense has already been disputed above. Indeed it is abhorrent that entirely innocent persons should be charged with others' sins, so that on account of imputed sins they are punished with a penalty which is truly sin, and are made inherently sinners, so that by this imputation they become liable to eternal death, when otherwise they would not be. This, I say, seems to me vehemently abhorrent to common sense, to Scripture, to reason, and to the very sense of conscience. What then? If someone were to say that the other sins of Adam, or of other patriarchs, are imputed to us all, would he not seem to be saying things abhorrent to common sense? Let some non-unjust imputation of another's sin be granted. Has it been proved for every case, and specifically for this immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin, than which none seems to me more unjust to invent?

units.la: Resp. 2. Hic notandam confessionem viri Docti: Si dictum fuisset ἐν ῥ, imputationem peccati inde manifeste concludi potuisse, quippe diserte commemoratam. Ita enim instantiam posteriores scripti contra hanc imputationem damnat, vbi pertenditur, etiamsi vertas, in quo, inde tamen nihil colligi posse pro causa imputationis. Miror ἀβλεψίαν viri docti, non videntis autorem illius rationis non ex sua, sed ex eorum, contra quos disputabat, mente sic fuisse locutum. Ita enim argumentantem decet ex Aduersariorum hypothelibus, potius quam ex suis ipsius, disputare, alioqui nihil promoturum.
units.tr: Second reply. Here we must note the confession of the learned man: If it had been said ἐν ᾧ, the imputation of sin could clearly have been inferred from it, since it would have been expressly mentioned. For the later writings thus condemn this objection against that imputation, where it is contended that even if you translate in which, nothing can be gathered from it in support of the cause of imputation. I marvel at the oversight of the learned man, who does not see that the author of that reasoning spoke in that way not from his own mind but from the mind of those against whom he was disputing. For one who argues should dispute from his opponents' premises rather than from his own; otherwise he will achieve nothing.

units.la: Resp. 3. vix ferendum videri, quod dicitur si Paulus imputationem docere voluisset, dicere potius ἐν ῥ dicere quàm ἐκ ῥ. Qui enim nos sumus, qui Apostolo præscribere audeamus loquendi ratione, & formulas, præsertim cum ἐπὶ & ἐν tam frequenter eundem sensum & significationem habeant?
units.tr: Third reply. It is hardly bearable that it is said: if Paul had wished to teach imputation, he would rather have said ἐν ᾧ than ἐφ' ᾧ. For who are we, that we dare to prescribe to the Apostle his manner and formulas of speech, especially since ἐπί and ἐν so often have the same sense and meaning?

units.la: Clementer quæso: abhorret enim fine dubio vehementer ab hujusmodi arrogantia rationis illius autor. Non præscribit Apostolo loquendi rationem & formulas, sed ab ejus sapientia & prudentia, quam summam fuisse constat, ducit argumentum. Quærebatur quid Apostolus significare voluit verbis ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον ? Aiunt quidam eum significare voluisse, primum Adami peccatum actuale omnibus hominibus imputatum fuisse, & quidem immediatè. Quoniam ergo hanc mentem Apostolo, non dicam præscribunt, sed tamen, quia ita ipsis placet, tribuunt; atque ad eam mentem verba ejus minus accommodata paululum inflectunt, ἐπὶ pro ἐν positum nulla reddita ratione, affirmantes. Ille objicit, hoc sapientiæ Apostolicæ minùs convenire. Cùm enim ejufmodi doctrina fit admodum ardua, & à sensu communi abhorrens, & alibi non doceatur in Scriptura, confentaneum erat, vt saltem hoc vno in loco doceretur aperte, & verbis disertis, aut saltem iis, quæ salsò quidem, sed tamen pro disertis ab iis habentur qui a nobis in hac causa dissentiunt. Si saltem dixisset ἐν ᾧ non fuisset opus recurrere ad enallagem præpofitionis ἐπὶ positæ pro ἐν & minùs fuisset ambigua vocum ἐν ᾧ significatio: multò enim rarius, quàm ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, significant eo quod, quatenus &c. Cùm ergo Apostolus confulto dicere maluerit ἐφ᾽ ᾧ quàm ἐν ᾧ, ac, quantum fieri potuit, ab illis remouerit, & pluribus interpositis separauerit nomen ἀνθρώπῳ; atque ita impediuerit ne ad id tanquam antecedens relatiuum ᾧ referretur, cur fine necessitate, fine ratione, malumus eius verbis & verborum collocationi vim aliquam inferre, vt id dicere aliquomodo videantur quod ex eis colligi nequit, quàm retenta verborum ℓᵩ' ᵩᶠ proprietate, & Apostolico commatum situ eam sententiam verborum eius admittere, quam in se veram esse nemo non Pelagianus negare potest? Sed quid, inquit, impediet, quominus Pelagius aut Socinus eadem ratione objicere possint; Si Scriptura docere voluisset, vel peccatum generatione propagari, vel Christum esse Mediatorem merito & satisfactione; id expressuram fuisse, vel exprimere debuisse verbis claris & perspicuis, cum res sit ardua, nec satis ad communem hominum sensum accommodata? Omnino nihil impediet quominus hoc possint objicere, si velint, Pelagij & Socini sequaces; Sed nihil impediet etiam, quominus objicientibus respondeamus, non id quod vult D. G. nostrum non esse, Deo loquendi rationes & modos praescribere: Hoc enim, cum Dei mens & sententia versatur in quæstione, sophisticum videri possit; Sed quod res est, id neque à sensu conscientiæ ullo modo abhorrere, & tam disertis ac claris verbis in Scriptura exprimi, ut, nisi iis magna vis afferatur, in alium sensum detorqueri nequeant.
units.tr: I ask you to be gentle, for the author of that argument surely shrinks from such arrogance. He does not prescribe to the Apostle a manner or formulas of speaking. He draws his argument from the Apostle's wisdom and prudence, which is known to have been supreme. The question was what the Apostle meant by the words ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον [because all sinned]. Some say he meant that the first actual sin of Adam was imputed to all men, and indeed immediately. Since they do not, I say, prescribe this meaning to the Apostle, but nonetheless, because it pleases them, attribute it to him, and bend his words, which fit it poorly, a little towards it, asserting that ἐπί stands for ἐν without giving any reason, the other objects that this is less consistent with apostolic wisdom. Since such a doctrine is very difficult and abhorrent to common sense, and is not taught elsewhere in Scripture, it was fitting that at least in this one place it should be taught openly and in express words, or at least in words which are wrongly, yet still, regarded as express by those who dissent from us in this matter. If he had at least written ἐν ᾧ, there would have been no need to resort to the figure by which the preposition ἐπί is put for ἐν, and the meaning of ἐν ᾧ would have been less ambiguous, since it signifies because, inasmuch as, and so on far more rarely than ἐφ' ᾧ. Since the Apostle therefore deliberately preferred ἐφ' ᾧ to ἐν ᾧ, removed it as far as possible from those words, and separated the noun ἀνθρώπῳ [man] by several intervening words, so as to prevent ᾧ from being referred to it as its antecedent, why, without necessity and without reason, do we prefer to do violence to his words and their arrangement, so that they seem to say something that cannot be gathered from them? Why not retain the proper sense of the words and the Apostolic order of the clauses, and admit that sense of his words which no one who is not a Pelagian can deny is true in itself? But, he says, what will prevent Pelagius or Socinus from objecting on the same ground: if Scripture had wished to teach either that sin is propagated by generation, or that Christ is Mediator by merit and satisfaction, it would have expressed this, or ought to have expressed it in clear and perspicuous words, since the matter is difficult and not sufficiently adapted to common human sense? Certainly nothing will prevent the followers of Pelagius and Socinus from raising this objection, if they wish. But nothing will prevent us either from answering the objectors that it is not ours, as Dr. G. says, to prescribe to God modes and manners of speaking. This might seem sophistical, since God's mind and judgement is the very question. But the matter is such that it in no way shrinks from the sense of conscience, and it is expressed in Scripture in words so express and clear that they cannot be twisted into another sense unless great force is applied to them.

units.la: Tertia ratio. Locus non postulat ut ita vertatur: cum enim causa certa sit, cur Apostolus dixerit, mortem in omnes homines pervasisse, nempe quia omnes peccaverunt, quid opus est confugere ad causam incertam & remotam, idque contra verborum vim naturalem? Respondet quatuor: sed, quia vim argumenti non perceperat, ἀπροσδιόνυσα. Dixit Apostolus, mortem in omnes homines pervasisse: causa sine dubio est quia omnes peccaverunt. Sed quod peccatum intelligi debeat quæritur. Alij peccatum intelligi volunt habituale omnibus inhærens, alij peccatum actuale Adami omnibus ordine naturæ priusquam vitiosi sint imputatum. Peccatum habituale inhærens ab Adamo in omnes propagatum causa est certa, hoc est, confessa ab omnibus orthodoxis. De eo enim vitio quin sit, & causa sit mortis; quippe veré peccatum, veré reos mortis nos efficiens, nulla est inter nos controuersia. Id enim est communi confessione fidei verbis clarissimis & difertissimis confirmatum. De peccato verò actuali Adami, an ante corruptionem imputetur, & an illa imputatio sit causa cur in omnes mors peruaserit, res certa non est & liquida: id enim est quod nunc inter nos controuertitur. Rursus vitium vnicuique nostrum inhærens causa est mortis nostræ propinquior, quàm primum Adami peccatum actuale, quod nobis imputatum dicitur, non modò prius ordine naturæ quàm effemus corrupti, sed etiam aliquot annorum millibus antequam esse & viuere incepissemus. Itaque cùm duæ illæ causæ inter se conferuntur, illa est certa, quia non controuersa, hæc incerta, quia controuersa: illa est proxima in eodem cum suo effectu, hoc est, morte, subiecto, hæc remota, quia in alio subiecto, à nobis non modo naturæ generantis ordine, sed tempore etiam valdè remota, ac inter quam & mortem interposita est causa propinquior, nimirum corruptio. Iam, opinor, Lector humanissime, vides argumenti vim, & ab ea quàm aberrent viri docti responsiones ipse per te intelligis. Cùm enim certum sit ac nullo modo inter nos controuersum, omnibus inhærere peccatum quod meretur mortem, & ob quod omnes moriuntur, cur de eo peccato verba Apostoli, quibus causa mortis omnium hominum continetur, omnes peccauerunt, non accipimus? Cur eo peccato, quasi nullum effet, insuper habito, confugimus ad aliud imputatum, quod & controuertitur, & ab illo effecto est remotius, praesertim verbis Apostolii & verborum situ repugnantibus? Praeter aberrationem ab argumento sunt alia vitia in responsionibus tribus D. G. quae paucis indicabo.
units.tr: Third reason. The passage does not require that it be translated thus. For since the cause is certain, why the Apostle said that death passed upon all men, namely because all sinned, what need is there to flee to an uncertain and remote cause, and that against the natural force of the words? He gives four answers, but since he had not grasped the force of the argument, they are beside the point (ἀπροσδιόνυσα [irrelevant]). The Apostle said that death passed upon all men. The cause is without doubt that all sinned. The question is what sin ought to be understood. Some want it understood as the habitual sin inhering in all, others as Adam's actual sin imputed to all, in the order of nature, before they were corrupt. The habitual sin inhering in us, propagated from Adam to all, is a certain cause, that is, one confessed by all the orthodox. That this sin exists and is a cause of death is no controversy between us, for it is truly sin, and it makes us truly liable to death. This is confirmed by the common confession of faith in the clearest and most express words. But whether Adam's actual sin is imputed before corruption, and whether that imputation is the cause by which death passed upon all, is not certain or clear. This is precisely what is now disputed between us. Again, the vice inhering in each of us is a nearer cause of our death than Adam's first actual sin, which is said to be imputed to us. That sin is not only prior in the order of nature to our being corrupt, but also many thousands of years before we began to exist and live. So when these two causes are compared, the one is certain, because it is not disputed, the other uncertain, because it is disputed. The one is nearer, being in the same subject as its effect, that is, death; the other is remote, being in another subject, and remote from us not only in the order of generation but even in time. Between it and death lies the nearer cause, namely corruption. Now, most learned reader, I think you see the force of the argument, and you understand for yourself how far the learned men's replies are from it. For since it is certain, and in no way disputed among us, that sin which deserves death, and on account of which all die, inheres in all, why do we not take the Apostle's words because all sinned, by which the cause of death for all men is stated, as referring to that sin? Why, as if it were nothing, do we pass over that sin and flee to another, imputed sin, which is both disputed and more remote from the effect, especially when the Apostle's words and their order are against it?

units.la: I. Ἡ̈os, inquit, pertendimus certam fuisse causam, quare de imputatione illa loqueretur Apostolus. Nam cum dixisset, vnius hominis peccato mortem fuisse introductam in mundum, quaeri potuit, vnde ea vis illi peccato, vt tantum mali non in vnum aut alterum, sed in omnes inuexerit. Respondet Paulus, illud inde factum, quod vno illo peccato omnes rei facti sint, siue quod vno illo peccante omnes in illo & cum illo peccasse intelligendi sunt. Haec responsio, praeter quam quod non tangit neruum argumenti, Apostolum facit nugantem, & mutatis tantum verbis idipsum quod quaerebatur respondentem, ac pro causa effectus ipsum effectum, cuius causa quaerebatur, afferentem. Quid enim est huius responsionis autori, peccatum in mundum introiisse? nihil, nisi peccatum actuale omnibus hominibus imputatum fuisse. Id patet clarissime ex hoc ipso ejus cap. 8. §. 8. p. 217. & aliis aliquot locis. Quid rursus ei est in Adamo omnes peccauisse? id sane, inquit, melius exponi non poteft, quam si dicamus peccatum Adae omnibus imputari. eodem cap. §. 10. p. 222. Quaerenti ergo cur peccatum actuale Adami omnibus imputetur ad mortem, Respondebit Apostolus, quia omnibus imputatur. Quaerenti, unde ea vis illi peccato, vt imputetur non vni aut alteri, sed omnibus, respondet illud inde factum, quod illud imputetur omnibus. Quid est nugari, si hoc non est? Ad duo ista vitia accedit etiam tertium. Sibi enim ipse repugnat. Nam si ea fuit mens Apostoli quam ei tribuit haec responsio, certè verba ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον construi debent, post antecedentia omnia, peccatum in mundum introiit, & per peccatum mors, & ita mors in omnes pertransiit: responsio enim esset ad quaestionem, quae ex verbis illis immediatè praecedentibus exoriri poterat. Id quod versionem in quo euertit. Ea enim posita construi debent verba in quo omnes peccaverunt, ante illa omnia: cohaerent enim immediatè cum nomine ἀνθρώπῳ & est trajectio. Sic ergo construi deberent, Sicut per unum hominem, in quo omnes peccaverunt, peccatum in mundum introiit, & per peccatum mors, & ita in omnes homines mors pertransiit.
units.tr: I. "Let us grant," he says, "that there was a certain cause why the Apostle spoke of this imputation. For when he had said that death was introduced into the world by the sin of one man, it could be asked whence that sin had the power to bring so much evil not upon one or another, but upon all. Paul answers that this came about because all were made guilty by that one sin, or because all are to be understood to have sinned in and with the one who sinned." This answer, apart from not touching the heart of the argument, makes the Apostle trifle, and by changing only the words it simply repeats what was asked, and offers the effect itself as the cause of the effect whose cause was sought. For what does this answerer mean by the sin entered into the world? Nothing except that the actual sin was imputed to all men. This is quite clear from this same author's chapter 8, §8, p. 217, and from several other places. And what does he mean by all sinned in Adam? "Indeed," he says, "this cannot be better explained than by saying that the sin of Adam is imputed to all." The same chapter, §10, p. 222. So to one who asks why the actual sin of Adam is imputed to all unto death, the Apostle will answer: because it is imputed to all. To one who asks whence that sin has the power to be imputed not to one or another, but to all, he answers that this came about because it is imputed to all. What is this but trifling? To these two faults a third is added. For he contradicts himself. If the Apostle's mind was what this answer attributes to him, then certainly the words [ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον] in whom all sinned ought to be construed after all the preceding clauses: sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death passed upon all men; for the answer would then be to the question that could arise immediately from those preceding words. This overturns the rendering in whom. For on that reading the words in whom all sinned must be construed before all those clauses, since they stand directly with the noun ἀνθρώπῳ [man], and there is a transposition. So they would have to be construed thus: As through one man, in whom all sinned, sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death passed upon all men.

units.la: Secunda similiter responsio peccat ignoratione argumenti, causamque incertam aliter quàm debuit accipit, & praeterea nonnulla habet minùs rectè dicta. Quis dixerit, inquit, incertam causam à Paulo proponi cùm 1. Cor. xv. 22. ad Adamum usque protoplastam confcendit, & nos omnes decit in Adamo mori? Quorsum hoc spectat? Ibine causam aliquam affert Apostolus, cur omnes vi communionis quam habent cum Adamo moriantur? aut suntne illa verba, in Adamo omnes moriuntur, etiam imputatiue, ut loquuntur, intelligenda? Deteriora sunt quae sequuntur. Nimirum, inquit, neque ibi, neque hic Apostolus proprie ad causas particulares respicit, quae residere possunt in unoquoque individuo generis humani, & propter quas fit ut moriantur: sed causam generalem exponit quae omnes in genere ex aequo respiciat &c. Perinde loquitur, quasi corruptio haereditaria non esset causa generalis omnes homines ex aequo respiciens: Cùm illa tamen tam fit communis, quàm communis est eorum qui peccauerunt mors, quàm communis est illis natura humana, immò quàm communis dicitur esse imputatio. Ita paulatim doctrina de corruptionis hæreditariæ vi & reatu, quam summo studio primi reformatores tuebantur, negligitur ac prope obliteratur, vt det locum illi imputationi, quam magni illi viri, aut ignorarunt prorsus, aut etiam refutarunt. Neque par est, addit, vt eam causam dicamus esse remotam & longinquam, quia hic non ad annorum & sæculorum spatia, sed ad rei efficacitatem respiciendum est. Quid? an injustitia, quæ in me non hæsit, sed in solo Adamo, tot annorum millibus antequàm effem mortuo, causa est æquè immediata ac proxima mihi vel morti meæ, ac illa quæ in me hæret intimè, & est omnium confeffione mortis meæ causa? Annon etiam peccatum Adami fequuta est corruptio, & hanc mors? est igitur corruptio causa propinquior mortis quàm peccatum quod in solo hæsit Adamo. Neque vero, subjungit, qui corruptionem ab Adamo deriuari dicunt, Adamum ideo proponunt, tanquam causam remotam & difsitam corruptionis illius, nimirum, quia est nobis cum eo ratione sanguinis proxima vnio, etsi non ratione perfonæ. Immo eum proponunt, tanquam causam corruptionis illius remotam & dissitam, hoc est, primam, vnde ad alios omnes dimanauit. Itaque quod sanguis hic à persona distinguitur, & illius, non hujus, ratione nobis esse dicitur proxima cum Adamo vnio, id equidem non intelligo. Tam enim sanguis meus à sanguine, & natura mea à natura, quàm persona à perlona Adami differt: differentia est vtriusque pariter numerica, non fpecifica: Et quàm personam meam, tam naturam etiam meam per omnes meos intermedios parentes ab Adamo traxi. Est enim Adamus pater noster non proximus, sed primus; nihil que ab eo nisi per proximos meos parentes, accepi, aut accipere potui. Sed, inquit, cum hic instituatur inter Christum & Adamum comparatio, non magis dicendum est inobedientiam ab Adamo commissam, esse causam remotam nostrae condemnationis, quam obedientiam a Christo praestitam, esse causam remotam nostrae justificationis. Quasi vero non possit comparatio inter duas causas effectuum oppositorum instituì, cum sunt in suo genere primae, nisi utraque sit pariter proxima ! Quis nescit obedientiam Christi esse justificationis nostrae causam adaequatam & unicam, inobedientiam vero Adami condemnationis nostrae nonnisi inadaequatam & partialem? damnamur enim non ob solum peccatum actuale Adami, sed etiam ob inhaerentem nobis corruptionem haereditariam, & alia omnia nostra peccata sive actualia sive habitualia; cum tamen ob unam Christi obedientiam, nullo autem modo ob nostram, justificemur. Haec igitur, cum sola & unica justificationis causa sit, eadem & prima & proxima est; illa vero cum non sola sit, sed una cum ea aliae multae sint causae condemnationis, ita prima est, ut nihil necesse sit proximam esse. Quid? nonne peccatum & per peccatum condemnationem trahimus ab Adamo propagatione naturali? Nonne & Patres olim, & primi nostri Reformatores imitationi Pelagianae opponere solebant propagationem peccati, nulla imputationis facta mentione? Atqui propagationis naturalis, in suo quidem genere, prima est causa Adamus, sed cujusque nostrum proxima aut immediata prosecto non est. Hic ergo maximum cernitur Adamum inter & Christum discrimen. Adamus est generationis nostræ causa remotissima , cùm regenerationis nostræ Christus sit causa proxima. Filij sumus Adami non proximi sed remoti : inter nos enim & Adamum alij multi interjecti sunt ; Filij vero Christi proxi- mi sumus, quotquot in eum credimus. Per fidem enim vnimur Christo recta & immediatè, necnon per ejus Spiritum, qui cùm vnus tantùm numero sit & in Christo & in omnibus nobis, nos Christo tam immediatè copulat, vt inter Christum & fidelem intermedius nemo sit. Hæc cùm non ignoraret Vir Doctus, qui potuit sic loqui? Deniq; in causis meritoriis, inquit, quales sunt de quibus agimus, semper est proximitas, quia meritum illud semper ἐνεργὰ & efficaciter agit. Egregium argumentum ! quasi non possit pariter efficacia, ac causa, distingui in remotam & proximam! sua enim cuique causæ vis &, cùm sequitur effectum, efficacia est; alioqui non esset causa. Annon Adamus efficaciter naturam suam & corruptionem in nos propagauit ? Attamen naturæ & corruptionis nostræ causa non est nisi remota. Non est autem ipse causa meritoria condemnationis nostræ, sed hujus causæ causa; manauit enim ab eo corruptio hæreditaria nostræ condemnationis causa proxima seu immediata,hujus autem causa fuit peccatum actuale Adami. Possumus-ne similiter dicere, obedientiam Christi causam fuisse alicujus virtutis vel obedientiæ , quæ sit causa justificationis nostræ ? Eatenus igitur inter Christi obedientiam & Adami inobedientiam discrimen est memorabile, & illa proxima justificationis, hæc remota condemnationis nostræ ( corruptio enim interponitur) causa dicenda est. Alioqui quomodo peccatum actuale Adami causa esse posset condemnationis nostræ meritoria & proxima? Primùm si non est nostrum nisi per imputationem, non meretur condemnationem nostram nisi imputationis interuentu. Non est igitur causa meritoria nostræ condemnationis per se, sed per accidens tantùm, ratione illius imputationis, quæ est actio diuina, atque adeò supernaturalis & voluntaria: cùm tamen obedientia Christi sit causa meritoria justificationis nostræ per se; quippe, eo fine ac consilio à vade nostro loco nostro prælita. Quo posito sequitur, quod sumus peccatores & condemnamur, id esse diuinæ illi actioni per se ascribendum, peccato verò Adami nonnisi per accidens, id quod ut credam vel faciam adduci me mea nullo modo patitur conscientia. Deinde qui imputat alicui homini peccatum, supponit illum hominem esse, qui damnat ad mortem supponit eum quem damnat viuere. Cùm ergo nostri esse & viuere, quod natura condemnationem nostram antecedit, non sit Adamus causa nisi remota, qui potest esse condemnationis nostræ causa proxima?
units.tr: A second answer likewise errs by ignoring the argument, takes the uncertain cause in a different sense from what it should have, and also contains some things said too loosely. Who would say, he says, that Paul proposes an uncertain cause when in 1 Cor. 15:22 he goes back as far as Adam the first-formed, and says that we all die in Adam? What does this have to do with the matter? Does the Apostle there give some cause why all die by virtue of their communion with Adam? Or are the words in Adam all die to be understood even imputatively, as they say? What follows is worse. Certainly, he says, neither there nor here does the Apostle properly look to particular causes, which may reside in each individual of the human race and on account of which they die, but he sets forth a general cause that bears equally on all in the mass, etc. He speaks as though hereditary corruption were not a general cause bearing equally on all men, when yet it is as common as the death of those who sinned, as common as human nature is to them, indeed as common as imputation is said to be. Thus little by little the doctrine of the power and guilt of hereditary corruption, which the first Reformers defended with the greatest zeal, is neglected and almost blotted out, so as to give room to that imputation which those great men either quite ignored or even refuted. Nor is it fitting, he adds, that we should call that cause remote and distant, because here we must look not to spans of years and centuries but to the efficacy of the thing. What then? Is the injustice which did not cling to me but to Adam alone, many thousands of years before I was even born, an equally immediate and proximate cause of my death as that which clings inwardly to me and is, by everyone's confession, the cause of my death? Does not corruption also follow Adam's sin, and death follow corruption? Corruption is therefore a nearer cause of death than the sin which stayed in Adam alone. Nor indeed, he adds, do those who say that corruption is derived from Adam put Adam forward as a remote and distant cause of that corruption, namely because we have a close union with him by reason of blood, though not by reason of person. Rather they put him forward as a remote and distant cause of that corruption, that is, as the first cause, from whom it flowed to all others. So I do not understand how it is said that blood is distinguished here from person, and that our close union with Adam is said to be by reason of the one and not the other. For my blood differs from his blood, and my nature from his nature, just as my person differs from Adam's person; the difference is numerical in each case, not specific. And just as I have drawn my person from Adam, so too I have drawn my nature from him through all my intervening parents. For Adam is our father not as the nearest but as the first; and I have received nothing from him except through my nearer parents, nor could I have received anything otherwise. But, he says, since a comparison is here set up between Christ and Adam, we must no more say that the disobedience committed by Adam is a remote cause of our condemnation than that the obedience rendered by Christ is a remote cause of our justification. As if a comparison could not be set up between two causes of opposite effects, when both are first in their own kind, unless each were equally proximate! Who does not know that the obedience of Christ is the adequate and sole cause of our justification, whereas the disobedience of Adam is cause of our condemnation only inadequately and partially? For we are condemned not only on account of Adam's actual sin but also on account of the hereditary corruption inhering in us and all our other sins, whether actual or habitual, whereas we are justified on account of the one obedience of Christ and in no way on account of our own. Therefore, since the one obedience of Christ is the sole and only cause of justification, it is both first and proximate; but since Adam's sin is not the sole cause of condemnation, but there are many other causes of condemnation along with it, it is first in such a way that it need not be proximate. What then? Do we not also draw sin, and through sin condemnation, from Adam by natural propagation? Did not the Fathers of old, and our first Reformers, use to oppose to the Pelagian imitation the propagation of sin, without any mention of imputation? Yet Adam is the first cause of natural propagation in its own kind, but he is certainly not the proximate or immediate cause of each one of us. Here, then, the greatest difference between Adam and Christ is seen. Adam is the most remote cause of our generation, whereas Christ is the proximate cause of our regeneration. We are sons of Adam not as nearest but as remote; for many others are interposed between us and Adam. But we are the nearest sons of Christ, as many as believe in him. For through faith we are united to Christ directly and immediately, and likewise through his Spirit, who, being one only in number and in Christ and in all of us, joins us to Christ so immediately that no one is intermediate between Christ and the believer. Since the learned man did not ignore these things, who could have spoken thus? Finally, in meritorious causes, he says, such as those we are discussing, there is always proximity, because that merit always acts energetically [ἐνεργὰ] and effectively. A fine argument! As if efficacy and cause could not equally be distinguished into remote and proximate! For each cause has its own power and, when it produces its effect, its efficacy; otherwise it would not be a cause. Did not Adam efficaciously propagate his nature and corruption into us? Yet the cause of our nature and corruption is only remote. Nor is he himself the meritorious cause of our condemnation, but the cause of this cause; for hereditary corruption flowed from him as the proximate or immediate cause of our condemnation, but the cause of that corruption was the actual sin of Adam. Could we likewise say that the obedience of Christ was the cause of some virtue or obedience which is the cause of our justification? So in this respect the difference between the obedience of Christ and the disobedience of Adam is remarkable: the one is the proximate cause of justification, the other must be called the remote cause of our condemnation (for corruption intervenes). Otherwise, how could the actual sin of Adam be the meritorious and proximate cause of our condemnation? First, if it is ours only by imputation, it merits our condemnation only through the intervention of imputation. It is therefore not a meritorious cause of our condemnation in itself, but only by accident, by reason of that imputation, which is a divine action and therefore supernatural and voluntary; whereas the obedience of Christ is the meritorious cause of our justification in itself, since it was undertaken for this end and purpose, in our place and on our behalf. Given this, it follows that the fact that we are sinners and are condemned must be ascribed in itself to that divine action, and to Adam's sin only by accident, which my conscience in no way allows me to believe or do. Next, whoever imputes sin to any man supposes that man to exist, and supposes that the one he condemns to death is alive. Since, then, our existence and life, which nature precedes our condemnation, are caused by Adam only remotely, how can he be the proximate cause of our condemnation?

units.la: Sequitur ratio quarta. Scopus Apostoli non patitur vt ita vertantur; cœpit enim Apostolus verf. 12. comparationem inter Christum & Adamum instituere eo modo, vt affirmaret per vnum hominem peccatum introiisse, & per peccatum mortem, adeo vt mors in omnes homines peruagata sit. Quia vero mirum videri potuit, tantam fuisse in vnius hominis vno peccato vim atque efficacitatem, vt totam hominum multitudinem morti addiceret, ne quis indignè quicquam de Deo suspicaretur, addit, id mirum videri non debere, cùm omnes peccauerint. Vt igitur Adam in mortem incidit, quia peccauit; sic & omnes pariter in mortem incidunt, quia omnes peccauerunt. Quid reponit vir doctus? Primo, inquit, notetur respondentis confessio: Nam dum agnoscit peccatum illud, quod per vnum hominem introiisse dicitur, esse vnum vnius hominis, nempe Adami peccatum, eadem ratione omnia illa argumenta confutat & conuellit, quibus supra moliebatur alius confirmare, hic peccati nomine non ipsius Adami peccatum, sed nostram internam & originalem corruptionem tantum intelligendam esse. Itâ-ne, omnia illa argumenta confutat & conuellit? Possunt-ne vnius simplici affirmatione, alterius argumenta & multa, & valida, & diu post illam affirmationem excogitata & proposita confutari & conuelli? Si est ita, nullum est argumentum vsque adeò necessarium, & demonstratiuum, quod non possit ea ratione facillimè confutari & conuelli. Argumenta autem illa, quia sunt posterioris manuscripti, quàm sint valida & inuicta, tum fiet manifestum, cum instituetur manuscripti illius cum libro D. Gar. comparatio. Quid verò dices, candide Lector, si id non confitetur doctissimus autor illius rationis, quod hic confiteri dicitur? Certè non agnoscit peccatum illud, quod per vnum hominem introiisse dicitur, esse vnum vnius hominis, nempe Adami peccatum: id non sentit: id neque totidem verbis dixit, neque æquipollentibus. Dixit tantum in vno vnius peccato tantam fuisse vim, vt totam hominum multitudinem morti addiceret: sed non dixit illud vnum vnius peccatum idem numero in omnes homines ingressum esse, & proximè mortem inuexisse. Nempe peccatum quod introijt in mundum est vnius peccati vnius hominis effectum, & per vnum hominem peccatum introiit in mundum & mors vi vnius peccati, quo1 sese propagatione naturali diffudit,& multiplicauit, & cum natura humana, cui inhæret,propagauit. Itaque totam hominum multitudinem morti addixit fui in omnes homines propagatione, ac secundùm numerum multiplicatione. Hæc est præstantissimi illius viri mens, neque sibi, neque Placeo contradicentis. Hæc prima fuit D. G. respondsio. 2. Ad dubium, inquit, quod emergere potuit in lectorum animis, nulla esset plane Apostoli responsio legitima, si talem daret, qualem vult Vir Doctus. Dubium enim hoc est, quomodo tanta sit vis in vno vnius Adami peccato, vt totam hominum multitudinem morti addicat. Responsio dicitur esse, id inde fieri, quod omnes peccauerint in sua propria persona. Hoc verò ludere est, non dubio satisfacere. Nam hæc quidem ratio esse potest, propter quam morti omnes addicantur, quia omnes peccarunt. Sed hic non quaeritur, quare omnes morti addicantur, verum hoc potius, cur in vno vnius Adami peccato tanta vis sit, vt hunc effectum producat, nempe mortem. Responsio igitur debet agere de peccato illo Adami, non de nostro vniuscujusque, de quo nihil dictum fuerat in dubio propósito. Itaque vt appósita sit responsio, necessarium est, vt illud ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον, interpretemur de peccato ipsius Adami, quod omnes morti addicat, propterea quod ejus reatus in omnes descendit, sive quia propter imputationem commune sit omnibus. Hoc ita clarum est & cuidens, vt hic oporteat valde festinasse disputatorem.Festinauit quidem fortasse autor hujus rationis, sed non nimis: optimè enim disputat. Sed an festinauerit D. G. nescio, illud certè mihi constat, eum hic, vt alibi passim, haud rectè disputare. Non ludit, sed revera dubio satisfacit Responsio. Duobus enim modis in vnius hominis vno peccato tantam vim fuisse, vt totam hominum multitudinem morti addiceret, intelligi poterat, vno, si ponatur, quod facit hoc loco D. G. Deum toti hominum multitudini vnum illud vnius hominis peccatum immediatè imputasse, atque ob illud imputatum eam morti addixisse. Altero, si intelligatur, peccatum illud sese naturali quodam contagio, ab vno homine in alios omnes propagasse & multiplicasse, atque ita, quoniam omnes peccaverunt, morti addictos fuisse. Apostolus ne Lector priorem modum cogitans, ind'gnè quicquam de Deo sci'sp'cantur, posteriorem docet, affirmans omnes homines morti fuisse addictos, non quia vnus tantùm peccavit, sed quia omnes peccaverunt; non proximè ob vnius vnum peccatum, sed ob suum quisque sibi insitum, ab illo vno propagatum, quæ propagatio vocibus & ita, non minus ad peccatum quàm ad mortem pertinentibus, satis innuitur.
units.tr: The fourth argument follows. The purpose of the Apostle does not allow it to be rendered thus. For the Apostle, in Rom. 5:12, began to draw a comparison between Christ and Adam, in such a way as to affirm that sin entered through one man, and death through sin, so that death spread to all men. But because it might seem strange that such great power and efficacy lay in the one sin of one man, that it condemned the whole multitude of men to death, lest anyone should unworthily suspect anything of God, he adds that this should not seem strange, since all have sinned. Therefore, just as Adam fell into death because he sinned, so all likewise fall into death because all have sinned. What does the learned man reply? First, he says, let the admission of the respondent be noted. For while he acknowledges that the sin which is said to have entered through one man is the one sin of one man, namely Adam's sin, by the same reasoning he refutes and overturns all those arguments with which another laboured above to confirm that by the name of sin is to be understood not Adam's own sin, but only our inner and original corruption. So he refutes and overturns all those arguments? Can the arguments, many and strong, devised and proposed long after that affirmation, be refuted and overturned by a single simple assertion of the other side? If so, there is no argument so necessary and demonstrative that it cannot be very easily refuted and overturned in this way. As for those arguments, how strong and unconquerable they are, given that they belong to a later writing, will become plain when the comparison of that writing with the book of Dr. G. is carried out. But what will you say, candid reader, if the most learned author of that reasoning does not confess what he is said to confess here? Certainly he does not acknowledge that the sin which is said to have entered through one man is the one sin of one man, namely Adam's sin. He does not think this; he has said it neither in these exact words nor in equivalent ones. He has said only that in the one sin of one man there was such power that it condemned the whole multitude of men to death; but he has not said that this one sin of one man, numerically the same, entered into all men and immediately brought in death. Indeed, the sin that entered the world is the effect of one sin of one man, and through one man sin entered the world, and death by the power of the one sin, which spread itself by natural propagation, multiplied, and passed on together with human nature, to which it clings. Thus it condemned the whole multitude of men to death by its spreading into all men through propagation, and by its multiplying according to their number. This is the mind of that most distinguished man, who contradicts neither himself nor Place. This was Dr. G.'s first reply. 2. To the doubt, he says, which could arise in the minds of readers, there would be no legitimate answer of the Apostle at all, if he gave such an answer as the learned man wishes. For the doubt is this: how is there such power in the one sin of one Adam that it condemns the whole multitude of men to death? The answer is said to be that this happens because all have sinned in their own person. But this is trifling, not satisfying the doubt. For this reason may indeed be the cause on account of which all are condemned to death, because all have sinned. But here it is not asked why all are condemned to death, but rather this: why there is such power in the one sin of Adam that it produces this effect, namely death. The answer, therefore, ought to deal with that sin of Adam, not with the sin of each one of us, about which nothing had been said in the doubt proposed. So that the answer may be apt, it is necessary that we interpret the words ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον [on which all sinned] of the sin of Adam himself, which condemns all to death, because its guilt descends upon all, or because by imputation it is common to all. This is so clear and evident that the disputant here must have been very hasty. The author of this reasoning was perhaps indeed hasty, but not too much; for he argues very well. But whether Dr. G. was hasty I do not know; this at least is certain to me, that he here, as elsewhere throughout, does not argue correctly. The answer does not trifle, but in truth satisfies the doubt. For there were two ways in which the great power of the one sin of one man, condemning the whole multitude of men to death, could be understood. The first, which Dr. G. here assumes, is that God immediately imputed that one sin of one man to the whole multitude of men, and on account of that imputed sin condemned them to death. The second is that the sin spread and multiplied from one man into all others by a certain natural contagion, and thus, since all have sinned, they were condemned to death. Lest the reader, thinking of the first way, should unworthily suspect anything of God, the Apostle teaches the second, affirming that all men were condemned to death not because one alone sinned, but because all sinned; not immediately on account of the one sin of one man, but on account of each one's own sin, implanted in him and propagated from that one; and this propagation is sufficiently indicated by the words so and as, which pertain no less to sin than to death.

units.la: Audi, quæso humanissime Lector, Caluinum, à cujus doctrina recedant necesse est qui nos innouatæ doctrinæ accusant, Comm. in Rom. 5. 12. Obscrua quem hic ponat ordinem. Peccatum enim præcessisse dicit: ex eo sequitur esse mortem. Sunt enim qui contendunt, nos in peccato Adæ esse perditos ac si nulla nostra culpa periremus, ideo tantum quasi ille nobis peccasset. (Vix potuit clarius imputatio antedens describi, quam sequi putantur mors animæ, id est, corruptio hæreditaria, & mors corporis ac æterna, tanquam poenæ propriedictæ.) Atqui diserte affirmat Paulus, in omnes propagatum esse peccatum, qui ejus pœnam luunt. Atque id deinde propius urget, quum rationem assignat paulo post, cur omnis Adæ posteri, tus subjaceat mortis imperio. Nempe,
units.tr: Hear, I beg you, most kind reader, Calvin, from whose teaching those must depart who accuse us of a novel doctrine, Comm. on Rom. 5:12. Observe what order he puts here. For he says that sin came first; from it, he says, follows death. For there are those who contend that we perished in the sin of Adam as if without any fault of our own, but only because he sinned, as it were, on our behalf. (Hardly could imputation that precedes be described more clearly, when they think that the death of the soul, that is, hereditary corruption, and the death of the body and eternal death follow as punishments justly imposed.) Yet Paul affirms plainly that sin was propagated into all who bear its punishment. And he presses this more closely when he assigns the reason, shortly afterwards, why all the posterity of Adam is subject to the dominion of death. Namely,

units.la: P inquit, quoniam omnes peccauimus. Porro istud peccare, est corruptos esse & vitiatos. Illa enim naturalis prauitas quam e matris vtero afferimus, tametsi non ita cito fructus suos edit, peccatum tamen est coram domino, & ejus vltionem meretur. Atque hoc est peccatum quod vocant Originale. Et paulo post, Peccauimus igitur omnes, quia naturali corruptione omnes imbuti fumus. Et iterum, Sequitur ergo prauitatem nobis ingenitam, & hereditariam notari. Nihil potuit dici clarius & difertius. Gratulatur sibi Placeus cum videt per latus suum peti Caluinum, feque cum eo pariter oppugnari, & desertae antiquae doctrinae, aut potius eam deferentium vices luget. Notetur hic rursus noua, &, vt mihi quidem videtur, Deo injuriosa doctrina, peccatum Adami propter imputationem commune fieri om nilus. Quod igitur commune est omnibus id non vi aut contagio aut naturali propagationi illius peccati ascribendum est, sed Deo, cui libuit imputando facere omnibus commune, quod alioqui commune non fuisset. Vnde igitur nostra perditio, nisi ex Deo, qui nos fecit peccatores alienum peccatum efficiendo nostrum? Et cur peccatum illud nobis imputauit, & fecit nostrum, nosque peccatores? Nulla causa affertur, aut afferri potest, nisi quia ita ei libuit. Non excitatur confcientia tua, pie Lector? non refugit talem doctrinam? non exhorrescit? Sed pergamus.
units.tr: P says, since all have sinned. Moreover, to sin in that way is to be corrupted and vitiated. For that natural depravity which we bring from the womb of our mother, although it does not put forth its fruits so quickly, is nevertheless sin before the Lord, and deserves his vengeance. And this is the sin that they call Original. And a little later, We have all therefore sinned, because we have all been imbued with natural corruption. And again, It follows, therefore, that inborn and hereditary depravity is noted. Nothing could have been said more clearly and plainly. Place rejoices to see Calvin attacked alongside himself, and laments the abandonment of the old doctrine, or rather those who desert it. Let it be noted here again that this new doctrine, and, as it seems to me, injurious to God, makes the sin of Adam common to all because of imputation. What is therefore common to all is to be ascribed not to force, or contagion, or natural propagation of that sin, but to God, who chose by imputation to make common to all what otherwise would not have been common. Whence then is our perdition, if not from God, who made us sinners by making another's sin ours? And why did he impute that sin to us, and make it ours, and us sinners? No cause is given, or can be given, except that so it pleased him. Is your conscience not stirred, godly reader? Does it not shrink from such a doctrine? Does it not shudder? But let us go on.

units.la: Quinta & vltima ratio his verbis concepta est § xr. pag. 224. Ea interpretatio confirmatur verf. 13. sequenti, qui per particulam γὰρ connectitur cum precedenti. Dubitare enim aliquis potuit, an omnes homines revera peccauerint; Id igitur Apostolus probat eo argumento, quod vbicunque mors est, ibi necesse est esse peccatum. Mors autem non extitit modo, sed & regnauit in omnes illos qui vixerunt ij s temporibus, qua inter primum peccatum Adami & legem interfluxerunt : omnes illi ergo fuerunt peccato obnoxij. Respondeo inquit D. G. Absit vero vt ejusmodi analysim accipiamus, qua ex diuino Apostolo facit ineptum circulatorem. Bona verba : ineptum circulatorem! Absit à nobis tam grande crimen. Quomodo vero id probat? Nam, inquit, Apostolus versu 12. probat omnes esse addictos morti, quia peccauerunt, postea verf. 13. probat omnes peccasse, quia morti addicti sunt, & mors in omnes regnat. Hoc scilicet est esse ineptum circulatorem. Atqui non dixit illius rationis eruditissimus autor, Apostolum versu 12. probare, omnes esse addictos morti? Relege quaeso & considera rationem, quemadmodum ab ipso Gariffolio recitata fuerat § xi. & à me exscripta. Num tale quid in ea animaduertis? aut ex ea bona consequentia deduci potest? Eccur vero Apostolus id probare instituisset, quod Scriptura, & omnium seculorum experientia, genusque adeo humanum vniuersum perpetuò confitetur & clamat? Ecquis etiam credat, Apostolum probare voluisse clarius per obscurius? Clarius enim est omnes mori, quàm omnes peccasse. Non igitur probat, sed ne viderentur omnes homines ob vnicum vnius hominis peccatum eis imputatum mori, affirmat per vnum hominem ita mortem ingressam esse in genus humanum, vt non sola in omnes homines inuaserit, sed ejus etiam causa, peccatum. Itaque mori omnes non proximè ob vnum illud actuale vnius hominis peccatum, sed ob suum quemque sibi insitum, ab illo deriuatum. Fingit ergo D. G. probationem circularem vbi nulla est; quanquam si esset, non tam circulus à
units.tr: The fifth and last argument is expressed in these words (§ xr., p. 224): "This interpretation is confirmed by the following verse 13, which is connected with the preceding by the particle γὰρ. For someone might doubt whether all men have really sinned. The Apostle therefore proves this by the argument that wherever there is death, there must of necessity be sin." But death not only existed, it also reigned over all those who lived in the times that flowed between the first sin of Adam and the law: therefore all of them were subject to sin. "I reply," says D. G. "Far be it from us to take this as the kind of analysis which makes the divine Apostle an inept circulator." Fine words: an inept circulator! Far be it from us to commit so grave a fault. But how does he prove this? "For," he says, "the Apostle in verse 12 proves that all are given over to death because they sinned; afterwards in verse 13 he proves that all sinned because they are given over to death, and death reigns over all." This, of course, is to be an inept circulator. But did that most learned author not say that the Apostle in verse 12 proves that all are given over to death? Please reread and consider the argument as Gariffolius himself recited it in § xi., and as I copied it out. Do you notice anything of the kind in it? Or can any sound consequence be drawn from it? Why, moreover, would the Apostle have undertaken to prove what Scripture, and the experience of all ages, and the whole human race constantly confess and proclaim? Who would also believe that the Apostle wished to prove the clearer by the more obscure? For it is clearer that all die than that all sinned. Therefore he does not prove this, but, lest all men should seem to die because of the single sin of one man imputed to them, he affirms that through one man death has so entered into the human race that it has not only invaded all men, but sin also is its cause. Thus all men die not immediately because of that one actual sin of one man, but each because of the sin implanted in him and derived from that man. So D. G. invents a circular proof where there is none; yet even if there were, it ought to be called not so much a circle condemned by the philosophers as a regress praised by them: for it would consist of two demonstrations, one τὸ διότι, the other τὸ ὅτι, the former giving distinct knowledge of the effect, the latter confused knowledge of the cause.

units.la: Philosophis damnatus, quàm regressus ab iisdem laudatus dici deberet: constaret enim ex duabus demonstrationibus, altera τὸ διότι, altera τὸ ὅτι, illa pariente distinctam effectus, hac confusam causæ notitiam. Eandem autem circulationem cùm ipse sibi objecisset D. G. expedire sese ex ea non potuit. Posteriorem enim tantùm rationem attigit, priorem, ex qua pendebat circulus, alto inuoluit silentio. Peto igitur ex ejus mente, num Apostolus probet Rom. 12. omnes esse morti addictos, quia peccatum Adæ ipsis imputatur? Si ais, manet circularis argumentatio: statim enim Rom. 13. & 14. probabit omnibus peccatum Adæ imputari, quia omnes sunt morti addicti. Si negas, tollis quidem circulum; sed neque id negauit D. G. neque ut se ex eo circulo educeret, quicquam ejusmodi tentauit: fecit ergo id, cujus nos falsò accusabat, ex Apostolo diuino ineptum, vt loquitur, circulatorem.
units.tr: When D. G. had himself raised this same circularity as an objection, he could not extricate himself from it. For he touched only on the later reason, and wrapped the earlier one, on which the circle depended, in deep silence. I ask therefore, in his own mind: does the Apostle prove in Romans 12 that all are given over to death because Adam's sin is imputed to them? If you say yes, the argument remains circular: for immediately in Romans 13 and 14 he will prove that Adam's sin is imputed to all, because all are given over to death. If you say no, you indeed remove the circle; but D. G. neither denied this nor attempted anything of the kind to lead himself out of that circle. He therefore did the very thing of which he falsely accused us: he made himself, as he puts it, an inept circulator, from the divine Apostle.

units.la: Sed tamen inde hoc argumentum elicit. Quibus irrogatur pœna mortis propter peccatum, iis peccatum imputatur. Atqui infantibus irrogata est ante legem pœna mortis propter peccatum Adæ. Ergo iis peccatum Adæ imputatum est. Resp. Peccatum Adæ duobus modis accipi: 1. pro eo peccato, quod ab eo in posteros propagatum & fecundum hominum numerum multiplicatum, caro & vetus Adam appellatur. 2. pro causa peccati illius propagati, nempe actuali Adæ inobedientia. Si priore modo accipitur, concedo totum argumentum. Fateor enim peccatum illud, quia intra nos est, nobis omnibus, etiam infantibus, merito imputari. Si posteriore modo, distinguo præpositionem propter: nam vel causam proximam seu immediatam, vel remotam tantùm seu mediatam significat. Si prius, nego minorem propositione: irrogata est infantibus poena mortis proximè ob inhærens vitium, remotè ob Adami actuale peccatum. Si posterius, inde sequitur duntaxat peccati illius actualis imputatio mediata, quam vltrò concedo. Hoc me docuit Caluinus, quia, inquit, ejus peccatum peccati nostri causa est, exitium nostrum illi Paulus ascribit. Peccatum nostrum voco, quod nobis ingenitum est, & cum quo nascimur. Et Bullingerus, non nocceret nobis Adæ lapsus, nisi talis ex eo peruerfitas seu corruptio nobis innata fuisset, quæ Dei judicium promereretur.
units.tr: Yet from this he draws the following argument: "Those on whom the penalty of death is inflicted on account of sin, to them sin is imputed. But the penalty of death was inflicted on infants before the law on account of Adam's sin. Therefore Adam's sin was imputed to them." Reply: the sin of Adam may be taken in two ways: (1) for that sin which, propagated from him to his posterity and multiplied according to the number of men, is called flesh and the old Adam; (2) for the cause of that propagated sin, namely Adam's actual disobedience. If it is taken in the former way, I grant the whole argument. For I confess that this sin, because it is within us, is rightly imputed to all of us, even to infants. If it is taken in the latter way, I distinguish the preposition "on account of": for it signifies either a proximate or immediate cause, or only a remote or mediate one. If the former, I deny the minor premise: the penalty of death was inflicted on infants immediately on account of the inherent vice, remotely on account of Adam's actual sin. If the latter, it follows only that the mediate imputation of that actual sin, which I freely concede. Calvin taught me this: "because," he says, "his sin is the cause of our sin, Paul ascribes our ruin to it. I call it our sin, which is innate in us, and with which we are born." And Bullinger: "the fall of Adam would not harm us unless such perversity or corruption, innate to us from it, had been present, which would deserve the judgment of God."

units.la: Sic vindicata est versio Gallica, qua vtuntur Ecclesiæ nostræ. Quod autem subjungit D. G. Sic acriter disputatum fuisse, &c, sed ab eo tempore deferbuisse impetum,& in posterioribus scriptis mutata esse velificationem &c, Fallitur vehementer. Eadem enim perpetuò Placei sententia fuit, & melius verti voces ἐφ' ᾧ εὸ quod, quàm in quo, Et tamen ne hanc quidem versionem obesse sententiæ suæ, ob eas rationes, quas thesibus suis aliquot annis, priusquam Manuscriptum illud prius fieret, editis, inseruerat. Non viderat illud manuscriptum, cùm suum istud fecit quod D. G. posterius appellat, nec cur mutaret, vt loquitur vir Doctus, velificationem causa vlla erat. Nemo enim ei tum quicquam objecerat, quo recepta, quam sequitur, vocularum ἐφ' ᾧ versio impugnaretur. De nostra confessione, quàm præter rationem triumphet hoc loco D. G. patet ex dictis pag. hujus lib. 73. Quæ tamen si vlla fuisset, Placeo obesse non posset, quo inscio nec consentiente facta fuisset. Sed de illa versione jam fortasse plus satis.
units.tr: Thus the Gallic version, which our Church uses, is vindicated. As for what D. G. adds, that "the dispute was so sharp... but the zeal cooled after that time, and in the later writings the sails were trimmed..." etc., he is gravely mistaken. For Placaeus's opinion was always the same, and the phrase ἐφ' ᾧ is better rendered "because" than "in whom." And yet not even this translation harms his opinion, on account of the reasons which he had inserted in his theses published some years before that manuscript was made. He had not seen that manuscript when he made what D. G. calls the later version; nor was there any cause for changing, as the learned man puts it, the course of the sails. For no one had then objected anything to him by which the accepted version, which he follows, of the words ἐφ' ᾧ might be assailed. That D. G. triumphs here beyond reason over our confession is plain from what was said on page 73 of this book. Yet even if there had been any such thing, it could not have harmed Placaeus, since it would have been made without his knowledge and consent. But perhaps enough has been said about that version.

units.la: Redeo ad argumentum supra pag. 70. ita propositum, ut ejus tres lineæ à Typographo repetitæ fuerint, nec à Corrector, adeo aliis distractus negotiis tunc festinabat, deletæ. Id sic habet. Qui, cum nondum essent in rerum natura, dicuntur in alio peccasse, censentur proculdubio eo committente peccatum, & ipsi etiam commisisse, quod euidenter ad imputationem pertinet. Atqui homines omnes cum nondum essent, dicuntur in Adamo peccasse. Ergo censentur eo committente peccatum, & ipsi commisisse, quod ad imputationem peccati Adæ manifeste pertinet. Primo nego id euidenter ad imputationem pertinere quam antecedentem seu immediatam voco. Cur enim non pertineat potius ad propagationem peccati inhærentis, quod reatus & imputatio sequitur? Deinde nego majorem. An enim qui dicuntur in alio fuisse, vel mortui fuisse, censentur eo existente vel moriente & ipsi extitisse, & mortui fuisse? Morimur certe in Adamo, sed sua quisque morte; sicut resurgimus in Christo sua quisque resurrectione. Sic peccamus in Adamo, sed suo quisque peccato. Notatur tantum peccati & mortis primus autor & fons, unde ad nos omnes dimanarunt. Denique negò minorem. Non enim dixit Apostolus, omnes homines, cum nondum essent, in Adamo peccasse. Iam offendi, ἐφ' ᾧ non significare hoc loco in quo. Dixit quidem per unum hominem peccatum ita in mundum intrasse, ut omnes homines peccauerint, sed non dixit, peccasse in uno illo homine: Multò vero minus dixit tunc peccasse cum nondum essent in rerum natura. Hoc enim mihi videtur manifestam contradictionem implicare, Quis enim contradictionem implicari non videat, si quis dicat, prius esse accidens quàm subjectum, prius homines fuisse peccatores quàm homines, mortuos quàm viuentes, imò prius peccasse quàm fuisse?
units.tr: I return to the argument set out above on page 70, which the printer repeated in three lines and which the corrector, who was then hurrying, distracted by other business, deleted. It reads thus: "Those who, when they did not yet exist in nature, are said to have sinned in another, are without doubt considered to have sinned through that other's committing the sin, and to have committed it themselves, which evidently pertains to imputation. But all men, when they did not yet exist, are said to have sinned in Adam. Therefore they are considered to have committed it through his committing the sin, and to have committed it themselves, which clearly pertains to the imputation of Adam's sin." First, I deny that this evidently pertains to imputation, which I call the antecedent or immediate. For why should it not rather pertain to the propagation of inherent sin, which guilt and imputation follow? Next I deny the major premise. For do those who are said to have been in another, or to have died in another, count as having existed or died themselves when that other existed or died? We certainly die in Adam, but each by his own death; just as we rise in Christ, each by his own resurrection. So we sin in Adam, but each by his own sin. Only the first author and source of sin and death is noted, from whom they flowed down to us all. Finally I deny the minor premise. For the Apostle did not say that "all men, when they were not yet, sinned in Adam." I have already objected that ἐφ' ᾧ does not here mean "in whom." He indeed said that through one man sin entered the world so that all men sinned; but he did not say that they sinned in that one man; still less did he say that they sinned then "when they were not yet in nature." For this seems to me to involve a manifest contradiction. For who would not see the contradiction if someone said that the accident is prior to the subject, that men were sinners before they were men, dead before they were living, or indeed that they sinned before they existed?

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Argumenta D. Gar. ex Rom. v. versibus 14. 15. 16. 17. 18. 19. expenduntur.
units.tr: The arguments of D. Gar. from Romans 5:14–19 are examined.

units.la: EX versu 14. hunc nectit Syllogismum. Ea est inter typum & τὸ τυπωθὲν convenientia, ut quod in re per typum repræsentatâ exhibetur, illud in typo præcessisse oportuerit. Atqui Adamus proponitur ut typus Christi in iis quæ ad rationem justificationis pertinent; ut nempe simili modo condemnationem habeamus in Adamo, quo justificationem habemus in Christo. Itaque cum ea sit ratio justificationis nostræ per Christum, ut ejus justitiâ nobis per imputationem communicatâ justificemur, sive pro justis habeamur apud Deum; Eam etiam oportet esse condemnationis per Adamum nostræ rationem, ut illius peccato nobis per imputationem communicato condemnemur, & pro peccatoribus ac reis habeamur apud Deum. Principio quæcunque sit hujus argumenti vis, eo nonnisi consequens seu mediata imputatio concludi potest. Nam ut imputatio justitiæ sequitur fidem nostram, sic imputatio peccati sequitur corruptionem nostram. Hoc si sufficit, pax esto. Deinde nullo negotio dissolui potest hoc argumentum. Ad majorem enim quod attinet, propositio, Quod in re per typum repræsentatâ exhibetur, illud in typo præcessisse oportuit. Eget hac limitatione, si nempe ad id repræsentandum typus fuit comparatus. Nam alioqui sæpenumero multa in re repræsentatâ exhibita fuerunt, quæ non potuerunt vno typo repræsentari; quapropter multi ad eandem rem adumbrandam adhibiti sunt. Deinde etiam adhibitâ illâ limitatione propositio vera non est, nisi quantum pati potest ejus rei, quæ typus est, natura, seruatâ inter Typum & τὸ τυπωθὲν, vmbram & corpus differentiâ. Itaque melior est à typo ad rem adumbratam, quàm ab hac ad illam argumentatio. Ad minorem autem quod spectat, jam aliquoties negauimus vrgeri debere similitudinem in modo, quo ab Adamo condemnationem, & à Christo justificationem habemus. Idque cum autoritate magnorum virorum, tum aliquot exemplis comprobauimus.
units.tr: From verse 14 he constructs this syllogism: "There is such a correspondence between the type and the antitype [τὸ τυπωθὲν] that what is exhibited in the thing represented by the type must have preceded in the type. But Adam is set forth as a type of Christ in those things which pertain to the manner of justification, namely that in the same way we have condemnation in Adam as we have justification in Christ. Therefore, since the manner of our justification through Christ is that we are justified by his righteousness communicated to us through imputation, or are held as righteous before God, the manner of our condemnation through Adam must also be that we are condemned by his sin communicated to us through imputation, and are held as sinners and guilty before God." First, whatever the force of this argument, it can conclude only a consequent or mediate imputation. For just as the imputation of righteousness follows our faith, so the imputation of sin follows our corruption. If that is enough, let there be peace. Second, this argument can be easily dissolved. As for the major premise, "What is exhibited in the thing represented by the type must have preceded in the type," it needs this qualification: that the type was compared to it for the purpose of representing that thing. For otherwise many things exhibited in the thing represented often could not be represented by one type alone; that is why several types were used to shadow forth the same thing. Moreover, even with that qualification the proposition is true only so far as the nature of the type allows, the difference between shadow and body being preserved between the type and [τὸ τυπωθέν]. Therefore the argument from the type to the thing shadowed is better than the argument from the thing to the type. As for the minor premise, we have already several times denied that the likeness in the manner by which we have condemnation from Adam and justification from Christ should be pressed. We have proved this both by the authority of great men and by several examples.

units.la: Audi, si placet, Caluinum, Porrò duas hic differentias inter Christum & Adamum edmtare cpere pretium est: quas non ideo subticuit Apostolus, quia negligendas censeret, sed quia præsentis argumenti nihil referebat eas enumerare. Prior est quod peccato Adæ non per solum imputationem damnamur, ac si alieni peccati exigeretur à nobis pœna: sed ideo pœnam eius sustinemus, qui ia & culpæ sumus rei, quatenus scilicet natura nostra in ipso vitiata, iniquitatis reatu obstringitur apud Deum. At per Christi iustitiam alio modo in salutem restituimur, neque enim ideo nobis accepta fertur, quia intra nos sit: sed quod Christum ipsum cum bonis suis omnibus, Patris largitate nobis donatum possidemus. Itaque donum iustitiæ, non qualitatem qua nos Deus imbuat, ut perperam quidam interpretantur, sed gratuitam iustitiæ imputationem significat. Placet-ne etiam audire Rodolphum Gualterum? Sensus ergo est, in hoc quidem comparari inter se posse Adamum & Christum, quod uterque quod suum erat in suos propagarit , In ceteris vero Multiplex esse discrimen, neque eandem esse rationem offensa aut peccati per Adamum inuectli, & beneficij nobis in Christo exhibiti &c. & paulo post. Videtur autem duplex discrimen his verbis annotari , vt primo quidem Natura corrupta & gratia Dei opponantur , eo quod Adam quidem propter naturae corruptionem, quam ex suo lapsu contraxit, peccatum in omnes posteros propagarit, adeo vt peccatores ex ipso matris vtero nascantur : Christus vero nobis ex gratia datus sit, vt eius iustitia siue obedientia in multos, id est, in omnes redundaret. Quod ergo peccatores & propter peccatum morti obnoxij sumus, hoc ex natura ceu proprium habemus : quod vero iusti & vitae consortes facti sumus, id gratuitum Dei beneficium est, qui Filij sui iustitiam nobis imputat propter fidem , qua hunc apprehendimus. His duobus tertium adjungam Petrum Martyrem Com.in Rom.5.​f.14. ad verba qui est typus futuri. Similitudo haec accipienda est in genere quod sicut omnes ab Adamo , ita omnes a Christo iuxta ordinem suum pendeant : quodque quemadmodum alter meritus est suis omnibus, ita etiam alter. Sed particulariter & quoad species magnum est discrimen. Nam Adamus peccatum , mortem , & damnationem inuexit : Christus vero iustitiam , vitam & gratiam. Est etiam discrimen in propagatione. Adamus enim mala sua per carnis generationem in homines transfudit. Christus autem per fidem. Ideo Paulus cum dixisset , Adamum typum fuisse futuri, quasi per correctionem subiecit. At non vt peccatum , ita & donum. Quamobrem inter Adamum & Christum potius analogia quaedam & proportio, quam vera similitudo constituenda est. Vides nos Magnorum virorum doctrinam aduersus D. Gariffolij impetum defendere. Noli nos igitur quaeso, candide
units.tr: Listen, if you please, to Calvin: "It is worth while to point out here two differences between Christ and Adam. The Apostle did not pass over these because he thought them to be neglected, but because it did not matter to the present argument to list them. The first is that we are not condemned by the sin of Adam merely through imputation, as if the penalty of another's sin were exacted from us; rather we bear his penalty because we are also guilty of the fault, inasmuch as our nature, corrupted in him, is bound over to the guilt of iniquity before God." But through the righteousness of Christ we are restored to salvation in another way: it is not credited to us because it is inside us, but because we possess Christ himself with all his goods, given to us by the bounty of the Father. Therefore the gift of righteousness signifies not a quality with which God imbues us, as some wrongly interpret, but the free imputation of righteousness. Shall I also have you hear Rudolph Gwalther? "The sense, then, is that Adam and Christ can be compared with each other in this respect, that each has propagated what was his own into his own people. But in other respects there is a manifold difference, and the rationale of the offence or sin brought in through Adam is not the same as that of the benefit exhibited to us in Christ, etc." And a little later: "A twofold difference seems to be noted in these words, so that first, corrupted nature and the grace of God are set against each other: because Adam, on account of the corruption of nature which he contracted from his fall, has propagated sin to all his posterity, so that sinners are born from the womb itself; but Christ was given to us by grace, so that his righteousness or obedience might overflow to many, that is, to all. Therefore that we are sinners and liable to death on account of sin, we have from nature as our own; but that we have been made righteous and partakers of life is the free benefit of God, who imputes to us the righteousness of his Son through the faith by which we apprehend him." To these two I will add a third, Peter Martyr, in his commentary on Romans 5, on the words "who is a type of the one to come": "This likeness is to be understood in general, in that as all depend on Adam, so all depend on Christ in their own order; and as the one merited for all his people, so does the other. But in particulars and in kind the difference is great. For Adam brought in sin, death and condemnation; Christ brings righteousness, life and grace. There is also a difference in propagation: Adam transmitted his evils to men by the generation of the flesh, but Christ by faith. Therefore Paul, having said that Adam was a type of the one to come, added by way of correction..." But not as sin, so also the gift. "Wherefore between Adam and Christ there is to be established rather a certain analogy and proportion than a true likeness." You see that we defend the doctrine of great men against the attack of D. Garissolius. Do not, therefore, I beg you, kind reader, condemn us for novelty.

units.la: Q ledor, nouitatis damnare.
units.tr: Kind reader, do not condemn us for novelty.

units.la: II. Ex Vf. 15. At non vt ipsus, ita etiam donum &c, sic colligit; Qui Adami actuali peccato morti facti sunt obnoxij, illi poenam ferunt illius peccati, adeoque peccatum illud ipsis imputatur. Atqui omnes homines actuali Adami peccato facti sunt morti obnoxij. Ergo omnes homines ferunt poenam illius peccati, adeoque peccatum illud ipsis imputatur. Facilis est responsio. Qui Adami actuali peccato morti facti sunt obnoxij proximè seu immediate, illi poenam ferunt illius peccati proximè seu immediate. Qui eo peccato facti sunt morti obnoxij tantùm remote seu mediate, hoc est, mediante corruptione, illi ferunt poenas illius peccati tantùm remote seu mediate,hoc est,mediante corruptione. Atqui omnes homines actuali Adami peccato facti sunt morti obnoxij proximè seu immediate, Nego: mediante corruptione, Concedo, Ergo omnes homines ferunt poenam illius peccati, adeóque peccatum illud ipsis imputatur, immediate, nego: mediante corruptione nobis inhaerente, Concedo. Nonne omnia D. Gar. argumenta hac vna fidelia dealbari possunt? Deinde, inquit, opponuntur ab Apostolo τὸ παράπτωμα Adami & τὸ χάρισμα Christi. At per χάρισμα intelligitur iustitia illa Christi, quae gratiosa imputatione fit nostra, & quae sanctificationem, sive iustitiam inhaerentem ex se necessario fundit. Ergo & παράπτωμα intelligitur peccatum illud Adami, quod imputatione nostrum fit, & quod corruptio nostra naturalis necessario & infallibiliter sequitur. Omnino opponuntur ab Apostolo τὸ παράπτωμα Adami & τὸ χάρισμα Christi. Quid inde sequitur? Nonne jam aliquoties argumento ducto ab hac oppositione occurrimus? Caeterum aut anomalus est hic fyl-
units.tr: II. From verse 15, "But not as the trespass, so also the gift," he concludes thus: "Those who have been made liable to death by Adam's actual sin bear the penalty of that sin, and therefore that sin is imputed to them. But all men have been made liable to death by Adam's actual sin. Therefore all men bear the penalty of that sin, and therefore that sin is imputed to them." The answer is easy. Those who have been made liable to death by Adam's actual sin proximately or immediately bear the penalty of that sin proximately or immediately. Those who have been made liable to death by that sin only remotely or mediately, that is, through corruption, bear the penalties of that sin only remotely or mediately, that is, through corruption. But all men have been made liable to death by Adam's actual sin proximately or immediately: I deny it. Through corruption: I grant it. Therefore all men bear the penalty of that sin, and therefore that sin is imputed to them immediately: I deny it. Through corruption inhering in us: I grant it. Could not all the arguments of D. Gar. be whitewashed by this one thing? Next, he says: "The trespass [παράπτωμα] of Adam and the gift [χάρισμα] of Christ are set against each other by the Apostle.
