But by the χάρισμα is understood that righteousness of Christ which becomes ours by gracious imputation, and which of itself necessarily pours forth sanctification, or inherent righteousness. Therefore by the παράπτωμα is also understood that sin of Adam, which becomes ours by imputation, and which our natural corruption necessarily and infallibly follows." Certainly the trespass of Adam and the gift of Christ are set against each other by the Apostle. What follows from this? Have we not already several times met an argument drawn from this opposition? Moreover, either this syllogism is anomalous and has no force of concluding anything, or a proposition has been omitted which, if conceived universally, as it ought to be, would undoubtedly be false.

units.la: Supr p. 56. & 63 logismus, nec vim vllam concludendi habet, aut omissa est propositio, quæ si vniuersaliter, vt debet, concipiatur, erit falsa procul dubio. Admonet autem nos oppositio inter <bl>ἀρχαῖος</bl>? Adami & χάρισμα Christi, longè aliter hoc nostrum esse quàm illud. Non enim, vt hoc nostrum est dono Christi, sic illud est nostrum dono Adami. Alterum ergo alteri opponit Apostolus in modo quo fit nostrum. Quomodo igitur ex hac oppositione concludere potest D. G. vtrumque eodem modo nostrum fieri? Dicet-ne imputationem, qua aliquid nostrum fit, alioqui non nostrum, esse donationem quandam. Est igitur Adami peccatum donum quoddam, non Adami, hic enim non imputat, sed, horresco pronuncians, ipsius Dei.
units.tr: Moreover, the opposition between the trespass of Adam [παράπτωμα] and the gift of Christ [χάρισμα] reminds us that the one is ours in a very different way from the other. For just as this is ours by the gift of Christ, so that is not ours by the gift of Adam. Therefore the Apostle sets the one against the other in the manner in which each becomes ours. How, then, can D. G. conclude from this opposition that both become ours in the same way? Will he say that the imputation by which something becomes ours, otherwise not ours, is a kind of donation? Then Adam's sin is a certain gift, but not Adam's; for here Adam does not impute, but, I shudder to say it, it is God's own. (Supra p. 56 & 63.)

units.la: Hic D. G. insignem Caluini locum jam à nobis laudatum pag. 20. contra se citat. Quod vnius delicto periisse nos tradit, sic accipe, quia ex ipso in nos corruptio transfusa fit. Neque enim sic perimus eius culpâ, quasi extra culpam ipsisimus; Sed quia eius peccatum peccati nostri causa est, exitium nostrum illi Paulus adscribit. Non potuit apertius significare, peccatum Adami causam esse exitij nostri non proximam sed remotam, non immediatam, sed mediatam. Causa enim causæ est causa etiam effectus, sed remota duntaxat. Conatur tamen tam claro loco tenebras offundere D. G. Quibus verbis, inquit, non negatur nos Adami ipsius actuali peccato perire, nec hoc etiam negat, aut negauit vnquam Placeus: Sed significatur, non esse illud Adami peccatum a nostra corruptione separandum, quippe cum ex utroque consurgat idem reatus.
units.tr: Here D. G. cites against himself the notable passage of Calvin that we have already praised on p. 20: "That he tells us we perished through the one offence of one man, understand it this way: because corruption has been poured from him into us. For we do not perish through his fault as though we ourselves were outside the fault; rather, because his sin is the cause of our sin, Paul ascribes our ruin to him." He could not have indicated more plainly that Adam's sin is the cause of our ruin not proximately but remotely, not immediately but mediately. For a cause of a cause is also a cause of the effect, but only a remote one. Yet D. G. tries to cast darkness over so clear a passage. "By these words," he says, "it is not denied that we perish through Adam's actual sin." Nor does Placaeus deny this, or ever has denied it. "But it is signified that Adam's sin is not to be separated from our corruption, since the same guilt arises from both together."

units.la: An id verbis illis significetur, eaque ratio afferatur, iudicium esto penes Lectorem. Illud mihi satis est,
units.tr: Whether these words signify this, and whether this reason is what is being offered, let the reader judge. For my part, it is enough that

units.la: ideo exitium nostrum Adami peccato adscribi, quia est causa peccati nostri, non dicit, quia nobis imputatur, aut quia imputatione nostrum est: sed illud distinguit à peccato nostro tanquam causam ab effectu. Est igitur à peccato Adami peccatum nostrum, & ab hoc exitium nostrum. Ita ex vtroque consurgit idem reatus, ex peccato nostro proximè, ex peccato Adami remotè. Exponit mentem suam alibi Caluinus, Peccatum originale; inquit, est natura nostra prauitas ac corruptio, quæ primùm reos facit nos ira Dei, tum etiam opera in nobis profert quæ Scriptura vocat opera carnis. Sequitur ergo reatus corruptionem vt effectus causam, & quidem causam, vt loquuntur, adæquatam: subjungit enim continuò. Hæc itaque duo distinctè obseruanda: nempe quod sic omnibus natura nostræ partibus vitiati peruersíque, jam ob talem duntaxat corruptionem damnati merito conuiciíque coram Deo tenemur. Quæ eadem verba, adeò tanto viro placebant, bis extant in ejus institutione, semel. lib. 2. cap. 1. §. 8. & iterum lib. 4. cap. 15. §. 10. Addit quoque in priore loco vberioris explicationis gratia hæc verba. Neque ista est alieni delicti obligatio: quod enim dicitur, nos per Adæ peccatum obnoxios esse factos Dei judicio: non ita est accipiendum, ac si insontes ipsi & immerentes culpam delicti ejus sustineremus: sed quia per eius transgressionem maledictione induti sumus omnes, dicitur ille nos obstrinxisse. Ab illo tamen non sola in nos pœna grassata est, sed instillata ab ipso lues in nobis residet cui iure pœna debetur. Quare Augustinus vtcunque alienum peccatum sæpe vocet (quo clarius ostendat propagine in nos deriuari) simul tamen & proprium vnicuique asserit. Et Apostolus ipse disertissimè testatur, ideo mortem in omnes peruagatam, quod omnes peccarint, id est, inuoluti sint originali peccato, & eius maculis inquinati. Atque adeo infantes quoque ipsi, dum suam secum damnationem a matrix vtero afferunt, non alieno, sed suo ipsorum vitio sunt obstricti. Reatus igitur & damnatio & mors, sequuntur corruptionem haereditariam vt effectus causam, & ob eam duntaxat non autem ob peccatum actuale Adami (nisi remote & mediate) morti sumus addicti.
units.tr: the ruin of us all is ascribed to Adam's sin because it is the cause of our sin; the passage does not say that it is because it is imputed to us, or because we are his by imputation. Rather, it distinguishes his sin from our sin as cause from effect. Our sin therefore is distinct from Adam's sin, and our ruin from our sin. So the same guilt arises from both together: from our sin proximately, from Adam's sin remotely. Calvin explains his own mind elsewhere: "Original sin is the depravity and corruption of our nature, which first makes us guilty before the wrath of God, and then also produces in us those works which Scripture calls the works of the flesh." Guilt therefore follows corruption as effect follows cause, and indeed, as they say, an adequate cause. For he goes on at once: "These two things are to be observed distinctly: namely, that since all parts of our nature are thus vitiated and perverted, we are held by right to be condemned and convicted before God on account of such corruption alone." These same words so pleased so great a man that they occur twice in his Institutes: once in book 2, chapter 1, §8, and again in book 4, chapter 15, §10. In the earlier place, for the sake of a fuller explanation, he also adds these words: "Nor is this an obligation for another's offence. For when it is said that we were made liable to the judgment of God through Adam's sin, this is not to be understood as though we, innocent and undeserving, bore the guilt of his offence; rather, because through his transgression we were all clothed with the curse, he is said to have bound us. Yet the punishment did not rage only against us from him; the plague instilled by him remains in us, to which punishment is rightly owed. Therefore, although Augustine often calls it another's sin (so that he may show more clearly that it is derived into us by propagation), he at the same time asserts that it is each one's own. And the Apostle himself testifies most plainly that death has passed over to all for this reason, that all have sinned, that is, have been involved in original sin and polluted by its stains. And so even infants, while they bring their own damnation with them from the mother's womb, are bound not by another's fault but by their own vice." Guilt, therefore, and condemnation and death follow hereditary corruption as effect follows cause, and we are doomed to death on account of that alone, and not on account of Adam's actual sin (except remotely and mediately).

units.la: III. Ex verf. 16. sic ratiocinatur.
units.tr: III. He reasons thus from verse 16.

units.la: Hic κρίμα, iudicium sive reatus ex Adamo, opponitur χάρισμα Christi. Ergo vt χάρισμα non significat qualitatem aliquam nobis inhaerentem, sed quod in Christo est, & in Christo nobis gratis imputatur; Ita κρίμα aliquid significare debet, quod sit extra nos, nempe culpam ab Adamo patratam, vnde reatum & condemnationem trahimus. Colli'ge. Cuius culpa est in omnium condemnationem, eam omnibus imputari oportet. Atqui culpa Adami est in omnium condemnationem. Ergo eam omnibus imputari oportet. Nihil roboris in hoc argumento video, quod non extet in superioribus jam abunde refutatis. Quae enim & quam imbecilla est haec collectio; Hic κρίμα iudicium sive reatus ex Adamo, opponitur χάρισμα Christi. Ergo vt hoc non significat qualitatem nobis inhaerentem, sic nec illud? Quid enim prohibet, vitium inhaerens quatenus nos facit reos & poena dignos ei justitiae opponi, quae nos ab eo reatu & poena liberat, vti vidimus censuisse maximos viros? Id non modo nihil prohibet, sed ipsa illa oppositio exigit. Est enim κρίμα ex justitia, χάρισμα ex gratia. Iustitia nonnisi suum cuique tribuit; gratia donat id quod alioqui nostrum non erat, sed alienum. Hoc accepi a Chamiero, Si nihil, inquit, habent infantes peccati proprij, cur propria morte pereunt? Nam propter alienam culpam, quæ tantum aliena fit, non fert iustitia diuina. Habuerint sane aliquando homines eum morem, vt patris seruitus, filijs effet hereditaria: at eiusmodi nihil erat in populo Dei, ex diuinis legibus: quanto minus in Deo: qui irascitur in eos, quibus erat in ore proverbium, Patres nostri vuas acerbas comederunt : Filiis autem dentes stupent; Quod si excipiat quis, seruari fideles propter iustitiam non suam, sed Christi: itaque posse etiam damnari, propter alienam iniustitiam, is vero non videt comparari valde diuersa. Nam damnatio est a iustitia, salus autem a gratia. Nam si esset etiam ipsa a iustitia, non posset nos aliena iusti tia seruare: quare ne aliena quidem culpa damnare. Nihil, opinor, desiderari potuit difertius.
units.tr: "Here judgment [κρίμα], that is, judgment or guilt from Adam, is set against the gift [χάρισμα] of Christ. Therefore, just as the gift [χάρισμα] does not signify some quality inhering in us, but what is in Christ and is freely imputed to us in Christ, so the judgment [κρίμα] must signify something outside us, namely the fault committed by Adam, from which we derive guilt and condemnation. Infer: the one whose fault brings condemnation upon all, that fault must be imputed to all. But Adam's fault brings condemnation upon all. Therefore that fault must be imputed to all." I see no strength in this argument that does not already appear in the earlier points, which have been sufficiently refuted. For how weak is this inference: here judgment [κρίμα], that is, judgment or guilt from Adam, is set against the gift [χάρισμα] of Christ; therefore, just as this does not signify a quality inhering in us, neither does that? For what prevents an inhering vice, insofar as it makes us guilty and worthy of punishment, from being set against that righteousness which frees us from that guilt and punishment, as the greatest men have judged? Not only does nothing prevent this, but the very opposition demands it. For judgment [κρίμα] comes from justice, the gift [χάρισμα] from grace. Justice gives each his own; grace gives what otherwise was not ours but another's. I have taken this from Chamier: "If infants have nothing of their own sin, why do they perish by their own death? For divine justice does not bear with punishment on account of another's fault, which is only another's. Men may indeed have sometimes had the custom that a father's servitude was hereditary for his sons; but nothing of this kind existed among God's people by divine laws, and still less in God, who is angry with those who have the proverb in their mouths: 'The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge.' But if anyone objects that the faithful are saved by a righteousness not their own, but Christ's, and so they could also be condemned on account of another's unrighteousness, he does not see that very different things are being compared. For condemnation comes from justice, but salvation from grace. For if condemnation too came from justice, another's righteousness could not save us; and so neither could another's fault condemn us." Nothing, I think, could have been stated more clearly.

units.la: IV. Veniamus igitur ad verf. 17. Ex eo simile, inquit D. G. argumentum emergit.
units.tr: IV. Let us come, then, to verse 17. From this, says the Reverend G., an argument arises by analogy.

units.la: Cuius delicto & lapsu mors semper regnauit & regnatura est in finem seculi, eius delicti poena peruadit in omnes. Mors enim certe ab Apostolo ponitur, tanquam causa illius effectum. At vno Adami delicto mors hactenus in omnes regnauit, & porro regnatura est vsque ad finem seculi. Igitur delicti & lapsus illius Adæ poena in omnes peruagatur. Concedo totum arg. Quis enim nostrum vnquam negauit, lapsus Adæ poenam in omnes esse peruagatam? Tantum contendimus, inter eam & lapsum Adæ interuenisse vitium originale cui proximè poena debetur. Est igitur lapsus Adæ prima causa regni mortis, sed proxima est ab illo productum peccatum omnibus inhærens, quod quia regnat, etiam mors regnat. Certe peccatum quod in hominibus non modò est, sed viuit, non modò viuit sed regnat, cui seruiunt, cui obediunt, cujus lex est in membris, id non est peccatum actuale Adami, sed hujus effectum, corruptio inhærens.
units.tr: By the offence and fall of one man, death has always reigned and will reign until the end of the world; the punishment of that offence spreads to all. For death is certainly set down by the Apostle as the effect of that cause. But by the one offence of Adam, death has hitherto reigned over all, and will reign on until the end of the age. Therefore the punishment of Adam's offence and fall passes over to all. I grant the whole argument. For which of us has ever denied that the punishment of Adam's fall has passed over to all? We only contend that between that fall and the punishment there has intervened the original sin, to which the punishment is most immediately owed. So Adam's fall is the first cause of the reign of death, but the proximate cause is the sin produced from it and clinging to all men, and because this sin reigns, death also reigns. Certainly the sin which is not merely in men but lives, which not merely lives but reigns, which they serve and obey, whose law is in their members: that is not Adam's actual sin, but its effect, the inherent corruption.

units.la: V. Ex verf. 18. similli ratione ac supra colligit. Per cuius delictum condemnatio in omnes homines venit, propter illius delictum pœna irrogatur omnibus: ⌣Atqui per unius Adæ delictum condemnatio venit in omnes. Ergo propter unius Adæ delictum, pœna irrogatur omnibus ejus posteris. Primum negari potest major propositio. aliud enim est per aliquem esse aliquid, aliud propter aliquem; per calamum scribo, non tamen propter calamum; per judicem est condemnatio, non tamen propter judicem. Deinde distinguo propter ut supra. Nam vel causam remotam designat, vel proximam. Si illam, conceditur totum argumentum; si hanc, negatur propositio. Est enim, ut multoties inculcaui, primum Adami peccatum actuale causa nostri peccati inhærentis, & hoc causa mortis: quod autem est causa causæ, id causa est etiam effectus. Aut cum Pelagio, Pighio, & Socino negandum est peccatum inhærens ejusque reatus, aut impossibile est ex verbis Apostoli imputationem peccati Adæ actualis antecedentem seu immediatam efficere.
units.tr: V. From verse 18 he draws a conclusion by the same reasoning as above: Through whose offence condemnation came upon all men; on account of his offence punishment is inflicted on all. But through the offence of the one Adam, condemnation came upon all. Therefore, on account of the offence of the one Adam, punishment is inflicted on all his posterity. First, the major premise can be denied. For it is one thing for something to be through someone, another for it to be on account of someone: I write through a pen, but not on account of the pen; condemnation is through a judge, but not on account of the judge. Next, I distinguish the word on account of, as above. For it designates either a remote cause or a proximate cause. If the former, the whole argument is granted; if the latter, the proposition is denied. For, as I have very often insisted, Adam's first actual sin is the cause of our inherent sin, and this is the cause of death; but what is the cause of a cause is also the cause of the effect. Either we must deny with Pelagius, Pighius, and Socinus both inherent sin and its guilt, or it is impossible to establish from the words of the Apostle an immediate or antecedent imputation of Adam's actual sin.

units.la: VI. Sed fortasse illa tandem aliquando emerget ex verf. 19. Sicut per unius inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita per unius obedientiam justi constituentur multi: Nullo certe modo. Argumentatur ex eo D. G. non uno modo, & primo quidem sic. Idem Apostolus agit hoc versu quod reliquis illis diffusius prosecutus fuerat. ⌣Atqui hoc versu man siste agit de imputatione. Ergo & de eadem imputatione superiora intelligenda sunt. Respondeo ad minorem, Apostolum hoc versu non agere de imputatione : aut fi agit de imputatione, non agere de imputatione immediata seu antecedente, quam solam nego. Nam fi idem agit hoc versu quod in superioribus, in quibus de ista imputatione eum non egisse patuit, consequens est, eum de ista imputatione non agere in isto versu.
units.tr: VI. But perhaps that imputation will at length emerge from verse 19: As by the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one many will be made righteous. By no means! The Reverend G. argues from this in more than one way, and first in this manner: The same Apostle in this verse deals with what he had treated more fully in those preceding. But in this verse he plainly deals with imputation. Therefore the preceding verses must be understood to deal with the same imputation. I answer to the minor premise: the Apostle in this verse does not deal with imputation; or, if he does deal with imputation, he does not deal with immediate or antecedent imputation, which alone I deny. For if he in this verse deals with the same thing as in the preceding verses, in which it has been shown that he did not deal with that imputation, it follows that he does not deal with that imputation in this verse.

units.la: Deinde, inquit, vix difertius & efficacius poterat ⌣Apoftolus imputationem Adamici peccati significare, quam factum est his verbis, claram oppofitionem continent bus inter Adami inobedientiam,& obedientiam Christi.Qui factum est igitur, vt maximi viri versum illum exponentes, imputationem illam in Apostoli verbis non animadverterint, sed rejecerint potius? verum pergat, Obedientiam Christi actualem significat, qua Christus factus est obediens Patri vsque ad mortem crucis, Phil. 2. 8. Ergo & obedientiam ⌣Adami actualem, qua Dei mandatum violauit : vt mirum fit qua ratione neget Vir doctus hic πεφαλης voce ab ⌣Apostolo designari peccatum ⌣Adami actuale. Nam quod addit, non designari peccatum actuale praecisum a corruptione, quam in ⌣Adamo peperit, hoc parum moramur. Quid, affirmare voce πεφαλης solum peccatum ⌣Adami significari, non quidem actuale praecisum ab habituali, sed simul cum habituali, quae sunt Placei verba, estne negare, ea voce designari peccatum Adami actuale? Cur vero id non moratur? Etenim, inquit, fiue praecisum ab illa corruptione, fiue coniunctum cum ea, semper tamen designari intelligitur, quod ad causam noftram fatis est. Immo vero fi causam defendis imputationis immediatae, id non fatis est. oportet enim sic imputari peccatum actuale praecisum a corruptione, siquidem haec est illius imputati poena proprie dicta. non potest enim idem peccatum esse poena fui ipsius,
units.tr: Next, he says, the Apostle could hardly have signified the imputation of Adam's sin more clearly and effectively than he has done by these words, which contain a plain opposition between the disobedience of Adam and the obedience of Christ. How is it, then, that such great men, expounding that verse, did not notice that imputation in the Apostle's words, but rather rejected it? But let him go on: The obedience of Christ means His actual obedience, by which Christ became obedient to the Father unto the death of the cross (Phil. 2:8). Therefore Adam's actual obedience also is meant, by which he violated God's command. So it is a wonder by what reasoning this learned man denies that the word head [κεφαλῆς] designates Adam's actual sin by the Apostle. As for what he adds, that the actual sin is not designated as separated from the corruption which it begat in Adam, we give this little attention. What? Does to affirm that by the word head [κεφαλῆς] only the sin of Adam is signified, not indeed the actual sin separated from the habitual, but together with the habitual (these are Place's own words), amount to denying that Adam's actual sin is designated by that word? Why then does he not dwell on this? For, he says, whether it is taken as separated from that corruption or as joined with it, it is always understood to be designated, which is enough for our cause. Indeed, if you defend immediate imputation, it is not enough. For it is necessary that the actual sin be imputed as separated from the corruption, since this is the punishment of that imputed sin, properly so called. For the same sin cannot be the punishment of itself,

units.la: C̄ap.IX M.P. præsertim pœna proprie dicta.
units.tr: Chap. IX. [Running head.] Especially punishment properly so called.

units.la: Hinc duplex argumentum se posse putat colligere: primum ex vi oppositionis. Eadem ratione constituimur peccatores in Adamo, quâ iusti constituimur in Christo. Atqui in Christo iusti constituimur per iustitiæ ipsius imputationem. Ergo & peccatores in Adamo perpecati ipsius imputationem. Etsi nobis conclusio non nocet imputationem mediatam agnoscentibus, tamen major propositio falsa est. In eo enim ipso, de quo agitur, discrimen observatum est à viris maximis, vti patuit ex superioribus nostris responsionibus. Constituti enim sumus peccatores propagato in nos peccato inhærente quod meretur mortem, non sumus constituti iusti iustitiâ inhærente quæ mereatur vitam.
units.tr: From this he thinks he can draw a double argument, first from the force of the opposition: We are constituted sinners in Adam by the same reasoning by which we are constituted righteous in Christ. But in Christ we are constituted righteous through the imputation of His righteousness. Therefore we are also constituted sinners in Adam through the imputation of his sin. Although the conclusion does not harm us, since we acknowledge a mediate imputation, the major premise is nevertheless false. For this very distinction, which is at issue, has been observed by very great men, as appeared from our earlier replies. For we are constituted sinners by inherent sin propagated into us, which merits death; we are not constituted righteous by an inherent righteousness which merits life.

units.la: Deinde, inquit, ex verbis per inobedientiam Adæ peccatores constituimur. Nam per actualem alterius inobedientiam constituti non possumus peccatores, nisi imputatione, quia quod alterius est personaliter, nostrum fieri nequit, neque nos inde denominari, nisi imputationis interventu. Atqui per actualem Adami inobedientiam constituimur peccatores. Ergo imputatione. Quid est negare propagationem peccati inhærentis, si hoc non est? Audiamus ergo potius ejus Antecessorem Chamierum, Illud etiam non omittendum: per unius inobedientiam multos esse constitutos peccatores ἁμαρτωλούς: quod vocabulum in Scripturis sumitur pro iis in quibus est re vera peccatum contrarium legi Dei. Et paulo post. Vno verbo. Nunquam ἁμαρτωλὸς dicitur de simplici reatu, & absque ullo vitio aut peccato. Ergo, cum dixit Paulus multos esse constitutos peccatores per unius inobedientiam: NIHIL ALII D intellexit, nisi eo Adami peccato effectum esse, ut
units.tr: Next, he says, from the words "through Adam's disobedience we are constituted sinners": For we cannot be constituted sinners by another's actual disobedience except through imputation, because what is personally another's cannot become ours, nor can we be denominated from it, except by the intervention of imputation. But we are constituted sinners by Adam's actual disobedience. Therefore by imputation. What is this but denying the propagation of inherent sin, if it is not that? Let us rather hear his predecessor Chamier: This also must not be omitted: that through one man's disobedience many were constituted sinners [ἁμαρτωλούς], a word which in the Scriptures is used of those in whom there is really sin contrary to the law of God. And shortly after: In one word: [ἁμαρτωλὸς] is never said of mere guilt, apart from any vice or sin. Therefore, when Paul said that many were constituted sinners through the disobedience of one, he understood nothing else than that by that sin of Adam it was brought about that

units.la: Lib I. de hom corrup. cap 5. § VII. omnes homines re vera, & in se se peccatores essent. Et alio loco, A Paulo autem docceri vnicum esse numero in omnibus peccatum originale, hoc vero insigniter falsum. Nam contra. Per vnius inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi. Eodem capite. Peccator autem est, qui ipse habet peccatum suum: non autem cui alienum imputatur. Et rursus. In Adamo peccauimus omnes: quia Adamus primus peccauit: & inde initium factum peccati in omnibus hominibus: at in nobis etiam peccamus: quia eius peccato constituti sumus peccatores: id est, ab eo in nos peccatum propagatum. Et illius inobedientia eodem modo sumus omnes constituti peccatores: quo nostra etiam propria iam vere sumus peccatores: alioqui falsum efficit, nos illius inobedientia constitutos esse peccatores. Alio loco ait nos per inobedientiam Adami constitutos esse peccatores, non formaliter, sed causaliter, quia est causa efficiens qualitatis illius per quam sumus formaliter peccatores: Sicut, inquit, podagrici causa est parens podagricus, sive podagra in parente: qua tamen non est podagra filij. Audiamus etiam Petrum Martyrem contra argumentantem. Hic, inquit, annotabimus, cum Apostolus dicit, Per vnius inobedientiam peccatores multos esse constitutos, ex his verbis argumentum habeti aduersus eos, qui putant peccatum originis non esse cuique proprium: sed vnum tantum extitisse, illudque fuisse in Adamo, quo nos nexi & obligati sumus ad mortem & damnationem. Quum enim dicantur peccatores constituti, oportet, ut ipsi aut peccatum habeant, aut saltem habuerint. Nam alieno vitio nemo dicitur peccator.
units.tr: Book I, On the Corruption of Man, chap. 5, § VII. all men really and in themselves were sinners. And in another place: It is taught by the Apostle that original sin is one in number in all men; but this is notoriously false. For against it: "Through the disobedience of one many were made sinners." In the same chapter: But he is a sinner who himself has his own sin, not one to whom another's sin is imputed. And again: In Adam we all sinned, because Adam first sinned, and thence a beginning of sin was made in all men; but in us also we sin, because we are constituted sinners by his sin, that is, sin propagated from him into us. And we are all constituted sinners by his disobedience in the same way as we are now truly sinners by our own; otherwise it would make it false that we are constituted sinners by his disobedience. In another place he says that we are constituted sinners through Adam's disobedience not formally but causally, because he is the efficient cause of that quality through which we are formally sinners: Just as, he says, the cause of gout is the gouty parent, or the gout in the parent, which nevertheless is not the gout of the child. Let us also hear Peter Martyr arguing against this: Here we shall note, with the Apostle, that when he says "through the disobedience of one, many were constituted sinners," we have from these words an argument against those who think that original sin is not proper to each person, but that only one existed, and that it was in Adam, by which we were bound and obligated to death and condemnation. For since they are said to be constituted sinners, it is necessary that they either have sin themselves, or at least have had it. For no one is called a sinner through another's fault.

units.la: CAPVT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Declaratio doctrinæ de Imputatione primi peccati, Ex Hebr. cap. 7. verf. 9. 10. de decimatione Leui in lumbis Abrahæ, vocatur ad examen.
units.tr: A declaration of the doctrine of the Imputation of the First Sin, from Heb. 7:9-10, on the tithing of Levi in the loins of Abraham, is brought to examination.

units.la: I. DOctrinam de imputatione primi peccati antecedente seu immediata nullis Scripturæ fundamentis innixam esse jam, opinor, patet. Num ea saltem illustrari possit, nam prbari certè non potest, ex Hebr. vii. 9. 10. vbi dicitur Leui decimatus in lumbis Abrahæ, paucis videamus. Ait D. G. Originalis peccati in nos ex Adamo transeuntis naturam & rationem ex hoc loco declarare Theologis solemne esse. Bene dixit originalis peccati: Nominat enim quosdam qui imputationem immediatam non modò non docent, sed apertè damnant. Possem ex Augustino, Bucero, Martyre, Gualtero, Gerhardo, &c. multa loca proferre: sed ne in re clara æquo longior videar, vnius Anselmi his verbis ero contentus. Non portant (infantes qui non seruantur) peccatum Adæ sed suum. Nam aliud fuit peccatum Adæ, aliud infantum, quia differunt vt dictum est. Illud enim fuit causa, istud est effectus. Et paulò post. Cùm dicit Apostolus, quod supra posui, quia mors regnauit ab Adam vsque ad Mosem, etiam in eos qui non peccauerunt in similitudinem prævaricationis Adæ, sicut significat infantum minus esse quàm Adæ peccatum, ita aperte monstrat aliud esse. Quapropter cùm damnatur infans pro peccato
units.tr: I. That the doctrine of the imputation of the first sin, antecedent or immediate, rests on no foundation of Scripture is now, I think, plain. Whether at least it can be illustrated, since it certainly cannot be proved, from Heb. 7:9-10, where it is said that Levi was tithed in the loins of Abraham, let us briefly consider. D. G. says: it is customary for theologians to explain from this passage the nature and reason of original sin passing over to us from Adam. He spoke well of original sin, for he names certain men who not only do not teach immediate imputation but openly condemn it. I could cite many passages from Augustine, Bucer, Martyr, Gualther, Gerhard, and others; but lest I seem overly long on a clear matter, I will be content with the words of Anselm alone. Infants who are not saved do not bear the sin of Adam but their own. For the sin of Adam was one thing, that of infants another, because they differ, as has been said. The former was the cause, the latter is the effect. And a little later: When the Apostle says, as I quoted above, that death reigned from Adam to Moses even over those who had not sinned, in the likeness of the transgression of Adam, it signifies that the sin of infants is less than Adam's, and so it plainly shows that it is other. Therefore when an infant is condemned for original sin

units.la: Lib. de concep. Virg. & peccato originali, damnatur non pro peccato Adæ, sed pro suo. Nam si ipse non habuisset suum peccatum, non damnaretur. Ita ergo non portat iniquitatem Adæ sed suam, quamvis ideo dicatur portare, quia iniquitas illius peccati ipsius causa fuit.
units.tr: ...it is condemned not for the sin of Adam but for its own. For if it had not had its own sin, it would not be condemned. So it does not bear the iniquity of Adam but its own, although it is said to bear it because the iniquity of that sin was the cause of it. (From the book On the Conception of the Virgin and Original Sin.)

units.la: I I. Sed quid ex decimatione Leui colligit D. Garissolius ? Sicut, inquit, Abrahamus originarium fuit principium Gentis Leuiticæ, quæ secundum rationem seminalem ab eo propagata est, ita & Adam principium est materiale totius generis humani, quod ad generationem naturalem attinet. Itaque si recte dictum est ab Apostolo Leuiticos sacerdotes decimatos fuisse in Abrahamo, quia in ejus lumbis erant, quando scilicet Abrahamus Dei sacerdoti Melchisedeco decimas persoluit; nihil mirum videri debet, aut inusitatum, quod dicuntur omnes homines peccasse in Adamo, & in eo perditi ac damnati fuisse, quatenus omnes in ejus peccantis lumbis fuerunt. Quid vetat me hoc totum concedere, negantem imputationem primi Adæ peccati actualis immediatam ? Fayus certè verba ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον vertit in quo omnes peccaverunt, ut hoc, inquit, intelligatur de Adamo, cujus peccatum fuit commune omnium; sicut communis est omnium pœna siue mors.
units.tr: II. But what does D. Garissolius gather from the tithing of Levi? Just as Abraham, he says, was the originating principle of the Levitical race, which was propagated from him according to a seminal reason, so also Adam is the material principle of the whole human race, as far as natural generation is concerned. Therefore if it was rightly said by the Apostle that the Levitical priests were tithed in Abraham, because they were in his loins, when Abraham paid tithes to Melchizedek, the priest of God, nothing should seem strange or unusual that all men are said to have sinned in Adam and to have been lost and condemned in him, inasmuch as all were in the loins of him who sinned. What prevents me from granting all this while denying the immediate imputation of Adam's actual sin? Fayus at any rate translates ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον [in whom all sinned], so that, he says, it is understood of Adam, whose sin was common to all, just as punishment or death is common to all.

units.la: Hæc autem non imputatione communis est omnium, sed propagatione tantum. Idem ergo de peccato dicendum est. itaque illud omnes peccaverunt, exponit de peccato, quod non committitur actu, sed habitu quodam in nobis adhæret. Et iterum alio loco. Peccaverunt autem in Adamo: sed non in similitudinem prævaricatoris Adami: quia non propter cupiditates suas peccarunt, quas in se nullas habebant, cum essent pueruli vel infantuli: ergo propter peccatum aliud à peccato Adæ. qua de re in Arausicano concilio sic legitur, Iniustitiam Deo dat qui mortem, quæ est peccati pœna, sive peccato, quod est meritum mortis, ad nos transiisse dicit. Dicantur ergo omnes homines peccasse in Adamo, modò id accipiatur de peccato habituali seu corruptione, quid hoc juuat imputationem antecedentem? Aut quid opus est ad talem illustrationem peccati originalis nobis nullo modo nocentem, nos respondere?
units.tr: But this is common to all not by imputation but by propagation only. So the same must be said of sin. Thus he explains all sinned as of sin, which is not committed actually but cleaves to us by a certain habit. And again in another place: They sinned in Adam, but not in the likeness of the transgression of Adam, because they did not sin on account of their own lusts, which they did not have, being little children or infants. Therefore they sinned on account of a sin other than Adam's sin. Hence in the Council of Orange it is read thus: he attributes injustice to God who says that death, which is the punishment of sin, or sin, which is the merit of death, passed over to us. Let all men therefore be said to have sinned in Adam, provided that this is understood of habitual sin or corruption; what does this help the antecedent imputation? Or why is it necessary, in such an illustration of original sin which in no way harms us, for us to reply?

units.la: Pertendit tamen Placeus in Thesibus de statu hominis lapsi ante Gratiam, non magis inde colligi Adami peccatum nobis imputari, quàm colligi potest, aut peccata Abrahami, aut ejus fidem & bona opera eidem Leui imputata fuisse, quæ tamen ei imputata fuisse nemo dixerit. Hoc confitetur D. Garissolius: Sed negat eo fine hoc Apostolicum Testimonium à tot & tantis Theologis in hoc negotio vsurpari. Non enim, inquit, inde directè quisquam colligit Adami peccatum nobis imputari. Habet igitur Placeus quod voluit, imputationem immediatam (de qua sola eum agere patet ex Th. vii.) non posse probari ex hoc loco. Ille enim sic argumentabatur. Quæ doctrina ad religionem spectans non potest probari ex sacris literis, ea est reijcienda. Doctrina de imputatione immediata inobedientiæ actualis Adami non potest probari ex sacris literis. Ergo est reijcienda.
units.tr: Nevertheless Placaeus, in his Theses on the state of fallen man before grace, contends that no more can be gathered from this passage that Adam's sin is imputed to us than can be gathered that either Abraham's sins, or his faith and good works, were imputed to that Levi, which yet no one would say were imputed to him. D. Garissolius concedes this, but he denies that this Apostolic testimony is used for that purpose by so many great theologians in this matter. For, he says, no one directly draws from it that Adam's sin is imputed to us. Placaeus therefore has what he wanted: that immediate imputation (which alone he clearly treats, from Thesis 7) cannot be proved from this passage. For he argued thus: Doctrine which pertains to religion and cannot be proved from the Holy Scriptures is to be rejected. The doctrine of the immediate imputation of Adam's actual disobedience cannot be proved from the Holy Scriptures. Therefore it is to be rejected.

units.la: Major non potest à Reformato vocari in dubium. Minor ab eo sic probabatur. Si quæ sunt sacræ literæ, ex quibus illa imputatio probari possit, illæ petuntur præcipuè ex cap. v. Epist. ad Rom. Vf.12. & seqq. & Hebr. vii. Vf. 9. 10. Sed ex illis locis non potest illa imputatio probari. Ergo non potest probari ex sacris literis.
units.tr: The major premise cannot be called in doubt by a Reformed man. The minor was proved by him thus: If there are any Holy Scriptures from which that imputation can be proved, they are sought chiefly in Rom. 5:12ff. and Heb. 7:9-10. But that imputation cannot be proved from those passages. Therefore it cannot be proved from the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: Sed fortasse ex hoc loco colligere potest aliquis indirectè, peccatum Adami actuale nobis imputari immediatè. Nam, inquit D. G. Si quod fecit Abrahamus decimas dando, fecisse censentur tot postea seculis nati Leuita, nec tamen est in eiusmodi imputatione aliquid à ratione, aut Dei iustitia alienum, nemo causam dicet, quare qui afferunt Adæ peccatum censeri posterorum peccatum, ita vt in eo dicantur peccaffe ac damnati fuisse, habendi sint pro absurditatum hamaxarijs, aut rectæ rationis & diuinæ iustitiæ aducrfarijs. Rursus potest hoc totum concedi, absque vllo caulæ quam ago dispendio. Fateor enim Adæ peccatum censeri posterorum peccatum ob vitium illis inhærens ab eo deriuatum. Fateor in eo dici posse posteros ejus peccaffe ac damnatos fuisse, quia nimirum ab eo peccatum inhærens & per peccatum damnationem suam traxerunt. Sed nego peccatum actuale Adami ita nobis omnibus ejus posteris imputari, vt ea imputatione nostrum fiat, alioqui non nostrum, & vt sic imputatum puniatur, corruptionem hæreditariam, quæ vere peccatum est, tanquam poenam propriedictam, ac vt justitia fiat, infligi, nec-non mortem corporis & æternam. Hoc est quod absurditatibus cumulamus, à quibus liberari non potest per decimationem Leui in Lumbis Abrahæ. An enim ex eo quod decimatus dicitur Leui in Lumbis Abrahæ, consequitur, imputationem illam posse probari ex sacris literis, non pugnare cum oraculo, Filius non fert iniquitatem Patris, non facere Deum autorem peccati, & Christum peccatorem &c. ? Impedit-ne ne sint bona & solida argumenta, quibus imputationem illam oppugnamus ? Nullo modo. Quid igitur imputationem illam juuat hæc decimatio ? Nihil prorsus. Vin' præterea ostendam quàm male ratiocinetur D. Gariffolius ? Si quis in prætereuntem rosas projiciat, nihil sequetur absurdi : hæ enim minimè nocent. An ergo similiter, si quis in prætereuntem lapides aut lutum projiciat, nihil sequetur absurdi? Se habet autem solutio decimarum vt rosa quæ non potuit nocere Leui : At peccatum Adami non solum vt lapis, sed vt summum malum. Non fuerit igitur alienum à justitia, si solutio decimarum ab Abrahamo facta tribuatur Leui; quia id ei nullo modo nocuit, aut nocere potuit: An sequitur inde, non esse alienum à justitia, si peccatum ab Adamo commissum ejus posteris tribuatur, atque ita malum maximum illis inferatur? Non admodum opus est aliis responsionibus; quatuor tamen alias nobis D. Gariffolius tribuit, quas fortasse ex Priore, quod vocat, Manuscripto exprompsit, & prolixè admodum refellere conatur, sed, pro suo more, conatu infœlici.
units.tr: But perhaps someone can gather from this passage, indirectly, that Adam's actual sin is imputed to us immediately. For, says D. G., if what Abraham did in giving tithes is considered to have been done by the Levites born so many ages later, and yet there is nothing in such imputation foreign to reason or to God's justice, no one will say what cause there is why those who assert that Adam's sin is counted as the sin of his posterity, so that in it they are said to have sinned and been condemned, should be held to be purveyors of absurdities or adversaries of right reason and divine justice. Again, all this can be granted without any loss to the cause I am pursuing. For I confess that Adam's sin is counted as the sin of his posterity on account of the corruption inhering in them, derived from him. I confess that in it his posterity can be said to have sinned and been condemned, since indeed they drew from him inhering sin and, through sin, their condemnation. But I deny that Adam's actual sin is imputed to all of us, his posterity, in such a way that by that imputation it becomes ours, otherwise not ours, and that, thus imputed, it is punished by inflicting hereditary corruption, which truly is sin, as a punishment that is our own, so that justice may be done, together with bodily death and eternal death. This is what we heap absurdities upon, and from which it cannot be freed by the tithing of Levi in the loins of Abraham. For does it follow, from the fact that Levi is said to have been tithed in the loins of Abraham, that this imputation can be proved from Holy Scripture, that it does not conflict with the oracle The son does not bear the iniquity of the father, does not make God the author of sin, and Christ a sinner, and so on? Do not the good and solid arguments by which we oppose that imputation remain intact? In no way do they fail. What then does this tithing help that imputation? Nothing at all. Moreover, shall I show how badly D. Garissolius reasons? If someone throws roses at a passer-by, nothing absurd follows, for these do no harm at all. Does it then likewise follow, if someone throws stones or mud at a passer-by, that nothing absurd follows? The payment of tithes stands to Levi as a rose, which could not harm him; but Adam's sin is not like a stone only but like the greatest evil. It would not therefore be foreign to justice if the payment of tithes made by Abraham were attributed to Levi, since it in no way harmed him, or could not harm him. Does it follow from this that it is not foreign to justice if the sin committed by Adam is attributed to his posterity, and so the greatest evil is inflicted upon them? There is no great need for other replies. Nevertheless D. Garissolius attributes four others to us, which he perhaps drew from the so-called Prior Manuscript, and he tries at length to refute them, but, after his usual manner, with an unhappy effort.

units.la: Responsio igitur secunda, eo referente, est, Apostolum, quia præuidebat fore, vt durum videretur, quod dicturus erat de decimatione Leui in Abrahamo, præoccupasse dicendo, In Abrahamo decimatus est & ipse Leui, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, vt ita loquar. Quæ ratio molliendi non vsurpatur, nisi vbi locutio audacior est, aut inusitatior, quàm vt eam liceat vrgere vehementius, aut ex ea quippiam colligere ratiocinando. Hoc igitur non debet eò traduci, vt inde colligatur peccatum Adami omnibus imputari, aut vt tanquam fundamentum substernatur rei, quæ ipsa per se vel obscura est, vel omninò fidem ipsa sibi derogat. Huic responsioni multa reponit. 1. Locum hunc non tanquam fundamentum substerni, sed tanquam testimonium proponi declarandæ & illustrandæ doctrinæ de imputatione peccati Ada valde appositum. An fit appositum declarandæ imputationi immediatæ partim ex superiori, partim ex hac & sequentibus responsionibus manifestum fiet. Quod subjungit fundamentum illius desumi ex Rom. V. quàm fit falsum partim ex dictis, partim ex Manuscripto posteriore comprobatur. Quod ait Augustinum & Caluinum imputationem illam amplecti, sine dubitatione pro falso habeo. Sed pergat. 2. Frustra, inquit, confugium quaeritur in verbis, ὡς ἐπος εἰπεῖν. Quid enim si verti debeant, vt breuiter dicam, potius quàm, vt ita dicam? Sic enim sane praecludetur istud confugium. Omnino praecludetur, si probet sic debere verti hoc loco. Sed quo argumento id euincet? Nos enim nunc tantum respondemus: ejus est argumentari: respondemus autem consentanea receptæ versioni, quæ refelli non potest. Quis etiam credat Apostolum, qui non breuius hoc loco quàm alibi passim loquitur, voluisse hoc vno loco verba illa vsurpare, vt breuiter dicam, quibus alibi nunquam vtitur? nempe perpetuo breuiter loquitur. Quid si, addit, ita vertas, ὡς ἐπος εἰπεῖν, vt aliquid majus & mirabilius dicā: Praecludetur iterum hæc disputatoris euasio. Quomodo inquam praecludetur, nisi probetur (id quod est impossibile) sic esse vertendum? Et cùm maxima mirabilissimáque passim doceant Apostoli, qui factum effet, vt hoc vno dutaxat loco hujusmodi praefatio, potius quàm alibi, vsurparetur? Diciturne hic aliquid majus & mirabilius, quàm alijs aut capitis aut Epistolæ locis? Si præmollitio vel correctio est, aliquid est in sequenti sententia, vel emolliendum, vel corrigendum, nec, nisi adhibita emollitione vel correctione, vrgendum. Præmissa hac inutili vclitatione, subjungit, 3. Ἀλλ' ταmen men facile expositionem communiorem sequimur, ὡς ἐπὶ τὸν, vt ita dicam. Verba sint ergo molliendo dicto Apostoli apposita. Hoc quidem causa nostra nihil praeiudicat. Illa enim molliendi ratio, non rem ipsam spectat, sed potius ad verbum decimandi referenda est. Non enim personae proprie decimantur, sed bona, vt notum est, cum ex eis decima pars excerpitur. Ergo quia quaedam improprietas est in eo quod Leui decimatus dicitur, pro eo quod est, decimas ex Leui acceptas fuisse, ideo exstimauit Apostolus hanc εἶναι esse leniendam per voculas, ὡς ἴσως ἐπὶ τὸν. Miror hoc excidisse Viro docto. Non videtur inspexisse locum. Vidisset enim Apostolum jam bis absque vlla emollitione verbum illud eodem modo vsurpasse, semel Ἰ. 5. ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀὴρ λαὸν decimandi populum & iterum Ἰ. 6 Δεκάτωσε τὸν Ἀβραὰμ decimaut Abrahamum. Non igitur decimandi verbum sic vsurpatum emollire voluit Apostolus. 4. Fac, inquit, etiam phrasim illam ad molliendam totam sententiam pertinere, Leui decimatus est in Abrahamo, quid hoc iuuat causam aduersariam? Certe enim decimarum persolutio fuit actio propria & personalis solius Abrahami. Ergo cum ea Leuitis etiam tribuitur, est agnoscenda quaedam sermonis improprietas; non enim proprie & personaliter, sed interpretatiue & per imputationem eis tribuitur, quatenus illi reputantur fecisse, quod Abrahamus solus fecerat; Neque enim quae praestita sunt ab aliis & nobis imputantur, ita proprie nostra dicuntur, sicut ea quae ipsi fecimus, iuxta illud Poetae, Et quae non fecimus ipsi, vix ea nostra voco. Primum autem oblitus videtur quas agere partes debeat. Respondet enim, cum probare debeat. Nos certe verba illa Apostoli non afferimus; allatis & obiectis respondemus duntaxat, ac palam facimus ea causæ nostræ nullo modo obesse : id quod nobis fatis est. Interim concedit quod volumus, esse sermonis improprietatem quandam egentem emollitione. Ejus igitur erat ostendere & probare hujusmodi improprietatem non impedire, quominus illius loci verba sic vrgeantur, vt ab iis fit qui nos oppugnant. Hoc vero minime facit. Cæterum ex ejus verbis sic colligo : Si par effet ratio illius sententiæ, in Adamo omnes peccauerunt, ac hujus, in Abrahamo Leui decimatus est, par effet vtriusque improprietas seu durities, ac proinde aut neutri, aut vtrique pariter emollitio illa præmittenda fuisset. Vel igitur Apostolus non dixit omnes in Adamo peccasse; vel si dixit, dispar est propositionis illius, ac hujus, in Abraham Leui decimatus est, ratio. Aliud etiam Colligo. Nam, si actio criminosa primi hominis fuit proprie actio ipsius solius, & nostra minus proprie, nimirum per imputationem, qui nos, æquè ac Adamum, facit proprie reos ac morti obnoxios coram Deo iudiciissimo judice. Debet enim similiter nos facere reos minus proprie ? Id tamen comparatione illustrat. Sicut peccata nostra non proprie, sed tantum per imputationem fuerunt in Christo, & sufficit tamen ea imputatio, ut Christus peccatorum nostrorum pœnas vere ac reapse lueret. An igitur vt nos in Adamo, sic Christus in nobis dici potest peccasse ? An ei peccata nostra sunt ita imputata, vti nobis imputatum dicitur peccatum Adæ ? Si ais, igitur, quod vel cogitare horret animus, peccator fuit, & quidem magis quam alius quisquam : quippe cui plura fuerint imputata peccata. Si negas, quid facit πρὸς ὑπος dissimile exemplum ? Potuit quidem sufficere imputatio, vt pœnas peccatorum nostrorum Christus lueret tanquam vas noster; at non vt eas lueret tanquam peccatorum caussa. Agitur autem hoc loco de imputatione, qua fiat vt censeamur causæ peccati, quod solius Adami proprie actio fuit, & quidem causæ ita proprie & vere, vt non minus proprie & vere quàm ipse Adamus puniri mereamur. Id quod ajo à veritate & justitia omnino esse alienum.
units.tr: The second answer, according to him, is that the Apostle, foreseeing that it would seem harsh, what he was about to say about the tithing of Levi in Abraham, anticipated it by saying, In Abraham even Levi himself was tithed, so to speak (ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν), as I may put it. [ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν] This softening device is used only where the expression is bolder or more unusual than one may press vigorously or draw an inference from by reasoning. So this should not be taken to mean that from it one may conclude that the sin of Adam is imputed to all, or that it is laid down as a foundation for a matter which is itself obscure or which in itself undermines its own credibility. He raises many objections to this answer. 1. That this passage is not set down as a foundation, but offered as a testimony very apt for declaring and illustrating the doctrine of the imputation of Adam's sin. Whether it is apt for declaring immediate imputation will become clear partly from what has been said above and partly from the following answers. As for what he adds, that its foundation is drawn from Rom. 5, how false this is is shown partly from what has been said and partly from the later manuscript. That he says Augustine and Calvin embrace that imputation I hold without hesitation to be false. But let him proceed. 2. In vain, he says, is refuge sought in the words ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν. For what if they ought to be rendered, to put it briefly, rather than, as I may say? For in that way this refuge would certainly be closed off. It would indeed be closed off entirely, if he proved that they must be rendered so in this place. But by what argument will he establish that? For we are now only answering: it is his business to argue; we answer by what agrees with the accepted version, which cannot be refuted. Who, moreover, would believe that the Apostle, who does not speak more briefly in this place than he does everywhere else, wished to use those words, to put it briefly, in this one place only, words which he never uses elsewhere? Indeed he speaks briefly throughout. What if, he adds, you render it so, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, so that I may say something greater and more wonderful: this evasion of the disputant will again be closed off. How, I ask, will it be closed off, unless it is proved (which is impossible) that it must be rendered so? And since the Apostles everywhere teach very great and most wonderful things, how came it about that such a preface should be used in this one place only, rather than elsewhere? Is anything greater and more wonderful said here than in other passages of this chapter or of the Epistle? If it is a softening or a correction, then something in the following sentence must either be softened or corrected, and it must not be pressed unless that softening or correction is applied. With this useless flourish set aside, he adds, 3. But we more readily follow the more common explanation, ὡς ἐπὶ τὸν [ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν], as I may say. Let the words therefore be taken as a softening placed alongside the Apostle's statement. This indeed does nothing to prejudice our cause. For that mode of softening does not concern the thing itself, but rather refers to the word to tithe. For persons are not properly tithed, but goods, as is well known, since a tenth part is taken out of them. Therefore, because there is a certain impropriety in saying that Levi was tithed, for what is really meant, that tithes were received from Levi, the Apostle thought that this ἐν [expression] should be softened by the little words ὡς ἴσως ἐπὶ τὸν [as it were, so to speak]. I am surprised that this has escaped a learned man. He does not seem to have examined the passage. For he would have seen that the Apostle had already twice used that word in the same way without any softening: once in Heb. 7.5, to tithe the people [ἀποδεκατοῦν τὸν λαόν], and again in Heb. 7.6, he tithed Abraham [Δεκάτωσε τὸν Ἀβραάμ]. The Apostle therefore did not wish to soften the word to tithe when so used. 4. Grant, he says, that this phrase too pertains to softening the whole sentence, Levi was tithed in Abraham: what does this help the opposing cause? For certainly the payment of tithes was the proper and personal action of Abraham alone. Therefore when it is also attributed to the Levites, a certain impropriety of speech must be recognised; for it is attributed to them not properly and personally, but by interpretation and imputation, inasmuch as they are reckoned to have done what Abraham alone had done. For what has been performed by others and is imputed to us is not called ours in the same proper way as what we ourselves have done, according to the saying of the poet, "And what we have not done ourselves, I can scarcely call ours." But first he seems to have forgotten what part he ought to play. For he is answering, when he ought to be proving. We certainly do not bring forward those words of the Apostle; we only answer what is brought forward and objected, and we make plain that these do no harm to our cause in any way, which is enough for us. Meanwhile he concedes what we want, that there is a certain impropriety of speech in need of softening. It was therefore his task to show and prove that such an impropriety does not prevent the words of that passage from being pressed in the way our opponents press them. This he does not do at all. Otherwise, I infer from his words as follows: if the reasoning of that statement, in Adam all sinned, were the same as that of this, in Abraham Levi was tithed, then the impropriety or harshness of both would be equal, and accordingly that softening would have had to be prefixed either to neither or to both alike. Therefore either the Apostle did not say that all sinned in Adam, or, if he did say it, the reasoning of that proposition differs from that of this, in Abraham Levi was tithed. I also infer another point. For if the criminal act of the first man was properly the act of him alone, and ours only improperly, namely by imputation, does it not make us, just as much as Adam, properly guilty and liable to death before God, the most righteous Judge? For must it not similarly make us guilty in an improper sense? Yet he illustrates this by comparison: Just as our sins were not in Christ properly, but only by imputation, and yet that imputation suffices for Christ truly and really to pay the penalties of our sins. Can it then be said that as we sinned in Adam, so Christ sinned in us? Were our sins imputed to him in the way that the sin of Adam is said to be imputed to us? If you say yes, then the mind shudders even to think it: he would have been a sinner, and indeed more than anyone else, since more sins would have been imputed to him. If you deny it, what does an unlike example accomplish, πρὸς ὑπος [to the point]? Imputation could indeed suffice for Christ to pay the penalties of our sins as our surety, but not for him to pay them as the cause of sins. Yet in this place we are dealing with an imputation by which we are made to be counted as the cause of a sin which was properly the act of Adam alone, and indeed as the cause so properly and truly that we deserve to be punished no less properly and truly than Adam himself. This I affirm to be wholly alien from truth and justice.

units.la: Supersunt tres aliæ responsiones, quas ne nimia, nec necessaria, prolixitate tædium afferam lectori, prætermittendas duco, tantùm addam, non videri, ex verbis in Abrahamo decimatus est Leui, concludi posse, actionem illam Abrahami imputatam fuisse Leui. Nam si fuit imputata; idque probatum est ab Apostolo ea ratione,quam,aut nullam esse,aut hanc esse D.G.asserit Qui est in lumbis alterius,tanquam originarij principij sui, illi non absonum si tribuantur quæ facta sunt ab eo,in cujus lumbis fuit. Atqui Leui fuit in lumbis Abrahæ tanquam originalis sui principij.Ergo recte Leui possunt attribui, quæ dicuntur de Abrahamo persoluente decimas Pontifici Melchisedecho, nulla erit patris actio, quæ imputari filio rectè non possit.Cùm enimSyllogismus sit in prima figura, valere non potest, nisi major sit vera vniuersaliter. Quo posito, manente eadem minore, concludam; Ergo recte Leui possunt attribui, quæ dicuntur de Abrahamo credente Deo, aut fugiente in Æ-gyptum, aut dicente de vxore soror mea est &c. Cùm igitur ex iisdem illis præmissis conclusio effici possit, vel ipso D. Garissolio confitente cap. x. § 2. falsa, & minorem constet esse veram, necesse-est vt falsa sit major, & ab Apostoli mente aliena.
units.tr: Three other answers remain, which, so as not to weary the reader with excessive and unnecessary length, I consider should be passed over. I will only add that it does not seem possible to conclude from the words in Abraham Levi was tithed that that act of Abraham was imputed to Levi. For if it was imputed, and this has been proved by the Apostle by that reasoning which D. G. asserts is either no argument at all or is this one: He who is in the loins of another, as of his originating principle, it is not absurd if the things done by him in whose loins he was are attributed to him. But Levi was in the loins of Abraham as of his originating principle. Therefore those things which are said of Abraham paying tithes to the priest Melchizedek can rightly be attributed to Levi, there will be no action of the father which cannot rightly be imputed to the son. For since the syllogism is in the first figure, it cannot hold unless the major premise is true universally. With this laid down, and the same minor premise remaining, I will conclude: Therefore those things which are said of Abraham believing God, or fleeing into Egypt, or saying of his wife, she is my sister, etc., can rightly be attributed to Levi. Since therefore from those same premises a conclusion can be drawn which is false, as D. Garissolius himself admits in chap. 10, § 2, and since the minor premise is plainly true, it is necessary that the major is false and alien to the mind of the Apostle.

units.la: Quænam igitur, inquies, est Apostoli ratiocinatio ? Scopus est probare Sacerdotij Leuitici quàm Melchisedecici dignitatem esse minorem. Argumentum ex eo ducit, quòd Melchisedeco decimæ sunt ab Abrahamo solutæ. Quod vt explicet, atque proferat in lucem, comparationem instituit inter Leui & Melchisedecum habita ratione muneris ipsorum Sacerdotalis. Leui autem nomine Sacerdotes Leuiticos, totumque eorum sacerdotium completitur. Si Melchisedecus decimas accepit, etiam ipsi sacerdotes Leuitici decimas accipiebant. Hactenus igitur quodammodo pares erant. Sed quatuor obseruat Apostolus differentias Melchisedecum supra Sacerdotes Leuiticos, immane quantum, extollentes. Prima est, quòd his datum erat mandatum accipiendi decimas, cùm de illo nullum extet ejusmodi mandatum. Altera, quòd hi decimas accipiebant à fratribus suis, egressis è lumbis Abrahæ, ac proinde natura & origine sibi æqualibus; Ille verò, cùm non esset ex eodem genere, decimas accepit, non à Leuitarum fratribus, sed ab ipso eorum patre, Abrahamo, habente promissiones. Itaque hi ab Abrahamo sacerdotium ac dignitatem suam tanquam illius hæredes acceperunt; Ille suam aliunde habuit. Hi suam omnem benedictionem quam fratribus impertierunt ab Abrahamo habente promissiones traxerunt, Ille verò benedictionem non accepit ab Abrahamo, sed contrà Abrahamus ab ipso, cùm tamen hic promissiones haberet. Tertia, quòd hi accipiant decimas tanquam homines morti obnoxij, ac proinde eis egentes, Ille verò tanquam is, quem perpetuò viuere, seu immortalem esse Scriptura testatur: vt non potuerint ei decimæ dari, nisi declarandæ ejus dignitatis gratia. Quarta denique quod etiam ipse Leui, qui decimas accipit, per Abrahamum decimatum quodammodo decimatus fuisse à Melchisedeco dici possit.
units.tr: What, then, you will ask, is the Apostle's line of reasoning? His aim is to prove that the dignity of the Levitical priesthood is less than that of the priesthood of Melchizedek. He draws the argument from the fact that tithes were paid to Melchizedek by Abraham. To explain and bring this out into the light, he compares Levi with Melchizedek, taking into account their priestly office. By the name of Levi he means the Levitical priests and their whole priesthood. If Melchizedek received tithes, then the Levitical priests themselves also received tithes. So far, then, they were in a sense equal. But the Apostle notes four differences by which he raises Melchizedek immeasurably above the Levitical priests. The first is that these were commanded to receive tithes, whereas no such command exists concerning him. The second is that these received tithes from their brothers, who had sprung from the loins of Abraham and were therefore equal to them in nature and origin; but he, since he was not of the same stock, received tithes not from the brothers of Levi but from their father himself, Abraham, who held the promises. Thus the Levites received their priesthood and their dignity from Abraham as his heirs, whereas Melchizedek had his from elsewhere. The Levites derived every blessing they bestowed on their brothers from Abraham, who held the promises; but Melchizedek did not receive a blessing from Abraham, rather Abraham received one from him, although Abraham held the promises. The third is that these receive tithes as men subject to death, and therefore in need, whereas he receives them as one whom Scripture testifies lives forever, or is immortal; so tithes could be given to him only to declare his dignity. Finally, the fourth is that Levi himself, who receives tithes, can be said to have been in a sense tithed by Melchizedek through Abraham.

units.la: Nam is adhuc erat in lumbis patris, cùm Abrahamo occurreret Melchisedecus. Hoc enim euenit antequam Isaacus esset genitus. Id quod non casu, sed singulari Dei prouidentia sine dubio accidit, ne separato eb eo Leui, videretur etiam ab eo tunc seporata fuisse Leuitici sacerdotij dignitas. Itaque id tempus elegit Deus, cùm in vno Abrahamo nondum vlla ab eo facta hæredum seperatione, omnis posteritatis ejus secundum carnem vnita continearetur dignitas, quæ suo tandem tempore inter ejus filios ita est distributa, vt sacerdotalis dignitatis Leui, regiæ Iuda hæres fieret. Quod si quis à me flagitet, vt rationem Apostoli Syllogisimi forma induam: is sic poterit concipi. Qui singulari Dei prouidentia tunc est decimatus, cùm adhuc in sese sacerdotij Leuitici dignitatem, nondum vllâ factâ ab eo separatione, totam contineret, in eo decimato ipsum sacerdotium Leuiticum, seu ipsi Leuitæ sacerdotes, vt ita loquar, decimati fuerunt. Atqui singulari Dei prouidentiâ tunc est decimatus Abrahamus, cum adhuc in sese Sacerdotij Leuitici dignitatem, nondum vllâ factâ ab eo separatione, totam contineret. Ergo in eo decimato Leuitæ sacerdotes, vt ita loquar, decimati fuerunt. Hoc enim, vt ita dicam, homagium Sacerdotium Leuiticum per Abrahamum, in quo continebatur, Melchisedeco exhibuit. Non enim aliud habuit Leui sacerdotium, quàm quod ab Abrahamo hæreditario iure acceptum, Deo attribuente & formante, ipsi indultum fuit. Hinc, opinor, Lector benevole perspicis, cum inuictam esse rationem Apostoli, tum ineius verbis nullam proprie dictam imputationem haberi, nisi forte mediatam. Nam vt in Abrahamo fuit Sacerdotium Leuiticum, ex eoque ad Leui est deriuatum, sic in Adamo fuit peccatum, ex eoque in nos est propagatum. Itaque vt idem de Leui sacerdote ac de Abrahamo sacerdote faciendum, quantum ad dignitatem sacerdotij spectat, judicium fuit, sic de Adamo peccatore & nobis ob tractum ab eo inhaerens vitium peccatoribus, idem, quoad reatum, faciendum judicium est. Si diceretur aliquis Domino feudi in suo patre,cum in eius lumbis adhuc delitesceret,vt ita loquar,homagium quod vocant praestitisse, itaque Domini illius, vt loquuntur, vasallum esse, nonne recte procederet argumentum? Et tamen non imputaretur praestitum a patre homagium filio: nam si imputaretur, non magis a filio exigi posset vt id ipse denuo praestaret, quam id poterat a parente exigi.
units.tr: For Levi was still in the loins of his father when Melchizedek met Abraham. This happened before Isaac was born. This did not happen by chance, but without doubt by the singular providence of God, so that Levi should not appear to have been separated from him and the dignity of the Levitical priesthood to have been separated from him at that time. Therefore God chose that time, when in Abraham alone, with no separation yet made from him of his heirs, the dignity of his whole posterity according to the flesh was contained in unity; this dignity was at its proper time so distributed among his sons that the priestly dignity became the inheritance of Levi and the royal of Judah. But if anyone should ask me to put the Apostle's reasoning into the form of a syllogism, it could be framed thus: He who by the singular providence of God was tithed at the time when he still contained within himself the whole dignity of the Levitical priesthood, with no separation yet made from him, in him the Levitical priesthood itself, or, so to speak, the Levitical priests themselves, were tithed. But by the singular providence of God Abraham was tithed at the time when he still contained within himself the dignity of the Levitical priesthood, with no separation yet made from him. Therefore in him the Levitical priests, so to speak, were tithed. For Abraham, so to speak, offered this homage, the Levitical priesthood contained in him, to Melchizedek. For the Levitical priesthood had no other standing than what, received by hereditary right from Abraham, was granted to it, God bestowing and shaping it. From this, I think, kind reader, you perceive that the Apostle's argument is unanswerable, and that in his words there is no imputation properly so called, unless perhaps a mediate one. For just as the Levitical priesthood was in Abraham and from him was derived to Levi, so sin was in Adam and from him has been propagated to us. Therefore, just as the same judgment must be made concerning Levi the priest and Abraham the priest, as far as the dignity of the priesthood is concerned, so the same judgment must be made concerning Adam the sinner and us sinners, on account of the fault inhering in us that was drawn from him, as far as guilt is concerned. If someone were to say that he had rendered homage, as they call it, to the lord of a fief in his father, while he still lay hidden, so to speak, in his father's loins, and that he was therefore the vassal of that lord, as they say, would the argument not proceed rightly? And yet the homage rendered by the father would not be imputed to the son; for if it were imputed, it could no more be demanded of the son that he render it again himself than it could be demanded of the parent.

units.la: CAPVT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Imputationem primi Adae peccati actualis antece- dentem seu immediatam nullis rationibus aliqui posse.
units.tr: That no arguments can establish the antecedent or immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin.

units.la: PVtasne, Lector, hanc imputationem, cum absit a Scriptura, rationibus posse aliqui? Audiamus tamen, si quae afferuntur, rationes. Persuasum enim est nobis perpetuo cum Scriptura rectam consentire rationem. Agnosco, Quae Deus Adamo largitus erat, non ipsi soli, sed etiam toti posteritati ipsius fuisse data; ac proinde nos in ipsius persona omnibus illis bonis spoliatos in omnem hanc miseriam & maledictionem incidisse. Quid inde pro illa imputatione rationis elici poteit? Erantne posteris omnibus imputanda, quæ Deus Adamo largitus fuerat bona? Aut est-ne imputanda nobis illorum omnium bonorum Adamo conueniens spoliatio? Vtinam hæc spoliatio nobis nonnihil imputatiuè conueniret!
units.tr: Do you think, Reader, that this imputation can be supported by arguments, since it is absent from Scripture? Let us nevertheless hear what arguments are brought. For we are persuaded that sound reason always agrees with Scripture. I grant that what God had bestowed on Adam was given not to him alone, but to his whole posterity; and therefore we, in his person, stripped of all those goods, fell into all this misery and curse. What argument for that imputation can be drawn from this? Were all the goods that God had bestowed on Adam to be imputed to his posterity? Or is the loss of all those goods, which befell Adam, to be imputed to us? Would that this deprivation applied to us in some measure by imputation!

units.la: Qui, inquit, propter parentum crimen actuale aliquod, иjs beneficijs priuantur, quæ parentes illi & pro se & pro liberis suis acceperant; illi paterni criminis pœnas luunt, atque adeo paternum crimen illis imputatur. Atqui posteri omnes Adami propter primam illam ejus inobedientiam qua se pollluit, priuantur ijs beneficijs, quæ Adamus pro se & pro posteris suis acceperat, nimirum, justitia & recti tudine naturali. Ergo posteri omnes naturales Adami paterni criminis pœnas luunt, adeoque paternum illis crimen imputatur. Quid si hanc conclusionem concedam? Paternum enim crimen vel vitium hæreditarium intelligitur, vel causa illius vitij, actualis inobedientia Adami. Si prius, imputatur, & quidem immediatè. Si posterius, imputatur id quoque, sed mediante inhærente vitio. Luimus pœnas proximè peccati nostri in nos propagati, remotè verò peccati ab Adamo olim admissi. Quod si dicat aliquis, nos omnes transgressoris Adæ nasci obnoxios, immediatè, hoc est, non propter aliquod vitium, aut culpam, aut depravationem, quam in nobis habeamus, is meminerit sic tuisse Pighij errorem à Petro Martyre explicatum: atque his argumentis in primis confutatum: quæ considera Lector si placet, annon pugnent cum D. G. sententia &c. argumentis. Verum, inquit, contra hanc sententiam in primis illud facit, quod jam bis diximus : videlicet, infantes mori. Mors enim nihil iuris habet vbi non est peccatum. Nisi dicere velimus Deum punire innocentem. Confirmatur autem hæc ratio ex argumento Pauli, quo probauit, peccatum fuisse ante Legem. Quia mors, inquit, regnauit ab Adamo vsque ad Mosem. Atqui juxta Pighij sententiam hæc ratio hebetissima videri possit. Diceret enim quispiam, etsi illi mortui fuerint, tamen ex eo non sequitur, illos habuisse peccatum. Mors enim illis contigit propter Adamum, ob cujus peccatum redditi sint mortales. Vides, Lector, & peccatum intelligi, non actuale Adami, vt vult D. Gariffolius, sed habituale nostrum, & pro causa Pighij eius argumenta militare aduersus nostros. Quod vt fiat manifestius, subjungam aliud argumentum Martyris. Postremo, inquit, habemus a Paulo per inobedientiam vnius hominis multos constitutos esse peccatores : quod indicat, in illis, qui nascuntur ex Adamo, esse vitium, propter quod peccatores dici possint. Sed hoc putat Pighius se posse eludere, quod peccatores interdum dicantur propter reatum, quamvis actio peccandi praeterierit, neque amplius extet. Quamvis hoc ita sit, nunquam tamen ostendere potest e Scripturis, quenquam peccatorem appellari, quin aut in ipso vitium habeat, aut certe antea admiserit : nisi dicere velit, Deum homines reos facere absque ipsorum aliquo peccato. Num quid flagitare difertius tua potest, Lector, æquitas? Sed redeamus ad Argumentum nobis objectum. Quamvis causæ nostræ non obsit conclusio, tamen Minor distingui debet. Nam si vult nos priuari iustitia naturali propter primam Adæ inobedientiam nobis imputatam, petitio est, vt loquuntur, principij: id ipsum enim assumit quod versatur in quæstione: quare negatur minor. Sin vult nos priuari iustitia propter inobedientiam illam in nos, (non quidem secundum actum, sed secundum habitum) naturaliter propagatam, concedi potest. Nam inobedientia actualis Adamum iustitiâ priuauit, quam amissam cum posteris communicare non potuit: Nemo enim dat quod non habet. Negamus igitur nos priuari iustitia naturali ob peccatum Adami nobis imputatum: Concedimus nos ea priuari ob peccatum Adami in nos propagatum.
units.tr: He says: those who, on account of some actual crime of their parents, are deprived of those benefits which their parents had received both for themselves and for their children, bear the penalties of the parent's crime; and so the parent's crime is imputed to them. But all Adam's posterity, on account of that first disobedience by which he defiled himself, are deprived of those benefits which Adam had received for himself and for his posterity, namely original justice and natural uprightness. Therefore all Adam's natural posterity bear the penalties of the parent's crime, and so the parent's crime is imputed to them. What if I concede this conclusion? For the "parental crime" is understood either as hereditary vice, or as the cause of that vice, Adam's actual disobedience. If the former, it is imputed, and indeed immediately. If the latter, it is imputed too, but through the inherent vice. We bear the penalties proximately for the sin propagated into us, and remotely for the sin committed long ago by Adam. But if anyone says that we are all born liable to the transgressor Adam immediately, that is, not on account of any vice, or fault, or depravity that we have in ourselves, let him remember that the error of Pighius was thus explained by Peter Martyr, and refuted chiefly by these arguments. Let the reader consider, if he pleases, whether they do not clash with the opinion and arguments of D. G. etc. But, he says, against this opinion, above all, stands what we have already said twice: namely, that infants die. For death has no right where there is no sin. Unless we wish to say that God punishes the innocent. This argument is confirmed by Paul's argument, by which he proved that sin existed before the Law. For death, he says, reigned from Adam to Moses. But according to Pighius' opinion this argument might seem very dull. For someone might say: even if those men died, it does not follow that they had sin. For death came upon them on account of Adam, through whose sin they were made mortal. You see, Reader, that the sin understood here is not Adam's actual sin, as D. Garissolius wishes, but our habitual sin; and that Pighius' arguments fight for his cause against ours. To make this clearer, I will add another argument of Martyr. Lastly, he says, we have from Paul that through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners; which indicates that in those who are born of Adam there is a vice on account of which they can be called sinners. But Pighius thinks he can evade this, because sinners are sometimes so called on account of guilt, although the act of sinning has passed and no longer exists. Although this is so, he can never show from Scripture that anyone is called a sinner unless he either has the vice in himself or has certainly committed it earlier; unless he wishes to say that God makes men guilty without any sin of their own. Can your fairness, Reader, demand anything plainer? But let us return to the argument put against us. Although the conclusion does no harm to our cause, the minor premise must still be distinguished. For if he means that we are deprived of natural justice on account of Adam's first disobedience imputed to us, this is, as they say, a petitio principii: he assumes the very thing in question; therefore the minor is denied. But if he means that we are deprived of justice on account of that disobedience propagated into us by nature (not indeed as an act, but as a habit), this can be conceded. For Adam's actual disobedience deprived him of justice, which, once lost, he could not communicate to his posterity: for no one gives what he does not have. We therefore deny that we are deprived of natural justice on account of Adam's sin imputed to us; we concede that we are deprived of it on account of Adam's sin propagated into us.

units.la: Instat D. Garissolius. Quid dico instat? Respondeo, inquit, nempe responsioni responsionem opponit. Sed quid tamen respondet? Resp. inquit, 1. Non si propagatio peccati & eius transmissio per generationem naturalem concedenda est, vt est certissima, propterea imputationem negari, aut tolli consentaneum est; neque enim ab illius positione ad huius negationem consequentia vlla legitima duci potest, vtraque potius in causâ peccati originalis coniungenda est, sicut à nostris Theologis communiter obseruari certum est. Atqui, inquam, nostræ, nunc quidem, partes sunt respondere, eius probare. Ponimus autem, id quod est in confesso, propagari peccatum Adami per generationem naturalem. An eam antecedat imputatio peccati Adamici, necne, id ipsum est quod inter nos controuertitur, quodque probandum suscepisse videbatur. Nunc probationis loco contentus est dicere ab illius positione ad huius negationem nullam esse consequentiam. Fac ita esse, an propterea imputationem illam astruxit? probet igitur non sufficere propagationem naturalem, nisi eam antecedat imputatio, alioquin aërem diuerberat.
