Atque hoc est quod intendit probare.
units.tr: D. Garissolius presses the point. What do I mean by "presses"? I answer, he says; that is, he sets a reply against a reply. But what does he actually answer? Answer, he says, 1. It does not follow that, if the propagation of sin and its transmission by natural generation are to be conceded, as is most certain, imputation must therefore be denied or removed; for no legitimate inference can be drawn from the positing of the one to the denial of the other. Rather, both should be joined together in the cause of original sin, as our theologians commonly observe, and this is certain. Yet, I say, it is now our part to answer and his to prove. But we posit what is admitted, that Adam's sin is propagated by natural generation. Whether the imputation of Adam's sin precedes that generation or not is precisely what is disputed between us, and what he seemed to have undertaken to prove. Now, instead of proof, he is content to say that there is no consequence from the positing of the one to the denial of the other. Grant that it is so: does he therefore establish that imputation? Let him then prove that natural propagation is not sufficient unless imputation precedes it; otherwise he is beating the air. And this is what he intends to prove.

units.la: Addit enim. 2. Nec satis est, fi dicas Adamum, quæ amiserat communicare non potuisse, eo quod nemo dat, quod non habet, quia hic ratio reddenda est, quare anima Adami iustitiæ originalis decoramentis ornata fuerit; & quare posterorum ipsius animæ, quæ non traducuntur propagatione naturali, sed a Deo infundendo creantur, & creando infunduntur, eodem ornatibus ipsa sua creatione careant, adeoque perfectione illa prima patris Adami destitutæ in corpus a Deo inducantur, quod tamen aliter futurum fuit, si Adam in integritate sua perstitisset. Hic enim non est simpliciter recurrendum ad propagationem, cum anima non propagentur, aut traducantur; Neque ad legem naturæ, quia morbosi morbosos generant, quia anima non generatur, & tamen ab initio sui esse, priuata est primis illis beneficijs.
units.tr: For he adds, 2. Nor is it enough to say that Adam could not communicate what he had lost, because no one gives what he does not have. For here a reason must be given why Adam's soul was adorned with the ornaments of original righteousness; and why the souls of his posterity, which are not transmitted by natural propagation but are created and infused by God at the moment of creation, lack those same ornaments from their very creation, and so, destitute of that first perfection of father Adam, are brought by God into the body, which would otherwise have been the case had Adam persisted in his integrity. For here we must not simply have recourse to propagation, since souls are not propagated or transmitted; nor to the law of nature, because diseased parents beget diseased children, since the soul is not begotten, and yet from the beginning of its existence it is deprived of those first benefits.

units.la: 3. Quia non bene comparatur qualitas physica in carne sola hærens, qualis est morbus aut lepra, cum qualitate morali, qualis est corruptio siue peccatum originale. Neque sequitur, si vere naturale est, vt leprosus leprosum, aut elephantiacus elephantiacum generet, vt putandum sit a sola natura propagationis esse, citra omnem respectum imputationis, quod ex Adam moraliter corrupto generantur homines moraliter itidem corrupti. Primum quod ait, rationem reddendam esse quare anima Adami iustitiæ originalis decoramentis ornata fuerit, ea ratio est in prompto: cum enim rationalis & capax iustitiæ esset, creari a Deo optimo expers iustitiæ & sanctitatis, hoc est, iniusta & immunda non potuit. Sed quare posterorum eius animæ eadem iustitia, cum producuntur non ornantur? etiam obuia est responsio, quia immundus Adamus mundum generare non potuit: genuit enim sibi similes. Quid opus est, vt tibi ratione reddâ,
units.tr: 3. Because a physical quality that inheres only in the flesh, such as disease or leprosy, is not fitly compared with a moral quality, such as original corruption or sin. Nor does it follow, if it is truly natural that a leper begets a leper or an elephantiac begets an elephantiac, that it must be thought to arise from the nature of propagation alone, without any regard to imputation, that men morally corrupt are begotten from Adam, who was himself morally corrupted. As for the first point, that he says a reason must be given why Adam's soul was adorned with the ornaments of original justice, that reason is ready to hand: since it was rational and capable of justice, it could not have been created by the best God lacking justice and holiness, that is, unjust and unclean. But why are the souls of his posterity not adorned with the same justice when they are produced? The answer is also obvious: because unclean Adam could not beget clean offspring; for he begot children like himself. What need is there for me to give you a reason,

units.la: quare lupus lupum gignit? vt enim, inquit Galterus, lupi lupos generant, ita Adam peccator peccatores genuit:& vt luporum catuli lupinam ingluuiem non obscuris argumentis produnt, ita in infantibus quoque peccatum tunc quoque vires suas exerit, quando per aetatem opus adhuc nullum possunt perficere. At inquis, Hic non est simpliciter recurrendum ad propagationem, cum anima non propagentur aut traducantur. Ego vero publicae noštrae confessionis fidei non sum immemor. Art. 10. Nec putamus necessarium esse inquirere, quinam peccatum potsit ab vno ab alterum propagari. Praeclara sunt etiam Petri Martyris, vt alios omittam, haec verba. Res quidem, inquit, obscura est, & perdifficilis: eoque minus arbitror de ea esse laborandum. Nam cum peccatum ipsum originis extare, & ad posteros transmitti, verbum Dei luculentissime doceat, quamvis modum, & rationem, qua transfundatur non intelligamus, tamen veritati cedendum est: de modo autem qui difficulter sciri, & sine jactura ignorari potest, non nimis sollicite, atque anxie disputandum. Re vera constat, multa esse, quae, quomodo producta fuerint, ignoramus. Praestat modesta ignorantia audaci & incertae scientiae.
units.tr: Why does a wolf beget a wolf? "For just as wolves beget wolves, so Adam, a sinner, begot sinners," says Galterus, "and just as the whelps of wolves reveal their wolfish greed by no obscure signs, so too in infants sin exerts its strength even then, when by age they cannot yet perform any work." But you say, "Here we must not simply have recourse to propagation, since souls are not propagated or transmitted." I am indeed not unmindful of our public confession of faith. Art. 10: "Nor do we think it necessary to inquire how sin can be propagated from one to another." The words of Peter Martyr, to omit others, are also excellent: "The matter, indeed, is obscure and very difficult; therefore I think we should not labour over it the more. For while the Word of God most clearly teaches that original sin itself exists and is transmitted to posterity, however much we do not understand the manner and mode by which it is transfused, yet we must yield to the truth; but concerning the mode, which can be known with difficulty and can be left unknown without loss, we should not dispute too anxiously and worriedly." It is indeed certain that there are many things whose mode of production we do not know. Modest ignorance is better than bold and uncertain knowledge.

units.la: Sed quoniam nobis per Viri docti ratiocinationem non licet ita sobrie sapere, Peto, an peccatum haereditarium propagetur naturaliter, nec-ne? Propagatur, inquit, quia mundum ex immundo nemo elicerepotest, quia corruptus Adam corruptos genuit, quia Deus permisit labem illam a primis parentibus peccato contractam haerere in femine, & ad posteros promanare. Ita est, neque aliquis nostrum erit, qui non totum illud prolixissime largiatur. Hoc sane verissimum est, & aduersus Pelagianos ab omnibus orthodoxis constanter assertum.
units.tr: But since, by the reasoning of this learned man, we are not permitted to be so sober in our judgement, I ask: is hereditary sin propagated naturally or not? "It is propagated," he says, "because no one can draw a clean thing out of an unclean one; because corrupt Adam begot corrupt children; because God permitted that stain, contracted from sin by our first parents, to cling to the seed and to pass down to posterity. So it is, and there will be none of us who does not grant the whole of this most fully." This is certainly most true, and it has been constantly asserted by all orthodox writers against the Pelagians.

units.la: Considera ergo, Lector, quid possis respondere has ipsas D. Gariffolij, quibus nos oppugnat, rationes, in illam propagationem retorquenti. Quomodo propagatur peccatum hæreditarium, cùm animæ, quibus inhæret, non propagentur, aut traducantur? Non potes confugere ad legem naturæ, qua morbosi morbosos generant, quia anima non generatur, & tamen ab initio sui esse priuata est iustitiâ & corrupta. Quomodo etiam potest labes illa, cùm non fit qualitas physica, sed moralis hærere in femine? Aut ego vehementer fallor, aut non poteris his rationibus, quatenus simpliciter propagationem peccati impugnant, occurrere, quin eâdem operâ nos ab eis præstes immunes. Nam fi recurras ad imputationem, nihil proficies. Imputatio enim est actio non hominis generantis, sed Dei judicantis. Deinde, vult D. Gariffolius imputationem illam tunc fuisse factam, cùm primùm peccauit Adamus, diu antequam propagatio seu generatio fieret: vt quomodo propagationis naturalis pars aliqua dici possit, haud equidem intelligam. Quod fi per imputationem pœnæ irrogationem ob Adami peccatum intelligis, illa ipsa irrogatio Dei actio est, non autem naturæ aut hominis gignentis. Deinde illa pœna, quæ eadem peccatum est, vel producitur à gignente, vel non. Si producitur, redeunt superiores rationes, quomodo enim potest ab homine gignente produci peccatum in anima quæ ab eo non gignitur? Si non producitur, certè non propagatur. Vides ergo à D. Gariffolio propagationis peccati nomen retineri, rem verò fignificatam tolli. Cùm igitur in confesso fit, peccatum per generationem carnalem propagari, juxta illud quod ex carne natum est, caro est; Et rationes illæ à Pelagianis aduersus orthodoxos centies sint objectæ, nihil opus est vt iis soluendis remoremur lectorem. Consuli possunt Augustinus, Martyr, Chamierus, alijque plurimi, qui de propagatione peccati diligenter scripserunt. Sic se habuit prima D. Gariffolij ratio.
units.tr: Consider then, reader, what you can answer to these very reasons of Master Gariffolius, with which he assails us, turning them back upon that propagation. How is hereditary sin propagated, when the souls in which it inheres are not propagated or transmitted? You cannot flee to the law of nature, by which the diseased beget the diseased, because the soul is not begotten, and yet from the beginning of its being it was deprived of righteousness and corrupted. How can that stain, since it is not a physical quality but a moral one, cling to the seed? Unless I am greatly mistaken, you will not be able, with these reasons, insofar as they simply attack the propagation of sin, to meet them without at the same time exempting us from them. For if you have recourse to imputation, you will achieve nothing. Imputation is the act not of the man who begets but of God who judges. Next, Master Gariffolius wants that imputation to have been made when Adam first sinned, long before propagation or generation took place; how any part of natural propagation can be said to be this, I certainly cannot understand. But if by the imputation of punishment for Adam's sin you mean the infliction of punishment, that infliction is itself an act of God, not of nature or of the begetting man. Next, that punishment, which is itself sin, is either produced by the begetter or it is not. If it is produced, the earlier reasons return: for how can sin be produced in a soul by a begetting man when the soul is not begotten by him? If it is not produced, then certainly it is not propagated. You see, then, that Master Gariffolius retains the name of propagation of sin while removing the thing signified. Since therefore it is agreed that sin is propagated through carnal generation, according to that saying, "that which is born of the flesh is flesh," and since those reasons have been objected by the Pelagians against the orthodox a hundred times, there is no need to detain the reader in solving them. Augustine, Martyr, Chamier, and very many others who have written diligently on the propagation of sin can be consulted. Thus stood the first reason of Master Gariffolius.

units.la: Adjungo, inquit, alteram. Etenim nisi ad imputationem confugias, eamque à Dei voluntate, iustoque iudicio dependentem, vix est, vt idonea ratio reddi possit, quare labes originalis peccati in naturales omnes Adami filios ab initio decurrerit, & vsque ad seculi finem d' manatura fit: sine, quare corruptio primi parentis, propagatione descendat in totam sobolem, potius quam peccata reliquorum parentum, quibus ortum nostrum non minus quam Adamo debemus, imo quos propinquius attingimus. Nam si ea est ipsius natura lex, vt corrupti corruptos generent, sicut leprosi generantur à leprosis, unde fit, vt parentes, qui peccatis variis se commaculant, inquinamenta illa peccatorum suorum non semper transmittant in liberos? Cur Adamus inobediens filios generat rebelles Deo, & natura contumaces? Et Achas idololatra non generat Ezechiam fili similem? Aut cur adulteri, ebriosi, prædones, non semper progignunt filios in eadem vitia præcipites? Aut cur vitium tam vetus propagetur, non propagantur recentiora, & quæ tanto temporis spatio non distant ab nobis? Aut cur denique corruptio ex primo peccato sobolescens seminatur, & quæ ex sequentibus Adami peccatis cumulari potuit, non deriuatur in posteros? Doctrinam imputationis reyce, harebit aqua, nec, quoquo te vertas, idoneam redditurus es eius differentiæ rationem. Doctrinam imputationis pone, crit tibi certa causa illius diuersitatis præ manibus; Nimirum discrimen inde procedit, quod primi parentis culpam voluit Deus in omnes imputatione transfire: aliorum parentum ita transfmitti non voluit. Eam veram & solidam & unicam ejus rei causam agnoscunt Theologi &c. Primum satis mirari nequeo viri docti ἀβλεψίαν, non animaduertentis, nos pariter à Dei voluntate hujus discriminis rationem petere posse. Quid enim facilius quàm respondere, ejusmodi esse omnis vitij contagium, vt instar pestis, vel veneni, vel fermenti sese diffundere & propagare possit, nisi Dei vel prouidentia vel gratia obicem ponat. Discrimen igitur inde procedere, quod primi parentis vitium Deus, quominus per carnalem generationem propagaretur, noluit impedire: Aliorum vero parentum alia vitia, ne similiter propagatione naturali multiplicarentur, inhibere voluit; vt in illo quæ peccati & naturæ; in his quæ Dei prouidentiæ & gratiæ vis effet, perspici posset. Quærenti ergo, vnde fit, vt parentes, qui peccatis variis sese commaculant, inquinamenta illa peccatorum suorum non semper transmittant in liberos? Respondeo verbis Petri Martyris, quia Deus modum præfixit, ne malum grassctur in immensum, & hanc mali propagationem suspendit. Cur Adamus inobediens filios generat rebelles Deo, & natura contumaces? Respondeo, quia Deus voluit permittere, hoc est, non impedire lapsum Adami & lapsus propagationem. Cur Achas idololatra non generat Ezechiam sibi similem? Quia Deus, qui Ezechiam elegerat, eum a paterna idololatria Spiritus sancti virtute liberauit. Cur adulteri, ebriosi, prædones, non semper gignunt filios in eadem vitia præcipites? Quia vitia illa, vel non propagantur impediente Dei prouidentia, quæ humani generis conseruationi proipicit, vel propagata tolluntur regenerationis gratia. Itaque vitium tam vetus propagatur, quia Deus noluit quominus propagaretur impedire: non propagantur recentiora, quia Deus voluit ne propagarentur impedire. Vno verbo, voluit permittere propagationem lapsus Adami, non aliorum peccatorum. Vides, opinor jam æquissime Lector, nobis aquam nullo modo hærere. Aliam ejusmodi discriminis rationem Placeus cum in Thesibus, tum in Manuscripto posteriore reddiderat abipsa primi Adæ peccati natura petitam, quæ suo loco ab exceptionibus D. Gariffolij Deo dante vindicabitur. Nunc enim mihi satis est ostendisse, quam ipse hujus discriminis rationem reddit, eam, non minus propagationi quam imputationi applicari posse: Est que nostra quàm eius causa melior. Nihil enim sic respondendo dicimus quod possit negari. Convenit enim inter nos propagari peccatum originale, non perpetuo propagari alia vitia, nihilque fieri posse Deo prorsus inscio & inuito. Ille vero sic respondendo, supponit imputationem antecedentem, quam nos negamus, & probare debebat, Deoque voluntatem sic imputandi primi Adæ peccati actualis tribuit: quam tamen voluntatem Deus neque per naturam, neque per Scripturam patefecit. Id quod peccato vacare non videtur. Adde quod, si rei illius vera & solida, & unica causa est Dei voluntas, cui sic libuit nobis omnibus primum Adami peccatum imputare; nec libuit aut sequentia Adami, aut aliorum parentum peccata imputare, fatendum est (id quod vehementissime refugit conscientia) veram & solidam & unicam causam cur simus peccatores & perditi, Dei voluntatem esse, contra oraculum, Ex te perditio tua ǵ Israël. Fateor equidem cum propagatione vitij originalis imputationem, nisi Dei misericordia intercedat, cohærere, sed ea imputatio sequitur propagationem, non antecedit, nec est vllo modo propagationis causa. At ponere imputationem, qua peccatum actuale Adami nostrum fiat, qua fiamus peccatores & rei mortis æternæ, quæ fit causa propagationis peccati, & hujus imputationis vnicam esse causam Dei voluntatem, quid est facere Deum perditionis nostræ autorem, si hoc non est? Sed fortasse exigebat justitia, vt Deus vellet primum illud peccatum imputare potius quàm alia peccata? Cur ergo, inquam, hanc causam non attulit? cur dixit illius rei vnicam esse causam, Dei voluntatem? Aut quomodo probabitur (nos enim nunc quidem respondentium partes tuemur) id justitiam exegisse? Si consugias ad conjunctionem quæ nobis cum Adamo intercedit, ea-ne major fuit cum primum peccaret quàm postea, aut cum eo, quàm cum propinquioribus nostris parentibus? Si ad nescio quoddam fœdus, cujus hæc fuerit conditio, vt si peccaret, primum eius peccatum omnibus eius posteris ad duas istas poenas imputaretur, peccatum inhærens & mortem æternam, probandum erit illud fœdus e Scriptura; id quod est prorsus impossibile. Cauendum est autem nobis quàm diligentissimè ne quid præter Scripturam Deo tribuamus, præsertim ejusmodi, quod virtutes eius obscuret; id enim non potest non graue peccatum esse.
units.tr: "I add another," he says. "For unless you flee to imputation, and make it depend on the will of God and his just judgement, it is hardly possible to give a suitable reason why the stain of original sin has run down from the beginning into all the natural sons of Adam and will flow on until the end of the world; in other words, why the corruption of the first parent descends by propagation into the whole offspring, rather than the sins of the other parents, to whom we owe our origin no less than to Adam, indeed whom we more closely touch. For if it is the very law of nature that the corrupt beget corrupt, as lepers are begotten by lepers, whence is it that parents who defile themselves with various sins do not always transmit those pollutions of their sins to their children? Why does disobedient Adam beget sons rebellious against God and stubborn by nature? And why does idolatrous Ahaz not beget a son like Hezekiah? Or why do adulterers, drunkards, and robbers not always beget sons who rush headlong into the same vices? Or why is so ancient a vice propagated, while more recent ones, which are not so far removed from us in time, are not propagated? Or why, finally, is the corruption that grew up from the first sin sown, while that which could have accumulated from Adam's later sins is not derived to posterity? Reject the doctrine of imputation, the water will stick, and whichever way you turn you will not be able to give a suitable account of that difference. Lay down the doctrine of imputation, and you will have a sure cause of that diversity at hand: namely, the difference proceeds from this, that God willed the guilt of the first parent to pass over to all by imputation; he did not will the guilt of other parents to be transmitted in this way. Theologians acknowledge this as the true, solid and sole cause of that matter, etc." First, I can scarcely wonder enough at the blindness [ἀβλεψίαν] of this learned man, who does not notice that we too can seek the reason for this difference from the will of God. For what is easier than to answer that every contagion of vice is of such a kind that, like a plague or poison or leaven, it can spread and propagate itself, unless God by his providence or grace places an obstacle? The difference therefore proceeds from this: God did not wish to prevent the vice of the first parent from being propagated by carnal generation; but he wished to restrain the other vices of other parents, lest they likewise be multiplied by natural propagation; so that in the one case the force of sin and of nature, and in the others the force of God's providence and grace, might be seen. To the question, then, why parents who defile themselves with various sins do not always transmit the pollutions of their sins to their children, I answer in the words of Peter Martyr: "God has fixed a limit, lest evil should spread without measure, and he suspends this propagation of evil." Why does disobedient Adam beget sons rebellious against God and stubborn by nature? I answer: because God willed to permit, that is, not to prevent, Adam's fall and the propagation of that fall. Why does idolatrous Ahaz not beget a son like himself, Hezekiah? Because God, who had chosen Hezekiah, freed him from his father's idolatry by the power of the Holy Spirit. Why do adulterers, drunkards and robbers not always beget sons who rush headlong into the same vices? Because those vices either are not propagated, God's providence, which looks after the preservation of the human race, preventing it, or, when propagated, they are removed by the grace of regeneration. Thus so ancient a vice is propagated because God did not will to prevent its propagation; more recent ones are not propagated because God willed to prevent their propagation. In one word, he willed to permit the propagation of Adam's fall, not that of other sins. I think you now see, most fair reader, that the water does not stick for us in any way. Placeus, both in his Theses and in his later manuscript, gave another reason for this difference, drawn from the very nature of the first sin of Adam; this, God willing, will be defended in its place against the objections of Master Gariffolius. For now it is enough for me to have shown that the reason he himself gives for this difference can be applied no less to propagation than to imputation; and our answer is better than his. For in answering thus we say nothing that can be denied. For we agree that original sin is propagated, but other vices are not perpetually propagated, and nothing can happen wholly without God's knowledge and against his will. But he, in answering thus, presupposes an antecedent imputation, which we deny, and ought to have proved it; and he attributes to God a will to impute the first sin of Adam in this way, which nevertheless God has revealed neither by nature nor by Scripture. This does not seem to be free of sin. Add that, if the will of God is the true, solid and sole cause of this matter, namely that it so pleased him to impute to all of us the first sin of Adam, and it did not please him to impute the later sins of Adam or the sins of other parents, it must be confessed (which conscience most vehemently shrinks from) that the will of God is the true, solid and sole cause why we are sinners and lost, contrary to the oracle, "Your destruction is from yourself, O Israel." I grant indeed that the imputation of original sin is bound up with its propagation, unless the mercy of God intervenes; but that imputation follows propagation, and does not precede it, nor is it in any way the cause of propagation. But to posit an imputation by which the actual sin of Adam becomes ours, by which we become sinners and liable to eternal death, and which is the cause of the propagation of sin, and to say that the sole cause of this imputation is the will of God, what is this but making God the author of our destruction, if it is not? But perhaps justice required that God should will to impute that first sin rather than other sins? Why then, I ask, did he not bring forward this cause? Why did he say that the sole cause of that matter is the will of God? Or how will it be proved (for we are now taking the part of those who answer) that justice required it? If you flee to the conjunction that we have with Adam, was that conjunction greater when he first sinned than afterwards, or when we were with him than when we were with our nearer parents? If you flee to I know not what covenant, the condition of which was that if he sinned, his first sin should be imputed to all his posterity for those two punishments, inherent sin and eternal death, it will have to be proved from Scripture that such a covenant exists; and that is utterly impossible. We must take the greatest care, however, not to attribute to God anything beyond Scripture, especially something of such a kind as obscures his virtues; for this cannot but be a grave sin.

units.la: Hac ratione sic proposita Theologorum auxilium sibi adjungit, & Vitakerum, Chamierum, Sixtum senensem, & Bellarminum nominat. Nostros cur laudet non miror: ita enim in hac causa vsuenit, nouitatis suspicionem amoliendi causa: Sed cur Pontificios ? cur Bellarminum ? Nosne putauit eorum autoritate moueri posse ? Non arbitror: Sed suis rationibus coniungere voluit ad nos oppugnandos Bellarmini rationes. Eum enim dicit non contemnendis ad firmandam hanc sententiam rationibus fultum procedere in medium lib. 5. de Amiff. Grat. & Stat. pecc. cap.18. Age igitur huius etiam soluamus rationes, eóque majore animo quòd fi quid intelligo, receptæ in Ecclesijs nostris doctrinæ de peccato originali non obscurè aduersantur. Nisi ponamus, inquit, nos in Adamo, & cum Adamo vere peccasse, nulla ratione explicari poterit, quomodo in parvulis recens natis fit aliqua vera culpa, & hoc Catholicum dogma, non tam supra rationem, quam contra rationem esse videbitur. Antequam progrediamur, quid est in & cum Adamo peccare ? Figuratam enim profecto locutionem esse oportet. Fortasse est nobis Adami peccatum imputari. Hoc posito, propositionem illam nego. Eam probat Bellarminus, Nam, inquit, quicquid dicamus in parvulis ex peccato haerere, sine reatum, sine auersionem, sine gratiæ priuationem, sine quid aliud; nullo modo parvulis vitio dari, ac ne esse quidem poterit, nisi processerit ab actione libera, cuius actionis illi aliquomodo participes fuerint. Nonne hoc est negare, vitium hæreditarium, infantibus inhærens, esse verè peccatum ijs damnandis sufficiens, vti nostra pronunciat Confessio Artic. xi. Sed pergat. Nam primò, reatus, cum sit relatio consequens actionem, qui fieri potest ut existat in eo, qui non est particeps actionis ? Valeret sanè hoc argumentum, si nullum esset peccatum nisi actuale, nullus reatus nisi proximè actionem consequens. Nunc autem est etiam peccatum habituale, & reatus. consequens habitum. Secundo ( recito enim has rationes vt apud D. Gariffolium extant) auersio habitualis , nisi praecesserit actualis , ne intelligi quidem potest. Hoc vero insigniter falsum est, si actualis auersio ipsorum paruulorum intelligitur. Alioqui quis negat auersionem actualem Adami praecessisse habitualem in ipso, & hanc esse in paruulos propagatam ? Prosecto auersio a Deo, in quocunque sit, hoc ipso quod est auersio a Deo , peccatum est. Tertio, fingamus paruulum aliquem habere auersionem & reatum , & tamen non peccasse cum Adamo, quis capere poterit, eum merito reprehendi, & puniri debere. Quam culpam habet in eo, quod ita generatus est ? Num impedire potuit, ne sic gigneretur ?
units.tr: Having set out the argument in this way, he calls in the help of the theologians: he names Whitaker, Chamier, Sixtus of Siena and Bellarmine. I am not surprised that he praises our own men, since that is the usual practice in this controversy, to remove the suspicion of novelty. But why the Papists, and why Bellarmine? Did he think that we could be moved by their authority? I do not think so. He wanted to join to his own reasons Bellarmine's arguments for attacking us. He says that Bellarmine comes forward with arguments that are not to be despised in support of this opinion, in book 5 of De amissione gratiae et statu peccati, chapter 18. Let us then answer these arguments too, and with more courage, because, so far as I understand, they plainly oppose the doctrine of original sin taught in our churches. "Unless we hold," he says, "that we sinned in Adam and with Adam, no account can be given of how there is any real guilt in newborn infants, and this Catholic dogma will seem not so much above reason as against reason." Before we go further, what does to sin in and with Adam mean? It must surely be a figurative expression. Perhaps it means that Adam's sin is imputed to us. Granting this, I deny the proposition. Bellarmine tries to prove it: "For, he says, whatever we say about sin clinging to infants, whether guilt, or aversion, or deprivation of grace, or anything else, it can in no way be a fault in infants, nor could it even exist, unless it had proceeded from a free act in which those infants in some way took part." Is this not to deny that hereditary vice, clinging to infants, is truly sin sufficient to condemn them, as our Confession declares in article 11? But let him go on. "First, guilt, since it is a relation following an action, how can it exist in one who did not take part in the action?" This argument would hold good if there were no sin except actual sin, and no guilt except guilt immediately following an action. But now there is also habitual sin, and guilt following a habit. "Second" (for I quote these arguments as they stand in Garrigou... in Gariffolius), "habitual aversion cannot even be understood unless actual aversion has gone before." But this is notably false, if the actual aversion of the infants themselves is meant. Otherwise, who denies that the actual aversion of Adam went before the habitual aversion in him, and that this has been propagated into his offspring? Surely aversion from God, in whomever it is, is sin for the very reason that it is aversion from God. "Third, let us suppose some infant to have aversion and guilt, and yet not to have sinned with Adam; who can grasp how he is rightly to be blamed and ought to be punished? What fault does he have in the fact that he was so begotten? Could he have prevented being so begotten?"

units.la: Ex mente D Gariffolij peccasse cum Adamo est peccatum imputari , & quidem imputatione vitium inhaerens antecedente: alioqui nos istae rationes non oppugnarent. Iam autem sublata ista imputatione, poteftne auersio a Deo, in quocunque sit, non digna esse reprehensione ? Culpa quidem eius non est quod ita generatus est, sed quod ita comparatus est, quod nequam, quod impius, quod Dei aduersarius est, haec est profecto magna culpa, non quidem, ut loquuntur, culpa actualis, sed tamen habitualis. Ab actuali inobedientia causa a qua est, extrinsece ; ab habituali vero subjectum in quo est, intrinsece denominatur inobediens. Non est igitur paruulus reus ab actione proximè sed ab habitu : non quia malam aliquam actionem commiserit , sed quia ipse malus est , & ad male agendum comparatus. Quarto, non satis est ad culpam, ut aliquid sit voluntarium habituali voluntate, sed requiritur, ut processerit ab actu etiam voluntario; alioqui voluntarium illud voluntate habituali naturale esset, & misericordia, non reprehensione dignum. Immò inquam, id satis est ad culpam habitualem. Non enim vitium originale dicitur voluntarium, quia est à voluntate, sed quia est in voluntate: illo modo voluntarius est actus, isto habitus: Nimirum vitium illud est ipsius voluntatis malitia & prauitas, à qua, licet naturalis sit, mala dicitur. Quo magis autem naturaliter mala est voluntas, eo est pejor, & odio dignior. Cæterum quis non videt has rationes posse retorqueri? Reatus enim est relatio consequens actionem eius cuius est reatus, non autem alterius: & habitus sequi solet actionem eius cuius est habitus, non autem actionem alterius: Et, Num impedire potuimus, aut debuimus ne peccaret Adamus? Et, quomodo est voluntarium respectu voluntatis nostræ, quod tanto tempore, antequam vllam haberemus voluntatem factum est? Et, facit-ne illa imputatio, vt peccatum illud actuale Adami processerit ab actu voluntario nostro? aut sumus-ne minùs necessario rei, quàm corrupti? Num sumus commeriti, vt tales gigneremur? Legantur Theologi nostri, aduersus vel Pelagium, vel Pighium, vel ipsum Bellarminum disputantes, præsertim cùm tractant controuersiam de peccato originali & concupiscentia, an sit peccatum, etiam post susceptum baptismum.
units.tr: According to the mind of Gariffolius, to have sinned with Adam is to have his sin imputed, and indeed imputed as an inherent vice that comes before; otherwise these arguments would not attack us. But now, if that imputation is removed, can aversion from God, in whomever it is, fail to be worthy of reproof? Its fault is not, to be sure, that he was so begotten, but that he was so constituted: that he is worthless, wicked, an adversary of God. This is certainly a great fault, not indeed, as they put it, an actual fault, but nonetheless a habitual one. A person is named disobedient from actual disobedience extrinsically, by the cause from which it comes; but from habitual disobedience he is named disobedient intrinsically, by the subject in which it is. The infant therefore is not guilty immediately from an act, but from a habit: not because he has committed some wicked act, but because he himself is wicked and disposed to act wickedly. "Fourth, it is not enough for guilt that something be voluntary with a habitual will; it is required that it proceed from an act that is also voluntary; otherwise that voluntary thing, being voluntary by a habitual will, would be natural and worthy of pity, not of reproof." But I say, on the contrary, that this is enough for habitual guilt. For original vice is not called voluntary because it comes from the will, but because it is in the will. An act is voluntary in the one way, a habit in the other. Indeed that vice is the very malice and perversity of the will itself, and it is called evil although it is natural. Yet the more naturally evil the will is, the worse it is and the more worthy of hatred. Moreover, who does not see that these arguments can be turned back upon their author? For guilt is a relation following the action of him whose guilt it is, and not of another; and a habit usually follows the action of him whose habit it is, and not the action of another. And: could we have prevented, or ought we to have prevented, Adam from sinning? And: how is that voluntary with respect to our will which was done long before we had any will at all? And: does that imputation make Adam's actual sin proceed from our voluntary act? Or are we less necessarily guilty than corrupted? Have we deserved to be begotten such? Let our theologians be read, when they dispute against Pelagius, or Pighius, or Bellarmine himself, especially when they treat the controversy about original sin and concupiscence, whether it is sin even after baptism has been received.

units.la: Superest vltima eius ratio ducta ab imputatione Iustitiæ Christi. Eam sic concipit. Quod doctrinam de imputatâ Christi justitiâ vel tonuellit, vel labefactat, neque admittendum, neque tolerandum est, sed amolendum omnino ac rejiciendum. Atqui dogmate de Non imputatione peccati Adæ, doctrinam de imputatione justitiæ Christi, non parùm labefactari certum est, cùm ex negatione prioris facillimus fit lapsus ad posterioris negationem. Nam cum in Christo tanquam secundo Adamo, remedium habeamus certissimum adversus ea mala & damna, quae sunt in genus humanum a primo Adamo inuecta; Remedium autem morbis, quibus sanandis paratum est, justa proportione respondere debeat; qui praeter natiuam corruptionem, nihil nos damni ex Adamo trahere existimabit, & huic corruptioni considerabit ex adverso respondere donum sanctificationis, facile in eam sententiam deveniet, cum nullus sit in nobis propter Adae inobedientiam reatus labe nostra originali prior, neque opus esse ulla justitiae Christi imputatione, quae sanctificationem ordine naturae praecedat: quia ubi nullum est malum, nullo etiam opus est remedio. Nego dogma de Non-imputatione peccati Adae antecedente seu immediata vllo molo doctrinâ de imputatione justitiae Christi labefactare; mihique valdè dolet, quod videam virum doctum, ut id probet, deserere doctrinam de corruptionis natiuae reatu, publicis fidei confessionibus Ecclesiarum protestantium declaratam, & confirmatam. Corruptio natiua duobus modis spectari potest: vno forensi, altero morali. Priori modo consideratur ut peccatum nobis damnandis sufficiens: Posteriori vero ut qualitas nos sua inhaerentia polluens. Quatenus est peccatum nos irae Dei addicens, ei respondet justificatio: quatenus vero est qualitas foeda nobis inhaerens, ei respondet sanctificatio. Tolli autem illa qualitas non potest, nisi prius tollatur ejus reatus. Itaque sanctificationem ordine naturae justificatio praecedit. Cum igitur corruptio duplicem illum respectum habeat, unum forensem; quo fit, ut, nisi condonetur, imputetur ad mortem; alterum moralem seu philofophicum, quo subjectum reddit habile ad peccandum, duplici nobis remedio opus fuit, imputatione justitiæ Christi, quæ mederetur reatui corruptionis, & vi Spiritus, qua è subjecto reuelleretur. Nonne orthodoxa est hæc doctrina, & ab omnibus prioribus Ecclesiis confessa? Miror igitur eam doctrinam à D. Gariffolio hoc loco fuisse negatam. Quanquam id non est admodum mirandum. Vix enim fieri poteft, quin in hunc scopulum incurrant ij, qui antecedentem imputationem probare student. Cæterum necessaria est imputatio iustitiæ non modò vt à reatu vitij inhærentis, verùm etiam vt ab omnibus aliis nostris peccatis justificemur. Id enim quod Deus gratificatur est ex multis lapsibus ad justificationem. Rom.5. 16. Possem etiam hanc rationem in suum autorem retorquere. Nam si vbi nullum est malum, nullo opus est remedio, & nullum sit malum, si nullus sit in nobis propter Adæ inobedientiam reatus labe nostra originali prior, & cur sit in nobis iste reatus vera & vnica causa est Dei voluntas, non intelligo quæ sit imputatæ justitiæ necessitas. Abstineat modò Deus ab imputatione primi Adæ peccati quemadmodum sibi temperat ab aliorum peccatorum, vel ipsius Adami, vel nostrorum majorum, imputatione, nullum erit malum, nec opus erit remedio. Nulla enim est causa, si D. Gariffolio fides habetur, cur Deus illud peccatum nobis potius quàm alia peccata, vel Adami, vel aliorum parentum, imputet, præter vnam eius voluntatem. Cùm ergo id pendeat ab eius voluntate vt imputet, vel non imputet, quid opus fuit, Christum tam dira pati, vt posset nobis illud peccatum non imputari? Possem etiam hoc loco contradictionem Domino Gariffolio objicere. Ait enim, si nullus sit reatus prior corruptione, non esse opus imputata Christi iustitia, & tamen alibi fatetur esse imputationem, & reatum corruptione posteriorem. Huic reatui qui corruptionem sequitur, quod justa proportione remedium respondet ?. sanctificatio ? non opponitur proprie reatui. Iustitia Christi imputata ? Haec igitur, posita imputatione consequente seu mediata, nobis necessaria est. Itaque non labefactatur a Placeo doctrina de justitia Christi imputata: agnoscit enim imputationem & reatum consequentem; atque adeo peccatum originale, & satisfactionis Christi necessitatem, nihilque habet cum erroribus Socinianorum, Arminianorum &c, conjunctum.
units.tr: There remains his last argument, drawn from the imputation of Christ's righteousness. He conceives it thus: "The doctrine of the imputed righteousness of Christ, whether it is shaken or weakened, is neither to be admitted nor tolerated, but must be removed and rejected altogether. But it is certain that by the dogma of the non-imputation of Adam's sin the doctrine of the imputation of Christ's righteousness is not a little weakened, since from the denial of the former the slide to the denial of the latter is very easy. For since in Christ, as the second Adam, we have a most certain remedy against those evils and losses which have been brought upon the human race by the first Adam; and since a remedy ought to correspond in just proportion to the diseases for whose healing it is prepared; whoever thinks that we derive no loss from Adam except native corruption, and considers that over against this corruption there stands the gift of sanctification, will easily come to that opinion, since there is in us no guilt, prior in order to our original stain, arising from Adam's disobedience, and there is no need of any imputation of Christ's righteousness, which would precede sanctification in the order of nature, because where there is no evil, there is no need of a remedy either." I deny that the dogma of the non-imputation of Adam's sin, whether antecedent or immediate, weakens in any way the doctrine of the imputation of Christ's righteousness; and it greatly grieves me that I see a learned man, in order to prove this, abandoning the doctrine of the guilt of native corruption, which has been declared and confirmed in the public confessions of faith of the Protestant churches. Native corruption can be regarded in two ways: in one, forensically; in the other, morally. In the first way it is considered as sin sufficient to condemn us; in the second, as a quality defiling us by its inherence. Insofar as it is sin binding us over to the wrath of God, justification answers to it; insofar as it is a foul quality inhering in us, sanctification answers to it. But that quality cannot be removed unless its guilt is first removed. Therefore justification precedes sanctification in the order of nature. Since corruption then has that twofold aspect, one forensic, whereby, unless it is forgiven, it is imputed to death; the other moral or philosophical, whereby it renders the subject apt to sin, we needed a twofold remedy: the imputation of Christ's righteousness, which heals the guilt of corruption, and the power of the Spirit, by which it is plucked out of the subject. Is this doctrine not orthodox, and confessed by all the earlier churches? I wonder, therefore, that Gariffolius denied it at this point. Yet this is not very surprising. For it is hardly possible that those who strive to prove an antecedent imputation should not run upon this rock. Moreover, the imputation of righteousness is necessary not only so that we may be justified from the guilt of inherent vice, but also from all our other sins. For that which God accepts is from many falls to justification. Rom. 5. 16. I could also turn this argument back upon its author. For if where there is no evil there is no need of a remedy, and if there is no evil, since there is in us no guilt prior in order to our original stain arising from Adam's disobedience, and if the true and only cause of why that guilt is in us is the will of God, I do not understand what the necessity of imputed righteousness is. Let God only abstain from imputing the first Adam's sin, just as He refrains from imputing the sins of others, whether of Adam himself or of our forebears, and there will be no evil, and there will be no need of a remedy. For, if Gariffolius is to be believed, there is no cause, apart from His one will, why God should impute that sin to us rather than other sins, either of Adam or of other parents. Since this therefore depends on His will to impute or not to impute, what need was there for Christ to suffer such dreadful things, so that that sin might not be imputed to us? I could also here object a contradiction to Master Gariffolius. For he says that if there is no guilt prior to corruption, there is no need of the imputed righteousness of Christ; and yet elsewhere he confesses that there is an imputation, and a guilt that comes after corruption. To this guilt, which follows corruption, what remedy corresponds in just proportion? Sanctification? It is not properly opposed to guilt. The imputed righteousness of Christ? This, then, on the supposition of a consequent or mediate imputation, is necessary to us. Therefore the doctrine of the imputed righteousness of Christ is not weakened by Placaeus: for he acknowledges both imputation and consequent guilt, and thus original sin and the necessity of Christ's satisfaction, and he has nothing in common with the errors of the Socinians, Arminians, etc.

units.la: CAPVT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: A Pelagianorum, Socinianorum, & Remonstran- tium in hoc negotio sententia Placeum esse alienum.
units.tr: The opinion of the Pelagians, Socinians and Remonstrants in this matter is foreign to Placeus.

units.la: VT nos reddat exosos, & grauissimis obruat praejudiciis, dolet nos cum Pelagianis & Socinistis patria facere. Sed dolendi causa nulla est: Nam ab hujusmodi hominum erroribus abhorremus, ut qui maxime.
units.tr: So that he may make us hateful and overwhelm us with the gravest prejudices, he complains that we make common cause with the Pelagians and Socinians. But there is no reason for complaint. For we shrink from the errors of such men as much as anyone.

units.la: Vetustissimorum, addit, haereticorum (Marcionitas puto, & Manichaeos, qui legem artiquam malam esse summa cum impietate afferebant) sententia fuit, nullam esse posse justam alieni peccati imputationem. Quid hoc ad rem? Nos-ne idem cum illis hæreticis sentimus ? Imò eis contradicimus. Aliquam enim esse posse justam alieni peccati imputationem credimus, & docemus; ipfiusque primi Adæ peccati imputationem admittimus consequentem seu mediatam. Adde quod non in ea sententia, sed in dogmate, quod inde probare satagebant, absurdissimo eorum sita erat hæresis. Itaque quos duos testes laudat D. G. Origenem hom. 8. in Exod. & Hieronymum Comm. in Ezech. xviii. 1. 2. eos ambos laudat contra se. Cùm enim Origenes protulisset illa verba, quæ D. G. recitat. Videamus quomodo reddi dicantur peccata patrum in filios in tertiam & quartam generationem. In hoc enim sermone solent nos hæretici suggillare, quod non sit boni Dei sermo, qui pro peccatis alterius alterum plecti dicat. Respondet-ne, id quod D. G. respondisset, hoc minimè esse injustum ? Imò cùm injustum id putaret, miniméque Deum decere, confugit ad sensum metaphoricum, & per parentes intelligi voluit Diabolum & angelos eius, per filios ac primam generationem eos quos Diabolus immediatè seducit, per secundam eos qui ab his proximè seducuntur, per tertiam & quartam eos quos hi vel socios, vel administros peccati sibi adjungunt. Hos autem homines filios diaboli corripi & puniri in hoc seculo, vt seruentur: diabolorum verò, qui sunt eorum parentes, supplicium differri in futurum seculum. Ad Hieronymum autem quod attinet, eius quidem ea sunt verba, quæ D. G. laudat. Sed quomodo nodum illum soluit ? quomodo verba Decalogi, qui reddo peccata patrum super filios &c. interpretatur ? Num ea, sicut D. G. de imputatione immediata accipit ? Nullo modo. Scandalum, inquit ibidem, patiebamur occultum, quod injustitia videretur Dei, alium peccare, & alium luere peccata. Si enim reddit peccata patrum super filios in tertiam & quartam generationem, injustum videtur ut alius peccet & alius puniatur. Sed ex eo quod sequitur: His qui me oderunt, comminationis sine praecepti scandalum soluitur. Non enim ideo puniuntur in tertia & in quarta generatione: quia deliquerunt patres eorum: cum patres potius qui fuerunt peccatores, puniri debuerint: sed quia patrum extiterunt aemulatores & oderunt Deum, haereditario malo & impietate in ramos quoque de radice crescente. Quid potuit dici nostrae sententiae accommodatius? Habet idem Hieronymus paulo post haec verba. Scriptum est in Proverbiis: Sicut vna acerba dentibus noxia est: & fumus oculis: sic iniquitas his qui vtuntur ea. Ex quo perspicuum est non aliorum dolere dentes & obstupere, sed eorum qui vnam acerbam comederint. Est autem loci istius hic sensus: Quomodo si quis velit dicere: Patres vnam acerbam comederunt, & dentes filiorum obstupuerunt: ridiculum est, & nullam habens consequentiam: sic iniquum est atque perversum peccare patres, & filios nepotesque cruciari. Quid contra imputationem antecedentem dici potuit difertius?
units.tr: He adds that the opinion of the most ancient heretics (I think the Marcionites and the Manichaeans, who asserted with the utmost impiety that the ancient law was evil) was that no just imputation of another's sin can be possible. What has this to do with the matter? Do we hold the same view as those heretics? On the contrary, we contradict them. For we believe and teach that some just imputation of another's sin is possible, and we admit the consequent or mediate imputation of the sin of the first Adam itself. Moreover, the heresy did not lie in that opinion but in the most absurd dogma which they tried to prove from it. So the two witnesses whom D. G. cites, Origen (Homily 8 on Exodus) and Jerome (Commentary on Ezekiel 18), both praise him against himself. For when Origen had brought forward the words which D. G. recites, "Let us see how the sins of the fathers are said to be rendered upon the children unto the third and fourth generation. For in this discourse heretics are accustomed to taunt us, that it is not the word of a good God, who says that one is punished for the sins of another." does he answer as D. G. would have answered, that this is by no means unjust? On the contrary, since he thought it unjust and unworthy of God, he takes refuge in a metaphorical sense, and wants the parents to be understood as the Devil and his angels, the children and the first generation as those whom the Devil seduces directly, the second as those who are seduced immediately by these, and the third and fourth as those whom these join to themselves as partners or agents of sin. These men, the sons of the devil, are corrected and punished in this age so that they may be preserved, but the punishment of the devils, who are their parents, is deferred to the age to come. As for Jerome, those are indeed his words which D. G. praises. But how does he loosen that knot? How does he interpret the words of the Decalogue, "who render the sins of the fathers upon the children etc."? Does he take them as D. G. takes them, of immediate imputation? By no means. "We were suffering," he says there, "a hidden scandal, that it would seem to be injustice in God for one to sin and another to pay for the sins. For if he renders the sins of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation, it seems unjust that one should sin and another be punished. But the scandal of a threat without a command is resolved by what follows: 'to those who hate me.' For they are not punished in the third and fourth generation because their fathers sinned, since rather the fathers, who were the sinners, ought to have been punished; but because they became imitators of their fathers and hated God, and the hereditary evil and impiety grew from the root into the branches also." What could have been said more suited to our view? The same Jerome says, a little after these words, "It is written in the Proverbs: As vinegar is hurtful to the teeth, and smoke to the eyes, so is iniquity to those who use it. From this it is plain that it is not the teeth of others that ache and are set on edge, but of those who have eaten the sour grape. The sense of that passage is this: as if someone should say, 'The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children's teeth were set on edge': it is ridiculous and has no consequence; so it is unfair and perverse for the fathers to sin and the sons and grandsons to be tormented." What could be said more plainly against antecedent imputation?

units.la: His ergo missis sibi non fauentibus accedit D. G. ad Pelagianos, & miratur Aegidij Hunnij ἀνισοφναν, pertendentis hanc fuisse Pelagianorum sententiam, Adami peccatum posteris imputari. Miratur etiam hallucinatum in eadem re virum doctum (Placeum designat) ita de hoc negotio in priuata quadam Epistola loquentem. Qui primi immediatam (nota immediatam: hanc enim solam, minime vero mediatam, Placeus constanter improbauit.) imputationem peccati Adae commenti sunt, ȳ Pelagiani fuerunt, qui hac ratione conati sunt anathematum aduersus Pelagium vibratorum impetum declinare. Negarunt enim corruptionem hereditariam, id est, originale peccatum: & ad praestringendos Ecclesiae oculos, hoc nomine donauerunt reatum imputati primi Adae peccati. Hoc D. G. falsum esse clamat. Fatetur tamen eos qui totam rationem peccati originalis sola imputatione peccati Adae definierunt, Pelagianis accensendos esse: sed accensendos, non quia imputationem posuerint, sed quia corruptionem negauerint, &c. Id quod Ægidij Hunnij & Placei sententiam confirmat potius quàm euertit. Non enim dogma de imputatione primi peccati immediata ipsi Pelagio aut omnibus Pelagianis ascripserunt: Sed illis duntaxat, qui cùm essent reuera Pelagiani, voluerunt non Pelagiani videri: quam ad rem inutile fuisset dogma de imputato Adae peccato, si id Pelagius aperte protulisset. Cùm enim viderent, qui negarent peccatum originale pro haereticis haberi, professi sunt se peccatum originale credere: sed hoc nomine non peccatum propagatum, ut reliqui omnes orthodoxi, sed peccatum actuale Adami omnibus imputatum intelligebant. Certe illi ipsi, qui aduersus Placeum imputationem immediatam vrgent, imprudentes quidem, sed tamen euitare non possunt, quin pelagianis accedant; vti jam in ipso D. Gariffolio aliquoties obseruaui. Posito enim peccato propagato seu inhaerente, quod vere peccatum sit, ac nobis damnandis sufficiat, quid opus est alio peccato nobis imputato? posita imputatione primi Adae peccati actualis mediata, quid opus est immediata? & quomodo potest immediata ex Scriptura probari?
units.tr: Having thus dismissed the witnesses who do not favour him, D. G. comes to the Pelagians, and marvels at the ἀνισοφναν of Aegidius Hunnius, who maintains that this was the opinion of the Pelagians, that the sin of Adam is imputed to posterity. He also marvels that a learned man (he means Placeus) has gone astray in the same matter, speaking thus about this question in a certain private letter: "Those who first devised the immediate (note immediate: for this alone, and by no means the mediate, Placeus consistently rejected) imputation of Adam's sin were Pelagians, who by this device tried to evade the blows of the anathemas hurled against Pelagius. For they denied hereditary corruption, that is, original sin; and to blind the eyes of the Church, they bestowed under this name the guilt of the imputed sin of the first Adam." D. G. cries out that this is false. Yet he admits that those who defined the whole account of original sin by the sole imputation of Adam's sin are to be counted among the Pelagians; but they are to be so counted not because they posited imputation, but because they denied corruption, and so on. This confirms the view of Hunnius and Placeus rather than overturning it. For they did not ascribe the dogma of the immediate imputation of the first sin to Pelagius himself or to all Pelagians, but only to those who, though they were in truth Pelagians, wished to seem not to be Pelagians. For it would have been useless for this purpose to have the dogma of Adam's imputed sin, if Pelagius had openly put it forward. For when those who denied original sin saw that they were regarded as heretics, they professed that they believed in original sin; but by this name they understood not transmitted sin, as all the other orthodox do, but the actual sin of Adam imputed to all. Certainly those very men who press immediate imputation against Placeus, though unwittingly, cannot avoid coming close to the Pelagians, as I have already observed more than once in the case of D. Gariffolius himself. For if transmitted or inherent sin is posited, which is truly sin and is sufficient for our damnation, what need is there of another sin imputed to us? If the mediate imputation of the actual sin of the first Adam is posited, what need is there of the immediate? And how can the immediate be proved from Scripture?

units.la: Hic D. Gariffolius multis verbis, ac prolatis aliquot testibus,confirmat Pelagium nullam imputationem Adamici peccati credidisse. Quorsum? nescio. Quis enim negat? An propterea Placeus paria facit cum Pelagio? Nonne Placei sententia Pelagianæ contradicit apertissimè? Pelagius omnem imputationem peccati Adæ damnabat, Placeus non omnem, sed immediatam duntaxat. Ille nullam imputationem peccati Adæ justam esse putabat, Placeus nonnullam esse arbitratur justam, nempe mediatam. Ille peccatum originale negabat, Placeus contrà peccatum originale confitetur & probat. Qui tantopere opponuntur, quomodo paria facere dicuntur? At negat Pelagius imputationem immediatam, quam etiam Placeus negat. At, inquam, in ea negatione nunquam sita fuit hæresis Pelagiana. Non quicquid aut negauit, aut affirmauit Pelagius, continuò hæreticum est. Percurramne illa omnia quæ D. Gariffolius Pelagianis tribuit § vi? Illi, inquit, 1. Iustitiam originalem deperditam fuisse negabant. Placeus contrà deperditam fuisse affirmat. Imo justitiam nullam originalem agnoscebat. Placeus justitiam originalem agnofcit. Sentiebant nos vt fine virtute sic fine vitio nasci. Sentit Placeus nos penitiffimè imbutos vitio nasci. Itaque infantes in illo statu esse in quo fuerat Adam anteprævaricationem. Itaque infantes non esse in eo statu in quo fuerat Adam ante præuaricationem, sed in multo deteriore. 2. Naturæ humanæ aliquam ab origine corruptionem inesse negabant. Placeus contrà affirmat. 3. Necessitatem moriendi non habebant pro pœna peccati, sed pro sequela & conditione naturæ. Docebant enim Adamum sine peccaffet, sine non peccaffet, moriturum. Placeus habet necessitatem moriendi pro necessitate subeundi poenam, non autem pro sequela & conditione naturæ. Docet enim Adamum, fi non peccaffet, non fuisse moriturum. 4. pœnæ æternæ infantes vllos damnari negabant, eas quippe non aliunde quam ex propria vniuscujusque injustitia prouenire. Placeus id non negat, quippe qui sciat poenas æternas etiam ex innata injustitia prouenire. Denique nullam omnino pœnam propter Adæ peccatum posteris irrogari putauerunt. Placeus contra aliquam poenam propter Adæ peccatum posteris irrogari putat, nempe mortem. Itaque imputationem agnoscit immediatam peccati Adæ habitualis propagati ac intra nos existentis, & mediatam peccati Adæ actualis extra nos olim producti. Vides igitur, Lector, Placeum nullo modo esse Pelagianum: Quorsum ergo D. G. hoc loco patientia lectoris ad id probandum quod nemo negat, Pelagium negasse imputationem peccati Adami, abutitur, ejusque errores enumerat, quasi illorum Placeus esset particeps?
units.tr: Here D. Gariffolius, with many words and several witnesses produced, confirms that Pelagius believed in no imputation of Adam's sin. To what end? I do not know. For who denies it? Does Placeus therefore make common cause with Pelagius? Does not Placeus's view contradict the Pelagian view most plainly? Pelagius condemned every imputation of Adam's sin; Placeus does not condemn every one, but only the immediate. Pelagius thought that no imputation of Adam's sin was just; Placeus thinks that some is just, namely the mediate. Pelagius denied original sin; Placeus, on the contrary, confesses and proves original sin. How can they be said to be alike, when they are so strongly opposed? But Pelagius denies immediate imputation, which Placeus also denies. But, I reply, the Pelagian heresy never lay in that denial. Whatever Pelagius either denied or affirmed is not immediately heretical. Shall I run through all those things which D. Gariffolius attributes to the Pelagians, §6? "They," he says, "1. Denied that original righteousness had been lost." Placeus, on the contrary, affirms that it was lost. "Indeed they recognised no original righteousness at all." Placeus recognises original righteousness. "They held that we are born without virtue, just as without vice." Placeus holds that we are born thoroughly steeped in vice. "Therefore infants are in that state in which Adam was before the transgression." Therefore infants are not in the state in which Adam was before the transgression, but in a much worse one. "2. They denied that there is any corruption inherent in human nature from its origin." Placeus affirms it. "3. They did not regard the necessity of dying as a punishment of sin, but as a consequence and condition of nature. For they taught that Adam would have died whether he had sinned or not." Placeus holds the necessity of dying to be the necessity of undergoing punishment, and not a consequence and condition of nature. For he teaches that Adam, if he had not sinned, would not have died. "4. They denied that any infants are damned to eternal punishments, since these come surely from nothing other than each one's own injustice." Placeus does not deny this, since he knows that eternal punishments also come from innate injustice. Finally, "they thought that no punishment at all is inflicted on posterity on account of Adam's sin." Placeus, on the contrary, thinks that some punishment is inflicted on posterity on account of Adam's sin, namely death. Therefore he recognises the immediate imputation of Adam's habitual sin, which is transmitted and exists within us, and the mediate imputation of Adam's actual sin, which was once produced outside us. You see then, reader, that Placeus is in no way a Pelagian. Why then does D. G., in this place, abuse the patience of the reader to prove what no one denies, that Pelagius denied the imputation of Adam's sin, and enumerates his errors as if Placeus were a partaker in them?

units.la: Interim quia obiter laudat ex Augustini opere imperfecto contra secundam Iuliani responsionem Lutetiæ edito anno hujus sæculi decimo septimo, locum, Qui, inquit, vel solus, si alius non extaret apud Augustinum, satis docet quid de hac imputatione & ipse & Ecclesia Catholica senserit, eum locum inspiciamus: Augustinus enim, si sibi constat, totus noster est. Quid est ergo quod clamas & dicis non posse Deum & dimittere peccata majoribus propter propria, & imputare parvulis aliena. (Videtur & delenda vox propter inutilis eo loco & incommoda, & sententia alio quodam modo laborare.Non dicebat enim Iulianus Deum non posse majoribus, hoc est, adultis propria dimittere peccata; sed dicebat non decere Deum, qui dimittit peccata majoribus propria, imputare paruulis aliena ) Nec vis attendere quod nonnisi in Christo renatis, vtraque; non renatis autem in Christo neutra dimittantur. ipsa sunt enim Christiana & gratia sacramenta abscondita sapientibus & prudentibus & reuelata paruulis. In quibus, o si esses, nec quasi magnus in tua virtute consideres profecto intelligeres, sic imputari generatis paruulis iniustitiam primi hominis ad subeundum supplicium, quemadmodum imput. tur paruulis regeneratis iustitia secundi hominis ad obtinendum regnum caelorum. Nobis hic locus minime nocet. Imputationem enim intelligit, quae generationem, atque adeo ingenitam corruptionem sequitur; cum imputatio, quam negamus, vt corruptionem sic generationem antecedere putetur; causa enim creditur esse, cur gignamur corrupti. Adde quod nihil prohibet per iniustitiam primi hominis, iniustitiam intelligere habitualem, quam ad paruulos primus homo per generationem transmisit. Certe enim cum Augustino obijceretur a Pelagianis, Qui fieri possit, vt Deus, qui pro sua bonitate nostra ipsorum peccata remittit, velit imputare aliena? Respondit, telte Martyre, Deum summe bonum esse, neque, quod isti assumunt, in culpa originis imputare nobis alienum peccatum, sed nostram ipsorum iniquitatem, quae nostra natura adhaeret iam inde ab ipsa origine. Addam aliud eiusdem Martyris de Augustino testimonium. Augustinus, inquit, in Enchiridio ad Laurentium capite 46. probabile ait esse, peccata et am proximorum parentum communicari cum filijs. Ad quod probandum componit inter se duo loca Scripturarum a nobis ante tractata: Quod Deus ait, se velle persequi peccata patrum in filios in tertiam, & quartam generationem : quum alio loco dicat, Filium non portaturum iniquitatem patris. Si filius, inquit, non portat iniquitatem patris, sed suam, & tamen Deus persequitur in eo peccatum patris, oportet, ut filius ipse peccatum illud in se habeat : Alioqui haec loca inter se non convenirent. Num haec dixisset Augustinus, si peccati paterni imputationem antecedentem seu immediatam credidisset, qua scilicet filius fit peccator & reus, alioqui non peccator, nec reus?
units.tr: Meanwhile, because he cites in passing a passage from Augustine's unfinished work against the second answer of Julian, published at Paris in the seventeenth year of this century, which alone, he says, if no other passage survived in Augustine, sufficiently shows what both he and the Catholic Church thought about this imputation; let us look at that passage: For Augustine, if he is consistent with himself, is wholly ours. What then is it you cry out, saying that God cannot forgive the sins of adults for their own sins, and impute the sins of others to infants? (The word propter seems to be superfluous and awkward in that place, and the sense seems to labour in some way. For Julian did not say that God cannot forgive the sins of adults, that is, of grown men, for their own sins; he said it was not fitting for God, who forgives the grown men their own sins, to impute the sins of others to infants.) Nor do you attend to the fact that both are forgiven only to those reborn in Christ, and neither to those not reborn in Christ. For these are the Christian and hidden sacraments of grace, which are hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to infants. If you were among them, and did not consider yourself great in your own strength, you would surely understand that the unrighteousness of the first man is so imputed to born infants, so that they undergo punishment, as the righteousness of the second man is imputed to reborn infants, so that they obtain the kingdom of heaven. This passage does us no harm at all. For it speaks of an imputation that follows generation, and therefore inborn corruption; whereas the imputation we deny is thought to precede corruption, as its cause, so that we are born corrupt. Add that nothing prevents us from understanding by the unrighteousness of the first man a habitual unrighteousness, which the first man transmitted to his infants by generation. Indeed, when the Pelagians objected to Augustine, How can it be that God, who for his goodness forgives our own sins, should wish to impute what is another's? he answered, as the martyr witnesses, that God is the highest good, and does not, as they assume, impute to us in the guilt of origin another's sin, but our own iniquity, which has clung to our nature from the very origin. I will add another testimony of the same martyr concerning Augustine. Augustine, he says, in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 46, says it is probable that the sins even of the nearest parents are communicated to their children. To prove this he sets side by side two passages of Scripture that we have treated before: that God says he will pursue the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation; and in another place he says that the son will not bear the iniquity of the father. If the son, he says, does not bear the iniquity of the father, but his own, and yet God pursues in him the sin of the father, it must be that the son himself has that sin in him; otherwise these passages would not agree with each other. Would Augustine have said this, if he had believed in an antecedent or immediate imputation of the father's sin, by which the son becomes a sinner and guilty, and otherwise is neither sinner nor guilty?

units.la: De Socinianis, cum nihil differant a Pelagianis, quid opus est dicere? Ad Arminianos autem quod spectat, ab eorum etiam erroribus, Dei beneficio, abhorret Placeus. Qui autem pro Clariss. Molineo Respondit Coruino doctissimus VValaeus, is non dubitavit imputationem immediatam disertis verbis negare, uti a nobis observatum est supra, pag. 22. nec propterea partibus Remonstrantium fauere exististimatur. Atque haec fuerunt argumenta D.Garissolij.
units.tr: As for the Socinians, since they differ in nothing from the Pelagians, why need I say more? As for the Arminians, Placaeus, by God's favour, shrinks from their errors too. But as for the most learned Walaeus, who answered Corvinus on behalf of the very distinguished Molineus, he did not hesitate to deny immediate imputation in plain words, as we have noted above, p. 22; and yet he is not thought on that account to favour the party of the Remonstrants. And these were the arguments of D. Garissolius.

units.la: CAPVT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Imputationem antecedentem seu immediatam non esse probatam argumentis Dom. Daubuz.
units.tr: That the immediate or antecedent imputation is not proved by the arguments of Mr. Daubuz.

units.la: VNA cum libro D.Garissolij prodijt ad eum Epistola & carmen propempticum Caroli Daubuz V.D.in Ecclesia Neracensi Ministri, quibus vehementer eum laudat, & in Placeum invehitur. Affert autem pro imputatione peccati Adamici argumenta eadem, sed verbis paulo diuersis. Orditur autem a foedere inito cum Adamo, idque supponit non probat : Aitque nos cum Adamo fuisse ; & vt cum eo, ac per eum agentes & consentientes, pari pœna plectendos. At, amabo te, quomodo cum Adamo fuimus, qui tunc nulli fuimus ? Prius enim est nos esse, quàm esse cum alio. Quomodo cum eo egimus ? Non enim agit nisi qui est, & quidem persona vel suppositum : actiones enim sunt suppositorum. Quomodo cum eo & per eum consensimus ? Est enim consensio nostra voluntatis nostræ, quatenus ab Adamo differimus, actio. Quod si hanc consensionem nihil aliud vult esse quàm corruptionem hæreditariam nobis ingenitam, ex ea nihil conficietur præter imputationem mediatam, quam Placeus probat. Addit pro ratione, Quandoquidem ex Iurisconsultorum placitis, qui per alium facit, per se ipsum facere videtur. At, inquam, id erat non supponendum sed probandum, Nos per Adamum id fecisse, quod fecit Adamus. Auscultauitne voci vxoris suæ loco nostro? nos ne illi fuimus autores vt peccaret ? aut peccauitne vt minister noster, nos vt causæ principales ?
units.tr: Together with Mr. Garissolius' book there appeared a letter and a valedictory poem to him by Charles Daubuz, a learned man and minister of the church at Nérac, in which he praises Garissolius highly and attacks Placaeus. He offers the same arguments for the imputation of Adam's sin, though in somewhat different words. He begins from the covenant made with Adam, which he assumes without proving, and says that we were with Adam, and as with him, and acting and consenting through him, we are to be punished with the same penalty. But, I beg you, how were we with Adam, when we were then nobody? For to be comes before to be with another. How did we act with him? Only someone who exists acts, and indeed a person or subsistent being, for actions belong to subsistent beings. How did we consent with him and through him? For our consent is an action of our will, insofar as we differ from Adam. But if he means by this consent nothing other than the hereditary corruption implanted in us, then nothing follows from it except mediate imputation, which Placaeus proves. He adds as a reason: since by the opinions of the jurists, one who acts through another is seen to act himself. But, I reply, this was not to be assumed but proved: that we did through Adam what Adam did. Did he listen to his wife's voice in our place? Were we the authors of her urging him to sin? Or did he sin as our minister, and we as the principal causes?

units.la: Sed his missis argumentatur ex Scriptura, & primò ex verbis ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον. Peccauimus, inquit, in Adamo, Ergo illius peccati participes, rei; ergo imputabile iure, & imputatum delictum illud. Primùm esto, imputetur, modò id fieri intelligatur mediante corruptione, quid hoc contra nos? Deinde, negò verba ἐφ' ᾧ verti debere in quo. Id probare conatur autoritate eorum qui sic verterunt, quibus nominatis concludit, Hinc patere, quàm præcipitanter, aut quàm ofcitanter non nemo scripserit, nec ἐφ' ᾧ verti debere in quo, sed eo quòd. Quæ accusatio vna cum Placeo eos omnes petit, qui maluerunt eo quod, vel quatenus, vel quoniam, &c, quàm in quo, vertere : qui haud dubie, si putassent verti|deberein quo, versionem illam retinuissent; si non putassent verti debereeo quod &c,noneo quod vertissent. Caeterū & nobis respondentibus satis est posse verti eo quod &c, & sic debere reddi probatum est supra pag. 70.& seqq. Denique, ut dicamur peccasse in Adamo satis est, si peccatum Adami causa fuerit peccati nostri, sicut eius esse nostri esse causa fuit.
units.tr: But setting these aside, he argues from Scripture, and first from the words ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον [eph' hō pantes hēmarton]. We sinned, he says, in Adam. Therefore we are partakers of that sin and guilty; therefore that offence is imputable by right and has been imputed. First, grant that it is imputed; but if this is understood as taking place through corruption, what is that against us? Next, I deny that the words ἐφ' ᾧ ought to be rendered in quo [in whom]. He tries to prove this by the authority of those who translated thus, and after naming them he concludes: From this it is evident how hastily, or how carelessly, certain people have written, and that ἐφ' ᾧ ought to be rendered not in quo but eo quod [because]. This accusation, together with Placaeus, strikes all those who preferred to translate it eo quod, or quatenus, or quoniam, and so on, rather than in quo. Undoubtedly, if they had thought it should be rendered in quo, they would have kept that rendering; and if they had not thought it should be rendered eo quod and so on, they would not have rendered it eo quod. Moreover, for our part it is enough that it can be rendered eo quod and so on, and that it ought to be so rendered has been shown above, on page 70 and following. Finally, for us to be said to have sinned in Adam, it is enough that Adam's sin was the cause of our sin, just as his being was the cause of our being.

units.la: Demus tamen, inquit Vir doctus, illud gratis, an eius loci vim penitus infringunt ? Nequaquam certe : nam illud τὸ peccarunt in infantibus verissimum, peccatum quoddam actuale designat evidenter. Hoc nego, negarunt que ante me plurimi viri maximi, inter quos Calvinus & Martyr : ac, si me decet recriminari, de peccato actuali illud peccarunt exponebant Pelagiani. At quod quaeso peccatum peccauerit infans in matris utero latens, in cunis vagiens ? Peccauit certe non actu sed habitu, non peccatum actuale sed originale. Originale quidem, inquit, habet, sed πασσιν πνεῦμα potius & subjectiue, quam ἐνεργητικῶς. Nimirum non est actio sed qualitas potius : sese enim habet admodum habitus. An propterea minus vere peccatum est, nos reatu, nisi condonetur, obstringens ? Ergo, addit, quod morimur a teneris annis, ab ipsis unguiculis : imo quod vix nati denascimur, ideo fit (& fatemur) quia peccauimus; at peccare nisi in Adamo tunc non potuimus. Quid est negare vitium originale esse vere peccatum toti generi humano damnando (ut habet art. xi. Confessionis Fidei) sufficiens, si hoc non est ? Causam profecto Pighij vir hic doctus agit imprudens. Quid enim? Annon ab ipso utero materno peccatores in nobis ipsis fumus ? inhaerente peccato inuoluti ac contaminati ? incredulitate, malitia, &c, penitus imbuti, ac propterea iustificationis & regenerationis gratia egentes? Si fateris, quomodo negas nos peccasse, nos esse peccatores in nobis ipsis? Si negas, ijsdem tecum argumentis agere necesse erit, quibus olim aduersus Pelagium, & superiore seculo aduersus Pighium disputatum est. Quod tamen subjungit, Illam mortem culpam actualem mediate saltem præsupponere, ambiguum est. Si culpam actualem habituali opponit, quid inde sequi potest, nisi culpam actualem Adami mediate nobis imputari? id quod damus libenter. Sin culpam actualem opponit potentiali, etiam peccatum originale culpa actualis dici potest: est enim in nobis non potestate sed actu, eiusque reatus eo sensu non minus actualis dici potest quàm reatus peccati actualis. Affirmanti igitur D. Daubuz, nec probanti oppono Theodoretum, Ad omnes homines mors pervasit, quatenus omnes peccaverunt: Non enim propter primi parentis peccatum: sed propter suum vnusquisque mortis decretum suscipit. Oppono etiam Augustinum, Propter hoc ergo vitium, sicut in eo libro cui respondis, à me scriptum est, humana natura damnatur, & propter quod damnatur, damnabili diabolo subjugatur, quia & ipse diabolus spiritus immundus est.
units.tr: Let us grant, however, says the learned man, that point gratis: do they in any way overturn the force of that passage? Certainly not: for that they sinned [ἥμαρτον] clearly refers, in infants, to a certain actual sin, which is most true. This I deny, and many very great men before me have denied it, among them Calvin and Martyr; and if I may return the accusation, the Pelagians used to explain that they sinned of actual sin. But, I ask, what sin could an infant have committed while lying hidden in the mother's womb, crying in the cradle? It certainly sinned not in act but in state: not an actual sin but an original one. Indeed it has original sin, he says, but it is πάσχων πνεῦμα [paschōn pneuma, a passive state] rather, and subjectively rather than ἐνεργητικῶς [energētikōs, actively]. Of course it is not an action but rather a quality: for it is in the manner of a habit. Is it therefore any less truly sin, binding us to guilt unless it is forgiven? Therefore, he adds, that we die from our tender years, from our very fingernails; indeed that, scarcely born, we die, this comes about (and we admit it) because we have sinned; but we could not have sinned then except in Adam. What is it to deny that original vice is truly sin, sufficient to condemn the whole human race (as article 11 of the Confession of Faith has it), if this is not so? Certainly this learned man, without realising it, pleads the cause of Pighius. For what? Are we not sinners in ourselves from the very maternal womb? Wrapped up and defiled by indwelling sin, thoroughly steeped in unbelief, malice, and so on, and therefore in need of the grace of justification and regeneration? If you admit this, how do you deny that we have sinned, that we are sinners in ourselves? If you deny it, it will be necessary to argue with the same arguments with which disputes were once waged against Pelagius and, in the last century, against Pighius. What he adds, however, that that death presupposes actual guilt at least mediately, is ambiguous. If he sets actual guilt against habitual guilt, what can follow from this except that Adam's actual guilt is imputed to us mediately? This we gladly grant.
