But if he sets actual guilt against potential guilt, then original sin too can be called actual guilt: for it is in us not in potency but in act, and its guilt in that sense can be called no less actual than the guilt of actual sin. Therefore, to Mr. Daubuz, who affirms but does not prove, I oppose Theodoret: Death has passed upon all men, inasmuch as all have sinned: for it is not on account of the sin of the first parent, but each one receives the sentence of death on account of his own. I also oppose Augustine: On account of this vice, therefore, as I have written in that book to which you reply, human nature is condemned, and on account of which it is condemned it is subjected to the damnable devil, since the devil himself is an unclean spirit.

units.la: Vt tam debili argumento colorem aliquem conciliet obuiam it cuidam responsioni Placei. In eo, inquit, quod addunt illi, quibus ab aduersis partibus hic stare placuit, & fallendo falluntur, & ne hilum quidem proficiunt. Non est, inquiunt, cur in Adamo aliter peccasse, quam suisse aut mori dicamur. O nodum ἀδιάλυτον! Atqui in Adamo fuimus dupliciter ἡσυχῶς & φυσικῶς, scilicet representatiue & naturaliter; & tota quidem natura humana, quacitra citra dubium fuit in Adamo (vt ait Thom. in cap. 5. ad Rom. Lect. 3. circa finem; Nos fuimus in Adamo secundum corpulentam substantiam & secundum seminalem rationem) & per personam peccauit in Adamo, rea fuit & culpa tunc commissa, & pœna futura. Primum non argumentatur Placeus, sed respondet. Est-ne igitur illud quod respondet verum, an falsum? Si verum, non fallendo fallitur. Si falsum, falsitas ostendenda fuit. Id quod à viro docto non fit. Latebat autem in responsione illa Placei duplex argumentum, unum ab existentia, alterum à morte. Illud sic potest concipi; Non aliter in Adamo peccasse quàm fuisse dicimur. Atqui in Adamo non dicimur fuisse imputative; eius enim esse nobis non imputatur: sed tantum eius esse in nos est propagatum. Ergo nec peccasse dicendi sumus in Adamo imputative, sed reali peccati eius per propagationem naturalem communicatione. Item sic; Non aliter in Adamo peccauimus quàm fuimus. Atqui non fuimus in Adamo proximè seu immediatè, sed mediantibus parentibus nostris intermediis ab eo propagatis. Ergo non peccauimus in Adamo proximè seu immediatè, sed mediantibus parentum nostrorum ab eo propagatis originalibus vitiis. Argumentum verò ductum à morte, sic potest formari. Non aliter in Adamo peccasse quàm mori dicimur. Sed morimur in Adamo, non imputata nobis Adami morte, sed morte reapse in nos propagata. Ergo peccauimus in Adamo, non imputato eius peccato, sed peccato reapse in nos propagato. Probat-ne, aut respondet aliquid Vir doctus, quod hujusmodi argumenta destruat, aut aliquomodo infirmet? Nihil prorsus. Negat-ne an fatetur, nos non aliter in Adamo peccasse, quàm fuisse, aut mori dicimur? Nescio. Tantùm ait nos fuisse in Adamo dupliciter, repraesentatiue & naturaliter. Aitne ergo, an negat esse Adami nobis imputari? Saltem explicasset quid sibi voluit illa distinctione; & an similiter peccauerimus in Adamo repraesentatiuè & naturaliter, ac itidem in eo dupliciter mortui simus! Probatne igitur duplicem illum modum? Nequaquam. Tantùm Reformatus apud Reformatum agens pro testimonio Scripturae, pro ratione, Thomam Aquinatem laudat dicentem, Nos fuisse in Adamo secundum corpulentam substantiam & secundum feminalem rationem. Hoccine est esse in Adamo dupliciter, repraesentatiuè scilicet & naturaliter? Et, an similiter peccauimus in Adamo? Illustrat tamen hoc similitudine, Et si quondam verè dixit ille, in uno Caesare plures inesse Marios, quàm verius nobis dicere licet, in uno Adamo peccante plures, imò omnes (excepto Christo ἀνθρώπῳ) fuisse Adamos. Quid potuit afferri minus appositum? Num inde potuit colligi, aliquam Caesaris actionem pluribus Marijs imputandam fuisse? Num fuerunt plures Marij repraesentatiuè & naturaliter, vel secundum corpulentam subsistantiam & feminalem rationem, in Caesare? Non miseret te mei, Lector prudentissime, cui cum talibus disputatoribus tanti momenti negotium est?
units.tr: In order to lend some colour to so weak an argument, he comes up against a certain reply of Placaeus: In that which those on the opposing side, who here have chosen to stand, add to him, they are both deceived in deceiving and gain not the least advantage. They say there is no reason why we should be said to have sinned in Adam otherwise than to have been, or to die. O indissoluble knot! And yet we were in Adam in two ways, [ἡσυχῶς, in two ways], representatively and naturally; and indeed the whole of human nature was undoubtedly in Adam (as Thomas says on chapter 5 of Romans, lecture 3, near the end: We were in Adam according to bodily substance and according to seminal reason), and through the person he sinned in Adam, and the guilt committed then and the penalty to come were ours. First, Placaeus does not argue this but replies to it. Is then what he replies true or false? If true, he is not deceived in deceiving. If false, its falsity ought to have been shown. This the learned man does not do. But there lay hidden in that reply of Placaeus a twofold argument, one from existence and the other from death. The first may be framed thus: We are said to have sinned in Adam only in the way we were in him. But we are not said to have been in Adam imputatively; for his being is not imputed to us, but only his being has been propagated into us. Therefore we are not to be said to have sinned in Adam imputatively, but by the real communication of his sin through natural propagation. Likewise thus: We did not sin in Adam otherwise than we were in him. But we were not in Adam proximately or immediately, but through our parents as intermediaries propagated from him. Therefore we did not sin in Adam proximately or immediately, but through the original vices of our parents propagated from him. The argument drawn from death, however, can be framed thus: We are said to have sinned in Adam only in the way we are said to die. But we die in Adam, not by Adam's death being imputed to us, but by death actually propagated into us. Therefore we sinned in Adam, not by his sin being imputed, but by sin actually propagated into us. Does the learned man prove or answer anything that destroys or in any way weakens arguments of this kind? Nothing at all. Does he deny or concede that we are said to have sinned in Adam only in the way we were or died in him? I do not know. He says only that we were in Adam in two ways, representatively and naturally. Does he therefore say, or deny, that Adam's being is imputed to us? At least he should have explained what he meant by that distinction, and whether we sinned in Adam in the same way representatively and naturally, and whether in him we likewise died in two ways! Does he therefore prove that twofold mode? By no means. He merely, a Reformed man arguing against Reformed opponents, cites for testimony of Scripture, and for reason, Thomas Aquinas saying: We were in Adam according to bodily substance and according to seminal reason. Is this what it is to be in Adam in two ways, that is, representatively and naturally? And did we sin in Adam in the same way? Yet he illustrates this by a comparison: And though that man once truly said that many Mariuses were in the one Caesar, it is truer for us to say that in the one sinning Adam there were many, indeed all (except Christ the man [ἀνθρώπῳ]), who were Adams. What could have been brought forward that was less to the point? Could it be inferred from this that some action of Caesar was to be imputed to many Mariuses? Were there many Mariuses representatively and naturally, or according to bodily substance and seminal reason, in Caesar? Do you not pity me, most prudent reader, who have such a weighty matter to dispute with such disputants?

units.la: Porrò, inquit, adeant illi Docti viri, qui nonnisi nimiā subtilitatis & scientiae opinione nunc errant. Erremusne, necne, tuum esto, quisquis haec legis, iudicium. Nobisne infit nimia subtilitatis & scientiae opinio, is novit qui corda scrutatur: Nos certè, quantum possumus, abiecta eiusmodi opinione, ab eo uno pendemus. Sed pergat, Adeant, inquam, consulant tribunalia iudieum, subsellia Iurisconsultorum. Annon actores publici, legati, tabelliones, & eiusmodi homines, quipro alijs stant, eos etiam absentes referant, ceu praesentes sistant, repraesentent, ut hoc, etsi ambiguo, nunc vtar verbo. Et quanto magis in hoc fœdere ὁ πρωτόπλαστος, pater, stirps, caput, actor totius generis humani, posteros omnes in publico & communi pacto repraesentauerit? Egregia consequentia! scilicet Adamus erat legatus nostep, aut tabellio noster! Erat saltem pater, stirps, caput nostrum, nimirum postquam nos genuit: antequam enim inciperet gignere profecto pater non fuit. Decet ergo nos potius adire oracula diuina clamantia, neque patrem filij, neque filium patris iniquitatem laturum.
units.tr: Moreover, he says, let them go to those learned men who now err only through an excessive opinion of their own subtlety and learning. Whether we err or not, let it be your judgment, reader, whoever you are who reads this. Whether there is an excessive opinion of subtlety and learning in us, he knows who searches the hearts. For our part, as far as we can, we set aside any such opinion and rely on him alone. But let him continue: Let them go, I say, and consult the courts of the judges, the benches of the jurists. Do not public prosecutors, envoys, notaries and such men, who stand for others, bring absent people before the court as if they were present, and represent them? I use the word "represent" here, though it is an ambiguous one. How much more, then, in this covenant, did the first-formed man, the father, stock, head and agent of the whole human race, represent all his posterity in a public and common pact! A fine inference! So Adam was our envoy, or our notary! At least he was our father, stock and head, since he begot us; for before he began to beget, he certainly was not a father. It is better for us, then, to go to the divine oracles, which cry out that the father shall not bear the son's iniquity, nor the son the father's.

units.la: Ad fœdus quod spectat, qualenam intelligit? Gratiæ? Legale? Non arbitror. Naturæ? Id quale intelligitur velim mihi exponi. Video enim duplicem latam fuisse Adamo legem: Vnam per signa naturaliter significantia, Alteram per signa ex instituto significantia; illam naturæ insitam, hanc verbo reuelatam. Sub illa fuit Adamus, quatenus homo ac mundi incola; sub hac vero, quatenus incola paradisi. Vtra fœdus illud fuit? Non ista, vt opinor. His enim verbis concepta fuit, De omni arbore horti comedendo comedes. De arbore vero scientiæ boni & mali non comedes ex ea: Nam quocunque die comederis ex ea moriendo morieris. Quæ lex nec fœderis præ se fert naturam, & tunc lata est Adamo, cum defectu vxoris (quæ supernaturaliter creanda erat) pater esse non posset. Dices illam legem toti generi humano latam fuisse. Omnino lata fuit toti generi humano quod tunc extabat: at non ei, quod neque erat, neque paradisi vnquam incola fuit. Fuerit tamen lata toti generi humano, num illius prima violatio actualis profecta ab vno homine, omnibus illius hominis posteris, à quibus violata non est, imputari debuit? Nonne lex Mosaica toti populo Israelitico lata fuit? Et tamen prima illius legis violatio non est omnibus posteris eorum, quibus primum lata est, imputata. Nonne foedus diuinitus cum Abrahamo percussum fuit? Idque pro se & semine suo Abrahamus accepit? Num ergo Abrahami actio vel una, vel plures, omnibus eius posteris imputatur? Estne quicquam in illa lege, unde eiusmodi imputatio elici possit? Non est ergo lex illa tale foedus, quod talem imputationem importet. Sed neque etiam huiusmodi foedus est lex seu foedus quod vulgo naturae appellatur. Sub ea quidem nascuntur omnes homines: Sed in ea nihil potest deprehendi, unde primi Adae peccati actualis antecedens seu immediata imputatio colligi possit. Non magis enim pertinent ad omnes homines eius comminationes quam mandata: Nec minus tenentur posteri Adami pro se quisque eam observare, quam tenebatur olim Adamus. Sed fortasse diutius, quam par est, in nudis assertionibus, ac, ut loquuntur principij petitionibus refellendis immoror.
units.tr: As for the covenant, what kind do they mean? A covenant of grace? A legal one? I do not think so. A covenant of nature? I should like to have it explained to me what kind of covenant that is understood to be. For I see that a twofold law was given to Adam: one through signs that signify naturally, and the other through signs that signify by institution; the former implanted in nature, the latter revealed in words. Under the former Adam stood as a man and an inhabitant of the world; under the latter, as an inhabitant of paradise. Which of these was that covenant? Not the former, I think. For it was framed in these words: Of every tree of the garden you shall freely eat. But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat of it: for in whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by dying. This law does not bear the nature of a covenant on its face, and it was given to Adam at a time when, for lack of a wife (who was yet to be created supernaturally), he could not be a father. You will say that this law was given to the whole human race. It was indeed given to the whole human race that then existed; but not to that which neither existed nor was ever an inhabitant of paradise. Yet even granting that it was given to the whole human race, should the first actual violation of it, committed by one man, be imputed to all that man's posterity, who did not violate it? Was not the Mosaic law given to the whole Israelite people? And yet the first violation of that law was not imputed to all their posterity, to whom it was first given. Was not a covenant struck with Abraham by God? And did Abraham not receive it for himself and his seed? Is then the action of Abraham, whether one or many, imputed to all his posterity? Is there anything in that law from which such an imputation could be drawn? That law, therefore, is not such a covenant as would imply such an imputation. But neither is that law or covenant which is commonly called the law of nature of this kind. Indeed, all men are born under it; but nothing can be discovered in it from which the antecedent or immediate imputation of the first Adam's actual sin could be inferred. Its threatenings pertain no more to all men than its commands do; nor are the posterity of Adam less bound each for himself to observe it than Adam himself was once bound. But perhaps I dwell longer than is fitting on bare assertions and, as they say, on refuting petitions of principle.

units.la: Transit ille Vir doctus ad verf. xix. Exeoque sic argumentatur. Constituti sumus peccatores per inobedientiam Adami; Ergo nobis imputata fuit. Mediante corruptione hereditaria, Concedo: Immediate, Nego. Videtur probare velle consequentiam. Nam qui quasi, inquit, illa παράβασις, illa ἁμάρτημα, illud παράπτωμα, nos potuit reos constituere, κρίμα, κατάκριμα Rom. verf.18. (quod quidem est actus iudiciarius, iustitiae Dei effatum, & essectum, damnatio, condemnatio) in nos inducere citra peccaNum actuale, vel proprium, vel imputatum? Apage hoc delirium. Facilis est responsio. Potest nos reos conftituere, vt loquitur Chamierus, causaliter, produćto & propagato in nos peccato originali. Neque id est delirium; sed constans Ecclesiæ doćtrina, quam veram esse Scriptura & experientia contestantur. Quomodo, subjungit, constitui peccatores, scilicet actu, fine peccato? Quod cum non possit esse originale, quippe quod tantum adhuc habituale, præsertim in recens conceptis aut natis, superest vt fit quoddam actuale peccatum. Refpondeo, constitui peccatores non fine peccato: nam peccatum originale est vere peccatum. At non est actu. Imo est actu peccatum habituale: actu inhæret infantibus: actu nos facit reos iræ diuinæ. Hoc fi negas, à Pighij opinione vix distas.
units.tr: That learned man passes on to verse 19 and reasons thus: We have been made sinners through the disobedience of Adam; therefore it was imputed to us. Through hereditary corruption, I grant; immediately, I deny. He seems to want to prove the consequence. For he who could, as he says, bring upon us, apart from actual or proper or imputed sin, those trespasses, that sin, that false step [παράβασις, ἁμάρτημα, παράπτωμα], to make us guilty, the judgment, the condemnation [κρίμα, κατάκριμα] (Rom. 18), which is indeed a judicial act, the effect and result of God's justice, a damnation and condemnation? Away with such madness. The answer is easy. Adam could make us guilty, as Chamier puts it, causally, the original sin having been produced and propagated in us. This is no madness, but the constant doctrine of the Church, which Scripture and experience attest to be true. How, he adds, can they be made sinners, namely in act, without sin? Since this cannot be original sin, being as yet only habitual, especially in those newly conceived or born, it remains that it must be some actual sin. I answer that men are made sinners not without sin, for original sin is truly sin. But it is not in act. Indeed, it is habitual sin in act: it actually inheres in infants; it actually makes us guilty before the wrath of God. If you deny this, you differ little from the opinion of Pighius.

units.la: Suggillat etiam nostram refponfionem, In reftam esse similitudinem oppofitionis, non in rei modo; ac dicit nos Socini potius quam Caluinipartes tueri: cum tamen ipse revera discedat à Caluino, cui nos arcte adhæremus. Quomodo autem illam refponfionem, quam supra & autoritate & ratione comprobauimus, refutat? petit, cur ergo noftrates iustificationis nostræ modum, nempe per imputationem iustitiæ Christi hinc eliciunt? Hæc est scilicet egregia refutandi ratio! Quinam vero sunt illi noftrates qui id hinc eliciunt? Caluinus? Martyr? Bucerus? Bullingerus &c? Nequaquam certe; sed recentiores, ab eorum vestigiis ea in re deflećtentes. At, inquit, non vident quantum communem causam lædant, qui hoc sibi inuićtum argumentum non solum cripi patiuntur, sed & nobis, vt aduersæ causæ faveant, quantum in eis situm est, eripiunt. Et fi cur hunc locum ita luxent, anquiramus, id in gratiam Pelagianorum, Arminianorum, Socinianorum, Anabaptistarum fieri certò comperiemus. Imò verò videmus quantum causam communem lædant, qui bene argumentari, vel nesc).iunt vel nolunt, argumentaque nullius roboris pro inuiditis obtrudunt, & interim fratres suos calumniis obruunt. Hoc certè & videmus & dolemus. Cætera prætermitto, nudas sine ratione affirmationes: illud tantùm subiungam, quod & speciem aliquam præ se fert argumenti, & quàm à publica fidei nostræ Confessione recedant & ad Pighianismum accedant illi qui nos accusant, prodit. Si peccatum, inquit, primi parentis non imputatur, quid opus imputatione meritorum Christi? Si vel peccatum originale intelligeret, vel imputationem mediatam, nihil diceret causæ, quam agimus repugnans, diceret tantùm aliquid salsum, & Theologo indignum, ne dicam Christiano. Opus enim nobis est imputatione iustitiæ Christi, ut etiam ab aliis peccatis nostris, quæ nimium multa sunt, iustificemur: Sed cùm peccatum actuale Adami intelligat, illiusque imputationem immediatam, quis non videt ab eo peccati originalis reatum negari? Idque peccatum, quantum ad condemnationem vel justificationem attinet, pro nullo haberi? Sufficit, addit, sanctificatio quæ tollat illum morbum. Est-ne igitur, inquam, ita morbus ut non sit peccatum? ut non damnet? Confer quæso cum hujusmodi hominum doctrina articulum xi. Confessionis fidei; Credimus hoc vitium esse verè peccatum, quod omnes & singulos homines, neparuulis quidem exceptis adhuc in utero matrum delitescentibus, æternæ mortis reos coram Deo peragit. Affirmamus quoque hoc vitium, etiam post baptismum esse verè peccatum, quod ad culpam attinet, quamvis qui filij Dei sunt, minime idcirco condemnentur, quoniam videlicet Deus pro gratuita sua bonitate & misericordia illud ipsis non imputat. Dicimus praeterea hanc peruersitatem semper edere fructus aliquos malitia & rebellionis, &c. Vides hoc vitium esse vere peccatum, omnes homines aeternae mortis reos coram Deo peragere, nisi condonetur, imputari, & negabis nobis opus esse imputatione meritorum Christi vt iustificemur ab hoc vitio? Ita qui nobis in hac causa aduersantur ejus culpae rei sunt, cujus nos falso accusant: discedunt enim à recepta doctrina. Quod ergo addit, & sic tota illa nostrae justificationis evangelicae doctrina, quam eximia, quam admiranda! ex horum ὑπομνήσεων aut corruet tota, aut saltem inutilis reddetur; cernis, vt opinor, Lector, quàm falsum & calumniosum sit.
units.tr: He also disparages our answer, which says that the likeness of opposition is correct, not only in the thing, and says that we defend the parts of Socinus rather than of Calvin; yet he himself in fact departs from Calvin, to whom we closely adhere. But how does he refute the answer which we above proved both by authority and by reason? He asks: why then do our people derive the manner of our justification from this, namely by the imputation of Christ's righteousness? This, forsooth, is an excellent method of refutation! But who are these "our people" who derive it from this? Calvin? Martyr? Bucer? Bullinger, etc.? Certainly not; but more recent writers, who in this matter have departed from their footsteps. But, he says, they do not see how greatly they harm the common cause, those who not only allow this invincible argument to be snatched from them, but also, as far as in them lies, snatch it from us, to favour the opposing cause. And if we ask why they so distort this passage, we shall surely find that it is done for the sake of the Pelagians, Arminians, Socinians and Anabaptists. Indeed, we do see how greatly they harm the common cause who either cannot or will not argue well, and who thrust arguments of no force upon the unwilling, and meanwhile overwhelm their brothers with calumnies. This indeed we both see and lament. I pass over the rest, bare assertions without reason; I shall add only this, which has some semblance of an argument and shows how far from our public Confession of faith those who accuse us depart, and how close they come to Pighianism. If the sin of the first parent is not imputed, he says, what need is there for the imputation of the merits of Christ? If he understood either original sin or mediate imputation, he would say nothing that conflicts with the cause we are pleading; he would only say something false and unworthy of a theologian, not to say of a Christian. For we need the imputation of Christ's righteousness so that we may be justified also from our other sins, which are far too many. But since he means the actual sin of Adam and its immediate imputation, who does not see that he thereby denies the guilt of original sin? And that this sin, so far as condemnation or justification is concerned, is held to be nothing? It is enough, he adds, that sanctification removes that disease. Is it then, I ask, such a disease that it is not sin? That it does not condemn? Please compare with the teaching of such men article xi of the Confession of faith: We believe that this vice is truly sin, which renders all and each men, not even the infants excepted who still lurk in the wombs of their mothers, guilty of eternal death before God. We affirm also that this vice, even after baptism, is truly sin as regards guilt, although those who are sons of God are by no means condemned for it, because God, out of his free goodness and mercy, does not impute it to them. We say moreover that this perversity always produces some fruits of malice and rebellion, etc. You see that this vice is truly sin, rendering all men guilty of eternal death before God unless it is forgiven, and imputed; and will you deny that we need the imputation of Christ's merits to be justified from this vice? Thus those who oppose us in this cause are guilty of the very thing of which they falsely accuse us: for they depart from the received doctrine. As for what he adds, and so that whole doctrine of our evangelical justification, how excellent, how admirable! will either collapse entirely, or at least be rendered useless by these remonstrances [ὑπομνήσεων]; you perceive, I think, reader, how false and calumnious this is.

units.la: Idem accidit Clarissimo viro D. Steph. Blanco, cujus Disputatio Theologica de animae humanae origine, & modo quo propagatur peccatum originale prodiit in lucem eodem anno 1648. Is enim Th. XLII. sic disputat. Omnes peccauerunt peccato scilicet illo, quod per vnum hominem introiit in mundum; at non peccauerunt peccato illo in sua persona, quia non extiterunt. Ergo peccauerunt in Adamo, quippe in quo mortui sunt 1. Cor. 15. 22. Quanquam enim admitti posset conclusio, si recte intelligeretur; tamen minor propositio nihil aliud esse videtur, quàm eius negatio, quod articulo illo XI. ab Ecclesiis nostris asseritur. Negat enim vitium illud esse peccatum quod per vnum hominem in mundum, id est, in omnes homines introiit, quod tamen vitium in illo articulo & vere peccatum esse, & omnes & singulos homines reos mortis aeternae coram Deo peragere dicitur; quod efficere non posset, nisi in omnes & singulos homines introiisset. Quod etiam subjungit, quippe in quo mortui sunt, confirmat noftram sententiam: non enim cùm in Adamo mori omnes dicuntur, mors ipsius Adami intelligitur, vna numero, omnibus imputata; sed mors secundum hominum numerum multiplicata, ac sua cuiq; propria.
units.tr: The same happens to the most distinguished man, D. Stephen Blanc, whose Theological Disputation on the origin of the human soul and the manner in which original sin is propagated came out in 1648. In Thesis XLII he argues thus: All sinned with that sin, namely the one that entered the world through one man; but they did not sin that sin in their own person, because they did not yet exist. Therefore they sinned in Adam, in whom indeed they died, 1 Cor. 15:22. Although the conclusion could be admitted if it were rightly understood, the minor premise seems to be nothing other than the denial of what is asserted in the eleventh article of our Churches. For he denies that the vice which entered the world through one man, that is, into all men, is sin, whereas in that article this vice is said to be truly sin, making all and each man guilty of eternal death before God; and this could not be brought about unless it had entered into all and each man. What he adds, in whom indeed they died, confirms our view: when all are said to die in Adam, the death meant is not the death of Adam himself, one in number, imputed to all, but death multiplied according to the number of men, and proper to each one.

units.la: Addit, & mortui vnius illius hominis offensa Rom. 5. 15. unde, inquit, promptum est colligere, illam offensam fuisse omnium offensam, puta imputatione: repugnat enim justitiæ diuinæ vt quis alienæ pœnæ fit particeps, & non fit vllo modo particeps culpæ. Si quis similiter diceret, nos fuisse productos vnius illius hominis operatione vel virtute, num inde sequeretur, illam operationem vel virtutem fuisse omnium communem imputatione? Si repugnat justitiæ diuinæ, vt quis alienæ pœnæ sit particeps, & non sit vllo modo particeps culpæ, certè eidem etiam justitiæ repugnat, vt fiat particeps culpæ judicis imputatione, is, qui alioqui non esset culpæ particeps. Si judex facit injustè ei pœnam irrogans, qui nullo modo est particeps culpæ, quanto major erit injustitia, si non modò pœnam irroget, sed eum faciat etiam sua actione & judiciaria imputatione participem culpæ, atque adeò peccatorem & reum, alioqui non peccatorem nec reum? Miror hoc à viris piis & doctis non considerari. Quis enim innocens puniri juste non poterit, si facit imputatio commune esse peccatum quod alioqui non fuisset commune, & esse verè peccatorem & reum, qui alioqui peccator non fuisset?
units.tr: He adds, And by the offence of that one man many died, Rom. 5:15. Whence, he says, it is easy to conclude that that offence was the offence of all, by imputation: for it is repugnant to divine justice that someone should partake of another's punishment and in no way partake of the guilt. If someone were similarly to say that we were produced by the operation or power of that one man, would it follow that that operation or power was common to all by imputation? If it is repugnant to divine justice that someone should partake of another's punishment and in no way partake of the guilt, then surely it is equally repugnant to that same justice that someone should be made a partaker of guilt by the judge's imputation when he otherwise would not have been a partaker of it. If a judge acts unjustly in inflicting punishment on one who in no way shares the guilt, how much greater the injustice if he not only inflicts the punishment but also, by his own act and judicial imputation, makes him a partaker of guilt, and so a sinner and guilty, when otherwise he would be neither? I marvel that pious and learned men do not consider this. For who could be justly punished as innocent, if imputation makes common a sin that otherwise would not have been common, and makes a man truly a sinner and guilty who otherwise would not have been a sinner?

units.la: Tandem, ait vir doctus, vox illa ἁμαρτία in loco Pauli non nonsignificat habitum peccati, seu habitualem corruptionem, quæ ipsis etiam infantibus inest, sed actum peccandi, cumque eumque praeteritum, quo non potest intelligi aliud praeter primum Adami peccatum. Hoc vero est Calvino & aliis viris maximis, quos sequimur, contradicere, illud peccauerunt de vitio originali exponentibus. Affert tamen rationes, Quia 1. inquit, loquitur Paulus de peccato quod introiit in mundum. 1. in omnes homines, per Adamum, quem vocat unum hominem. Supponit vitium originale, aut non esse peccatum, aut non introiisse in omnes homines per unum illum hominem naturaliter procreatos. 11. quia, hoc peccato inuoluuntur etiam infantes: sunt enim in censu hominum, & ex eorum numero, in quos mors transiit, nec moriuntur propter aliud peccatum actuale quam imputatum, quia aliud actuale in eos non cadit: actuale autem imputatum non est aliud praeter primum Adami peccatum. Non moriuntur quidem infantes propter aliud peccatum actuale quam primum illud Adami: sed cur non moriuntur proximè propter vitium illud habituale, quod omnes & singulos homines reos mortis æternæ coram Deo peragit? Hoc est quod jam non semel obseruaui, non posse imputationem immediatam primi Adæ peccati actualis aliter, nisi negato habitualis vitij reatu. 111. inquit, cum Paulus dicit verf. 17. mortem regnasse per unam offensam & verf. 19. multos esse constitutos peccatores unius hominis inobedientia; verba ista una offensa, & unius hominis inobedientia, non possunt aliud respicere quam ipsum factum Adami. 1. diuini mandati violationem. Esto, quid tum postea? Num inde sequitur; verbum ἁμαρτωλοί non significare habitum peccati? aut primum Adami peccatum actuale nobis imputari immediatè, seu prius quam nascamur corrupti? Mors regnat per unam offensam ita secundum habitum propagatam in omnes, vt in omnibus regnet mors, quia regnat peccatum. Vnius hominis inobedientia secundum habitum propagatá & multiplicata multi sunt constituti peccatores. Cur proximam mortis nostræ causam in alio quærimus, cùm se prodat ipsa in nobis, in corpore nostro, ac membris nostris, inhærens nempe illud peccatum, quod nisi crucifigatur gratia Christi; tam impotenter in nobis regnat?
units.tr: Finally, says the learned man, the word ἁμαρτία in Paul's passage does not signify the habit of sin, or habitual corruption, which is inherent even in infants, but the act of sinning, past, whichever it is, which can be understood as nothing other than the first sin of Adam. But this is to contradict Calvin and other very great men, whom we follow, who explain "they sinned" of original vice. He nevertheless offers reasons. (1) Paul speaks, he says, of the sin which entered the world, into all men, through Adam, whom he calls one man. He supposes that original vice is either not sin, or did not enter into all men through that one man naturally procreated. (2) Infants too are involved in this sin: for they are in the census of men, and among those into whom death passed; nor do they die on account of any other actual sin than an imputed one, since no other actual sin falls upon them; but an imputed actual sin is nothing other than the first sin of Adam. Indeed infants do not die on account of any other actual sin than that first sin of Adam; but why do they not die immediately on account of that habitual vice which makes all and each man guilty of eternal death before God? This is what I have already observed more than once: the immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin cannot be had except by denying the guilt of habitual vice. (3) When Paul says in verse 17 that death reigned through one offence, and in verse 19 that many were constituted sinners by the disobedience of one man, those words, one offence and the disobedience of one man, can refer to nothing other than the very deed of Adam, the violation of a divine command. Granted; what follows from this? Does it follow that the word sinners [ἁμαρτωλοί] does not signify a habit of sin? Or that the first actual sin of Adam is imputed to us immediately, before we are born corrupt? Death reigns through one offence, spread by habit into all, so that death reigns in all because sin reigns. The disobedience of one man, propagated and multiplied by habit, has constituted many sinners. Why do we seek the proximate cause of our death in another, when it reveals itself in us, in our body and our members, namely that sin dwelling within, which, unless it is crucified by the grace of Christ, reigns so powerfully in us?

units.la: Subjungit th. xliii. Mortem illam, quæ per vnum hominem in omnes homines pertransùt &c, includere sua significationis ambitu mortem spiritualem, scu animæ, quæ nihil aliud est, quàm priuatio justitiæ originalis cum positione contrariæ corruptionis habitualis &c: Hoc qua facilitate affirmatur, eâdem negari potest; itaque probandum erat: quod vir doctus ne conatur quidem. De sola corporis & æterna morte Confessio Heluetica,omnesque melioris notæ interpretes mortem illam accipiunt, esséque accipiendam probabitur alio loco. Quod subjicit, sine imputatione inobedientiæ Adami deriuationem habitualis naturæ humanæ corruptionis non posse esse justam, id quomodo verum esse possit considerare oportet. Deriuatio enim illa, cùm fit aliud nihil quàm contagium peccati & propagatio injustitiæ, ipsa per se justa non est, nec esse potest. Non enim justum est propagare & multiplicare injustitiam. Sed illius deriuationis permissio seu non impeditio diuina justa est, nihilque habet justitiæ repugnans. Quam adjungit rationem, Quâ enim justitiâ & æquitate sustineremus omnes illius peccati pœnam, nempe mortem spiritualem, si peccatum illud nobis non imputatur? Ea primùm supponit, id quod inter nos controuertitur, vitium originale nobis à Deo infligi, & esse pœnam propriedictam. Deinde imputatio peccati alieni, qua nostrum fiat, non tollit injustitiam; sed auget potius: quasi Deus æquissimus & sanctissimus omnibus hominibus primùm imputaret alienum peccatum, quò eos faceret imputatiuè peccatores & reos, deinde vt illud imputatum puniret eos faceret inhærenter peccatores. Ita vnum tantùm hominem Diabolus tentatione sua fecisset peccatorem, Deus sua actione, id est, imputatione, fecisset omnes homines peccatores & perditos. Quomodo fieri potest, vt pia conscientia tale dogma non detegetur?
units.tr: He adds in Thesis XLIII: That death which passed through one man into all men, etc., includes in the scope of its meaning spiritual death, or death of the soul, which is nothing other than privation of original righteousness together with the positing of the contrary habitual corruption, etc. With what ease this is affirmed, it can equally be denied; so it needed proof, which the learned man does not even attempt. The Helvetic Confession and all interpreters of better repute understand that death to be bodily and eternal death alone, and that it must be so understood will be shown in another place. As to what he adds, that without the imputation of Adam's disobedience the derivation of the habitual corruption of human nature cannot be just, we must consider how this could be true. For that derivation, since it is nothing other than the contagion of sin and the propagation of injustice, is not just in itself, nor can it be. For it is not just to propagate and multiply injustice. But the divine permission, or non-hindrance, of that derivation is just and has nothing repugnant to justice. As for the reason he adds: For by what justice and equity would we all sustain the punishment of that sin, namely spiritual death, if that sin is not imputed to us? First, this assumes what is disputed between us, that original vice is inflicted on us by God and is a punishment properly so called. Next, the imputation of another's sin, by which it becomes ours, does not remove injustice but rather increases it: as if the most equitable and most holy God first imputed the alien sin to all men, making them sinners and guilty by imputation, and then, in order to punish that imputed sin, made them sinners inherently. Thus the Devil by his temptation would have made one man a sinner, while God by his act, that is by imputation, would have made all men sinners and lost. How can it be that a pious conscience does not detect such a dogma?

units.la: Nihil amplius argumenti apud hunc autorem reperio, quod non fit jam satis refutatum, vt nihil opus sit inani repetitione fastidio esse Lectori. Tantùm, quod pené præterieram, illud sine aliqua censura dimittendum non videtur, quod ait Th.xli. Palam est, quicquid delinquit aliquis vt caput alicuius societatis, aut multitudinis, illud iustè toti communitati imputari. Nam si id verum est, malè omnino agebatur cum Romanis, cùm eorum caput esset Nero aut Caligula: quippe quibus omnibus & singulis iustè imputari poterat quicquid scelerati illi imperatores delinquebant: ita nullus erat in toto imperio Romano, qui non esset parricida, siquidem parricidium à capite commissum omnibus Romanis iustè imputabatur.
units.tr: I find nothing further of argument in this author that has not already been sufficiently refuted, so there is no need to weary the Reader with empty repetition. Only one point, which I had almost passed over, does not seem to be let go without some censure: what he says in Thesis XLI: It is plain that whatever wrong one commits as head of some society or multitude is rightly imputed to the whole community. For if that is true, things would have gone very badly for the Romans when their head was Nero or Caligula: for whatever those wicked emperors committed could justly be imputed to each and every one of them; so there would have been no one in the whole Roman empire who was not a parricide, since parricide committed by the head would have been justly imputed to all Romans.

units.la: CAPVT XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Nullam extare in Manuscriptis libellis rationem quæ peccati Adamici imputationem immedia- tam seu antecedentem probare possit.
units.tr: That the manuscript treatises contain no argument capable of proving the immediate or antecedent imputation of Adam's sin.

units.la: DE Argumentis typis excusis, quæ mihi legere contigit, dictum est, vt ego arbitror, satis. Manuscripta vidi complura: Sed in quibus nihil fere animaduerti, quod non legatur in scriptis Typographorum opera publicatis; si primum illud excipias, cui Placeus manuscripto illo respondit, quod D. Gariffolius posterius appellauit, &in quo refellendo magnam partem libri sui consumpsit. Quare nihil mihi videtur consultius, quàm vt manuscriptum illud Placei tibi, Lector, exhibeam (Cur enim in illis argumentis vel proponendis,vel refutandis operam meam ponerem, cùm id jam fuerit ab ipso Placeo præstitum?) ac, quando id refutare voluit D. Gariffolius, ejusque passim fruftula & lacinias transcripsit in suum librum, &, quantum potuit, confutauit, subjiciam singulis illis particulis viri illius reprehensiones, hisque ipsis Placei defensiones. Ita poteris, Lector æquissime, admodum facile, & citra errandi aleam, de tota hac causa cognoscere, & judicium ferre. id quod alioqui difficile, ne dicam impossibile, foret. Vix enim qua mente, quo sensu quidque dictum fuerit, bene perspici potest, cùm lacerae tantùm, & suis locis reuulsæ, ac veluti luxatæ & dissipatæ partes sermonis legenti offeruntur. Neque est quòd quisquam propterea offendatur. Si quid enim in eo scripto reprehensione dignum est, id in iis potissimùm partibus habere locum putandum est, quæ jam sunt à D. Gariffolio vulgatæ. Non eo quidem consilio à Placeo compositum fuerat vt ederetur, & ex nimia festinatione irrepsere fortasse nonnulla, si per otium licuisset autori, emendanda atque expolienda: tamen ne voculam quidem tollere, addere, aut mutare voluimus, ne quis de nostra fide vel synceritate conqueri posset. Qualecunque est, Tu æquissime Lector, illud æqui bonique consules, quodque ejus integri legendi, totiusque istius controuersiæ dijudicandæ copiam tibi facimus, aut habebis nobis gratiam, aut saltem non iniquo animo feres.
units.tr: I think I have said enough about the printed arguments that I have happened to read. I have seen several manuscripts, but in them I have found almost nothing that is not also found in the works the printers have published, except the first, to which Placeus replied in that manuscript, which D. Gariffolius later called the "posterior" one, and in refuting which he spent a large part of his book. It therefore seems to me most sensible to set before you, reader, that manuscript of Placeus itself. Why should I take the trouble to propose or refute those arguments, when Placeus has already done so himself? And since D. Gariffolius wanted to refute it, and has copied its scraps and shreds here and there into his book and answered them as well as he could, I will append to each of those passages the criticisms of that man and, in turn, Placeus's defences. In this way you, most fair reader, can learn the whole of this cause quite easily, without risk of error, and pass judgement, which would otherwise be difficult, not to say impossible. For it is hardly possible to grasp with what mind and in what sense anything was said when only torn fragments, pulled from their places and as it were dislocated and scattered, are presented to the reader. Nor should anyone take offence at this. For if there is anything in that writing deserving of censure, it must be supposed to lie chiefly in those parts which D. Gariffolius has already made public. Placeus did not compose it with the intention that it be published, and perhaps some things crept in through excessive haste, which the author would have emended and polished had he had leisure. Yet we have not wished to remove, add or change even the smallest word, lest anyone be able to complain of our good faith or sincerity. Whatever its quality, you, most fair reader, will take it in fair and good part; and since we are giving you the opportunity to read it whole and to judge this entire controversy, you will either be grateful to us or at least bear it without ill will.

units.la: MANVSCRIPTVM POSTERIVS, HOC EST, EXAMEN
units.tr: MANUSCRIPT SECOND, THAT IS, EXAMINATION

units.la: Tractatus singularis, De peccato originis, In quo demonstratur primum primi hominis peccatum omnibus hominibus imputari, oppositi Thesibus de statu hominis lapsi ante gratiam, disputatis Salmurij die 16. Martij An. 1640. sub Præsidio Josue Placei S.Theologiæ Professoris in Academia Salmuriensi.
units.tr: A Separate Treatise, On Original Sin, in which it is demonstrated that the first sin of the first man is imputed to all men, opposed to the Theses on the state of fallen man before grace, disputed at Saumur on 16 March 1640, under the presidency of Josue Placaeus, Professor of Sacred Theology in the Academy of Saumur.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Capita doctrinæ de Peccato originali de quibus inter nos conuenit.
units.tr: The heads of doctrine concerning original sin on which we agree.

units.la: LICEAT mihi, quæso, Vir reuerende, te, perinde ac si coram sermone res ageretur, compellare & alloqui : Sic enim, vti spero, tua, velut oculis meis obuersantis præsentia me torpentem excitabit, & ad tui majorem reuerentiam componet.
units.tr: Let me, I beg you, reverend sir, address you and speak to you as if the matter were being discussed face to face. In this way, I hope, your presence, as if standing before my eyes, will rouse me from my drowsiness and make me more mindful of showing you respect.

units.la: Tu quidem pro tua singulari prudentia voluisti tibi viam ad statum controuersiæ constituendum munire, præstratis iis de quibus inter nos conuenit. Quod tuum consilium valdè probo ; sed (quod cum tua bona venia dictum velim) visus es mihi neutrum præstitisse satis accuratè & enucleatè. Patere igitur vt vtrumque tuo exemplo faciam breuiter quidem, sed ita tamen, vt ab hac nostra amica collatione omnis, si fieri possit, tollatur confusio, omnis ambiguitas.
units.tr: For your part, with your characteristic good sense, you chose to prepare the way to fixing the state of the controversy by first setting out the points on which we agree. I greatly approve of that plan. But, with your good leave, I must say that you seemed to me to have done neither task with sufficient precision and clarity. Allow me, then, to do both briefly, following your example, but in such a way that, if possible, all confusion and all ambiguity may be removed from this friendly discussion of ours.

units.la: Ego arctè teneo, accuratèque defendo quicquid de peccato originali Ecclesia verè Christiana aduersus veteres nouosque Pelagianos, & Semipelagianos cum definiuit olim, tum his postremis seculis suis publicis confessionibus se credere professa est. Id autem vniuersum Daniel Chamierus, vir suo merito magni apud Ecclesias nostras nominis, statum controuersiæ inter nos & Pighium ac Salmeronem constituens ad tria capita reuocauit. Catholici, inquit, (Protestantes intelligit) certis argumentis docent, ipsi humanæ naturæ inesse corruptionem, seu prauitatem cuilibet homini propriam, aliam ab actibus peccati. Secundò, etiam nascenti homini cuilibet eandem inesse. Tertiò eandem ab Adamo ortum ducere, & per propagationem deriuari in posteros. Quamvis autem subjungat, hæc tria capita continere vniuersam peccati originalis naturam. Itaque iis demonstratis nihil fore reliqui factum; tamen vberioris explicationis causa duo addam: vnum, hanc corruptionem omnes animæ nostræ facultates ita depraualse, vt nisi ex aqua & Spiritu renati fuerimus, neque vllum fructum verè bonum proferre, neque ad Deum conuerti valeamus. Alterum, hanc corruptionem verè peccatum esse, omnes Adami posteros, solo Christo, in quo nunquam fuit, excepto, mortis æternæ reos peragens.
units.tr: I hold firmly and defend carefully whatever the truly Christian Church, against the old and new Pelagians and Semipelagians, has defined about original sin, and whatever it has professed in its public confessions in these later centuries. Daniel Chamier, a man of great reputation among our churches, set out the state of the controversy between us and Pighius and Salmeron, and reduced all of this to three heads. Catholics, he says, (by which he means Protestants) teach by sure arguments that a corruption or depravity belonging to every man is present in human nature itself, apart from the acts of sin. Second, that the same is present in every man at birth. Third, that it derives from Adam and is passed on by propagation to his posterity. Although he adds that these three heads contain the whole nature of original sin, so that once these are demonstrated nothing will remain to be done, still, for the sake of a fuller explanation, he adds two things: first, that this corruption has so depraved all the faculties of our soul that, unless we are born again of water and the Spirit, we can bring forth no truly good fruit and cannot turn to God; and second, that this corruption is truly sin, making all Adam's posterity, except Christ alone, in whom it never was, liable to eternal death.

units.la: GARISSOLIVS. Chamierus duo in Peccato originali manifestè distinguit, quòd pœna est peccati primi, & quòd vitium est internum in nobis hærens. Sed prius non veniebat in controuersiam cum Pighio, & aliis quos eo libro refutat; itaque eam considerationem non vrget hoc loco. Sed quærebatur tantum, an peccatum originale veram haberet rationem vitij & corruptionis. Affirmat Chamierus, & probat; Et peccatum originale considerans jam, qua vitium est, haud immeritò ejus naturam in illis tribus constituit.
units.tr: Garissolius. Chamier clearly distinguishes two things in original sin: that it is the punishment of the first sin, and that it is an internal vice clinging to us. But the former did not come into dispute with Pighius and the others whom he refutes in that book, so he does not press that consideration here. The only question was whether original sin has the true character of a vice and corruption. Chamier affirms this and proves it; and, considering original sin now insofar as it is a vice, he not unreasonably constitutes its nature in those three points.

units.la: PLACEVS. Quorsum spectet ista distinctio, nescio? Quis enim vnquam peccatum originale dixit esse duplex: vnum, pœnam peccati primi actualis, alterum, vitium inhærens; aut duas esse peccati originalis partes: vnam pœnam peccati primi, alteram peccatum internum in nobis hærens? Sed qui imputationem primi Adæ peccati actualis immediatam docent, illi, vel duplex esse dicunt peccatum originale: vnum imputatum, alterum inhærens; vel duas peccati originalis partes; primariam & præcipuam peccatum actuale Adami imputatum, minùs præcipuam corruptionem hæreditariam. In qua opinione si fuit Chamierus, quomodo in illis tribus, quæ commemorauit, vniuersam peccati originalis naturam contineri asseruit? Quomodo addidit; Itaque iis demonstratis nihil erit reliqui factum? Omisisset enim præcipuam peccati originalis partem. Adde quod si hæresis Pelagianæ in imputationis illius negatione pars sita fuit, vt voluit D. Garissolius, decuit Catholicos eam imputationem inprimis demonstrare, præsertim cùm à Stapletono, aliisque nonnullis Pontificiis, aperte negata fuisset. Sed de Chamiero, si opus erit, alibi disputabitur.
units.tr: PLACAEUS. I do not know what bearing that distinction has. For who has ever said that original sin is twofold: one, the punishment of the first actual sin, and the other, an inherent vice? Or that original sin has two parts: one the punishment of the first sin, and the other the internal sin clinging to us? But those who teach that the first actual sin of Adam is imputed immediately either say that original sin is twofold, one imputed and the other inherent, or they say that it has two parts: the primary and chief part is Adam's actual sin imputed, and the less principal part is hereditary corruption. If Chamier held that opinion, how could he assert that the whole nature of original sin is contained in those three points he mentioned? How could he add, "So, once these are demonstrated, nothing will remain to be done"? For he would then have omitted the chief part of original sin. Add to this that if the heresy of the Pelagians lay in the denial of that imputation, as Mr Garissolius wishes, Catholics ought above all to have demonstrated that imputation, especially since it had been openly denied by Stapleton and some other Papists. But if there is need, Chamier will be discussed elsewhere.

units.la: Tu quidem, obseruäde Symmysta, superiora credis. Sed de hoc vltimo quid sentis? Conceptum est verbis cofessionis Ecclesiarum noftrarū Art. xi. quæ tu ipse laudas Cap. vii. Credimus hoc vitium esse verè peccatum , quod omnes & singulos homines, ne parvulis quidem exceptis adhuc in utero matrum delitescentibus, aeterna mortis reos coram deo peragat. Affirmamus quoque hoc vitium, etiam post baptismum, esse vere peccatum, quod ad culpam attinet. Hoc ego ex animo credo ut sacris literis consentaneum, immo rationi, neque euerti potest, quin eo ipso thesium mearum quas oppugnas compactio & contextus luxetur. Tu vero num id credis ? videris tale quid affirmare Cap. 1. & 2. tui tractatus, & aliis aliquot locis: sed vereor ne ita loqueris occultandae opinionis tuae gratia: Id enim aliis quibusdam locis exserte negas, eaque negatione tanquam fundamento pars non contemnenda huius tuae disputationis nititur. Recognosce tua verba: non enim grauabor huc transferre. Cap. v. sic colligis, Vbi mors regnat, nec est reatus ex peccato proprio actuali, ibi necessario est imputatio reatus primi peccati. Item, mors regnauit in infantes. Ergo infantibus reatus primi peccati necessario fuit imputatus. Cum autem videres tibi responderi posse, reatum, in illis esse a vitio inhaerente & depravatione haereditaria, tu hanc responsionem cauillum appellasti, & contra sic conclusisti, si pueri in utero matrum, aut recens nati, sunt peccatores, idco sunt, vel quod actu peccauerint, vel quod primum peccatum primi parentis ipsis imputetur. Tertium siquidem dari non potest, quod illos constituat peccatores. Nam peccator quis dicitur ob peccatum; Nec vllum aliud peccatum potest imputari, nisi illud primum. Relege, si placet, quae sequuntur. Cap. ix. mentem tuam plenius aperis. Non video, inquis, quid sit peccatum originis si negetur ejusmodi imputatio. Potuisset-ne Pighius suam sententiam exprimere clarius? Subjicis rationem, nam qui-nam nam mors regnauit tunc in eos quoque qui non peccauerunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adam, si hoc peccatum Adami non fuit illis imputatum? Finge puerum recens natum vel in vtero ipso matris morientem, quid in illo est quod peccatum dici possit? voluntas in ipso ab omni actione vacat, nec potest propria voluntate peccare. Habet in se, inquies, feminā peccati, valeat, sed nondum peccatum proprie, nisi peccatum illud originis, quat: in Adamo peccauit. Ergo peccatum illius non in ipso, vel ex seipso, sed in prima origine, id est, in primo parente quærendum est: Nec est aliud peccatum illud quàm inobedientia illa voluntaria Adami &c. Tu igitur nullum peccatum originale agnoscis præter primum illud peccatum actuale Adami nobis imputatum, nullum reatum in infantibus præter eum qui immediatè ex illa imputatione existit. Quo ergò vel animo, vel sensu, corruptionem inhærentem modò simpliciter peccatum, modò cum epitheto peccatum originale appellas? sic enim in hanc tuam disputationem ambiguitatem & consusionem intulisti, noxiam mihi futuram nisi eam deprehendissem, ac, quod facio, sustulissem. Hic subit animum meum mirari, vir reuerende, qui, cùm tàm aperte à confessione Ecclesiæ nostræ abeas, potueris inducere in animum tuum, vt mihi, qui illi religiosè adhæreo, quasi ab ea desciuissem, grandem dicam scriberes. Dolet etiam mihi quod te aliis doctrina & sanctitate præluicentem, & quem ex animo diligo, tueri non possim vel ab inconstantia, vel à dissimulatione: ab inconstantia quidem si corruptionem inhærentem verè peccatum esse, reatum mortis æternæ ex sese fundeas modò sensisti, modò non sensisti; à dissimulatione verò, si cùm sentires constanter non esse peccatum, tu tamen peccatum esse aliquot locis dixisti & inculcasti, perinde ac si revera & proprie peccatum esse crederes, nec eo contentus, affirmasti inter nos ea de re nullam esse differentionem, cum te fugere non posset, non solum me, quem refutandum sumpseras, sed Ecclesias etiam nostras vitium illud formaliter & proprie, &, ut loquitur confessio fidei, vere peccatum esse statuere; & eos ipsos, qui tecum imputationem primi peccati vrgent, solitos esse peccatum originale in duo peccata dispescere, imputatum & inhaerens, ac suum utrique proprium Mortis aeternae reatum attribuere. Laudarem testimonia nisi libri omnibus noti essent, omnium triti manibus. Hic igitur aut consentis corruptionem haereditariam, sepposito peccato Adami imputato, esse vere peccatum damnando generi humano sufficiens, aut dissentis. Si consentis, revoca eas rationes & solutiones, quas in progressu hujus tui tractatus contrariae hypothesi superstruxisti. Si dissentis, haec erit inter me teque unum singularis controversia, quam libentissime suscipiam pro tuenda confessione Ecclesiarum nostrarum, quae mihi videtur verissima.
units.tr: You, fellow-initiate whom I respect, believe the earlier points. But what do you think about this last one? It is set out in the words of the confession of our Churches, Article 11, which you yourself praise in chapter 7: We believe that this vice is truly sin, which makes all and single men, not even infants excepted, still hidden in their mothers' wombs, liable to eternal death before God. We affirm also that this vice, even after baptism, is truly sin, so far as guilt is concerned. I sincerely believe this as agreeing with Holy Scripture and indeed with reason, and it cannot be overturned without dislocating the structure and connection of my theses, which you are attacking. But do you believe it too? You seem to affirm something of the kind in chapters 1 and 2 of your treatise, and in several other places; but I fear you speak so only to conceal your opinion. For in some other places you plainly deny it, and your denial serves as the foundation on which a not inconsiderable part of this disputation of yours rests. Let me recall your words, for I shall not hesitate to transfer them here. In chapter 5 you conclude thus: Where death reigns, and there is no guilt from one's own actual sin, there is necessarily imputation of the guilt of the first sin. Likewise: death reigned over infants. Therefore the guilt of the first sin was necessarily imputed to infants. But when you saw that it could be answered that the guilt in them comes from an inherent vice and hereditary depravity, you called this answer a cavil, and against it you concluded thus: if children in their mothers' wombs, or newly born, are sinners, they are so either because they have sinned actually or because the first sin of the first parent is imputed to them. For a third option cannot be given that would make them sinners. For a man is called a sinner because of sin; and no other sin can be imputed except that first one. Please reread what follows. In chapter 9 you open your mind more fully: I do not see, you say, what original sin is if such imputation is denied. Could Pighius have expressed his opinion more clearly? You add the reasoning: for how could death have reigned even over those who did not sin after the likeness of Adam's transgression, if that sin of Adam was not imputed to them? Imagine a child newly born, or dying in its mother's womb: what is there in it that can be called sin? The will in it is free from every act, nor can it sin by its own will. It has in itself, you will say, the seed of sin, be that as it may, but not yet sin properly, except that original sin by which it sinned in Adam. Therefore that sin is to be sought not in the child itself, nor from itself, but in the first origin, that is, in the first parent; and that sin is nothing other than Adam's voluntary disobedience, and so on. Therefore you acknowledge no original sin except that first actual sin of Adam imputed to us, and no guilt in infants except that which arises immediately from that imputation. With what intention, then, or in what sense do you sometimes call the inherent corruption simply sin, and sometimes original sin with an added epithet? For in this way you have introduced into your disputation an ambiguity and confusion, which would have been harmful to me had I not detected it and, as I am doing, removed it. Here, reverend sir, I am moved to wonder how, although you depart so openly from the confession of our Church, you could bring yourself to write of me, who adhere to it faithfully, as if I had revolted from it. I am also grieved that I cannot defend you, whom I dearly love and who surpass others in learning and holiness, against charges of inconsistency or of dissimulation. Inconsistency, if you at one time thought that inherent corruption is truly sin and that it derives from itself the guilt of eternal death, and at another time did not think so. Dissimulation, if, while you thought it was constantly not sin, you nevertheless said and insisted in several places that it is sin, as though you believed it really and properly to be sin; and not content with that, you asserted that between us there is no difference on this matter, when you could not escape notice that you were not merely opposing me, whom you had taken up to refute, but also setting our Churches against you in holding that vice formally and properly to be, as the confession of faith puts it, truly sin. You also set against yourself those very men who press the imputation of the first sin along with you, who are accustomed to divide original sin into two sins, imputed and inherent, and to assign to each its own proper guilt of eternal death. I would quote testimonies, were the books not known to all and worn thin in everyone's hands. Here, therefore, you either agree that hereditary corruption, apart from the imputed sin of Adam, is truly sin sufficient to condemn the human race, or you disagree. If you agree, retract those arguments and solutions which you built up against the contrary hypothesis in the course of this treatise of yours. If you disagree, this will be a single and distinct controversy between you and me, which I will take up most willingly in defence of the confession of our Churches, which seems to me most true.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: Status Quaestionis.
units.tr: Status Quaestionis.

units.la: VENIO nunc ad statum quaestionis. Eum non incommode constituisses si poenae nomini, quod in eam introduxisti, ambiguitatem vel non inclusisses, vel suffulisses. Enimvero poenae nomine corruptionem hæreditariam completi vel voluisti,vel noluisti. Si noluisti : debuisti id significare, alioqui erraturo lectori, quippe cùm hoc primo capite innuas, & secundo clames, & aliis inculces, corruptionem illam poenam esse primi peccati. Si voluisti ; vel putasti corruptionem illam esse poenam proprie dictam primi peccati, non solùm quatenus in ipso Adamo fuit, sed etiam quatenus inest in nobis ; vel non: Si prius, quæstionem non admitto : Præsupponit enim vt certum, vt inter nos confessum, id quod ego thesibus meis refutaui, quodque versatur in quæstione, nimirum corruptionem hæreditariam esse, proprie & strictè loquendo, poenam primi peccati, non solùm quatenus fuit in Adamo sed etiam quatenus nobis propagata inest. Si poenam quidem esse voluisti, sed non propriedictam, nec stricta hujus vocabuli significatione, saltem quatenus est in nobis, decuit te mentem tuam explicare, quoniam apparet ex multis hujus tui tractatus locis te corruptionem illam putare poenam esse sensu strictissimo, maximèque proprio. Misso igitur poenæ nomine, potuisses sic quæstionem instituisse sine vlla ambiguitate, Cur nascamur obnoxij miseriis hujus vitæ, morti corporis, & morti æternæ? an quia nobis imputetur proximè & immediatè primum peccatum actuale Adami? aut quia sine ejusmodi imputatione, vitiositas eius ab eo in nos deriuata est, & per propagationem naturalem transfusa? Tu prius affirmas, ego posterius. Vel sic, Cur trahimus ab Adamo corruptionem moralem hæreditariam, quæ peccatum originale dici solet? An quia nobis à Deo Iudice primum peccatum actuale Adami imputetur, ac in eius imputati poenam, vt vindicetur, & justitiæ satisfiat, infligatur illa corruptio moralis, quæ & ipsa peccatum est, & fons aliorum peccatorum? Aut vero quia, sine ejusmodi imputatione, hæc est naturæ lex ante peccatum constituta, vt sui quæque res similem gignat, homo hominem, corruptus corruptum, vitiosus vitiosum, leprosus leprosum? Tu rursus prius afferis, ego posterius. Quamvis autem status quæstionis, ita propositus accommodatè ad mentem tuam, non prorsus incommodus fit, nondum tamen mihi omni ex parte satisfacit: exprimit enim potius partes quæstionis, quàm ipsam quæstionem vniuersam.
units.tr: I now come to the state of the question. You would not have framed it badly if you had either left out the ambiguity of the word "punishment," which you introduced, or had at least guarded it. As it stands, you have either meant or not meant hereditary corruption to be included under the name of punishment. If you did not mean it, you ought to have said so, since otherwise the reader will be misled, given that in this first chapter you hint at it, in the second you proclaim it, and elsewhere you keep pressing it: that this corruption is the punishment of the first sin. If you did mean it, then either you thought that corruption is the punishment of Adam's first sin properly so called, not only as it was in Adam himself but also as it inheres in us; or you did not think so. If the former, I do not admit the question. For it presupposes as certain, as agreed between us, what I have refuted in my theses, and what is the very point in dispute: namely, that hereditary corruption is, properly and strictly speaking, the punishment of the first sin, not only as it was in Adam but also as it is transmitted to us and inheres in us. If you meant it to be a punishment, but not in the proper sense or the strict meaning of the word, at least as it is in us, you ought to have explained your meaning, since it appears from many passages of this treatise that you think that corruption is a punishment in the strictest and most proper sense. Setting aside, then, the word "punishment," you could have framed the question without any ambiguity thus: Why are we born subject to the miseries of this life, to bodily death and to eternal death? Is it because the first actual sin of Adam is imputed to us immediately and directly? Or is it because, without any such imputation, his viciousness was derived from him into us and passed on by natural propagation? You affirm the former, I the latter. Or again: Why do we draw from Adam that hereditary moral corruption which is commonly called original sin? Is it because the first actual sin of Adam is imputed to us by God the Judge, and that corruption, which is itself both sin and the source of other sins, is inflicted on us in punishment of that imputed sin, so that it may be avenged and justice satisfied? Or is it rather because, without any such imputation, this is the law of nature established before sin, that each thing begets its like: man begets man, the corrupt begets the corrupt, the vicious the vicious, the leprous the leprous? Again you assert the former, I the latter. Although the state of the question, as proposed in this way, is not altogether unsuitable to your mind, it does not yet fully satisfy me; for it sets forth parts of the question rather than the whole question itself.

units.la: Vt igitur, quando de mea sententia agitur, quid sentiam distinctè aperiam, atque statum quæstionis, quoad eius fieri à me poterit, dilucidè & enucleatè cõstituam, eam diuidam in duas, quarum altera est de imputatione primi peccati Adami, altera de pœna, qua imputatum vindicari dicitur. Quæritur enim primum, Vtrum primum peccatum Adami omnibus eius posteris, Christo excepto, imputetur? Deinde, Vtrùm corruptio hæreditaria nobis infligatur à Deo Iudice, vt fiat justitia?
units.tr: So, in order that, since my opinion is under discussion, I may state clearly what I think, and set out the state of the question as clearly and plainly as I can, I will divide it into two parts. One concerns the imputation of Adam's first sin, the other the punishment by which the imputed sin is said to be avenged. For first the question is: Is Adam's first sin imputed to all his posterity, Christ excepted? Then: Is hereditary corruption inflicted on us by God the Judge, so that justice may be done?

units.la: Priori quæstioni, quia laborat homonymia, non possum per simplicem affirmationem, aut negationem respondere. Distinguendum enim eius est cum subjectum, tum attributum. Subjectum est primum peccatum Adami: in quo duo distinguenda, Actio tam interna quàm externa, qua diuinum interdictum violauit, & Corruptio moralis, quam illa actio in Adami naturam intulit. Quæ corruptio ipsa quoque spectari potest duobus modis, vno vt fuit in Adamo; altero, vt est in nobis profecta ab Adamo. Hinc fit vt primum peccatum Adami vsurpetur quatuor modis. 1. pro actione qua dei legem est transgressus, quæ primum fuit peccatum actuale. 2. pro eadem illa actione non præcisè accepta, sed simul cum habituali corruptione quam peperit: habent enim se hæc duo velut calefactio & calor, actus & habitus, mutatio actualis & mutatio habitualis. Itaque vtrumque conjunctim idem nomen peccati Adami, vel primi peccati nonnunquam complectitur. 3. pro corruptione, quam actualis inobedientia genuit in Adamo, quæque fuit eius primum peccatum habituale. 4. denique pro eadem illa corruptione in nos transmissa & propagata, quæ nostrum quidem peccatum est, quia nobis inhæret, nos afficit, & denominat; dicitur tamen peccatum Adami vt authoris, vt primi veluti possessoris, vt fontis unde ad nos defluxit. Si hoc ultimo modo sumatur primum Adami peccatum, aio illud omnibus Adami posteris (uno, in quo locum nullum habuit, Christo excepto) imputari, donec ab eo per Christum justificentur, eorumque sententiam jure damnatam a Synodo Carentonensi arbitror, qui hoc quidem peccatum agnoscere se profitentur, nulli tamen imputari, quamtumvis infideli: esse enim hoc sæculo qui id doceant editis libris testatur & deplorat paulo ante obitum suum in quadam Epistola doctissimus VValæus. Similiter si tertio modo sumatur, fateor nobis imputari, non tamen qua hæsit in Adamo, sed qua in nos transiit, ac, ut verbis vtar Caluini, quia intra nos est: est enim nostra corruptio hæreditaria eadem specie cum illa, quæ olim fuit in Adamo; ac quàm suam naturam, tàm suam corruptionem moralem nobiscum Adamus communicauit. Idem de fecundo modo dicendum : quàm enim verè dicitur peccatum Adami in nos transiisse, deriuatum, transmissum, propagatum esse, tàm verè etiam dicitur nobis imputari.Propagatum est autem, non quâ fuit actio transiens, sed quâ fuit vitiofitas permanens, non quâ fuit peccatum personæ, sed quâ fuit peccatum naturæ, non quâ olim esse desijt in rerum natura, sed quâ naturæ humanæ adhæret, cumque ea multiplicatur & propagatur. Porrò vt natura mea propagata & deriuata ab Adamo differt numero à natura Adami, sic peccatum ab Adamo deriuatum & propagatum differt numero à peccato Adami. Hactenus, nisi me fallit animus, inter nos fummus est consensus, modò nolis negare corruptionem hæreditariam esse verè peccatum irregenitis imputabile, vel potius imputandum ad condemnationem. Quod si id neges, hæc tertia exorietur inter me & te controuerfia, quæ quamvis proprijs argumentis confici poterit, tamen ijs nihil opus erit: nam refutatis (quod feci in Thesibus) exceptionibus Socini, Pelagij, & Pighij, necesse est fateri, vniuersam illam condemnationem, quam Apostolus ad Rom.v.12. inculcat, ex sola illa corruptione, quæ à lapsu Adami fluxit, proximè enafci.
units.tr: I cannot answer the first question with a simple yes or no, because it is ambiguous. Its subject and its predicate must both be distinguished. The subject is Adam's first sin, in which two things must be distinguished: the action, both inward and outward, by which he violated the divine prohibition, and the moral corruption which that action brought into Adam's nature. This corruption itself may be considered in two ways: as it was in Adam, and as it has come from Adam into us. Hence Adam's first sin is used in four senses. (1) For the action by which he transgressed God's law, which was the first actual sin. (2) For that same action, not taken precisely, but together with the habitual corruption it produced; for these two stand to each other as heating and heat, act and habit, actual change and habitual change. So the name of Adam's sin, or of the first sin, sometimes embraces both together. (3) For the corruption which the actual disobedience produced in Adam, and which was his first habitual sin. (4) Lastly, for that same corruption transmitted and propagated into us, which is indeed our sin, because it inheres in us, affects us and characterises us; yet it is called Adam's sin as its author, as its first possessor, as the source from which it has flowed down to us. If Adam's first sin is taken in this last sense, I affirm that it is imputed to all Adam's posterity (save Christ, in whom it had no place) until they are justified from it through Christ. I think the Synod of Charenton rightly condemned those who profess to acknowledge this sin, yet deny that it is imputed to anyone, even to the unbelieving. That there are people in this age who teach this, the most learned Walaeus testifies and laments in his published books, and in a certain letter shortly before his death. Similarly, if it is taken in the third sense, I grant that it is imputed to us, not as it clung to Adam, but as it passed into us, and, to use Calvin's words, because it is within us. For our hereditary corruption is of the same kind as that which once existed in Adam; and Adam communicated to us his moral corruption just as he communicated his nature. The same must be said of the second sense. For just as truly as Adam's sin is said to have passed into us, to have been derived, transmitted and propagated, so truly is it also said to be imputed to us. It is propagated not as a transient action, but as a lasting viciousness; not as the sin of a person, but as the sin of nature; not as that which has ceased to exist in the world of things, but as that which clings to human nature and is multiplied and propagated with it. Moreover, just as my nature, propagated and derived from Adam, differs in number from Adam's nature, so sin derived and propagated from Adam differs in number from Adam's sin. Thus far, unless I am mistaken, there is the fullest agreement between us, provided you do not deny that hereditary corruption is truly sin, imputable to the unregenerate, or rather to be imputed to them for condemnation. But if you deny this, a third controversy will arise between you and me. This could be settled by its own arguments, yet none will be needed; for once the objections of Socinus, Pelagius and Pighius are refuted (as I did in my theses), it must be admitted that the whole condemnation, which the Apostle inculcates in Rom. v. 12, arises immediately from that corruption alone which flowed from Adam's fall.

units.la: PLAC. Has tres vltimas peccati Adamici acceptiones D. Gar. mirum in modum exagitat : qua mente? nescio. Nihil enim id juuat statum quæstionis, aut causam quam agit, & Lectorem inutiliter moratur. Quid enim in ea nominis distinctione reprehendit? Num eam falsitatis arguit? minimè. Num negat in ea re consensum esse? sequaquam. Quid ergo agit? ipsum audi.
units.tr: PLACAEUS. The Doctor Garissolius criticises these three last senses of Adam's sin in a remarkable manner. With what intent, I do not know. For this distinction of meanings contributes nothing to the state of the question or to the cause he is pursuing, and it detains the reader to no purpose. What does he find to blame in this distinction of the name? Does he charge it with falsehood? Not at all. Does he deny that there is agreement on this point? By no means. What then is he doing? Hear him for yourself.

units.la: GAR. Primùm quidem est, quod suam præstanti Theologo confessionem gratulemur, qui, etsi negat imputari posteris primam illam Ada actionem, qua Dei mandatum violauit, si eam pracisè ac seorsim spectemus; agnoscit tamen illam imputari, acceptam simul cum corruptione quam peperit. Hoc enim inde certò consequitur, ergo ipsam criminosam Adami actionem posteris imputari: quoniam quod simul & conjunctim cum alio spectatum imputatur, non eo tantum minùs imputari censendum est. Iam verò si Adami actio, non pracisè sumpta, sed simul cum corruptione consequenti, imputatur; nemo non videt, eas omnes rationes vna veluti litura expungendas, quibus aduersus actionis Adamica imputationem hactenus Viri Docti disputarunt. Illa enim omnes id efficiunt, si quid efficiunt, nos nullo modo esse posse reos propter inobedientiam & actionem injustam alterius nobis imputatam, sine pracisè, sine vna cum alio vel actu, vel habitu illam considerare libeat. Illud autem si fixum maneat, actionem Adami simul cum corruptione, quam peperit acceptam vnicuique posterorum imputari, pax facilè componetur.
units.tr: GARISSOLIUS. First, we congratulate our distinguished theologian on his confession. Although he denies that the first action of Adam, by which he violated God's command, is imputed to posterity, if we consider it precisely and in isolation, he nevertheless acknowledges that it is imputed when taken together with the corruption which it produced. For this follows with certainty: therefore the criminal action of Adam itself is imputed to posterity; since what is imputed when considered together and conjointly with another is not thereby to be judged less imputed. Now indeed, if Adam's action is imputed, not as taken precisely, but together with the corruption that follows, everyone sees that all those arguments which learned men have hitherto advanced against the imputation of Adam's action must be struck out, as it were with one stroke. For all those arguments, if they prove anything, prove that we cannot in any way be guilty on account of the disobedience and unjust action of another imputed to us, whether we consider that action precisely, or together with some act or habit of his. But if this point stands fixed, that Adam's action, taken together with the corruption which it produced, is imputed to each of his posterity, peace will easily be made.

units.la: PLAC. In elogio præstantis theologi, quo me ornat indignum, iudicium charitatis agnosco. In reliquis eius verbis quatuor mihi apparent οφάλματα. Primùm enim sententiam mihi tribuit, quæ mea non est. Nunquam enim negaui ipsam criminosam actionem Adami posteris eius imputari. Nunquam affirmaui nos nullo modo esse posse reos propter inobedientiam Adami. Tantummodò negaui illam actionem posteris imputari immediatè, & nos esse reos propter illam immediatè. Nam illam imputari mediatè, propter illam nos esse reos mediatè, id est, mediante corruptione ab illa in nos descendente, ego toties dixi, repetiui, inculcaui, vt mirum fit virum doctum ad has meas voces toties iteratas obsurduisse. Deinde, non modò perdit operam in eo contra me probando quod passim affirmo, sed, quod deterius est, id inde elicere conatur, vbi non latet. Etsi enim verba mea prima fronte fauere videantur eius collectioni, tamen ei præscindit omnem ansam, quæ continuò sequitur explicatio, quam ipse libri sui pag. 33. sic contraxerat, quia, quàm vere peccatum Adami in nos transiit, tam vere nobis imputari dicitur. Atqui transiit & propagatum est, non qua fuit actio transiens, sed qua fuit vitiofitas permanens, nec qua fuit peccatum persona, sed qua fuit peccatum natura, quodfcilicet natura humana adhaeret, & cum ea multiplicatur atque propagatur. Tertio, falsum est nostras omnes rationes, fi quid efficiunt, efficere nos nullo modo esse reos propter inobedientiam Adami : Eas enim imputationem illius inobedientiæ mediatam nullo modo impugnare tam clare ostendi datis ad eum literis, vt ab eo responsionem nulla efflagitatione impetrare potuerim.
