Quarto denique falsum est, id quod ait, fi fixum maneat, actionem Adami simul cum corruptione, quam peperit, acceptam vnicuique posterorum imputari, pacem facile compositum iri. Restabit enim integra quæstio, vtrum illa actio præcise sumpta immediate imputetur, hoc est, ita, vt illius imputatæ corruptio sit pœna proprie dicta. Id quod vnum duntaxat & constanter negaui, & negatum volui. Præcisam enim à corruptione, quæ in Adamo & nobis hæsit, imputari oportet, si quidem illam imputationem corruptio sequitur vt pœna.
units.tr: PLAC. In the commendation of an outstanding theologian, which honours me though I do not deserve it, I recognise a judgement of charity. In the rest of his words I see four errors [σφάλματα]. First, he attributes to me an opinion that is not mine. I have never denied that Adam's criminal act is imputed to his posterity. I have never affirmed that we cannot in any way be guilty because of Adam's disobedience. I have only denied that that act is imputed immediately, and that we are guilty of it immediately. That it is imputed mediately, and that we are guilty of it mediately, that is, through the corruption which descends from it into us, I have said, repeated and insisted on so often that it is strange a learned man should have grown deaf to these words of mine, repeated so many times. Second, he not only wastes effort in proving against me what I affirm everywhere, but, what is worse, he tries to draw from it a conclusion where none lies hidden. Although my words may at first sight seem to favour his inference, the explanation that follows immediately cuts off every occasion for it. He himself had summed this up on page 33 of his book: as truly as Adam's sin passed over into us, so truly is it said to be imputed to us. And yet it passed over and was propagated not as a transient act, but as a permanent vitiation; not as a sin of the person, but as a sin of the nature, which of course clings to human nature and is multiplied and propagated along with it. Third, it is false that all our arguments, if they prove anything, prove that we cannot in any way be guilty because of Adam's disobedience. I have shown so clearly, by the letters I sent him, that our arguments do not in any way oppose the mediate imputation of that disobedience, that I could not obtain from him any reply, however much I pressed for one. Fourth and finally, it is false that, as he says, if this stands fixed, peace will easily be made, namely that Adam's act, together with the corruption which it produced, is imputed to each of his posterity. For the question will remain entire, whether that act, taken precisely by itself, is imputed immediately, that is, in such a way that the corruption imputed from it is punishment properly so called. This one thing alone I have consistently denied, and I wish it denied. For the act must be imputed apart from the corruption which clung to Adam and to us, if indeed the corruption follows that imputation as punishment.

units.la: GAR. Obseruo deinde, nulla necessitate, vel magna vtilitate compulsum Virum Doctum, vt ita anxie & scrupulose subjectum in quatuor significata distinguteret; cum quicunque hactenus de primi peccati imputatione locuti sunt, nihil aliud eo nomine intellexerint, vt ex ipsorum scriptis satis patere potest, quàm ipsius primi hominis actualem illam transgressionem, qua Dei mandatum de non gustando fructu arboris interdicta violauit. Vt quid igitur opus erat per operosas ambages lectoris animum circumducere, & de peccato in nobis inhærente, sive corruptione nostra originali, deque imputatione ac pœna reatu ipsam consequente verba facere, de qua in hac disputatione nequaquam agi satis notum est? Non enim quaeritur, vtrum nobis omnibus insita sit corruptio, propter quam Deus pœnas à nobis exigere merito posset, aut eam nobis imputare, quod nemo Euangelicorum vnquam reuocauit in dubium : Illud vnum in Quastionem hodie vocari quibusdam volupe est, vtrum ex primo illo actuali Adæ peccato aliquis reatus, & aliqua pœna dignitas posteris incumbat.
units.tr: GAR. I observe further that the learned man was compelled by no necessity, nor by any great usefulness, to divide the subject so anxiously and scrupulously into four meanings, since all who have hitherto spoken of the imputation of the first sin have understood by that name nothing other than the actual transgression of the first man himself, by which he violated God's command not to eat the fruit of the forbidden tree, as can sufficiently be seen from their writings. Why then was it necessary to lead the reader's mind through laborious detours, and to speak of the sin dwelling in us, or of our original corruption, and of the imputation and the guilt of punishment that follows from it, which, as is well known, is not at all the subject of this dispute? For the question is not whether corruption is inborn in all of us, on account of which God could justly exact punishment from us, or whether it is imputed to us, which none of the Evangelicals has ever called into doubt. The only thing that some are glad to have called into question today is whether any guilt, and any worthiness of punishment, rests upon posterity from that first actual sin of Adam.

units.la: PLAC. Primùm esto ; nulla necessitate , vel magna vtilitate compulsus peccatum Adæ sic distinxerim , modò distinctio non sit falsa, nec noxia, nec prorsus inutilis, mihi satis est. Vtinam in eius libro nihil minùs verum , minùs vtile occurreret ! Deinde verum non est, quod ait, quicunque de peccati Adæ imputatione locuti sunt , eos nihil aliud eo nomine intellexisse , quàm ipsius actualem transgressionem : cujus rei eum admonere debuerunt verba illa mea, ac vt verbis vtar Caluini , quia intra nos est, quæ, quia causæ suæ oberant, consultò omisit. Habentur autem illa Caluini verba Comm. in Rom. 5. ꝟf. 17. integrum locum habes supra p. 92. Perit enim differentia quam illic obseruat inter Christum & Adamum, nisi peccatum Adæ , quod nobis imputatur, intra nos sit, ieque habeat vt qualitas nobis inhærens. Tertiò , Quod addit de peccato inhærente ejusque imputatione in hac disputatione non agi, id ipsum dico hoc loco, ac vt dicerem distinctionem illam adhibui. Separandum enim fuit id quod non est inter nos controuersum ab eo quod controuersum est, remouendaque ab hac quæstione omnis ambiguitas & confusio. Quo neglecto qui mihi in hac causa aduersantur non me oppugnant, sed vmbram suam. Denique quod dicit in quæstionem vocari, vtrum ex primo illo actuali Adæ peccato aliquis reatus & aliqua pœnæ dignitas posteris incumbat, vel falsum est, vel ad me non spectat: Doceo enim constanter ex illo peccato aliquem reatum & aliquam pœnæ dignitatem, si tamen dignitas appellanda est, posteris incumbere : tantùm volo non immediatè sed mediante corruptione quam peperit, incumbere.
units.tr: PLAC. Granted first: I need no necessity or great usefulness to have distinguished Adam's sin in this way; it is enough for me if the distinction is not false, nor harmful, nor altogether useless. I wish nothing less true or less useful occurred in his book! Next, it is not true what he says, that those who have spoken of the imputation of Adam's sin understood by that name nothing other than his actual transgression. The words I used should have warned him of this, and, to use Calvin's words, because it is within us, which he deliberately left out because they are against his cause. Calvin's words are found in his Commentary on Romans 5:17; you have the full passage above on page 92. The difference Calvin observes there between Christ and Adam is lost unless Adam's sin, which is imputed to us, is within us and has the character of a quality inhering in us. Third, what he adds, that the inherent sin and its imputation are not treated in this dispute, is exactly what I say here, and I introduced that distinction precisely to say it. For what is not in controversy between us had to be separated from what is in controversy, and all ambiguity and confusion removed from this question. If this is neglected, those who oppose me in this cause are not attacking me but their own shadow. Finally, when he says that it is called into question whether any guilt and any worthiness of punishment rests upon posterity from that first actual sin of Adam, this is either false or does not concern me. For I consistently teach that some guilt and some worthiness of punishment, if indeed it may be called worthiness, rests upon posterity from that sin; I only want it to rest not immediately but through the corruption which it produced.

units.la: GAR. Dicant verò , qui eam præ se ferunt in explicanda Quæstione diligentiam, annon ludificationi deputaturi sint, & præstigiarum loco habituri, si quis ex Nouis illis Pontificiorum Doctoribus, qui pacificationis studio prouincias & vrbes obire credi volunt, blandulus accedat, & in causa momentosa, justificationis puta negocio, consensum cum Euangelicis profiteatur : se nimirum haud inuito animo doctrinam ampleti de justificatione per imputatam Christi Domini nostri justitiam , dummodò distinctione adhibi-
units.tr: GAR. But let them say, those who make such a show of diligence in explaining the question, whether they will not count it mockery and regard it as sleight of hand if someone from those new Papist teachers, who are believed to travel through provinces and cities out of zeal for peace, comes up to us smoothly and professes agreement with the Evangelicals on a weighty matter, the business of justification for instance: namely that he does not unwillingly embrace the doctrine of justification by the imputed righteousness of Christ our Lord, provided that he is allowed to explain the matter by a distinction

units.la: Bb ta rem explicare liceat; Quia scilicet justitia Christi variis modis accipi possit. 1. Pro actionibus illis ad legis divinæ regulam exactissimis, quibus Christus & viuens & moriens plenissimum Patris sui mandatis obsequium præstitit. 2. Pro habituali illa & inhærente justitia, quæ Christi anima splendidissime enituit. 3. Pro justitia interna & habituali, quæ vnicuique fidelium subjectiue inest, sed quæ justitia Christi merito dici possit, quoniam à Christo, Christique Spiritu, tanquam autore, in nos defluit. Hoc ergo vltimo sensu, agnoscere se, in controuersia justificationis, imputationem justitiæ Christi: at vero si prima & secunda significatione Christi justitiam accipiamus, se justitiæ Christi imputationem nullam agnoscere, sed tanquam absurdam rejicere. Consensum certe in hoc negocio ita explicatum, nemo est, qui non conqueratur ludibrium esse, potius quam consensum. &c.
units.tr: Bb: namely, that the righteousness of Christ can be taken in various ways. 1. For those actions most exactly conforming to the rule of the divine law, by which Christ, both living and dying, rendered the fullest obedience to his Father's commands. 2. For that habitual and inherent righteousness which shone most splendidly in Christ's soul. 3. For the inner and habitual righteousness which inheres subjectively in each of the faithful, but which can rightly be called the righteousness of Christ, because it flows down into us from Christ, and from Christ's Spirit, as its author. In this last sense, then, he acknowledges in the controversy on justification the imputation of Christ's righteousness; but if we take the righteousness of Christ in the first and second senses, he acknowledges no imputation of Christ's righteousness, but rejects it as absurd. Certainly there is no one who would not complain that agreement in this business, explained in this way, is a mockery rather than agreement, etc.

units.la: PLAC. Hoc simile non est appositum, sed oppositum.
units.tr: PLAC. This simile is not apt; it is opposed.

units.la: Huic enim blandulo præstigiatori tam sum dissimilis quàm album nigro. Primò ille se enumerasse præ se ferret omnes acceptiones justitiæ Christi, cùm tamen vnam omitteret in justificationis negotio maximè momentosam, qua justitia Christi accipitur pro singulari illa obedientia quam præstitit patiendo mortem, mortem, inquam, crucis; quæ vulgo justitia passiua appellatur, & imputari fidelibus ab omnibus Protestantibus sine dubitatione creditur, cùm de imputatione justitiæ actiuæ, quam solam D. Gar. commemorauit, fit aliqua sententiarum discrepantia, quæ pacem Ecclesiæ non turbat. Ego vero primi Adæ peccati acceptiones omnes recensui, nullam prætermisi. Secundò ille Christi justitiam eo sensu acceptam imputari diceret, quo sensu accepta imputari negatur constanter ab omnibus Protestantibus. Ego vero peccatum Adami eo sensu posteris imputari affirmaui, quo sensu iis imputari omnes Protestantes constanter tenent. Itaque ille consensum fingeret cum Euangelicis plane falsum: Quis enim vnquam Euangelicorum docuit justitiam inhærentem, quam habemus à Christo, nobis ad justificationem imputari? Quem autem ego profiteor consensum, is verus est, neque negatur, aut negari potest à quoquam non Pelagiano. Tertiò denique; Ille præ se ferret tertiam illam justitiæ Christi acceptionem pro justitia nobis inhærente, esse eam, quæ intelligitur, cùm quæritur, vtrum justitia Christi nobis imputetur, necne? Id quod falsum est. Opponitur enim justitia Christi in ea quæstione nostræ justitiæ nobis insitæ. Ego verò contrà istas acceptiones peccati Adamici, quibus illud imputari, dixi consensum esse, remoui à statu quæstionis inter nos agitandæ, & quidem disertissimis verbis. Quare ab omni ludificatione alienissimus fui.
units.tr: For I am as unlike this smooth-tongued trickster as white is to black. First, he would have it appear that he had listed every sense of the righteousness of Christ, yet he omitted one that is most important in the matter of justification: the sense in which the righteousness of Christ is taken for that singular obedience which he rendered by suffering death, the death, I say, of the cross. This is commonly called passive righteousness, and all Protestants without doubt believe it is imputed to the faithful. Whereas concerning the imputation of active righteousness, the only sense D. Gar. mentioned, there is some difference of opinion that does not disturb the peace of the Church. But I have reviewed every sense of the first sin of Adam, and omitted none. Second, he would say that the righteousness of Christ is imputed in the sense in which all Protestants consistently deny that it is imputed. But I have affirmed that the sin of Adam is imputed to posterity in the sense in which all Protestants firmly hold that it is imputed to them. So he would feign an agreement with the Evangelicals that is plainly false: for who among the Evangelicals ever taught that the inherent righteousness we have from Christ is imputed to us for justification? The agreement I profess is true, and it is not denied, nor can it be denied, by anyone who is not a Pelagian. Third and finally, he would present that third sense of the righteousness of Christ, the righteousness inherent in us, as the one understood when it is asked whether the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us or not. This is false. In that question the righteousness of Christ is set over against our own righteousness implanted in us. But I, on the contrary, have removed those senses of Adamic sin, to which I said agreement attaches, from the state of the question to be debated between us, and that in the plainest words. Therefore I was most remote from any mockery.

units.la: GAR. Quod si aliqua esset in voce peccati Adæ, homonymia & ambiguitas, illa tamen omnino sublata est, cùm imputatio primi peccati Adæ nuncupatur.
units.tr: GAR. But if there were any ambiguity or equivocation in the phrase "sin of Adam", it has been entirely removed by calling it the imputation of the first sin of Adam.

units.la: Ita enim vnusquisque per se facile intelligere potest, cum plura fuerint Adami peccata, de vno illo quæri, quod inter omnia primum fuit, & quo non aliud est in genere humano prius. Vbi enim de numero vel ordine agitur, primum illud dici omnes intelligunt, vnde ducitur numeri ordinisque principium, & quo prius nihil est in illo ordine. Itaque non erat hic istis distinctionum argutiis distinendus, id est obturbandus magis, quàm instruendus Lector.
units.tr: For each person can easily understand for himself that, since Adam's sins were many, the question concerns that one which was first among them all, and before which there was no other in the human race. For where number or order is at issue, everyone understands that "first" is the point from which number and order begin, and before which nothing comes in that order. Therefore the reader was not to be distracted by those subtle distinctions here, that is, thrown into confusion rather than instructed.

units.la: PLAC. Parum abest quin credam, hanc primi peccati Adæ distinctionem Viro Docto commouisse bilem: adeò eam omni ex parte adoritur & sollicitat. Quid autem probare instituit? illam non necessariam fuisse. Fac ita esse; modò non sit falsa, non sit absurda, non sit causæ meæ noxia, causam non video, cur tantopere debeat exagitari. At distinet & obturbat Lectorem. Distinet forte, sed non diu. Obturbat autem neminem, nisi si quis me damnatum velit & confutatum. Lux distinguit & recreat: tenebræ confundunt & turbant. Præterea nego non fuisse necessariam illam distinctionem. Ita enim distinctis subjecto & attributo quæstionis irritus fit eorum labor, qui meam sententiam tanto molimine oppugnant: quæ causa videtur esse, cur hæ distinctiones eis tantopere ingratæ fuerint. Sed, inquit, vnusquisque per se facilè intelligere potest, cùm plura fuerint Adami peccata, de vno illo quæri, quod inter omnia primum fuit. Ergo id expressi, quod quisque per se facilè intelligere potest: Grande scilicet crimen, & quod magnam reprehensionem meretur ! At, inquam, hoc non sufficit. Progredi longius oportet. Peccatum enim Adami inter omnia primum duo complectitur, peccatum actuale, & peccatum habituale : illud omnium peccatorum actualium, hoc omnium habitualium primum : illud transiit, hoc manet, & in posteros propagatum est, & quin nobis proxime seu immediate, cum intra nos sit, imputetur, nemo non Pelagianus ambigit. De altero illo an imputetur immediate, omnis est inter nos excitata controversia. Haec distinctio, quia audientis nominari primum Adae peccatum non statim veniebat in mentem, multumque habebat ad decidendam quaestionem momenti, constituenda fuit ob oculos Lectoris. *
units.tr: PLAC. I almost believe that this distinction concerning the first sin of Adam has stirred the learned man's bile, so fiercely does he attack and harass it on every side. But what does he set out to prove? That it was not necessary. Granted that it is so, provided it is not false, not absurd, and not harmful to my cause, I do not see why it should be so vigorously assailed. But, he says, it distracts and confuses the reader. It may distract, but not for long. It confuses nobody, unless someone wishes to condemn and refute me. Light distinguishes and refreshes; darkness confounds and disturbs. Moreover, I deny that the distinction was unnecessary. For once subject and predicate of the question are distinguished, the labour of those who attack my opinion with such great effort is rendered futile, which seems to be the reason why these distinctions have been so unwelcome to them. But, he says, each person can easily understand for himself that, since Adam's sins were many, the question concerns that one which was first among them all. So I have stated what each person can easily understand for himself: a great crime, deserving great reproach! But, I say, this is not enough; one must go further. For the first of all Adam's sins comprises two things: actual sin and habitual sin. The former is the first of all actual sins, the latter the first of all habitual sins. The former has passed away, the latter remains and has been propagated to posterity. That it is imputed to us immediately, or proximately, since it is within us, no one doubts who is not a Pelagian. Concerning the other, whether it is imputed immediately, a whole controversy has been stirred up between us. This distinction, since at the mention of the first sin of Adam it did not come to the hearer's mind at once, and since it carried much weight in settling the question, had to be set before the eyes of the reader.

units.la: GAR. Sed & in hac subjecti distinctione nonnulla continentur, quae bene perpendenti vix est ut probari valeant. Nam 1. Quo fructu secunda peccati Adae significatio distinguitur a tertia, cum quicquid de peccato Adae in secunda significatione hic dicitur, ei reapse convenire asseratur, non quatenus est actio transiens, sed quatenus est corruptio habitualis & permanens? Ita enim peccatum Adae secundo & tertio modo dictum in idem revera coincidunt.
units.tr: GAR. But in this distinction of the subject too, some matters are contained which, on careful consideration, can hardly be proved. For, first: what is the advantage of distinguishing the second signification of the sin of Adam from the third, since whatever is said here about the sin of Adam in the second signification is asserted to belong to it in fact, not insofar as it is a transient act, but insofar as it is a habitual and lasting corruption? For thus the sin of Adam, taken in the second and third way, in fact coincide.

units.la: PLAC. Magnas habeo Viro docto gratias non patienti quicquam a me dici absque fructu. Quanquam fructu, vti spero, non carebit haec distinctio suo tempore & loco. Coincidunt quidem secunda & tertia acceptio in eandem imputationem, sed differunt modo loquendi, & sunt eiusdem nominis acceptiones diversae. Distinguere autem nomen, non rem ipsam, volui. Si quis dicat, id quod verum est, peccatum Adae diuidi posse in primum peccatum actuale, & primum peccatum habituale; diuidendum erit peccatum Adae acceptum secundo modo : diuisi primum membrum erit peccatum Adae sumptum primo modo, & secundum membrum erit peccatum Adae tertio modo. Quibus si addas propagatam in nos corruptionem, quae vetus Adam solet nuncupari, etiam peccatum Adae vocari posse, habebis omnes illas acceptiones quas enumeraui, nihil vt sit, quare tanto conatu rejiciantur.
units.tr: PLAC. I am greatly obliged to the learned man, who does not allow anything to be said by me without profit. Yet, as I hope, this distinction will not lack profit in its own time and place. The second and third senses indeed coincide in the same imputation, but they differ in their mode of speaking, and they are different senses of the same name. I wished to distinguish the name, not the thing itself. If someone says, and this is true, that the sin of Adam can be divided into the first actual sin and the first habitual sin, then the sin of Adam taken in the second way must be divided: the first member of the division will be the sin of Adam taken in the first way, and the second member the sin of Adam taken in the third way. If to these you add the corruption propagated into us, which is customarily called the old Adam and can also be called the sin of Adam, you will have all those senses which I have enumerated, so that there is nothing for which they should be rejected with such effort.

units.la: GAR, 2. Quomodo ista componi possunt inter se ? Peccatum Adæ imputatur nobis, non quâ hæsit in ipso, & peccatum Adæ imputatur nobis qua fuit vitiositas permanens in ipso: nam hærere in Adamo, & esse permanens in Adamo, quid hic differant, ego quidem non video.
units.tr: GAR, 2. How can these be put together with one another? The sin of Adam is imputed to us not in that it inhered in him, and the sin of Adam is imputed to us in that it was a permanent vitiosity in him. For to cleave to Adam and to be permanent in Adam, what difference there is here, I indeed do not see.

units.la: PLAC. Propositio, Peccatum Adæ imputatur nobis, non qua hæsit in ipso, mea quidem est; sed illi opposita, Peccatum Adæ imputatur nobis qua fuit vitiositas permanens in ipso, mea non est. Voces enim in ipso, quæ contradictionem efficiunt, non inuenit in meis scriptis, sed de suo Vir doctus addidit hoc loco: neque verò illæ comparent in sententiæ meæ expositione quam ipse præmiserat § x. Contradictionem igitur istam ipse fecit ac finxit, mihique falsò tribuit.
units.tr: PLAC. The proposition "The sin of Adam is imputed to us, not in that it cleaved to him" is indeed mine. But the opposite, "The sin of Adam is imputed to us in that it was a permanent vitiosity in him," is not mine. The words "in him", which produce the contradiction, the learned man did not find in my writings; he added them here on his own, and they do not appear in the exposition of my view which he himself had set out in § x. He therefore made and invented this contradiction himself, and falsely attributed it to me.

units.la: GAR. 3.
units.tr: GAR. 3.

units.la: Quando dicitur primi nostri parentis corruptio nobis posteris illius imputari, non quatenus hæsit in ipso Adamo, sed quatenus transfuit in nos: quænam est illa, quæ statim profertur, hujus rei ratio; quòd scilicet corruptio nostra hereditaria, sit ejusdem speciei cum corruptione, quæ fuit in Adamo? An igitur specifica illa duarum corruptionum identitas id efficit, ut prior nobis imputetur? Quod si est, nihil causæ dici potest, cur non omnium nostrorum majorum corruptio nobis imputari dicenda sit &c.
units.tr: When it is said that the corruption of our first parent is imputed to us his posterity, it is not as it cleaved in Adam himself, but as it passed over into us. What is the reason immediately offered for this? Namely, that our hereditary corruption is of the same species as the corruption that was in Adam. Does that specific identity of the two corruptions bring it about that the former is imputed to us? If so, no reason can be given why the corruption of all our ancestors should not be said to be imputed to us, and so on.

units.la: PLAC. Hic quoque monstrum sibi fingit, quod debellet. Meam enim istam rationem & truncat, & perperam interpretatur. Truncat: omittit enim & verba immediatè præcedentia, ac ut verbis vtar Calvini, quia intra nos est, & sequentia, ac quàm suam naturam, tam suam corruptionem morralem nobis cum Adamus communicavit. Male interpretatur: Non enim verbis illis, Est enim corruptio nostra hereditaria eadem specie cum illa quæ olim fuit in Adamo, rationem reddere volui, cur peccatum Adami tertio modo acceptum nobis imputetur; sed cur dicatur intra nos esse. Quare imputetur ostendi, cum dixi, ac ut verbis vtar Calvini, quia intra nos est: id quod causalis quia monere eum potuisset, si voluisset attendere. Dixi ergo cum Calvino ad Rom 5. 17. ideo imputari, quia intra nos est: Posse autem intra nos dici, quia corruptio nostra hereditaria est eadem specie cum illa quæ fuit in Adamo. Idque illustraui similitudine ducta ab ipsa natura nostra, quæ, quia specie eadem est cum natura Adami, & ab ea propagata, inde fit vt dici posset Adamus naturam suam nobiscum communicasse : non minus autem nobiscum communicauit corruptionem suam , seu peccatum. Potest igitur dici peccatum Adami in nos propagatum, in nos introiisse, intra nos esse. Hæc est ratiocinij mei vis : a qua vides, Lector, quàm aberret D. Garissolius.
units.tr: PLAC. Here too he invents a monster for himself, in order to slay it. For he both truncates my argument and misinterprets it. He truncates it, since he leaves out the words immediately before, and, to use Calvin's words, because it is within us, and the words that follow, and just as he communicated his nature to us, so Adam communicated his moral corruption to us as well. He misinterprets it: I did not wish to give, in those words, For our hereditary corruption is of the same species as that which once was in Adam, the reason why the sin of Adam, taken in the third way, is imputed to us. I wished to show why it is said to be within us. I showed why it is imputed when I said, and, to use Calvin's words, because it is within us. The causal because could have reminded him of this, had he chosen to attend. So I said, with Calvin on Rom. 5:17, that it is imputed because it is within us; and that it can be said to be within us because our hereditary corruption is of the same species as that which was in Adam. I illustrated this by a likeness drawn from our very nature: since it is of the same species as Adam's nature, and is propagated from him, it follows that Adam could be said to have communicated his nature to us. Yet he communicated his corruption, or sin, to us no less. So the sin of Adam can be said to have been propagated into us, to have entered into us, to be within us. This is the force of my reasoning, and from it you see, reader, how far Mr Garissolius is wrong.

units.la: Est igitur quæstio inter nos instituta duntaxat de primo peccato Adami sumpto primo modo, hoc est, de actuali ejus inobedientia, de actione illa interna & externa, qua Dei legem transgressus est actu, præcisa ab habituali corruptione , quæ actionem illam sequuta est; num ea nobis nascentibus imputetur ? Cui quæstioni nondum negatione simplici, sed distinctione rursus satisfaciendum videtur. Est enim ejus distinguendum attributum. Potest enim animo concipi duplex imputatio. Immediata & Mediata, vel (vt idem alijs verbis dicam) Antecedens & Consequens. Immediatam voco eam, quam solam thesibus, quas tu refutandas tibi sumpsisti, negare volui; qua putatur actio illa Adami, hoc est, vetiti fructus Manducatio ejus posteris omnibus (Christo excepto) proximè, immediatè, hoc ipso quod filij sunt Adami, imputari ad duas istas pœnas proprie dictas, priuationem iustitiæ originalis quam mortem spiritualè appellas, & mortem æternam. Hanc solam imputationem actionis illius ego negaui, quia non docetur in sacris literis adæquatâ fidei nostræ normâ, quia pugnat cum sacris literis, quia Deum facit authorem peccati, quia Dei iustitiam dehonestat, quia sequitur ex ea Christum esse naturâ sua peccatorem, quia alia nonnulla trahit secum absurda, mirabilem religionis Christianæ puritatem & splendorem obscurantia, quæ vtinam fratres & conferui nostri à me per theses moniti, aut non prorsus contempsissent, aut non contemptim expendissent!
units.tr: The question between us, then, is only about the first sin of Adam taken in the first way, that is, about his actual disobedience, that inward and outward act by which he actually transgressed God's law, apart from the habitual corruption that followed that act: whether that act is imputed to us at our birth. To this question I think an answer should be given not by a simple denial but by a further distinction. For its attribute must be distinguished. For a twofold imputation can be conceived in the mind: immediate and mediate, or (to say the same in other words) antecedent and consequent. I call immediate that imputation which I alone wished to deny in the theses you took upon yourself to refute: the view that that act of Adam, that is, the eating of the forbidden fruit, is imputed to all his posterity (Christ excepted) directly and immediately, simply because they are sons of Adam, for the two punishments properly so called: the privation of original righteousness, which you call spiritual death, and eternal death. I alone denied this imputation of that act, because it is not taught in the sacred letters, which are the adequate rule of our faith; because it conflicts with the sacred letters; because it makes God the author of sin; because it dishonours the justice of God; because it follows from it that Christ is by nature a sinner; and because it brings with it several other absurdities that obscure the wonderful purity and splendour of the Christian religion. Would that our brothers and fellow servants, warned by me through the theses, had either not utterly despised them or not weighed them with contempt!

units.la: Mediatam seu consequentem appello eam, quæ hæreditariæ corruptionis in nos ab Adamo deriuatæ intuitum consequitur, eâque mediante fit. Hujus enim corruptionis participatione communicamus peccato Adami, eique, vt ita loquar, habitualiter consentimus; ac propterea digni fumus, qui Adamo peccatori annumeremur. Id me Chamierus docuit Panftr. tom. 3. lib. 6. cap. 4. de pœnis peccati § xvi. & xvii. Locum, fi placet, quære & lege. Huc transcripfiffem (nam est insignis) nisi consulerem breuitati. Sed tenere me non possum quin Ægidij Hunnii Auguftanæ confessionis Theologi celebris verba subijciam, quibus hanc imputationem mediatam docet & explicat, Ostendit ergo (Apostolus Paulus) lapsum Adami non immediatè & per fe, sed mediatè & propter aliud nobis ejus posteris imputari, quia videlicet per lapsum illum polluta est natura primorum parentum, vt nonnisi peccato corruptos & vitiatos liberos procreare possent, sicut fcriptum est, genuit Adam filium ad imaginem suam Gen. 5. Alias fi fieri potuisset, vt in posteros non vitium proprium deriuaretur à primis parentibus, tum lapsus ille tanquam peccatum alienum eis plane non imputaretur. Palam igitur ostendit Paulus vnum illud delictum nobis ad condemnationem cedere tantum Mediatè, quatenus per delictum illud actuale introducta est in naturam horribilis corruptio, quam per carnalem generationem propagauit in ipsos posteros. Ita vt à lapsu corruptio Naturæ, à corruptione naturæ in nos deriuata mors & damnatio peruenit, quat: omnes peccaimus, inquit, id est quat: ipsi in possessionem illius hæreditariam deuenimus..
units.tr: I call mediate or consequent that imputation which follows upon regard for the hereditary corruption derived from Adam into us, and comes about through that corruption. For by sharing in this corruption we are made partakers of Adam's sin, and, so to speak, consent to it habitually; and for that reason we are rightly reckoned among Adam the sinner. Chamier taught me this in his Panstratia, vol. 3, book 6, chapter 4, on the punishments of sin, sections 16 and 17. If you please, look it up and read it. I would have transcribed it here (for it is striking) had I not been mindful of brevity. But I cannot refrain from adding the words of Ægidius Hunnius, a famous theologian of the Augsburg Confession, in which he teaches and explains this mediate imputation: Therefore the Apostle Paul shows that the fall of Adam was imputed to us his posterity not immediately and in itself, but mediately and on account of something else, namely because by that fall the nature of our first parents was polluted, so that they could beget children only corrupted and vitiated by sin, as it is written, Adam begat a son in his own image, Gen. 5. Otherwise, if it could have been that no proper vice was derived from the first parents into their posterity, then that fall would not have been imputed to them at all, as another's sin. Paul therefore plainly shows that that one offence comes to our condemnation only mediately, insofar as through that actual offence a horrible corruption of nature was introduced, which it propagated by carnal generation into the posterity themselves. So that from the fall comes the corruption of nature, and from the corruption of nature derived into us comes death and damnation, inasmuch as, he says, all have sinned, that is, inasmuch as we have come into possession of that hereditary corruption.

units.la: Vt igitur rem verbo absoluam, quæritur, vtrum primum peccatum actuale Adami præcisè sumptum nobis ejus posteris imputetur à Deo Iusto Iudice proximè, immediatè ac ordine naturæ prius quàm inhærenter corrupti simus? Tu venerande frater affirmas: Ego Nego. Vter rectius, sequens disputatio, vti spero in Domino, planum faciet.
units.tr: So, to sum the matter up in a word, the question is this: whether the first actual sin of Adam, taken precisely by itself, is imputed to us his posterity by God the just Judge directly and immediately, and in the order of nature before we are corrupted inherently? You, honoured brother, affirm it; I deny it. Which of us is more correct, the following disputation, as I hope in the Lord, will make plain.

units.la: GAR. Distinguitur imputatio peccati in Priorem, siue Antecedentem, aut Immediatam; & Posteriorem, siue Consequentem, aut Mediatam. Haud incommodè sanè; nec dubito, si modo recta explicatio adhiberetur, consensum hic facile stabiliri posse: si nempe utraque imputatio eodem referretur, id est, si intelligeretur de peccato Adami eadem significatione accepto, siue de actione, qua primùm Adamus reum se fecit læsæ Diuinæ Majestatis.
units.tr: GAR. The imputation of sin is distinguished into prior, or antecedent, or immediate; and posterior, or consequent, or mediate. Certainly this is not inappropriate; nor do I doubt that, if only a correct explanation were applied, agreement could easily be established here: namely, if both imputations were referred to the same thing, that is, if it were understood of the sin of Adam taken in the same sense, namely of the act by which Adam first made himself guilty of offending the divine majesty.

units.la: PL. Cur ergo consensus non stabilitur? Cur oppugnor? utramque enim illam imputationem eodem retuli, ac nonnisi de illa actione qua primum Adamus peccavit, intellexi. Id sole meridiano clarius est, & miror vocari potuisse in dubium. Illa enim ipsa distinctio, ut alia omittam, hoc clarum facit: non potest enim de peccati habitualis seu corruptionis imputatione accipi. Quis enim dicat corruptionem ante corruptionem, aut post corruptionem; mediante corruptione, aut ea non mediante imputari?
units.tr: PL. Why then is agreement not established? Why am I opposed? For I referred both imputations to the same thing, and understood them only of that act by which Adam first sinned. This is clearer than the noonday sun, and I am surprised it could be called in doubt. For that very distinction, to omit other points, makes it clear: it cannot be understood of the imputation of habitual sin or corruption. For who would say that corruption is imputed before corruption, or after corruption; through corruption, or not through corruption?

units.la: GAR. Ita enim paria fermè faceret cum ea, quam præmisimus, imputationis distinctione in communem & singularem: ut priorem & immediatam intelligeremus, communem illam quam diximus; posteriorem & mediatam quam propriam sive singularem nominauimus. Nam certè communis illa sive immediata, quemadmodum posterior fuit prima actuali Adæ transgressione, ita prior fuit personali cujusque hominis ex Adamo prognati existentia, atque adeò etiam corruptione illa, qua in singulos naturali generatione descendit; quatenus ab initio rei fuerunt omnes communiter in Adamo, quo sensu dictum est à Bernardo, Adamum & Euam fuisse prius nostros peremptores quàm parentes, At imputatio singularis, propria, personalis & mediata, recte dici posšit corruptione nobis inhærente posterior.
units.tr: GAR. For in this way he would make almost the same distinction as the one we set out earlier, between common and singular imputation: so that we understand the prior and immediate to be that common imputation we spoke of, and the posterior and mediate, which we named proper or singular. For certainly that common or immediate imputation, just as it was posterior to the first actual transgression of Adam, so it was prior to the personal existence of each man born of Adam, and therefore also prior to that corruption which descends by natural generation upon each individual; inasmuch as all were from the beginning in Adam together, in which sense Bernard said that Adam and Eve were our destroyers before they were our parents. But the singular, proper, personal and mediate imputation can rightly be said to be posterior to the corruption inhering in us.

units.la: § XVII. rior, quatenus nemini perfonaliter imputari potest peccatum istud, nisi filius sit Adami, adeòque nisi personaliter existat: neque potest aliquis personaliter existere, & pro filio Adami haberi, nisi postquam anima & corpus in vnam personam coaluerunt: quæ partium hominis essentialium coalitio atque conjunctio, sine dubio conceptione posterior est &c. Ergo in conceptione primâ nondum adest anima, nondum homo est, nondum filius Adami: & ta-men ab ipso conceptionis momento inest vitiofitas in semine, quippe quod habet fomitem illum peccati, quem definiunt, inordinatam carnis qualitatem ex peccato primorum parentium traductam in posteros, &c.
units.tr: § XVII. later, inasmuch as that sin cannot be imputed personally to anyone unless he is a son of Adam, and therefore unless he exists as a person: nor can anyone exist personally and be regarded as a son of Adam until soul and body have come together into one person. That coalition and conjunction of the essential parts of a man is without doubt later than conception, etc. Therefore at the first conception the soul is not yet present, the man is not yet there, the son of Adam is not yet there; and yet from the very moment of conception there is vitiation in the seed, since it has that fomes of sin, which they define as the disordered quality of the flesh handed down from the sin of our first parents to their posterity, etc.

units.la: PLAC. Si paria facit, cur non contentus illa distinctione jam recepta & commoda excogitauit nouam & incommodam? Melior enim est imputationis distinctio in immediatam & mediatam,quàm in communem & singularem. Primò quia illa jam fuerat vsurpata ab Ægidio Hunnio & VValæo, hæc verò à quo fuerat vsurpata? Deinde, quia illa est in membra non re modò, sed nomine etiam opposita; quæ bonæ distinctionis nota in hac desideratur. Nam imputatio illa singularis dici potest communis, & vice versa communis singularis. Quid enim? nonne humana natura, corruptio hæreditaria, existentia, &c sunt omnium hominum communes? Atqui imputatio singularis, propria, personalis non minùs communis est quàm natura humana, quàm corruptio, quàm existentia (Christum semper excipio) quomodo ergo imputationi communi opponitur? Nam membrorum oppositorum alterum alterius negationem importat. Rursus imputatio communis potest etiam ipsa dici singularis, propria, personalis, siquidem communis dicitur distributiue: de singulis enim personis posterorum Adæ singulatim prædicatur. Quod si dicitur communis collectiue, vtraque dici debuit communis, altera collectiue, altera distributiue. Deinde quod commune est collectiuè posteris Adami, id quidem de tota collectione posterorum cjus prædicari potest, sed de iis singulis, nullo modo; sicut Apostolis commune fuit collectiuè esse duodecim; ac propterea eorum nullus fuit duodecim. Præterea, cùm per imputa-
units.tr: PLAC. If they make no difference, why did he not rest content with that distinction, already accepted and convenient, and devise a new and inconvenient one? The distinction of imputation into immediate and mediate is better than the one into common and singular. First, because the former had already been used by Aegidius Hunnius and Walaeus, whereas who has used the latter? Next, because the former is opposed to its members not only in fact but also in name, and this mark of a good distinction is missing here. For that imputation which is called singular can be called common, and conversely common can be called singular. For what? Are not human nature, hereditary corruption, existence, and so on, common to all men? Yet singular, proper, personal imputation is no less common than human nature, than corruption, than existence (I always except Christ). How then is it opposed to common imputation? For of two opposed members one imports the negation of the other. Again, common imputation can itself also be called singular, proper, personal, since it is called common distributively: it is predicated of the individual persons of Adam's posterity one by one. But if it is called common collectively, both should be called common, the one collectively and the other distributively. Next, what is common to Adam's posterity collectively can indeed be predicated of the whole collection of his posterity, but of the individuals in no way; just as it was common to the apostles collectively to be twelve, yet none of them was twelve. Moreover, since the learned man understands by imputa-

units.la: Cc tionem vir doctus intelligat, vel actum Iudicis declarantis aliquem reum, poenaque dignum, vel ipsam poenæ inflictionem, palam est inflictionem poenæ esse singularem: seu enim illa sit corruptio,seu mors corporis vel æterna, infligitur singulis. Si igitur imputatio communis est poenæ inflictio, vtique singularis est. Inflictioni autem poenæ respondet condemnatio, seu declaratio Iudicis aliquem esse reum & poena dignum. Quæro etiam, quo sensu imputatio dicatur communis & opponatur singulari? An quo sensu solet commune seu vniuersale opponi singulari? Non differt ergo imputatio communis à singulari, nisi vt species ab indiuiduo suo. Non est autem species nisi in aliquo indiuiduo suo. Extra aut ante indiuidua sua frustra quæritur. Attamen vult Vir doctus imputationem communem diu antequam esset singularis, adeoque extra singularem fuisse. Mitto alia discrimina. Quod si alio sensu, quàm fert vsus, communem singulari Vir doctus oppositit, singularitatem, ipse & obscuritatem affectauit, sibique potius quàm Lectori scripsit. Adde quod communis videtur magis communis esse debere quàm singularis: alioqui cur id nomen huic opponitur? Attamen non est magis communis, nisi velis etiam iis communem esse hominibus, qui nunquam fuerunt, nec futuri sunt. Plura non addam; nisi hoc vnum, quod praetermitti non debet. Ex ratione Viri docti, qua probat imputationem singularem, propriam, personalem corruptione nobis inhærente posteriorem esse, sequi, imputari posteris peccatum Adæ imputatione illa communi, antequam sint filij Adæ, & profiliis Adæ habeantur. Quod quomodo verum & iustum esse possit, tibi prudens Lector, considerandum relinquo.
units.tr: tion either the act of a judge declaring someone guilty and worthy of punishment, or the infliction of the punishment itself, it is plain that the infliction of punishment is singular: for whether it be corruption, or bodily death, or eternal death, it is inflicted on individuals. If therefore common imputation is the infliction of punishment, it is surely singular. Now to the infliction of punishment corresponds condemnation, or the judge's declaration that someone is guilty and worthy of punishment. I ask also in what sense imputation is called common and opposed to singular? In the sense in which common or universal is usually opposed to singular? Common imputation therefore differs from singular only as a species differs from its individual. But a species exists only in some individual; outside or before its individuals it is sought in vain. Yet the learned man wants common imputation to have existed long before it was singular, and so outside the singular. I pass over other distinctions. But if he opposed common to singular in a sense other than usage bears, he has himself courted obscurity and written for himself rather than for the reader. Add that common ought to seem more common than singular; otherwise why is this name opposed to that one? Yet it is not more common, unless you also make it common to men who have never existed and never will. I will add no more, except this one thing, which must not be passed over. From the learned man's reasoning, by which he proves that singular, proper, personal imputation is posterior to the corruption inhering in us, it follows that Adam's sin is imputed to posterity by that common imputation, before they are sons of Adam and are regarded as sons of Adam. How this can be true and just, I leave, prudent reader, for you to consider.

units.la: GAR. Eam existimo fuisse mentem illis Theologis, qui peccatum Adæ docent nobis imputari mediate, sine mediante corruptione & vitiositate nostra. Ægid. Hunnius artic. de pecc. Quaest. 7. Valaus Defens. Molin. cap. 8. Enimuero longe alius Doctis Viris sensus, qui hac prioris & posterioris imputationis distinctione vtuntur. Quandoquidem 1. eam, quam diximus communem, priorem & immediatam, absolutè negant &c. 2. Quia posteriorem & mediatam sive singularem longè aliter exponunt, ita scilicet vt eam pertendant nulla ratione ad ipsum actuale & personale Adami peccatum respicere, sed ad nostrum ipsorum duntaxat originale vitium natiuamque & hereditariam corruptionem referri debere.
units.tr: GAR. I think this was the mind of those theologians who teach that Adam's sin is imputed to us mediately, without any mediating corruption or vitiosity in us. Aegid. Hunnius, article on sin, question 7. Walaeus, Defence against Molina, chapter 8. But the sense of learned men who use this distinction between prior and posterior imputation is quite different. For, first, they flatly deny that which we have called common, prior and immediate. Second, because they expound the posterior or mediate, that is the singular, in quite another way, so that they maintain it refers in no way to Adam's actual and personal sin, but must be referred only to our own original vice and innate and hereditary corruption.

units.la: P L A C. Vtrumque hoc discrimen aperte falsum est. Et primum quidem: Negarunt enim imputationem immediatam Ægidius Hunnius & V Valæus tam diserte, vt disertius non potuerint. Ille air lapsum Adami non immediate & per se, sed mediate & propter aliud nobis ejus posteris imputari. Item, vnum illud delictum nobis ad condemnationem cedere tantum mediate. Quid sibi vult illa negatio, non immediate & per se? Quid exclusiua, Tantum mediate? Quid est negare imputationem immediatam, si hoc non est? Hic vero imputationis illius possibilitatem negat, suamque negationem firmat ducto a Dei justitia argumento. Locum habes supra pag. 22. vti superiorem pag. 20. Secundum etiam tam aperte falsum est, vt satis mirari non possim, quomodo a se vir Doctus impetrare potuerit, vt id proferret. Contra enim pertendo imputationem mediatam ad ipsum actuale & personale Adami peccatum respicere; nec de alio peccato a me vnquam vsurpatam fuisse, aut, quod amplius est, vsurpari potuisse.
units.tr: PLAC. Both of these distinctions are plainly false. And first: Aegidius Hunnius and Walaeus denied immediate imputation so plainly that they could not have done so more plainly. The former says that the fall of Adam is imputed to us his posterity not immediately and through itself, but mediately and on account of something else. Likewise, that one offence comes to our condemnation only mediately. What does that negation mean, not immediately and through itself? What does the exclusive only mediately mean? What is it to deny immediate imputation, if this is not? The latter denies the possibility of that imputation, and confirms his denial by an argument drawn from the justice of God. You have it above on page 22, as well as the earlier passage on page 20. Second, this is also so plainly false that I cannot sufficiently wonder how the learned man could bring himself to put it forward. For I maintain that mediate imputation relates to the actual and personal sin of Adam itself; and I have never used, or could even have used, it of any other sin.

units.la: G A R. Tum in nomine imputationis peccati varie Inditur. Nam disputationis initio consenseramus, per imputationis vocem in hoc negotio intelligendum, vel actum judicis declarantis aliquem reum poenaque dignum, vel ipsam poenae inflictionem. Nunc in alia omnia itur. Quaeritur enim, an ipsius Adae actuale peccatum posteris imputetur. Agnoscunt Viri Docti verbotenus; sed explicationem audi: ita scilicet, inquiunt, vt imputari dicatur illa transgressio eodem significatu, quo dixit Apostolus, praeputium imputari in circuncisionem, id est, eodem loco haberi ac si circumcisum esset: Nos enim, ob peccatum nobis ab origine inhaerens, dignos esse, qui eo loco habeamur, ac si actualem ipsam inobedientiam commisissemus. Quod aliquis sane haud immerito tergiuersationi deputari debere pertenderit. Conuenerat enim, imputare peccatum hoc loco non aliud esse, quam alicui peccatum ita adscribere, vt propter illud, & ejus consideratione reatum subeat, & vel poenas det, vel certe poenis dignus existimetur. At quàm remotum sit illud ab eo imputationis significatu, quem hic proponunt, nemo non videt.
units.tr: GAR. Then the name of imputation of sin is variously used. For at the beginning of the disputation we agreed that by the word imputation in this matter is to be understood either the act of a judge declaring someone guilty and deserving punishment, or the infliction of punishment itself. Now they go off in every other direction. For the question is whether the actual sin of Adam himself is imputed to his posterity. The learned men acknowledge it in words, but hear their explanation: namely, they say that the transgression is said to be imputed in the same sense in which the Apostle said that uncircumcision is imputed for circumcision, that is, that it is held in the same place as if it had been circumcised. For we, because of sin inhering in us from our origin, are worthy to be held in the same place as if we had ourselves committed the actual disobedience. Someone may fairly argue that this must be counted as evasion. For it had been agreed that to impute sin here means nothing other than to ascribe sin to someone in such a way that, on account of it and in consideration of it, he incurs guilt and either suffers punishments or at least is judged worthy of them. But how far that is from the meaning of imputation which they propose here, everyone sees.

units.la: PLAC. Quod ait me, in nomine imputationis varie lusisse, ab eo longissimè abfui, & quàm maximè potui ferio egi,vt veritatis & pacis decebat studiosum. Abhorrui etiam ab omni tergiuersatione, & nihil mihi prius fuit quàm vt statum quæstionis purgarem ab omni impedimento, & clarum facerem & liquidum, ne vllus vel rergiuersatiouni, vel dissimulationi, vel declinationi locus esse posset. Quod autem me accusat, quasi conuentis non steterim, satis mirari nequeo. Quomodo enim consenseramus Disputationis initio, aut conuenerat inter nos de vocis imputationis significatu, qui nunquam ea de re inter nos disputauerami̅us? Virum enim Doctum mihi nunquam datum est, videre, aut coram alloqui. Vt autem de hac quæstione mecum conferre vellet, impetrare nulla ratione potui. Cùm autem dicit, Nunc in alia omnia itur, putas fortasse, Lector, cum hoc meum manuscriptum posterius aut saltem tempus quo scriptum est, designare. At non ita est. Quæ enim subjungit verba mea non petuntur ex hoc meo Manuscripto, sed partim ex Thesibus meis de statu hominis lapsi ante gratiam, quinquennio, antequam inciperet illa controuersia, publicatis, partim ex duarum epistolarum quas solas ad eum scripsi, posteriore, duobus aut tribus à Synodo postrema Nationali mensibus: In priore autem nihil disputabam, tantùm ex ipso quærebam modestè, qua de imputatione Decretum Synodi esset intelligendum, de Mediata, an de Immediata? In posteriore verò breuiter ostendebam, nec rationes à me in thesibus allatas mediatam oppugnare imputationem, nec defuisse magnos Theologos qui immediatam negarent confessâ mediatâ. Illud enim vtrumque rescripserat ostendendum esse, quod vbi à me factum est, aliquamdiu respondere mihi renuit, tandem verò datis ad me secundis literis protestatus est se mihi ea de re non responsurum, neque mecum aut cum alio vllo eo de negotio disputaturum, nisi in proxima Synodo Nationali. Atque ita finem scribendarum inuicem literarum fecimus. Vbi igitur aut quando inter nos ea facta fuerit conuentio, diminare non possum. Fac tamen fuisse factam, quid dixi, quod ei vocis imputationis significatui repugnet?
units.tr: PLAC. As for his saying that I have trifled with the name of imputation in various ways, I was very far from that, and I was as serious as I could be, as befits a student of truth and peace. I also shrank from every evasion, and nothing was more important to me than to clear the state of the question of every hindrance, and to make it clear and plain, so that there could be no place for any evasion, dissimulation, or shifting. As to his accusing me, as if I had not kept to what was agreed, I can hardly wonder enough. For how had we agreed at the beginning of the disputation, or how had we come to an agreement between ourselves about the meaning of the word imputation, when we never disputed about that matter between ourselves? For it was never granted to me to see the learned man or to address him face to face. And I could by no means prevail upon him to be willing to confer with me on this question. But when he says, Now they go off in every other direction, perhaps you think, reader, that he is pointing to this manuscript of mine as later, or at least to the time when it was written. But that is not so. For the words he adds are not taken from this manuscript of mine, but partly from my Theses on the state of fallen man before grace, published five years before that controversy began, and partly from the later of the only two letters I wrote to him, written two or three months before the last National Synod. In the earlier I disputed nothing; I only asked him modestly in what sense the decree of the Synod was to be understood, of mediate or of immediate imputation? In the later I showed briefly that the reasons I had given in my Theses did not oppose mediate imputation, and that there were not lacking great theologians who denied immediate imputation while confessing mediate imputation. For he had written back that both points needed to be shown; and when I had done so, he refused for some time to answer me, and finally, when I had sent him a second letter, he protested that he would not answer me on this matter, nor dispute with me or with anyone else about this business, except at the next National Synod. And so we brought the exchange of letters to an end. Where or when any agreement was made between us, I cannot tell. Yet suppose it was made: what have I said that contradicts that meaning of the word imputation?

units.la: Scripsi in Thesibus supra dictis § vii. Actualem inobedientiam Adami dici posse nobis imputari, hoc sensu, quod ob peccatum nobis ab origine inhærens digni sumus, qui eodem loco habeamur, ac si inobedientiam illam admisissemus. Est-ne id verum, an salsum? Si falsum, debuit ostendere falsitatem. Si verum, utique non repugnat imputationi mediatæ, quam esse verum ipse vir doctus non diffitetur: verum enim vero non repugnat. Imo nihil aliud est quàm descriptio imputationis mediatæ, quam oppositi opinioni Pighij, culpam originis vnicam statuentis transgressionem Adami. Cui vni, inquit Martyr, nos omnes vult nasci obnoxios, non propter aliquod vitium, aut culpam, aut depravationem, quam in nobis habeamus. Dixi in Epistola, cùm vitium hæreditarium nos æque morte dignos ac Adamum faciat, nihil obstare, quominus peccatum Adami nobis eo sensu dicatur imputari, quo dixit Apostolus, si quis legem fervauerit, illius præputium in circumcisionem imputari. Est-ne id verum, nec-ne? Neque ait, neque negat D. Gariffolius. Quid igitur facit? eum audi.
units.tr: I wrote in the Theses cited above, §7: The actual disobedience of Adam can be said to be imputed to us in this sense, that because of the sin inherent in us from our origin we are worthy to be held in the same position as if we had committed that disobedience. Is that true or false? If false, he ought to have shown the falsity. If true, it certainly does not conflict with mediate imputation, which the learned man himself does not deny to be true; for a truth does not conflict with a truth. Indeed it is nothing other than a description of mediate imputation, set against the opinion of Pighius, who holds that the one guilt of origin is the transgression of Adam alone. To that one, says Martyr, he wants all of us to be born liable, not on account of any vice, fault or corruption that we have in ourselves. In my letter I said: Since hereditary vice makes us as worthy of death as Adam, there is nothing to prevent Adam's sin from being said to be imputed to us in the sense in which the Apostle said, if anyone keeps the law, his uncircumcision is imputed as circumcision. Is that true or not? Gariffolius neither affirms nor denies it. What then does he do? Let us hear him.

units.la: GAR. Dixerit ergo Paulus, imputari præputium in circumcisionem, quia eodem loco habeatur ac si circumcisum esset. At hic non de imputatione cujusuis rei agitur, sed de imputatione peccati alieni. Quis autem hactenus vel docuit, vel sibi persuasit, per imputationem illam peccati, intelligendam collationem diuersorum peccatorum à diuersis personis patratorum, vel paritatem inter diuersa peccata ratione pœnæ aut reatus? Hoc neque Scriptura, neque communis ipse loquendi vsus admittit.
units.tr: GAR. Paul would therefore say that uncircumcision is imputed as circumcision, because it is held to be in the same position as if it had been circumcised. But here we are not dealing with the imputation of any thing whatever, but with the imputation of another's sin. Now who has hitherto taught, or persuaded himself, that by that imputation of sin is to be understood a comparison of different sins committed by different persons, or an equality between different sins in respect of punishment or guilt? Neither Scripture nor common usage of speech admits this.

units.la: PLAC. Sumpsisse verbum imputandi eo sensu quo illud Paulus sumpsit, cùm dixit præputium imputari in circumcisionem, nec-ne? Non negat Vir doctus. Ergo in eo verbo non lusi, nisi velit in eodem verbo similiter lusisse Apostolum. In ea enim significatione illud vsurpaui, cujus grauissimum habeo autorem, ipsum Paulum. At hic, inquit, non de imputatione cujusuis rei agitur, sed de imputatione peccati alieni. Quid tum postea? Est-ne aliquid quod prohibeat illud verbum, quo sensu de alia aliqua re vsurpatur, eodem etiam vsurpari de peccato? At per imputationem peccati non est intelligenda collatio diuersorum peccatorum a diuersis personis patratorum vel paritas inter diuersa peccata. Quid hoc ad me? An per imputationem inobedientiæ Adami talem intellexi vel collationem, vel paritatem? Non certè. Diuersa peccata a diuersis personis patrata sunt ambo peccata actualia; vitium nobis ab origine inhærens non est peccatum actuale, sed habituale tantum. Illorum peccatorum diuersorum vnum non est causa alterius: cùm tamen inobedientia actualis nobis inhærentis habitualis causa fuerit. Itaque conferuntur illa diuersa peccata, tanquam vt, ita loquar, coordinata, hæ verò inobedientiæ tanquam subordinatæ. Cùm ergo inobedientia Adami sit causa vitij nobis inhærentis, & hoc sit causa reatus nostri, necesse est inobedientiam Adami causam esse nostri reatus, saltem mediatam. Itaque nos esse reos ob vitium nobis inhærens immediatè, eoque mediante ob inobedientiam illam actualem Adami, cujus vitium illud inhærens habitualis quædam est consensio & approbatio, & communio: vt ob eam causam magis proprie nobis in peccatum dici possit imputari, quàm præputium in circumcisionem, ob seruata Legis δικαιώματα. Cæterum quod ait in Scriptura nullibi ostendi posse imputationem peccati eo sensu vsurpatam, conturbare nos non debet: nam phrasis imputare vel imputari peccatum admodum rara est in Scriptura, nec forte nisi cum negatione adjuncta vspiam occurrit. Considera autem, humanissime Lector, quo sensu phrasis æquipollens ab ipso Domino nostro Iesu Christo vsurpata fuerit Matth. 23. 34. Propterea ecce ego mitto ad vos Prophetas & sapientes, & scribas, & ex ipsis quosdam trucidabitis & crucifigetis, & ex ipsis aliquos flagellabitis in Synagogis vestris, & persequemini ex vrbe in vrbem, vt veniat super vos omnis sanguis justus effusus super terram, a sanguine Abel justi vsque ad sanguinem Zachariæ filij Barachiæ, quem occidistis inter templum & altare: hoc est, exponente Luca cap. xi. 50. vt à gente ista requiratur sanguis omnium Prophetarum effusus a facto mundi fundamento. Quin enim illis verbis significata fuerit imputatio peccati negari nequit. Itaque sic in verba illa commentatus est Calvinus, Tametsi Abel non a Iudaeis occisus est, ejus tamen necem ipsis imputat Christus, quia inter ipsos & Cain quaedam erat impietatis cognatio. Facit autem vitiositas inhaerens, ut nobis cum Adamo peccante non qualiscunque cognatio peccati, sed consanguinitas interfit. Imo vitium nostrum inhaerens nihil aliud est quam peccatum Adami secundum habitum in nos propagatum, vel instar pestis aut veneni naturali contagio diffusum. Quid est igitur, cur ob illud vitium nobis imputari dici non possit? Vide ergo, Lector, an me potius hoc loco quam ipsum Dominum, Vir Doctus impugnet.
units.tr: PLAC. Did he take the word imputing in the sense in which Paul took it when he said uncircumcision is imputed as circumcision, or not? The learned man does not deny it. So I have not played with the word, unless he wants to say that the Apostle played with the same word in the same way. For I used it in that meaning, of which I have the most weighty authority, Paul himself. But, he says, here we are not dealing with the imputation of any thing whatever, but with the imputation of another's sin. What follows from that? Is there anything that forbids the word, when it is used in one sense of some other thing, from being used in the same sense of sin as well? But by the imputation of sin is not to be understood a comparison of different sins committed by different persons, or an equality between different sins. What has this to do with me? Did I understand by the imputation of Adam's disobedience any such comparison or equality? Certainly not. Both the different sins committed by different persons are actual sins; the vice inherent in us from birth is not an actual sin, but only a habitual one. One of those different sins is not the cause of the other, whereas actual disobedience was the habitual cause of the disobedience inherent in us. So those different sins are compared as, so to speak, coordinate, but these disobediences as subordinate. Since therefore the disobedience of Adam is the cause of the vice inherent in us, and this is the cause of our guilt, it is necessary that the disobedience of Adam be the cause of our guilt, at least mediately. Thus we are guilty immediately because of the vice inherent in us, and through that mediately because of that actual disobedience of Adam, of which the inherent vice is a certain habitual consent, approval and communion; so that for that reason it can be said more properly that sin is imputed to us than that uncircumcision is imputed for keeping the law's ordinances [δικαιώματα]. Moreover, that he says that the imputation of sin in this sense cannot be shown anywhere in Scripture should not disturb us: for the phrase to impute or to be imputed sin is very rare in Scripture, and perhaps it occurs nowhere except with a negation attached. But consider, most kind reader, in what sense the equivalent phrase was used by our Lord Jesus Christ himself, Matthew 23:34: Therefore, behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes, and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues, and persecute from city to city, so that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar. That is, as Luke explains in chapter 11, verse 50: that the blood of all the prophets shed from the foundation of the world may be required of this generation. That by those words the imputation of sin is meant cannot be denied. So Calvin commented on those words: Although Abel was not killed by the Jews, Christ nevertheless imputes his death to them, because there was a certain kinship of impiety between them and Cain. But the inherent vitiation makes it so that between us and Adam sinning there is not just any kind of kinship of sin, but a blood relationship. Indeed our inherent vice is nothing other than the sin of Adam propagated into us according to habit, or spread by natural contagion like a plague or poison. What reason is there, then, why it cannot be said to be imputed to us because of that vice? See therefore, reader, whether the learned man is attacking me here rather than the Lord himself.

units.la: GAR. Denique Socinista imputationem peccati Adae exerte negant, & agnoscunt tamen nos propter nostrum peccatum eodem loco haberi, ac si Adami actualem inobedientiam commisissemus, quia nimirum imputationem peccati sic explicatam agnoverunt, nullam esse veri nominis imputationem.
units.tr: GAR. Finally, the Socinians openly deny that the sin of Adam is imputed, and yet they acknowledge that we are held in the same position on account of our own sin as if we had committed Adam's actual disobedience; because they acknowledged that imputation of sin so explained is no imputation in the proper sense of the word.

units.la: PLAC. Hic quoque nos traducendi cupido tenebras offudit animo Viri Docti. Ait enim Socinistas agnoscere nos propter nostrum peccatum eodem loco haberi, ac si Adami actualem ipsam inobedientiam commisissemus. Id quod falsum est. Volunt enim nos quidem eodem cum Adamo loco haberi, at non propter peccatum nostrum; (peccatum enim ab origine nobis inhaerens nullum agnoscunt) sed quia sumus ab eo procreati, & de liberis idem quod de patre judicium fit. Itaque ab eorum sententia abest nostra toto caelo. Caeterum imputationem peccati Adami Socinus verbis negat, reponit. Nam si idem fit de filio quod de Patre judicium, & hic judicatur peccator & dignus poena, judicatur etiam poena dignus esse filius: Ille quidem quia ipse peccavit, hic vero quia ejus pater peccavit. Id quod, ipso Viro Docto teste, est peccatum patris filio imputare, & quidem imputatione immediata; quippe cum haereditariam corruptionem neget Socinus, sine qua mediata imputatio esse non potest. Adde quod eadem mors infligitur posteris Adami & Adamo. Ipsa autem poena inflictio est Viro Docto peccati imputatio. Reuera igitur Socinus negat imputationem mediatam quam agnosco ; immediatam quam impugno verbotenus tantum negat, re autem ipsa affirmat.
units.tr: PLAC. Here too the desire to find fault has cast a shadow over the mind of the learned man. For he says that the Socinians acknowledge that we are held in the same position on account of our own sin as if we had committed Adam's very actual disobedience. This is false. For they want us indeed to be held in the same position as Adam, but not on account of our sin (for they acknowledge no sin inherent in us from origin); but because we are begotten of him, and the judgment passed on children is the same as that passed on the father. So our view is totally remote from their opinion. Moreover Socinus denies in words the imputation of Adam's sin, but in fact restores it. For if the judgment on a son is the same as on the father, and the father is judged a sinner and worthy of punishment, the son too is judged worthy of punishment: the father indeed because he himself sinned, the son because his father sinned. This, by the learned man's own testimony, is to impute the father's sin to the son, and indeed by immediate imputation; since Socinus denies hereditary corruption, without which mediate imputation cannot exist. Add that the same death is inflicted on Adam's posterity as on Adam. But the infliction of the penalty itself is, for the learned man, the imputation of sin. Truly, therefore, Socinus denies mediate imputation, which I acknowledge; immediate imputation, which I oppose, he denies only in words, but in fact affirms it.

units.la: G A R. Alio deinde colore hanc posteriorem suam imputationem pingunt, cum addunt, nihil obstare, quominus Adami peccatum nobis imputari dicatur, quatenus vitium nostrum hareditarium habitus est, quem primum actuale peccatum reliquit in Adami anima ; deinde inclinatio ad similia peccata ; tertio consensus habitualis ad illud peccatum. Hæc verba ex secunda, quam ad cum scripsferam, epistola vir Doctus deprompsit: sed de suo addidit voces quatenus, deinde, tertio, diuidens ea quæ conjunxi, ac ex vna ratione tres conficies præter mentem meam. Locum ex illa epistola Gallice scripta integrum ex scribam. Peccatum Adami dici potest nobis eius posteris imputari tribus modis. Primo, quia ( vt innuit Caluinus, vitium quod ab Adamo in nos defluxit peccatum Adami vocans ) intra nos est. Secundo, quia cum vitium hæreditarium nos æquè morte æterna dignos ac Adamum faciat, nihil obstat, quominus peccatum Adami nobis eo sensu dicatur imputari, quo dixit Apostolus, si quis legem seruauerit, illius præputium in circuncisionem imputari, hoc est, eodem loco eum haberi ac si fuisset circuncisus. Tertio, quia corruptio hæreditaria est habitus, quem primum peccatum in Adami anima reliquit, & peruersa inclinatio ad simile peccatum ; ac proinde consensus habitualis ad illud peccatum, nihil video quod impediat, quominus nobis imputari dicatur. Hunc vltimum modum, hanc vltimam rationem, Vir Doctus in tres discerpit, ac mutat quia in quatenus. Sed eum audiamus.
units.tr: GAR. Then they paint this later imputation of theirs with another colour, when they add that there is nothing to prevent Adam's sin from being said to be imputed to us, in so far as our hereditary vice is a habit which the first actual sin left in the soul of Adam; then an inclination to similar sins; thirdly a habitual consent to that sin. The learned man has drawn these words from my second letter written to him; but on his own account he has added the words in so far as, then, thirdly, dividing what I joined together, and you will make three reasons out of one, contrary to my intention. I will write out the whole passage from that letter, written in French. The sin of Adam can be said to be imputed to us his posterity in three ways. First, because (as Calvin hints, calling the vice which flowed from Adam into us the sin of Adam) it is within us. Second, because since hereditary vice makes us as worthy of eternal death as Adam, there is nothing to prevent Adam's sin from being said to be imputed to us in the sense in which the Apostle said, if anyone keeps the law, his uncircumcision is imputed as circumcision, that is, he is held to be in the same position as if he had been circumcised. Third, because hereditary corruption is a habit which the first sin left in the soul of Adam, and a perverse inclination to a similar sin; and accordingly a habitual consent to that sin: I see nothing that would prevent it from being said to be imputed to us. This last way, this last reason, the learned man tears into three and changes because into in so far as. But let us hear him.

units.la: G A R. Vbi primum illud mirari subit, quod imputari agnofcunt peccatum Ada, quatenus corruptio nostra est habitus in Adami anima relictus. Hæc enim verba præferre videntur imputationem ipsius habitualis peccati Ada. Quid autem horridius aut absurdius est, in eo quod dicimus, imputari nobis peccatum Adami actuale, quam quod hic verbis fatentur, imputari peccatum habituale ; præsertim cum imputatio potius ad actus videatur referenda quam ad habitus ?
units.tr: G A R. My first surprise is that you acknowledge Adam's sin to be imputed insofar as our corruption is a habit left in Adam's soul. These words seem to put forward the imputation of Adam's habitual sin itself. What is more horrid or absurd than this? When we say that Adam's actual sin is imputed to us, you here confess in words that his habitual sin is imputed. This is especially so since imputation seems to refer to acts rather than to habits.

units.la: PLAC. Primùm non dixi, imputari peccatum Adæ, quatenus corruptio nostra est habitus in Adami anima relictus. Tantùm dixi, quia corruptio hæreditaria est habitus quem primum peccatum in Adami anima reliquit, & pernersa propensio ad ejusmodi peccatum, atque adeò consensus habitualis ad illud peccatum, causam me non videre, cur non possit dici nobis imputari, nimirum primum illud peccatum, quod corruptionem, quæ hæreditaria vocatur, in Adami anima reliquit. id autem aliud esse non potest quàm primum illud Adæ peccatum actuale. Aliud enim nullum illam depravationem in Adami anima reliquit. Vides Lector, me imputationem illam, quam mediatam appello, referre ad peccatum Adæ actuale, ac rationem reddere, cur ob hæreditariam illam corruptionem dici possit nobis imputari. Sed quandoquidem Vir Doctus probat corruptionem, quatenus in Adami anima fuit, nobis imputari, vide quæso quid consequatur. Primùm illa nostra erit, vt peccatum actuale, per imputationem; hoc enim est illius sententiæ consentaneum. Vultne igitur posteros Adami corruptos esse, vt loquitur, interpretatiue, seu imputatiue? Deinde, peto an corruptio, quatenus nobis inhæret, nobis imputetur, necne? Si negas; igitur non est verè peccatum, non peragit nos reos. Si ais; igitur bis corruptio nobis imputatur, semel quatenus fuit in Adamo, iterum quatenus est in nobis. Ita magis rei sumus quàm Adamus. Quis hoc credat? Denique peto an corruptio, quatenus hæsit in Adamo, imputetur nobis immediatè, an mediante corruptione? Si hoc, cur idem non dicitur de peccato actuali? Si illud, Ergo illius corruptionis Adæ, nostra corruptio pœna est: Cur enim non æquè imputati habitualis pœna sit, ac imputati actualis? Si ergo illius imputati pœna est, magis punitur in nobis peccatum habituale Adami, quàm in ipso Adamo punitum est. In nobis enim, si viro Docto fides habetur, punitur inflicta corruptione, cum cà pœnà non fuerit corruptio Adami in Adamo punita. Postremò, Si nobis imputatur corruptio vt fuit in Adamo, vel nobis imputatur simul cum eius peccato actuali, vel ante, aut post illud peccatum. Cur ante aut post illud imputetur, causa dici non potest. Si nobis simul imputatur, etiam simul cum actuali imputata fuit Adamo, cur non enim æque simul illi ac nobis duo illa eius peccata imputata fuissent? Si ergo simul imputata fuerunt ipsi Adamo, eius corruptio non fuit pœna peccati actualis: fuisset enim semetipsa prior: antecedit enim imputatio pœnam; & prius imputata fuisset Adamo, quàm in eo fuisset. Id quod non obscurè contradictionem implicat. Sed pergat.
units.tr: PLAC. First, I did not say that Adam's sin is imputed insofar as our corruption is a habit left in Adam's soul. I only said that, since hereditary corruption is a habit which the first sin left in Adam's soul, and a perverse propensity to that kind of sin, and therefore a habitual consent to that sin, I see no reason why it cannot be said to be imputed to us. Namely, that first sin, which left in Adam's soul the corruption called hereditary. This can be nothing other than Adam's first actual sin, for no other thing left that depravity in Adam's soul. You see, reader, that I refer that imputation, which I call mediate, to Adam's actual sin, and I give the reason why hereditary corruption can be said to be imputed to us. But since the learned man proves that the corruption, insofar as it was in Adam's soul, is imputed to us, please see what follows. First, it will be our actual sin, through imputation, for this agrees with his opinion. Does he therefore want Adam's posterity to be corrupt, as he puts it, interpretatively or imputatively? Next, I ask whether corruption, insofar as it inheres in us, is imputed to us or not. If you deny it, then it is not truly sin and does not make us guilty. If you affirm it, then corruption is imputed to us twice: once insofar as it was in Adam, and again insofar as it is in us. So we would be more guilty than Adam. Who could believe this? Finally, I ask whether the corruption, insofar as it clung to Adam, is imputed to us immediately, or through the medium of corruption. If the former, why is the same not said of actual sin? If the latter, then our corruption is the punishment of Adam's corruption. For why should the punishment of imputed habitual sin not be as much as that of imputed actual sin? If, then, it is the punishment of that imputed sin, the habitual sin of Adam is punished more in us than it was punished in Adam himself.
