For in us, if the learned man is to be believed, it is punished by the infliction of corruption, whereas Adam's corruption was not punished in Adam with that punishment. Lastly, if corruption as it was in Adam is imputed to us, it is imputed either together with his actual sin, or before or after that sin. Why it would be imputed before or after that sin cannot be given as a reason. If it is imputed together with it, then it was imputed to Adam himself together with the actual sin as well. For why would those two sins of his not have been imputed to him and to us equally together? If, then, they were imputed together to Adam himself, his corruption was not the punishment of his actual sin, for it would have been prior to itself. For imputation precedes punishment, and it would have been imputed to Adam before it was in him. This plainly involves a contradiction. But let him go on.

units.la: GAR. Deinde, quâ ratione habitus ille in Adami anima relictus, dici potest peccatum nostrum hæreditarium? habitus ille in Adami anima, nonne diu est cum esse desijt? Quomodo igitur esse amplius potest, aut nobis subjectiuè inhærere? imo qui fieri potest, vt vnicus habitus, id. vnum idemque numero accidens, in tam diuersa, adeoque infinita pœne subjecta transeat?
units.tr: GAR. Next, in what sense can that habit left in Adam's soul be called our hereditary sin? That habit in Adam's soul, has it not long since ceased to exist? How, then, can it any longer exist, or inhere in us as its subject? Indeed, how can it happen that a single habit, one and the same accident numerically, passes into so many different, indeed almost infinite, subjects?

units.la: PLAC. Dixi in genere corruptionem hæreditariam esse habitum, quem primum peccatum in Adami anima reliquit; nempe vt in suo fonte, vnde ad nos omnes propagatione naturali manauit. Nonne hoc verum est? Atqui diu est cum esse desijt, nempe in Adamo. Sed nondum esse desijt in Adami posteris. At quomodo habitus in Adami anima relictus dici potest peccatum nostrum? Eo modo, inquam, quo peccatum Adami dicitur à Caluino intra nos esse, & peccatum hæreditarium dicitur vetus Adam, & natura Adami dicitur natura nostra, & quod seminatur esse id quod metitur. Nimirum habitus ille in Adamo relictus ab eo in nos propagatus est. Differt igitur numero peccatum nostrum ab Adami peccato, sed est idem specie, nec id tantum, sed ab eo ducit originem quodam quasi naturali contagio. Si dixero naturam humanam esse illam quæ creata est in Adamo, num inde sequetur, naturam humanam Adami, & nostram non differre numero?
units.tr: PLAC. I said in general that hereditary corruption is the habit which the first sin left in Adam's soul, namely as in its source, from which it flowed by natural propagation to all of us. Is this not true? Yet it has long since ceased to exist, namely in Adam. But it has not yet ceased to exist in Adam's posterity. But how can the habit left in Adam's soul be called our sin? In the way, I say, that Calvin says Adam's sin is within us, and hereditary sin is called the old Adam, and Adam's nature is called our nature, and what is sown is the same as what is reaped. Clearly that habit left in Adam was propagated from him into us. Our sin, therefore, differs numerically from Adam's sin, but is the same in kind, and not only this, but it derives its origin from him by a kind of natural contagion. If I say that human nature is that which was created in Adam, will it follow from this that Adam's human nature and ours do not differ numerically?

units.la: GAR. Est inclinatio ad peccata similia peccato illi primo Ada. Sane vero; Sed & ad alia Adami peccata. An ideo dicemus, reliquum itidem Adami peccata nobis imputari? Imo nequaquam sufficiens est alieni peccati imputationis causa, vt nostrum peccatum eodem animum nostrum inclinet & fleteat. Multi enim inclinationem,& naturalem quendam impetum habent ad similia aliorum peccata, sine omni omnino illorum imputatione. &c.
units.tr: GAR. There is an inclination to sins similar to that first sin of Adam. Certainly; but also to the other sins of Adam. Shall we therefore say that the remaining sins of Adam are likewise imputed to us? No, by no means is it sufficient reason for the imputation of another's sin that our sin inclines and bends our mind to the same. For many have an inclination and a certain natural impulse to the similar sins of others, without any imputation of those sins at all. Etc.

units.la: PLAC. Primò tribuit mihi argumentationem non meam. Hoc enim, vt dixi, conjunxi cum superiori, vt ex duobus illis tertium colligerem, in quo ratio imputationis potissimum consistit. Id quod ex tertia illa ratione, quam ex literis meis se collegisse profitetur hoc eodem cap. 2. §. x. pag. 35. 36. liquere poterit. In ea enim copulantur ista tria quæ hoc loco diuisit sic vt duplex mutatio notari posset. Primò enim pro corruptione hereditaria reposuit vitium in nobis inexistens. Deinde omisit conjunctionem causalem proinde, adeo, aut similem, respondentem eo loco vocibus gallicis par consequent, quibus in illa epistola vsus fueram, & ex quibus apparet, rationem imputationis me petere à consensu habituali ad illud peccatum in corruptione hereditaria incluso : hunc autem consensum ex eo colligere, quòd illa corruptio nihil aliud est quàm primi illius peccati actualis prauitas habitualis, quam in Adami anima reliquit, & quæ in nos propagata nos ad simile peccatum inclinat. Cæterum nescio, annon etiam hoc loco aduersus ipsius Domini verba disputare videatur, quæ habentur Matth. 23. 34. & Luc. xi. 50. 51. Quid est enim, cur, exempli causa, non possint aliquomodo crudelia facinora Neronis ei, qui sit animo æquè crudeli & immani, imputari, quandoquidem quominus eadem perpetret per ejus voluntatem non stat, æquè videlicet crudelem?
units.tr: PLAC. First, he attributes to me an argument that is not mine. For, as I said, I joined this with the previous point, so that from those two I might draw a third, in which the principal ground of imputation consists. This can be seen from that third reason, which he professes he has gathered from my letters, in this same chapter 2, §10, pages 35 and 36. For in it these three things are joined, which he here has divided, so that a double change could be noted. For first, he has put vice inhering in us in place of hereditary corruption. Then he has omitted the causal conjunction therefore, and so, or a similar one, corresponding in that place to the French words par consequent, which I had used in that letter, and from which it appears that I seek the ground of imputation from habitual consent to that sin included in hereditary corruption, and that I infer this consent from the fact that this corruption is nothing other than the habitual depravity of that first actual sin, which it left in Adam's soul, and which, propagated into us, inclines us to a similar sin. For the rest, I do not know whether he does not also seem here to dispute against the very words of the Lord, which are found in Matthew 23:34 and Luke 11:50-51. For why, for example, could the cruel crimes of Nero not in some way be imputed to one who is of an equally cruel and savage mind, since the fact that he does not commit the same deeds is not due to his will, which is equally cruel?

units.la: GAR. De habituali consensu quod vltimo loco dicitur, ad rem præsentem magis pertinet, sed tale tamen est, vt Virorum Doctorum causam euertat potius quàm stabilit. Contendunt enim acriter ipsam Adami actualem inobedientiam nemini posterorum imputari, neminem ejus poenas ferre, neminem propter eam reum haberi posse, & tamen fatentur esse in omnibus Adami posteris consensum habitualem ad illud peccatum. Quis non inde consequi videt, eam igitur inobedientiam primi parentis merito posse posteris imputari? Nam consensus in peccatum alterius, justa causa esse potest imputationis illius peccati, juxta dictum Apostolicum, esse dignos morte, non modò qui mala ipsi patrant, sed & qui mala patrantibus consentiunt. Rom 1.32. Unde colligitur hac argumentatio. Omnis consensus in alienum peccatum, justa causa esse potest imputationis illius peccati. At consensus habitualis omnium posterorum Adæ, est aliquis consensus in peccatum actuale primum Adami. Ergo consensus habitualis, justa ratio & causa esse potest, quare primum Adami peccatum omnibus ipsius posteris imputetur.
units.tr: GAR. What is said in the last place about habitual consent bears more on the present matter, but it is of such a kind that it overturns the cause of the learned men rather than establishing it. For they strenuously contend that Adam's actual disobedience is imputed to none of his posterity, that none bears its punishment, that none can be held guilty on account of it, and yet they confess that there is habitual consent to that sin in all Adam's posterity. Who does not see that it follows from this that that disobedience of the first parent can rightly be imputed to his posterity? For consent to another's sin can be a just cause of the imputation of that sin, according to the apostolic saying, that they are worthy of death, not only those who commit evil themselves, but also those who consent to those who commit it. Romans 1:32. Whence this argument is drawn. Every consent to another's sin can be a just cause of the imputation of that sin. But the habitual consent of all Adam's posterity is some consent to Adam's first actual sin. Therefore habitual consent can be a just reason and cause why Adam's first sin is imputed to all his posterity.

units.la: P L A C. Itáne argumentatio, quæ tota mea est, causam meam evertit? Itáne contendo acriter ipsam Adami actualem inobedientiam nemini posterorum imputari, neminem ejus pœnas ferre, neminem propter eam reum haberi posse? Quid clarius, quàm me potiùs contendere eam Adami posteris imputari, eos eius pœnas ferre, propter eam reos haberi? Alioqui, quorsum seposui corruptionem hæreditariam à statu quæstionis? Cur imputationis immediatæ & mediatæ distinctionem attuli? Cur sic distinguendum censui attributum quæstionis, Utrùm actualis inobedientia Adami nobis nascentibus imputetur? Cur constituens statum controversiæ ei limitationem ab illa distinctione petitam adhibui? Quorsum etiam pertinent istæ ipsæ rationes, quas coniunctim propositeram & Vir Doctus disjunxit? Volui certè rationem reddere, cur peccatum aliquod nobis imputetur, nonne? Nimis diserta sunt verba mea quàm ut id possit negari. Quod ergo peccatum intellexi? Nullum potui, præter actuale primum Adami. Dixi corruptionem hæreditariam esse habitum, quem primum peccatum reliquit in Adami anima. nonne vides me aliud primum peccatum intelligere non posse, quàm actuale illud primum? Dixi illam corruptionem esse propensionem ad similia peccata, nempe similia illi primo actuali, alia intelligi non possunt. Dixi eam esse consensum habitualem ad illud peccatum. Quis non videt per illud peccatum me corruptionem non intelligere, sed actuale illud primum quo se ipse Adamus corrupit? Eandem rationem imputationis mediatæ in hoc ipso Manuscripto propositi his verbis. Hujus enim corruptionis participatione communicamus peccato Adami, eique, ut ita loquar, habitualiter consentimus. Quis non videt me peccatum Adami cui communicamus, cui habitualiter consentimus, distinguere à corruptione quâ ei communicamus & consentimus? Id autem aliud esse non potest quàm primum illud actuale Adami. Hoc igitur volui nobis imputari, & quidem ob istum ipsum habitualem consensum. Non igitur me mecum committit Vir doctus, sed cum animi sui figmento.
units.tr: PLACAEUS. So then, does the argument, which is entirely mine, overthrow my cause? Do I so vehemently contend that Adam's actual disobedience is imputed to none of his posterity, that none of them bears its punishment, and that none can be held guilty on account of it? What is clearer than that I contend the opposite: that this disobedience is imputed to Adam's posterity, that they bear its punishment, and that they are held guilty on account of it? Otherwise, why did I set hereditary corruption apart from the state of the question? Why did I introduce the distinction between immediate and mediate imputation? Why did I think the question should be divided in this way, Whether Adam's actual disobedience is imputed to us at our birth? Why did I apply to the statement of the controversy a limitation drawn from that distinction? And what bearing have those very reasons, which I set out together and which the learned man has separated? I certainly meant to give a reason why some sin is imputed to us, did I not? My words are too plain for this to be denied. What sin, then, did I understand? I could understand none except Adam's actual first sin. I said that hereditary corruption is a habit which the first sin left in Adam's soul. Do you not see that I can understand no other first sin than that actual first one? I said that this corruption is a propensity to like sins, namely like that first actual sin; other sins cannot be meant. I said that it is a habitual consent to that sin. Who does not see that by that sin I do not mean the corruption, but that actual first sin by which Adam himself was corrupted? I set out the same reason for mediate imputation in this very manuscript, in these words: For by participation in this corruption we are made partakers of Adam's sin, and, so to speak, habitually consent to it. Who does not see that I distinguish the sin of Adam, in which we participate and to which we habitually consent, from the corruption by which we participate in it and consent to it? That sin can be nothing other than Adam's first actual sin. This, then, is what I meant to be imputed to us, and indeed on account of that very habitual consent. The learned man therefore is not contending with me, but with a figment of his own mind.

units.la: Posterior quæstio de hujus peccati imputati pœna etiam ipsa aliquam explicationem desiderat. Primùm autem pœna distinguenda est; deinde separandus à nobis Adamus. Pœna dicitur vel proprie, vel improprie. Proprie rursus multipliciter: sed nihil opus est omnia pœnarum genera quæ te nosse arbitror, enumerare, id enim cum longum esset, tum ad rem quam agimus inutile. Satis est tenere quo sensu corruptio hæreditaria pœna dicatur à te aliisque fratribus nostris, quorum sententiam aduersus me tueri vis. Nempe statuis esse pœnam strictissimè ac propriissimè sic dictam, cujus hæ sunt conditiones. 1. Lex eam comminatur. 2. Iustitia ut infligatur à iudice exigit. 3. Iudex eam infligit ut fiat justitia, siue ut justitiæ satisfiat. Itaque Vrsinus in explicat. Catechet. Cum sibi objecisset non debuisse Deum culpam Adami tali pœna punire, respondit fiat justitia & pereat Mundus. Ego verò talem esse pœnam & negaui in Thesibus & non possum impetrare à conscientia mea ut nunc quoque non negem. Scio hanc corruptionem seu cōcupiscentiam pœnam à Patribus appellari, necnon alicubi à Caluino, sed nego sensu ita proprio, ita stricto. Sed ob similitudinem quandam pœnæ nomen ei accommodatur. Vt enim pœna sequitur culpam & cum ea cohæret, sic corruptio hæreditaria secuta est culpam Adami atque ex ea nata est. Vt non est in eius qui punitur potestate pœnam admittere, vel non admittere aut etiam excutere, sic ab alio corruptione ista afficimur, nec in nobis situm est eam non admittere, aut excutere. Vt pœna ejus cui infligitur conditionem mutat in deteriorem, sic hac corruptione inquinatus Adamus deterior, ignobilior, fœdior, miserior, quàm alioqui fuisset, euasit. Denique vt qui inflictam pœnam sentit, ingemiscit, & ab ea liberari percupit; sic qui hanc in se corruptionem deprehendunt & agnoscunt serio, vehementer indolescunt & ægre ferunt se hujus mali vinculis illigari. Has ob similitudines merito tetrum istud & horrendum malum pœna dici potuit & dicitur à multis? Sed quæritur inter nos duntaxat, num sit pœna sensuillo, quem explicaui, maximè proprio & stricto. Has duas quæstiones, quia tu non separasti, vt feret occasio, tua sequens vestigia, Deo fauente, tractabo.
units.tr: The second question, concerning the punishment of this imputed sin, also requires some explanation. First, the punishment must be distinguished; then Adam must be separated from us. Punishment is spoken of either properly or improperly. Properly, again, in many ways; but there is no need to enumerate all the kinds of punishment which I suppose you know, for that would be both lengthy and useless for the matter we are dealing with. It is enough to grasp in what sense hereditary corruption is called a punishment by you and by our other brethren, whose opinion you wish to defend against me. Namely, you hold that a punishment in the strictest and most proper sense is one with these conditions: (1) the law threatens it; (2) justice demands that it be inflicted by a judge; (3) the judge inflicts it so that justice may be done, or that justice may be satisfied. Thus Ursinus, in his explanation of the Catechism, when someone objected to him that God ought not to punish Adam's guilt with such a punishment, answered: let justice be done, though the world perish. I, however, have both denied in my Theses that such a punishment exists, and I cannot bring my conscience to refrain from denying it now as well. I know that the Fathers call this corruption, or concupiscence, a punishment, and that Calvin does so somewhere too; but I deny that it is a punishment in that proper and strict sense. It is given the name because of a certain likeness to punishment. For as punishment follows guilt and coheres with it, so hereditary corruption has followed Adam's guilt and been born from it. As it is not within the power of the one who is punished to admit or not admit the punishment, or even to shake it off, so we are afflicted by that corruption from another, and it does not lie in us to refuse it or shake it off. As punishment changes the condition of the one on whom it is inflicted for the worse, so Adam, defiled by this corruption, became worse, less noble, more foul and more wretched than he otherwise would have been. Finally, as one who feels an inflicted punishment groans and earnestly wishes to be freed from it, so those who perceive and seriously acknowledge this corruption in themselves are deeply grieved and bear it with difficulty, being bound in the chains of this evil. Is it because of these likenesses that this foul and dreadful evil could rightly be called, and is called by many, a punishment? But the question between us is only whether it is a punishment in the most proper and strict sense which I have explained. Since you have not separated these two questions, I shall, as occasion allows, treat them in turn, following your footsteps, God willing.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Obseruata quædam in primo & secundo Capite Tractatus, & alia laudata, alia refutata.
units.tr: Certain points noted in the first and second chapters of your treatise: some commended, others refuted.

units.la: PRIMO Capite tui tractatus statum quæstionis constituisti. Eo constituto Capite secundo digrederis ad probandum, omnes homines esse infectos peccato originali, & ideo omnibus hujus vitæ miserius & morti obnoxios. quo consilio, equidem nescio. Nam tu ipse fateris extremis verbis cap. 2. nullam ea de re inter nos esse controuersiam: Et vero id ipsum Thesibus quas oppugnas probaueram, paucis quidem verbis, sed argumentis multis & validis, robore & numero præstantibus, quorum quædam expoliuisti, quædam prætermisisti. Notaui autem inter legendum nonnulla digna obseruatu, vel quia vera sunt, sed causæ quam agis repugnantia, vel quia tam veritati quàm meæ sententiæ aduersari mihi videntur.
units.tr: In the first chapter of your treatise you set out the state of the question. Having done so, you go on in the second chapter to prove that all men are infected with original sin, and therefore subject to every misery of this life and liable to death. I honestly do not know what purpose this served. For you yourself admit in the closing words of chapter 2 that there is no controversy between us on this point. Indeed, my Theses, which you attack, had already proved this same point, in few words but with many strong arguments, excellent in force and number. Some of these you have polished, and others you have passed over. In reading, I noted several things worth observing, either because they are true but inconsistent with the cause you defend, or because they seem to me to bear against the truth no less than against my own opinion.

units.la: Laudo in primis quæ scripsisti non procul à fine Cap. 2. peccatum illud Adami omnium malorum scaturigo, actuale & PERSONALE fuit in ipso, sed infecit naturam: & omnes homines eo inficiuntur, quia sunt ab eo secundum ordinem naturæ &c. Dic mihi, amabo te, si peccatum illud personale fuit in Adamo, quo jure illud idem numero quod in Adamo fuit nobis omnibus imputetur? Tu Cap. x. dicis Deum in verbis illis Ezechielis, filius non feret iniquitatem Patris, loqui tantum de peccatis externis & actualibus, & cum ejusmodi peccata sint personalia, personam tantum spectare. Iam autem tu affirmas hoc loco peccatum illud Adami fuisse actuale & personale. Quis non inde concludat ergo peccatum illud tantum Adami personam spectabat, nec illud ferre filij eius debent? Quid sibi etiam volunt illa verba in ipso? opponunturne his in ejus posteris, vel in nobis? certè in nobis peccatum Adami non est personale, sed totius generis humani, (vno excepto Christo) commune: sed in nobis nihil aliud est quàm hæreditarium illud vitium, quo omnes infecti nascimur, quodque omnibus, nisi condonatum fuerit per Christum, imputatur.
units.tr: First, I commend what you wrote not far from the end of chapter 2: that sin of Adam, the fountain of all evils, was actual and PERSONAL in him, but it infected nature; and all men are infected by it, because they are from him according to the order of nature, and so on. Tell me, I beg you: if that sin was personal in Adam, by what right is that same sin, numerically the same as it was in Adam, imputed to all of us? In chapter 10 you say that God, in those words of Ezekiel, "the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father," speaks only of external and actual sins, and since such sins are personal, they concern only the person. Yet here you affirm that the sin of Adam was actual and personal. Who would not conclude from this that the sin concerned only the person of Adam, and that his sons ought not to bear it? What do the words in ipso ("in him") mean? Are they set against in his posterity or in us? Certainly the sin of Adam is not personal in us, but common to the whole human race (with the one exception of Christ). In us there is nothing else but that hereditary vice with which we are all born infected, and which is imputed to all of us unless it is pardoned through Christ.

units.la: Minùs commodè idem dixeras. Cap. 1. hæc culpa vnius hominis fuit, sed pœna omnibus hominibus est communis &c. Hoc discrimen obseruas inter culpam Adami & pœnam, quod culpa vnius hominis fuit, pœna vero communis omnibus. Nonne vides quid sequatur, nimirum poenam non respondere culpae; quippe, culpam enim non communem vindicari poena communi: poenam ijs irrogari, quorum non sit culpa. Certe si poena est omnium, culpa tantùm vnius, omnes, vno excepto, culpa vacant, quomodo igitur puniuntur iustè? Si culpa vnius hominis est, nec est communis omnibus, cur omnibus imputatur? Si eam dicas, cùm vnius sit, imputatione fieri communem omnibus, non euades, primùm enim quæ mea culpa non est, ea mihi imputari non debet. Non enim ideo mihi imputatur vt sit mea, sed contrà quia mea est, idcirco mihi imputatur: alioqui mihi imputatur falsò & iniustè. Deinde si culpa Adami mea non est nisi imputatione, fecit me Deus Iudex (cogitans horresco) sua imputatione peccatorem, non inuenit: est enim imputatio judicis actus, non meus. Tolle imputationem, culpâ illâ vaco; mea enim non est, sed fuit vnius hominis Adami: me igitur (vide quo ducat ista imputatio & mecum cohorresce) judex, hoc est, Deus fecit peccatorem ac reum, & causa est primi mei peccati, primi mei reatus. Denique de jure non magis ad me poena Adami pertinet quàm culpa. Si igitur culpa eius mea non est reipsa, sed tantum imputatione, idem etiam de poena dicendum est. His ego absurdis non vrgeor, qui culpam volo esse tam communem omnibus, quàm poenam: communem inquam reapse, non imputatione sed propagatione, ac nobis imputari, quia intra nos est. Culpa autem illa est vitium originale nobis singulis inhærens, quam ipsam nolo proprie loquendo poenam esse ob eas causas, quas mox aperiam cap. sequente. Laudo etiam hæc tua verba, Quemadmodum fons infectus rivos etiam inficit, & sicut radix producit surculos secundum speciem suam, malos scilicet, si mala est, EODEM PRORSVS MODO primus homo corruptus & peccator genuit & protulit filios corruptos & peccatores. Subsumo, atqui fons infectus inficit rivos & radix mala profert malos surculos ea tantummodo lege Naturæ, qua sibi quodque simile gignit. Cur igitur non idem statuis de primo homine, si nos eodem prorsus modo corruptus corruptos genuit? Si lex ista naturæ sufficit ad peccati originalis propagationem ante peccatum constituta & fancita, quid est quamobrem eam dei justitiæ, dei judicis sententiæ imputes non sine magno meo scandalo, qui sic magnam Dei justitiæ fieri iniuriam queror? atque huius rei ipsum propagationis nomen admonere potuit: est enim propagatio opus naturæ, quæ suas in ea leges sequitur, Deo, vt est naturæ author & conseruator, Leges illas suo concursu conseruante & constabiliente, pendent enim ex decreto, quod ordine naturæ decretum de lapsu permittendo mihi videtur antecessisse. Itaque posteriore decreto rescindi nec potuerunt, nec debuerunt.
units.tr: You had said the same thing less aptly in chapter 1: this guilt was of one man, but the punishment is common to all men, and so on. You note this difference between the guilt of Adam and the punishment: the guilt was of one man, but the punishment is common to all. Do you not see what follows? Namely, that punishment does not correspond to guilt; for a guilt that is not common is not avenged by a common punishment, and punishment is inflicted on those who have no guilt. Certainly, if the punishment belongs to all but the guilt to one only, then all men except one are free of guilt, and how then are they justly punished? If the guilt is of one man and is not common to all, why is it imputed to all? If you say that, since it belongs to one man, it becomes common to all by imputation, you will not escape. For first, what is not my guilt ought not to be imputed to me. It is not imputed to me because it is mine, but on the contrary it is mine because it is imputed to me; otherwise it is imputed to me falsely and unjustly. Next, if the guilt of Adam is not mine except by imputation, then God the Judge (I shudder to think it) made me a sinner by his imputation, and did not find me one. For imputation is an act of the judge, not of mine. Take away the imputation, and I am free of that guilt; for it is not mine, but was the guilt of one man, Adam. So the judge, that is God, has made me a sinner and guilty (consider where this imputation leads, and shudder with me), and is the cause of my first sin and my first guilt. Finally, by right the punishment of Adam belongs to me no more than the guilt does. If, therefore, his guilt is not really mine, but only by imputation, the same must be said of the punishment. I am not troubled by these absurdities, since I hold that guilt is as common to all men as punishment is: common, I say, in reality, not by imputation, but by propagation; and it is imputed to us because it is within us. That guilt, however, is the original vice inhering in each of us, which I do not wish to call properly a punishment, for the reasons I will set out in the following chapter. I also commend these words of yours: just as a poisoned spring poisons the streams, and as a root produces shoots according to its kind, evil shoots, namely, if it is evil, in exactly the same way the first man, corrupt and a sinner, begot and brought forth corrupt and sinful children. I reason thus: a poisoned spring poisons its streams, and an evil root produces evil shoots only by that law of nature by which each thing begets what is like itself. Why, then, do you not hold the same of the first man, if he begot corrupt children in exactly the same way? If that law of nature, established and sanctioned before the sin, is enough for the propagation of original sin, why do you impute it to the justice of God and the sentence of the Judge, to my great offence, since I complain that such an imputation does great injury to the justice of God? The very name of propagation could have warned you: propagation is a work of nature, which follows its own laws in it, while God, as author and preserver of nature, keeps and maintains those laws by his concurring action; for they depend on a decree which, in the order of nature, seems to me to have preceded the decree to permit the fall. Therefore they could not, and ought not, be annulled by a later decree.

units.la: Placet etiam mihi valde, quod hanc labem & corruptionem in omnes homines transfusam & transmissam fuisse clare nos doceri affirmas Rom. 5. 12. 14. 15. 16. 19. quibus versibus græcè & latinè pro tuo more citatis, concludis hæc manifeste probare primum illud hominis peccatum in omnes homines transfusum, & transmissum vniuersos infecisse, & morti addixisse. Nam si illis versibus clare docetur in omnes homines transfusa corruptio, contendo ex ijsdem illis versibus nulla arte concludi posse, primum Adami peccatum actuale toti eius posteritati proxime & immediate imputari. Id quod hæc nostra disputatio, Deo fauente, faciet liquidum. Interim quid est primum illud primi hominis peccatum in omnes homines transfusum & transmissum, nisi inhærens omnibus ab ipso ortu labes & corruptio ab ea, quæ fuit in Adamo, numero differens? nam, neque ejus actio, quæ simul ac commissa est esse desiit, in nos transfundi, neque imputatio, extra nos in dei mente facta, transfusio & transmissio in nos dici, neque inhærens Adamo corruptio de subjecto in subjectum eadem numero migrare potuit. Memineris igitur te primi Adæ peccati nomine hereditariam corruptionem insigniuisse.
units.tr: I am also very pleased that you affirm that this stain and corruption, transfused and transmitted into all men, is clearly taught to us in Romans 5:12, 14, 15, 16, 19. Having cited these verses in Greek and Latin, as is your custom, you conclude that these verses manifestly prove that the first sin of man, transfused and transmitted into all men, infected them all and delivered them to death. For if the corruption transfused into all men is clearly taught in those verses, I contend that from those same verses it cannot be concluded by any art that the actual first sin of Adam is imputed to his whole posterity proximately and immediately. This present disputation of ours, God willing, will make that plain. Meanwhile, what is that first sin of the first man, transfused and transmitted into all men, except the stain and corruption inhering in all from their very birth, differing in number from that which was in Adam? For neither his act, which ceased to exist as soon as it was committed, can be transfused into us, nor can an imputation, made in the mind of God outside us, be said to be a transfusion and transmission into us; nor could the corruption inhering in Adam pass from subject to subject and remain numerically the same. Remember, then, that by the name of the first sin of Adam you have marked hereditary corruption.

units.la: Laudo denique quod hoc vitium, & peccatum appellas, & sic vocatum ab Apostolo agnoscis, & mortis homines vniuersos addixisse fateris, teque hortor vt in ea doctrina, quam Scriptura, & secundum scripturam Ecclesiæ omnes protestantium vnanimi consensu docent, perseueres constanter.
units.tr: Finally, I commend your calling this a vice and a sin, and your acknowledging that it is so called by the Apostle, and your confessing that it has delivered all men to death. I exhort you to persevere constantly in that doctrine which Scripture, and the Church according to Scripture, teaches with the unanimous consent of all Protestants.

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Rursus quædam obseruata & reprehensa in eodem Cap. II.
units.tr: Further points observed and criticised in the same Chapter II.

units.la: LAVDAVI quædam, Reuerende & dilectissime in Christo Frater, in secundo Capite Tui tractatus, Patere me etiam quædam refellere. Dicis enim quædam de spiraculo vitæ, de ligno vitæ, deque morte interminata Adamo, quæ, nec probo, nec quid momenti ad id conferant, quod tu eo capite probare instituisti, satis assequor, refutata autem meam causam juuare possunt. Rem ab ouo vt aiunt exorsus observas, Deum infpirasse homini spiraculum triplicis vitæ, animalis, quæ est corporis per vnionem animæ illud viuificantis, spiritualis, quæ est animæ per vnionem Spiritus sancti illam sanctificantis, & beatæ, quæ est animæ & corporis per vnionem cum Deo vtrumque beatum reddentis. Idque hoc vno argumento probas, quia textus hebræus habet in plurali Numero םימ vitas. Quod mihi videtur debilissimum: passim enim vsurpatur plurale illud pro singulari, pro ea vna vita, quam tu animalem vocas: obuia sunt exempla: vide Gen. 3. 14. & 23. 1. & 25. 7. 17. & 27. 45. Pf. 17. 14. & 31. 11. Eccles. 2. 17. & 9. 9. Et passim alibi. Immo pro ea imperfecta, qualis est brutorum vt Gen. 7. 15. 27. quibus locis etiam brutis animantibus tribuitur םימ חור spiraculum, vt tu loqueris, vitarum, nec tamen, opinor, alia vita quam animalis, & quidem destituta ratione. Itaque interpretes omnes quos viderim, vitam verterunt non vitas, & vel nihil mysterij in plurali םימ quesierunt, vel putarunt eo innui eas vitas, quæ ad hominis essentiam & naturam sunt absolute necessarias, vegetatiuam, sensitiuam, & rationalem, quæ Zanchij & Parei opinio est non contemnenda: quàm enim formatio Corporis, tam hæc quoque םימ חור inspiratio ad hominis fabricationem & compositionem, ac constitutionem pertinebat, ad quam etiam sanctitatem & beatitudinem, introductione Adami, postquam creatus fuit, in paradisum, autam, libenter refero. Habebat enim se sanctitas ad animam, vt sanitas ad corpus. Itaque quemadmodum in corpore non erat duplex vita, quarum altera posita esset in sanitate, sic non arbitror sanctitatem animæ augere numerum vitarum, quibus præditus fuit Adamus. Magnum enim discrimen observuo inter Adami & nostram in Christo sanctitatem. Illa naturalis fuit simul cum natura humana & creata, &, nisi amissa fuisset, propaganda secundum leges naturæ, ac propterea mutabilis: hęc vero pendet ex dono supernaturali Spiritus Sancti à Christo capite in nos eius membra delapsi, quo regeneramur, vivificamur, & veluti animamur ac regimur. Sanctitas Adami conditio erat eius vitæ Adami, quam animalem appellas, sine qua creari non potuit à Deo justissimo sanctissimóque, & qua fiebat ut Adamus esset bene comparatus ad objecta naturalia. Nostra tota pendet à reuelatione supernaturali, tota tendit in objectum supernaturale, nolque supra conditionem illam naturalem & animalem & mutabilem Adami longè euehit. Itaque natura diuina à Petro appellatur, & imago gloriæ Christi à Paulo. Sed hæc obiter: nihil enim faciunt ad rem quam agimus.
units.tr: I have praised some things, most reverend and dearly beloved brother in Christ, in the second chapter of your treatise, but allow me to refute some others. You say certain things about the breath of life, the tree of life, and the death threatened to Adam, which I do not approve, and which do not contribute anything of weight to what you set out to prove in that chapter. I can follow that much, but their refutation can help my cause. Beginning at the egg, as they say, you observe that God breathed into man a breath of threefold life: animal life, which is the life of the body through the union of the soul that quickens it; spiritual life, which is the life of the soul through the union of the Holy Spirit who sanctifies it; and blessed life, which is the life of soul and body through union with God, making both blessed. You prove this by one argument alone: the Hebrew text has the plural lives [חיים] in the phrase "breath of lives" [רוח חיים]. This seems to me a very weak argument. For that plural is used everywhere for the singular, for that one life which you call animal. Examples are at hand: see Gen. 3. 14, 23. 1, 25. 7, 17, 27. 45, Ps. 17. 14, 31. 11, Eccles. 2. 17, 9. 9, and passim elsewhere. Indeed it is used even for that imperfect life which belongs to the brutes, as in Gen. 7. 15, 27, where the breath of lives [רוח חיים] is attributed to living creatures as well, as you put it, the breath of lives; yet I suppose this is nothing other than animal life, and indeed life lacking reason. Therefore all the interpreters I have seen have translated life, not lives, and either have sought no mystery in the plural, or have thought that by it are signified those lives which are absolutely necessary to the essence and nature of man: the vegetative, the sensitive and the rational. This is the opinion of Zanchius and Pareus, and it is not to be despised. For just as the formation of the body, so also this breathing of the breath of life pertained to the making, composition and constitution of man. To this too I gladly refer holiness and blessedness, which were brought into paradise by Adam after he had been created. For holiness related to the soul as health does to the body. Therefore, just as in the body there was not a double life, one of which lay in health, so I do not think the holiness of the soul increases the number of lives with which Adam was endowed. For I observe a great difference between Adam's holiness and our holiness in Christ. The former was natural, arising together with human nature and created with it, and, unless it had been lost, would have been propagated according to the laws of nature, and for that reason was mutable. The latter, however, depends on the supernatural gift of the Holy Spirit, which has descended from Christ the head upon us his members, by which we are regenerated, quickened, and as it were animated and ruled. Adam's holiness was the condition of that life of Adam which you call animal, without which it could not have been created by the most just and most holy God, and by which Adam was rightly equipped for natural objects. Ours depends wholly on supernatural revelation, aims wholly at a supernatural object, and lifts us far above that natural, animal and mutable condition of Adam. Hence the divine nature is called by Peter, and the image of the glory of Christ by Paul. But these are incidental remarks, for they have nothing to do with the matter we are treating.

units.la: Eodem nixus plurali םיִנּח vis arborem vitæ certam spem fecisse Adamo harum vitarum continuandarum. Atqui non potuit certam spem fecisse continuandæ sanctitatis, in qua vitam spiritualem ponis. Hanc enim continuationem Deus ab Adamo exigebat, non ipsi promittebat: qui si eam promisisset: fecisset procul dubio Adamum impeccabilem: fuisset enim promissio ridicula, efficiam ut perseueres in sanctitate & justitia, modò ne pecces.
units.tr: Relying on the same plural [חיים], you say that the tree of life gave Adam a sure hope of continuing these lives. But it could not have given a sure hope of continuing holiness, in which you place spiritual life. For God required this continuation of Adam; he did not promise it to him. Had he promised it, he would doubtless have made Adam impeccable. For the promise would have been absurd: "I will make you persevere in holiness and righteousness, provided only that you do not sin."

units.la: Huic triplici vitæ triplicem opponis priuationem seu mortem denunciatam à Deo Adamo vt pœnam verbis, morte morieris, afferisque hominem, prout Deus minatus fuerat, mortuum esse. Ego vero (pace tua & aliorum, qui sic tecum sentiunt, ) non possum verba illa morte morieris ad mortem spiritualem seu privationem justitiæ & sanctitatis transferre. Audi, si placet, rationes meas, & expende: nam, nisi me fallit animus, non sunt de nihilo.
units.tr: To this threefold life you oppose a threefold privation, or death, threatened by God to Adam as a punishment in the words you shall surely die, and you assert that man, as God had threatened, has died. But I cannot (with your leave and that of others who think with you) transfer those words you shall surely die to spiritual death, or the privation of righteousness and holiness. Please hear my reasons and weigh them, for unless I am mistaken they are not without foundation.

units.la: Prima ratio. Comminatio opponitur tacitæ promissioni, poena præmio, mors denunciata vitæ promissæ. Atqui vita tacitè promissa Adamo non erat justitia seu sanctitas, nisi velis promissionis conditionem cum re promissa confundere. Ergo mors denunciata non erat privatio justitiæ.
units.tr: First reason. A threat is opposed to a tacit promise, a punishment to a reward, a threatened death to a promised life. But the life tacitly promised to Adam was not righteousness or holiness, unless you wish to confuse the condition of the promise with the thing promised. Therefore the threatened death was not the privation of righteousness.

units.la: G A R. Resp. Minorem non esse simpliciter veram, si audiatur Camero præleCt. de verbo Dei cap. 7. Summum hominis bonum est § 33 animi & corporis, adeoque totius hominis status perfectus atque omnibus numeris absolutus, nihil ut ultra requiri vel debeat, vel possit amplius. Hic vero status & conditio est imago Dei. Caterum imago Dei in duobus sita est, in sanctitate, & qua sanctitatem sequitur, beata immortalitate. Si vita promissa Adæ erat status ipsius perfectus, & ea vita consistit in sanctitate. Ergo vita promissa consistebat in sanctitate. Nec aliter Clar. Amyraldus, De trib. fœder. Thef. 11. Promissio fœderis illius primi consistere debuit in vita perpetua, & affluente omni bonorum genere, quæ tum in animum, tum in corpus hominis competere potuissent. Justitia autem & sanctitas nonne inter animi bona censeri debent?
units.tr: GAR. Reply: The minor premise is not simply true, if we listen to Cameron, in his lectures on the Word of God, chapter 7: "The highest good of man is of soul and body, and so the perfect state of the whole man, complete in every respect, so that nothing more ought or can be required. This state and condition is the image of God. Moreover, the image of God consists in two things: in holiness, and, following holiness, in blessed immortality. If the life promised to Adam was his perfect state, and that life consists in holiness, then the promised life consisted in holiness." Clarissimus Amyraldus says the same, in his De tribus foederibus, thesis 11: "The promise of that first covenant ought to have consisted in perpetual life, and in an abundance of every kind of good, which could have belonged both to the soul and to the body of man. But are not righteousness and holiness rightly counted among the goods of the soul?"

units.la: PLAC. Quis non videt à præstantissimo Camerone describi eo loco, non vitam quatenus promissa Adamo sub perfectæ obedientiæ conditione fuerat, sed absolutè summum hominis bonum, quale Dei verbo seu Euangelio promittitur? Differt autem admodum id quod fœdere gratiæ promittitur, ab eo quod fœdere naturæ promittebatur Adamo. Quis etiam non videt, Clariss. Collegam D. Amyraldum bona intelligere, ut ita loquar, physica, non autem ea quæ merè moralia erant, quorumque continuatio exigebatur ab Adamo? Itaque inseruerat hæc verba, in statu integra natura constituti, & subjunxerat ista eaque in paradiso Terrestri fruenda, quæ cur sint à Viro Docto omissa, aliis judicandum relinquo. Innuunt certè supponi integritatis moralis Naturæ conseruationem, promitti reliquorum omnium bonorum in paradiso Terrestri fruendorum continuationem. Nam, ut Minorem negatam probem, si comminabatur Deus Adamo tanquam pœnam, amissionem seu privationem justitiæ originalis, certè pollicebatur tanquam præmium, non-amissionem seu conseruationem justitiæ originalis, quomodo igitur fieri potuit ut eam Adamus amitteret? Pollicebatur, inquies, sub conditione. Quanam? si perseveraret in integritate & justitia? Si permaneret in obedientia erga Deum? Si non peccaret? Quocunque nomine eam voces, idem erit cum re promissa, & conditio promissionis cum re promissa confundetur.
units.tr: PLAC. Who does not see that the most excellent Cameron, in that passage, describes not the life as it was promised to Adam under the condition of perfect obedience, but absolutely the highest good of man, such as is promised in the word of God or the gospel? But what is promised in the covenant of grace differs greatly from what was promised to Adam in the covenant of nature. Who also does not see that our most distinguished colleague, Mr. Amyraldus, means by goods, so to speak, physical goods, and not those which were purely moral, and whose continuation was required of Adam? So he had inserted the words constituted in a state of integral nature, and added and to be enjoyed in the earthly paradise. Why the learned man has omitted these, I leave to others to judge. They certainly imply that the preservation of the moral integrity of nature was presupposed, and that the continuation of all the other goods to be enjoyed in the earthly paradise was promised. For, to prove my denied minor premise: if God threatened Adam, as a punishment, the loss or privation of original righteousness, then surely he promised, as a reward, the non-loss or preservation of original righteousness. How then could Adam have lost it? "He promised it," you will say, "under a condition." What condition? That he would persevere in integrity and righteousness? That he would remain in obedience towards God? That he would not sin? Whatever name you give it, it will be the same as the thing promised, and the condition of the promise will be confused with the thing promised.

units.la: GAR. Hoc iterum inficiamur. Quia justitia & sanctitas Adami duplex constitui potest. Altera naturalis, altera supernaturalis: altera viæ, altera patriæ; altera hominis creati, altera hominis glorificati. Iustitia naturalis & hominis creati quæ justitia via dici potest, erat conditio promissionis; sed supernaturalis, & hominis glorificati, quam dicimus justitiam patriæ erat res promissa.
units.tr: GAR. We deny this again. For the righteousness and holiness of Adam may be considered as twofold: one natural, the other supernatural; one of the way, the other of the homeland; one of created man, the other of glorified man. The natural righteousness of created man, which may be called the righteousness of the way, was the condition of the promise; but the supernatural righteousness of glorified man, which we call the righteousness of the homeland, was the thing promised.

units.la: PLAC. Hac responsione sibi Vir Doctus aperte contradicit, & cum videatur respondere, non respondet tamen, sed dat manus. Agebatur enim de justitia originali, ut patet ex meo argumento. Vtra igitur duarum illarum, quas distinxit, justitiarum est justitia originalis? Num illa supernaturalis, patriæ, hominis glorificati? Non certè. Non enim illa Adamus priusquam peccaret præditus erat: non illam erat propagaturus in posteros. Est igitur justitia naturalis, viæ, hominis creati, justitia originalis de qua agebatur in argumento? Atqui Vir doctus confiterur hanc Iustitiam suisse conditionem promissionis. Confitetur ergo non fuisse promissam: id quod probare instituerat, & ipse negaverat. Quod si non fuit promissa, eius privatio non fuit mors comminatione denunciata. Id quod mihi probandum incumbebat. Caeterum libenter quaesiuerim, unde habuerit Vir Doctus foedere naturae, cujus conditio fuit justitia naturalis, promissam fuisse justitiam supernaturalem? Id ne alicubi dicit Scriptura? An potest ratiocinando ex Naturae contemplatione colligi? Quaero etiam unde habuerit, Adami, qui e terra fuit, terrenus, & cujus paradisus fuit in terra, patriam non fuisse terram? Tollere certe videtur discrimen inter foedus naturae & foedus gratiae, primum hominem & secundum, & aliquid docere, immo Dei voluntatem quandam & promissionem confingere praeter Scripturam. Id quod omni Christiano, praecipue inter Reformatos Theologiae profesori summa cura vitandum est.
units.tr: PLAC. In this reply the learned man openly contradicts himself. And although he seems to answer, he does not answer; rather he gives up the fight. For the question concerned original righteousness, as is clear from my argument. Which, then, of the two righteousnesses he has distinguished is original righteousness? Is it the supernatural, of the homeland, of glorified man? Certainly not. Adam did not possess that before he sinned, nor was he going to propagate it to his posterity. Therefore original righteousness, the one under discussion in the argument, is the natural, of the way, of created man? But the learned man admits that this righteousness was the condition of the promise. He therefore admits that it was not promised, which is what he had set out to prove, and what he himself had denied. But if it was not promised, its privation was not death threatened by a warning, and this is what I had to prove. Moreover, I would gladly ask where the learned man got the idea that, under the covenant of nature, whose condition was natural righteousness, supernatural righteousness was promised. Does Scripture say this anywhere? Or can it be gathered by reasoning from the contemplation of nature? I also ask where he got the idea that the homeland of Adam, who was of the earth, earthly, and whose paradise was on earth, was not the earth? He certainly seems to remove the distinction between the covenant of nature and the covenant of grace, the first man and the second, and to teach something, indeed to invent a certain will and promise of God, beyond Scripture. This must be avoided with the greatest care by every Christian, and especially by a professor of theology among the Reformed.

units.la: Secunda; Hoc potest illustrari & confirmari promissione & comminatione foederis legalis. Pollicebatur vitam, hoc fac & vives. Quam? spiritualem illam positam in justitia & sanctitate? nihil minus: eius nec initium, nec progressum, nec continuationem lex promittebat, sed exigebat. Promissiones foederis legalis erant conditionales. Conditio erat perfecta Iustitia perpetuo conseruata. Sub hac conditione promittebatur vita. Quare vita promissa non potuit sita esse in praesentia justitiae. Iam autem mors, quam lex comminabatur, opposita erat formaliter non conditioni, sed vitae promissae: non consistebat igitur in absentia seu priuatione justitiae.
units.tr: Second: this can be illustrated and confirmed by the promise and the threat of the legal covenant. It promised life: do this and you will live. But what life? That spiritual life founded in righteousness and holiness? Far from it. The law neither promised nor demanded its beginning, its progress, or its continuation. The promises of the legal covenant were conditional, and the condition was perfect righteousness perpetually preserved. Life was promised under this condition. Therefore the promised life could not consist in the presence of righteousness. Death, however, which the law threatened, was formally opposed not to the condition but to the promised life. It did not consist, then, in the absence or privation of righteousness.

units.la: PLAC. Hanc secundam rationem D. Gariffolius alto Silentio praeteriit.
units.tr: PLAC. Garissolius passed over this second argument in deep silence.

units.la: Tertia; violatio conditionis sive praecepti non est poena transgressori denunciata. Sed priuatio justitiae est violatio conditionis seu praecepti. Ergo non est poena transgressori denunciata. Major probatione non eget: Minorem sic demonstro. Quod lex prohibet, id legis violatio est. At lex prohibet absentiam justitiæ in homine ( tàm certè quàm jubet homini justitiam inesse. ) Ergo absentia justitiæ (quæ tibi mors est spiritualis ) violatio est legis.
units.tr: Third: a violation of the condition or precept is not a penalty denounced on the transgressor. But the privation of righteousness is a violation of the condition or precept. Therefore it is not a penalty denounced on the transgressor. The major needs no proof. I demonstrate the minor thus: what the law forbids is a violation of the law. But the law forbids the absence of righteousness in a man, just as surely as it commands that righteousness be present in him. Therefore the absence of righteousness (which for you is spiritual death) is a violation of the law.

units.la: GAR. Respond. De majore litem hîc non moueo : disputabitur inferius, an violatio præcepti diuini, quæ peccatum est, possit esse pœna peccati. Ad minorem dico, distinguendam esse priuatio-nem justitiæ, vt aliam actiuam nominemus, aliam passiuam. Actiua est, quâ homo ipse malè agendo justitia seipsum spoliat, qua Deus illum impertiuerat : passiua qua Deus hominem justitia priuat, & donis quibus ipsum cumulárat. Si ergo agnoscimus priuationem actiuam justitiæ idem esse cum violatione legis; de priuatione tamen passiua id merito negabitur.
units.tr: GAR. Reply. I do not raise a dispute here about the major: it will be discussed below whether a violation of a divine precept, which is sin, can be the punishment of sin. To the minor I say that the privation of righteousness must be distinguished, so that we may call one active and the other passive. The active is that by which a man, by acting badly, strips himself of the righteousness with which God had endowed him. The passive is that by which God deprives man of righteousness and of the gifts with which he had heaped him. If therefore we acknowledge that the active privation of righteousness is the same as a violation of the law, yet concerning the passive privation this will rightly be denied.

units.la: PLAC. Quod de majore litem hîc non mouet, prudenter facit : nam præter tres illas rationes, quæ sequuntur in Manuscripto, ad quas nihil respondit, violatio conditionis seu præcepti prima nec antecedentis peccati pœna esse potest, cùm sit peccatum primum, nec sui ipsius, cùm non possit posterior esse seipsa : & ridiculè apponeretur præcepto comminatio, quæ minaretur fore vt violetur præceptum, si violetur. Minorem argumento confirmaueram, quod illi visum est tutius silentio tegere, quàm attingere. Potest etiam sic probari. Peccatum est violatio legis. Priuatio justitiæ in homine, est peccatum. Ergo priuatio justitiæ est violatio legis. Quid clarius? At ille distinguit priuationem justitiæ in actiuam & passiuam : illam qua homo ipse malè agendo justitia seipsum spoliat, hanc qua Deus hominem justitia priuat : illam fatetur esse violationem legis, hanc negat. Ex quo sequitur, hanc, non illam, legem esse suo violatori comminatam. Consideremus igitur paulò attentius illam distinctionem. Rectè sanè priuatio justitiæ actiua dicitur respectu priuantis se justitiâ hominis : actiua enim dicitur respectu agentis. Sed passiua, cur non similiter dicitur respectu priuati seu patientis hominis? Nam vt priuans respondet priuato, agens patienti, actio passioni, ita videtur priuatio actiuè sumpta esse priuantis, passiuè verò priuati? Cur ergo passiua tribuitur Deo, qui priuat hominem justitia, non priuatur vllo modo? Hoc primum. Dein-de de si se homo ipse priuat iustitia, nonne hoc satis est vt sit iustitia priuatus? Quid opus est, vt postquam sese ipse priuauit iustitia, Deus eum priuet iustitia? oportet enim hanc priuationem illa posteriorem esse, siquidem illa est violatio legis, haec illam violationem consequens poena. Praeterea, quaero, priuatio iustitiae originalis quatenus fuit in Adamo, aut est in nobis omnibus, qualis sit priuatio? si est actiua, habeo quod volo, est violatio legis, non autem poena lege denunciata. Si est passiua, non est violatio legis, non est peccatum, sed poena tantum. Id quod est negare peccatum originale. Denique, Docet-ne alicubi Scriptura Deum priuasse Adamum iustitia? Quomodo ergo ausus est Vir Doctus id afferere? Certe, qua ducor erga Deum reuerentia, ferre non potest mea conscientia illam assertionem. Nam qui priuat hominem iustitia, facit eum injustum ejusque injustitiae causa est. Id quod vel suspicari de Deo mihi nefas esse videtur. Sed secundam affert Vir Doctus responsionem, qua tollit id quod dedit: eam audiamus.
units.tr: PLAC. He prudently does not dispute the major here. For besides those three arguments which follow in the manuscript, to which he has made no reply, a violation of a condition or precept can be neither the first penalty for an antecedent sin (since it is itself the first sin), nor a penalty of itself, since a later thing cannot be itself. Moreover, it would be ridiculous to attach to a precept a threat that it will be violated, if it is violated. I had confirmed the minor by argument, which he thought it safer to cover with silence than to touch. It can also be proved thus: sin is a violation of the law. The privation of righteousness in a man is sin. Therefore the privation of righteousness is a violation of the law. What could be clearer? But he distinguishes the privation of righteousness into active and passive: the active, by which a man strips himself of righteousness by acting badly, and the passive, by which God deprives man of righteousness. He admits that the former is a violation of the law but denies this of the latter. From this it follows that the law is threatened against the one who violates it in the latter sense and not in the former. Let us therefore consider that distinction a little more carefully. Rightly, indeed, the active privation of righteousness is so called with respect to the man who strips himself of righteousness, for it is called active with respect to the agent. But why is the passive not likewise called so with respect to the man who is stripped, that is, the patient? For just as the one who deprives corresponds to the one deprived, the agent to the patient, and action to passion, it seems that privation taken actively belongs to the one who deprives, and taken passively to the one who is deprived. Why, then, is the passive attributed to God, who deprives man of righteousness, while God is in no way deprived? This is the first point. Next, if man himself strips himself of righteousness, is this not enough for him to be deprived of righteousness? What need is there, after he has deprived himself of righteousness, for God also to deprive him of it? For this privation must be later than that one, since that one is a violation of the law and this one is a penalty following that violation. Furthermore, I ask: the privation of original righteousness, insofar as it was in Adam, or is in all of us, what sort of privation is it? If it is active, I have what I want: it is a violation of the law, not a penalty denounced by the law. If it is passive, it is not a violation of the law, it is not sin, but only a penalty. And this is to deny original sin. Finally, does Scripture anywhere teach that God deprived Adam of righteousness? How then has this learned man dared to assert it? Certainly, the reverence I feel toward God means my conscience cannot bear that assertion. For whoever deprives a man of righteousness makes him unrighteous, and is the cause of his unrighteousness. This, even to suspect of God, seems to me an impiety. But the learned man offers a second reply, by which he takes back what he has given. Let us hear it.

units.la: GAR. 2. Si rem diligenter attendimus, patebit priuationem actiuam iustitia, qua scil. homo amittit iustitiam & ea seipsum spoliat, non esse formaliter idem cum violatione praecepti diuini. Itaque verum quidem erit in sensu causali violationem diuini praecepti esse iustitiae priuationem, quia scilicet ex violatione consequitur illa priuatio; quo sensu dicitur dolor esse solutio continui, quia ad solutionem continui sequitur: sed in sensu formali non erit verum, ita scilicet vt reapse vnum idemque sint, nec differant, nisi nominibus.
units.tr: GAR. 2. If we attend carefully to the matter, it will be evident that the active privation of righteousness, by which a man loses righteousness and strips himself of it, is not formally the same as a violation of the divine precept. Therefore it will be true in a causal sense that a violation of the divine precept is the privation of righteousness, because that privation follows from the violation. In this sense pain is said to be the solution of continuity, because it follows the solution of continuity. But in a formal sense it will not be true, namely that they are really one and the same and differ only in name.

units.la: PLAC. Ego vero existimo, priuationem pro distinctione termini seu formae, cuius est priuatio, distingui debere. Est autem iustitia duplex, actualis nempe, & habitualis. Forma mali moralis, seu peccati solet collocari in priuatione boni. Iustitiae igitur actualis priuatio est formaliter peccatum actuale; iustitiae vero habitualis priuatio est formaliter malum seu peccatum habituale. Nonne? Cum ergo actualis violatio legis formaliter opponatur iustitiae actuali, hoc est, inobedientia obedientiae, necesse est vt actualis violatio legis sit formaliter actualis priuatio iustitiae, & cum habitualis violatio legis seu inobedientia formaliter opponatur habituali justitiae seu obedientiae, necesse est ut ipsa quoque sit formaliter privatio justitiae habitualis, atque adeo peccatum habituale. Sed contra disputat Vir Doctus tribus rationibus.
units.tr: PLAC. I, however, think that privation must be distinguished according to the term or form of which it is the privation. Righteousness is twofold: actual, namely, and habitual. The form of moral evil, or sin, is usually placed in the privation of good. Therefore the privation of actual righteousness is formally actual sin, and the privation of habitual righteousness is formally an evil or sin of habit. Is this not so? Since, then, actual violation of the law is formally opposed to actual righteousness, that is, disobedience to obedience, it must be that actual violation of the law is formally an actual privation of righteousness. And since habitual violation of the law, or disobedience, is formally opposed to habitual righteousness or obedience, it must be that it too is formally a privation of habitual righteousness, and so a habitual sin. But the learned man argues against this with three reasons.

units.la: GAR. Etenim 1. non unum idemque sunt, quorum unum idem homo eodem tempore velle potest, & alterum nolle. At ita habet in hac causa. Adamus enim de fructu interdicto comedens, volebat violare Dei praeceptum, sed nolebat justitiam suam & praerogativas amittere.
units.tr: GAR. For, first, things are not one and the same if one and the same man can at the same time will the one and not will the other. But so it is in this matter. For Adam, eating the forbidden fruit, was willing to violate God's precept, but was not willing to lose his righteousness and his prerogatives.

units.la: PLAC. Utraque propositio est falsa ; Major quidem ; potest enim unum idemque homo idem eodem tempore ob diversas rationes velle & nolle. Idque euenit frequenter: inde haesitatio, & deliberatio, & pugna nonnunquam inter cogitationes volitionesque nostras. Deinde est voluntas rectae rationi conformis, & est voluntas errans & rectae rationi repugnans : haec secum ipsa nonnunquam pugnat. Denique nemo vult malum qua malum formaliter, hoc est, quatenus est privatio boni. Itaque mirum videri non debet, si Adamus privationem justitiae formaliter non voluit. Ita enim peccatum suum voluisset sub ratione mali. Quod etiam in Minore ait, Adamum, voluisse violare Dei praeceptum, Materialiter tantum, ut sic loquar, non formaliter verum est. Voluit enim id quod erat violatio praecepti Dei, sed non sub ratione violationis praecepti divini, sed sub ratione magnae cujusdam bonitatis sibi falso apparentis. Quod si formaliter volebat violare Dei praeceptum, & tamen nolebat justitiam suam amittere, stultus erat, putans separari posse, quae separari nullo modo poterant.
units.tr: PLAC. Both propositions are false. The major, indeed: for one and the same man can at the same time will and not will one and the same thing, for different reasons. This happens often: hence hesitation, and deliberation, and sometimes conflict among our thoughts and volitions. Again, there is a will conformed to right reason, and there is a will that errs and resists right reason; these sometimes struggle with one another. Finally, no one wills evil as evil, formally, that is, insofar as it is the privation of good. So it should not seem strange if Adam did not formally will the privation of righteousness. For in that case he would have willed his sin under the aspect of evil. What he says in the minor, that Adam was willing to violate God's precept, is true only materially, so to speak, and not formally. For he willed that which was a violation of God's precept, but not under the aspect of a violation of the divine precept; he willed it under the aspect of some great good falsely appearing to him. But if he formally willed to violate God's precept, and yet was not willing to lose his righteousness, he was foolish, thinking that things could be separated which in no way could be separated.

units.la: GAR. 2. Ea non sunt unum & idem, quae reapse possunt separari. Atqui potest aliquis violare legem, qui tamen propter ea justitia sua habituali actu non privabitur, quod patet exemplo fidelium, qui subinde peccant, nec tamen privantur ea justitia, quam Deus spiritu suo in ipsorum cordibus operatus est.
units.tr: GAR. 2. Things are not one and the same if they can in fact be separated. But someone can violate the law and yet, for that very reason, will not be deprived of his habitual righteousness in act, as is shown by the example of the faithful, who sometimes sin and yet are not deprived of that righteousness which God has worked in their hearts by his Spirit.

units.la: PLAC. Conclusionem non expressit : haud enim ex duabus illis praemissis cocludi potest id quod ei probandum incumbebat. Agitur enim non de omni violatione legis, sed de tali, nempe prima illa Adami, nec de qualibet priuatione iustitiæ, sed de priuatione iustitiæ qua præditus erat ante lapsum Adamus. De hac enim violatione & priuatione intelligenda est argumenti mei propositio minor. Aut igitur vniuersalem esse oportebat Viri Docti Minorem, aut nominatim de illa priuatione & violatione intelligi. Neutrum cum sit factum, nihil potest concludi mihi repugnans. Deinde simili argumento possent infinitæ propositiones verissimæ refelli, etiam ista, homo est animal. Nam ea non sunt vnum & idem quæ reapse possunt separari. Atqui potest aliquid esse animal, nec tamen esse homo. Distinguo tamen vt supra iustitiæ priuationem. Est enim priuatio iustitiæ actualis & priuatio iustitiæ habitualis ? illa est violatio legis actualis, hæc habitualis. Sed rursus distinguenda est iustitia: accipi enim potest vel forensi significatione vel morali. Vtraque rursus vel est legalis vel euangelica. Iustitia forensis legalis, quia consistit in perfecta totius vitæ conformitate cum lege, vel vnica legis violatione amittitur. Vna enim ad condemnationem sufficit. Euangelicæ dispar est ratio: cum enim in remissione peccatorum consistat; Palam est violationem legis non excludere remissionem peccati. Iustitia vero morali sensu accepta opponitur, vt dixi, violationi legis, hoc est, injustitiæ, actualis quidem actuali, habitualis vero habituali. Sed quæritur an violatio actualis inducat necessario priuationem iustitiæ habitualis? Distinctione opus est. Dispar enim est ratio habitus iustitiæ naturalis seu legalis, qualis ponitur esse in Adamo, & habitus iustitiæ supernaturalis seu euangelicæ. Illa enim nec spem includit remissionis peccatorum, nec aliunde pendere videtur quam à facultate hominis naturali. Itaque violatione legis amittitur. Hæc vero quia fidem ac spem remissionis peccatorum includit, & pendet ab alio principio quam humano, nempe à Spiritu regenerationis Sancto, & Decreto electionis, simplici legis violatione non excutitur. Est etiam violatio legis duplex: vna est vniuersalis à Deo ἀπostasia, seu mutatio finis vltimi, altera, particulare quodvis peccatum. Illa habitum iustitiæ delet, hæc lædit quidem, at non destruit. Cum ergo justitia Adami legalis ac naturalis esset, ejusque peccatum vniuersalis quædam à Deo apostasia, seu finis vltimi mutatio, fieri non potuit, quin simul ac peccauit justitia priuaretur, nec opus fuit, vt Deus judiciaria aliqua actione eum justitia priuaret.
units.tr: PLAC. He has not stated the conclusion, for what he was bound to prove cannot be inferred from those two premises. The question is not about every violation of the law, but about that particular one, namely Adam's first sin, nor about any privation of righteousness, but about the privation of the righteousness with which Adam was endowed before the fall. My minor premise is to be understood of this violation and this privation. So either the learned man's minor premise ought to have been universal, or it should have been expressly understood of that privation and violation. Since neither has been done, nothing can be concluded that tells against me. Moreover, by a similar argument infinitely many most true propositions could be refuted, even this one: man is an animal. For those things are not one and the same which can in fact be separated, and yet something can be an animal without being a man. I distinguish, however, as above, the privation of righteousness. There is actual privation of righteousness and habitual privation of righteousness; the former is an actual violation of the law, the latter a habitual one. But again righteousness must be distinguished, for it can be taken in a forensic or a moral sense. Each of these is again either legal or evangelical. Forensic legal righteousness, since it consists in the perfect conformity of the whole of life with the law, is lost by a single violation of the law, for one is enough for condemnation. The evangelical case is different: since it consists in the remission of sins, it is plain that a violation of the law does not exclude the remission of sin. But righteousness taken in the moral sense is opposed, as I said, to violation of the law, that is, to unrighteousness: actual to actual, and habitual to habitual. But the question is whether actual violation necessarily brings about privation of habitual righteousness. A distinction is needed. For the case of the habit of natural or legal righteousness, such as is supposed to have been in Adam, is different from that of supernatural or evangelical righteousness. The former includes no hope of remission of sins and seems to depend on nothing but the man's natural faculty; therefore it is lost by violation of the law. The latter, since it includes faith and hope of remission of sins, and depends on a principle other than human, namely the Holy Spirit of regeneration and the decree of election, is not shaken off by a simple violation of the law. There is also a twofold violation of the law: one is a universal apostasy from God, or change of ultimate end [ἀπostasia]; the other is any particular sin. The former destroys the habit of righteousness, the latter injures it but does not destroy it. Therefore, since Adam's righteousness was legal and natural, and his sin was a certain universal apostasy from God, or change of ultimate end, it could not happen but that righteousness was taken away as soon as he sinned, nor was it necessary for God to deprive him of righteousness by some judicial act.

units.la: GAR. 3. Denique sicut actus illi, quibus habitus comparatur, non sunt ipsa habitus acquisitio, sed ad eos consequitur acquisitio : ita etiam actus, quibus excutitur habitus, non sunt ipsa habitus privatio, sed ad eos consequitur illa privatio. Frustra ergo jactat Vir Doctus in Thesibus suis de statu hom. lapsi ante Grat. Th. 24. Nos hoc ipso iustitia priuari, quod legem transgredimur & hac ipsa mutatione, qua corruptio introducta est in Adamum, ab eodem expulsam esse iustitiam. Etenim si intelligit transgressionem legis esse causam meritoriam privationis iustitiæ, facile agnoscimus. Si putat transgressionem legis & privationem iustitiæ, nihil inter se differre omnino, non probamus: quia transgressio legis est actio, privatio iustitiæ passio est: at pati & agere plusquam verbis differunt: Et Deus animas hominum creat iustitia originalis decoramento destitutas, qui tamen creando non facit legis prævaricatores. Sic expulsio iustitiæ est antecedens ad corruptionem, & corruptio consequens ad expulsionem iustitiæ: antecedens autem & consequens, nonnihil differunt inter se, vt opinor: Et Deus hominem concessis creatione donis spoliauit, quem tamen non corrupit.
units.tr: GAR. 3. Finally, just as those acts by which a habit is acquired are not the acquisition of the habit itself, but the acquisition follows upon them, so too the acts by which a habit is driven out are not the privation of the habit itself, but the privation follows upon them. Therefore the learned man vainly boasts in his Theses on the state of fallen man before grace, Thesis 24, that "we are deprived of righteousness by this very fact, that we transgress the law, and by this very change by which corruption was introduced into Adam, righteousness was expelled from him." For if he means that the transgression of the law is the meritorious cause of the privation of righteousness, we readily agree. If he thinks that the transgression of the law and the privation of righteousness differ in no way at all, we do not approve, because transgression of the law is an action, while privation of righteousness is a passion, and to suffer and to act differ more than in words. And God creates the souls of men destitute of the adornment of original righteousness, yet by creating them he does not make them transgressors of the law. Thus the expulsion of righteousness is antecedent to corruption, and corruption is consequent upon the expulsion of righteousness; but antecedent and consequent differ somewhat from one another, as I think. And God despoiled man of the gifts granted at creation, yet did not corrupt him.

units.la: PLAC. Aberrat etiam hæc responsio ab argumenti mei propositione minore, Cum enim dixi, priuationem justitiæ esse violationem conditionis seu præcepti, id ita accipi debuit, vt priuatio justitiæ actualis esse intelligeretur violatio actualis, & priuatio justitiæ habitualis, violatio habitualis. Sed videtur habituale peccatum Vir Doctus nullo fere loco habere. Itaque non frustra est quod me jactasse dicit in Thesibus: quo verbo, seu jactationem seu jactantiam significet, cur vteretur quam ei ansam præbuerim non possum videre. Diuisi autem quæ conjunxit, hocque dilemmate sum vsus. Si iustitia sumitur sensu forensi, nonne ea priuamur hoc ipso quod legem transgredimur? In hoc dilemmatis membro quid reprehendat, aut reprehendi possit, non intelligo. Sequitur alterum; Si sensu morali: Annon hac ipsa mutatione, qua corruptio contraria iustitia in Adamum introdu-sta est, ab eodem expulsa est iustitia, haud aliter quàm obtenebratione aëris expelluntur lumen, aut frigefactione calor? In his quoque verbis meis quid reprehendit? Si intelligo transgressionem legis esse causam meritoriam priuationis iustitiæ facilè agnoscit. Hoc verò si intelligerem mecum ipse pugnarem, qui hoc, de quo agitur, argumentum affero, vt probem priuationem iustitiæ originalis non esse pœnam proprie dictam. Certè transgressio legis injustitia seu priuatio justitiæ est; Iustitiæ, inquam, actualis si est actio vel actionis omissio, habitualis verò si est habitus: transgredimur enim legem non solùm actione, sed etiam habitu. Si puto transgressionem legis & priuationem iustitiæ nihil inter se differre omnino, non probat. Ego verò nihil aliud volo, quàm vt propositio mea vera sit, siue attributum & subjectum nihil omnino differant, siue differant nonnihil. Nam propositiones, homo est animal, homo est risibilis, veræ sunt, quamvis subjectum & attributum plusquàm nominibus differant. Sed quomodo probat differre? transgressio, inquit, legis est actio. Omnisne transgressio? non habitualis, vt opinor, nec ea actualis, quæ in omissione actionis consistit. Sed pergat. Priuatio iustitiæ passio est. At modò distinguebat priuationem in actiuam & passiuam. Est-ne igitur priuatio actiua passio? non fit veri simile. Passiua quoque, est ne passio? at dicitur respectu Dei qui omnis passionis est expers. Certè priuatio formaliter non est passio, sed reducitur ad prædicamentum formæ seu termini cujus est negatio. Hoc docent omnes Logici. Passio non minùs quàm actio transit; Priuatio verò permanet, etiam postquam actio & passio desierunt esse. Passio formaliter est ens reale, & per se est in prædicamento, priuatio nec formaliter est ens sed negatio potius, nec in prædicamento nisi reductiuè. Mitto alias differentias inter passionem & priuationem. Addo posita actione, cujus terminus sit accidens, poni necessariò passionem; hancque ab illa non realiter differre, sed respectu tantùm & ratione. Quod subjungit, Deus animas hominum creare iustitiæ originalis decoramento destitutas, qui tamen creando non facit legis prævaricatrices, illud quale fit considerari oportet. Nam creat quidem animas iustitia priuatas, sed sic tamen, vt huius priuationis autor non fit, eam ipsæ contrahant à corpore. Alioquin enim eas, si priuaret iustitia, faceret iniustas. Nam inter iustum & iniustum, sanctum & pollutum in subiecto capaci nullum est medium. Quid porrò est, quod addit, Sic expulsio iustitiæ est antecedens ad corruptionem, & corruptio consequens ad expulsionem iustitiæ? Primò enim expulsio iustitiæ, præsupponit iustitiam præexistentem in subiecto vnde expellitur. Non fuit autem originalis iustitia nisi in solo Adamo. Ab eo igitur solo expulsa est. Deinde quis credat Deum ab homine iustitiam expellere, ac proptere a quòd ab eo expulsa fit, ei irasci? Item Deum causam esse priuationis iustitiæ, nec tamen esse causam corruptionis? Perinde enim est, ac si eum dicerem, qui tollit à corpore rectitudinem, non esse causam obliquitatis, aut qui tollit à corpore humano sanitatem, morbi causam non esse. Mihi quidem certè videtur nec corruptio moralis absque priuatione iustitiæ, nec priuatio iustitiæ absque corruptione morali consistere vllo modo, aut intelligi posse? Nam siue priuatiuè iustitia & corruptio opponuntur, hæc illius priuatio est; sine contrariè, expellunt sese mutuò ex eodem subiecto capaci, & quidem immediatè. Nullum enim medium concipi animo potest inter iustitiam & iniustitiam, virtutem & vitium, rectitudinem & obliquitatem &c, in subiecto capaci.
units.tr: PLAC. This answer also strays from my minor premise. When I said that the privation of righteousness is a violation of the condition or precept, this had to be taken in such a way that the actual privation of righteousness is understood as actual violation, and the habitual privation of righteousness as habitual violation. But the learned man seems to have almost no regard for habitual sin. So it is not without reason that he says I have boasted in the Theses; I cannot see why he uses that word, whether it signifies boasting or bragging, or what occasion I have given him for it. He has separated what I joined together, and I have used this dilemma: If righteousness is taken in the forensic sense, are we not deprived of it by this very fact, that we transgress the law? I do not understand what he could find to censure, or what could be censured, in this member of the dilemma.
