The other follows: If in the moral sense: is righteousness not expelled from Adam by this very change by which corruption contrary to righteousness was introduced into him, just as light is expelled by the darkening of the air, or heat by cooling? What does he find to censure in these words of mine? He easily admits that, if I mean that the transgression of the law is the meritorious cause of the privation of righteousness. But if I were to mean that the transgression of the law and the privation of righteousness differ in no way at all, I would be contradicting myself, since I put forward this argument precisely to prove that the privation of original righteousness is not punishment properly so called. Certainly the transgression of the law is injustice, or privation of righteousness: of actual righteousness if it is an action or the omission of an action, and of habitual righteousness if it is a habit, for we transgress the law not only by action but also by habit. If I think that the transgression of the law and the privation of righteousness differ in no way at all, he does not prove it. I want nothing more than that my proposition be true, whether subject and predicate differ in no way at all or differ somewhat. For the propositions "man is an animal" and "man is capable of laughter" are true, although subject and predicate differ by more than their names. But how does he prove that they differ? "The transgression of the law," he says, "is an action." Is every transgression? Not habitual transgression, I think, nor that actual transgression which consists in the omission of an action. But let him go on. "The privation of righteousness is a passion." Yet a moment ago he was distinguishing privation into active and passive. Is active privation then a passion? That is not likely. Is passive privation a passion? But it is said with respect to God, who is free of all passion. Certainly privation formally is not a passion, but is reduced to the category of the form or term of which it is the negation. All logicians teach this. A passion, no less than an action, passes away; but privation remains even after action and passion have ceased to be. A passion is formally a real being and is in its own right in a category; privation is formally not a being but rather a negation, and it is in a category only by reduction. I set aside other differences between passion and privation. I add that, when an action whose term is an accident is posited, a passion is necessarily posited along with it, and that this passion does not differ really from that action, but only in respect and in reason. As for what he adds, that God creates the souls of men destitute of the adornment of original righteousness, yet by creating them he does not make them transgressors of the law, we must consider how this is. For he indeed creates souls deprived of righteousness, but in such a way that he is not the author of this privation, which they contract from the body. For otherwise, if he deprived them of righteousness, he would make them unrighteous; for between the righteous and the unrighteous, the holy and the defiled, in a capable subject there is no middle. What is the point of what he adds: Thus the expulsion of righteousness is antecedent to corruption, and corruption is consequent upon the expulsion of righteousness? For first, the expulsion of righteousness presupposes righteousness existing beforehand in the subject from which it is expelled. But original righteousness was present only in Adam alone; therefore it was expelled from him alone. Next, who would believe that God expels righteousness from a man, and is angry with him because it is expelled from him? Likewise, that God is the cause of the privation of righteousness yet not the cause of corruption? For it is just as if I said that one who takes uprightness from the body is not the cause of crookedness, or one who takes health from the human body is not the cause of disease. Indeed it seems to me certain that moral corruption cannot subsist, nor can it be understood in any way, without privation of righteousness, nor privation of righteousness without moral corruption. For whether righteousness and corruption are opposed as privative, the latter is the privation of the former; or as contraries, they drive each other out from the same capable subject, and indeed immediately. For no middle can be conceived in the mind between righteousness and unrighteousness, virtue and vice, uprightness and crookedness, and so on, in a capable subject.

units.la: Noli mihi obijcere peccatum esse interdum pœnam peccati. Primùm enim non est pœna quatenus peccatum, nisi velis duas species mali oppositas inter se confundere, sublato inter malum pœnæ & culpæ discrimine. Priuatio autem iustitiæ in nobis, quatalis, formaliter peccatum est; repugnat enim legi. Deinde id non est accipiendum de pœna proprie & strictè accepta, qualem lex comminatur & iustitia necessario exigit vt sibi satisfiat. Quis enim credat Iustitiam exigere vt iustitia violetur? satisfieri iustitiæ eo quo iustitia lædítur? solui pœnæ debitum eo, quo debitum illud augetur? Adiungi præcepto, ne violetur, comminationem pœnæ sitæ in violatione præcepti? pergo igitur.
units.tr: Do not object to me that sin is sometimes the punishment of sin. First, it is not punishment insofar as it is sin, unless you wish to confuse two opposed kinds of evil and abolish the distinction between the evil of punishment and the evil of guilt. The privation of righteousness in us, as such, is formally sin, for it contradicts the law. Second, this must not be understood of punishment properly and strictly so called, the kind the law threatens and justice necessarily demands so that it may be satisfied. For who would believe that justice requires that justice be violated? That justice is satisfied by that by which justice is injured? That the debt of punishment is paid by that by which the debt itself is increased? That the threat of punishment set in the violation of a precept is added to the precept so that it may not be violated? I go on, then.

units.la: Quarta ratio, pœna proprie dicta siue mors quam lex comminabatur sequi debuit quæstionem ac iudicium Dei de violatione illius legis. Sed priuatio iustitiæ siue mors spiritualis quæstionem ac iudicium Dei de violatione legis sequuta non est, sed antecessit: non fuit igitur pœna proprie dicta, siue mors quam lex comminabatur.
units.tr: The fourth reason: the punishment properly so called, or the death which the law threatened, ought to have followed God's examination and judgment concerning the violation of that law. But the privation of righteousness, or spiritual death, did not follow God's examination and judgment concerning the violation of the law; it preceded it. Therefore it was not the punishment properly so called, or the death which the law threatened.

units.la: Quinta denique ratio, (cæteras enim differre, & in alium locum conferre satius erit.) Si lex Adamo mortem sitam in priuatione iustitiæ comminabatur, Adamus (vt tu asseris) prout Deus minatus fuerat, Mortuus est. Id autem mihi falsum videtur. Nam primo, Tu, opinor, fateris Adamo condonatum fuisse primum illud peccatum, numerando alioquin inter damnatos: non igitur, prout Deus minatus fuerat, mortuus est. Pugnant enim hæc duo, condonari peccatum & puniri secundum legem. Deinde, Tu per mortem denunciatam comminatione tàm mortem corporis & æternam intelligis, quàm spiritualem illam. Pertinebat igitur æque ad veritatem comminationis & iustitiam, vt, quo die legem violauit, eodem tam corporeâ & æternâ morte, quàm spirituali moreretur. Tamen eodem die neutram passus est, æternam autem nunquam subijt, aut subibit. Cur non potuit Adamo mortis spiritualis æque ac æternæ pœna condonari? aut saltem differri? His accedat Scripturæ Testimonium: colligens enim summam annorum vitę Adami Gen. v. ℣f. 5. non contenta iis verbis, quibus in similibus computationibus solis vsa est constantissimè, interferuit hęc duo, ⸀ןשא, procul dubio nec frustra, nec temerè: quo tamen pertineant non video, nisi vt innuatur, Adamum, vt ferebat diuina comminatio, non fuisse mortuum, sed vixisse; quod aliunde quàm à Dei gratia, & domini nostri Iesu Christi satisfactione proficisci non potuit. Hoc ipsum etiam ex eo potest intelligi, quòd sententia Adamo lata in paradiso non fuit definitiua, sed quasi interloquutoria, dans spatium homini ad resipiscendum, dilato post mortem extremo judicio, ac interim conditionem hominis definiens, mediam quodammodo inter damnatum & absolutum. Hinc factum est, vt, neque Deus hominem pronunciauerit maledictum, quemadmodum serpentem, sed terram duntaxat. Et quamvis morti corporeæ eum addixerit sententia, tamen circunlocutione vsus fit, nec mortem eam appellare voluerit, ne videretur pertinere ad Comminationis legis executionem. Fuit igitur judicium illud, non extremum (hoc enim Adamo post mortem subeundum fuit iuxta illud Apoftoli, statutum est hominibus vt semel moriantur, postea vero judicium heb. 9.) sed præmissum extremo in aliud tempus dilato. Videsis Thesium mearum de lapsu Adami vltimam. Si igitur Deus pro summa sua misericordia & sapientia comminationis illius executionem distulit, ac suspendit ex alio judicio post separationem animæ à corpore futuro, fatendum est Adamum non fuisse, prout ferebat legis comminatio, Mortuum. Itaque comminationem illam de spirituali morte posita in priuatione iustitiæ non esse intelligendam, quam ego arbitror ipsa morte æterna deterius malum esse.
units.tr: Finally, the fifth reason (for it will be better to defer the others and reserve them for another place). If the law threatened Adam with death set in privation of righteousness, then Adam, as you assert, died as God had threatened. But this seems false to me. For first, you, I suppose, admit that this first sin was pardoned to Adam, otherwise he would be counted among the damned. Therefore he did not die as God had threatened. For these two things clash: a sin being pardoned and a sin being punished according to the law. Second, by the death declared in the threat you understand bodily and eternal death as much as that spiritual death. It would therefore have belonged equally to the truth of the threat and to justice that on the day he broke the law he should die with bodily and eternal death as well as with spiritual death. Yet on that same day he suffered neither, and he never underwent, nor will he undergo, eternal death. Why could the punishment of spiritual death not have been pardoned to Adam, as eternal death was, or at least deferred? To these let the testimony of Scripture be added. In summing up the years of Adam's life (Gen. 5 v. 5), Scripture did not stop with the words it used most consistently in such computations, but inserted these two words, undoubtedly neither without purpose nor carelessly. Yet I do not see what they bear on, except to hint that Adam, as the divine threat carried, did not die but lived. This could have come from nowhere other than God's grace and the satisfaction of our Lord Jesus Christ. This can also be understood from the fact that the sentence pronounced on Adam in paradise was not definitive but, as it were, interlocutory, giving man room to repent, with the final judgment deferred until after death, and meanwhile defining man's condition as somehow midway between condemned and absolved. Hence God pronounced no man accursed, as he did the serpent, but only the earth. And although the sentence assigned him to bodily death, God used circumlocution and was unwilling to call it death, lest it seem to belong to the execution of the law's threat. That judgment, then, was not the final one (for after death Adam had to undergo that, according to the Apostle's saying, "It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment," Heb. 9), but a preliminary one, placed before the final judgment and deferred to another time. See my last Thesis on Adam's fall. If therefore God, in his supreme mercy and wisdom, deferred and suspended the execution of that threat, by a further judgment after the soul's separation from the body, it must be admitted that Adam was not dead, as the law's threat carried. Thus that threat of spiritual death set in privation of righteousness is not to be understood as the kind of evil which, I hold, is worse than eternal death itself.

units.la: GAR. Additur & tertia ratio. Si lex Adamo mortem sitam in priuatione iustitiæ comminabatur, Adamus, prout Deus comminatus erat, mortuus fuerit, quod falsum; cùm inter damnatos non sit computandus. Item, cùm mors illa æternam, corporalem, & spiritualem completatur, qui nunquam sensit æternam, necessatim sensit temporalem, quomodo spiritualem, nempe priuationem iustitiæ statim incurrisset? Respond. 1. Qui mortuus est morte sita in priuatione iustitiæ, si in ea perseueret, vsque ad finem, inter damnatos computandus est. At non ita factum Adamo, qui fide in semen benedictum ex illa morte spirituali in vitam spiritualem excitatus est, vt sit omnibus electis, quos mortuos in peccatis placet Deo viuificare in Christo, Ephef. 2. 5. 6.
units.tr: GAR. A third reason is also added. If the law threatened Adam with death set in privation of righteousness, then Adam, as God had threatened, would have died, which is false, since he is not to be counted among the damned. Likewise, since that death is completed as eternal, bodily and spiritual, how could one who never felt eternal death necessarily have felt temporal death, or how could he have immediately incurred spiritual death, namely privation of righteousness? Reply 1. One who died with death set in privation of righteousness, if he persists in it to the end, is to be counted among the damned. But this did not happen to Adam, who by faith in the blessed Seed was raised from that spiritual death into spiritual life, so that he is among all the elect whom God is pleased to make alive together in Christ, when they were dead in sins, Eph. 2. 5. 6.

units.la: PLAC. Cur hanc rationem, cùm sit quinta, tertiam vocet, causam nullam video, nisi quia, cùm duas præteriisset, secundam & quartam, videri tamen noluit vllam prætermisisse. Quatuor etiam rationibus minorem huius argumenti quinti confirmaueram: ex quibus solas priores duas hibi objicit, sed ita contractas, præsertim primam, vt vix eam agnoscam. Adhibet autem responsiones duas, quibus argumentum firmare potius videtur, quàm infirmare. Priore rationem reddit, cur Adamus non fuerit damnatus. Concedit igitur, (quæ minoris argumenti mei confirmatio erat) eum non fuisse damnatum. Sic enim se habebat argumentum meum; Si lex Adamo mortem sitam in priuatione iustitiæ comminabatur, Adamus secundum legis comminationem punitus est. Atqui Adamus secundum legis comminationem punitus non est. Ergo Lex non comminabatur Adamo mortem sitam in priuatione iustitiæ. Quid respondet Vir Doctus ad Majorem? Num eam negat? Num distinguit? Num ei limitationem adhibet? Nihil prorsus responder. Eam igitur concedit. Ita videtur. Potest tamen limitari: cùm enim præter illam priuationem, etiam corporis & æternam mortem lex minaretur, Adamus secundum legis comminationem partim punitus fuisset, partim non fuisset Punitus fuisset illa priuatione seu morte spirituali, non fuisset punitus morte corporis & æterna. Sed hæc limitatio argumento nihil nocet. Punitus enim saltem fuisset poena aliqua propriedicta, seu judiciaria quam Lex comminabatur, & quidem poena maxima. Id autem est falsum. Fecit enim ei Deus gratiam peccati. Non punitur autem cui peccatum remittitur, cui peccatum non imputatur, qui justificatus est a peccato. Nam si partim puniretur, partim non puniretur, etiam ei partim peccatum remitteretur, partim non remitteretur, & partim iustificaretur, partim non justificaretur; imperfectaque esset justificatio, id quod Euangelicorum nemo dixerit. Cum tale sit argumentum meum, vides, lector, hanc priorem Viri Docti responsionem illius neque majorem, neque minorem labefactare. Pergat igitur.
units.tr: PLAC. I see no cause why he calls this reason the third when it is the fifth, except that, having passed over two, the second and the fourth, he did not want to seem to have omitted any. I had also confirmed the minor premise of this fifth argument by four reasons. Of these he objects only the first two, and even these so abbreviated, especially the first, that I scarcely recognise it. He uses two replies, which seem rather to confirm the argument than to weaken it. By the former reply he gives the reason why Adam was not condemned. He therefore concedes (which was the confirmation of my minor premise) that Adam was not condemned. My argument stood thus: If the law threatened Adam with death set in privation of righteousness, then Adam was punished according to the law's threat. But Adam was not punished according to the law's threat. Therefore the law did not threaten Adam with death set in privation of righteousness. What does the learned author reply to the major premise? Does he deny it? Does he distinguish? Does he add a qualification? He replies absolutely nothing. He therefore concedes it. So it seems. Yet it can be qualified. For since the law threatened, besides that privation, also bodily and eternal death, Adam would have been punished partly according to the law's threat and partly not. He would have been punished with that privation, or spiritual death, but not with bodily death and eternal death. But this qualification does nothing against my argument. For he would at least have been punished with some punishment properly so called, or judicial, which the law threatened, and indeed the greatest punishment. But that is false, for God granted him forgiveness of sin. Yet one whose sin is remitted, to whom sin is not imputed, who is justified from sin, is not punished. For if he were partly punished and partly not, then sin would also be partly remitted to him and partly not, and he would be partly justified and partly not justified. His justification would be imperfect, which no evangelical would say. Since my argument is of this kind, you see, reader, that this first reply of the learned author shakes neither the major premise nor the minor. Let him go on, then.

units.la: GAR. 1. Nihil in eo mirum quod Adamus & statim a peccato priuationem justitiae incurrit, & nec aeterna morte damnatus est, nec temporalem statim sensit. In spiritualem statim incurrit, ita volente Deo, ne si statim in eum non incurrisset vlla species mortis, videri posset Adamo verior Satana promissio, non moriemini omnino, quam Dei comminatio, morte moriemini; & in peccato consenescens Adamus de feria poenitentia & conuersione ad Deum forte non cogitasset: sed pupugit eum praesentis poena sensus, vt ad Deum respicendo rediret, quem rebellando deseruerat. Mortem vero temporalem non statim incurrit, vt poenitendi tempus ipsi concederetur, quod nullum est post mortem. Hanc poenam eodem quo peccauit die Adamus luisset, nisi vitum fuisset Deo ob futuram Christi satisfactionem, spatium dare generi humano ad agendam poenitentiam, inquit Vir Doctus Disput. de lapsu Adami Thef. ultima. Denique aeternam omnino non incurrit, quia erat inter electos Dei, in quos infernus, nihil habet juris. Apocal. xx. 6.
units.tr: GAR. 1. There is nothing surprising in this, that Adam both immediately incurred privation of righteousness upon sin, and was neither condemned to eternal death nor immediately felt temporal death. He immediately incurred spiritual death, God so willing, lest, if no kind of death had immediately fallen upon him, Satan's promise, "You shall not die at all," might have seemed truer to Adam than God's threat, "you shall surely die." And Adam, growing old in sin, might perhaps not have thought of repentance and of conversion to God. But the sense of present punishment pricked him, so that by looking back to God he might return to the one whom he had deserted by rebelling. Temporal death, however, he did not immediately incur, so that time for repentance might be granted him, for there is none after death. Adam would have paid this punishment on the very day he sinned, unless it had seemed good to God, on account of Christ's future satisfaction, to give the human race room to do penance, says the learned author in his Disputation on Adam's fall, last Thesis. Finally, he did not incur eternal death at all, because he was among God's elect, over whom hell has no right, Rev. 20. 6.

units.la: PLAC. Haec posterior responsio ad secundam Minoris argumenti mei confirmationem spectare videtur: Sed primo eam non attingit; Deinde sese ipsa contradictione implicat; Denique se praebet ridiculam. Sic enim se habebat illa confirmatio, vt eius vim explicem, Cui, quo die peccauit, non est inflicta mors corporis, nec aeterna, is non est eo die, sicut Deus minatus fuerat, mortuus. Atqui Adamo, quo die peccauit, non est inflicta mors corporis, nec aeterna. Ergo Adamus non est eo die, sicuti Deus minatus fuerat, mortuus. Nihil potest responderi, nisi, ei quidem inflictam non fuisse mortem corporis & æternam, sed tamen inflictam fuisse mortem animæ positam in priuatione justitiæ. Sed contrà sic insto. Si inflicta ei fuit mors animæ, ideò ei inflicta fuit, quia id exigebat comminatio. Sed non ideò ei inflicta fuit, quia id exigebat comminatio. Ergo ei inflicta mors illa non fuit. Majorem negari non poreft. Minorem probo. Si ideò ei inflicta fuit mors animæ, quia id exigebat comminatio, etiam ei inflictæ fuerunt mors corporis & æterna, quia hoc non minus exigebat comminatio. Attamen hæ mortes non sunt ei inflictæ. Ergo mors animæ non est ideò ei inflicta, quia id exigebat comminatio. De minore nulla lis esse potest. Major, quanquam aperte vera est, tamen eo confirmatur, quòd non minus mortem corporis & æternam Deus comminatus fuerat quàm fpiritualem. Hæc igitur fi Dei veritas, & iustitia exigebant vt eo die Adamo infligeretur, eadem, veritas & iustitia, non minus exigebant, vt illæ etiam mortes infligerentur eadem die; par, vti vides, ratio est. Quod huic argumentationi diffoluendæ accommodatum fit, nihil animaduerto in refponfione Viri Do�similti. Ea autem, quod fecundum erat eius peccatum, sese contradictione inuoluit. Nam qui potuisset Adamus retinens iustitiam originalem, quæ fine dubio injustitiæ seu peccato opponitur, consenescere in peccato, manere à Deo auersus, Dei defertor, Deo rebellis? Quid enim erat iustitia illa, nisi conuersio cordis ad Deum, obedientia habitualis Dei mandatis, constans voluntas obediendi Deo, iusque illi suum tribuendi, qua, hoc ipso quod ipsi inerat, iustus erat Adamus? Quis ergo futurum fuisse credat, vt Adamus, nisi amitteret iustitiam, consenesceret in peccato? Contrà enim consenuisset in justitia, fi quidem iustitiam non amisisset. Se quoque ridiculam præbet hæc refponfio, cùm fingit ablatam fuisse Adamo iustitiam, vt ad Deum resipiscendo rediret. Tantùm enim abest, vt mors spiritualis medium fit ad refipifcentiam, & conuersionem ad Deum, vt eam homini reddat impossibilem, eumque à Deo longissimè abducat. Ridiculum etiam mihi videtur, quod dicitur, pupugisse Adamum præfentis illius pœnæ sensum. Habitus enim non sunt qualitates sensibiles, neque sentiuntur, aut intelliguntur a nobis, nisi quatenus ex antecedentibus aut consequentibus actibus inesse deprehenduntur. Adde quod mors spiritualis, quantum ad veram pietatem attinet, hominem sensu priuat, & facultate bene agendi, cumque ad omne bonum opus ineptum, ad omne malum pronum, auersum a Deo, conuersum autem ad carnem & ea quæ Deus odit, efficit.
units.tr: PLAC. This second reply seems to bear on the second confirmation of my minor premise. But, first, it does not touch it; second, it entangles itself in contradiction; and finally, it makes itself ridiculous. My confirmation ran thus, so that I may explain its force: he to whom neither bodily nor eternal death was inflicted on the day he sinned has not died on that day, as God had threatened. But neither bodily nor eternal death was inflicted on Adam on the day he sinned. Therefore Adam did not die on that day, as God had threatened. Nothing can be answered, except that indeed bodily and eternal death were not inflicted on him, but that the death of the soul, consisting in the privation of righteousness, was inflicted. But I argue against this thus. If the death of the soul was inflicted on him, it was inflicted because the threatening required it. But it was not inflicted on him because the threatening required it. Therefore that death was not inflicted on him. The major premise cannot be denied. I prove the minor. If the death of the soul was inflicted on him because the threatening required it, then bodily and eternal death were also inflicted on him, since the threatening required these no less. Yet these deaths were not inflicted on him. Therefore the death of the soul was not inflicted on him because the threatening required it. There can be no dispute about the minor. The major, though it is plainly true, is confirmed by the fact that God threatened bodily and eternal death no less than spiritual death. If therefore the truth and justice of God required that this death be inflicted on Adam that day, the same truth and justice required no less that those other deaths also be inflicted the same day; the reasoning is equal, as you see. As for what would suit the dissolving of this argument, I notice nothing in the learned man's reply. But his second answer entangles itself in contradiction. For how could Adam, retaining original righteousness, which without doubt is opposed to unrighteousness or sin, have grown old in sin, remaining turned away from God, a deserter of God, a rebel against God? For what was that righteousness but the turning of the heart to God, habitual obedience to God's commands, a constant will to obey God and to render him his due, by which Adam was righteous simply because it was in him? Who then can believe that Adam, unless he lost his righteousness, would have grown old in sin? On the contrary, he would have grown old in righteousness, if indeed he had not lost his righteousness. This reply also makes itself ridiculous when it imagines that righteousness was taken away from Adam so that he might return to God by repentance. Spiritual death is so far from being a means to repentance and conversion to God that it makes this impossible for a man and drives him very far from God. It also seems ridiculous to me that it is said that Adam felt the pain of that present punishment. For habits are not sensible qualities, nor are they perceived or understood by us, except insofar as they are detected to be present from the acts that go before or follow. Add that spiritual death, as far as true godliness is concerned, deprives a man of sense and of the ability to do good, and makes him unfit for every good work, prone to every evil, turned away from God, and turned instead to the flesh and to those things which God hates.

units.la: Temperare mihi non possum quin sextam rationem superioribus adjungam, ductam primum a phrasi illa morte morieris: Nam nullus quod sciam locus extat in scriptura, vbi phrasis illa morte mori de figurata illa morte fit accipienda, quæ nihil aliud est quàm absentia sanctitatis in anima. Deinde ab ipso nomine mortis, quod in vetere Testamento mihi non occurrit eo sensu, Immo ne in Nouo quidem absolutè, & sine additamento, nisi forte Luc. ix. 60. sine vt mortui sepeliant suos mortuos: quo tamen loco non videtur Dominus ad priuationem originalis iustitiæ communem omnibus respexisse, sed ad incredulitatem & contumaciam. Cùm enim qui non credit jam sit condemnatus Ioh. 3. 18. & super eum ira Dei maneat. Ioh. 3. 36. nihil prohibet credentem mortuum appellari. Fac tamen eum ad priuationem illam respexisse, folemne ei est vocabula transferre à propria & communiter vsitata significatione ad spiritualem & metaphoricam lucis Euangelicæ ad tempus tegendæ causa, in quo eum imitari non debuerunt Apostoli.
units.tr: I cannot refrain from adding a sixth reason to the foregoing, drawn first from the phrase morte morieris, "you shall surely die." For there is no passage in Scripture, so far as I know, where the phrase to die the death is to be taken of that figurative death, which is nothing other than the absence of holiness in the soul. Next, from the very word death, which in the Old Testament I have not met in that sense, nor indeed in the New Testament absolutely and without addition, except perhaps Luke 9:60, Let the dead bury their dead; yet in that place the Lord does not seem to have looked to the privation of original righteousness common to all, but to unbelief and obstinacy. For since he who does not believe is already condemned, John 3:18, and the wrath of God remains upon him, John 3:36, nothing prevents the believer from being called dead. But grant that he looked to that privation: it is customary for him to transfer words from their proper and commonly used meaning to a spiritual and metaphorical sense, for the sake of concealing the light of the Gospel for a time; the Apostles ought not to imitate him in this.

units.la: Iam quis credat primam illam dei legem & commination em conceptam verbis vsitatissimis morte moriens, intelligendam esse sensu prorsus inusitato, & quidem ita vt idem vocabulum semel positum, semel intelligendum, accipiatur simul & proprie, & metaphoricè. Possem te obruere aliis argumentis, sed non sunt omnia simul ac semel effundenda.
units.tr: Now who would believe that the first law of God and its threatening, framed in the most common words, dying you shall die, is to be understood in a wholly unusual sense, and indeed in such a way that the same word, placed once, is to be understood once, and is taken at once both properly and metaphorically? I could overwhelm you with other arguments, but not everything is to be poured out at once.

units.la: GAR. Vltimò sic argumentatur. Mors spiritualis est mors metaphoricè dicta; mors corporalis proprie. Quis autem existimet in lege, quæ debuit verbis vsitatissimis concipi, vocabulum vnum idémque debere accipi simul & proprie & metaphoricè? præsertim cùm morte mori figurato sensu, nusquam accipiatur, nisi forte Luc. IX. 60.
units.tr: GAR. Lastly he argues thus. Spiritual death is death said metaphorically; bodily death is death said properly. But who would think that in a law, which ought to be framed in the most common words, one and the same word must be taken at once both properly and metaphorically? Especially since to die the death is nowhere taken in a figurative sense, except perhaps Luke 9:60.

units.la: PLAC. Vides, vt meam istam rationem contrahit, vt magna sui parte truncat, vt mihi tribuit, id quod non dixi, morte mori vsurpari Luc IX. 60. Pergat tamen.
units.tr: PLAC. You see how he contracts my argument, how he cuts it short in great part, how he attributes to me what I did not say, that to die the death is used at Luke 9:60. Let him go on nonetheless.

units.la: GAR. Resp. Agnoscit Vir doctus, mortis nomine, tum mortem corporalem, tum etiam æternum inferorum cruciatum intelligi, vt audiuimus. Quid ergo respondurus est, si quis hoc argumentum ipsi reponat; vocem eandem in lege, quæ debeat verbis vsitatis concipi, non posse simul proprie & metaphoricè sumi: cruciatum autem inferorum, quem pascuri sunt reprobi corpore & animâ, esse mortem metaphoricè dictam; cùm sola corporalis sit mors propriè dicta: ergo non posse his verbis intelligi cruciatum illum.
units.tr: GAR. Reply. The learned man acknowledges that by the name of death both bodily death and also the eternal torment of hell are understood, as we have heard. What then will he answer if someone should bring this argument against him: that the same word in a law, which ought to be framed in common words, cannot be taken at once properly and metaphorically; but the torment of hell, which the reprobate suffer in body and soul, is death said metaphorically, since bodily death alone is death properly so called; therefore that torment cannot be understood by these words?

units.la: PLAC. Ego verò respondebo, cùm de foro Dei agitur nullam magis proprie mortem dici quàm æternam: à qua si corporalis sejungitur, ne mors quidem amplius vocari debet ipso Christo autore: Eam enim non comminatur lex, nisi quatenus est jactura omnium huius vitæ bonorum. Iactura autem non est, cùm in eorum locum succedunt meliora. Adde quod mors æterna corporalem includit, id est, huius vitæ priuationem, vt illam comminari lex non potuerit, quin istam simul co nminarerur.
units.tr: PLAC. I shall answer that, when we are dealing with the tribunal of God, no death is called more properly than eternal death; if bodily death is separated from it, not even the name of death ought any longer to be applied, Christ himself being the author. For the law threatens it only insofar as it is the loss of all the good things of this life. But it is not a loss when better things succeed in their place. Add that eternal death includes bodily death, that is, the deprivation of this life, so that the law could not threaten the former without threatening the latter at the same time.

units.la: GAR. 2. Cùm Deus hic omnem mortem comminatus sit, quâ dignum erat peccatum Adæ, quidni dicamus & corporalem & spiritualem & æternam fuisse comminatum, cùm ijs omnibus subjacere commereatur peccator?
units.tr: GAR. 2. Since God here threatened every death by which Adam's sin deserved to be punished, why should we not say that bodily, spiritual and eternal death were all threatened, since the sinner deserves to be subject to all of them?

units.la: PLAC. Omnis mors, qua dignum est peccatum, est mors diuersa à peccato. Mors autem spiritualis est peccatum, & meretur mortem.
units.tr: PLAC. Every death by which sin deserves to be punished is a death different from sin. But spiritual death is sin, and it deserves death.

units.la: GAR. 3. Nec verò Scripturis inusitatum est mortis nomine, mortem spiritualem designare, cùm contrarium pateat, non modò ex Luc 9. 60. sed etiam ex frequentibus testimonijs, quorum etiam nonnulla jam produximus.
units.tr: GAR. 3. Nor is it unusual in Scripture to designate spiritual death by the name of death, since the contrary is plain, not only from Luke 9:60, but also from frequent testimonies, some of which we have already brought forward.

units.la: PLAC. Non dixi inusitatum esse Scripturis nomen mortis pro morte spirituali : Dixi tantùm inusitatum esse Scripturæ veteris Testamenti, dixi toti Scripturæ inusitatam esse phrasim, morte morieris eo sensu. Id ad meam istam rationem satis erat. Testimonia é veteri Testamento duo quidem paulò ante §. 32. pag. 171. laudauerat, vnum ex Ezech. 3. 18. alterum ex Hos. 13.1. sed frustrà : nam vt ne ei opponam interpretes neutrum locum de morte spirituali accipientes, reclamat ipsa res. Agitur enim in illis locis de morte, quæ non est omnium hominum communis, sed de morte in quam incurrunt quidam ob sua quædam peccata actualia, cùm mors spiritualis omnium sit homi um, & quidem ab ipso eorum ortu, antecedens omnia ipsorum actualia peccata. Itaque non possunt loca illa de spirituali morte, in priuatione justitiæ originalis sitâ accipi.
units.tr: PLAC. I did not say that the name death is unusual in Scripture for spiritual death. I said only that the phrase you shall surely die in that sense is unusual in the Scripture of the Old Testament, and unusual in all Scripture. That was enough for my argument. He had indeed cited two testimonies from the Old Testament a little before, §. 32, p. 171, one from Ezekiel 3:18 and the other from Hosea 13:1; but in vain. For, not to set against him the interpreters who take neither passage of spiritual death, the matter itself cries out against it. For in those places it is a question of a death which is not common to all men, but of a death which some incur on account of certain actual sins of their own; whereas spiritual death is common to all men, and indeed from their very origin, preceding all their actual sins. Therefore those places cannot be understood of spiritual death, consisting in the privation of original righteousness.

units.la: GAR. 4. Verbis vsitatis, id est, vulgò notis leges concipi debere fatemur. Sed quis dicat verba metaphorica & impropria non esse vsitata? Imò metaphoris nihil communius, etiam in legibus sanciendis, quæ sæpè vnâ voce multa compleƈtuntur, eaque diuersissima, vt ad vnius vocabuli proprietatem reduci non possint, sicuti patet in præceptis Decalogi.
units.tr: GAR. 4. We grant that laws ought to be framed in customary words, that is, words commonly known. But who would say that metaphorical and improper words are not customary? Indeed, nothing is more common than metaphor, even in enacting laws, which often comprise many very different things in one word, so that they cannot be reduced to the proper sense of a single term, as is clear in the precepts of the Decalogue.

units.la: PLAC. Dixine verba metaphorica, & impropria non esse vsitata? Dixi tantum nomen mortis eo sensu metaphorico & improprio, quo significat mortem spiritualem, seu priuationem iustitiæ originalis, non esse vsitatum in vetere Testamento. Non negaui quin vsurpentur interdum metaphoræ in legibus, tantùm negaui eas vsurpari, quæ sunt eo tempore, quo leges feruntur, inusitatæ: negaui etiam eandem vocem in eadem lege semel vsurpatam, simul & proprie & metaphoricè intelligi debere. Tum enim demum accipi debet metaphoricè, cùm aliquid obest, quominus accipi possit aut debeat proprie. Neque propterea duplicem sensum Scripturæ nego, literalem & mysticum: ille enim est verborû,hic potiùs rerum. In præceptis Decalogi nullam vocem video, quæ simul & proprie & improprie, seu metaphoricè debeat exponi.
units.tr: PLAC. Did I say that metaphorical and improper words are not customary? I said only that the noun death, in the metaphorical and improper sense in which it signifies spiritual death, or the privation of original righteousness, is not customary in the Old Testament. I did not deny that metaphors are sometimes used in laws. I denied only that metaphors are used which were unusual at the time the laws were given. I also denied that the same word, used once in the same law, must be understood both properly and metaphorically. A word is to be taken metaphorically only when something prevents it from being taken properly, or from being taken properly as it ought to be. Nor for this reason do I deny a twofold sense of Scripture, literal and mystical: the former belongs to words, the latter rather to things. In the precepts of the Decalogue I see no word that must be explained both properly and improperly, or metaphorically.

units.la: GAR. Denique pari argumento vtuntur Pontificij, vt probent illa verba, hoc est corpus meum, non esse intelligenda figurate, quia pactum, sacramentum, lex, requirunt propriam non figuratam locutionem: ita enim Bellarminus & Costerus. Nostri respondentes negant, vt videre est apud Chamierum lib. 10. de Eucharist. cap. 15. n. 60. 61.
units.tr: GAR. Finally, the Papists use the same argument to prove that the words This is my body are not to be understood figuratively, because a covenant, a sacrament and a law require a proper, not figurative, mode of speech. So Bellarmine and Costerus. Our men, answering them, deny this, as may be seen in Chamier, book 10 on the Eucharist, chapter 15, nn. 60, 61.

units.la: PLAC. Si dicerent Pontificij in verbis hoc est corpus meum, non esse metaphoram inusitatam, aut non esse eandem vocem simul proprie & non proprie seu improprie accipiendam, quia id non ferat pactum, Sacramentum, lex, recte procederet comparatio, neque nostros haberent repugnantes. Nunc cum ab illis verbis, omnique pacto, sacramento, & lege omnem excludant metaphoram, etiam admodum tritam & perspicuam, quid est illis mecum commune? Certe eos refutaui Exam. rat. pro & contra Sacr. Miss� part. 1. c. xiv. pag. 429. & seqq. negari autem non potest, quin verbis morte morieris, proprie dicta mors designata fuerit. Sic meas deffendi rationes. Suas etiam quasdam habet Vir Doctus, quibus probet, mortem, quam Deus illa lege comminatus est, non tantum esse mortem corporis, verum etiam mortem animae, id est, amissionem justitiae originalis, & imaginis Dei priuationem. Eas expendi par est.
units.tr: PLAC. If the Papists said that in the words This is my body there is no unusual metaphor, or that the same word must not be taken both properly and improperly, because a covenant, a sacrament and a law do not allow this, the comparison would be sound and they would not be opposing our people. But now, since they exclude from those words, and from every covenant, sacrament and law, every metaphor, even a very common and obvious one, what do they have in common with me? Certainly I refuted them in Examen rationum pro et contra Sacrificium Missae, part 1, chapter 14, p. 429 and following. But it cannot be denied that by the words you shall surely die the death properly so called is meant. Thus I have defended my arguments. The learned man also has some arguments of his own, by which he tries to prove that the death with which God threatened him in that law is not only the death of the body but also the death of the soul, that is, the loss of original righteousness and the privation of the image of God. These it is right that I weigh.

units.la: GAR. Rationem triplicem producimus. Primum enim. Non alia mala & damna rebellione sua homo incurrit, quam qua interminatus fuerat ei Deus sua legis sanctione; quem enim ab inobedientia & praeuaricatione legis abstherre voluit, quidni precipitia ei posfuisset ob oculos, in qua erat sua legis diuina violatione deturbandus? Atqui homo, sua obsequij denegatione, non mortem modo corporalem, & calamitates externas sibi accersiuit, verum & omissionem spiritualium donorum, & facultatum omnium peruerfionem, & damnationis aeterna reatum incurrit. Omnia ergo Deus sua illa mortis declaratione comminatus fuerat.
units.tr: GAR. We bring forward a threefold argument. First: by his rebellion man incurred no evils and losses other than those with which God had threatened him in the sanction of his law. For why, when God wished to deter him from disobedience and transgression of the law, should he not have set before his eyes the precipice into which he would be cast by violating the divine law? But man, by refusing obedience, brought upon himself not only bodily death and external calamities, but also the loss of spiritual gifts, the perversion of all his faculties, and the guilt of eternal damnation. Therefore God by that declaration of death threatened all of these.

units.la: PL. Distinguo mala. Alia enim sunt culpae, alia poenae. Illa Deus lege sua vetuerat, non comminatus fuerat: hæc comminatus fuerat, non autem vetuerat. Est autem mors spiritualis seu priuatio justitiae originalis malu culpae, non poenae proprie dictae. Negatur igitur Major, si de culpae malis intelligitur. Quaquam ne de malis quidem pœnæ intellecta vniuersaliter vera est. Distinguì enim debent mala pœnæ in ea quæ sunt pœnæ, vt loquuntur, satisfactoriæ, & ea quæ se habet aliquomodo vt carceris pœdor & molestiæ, vel vt castigationes paternæ. Illas solas lex comminabatur. Incurrit autem in has homo per peccatum suum, quia propter Christi satisfactionem datum est ei ad refipiscendum spatium, & tractatur à Deo, vt solet à patre filius puer.
units.tr: PL. I distinguish the evils. For some are faults, others are punishments. God had forbidden the former by his law; he had not threatened them. He had threatened the latter, but had not forbidden them. Now spiritual death, or the privation of original righteousness, is an evil of fault, not properly a punishment. Therefore I deny the major premise, if it is understood of evils of fault. Yet even understood of evils of punishment it is not universally true. For the evils of punishment must be distinguished into those which are, as they say, satisfactory punishments, and those which are in some way like the squalor and discomfort of a prison, or like a father's chastisements. The law threatened only the former. Man, however, incurs the latter through his sin, because a space for repentance was given him on account of Christ's satisfaction, and God deals with him as a father customarily deals with a young son.

units.la: GAR. 2. Adamus in integritate perseuerans, bonorum & corporalium, & spiritualium continuatione & augmento donandus erat: Ergo & ab ea integritate deficiens, vt malis subiaceret, & corporalibus, & spiritualibus, consentaneum erat: quidni ergo Deus ea significata voluerit mortis nomine?
units.tr: GAR. 2. Adam, persevering in integrity, was to be granted the continuation and increase of goods both bodily and spiritual. Therefore, falling away from that integrity, it was fitting that he should be subject to evils, both bodily and spiritual. Why then should God not have willed those things to be signified by the name of death?

units.la: PLAC. Atqui perseuerantia in integritate & continuatio integritatis idem sunt. Integritas autem originalis & iustitia originalis quid differunt? Erat igitur donandus continuatione, non iustitiæ originalis (hæc enim continuatio exigebatur vt conditio) sed aliorum omnium bonorum. Porrò integritas opponitur corruptioni immediate: deficere ab integritate est corrumpi, amittere integritatem est acquirere corruptionem. Confundit ergo Vir doctus conditionem promissionis cum re promissa: nec verum est argumenti eius antecedens, nisi de bonis intelligatur physicis, seu ab ipsa integritate seu iustitia diuersis.
units.tr: PLAC. But perseverance in integrity and the continuation of integrity are the same thing. What, then, is the difference between original integrity and original righteousness? Adam was therefore to be granted continuation not of original righteousness (for this continuation was required as a condition) but of all the other goods. Moreover, integrity is opposed immediately to corruption: to fall away from integrity is to be corrupted, and to lose integrity is to acquire corruption. The learned man therefore confuses the condition of the promise with the thing promised. Nor is the antecedent of his argument true, unless it is understood of physical goods, that is, goods distinct from integrity itself or from righteousness.

units.la: GAR. 3. Nulla ratio dici potest, quare non mortis nomen in tota sua latitudine hoc loco sumatur; atqui mortis nomen in Scripturis non ad corpus modò, sed & ad animam, & spiritualia referri patet ex frequentibus Scripturæ testimoniis. Vide Ezech. 3. 18. Of. 13. 1. Matth. 8. 22. Luc. 9. 60. & 15. 24. Ephef. 5. 14. 1. Tim. 5. 6. Apoc. 3. 1. &c.
units.tr: GAR. 3. No reason can be given why the name of death should not be taken in this place in its whole breadth. But that the name of death in the Scriptures refers not only to the body but also to the soul and to spiritual things is plain from the frequent testimonies of Scripture. See Ezek. 3. 18; Hos. 13. 1; Matt. 8. 22; Luke 9. 60; 15. 24; Eph. 5. 14; 1 Tim. 5. 6; Rev. 3. 1, etc.

units.la: PLAC. Ratio est in promptu, quia mors spiritualis est peccatum, non autem proprie loquendo peccati pœna. Comminatur autem Lex non peccatum, sed proprie dictam duntaxat peccati pœnam. Quod autem ait, non deesse auctoritates grauium virorum, nec desunt etiam mihi non minus grauium virorum auctoritates, & jam supra Helueticam laudaui confessionem Art. 8. Sed quid opus est humanis pugnare testimoniis, vbi rationes adsunt illis multò validiores? Caeterum vides quid hinc sequatur: nam si priuatio iustitiæ non est pœna lege denunciata, certè pœna propriedicta non est. Quare non est adscribenda iustitiæ vindici nobis peccatum illud actuale Adami imputantis.
units.tr: PLAC. The reason is at hand: spiritual death is sin, not properly speaking the punishment of sin. But the law threatens not sin, but properly speaking only the punishment of sin. As for his saying that the authorities of weighty men are not lacking, the authorities of no less weighty men are not lacking to me either, and I have already cited above the Helvetic Confession, art. 8. But why is there need to contend with human testimonies where there are reasons far more powerful than these? Moreover, you see what follows from this: for if the privation of righteousness is not a punishment threatened by the law, then certainly it is not a punishment properly so called. Therefore that actual sin of Adam is not to be ascribed to us, as the avenger of righteousness imputing it.

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Examen Cap. iii. In quo disquiritur, Quid sit imputari vel non imputari peccatum.
units.tr: Examination of Chapter III, in which it is inquired what it is to impute or not to impute sin.

units.la: CApite tertio rursus constituis statum controuersiæ, eoque constituto iterum digredeiis, ac tibi sumis illustrandum, quid sit imputare & imputari, ac primum verbum hebræum, deinde verbum græcum expendis, laudatis in eum finem aliquot Scripturæ locis: quorsum, aut quo consilio, nescio, nisi forte, vt tui tractatus molem augeres, ac tuorum argumentorum paucitatem tegeres: vtilis quidem fortasse tua hæc illustratio foret ad controuersiam de iustificatione: quoniam Scriptura eam solita est modò imputatione fidei & iustitiæ, modò non imputatione peccati describere: ad hanc verò, quæ inter nos agitatur, quæstionem quid valeat non video: Nullus enim extat in tota Scriptura locus, in quo peccatum Adami nobis imputari dicatur. Itaque non quæritur inter nos, quo sensu Scriptura vsurpet in hac quæstione verbum imputandi; nunquam enim vsurpat, sed quo sensu in meis thesibus (quandoquidem tu eas refutare aggressus es) negauerim peccatum Adami nobis imputari, vt mea illa negatio, qualis sit, verane an falsa cognoscatur, ac vitetur λοχμαχία. Tandem concludis, peccatum imputari, cum attribuitur, consideratur, & pro peccato habetur & punitur vt peccatum; Ex opposito peccatum non imputari, cùm non consideratur vt peccatum, sed tegitur, condonatur & remittitur. Quod certè non est accómodatum ad quæstionem nostram. Cùm enim affirmo, peccatum actuale Adami nobis non imputari, non hoc volo peccatum illud non considerari vt peccatum, sed tegi, condonari, & remitti nobis. ( vides alienam esse hanc tuam non imputandi explicationem à mea mente, & ab hac cuæstione, non quæritur inter nos, vtrum peccatum Adami nobis condonetur : talis non imputatio est à misericordia ; sed quæritur inter nos, vtrum de jure, ex iustitia nobis imputetur, necne ? Tu proculdubio statuis non imputari, hoc est, remitti fidelibus : attamen idem contendis me aduersus omnibus hominibus imputari, & quidem ita imputari, vt in omnibus puniatur actu : non quæro hoc loco quomodo ista punitio consistat cum justificatione seu remissione, & non imputatione illius peccati. Sed, quicquid sit, Contendo peccatum illud Adami actuale nostrum peccatum non esse. Itaque nobis jure imputari non posse.
units.tr: In the third chapter you again set out the state of the controversy, and, having set it out, you digress again, undertaking to illustrate what it is to impute and to be imputed. You weigh first the Hebrew word and then the Greek, citing several passages of Scripture for that purpose. To what end, or with what design, I do not know, unless perhaps to swell the bulk of your treatise and to cover the paucity of your arguments. This illustration of yours might perhaps be useful for the controversy about justification, since Scripture is accustomed to describe justification sometimes by the imputation of faith and righteousness, sometimes by the non-imputation of sin. But as to the question now debated between us, I do not see what it contributes. For there is no place in the whole of Scripture where it is said that Adam's sin is imputed to us. Therefore the question between us is not in what sense Scripture uses the word "to impute" in this matter, for it never uses it so; the question is in what sense, in my theses (since you have undertaken to refute them), I denied that Adam's sin is imputed to us, so that my denial, whether true or false, may be recognised and logomachy [λογομαχία] avoided. Finally you conclude: sin is imputed when it is attributed, considered, and held to be sin and punished as sin; conversely, sin is not imputed when it is not considered as sin, but is covered, pardoned and remitted. This certainly does not fit our question. For when I affirm that Adam's actual sin is not imputed to us, I do not mean that the sin is not considered as sin but is covered, pardoned and remitted to us. (You see that this explanation of yours of non-imputation is foreign both to my meaning and to this question. The question between us is not whether Adam's sin is pardoned to us; such non-imputation comes from mercy. The question between us is whether it is imputed to us by right, from justice, or not.) You doubtless hold that it is not imputed, that is, that it is remitted to believers; yet at the same time you contend that I maintain it is imputed to all men, and indeed imputed in such a way that it is actually punished in all of them. I do not ask here how that punishment agrees with justification or remission and the non-imputation of that sin. But whatever the case, I contend that Adam's actual sin is not our sin, and so cannot be imputed to us by right.

units.la: Fateor imputare esse tribuere, attribuere, adscribere : sed quædam sunt hoc loco obseruanda, in primis distinctio illa imputationis in antecedentem & consequentem seu immediatam & mediatam, quam, dum statum quæstionis constituerem, Cap. 2. explicaui, nec hic repeto : ejus vt memineris te rogo. Deinde illud etiam cogitationi nostræ obuersari debet, agi inter nos de imputatione non qualibet, sed judiciaria, quam punitio iusta sequatur. Est autem ejusmodi imputatio peccati, actus judicis sententia sua peccatum alicui tribuentis, hoc est, aliquem certi cujusdam peccati reum esse pronunciantis, ac propterea poena afficiendum. Tributur autem alicui peccatum vel tanquam peccatori, vel tanquam peccatoris personam vltro sustinenti, vadi: illi vt suum, huic vt alienum. Nobis ii peccatum Adami actuale imputatur, tribuitur, non vt alienum, sed vt nostrum: suam enim quisque nostrum, cum concipitur & nascitur, personam, non Adami, cujus vas non est, gerit. Consldera igitur mecum, quaeso, & perpende, quomodo nobis peccatum illud primum actuale, possit imputari vere an falso, iuste an iniuste? Fuit actio quaedam singularis, quae non potuit reum peragere, nisi aut imperantem, aut exequentem, aut consentientem. Eam autem neque imperauimus, aut suasimus Adamo, neque ipsi, qui non eramus, commisimus, neque ei, vel antequam essemus, vel in vtero materno delitescentes actu consensimus. dic igitur, amabo te, quomodo nobis vere & iuste singulis attribuatur & adscribatur? Si respondeas, vitium illud hereditarium, quod ab illa actione productum in nos manauit, esse peccati illius veluti reliquias & semen, & habitualem, vt ita loquar, voluntatis nostrae consensum; Itaque iure nobis imputari, descendes in meam sententiam, qui imputationem mediatam, quae hereditariam corruptionem sequatur, & in ea fundata sit, vltro agnosco, & doceo.
units.tr: I grant that to impute is to assign, attribute or ascribe. But certain things must be observed here, above all that distinction of imputation into antecedent and consequent, or immediate and mediate, which I explained in chapter 2 when setting out the state of the question, and which I do not repeat here; I ask you to remember it. Next, this too should be borne in mind: the question between us concerns not any imputation whatever, but judicial imputation, which is followed by just punishment. Such an imputation of sin is an act of a judge who, by his sentence, assigns a sin to someone, that is, pronounces him guilty of a certain sin and therefore to be punished. Now sin is assigned to someone either as to a sinner, or as to one who has voluntarily taken on the person of a sinner, as surety: to the former as his own, to the latter as another's. Adam's actual sin is imputed to us, assigned, not as another's but as our own. For each of us, when he is conceived and born, bears his own person, not Adam's, whose vessel he is not. Consider then with me, I beg you, and weigh how that first actual sin can be imputed to us truly or falsely, justly or unjustly. It was a single action, which the guilty party could not have committed except by commanding, executing or consenting. But we neither commanded nor advised Adam to it, nor did we commit it ourselves, since we did not yet exist; nor did we consent to it actually, either before we existed or while we lay hidden in the mother's womb. Tell me then, I pray you, how is it truly and justly assigned and ascribed to each of us? If you answer that the hereditary corruption which flowed into us from that action is the remnant and seed of that sin, and, so to speak, the habitual consent of our will, and that therefore it is rightly imputed to us, then you come down to my opinion. For I willingly acknowledge and teach a mediate imputation, which follows hereditary corruption and is founded upon it.

units.la: CAPVT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Examen Cap. IV.
units.tr: Examination of Chapter IV.

units.la: RVRSVM Cap. iv. tui tractatus manum admoues statui quaestionis constituendo, expoliendo, illustrando; inque ea re totum Cap. iv. consumis. Doleo nos tamdiu detineri à te in vestibulo famelicos & appetentes tuarum rationum, ad quas percipiendas nos tui tractatus Cap. primo inuitaueras. Hic tamen decet me tecum paulisper commorari, & colloqui. Quaeritur, inquis, quomodo peccatum illud actuale, quod fuit persona, sufficiat ad condemnationem omnium hominum? Sufficere praesupponis, quomodo sufficiat quaeris. Atqui prius illud non fuit absque distinctione praesupponendum: in eo enim ipso vertitur cardo huius controuersiae: nam si hoc vis, peccatum illud actuale per se ipsum vnum immediate sufficere ad condemnationem omnium hominum, id praesupponis quod versatur in quaestione, quodque ego pernego. Sin vis sufficere ad eam condemnationem mediante corruptione, quam produxit, propagatâ in omnes homines, tibi assentior. Sed tuam responsionem audiamus. Respondeo, inquis, omnes homines ex Adamo natos considerari tanquam vnum hominem in Adamo & omnes peccasse in illo, ita vt primum peccatum, quod actualiter commisit, illis imputetur, & tribuatur, & satis sit vt habeantur pro peccatoribus, & morti adjudicentur. Licet-ne mihi quaerere, vnde id habeas, ex Scriptura, an aliunde? nam à quo vis considerari omnes homines tanquam vnum hominem, nisi à Deo? Vnde igitur tibi iste mentis diuinæ internus actus innotuit? Tacet scriptura, reclamat ratio: nam quomodo omnes homines considerantur tanquam vnus homo in Adamo? an quomodo dixit Porphyrius participatione speciei multos homines esse vnum, vnitate scilicet specifica? at id iuuare non potest imputationem peccati actualis Adami omnibus hominibus: actiones enim sunt suppositorum, non autem generis, aut speciei: nec positis, quibus inter se distinguuntur, differentiis propriis omnes homines magis sunt Adamus, quàm alius quilibet homo: continetur enim sub hominis specie Adamus haud secus quàm reliqui indiuidui homines. An vis omnes homines consideratos fuisse tanquam vnum numero hominem in Adamo? nihil fingi posset salsius ista consideratione. Quid igitur tibi vis hac propositione? ea, fateor ingenuè, non intelligo quem sensum non ineptum habere possit. Explica te, quæso, dilucidius: cupio enim mentem tuam assequi: connitar adhuc: Visne omnes homines consideratos fuisse tanquam oriundos ex vno homine, ex vno fonte, vna stirpe, Adamo? non video quomodo inde sequatur peccatum actuale Adami sufficere ad condemnationem omnium hominum, aut debere omnibus hominibus immediatè imputari; sed ea de re postea.
units.tr: Returning to Chapter IV of your treatise, you take up the task of setting out, refining and clarifying the question, and you spend the whole chapter on this. I regret that you keep us so long in the vestibule, hungry and eager for your reasons, which you had promised in the first chapter of your treatise that we would receive. Still, it is fitting that I pause with you for a little while and talk it over. You ask, you say, how that actual sin, which was committed by one person, is sufficient for the condemnation of all men? You presuppose that it is sufficient, and then ask how it is sufficient. But that should not have been presupposed without distinction, for the hinge of this controversy turns on exactly that point. If you mean that this actual sin, by itself and immediately, is sufficient for the condemnation of all men, then you presuppose what is in dispute, and what I flatly deny. But if you mean that it is sufficient for that condemnation through the corruption which it produced and which was passed on to all men, I agree with you. Let us, however, hear your answer. I answer, you say, that all men born of Adam are considered as one man in Adam, and that all sinned in him, so that the first sin, which he committed in act, is imputed and ascribed to them, and it is enough that they are held to be sinners and adjudged to death. May I ask where you get this, from Scripture or from somewhere else? For by whom would you have all men considered as one man, if not by God? Where, then, has this inward act of the divine mind become known to you? Scripture is silent, and reason cries out against it. For in what way are all men considered as one man in Adam? Is it as Porphyry said, that many men are one by participation in the species, that is, by specific unity? But that cannot help the imputation of Adam's actual sin to all men, for actions belong to individuals, not to a genus or a species; and even with the proper differences by which they are distinguished from one another, all men are not more Adam than any other man is: Adam is contained under the species of man no less than the other individual men. Or do you mean that all men were considered as one man numerically in Adam? Nothing more absurd could be imagined than that view. What then do you mean by this proposition? I frankly confess that I do not understand what sense it could have that is not nonsensical. Please explain yourself more clearly, for I wish to grasp your mind, and I will try again. Do you mean that all men were considered as descended from one man, one source, one stock, Adam? I do not see how it follows from that that Adam's actual sin is sufficient for the condemnation of all men, or must be imputed to all men immediately; but I will return to that matter later.

units.la: GAR. Respons. 1. omnes homines fuisse vnum hominem in Adamo, non commentum recens est, sed vetus Catholicorum, ac nominatim Augustini aduersus Pelagianos disputantis doctrina, quam sæpius in operibus suis repetit. Sufficiat nunc vnus ille locus ex Epist. 106. ad Bonifac. Quicunque ex illo vno multi in seipsis futuri erant, in illo vnus homo erant, Si ab Augustino quaras, unde id habeat, respondebit ex Apostolo se habere, ubi testatur omnes in Adamo peccasse. In Adamo peccarunt: itaque unum fuerunt in Adamo. Quod & Martyr, unus ex grauissimis Theologis, quorum autoritatem obtendit in hoc negotio vir doctus, evidenter significauit ubi scripsit, Adamo peccante idem fuisse, ac ii omnes praesentes fuissent, & cum Adamo peccauissent.
units.tr: GAR. Answer 1. That all men were one man in Adam is not a recent invention but the old teaching of the Catholics, and especially of Augustine, who disputed against the Pelagians and repeats it often in his works. For now let that one passage from Letter 106 to Boniface suffice: "All who were to be many in themselves out of that one were one man in him." If you ask Augustine where he gets this, he will answer that he has it from the Apostle, where he testifies that all sinned in Adam. They sinned in Adam; therefore they were one in Adam. Martyr also, one of the most weighty theologians, whose authority the learned man cites in this matter, clearly expressed the same when he wrote that, with Adam sinning, it was the same as if they had all been present and had sinned with Adam.

units.la: PLAC. Aliud quaesiui, aliud respondet. Non enim quaesiui, unde haberet, omnes homines fuisse unum hominem in Adamo; sed unde haberet, Deum considerasse omnes homines tanquam unum hominem in Adamo, ita ut illis primum illud peccatum actuale Adami imputauerit immediate? De illa consideratione, de illo interno mentis diuinae actu agebatur: de quo tamen altum in hac responsione silentium. Deinde quaesiui, unde haberet, hoc est, ex qua diuina Scriptura. Talis enim actus mentis diuinae aliunde quam ex Dei revelatione cognosci nequit. Ille vero confugit ad Augustinum, & Martyrem, quibus talis diuinus actus non est, opinor, nominatim coelitus revelatus. Tum non negaui omnes homines aliquomodo unum fuisse in Adamo, nempe unitate speciei, & originis, tantum negaui inde sequi fuisse ita a Deo tanquam unum consideratos, ut illis primum Adami peccatum actuale immediate imputauerit. Negaui etiam fuisse consideratos tanquam unum numero, seu indiuidum hominem. Itaque ille probat quod concedo, quod nego ne attingit quidem.
units.tr: PAPISTS? No: PLAC. You have asked one thing and he answers another. I did not ask where he gets the claim that all men were one man in Adam; I asked where he gets the claim that God considered all men as one man in Adam, so that He imputed to them immediately that first actual sin of Adam. It was that consideration, that inward act of the divine mind, that was at issue, and about it this answer keeps a deep silence. Next, I asked where he gets it, that is, from which divine Scripture. For such an act of the divine mind cannot be known from anywhere but God's revelation. He, however, takes refuge in Augustine and Martyr, to whom, I suppose, such a divine act was not specifically revealed from heaven. Furthermore, I did not deny that in some way all men were one in Adam, namely by unity of species and of origin; I only denied that it follows that they were so considered by God as one that Adam's first actual sin was imputed to them immediately. I also denied that they were considered as one numerically, or as one individual man. So he proves what I concede, and does not even touch what I deny.

units.la: GAR. 2. Cum Apostolica verba, in quo omnes peccauerunt, imputationem Adamici peccati denotent, ut est supra confirmatum: imputatio autem illa fit actus Dei declarantis omnes ob Adami peccatum reos, consequens est, ut, si ea verba significent omnes in Adamo consideratos ut unum hominem, designent eadem ratione, a Deo ita fuisse consideratos.
units.tr: GAR. 2. Since the apostolic words, "in whom all sinned," denote the imputation of Adam's sin, as has been confirmed above, and since that imputation is an act of God declaring all guilty on account of Adam's sin, it follows that, if those words mean that all were considered in Adam as one man, they also signify that they were so considered by God for the same reason.

units.la: PLAC. Nec Apostolus dixit omnes in Adamo peccasse; Nec si id dixisset, verba illa denotarent imputationem Adamici peccati, saltem immediatam, vti & supra ostendimus, & infra confirmabimus.
units.tr: PLAC. Nor did the Apostle say that all sinned in Adam; and even if he had said so, those words would not denote the imputation of Adam's sin, at least not an immediate imputation, as I have shown above and will confirm below.

units.la: GAR. 3. Vnus homo dicuntur omnes in Adamo fuisse, non vnitate vel specifica, vel numerica. Sed tum vnitate originis, quia omnes ex vno sunt sanguine, Actor. XVII. 26. & omnis homo terrenus nihil est origine, nisi Adam, ut loquitur Augustinus Retract. lib. 1. cap. 15. Tum vnitate repræsentationis: ab vno enim Adamo sunt omnes repræsentati, quia vnus Adamus omnium personam sustinebat, ut & Theologi consentienter docent, & non diffitetur Clarif. Amyraldus Thesib. de trib. fœder. Thes. 8. Ex illa duplici vnitate colligitur peccati Adæ imputatio. Nam propter vnitatem originis habent omnes naturalem conjunctionem cum Adamo. At naturalis conjunctio idonea causa esse potest, cur aliquis pro alterius crimine pœnis subjaceat, vt antea dictum: propter vnitatem repræsentationis, Adamo peccante idem fuit, ac si omnes peccatum commisissent.
units.tr: GAR. 3. All are said to have been in Adam as one man, not by specific or numerical unity, but both by unity of origin, because "all are of one blood," Acts 17.26, and "every earthly man is nothing in origin but Adam," as Augustine says in the Retractations, book 1, chapter 15; and by unity of representation, for all were represented by the one Adam, because the one Adam bore the person of all, as the theologians teach with one voice, and as the distinguished Amyraldus does not deny in Thesis 8 of his Theses on the two covenants. From that twofold unity the imputation of Adam's sin is inferred. For because of the unity of origin all have a natural connection with Adam. But a natural connection can be a fitting cause why one should undergo punishments for another's crime, as was said before; and because of the unity of representation, with Adam sinning it was the same as if all had committed the sin.

units.la: PLAC. Agnosco vnitatem originis: quanquam aliud est omnes homines esse vnum hominem, aut considerari tanquam vnum hominem, aliud omnium hominum esse vnam originem, hoc est, stirpem, seu principium. Hoc ex vnitate originis sequitur, non illud. Sed vnitatem repræsentationis probari mihi è Scriptura cupio, vt & illud quod adfert probationis loco, vnum Adamum peccando omnium hominum personam sustinuisse. Hoc enim ipsum vndè habeatur, scire aueo. Ponitur enim à quibusdam, sed probatur à nemine. Idne igitur reuelauit Deus in Scriptura? Proferatur locus. potestne ex natura colligi? adferatur ratio. Affirmanti enim aliquid ejusmodi, præter naturæ & Scripturæ librum assentiri nec teneor, nec expedit. Nec verò id ex Augustini aut Clarif. Amyraldi verbis colligi potest. Quæ enim consequentia, omnis homo nihil est origine nisi Adam. Ergo omnes homines fuerunt à Deo considerati tanquam vnus homo in Adam. Vel, Ergo Adamus in peccando sustinebat omnium hominum personam? Eamne etiam sustinebat, cùm alia agebat? Minimè; imposita illi scilicet est hæc omnium persona, tantummodò vt pro omnibus peccaret. Dixit quidem Clarif. Amyraldus illa Thesi Adamum, quâ primus homo fuit, vniuersum genus humanum, quod ex eo nasciturum erat, veluti repræsentasse: Sed eam locutionem, quia dura videbatur, emolliuit præmissâ voce veluti, innuens non esse illam locutionem propriam, nec vrgendam vt propriam. Quod ait Vir Doctus, naturalem conjunctionem idoneam causam esse posse, cur aliquis pro alterius crimine poenis subjaceat, verum non est in foro diuino nisi aut sit etiam inter eos conjunctio peccati, aut saltem sit in eo, qui punitur, peccatum dignum illa poena, aut sit ipse peccatorum vas. Quod subjungit, propter vnitatem repraesentationis, Adamo peccante idem fuisse, ac si omnes peccatum commisissent, probatione eget. Non enim quicquid facit qui alterum repraesentat, huic continuo siue consentiat, siue non consentiat, imputandum est. Pepigit Deus foedus cum genere humano in Noacho, & cum Israelitis in Abrahamo, neutrius tamen, opinor, aut bona opera aut peccata posteris imputata sunt.
units.tr: PLAC. I acknowledge the unity of origin, although it is one thing for all men to be one man, or to be considered as one man, and another for all men to have one origin, that is, one stock or principle. It follows from the unity of origin that all men have one origin, not that they are one man. But I long to have the unity of representation proved to me from Scripture, and likewise the claim, which he adduces as proof, that by sinning the one Adam bore the person of all men. I want to know where this itself is to be got, for it is asserted by some but proved by no one. Did God indeed reveal this in Scripture? Let the passage be produced. Can it be gathered from nature? Let the argument be given. For I am neither bound nor advised to assent to such a claim apart from the book of nature and the book of Scripture. Nor can it be gathered from the words of Augustine or of Amyraldus. For what sort of inference is this: "every man is nothing in origin but Adam; therefore all men were considered by God as one man in Adam"? Or this: "Therefore Adam in sinning bore the person of all men"? Did he also bear that person when he was doing other things? By no means; this person of all men was evidently laid upon him only so that he might sin on behalf of all. Indeed Amyraldus, in that thesis, said that Adam, as the first man, had as it were represented the whole human race that was to be born from him; but because that expression seemed harsh, he softened it by prefixing the word "as it were," signalling that this is not a proper expression and should not be pressed as proper. What the learned man says, that a natural connection can be a fitting cause why one should undergo punishments for another's crime, is not true in the divine court unless there is also a connection of sin between them, or at least the one punished has a sin worthy of that punishment, or is himself a vessel of sins. What he adds, that because of the unity of representation, with Adam sinning it was the same as if all had committed the sin, needs proof. For whatever the one who represents another does, it is not straightway to be imputed to those represented, whether they consent or do not consent. God made a covenant with the human race in Noah, and with the Israelites in Abraham, yet neither their good works nor their sins, I suppose, were imputed to their posterity.

units.la: GAR. 4. Imputatio primi peccati colligitur non ex eo simpliciter, quod omnes sunt ab Adamo oriundi, sed ex eo quod ita docemur ab Apostolo Roman. v. ut audivimus, & quod per peccatum illud excussit Adamus gratiam omnem foederis illius primaui, quod in ipso cum omnibus hominibus initum fuerat, ut supra dictum.
units.tr: GAR. 4. The imputation of the first sin is inferred not simply from the fact that all are descended from Adam, but from the fact that we are taught this by the Apostle in Rom. 5, as we have heard, and because by that sin Adam cast away all the grace of that first covenant, which had been made with all men in him, as said above.

units.la: PLAC. Non docemur ab Apostolo Rom.5. imputationem immediatam primi peccati. Id hactenus neque vir doctus, neque alius quisquam probauit, vt partim ex dictis, partim ex dicendis cernere est. Addit alteram rationem, sed eam non intelligo. Velim enim mihi exponi quale foedus in Adamo cum omnibus hominibus initum intelligat. Nam si ea fuisse conditione censet, vt, si peccaret Adamus imputaretur ejus primum peccatum actuale omnibus ejus posteris immediate; id foedus adferendum non fuit ad probandam imputationem immediatam. Non enim minus in quaestione versatur quam illa ipsa imputatio: deque eo merito quaeri potest, vnde nam habeatur? Ex naturae inspectione? An ex diuina per Scripturam reuelatione? Aliunde enim si habetur, ob id ipsum reijci debet.
units.tr: PLAC. The Apostle in Rom. 5 does not teach us an immediate imputation of the first sin. Neither the learned man nor anyone else has yet proved this, as can be seen partly from what has been said and partly from what is still to be said. He adds a second argument, but I do not understand it. I would like to be told what sort of covenant he means to have been made with all men in Adam. For if he thinks it was on this condition, that if Adam sinned his first actual sin would be imputed immediately to all his posterity, then that covenant ought not to have been brought forward to prove immediate imputation. It is no less in question than imputation itself, and so one may fairly ask where it is got from. Is it from the observation of nature? Or from a divine revelation through Scripture? For if it is got from elsewhere, it must for that very reason be rejected.

units.la: Visne omnes homines considerari vt vnam rempublicam, vnum corpus, cujus caput sit Adamus, reliqui autem homines singuli membra? Fuit igitur Adamus caput sine corpore, vt nos hodie membra sine capite.
units.tr: Do you want all men to be considered as one commonwealth, one body, whose head is Adam, and the other men individually as members? Then Adam was a head without a body, just as we today are members without a head.

units.la: GAR. Hoc rationis genus, si L. Crasso venisset in mentem ea differtatione quam habuit cum Q. Mutio Scaevola apud Tullium lib. 1. de Oratore, na poterat ille plausibili argumento dictum Scaevola traducere, Socratem vocantis fontem & caput Philosophorum, qui longa serie post exemptum humanis Socratem in Gracia floruerunt: nimirum, quia & Socrates ante natos illos Philosophos fons fuisset sine riuulis, & caput sine membris; & illi post Socratem Philosophi, riui fuissent absque fonte, & membra sine capite.
units.tr: GAR. If this kind of reasoning had come to L. Crassus in that debate which he had with Q. Mucius Scaevola in Cicero, De Oratore, book 1, he could have made the plausible argument that Scaevola was wrong to call Socrates the fountain and head of philosophers, since those who flourished long afterwards in Greece, after Socrates was taken from men, were philosophers too. Namely, because Socrates would have been a fountain without streams and a head without members before those philosophers were born; and those philosophers after Socrates would have been streams without a fountain, and members without a head.

units.la: PLAC. Egregiam refutationem! Agebatur de Adamo relate ad id tempus, quo primum peccauit, diu antequam nobis gignendis operam daret. Dixi eum tunc nondum fuisse caput nostrum, quomodo exercitus caput est dux, reipublicae magistratus, regni rex: quia caput fuisset sine membris. Num eo tempore Socratem Scaevola fontem & caput appellauit? Num ejus temporis respectu, cum nondum vilus esset ejus auditor, vllusue alius praeter eum philosophus? Num propterea aliqua Socratis actio omnibus aliis philosophis imputari immediate potuit aut debuit? Nihil quicquam a Socrate in sequentes philosophos imputatione descendit.
units.tr: PLAC. A splendid refutation! The question was about Adam in relation to the time when he first sinned, long before he set about begetting us. I said that he was not yet our head at that time, in the way that a general is the head of an army, a magistrate the head of a commonwealth, or a king the head of a kingdom, because then he would have been a head without members. Did Scaevola at that time call Socrates the fountain and head? Was there then any philosopher besides him, or any hearer of his, with respect to that time, when he had not yet had even one listener? Was any action of Socrates for that reason able, or bound, to be imputed immediately to all the other philosophers? Nothing at all of Socrates descended by imputation to the philosophers who followed.

units.la: GAR. Atqui si rem serio agimus, quidni vulgatissimam distinctionem in memoriam renocamus, vt caput proprie dictum discernatur ab improprie dicto, id est, physicum a morali? Namin physico certe capite, quod natura suis nervis & vinculis cum reliquo corpore colligauit, ita res habet, vt neque caput dicatur, nisi cum adsunt membra; neque membra νψωνύμως vocentur, nisi qua actu cum capite conjuncta sunt. At vero cum Adamum dicunt Theologi esse generis humani caput, impropriam sine dubio significationem vsurpant, vt denotent originem esse & principium seminale generis humani, vnde scilicet humana natura sumpserit initium. Quomodo scilicet Abrahamus Iudaica gentis caput dicitur. Quis autem non eum riserit, qui propterea negare sustineat Abrahamum esse Iudaeorum caput; quod & ipse dicendus esset caput sine corpore, cum Iudai nondum essent; & Iudai membra sine capite, quia non amplius erat Abrahamus?
