Caput ergo generis merito dicitur Adamus, quia Deus eum constituit, vt radicem, fontem, & principium indiuiduale, vnde orituri essent homines, vt rivi, vt rami, vt γεννήματα ex eo principio.
units.tr: GAR. But if we are dealing with the matter seriously, why should we not call to mind the very common distinction, so that the head properly so called is distinguished from the head improperly so called, that is, the physical from the moral? For in a physical head, indeed, which nature has joined to the rest of the body by its nerves and sinews, the case is such that it is not called a head unless the members are present, and the members are not called by the same name unless they are actually joined to the head. But when the theologians call Adam the head of the human race, they use the term in an improper sense, to signify that he is the origin and seminal principle of the human race, from which human nature, of course, took its beginning. In the same way Abraham is called the head of the Jewish nation. But who would not laugh at the man who ventured to deny that Abraham is the head of the Jews, on the ground that he would then have to be called a head without a body, since the Jews did not yet exist, and the Jews would be members without a head, since Abraham was no longer there? Adam is therefore rightly called the head of the race, because God appointed him as the root, fountain and individual principle from which men were to arise, as streams, as branches, as offspring from that principle.

units.la: PLAC. Putauitne Vir D ɔctus me ita infamauisse vt caput proprie dictum intellexerim, qui disertis verbis dixi corpus improprie dictum, seu morale, tanquam rempublicam? Manifestum enim est rempublicam non esse corpus physicum: Et tamen, quamuis natura rempublicam cum capite suo rege, vel magistratu non colligauerit neruis & vinculis, nemo dixerit hominem tunc fuisse caput reipublicæ, cum ipse viueret priuatus, nondum nata republica: neque respublica quæ nunc est corpus dicetur illius principis, qui ante centum aut mille annos desijt esse in viuis. Tale caput, tale corpus politicum intellexi. Nam alioqui non nego, neque negaui vnquam, quin sit Adamus caput generis humani eo sensu quem Vir doctus hoc loco exponit. Sed quid ad immediatam imputationem peccati Adamici facit ista capitis ratio? An sic caput fuit Adamus duntaxat dum peccauit? An propterea quod Abrahamus gentis Iudaicæ caput fuit, eo modo ejus aliqua actio omnibus & singulis Iudæis imputatur?
units.tr: PLAC. Does the learned man think that I have been so ignorant as to understand the head in the proper sense, when I explicitly said that the body is used in an improper sense, or moral, like a commonwealth? For it is plain that a commonwealth is not a physical body. And yet, although nature does not bind a commonwealth to its head, its king or magistrate, by nerves and sinews, no one would say that a man was the head of a commonwealth at a time when he lived as a private person and the commonwealth had not yet come into being; nor would the commonwealth that now exists be called the body of a prince who ceased to be among the living a hundred or a thousand years ago. It was such a head, and such a political body, that I meant. For otherwise I do not deny, nor have I ever denied, that Adam is the head of the human race in the sense which the learned man sets out here. But what does that account of the head have to do with the immediate imputation of Adam's sin? Was Adam the head in this way only while he was sinning? Or is any action of Abraham imputed in that way to all and each of the Jews because Abraham was the head of the Jewish nation?

units.la: Et omnia peccata Adami nobis, nostra vicissim omnia Adamo imputari debuerunt; par enim est ratio: conueniunt enim toti corpori & quæ capitis, & quæ aliorum membrorum sunt. Me etiam perturbant ista verba, considerantur tanquam vnus homo in Adamo, videris enim illum vnum hominem ab Adamo distinguere. Porrò quæcunque illa consideratio fuerit, cum ea extra nos esset, nec quicquam vel in Adamo, vel in nobis poneret, capere animo non possum, quid ad hoc contulerit, vt nos reuera commiserimus peccatum illud actuale Adami tanto ante quàm essemus. Adde quod si committente alia peccata Adamo perdurauit, quid est quamobrem illa quoque nobis pariter non imputentur? Sin dum solum primum illud admitteret, obtinuit, mirabor, aut desijsse nos esse in Adamo confestim post primum illud peccatum admissum, aut, quamvis in eo sicut antea essemus, non fuisse tamen amplius consideratos tanquam vnum hominem in ipso.
units.tr: And all the sins of Adam ought to be imputed to us, and all ours in turn to Adam; for the reason is the same, since what belongs to the head and what belongs to the other members agrees with the whole body. The words considered as one man in Adam also trouble me, for you seem to distinguish that one man from Adam. Moreover, whatever that consideration may be, since it lies outside us and places nothing either in Adam or in us, I cannot grasp how it contributes to our really having committed that actual sin of Adam so long before we existed. Add that if Adam persisted in committing other sins, why are those not likewise imputed to us? But if he obtained this result by admitting only that first sin, I shall be surprised either that we ceased to be in Adam immediately after that first sin was committed, or, if we were in him as before, that we were not afterwards considered as one man in him.

units.la: Subijcis nos peccasse in Adamo. Vide quàm non sim difficilis, tibi id concedo, modo hoc etiam mihi concedas nos eo modo peccasse in Adamo, quo in eo fuimus. In eo autem fuimus, non quia ejus esse nobis imputetur, aut sit causa meritoria cur sumus, sed quia nos propagatione naturali per intermedios nostros parentes genuit : Eodem modo nos in eo peccasse confiteor, quia peccatum ejus nostrum peccatum longa propagationum serie procreauit.
units.tr: You add that we sinned in Adam. See how unreasonable I am not to concede this to you, provided you also concede to me that we sinned in Adam in the way in which we were in him. We were in him, however, not because his being is imputed to us, or because he is the meritorious cause of our existence, but because he begot us by natural propagation through our intermediate parents. In the same way I confess that we sinned in him, because his sin produced our sin through a long series of propagations.

units.la: Caeterum hanc tuam responsionem interrogationibus firmas. Nam, inquis, quipotest aliter reddi ratio huius infectionis & reatus? cur quasi Adam peccando perdidit, & morti subjecit, non tantum personam, sed etiam totam naturam humanam: Cum caeteri homines peccatis suis actualibus laedant personas, & se mortis reos efficiant, sed naturam non faciant pejorem, aut magis ream? Si vicíssim quæram, qui fieri potuit, vt nos cum nondum essemus, immo aliquot annorum millibus antequam esse inciperemus, peccaremus peccato actuali? qui potest nobis peccatum actuale juste imputari, quod neque fecimus ipsi, neque jussimus, neque suasimus, neque vllo voluntatis nostrae consensu probauimus, quodque nostro respectu nullo modo voluntarium fuit? Horumne tu rationem reddere potes? Annon igitur satius esset propagationem corruptionis inhaerentis & reatus qui eam sequitur, docente scriptura, contestante experientia, firmiter credere; modum autem quem non capis Deo permittere, quam præter & contra Scripturam imputationem excogitare æque, aut magis difficilem captu, ac Dei justitiam peruertentem, & maculantem? Subjungis hoc cogit nos fateri, primum illud Adami peccatum fuisse alio modo consideratum, & justo Dei judicio imputatum, & adscriptum toti naturae humanae, Mallem fateri meam ignorantiam: neque huius confessionis me puderet: caecum enim esse arbitror qui non sentit se multo plura quam scit ignorare. Quam multa sunt in natura, quorum rationes cur sic fiant reddere nequimus? Satius mea sententia id esset, quam in Dei arcana mentem irrumpentes, ei considerationem & judicium sine ulla revelatione tribuere, quod forte nec fuit, nec eum decet. Nosti enim illud Esai. 55. cogitationes meae non sunt ut cogitationes vestrae. Quanam alti sunt coeli supra terram, tam altae sunt cogitationes meae supra cogitationes vestras: Et illud, quis novit mentem Domini?
units.tr: Moreover, you strengthen this reply of yours with questions. For, you say, how else can the reason for this infection and guilt be given? Why is it that Adam by sinning ruined and subjected to death not only his person but the whole of human nature, when other men by their actual sins harm their persons and make themselves liable to death, but do not make nature worse or more guilty? If in turn I were to ask: how could it happen that we, when we did not yet exist, nay, some thousands of years before we began to exist, sinned an actual sin? How can an actual sin be justly imputed to us, which we neither committed, nor commanded, nor persuaded anyone to do, nor approved by any consent of our will, and which with respect to us was in no way voluntary? Can you give an account of these things? Would it not then be better to believe firmly, as Scripture teaches and experience attests, that the corruption inhering in us is propagated, together with the guilt that follows it; and to allow God the mode which we do not grasp, rather than to devise an imputation which is beyond and against Scripture, equally or more difficult to grasp, and which subverts and stains the justice of God? You add that this compels us to admit that the first sin of Adam was considered in another way, and imputed by the just judgment of God, and ascribed to the whole of human nature. I would rather admit my ignorance, and I am not ashamed of this confession, for I think that man is blind who does not feel that he is ignorant of far more than he knows. How many things are there in nature whose reasons we cannot give for why they happen as they do? In my view it would be better than to force our way into God's secrets and attribute to him, without any revelation, a consideration and a judgment which perhaps never existed and which do not become him. For you know that passage in Isaiah 55: My thoughts are not your thoughts. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my thoughts higher than your thoughts; and that other: Who has known the mind of the Lord?

units.la: G A R. Hic vero inprimis ego quoque profiteor, malle me credere, hanc non esse affectatam ignorantiam, de qua dicunt illi apud Iobum cap. 21. 14. Recede a nobis, sc enim viarum tuarum nolumus, quam sinistram aliquam de Viro docto opinionem fovere.
units.tr: GAR. Here indeed I too must first declare that I would rather believe this is not the affected ignorance of which those men in Job 21 (v. 14) speak: "Depart from us, for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways." I would not wish to foster some sinister opinion of a learned man.

units.la: P L A C. Ecquam quaeso veri is illis sinistram de me opinionem fovendi ansam praebui, aut quid est in mea ista moderata & religiosa ignorantia, qua nolo sapere praeter Scripturam, simile abominandae illorum apud Iobum sceleratorum impietati?
units.tr: PLAC. I ask you, what occasion have I given those men for fostering any sinister opinion of me? Or what is there in my moderate and religious ignorance, by which I am unwilling to be wise beyond Scripture, that resembles the abominable impiety of those wicked men in Job?

units.la: G A R. Miror solum, qua ratione ductus, eos arbitretur in arcanam Dei mentem irrumpere, qui corruptionis Originalis, & omnium poenarum in posteros ab ipsa natiuitate incumbentium causam quarunt in imputatione, adeoque participatione primi peccati; cum non ignoret veteres & Recentiores Theologos, hoc & docere, & profiteri se haussisse ex Apostoli doctrina Roman. v. Sicut postea frequentissimis testimoniis probabitur. Hos omnes grauissima accusatione vrgere, quasi in arcanam Dei mentem temerario ausu irrumpentes, & limites illos transilientes, quos Deus homini praefiluit Deuter. xxix. 29. nescio an sit decoro satis consentaneum &c.
units.tr: GAR. I only wonder by what reasoning he is led to think that those men break into the secret counsel of God who seek the cause of original corruption, and of all the punishments that fall upon posterity from birth itself, in imputation, and thus in the participation of the first sin. He cannot be unaware that both the ancient and the more recent theologians teach this, and profess that they have drawn it from the teaching of the Apostle in Romans 5, as will be shown later by very many testimonies. I do not know whether it is at all fitting for a gentleman to press all these men with the most serious accusation, as if they, with rash daring, broke into the secret counsel of God and overstepped those limits which God has set for man in Deuteronomy 29 (v. 29).

units.la: PLAC. Primùm agebatur de eo Dei actu interno, quo dicebatur Deus omnes homines considerasse tanquam unum hominem in Adamo. Idne veteres & Recentiores Theologi dixerunt? Idne colligi potest ex Apostoli doctrina Roman. v? Attulitne Vir doctus frequentissima testimonia vt id probaret? Tribuere Deo considerationem, actum quendam mentis & voluntatis internum praeter Scripturam, praeter rationem, quid est irrumpere in arcanam Dei mentem, si hoc non est? Idem, fateor, de immediata illa imputatione, in qua causa quaeritur originalis corruptionis, dici potest, si quidem ex sacris literis colligi nequit. Est enim ipsa quoque internus diuinae mentis & voluntatis actus. Frustra me praeiudiciis grauat; frustra Theologorum in me animos irritat: neque enim eos accuso, sed fraterne moneo, vt caveant sibi ab hoc scopulo. Humanum enim est errare, sed monitum in errore perseuerare, turpe admodum, & periculosum est. Miror autem Theologos Reformatos talibus vti aduersus fratres suos praejudicijs, quibus olim, & hoc tempore nihil veritati cognoscendae magis obfuit. Non enim quod hic, aut ille docuit, regula est fidei nostrae, sed id tantum, quod vnicus noster doctor per suos Apostolos & Prophetas docuit. Illam autem imputationem neque Scriptura, neque plerique veteres Theologi, neque recentiores quidam magni nominis docuerunt: Et quosdam ipse contra se Vir doctus laudat. Exemplo sit Ludovicus Lavaterus insignis Theologus Tigurinus (vaum enim attulisse exemplum sufficiet hoc loco) cujus haec verba ex Comm. in 2. paralip. 2. 4. 5. citat cap. xviii. pag. 629. Quisque sceleTum suorum poenas luat. Hac lege Deus non obstringitur. Iuste enim punit in omnibus hominibus peccatum primorum parentum, quod vitio originis sit cuique proprium. Quid potest magis opponi doctrinae Viri docti, palam affirmantis, peccatum primorum parentum nonnisi imputatione fieri nostrum?
units.tr: PLAC. First, the question was about that internal act of God by which it was said that God considered all men as one man in Adam. Did the ancient and more recent theologians say this? Can this be gathered from the teaching of the Apostle in Romans 5? Has the learned man brought very many testimonies to prove it? To attribute to God a consideration, an internal act of mind and will, apart from Scripture and apart from reason, what is this if not breaking into the secret counsel of God? I admit the same can be said of that immediate imputation, in which the cause of original corruption is sought, if indeed it cannot be gathered from the holy letters. For it too is an internal act of the divine mind and will. In vain does he burden me with prejudices; in vain does he stir up the minds of theologians against me. For I do not accuse them, but as a brother I warn them to beware of this rock. It is human to err, but to persist in error once warned is very shameful and dangerous. I am surprised, moreover, that the Reformed theologians use against their brethren such prejudices as, both formerly and at this time, have done nothing more to hinder the knowledge of the truth. For what this or that man has taught is not the rule of our faith, but only what our one Teacher has taught through his Apostles and Prophets. Now that imputation neither Scripture, nor most of the ancient theologians, nor certain recent men of great name have taught; and the learned man himself praises some who were against him. Let Ludovicus Lavaterus, the notable Zurich theologian, serve as an example (one example will suffice here), whose words the author quotes from his commentary on 2 Chronicles 2, 4, 5, at chapter 18, page 629: Let each man bear the punishments of his own crimes. God is not bound by this law. For he justly punishes in all men the sin of the first parents, which is proper to each one by the vice of origin. What can be set more directly against the teaching of the learned man, who plainly affirms that the sin of the first parents becomes ours only by imputation?

units.la: Quid si quaeram ex te rationem, cur primum illud peccatum fuerit alio modo, quàm alia peccata consideratum à Deo, & cur fuerit imputatum toti naturae humanae? Eamne poteris reddere? Vtinam! Prorsus enim me fugit. Quanquam eam vltrò necrogatus videris reddere voluisse, addis enim hæc verba, quia sc. Adam fuit primus homo, origo & stirps, seu radix omnium hominum. Agnosco, hinc intelligo potuisse vna cum natura humana suum propagare vitium in posteros : at nego propterea eius peccatum actuale nostrum fuisse, aut nobis debuisse imputari : nego inde considerationem illam & iudicium, quod tu Deo tribuis, posse confici. Ego non video, quomodo peccatum illud actuale Adami, actio illa singularis magis nostra actio, nostrum peccatum fuerit, quàm eius persona fuit nostra persona. Siid vides, ostende quæso mihi & explica : magnam tibi habebo gratiam.
units.tr: What if I ask you for the reason why this first sin was considered by God in a different way from other sins, and why it was imputed to the whole of human nature? Can you give that reason? I wish you could! For it has altogether escaped me. Although you seem to have been willing to give it when asked, you add these words: because Adam was the first man, the origin and stock, or root, of all men. I acknowledge this; from it I understand that he could, together with human nature, transmit his vice to his posterity. But I deny that on that account his actual sin was ours, or ought to have been imputed to us; I deny that that consideration and judgment, which you attribute to God, can be inferred from this. I do not see how that actual sin of Adam, a single action, is more our action than his person was our person. If you see it, please show and explain it to me; I shall be greatly obliged to you.

units.la: GAR. Huic argutandi rationi ego libenter similem hanc reposuerim. Si actio illa prima inobedientia, non quidem præcise sumpta, sed vna cum corruptione quam effecit in Adamo nobis imputatur, sicut supra vir doctus agnoscebat, erit sanè etiam per eam imputationem nostra. Quidni ergo & Adami persona nobis imputetur, & dicatur etiam fuisse persona nostra? Aut hoc vir doctus concedat, aut suam argumentandi rationem condemnet & eliminet : & fateatur quod res est, nunquam auditum alienas personas imputari, sed actionum imputationem rem esse omnium ore atque sermone tritam, &c.
units.tr: GAR. To this subtle reasoning I would gladly reply with this one. If that first act of disobedience, not taken precisely by itself but together with the corruption which it produced in Adam, is imputed to us, as the learned man above acknowledged, it will certainly be ours through that imputation too. Why then should not Adam's person also be imputed to us, and be said to have been our person too? Let the learned man either concede this, or condemn and discard his own mode of arguing, and admit what is the case: that the imputation of alien persons has never been heard of, but that the imputation of actions is a matter worn threadbare on everyone's lips and in their talk, etc.

units.la: PLAC. Quo sensu dixerim, & quàm is minimè causæ quam ago obsit, actionem illam primam inobedientiæ cum corruptione quam peperit nobis imputari, supra expositum est pag. 162. 163. Quod inde colligit, illam actionem etiam per eam imputationem nostram esse ; non agnosco. Nam corruptio nostra est, quia in nos propagata est. Actio autem illa nostra fit non imputatione, sed, vt dicebat Lauaterus, vitio originis: quia nempe vitium originis seu corruptio est inobedientiæ illius communicatio, & habitualis in eam consensio. Itaque non est nostra, quia nobis imputatur; sed contrà nobis imputatur, quia nostra est. Iustitia enim non modò non exigit, sed ne patitur quidem, vt iudiciaria imputatione peccatum fiat eius peccatum, cuius alioqui peccatum non fuisset. Faceret enim peccatorem iudex, alioqui non peccatorem. id quod cum iudicis officio pugnat, vt quod maximè. Itaque frustra obseruat vir doctus alienas personas non imputari, sed actiones. Non enim sic argumentabar; si actio Adami nobis imputatur, etiam nobis imputatur eius persona: Sed contendebam nullam reddi posse causam idoneam, cur illa actio nobis imputetur immediatè; ac inter cæteras hanc excludebam, nostram esse actionem illam Adami: ac proinde nobis iure imputari. Intelligebatur igitur esse nostra, non per imputationem immediatam, sed ante illam. quo modo dici non potest, cur magis nostra sit, quàm ipsa persona Adami. Non igitur id quod dixi vir doctus oppugnat, sed aliud quid. Certè Chamierus negauit actionem illam Adami esse nostra actionem, lib.1. de hom. corrupt. c.8. §. 9. Dico, inquit, nullum peccatum vnum numero posse esse commune omnibus hominibus. Nam peccatum, vel qualitas est, vel actio. Qualitas, vt peccatum originale. Actio, vt peccatum quodlibet actuale. At nulla qualitas, vna eademque numero potest pluribus subiectis communicari: vt candor qui est in niue, idem numero non potest esse in Cygno, aut lana. Actiones autem sunt suppositorum. Quare idem homicidium à Caino patratum non potest esse à Lamecho. Itaque nego peccatum illud Adami esse peccatum Originale. Non enim potest omnibus esse commune, siue numero, quia est actio: siue specie, quia est indiuiduus actus. Et rursus eodem capite §.xi. Omne peccatum vel qualitas est, vel actio, vt diximus, eius cuius dicitur peccatum. At hic actus Adami, neque qualitas est nostra: nam ne est quidem: ac proinde non potest esse qualitas: tum actio, qualitasque longè differunt: neque est etiam actus noster: quia idem numero actus non est variorum suppositorum. Ergo is actus Adami non est nostrum peccatum: nedum sit nostrum originale. Hæc eius ratio eadem est cum hac mea, si actio Adami est nostra, eius suppositum est nostrum; Sunt enim actiones suppositorum.
units.tr: PLAC. In what sense I could say, and how little this is against the cause I am pursuing, that the first act of disobedience, together with the corruption which it brought forth, is imputed to us, has been explained above, on pages 162 and 163. That he infers from this that the act is ours also through that imputation, I do not acknowledge. For our corruption is ours because it has been propagated into us. That act, however, becomes ours not by imputation, but, as Lavaterus said, by the vice of origin: namely because the vice of origin, or corruption, is the communication of that disobedience and a habitual consent to it. Therefore it is not ours because it is imputed to us; rather it is imputed to us because it is ours. For justice not only does not require, but does not even permit, that by judicial imputation the sin of one person should become the sin of another, of whom it otherwise would not have been a sin. For the judge would make a sinner of one who otherwise would not be a sinner; which is utterly at odds with the office of a judge. So the learned man is wrong to observe that it is not alien persons that are imputed but actions. For I did not argue thus: if Adam's action is imputed to us, then his person is imputed to us too. Rather I contended that no adequate cause can be given why that action is imputed to us immediately; and among the other causes I excluded this one, that the action of Adam is ours, and therefore rightly imputed to us. It was understood, then, that it is ours not through immediate imputation but before it; and in what way it cannot be said why it is more ours than the very person of Adam. So the learned man is not attacking what I said, but something else. Certainly Chamier denied that the action of Adam is our action, in book 1 on the corruption of man, chapter 8, section 9: I say, he writes, that no single sin numerically one can be common to all men. For sin is either a quality or an action. A quality, like original sin; an action, like any actual sin. But no quality, one and the same in number, can be communicated to several subjects: as the whiteness which is in snow cannot be numerically the same in a swan or in wool. Actions, however, belong to persons. Hence the same homicide committed by Cain cannot be committed by Lamech. Therefore I deny that the sin of Adam is original sin. It cannot be common to all, either numerically, since it is an action, or in kind, since it is an individual act. And again in the same chapter, section 11: Every sin is either a quality or an action, as we have said, of the one to whom the sin is attributed. But this act of Adam is neither our quality, for it is not even a quality, and so cannot be a quality; and action and quality differ greatly; nor is it our act, since one and the same act in number does not belong to several persons. Therefore that act of Adam is not our sin, much less our original sin. This his argument is the same as mine here: if Adam's action is ours, then its person is ours; for actions belong to persons.

units.la: Interim quæro dum alia peccata committeret (com-
units.tr: Meanwhile I ask: while he was committing other sins (

units.la: milisse enim haud dubie non negabis) an non fuerit etiam tum primus homo, origo, stirps, seu radix omnium hominum? fuisse proculdubio concedes: fueruntne igitur ea quoque eodem modo considerata, & iusto Dei iudicio omnibus hominibus imputata? Si negas, fatearis oportet huius considerationis iudicij & imputationis primi peccati, quæ protulifti in medium, rationem hanc non esse, quia Adam primus homo fuit, & origo, & stirps omnium hominum. Si affirmas, Reuincet te Apostolus Rom.v. tam peccati quàm hominis vnitatem inculcans. Quærerem etiam libenter de Setho, de Noacho, aliisque eiusmodi stirpibus totius, quod extat, generis humani, num eorum quoque peccata eodem modo fuerint & considerata, & imputata posteris? Si fuerunt, multos homines dicere debuit Apostolus Rom.v. non vnum, &, nos antequam nascamur miserrimi, qui tot peccata commisimus. Si non fuerunt, discriminis peto rationem: sed vereor ne sim longior hoc loco quàm necesse est.
units.tr: For you will not deny, I think, that he undoubtedly sinned at that time. Was the first man not then also the origin, stock, or root of all men? You will concede that he certainly existed: but were those things likewise considered in the same way, and imputed to all men by the just judgment of God? If you deny it, you must admit that the reason for this consideration, judgment and imputation of the first sin, which you have brought forward, is not this: that Adam was the first man and the origin and stock of all men. If you affirm it, the Apostle will refute you in Rom. 5, insisting on the unity of sin as well as of man. I would also gladly ask about Seth, Noah, and other such stocks of the whole human race that exists: were their sins likewise considered and imputed to their posterity in the same way? If they were, the Apostle ought to have said "many men" in Rom. 5, not "one," and we, most wretched before we are born, who have committed so many sins. If they were not, I ask for the reason of the difference; but I fear I am being longer on this point than is necessary.

units.la: G A R. Quod vero decent Theologi Adamum peccasse vt ca-put hominum, & iure posteris imputari primam illam eius inobe-dientiam, variis quastionum & erotematum machinis quatit, quibus & alij nonnulla etiam addunt, qua omnia hic in vnum fasci-culum compingemus.
units.tr: G A R. As for the fact that the theologians contend that Adam sinned as the head of mankind, and that his first disobedience is rightly imputed to posterity, they shake it with various machines of questions and erotemata, to which others also add some points of their own, all of which we shall here gather into one bundle.

units.la: P L A C. Nec Adamo elogium capitis hominum detraho, nec iure posteris imputari primam illam eius inobedientiam nego, si imputari intelligatur mediante corruptione ex ipsa in nos propagata. Tantùm nego ita Adamum vt caput hominum peccasse, vt nobis possit, aut debeat prima eius inobedientia imputari immediatè. Sunt autem hæ quæstiones partim e Thesibus meis, partim ex hoc posteriore Manuscripto omnes, præter vnam, excerptæ. Itaque non omnes sunt huius loci; non erit tamen inutile eas hoc loco à refponsionibus viri doƈti cutas præstare: quoniam in illis de causa agitur, ob quam peccatum illud immediatè dicitur imputari; cui inuestigandæ hoc caput destinatum est.
units.tr: PLAC. I do not detract from Adam the title of head of men, nor do I deny that his first disobedience is rightly imputed to posterity, provided it is understood to be imputed through the corruption propagated from it into us. I only deny that Adam sinned as the head of men in such a way that his first disobedience can be, or ought to be, imputed to us immediately. All these questions, except one, are excerpted partly from my Theses and partly from this later manuscript. So not all of them belong to this place; yet it will not be useless to answer them here, using the learned man's replies, since those replies debate the cause on account of which that sin is said to be imputed immediately, and this chapter is devoted to investigating that cause.

units.la: GAR. 1. Si peccauit vt caput generis humani, cur non etiam puniri debuit eo nomine? 2. Cur potius Adami peccatum posteris, quàm posterorum Adæ imputatur? 3. Cùm Adamus post illud peccatum, confessim non desierit esse caput, cur non sequentia Adami peccata æque posteris imputantur atque primum? 4. Cur potius actuale peccatum, quæ est actio transiens, imputari dicitur, quàm habituale, quod fuit vitium permanens? 5. Si primus actus peccandi fuit actus naturæ, cur non etiam primus actus generandi? Nemo tamen dixerit nos in Adamo Caïnum aut Sethum genuisse? 6. Si vt Christi iustitia nobis imputatur, ita & peccatum Adæ nostrum est imputatione, cur non, vt Christus dicitur, iustitia nostra, dicitur etiam Adamus peccatum nostrum? 7. Cùm dicimur peccasse in Adamo, estne propria, an impropria locutio? Propria dici non potest, nisi dicamus, aliquid simul esse & non esse: proprie enim loquendo, tum cùm Adamus peccauit, fuissemus, & non fuissemus. Si propria non est, renocanda est ad propriam. Quid autem significat proprie nos fuisse in Adamo, nisi nos ducere ab Adamo originem, vel esse Adami esse causam nostri esse? Est autem causa non essentialis & proxima, sed accidentalis & remota, & quæ ad nos gignendos non magis per se contulit, quàm ad multos gignendos, qui gigni quidem potuerunt, sed tamen defectu causæ proximæ geniti non sunt: quibus libenter quæsierim, an non etiam imputari debeat peccatum Adamí? Potuit enim Adamus eos mediatè & remotè, vt nos, gignere: & vix potest intelligi, quomodo, vt quis ante quinque annorum millia fuerit, vel non fuerit, pendere possit ab hodierna, vel crastina actione.
units.tr: GAR. 1. If he sinned as the head of the human race, why was he not also punished on that account? 2. Why is Adam's sin imputed to posterity, rather than the posterity's sins to Adam? 3. Since Adam did not cease at once to be head after that sin, why are his subsequent sins not imputed to posterity just as much as the first? 4. Why is the actual sin, which is a transient act, said to be imputed, rather than the habitual sin, which was a permanent vice? 5. If the first act of sinning was an act of nature, why was the first act of begetting not also one? Yet no one would say that we begot Cain or Seth in Adam. 6. If, as Christ's righteousness is imputed to us, so also Adam's sin is ours by imputation, why, as Christ is called our righteousness, is Adam not also called our sin? 7. When we are said to have sinned in Adam, is this a proper or an improper expression? It cannot be proper, unless we say that something is at once both existing and not existing; for properly speaking, when Adam sinned, we both were and were not. If it is not proper, it must be referred back to the proper sense. But what does it mean properly to have been in Adam, except to derive our origin from Adam, or for Adam's being to be the cause of our being? The cause is not essential and proximate, but accidental and remote, and it contributed no more per se to our begetting than to the begetting of many who could indeed have been begotten but, for lack of a proximate cause, were not. To them I would gladly put the question whether Adam's sin ought not also to be imputed to them? For Adam could have begotten them mediately and remotely, as he did us; and it can hardly be understood how someone's being or not being five thousand years ago could depend on today's or tomorrow's action.

units.la: VII. Nos vero respondemus. 1. Generaliter. Si eiusmodi interrogationum punctulis locus esse debeat, non minus speciosè sollicitari posse doctrinam de corruptione Originali à Pelagij aut Socini sectatoribus, quàm hac de imputatione doctrina hic vexatur. Quaretur enim 1. Cur Adami corruptio moralis posteros potius infecit, quàm corruptio posterorum inquinauit Adamum? 2. Cur Adami peccatum in posteros necessario descendit, cæterorum patrum non ita descendit? 3. Cur Adami peccatum Caino nocuit, Caini peccatum Adamo minime nocuit ? 4. Cur primum peccatum nos potius corrupit, quam sequentia Adami peccata ? 5. Cur Adamus ab illa corruptione liberatus est, quam sua actione sibi comparauit; infantes omnes, qui nihil mali egerunt, non liberantur ? 6. Cur Christus justitia & sanctificatio nostra dicitur, Adamus non dicitur peccatum & corruptio nostra ? Hæc & alia aduersus doctrinam de corruptione ingenita quæri possunt, quasi non obstant quominus Viri docti corruptionem illam agnoscere debeant; neque debent quastiuncula illa impedimento nobis esse, quominus in antiqua & Catholica imputationis fide perseueremus.
units.tr: VII. We respond. 1. In general: if room must be given to such little points of questioning, the doctrine of original corruption can be attacked no less plausibly by the followers of Pelagius or Socinus than this doctrine of imputation is harassed here. For it will be asked: 1. Why did Adam's moral corruption infect posterity rather than the corruption of posterity defile Adam? 2. Why did Adam's sin descend necessarily to posterity, while the sins of the other fathers did not descend so? 3. Why did Adam's sin harm Cain, while Cain's sin did not harm Adam at all? 4. Why did the first sin corrupt us rather than Adam's subsequent sins? 5. Why was Adam freed from that corruption, which he procured for himself by his own action, while all infants, who have done no evil, are not freed? 6. Why is Christ called our righteousness and sanctification, while Adam is not called our sin and corruption? These and other things can be asked against the doctrine of innate corruption, as if they stood in the way of learned men acknowledging that corruption; nor ought these little questions to hinder us from persevering in the ancient and catholic faith of imputation.

units.la: PLAC. Itáne antiqua & catholica est imputationis immediatæ fides? Id neque probatum est haftenus, neque probari potest. Frustra autem istas de corruptione originali quæstiones nostris opponit: non enim sunt pares, nec illam prorsus probandi vim habent. Respondeo ad primam, Cur Adami corruptio moralis posteros potius infecit, quam corruptio posterorum inquinauit Adamum ? quia corruptio moralis non aliter quàm per generationem carnalem propagatur: sunt autem posteri Adami ab eo geniti, non autem Adamus ab illis. Ad 2. Cur Adami peccatum in posteros necessario descendit, caeterorum patrum non ita descendit ? quia peccatum Adami fuit mutatio finis vltimi, atque adeo vniuersalem in Adami naturam corruptionem induxit: immundus autem non potuit non immundum, caro non carnem gignere. Peccata vero aliorum patrum, hujusmodi corruptionis causæ esse non potuerunt, cùm jam effet in eis producta, sed effecta quibus ipsa sese exeruit, & confeeruauit. Itaque quamuis à proximis parentibus eam proximè traxerimus, tamen Adamo, vt illius primo autori & scaturigini ascribi debet. Ad 3. Cur Adami peccatum Caino nocuit, Caini peccatum Adamo minime nocuit ? quia Adamus genuit Cainum, non Cainus Adamum. Ad 4. Cur primum peccatum nos potius corrupit, quam sequentia Adami peccata ? quia illud naturam Adami corrupit, ita corruptionem iam factam confequuta sunt vt causam effecta. Ad 5. Cur Adamus ab illa corruptione liberatus est, quam sua actione sibi comparauit; infantes omnes, qui nihil mali egerunt, non liberantur ? Liberatus est ab illius corruptionis i entu gratia iustificationis, & ab inhærentia paulat m graria it gt nei ationis, quia credidit & refi puit; credidit autem, quia fuit electus. Idem evenit aliis omnibus electis. Cur autem, hic potius quàm ille fuerit electus, alij causæ quàm liberrimæ Dei voluntati, de suo quod vult facientis, tibui nequit. Genu:t autem non secundum gratiam, sed secundum naturam, corruptus corruptos, sicut arte circuncisus gigre'at in circunfos. Ad 6. Cur Christus justitia & sanctificatio nostra dicitur, Adamus non dicitur peccatum & corruptio nostra? ua nulla alia justi ca justificamur, nulla alia virtute sanctificamur, quàm Christi. Itaque in eo omnis nostra justitia & sanctificatio quærenda. Non possumus similiter dicere, nullo nos peccato damnari, quàm Adami. Nam & multorum aliorum iumus rei, & ad vniuersalem corruptionem, quam ab Adamo traximus, multo habitus, seu particulares ad certa objecta determinationes nimis sæpe adjungimus, & illud ipsum Adami peccatum non est nostrum donatione, aut imputatione vt Christi justitia, sed ratione propagati ex eo vitij nobis inhærentis, quod vim habet nos condemnandi, non quia est Adami, aut profectum ab Adamo, sed quia natura sua vitium est legi Dei repugnans. Ejus pro Pelagio & Socino quæstiunculis respondi: nunc videamus quomodo respondeat nostris.
units.tr: PLAC. So is the faith in immediate imputation ancient and catholic? That has neither been proved so far nor can it be proved. He vainly opposes to ours these questions about original corruption, for they are not equal, and they have no force to prove that doctrine. I answer the first: why did Adam's moral corruption infect posterity rather than the corruption of posterity defile Adam? Because moral corruption is propagated only through carnal generation; Adam's posterity were begotten by him, but Adam was not begotten by them. To the second: why did Adam's sin descend necessarily to posterity, while the sins of the other fathers did not? Because Adam's sin was a change of his ultimate end, and so it introduced a universal corruption into Adam's nature; an unclean thing could not but beget unclean, flesh could not but beget flesh. The sins of the other fathers, however, could not be causes of such corruption, since it had already been produced in them; they were effects by which it put itself forth and was preserved. Thus, although we have derived it immediately from our nearest parents, it must still be ascribed to Adam as its first author and fountainhead. To the third: why did Adam's sin harm Cain, while Cain's sin did not harm Adam at all? Because Adam begot Cain, not Cain Adam. To the fourth: why did the first sin corrupt us rather than Adam's subsequent sins? Because the first sin corrupted Adam's nature; the later sins followed upon the corruption already made, as effects follow a cause. To the fifth: why was Adam freed from that corruption, which he procured for himself by his own action, while all infants, who have done no evil, are not freed? He was freed from the guilt of that corruption by the grace of justification, and gradually from its inherence by the grace of regeneration, because he believed and repented; and he believed because he was elect. The same happens to all the other elect. Why this one rather than that one was chosen cannot be assigned to any cause other than God's most free will, which does what it wills on its own authority. Adam begot, however, not according to grace but according to nature, corrupt beings who were corrupt, just as a circumcised man begets the circumcised. To the sixth: why is Christ called our righteousness and sanctification, while Adam is not called our sin and corruption? Because we are justified by no other righteousness and sanctified by no other virtue than Christ's; therefore all our righteousness and sanctification is to be sought in him. We cannot similarly say that we are condemned by no sin other than Adam's. For we are also guilty of many other sins, and to the universal corruption which we drew from Adam we very often add particular habits, or determinations to certain objects. That very sin of Adam is not ours by gift or imputation as Christ's righteousness is, but by reason of the propagation of that vice which inheres in us, and which has the power to condemn us, not because it is Adam's or came from Adam, but because by its nature it is a vice repugnant to God's law. I have answered the little questions of Pelagius and Socinus; now let us see how he answers ours.

units.la: GAR. Nobis certa responsio suppetit, imputationem primi peccati esse actionem Dei liberam & voluntariam, ex certo Dei consilio judicioque, non ex solius naturæ ordine dependentem. Neminem autem fuisse Dei consiliarium, qui ea nosse, & de iis respondere teneatur, qua Deus in verbo suo reuelare noluit. Sufficere nobis ipsius rei notitiam, omnes scilicet in Adamo peccasse, & ipsius reatum super omnes venire in condemnationem, atque ita primum illud peccatum in omnes imputatione descendere. Rationes illius iudicij penes Deum esse cujus viæ sunt impetrestigabiles, & eius iudicia abyssus multa. Rom. xi. 33. Psalm. xxxvi. 7. &c.
units.tr: GAR. We have a ready answer: the imputation of the first sin is a free and voluntary act of God, proceeding from God's certain counsel and judgment, and not depending solely on the order of nature. No one, however, was God's counsellor, bound to know and answer for those things which God has chosen not to reveal in his Word. It is enough for us to know the fact itself: that all sinned in Adam, that his guilt comes upon all to condemnation, and that the first sin thus descends by imputation to all. The reasons for that judgment rest with God, whose ways are unsearchable and whose judgments are a great deep. Rom. xi. 33. Psalm. xxxvi. 7. &c.

units.la: P L A C. Si immediata imputatio primi peccati est actio Dei libera & voluntaria, ea nisi in Scriptura reuelata fuerit, sciri non potest. Atqui non est in Scriptura reuelata, neque ad eam probandam vllam vim habent loca à viro docto hic repecita, vt partim iam patuit, partim ex dicendis manifestum fiet. Deinde si est actio Dei libera, quomodo est actio Dei iudiciaria? liberam enim, opinor, intelligit, quae potest absque vlla iustitiae aut legis violatione omitti. Quomodo ergo iudiciaria dicitur, si eam a Iudice neque lex, neque iustitia exigit? Si nemo tenetur ea nosse, quae Deus in verbo suo reuelare noluit, certe nemo tenetur illam imputationem nosse, siquidem, vt contendo, Deus eam non reuelauit in verbo suo. Caeterum quaestionibus illis oppugno potissimum rationes, quae reddi solent, cur vnum illud peccatum primum nobis omnibus immediate imputetur. Iis igitur renunciandum est, ac ad solam Dei voluntatem confugiendum, cui placuit illud vnum, non alia, imputare, aut nostris istis interrogatis respondendum. Denique cum Deus nihil faciat nisi sapientissime, & iustissime, & optime, si eiusmodi imputatio aut iustitiae, aut sapientiae, aut bonitati repugnare videatur, quominus tribuatur Deo pia refugit conscientia, nec potest id a se impetrare, nisi, vel tollatur illa repugnantia, vel disertis Scripturae testimoniis, quae profecto nulla sunt, ad eam credendam aliquo modo cogatur. Quaecunque enim docentur in sacris literis, ea mihi egregie concordare cum recta ratione videntur, vbique diuinae virtutes conspicuae sunt. Quis ergo credat in actione diuina tanti momenti, vnde omnium hominum pendet condemnatio, & mortis Christi necessitas, nullam bonitatis, nullam iustitiae, nullam sapientiae. vel minimam scintillam posse animaduerti, sed repugnantiam tantum rationi, quantum capere possumus, rectae?
units.tr: PLAC. If the immediate imputation of the first sin is a free and voluntary act of God, it cannot be known unless it has been revealed in Scripture. But it is not revealed in Scripture, and the passages here gathered by the learned man have no force to prove it, as has partly already become clear and will partly become clear from what follows. Next, if it is a free act of God, how is it a judicial act of God? For by "free" he means, I suppose, what can be omitted without any violation of justice or law. How then is it called judicial, if neither law nor justice requires it of the Judge? If no one is bound to know what God has chosen not to reveal in his Word, then surely no one is bound to know that imputation, since, as I maintain, God has not revealed it in his Word. Moreover, in these questions I chiefly attack the reasons usually given for why that one first sin is imputed to us all immediately. These, therefore, must be renounced, and we must take refuge in the sole will of God, who was pleased to impute that one sin and not another; or else our questions must be answered. Finally, since God does nothing except most wisely, most justly and most well, if such an imputation seems to conflict with justice, or wisdom, or goodness, a pious conscience shrinks from ascribing it to God, and cannot bring itself to do so unless that conflict is removed or it is compelled to believe it by clear testimonies of Scripture, of which there are assuredly none. For whatever is taught in the sacred letters seems to me to agree admirably with sound reason; everywhere the divine virtues are conspicuous. Who, then, would believe that in a divine act of such great importance, on which the condemnation of all men depends and the necessity of Christ's death, no trace of goodness, no trace of justice, no trace of wisdom can be perceived, but only a contradiction to reason, so far as we are able to grasp what is right?

units.la: GAR. Neque tamen quaestionum nodi putandi sunt infolubiles. Itaque nunc secundo loco Erotemata singula considereмus. Quaeritur primo. Si Adam peccauit, vt caput generis, cur non puram debeat vt caput? Resp. Adamo cum tribuitur capitis nomen, rationem haberi non tantum originis carnalis, sed etiam foederis vniuersalis illius, quod in Adamo Deus cum humano genere iniuit. Cum ergo peccasse dicitur vt caput, non tantum denotatur, eum fuisse principium radicale totius generis, verum etiam ea conditione constitutum fuisse generis caput & principium, vt quamprimum ab obedientia praescripta defleeteret, non ipse tantum peccati fui reatu obstringeretur, sed & posteros omnes reos efficeret, ac proinde poena dignos. Hoc est ergo peccasse vt caput, & se & posteros ob peccatum illud reatu innoluisse.
units.tr: GAR. Yet the knots of these questions are not to be thought insoluble. Therefore, now in the second place, let us consider the individual questions. The first question is: If Adam sinned as the head of the race, why was his sin not imputed to him as head? Answer: when the name of head is given to Adam, account is taken not only of carnal origin but also of that universal covenant which God made with the human race in Adam. Therefore, when he is said to have sinned as head, it is meant not only that he was the radical source of the whole race, but also that under that condition he was constituted head and principle of the race, so that as soon as he turned aside from the prescribed obedience, he would not only himself be bound by the guilt of his sin, but would also make all his posterity guilty, and so worthy of punishment. This, then, is to have sinned as head: to have involved himself and his posterity in the guilt of that sin.

units.la: PLAC. Ita nodus non soluitur, sed augetur alio nodo. Nam praeter liberam & voluntariam illam actionem, quae Deo sine Scriptura tribuebatur, ecce aliam, nempe foederis cujusdam vniuersalis pactionem, de qua ne χῦ quidem in Scriptura; & quod deterius est, conditio fingitur Deo haud satis digna. Si quod enim foedus cum homine contrahit, id facit hominis causa, & quia bonum est homini. Hoc vero foedus, cuius ea esset, quam Vir Doctus declarat, conditio, non poterat non esse Adami posteris damnosum. Multo plus enim ex eo erat metuendum mali, quam sperandum boni: nam vt inde ad nos aliqua vtilitas rediret, opus erat vt Adamus toto vitae curriculo perseueraret in obedientia & fide erga Deum: nec tamen propterea, si Viro Docto fides habetur, nobis eius imputata fuisset obedientia, tantum qualis fuisset, tales nos genuisset: at, si vel semel ab obedientia declinaret, prima eius inobedientia nobis omnibus imputanda erat ad mortis aeternae reatum, nec id tantum, sed vt ob imputatum illud peccatum puniremur infligenda nobis erat corruptio illa hereditaria quae vere peccatum est, & fons peccatorum. Qui factum est, vt Deus, qui ipsa bonitas est, & genus humanum amabat, aequiorem ei non tulerit conditionem, & qui Adamus non rogauit Deum, quandoquidem contrahebat cum Deo vt totius generis humani procurator, vt ab eo conditionem impetraret tolerabiliorem? Nam certe talis conditio ab odio potius quam ab amore profecta videri possit; nec quid ad Dei gloriam, vt omnia quae facit Deus, per se conferre possit vllo modo intelligitur. Adde quod ea ratione aliter ad Adamum pertinuisset mandatum, aliter comminatio: illud vt ad caput generis humani, haec vt ad priuatam personam: & vice versa ad nos pertinuisset comminatio, non item mandatum. Denique cur non ea conditione contractum est istud foedus, vt quemadmodum peccaret, sic etiam puniretur vt caput generis humani? Si recurras ad voluntatem Dei, quid opus erat ad has quaestiones alia responsione, quam generali ista, quia Deus ita voluit? Sed vide ne ei voluntatem attribuas pro tuo ingenio eius virtutibus minime conuenienter, ac praeter Scripturam.
units.tr: PLAC. So the knot is not untied but tied tighter with another knot. For besides that free and voluntary act, which was attributed to God without Scripture, behold another: the making of a certain universal covenant, of which there is not even a trace [χῦ] in Scripture. And what is worse, a condition is invented that is scarcely worthy of God. For if anyone contracts a covenant with a man, he does so for the man's sake, and because it is good for him. But this covenant, whose condition was such as the learned man describes, could not fail to be harmful to Adam's posterity. For far more evil was to be feared from it than good hoped for. For some benefit to come back to us from it, Adam had to persevere through the whole course of his life in obedience and faith towards God; yet even so, if the learned man is to be believed, his obedience would not have been imputed to us, but he would only have begotten us such as he himself was. But if he had turned aside from obedience even once, his first disobedience was to be imputed to all of us for the guilt of eternal death; and not only that, but in order that we be punished for that imputed sin, that hereditary corruption, which truly is sin and the fountain of sins, was to be inflicted upon us. How has it come about that God, who is goodness itself and loved the human race, did not grant a fairer condition? And why did Adam not ask God, since he was contracting with God as procurator of the whole human race, to obtain from him a more tolerable condition? For surely such a condition could seem to proceed from hatred rather than from love; nor is it understood in any way how it could contribute to God's glory, as all that God does ought to. Add that on this reasoning the commandment would pertain to Adam in one way and the threat in another: the former to him as head of the human race, the latter to him as a private person; and conversely the threat would pertain to us, but not the commandment. Finally, why was this covenant not contracted on the condition that, just as he sinned, so he should also be punished as head of the human race? If you have recourse to the will of God, what need was there for any other answer to these questions than that general one, that God so willed? But take care that you do not attribute to him a will that, according to your own wit, is very unbefitting his virtues, and beyond Scripture.

units.la: GAR. Quaritur secundo, Cur potius Adami peccatum posteris, quàm posterorum Adamo imputatur? R sp. 1. Hoc inde esse, quod posteri omnes in Adamo radicaliter & seminaliter fuerunt. Adamus in posteris hoc modo non fuit. 2. Quod peccatum imputari, est poenam propter peccatum irrogari. Atqui poena peccatum ordine naturae semper insequitur, nunquam antecedit. Non potuit igitur Adamus poenas dare peccatorum, quae nondum erant, praesertim cum non ipse, sed Christus peccata hominum portare debuerit, & portando expiare.
units.tr: GAR. The second question: Why is Adam's sin imputed to his posterity, rather than the posterity's sin to Adam? Answer 1: This is because all his posterity were radically and seminally in Adam; Adam was not in his posterity in this way. 2. To impute a sin is to inflict punishment on account of sin. But in the order of nature punishment always follows sin and never precedes it. Adam therefore could not pay the penalties of sins which did not yet exist, especially since it was not he but Christ who ought to bear the sins of men and expiate them by bearing them.

units.la: PLAC. Hac interrogatione non oppugnaui immediate imputationem immediatam primi peccati, sed rationem qua firmabatur, ideo scilicet primum illud Adami peccatum omnibus eius posteris imputari, quoniam Adamus componebat cum suis posteris vnum corpus, cuius ipse caput erat, nos omnes eius posteri membra, quod autem facit caput toti corpori imputatur: objiciebam, si valet haec ratio, causam non esse, cur non itidem quae faciunt membra capiti, aut etiam toti corpori imputentur, quia reciproca est capitis & membrorum relatio. Itaque non attendens ad mentem meam, & loci, vnde hanc interrogationem deprompsit, circunstantiam, Vir Doctus non ad rem respondet. Nam ad primam eius responsionem quod spectat, primo non est de ratione capitis vt sint in eo membra radicaliter & seminaliter. Deinde si de propagationeageretur naturali, optima quidem esset ratio, cur propagatum fuerit peccatum ab Adamo in posteros, potius quàm a posteris in Adamum, quia nempe posteri sunt ab Adamo, non Adamus a posteris: sed cùm agatur de imputatione immediata, quae sit libera Dei actio, si spectauit posteros Adami tanquam eius membra vnum cum eo corpus componentes, cur non potuit Deus aeque posterorum Adamo, atque Adami posteris peccatum imputare, praesertim cùm posteri nullo modo causa fuerint peccati Adami, Adamus vero causa fuerit peccati posterorum? Ad alteram autem eius responsionem quod attinet, primùm viuente Adamo eius filij & nepotes peccauerunt. Deinde vltimi diei judicium quae sequetur poena posterios erit peccatis posterorum Adami, & quidem omnium. Tertiò cum imputatio fit actio Dei, & Deus tum habuerit praesentes omnes Adami posteros, habuit etiam praesentia eorum peccata, cur ergo ea imputare non potuit? Denique, si poena peccatum ordine naturae semper insequitur, nunquam antecedit, certè etiam peccatum ordine naturae semper insequitur existentiam eius cui imputatur, nunquam antecedit.
units.tr: PLAC. By this question I did not attack directly the immediate imputation of the first sin, but the reason by which it was supported: namely, that this first sin of Adam is imputed to all his posterity because Adam made one body with his posterity, of which he was the head, and we all his posterity the members; and what the head does is imputed to the whole body. I objected: if this reasoning holds, there is no reason why what the members do should not likewise be imputed to the head, or even to the whole body, since the relation of head and members is reciprocal. Therefore, not attending to my meaning, and to the circumstance of the passage from which he took this question, the learned man does not answer to the point. As far as his first answer is concerned: first, it is not of the nature of a head that members should be in it radically and seminally. Next, if we were dealing with natural propagation, there would indeed be an excellent reason why sin was propagated from Adam to his posterity rather than from posterity to Adam, namely that the posterity are from Adam, not Adam from the posterity. But since we are dealing with immediate imputation, which is a free act of God, if he regarded Adam's posterity as his members making up one body with him, why could God not impute the posterity's sin to Adam just as well as Adam's sin to the posterity? This is especially so since the posterity were in no way the cause of Adam's sin, whereas Adam was the cause of the posterity's sin. As for his second answer: first, while Adam was still alive his sons and grandsons sinned. Next, the judgment of the last day, which will follow, will be the punishment of Adam's posterity for the sins of his posterity, and indeed of all of them. Thirdly, since imputation is an act of God, and God then had all Adam's posterity present, he also had their sins present; why then could he not impute them? Finally, if punishment always follows sin in the order of nature and never precedes it, then surely sin also always follows in the order of nature the existence of the one to whom it is imputed, and never precedes it.

units.la: G A R. Quaeritur tertio. Cum Adamus post peccatum illud primum confestim non desierit esse caput generis humani, cur non sequentia eius peccata aeque imputantur ac primum? Resp. 1. Quia vnam vnius offensam & inobedientiam, non plures memorat Apostolus, ob quam homines peccatores constituti fuerint. 2. Quia Adamus per primum illud peccatum suum, excusstus est beneficio foederis illius, quod Deus cum toto genere in Adami persona pactus fuerat. Itaque etiamsi non desierit esse caput relatione originis, desijt tamen esse relatione foederis. Ad imputationem autem de qua loquimur, utrumque necessarium fuit, ut scilicet Adamus, & radix esset, unde genus humanum oriretur, & foederis depositarius, quod sibi & suis, aut conseruaret, aut amitteret. Cum ergo posterior haec relatio capitis cessauerit per primum illud inobedientiae peccatum, nihil mirum si peccata Adami sequentia non imputentur, cum in eorum patratione priorem illam personam non amplius sustineret, neque caput esset eo modo, quo Deus ipsum initio constituerat.
units.tr: GAR. The third question is: since Adam did not at once cease to be the head of the human race after that first sin, why are his later sins not imputed just as the first was? Answer 1: Because the Apostle mentions one offence and one disobedience of one man, not several, on account of which men were constituted sinners. 2. Because by that first sin Adam was stripped of the benefit of the covenant which God had made with the whole race in Adam's person. So although he did not cease to be head by relation of origin, he did cease to be head by relation of covenant. Both were necessary for the imputation we are discussing: Adam had to be both the root from which the human race springs and the depositary of the covenant, which he would either keep or lose for himself and his own. Since this latter relation of headship ceased through that first sin of disobedience, it is no wonder that his later sins are not imputed, for in committing them he no longer sustained that former person, nor was he head in the way God had originally appointed.

units.la: P L A C. Apostolus vnam vnius offensam & inobedientiam memorat, quia vna illa offensa corrupit naturam vnius, qualem autem iste vnus habuit naturam, talem in suos posteros propagauit. Sed quid hoc ad imputationem antecedentem, quam Apostolus non docuit, & quae omnem propagationem naturalem antecedere putatur, & a Dei duntaxat voluntate pendere? Manet ratio, si ideo imputatur prima illa inobedientia, quia Adamus cum eam committeret nostrum erat caput, quando cum alias committebat nostrum etiam erat caput, debuerunt etiam aliae eius inobedientiae nobis imputari: eadem enim utrobique ratio est. Ad alteram responsionem, quam rursus a nescio quo foedere, cuius iam aliquoties memnerat, arcessit, dico illud foedus nec in sacris literis doceri, nec Deum decere, nec eius vllum fuisse beneficium, contra nos, non pro nobis constituti: & quamuis eius beneficio, fi quod erat, excussus fuiflet Adamus, tamen remansisset vis obligandi ad obedientiam, & fi minus ea præstaretur, ad augendam pœnam. Alioqui quod fuit illud fœdus? idem cum fœdere quod vocant natura, an ab eo diuersum? Si idem, mansit obligatus Adamus ad obsequendum legi fœderis naturæ, eiusque omnia peccata fœderis illius violationes fuerunt: cur ergo etiam illius fœderis relatione caput generis non permansit? Si diuersum, duo igitur cum Adamo, atque genere humano contracta sunt fœdera, vnum naturæ, alterum quomodo appellabitur, (gratiæ enim certe quidem non fuit) & cur huius violatio potius imputetur toti generi humano, quam illius, quod cùm fit naturæ, ad naturam hominum totam pertinet? Adde quod non intelligo, quare id fœdus hominum caput conftituerit Adamum, quod diu esse desiit, antequam Adamus quenquam gigneret? Nec quomodo Adamus dicatur caput generis humani relatione ad id fœdus, sub quo eius posteri nunquam fuerunt? Certè caput non fuit posterorum, fi antequam vlli fuerint eius posteri, definit esse eorum caput: nec opinor, dicitur caput relatione fœderis, sed potius relatione ad posteros fundata in generatione. Ita non fuiflet caput, nisi quo momento peccauit, hoc est, non fuiflet caput nisi quando ij nondum fuerunt quorum diceretur caput, quando fuerunt non fuiflet amplius eorum caput, quod concoquat quipotest, ego certè concoquere non possum.
units.tr: PLAC. The Apostle mentions one offence and one disobedience of one man because that one offence corrupted the nature of that one man, and whatever nature he had, he propagated the same into his posterity. But what has this to do with the antecedent imputation, which the Apostle did not teach, and which is thought to precede all natural propagation and to depend on God's will alone? The reasoning stands: if that first disobedience is imputed because Adam was our head when he committed it, then, since he was also our head when he committed other sins, those other disobediences should be imputed to us too, for the reason is the same in both cases. As to the second answer, which he again derives from I know not what covenant, mentioned several times already, I say that this covenant is taught neither in Holy Scripture nor in keeping with God's character, and it was no benefit of his, since it was established against us, not for us. Even if Adam had been stripped of its benefit, whatever it was, the force of obliging him to obedience would have remained, and if that obedience were not rendered, it would serve to increase the punishment. Otherwise, what was that covenant? Is it the same as the covenant they call nature, or different from it? If the same, Adam remained bound to obey the law of the covenant of nature, and all his sins were violations of that covenant; why then did he not remain head of the race by relation to that covenant too? If different, then two covenants were made with Adam and the human race, one of nature and the other, which we may call what? (It was certainly not a covenant of grace.) And why is the violation of the latter imputed to the whole human race rather than the former, which, being of nature, pertains to the whole nature of men? Add that I do not understand why that covenant should have made Adam head of mankind, when it ceased to exist long before Adam begat anyone. Nor how Adam can be called head of the human race by relation to a covenant under which his posterity never existed. Surely he was not head of posterity if he ceased to be their head before any of them existed. I do not think he is called head by relation to a covenant, but rather by relation to posterity founded in generation. Thus he would not have been head except at the moment he sinned; that is, he would have been head only while those of whom he is called head did not yet exist, and once they existed he would no longer have been their head. Whoever can digest that can digest more than I can.

units.la: GAR. Quæritur quarto. Cur actuale peccatum Adami tanquam capitis imputetur, quæ tamen fuit actio transiens; & non imputetur habituale, fiue corruptio Adæ, quæ fuit vitium permanens? Refp. 1. Hoc ab Apostolo petendum, qui in hoc negotio lapsum & inobedientiam actualem proponit, non autem proponit habitum corruptionis ex illa inobedientia confequentem.
units.tr: GAR. The fourth question is: why is Adam's actual sin imputed as head, since it was a transient act, while his habitual sin, that is, the corruption of Adam, which was a lasting vice, is not imputed? Answer 1: This must be asked of the Apostle, who in this matter sets forth the fall and the actual disobedience, but does not set forth the habit of corruption that follows from that disobedience.

units.la: PLAC. Cur ab Apostolo id peterem, qui illam imputationem quam impugno non docuit? Deinde fi nullum Apostolus proponit habitum corruptionis ex illa inobedientia consequentem, non potest ex Apostolo Pighius refelli, nec probari habitualis
units.tr: PLAC. Why should I ask this of the Apostle, who did not teach the imputation I am opposing? Further, if the Apostle sets forth no habit of corruption following from that disobedience, then Pighius cannot be refuted from the Apostle, nor can habitual corruption be proved from him.

units.la: J habitualis corruptio. quod quàm sit alienum à doctrina eorum, quorum opera Deus visus est ad reformandam Ecclesiam, nemo in eorum libris non plane hospes non facile perspicit.
units.tr: Habitual corruption. How far this is alien to the teaching of those through whose work God was pleased to reform the Church, no one who is at all a stranger to their books fails to see readily.

units.la: GAR. 2. Cum in alieni peccati imputatione, non habitus, sed actiones imputentur, sicut patere potest omnia illa exempla percurrenti, quæ supra magno numero producta sunt, quid mirum, si et am in ista causa non habitus, sed actio tantum Adami memoratur?
units.tr: GAR. 2. Since in the imputation of another's sin it is not habits but actions that are imputed, as can be seen by running through all those examples brought forward in great number above, what wonder if in this case too only Adam's action is mentioned and not his habit?

units.la: PLAC. Si habitus sunt peccata, si reos faciunt eos in quibus iunt, quid est cur non possint imputari? Certè, non minus quàm actualia nostra, imputata sunt vadi nostro, ut pro eorum reatu satisfacerer. Alienorum autem peccatorum si qua facta est imputatio, unde habes separata ab habitualibus imputata fuisse peccata actualia? Et ut id probari posset, tamen peculiaris est ratio habitus corruptionis Adami, qui fuit peccatum naturæ, cum eius causa inobedientia actualis fuerit potius peccatum personæ; Ille propagatur cum natura, hæc non item.
units.tr: PLAC. If habits are sins, if they make guilty those in whom they dwell, why can they not be imputed? Certainly they were imputed to our surety no less than our actual sins, so that he might make satisfaction for their guilt. But if any imputation of others' sins has been made, how do you know that actual sins were imputed separately from habitual ones? And even if that could be proved, there is a peculiar reason for Adam's habit of corruption, which was a sin of nature, whereas his actual disobedience was rather a sin of the person. The former is propagated along with nature; the latter is not.

units.la: GAR. 3. Imputare alicui peccatum alienum, est ipsum eodem loco habere, ac si in propria persona ipsemet peccatum patrafset, aut commisisset. Atqui habitus non patrantur, neque committuntur. Itaque nec imputantur.
units.tr: GAR. 3. To impute another's sin to someone is to hold it in the same position as if he himself had perpetrated or committed the sin in his own person. But habits are not perpetrated or committed. Therefore they are not imputed either.

units.la: PLAC. Quid igitur fiet de peccato omissionis? neque enim proprie patratur aut committitur: immo omissio commissioni opponitur. Vides etiam lector hinc sequi peccatum originis habituale seu corruptionem non esse verè peccatum: omne enim verè peccatum imputatur, nisi condonetur: condonare enim est non imputare peccatum.
units.tr: PLAC. What then will become of the sin of omission? For it is not properly perpetrated or committed; indeed omission is opposed to commission. The reader also sees from this that habitual sin of origin, or corruption, is not truly sin: for every true sin is imputed unless it is pardoned, and to pardon is not to impute sin.

units.la: GAR. 4. Ea ratione fœdus à Deo cum Adamo conceptum est, ut quamprimum illud violaret, se & suos illo reatu obstringeret. Violavit autem prius quam habitum corruptionis induisset: & fuit illud actuale peccatum natura prius illo habitu. Ideo actio imputata, non imputatus habitus.
units.tr: GAR. 4. On this principle God made the covenant with Adam, that as soon as he violated it, he would bind himself and his own to that guilt. But he violated it before he had put on the habit of corruption, and that actual sin was prior in nature to that habit. Therefore the act was imputed, not the habit.

units.la: PLAC. Vtinam vir doctus verba retulisset quibus illud fœdus fuit conceptum! Nam si ea nescius, qui scire potuit illud ea ratione fuisse conceptum? Quid est facilius quam sic rationes fingere: Quod si vox quam primum abfuit ab illis verbis quibus conceptum fuit, cur eam vir doctus de suo inseruit & addidit? Si in concipiendo illo foedere Deus illa voce vsus est, vnde habet vir doctus eam significatione tam praecisa esse accipiendam, vt excludat habitum ideo, quia fi non temporis forte aliquo naturae momento fequutus est actuale peccatum?
units.tr: PLAC. Would that the learned man had reported the words in which that covenant was framed! For if he does not know them, how can he know that it was framed on this principle? What is easier than to invent reasons in this way? If the phrase "as soon as" was absent from the words in which the covenant was conceived, why did the learned man insert and add it on his own? If God used that phrase in framing the covenant, whence does the learned man have it that it must be taken in so precise a sense as to exclude the habit, on the ground that the habit followed the actual sin by no moment of natural time?

units.la: GAR. Si comparatio instituatur actualis inobedientia Adami, & consecuta corruptionis habitualis, videbimus hanc corruptionem fuisse effectum illius inobedientia, atque adeo poenam iusto Dei iudicio illius peccati actualis. Poena vero non imputatur, sed peccatum potius quod est illius poena causa meritoria. Quid ergo mirum, fi illa inobedientia potius imputata est, quam ipsa corruptio?
units.tr: GAR. If we compare Adam's actual disobedience with the habitual corruption that followed, we shall see that this corruption was an effect of that disobedience, and so a punishment of that actual sin by God's just judgment. But punishment is not imputed; rather the sin, which is the meritorious cause of the punishment, is. What wonder, then, if that disobedience was imputed rather than the corruption itself?

units.la: PLAC. Hic rursus negatur corruptio imputari, esse peccatum, & doctrina tam opposita confessionibus fidei Protestantium inculcatur. Quod autem ait corruptione n esse illius inobedientiae actualis effectum, fi effectum accipit significatione paulo laxiore admitti potest? Se habet enim ad illam inobedientiam vt calor ad calefactionem per quam producitur. Quod vero inde deducit, eam esse poenam illius inobedientiae, non consequitur necessario: non enim omne peccati effectum illius poena est. Certe habitus neque bonarum actionum praemia, neque malarum poenae esse proprie solent. Quomodo autem corruptio poena fit, & iusto Dei iudicio tribui possit, & supra explicatum est, & infra etiam explicabitur. Caeterum quocunquefenfu poena dicatur, id non impedit, quin fit peccatum dignum alia poena, ac proinde imputabile.
units.tr: PLAC. Here again it is denied that corruption is imputed or is sin, and a doctrine so opposed to the confessions of the Protestant faith is pressed upon us. As to his saying that corruption is an effect of that actual disobedience, if "effect" is taken in a somewhat looser sense, it can be admitted: for it stands to that disobedience as heat stands to the heating by which it is produced. But what he deduces from this, that corruption is the punishment of that disobedience, does not follow necessarily, for not every effect of sin is its punishment. Certainly habits are not properly the rewards of good actions or the punishments of evil ones. How corruption becomes a punishment, and can be assigned to God's just judgment, has been explained above and will be explained below. However, in whatever sense it is called a punishment, this does not prevent it from being a sin worthy of another punishment, and therefore imputable.

units.la: GAR. Quinto quaeritur. Si primus actus peccandi fuit actus naturae, cur non & primus actus generandi, vt in Adamo dicamur Cainum, aut Sethum generaffe? Refp. Mitto viri doctii Sethi genituram primo actui, quo Adamus generauit, attribuenti, qui tamen nonnisi tertius esse potuit, Gen. iv.
units.tr: GAR. Fifthly, it is asked: if the first act of sinning was an act of nature, why is the first act of begetting not also imputed, so that we are said to have begotten Cain or Seth in Adam? Answer: I pass over the learned man's attribution of Seth's begetting to the first act by which Adam begat, which could only have been the third, Gen. iv.

units.la: PLAC. Quale quaeso, est hoc? Vereor ne id potius Viro docto tribui debeat, qui animaduertisse non videtur vtin disjunctiuae aut qua vsus fueram; nempe duplex fuit actus generandi Adami, vnus absolute primus, alter primus in genere eorum vnde orti sumus. Ille fuit actus quo Cainum genuit, hic quo Sethum: Ex Setho enim, minime vero ex Caino, nos omnes originem ducimus: vtrumque, ne quod pateret effagium, complexus sum.
units.tr: PLAC. What, I ask, is this? I fear it should rather be attributed to the learned man, who does not seem to have noticed which disjunctive "or" I had used. Adam's act of begetting was twofold: one was absolutely first, the other first in the kind of those from whom we have sprung. The former was the act by which he begat Cain, the latter the act by which he begat Seth, for we all trace our origin from Seth, by no means from Cain. I included both, lest any escape be left open.

units.la: GAR. Ad rem ipsam dico, non quemlibet primum actum natura fuisse posteris imputandum (hoc enim Scriptura neque aperte testatur, neque vel leuissime insinuat) sed primum tantum actum naturae deficientis ab ea perfectione, quam ipsi Deus creatione indiderat, idque iuxta comminationem, quo die primum de fructu vetito comederis, moriendo morieris. Cum igitur primus actus generandi, nullus fuerit per se actus natura rebellantis ac deficientis a creatore, magis quam primus actus respirandi, concoquendi, ambulandi, &c. Sed prima illa inobedientia fuerit primus deficientis naturae actus, quo scilicet Adamus a primo anno: foedere desciuit turpissime, nemo mirari debet, si & primus peccandi actus posteris imputetur, & primus generandi actus non imputetur.
units.tr: GAR. As to the matter itself, I say that not every first act of nature is to be imputed to posterity (for Scripture neither clearly testifies to this nor even faintly hints at it), but only the first act of nature falling away from that perfection which God had bestowed on it at creation, and this according to the threat, "on the day you eat of the forbidden fruit, dying you shall die." Since the first act of begetting was therefore in itself no act of nature rebelling and falling away from its Creator, any more than the first act of breathing, digesting, walking, and so on, but that first disobedience was the first act of a failing nature, by which Adam from his first year most basely deserted the covenant, no one ought to wonder if the first sinful act is imputed to posterity and the first act of begetting is not imputed.

units.la: PLAC. Non igitur imputatur nobis inobedientia illa Adami, qua est actus Adami: alij enim multi eius actus non imputantur: nec qua est primus eius actus, non enim absolute primus fuit, sed tantum in suo genere, nec qua est in suo genere primus actus naturae; hoc enim aliis quoque actibus conuenit, sed qua est actus naturae deficientis. Iam hoc quaeritur, quare actus naturae deficientis nobis potius imputari debeat, quam actus naturae non deficientis? id enim, vt video, a defectione est naturae, non ab ipsa natura. Quid est enim cur, cum caetera sunt paria, malum potius nobis imputetur, quam bonum? Nam si peccare sequitur esse, vt certe debet (non entis enim non sunt accidentia) actus generandi is est cuius vi primum fumus, hunc sequi debere videtur, & in eo fundari is actus cuius vi primum peccatores sumus; saltem hic nos non facit peccatores, nisi illo mediante: itaque illum praesupponit: peccare enim praesupponit esse, & prius est naturae ordine nos fieri, quam fieri peccatores. Si ergo fuimus peccatores imputatione alieni peccati qua fit nostrum, ea imputatio sequi debet aliquid quo fuimus homines, siquidem ordine naturae prius sumus homines quam peccatores, prius est subjestum quàm eius accidens. Is autem actus, quo primo facti fumus homines, est actus ille generandi, quo Adamus Sethum genuit: quare imputatio peccati primi antecedens seu immediata supponit illum actum. Prius igitur fuit nos haberi pro genitis ab Adamo, quàm pro peccatoribus, & primus ille actus quo geniti sumus prius ad nos pertinuit, quàm ille quo facti sumus peccatores. Imputatur enim nobis peccatum Adæ, quia sumus eius posteri: sumus autem eius posteri, quia nos genuit: nos autem genuit, quatenus genuit Sethum. Actus ergo quo genuit Sethum ordine naturæ antecedit imputationem peccati. Sed tamen, si viro docto fides habetur, imputatum est nobis peccatum Adami diu antequam Sethum genuisset, illo ipso tempore quo commissum est: aut igitur antecedit etiam generationis imputatio, aut ostendendum est quomodo potuerimus priùs considerari vt peccatores quàm vt homines, & posteri Adami.
units.tr: PLAC. Therefore that disobedience of Adam is not imputed to us insofar as it is an act of Adam, for many of his other acts are not imputed; nor insofar as it is his first act, for it was not absolutely first but only first in its kind; nor insofar as it is the first act of nature in its kind, for this belongs to other acts as well; but insofar as it is the act of a failing nature. Now the question is why the act of a failing nature should rather be imputed to us than the act of a non-failing nature.
