For that, as I see it, comes from the defection of nature, not from nature itself. Why, when other things are equal, should evil rather be imputed to us than good? For if to sin follows to be, as it certainly must (since accidents do not belong to non-beings), then the act of begetting, by whose power we first exist, ought to come first, and the act by whose power we first become sinners ought to be founded on it. At least this act does not make us sinners except through it, so it presupposes it, for to sin presupposes to be, and in the order of nature we become men before we become sinners. If therefore we were made sinners by the imputation of another's sin, which becomes ours, this imputation must follow something by which we were men, since in the order of nature we are men before we are sinners, and the subject is prior to its accident. But the act by which we were first made men is that act of begetting by which Adam begat Seth; wherefore the imputation of the first sin, whether antecedent or immediate, presupposes that act. Therefore it was prior that we were regarded as begotten by Adam than that we were regarded as sinners, and that first act by which we were begotten pertained to us earlier than that by which we became sinners. For Adam's sin is imputed to us because we are his posterity; we are his posterity because he begat us; and he begat us insofar as he begat Seth. The act by which he begat Seth therefore precedes, in the order of nature, the imputation of sin. Nevertheless, if credence is given to the learned man, Adam's sin was imputed to us long before he begat Seth, at the very time it was committed. Either, therefore, the imputation of generation precedes as well, or it must be shown how we could be regarded as sinners before we were regarded as men and as Adam's posterity.

units.la: G A R. Quæritur sexto. Si vt Christi iustitia nobis imputatur, ita & peccatum Adæ nostrum fit imputatione, cur non, vt Christus dicitur iustitia nostra, ita & Adamus dicitur peccatum nostrum? Resp.1. Deum loqui vt vult; nostrum esse iis phrasibus esse contentos, quæ in Scripturis occurrunt, quæque Dei mentem, quantum salutis nostræ interest, fatis euidenter exponunt. Quanquam ergo non dicit Scriptura Adamum esse peccatum nostrum; eas tamen locutiones adhibet, quæ imputationem manifeste designant, de quo fuse dictum est antea.
units.tr: GAR. Sixthly, it is asked: if, as Christ's righteousness is imputed to us, so also Adam's sin becomes ours by imputation, why, as Christ is said to be our righteousness, is Adam not said to be our sin? Answer 1: God speaks as he wills. It is for us to be content with those phrases which occur in the Scriptures, and which set forth God's mind, so far as it concerns our salvation, quite clearly enough. Although, therefore, Scripture does not say that Adam is our sin, it nonetheless uses those expressions which plainly designate imputation, as has been explained at length above.

units.la: P L A C. Hac ratione seu interrogatione vsum esse me non memini, nec cuius sit nouï: siue tamen mea, aut alterius sit, accommodata fuisse videtur ad refellendam maiorem argumenti, quo solet imputatio immediata maximè niti, Quemadmodum constituimur iusti per Christum, eodem modo constituti sumus peccatores per Adamum: ostendit enim inter Christum & Adamum memorabile discrimen: Non est autem verbum dicitur in hac interrogatione accipiendum relatè ad solam Scripturam, vt facit vir doctus, sed relatè ad Scripturam & omnes Theologos, qui nunquam dixerunt Adamum esse peccatum nostrum, aut innustitiam nostram, aut nos esse iniustitiam in Adamo. Diuersitas enim phrasium cum de Christo & Adamo agitur in negotio iustificationis & condemnationis arguit inter utrumque diuersitatem atque disparitatem. Itaque nos quidem decet iis phrasibus esse contentos, quae in Scriptura occurrunt, & vero nos iis admodum contenti sumus, sed decet nos tamen eas phrases attente considerare, & rationes expendere, quare sic vel sic Deus mentem suam expresserit, vel non expresserit; in quo nobis suo exemplo praeiuerunt Apostoli, ipsum etiam Scripturae silentium interdum vrgentes. Nullae autem sunt apud Apostolum locutiones quae imputationem immediatam manifeste designent, immo ne obscure quidem quae designent, vllae sunt.
units.tr: PLAC. I do not recall having used this argument or question, nor whose it is new. Whether it is mine or another's, it seems to have been framed to refute the major premise on which immediate imputation chiefly rests: "As we are constituted righteous through Christ, so in the same way we are constituted sinners through Adam." For it shows a memorable difference between Christ and Adam. But the word "is said" in this question is not to be taken relatively to Scripture alone, as the learned man does, but relatively to Scripture and all theologians, who never said that Adam is our sin, or our unrighteousness, or that we are unrighteousness in Adam. For the diversity of phrases, when Christ and Adam are treated in the matter of justification and condemnation, shows a diversity and disparity between the two. Thus indeed it becomes us to be content with the phrases which occur in Scripture, and truly we are quite content with them; but it becomes us also to consider those phrases attentively and to weigh the reasons why God has or has not expressed his mind thus or so. In this the Apostles have gone before us by their example, sometimes even urging the very silence of Scripture. But there are no expressions in the Apostle that clearly designate immediate imputation, indeed none that designate it even obscurely.

units.la: GAR. 2. Locis illis, vbi dicitur Christus iustitia nostra, nulla inter Adamum & Christum instituitur comparatio: quae si instituta fuisset, vt factum est Roman. 5. quis nouit annon ea phrasi vsurus fuerit Paulus, quae doceret Adamum esse peccatum nostrum, sicut Christus est iustitia nostra, etsi non eadem omnino ratione.
units.tr: GAR. 2. In those passages where Christ is called our righteousness, no comparison is drawn between Adam and Christ. If one had been drawn, as is done in Romans 5, who knows whether Paul would not have used that phrase which would teach that Adam is our sin, as Christ is our righteousness, although not altogether in the same way?

units.la: PLAC. Ego vero inde argumentor, quod vbi nullam instituit Apostolus comparationem Christi inter & Adamum vsurpat illam de Christo locutionem, vbi autem aliquam inter vtrumque instituit comparationem ab ea abstinet. Quanquam, vt dixi, non ad solam Scripturam, sed etiam ad Theologos omnes habetur respectus, qui locutionem illam nunquam vsurpant de Adamo.
units.tr: PLAC. I for my part argue from this that where the Apostle draws no comparison between Christ and Adam, he uses that expression about Christ, but where he draws some comparison between the two, he abstains from it. Although, as I said, regard is had not only to Scripture alone but also to all theologians, who never use that expression of Adam.

units.la: GAR. 3. Probabilis tamen ratio reddi poterit, quare Adam non dicatur peccatum nostrum, sicut Christus iustitia nostra nominatur. Ita nempe vocatur Christus, vt significetur, nihil esse internum & inhaerens in nobis, cuius vi & virtute coram Dei tribunali consistere, aut absolutionem & remissionem peccatorum impetrare valeamus: itaque extra nos esse totum illud, quod est nostrae iustificationis meritorium, iustitia nimirum quae Christi est propria, nostra non est nisi imputatione. Atqui tale aliquid de Adamo dici non poterit. Nam praterquam quod Adami peccatum actuale meritorium est poenarum, quae nobis incumbunt; est etiam internum aliquid & in nobis inhaerens, cuius merito etiam condemnationi subiacemus, nimirum natiua nostra corruptio, quae vna cum imputato Adae peccato facit vnum veluti corpus reatus, quo Deus iudicio sito nos tenet obnoxios. Ea igitur causa esse poterit, quare non dixerit Scriptura Adamum esse peccatum nostrum, sicut dixit Chriftum esse iuffitiam nostram.
units.tr: GAR. 3. Yet a probable reason can be given why Adam is not called our sin, as Christ is named our righteousness. Christ is so called to signify that there is nothing internal and inhering in us by whose power and virtue we can stand before God's tribunal or obtain absolution and remission of sins. Thus all that is meritorious of our justification lies outside us, namely the righteousness which is proper to Christ, and it is ours only by imputation. But something of this kind cannot be said of Adam. For besides the fact that Adam's actual sin is meritorious of the punishments which lie upon us, there is also something internal and inhering in us, by whose merit we too are subject to condemnation: namely our native corruption, which together with the imputed sin of Adam makes, as it were, one body of guilt, by which God, by a just judgment, holds us liable. That may therefore be the reason why Scripture has not said that Adam is our sin, as it has said that Christ is our righteousness.

units.la: PLAC. Agnoscit ergo vir doctus non eodem prorsus modo per Adami inobedientiam nos coram tribunali Dei conftitui peccatores, quo per Christi obedientiam constituimur iusti: taque non esse vrgendam illam similitudinem, quasi nullum effet in modo discrimen: hoc vero est totum, quod hac interrogatione, siquidem ea fumus vsi, probare instituimus. Quare pro nobis, non contra nos haec eius militat responsio. Videntur tamen in ea quaedam digna reprehensione. Illud in primis, quod ait, iustitiam Christi nostram non esse nisi imputatione: nam si similiter, vt passim contendit, peccatum Adami nostrum non est nisi imputatione, eodem modo ambo nostra sunt, nec ea in re vllum est discrimen. id quod pugnat cum Apostolo, maximum in modo, quo nostrae sunt, iustitia Christi & iniustitia Adami, discrimen innuente, cum illam appellat donum, & gratiam, & donationem quae est ex gratia: sic enim modum significat quo fit nostra: quo modo nostrum nec factum est, ne fieri potuit Adami peccatum. Deinde quorsum obseruat hoc loco, iustitiam Christi propriam, non esse nostram nisi imputatione, si idem censet de peccato quod Adami est proprium, id similiter non esse nostrum nisi imputatione? Quid enim hoc facit ad discrimen inter Christum & Adamum explicandum? Quod si id non censet, sibi ipse contradicit, quippe qui id aliquoties inculcauit. Praeterea, si est aliquid in nobis internum & inhaerens cuius merito condemnationi subiacemus, cur eo merito eaque condemnatione non contenti, volumus aliud peccatum extra nos positum immediate imputari? Nempe, inquies, vt fit huius interni causa, quo alioqui careremus. Deleatur igitur Deus hoc interno peccato, quippe qui sine vlla necessitate libere nobis illud extra nos positum peccatum imputat, vt vi illius imputationis producatur internum illud in nobis peccatum, quod alioqui non posset produci. Hoccine est glorificare Deum, & non potius cum facere, (quod sine horrore conscientiae pronunciare non possum,) autorem peccati nostri? Denique, quomodo imputatum illud peccatum & corruptio natiua faciunt vnum veluti corpus reatus, si hæc illius est pœna proprie dicta? Antecedit enim reatus pœnam; & qui adeo reos facit imputatum peccatum, vt simus illa corruptione & morte æterna dignii eius reatus non dimidiatus videtur reatus, sed perfectus & integer. Quod si vnum componunt corpus reatus, vel eum reatum integrum intellexit Apostolus Rom.v. atque ita alio modo condemnamur per Adamum, quàm iustificamur per Christum, quod passim negat vir doctus, vel intellexit dimidiam tantùm illius reatus partem, id quod, opinor, nemo dixerit. Vlitimam quæstionem visum est differre in suum, qui mox occurret, proprium locum.
units.tr: PLAC. So the learned man admits that we are constituted sinners before the tribunal of God not in exactly the same way as we are constituted righteous through the obedience of Christ. Therefore that comparison should not be pressed, as though there were no difference in the manner. But this is the whole point we set out to prove by this question, if we have used it correctly. So his answer supports us and does not work against us. Yet some things in it deserve blame. First, he says that the righteousness of Christ becomes ours only by imputation. If, as he argues everywhere, the sin of Adam becomes ours only by imputation, then both are ours in the same way, and there is no difference between them in this respect. This contradicts the Apostle, who points to the greatest difference in the manner in which the righteousness of Christ and the unrighteousness of Adam become ours, when he calls the one a gift, a grace, and a donation that comes by grace. That word signifies the manner in which it becomes ours. In that manner Adam's sin neither was nor could be ours. Next, why does he observe here that the righteousness of Christ, which is proper to Christ, is ours only by imputation, if he holds that the sin which is proper to Adam likewise is ours only by imputation? For what does this contribute to explaining the difference between Christ and Adam? If he does not hold this, he contradicts himself, since he has pressed it many times. Moreover, if there is something internal and inherent in us, on account of which we are liable to condemnation, why, not content with that merit and that condemnation, do we want another sin, placed outside us, to be imputed to us immediately? You will say, of course, that this is so that the internal sin may have a cause, which otherwise we would lack. Then let God be relieved of this internal sin, since he imputes to us, without any necessity and freely, a sin placed outside us, so that by the force of that imputation the internal sin may be produced in us, which otherwise could not be produced. Is this to glorify God, or rather to make him (which I cannot say without horror of conscience) the author of our sin? Finally, how do the imputed sin and innate corruption make up one body of guilt, if the latter is properly speaking the punishment of the former? For guilt precedes punishment. And if the imputed sin makes us so guilty that we deserve that corruption and eternal death, then this guilt is not half, but complete and whole. But if they make up one body of guilt, then either the Apostle in Rom. 5 understood that whole guilt, and so we are condemned through Adam in a different way from how we are justified through Christ, which the learned man everywhere denies; or else he understood only a half part of that guilt, which, I suppose, no one would say. I have thought it best to defer the last question to its own proper place, which will come up shortly.

units.la: Pergis quærendo; Quæ enim, inquis, ratio assignari potest, cur paruuli, qui nondum peccarunt actualiter, moriantur, vel in vtero matrum, vel nascendo, vel statim post natiuitatem, nisi hoc, quod peccatum Adami, per quod mors peruasit in omnes homines, illis imputetur? Ego contrà quæro, quæ ratio assignari possit, cur paruulis peccatum actuale Adami, tantò antequam esse inciperent admissum, nondum vsum rationis assequutis imputetur ad mortem? Interim tuæ quæstioni satisfacio: assigno rationem, vitium illis inhærens à conceptione. testem laudo Confessionem Fidei Art. XI. Credimus hoc vitium esse vere peccatum, quod omnes & singulos homines, ne paruulis quidem exceptis, adhuc in vtero matrum delitescentibus æternæ mortis reos coram Deo peragat.
units.tr: You go on asking: For what reason, you say, can be given why little children, who have not yet actually sinned, die, either in their mothers' wombs, or at birth, or immediately after birth, unless it be that the sin of Adam, through which death came upon all men, is imputed to them? I, on the contrary, ask what reason can be given why the actual sin of Adam, committed long before they began to exist, is imputed to little children, who have not yet attained the use of reason, for death? Meanwhile I satisfy your question: I assign the reason, namely the vice inhering in them from conception. I cite the witness of the Confession of Faith, Art. XI: We believe that this vice is truly sin, which renders all and each of mankind, not even little children excepted, while still lurking in their mothers' wombs, guilty of eternal death before God.

units.la: Videras hanc rationem, cur ei non acquieuisti? Non satisfit, inquis, si quis dicat esse peccatores, & quia peccato inquinatos, esse mortales. Id quidem verum est, sed necessariò admittendum est, eos nullum habere peccatum, nisi illud originale, quod non est peccatum ipsorum, nisi quatenus sunt filij Adami; & quat: ab ipso orti & procreati, in ipso peccauerunt, & inobedientia & culpa illius ipsis imputatur.
units.tr: You have seen this reason; why did you not accept it? It is not enough, you say, if someone says that they are sinners, and because they are polluted by sin, that they are mortal. That is indeed true, but it must be granted of necessity that they have no sin except original sin, which is not their own sin, except insofar as they are sons of Adam; and insofar as they were born and begotten of him, they sinned in him, and his disobedience and guilt are imputed to them.

units.la: Aut te non intelligo, aut hic incipis quod sentis apesire, nullum esse peccatum originale praeter illud actuale Adami nobis imputatum: Quae Pighij & Catharini, & Salmeronis fuit sententia ab Ecclesijs nostris iure damnata: nam si credis in infantibus vitium esse originale inhærens, quod vere peccatum sit, quod generi humano damnando sufficiat, quod infantes in utero materno delitescentes æternæ mortis reos coram Deo peragat, cur tibi quærenti, cur infantes moriantur, non satisfacit qui respondet, in illis causam esse mortis vitium seu peccatum hæreditario inhærens? Hoc enim est mortis infantium proximam causam afferre, cujus remota est lapsus Adami. Si rursus quæras, cur hoc vitium puerulis infit, Respondebo cum Iobo, ex immundo fieri mundum non posse, Et cum ipso Christo, quod ex carne natum est, carnem esse, Quàm homo hominem, tam immundus immundum, corruptus corruptum genuit. secundum leges naturæ. Quid est quamobrem hæc responsio tibi non satisfacit? an quia non capis quomodo vitium propagari possit & à parente in prolis animam transfundi? atqui nihil in ea re est difficultatis, præter eam quæ oritur ex creatione animæ rationalis: quam difficultatem tribus meis tollere conatus sum ea ratione, quam tu, quia non intellexisti, carpis quidem in extremo tui tractatus Capite, sed nullo modo refutas. Frustra enim laboratur in refutando id, quod non intelligitur. Ad eum locum cum peruenero, Deo bene iuuante, meipsum explicabo. An quia non capis, quomodo vnum actuale peccatum inuehere potuerit in Adamum corruptionem moralem vna cum natura propagandam? Atqui hujus rei rationem in thesibus reddideram, quam à te reiectam aut reprehensam in toto
units.tr: Either I do not understand you, or here you begin to reveal what you think: that there is no original sin besides the actual sin of Adam imputed to us. This was the opinion of Pighius, Catharinus and Salmeron, which our churches have rightly condemned. For if you believe that in infants there is an inherent vice, which is truly sin, sufficient to condemn the human race, which renders infants, while still lurking in their mothers' wombs, guilty of eternal death before God, then why, when you ask why infants die, is the answer not satisfying to you, which says that the cause of their death is the vice or sin inherent by inheritance? For this is to give the proximate cause of infants' death, whose remote cause is the fall of Adam. If again you ask why this vice comes to be in little children, I will answer with Job, that what is unclean cannot become clean, and with Christ himself, that what is born of the flesh is flesh. As man begets man, so the unclean begets the unclean, the corrupt the corrupt, according to the laws of nature. Why is this answer not satisfying to you? Is it because you do not grasp how a vice can be propagated and its soul transmitted from parent to offspring? Yet in this matter there is no difficulty except that which arises from the creation of the rational soul. I have tried to remove this difficulty in my three [theses] by the method which you, because you did not understand it, criticise at the end of your treatise, but in no way refute. For it is vain to labour in refuting what is not understood. When I come to that place, with God's good help, I will explain myself. Or is it because you do not grasp how one actual sin could bring into Adam a moral corruption to be propagated along with nature? Yet I had given the reason for this in my theses, which in your whole treatise I have not found rejected or criticised.

units.la: Quae Pighij toto isto tuo tractatu non legi.
units.tr: Which opinion of Pighius I have not read in all that treatise of yours.

units.la: Vis dicam ingenuè quid interfit inter tuam sententiam & meam? Ego eò tendo, vt omnium malorum generis humani fons & causa in ipsum genus humanum, non autem in Deum referatur. Tua verò sententia eò spectat, vt ipsi Deo attribuatur. quod ego, qua erga Creatorem & Redemptorem meum ducor reuerentia, pati non possum. Vitium inhærens fons est omnium peccatorum actualium. Constat inter nos id ducere originem à primo peccato actuali Adami. Sed quæritur primò, quæ sit ratio, cur primum peccatum actuale Adamum corruperit? Ego id ascribo ipsi illius primi peccati naturæ, quod fuit mutatio summi boni, seu finis vltimi, hoc est, apostasia à Deo, tanquam inuido & maleuolo, & conuersio ad creaturas tanquam ad summum bonum, seu finem vltimum, contra Dei verbum. Quoniam autem quicquid appetimus est, aut finis, aut medium ad finem, & media omnia, omnesque fines subordinatos finis vltimus continet sibi colligatos, eo mutato sequuta est vniuersalis mutatio eorum omnium, quæ in Adamo moralia fuerunt, quam mutationem subsecuta mala conscientia Deum refugiens & horrens, vt offensum, vt iratum, vt iudicem, vt hostem, auxit & confirmauit. Tu verò non dubitas id, quicquid est, ipsi Deo adscribere, qui iustitiam substraxerit Adamo, eumque priuauerit rectitudine & sanctitate, vt sic puniret peccatum actuale, & iustitiæ suæ satisfaceret.
units.tr: Shall I tell you frankly what the difference is between your view and mine? I aim to refer every source and cause of the evils of the human race to the human race itself, and not to God. Your view, on the other hand, tends to attribute these to God himself. This I cannot bear, out of the reverence I owe to my Creator and Redeemer. The inherent vice is the source of all actual sins. We agree that this derives its origin from the first actual sin of Adam. But first the question arises: what was the reason why the first actual sin corrupted Adam? I ascribe this to the very nature of that first sin, which was a change of the highest good, or of the ultimate end, that is, apostasy from God, as though he were envious and malevolent, and a turning to creatures as to the highest good or ultimate end, contrary to the Word of God. Now whatever we desire is either an end or a means to an end, and the ultimate end contains within itself all means and all subordinate ends bound together. When this was changed, there followed a universal change of all those things which were moral in Adam. After this change, an evil conscience, fleeing from God and shuddering at him as offended, angry, a judge, and an enemy, increased and confirmed that change. But you do not hesitate to ascribe to God himself whatever exists, as one who withdrew righteousness from Adam and deprived him of uprightness and holiness, so that he might punish the actual sin and satisfy his own justice.

units.la: Quæritur secundò, cur peccato corruptus ac vitiatus Adamus filios genuerit similiter corruptos? Ego corruptionis illius naturæ id tribuo, quæ vniuersalis cum effet, ipsam vim generatricem, quatenus moralis quaedam facultas est, corrupit, & infecit, & convertit ad generationem, non vt ad medium, sed vt ad finem vltimum. Porrò finis vltimus, cum ab alio non definiatur, aut pendeat, sed ab eo omnia, natura sua infinitus est. Itaque in eum feruntur facultates sine limitatione, aut modo, quodammodò infinitè. Postquam igitur in locum veri finis vltimi, hoc est, Dei succeßit falsò apparens, fallax nempe fœlicitatis species reperiendæ in creaturis, immoderatè, absque fræno, absque limitatione, corruptè, deprauatéque circa generationem versata est, tanquam circa finem vltimum facultas generandi, parte animæ superiore, eódem conuersa vnà cum appetitu sensitiuo, non cohibente, sed impellente. A facultate sic corrupta ac deprauatè agente elaboratum est semen corruptum, hoc est, consentaneum ac congruens cum depravatæ facultati generatrici, tum etiam aliis facultatibus quas generatrix femine adumbrare & exprimere quàm accuratissimè conatur. Quomodo autem hæc vitiositas à femine ad animam rationalem transfeat, suo loco, hoc est, ad Cap. vltimum tractatus tui Deo dante exponam.
units.tr: Second, why did Adam, corrupted and vitiated by sin, beget sons who were similarly corrupt? I attribute this to that corruption of nature which, being universal, corrupted and infected the generative power itself, insofar as it is a certain moral faculty, and turned it to generation, not as a means but as its ultimate end. The ultimate end, since it is not defined or dependent on anything else but everything depends on it, is by its nature infinite. Faculties are therefore carried toward it without limit or measure, in a way infinitely. Since the false appearance of happiness to be found in creatures took the place of the true ultimate end, that is God, the generative faculty, together with the sensitive appetite, which does not restrain but drives it, has been directed immoderately, without bridle or limit, corruptly and perversely toward generation, as if toward its ultimate end, and the higher part of the soul has turned with it. The seed, elaborated by a faculty so corrupted and acting perversely, is itself corrupt: it is consonant and congruent both with the depraved generative faculty and with the other faculties which the generative faculty strives as accurately as it can to shadow forth and express in the seed. How this vitiation passes from the seed into the rational soul I will explain in its place, that is, in the last chapter of your treatise, God willing.

units.la: G A R. Primum id ab eo quaerimus, quod ipse à nobis alibi, Vnde id habes? Ex Scripturisne, an aliunde? aut quomodo demonstras, hoc non esse interfigmenta habendum, quæ inani subtilitatis umbra curiosulos delectant?
units.tr: GAR. First we ask him this, which we have asked him elsewhere: Where do you have it? From Scripture, or from somewhere else? And how do you show that this is not to be held as one of those fictions which delight the overcurious with the empty shadow of subtlety?

units.la: P L A C. Quaeliun unde haberet is, qui cum disputabam, quod dicebat de interno quodam mentis & voluntatis diuinæ actu, non aliunde quam ex reuelatione diuina noscendo. Hic vero quid dixi eiusmodi, quod non vel Scriptura, vel ratione, vel experientia ipsa firmari possit?
units.tr: PLAC. The question is where he had it, who was disputing with me, when he spoke of some internal act of the divine mind and will, knowing it from nothing but divine revelation. But what have I said of this kind that cannot be confirmed by Scripture, by reason, or by experience itself?

units.la: G A R. Ego vero vix oculis meis credidi cum legerem facultatem genitricem inter facultates morales locum habere posse : An etiam vt eam physicis & medicis tanquam malæ fidei poffeffboribus ereptam, moralis philosophia in possessum sibi tanquam proprium peculium vindicet? Quid vero habet facultas ista, quare potius ad moralium dignitatem euehi debeat, quam concoctrix, vel altrix, vel augmentatrix, quas hactenus docuerunt Philosophi non esse rationis participes, sed natura sua brutas ac sui nescias, quaeque homini conueniant, non qua homo est, sed qua naturam habet cum aliis animalibus communem? Denique qua lex erit Decalogi, cuius praecepto facultas generandi subiacere credenda sit? Moralia enim Decalogo circumscribi omnes, vt spero, consentiunt. At saltem moralibus subiecta est. Imo neque hoc simpliciter verum, alioqui ex imperio voluntatis semper moueretur, quod saepe aliter fieri certum. Neque foemina semper vel concipit, cum vult, vel non concipit, quando non vult.
units.tr: GAR. Indeed, I could scarcely believe my eyes when I read that the generative faculty can hold a place among the moral faculties. Does moral philosophy claim as its own property what the physicians and natural philosophers have snatched away as from a dishonest possessor? What does that faculty have, that it should be raised to the dignity of the moral, rather than being the digestive, nourishing, or augmenting faculty, which the philosophers have hitherto taught are not sharers in reason, but by their nature brute and unaware of themselves, and which belong to man not as he is man but as he has a nature common with the other animals? Finally, under what law of the Decalogue is the generative faculty to be thought subject? For all agree, as I hope, that moral matters are circumscribed by the Decalogue. But is it at least subject to the moral? No, not even this is simply true; otherwise it would always be moved by the command of the will, which is certainly often not the case. Nor does a woman always conceive when she wishes, or fail to conceive when she does not wish.

units.la: PLAC. Egone simpliciter dixi, facultatem genitricem esse facultatem moralem? tantum dixi corruptionem naturae universalis cum esset, etiam ipsam facultatem genitricem, quatenus moralis quaedam facultas est, corrupiile, significaui igitur non absolute moralem esse, sed quodam respectu. Tribus autem modis spectari potest, vno, vt est facultas quaedam seu proprietas generica: quo modo spectata facultas est animae vegetatiuae mere physica & bruta: nihilque intendit gignere, nisi rem vegetantem. Altero, vt est facultas animalis moliens generationem animalis, atque adeo ipsius animae sensitiuae productionem: quomodo dici potest facultas animae sensitiuae, cuius appetitu sensitiuo excitatur ad generandum, & applicatur. Denique spectari potest vt est facultas hominis pendens aliquomodo non solum ab appetitu sensitiuo, sed etiam a voluntate, & intendens generationem non canis, aut leonis, aut alius animalis bruti, sed hominis. Eatenus dici potest moralis, quatenus elaborat femen vt producatur animal rationale praedictum facultatibus moralibus, & excitatur ac applicatur ad eam rem facultatibus moralibus, voluntate & appetitu sensitiuo. Sicut ergo appetitus sensitiuus, quamuis genere suo non nisi sensitiuus sit, tamen in homine spectari potest, quatenus est aliquo modo rationalis, &, vt loquitur Ariftoteles, λόγῳ μετέχει πως, atque ita & virtutis capax est, & lege regi potest; Sic facultas generatrix, licet generice fpecìata nullo modo moralis fit, tamen quatenus est facultas hominis, cuius & appetitu aliquomodo regitur, & generationem molitur, quid est cur eatenus moralis aliquomodo dici non possit? Id quod ipse vir doctus innuere fatis videtur cùm ait, eam imperio voluntatis sæpe non moueri: concedere enim videtur, eam imperio voluntatis aliquando moueri. Quid est igitur quamobrem eatenus non possit appellari moralis? Nihil igitur aliud volui, nisi eam quatenus ab appetitu seu libidine dependet, & elaborat femen accommodate ad facultates morales, eatenus corruptam fuisse, atque, vt ratione naturæ tendit ad productionem hominis, sic ratione corruptionis tendit ad productionem hominis corrupti. Quid est ea in re, dignum tam acri reprehenfione? Est quidem facultatis generatricis, fi fecundum rationem illam suam genericam spectetur, eademque altricis, aut auctoris ratio: non vero, fi fecundum fpecificam, quam habet in homine, cuius ab appetitu dependet. Non enim concoctrix qua concoctrix, aut altrix qua altrix vllo modo dependet à voluntate, sed tantum per accidens, quatenus vtraque cibi sumptionem sequitur pendentem à voluntate. Sed generatio qua talis aliquomodo in potestate est voluntatis seu appetitus: Nam nec generant vnquam patres non concurrente appetitu, & possunt à generando etiam perpetuo abstinere fi velint. Quid igitur est, cur, vt manducandi, sic generandi facultas lege regi non possit? Et quo pertinet mandatum Decalogi, non concupisces?
units.tr: PLAC. Did I simply say that the generative faculty is a moral faculty? I said only that the corruption of universal nature, since it was universal, corrupted also the generative faculty itself insofar as it is a certain moral faculty. So I signified that it is moral not absolutely but in a certain respect. It can be considered in three ways. First, as a faculty or generic property: so considered it is a faculty of the vegetative soul, purely physical and brute, which intends nothing but to beget a living thing. Second, as the faculty of an animal, working toward the generation of an animal and so toward the production of the sensitive soul itself: thus it can be called a faculty of the sensitive soul, which by its sensitive appetite is stirred up and applied to generating. Finally, it can be considered as the faculty of man, depending in some way not only on the sensitive appetite but also on the will, and aiming at the generation not of a dog, a lion, or some other brute animal, but of a man. So far it can be called moral, insofar as it works up the seed so that a rational animal, endowed with moral faculties, is produced, and it is stirred up and applied to this task by moral faculties, namely the will and the sensitive appetite. Just as, therefore, the sensitive appetite, though in its kind it is only sensitive, can nevertheless be considered in man insofar as it is in some way rational, and, as Aristotle speaks, partakes of reason in some way [λόγῳ μετέχει πως], and so is capable of virtue and can be ruled by law; so the generative faculty, though considered generically it is in no way moral, nevertheless, insofar as it is the faculty of man, by whose appetite it is in some way governed and which it serves toward generation, why can it not in that respect be called moral in some way? The learned man himself seems sufficiently to hint at this when he says that it is not often moved by the command of the will, for he seems to concede that it is sometimes moved by that command. Why then can it not in that respect be called moral? I wished to say nothing else than that, insofar as it depends on appetite or lust and elaborates seed fitted to the moral faculties, it was corrupted in that respect, and that, just as by reason of nature it tends to the production of man, so by reason of corruption it tends to the production of corrupt man. What in this is worthy of such sharp reproof? Indeed, if the generative faculty is considered according to its generic nature, it has the same account as the nourishing or the augmenting faculty; but not if it is considered according to the specific nature it has in man, on whose appetite it depends. For the digestive faculty as digestive, or the nourishing faculty as nourishing, depends in no way on the will, but only accidentally, insofar as both follow the taking of food, which depends on the will. But generation as such is in some way within the power of the will or appetite: fathers never generate without the concurrence of appetite, and they can abstain from generating for ever if they wish. Why then can the faculty of generating not be ruled by law, just as the faculty of eating can? And to what does the command of the Decalogue, Thou shalt not covet, pertain?

units.la: GAR. Verum his missis, quid est, quod dicitur Adæ corruptio conuertisse facultatem generatricem ad generationem tanquam finem vltimum? Nam illa certè corrupta, cùm fit vniuersalis, alias etiam facultates infecit non minus quàm istam. Quidni ergo cateras facultates ad actus suos, concoctricem ad concoctionem, altricem ad nutritionem, &c. tanquam finem vltimum conuertisse dicatur? vt fit pro facultatum numero etiam finium vltimorum numerus. Quod quis ferat eorum qui norunt finem vltimum homini non posse esse nisi vnum?
units.tr: GAR. Setting these matters aside, what is meant by saying that the corruption of Adam turned the generative faculty to generation as its ultimate end? For that corruption, since it is universal, infected the other faculties no less than this one. Why then should it not be said that the others too were turned to their acts as ultimate ends, the digestive faculty to digestion, the nourishing faculty to nourishment, and so on, so that the number of ultimate ends matches the number of faculties? Who could bear this, among those who know that a man can have only one ultimate end?

units.la: PLAC. Et viuerfalis est illa corruptio, & alias etiam facultates infecit, sed ad prepofitum sola generans faciebat, quia de propagatione hominis, per quam propagatur illa corruptio, agebatur. Sed neque, vt iam monui, concoctio & nutritio sunt, vt actus generandi, infecti libidine, & facultas generandi caeteras facultates conatur quales sunt, propagare. Interim certum est non tam perfecte suas obire functiones concoctricem & altricem post peccatum admissum quam ante, itaque morbis variis & morti, etiam ab infantia omnes sunt obnoxij homines, nec tamen concoctio aut nutritio sunt vltimi fines, sed subordinati tantum conseruationi indiuidui & propagationi speciei. Finis vltimus verus non potest esse nisi vnus, nimirum Deus. Sed finis vltimus falsus genere tantum vnus est, specie autem & numero multiplex; vel enim voluptas quaeritur, vel vtilitas, vel honor, horumque etiam pro variis rebus in quibus quaeruntur, magna est varietas.
units.tr: PLAC. That corruption is universal, and it infected the other faculties too; but for the matter in hand the generative faculty alone was in view, since the propagation of man was being discussed, through which that corruption is propagated. But, as I have already said, digestion and nourishment are not infected with lust as the act of generating is, nor does the generative faculty strive to propagate the other faculties, whatever they are. Meanwhile it is certain that the digestive and nourishing faculties do not discharge their functions as perfectly after the sin was committed as before, and therefore all men from infancy are subject to various diseases and to death. Yet digestion and nourishment are not ultimate ends, but are merely subordinate to the preservation of the individual and the propagation of the species. The true ultimate end can be only one, namely God. But the false ultimate end is one in kind only, and manifold in species and in number; for either pleasure is sought, or utility, or honour, and there is also great variety of these according to the various things in which they are sought.

units.la: GAR. Praterea, Cum finis vltimus relationem habeat ad fines intermedios & subalternos, eorum erit proprie finis vltimus, qui finium subalternorum, & vltimi distinctionem nosse possunt; quodcum neque in corruptionem vniuersalem illam, neque in facultatem generatricem, aut aliam simpliciter physicam connenire potest, quomodo dicetur facultas genitrix a corruptione conuerti ad generationem tanquam ad finem vltimum? Distinguendum potius fuerit inter facultatem, & hominem, qui facultate vtitur. Hic enim poterit sane intelligentia ac voluntate sua finem vltimum sibi praestituere: sed ipsa facultas physica, finem habet ad quem ab Autore natura determinata est, quem semper respicit, quicquid homo corruptus moliatur, vt concoctrix concoctionem, genitrix generationem, &c. PLAC. Si bene ratiocinatur vir doctus sola mens agit propter finem, non voluntas: haec enim non cognoscit proprie, nedum vt distinctionem cognoscat inter finem vltimum & subordinatos. Phantasia quoque & appetitus sensitiuus eam distinctionem non norunt. Quod si vt facultas agat propter finem vltimum, oportet distinctione finis vltimi a subordinatis illam facultatem nosse, necesse etiam erit vt eandem distinctionem cognitam habeat facultas quae tendit in finem subordinatum vltimo : itaque nulla, vt dixi, hominis facultas, praeter vnam mentem aget propter finem. Idem de vniuersa natura, quam propter finem agere, à Philosophis demonstrari solet. Nihil igitur salsius illa viri docti propositione. Porro cum homo mente & voluntate tendit in verum vltimum finem, eodem etiam omnia hominis tendunt, & ab eo referuntur: at cum à vero fine vltimo aberrat, ab eodem etiam fine eius omnes aberrant facultates. Quis autem nescit quàm libidine proclivius sit ad facultate generandi abutendum ad voluptatem? Et quando illa tributa est à Deo ac destinata ad procreationem similis, posita in generante vniuersali corruptione, fieri non potest quin, non Dei, sed corrupti generantis vitio, generet corruptum, sicut facultas genitrix leprosi generat leprosum: determinatur enim eam ad rem non ab autore naturae, sed à depravatione eius cuius est facultas.
units.tr: GAR. Moreover, since the ultimate end stands in relation to intermediate and subordinate ends, the proper ultimate end belongs to whoever can know the distinction between subordinate ends and the ultimate end. That cannot apply either to the universal corruption or to the generative faculty, or to any other purely physical thing. How, then, can it be said that the generative faculty, under corruption, is turned to generation as its ultimate end? A distinction should rather be drawn between the faculty and the man who uses it. For he can certainly set an ultimate end for himself by his understanding and will, but the physical faculty itself has the end to which nature, its Author, has determined it, and it always aims at that end, whatever the corrupt man attempts: the digestive faculty at digestion, the generative faculty at generation, and so on. PLAC. If the learned man reasons well, only the mind acts for an end, not the will. The will does not know the end properly, let alone know the distinction between the ultimate end and the subordinate ones. Imagination and the sensitive appetite do not know that distinction either. And if a faculty is to act for the ultimate end, it must know that distinction between the ultimate end and the subordinate ones; and the faculty that tends to a subordinate end must likewise have that distinction known to it in relation to the ultimate end. So, as I said, no faculty of man except the mind alone acts for an end. The same holds for all of nature, which philosophers usually demonstrate acts for an end. Nothing, therefore, is more false than that proposition of the learned man. Further, when a man tends with mind and will toward the true ultimate end, all his faculties also tend toward it and are referred to it; but when he strays from the true ultimate end, all his faculties also stray from its end. Who does not know how much more readily lust abuses the generative faculty for pleasure? And since that faculty was given by God and destined to produce like offspring, but with universal corruption present in the begetter, it cannot be otherwise than that, through the fault not of God but of the corrupt begetter, it generates the corrupt, just as the generative faculty of a leper generates a leper. For it is determined to that act not by the Author of nature but by the depravity of the one whose faculty it is.

units.la: GAR. Deinde cum finem vltimum vir doctus proponat, qui in veri finis locum succedere rit, falsò apparentem, nempe fallacem felicitatis speciem in creaturis reperiendam, quomodo statim defilit ad generationem, hoc est, à generali fine ad singularem? Non enim qui agnoscit succedere, in locum veri finis vltimi finem alium falsò apparentem, ideò statim concludere cogitur, eum finem esse debere generationem. Cur enim potius quàm scientiam, vel voluptatem, vel bona externa, &c. nisi aliunde pateat ratio, quare potius succedere dicatur in locum veri finis vltimi generatio, quàm aliud quodlibet?
units.tr: GAR. Next, since the learned man proposes an ultimate end to take the place of the true ultimate end, namely a falsely apparent end, a deceptive semblance of happiness to be found in creatures, how does he at once leap from generation, that is, from a general end to a particular one? For one who admits that another, falsely apparent end takes the place of the true ultimate end is not thereby forced to conclude at once that this end must be generation. Why generation rather than knowledge, or pleasure, or external goods, and so on? Unless it is clear from elsewhere why generation rather than any other thing is said to take the place of the true ultimate end.

units.la: PLAC. Ludere mihi potius videtur vir doctus his verbis, & sequentibus, quàm ferò argumentari. Nonne enim fallax illa fœlicitatis species multis in rebus quaeritur? At cur non potius voluptatem dixi quàm generationem? nempe quia coitus voluptatem sic visum est honestè significare, id quod miror aut non animaduertisse virum doctum, aut, si animaduertit, dissimulasse. Quis enim quaeso concupiscentiae carnalis & libidinis est scopus? gloria Dei? aedificatio proximi? certè nihil nisi fallacem sequitur fœlicitatis & voluptatis vmbram. id quod in iis cernere est qui huiusmodi concupiscentiis laxant frena: aliud enim nihil quaerunt quàm cupitis potiri, & libidinem explere. Itaque quae vir doctus subjungit, non videtur mihi vlla egere refponsione. GAR. Sed fac omnia haud aliter habere, quàm quomodo viro doêto libuit: vim generatricem esse facultatem moralem, corruptionem Adæ eam conuertisse ad generationem tanquam finem vltimum, eodem conuersam fuisse totam partem superiorem animæ cum appetitu sensitiuo, id est, totum Adamum; ex iis promanasse corruptum Iemen. Hæc omnia tamen non effecerint, vt corruptio illa prima prognatos ex Adamo inquinet, nisi aliud aliquid adjungatur. Nam & idem in aliis accidere potest. Homo sæperjuriis, adulteriis, homicidiis, &c. contaminabit, & pessimos habitus inde contrahet: vim genitricem suam, & appetitum sensitiuum, & partem animæ superiorem, & se totum, quantus quantus est, ad generationem conuertet, tanquam finem vltimum: & tamen, vitia sua illa, quibus iustam condemnationem in caput suum accersiuit, propagatione naturali non deriuabit in posteros, sicut Adamo factum. Aliud ergo quippiam intercesse necessum est in primo illo peccato, quod in aliis patrum peccatis non ita habet. Nimirum Deus, cuius est absolutum in creaturas suas, primum illud πρῶτον ἁμάρτημα peccatum iustissimo iudicio imputatum voluit omnibus ipsius posteris: aliorum peccata non ita vult in omnes posteros descendere.
units.tr: PLAC. The learned man seems to me to be playing with these words and those that follow, rather than arguing seriously. For is not that deceptive semblance of happiness sought in many things? But why did I say generation rather than pleasure? Because it has seemed right to describe intercourse decently as pleasure. I wonder that the learned man either failed to notice this or, if he noticed it, pretended not to. For what, I ask, is the aim of carnal desire and lust? The glory of God? The edification of one's neighbour? Surely it pursues nothing but the deceptive shadow of happiness and pleasure. This can be seen in those who loosen the reins on such desires: they seek nothing else than to possess what they crave and to satisfy their lust. Therefore what the learned man adds does not seem to me to need any answer. GAR. But grant that everything is no different from how the learned man wished: that the generative power is a moral faculty, that Adam's corruption turned it to generation as its ultimate end, and that the whole superior part of the soul, together with the sensitive appetite, was turned in the same way, that is, the whole Adam; and that the corrupt offspring sprang from these. Yet all this would not have the effect of making that first corruption defile those born of Adam, unless something else were added. For the same can happen in others. A man often defiles himself with perjuries, adulteries, homicides, and so on, and thereby contracts the worst habits. He turns his generative power, his sensitive appetite, the superior part of his soul, and himself entire, however great he is, to generation as his ultimate end. And yet those vices of his, by which he has drawn just condemnation upon his own head, he does not pass on to his posterity by natural propagation, as happened with Adam. Something else, therefore, must have intervened in that first sin, which is not so in the other sins of the forefathers. Namely, God, whose dominion over his creatures is absolute, willed that this first sin, the first transgression, be imputed by most just judgment to all his posterity. He does not will the sins of others to descend in this way upon all posterity.

units.la: PLAC. Quo sensu facultas genitrix à me dicatur aliquatenus moralis, iam exposui, nimirum ratione concupiscentiæ seu libidinis, & destinationis ad procreandum morum subiectum. Patet etiam quo sensu dixerim eam coüersam fuisse ad actu generandi tanquam ad vltimum finem, nempe quia aliud non spectat libido, quàm voluptatem: Eatenus etiam corrupta à me dicitur, quatenus non solum ad propagationem facultatum hominis tendit, sed etiam ad propagandam corruptionem, in quo à scopo, cuius gratia creata fuit, recedit. Hac immunditie posita necessariò sequitur prognatos ex Adamo inquinari. At cur idem non accidit in aliis peccatis? quia alia peccata non induxerunt in parentes vniuersalem corruptionem, sed ex ea profecta sunt, nihilque addiderunt præter vniuersalis illius corruptionis particulares quasdam determinationes ad quærendam fœlicitatem potius in tali re quàm in alia, in tali voluptate quàm in aliqua alia. Itaque mirum videri non debet si corruptio vniuersalis propagatur, non propagantur continuò. particulares determinationes seu habitus. Est enim ; nostrâ quidem sententia, vniuersalis illa corruptio posita in propensione ad falsum finem victimum, & auersione à vero fine. Est enim appetitus finis victimi necessarius, quia primò omnium appetitur. itaque creari hominem oportuit cum appetitu veri finis, & nunc nasci necesse est cum appetitu finis falso apparentis, si non actu, saltem propensione, ob inductam in naturam nostram per lapsum Adami finis victimi mutationem : quæ mutatio per perjuria, adulteria, & homicidia non fit, itaque non propagantur. Hinc est quod particulares eiusmodi habitus seu determinationes aliquomodo corrigi & mutari possunt, & non raro ab vno vitio in oppositum flectimur : Sed vniuerfalis illa corruptio nisi per gratiam regenerationis auferri à nobis nequit. Quod si hæc nostra non placet responsio, malim saltem dicere, huius discriminis hanc esse causam, quòd noluerit Deus impedire quominus primum illud Adami peccatum propagaretur, alia verò eius & aliorum patrum peccata, quominus etiam ipsa propagarentur, voluerit impedire. Hoc enim factus videtur quàm imputationem antecedentem comminisci, quæ tamen non obstet, quin ad Dei voluntatem discrimen illud totum referendum sit. Cæterum hîc mihi videntur coniungi duo non satis bene cohærentia, cùm imputatio illa Adamici peccati fieri à Deo dicitur pro absoluto suo in creaturas iure, & tamen iustissimo iudicio. Quæ enim Deus facit vt iudex, ea facit secundum latam à se legem & iustitiæ normam; quæ verò facit vt absolutum habens in creaturas suas ius, ea facit pro liberrimo suo beneplacito, non autem secundum aliquam legem præstitutam, poscente iustitia.
units.tr: PLAC. In what sense I have called the generative faculty in some measure moral, I have already explained: namely by reason of concupiscence or lust, and of its being destined to produce a subject of morals. It is also clear in what sense I said it was turned to the act of generation as to its ultimate end: because lust aims at nothing but pleasure. In that respect too I call it corrupt, insofar as it tends not only to the propagation of human faculties but also to the propagation of corruption, and so departs from the purpose for which it was created. With this uncleanness posited, it necessarily follows that those born of Adam are defiled. But why does the same not happen with other sins? Because other sins did not bring universal corruption into the parents; they proceeded from it, and added nothing except certain particular determinations of that universal corruption: to seek happiness in this thing rather than that, in this pleasure rather than another. It should not seem strange, therefore, if universal corruption is propagated while particular determinations or habits are not continually propagated. For in our view that universal corruption consists in a propensity toward the false ultimate end and an aversion from the true ultimate end. An appetite for an ultimate end is necessary, because it is desired first of all. Thus man had to be created with an appetite for the true end, and now must be born with an appetite for the falsely apparent end, if not in act, at least in propensity, because through Adam's fall a change of ultimate end has been introduced into our nature. This change does not come about through perjuries, adulteries and homicides, and so these are not propagated. Hence such particular habits or determinations can in some measure be corrected and changed, and we often turn from one vice to its opposite. But that universal corruption cannot be removed from us except through the grace of regeneration. But if this answer of ours does not please, I would rather say at least that the cause of this difference is that God did not will to hinder the propagation of Adam's first sin, while he willed to hinder the propagation of his other sins and those of the other fathers. For this seems to be to invent an antecedent imputation, which nevertheless does not prevent that whole difference from being referred to the will of God. Moreover, here two things that do not cohere well seem to me to be joined: that the imputation of Adam's sin is said to be made by God by his absolute right over creatures, and yet with most just judgment. For what God does as judge, he does according to the law he has laid down and the standard of justice; but what he does as one having absolute right over his creatures, he does by his most free good pleasure, not according to some prescribed law, which justice would demand.

units.la: GAR. Nos hanc rationem vrgemus &c. Malum, quod iam à tempore primæ transgressionis Adæ in omnes ipsius posteros ita deriuatur, vt non prius incipiant esse, quàm illo malo affici, est ex singulari iudicio Dei, siue ex voluntate & consilio Dei tanquam supremi iudicis in pœnam peccati illius quod in Adamo praecesserat. Atqui labes Originalis est malum, quod à tempore transgressionis Adæ in omnes eius posteros ita deriuatur, vt non prius esse incipiant, quàm illo malo affici. Labes igitur originalis inest in omnibus Adæ posteris ex ratione singularis iudicij Dei, in pœnam primæ illius transgressionis Adæ; unde per se consequitur illius imputatio. De mirore nemo dubitat. Maioris veritas etiam certa est. Nam cum iam supra demonstratum sit, eam corruptionem moralem in omnes ex Adamo descendentem non posse soli naturæ adscribi, nemo causam dicere potest, cur non ad singulare Dei consilium atque iudicium conscendendum fit: Quod autem malum est à Deo tanquam iusto iudice, est sine dubio in poenam alicuius peccati praecedentis. At in ipsis posteris primulum conceptis aut nascentibus non est aliud peccatum, quod praecedat eam labem originalem. Deuceniendum est igitur ad ipsius Adæ peccatum, propter quod Deus illud malum in posteros descendere voluerit.
units.tr: GAR. We press this argument, etc. The evil that, from the time of Adam's first transgression, is derived into all his posterity in such a way that they do not begin to exist before being affected by it, comes from a singular judgment of God, that is, from the will and counsel of God as supreme judge, in punishment of the sin that preceded in Adam. But original sin is an evil that, from the time of Adam's transgression, is derived into all his posterity in such a way that they do not begin to exist before being affected by that evil. Therefore original sin inheres in all Adam's posterity by reason of a singular judgment of God, in punishment of that first transgression of Adam; from which imputation of it follows directly. No one doubts the minor premise. The major premise is also certain. For since it has already been demonstrated that this moral corruption, descending from Adam into all, cannot be ascribed to nature alone, no one can say why it should not be traced up to the singular counsel and judgment of God. What evil comes from God as just judge is without doubt in punishment of some preceding sin. But in the posterity themselves, at the moment of conception or birth, there is no other sin that precedes that original stain. We must therefore come to Adam's own sin, on account of which God willed that evil to descend upon his posterity.

units.la: PLAC. Quid est aliud haec ratio, quàm, vt loquuntur, petitio principij? Affertur enim pro argumento illud quod plane idem est cum eo quod vertatur in quæstione. itaque negatur maior: nec probatur ex eo quod ait vir doctus iam supra demonstratum esse: id enim nusquam demonstratum est, nec, vt arbitror, potuit demonstrari. Quanquam si accuratè loqui volumus, propagatio corruptionis non solì naturæ, sed eius depravationi debet adscribi: quæ natura suâ contagiosa est vt quod maximè. Potest etiam maior distingui: & concedi si malum intelligitur à prima Adæ transgressione actuali & habituali diuersum; sin minùs, negari.
units.tr: PLAC. What else is this argument but, as they say, begging the question? For what is put forward as the proof is plainly the same as what is in dispute. So the major premise is denied; nor is it proved by what the learned man says, that it has already been demonstrated: for that has nowhere been demonstrated, nor, as I think, could it be. Although, to speak accurately, the propagation of corruption should be ascribed not to nature alone but to its depravity, which nature, by its own character, is as contagious as possible. The major premise can also be distinguished, and granted if "evil" is understood as different from Adam's first actual transgression and from the habitual state; otherwise it is denied.

units.la: Huius ergo corruptionis propagationem in omnes Adami posteros soli naturæ vitiosæ adscribo, ex qua nihil potest gigni nisi vitiosum. Tu vero eam Deo adscribis imputanti peccatum actuale vnius Adami omnibus hominibus, illiisque singulis & omnibus corruptionem illam, vt peccatum illud puniat, infligenti. Quod si Deus noluisset, vel primum peccatum actuale primi hominis nobis imputare, quemadmodum cætera eiusdem hominis peccata nobis non imputat; aut si imputatum noluisset punire ea poena, quæ peccatum est, ac fons omnium aliorum peccatorum, nasceremur absque peccato incorrupti: cur autem vtrumque illud voluit? Confugitis ad iuditiam, quæ scilicet exigebat vt peccatum illud actuale, & nobis tot post fæcula nasciturisimputaretur, & imputatum sic puniretur. Eiusmodi iustitiam vnde habeatis nescio, nec cur iustitia appelletur intelligo, & mihi videtur cum ipsa iustitiæ notione pugnare. Sed de hac re alibi.
units.tr: I therefore ascribe the propagation of this corruption into all Adam's posterity to vicious nature alone, from which nothing but what is vicious can be begotten. But you ascribe it to God, who imputes the actual sin of the one Adam to all men, and inflicts that corruption on them, each and all, in order to punish that sin. But if God had not wished either to impute to us the first actual sin of the first man, as he does not impute to us his other sins; or if, having imputed it, he had not wished to punish it with that penalty which is sin and the source of all other sins, we would be born uncorrupted and without sin. Why then did he will both? You take refuge in justice, which, you say, required that that actual sin be imputed to us, born so many ages later, and so punished once imputed. I do not know where you get such a justice, nor do I understand why it is called justice; it seems to me to conflict with the very notion of justice. But of this matter, elsewhere.

units.la: Quid, inquiet aliquis, factum ne est igitur absque Dei iudicio, eodemque iusto, vt vitium illud inhærens in Adamum inuaserit, & ab eo in omnes homines permanarit? Non sane. neque enim aut corrumpi Adamus, aut corruptus suam in posteros corruptionem transfundere Deo vel inscio vel inuito potuit. Factum est igitur vtrumque Deo sapienter & iuste permittente. Cur lapsum Adami permiserit nunc non inquiro. lapsu permissio non potuit Adamus sine miraculo non corrumpi. motu enim posito ponitur necessario motus terminus. posito lapsu e loco superiori in inferiorem, eo finito, quod lapsum est in loco inseriore necesse est esse. Itaque fieri non potuit quin post actualem a Deo auersionem & conuersionem ad creaturas Adamus non esset a Deo auersus & ad creaturas conuersus. fieri etiam non potuit quin deinceps mala vteretur conscientia, deumque exhorresceret. non erat autem consentaneum vt permissio lapsu Deus rerum naturam turbaret impedito lapsus termino, (si tamen absque contradictionis implicatione impediri potuit,) aut eum productum statim destrueret restituto in pristinum statum Adamo. merebatur autem Adamus suo illo actuali peccato vt a Deo desereretur, nec condonari id peccatum potuit nisi ex gratia ob futuram Iesu Christi satisfactionem & mortem. Itaque corruptio Adami tribuitur iusto Dei iudicio & poena vocatur, quia non accidit Adamo fine diuina permissione ac desertione, Deo non impediente peccati actualis naturalem efficaciam & sequelam, tum quia impediri non potuit nisi contra ordinem naturæ, tum quia suo ipso peccato actuali dignus fiebat Adamus quem Deus desereret. Iudicauit igitur & constituit iustissimè non impedire corruptionis illius productionem in Adamo. Posita autem corruptione Adami & procreatione liberorum secuta est propagatio illius corruptionis in posteros naturæ vi & lege, non tamen sine Dei permissione.
units.tr: What, someone will say, has it happened then without the judgment of God, and that a just one, that this vice inhering in Adam invaded him and flowed from him into all men? Certainly not. For neither could Adam be corrupted, nor, once corrupted, could he transfuse his corruption into his posterity without God either knowing or being unwilling. Both things therefore happened, God permitting them wisely and justly. Why he permitted Adam's fall I do not now inquire. By the permission of the fall, Adam could not have remained uncorrupted without a miracle. For once motion is posited, the terminus of the motion is necessarily posited: once a fall from a higher place to a lower is posited, when the fall is ended, it must necessarily be in the lower place into which it fell. Thus it could not but be that after Adam's actual turning away from God and turning toward creatures, he would be turned away from God and turned toward creatures. Nor could it be that from then on he would not experience a bad conscience and shudder before God. Nor was it fitting that God, by permitting the fall, should disturb the nature of things by hindering the terminus of the fall (if indeed it could be hindered without implying contradiction), or, having brought it about, should at once destroy it by restoring Adam to his former state. But by that actual sin Adam deserved to be forsaken by God, and that sin could not be pardoned except by grace, on account of the future satisfaction and death of Jesus Christ. Thus Adam's corruption is attributed to the just judgment of God and is called a punishment, because it did not happen to Adam without divine permission and desertion, God not hindering the natural efficacy and consequence of the actual sin; both because it could not have been hindered except against the order of nature, and because by his own actual sin Adam was becoming worthy to be forsaken by God. God therefore judged and decreed, most justly, not to impede the production of that corruption in Adam. But once Adam's corruption was posited and children were procreated, the propagation of that corruption into the posterity followed by the force and law of nature, yet not without God's permission.

units.la: hæc permissio præter eas rationes ob quas Deus vel Angelorum vel Adami lapsum permisit hanc habet propriam, quod necesse fuisset ad eam impediendam rescindere atque euertere leges naturalis propagationis decreto de creando mundo constitutas, quod decretum quia naturæ ordine prius est decreto de permittendo lapsu, necnon decreto de reparando per Christum genere humano, non potuit nec debuit per posteriora decreta rescindi, vt iam semel monueram.
units.tr: This permission, apart from the reasons for which God permitted the fall of the angels or of Adam, has this particular reason: to impede it would have required rescinding and overturning the laws of natural propagation, which were established by the decree concerning the creation of the world. Since that decree is prior in the order of nature to the decree concerning the permission of the fall, and to the decree concerning the restoration of the human race through Christ, it could not, and ought not, be rescinded by later decrees, as I have already warned.

units.la: Est autem decretum de non impediendo seu permittendo lapsu iustum, quia nullo modo iustitiæ repugnat, & iustum fuit ac consentaneum leges non impedire naturæ: Itaque iis conseruaris alia ratione hominum saluti Deus sapientissimus & optimus consulere voluit, quæ naturam non euerteret sed seruaret.
units.tr: Now the decree not to impede, or to permit, the fall is just, since it in no way conflicts with justice; and it was just and fitting not to interfere with the laws of nature. Thus, by preserving those laws, God, most wise and best, willed to provide for human salvation by another way, one that would not overturn nature but preserve it.

units.la: Adde quod & in ipso generationis actu & conceptione durante parentes peccant, & Deum offendunt, vt iure merito eos quatenus sanctus est deserat & naturæ, quam benignè conseruat, permittat, nec in eorum vel operis cui incumbunt gratiam dignetur naturæ cursum impedire & leges refigere. quid est in hac mea sententia quod non fit, aut Scripturæ, aut rectæ rationi consentaneum? Tu ipse cap.1. conftituendo statum quæstionis fassus es propagationem vitij originis fieri lege naturæ, qua quisque sibi fimilem gignit: agnoscis igitur meæ sententiæ veritatem quid est cur ea non contentus causam nostri vitij originalis Deo certo modo peccatum actuale Adami consideranti & imputanti nobis & infligenti nobis illud vitium, imputes? Dic mihi quæso ii potes,quæ necessitas fuerit, cur nos omnes Deus consideraret tanquam vnum hominem in Adamo? cur primum Adami peccatum actuale consideraret alio modo quàm alia peccata? cur id nobis imputaret? cogeris proculdubio cum aliis quibusdam, quos nihil nominare opus est, id vniuersum in Dei voluntatem referre.
units.tr: Add that parents also sin and offend God in the very act of generation and while conception lasts, so that God rightly forsakes them, insofar as he is holy, and permits nature, which he kindly preserves, and does not deign, for the sake of their work or the grace of the work they undertake, to impede the course of nature or revoke its laws. What is there in my opinion that is not consistent with Scripture or with sound reason? You yourself, in chapter 1, in setting out the state of the question, confessed that the propagation of original vice happens by the law of nature, by which each begets what is like himself. You therefore acknowledge the truth of my opinion. Why then, not content with this, do you impute the cause of our original vice to God, who considers Adam's actual sin in a certain way, imputes it to us, and inflicts that vice upon us? Tell me, I ask you, what necessity there was for God to consider us all as one man in Adam? Why would he consider Adam's first actual sin in a different way from other sins? Why would he impute that one to us? You are without doubt compelled, along with certain others whom there is no need to name, to refer the whole matter to the will of God.

units.la: GAR. Primum, quæ de labe seu corruptione in ipso Adamo hærente, & ex actuali ipsius peccato professa hic dicuntur, sunt extra causam præsentem, vbi non aliud agitur, quàm vt norimus, an citra imputationem peccati primi, & singularis Dei iudicij consideratione, idonea causa reddi possit dismanationis eius, quæ corruptio moralis ex Adamo in omnes propagatur.
units.tr: GAR. First, what is said here about the stain or corruption inhering in Adam himself, and derived from his actual sin, lies outside the present question, where nothing else is being treated than whether, without the imputation of the first sin and apart from the consideration of God's singular judgment, a suitable cause can be given for the derivation of that moral corruption which is propagated from Adam into all.

units.la: PLAC. Nequaquam certè quæ hic à me dicuntur, sunt extra causam præsentem: agitur enim etiam vt norimus, quare primum peccatum, potiùs quam alia peccata, corruperit naturam Adami. Id enim qui mihi in hac causa adaersantur non minùs Dei voluntati scribunt, quàm illius corruptionis dismanationem in posteros. Inde etiam mihi exoritur argumentum: nam si corruptio in Adamo hærens non fuit pœna proprie dicta, sed secuta est necessariò peccatum actuale, vt terminus ad quem sequitur motum, consentaneum est rationi, vt eadem nobis inhærens, non sit etiam pœna proprie dicta. Cur enim puniretur in nobis peccatum Adami eo malo, quo punitum non fuit in Adamo?
units.tr: PLAC. By no means are the things I say here outside the present question. The question also concerns why the first sin, rather than other sins, corrupted the nature of Adam. For those who oppose me in this matter ascribe the transmission of that corruption to posterity no less to the will of God. From this an argument arises for me: if the corruption inhering in Adam was not punishment properly so called, but necessarily followed the actual sin as the terminus to which a motion leads, then it is consistent with reason that the same corruption, inhering in us, is also not punishment properly so called. For why would the sin of Adam be punished in us with that evil by which it was not punished in Adam?

units.la: GAR. Deinde, ita concedit vir doctus hic interuenire iustum Dei iudicium, vt sua tamen iusti iudicij explicatione id curare videatur, ne ad communem sententiam accedat.
units.tr: GAR. Further, the learned man here concedes that God's just judgment intervenes, but in his explanation of that just judgment he seems to take care not to agree with the common opinion.

units.la: PLAC. Id unum curo, ne quid dicam quod Dei verbo & gloriae non sit consentaneum. Non quid alij homines sentiant, sed quid sentire debeant, inquiro. Etiamsi vniuersus mundus uno ore clamaret, cur nascamur corrupti, vnicam causam esse Dei voluntatem, hoc tamen nihilon inus conscientia mea refugeret, vt quod maxime. Norma fidei meae est sacra Scriptura, non opiniones hominum.
units.tr: PLAC. I take care of only one thing: that I not say anything inconsistent with God's word and glory. I inquire not what other men think, but what they ought to think. Even if the whole world cried out with one voice that the only cause of our being born corrupt is God's will, my conscience would nonetheless shrink from this as much as possible. The norm of my faith is holy Scripture, not the opinions of men.

units.la: GAR. Etenim cum docent Theologi, non esse hic simpliciter haerendum in naturali hominis propagatione, sed altius attollendos animos ad singularem voluntatem atque dispensationem Dei, & iustum ipsius iudicium, quid putamus iusti iudicij nomine ipsos intelligere; quam opus illud Dei, quo poenam aliquam ex ratione iustitiae vindicatricis irrogat, quod Scriptura vocat iudicium Dei contra homines Ezech. 11. 9. Quid autem vir doctus? Iustum Dei iudicium hic agnoscit, quia nihil fiat, nescio vel inuito Deo, sed sapienter & iuste permittente. Itane? Et iustum iudicium Dei cum Scriptura Rom. 2. 5. 2. Thessalon. 1. 5. Apoc. xvi. 7. xix. 2. nihil aliud designat, quam cognitionem, iam scientiam, aut permissionem Dei? Imo vero iudicium Dei designat, quod vel poenas pro merito irrogat, vel praemia distribuit ex ratione iustitiae illius, quae ἀληθινή dicitur: provt & Apoc. xix. 2. Iusta Dei iudicia in eo constituta dicuntur, quod meretricem illam magnam, quae corrupit terram fornicatione sua, damnauit & vindicauit sanguinem seruorum suorum ex manu eius.
units.tr: GAR. For when the theologians teach that one should not stop simply at natural human propagation, but must raise our minds higher to the singular will and dispensation of God and his just judgment, what do we think they understand by the name of just judgment? It is that work of God by which he inflicts some punishment from the rationale of avenging justice, which Scripture calls the judgment of God against men (Ezek. 11. 9). But what does the learned man say? He acknowledges here a just judgment of God, because nothing happens without God's knowledge or against his will, but by his wise and just permission. Really? And does the just judgment of God, as in Rom. 2. 5, 2 Thess. 1. 5, Apoc. xvi. 7, xix. 2, designate nothing other than God's knowledge, or science, or permission? Indeed the judgment of God designates that which either inflicts punishment according to desert or distributes rewards from the rationale of that justice which is called true [ἀληθινή]; as also Apoc. xix. 2, where the just judgments of God are said to consist in this, that he condemned and avenged the blood of his servants at her hand, that great harlot who corrupted the earth with her fornication.

units.la: PLAC. Scriptura nunquam corruptionem, aut corruptionis propagationem iudicio Dei ascribit. itaque non agitur de locutione Scripturae, sed Theologorum, accipienda, pro eo ac pati potest analogia fidei & rei natura, in melius potius quam in deteriorem partem. Quod si iusti iudicij nomine nihil aliud intellexerunt, quam opus illud Dei, quo poenam aliquam ex ratione iustitiae vindicatricis irrogat, revera intellexerunt indicium Dei contra homines, Sed omne Dei iudicium contra homines quia sunt peccatores, supponit eos esse peccatores, non facit. Hic autem agitur de iudicio Dei, quod antecedit peccatum hominum, qui absque eo foret, peccatores non esfent. Non sunt igitur ad propositum quæ afferuntur exempla. In illis enim agitur de iudicio sequente eorum, quibus pœna irrogatur, peccatum. Hic vero quæstio est de iudicio, antecedente eorum qui puniuntur, peccatum. Deinde censuit ne vir doctus, hanc esse iudicij Dei perpetuam in Scriptura significationem, necne? Si censuit, erravit: non raro enim aliter accipitur, ut patet ex Psal.119. 7.12.19.29. &c. Si non censuit, quorsum eiusmodi loca laudauit? & quam vim habere possunt ad me refellendum?
units.tr: PLAC. Scripture never ascribes corruption, or the propagation of corruption, to the judgment of God. Therefore it is not a question of the language of Scripture but of the theologians, which is to be understood, so far as the analogy of faith and the nature of the matter allow, in the better rather than the worse sense. But if by the name of just judgment they understood nothing other than that work of God by which he inflicts some punishment from the rationale of avenging justice, they truly understood the judgment of God against men. But every judgment of God against men, because they are sinners, presupposes that they are sinners; it does not make them so. Here, however, the question concerns a judgment of God which precedes the sin of men, without which they would not be sinners. The examples adduced are therefore not to the point. For those examples concern a judgment following the sin of those who are punished. Here the question concerns a judgment preceding the sin of those who are punished. Further, did the learned man think that this is the constant meaning of judgment in Scripture, or not? If he thought so, he erred, for it is often taken otherwise, as is clear from Ps. 119. 7, 12, 19, 29, etc. If he did not think so, why did he cite such passages, and what force can they have to refute me?

units.la: GAR. Quid quod nihil est omnino in totius mundi gubernatione, quod insscio, vel inuito Deo fiat, quod sine permissione Dei euenit, vbi non Dei sapientia eluceat, quod non iuste, id est, ex immota & indeflexa Dei rectitudine administretur? Neque tamen propterea dicet aliquis hæc fieri ex occulto, iusto, admirabili, inscrutabili, Dei consilio, etiam cum arbores crescunt, & prata variegantur floribus, & animalia propagant speciem, & vermes ex terra formantur. Sunt enim certe illa omnia ex sapientia & prouidentia, eaque rectissima & consultissima. Sed justum, occultum, mirabile Dei consilium, non ad communem eiusmodi rerum creatarum administrationem Scriptura referre solet, sed ad singularem in certis operibus dispensationem & œconomiam: vt cum dicit Paulus Roman. xi. 33. Iudicia Dei esse inscrutabilia, & vias eius imperueltigabiles.
units.tr: GAR. What of the fact that nothing whatsoever in the government of the whole world happens without God's knowledge or against his will, that nothing occurs without God's permission, where the wisdom of God does not shine forth, and that nothing is not administered justly, that is, from the unchanging and unbending rectitude of God? Yet no one will therefore say that these things happen from the hidden, just, admirable, inscrutable counsel of God, even when trees grow, and meadows are variegated with flowers, and animals propagate their kind, and worms are formed from the earth. For all these things certainly come from wisdom and providence, and from a most upright and most wise providence. But Scripture is accustomed to refer the just, hidden, wonderful counsel of God not to the common administration of created things of this kind, but to his singular dispensation and economy in certain works, as when Paul says (Rom. 11. 33) that the judgments of God are inscrutable and his ways unsearchable.

units.la: PLAC. Primum non quaeritur hoc loco quid soleat Scriptura ad Dei iudicium referre: Non enim, ut iam obseruaui, vllo loco propagationem originalis peccati ad Dei iudicium retulit. Quæritur tantum quo sensu non repugnante Scripturæ, & ratione possit referri. Alium certe sensum, qui cum Scriptura & recta ratione conciliari possit, non video, præter eum, quem hoc loco & in fine cap. 12. & paulo ante medium cap. 13. huius ipsius Manuscripti exposui. Cæterum contra se vir doctus laudasse videtur verba illa Apostoli, iudicia Dei sunt inscrutabilia, & viæ eius imperuestigabiles. Constat enim eo loco per iudicia Dei non intelligi opera Dei, quibus pœnam ex ratione iustitiæ vindicatricis irrogat, vt vult vir doctus: nam neque de eiusmodi operibus agebatur eo loco, neque eiusmodi iudicia solent esse imperscrutabilia: quippe quorum ratio in Dei iustitia, & peccatis hominum est aperta. GAR. Tertio cum in hac causa Calvinus & Theologi haec duo opponunt, fieri ex vi naturae, &, fieri ex ratione iudicij diutius; quomodo vir doctus illud fieri dicit usto Dei iudicio, quod fit ita naturaliter, ut impe- diri non possit, nisi contra naturae ordinem, Et nisi euertantur leges naturalis propagationis,& nisi sistatur,& suffl aminetur peccati actualis sequela & efficacia naturalis?
units.tr: PLAC. First, it is not asked here what Scripture is accustomed to refer to the judgment of God. For, as I have already observed, it nowhere refers the propagation of original sin to the judgment of God. What is asked is only in what sense, not contrary to Scripture and reason, it can be referred.
