Certainly I see no other sense that can be reconciled with Scripture and sound reason, apart from the one I have set out here, at the end of chapter 12, and a little before the middle of chapter 13 of this very manuscript. Moreover, the learned man seems to have cited against himself those words of the Apostle, "the judgments of God are inscrutable, and his ways unsearchable." For it is clear that in that place "judgments of God" is not understood as the "works of God" by which he inflicts punishment from the rationale of avenging justice, as the learned man wishes. For neither were such works under discussion in that place, nor are such judgments wont to be inscrutable, since their rationale lies open in the justice of God and in the sins of men. GAR. Thirdly, since in this matter Calvin and the theologians oppose these two things, happening by the force of nature, and happening by the rationale of a judgment of God: how does the learned man say that it happens by the just judgment of God, which happens so naturally that it cannot be impeded unless against the order of nature, and unless the laws of natural propagation are overturned, and unless the sequel and natural efficacy of actual sin are halted and obstructed?

units.la: PLAC. Cum Calvinus opponit naturam iudicio Dei in hoc negotio, non id facit, ut neget naturali propagatione ab Adamo in posteros manasse corruptionem, nec per iudicium Dei intelligit iudiciariam imputationem peccati actualis Adami, aut poenae inflictionem. Dicimus, inquit, naturali hominem vitiositate corruptum, sed quae a natura non fluxerit. A natura fluxisse negamus, ut significemus adventitiam magis esse qualitatem, quae homini acciderit, quam substantialem proprietatem quae ab initio indita fuerit. Per iudicium, aut potius consilium, Dei intelligit illud, quo Deus permisit & praeordinavit ut lapsum Adami, sic lapsus propagationem; id quod a nobis cap. xiii. huius Manuscripti factis fuisse demonstratum est, nec ullibi refutatur a viro docto.
units.tr: PLAC. When Calvin opposes nature to the judgment of God in this business, he does not do so to deny that corruption flowed by natural propagation from Adam to posterity, nor does he understand by the judgment of God the judicial imputation of Adam's actual sin or the infliction of punishment. "We say," he says, "that man is corrupted by natural vitiosity," but one which has not flowed from nature. "We deny that it has flowed from nature, so as to signify that it is rather an adventitious quality that has befallen man than a substantial property that was implanted from the beginning." By the judgment, or rather the counsel, of God he understands that by which God permitted and foreordained that, just as Adam fell, so his fall should be propagated. This has been demonstrated by us in chapter 13 of this manuscript, and is nowhere refuted by the learned man.

units.la: GAR. An vero, cum Deus corruptionem personalem omnium hominum non permittat in posteros descendere, corruptionem, inquam, non natuam ex Adamo naturaliter omnibus insitam, sed adscitiam, & ex actualibus peccatis progerminantem, putandus est contra naturae ordinem agere, aut leges naturalis propagationis evertere, aut peccati actualis naturalem sequelam impedire? Vix dictum putem hactenus a quoquam, aut cogitatum.
units.tr: GAR. But when God does not permit the personal corruption of all men to descend to posterity, corruption, I say, not natural and implanted in all men from Adam by nature, but adventitious and sprouting from actual sins, is it to be thought that he acts against the order of nature, or overturns the laws of natural propagation, or prevents the natural sequel of actual sin? I would scarcely think that this has been said or thought by anyone hitherto.

units.la: PLAC. Iam ostendi, valde disparem esse rationem primi peccati actualis, & sequentium; illud corrupisse naturam, ista non item; nec non corruptionis vniuersalis in auersione a vero fine vltimo & conuersione ad finem vltimum salso apparentem sitae, & corruptionis illius particularis determinationis ad certa quaedam obiecta; illam enim naturaliter propagari, hanc non item; illam nonnisi per regenerationem tolli posse, hanc posse nonnunquam absque regeneratione aut tolli, aut etiam in oppositam mutari. Non igitur virum doctum supponere decuit, eandem esse utriusque rationem.
units.tr: PLAC. I have already shown that the reason of the first actual sin differs greatly from that of the subsequent ones: the former corrupted nature, the latter did not. Likewise, universal corruption, consisting in aversion from the true ultimate end and conversion to an apparently good end, differs from that particular corruption which is determined toward certain objects; for the former is propagated naturally, the latter is not; the former can be removed only through regeneration, whereas the latter can sometimes be removed without regeneration, or even changed into its opposite. Therefore the learned man ought not to have supposed that the reason of both is the same.

units.la: GAR. Denique de actu generationis quod additur, in quo hominies peccant, & Deum offendunt; & merito a Deo deferuntur, ad rem praesentem parum facere videtur : Quandoquidem hic non de iusto iudicio Dei erga generantes, sed erga genitos agitur : aut si iustum illud iudicium respicere dicatur filios, qui corrupti merito nascantur, quia genitores in actu generationis peccarunt & Deum offenderunt : quis non videt inde nobis emergere conclusionem, cui tam infestus est Vir doctus, peccati paterni poenas in filios descendere, id est, peccatum patris imputari filiis.
units.tr: GAR. Finally, as to the act of generation, which is added, in which men sin and offend God and are rightly punished by God, this seems to have little bearing on the present matter. For here we are not dealing with God's just judgment upon those who beget, but upon those who are begotten. Or if that just judgment is said to concern the sons, who are born corrupt by right, because the parents sinned in the act of generation and offended God, then who does not see emerging from this the conclusion to which the learned man is so hostile: that the punishments of a father's sin descend upon the sons, that is, that the father's sin is imputed to the sons?

units.la: PLAC. Facit hoc quidem non ad causam quam agit vir doctus, sed ad meam, qui reddere rationem volui, cur Deus propagationem peccati permiserit. Non tamen ideo enim non tenebatur impedire naturae cursum, sed ne impediret, obstabant constitutae ante lapsum leges, & ipsa generantium peccata desectionem promerentia. Hoc autem in consilium seu iudicium, cum spectet ad generantes eatenus suae naturae permittendos, aliquomodo ad genitos spectare dici potest : nec tamen propterea est iudicium, quo generantis peccatum imputatur generando. Nam aliud est decretum de non impediendo peccato, aut peccati contagio seu dimanatione a parente in liberos, aliud decretum de irroganda secundum legis comminationem poena. Hoc supponit existentiam & peccatum illius qui punitur. Imputare enim peccatum nondum existenti, punire nondum existentem, mihi paradoxum videtur.
units.tr: PLAC. This indeed has to do not with the cause which the learned man is pursuing, but with mine, since I wished to give an account of why God permitted the propagation of sin. Yet God was not for that reason bound to hinder the course of nature; rather, the laws established before the fall, and the sins of the parents themselves, which deserved desertion, stood in the way of his hindering it. Now this decree or judgment, since it concerns the parents, in that God permits them to follow their nature, can in some way be said to concern the begotten as well; yet it is not for that reason a judgment by which the parent's sin is imputed to the one who begets. For one thing is a decree not to hinder sin, or the contagion or transmission of sin from parent to children; another is a decree to inflict punishment according to the threat of the law. The latter presupposes the existence, and the sin, of the one who is punished. For to impute sin to one not yet existing, or to punish one not yet existing, seems to me a paradox.

units.la: CAPVT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Examen trium similitudinum, quibus imputatio primi peccati actualis Adami illustra- tur eodem Cap. IV.
units.tr: An examination of three similitudes by which the imputation of Adam's first actual sin is illustrated, in the same Chapter IV.

units.la: TV tamen istam tuam imputationem illustrare quibusdam similitudinibus, ac quodam probabilitatis fuco oblinere niteris, quas expendere est animus, & ostendere quàm ei non faueant. Primam fumis ab aulico Regis amico, qui infidelitatis & laesa-majestatis reus privatur titulis, dignitatibus, & fundis, quos sibi & suis acquisierat. Nunquid enim, inquis, verum est perditiße sibi & posteris haec omnia seruare, modo fidelis esset? Infidelitas ergo sive patris, sive aui, toti familiae obfuit. Et, si posteri considerentur illis bonis exuti, & infames facti, nonne dicetur delictum illius causa esse bonorum perditorum, & infamia, & toti familiae imputatum? nam sicut sibi & toti familiae acceperat sub conditione, sic in conditionem peccans tota familia in illo peccauit & cecidit. Haec similitudo miserè claudicat. Primùm conditio est fidelitas; bona tituli, dignitates, fundi. Itaque conditio, & bona sub illa conditione accepta sunt res admodum diuersae, & natura sua separabiles. Possunt enim bona illa bello, vel profusione, vel alea, vel litibus temerè suscepti, vel aliqua alia re amitti conseruatâ fide, aut hac violatâ retineri. Hîc verò bona sunt rectitudo, iustitia, sanctitas, conditio horum ipsorum bonorum conseruatio. Quid enim ab Adamo exigebatur, nisi, ut perseueraret in rectitudine, iustitia, sanctitate, fide, officio? Annon haec ipsa bona fidem includunt? obedientiam Deo continent. Quaenam autem fuit conditionis violatio, quod peccatum Adami? infidelitas, inobedientia, ambitio, superbia, ingratitudo, cupedia, curiositas, à Deo auersio, ad creaturas conuersio &c, quae, quomodo cum perfecta rectitudine, iustitia, sanctitate, innocentia consistere potuerint, equidem intelligere non possum. Hinc aliud nascitur discrimen, nam violata fide, ut bonis à Rege acceptis Aulicus priuetur, opus est Regis, vel iudicis actione, nempe iudicio, & iudicij executione. Alioqui tituli illi, dignitates, & fundi retinerentur ab Aulico. Adamus vero violata fide factus a Deo apostata, Deo rebellis, non potuit amplius integer, iustus, sanctus, rectus, bonus esse: nec ut priuaretur iustitia & rectitudine vllo Dei iudicio, vlla actione iudiciaria opus fuit: hoc ipso quod lapsus est desiit esse in eo, in quo collocatus fuerat, gradu: hoc ipso quod se a fine vltimo vero ad falso apparentem intorsit & incuruauit, desiit rectus esse, hoc ipso quod suum Deo ius reddere noluit infidelis & rebellis creatori suo & domino optimo, desiit iustus esse.
units.tr: YOU, however, try to illustrate this imputation of yours by certain similitudes, and to lend it a kind of gloss of probability. I intend to weigh them and to show how little they favour you. The first you take from a courtier, a friend of the King, who, guilty of disloyalty and treason, is stripped of his titles, dignities and estates, which he had acquired for himself and his own. For, you say, is it not true that he has lost all these things for himself and his posterity, which he would have kept had he remained faithful? The disloyalty therefore of father or grandfather harmed the whole family. And if the posterity are considered, deprived of those goods and made infamous, will it not be said that the crime of one man is the cause of the lost goods and of the infamy, and is imputed to the whole family? For just as he had received them for himself and his whole family under a condition, so the whole family, sinning against that condition, sinned in him and fell. This similitude limps miserably. First, the condition is fidelity; the goods are titles, dignities and estates. Thus the condition and the goods received under that condition are very different things, and separable by their nature. For those goods may be lost through war, extravagance, gambling, or lawsuits rashly undertaken, or through some other cause while fidelity is kept, or retained although fidelity has been violated. Here, however, the goods are rectitude, justice, holiness, and the condition is the preservation of these very goods. For what was required of Adam, but that he should persevere in rectitude, justice, holiness, faith and duty? Do not these very goods include faith? Do they not contain obedience to God? What, then, was the violation of the condition, what was Adam's sin? Unbelief, disobedience, ambition, pride, ingratitude, greed, curiosity, turning away from God, turning to creatures, and so on. How these could have coexisted with perfect rectitude, justice, holiness and innocence, I certainly cannot understand. Hence another difference arises. For when fidelity is violated, the courtier can be deprived of the goods received from the King only by the action of the King or a judge, namely by a judgment and its execution. Otherwise the courtier would keep those titles, dignities and estates. But Adam, having violated faith, was made an apostate from God and a rebel against him; he could no longer remain whole, just, holy, upright and good. Nor was any judgment of God, any judicial action, needed for him to be stripped of justice and rectitude. By the very fact that he fell, he ceased to be in the rank in which he had been placed. By the very fact that he turned and bent himself from the true final end to what falsely appeared to be one, he ceased to be upright. By the very fact that as an unfaithful and rebellious creature he refused to render to God, his Creator and best Lord, what was God's due, he ceased to be just.

units.la: GAR. Respondeo 1. nihil hic opus esse singularibus eiusmodi similitudinis capitibus; dummodo id obtineamus hoc exemplo, non esse quod putent homines, doctrinam de imputatione primi peccati continere aliquid, quod merito habendum sit pro absono aut iniquo. Cur enim decreto Dei iniustitiam adscribant, qui iudicum humanorum decretis in causa perduellionis non adscribunt? Eo impetrato, parum interest ad causam quae nunc agitur, secusne habeat, necne, imputatio peccati Adae, quam imputatio peccati perduellium. Nec vero nos y fumus, qui putemus esse in vtraque omnia similia.
units.tr: GAR. I reply, first, that there is no need for such separate chapters on similitudes, provided we obtain from this example that men should not think the doctrine of the imputation of the first sin contains anything which may rightly be held absurd or unjust. For why do they ascribe injustice to God's decree, when they do not ascribe injustice to the decrees of human judges in the case of treason? Once that is granted, it matters little to the present question whether or not the imputation of Adam's sin is like the imputation of the sin of traitors. Nor indeed are we such that we think everything is alike in both.

units.la: PLAC. Si de imputatione primi peccati mediata loquitur, facile do eam nihil continere absoni aut iniqui. Sin de immediata, nego id posse hoc exemplo obtineri, cum sit admodum difficile dissimulare, & quidem ea dissimilitudine, quae maxime ad rem facit de qua agitur.
units.tr: PLAC. If he speaks of mediate imputation, I readily grant that it contains nothing absurd or unjust. But if he speaks of immediate imputation, I deny that this can be secured by this example, since it is very hard to pass over the dissimilarity which bears most directly on the matter under discussion.

units.la: GAR. Secundo, quanquam in explicatione illa dissimilitudinum est, quod merito desideremus. Primum enim cum quatuor proposita fuerint, de bonis separabilibus, de aliis modis amittendi, de iudicis decreto, de filiis nascituris & nepotibus: tamen vbi dissimilitudinis capita explicantur, de primo membro nihil dicitur. Bona, inquis, perduellis iunt separato ita nomine ua. Quid igitur? Et bona Adami, quae pro se, & suis acceperat, non erant ab ipso separabilia natura sua? Imo non separabilia tantum fuerunt, sed & actu separata sunt, quippe amissa per primam illam inobedientiam. Ergo in hoc frustra dissimilitudo statutur. Nisi forte cum separabilia dicis, intelligis non modo separari posse, ita ut scilicet, amissis honoribus, remanere possint diuitiae, & amissa nobilitate, remanere possint affinitates. Quod si ita explicatur, quis non regerat, & bona Adami iuisse ieiunii abilia, quia & lumen naturale intellectus, & communes notiones, & opus legis scriptum in cordibus remanere potuit, & amitti tamen rectitudo, iustitia, justitas sint & factum esse nonimus. Et in hoc iterum similitudo consistit.
units.tr: GAR. Secondly, although there is in that explanation of the dissimilarities something we rightly miss. For when four points were put forward, concerning separable goods, concerning other ways of losing them, concerning the judge's decree, and concerning children to be born and grandchildren, yet when the heads of dissimilarity are explained, nothing is said about the first member. The goods, you say, of the traitor are separable from the condition under which they were received. What then? Were not Adam's goods, which he had received for himself and his own, separable from him by their nature? Nay, they were not only separable but actually separated, being lost through that first disobedience. So in this respect the dissimilarity is set up in vain. Unless perhaps when you say separable you mean not only that they can be separated, so that, the honours having been lost, riches may remain, and, nobility having been lost, kinship may remain. But if it is explained in that way, who would not reply that Adam's goods too could be separated, since the natural light of the intellect, common notions, and the work of the law written on the heart could remain, and yet rectitude, justice and holiness be lost? And in this again the similitude consists.

units.la: Ut ne tibi dissimilitudinis capita explicantur, de primo membro hi dicuntur? Aliquid non tamen illa quatuor membra a prioribus, ut in quatenus ordine singula explicata sunt, & iam in hac videtur in exemplo longus fuisse. Sed videtur vero dicitur perlecti verbis meis aliud quid mente agitasse, quod imperiit, cum minus ea & recte contraheret, & bene intelligere. Mentem enim a mea valde alienam mihi attingit.
units.tr: Why are these things said about the first member, as if those four members had not been explained one by one, in order, and this already seems long in this example? But it seems that, in reading my words, you have pondered something else in your mind, which you did not express, since you neither summarise it well nor rightly understand it. For you attribute to me a meaning very far from my own.

units.la: Dixi in exemplo perduellis bona separari posse a conditione sub qua accepta sunt, ille intellexit separari posse ab ipso perduelli, aut alia ab aliis. Itaque aliud dixi, ad aliud ille respondet. Scio bona Adami quibus excidit, potuisse ab eo separari, & separata fuisse. Scio potuisse eorum quaedam a se invicem separari. Scio ea in re similitudinem esse inter Adamum & aulicum perduellem: sed quid hoc ad rhombum? Non enim impedit, esse cam dissimilitudinem inter utrumque quam obseruaui. Bona enim Adami, hoc est, rectitudo, iustitia, integritas, separari non poterant a perfecta obedientia, seu conditione quae ab eo exigebatur. Perseuerare in perfecta obedientia erga Deum, & perseuerare in rectitudine, iustitia, integritate morali, res erant aut eadem prorsus, aut saltem inseparabiliter connexae: & similiter non perseuerare in obedientia erga Deum, & non perseuerare in rectitudine, iustitia, & integritate res erant vel eadem vel indiuulse cohaerentes. Nunc similiter cum fidelitate cohaerent nobilitas, opes, dignitatesque ciuiles? Num implicat contradictionem illa amissa, has saltem ad tempus retinere? Nonne igitur inter Adamum & eiusmodi perduellem ea in re est mirabilis dissimilitudo?
units.tr: I said that in the example of the traitor the goods can be separated from the condition under which they were received. He understood that they can be separated from the traitor himself, or from one another by others. So I said one thing and he answers another. I know that the goods of Adam which he lost could be separated from him, and were separated. I know that some of them could be separated from each other. I know that in this respect there is a similarity between Adam and the courtier-traitor; but what has this to do with the point? For it does not prevent there being the dissimilarity between the two which I observed. For Adam's goods, that is, rectitude, justice and integrity, could not be separated from perfect obedience, or from the condition required of him. To persevere in perfect obedience toward God and to persevere in rectitude, justice and moral integrity were either altogether the same thing or at least inseparably connected; and likewise, not to persevere in obedience toward God and not to persevere in rectitude, justice and integrity were the same thing or inseparably cohering. Now, do nobility, wealth and civil dignities cohere in the same way with fidelity? Does it involve a contradiction to lose the former yet keep the latter, at least for a time? Is there not, then, in this respect a remarkable dissimilarity between Adam and such a traitor?

units.la: GAR. Deinde, quomodo dicitur in iis quae acciderunt primo homini, nulla opus fuisse iudiciaria Dei actione? Annon homini adhuc integro legem Deus proposuerat, de non gustando fructu interdicto, addita grauissima comminatione, si secus faceret mortè moriturum. Gen. 2. 17. Quam comminationem Deus adimpleuit, & adimpleuit ut iudex, ac proinde in spoliando homine suis donis, & in varias miserias demergendo iudiciariam actionem exercuit? Hic quoque nihil dissimile.
units.tr: GAR. Then, how can it be said that in what happened to the first man no judicial action of God was needed? Did not God lay down a law for man while he was still whole, concerning not eating the forbidden fruit, adding the most grievous threat, that if he did otherwise he would die the death? Gen. 2. 17. Did not God fulfil that threat, and fulfil it as judge, and so, in stripping man of his gifts and plunging him into various miseries, exercise a judicial action? Here too nothing is dissimilar.

units.la: PLAC. Atqui, inquam, iam probaui verbis morte morieris non esse intelligendam mortem sicam in priuatione iustitiæ. Quid enim absurdius, quàm, aut legem comminari priuationem iustitiæ, aut iudicem spoliare eos quos iudicat iustitia? Probaui etiam Deum illam comminationem legis non adimpleuisse in Adamo, ob futuram Christi satisfactionem. Et quomodo potuit adimpleri, si verbis illis mors significabatur corporis & æterna? punire secundum legis comminationem & non punire: peccatum imputare & non imputare: iustificare reum & tamen in eo adimplere legis comminationem, si quid intelligo, ita pugnant, vt consistere simul nequeant. Abest igitur vt credam Deum fpoliasse Adamum iustitia originali, ac eum ex iusto fecisse iniustum.
units.tr: PLAC. But, I say, I have already proved from the words "dying you shall die" that death is not to be understood as mere privation of righteousness. For what could be more absurd than either for the law to threaten privation of righteousness, or for a judge to despoil those whom justice judges? I have also proved that God did not fulfil that threat of the law in Adam, on account of the future satisfaction of Christ. And how could it have been fulfilled, if by those words death was meant of the body and eternal? To punish according to the threat of the law and not to punish, to impute sin and not to impute it, to justify the guilty and yet in him to fulfil the threat of the law: if I understand anything, these clash so that they cannot stand together. Far be it, therefore, from me to believe that God despoiled Adam of original righteousness and made him from righteous unrighteous.

units.la: GAR. Neque est quod dicas, hominem eo ipso quod lapsus est, excidisse sua sanctitate & iustitia, adeoque nihil opus fuisse actione Dei iudiciaria, vt his donis spoliaretur. Quid enim? Non & Regius officiarius, qui bello aduersus Regem iusdcitando, vrbe, prouincia, Regno excedit, eo ipso excidit illo quod antea gesserat munere: nec tamen eo minus consequenti Regis iudicio abdicatur officio suo.
units.tr: GAR. Nor can you say that, by the very fact that man fell, he lost his holiness and righteousness, and so there was no need for a judicial act of God to strip him of these gifts. For what of this? Does not a royal officer who, by swearing an oath against the King, stirring up war, and leaving the city, province or kingdom, thereby lose the office he had held before? Yet he is no less removed from his office by the King's subsequent judgment.

units.la: PLAC. Omnino excidit munere, hoc est, commeritus est vt munere priuetur, idemque munus in alium conferatur; quam ad rem opus est Regis sententia: alioqui non liceret eo munere alium ornare. Censeretur enim is Regius officiarius suum in illud munus adhuc retinere. Aliud enim est bellum suscitare, vrbe, aut prouincia excedere, aliud munere priuari: Et sic nonnunquam admisso eiusmodi crimine, vt ad ali quod tempus differatur sententia iudiciaria, quo tempore eiusmodi officiarius nondum amisisse suum munus censetur. Sed quid hoc ad rem? Nonne enim ostendi, hoc ipso quod Adamus lapsus est, excidisse eum ex gradu, in quo antea erat, obedientiæ & iustitiæ? Poteratne simul forensi ratione iustus & iniustus esse? Poteratne simul esse legi Dei conformis & non conformis? perseuerare & non perseuerare in iustitia? Poteratne sese à Deo auertere & incuruare, & ita nen rectus permanere? Deum habere promendacì, inuido, maleuolo &c, & tamen conseruare amorem, fidem, obedientiam erga Deum, seu iustitiam?
units.tr: PLAC. He certainly loses the office, that is, he has deserved to be deprived of it and for that office to be conferred on another. For this a sentence of the King is needed; otherwise it would not be lawful to adorn another with that office, since the officer would still be considered to retain his office. For it is one thing to stir up war, or to leave the city or province, and another to be deprived of an office. Sometimes, when a crime of this kind has been committed, the judicial sentence is deferred for a time, and until then the officer is not considered to have lost his office. But what has this to do with the matter? Have I not shown that, by the very fact that Adam fell, he fell from the rank in which he had previously stood, that of obedience and righteousness? Could he be both righteous and unrighteous in the forensic sense? Could he at once conform and not conform to the law of God, persevere and not persevere in righteousness? Could he turn himself away from God and bend aside, and so not remain upright? Could he have God as a liar, envious, malicious, and so on, and yet keep love, faith and obedience towards God, that is, righteousness?

units.la: G A R. Et cum lapsu suo Adam non modo exciderit iustitia sua, sed in omnigenas calamitates incidere commeruerit; si quis agnoscat ad iustitiam amittendam nihil opus fuisse iudiciaria actione fatebitur saltem ad poenas subeundas eam interuenire oportuisse: hoc est enim precipue illud morte morieris.
units.tr: GAR. And since by his fall Adam not only lost his righteousness but also deserved to fall into calamities of every kind, if anyone acknowledges that no judicial act was needed for the loss of righteousness, he will at least admit that such an act had to intervene for the undergoing of the punishments; for this is especially what is meant by "you shall surely die".

units.la: P L A C. Id equidem fateor: Extat enim illa sententia Gen.3. Sed quid inde sequitur? Potestne ostendere vir doctus in Scriptura iudiciariam aliquam Dei sententiam, qua fuerit Adamus spoliatus iustitia? Et tamen non assentior viro docto poenas sententia lata Gen.3. 16.17. Euae & Adamo irrogatas, easfuisse, quas lex praecipue comminabatur verbis morte morieris. Id enim pugnat cum Christi satisfactione, & fidelium propter eam iustificatione plena & perfecta.
units.tr: PLAC. I indeed grant this, for that sentence stands in Genesis 3. But what follows from it? Can the learned man point to any judicial sentence of God in Scripture by which Adam was stripped of righteousness? Yet I do not agree with the learned man that the punishments pronounced in Genesis 3:16–17 and inflicted on Eve and Adam were those which the law especially threatened in the words "you shall surely die". For that conflicts with Christ's satisfaction and with the full and perfect justification of believers on account of it.

units.la: G A R. Adde quod fieri poterat, vt Adam peccando amitteret iustitiam meritorie, & tamen ex Dei benignitate eam conseruaret, quomodo nimirum in statu Gratia, peccando, meritorie amittimus Gratiam, fidem, charitatem, nec tamen actu ab eis excidimus, quia Dei gratia superabunda: Roman.5.2.
units.tr: GAR. Add that it could happen that Adam, by sinning, meritoriously lost his righteousness, and yet by God's kindness kept it, just as in the state of grace, by sinning, we meritoriously lose grace, faith and love, and yet do not actually fall from them, because the grace of God abounds: Romans 5:2.

units.la: P L A C. Primum quid est amittere iustitiam meritorie, nisi mereri non iustificari à iudice; sed condemnari? Nam mereri, vt pro poena iudex ab eo auferat iustitiae habitum, est mereri vt iudex tollat quod non est, & faciat id quod cum iustitia legis latoris & iudicis pugnare videtur. Tenetur enim potius iudex conseruare iustitiam, quàm destruere, & ab eo qui ea praeditus est, tollere. Nec enim eum decet eos, quos iudicat, facere iniustos & peccatores. Comparatio quam instituit inter fideles in statu gratiae, & Adamum in statu naturae, quà non fit apposita, nemo, opinor, non videt. Opponuntur enim inter se, tantum abest vt sint similes, status naturae lapsae, & status gratiae. Iustitia Adami erat donum naturale, iustitia nobis inhaerens est donum supernaturale. Status naturæ erat mutabilis, cùm status gratiæ fit incorruptibilis. Principium enim iustitiæ, seu sanctitatis nobis inhærentis, non est mutabilis natura ; sed immutabilis Spiritus Sanctus, vnio cum Christo indissolubilis, propositum iecundum electionem firmum ; itaque peccatum est à vetere homine, à carne, iustitia est à nouo homine, à Spiritu : non igitur mirum videri debet, si peccata quædam non pium nos habitu iustitiæ : quandoquidem illius habitus radices valde distant à radicibus peccati, & vita nostra spiritualis est æterna, & Gratia comparata est ad medendum peccato. Sed quid erat in Adamo, quod impediret, quominus actuales eius à Deo Apostasia expelleret habitualem obedientiam seu iustitiam? Mutato enim, vt dixi, fine vltimo, moralia mutari omnia necesse est. Id quod ipsum etiam cernere est, cum quis corde vel è falsa religione transit ad veram, vel è vera ad falsam. Quanta enim consequi solet studiorum & viuendi rationis commutatio?
units.tr: PLAC. First, what is it "to lose righteousness meritoriously", except to deserve not to be justified by the judge but to be condemned? For to deserve that the judge, as punishment, should take away from him the habit of righteousness is to deserve that the judge should remove what is not there, and do what seems to contradict the righteousness of the lawgiver and judge. For the judge is bound rather to preserve righteousness than to destroy it and take it from one who possesses it. Nor is it fitting for him to make those whom he judges unrighteous and sinners. The comparison he draws between believers in the state of grace and Adam in the state of nature, in so far as it is put forward, I think no one fails to see is not apt. For the state of fallen nature and the state of grace are set against each other, and so far from being alike, they are opposite. Adam's righteousness was a natural gift; the righteousness inhering in us is a supernatural gift. The state of nature was mutable, whereas the state of grace is incorruptible. For the principle of righteousness, or of holiness inhering in us, is not a mutable nature but the immutable Holy Spirit, union with Christ which is indissoluble, and a purpose fixed according to election. Thus sin comes from the old man, from the flesh, and righteousness from the new man, from the Spirit. It ought therefore not to seem strange if certain sins do not wholly strip us of the habit of righteousness, since the roots of that habit lie far from the roots of sin, our spiritual life is eternal, and grace has been provided to heal sin. But what was there in Adam that would have prevented his actual apostasy from God from driving out his habitual obedience or righteousness? For when the ultimate end is changed, as I have said, all moral matters must necessarily change. This is something that can be seen even in those who pass in heart, either from false religion to true, or from true to false. For what great change of studies and way of life usually follows?

units.la: Præterea priuato Aulico titulis, dignitatibus & fundis, ijsdem priuantur eius filij, Et nocet ijs patris infidelitas. Confiteor etiam lapsum Adami nobis obfuisse & quidem vehementer, & quàm ille fuit priuatus iustitia & rectitudine tam ijsdem nos priuatos ab eo gigni. Sed putasne crimen Aulici imputari à Iudice eius filijs nascituris & nepotibus?
units.tr: Moreover, a courtier who is deprived of his titles, dignities and estates has his sons deprived of the same things, and their father's unfaithfulness harms them. I also admit that Adam's fall harmed us, and indeed greatly; and that because he was deprived of righteousness and uprightness, we are begotten deprived of the same things by him. But do you think that a judge imputes the courtier's crime to his sons yet to be born and to his grandsons?

units.la: GAR. Denique falsum assumit, qui supponit parentum crimen nunquam nascituris, aut nepotibus imputari : cùm exempla in contrarium suppetant bene multa : Infamia enim, & honorum priuatio, & exilium etiam in nepotes perduellium non infrequenter descendunt. Quod & Scriptura exempla postea manifestum faciunt.
units.tr: GAR. Finally, he assumes falsely who supposes that the crime of parents is never imputed to children yet to be born or to grandchildren, since many examples to the contrary are at hand: for infamy, deprivation of honours, and even exile, not infrequently descend upon the grandchildren of traitors. Scripture's examples later make this plain.

units.la: PLAC. Si parentum crimen nascituris & nepotibus imputatur à Deo, id fit, quia illud crimen in nascituris & nepotibus etiam locum habet, maiorum traditiones & mores imitantibus, aut probantibus. Sic peccatum Ieroboami, eo mortuo, in decem tribubus permansit, & peccatum Iudæorum, qui Dominum gloriæ crucifixerunt, eorum posteri, hodie probant, & in seipsis fouent ac conseruant. Nec vnquam reperietur Deum iudicem, aut suo iudicio fecisse peccatorem eum, qui alioqui non fuisset peccator, aut sententia sua priuasse aliquem iustitia inhærente, aut puniuisse aliquem, in quo non esset peccatum, quod illam pœnam meruerat. Si quando nulla habita ratione peccati, pro summa sua in creaturas potestate, aliquem affligi permittit, vt Iobum, & cæcum illum cuius historia narratur Ioh. 9. id non facit vt iudex, nec vt iustitiæ satisfiat, nec vt legis comminatio adimpleatur, sed vt supremus creaturæ suæ Dominus, qui ea vti potest pro suo arbitrio ad gloriam suam, ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem, ad confusionem hostium suorum, ad probationem illius qui sic affligitur.
units.tr: PLAC. If the crime of parents is imputed by God to children yet to be born and to grandchildren, this happens because that crime also takes place in those yet to be born and in grandchildren, who imitate or approve the traditions and customs of their ancestors. So the sin of Jeroboam remained in the ten tribes after he died, and the posterity of the Jews who crucified the Lord of glory approve it today and cherish and preserve it in themselves. Nor will it ever be found that God, as judge, by his judgment made someone a sinner who otherwise would not have been a sinner, or by his sentence stripped someone of inherent righteousness, or punished someone in whom there was no sin that had merited that punishment. If at any time, with no account taken of sin, by his supreme power over his creatures, he permits someone to be afflicted, as Job and that blind man whose history is recounted in John 9, he does not do this as judge, nor so that satisfaction may be made to righteousness, nor so that the threat of the law may be fulfilled, but as the supreme Lord of his creature, who may use it at his will for his own glory, for the building up of the Church, for the confusion of his enemies, and for the proving of the one who is so afflicted.

units.la: Certè eiusmodi imputatione vt bonis illis priuentur nihil opus est. Sufficit enim ad id, parentem quæ non habet, quæ amisit, liberis suis dare non posse. Fac enim eadem illa vel belli calamitate, vel Domini iniustitia, vel vicini iniuria, vel aliqua alia ratione sine vllo infidelitatis crimine Aulicum amittere, aut etiam vendere, & pecuniam consumere: ijsdem illis bonis priuabuntur hæredes absque vlla infidelitatis imputatione, aut iudicis sententia, hac sola de causa, quoniam nemo dat quod non habet. Filij hæredes sunt bonorum paternorum. Quæ autem pater vel amisit, vel vendidit in bonis paternis non amplius sunt. Quod si humanus iudex paternum crimen filijs imputat, num idem Deus facere censendus est? Vtrum æquius est nostras de Dei iustitia cogitationes ad legū humanarum normam exigere, quàm ad ipsius Dei legem? non arbitror. Audi legem Dei. Deut. 24. 16.
units.tr: Certainly there is no need for such an imputation in order that they be deprived of those goods. For it is enough for this that a parent cannot give to his children what he does not have and has lost. For suppose that a courtier, by some calamity of war, or the injustice of his lord, or the injury of a neighbour, or some other cause, and without any crime of unfaithfulness, loses or even sells his estate and spends the money: his heirs will be deprived of those same goods without any imputation of unfaithfulness or sentence of a judge, for this sole reason, that no one gives what he does not have. Sons are heirs of their father's goods. But what their father has lost or sold is no longer among the paternal goods. If a human judge imputes a father's crime to his sons, is God to be thought to do the same? Is it more just to bring our thoughts about God's justice to the standard of human laws than to God's own law? I think not. Hear the law of God, Deuteronomy 24:16.

units.la: Ne morte afficiuntor patres pro filijs, ne filij morte afficiuntor pro patribus: quisque propter peccatum suum afficiuntor morte. Ac ne crimen infidelitatis, vel læsæ maiestatis excipias, obstat Scriptura, 2. Chr. 25. 3. Amatzia interfecit seruos suos qui percusserant Regem patrem suum : filios vero eorum non affecit morte : sed fecit sicut scriptum est in lege praecepisse Iehouam dicendo, ne moriuntur patres pro filijs & filij ne moriuntur pro patribus, sed quisque propter peccatum suum moriuntur. Quid quod ipse Deus vindicans suam iustitiam a Iudaeorum calumniis quid sit nobis de ea sentiendum praescripsit? Anima, inquit, quae peccat ipsa morietur. Filium non feret iniquitatem patris, & pater non feret iniquitatem filij &c.
units.tr: Let fathers not be put to death for their children, nor children put to death for their fathers: each shall be put to death for his own sin. Nor can you escape by pleading the crime of unbelief or treason, for Scripture stands in the way: 2 Chron. 25.3-4, Amaziah killed the servants who had struck down the king his father, but he did not put their children to death, but did as it is written in the law, where the Lord commanded, saying, the fathers shall not die for the children, nor the children for the fathers, but each shall die for his own sin. Moreover, God himself, defending his justice against the calumnies of the Jews, has prescribed what we ought to think of it: The soul that sins, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father bear the iniquity of the son, etc.

units.la: G A R. Atqui responsuris illud ante omnia clare fuerat explicandum, putentne in eiusmodi magistratuum iudiciis aliquid minus iustum aut crudele designari, quod secus fieri oportuerit, & cuius nomine in foro conscientia iusta possint accusatione percelli. Nam si iusta sunt ea Iudicum sententia, non dubium est quin suam apud Deum approbationem habeant, qui quae iusta sunt & bona non potest non approbare cum fiunt. Quae vero iusta & bona & sancta sunt, apud homines recte sentientes, cur tanquam absurda, & immania, & iniustitia plena traducantur, cum a Deo fieri dicuntur?
units.tr: GAR. But those who are going to answer should first of all have made clear whether they think that there is anything unjust or cruel in the judgments of magistrates of this kind, something that ought to have been done otherwise, and on account of which a good conscience in the court may be struck by accusation. For if those judgments of judges are just, there is no doubt that they have approval before God, who cannot fail to approve what is just and good when it is done. But what is just, good and holy among people who think rightly, why is it represented as absurd, monstrous and full of injustice when it is said to be done by God?

units.la: P L A C. Aut bona est mea responsio, aut mala. Si bona, cur eam non admisit Vir doctus? Si mala, debuit eius vitium ostendere, non aliam mihi respondendi rationem praescribere. Deinde illa ipsa responsionis ratio quam exigit potest in eum retorqueri: nam vel iustae sunt eiusmodi iudicum sententiae, vel iniustae. Si iustae, demonstrare debuit earum iustitiam, vel SCRIPTURAE aliquo testimonio, vel necessaria & evidenti ratione, unde constet similibus Deum delectari sententiis. Humana enim testimonia, cum de religione, & voluntate Dei agitur, haud satis cuta videntur. Si iniustae, quia ausus fuit eas esse non indignas Deo dicere? De sententiis iudicum sinte iustae, an iniustae, meum non est iudicare; Dei hae sunt partes, cui illi rationem iudiciorum suorum sunt reddituri. Coguntur nonnulli quia non sunt praemi Magistratus conferuandae Reipublicae causa nonnulla facere, quibus minime delectantur, sed quid hoc facit ad id de quo inter nos agitur? Siue iustae sunt, sive iniustae eiusmodi iudicia, annon tutius est de Dei voluntate & sententiis tentiis ex Scriptura iudicare, perfecta fidei nostrae regula, & plena voluntatis Dei erga nos reuelatione, quàm ex humano aliquo exemplo?
units.tr: PLAC. Either my answer is good or it is bad. If good, why has the learned man not accepted it? If bad, he ought to have shown its fault, not prescribed another way of answering me. Furthermore, that very method of answering which he demands can be turned back against him: for such judgments of judges are either just or unjust. If just, he ought to have demonstrated their justice either by some testimony of Scripture or by a necessary and evident argument, from which it would be clear that God takes delight in such sentences. For human testimonies, when the question concerns religion and the will of God, do not seem sufficiently reliable. If unjust, why did he dare to say that they are not unworthy of God? Whether the judgments of judges are just or unjust is not for me to decide; that is God's part, to whom those judges will have to render an account of their judgments. Some are compelled, because they are not rewarded, by the magistrate for the sake of preserving the commonwealth, to do some things in which they take no pleasure; but what has this to do with the matter in dispute between us? Whether such judgments are just or unjust, is it not safer to judge of God's will and sentences from Scripture, the perfect rule of our faith and the full revelation of God's will toward us, than from some human example?

units.la: GAR. Imò si forte sentiret aliquis, hoc ita fieri non debere ab hominibus, sed ijs iudiciorum suorum normam esse debere legem illam Iudaeis datam de filijs pro crimine patris non puniendis, Deut. 24. 16. tamen handquaquam inde consequeretur, Deum etiam in suis iudicijs ab eadem norma non posse discedere; cum ipse nullis legibus obstringatur, sed sua sit ipsi voluntas agendorum norma & lex.
units.tr: GAR. Indeed, even if someone should think that men ought not to act in this way, but that the law given to the Jews, that children are not to be punished for the crime of their parents (Deut. 24.16), ought to be the norm of their judgments, nevertheless it would by no means follow from this that God also cannot depart from the same norm in his judgments, since he is bound by no laws, but his own will is the norm and law of what he does.

units.la: PLAC. De potestate Dei hîc non quaeritur, sed de eius iustitia, quam partim datis legibus, partim sanctissimis sententiis, quibus eam à calumniis Iudaeorum vindicauit, qualis sit patefecit. Quid est, cur his eius reuelationibus non acquiescamus potius, quàm hominum iudiciis, aut opinionibus? Unde enim potius cognoscatur legislatoris iustitia, & quid probet, quàm ab eius lege? Nullis quidem legibus obstringitur Deus, nempe alterius, at suis ipsius legibus quid est quamobrem sese vltrò obstringere non possit? Sua ipsi voluntas est agendorum norma & lex; non certè praecise quatenus est voluntas, sed quatenus est optima, iustissima, sanctissima voluntas, eademque sapientissima, itaque nihil insipienter, nihil iniuste, nihil male velle, aut facere potest. Necessario enim volitio congruit cum voluntatis vniuersali perfectione. Determinatur igitur voluntas Dei ad bene volendum à sui ipsius iustitia &c: non potest enim suae ipsius perfectioni, hoc est, sibi ipsa repugnare.
units.tr: PLAC. Here we are not asking about the power of God, but about his justice, which he has revealed, partly by the laws he gave, partly by his most holy sentences, by which he defended it against the calumnies of the Jews. Why should we not rest in these revelations of his rather than in the judgments or opinions of men? For where is the justice of a lawgiver, and what it approves, more truly learned than from his law? God is indeed bound by no laws imposed by another, but why should he not be able to bind himself voluntarily by his own laws? His own will is the norm and law of what he does; not, certainly, precisely insofar as it is will, but insofar as it is the best, most just, most holy will, and at the same time most wise; therefore he can will or do nothing foolishly, nothing unjustly, nothing wickedly. For volition necessarily agrees with the universal perfection of the will. The will of God is therefore determined to will well by his own justice, etc.; for he cannot act against his own perfection, that is, against himself.

units.la: GAR. Sed quod secundo adjungimus, nobis legem illam aduersus perduelles in hoc negocio proponentibus non ea mens est, vt putemus cogitationes nostras De Dei iustitia ad legum humanarum normam exigendas esse. Nulla hactenus animum subiit cogitatio eiusmodi. Sed quia, qui peccati primi imputationem negant, hac inter alias ratione vtuntur, quod religio nostra Iudaeis & Ethnicis huius dogmatis assertione in odium adducatur, tanquam iniustum aliquid & crudele diuinitati attribuens, nos hoc exemplo docemus, illis iniustum aut barbarum videri non posse, quod ipsimet in suis publicis iudicijs tam frequenter obseruant. Non ergo ita colligimus. Homines perduellium liberis peccata paterna imputant. Ergo & Deus censendus est peccatum Adae posteris imputare. Sed ita potius. Hominibus sine Ethnicis, sine aliis non videtur iniustum, si in crimine laesae-Majestatis filius pro peccato patris poenas ferat. Quis igitur ex illis poterit Deum iniustitiae arguere, si peccatum Adae puniat in posteris? Ut exemplum non ad confirmandam veritatem vsurpetur, sed ad illustrandam tantum, & ab iniustitia aut immanitatis accusatione vindicandam.
units.tr: GAR. But as to what we add in the second place, the intention of our appeal to that law against those who oppose us in this matter is not that we think our thoughts about the justice of God ought to be measured by the norm of human laws. No such thought has entered our minds up to now. But because those who deny the imputation of the first sin use this argument among others, that our religion is brought into odium with Jews and Gentiles by the assertion of this doctrine, as if it attributed something unjust and cruel to the Deity, we teach by this example that what they themselves observe so frequently in their public judgments cannot seem unjust or barbarous to them. So we do not reason thus: men impute the sins of traitors to their children; therefore God too must be considered to impute the sin of Adam to his posterity. But rather thus: to men, apart from Gentiles and others, it does not seem unjust if, in the crime of treason against majesty, a son bears the punishment for his father's sin. Who among them, then, will be able to accuse God of injustice if he punishes the sin of Adam in his posterity? Let the example be used not to confirm the truth, but only to illustrate it, and to vindicate it from the accusation of injustice or cruelty.

units.la: PLAC. Si haec eius mens fuit quicum mihi res erat, aequum fuisset, ut eam innueret apertius: non enim sum Oedipus. Quicquid fit, praeter ea quae hactenus a me sunt obserwata, quominus ad id accommodatum fit hoc exemplum duo vel tria obstant, illud primo, quod in eo exemplo non agitur nisi de poena temporali, cum imputari dicatur peccatum Adae ad mortem aeternam, nec ad eam tantum, sed etiam ad poenam quae sit peccatum, & hominem in eo statu constituat, ut non possit deinceps non peccare. Hoc enim est quod potissimum repugnare iudicis & legis iustitiae nobis videtur. Deinde, si quidam ex hominibus criminis paterni imputationem liberis aut nepotibus approbauerunt, non defuerunt ex altera parte, & fortasse multo plures qui improbauerunt: Commemorat nonnullos ipse vir doctus pag. 81. 82. 83. potuisset multo plures si voluisset. Itaque non medetur scandalo similitudo nisi forte ex aliqua parte. Praeterea, quid simile afferri potest eiusmodi imputationi, quae etiamnum post aliquot annorum millia grassetur in omnes posteros, ne vno quidem excepto? Denique eiusmodi exempla vel ira extorsit, vel necessitas tuendae vitae principum & salutis reipublicae: quorum neutrum in re de qua agitur locum habet. Imo tantum abest ut imputatione illa immediata peccati Adami homines a peccando inhibeantur, ut contra priuentur bene agendi seu obediendi habitu, & subijciantur necessitati peccandi. id quod a fine legis & iustitiae vindicis vehementer abhorrere videtur.
units.tr: PLAC. If this was the intention of the man with whom I have to do, it would have been fair for him to indicate it more clearly; for I am no Oedipus. Whatever the case, apart from what I have observed so far, two or three things stand in the way of this example being suited to the purpose. First, that in that example only temporal punishment is in question, whereas the sin of Adam is said to be imputed unto eternal death, and not to that alone, but also to the punishment which is sin itself and places a man in that state in which he cannot thereafter avoid sinning. For this is what seems to us chiefly to conflict with the justice of a judge and of a law. Next, if some men have approved the imputation of a parent's crime to children or grandchildren, there were not lacking on the other side, and perhaps many more who disapproved. The learned man himself mentions some on pp. 81, 82, 83; he could have mentioned many more had he wished. Thus the likeness does not heal the offence, unless perhaps in some respect. Besides, what similar thing can be adduced for an imputation of this kind, which even now, after several thousand years, rages against all posterity, without exception of any one? Finally, such examples have been extorted either by anger or by the necessity of protecting the lives of princes and the safety of the commonwealth; neither of these has a place in the matter under discussion. Indeed, so far is that immediate imputation of Adam's sin from restraining men from sinning, that on the contrary it deprives them of the habit of doing well or obeying and subjects them to the necessity of sinning, which seems strongly contrary to the end of the law and the avenging of justice.

units.la: GAR. Denique nos in hoc negotio ad legem Dei respiciendum esse prolixe fatemur. Sed ad legem potius illam esse respiciendum contendimus, qua omnibus hominibus lata est, in qua testatur Deus se vindicare peccata patrum in filios Exod. xx. 5. quam ad particulare factum, quod Deus Iudaeis singulariter prascripsit, Deut.24.16. aut ad particularem oeconomiam, qua se in causa Iudaeorum vsurum significat Ezech.18.20. Sed de his locis fusius posthac dicendum erit.
units.tr: GAR. Finally, we freely admit that in this business we must have regard to the law of God at length. But we contend that we must rather have regard to that law which is given to all men, in which God testifies that he avenges the sins of the fathers upon the children (Exod. 20.5), than to the particular deed which God prescribed to the Jews singularly (Deut. 24.16), or to the particular economy by which he signifies that he will act in the case of the Jews (Ezek. 18.20). But we shall have to speak more fully about these passages later.

units.la: PLAC. Miror legem Deut.24.16. vocari a viro docto particulare factum, & oraculum, quo iustitiam suam Deus vindicat a calumniis Iudaeorum, Ezech.18. particularem oeconomiam; nec minus miror iis duabus legibus opponi legem Exod.20.5. quasi haec causae nostrae obesset. Nam & lex illa erat vniuersalis regula omnium iudiciorum, in quibus de crimine aliquo agebatur, & particularis oeconomia non potuisset, nisi respectu cuiusdam temporis, iustitiam Dei vindicare ab obiecta iniustitia, & lex Exod.20. si quam imputationem innuit, innuit tantum mediatam seu consequentem, cum declaratione dininae iustitiae Ezech.18. minime pugnantem. Proinde melius Augustinus (verba sunt Zanchij exponentis secundum Decalogi praeceptum) Tom.8. in Psal.108. qui locum hunc exodi interpretatur de illis impiorum filijs, qui parentum impietatem imitantur: ac proinde poenam etiam aeternam illis hoc loco denunciari docet, propter iniquitatem, qua ita parentum fuit, vt etiam facta fit propter imitationem & filiorum. Atque inde hoc probat, quod addit Deus, eorum qui oderunt me: odium enim hoc refertur tum ad patres tum ad liberos. Ita nihil pugnare locum Exodi cum loco Ezechielis vbi Dominus pronunciat, filium, nempe simpliciter innocentem non portaturum iniquitatem patris, nimirum neque aeternam neque temporalem. Exod. enim 20. sermonem esse de liberis non simpliciter innocentibus, sed qui patrum iniquitatem imitentur In his verbis habemus coniunctam duplicem autoritatem Augustini & Zanchij: Habes supra pag. 132. etiam Hieronymi; quibus consentiunt alij omnes, aut saltem prope omnes interpretes, vt mirum sit potuisse hanc Dei legem pro imputatione immediata a quoquam afferri.
units.tr: PLAC. I am surprised that a learned man calls the law of Deut. 24:16 a particular act, and the oracle by which God vindicates his justice against the slanders of the Jews, Ezek. 18, a particular dispensation. I am no less surprised that the law of Exod. 20:5 is set against those two laws, as if it harmed our cause. For that law was a universal rule for all judgments in which some crime was being tried. A particular dispensation could only have been, with respect to a certain time, the vindication of God's justice against the injustice charged to him. And the law of Exod. 20, if it implies any imputation, implies only a mediate or consequent one, which is by no means at odds with the declaration of divine justice in Ezek. 18. Therefore Augustine explains it better (these are the words of Zanchius, expounding the precept of the Decalogue) Tom. 8 on Ps. 108, who interprets this passage of Exodus as referring to those sons of the impious who imitate their parents' impiety. He therefore teaches that eternal punishment is also announced to them in this place, on account of the iniquity by which they were like their parents, and which is also made worse by the sons' imitation. And from this he proves what God adds, of those who hate me: for this hatred is referred both to the fathers and to the children. Thus the passage of Exodus does not conflict at all with the passage of Ezekiel, where the Lord pronounces that the son, namely the one who is simply innocent, will not bear the iniquity of the father, neither eternal nor temporal. For Exod. 20 speaks of children who are not simply innocent, but who imitate their fathers' iniquity. In these words we have the combined double authority of Augustine and Zanchius. You have above, p. 132, Jerome as well; with them agree all the others, or at least nearly all the interpreters, so that it is remarkable that this law of God could be advanced by anyone in support of immediate imputation.

units.la: Alteram similitudinem ducis a toto naturali, corpore scilicet humano, eamque Thomae Aquinatis verbis exprimis: non, opinor, vt eius authoritate sententiam tuam fulcias, aut me commoueas: scis enim quam apud Ecclesias nostras sit nulla, sed quia eius verba tibi visa sunt commoda & dilucida. Ego autem qua mente dicta sint a Thoma vtcunque intelligo &, quia intelligo, doctrinam continere a mente Ecclesiarum nostrarum diuersam, non recipio: quo vero consilio a te sint recitata hoc loco non assequor, nisi forte idem prorsus sentias de peccato originali cum Thoma: quod de te suspicari non audeo. Ponit Thomas peccatum per carnis originem vitiatam ab Adamo in nos traduci, siue, (vt habet in summa) primum peccatum primi hominis originaliter transfire in posteros; ac ostendit quomodo per semen ad animam rationalem perveniat. Sed concessa illa peccati traductione remanet dubitatio, quod defectus, qui ex vitiata origine trahuntur, non habent rationem culpae; non enim merentur poenam, sed magis misericordiam, sicut Philosophus dicit de eo qui nascitur caecus, vel quocunque alio modo aliter orbatus. Et hoc ideo, quia de ratione culpae est quod sit voluntaria, & in pestate hominis cui culpa imputatur. Quaestio igitur erat, quomodo defectus illi, vel, vt loquitur in summa, infectio, habeant rationem peccati, cum sint inuoluntarij in infantibus. Eius responsionem, quia a te laudatur, expendam per partes. Dicendum est, inquit, quod sicut peccatum actuale est peccatum personae, quod per voluntatem personae peccantis committitur; ita peccatum originale est peccatum naturae, quod per voluntatem principij humanae naturae commissum est. Distinguit duo peccata, vnum actuale, alterum originale: illud personae, hoc naturae. illud per voluntatem personae peccantis, hoc per voluntatem principij naturae humanae commissum. Erant ne igitur duae in Adamo voluntates, vna personae, altera principij naturae humanae? Et, an peccatum per voluntatem principij naturæ humanæ fuit actuale, necne? Si voluit distinguere peccatum actuale Adami à corruptione habituali, quam in eius facultatibus reliquit, bona est doctrina, sed non bene expressa. Cæterum peccatum actuale Adami, si fuit personæ, quomodo nobis imputatur? Sed pergamus, est enim, inquit, considerandum, quod sicut diuersa membra corporis partes sunt personæ vnius hominis, ita omnes homines sunt partes, & quasi quædam membra humanæ naturæ: unde Porphyrius dicit, quod participatione speciei plures homines sunt vnus homo. Diuersa membra corporis sunt partes integrantes totius hominis. Omnes vero homines non sunt partes integrantes naturæ humanæ. Non componitur natura ex multis hominibus. Alioqui cum mihi natura humana infit integra, inessent mihi omnes homines. Sed sunt partes Logicæ, siue subiectiuæ, vt vulgò loquuntur in scholis, & natura abstracta & præcisa ab indiuiduis, ac vniuersalitate donata totum est Logicum seu vniuersale: sed hanc rationem totius non habet à parte rei, sed per mentis nostræ operationem. Itaque Metaphysicè loquendo contrà res habet. Persona est totum, natura pars: persona est id quod agit, natura id quo agit. Addit Thomas, videmus autem quod actus peccati exercitus per aliquod membrum, puta per manum, vel pedem, non habet rationem culpæ ex voluntate manus vel pedis, sed ex voluntate totius hominis, à qua sicut à quodam principio deriuatur motus peccati ad singula membra. Et similiter à voluntate Adæ, qui fuit principium humanæ naturæ, tota inordinatio naturæ habet culpæ rationem in omnibus ad quos peruenit, quantum ad hoc quod suscepti sunt culpæ. Aducrte quæso quàm non bene procedat ista similitudo. In praecedentibus verbis componebat naturam cum persona, omnes homines cum membris corporis. Unde oriebatur haec similitudo, ut se habet persona ad membra corporis, sic se habet natura ad omnes homines. Satis, ut innui, male: Non enim ut persona est principium quod actionis, membrum quo; sic natura est principium quod, homines principia quibus peccat. Sed contra, ut iam dixi. Iam autem quomodo istam comparationem ad institutum accommodat? Actus, inquit, peccati exercitus per aliquod membrum non habet rationem peccati ex voluntate illius membri, sed totius personae. Expectabam ut concluderet, ergo actus peccati exercitus per aliquem hominem non habet rationem peccati ex voluntate illius hominis, sed ex voluntate naturae humanae. Verum ille mutatis terminis, loco actus exerciti per homines aut hominem, posuit totam inordinationem naturae, & pro voluntate naturae humanae posuit voluntatem Adae qui fuit principium naturae humanae. Atqui primum accurate loquendo falsum est, Adam fuisse principium naturae humanae: Immo contra potius, natura humana fuit principium Adami. Est enim natura quodammodo pars suppositi: pars autem principium aliquomodo eius quod componit. Et, ut Logici loquuntur, natura humana prior est Adamo existendi consequentia. Est igitur Adamus principium seu causa, non absolute naturae humanae, sed naturae humanae quae in eius posteris fuit: quomodo pater quilibet principium est naturae posterorum, non suae. Deinde voluntas Adae tam eius personae voluntas fuit, quam mea mea; nec intelligo cur naturae voluntas dici debeat. Nam si Adamus principium fuit naturæ humanæ, inde non sequitur eius voluntatem fuisse voluntatem naturæ, sequitur tantùm Adamum fuisse principium voluntatis naturæ humanæ, aut certè naturam humanam non habere voluntatem, aut ad summum voluntatem Adami fuisse principium voluntatis naturæ. Piget me diutius immorari in isto scholastico pulvere inanium subtilitatum, quibus tu me Thomæ operâ implicuisti, quem alioqui flabellis plurium rationum possem in suos autores dispellere, & dissipare: sed satis erit hoc loco duas huius similitudinis claudicationes observasse. Primùm enim ideò actus per membrum aliquod corporis exercitus non habet rationem culpæ ex voluntate illius membri, sed totius hominis, quia membro illi nulla est propria voluntas. At sua cuique homini propria est voluntas. Itaque membrum separatum nihil peccat, nihil agit. Homines singuli multa & agunt, & peccant separati ab Adamo, eorumque actiones peccata sunt, non quia profiscuntur à voluntate Adami, sed quia, prosecta à propria cuiusque voluntate, pugnant cum lege Dei. Deinde discere velim, cur hæc comparatio locum habeat duntaxat respectu primi illius peccati actualis, non autem sequentium? desiit ne simul ac peccavit Adamus, eius voluntas esse voluntas naturæ, aut Adamus esse principium naturæ humanæ? Effecerit igitur ista comparatio, ut, non minùs quàm primum, reliqua Adami peccata nobis imputentur, contradicente Apostolo Rom. 5. Addam & tertiam claudicationem, idcirco actiones membrorum corporis rationem culpæ habent ex voluntate totius hominis, quoniam membra corporis sunt voluntatis totius hominis organa, seu instrumenta, & eius imperio mouentur ; quo fit vt eorum actiones tribuantur voluntati personæ vt causæ principali, membris tantummodò vt causæ instrumentali. Nos autem, opinor, organa non fumus Adami, nec mouemur à voluntate Adami, nec ab eo imperantur actiones noftræ, nec, cùm quis generat, id facit vt causa instrumentalis, Adami voluntati obsequens.
units.tr: You bring forward a second comparison, drawn from the whole natural body, that is, the human body, and you express it in the words of Thomas Aquinas. I do not think you do this to shore up your opinion by his authority or to move me, for you know how little weight he carries in our Churches. Rather, his words seemed to you convenient and clear. As for me, I understand, in whatever way, the sense in which Thomas said these things, and because I understand it, I do not accept the doctrine, which is different from the mind of our Churches. But why you have quoted him here I do not grasp, unless perhaps you think exactly the same as Thomas about original sin, which I dare not suspect of you. Thomas holds that sin is transmitted through a corrupted origin of the flesh from Adam to us, or, as he puts it in the Summa, the first sin of the first man passes down to posterity by origin; and he shows how it reaches the rational soul through the seed. But even granting this transmission of sin, there remains a doubt, because the defects that are drawn from a corrupted origin do not have the character of guilt, for they do not deserve punishment but rather pity, as the Philosopher says of one who is born blind, or otherwise deprived in any other way. And this is because it belongs to the nature of guilt that it be voluntary and in the power of the person to whom the guilt is imputed. The question, then, was how those defects, or, as he puts it in the Summa, the infection, can have the character of sin when they are involuntary in infants. I shall weigh his answer part by part, since you praise it. It must be said, he says, that just as actual sin is the sin of the person, which is committed by the will of the person who sins, so original sin is the sin of nature, which is committed by the will of the principle of human nature. He distinguishes two sins, one actual and the other original: the one belongs to the person, the other to nature; the one is committed by the will of the sinning person, the other by the will of the principle of human nature. So were there two wills in Adam, one of the person and another of the principle of human nature? And was the sin committed by the will of the principle of human nature actual or not? If he meant to distinguish Adam's actual sin from the habitual corruption that he left in his faculties, the doctrine is sound, but it is poorly expressed. Moreover, if Adam's actual sin was the person's, how is it imputed to us? But let us go on. For it must be considered, he says, that just as the different members of the body are parts of the one person of a man, so all men are parts, and as it were certain members, of human nature; whence Porphyry says that by participation in the species many men are one man. The different members of the body are integral parts of the whole man. But all men are not integral parts of human nature. Nature is not composed of many men; otherwise, since human nature is whole in me, all men would be in me. They are rather logical or subjective parts, as they are commonly called in the schools; and nature, abstracted and separated from individuals and endowed with universality, is a logical or universal whole, but it has this character of a whole not from the thing itself but through the operation of our mind. So, speaking metaphysically, the matter is the reverse: the person is the whole, nature the part; the person is that which acts, nature that by which it acts. Thomas adds: We see that an act of sin carried out through some member, say the hand or foot, has the character of guilt not from the will of the hand or foot, but from the will of the whole man, from which the motion of sin is derived to the individual members as from a certain principle. Similarly, from the will of Adam, who was the principle of human nature, the whole disorder of nature has the character of guilt in all to whom it comes, insofar as they are subject to guilt. Please notice how badly this comparison holds together. In the preceding words he was setting nature alongside the person and all men alongside the members of the body; from this arose the comparison that as the person stands to the members of the body, so nature stands to all men. Enough of this, as I have hinted, is faulty: for the person is not the principle by which the act is done with the members as the instrument by which; nor is nature the principle by which, and men are the principles by which sin is committed. On the contrary, as I have already said. Now, how does he apply this comparison to his purpose? An act of sin carried out through a member, he says, has the character of sin not from the will of that member, but of the whole person. I expected him to conclude: therefore an act of sin carried out through a man does not have the character of sin from the will of that man, but from the will of human nature. But he changed the terms: in place of an act carried out through men or a man, he put the whole disorder of nature, and in place of the will of human nature he put the will of Adam, who was the principle of human nature. Yet first, speaking precisely, it is false that Adam was the principle of human nature; rather, on the contrary, human nature was the principle of Adam. For nature is in a way a part of the supposit, and a part is in some way the principle of that which it composes; and, as the logicians say, human nature is prior to Adam in the order of existence. Adam is therefore a principle or cause not absolutely of human nature, but of the human nature that was in his posterity; just as any father is a principle of the nature of his offspring, not of his own. Next, Adam's will was as much the will of his person as mine is mine; nor do I see why it should be called the will of nature. For even if Adam was the principle of human nature, it does not follow that his will was the will of nature; it follows only that Adam was the principle of the will of human nature, or else that human nature has no will, or at most that Adam's will was the principle of the will of nature. I am sorry to linger longer in this scholastic dust of empty subtleties, in which you have entangled me by means of Thomas, whom I could otherwise scatter and dissipate from his own authors with a fan of many arguments. But here it will be enough to note two limps in this comparison. First, the act carried out through some member of the body does not have the character of guilt from that member's will but from the will of the whole man, because that member has no will of its own. But each man has his own will. So a separated member neither sins nor acts. Individual men, separated from Adam, both act and sin in many ways, and their actions are sins, not because they proceed from Adam's will, but because, proceeding from each one's own will, they clash with the law of God. Next, I would like to learn why this comparison is said to hold only with respect to that first actual sin, and not to the sins that followed. Did Adam's will cease to be the will of nature as soon as he sinned, or did Adam cease to be the principle of human nature? The comparison would thus make the rest of Adam's sins imputed to us no less than the first, contrary to the Apostle, Rom. 5. I add a third limp: the actions of the members of the body have the character of guilt from the will of the whole man because the members of the body are the organs or instruments of the will of the whole man, and are moved by its command; hence their actions are attributed to the will of the person as principal cause, and to the members only as instrumental cause. But we, I think, are not Adam's organs, nor are we moved by Adam's will, nor are our actions commanded by him; nor, when someone begets, does he do so as an instrumental cause, obeying the will of Adam.

units.la: - Præter hos omnes defectus quos memoraui, laborat alio vitio hæc Thomæ Aquinatis similitudo & ratiocinatio, eóque maximo. Non enim propositæ difficultati vllo modo satisfacit. Vrgere enim id pofsum, quod etiam doctissimus Chamierus aduersus Pighium & Salmeronem vrget. Eius verba ascribam, Cùm peccatum dicitur esse voluntarium, intelligendum est de voluntate eius, cuius peccatum esse dicitur. At hoc certe sensu non potest dici in nobis peccatum illud Adami esse voluntarium, multo minus actus nostræ voluntatis. Neque enim est in nostra voluntate, neque à nostra voluntate: quia reipsa nostra voluntas nunquam fuit voluntas Adami. Si ergo nostræ voluntatis respectu voluntarium non est Adami peccatum, sed tantùm respectu voluntatis Adami, certè nostrum peccatum non est, sed solius Adami.
units.tr: Apart from all the defects I have mentioned, this comparison and reasoning of Thomas Aquinas suffers from another fault, and a very serious one. It does not satisfy the difficulty proposed. For I can press the point that the most learned Chamier also presses against Pighius and Salmeron. I will quote his words: When sin is said to be voluntary, it must be understood of the will of the person whose sin it is said to be. But in that sense it cannot be said that Adam's sin was voluntary in us, much less an act of our will. For it is neither in our will nor from our will, because in fact our will never was Adam's will. If therefore Adam's sin is voluntary not with respect to our will but only with respect to Adam's will, then certainly it is not our sin but Adam's alone.

units.la: Tu quidem ais, voluntatem Adami, cum peccauit, fuisse voluntatem omnium hominum: sed affirmanti, nec rationem afferenti oppono Chamierum, voluntas nostra nunquam fuit voluntas Adami. Cùm enim hæc propositio fit negans, conuertitur simpliciter in hanc, Voluntas Adami nunquam fuit voluntas nostra. Vin tui huius dicti protraham in lucem absurditatem?
units.tr: You say that Adam's will, when he sinned, was the will of all men. But against your affirmation, which offers no reason, I set Chamier: our will never was Adam's will. For since this proposition is negative, it converts simply into this one: Adam's will never was our will. Shall I bring out into the light the absurdity of your statement?

units.la: 1. Si voluntas Adami fuit voluntas omnium hominum ; igitur fuit voluntas vniuersalis. Atqui constat tam lingularem fuisse , quàm alius cuiusuis. 2. Si voluntas Adami fuit, exempli causa, mea voluntas, igitur etiam eius anima fuit mea anima, & eius corpus fuit meum corpus , & eius os fuit meum os, & eius vxor fuit mea vxor &c. 3. Si voluntas Adami fuit mea voluntas , igitur duas habeo voluntates, vnam aliquot millibus annorum antequam essem ; alteram creatam nuper, annis abhinc feré quinquaginta, alteram ab altera realiter, immò localiter, diuisam & separatam , vnam communem, alteram propriam. Porrò si duas voluntates habeo, etiam duas animas, duo corpora. Itaque qui me vnum hominem esse putabam , euasi in duos, vnum communem, alterum proprium ; illum pridem fato suo functum , hunc adhuc viuentem. Noli confugere ad figuras sermonis. Vis enim nobis omnibus veré & proprie imputari peccatum Adami, ac proinde nos illud veré & proprie commisisse. Non commisimus autem veré & proprie,nisi voluntas Adami qua commissum est veré & proprie nostra fuerit voluntas. 4. Si voluntas Adami fuit voluntas omnium hominum , igitur actus voluntatis Adami fuerunt actus omnium hominum : idem dicendum de actibus mentis. Quod si actus voluntatis eius eliciti fuerunt actus omnium hominum , etiam proculdubio actus eius voluntatis imperati. Cum loquebatur, loquebantur omnes homines ; cum ambulabat , ambulabant omnes ; cum edebat edebant omnes ; cum gignebat , gignebant omnes. Hoccine tibi probatur ? nisi fortasse vis hoc priuilegium habuisse voluntatem Adami vt nostra effet voluntas , pro eo duntaxat momento quo peccauit : mallem fuisset alio potius tempore.
units.tr: (1) If Adam's will was the will of all men, then it was a universal will. But it is clear that it was as singular as the will of anyone else. (2) If Adam's will was, for example, my will, then his soul was my soul, his body was my body, his mouth was my mouth, his wife was my wife, and so on. (3) If Adam's will was my will, then I have two wills: one that existed some thousands of years before I did, and another created only recently, about fifty years ago, the one divided and separated from the other really, and even locally; one common, the other my own. Moreover, if I have two wills, I also have two souls and two bodies. So I, who thought I was one man, have turned into two: one common, the other my own; the former long since dead, the latter still living. Do not take refuge in figures of speech. For you wish that the sin of Adam be truly and properly imputed to us all, and therefore that we truly and properly committed it. But we did not truly and properly commit it unless the will of Adam by which it was committed was truly and properly our will. (4) If Adam's will was the will of all men, then the acts of Adam's will were the acts of all men; the same must be said of the acts of his mind. And if the acts of his will were elicited acts of all men, then without doubt so too were the acts of his will that were commanded. When he spoke, all men spoke; when he walked, all walked; when he ate, all ate; when he begot, all begot. Does this seem proven to you? Unless perhaps you wish Adam's will to have had this privilege, that it should be our will only for that moment in which he sinned. I would have preferred that it had been at some other time.

units.la: GAR. Respondeo. Voluntatem Adæ fuisse voluntatem omnium, satis tritum est apud Theologos, neque Augustino ignoratum. Per vnius enim Adami voluntatem malam omnes in eo peccauerunt, quando omnes illi vnus fuerunt, inquit de Nupt. & Concup. lib. 1. cap 5. Et tamen hoc dictum non modo tanquam dubium, aut improbabile, aut falsum vir doctus exagitat; verum etiam, tanquam ineptum & fatuum, & anilium fabularum nugamenta superans, traducit, atque subsannat.
units.tr: GAR. I reply. That Adam's will was the will of all is quite a commonplace among the theologians, and it is not unknown to Augustine. For through the evil will of the one Adam all sinned in him, since all were that one, he says in On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 1, chapter 5. And yet this learned man not only attacks this saying as doubtful, improbable or false; he also, as silly and foolish, and surpassing the trifles of old wives' tales, twists it and mocks it.

units.la: PLAC. Negaui, praeeunte Chamicro praesenti Theologo, Adami voluntatem fuisse nostram voluntatem, & quae, si dicatur fuisse nostra voluntas, sequantur absurda, absque vllo afpectiore verbo, ostendi. Fecine ea in re quicquam praeter officium meum? At voluntatem Adae fuisse voluntatem omnium satis tritum est apud Theologos. Petamus, quos? Eorum certe autoritas non impediuit, quominus Chamierus, & ipse, opinor, Theologus, id negaret. Cur mihi quoque id negare non licuit? Opponitur mihi Augustinus, qui tamen totus meus est. Dixitne voluntatem Adami fuisse voluntatem omnium? Non, sed per vnius illius voluntatem malam omnes in eo peccasse, quando omnes illi (malum ille) vnus fuerunt, de quo propterea singuli peccatum originale traxerunt. Quando autem vnus fuerunt? nimirum quando ipsi non fuerunt, sed vnus fuit vnde suum esse traxerunt.
