Quomodo in eo tunc peccauerunt? nimirum ipsi tunc non peccarunt, sed ille peccauit cuius ex peccato suum singuli peccatum originale traxerunt. Id autem peccatum, non per voluntatem omnium, sed per voluntatem vnius illius commissum est. Cum ergo dicit fuisse voluntatem vnius illius, non affirmat, sed negat potius fuisse voluntatem omnium. At dicit omnes fuisse illum vnum, nempe quando ille vnus fuit, & ipsi non fuerunt. Simul enim ac ipsi esse coeperunt, non fuerunt amplius vnus, sed ab eo vno diuersi, id quod arguit vox quando: innuit enim quo tempore loquebatur, eos non esse amplius vnum. Si ex quo fumus, non fumus vnus ille homo, certe ex quo fumus eius voluntas non est noftra voluntas, nec ad eam similem habemus relationem ei quam habent membra ad voluntatem totius hominis, vt verbis Thomae asseuerabatis cum quo disputabam. Mihi igitur fauet potius Augustinus quàm nocet. Vis scire quomodo per voluntatem vnius peccauimus? Ex voluntate, inquit, peccatum est. Quaerit forte vtrum & originale peccatum. Respondeo prorsus & originale peccatum, quia & hoc ex voluntate primi hominis seminatum est, vt & in illo esset, & in omnes transiret. Putatne cum viro docto id per imputationem transire, & huius causam vnicam esse Dei voluntatem? Contra plane i contendit neque Deo, neque naturae humanae vt est a Deo, sed concupiscentiae seu libidini qua a parentibus in liberos transit per semen debere ascribi. Distinguit enim hac duo, & bonum laudanda coniunctionis, vnde filij generantur, & malum pudenda libidinis vnde qui generantur regenerandi sunt, ne damnentur. Distinguit natura in semine humano ab eius vitio. Illa quippe, inquit, habet authorem Deum, ex ipso autem trahitur originale peccatum. Nam si semen ipsum nullum habet vitium, quid est quod scriptum est &c. Et paulo post, Nunquid in Adam natura ista sic condita est? Absit, sed quia in illo vitiata sic per omnes iam naturaliter cucurrit & currit, vt ab hac perditione non liberet, nisi gratia Dei per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Hoc enim, inquit, traiecit parens in prolem carnalem quod & ipse carnaliter natus, non quod spiritualiter est renatus, quia id ipsum quod carnaliter natus est, quamuis reatu soluto non impediat fructum eius, tamen tanquam in semine oliua latet &c. Hac omnino concupiscentia, hac lex peccati habitans in membris &c. Hac, inquam, concupiscentia, qua solo sacramento regenerationis expiatur, profecto peccati vinculum generatione traycit in posteros, nisi ab illo & ipsi generatione soluantur. Hoc generi humano inflictum vulnus a Diabolo, quicquid per illud nascitur, cogit esse sub diabolo, tanquam a suo frutice fructum iure decerpat, non quod ab illo sit natura humana, qua non est nisi ex Deo, sed vitium quod non est ex Deo. Non enim propter seipsam qua laudabilis est, quia opus Dei est, sed propter damnabile vitium quo vitiata est, natura humana damnatur. Non vult immediate ab Adamo per imputationem vitium descendere, sed mediate, & a proxima cuiusque parentis vitio per carnalem generatione traiici in prolem. Cumque inquirat, quomodo quod dimissum est in parente trabatur in prolem, id quidem miris modis fieri dicit, sed tamen fieri: Et illustrat exemplo oliuæ ex qua nascitur oleaster. Mirum est ergo, inquit, quemadmodum à peccati vinculo per gratiam liberati: gignant tamen eodem vinculo obstrictos, quo, eodem modo oporteat liberari. Fatemur, mirum est. Sed quod latent fœtus oleastrorum etiam in feminibus olearum, quando & hoc credetur, nisi experientia probaretur? Proinde sicut gignitur ex oleastri femine oleaster, & ex olea femine nonnisi oleaster &c. Si idem cum viro docto sensisset, non confugiret ad naturam, non ad carnalem generationem, non ad vitium proximorum parentum, non ad oleastri exemplum, sed ad voluntatem Dei, cui placuit omnibus Adami posteris peccatum actuale immediate imputare, & vt illud imputatum puniret, & satisfieret iustitiæ, ipsis omnibus vitium illud originale infligere. Alter enim illius reirationem reddi non posse clamat vir doctus multis locis, ac nominatim cap.11. §.8. de quo supra pag.125.
units.tr: PLAC. Following the present theologian Chamier, I denied that Adam's will was our will, and I showed, without any more polished word, what absurdities follow if it is said to be our will. Did I in this matter do anything beyond my duty? But that Adam's will was the will of all is quite a commonplace among the theologians. Let us ask: which theologians? Certainly their authority did not prevent Chamier, and myself too, I think, a theologian, from denying it. Why was I not also allowed to deny it? Augustine is set against me, yet he is wholly on my side. Did he say that Adam's will was the will of all? No, but through the evil will of that one, all sinned in him, since all were that one (who was evil), from whom for that reason each one drew original sin. But when were they that one? Clearly when they did not yet exist, but that one existed, from whom they drew their being. In what way did they sin in him then? Clearly they did not then sin, but he sinned, from whose sin each one drew original sin. That sin, however, was committed not through the will of all, but through the will of that one alone. So when he says there was the will of that one alone, he does not affirm but rather denies that there was the will of all. But he says that all were that one, namely when that one existed and they did not. For as soon as they began to exist, they were no longer one, but diverse from that one, which the word when shows: for it indicates the time at which he was speaking, when they were no longer one. If from the time we exist we are not that one man, then certainly from the time we exist his will is not our will, nor do we bear to it the relation that the members bear to the will of the whole man, as you asserted in the words of Thomas, with whom I was disputing. Augustine therefore favours me rather than harms me. Do you want to know how we sinned through the will of one? Sin, he says, is from the will. Perhaps he asks whether original sin too is so. I reply: wholly and also original sin, because this too was sown from the will of the first man, so that it was both in him and passed into all. Does he think, with the learned man, that this passes by imputation, and that the sole cause of it is the will of God? On the contrary, he plainly contends that it must be ascribed neither to God nor to human nature as it is from God, but to concupiscence or lust, by which it passes from parents to children through the seed. For he distinguishes these two: the good of the praiseworthy union from which children are begotten, and the evil of shameful lust from which those who are begotten must be reborn, lest they be condemned. He distinguishes nature in human seed from its vice. For that, he says, has God as its author, but original sin is drawn from the seed itself. For if the seed itself has no vice, what is it that is written, etc.? And a little later: Was that nature thus created in Adam? Far from it, but because in him it was so vitiated that it has now run and runs through all naturally, so that it cannot be freed from this ruin except by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. For the parent, he says, passed on to the carnal offspring what he himself, born carnally, not what he was reborn spiritually, because that very thing which he was born with in the flesh, although once the guilt is loosed it does not hinder its fruit, yet lies hidden as in the seed of an olive, etc. This entirely concupiscence, this law of sin dwelling in the members, etc. This concupiscence, I say, which is cleansed only by the sacrament of regeneration, has certainly carried the bond of sin by generation to posterity, unless they too are loosed from it by generation. The wound inflicted on the human race by the Devil: whatever is born through it, it compels to be under the devil, so that he may rightfully pluck the fruit as from his own bush; not because human nature is from him, for it is from God alone, but because of the vice, which is not from God. For human nature is condemned not on account of itself, which is praiseworthy because it is God's work, but on account of the damnable vice by which it is vitiated. He does not wish that vice to descend immediately from Adam by imputation, but mediately, and from the nearest vice of each parent, passed on into the offspring by carnal generation. And when he asks how what was left in the parent is drawn into the offspring, he says that this indeed happens in wondrous ways, yet that it does happen, and he illustrates it by the example of the olive from which the wild olive is born. It is wonderful, therefore, he says, how those who are freed from the bond of sin through grace nevertheless beget offspring bound by the same bond, from which they ought in the same way to be freed. We admit it is wonderful. But how would it be believed that the offspring of wild olives lie hidden even in the seeds of olives, unless it were proved by experience? Therefore, just as a wild olive is begotten from the seed of a wild olive, and from the seed of an olive only a wild olive, etc. If he had thought the same as the learned man, he would not have fled to nature, nor to carnal generation, nor to the vice of the nearest parents, nor to the example of the wild olive, but to the will of God, who was pleased to impute to all the posterity of Adam the actual sin immediately, and, in order to punish that imputed sin and satisfy justice, to inflict that original vice on all of them. For the learned man cries out in many places that no other reason for that can be given, and especially in chapter 11, section 8, which I discussed above on page 125.

units.la: Vide amus tamen, an ista colligendi ratio, vt iocularis argutiola laudem habere potest, ita soliditatis habeat. Etenim respondeo, eam Adami voluntatem, de qua loquimur, & singularen fuisse, & vniuersalem. Singularem actus proprietate; vniuersalem repræsentationis iure. Singularem, quia ab vno ex indiuiduis humanis profecta est: vniuersalem, quia indiuiduum illud repræsentauit vniuersum genus, vt eo per voluntatem suam primum peccante, idem fuerit, ac si omnes per propriam suam voluntatem peccassent. 2. Voluntatem Adæ cum dicimus fuisse voluntatem omnium, non loquimur de voluntate prout significat facultatem illam λογικὴν, quæ Adamo ex natura principiis inerat, & sine qua ne homo quidem fuisset: sed voluntatis nomine intelligimus volitionem, siue actum illum volendi quem exercuit circa fructum arboris vetita, & quo se reum fecit inobedientia illius prima. Neque dicimus actum illum volendi fuisse omnium proprie, formaliter, aut personaliter, sed interpretatiue & per imputationem. Itaque quæ inde nectuntur conclusiuncula, Adami animam, corpus, vxorem fuisse nostra; nos habere duas voluntates, animas, corpora, & esse duos homines, ea loco possit habere aliquis, quo haberi voluit vir doctus illud Theologorum effatum.
units.tr: Let us nevertheless see whether this method of inference, though it may earn praise as a witty little subtlety, has any soundness. I answer that the will of Adam of which we speak was both singular and universal. Singular by the property of the act; universal by the right of representation. Singular, because it proceeded from one of the individual human beings; universal, because that individual represented the whole human race, so that when he sinned by his will, it was the same as if all had sinned by their own will. 2. When we say that the will of Adam was the will of all, we are not speaking of the will as signifying that rational faculty which was inherent in Adam by the principles of his nature, and without which man would not even be man. By the name of will we understand volition, or that act of willing which he exercised concerning the fruit of the forbidden tree, and by which he made himself guilty through his first disobedience. Nor do we say that this act of willing belonged to all properly, formally, or personally, but interpretively and by imputation. Therefore the little conclusions that follow from this, that Adam's soul, body and wife were ours, that we have two wills, two souls, two bodies, and are two men, may have whatever place anyone likes, in which the learned man wished the saying of the theologians to be held.

units.la: PLAC. Ergo, fi fides habetur viro doćto, cum voluntas Adami dicitur voluntas omnium, nihil aliud significatur, nisi voluntatem illam qua primum peccauit, hoc est, primam eius inobedientiam esse omnium per imputationem: id quod toto hoc libro refellimus. Sed quo iure est omnium? Est, inquit, vniuersalis repræfentationis iure. Estne igitur, vt loquuntur, vniuerlalis in repræsentando? Non, opinor, hoc voluit. Quid ergo voluit? nam quo fuit voluntas omnium, eo fuit voluntas vniuersalis; vniuersale enim & commune idem videntur significare. Fuit autem, fi illi creditur, omnium imputatione. Fuit ergo etiam vniuersalis imputatione. Cur ergo non dixit, fuisse vniuersalem imputationis iure? Placuit verborum copia, & distinćtionum speciosa multiplicatio retento tamen eodem sensu. Fortasse voluit, voluntatem Adami fuisse vniuerfalem repræfentationis iure, quo scilicet omnes nostras voluntates, seu potius volitiones (nam per voluntatem intelligit volitionem) repræsentauit. Sed quis vnquam dixerat, volitionem Adami repræfentaffe volitiones omnium hominum? Et quis tale ius excogitauerat? Probabilius est cum intellexiffe ius repræfentationis, quo scilicet Adamus repræsentauit omnes homines. At fi repræsentauit omnes homines, potuit non minus quàm sua voluntas, dici homo vniuersalis: quo tamen elogio nondum, vt opinor, à quoquam est insignitus. Deinde merito quæri potest, quo fundamento istiusmodi & repræfentatio, & repræfentationis ius nitatur. Proferetur fortaffe fœdus illud initum cum toto genere humano in Adamo, quod ad imputationem immediatam tuendam viri quidam docti præter Scripturam & naturam excogitarunt: Sed de eo & iam dićtum est, & nihil necesse est nunc disputare. Hæc enim obiter hoc loco obseruare volui: redeo ad id de quo agebatur in Manuscripto, & quod mihi videtur vir doćtus hac tua refponfione detorsisse in alienum sensum. Patet enim ex verbis Thomæ, quibus suam mentem is vir doćtus, quicum mihi res erat, exposuit, per voluntatem, non ipsam volitionem, sed volitionis principium intelligi, sicut per membra, non actio membrorum, sed huius principia significantur. Confiderantur enim à Thoma omnes homines tanquam partes seu membra naturæ humanæ, & voluntas Adami vt voluntas totius naturæ, vel, vt loquitur, principij naturæ humanæ: quæ comparatio flagitat, vt quemadmodum membra non significant actiones membrorum, sed illarum principia, sic voluntas non significet actionem voluntatis, sed eius principium. Natura per actum voluntatis principij sui traxit rationem culpæ, membra naturæ trahunt eam per actum naturæ qui est generatio. Id cui ratio illa culpæ inest est inordinatio naturæ. Discrimen inter meam & Thomæ sententiam hoc est, quod illam inordinationem naturæ volo per se culpæ rationè habere ex eo quod inest in voluntate & repugnat legi Dei, Thomas vero ex ordine quem habet ad volu ntatem Adami.
units.tr: PLAC. Therefore, if credit is given to the learned man, when the will of Adam is said to be the will of all, nothing else is signified than that the will by which he first sinned, that is, his first disobedience, belongs to all by imputation. This is what we refute throughout this whole book. But by what right is it of all? It is, he says, by the right of universal representation. Is it then universal in representing, as they say? No, I think he did not mean this. What then did he mean? For insofar as it was the will of all, it was a universal will, since "universal" and "common" seem to signify the same thing. But it was, if one believes him, of all by imputation. Therefore it was also universal by imputation. Why then did he not say that it was universal by the right of imputation? He preferred an abundance of words and a showy multiplication of distinctions, while keeping the same sense. Perhaps he meant that the will of Adam was universal by the right of representation, namely because it represented all our wills, or rather our volitions (for by will he understands volition). But who has ever said that the volition of Adam represented the volitions of all men? And who had devised such a right? It is more probable that he understood the right of representation by which Adam represented all men. But if he represented all men, he could be called universal man no less than his will could be called universal; yet, as I think, no one has yet honoured him with that title. Then it can rightly be asked on what foundation such a representation, and such a right of representation, rests. Perhaps there will be put forward that covenant made with the whole human race in Adam, which some learned men have devised, beyond Scripture and nature, to defend immediate imputation. But of this too has already been said, and there is no need to dispute it now. I wished to note these things in passing at this point. I return to what was under discussion in the manuscript, and what seems to me to have been twisted by that learned man in this reply of yours into an alien sense. For it is clear from the words of Thomas, by which that learned man, with whom I had the dispute, set out his own mind, that by will is understood not the volition itself but the principle of volition, just as by members are signified not the actions of the members but their principles. For all men are considered by Thomas as parts or members of human nature, and the will of Adam as the will of the whole nature, or, as he puts it, the principle of human nature. This comparison requires that, just as members do not signify the actions of members but their principles, so the will does not signify the action of the will but its principle. Nature, by the act of the will of its principle, drew the character of guilt; the members of nature draw it by the act of nature, which is generation. That in which this character of guilt inheres is the disorder of nature. The difference between my opinion and Thomas's is this: I want that disorder of nature to have the character of guilt in itself, because it inheres in the will and opposes the law of God; but Thomas holds it because of the order it has to the will of Adam.

units.la: · G A R. Quid si accedat aliquis de Socini schola, & arma mutuatus a viro doêto similibus conclusionum tormentis agat adversus id quod habet Gallica S. Cœna liturgia, vt tutem mortis Christi ad multiam nobis imputari, non minus quam si eam nos ipsi pertulissimus? Si actus ille voluntatis Christi, quo se in mortem obtulit, tam tuus est, quàm si tu actu proprio voluntatis tuæ te ipsum obtulisses, quidni etiam tua fuerit anima, corpus, mater Christi? Quidni duas voluntates habere dicaris, unam antequam esses, alteram post quam fuisti? &c.
units.tr: · G A R. What if someone from the school of Socinus should come forward, and borrowing arms from a learned man, should wage war with similar engines of argument against what the Gallican liturgy of the Holy Supper says, namely that the virtue of Christ's death is imputed to us no less than if we ourselves had suffered it? If that act of Christ's will by which he offered himself to death is as much yours as if you had offered yourself by your own act of will, why should not your soul, your body, and your mother also be Christ's? Why should you not be said to have two wills, one before you existed and another after you came to be? &c.

units.la: PLAC. Dixitne liturgia illa, voluntatem Christi fuisse voluntatem omnium nostrum? Aut actum illum voluntatis Christi, quo se in mortem obtulit, fuisse actum omnium nostrum? Minime: dixit tantum, virtutem mortis Christi ad iustitiam nobis imputari. Aliud autem est virtus mortis Christi, aliud voluntas Christi. Nihil igitur video in verbis liturgiæ unde tales consequentiæ deduci possint. Cur autem virtus mortis Christi nobis imputatur? Annon quia mortem luere tenebamur, ille, vt vas nostrum, eam loco nostro luit? Itaque nostra est Dei & Christi donatione, nostraque per fidem acceptione. Num similiter Adamus vas noster fuit, vt loco nostro peccaret? Aut eius peccatum factum est dono Dei, & Adami, & nostra acceptione, nostrum? Reliqua quæ addit hoc loco vir doctus egere non videntur refutatione præsertim, si meminerit, candide lector, eorum quæ dicta sunt a nobis supra pag. 163. Cum assertionem, voluntatem Adami fuisse voluntatem omnium oppugnaui, non putabam illius hunc esse sensum, volitionem, quam Adamus circa arborem vetitam exercuit, omnibus imputari.
units.tr: PLAC. Did that liturgy say that the will of Christ was the will of all of us? Or that that act of Christ's will, by which he offered himself to death, was the act of all of us? Not at all: it said only that the virtue of Christ's death is imputed to us for righteousness. But the virtue of Christ's death is one thing, and the will of Christ another. I see nothing, therefore, in the words of the liturgy from which such consequences could be deduced. But why is the virtue of Christ's death imputed to us? Is it not because we were bound to pay the penalty of death, and he, as our surrogate, paid it in our place? So it is ours by the gift of God and Christ, and ours by our acceptance through faith. Was Adam, likewise, our surrogate, to sin in our place? Or was his sin made ours by the gift of God and of Adam, and by our acceptance? The rest that the learned man adds here does not seem to need refutation, especially if, candid reader, you remember what has been said by us above at p. 163. When I attacked the assertion that the will of Adam was the will of all, I did not think its meaning was this: that the volition which Adam exercised concerning the forbidden tree is imputed to all.

units.la: Sequentia Thomæ verba quæ tu adscripsisti etsi verum continent, prætermittenda non sunt. Et sicut peccatum actuale, quod est peccatum per se trahitur ad singula membra per aliquem actum personalem, ita peccatum originale trahitur ad singulos homines per actum naturæ qui est generatio. Rursus peccatum actuale distinguit ab originali, & utrumque vult in Adamo fuisse: illud personæ, hoc naturæ. Necesse est igitur ut per originale corruptionem intelligat ex peccato actuali ortam. Quare non voluit peccatum actuale, quod personæ est, nobis imputari: immo nec vitium naturæ quatenus in Adamo hæsit, ut mox videbimus: alioqui imputanda etiam nobis esset generatio, qua secundum nostrum parentem Sethum Adamus genuit, quandoquidem illa Teste Thoma actus fuit natura. Subjicit, Et ita sicut per generationem humana natura trahitur, ita etiam per generationem traducitur desectus humanæ naturæ qui est consecutus ex peccato primi parentis. Nihil verius. Mea hæc est sententia. Unde concludo, quemadmodum natura humana trahitur per generationem absque imputatione naturæ Adami, sic trahi per generationem defectus naturæ humanæ absque imputatione peccati actualis Adami. Trahitur mente vitium naturæ per actum naturæ, non per actum Dei imputantis nobis peccatum Adami, & hos defectus infligentis.
units.tr: The following words of Thomas which you have added, although they contain truth, must not be passed over. And just as actual sin, which is sin in itself, is drawn to the individual members through some personal act, so original sin is drawn to the individual men through the act of nature, which is generation. Again he distinguishes actual from original sin, and wants both to have been in Adam: the former belonging to the person, the latter to nature. It is necessary, therefore, that by original corruption he means that which arose from actual sin. Hence he did not want actual sin, which belongs to the person, to be imputed to us; indeed nor the vice of nature insofar as it clung to Adam, as we shall soon see. Otherwise the generation by which Adam begot Seth, our parent, would also have to be imputed to us, since, according to the testimony of Thomas, that was an act of nature. He adds: And so, just as human nature is drawn by generation, so also by generation is drawn the defect of human nature which followed from the sin of the first parent. Nothing could be truer. This is my opinion too. From it I conclude that, just as human nature is drawn by generation without imputation of Adam's nature, so the defect of human nature is drawn by generation without imputation of Adam's actual sin. The vice of nature is drawn to the mind through the act of nature, not through an act of God imputing to us the sin of Adam and inflicting these defects upon us.

units.la: Adjunxisti alia eiusdem Thomæ verba in quibus occurrit verbum imputandi, quod tu majusculis literis pinxisti. Subit mirari qui in cæteris controuerfiis Thomæ Aquinatis,aliorumque fcholafticorū Pontificiorum authoritatē nullo loco habent, in hac quæstione ea apud eos niti qui eam ipsi quoque constenunt: nempe dogma istud de imputatione peccati actualis Adami omnibus hominibus nec antiquum est,& non aliunde primùm fluxit quàm ex lacunis quorundam scholasticorum , quos ne nominare quidem Lombardus Thomæ magister, adeò obscuri erant, voluit. Thomas autem quamuis & imputandi verbo vsus sit & tuæ causæ in speciem fauere videatur,tamen reuera abest à tua sententia haud parum , & mirum est te id non vidisse in his ipsis verbis quæ citas , Adam, inquit, peccans vitiauit naturam humanam , sed postmodum in alijs Natura vitiata ( non igitur imputatio peccati actualis Adæ) inficit personam , dum scilicet genito imputatur ad culpam ℨATVRAE VITIVM propter voluntatem primi parentis, vt dictum est. nonne vides verbi imputatur nominatiuum esse natura vitium? dabis autem proculdubio mihi vitium naturæ non esse peccatum actuale Adami , quod Thomas constanter docet fuisse peccatum personæ. Nempe omnis in eo erat Thomas vt ostenderet quomodo ista nobis inhærens naturæ infectio seu vitium culpæ rationem habere possit,cùm sit inuoluntaria. Affirmat igitur vt actus per membrum exercitus habet rationem culpæ & imputatur membro propter voluntatem non ipsius membri sed totius personæ , sic vitium tractum ab Adamo & genito inhærens culpæ rationem habere & imputari genito ad culpam , non propter voluntatem geniti cuius respectu inuoluntarium est , sed propter voluntatem primi parentis. Itaque addidit vt dictum est, nempe verbis præcedentibus. Quæ nos à tc à te citata expendimus. Id ipsum dilucidius exponit in sum. Theol.loco à te in margine notato, sed piget eius verba transcribere. Ausim affirmare imputationem peccati actualis Adami toti eius posteritati & inflictionem priuationis iustitiæ originalis omnibus hominibus in pœnam illius peccati imputati ignotas fuisse Thomæ Aquinati, & possem id si opus esset necessariis argumentis demonstrare.
units.tr: You have added other words of the same Thomas, in which the word "imputed" occurs, and you have printed it in capital letters. One is surprised that those who, in the other controversies, make no account of the authority of Thomas Aquinas and of the other Papist schoolmen, rest on it in this question, a question where they themselves also disagree. The doctrine that Adam's actual sin is imputed to all men is neither ancient, nor did it first arise from anywhere other than the obscure corners of certain schoolmen, whom Lombard, Thomas's own master, did not even wish to name, so obscure were they. Thomas, however, although he uses the word "imputed" and seems to favour your cause in appearance, is in reality quite far from your opinion, and it is strange that you did not see this in the very words you cite: Adam, he says, sinning vitiated human nature, but afterwards in others the vitiated nature (therefore not the imputation of Adam's actual sin) infects the person, namely when fault is imputed to the begotten on account of the vice of nature, through the will of the first parent, as has been said. Do you not see that the nominative of is imputed is the vice of nature? Surely you will grant me that the vice of nature is not Adam's actual sin, which Thomas consistently teaches was a sin of the person. Indeed, Thomas's whole aim was to show how this inherent infection of nature, which is involuntary, can nevertheless have the character of fault. He affirms, therefore, that just as an act carried out through a member has the character of fault and is imputed to the member on account of the will not of the member itself but of the whole person, so the vice drawn from Adam and inhering in the begotten can have the character of fault and be imputed to the begotten as fault, not on account of the will of the begotten, with respect to which it is involuntary, but on account of the will of the first parent. Hence he added as has been said, namely in the preceding words. These are the words you cite, which we have weighed. He explains the same thing more clearly in the Summa Theologiae passage you noted in the margin, but I am reluctant to transcribe his words. I would venture to affirm that the imputation of Adam's actual sin to his whole posterity, and the infliction on all men of the privation of original righteousness as the punishment of that imputed sin, were unknown to Thomas Aquinas, and I could demonstrate this by necessary arguments if it were needed.

units.la: Tertiam similitudinem petis à corpore ciuili. Ea bimembris est. Primum enim nobis ob oculos constituit Regem inferentem bellum vicinæ genti, qui non solum ipse qui inferre voluit, & in consilio decreuit, & armis persecutus est, habetur pro hoste, sed etiam omnes subditi, quorum plerique nec voluerunt, nec consenserunt huic bello, & quanquam non agunt, & domi maneant, si tamen in manus hostium veniant, excipiuntur incauti, concutiuntur, & iure belli interficiuntur. Attende, quæso, quàm non quadret hæc similitudo. Principiò si admittatur, fatendum erit, quemadmodum ab hoste capiuntur, & necantur qui nec bellum probant, nec in id consentiunt, nec vllo modo consilij Regis sunt participes, sic etiamsi nihil in nobis esset vitij, atque à peccato voluntas nostra abhorreret, tamen nobis imputari peccatum actuale Adami: quod qui tecum sentiunt multi non audent fateri. Deinde, consequens esset non solum primum peccatum Adami, sed reliqua etiam eius peccata actualia nobis esse imputanda: quippe cum generis humani caput fuerit quamdiu vixit. Tertiò, si peccatum Capitis imputatur corpori, cur non etiam peccatum corporis imputetur capiti? nam si Adam & reliqui homines vnum simul corpus siue totum constituunt, quàm toti corpori membra singula conueniunt, tam etiam singulorum membrorum attributa conueniunt toti: corpus enim non est vnum membrum, sed multa: nec si pes caput non est, consequens est pedem non esse ex corpore. Imputatur autem toti corpori non modò quod caput facit, sed etiam quod pes. Itaque cùm populum suum Deus consideraret vt vnum corpus in deserto, toti populo ob vnius Achan, qui populi illius caput non erat, iratus est. Si ergo omnes homines coalescunt cum Adamo in vnum corpus, non vnius Adami vnum peccatum, sed omnia Adami, omnia aliorum hominum peccata toti corpori imputanda sunt. Quod tamen nec Apostolus, nec tu secundum Apostolum probas. Quartò, quid obstat quominus hæc similitudo accommodetur etiam aliis stirpibus & parentibus respectu posterorum? Exempli causa, cur Noachus etiam non sit secundi mundi caput, Abrahamus Israëlitarum, & ita de reliquis? unde magna exurget moles peccatorum imputandorum? Caput enim dicitur Adamus, & regi comparatur, non quia primus homo fuit, sed quia ab eo ducimus originem. Negatione relationis ad priorem ad nos minimè refertur, sed relatione, quam generando sibi acquisiuit, ad posteros. Quintò, si quis in manus hostium incidat quem certò nouerint à bello fuisse & voluntate, & opere alienum, nec in id consensisse, hunc si interficiunt innocentem, mihi immanes & crudeles esse videntur. Alioqui quæ Regis est mens bellum inferentis, eadem præsumitur esse mens omnium subditorum. Transfugis autem, iisque qui se dedunt, parci solet. Sextò, Rex bellum infert vicinæ genti non per se solum, sed per subditos. Ipse imperat, subditi exequuntur. Ipse est causa principalis, subditi instrumentalis: ac illi ipsi, qui bello se non immiscent, subditi tenentur parere Regi, eumque pro viribus tueri & iuuare. Adamus vero peccauit solus, ipse sibi, non nobis peccatum illud suum imperauit; ipse solus quod sibi imperauit, mandauit executioni, & opere perfecit. Posterorum nemo actioni illi interfuit, aut mentem manumve admouit suam. Non igitur ipse causa principalis fuit illius peccati, posteri causae instrumentales. Non ad committendum illud peccatum nos ei vt membra, vt organa, vt subditi, vel famuli accommodauimus, sed ipse solus, vt tunc extabat in rerum natura, ita peccatum illud per se ipsum commisit, nec posterorum quisquam illi adfuit. Bellum est commune Regis & subditorum opus, fitque a corpore regni: peccatum actuale Adami, vt tu ipse loqueris, vnius personae fuit. Septimo, peccati imputatio, & poenae inflictio, actiones sunt iudiciariae. Fieri debent a iudice secundum leges. Lex autem est, Anima quae peccauerit ipsa morietur. Non feret iniquitatem filij pater, nec patris filius. Contra in bello leges silent, &, vt in statu perturbato, omnia vi fiunt: nec finis est vt fiat iustitia, sed victoria, cuius causa gens cui bellum infertur in id vnum intenta est, vt inferenti incommodet. Quoniam autem Regis potentia in subditorum multitudine & opibus sita est, eam vt atterant, & imminuant, & euertant, subditos Regi pro viribus, & bonis, & vita spoliare conantur: in quo scopus est & regi aegre facere, illique incommodare, & se tueri, ac opibus augere. Deus vero cum peccatum hominibus imputat & vindicat, Iudicis partibus fungitur, nihilque habet ob oculos praeter iustitiam, quae suum cuique tribuit. Itaque nulli alienum peccatum attribuit, nulli poenam irrogat ob peccatum, quod nec in se habuit, nec admisit: summa est iustitiae eius puritas, summus nitor, & splendor. Octavo, Rex cum bellum denunciat vel infert, actu Rex est, & qua Rex caput subditorum, & ad subditos relationem actu habet, & vicissim subditi ad eum. Itaque, cum actu & plures sint, & se mutuis relationibus respiciant, actu unum corpus constituunt, ex Rege & subditis constans. Adamus vero cum peccavit actu pater non erat, actu relationem ad nos nullam habebat, non erat actu caput nostrum, & vicissim nos ad eum nullam relationem actu habebamus. Tum demum nata est haec relatio, cum pater esse, & liberos habere coepit. Est autem, postquam creatus fuerat, centum & triginta annis demum Seth natus, ex quo nos omnes sumus. Itaque qui nulli tum eramus, cum eo coire in societatem, aut componere corpus non potuimus. Respondebis fortasse, nos in Adamo potentia fuisse. Ergo, inquam, discrepat similitudo subditi enim sunt actu, sunt actu subditi, actu Rex eorum est caput, actu eius imperata tenentur exequi, actu cum eo corpus componunt, actu eum vel consilio vel opibus, vel manu, vel saltem votis iuuant.
units.tr: You seek a third likeness from the civil body. It has two parts. First, it sets before us a king making war on a neighbouring people. Not only he himself, who wished to make war, decided on it in council and pursued it with arms, is held to be an enemy, but also all the subjects, most of whom neither wished nor consented to this war; and although they do not act and remain at home, yet if they fall into the hands of the enemy, the unwary are taken, struck down and killed by the right of war. Consider, I beg you, how little this likeness fits. In the first place, if it be admitted, it must be granted that just as those are taken and killed by the enemy who do not approve the war, do not consent to it, and are in no way partakers of the king's counsel, so even if there were no vice in us and our will shrank from sin, nevertheless Adam's actual sin would be imputed to us; and many who agree with you do not dare to admit this. Secondly, it would follow that not only Adam's first sin but also all his other actual sins would have to be imputed to us, since he was the head of the human race as long as he lived. Thirdly, if the sin of the head is imputed to the body, why is the sin of the body not also imputed to the head? For if Adam and the rest of men constitute one body or whole, then whatever belongs to the individual members belongs to the whole body just as the members belong to it; the body is not one member but many, and if the foot is not the head, it does not follow that the foot is not part of the body. Moreover, what the head does is imputed to the whole body, and so is what the foot does. Thus, when God regarded his people as one body in the wilderness, he was angry with the whole people on account of one Achan, who was not the head of that people. If, therefore, all men coalesce with Adam into one body, then not only one sin of Adam but all Adam's sins and all the sins of other men are to be imputed to the whole body. Yet neither the Apostle nor you, following the Apostle, prove this. Fourthly, what prevents this likeness from being applied also to other stocks and parents with respect to their posterity? For example, why is Noah not also the head of the second world, or Abraham of the Israelites, and so on for the rest? From where would a great mass of sins to be imputed then arise? Adam is called a head, and is compared to a king, not because he was the first man, but because we derive our origin from him. He does not relate to us by the denial of a prior relation, but by the relation which he acquired to his posterity by begetting them. Fifthly, if someone falls into the hands of enemies who are certainly known to have been, in will and in deed, alien from the war and not to have consented to it, then if they kill him as innocent, they seem to me savage and cruel. Otherwise, the mind of the subjects is presumed to be the same as the mind of the king who wages war. Deserters, moreover, and those who surrender are usually spared. Sixthly, a king does not wage war on a neighbouring people by himself alone, but through his subjects. He commands, the subjects carry out. He is the principal cause, the subjects the instrumental cause; and even those who do not mix themselves in the war are bound to obey the king and to defend and assist him to the best of their powers. But Adam sinned alone; he did not command that sin of his to us; he alone carried out what he commanded himself and accomplished it by deed. None of his posterity was present at that act, or applied mind or hand to it. Therefore he was not the principal cause of that sin and we the instrumental causes. We did not lend ourselves to committing that sin as members, as organs, as subjects or servants; but he alone, as he then existed in the nature of things, committed that sin by himself, and none of his posterity was with him. War is the common work of king and subjects, and is done by the body of the realm; Adam's actual sin, as you yourself put it, was the sin of one person. Seventhly, the imputation of sin and the infliction of punishment are judicial acts. They must be done by a judge according to the laws. The law is: The soul that sins, it shall die. The father shall not bear the iniquity of the son, nor the son the iniquity of the father. In war, on the contrary, the laws are silent, and, as in a state of disorder, everything is done by force; the aim is not that justice be done but victory, for which reason the people against whom war is waged is intent on this one thing, that it may harm the one who wages it. Since the power of a king lies in the multitude and resources of his subjects, the enemy try to wear down, diminish and overthrow that power by stripping the king's subjects of their goods, their lives and their strength; their aim is both to cause the king grief and harm, and to protect and enrich themselves. But God, when he imputes and avenges sin on men, performs the part of judge, and keeps before his eyes nothing but justice, which gives each his due. Therefore he assigns no one another's sin, and inflicts no punishment for a sin which the person neither had in himself nor committed; the sum of his justice is its purity, its highest brightness and splendour. Eighthly, when a king declares or wages war, he is king in act, and as king he is the head of his subjects and has an actual relation to them, and they likewise to him. Therefore, since they are actually many and regard one another in mutual relations, they actually constitute one body, made up of the king and his subjects. But Adam, when he sinned, was not actually a father; he had no actual relation to us; he was not actually our head, and we likewise had no actual relation to him. That relation arose only when he began to be a father and to have children. Now, after he had been created, Seth was born to him only a hundred and thirty years later, and from Seth we are all descended. Therefore, since we were none of us then in existence, we could not enter into fellowship with him or form a body with him. You will perhaps reply that we were in Adam potentially. Then, I say, the likeness is at odds: the subjects are subjects in act; they are subjects in act; their king is their head in act; they are bound in act to carry out his commands; they form a body with him in act, and in act aid him by counsel, by resources, by hand, or at least by prayers.

units.la: Deinde, an quia eramus in Adamo potentia, sequitur quod ille fecit nos fecisse, nobisque eius actiones imputari debere? Tu eras in eo potentia, an igitur fuisti vel actu, vel potentia maritus Euae primae parentis nostrae? An actu vel potentia genuisti Sethum secundum parentem generis humani? An in eo actu vel potentia resipuisti à peccato? Nempe illam vnam actionem tu in eo fecisti, concupiuisti scilicet fructum arboris vetitæ, gustasti eius suauitatem, blanditiis & suasionibus vxoris tuæ Euæ te persuaderi fiuisti, cupiditate sciendi bonum & malum flagrasti, diuinitatem quandam affectasti, manum arbori prohibitæ admouisti, fructum eius dentibus comminuisti. Equidem non capio cur istam vnam actionem in Adamo ediderimus, à cæteris autem eius actionibus abstinuerimus.
units.tr: Next, even if we were in Adam potentially, does it follow that what he did we did, and that his actions ought to be imputed to us? Were you in him potentially, or were you then actually or potentially the husband of Eve, our first parent? Did you actually or potentially beget Seth, the second parent of the human race? Did you in him actually or potentially repent of sin? Indeed, you alone did that one action in him: you desired the fruit of the forbidden tree, you tasted its sweetness, you let yourself be persuaded by the flatteries and urgings of your wife Eve, you burned with desire to know good and evil, you aspired to a certain divinity, you put your hand to the forbidden tree, and you crushed its fruit with your teeth. I certainly do not see why we should be said to have committed that one action in Adam, but to have abstained from his other actions.

units.la: Alterum similitudinis membrum, seu, si ita mauis, similitudinem integram his verbis expressisti. Eodem modo si in vrbe populus fit rebellis, & seditionem moueat in principis ministros, vel satellites, & eam ob causam princeps populum illum rebellionis damnet, & armis persequatur, seditio illa non tantum eorum esse censetur, qui se commouerunt primi, & iniuriam fecerunt satellitibus, sed etiam imputatur cœtui & toti communitati, seu societati ciuium. Omnes habentur rei & rebelles, bona proscribuntur, nec parcitur vitæ; quia sunt ex corpore, & societate illius vrbis rebellis. Sic seres habet in genere humano. Primus homo tanquam caput omnium hominum, rebellans Deo & peccans in Deum, iusto Dei iudicio punitus est; non tantum ipse in persona sua, sed tota natura humana & omnes homines, qui sunt tanquam vnum corpus, & coeunt in vnam societatem; Et hæc rebellio capitis, quæ totam naturam peruasit, tribuitur & imputatur omnibus hominibus. Quæ ad præcedentem similitudinem dicta sunt hanc ipsam quoque euertunt. Addam tamen pauca. Modò Adamum comparabas Regi bellum inferenti: Nunc eundem comparas populo rebellanti aduersus Regis ministros. At quid habet Adamus commune cum seditiosa & tumultuante plebe alicuius vrbis, in societatem rebellionis ipsos suos magistratus trahete,nisi eam coerceant pro virili, & fe Regi purgent. Hinc facilius concludas multitudinis hominum peccata ipsi Adamo, quàm vnius Adami primum peccatum actuale toti hominum multitudini imputari debere. Deinde, putasne iuftum & æquum Regem iis crimen illud rebellionis imputare, quos pro comperto habet in rebellionem non consensisse in illa vrbe? Discernit proculdubio pro sua æquitate inter rebelles & non rebelles, feditiosos & in officio constantes. Præterea, annon inde sequeretur multò propius & certius, multitudinis impiæ peccata imputari paucis inter improbos delitefcentibus piis, quàm vnius hominis peccatum vnum, nullo alio homine præsente, immo existente, commissum omnibus hominibus imputari? Attamen ab illa imputatione Dei iustitia abhorret. Absit tibi, dicebat Abraham Gen.13.28. Ut facias tale quidpiam, morti tradendo iustum cum iniusto, vt ita fit iusto sicut iniusto: Absit tibi; An iudex totius terræ non exerceret ius? Vides quantopere pater credentium pugnare cum diuina iustitia credebat, fi paucissimi iusti magnæ ciuitatis rebellis & peccatricis punitione cum ciuium multitudine inuoluerentur, & nos eius filij audebimus Deo eiusmodi iustitiam tribuere, quæ vnius hominis culpam imputet omnibus, non modò ad mortem æternam, sed etiam ad eam poenam quæ fit ipsa proprie malum culpæ, & causa omnium peccatorum? Absit, absit à nobis talis, de Deo nostro, de mundi iudice, cuius æquitas & φιλανθρωπία nobis notissima est, cogitatio!
units.tr: In the same way, if a people in a city becomes rebellious and stirs up sedition against the prince's ministers or guards, and for that reason the prince condemns that people as rebels and pursues them with arms, the sedition is considered not only that of those who first stirred and did injury to the guards, but is also imputed to the whole body and entire community, or society, of citizens. All are held guilty and rebels, their goods are confiscated, and their lives are not spared, because they are part of the body and society of that rebellious city. So it is with the seed in the human race. The first man, as the head of all men, rebelled against God and sinned against God, and was punished by the just judgment of God; not only he himself in his own person, but the whole human nature and all men, who are as one body and come together into one society. And this rebellion of the head, which pervaded the whole nature, is ascribed and imputed to all men. What was said about the previous comparison overturns this one too. I will add a few things nonetheless. Just now you compared Adam to a king waging war; now you compare him to a people rebelling against the king's ministers. But what does Adam have in common with the seditious and riotous common people of some city, who drag their very magistrates into the fellowship of rebellion, unless they restrain them as far as they can and clear themselves before the king? From this you may more easily conclude that the sins of a multitude of men ought to be imputed to Adam himself, than that the first actual sin of the one Adam ought to be imputed to the whole multitude of men. Next, do you think it just and fair for a king to impute that crime of rebellion to those whom he knows for certain did not consent to the rebellion in that city? Surely, in his fairness, he distinguishes between rebels and non-rebels, seditious and steadfast in their duty. Moreover, would it not follow much more closely and certainly that the sins of an impious multitude are imputed to the few pious who are hidden among the wicked, than that the one sin of one man, committed with no other man present, or rather with none existing, is imputed to all men? Yet God's justice shrinks from that imputation. Far be it from you, said Abraham (Gen.13.28), to do anything of this kind, to put the righteous to death with the wicked, so that the righteous is treated as the wicked: far be it from you. Shall not the judge of all the earth do right? You see how greatly the father of believers thought that divine justice would be violated if a very few just men in a great city were involved in the punishment of a rebellious and sinful city along with the multitude of its citizens. And shall we, his sons, dare to ascribe to God a justice of this kind, which imputes the guilt of one man to all, not only for eternal death, but also for that punishment which is properly the very evil of guilt and the cause of all sins? Far be it, far be it from us, to entertain such a thought about our God, the judge of the world, whose equity and [φιλανθρωπία] (love of mankind) are well known to us!

units.la: G A R. Mittamus nunc quidem Rhetoricationes, & quod de poena dicitur, quaesit ipsa specie malum culpa, quia de hoc & aliquid dictum est superius, & recurret postea ea de re fusius disputandi occasio. Argumenti duntaxat vim attendamus, quod ita pertexi potest. Iustos cum iniustis eadem condemnatione & morte innolui, alienum est a Dei iustitia, teste Abrahamo. Atqui in alieni peccati imputatione, iusti cum iniustis, eadem condemnatione & morte involuerentur. Ergo alieni peccati imputatio est a Dei iustitia aliena.
units.tr: G A R. Let us now set aside rhetorical flourishes, and what is said about punishment, whether it is itself by its kind an evil of guilt, since this has been touched on above and an opportunity to discuss the matter more fully will recur later. Let us attend only to the force of the argument, which can be framed thus: To involve the righteous with the unrighteous in the same condemnation and death is foreign to the justice of God, as Abraham testifies. But in the imputation of another's sin, the righteous would be involved with the unrighteous in the same condemnation and death. Therefore the imputation of another's sin is foreign to the justice of God.

units.la: P L A C. Qua occasione, & quàm appositè testimonium Abrahami fuerit a me allatum Lector prudens, si placer, considerabit. Interim Argumentum quod hic vir doctus contexuit libenter pro meo habebo modo in minore alieni peccati imputatio, non quaelibet intelligatur, sed ea duntaxat, de qua inter nos lis est, nempe antecedens omne peccatum nobis inhaerens aut a nobis commissum.
units.tr: P L A C. Let the prudent reader consider, if he pleases, on what occasion and how aptly I brought forward the testimony of Abraham. Meanwhile, I will gladly take as my own the argument this learned man has framed, with this qualification in the minor premise: that "another's sin" is not to be understood in any sense, but only in the sense about which we are in dispute, namely every preceding sin that cleaves to us or was committed by us.

units.la: G A R. Hic primo responderi posset, quae ab Abrahamo causa disceptatur, eam a Quaestione imputata Adami inobedientia longe abesse. Abrahamus enim de iis loquitur, qui non omnes eadem conditione agebant, sed alij iusti erant, alij iniustitia mancipati: & quorum ea erat ratio, ut non modo iusti propter impios, quibus commixti erant, in earundem poenarum consortium trahi possent, sed etiam impij propter iustos eiusdem beneficij & conservationis esse participes; unde Abrahamus utrumque a Deo precibus contendit, tum ut ne iusti propter impiorum scelera pereant, tum ut impijs propter iustos ignoscatur. Atqui longe aliter res habet in nostro negotio. Nam primo inter eos quibus Adae peccatum imputatur, hoc quidem respectu, nulla est iustitia iniustitiaeve distinctio; neque enim solus Adamus iniustus est; posteri vero iusti & innocentes, sed omnes natiua feminis corruptione polluti, sicut explicatum est cap. 2. Deinde nec quinquaginta, nec viginti, nec decem, ac ne unus quidem est in hoc ordine carnaliter generatorum, propter cuius iustitiam Deus cateris parcere aut velit, aut debeat. Itaque ex Abrahami verbis duci non potest legitima aduersus imputationem peccati Adae consequentia.
units.tr: G A R. Here it could first be answered that the cause which Abraham pleads is far removed from the question of the imputed disobedience of Adam. For Abraham speaks of those who were not all in the same condition, but some were righteous and others were given over to wickedness; and in such a case it was the rule that not only could the righteous, because of the wicked among whom they were mingled, be drawn into fellowship of the same punishments, but also the wicked, because of the righteous, could share in the same benefit and preservation. Hence Abraham begged God in prayer both that the righteous not perish because of the sins of the wicked, and that the wicked be forgiven for the sake of the righteous. But in our matter the case is very different. For first, among those to whom Adam's sin is imputed, there is in this respect no distinction of righteous and unrighteous; for Adam alone is not unrighteous; the posterity too are not righteous and innocent, but all are polluted by the corruption innate from women, as was explained in chapter 2. Next, neither fifty, nor twenty, nor ten, nor even one, is there in this order of those carnally begotten, for whose righteousness God would wish or ought to spare the others. Therefore no valid argument against the imputation of Adam's sin can be drawn from Abraham's words.

units.la: P L A C. Horum duorum discriminum prius quidem appositum est, si de imputatione mediata agitur, quae supponit & consequitur inhaerentem corruptionem seu iniustitiam: ideo enim eadem condemnatione & morte cum iniusto Adamo inuoluimur, quoniam & ipsi i n nobis ipsis iniusti fumus: sed fi de imputatione immediata, quam solam impugno, agitur, falsum est; antecedit eni o imputatio corruptionem hereditariam vt culpa poenam . itaque nostra iniustitia huiusmodi imputationem & condemnationem sequitur vt effectum, non antecedit vt causa. Non ideo eadem cum iniusto Adamo condemnatione inuoluimur, quia fumus iniusti, sed contra ideo fumus iniufti, quia eadem cum iniusto Adamo condemnatione inuoluimur : ita enim fimus imputatione peccati actualis ab Adamo commissi peccatores, id est, rei, & vt puniatur imputatum nobis illud peccatum fimus inhærenter iniusti. Seposita igitur hac imputatione seu condemnatione nocens est Adamus, nos innocentes. Quare illa imputatio seu condemnatio, iudice Abrahamo , pugnat cum Dei iustitia. Posterius discrimen quid ad rem faciat, de qua agitur, non video.
units.tr: P L A C. The former of these two differences is indeed relevant, if we are speaking of mediate imputation, which presupposes and follows inherent corruption or unrighteousness; for we are involved in the same condemnation and death as the unrighteous Adam precisely because we too are unrighteous in ourselves. But if we are speaking of immediate imputation, which alone I oppose, it is false; for imputation precedes hereditary corruption as guilt precedes punishment. Therefore our unrighteousness follows such imputation and condemnation as an effect, and does not precede it as a cause. We are not involved in the same condemnation as the unrighteous Adam because we are unrighteous; rather we are unrighteous because we are involved in the same condemnation as the unrighteous Adam. For by the imputation of the actual sin committed by Adam we are made sinners, that is, guilty, and that sin imputed to us is punished, and we are inherently unrighteous. Setting aside, then, this imputation or condemnation, Adam is guilty and we are innocent. Therefore that imputation or condemnation, by Abraham's judgment, is at odds with the justice of God. I do not see what bearing the latter difference has on the matter in question.

units.la: GAR. Verum ad iustam solutionem, progrediendum est vlterius in deprecationis huius Abrahamica consideratione. Dicimus ergo non esse simpliciter & absolute concedendum, abhorrere omnino a iustitia Dei vt iusti fiue perfonaliter innocentes eadem aliquando poena inuoluantur cum iniustis & criminosis, quantumuis inde sua deprecationis argumentum desumat Abrahamus. 1. quia Deus ipse expressis & disertis verbis testatur fe contrarium aliquando facere, Ita enim Prophetam suum alloquitur, Ezech. xxi. 8. 9. Dic terræ Israelis, Sic ait Iehoua; ecce ego exeram gladium meum e vagina sua, vt exscindam ex te iustum & improbum : vt exscindam ex te iustum & improbum : idcirco prodibit gladius meus e vagina sua contra omnem carnem a Meridie ad Aquilonem. 2. Quia eius diuina dispensationis exempla quaedam Abrahamus ignorare non poterat, qua Deus omnium oculis obiecerat, primo in diluuio generali, deinde in Sodomorum subuersione, tertio in Abimelechi familia, qua omnia supra suo loco produximus.
units.tr: GAR. But for a just solution we must go further in considering this plea of Abraham. We say, therefore, that it is not to be simply and absolutely conceded that it is wholly abhorrent to the justice of God that persons who are personally innocent should at any time be involved in the same punishment with the unrighteous and the guilty, however much Abraham draws his argument for his plea from it. (1) Because God himself testifies in express and plain words that he sometimes does the contrary. For thus he addresses his prophet, Ezech. xxi. 8. 9: Speak to the land of Israel, Thus says Jehovah: behold, I will draw my sword out of its sheath, to cut off from you the righteous and the wicked: to cut off from you the righteous and the wicked: therefore my sword shall go out of its sheath against all flesh from the south to the north. (2) Because Abraham could not be ignorant of certain examples of this divine dispensation, which God set before the eyes of all: first in the general deluge, then in the overthrow of the Sodomites, third in the family of Abimelech, all of which we have set forth in their proper place above.

units.la: PLAC. Hoc vero non est nodum soluere, sed secare. Quid fi Ezech. 21. per iustum intelligitur is, qui sibi, aut alijs iustus videtur, vt quibusdam placet interpretibus ? Quid fi iustus intelligitur per comparationem cum alijs nequioribus ? iuxta illud Mich. 7. 4. optimus eorum est similis spina ; rectissimus mus pra spineto est. Quid, quod nullus est omnino iustus, & qui non peccet: omnes peccauerunt & destituti sunt gloria Dei: ipsi infantes recens nati inhærente vitio polluti sunt; ac propterea illis pœnis digni quibus à Dei iustitia afficiuntur. Taceo communes pœnas aliter sese in pijs habere, aliter in impijs. Illorum enim respectu sunt castigationes, & pœnæ paternæ, & vitæ peccato & miseriæ obnoxiæ in perfectè sanctam ac beatam commutatio; itaque nulla ijs fit iniuria, vti nec impiorum liberis, qui ita ob peccatum originale, quo parentibus similes sunt, moriuntur, vt tamen à multis peccatis, quæ si prorogata illis vita fuisset, commisissent, & à multis calamitatibus in quas incidissent, præseruentur; id quod in aliquo beneficio reponi potest. Minimè igitur pugnat hoc Dei apud Ezech. oraculum cum Abrahami testimonio. Exempla diuinæ dispensationis quæ vir doctus subjungit, eius causæ obsunt. Non enim eådem cum impijs condemnatione Noachum in diluuio generali, nec Lothum in Sodomorum subuersione Dei iustitia inuoluit. Nouit enim Dominus pios è tentatione eripere, iniustos autem in diem iudicij pœnas dantes seruare: quanquam Sedomorum subuersio sequuta est non antecessit, vt memoria lapsus supponere videtur Vir doctus, istud Abrahami cum Deo colloquium. Idem de edito in Abimelechi familia exemplo dici debet: narratur enim eius historia demum Gen. cap. 20. & ita narratur, vt appareat idem cum Abrahamo sensisse Abimelechum de Dei iustitia.
units.tr: PLAC. But this is not untying the knot; it is cutting it. What if in Ezek. 21 "the just" means one who seems just to himself or to others, as some interpreters like to think? What if "the just" is understood by comparison with others who are more wicked, in line with Mic. 7:4: "The best of them is like a briar; the most upright is sharper than a thorn hedge"? Or what of the fact that there is absolutely no one just who never sins? "All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." Even newborn infants are polluted by inherent vice, and so they deserve those punishments with which God's justice afflicts them. I pass over the point that common punishments are one thing for the godly and another for the ungodly. For with respect to the godly they are chastisements and fatherly punishments, and a passage from a life subject to sin and misery into one that is perfectly holy and blessed. So no injury is done to them, just as none is done to the children of the impious, who die on account of the original sin by which they resemble their parents. Yet they are spared from many sins which they would have committed had their lives been prolonged, and from many calamities into which they would have fallen; this can be counted as a benefit. So this oracle of God in Ezekiel by no means conflicts with Abraham's testimony. The examples of divine dispensation which the learned man adds work against his own cause. For God's justice did not involve Noah in the universal deluge, nor Lot in the overthrow of Sodom, in the same condemnation as the impious. "The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, and to keep the unjust under punishment for the day of judgment" (2 Pet. 2). Although the overthrow of Sodom followed that conversation of Abraham with God, it did not precede it, as the learned man seems to suppose through a slip of memory. The same must be said of the example in the family of Abimelech. For its history is narrated only in Gen. 20, and it is narrated in such a way that it appears Abimelech thought the same as Abraham about God's justice.

units.la: GAR. Quomodo igitur, inquies, illud semel & iterum Abrahamus ingerit, abesse debere à Deo vt perimat iustum cum injusto? Resp. 1. De hac Abrahæ deprecatione ita iudicare nonnullos, vt non modo negent, vsquequaque certam esse, quam probat sententiam, sed affirment etiam multiplicem habere confutationem. Ita enim Pererius, qui vbi eam confutationem proposuit, concludit tandem in hac verba. Abraham similis oratori pessimam causam defendenti, & in omnes se partes versanti, vt, vndecunque possit, rapiat qualecunque defensionis præsidium, miscet verba, variatque sententias, inuoluit rationes etiam non admodum probabiles, nec proposito suo valde congruentes, omnem demum mouet lapidem, vt impetret quod à Deo postulat, non tam senten-
units.tr: GAR. "How then," you will ask, "does Abraham repeatedly insist that it must be far from God to destroy the just together with the unjust?" Reply 1. Some judge this prayer of Abraham in such a way that they not only deny that the opinion he defends is certain in every respect, but even affirm that it has many refutations. Thus Pererius, who after setting out that refutation, concludes in these words: "Abraham, like an orator defending a very bad cause and turning to every side so as to snatch from wherever he can any kind of defensive support, mixes words, varies his opinions, brings in arguments not very probable and not well suited to his purpose, and finally moves every stone to obtain what he asks of God. He deals with God not so much by the weight of opinions

units.la: Cap. 14 § 5. tiarum pondere, aut robore argumentorum cum Deo agens, quàm ardore charitatis & flagrantissimo pietatis erga miseros illos homines affectu.
units.tr: Cap. 14 § 5. or the strength of arguments as by the ardour of charity and the most burning affection of piety towards those wretched men."

units.la: PLAC. Probatne, an improbat Vir doctus illa Pererij verba? Si improbat, cur laudat? Si probat, miror eum probare potuisse tam audacia, tantoque Patriarchæ, patri credentium, tam iniuriosa Iesuitæ verba. Equidem qui me filium esse Abrahæ Dei beneficio maximo credo, & lætor, vix ferre possum tam inuerecundè de meo patre loquentem. Quantus enim erat Patriarcha, Dei confœderatus, Dei amicus, Dei colloquio tam sæpe dignatus, insignis Propheta? Quis credat eum voluisse apud Deum pessimam causam defendere, & rationibus tanquam necessariis vti minus probabilibus? Quid, quod Deus illam rationem non reprehendit, sed admisit, & nos decet credentes Patris credentium imitari fidem?
units.tr: PLAC. Does the learned man approve or disapprove those words of Pererius? If he disapproves, why does he praise him? If he approves, I wonder how he could approve words so audacious and so insulting to so great a patriarch, the father of believers, coming from a Jesuit. Indeed I, who believe by the greatest gift of God that I am a son of Abraham, and rejoice in it, can scarcely bear to hear someone speak so shamelessly of my father. For how great was the Patriarch: God's covenant partner, God's friend, so often deemed worthy of God's conversation, an outstanding prophet! Who would believe that he wished to defend a very bad cause before God, and used less probable arguments as if they were necessary? Moreover, God did not rebuke that reasoning but accepted it, and it becomes us, as believers, to imitate the faith of the father of believers.

units.la: GAR. 1. Abrahamo certa quidem fuit & immota hæc regula quam nullus fidelis non agnoscit, fieri nunquam omninò posse, vt Deus iniustè quidquam designet: sed in speciali videre non poterat, quomodo hæc innocentium clades cum iustitiâ Dei convenire posset. Quærit ergo non oblutandi animo, sed vt hunc scrupulum sibi eximat, an Deus iustum perditurus sit cum impio. &c.
units.tr: GAR. 1. Abraham indeed held this rule firm and unshaken, which no believer fails to acknowledge: it can never at all happen that God designs anything unjustly. But in the particular case he could not see how this slaughter of the innocent could agree with God's justice. He asks, therefore, not with a quarrelsome mind but to free himself of this scruple, whether God is going to destroy the just together with the impious, and so on.

units.la: PLAC. Suntne igitur illa verba dubitantis, aut simpliciter quærentis, Absit tibi vt facias tale quidpiam, morti tradendo iustum cum iniusto, vt ita fit iusto sicut iniusto: Absit tibi An index totius terra non exerceret ius? Quæ sunt assertiones vehementes ac fortes, tanquam certæ & indubitatæ, si hæ non sunt? Certò igitur sciebat, nec Deum posse quicquam iniquè designare, nec iustum esse apud Deum iudicem, vt pariter iustus ac iniustus damnetur, itaque hoc unum flagitabat, non modò vt Deus iustos propter impios non damnaret, id quod ei videbatur nimis à Dei iustitia alienum, sed vt propter paucos iustos parceret vel impiis, vel saltem ipsi loco seu urbi, id quod Dei bonitatem summam non dedecere videbatur. Agebatur enim non de qualicunque castigatione, sed de pœna iudiciaria, & quodammodo æterna: cuiusmodi pœna certum est nunquam iustos propter impios puniri. GAR. 3. Cum Deus in exequendis iudiciis suis, aliquando ex iustitia rigore agat, aliquando iustitiam aequitate temperet, dico Abrahamum, pro charitate sua in Sodomaos, percupiisse, ut Deus iudicium illud aliqua misericordia testificatione temperaret: Itaque seposito nunc quidem Dei τῷ ἀκριβοδικαίῳ, vnicè ha-buisse in ordinaria & communiori iustitia diuina dispensatione, cum praesertim alte animo ipsius insideret foedus illud cum ipso nuper initum Gen. 17. nimirum foedus gratiae, in quo Deus promisit se non imputaturum aliena peccata, Ierem. xxxi. 29. 30. Et cujus foederis nonnullam aliquando suavitatem etiam iis exhibet, qui ad illud non pertinent.
units.tr: PLAC. Are those words, then, the words of one who doubts, or of one who simply asks? "Far be it from you to do such a thing, to put the just to death with the unjust, so that the just is treated as the unjust. Far be it from you. Shall not the judge of all the earth do right?" These are vehement and strong assertions, as if certain and indubitable. If they are not, what are they? So he certainly knew both that God cannot designate anything unjustly, and that it is not just for God, the judge, to condemn the just and the unjust alike. So he asked for this one thing: not only that God not condemn the just on account of the impious, which seemed to him too alien to God's justice, but that for the sake of a few just he would spare either the impious or at least that place or city, which seemed not unworthy of God's supreme goodness. For the matter concerned not any chastisement whatever but judicial punishment, and in a sense eternal; and it is certain that the just are never punished in such a way on account of the impious. GAR. 3. Since God in carrying out his judgments sometimes acts with the rigour of justice and sometimes tempers justice with equity, I say that Abraham, out of his charity towards the Sodomites, desired that God would temper that judgment with some display of mercy. So, setting aside for the moment God's exact justice [τῷ ἀκριβοδικαίῳ], he had in view the ordinary and more common dispensation of divine justice, especially since that covenant newly made with him in Gen. 17 lay deep in his mind, namely the covenant of grace, in which God promised that he would not impute the sins of others (Jer. 31:29–30). And this covenant sometimes shows some sweetness even to those who do not belong to it.

units.la: PLAC. Duae sunt partes orationis Abrahami: altera asserit non conuenire iustitiae Dei, vt iustus pereat cum impio: altera petit à Deo, vt propter paucos iustos parcat vrbi; id quod, fateor, non ἀκριβοδίκαιον esse, sed testificationem potius misericordiae: itaque haec pars ad rem quam agimus non facit. Ab altera illa ductum est argumentum nostrum, quae est non aequitati modo, sed rigori etiam iustitiae, omni ex parte congruens. Quare quo spectet ista responsio, & quid argumento meo afferat noxae, nullus video. Illud tantum reponam, Si in foedere gratiae Deus promisit se non imputaturum aliena peccata, igitur cum nobis non imputare peccatum actuale primum Adami: Quomodo ergo nos ob illud peccatum punit, inflicta scilicet poena judiciaria, nempe corruptione originali? Caeterum non eo inficias, quin Deus nonnunquam eadem condemnatione temporali pios cum impiis involuat; quippe, nullus est ita pius & iustus, vt non peccet interdum, & pij non, vti par est, eorum, quibus admixti sunt, peccata detestantur fugiunt, redarguunt. Interim tamen huiusmodi calamitates cedunt pijs in castigationes paternas, quibus cauetur ne aeternum pereant cum impijs. Nos autem in hac causa de imputatione iudiciaria agimus & damnatione ad poenas propriedictas & iustitiae satisfactorias, quales illae sunt quas lex comminatur & iustitia, vt sibi satisfiat, exigit, quas ob aliena peccata portare innocentes minime nocentium vades, contendimus cum Abrahae testimonio, cum Dei iustitia & aequitate pugnare. Quarto, facefle aliquemRegem ea potentia praeditum, vt possit subditis suis, fi velit, animu rebellionis & inobedientiae immittere, putasne eum fi sapiens, fi iustus, fi bonus fit, ita fore comparatum, vt iis qui alioqui in vrbe illa fideles effent, primum imputet rebellium crimen, deinde vt illud puniat eos priuet iustitia & fidelitate, ac caeteris virtutibus, vt deinceps non possint non esse ipsi rebelles & scelesti? Noli igitur, quaeso, frater in Christo dilectissime, tales de Deo cogitationes fouere, quae mihi quidem certe horrorem incutiunt. Quinto denique, succurrant nobis Apostoli verba ad Gal.6.5. Vnusquisque suum onus portabit. Et ad Rom.14.12. Vnusquisque nostrum de seipso rationem reddet Deo. Putasne in illa die nobis omnibus & singulis reddendam esse rationem de peccato actuali Adami? Nonne nobis singulis suae cuique attributae sunt a Deo voluntates, facultates, actiones, dotes? De his quidem certe reddenda erit ratio singulis nobis, de Adami actione aliquot annorum millibus antequam esse inciperemus perpetrato non erit nobis, sed ipsi Adamo reddenda apud Deum ratio. Caeterum extrema huius tuae comparationis, necnon capitis, si bene intelligantur, verba mihi probantur, haec rebellio capitis quae totam naturam peruasit, tribuitur & imputatur omnibus hominibus. Nempe, rebellio actualis Adami suum ipsa per se naturali efficientia semen, virus, in omnes Adami facultates infeuit, atque medullitus infixit, idque malum serpsit, & per generationem naturalem se diffudit, & propagauit, & contagione sua posteros omnes infecit. Itaque, cum sit in singulis hominibus, merito iis tribuitur & imputatur.
units.tr: PLAC. Abraham's prayer has two parts. One asserts that it does not agree with God's justice that the just should perish with the impious; the other asks God to spare the city for the sake of a few just. The second, I grant, is not exact justice but rather a testimony of mercy, so that part has no bearing on the matter we are discussing. Our argument is drawn from the first part, which agrees not only with equity but with the rigour of justice in every respect. So I see no point in what this reply aims at, nor what harm it does to my argument. I will answer only this: if in the covenant of grace God promised that he would not impute the sins of others, then he does not impute to us the first actual sin of Adam. How, then, does he punish us on account of that sin, by inflicting judicial punishment, namely original corruption? Moreover, I do not deny that God sometimes involves the godly with the impious in the same temporal condemnation. There is no one so pious and just that he never sins at times, and the godly do not, as is fitting, detest, shun and rebuke the sins of those among whom they live. Yet such calamities turn for the godly into fatherly chastisements, by which care is taken that they do not perish eternally with the impious. But in this cause we are speaking of judicial imputation and of condemnation to punishments properly so called, which are satisfactions owed to justice, such as those the law threatens and justice demands be paid. We contend that the innocent, who are by no means sureties for the guilty, bearing these for the sins of others, conflicts with Abraham's testimony, with God's justice and with his equity. Fourth, suppose a king had such power that, if he wished, he could instil a spirit of rebellion and disobedience in his subjects. Do you think that such a king, if he were wise, just and good, would be so disposed as first to impute the crime of the rebels to those in that city who were otherwise faithful, and then to punish it by depriving them of justice, fidelity and the other virtues, so that thereafter they could not help being rebels and wicked themselves? Do not, I beg you, dearest brother in Christ, foster such thoughts about God, which indeed strike horror into me. Fifth and finally, let the words of the Apostle come to our aid, Gal. 6:5: "Each one will bear his own burden," and Rom. 14:12: "Each of us will give account of himself to God." Do you think that on that day an account of Adam's actual sin must be rendered by all of us and each of us? Has not each of us been given by God his own wills, faculties, actions and gifts? Of these indeed an account will certainly be owed by each of us. An account of Adam's action, committed some thousands of years before we began to exist, will not be owed by us, but by Adam himself to God. Moreover, the final words of this comparison of yours, and of the chapter, if rightly understood, please me: "This rebellion of the head, which has pervaded the whole of nature, is attributed and imputed to all men." Namely, Adam's actual rebellion, by its own natural efficacy, spread its seed and poison through all of Adam's faculties and fixed itself deep within them; and that evil crept on, spread itself and was propagated by natural generation, infecting all his posterity by its contagion. Thus, since it is present in each individual man, it is rightly attributed and imputed to each.

units.la: CAPVT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Responsio ad argumenta quae pro Imputatione peccati Actualis Adami ducuntur ex Vetere Testamento Cap. V.
units.tr: Reply to the arguments drawn for the imputation of Adam's actual sin from the Old Testament, Chapter V.

units.la: CONSTITVTO & illustrato, prout tibi visum est, quaestionis statu, tandem, Vir Clarissime, Capite tui tractatus quinto copias argumentorum tuorum educis in aciem, & explicas. Prodeunt autem omnium prima pauca quaedam e Veteri Testamento depromta.
units.tr: Having set out and clarified, as seemed good to you, the state of the question, most distinguished sir, you finally bring forward in the fifth chapter of your treatise the forces of your arguments and marshal them. The first to appear are a few drawn from the Old Testament.

units.la: Primum erumpit ex interdicto arboris scientiae boni & mali, & sic procedit. Si interdictum illud, inquis, & comminatio non tantum primos parentes spectauit, sed etiam totum genus humanum, sequitur transgressionem illius Mandati non tantum primos parentes morti obnoxios fecisse, sed etiam totum genus humanum. Atqui verum prius, Ergo & posterius. Prima pars maioris (quae est de interdicto) extra controversiam est: nam quis inficias ibit dominum legem dedisse non tantum Adamo, sed etiam posteris omnibus? quis negabit lege illa interdictum omnibus hominibus esum illius fructus? Consequentia vero manifesta est ex eventu: Nam violato interdicto, & Adam & omnes posteri morti obnoxij facti sunt. Principio huius tui argumenti conclusionem concedo: est enim tam meae quam tuae sententiae amica. Credo tecum firmiter, transgressionem Adami non tantum primos parentes morti obnoxios fecisse, sed etiam totum genus humanum. Sed quaestio est inter nos duntaxat de modo, quo transgressi{a} illa totum genus humanū morti obnoxium fecit. Tu hoc adfcribis Iustitiæ Dei, quæ transgressionem illam præcisam ab insecuta corruptione nobis omnibus, hoc ipso quod Adami filij fumus, imputet immediate, non secus ac fi illam ipsi, qui tum nulli eramus, admissemus, ac consequenter nos primùm inflicta corruptione morali quæ peccatum est, & causa omnium nostrorum peccatorum, deinde morte corporis & æterna, puniat. Itaque vis transgressionem illam actualem nos fecifle morti obnoxios interuentu eiufmodi imputationis. Ego verò absque tali imputatione aio transgressionem illam naturali efficientia & sequela vitiaffe facultates Adami, etiam illam qua nos genuit, eas vero vitiatas genuisse prolem vitiatam, hanc aliam, & ita vitium propagatum & multiplicatum vna cum natura humana ad omnes homines, vno Christo excepto, peruenisse sola lege naturæ, qua fui quodque simile gignit, quam generalem legem non ad homines solùm, sed ad alias etiam Creaturas, quotquot generandi facultate præditæ sunt, pertinentem, & decreto antecedente de creando mundo & natura constituenda politam & fancitam, non decuit Deum ob Adami transgressionem vel abrogare, vel infringere. Itaque laudo hæc verba Thomæ Aquinatis, dicendum, quod infectio originalis peccati nullo modo causatur à Deo, sed ex solo peccato primi parentis per carnalem generationem. Hoc autem vitium, quod in singulis nobis medullitus inest verè & proprie peccatum est, non quidem actuale, sed, vt ita loquar, habituale, dignum non temporali modo morte, sed æterna etiam, quod nostri aduersus Pontificios solent multis argumentis euincere, quæ tu proculdubio & legisti, & probas. Nos ergo transgressio Adami fecit obnoxios morti corporali & æternæ interuentu inhærentis vitij & culpæ, quo nos infecit. Hoc autem vitium in Adamo naturali sequela produxit ab Adamo verò in nos haud aliter quàm ipsa natura humana propagatum est generatione carnali. Volui statum quæstionis hoc loco repetere, quoniam eum purgatum & enucleatum habere perpetuò ob oculos nos decet, ne ab eo aliquando aberrantes in inanes κενοφωνίας prolabamur.
