units.tr: The first arises from the prohibition concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and proceeds thus: If that prohibition and threat, you say, looked not only to the first parents but also to the whole human race, it follows that the transgression of that command made not only the first parents liable to death but the whole human race as well. But the first is true, therefore the second too. The first part of the major premise (that concerning the prohibition) is beyond dispute: for who will deny that the Lord gave the law not only to Adam but to all his posterity? Who will deny that by that law the eating of its fruit was forbidden to all men? The consequence is clear from the outcome: for once the prohibition was violated, both Adam and all his posterity were made liable to death. At the start of this argument I concede the conclusion, for it is friendly to my view as much as to yours. I firmly believe with you that the transgression of Adam made not only the first parents liable to death, but the whole human race. But the question between us is only about the manner in which that transgression made the whole human race liable to death. You ascribe this to the justice of God, which imputes that transgression, considered apart from the corruption that followed, to all of us immediately, by the very fact that we are Adam's sons, just as if we ourselves, who at that time did not yet exist, had committed it; and so it punishes us first with the moral corruption which is sin and the cause of all our sins, and then with bodily and eternal death. Thus you hold that the actual transgression made us liable to death through the intervention of such imputation. But I say, without any such imputation, that the transgression by natural efficacy and consequence corrupted Adam's faculties, including that by which he begat us, and that he, being so corrupted, begot corrupted offspring, and thus the corruption, propagated and multiplied together with human nature, has come to all men, Christ alone excepted, by the sole law of nature, by which each thing begets its like. This general law pertains not only to men but to all other creatures endowed with the power of generation, and was established and sanctioned by the prior decree concerning the creation of the world and the constitution of nature. It was not fitting that God, because of Adam's transgression, should abrogate or infringe it. Therefore I commend these words of Thomas Aquinas: It must be said that the infection of original sin is in no way caused by God, but arises solely from the sin of the first parent through carnal generation. This corruption, which inheres deep within each of us, is truly and properly sin, not indeed actual but, if I may so speak, habitual, deserving not only temporal death but eternal death as well. Our writers commonly prove this against the Papists by many arguments, which you have doubtless both read and approve. Therefore Adam's transgression made us liable to bodily and eternal death through the intervention of the inherent corruption and guilt with which it infected us. Now this corruption was produced in Adam by natural consequence, and from Adam it was propagated to us in no other way than human nature itself is propagated, by carnal generation. I have wished to repeat the state of the question here, since it befits us always to keep it cleansed and clearly set out before our eyes, lest, straying from it at some point, we fall into empty babblings [κενοφωνίας].

units.la: Quamuis autem conclusionem huius tui syllogismi admittam, tamen non sunt ita liquidæ præmissæ, quin aliqua distinctione egeant, ad rem quam agimus, vtili. Nam quomodo, quæso, intelligis has propositiones, Dominum legem illam dedisse non tantum Adamo, sed etiam posteris omnibus; lege illa interdictum fuisse hominibus ejus illius fructus? Distinguenda certè sunt tempora. Nam si Adamus in paradiso liberos genuisset, eos, postea quàm geniti fuissent, interdictum illud obligasset; nisi forte interdictum illud Deus tandem abrogasset; quis enim nouit mentem Domini? Positiua lex fuit, libertatem arbitrij Adami circa rem natura sua indifferentem circumscribens, ac proinde potuit ad tempus præscribi, eoque tempore elapso abrogari, quemadmodum leges de ciborum delectu, quas Deus olim tulerat populo suo. Quis nostrum scire potest, vtrum Deus voluisset interdictum illud perpetuò vigere, an verò ad certum quoddam tempus duntaxat, quo exacto, & probata abundè hominis obedientia, illud sustulisset, facta homini copia vtendi in posterum illa arbore?
units.tr: However, although I admit the conclusion of this syllogism of yours, the premises are not so clear that they do not need some distinction, useful to the matter we are treating. For I ask, how do you understand these propositions: that the Lord gave that law not only to Adam but to all his posterity; that by that law the eating of its fruit was forbidden to men? Certainly the times must be distinguished. For if Adam had begotten children in paradise, the prohibition would have bound them after they were born, unless perhaps God had at length abrogated that prohibition; for who knows the mind of the Lord? It was a positive law, limiting Adam's freedom of choice with regard to a thing indifferent by its nature, and therefore it could have been prescribed for a time and abrogated when that time had passed, as were the laws concerning the choice of foods which God once gave to his people. Which of us can know whether God wished that prohibition to remain in force forever, or only for a certain time, after which, when man's obedience had been sufficiently proved, he would have lifted it, granting man the opportunity to eat of that tree in the future?

units.la: Haud enim decet nos in Dei arcana irrumpere, aut ea quæ ignoramus confidenter asseuerare. Concedo tamen libenter futurum fuisse vt obligaret posteros Adami quo tempore fuissent, at quo tempore non fuissent, eos tunc ad id obseruandum fuisse obligatos nullo modo concedere possum. Ipsa naturæ lex àqua, nemo eximi potest, non obligat ad obedientiam, nisi eos, qui sunt in rerum natura, & quamdiu sunt in rerum natura. Qui nondum sunt in Mundum ingressi, nondum tenentur obseruare leges latas ijs qui sunt in Mundo. Acceperant Israëlitæ olim legem in deserto pro se & posteris, quis credat eo tempore, quo peregrinabantur in eodem deserto, Dauidem, aut Mariam Virginem debuisse iam tunc legem illam obseruare? aut propterea eorum qui primi legem acceperunt, peccata fuisse posteris imputanda omnibus ad sæculorum vsque consummationem? Infanti in vtero materno putasne ea peccata imputari, quæ si vixisset, & ad senium peruenisset toto vitæ tempore facturus fuisset? non arbitror. Cur igitur ei vis imputari peccatum actuale tunc admissum cum nondum erat, immò aliquot annorum millibus antequam esset, quodque adeo ipse nec actu, nec potentia commisit; non actu, quia non erat; non potentia, quia cum committeretur, non poterat tunc esse, hoc volo, non poterat esse respectu illius temporis quo peccatum illud perpetratum est, vsque adeo vt implicet contradictionem illud idem numero quod vis nobis imputari à nobis fieri, aut factum esse. Nunquam illud fecimus, nec facere potuimus, nec ex quo nati sumus ficere possumus. Præclarè author Hypognosticon Contra pelag. siue is fit Augustinus, siue alius, Deus, inquitû, prəscies operum eius malorum, quæ factypus erat ætate perfectâ, periturum dixit de populo suo. Itane pelagiane insane, Deus qui iustus est in omnibus vîs suis & sanctus in omnibus operibus suis, pro huiusmodi credendus incircuncifum puerulum iudicare, vt tanquam factorem pro non factis sceleribus puniat, tempus imputet quoddam vbi vita non vixerit, vbi velle & nolle non fuit voluntatis ? Absit hoc apud iudicem iustum &c. Vide quantopere pius vir ab ista cogitatione abhorreat, Deum puerulo tempus imputare quoddam vbi vita non vixerit, quamuis potuerit viuere; quàmq; id existimet non cõuenire dei iustitiæ; quid ergo diceret de eo tempore quum puerulus non modo vita non viuebat, sed ne poterat quidem viuere; deque peccato quod non modo non fecit, sed neque potuit vnquam facere? Quod si Apostoli exemplo in Epistolis ad Gal. & ad Heb. velimus scripturæ verba & silentium, accuratè perpendere, quid est quamobrem non obseruemus in Interdicto, in sententia post violatum interdictum Adamo pronunciata nullam esse posteritatis factam mentionem? Cauit nimirum Deus iam tum, ne vobis vllam præberet ansam ita de iustitia sua, vt facitis, sentiendi. Sed fac interdictum illud nos ad obedientiam obligasse pro eo tempore quo nondum eramus, quo solus erat cum vxore in paradiso Adamus, quid à nobis requirebat? Vt ne ederemus de fructu arboris scientiæ boni & mali? Paruimus: nam qui edere tum temporis non poteramus, profecto non edimus. Edimus, inquies, in Adamo. bene habet: non igitur edimus in nobis. Quandoquidem igitur in vno Adamo manducauimus illum fructum, decuit nos etiam puniri in vno. Adamo: ac cum in nostris personis non manduuerimus, non oportuit nos puniri in nostris personis. Scire velim quomodo ad nos interdictum spectabat, vtrum quatenus fumus personæ distinctæ à persona Adami, an duntaxat quatenus nihil aliud eramus quàm ipse Adamus? nostri enim tunc certè pars nulla erat, immò ne femen quidem vnde procreati fumus, immò ne femen quidem ex quo Centesimus à nobis parens noster ortus est. Prius non dixeris. Posterius fi affirmas, quid est quamobrem ad nos non spectauerit interdictum, illius temporis respectu, nisi quatenus eramus nihil nisi ipse Adamus, velis autem comminationem adjunctam interdicto ad nos spectare quatenus personæ fumus ab Adamo diuersæ & separatæ? Equidem non intelligo cur ad nos alio modo interdictum, alio comminatio pertineat.
units.tr: For it does not befit us to break into the secrets of God, or to assert confidently what we do not know. Yet I readily grant that the prohibition would have bound Adam's posterity at the time when they existed; but that it bound them at a time when they did not exist, I can in no way concede. The law of nature itself, from which no one can be exempted, binds to obedience only those who are in the order of things, and only so long as they are in it. Those who have not yet entered the world are not yet bound to observe the laws given to those who are in the world. The Israelites once received the law in the desert for themselves and their posterity; who would believe that at the time when they were wandering in that same desert, David or the Virgin Mary were already bound to observe that law? Or that, on account of the sins of those who first received the law, the sins were to be imputed to all posterity until the end of the ages? Do you think that sins are imputed to an infant in its mother's womb, sins which, had it lived and reached old age, it would have committed during the whole course of its life? I do not think so. Why then do you wish an actual sin to be imputed to him, committed at a time when he did not yet exist, indeed some thousands of years before he existed, a sin which for that reason he himself committed neither actually nor potentially? Not actually, because he did not yet exist; not potentially, because when it was committed he could not yet exist. I mean that he could not exist with respect to the time in which that sin was perpetrated, so much so that it implies a contradiction that the same numerical sin should be imputed to us as something we did or have done. We never did it, nor could we do it, nor can we do it since we were born. The author of the Hypognosticon against the Pelagians, whether it is Augustine or another, writes well: God, it says, foreknowing the evils of his works, which he said would perish from his people when they were grown, must we believe that God, who is just in all his ways and holy in all his works, judges like this, that he punishes an uncircumcised little child as though it were the doer of crimes it did not commit, imputing to it a time in which it did not live, when it neither willed nor was unwilling? Far be it from a just judge, etc. See how greatly that pious man shrinks from this notion, that God should impute to a little child a time in which it did not live, even though it could have lived; and how he judges that this does not agree with the justice of God. What then would he say about that time when the little child not only did not live but could not even live; and about a sin which it not only did not commit but could never have committed? But if, following the Apostle's example in the Epistles to the Galatians and the Hebrews, we wish to weigh carefully the words and the silence of Scripture, why do we not observe that in the prohibition, and in the sentence pronounced on Adam after the prohibition was violated, no mention of posterity is made? God doubtless took care at that time that he should not give you any occasion to think of his justice as you do. But suppose the prohibition bound us to obedience at a time when we did not yet exist, when Adam alone was in paradise with his wife: what did it require of us? That we should not eat of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil? We obeyed, for since we could not eat at that time, we certainly did not eat. "We ate," you will say, "in Adam." Well and good: then we did not eat in ourselves. Since therefore we ate that fruit in Adam alone, it was fitting that we should be punished in Adam alone; and since we did not eat in our own persons, it was not fitting that we should be punished in our own persons. I should like to know how the prohibition applied to us: whether insofar as we are persons distinct from the person of Adam, or only insofar as we were nothing other than Adam himself? For at that time we were certainly no part of him; indeed we did not even exist as seed, nor even as the seed from which we were procreated, nor even as the seed from which our parent was born, a hundredth generation before us. You could not say the former. If you affirm the latter, why was the prohibition not addressed to us at that time, except insofar as we were nothing but Adam himself? But if you wish the threat attached to the prohibition to apply to us insofar as we are persons distinct and separate from Adam, I do not see why the prohibition applies to us in one way and the threat in another.

units.la: Verùm tu argumentaris ab euentu. Hoc enim violato interdicto & Adam, & omnes posteri morti obnoxij facti sunt. Certè, sed Adam immediatè ob violatum à se interdictum, posteri ob vitium & peccatum quod singulis ab Adamo propagatum inhæret.
units.tr: But you argue from the outcome: "For once the prohibition was violated, both Adam and all his posterity were made liable to death." Certainly, but Adam was subject to death immediately because of the prohibition he himself violated, while his posterity are subject to it because of the vice and sin that is propagated from Adam to each individual and clings to them.

units.la: Pergis & ducis argumentum à sententia, quam Deus Adamo prolapso in peccatum pronunciauit his verbis, quia paruisti voci vxoris tuæ, & comedisti ex arbore &c. vnde sic argumentaris, Si pœna fuit communis, peccatum debuit etiam esse commune. Atqui pœna fuit communis. Ergo etiam peccatum. Majorem probas hoc syllogismo, iustus Iudex non infligit pœnam communem omnibus hominibus, nisi ob commune peccatum omnium. Subjit animum tuum hoc totum posse à me concedi, qui agnosco peccatum commune omnium hominum, nempe vitium hæreditarium dignum communibus poenis. Itaque longius proueheris, Iam, inquis, subsumo, primum illud peccatum quod omnes homines addixit poena commune est omnibus, vel actu proprio, vel imputatione: Non actu proprio, quia solus Adamus actu peccauit. Ergo imputatione, quia scilicet omnibus imputatur. Cur tertium membrum omisisti tantopere aduersus Pelagianos decantatum, vel propagatione naturali, Constat enim primum peccatum in nos transiisse (non qua fuit actio transiens, sed qua fuit auersio a Deo & conuersio ad creaturas vt ad finem vltimum, permanens in Adamo) transiisse inquam non imputatione quae extra nos est, sed vera communicatione & propagatione. Ob hoc peccatum commune omnium communes irrogantur omnibus poenae: non satisfactoriae quidem illae in hac vita, saltem respectu fidelium, sed tamen poenae: irrogatur etiam, nisi gratia Christi intercedat, poena satisfactoria, sed quae nunquam satisfactionem absoluit, mors aeterna. Ego igitur inter actum primi peccati & imputationem interpono in omnibus Adami posteris corruptionem haereditariam quae imputetur nobis ad illas poenas. Cur tam longe quaeris causam proximam malorum quae omnes patimur, cum occurrat in proximo? Cur eam quaeris in Adamo cum in nobis singulis se prodat? Cur opus est vt Deus nobis imputet peccatum alienum, cum in nobis inueniat peccatum quod illas poenas meretur? Cur imputet actuale quod neque actu neque potentia fecimus, eum videat in singulis nobis vitium actu inhaerens dignum illis poenis? Repones fortasse miserias huius vitae & mortem corporis inflictas fuisse Adamo ob peccatum actuale, quia, inquit Deus, paruisti voci uxoris tuæ & comedisti ex arbore quam præcepi tibi dicendo &c. Et sic colliges, cujus peccati pœnas luimus, id peccatum nostrum est. Peccati actualis Adami pœnas luimus. Nostrum est igitur; quomodo, nisi imputatione? Quid si concedam (quod feci in constituendo statu quæstionis) nobis peccatum Adami imputari ac nostrum esse, sed mediatè tantùm; quia illi participatione vitiositatis, quam in Adamo reliquit, communicamus, & habituali voluntatis prauitate ab eo deriuata ei consentimus? Tria enim ista sese ordine consequuntur, peccatum actuale Adami corruptio nobis inhærens, pœna. Hæc nascitur proximè à corruptione nobis inhærente, corruptio à peccato actuali Adami. Relege, si placet, verba Ægidij Hunnij, quæ Cap. 2. dum statum quæstionis constituerem, adscripsi, necnon Chamieri, quorum locum ibidem notaui. Formaliter etiam ad præmissas respondeo hac distinctione, Cujus peccati pœnas luimus proximè, seu immediatè, Id peccatum nostrum est. Concedo. Cujus vero peccati pœnas luimus tantùm mediatè, alio scilicet mediante peccato, id peccatum nostrum est, Nego. Satis enim est, si sit causa nostri peccati. Nofti enim tritum illud in scholis, quod est causa causa, id etiam est causa causati. Atqui peccati actualis pœnas luimus proximè, Negò; Mediatè, Concedo. Est igitur nostrum peccatum, non sequitur; sed bene, est causa peccati nostri. Quid enim? putasne ista verba, quia paruisti voci vxoris tuæ tibi, tuæ, inquam, personæ dicta esse, & ad te immediatè spectare? Nonne vides quàm personale fuit, & proprium Adamo, maritum fuisse Euæ, tàm ad eius personam accommodata esse hæc verba? Potuitne Dei sententia verbis concipi magis, vt ita loquar, personalibus, magis propriis personæ Adami, minùs communibus generi humano? Id autem noli putare factum esse ab eo temerè. Si Deus actuale illud peccatum Adami imputauisset hominibus nondum existentibus, eosque omnes immediatè ob illud peccatum sua sententia pœnis illis adjudicasset, qua est sapientia communem sententiam verbis communibus, &c, quæ omnibus & singulis hominibus applicari possent, concepisset, aut posterorum Adami aliquam mentionem injecisset. Nunc autem Contrarium fecit, quorsum, nisi vt intelligamus decretas ea sententia pœnas ad nos non pertinere, nisi quia Adamus nobiscum eas communicauit, communicata, quæ illas meretur, per carnalem generationem peccati sui malitia? atque ita causam cur eas pœnas luamus, non quæramus in Deo nobis actionem, quam nullo modo commisimus, imputante, vt nos puniat, sed in Adamo solo, & natura peccati ipsius, quod, vt fermentum quoddam massæ generis humani immissum, eam totam, non per Dei imputationem, sed per carnalem generationem corrupit, ac malitia infecit. Vides me Dei causam agere, noli quæso ei adversari.
units.tr: You go on and draw an argument from the sentence that God pronounced on Adam after his fall, in these words: "Because you have listened to the voice of your wife, and eaten of the tree, etc." From this you argue as follows: "If the punishment was common, the sin must also have been common. But the punishment was common. Therefore the sin was too." You prove the major premise with this syllogism: "A just judge does not inflict a punishment common to all men unless it is on account of a sin common to all." Let me grant at once that I concede all of this, since I acknowledge a sin common to all men, namely the hereditary vice that deserves the common punishments. But you go further: "Now," you say, "I assume: that first sin which made all men liable to punishment is common to all, either by their own act or by imputation. Not by their own act, since Adam alone sinned in act. Therefore by imputation, since it is imputed to all." Why have you left out the third member, so often sung against the Pelagians, "or by natural propagation"? For it is established that the first sin passed over to us, not in the sense that it was a passing action, but in the sense that it was an aversion from God and a turning to creatures as to the ultimate end, remaining in Adam; it passed over, I say, not by an imputation that is outside us, but by a real communication and propagation. Because of this sin common to all, common punishments are inflicted on all: not indeed those satisfactory punishments in this life, at least in the case of the faithful, but still punishments. There is also inflicted, unless the grace of Christ intervenes, a punishment that is satisfactory, yet never brings satisfaction to an end, eternal death. I therefore place between the act of the first sin and its imputation a hereditary corruption in all the posterity of Adam, which is imputed to us for those punishments. Why do you seek so far away the proximate cause of the evils that we all suffer, when it lies close at hand? Why do you seek it in Adam, when it reveals itself in each one of us? Why is it necessary that God impute to us another's sin, when he finds in us a sin that deserves those punishments? Why should he impute an actual sin which we have committed neither in act nor in potentiality, when he sees in each of us a vice actually inhering that deserves those punishments? You will perhaps reply that the miseries of this life and the death of the body were inflicted on Adam on account of his actual sin, "because," says God, "you have listened to the voice of your wife and eaten of the tree which I commanded you," etc. And so you will conclude: the sin for whose penalties we suffer is our sin; we suffer the penalties of Adam's actual sin; therefore it is ours. How, then, except by imputation? But what if I grant (as I did when setting out the state of the question) that Adam's sin is imputed to us and is ours, but only mediately, because we share in the vitiated condition that he left in himself, and by a habitual perversity of will derived from him we consent to him? For these three things follow one another in order: Adam's actual sin, the corruption inhering in us, and the punishment. The punishment arises immediately from the corruption inhering in us; the corruption arises from Adam's actual sin. Please reread the words of Ægidius Hunnius that I quoted in chapter 2, when I was setting out the state of the question, and likewise those of Chamier, whose passage I noted there. I also answer your premises formally with this distinction: "For whose sin we suffer the penalties proximately or immediately, that sin is ours": I grant it. But "for whose sin we suffer the penalties only mediately, that is, with another sin as intermediary, that sin is ours": I deny it. For it is enough that it be the cause of our sin. For you know the familiar saying in the schools: "What is the cause of a cause is also the cause of what is caused." Now we suffer the penalties of actual sin proximately: I deny it; mediately: I grant it. Therefore it is our sin does not follow; but it is indeed the cause of our sin. For what do you think? Do you suppose that these words, "because you have listened to the voice of your wife," were spoken to you, to your person, I say, and apply to you immediately? Do you not see how personal and proper to Adam it was, that he was the husband of Eve, and how these words are so fitted to his person? Could God's sentence have been framed in words more personal, as I may say, more proper to the person of Adam, and less common to the human race? Yet do not think that this was done by him carelessly. If God had imputed that actual sin of Adam to men not yet existing, and had by his sentence immediately adjudged all of them to those punishments, he would have framed a common sentence in common words, such as could be applied to all and each of mankind, or would have made some mention of Adam's posterity. But he has done the contrary. To what end, except that we should understand that this sentence assigns those punishments not to us except because Adam has communicated them to us, since by carnal generation he communicated to us the malice of his sin, which deserves them? And so we should not seek the cause why we suffer those punishments in God, as if he imputed to us an action we never committed, in order to punish us, but in Adam alone and in the nature of the sin itself, which, like a leaven put into the mass of the human race, has corrupted and infected the whole of it, not through God's imputation but through carnal generation. You see that I am defending God's cause; please do not oppose him.

units.la: Me enim vehementer offendit, quòd tu, & alij quidam fratres nostri, dicitis, Deum omnes homines, etiam puerulos, punire morte corporis (& æterna) immo morte animæ, quæ formaliter peccatum est, ob peccatum actuale quod eorum non est vllo modo, nisi imputatione, quia Deus illud ipsis imputat. Id vel cogitare horret conscientia, ac vt aliam tibi & illis mentem det, Dominum supplex ex animo precor.
units.tr: For it greatly offends me that you and certain other brothers of ours say that God punishes all men, even little children, with bodily death (and eternal death), indeed with death of the soul, which is formally sin, on account of an actual sin which is in no way theirs except by imputation, because God imputes it to them. Conscience shudders even to think of this, and I pray to the Lord from my heart, as a suppliant, that he may give you and them another mind.

units.la: Quo enim jure, vt ait alicubi Bellarminus (cui tecum hæc causa est communis) mihi imputatur, quod meum non est? quæ hæc iustitia, peccatum quod alioqui omnium commune non est, imputando omnibus commune facere, ac propterea omnes homines tam seuere punire? Non est, inquis, primum illud peccatum commune omnibus, nisi imputatione, quia scilicet omnibus imputatur. Ergo inquam, antequam imputetur omnibus, commune non est omnibus. Quod igitur commune est omnibus, id soli isti imputationi, quæ scilicet actio Dei est iudiciaria, imputandum est. Consídera, quæso, quæ sit falsa & iniusta imputatio, si hæc non est; Et, an conueniat Deo actio, quæ nos alioqui non peccatores, peccatores faciat, & quidem formaliter, & per se, & annon hoc fit causam omnium nostrorum peccatorum & malorum in Deum referre; & da gloriam creatori tuo & redemptori. Reuoca in animum quæ dixi Cap. 3. hujus examinis §. iii. Neque puta tuam illam sententiam esse ex fontibus vel patrum antiquorum, vel eorum qui primi & præcipuè manum admouerunt Ecclesiæ Reformandæ sæculo superiore, haustam & deductam. Longè aliter illi senserunt, vt, Deo dante, faciam alio Capite manifestum. Nunc mihi satis est tuorum argumentorum nodos soluere.
units.tr: "For by what right," as Bellarmine says somewhere (who shares this cause with you), "is that imputed to me which is not mine?" What justice is this, to make a sin, which otherwise is not common to all, common to all by imputing it, and therefore to punish all men so severely? "The first sin," you say, "is not common to all except by imputation, since it is imputed to all." Therefore, I say, before it is imputed to all, it is not common to all. What is common to all must therefore be attributed to that imputation alone, which is clearly a judicial action of God. Consider, I beg you, what false and unjust imputation this is, if it is not this; and whether it befits God to make us, who otherwise are not sinners, sinners, and indeed formally and in themselves; and whether this is not to refer the cause of all our sins and evils to God. Give glory to your Creator and Redeemer. Recall what I said in chapter 3, section 3, of this examination. And do not think that your opinion was drawn from the sources either of the ancient Fathers or of those who first and chiefly put their hand to the reformation of the Church in the previous century. They thought quite otherwise, as, God willing, I shall make clear in another chapter. For now it is enough for me to untie the knots of your arguments.

units.la: Addis, idem demonstrari ex promissione Euangelij illic, inserta verf. 15. de semine mulieris, Christo scilicet vindice generis humani, contrituro caput serpentis. Quemadmodum expœna communi asseritur peccatum fuisse commune, sic ex Remedio comuni ad delendum illud peccatum, sequitur illud peccatum fuisse omnibus commune. At primum commune fateor peccatum, sed situm, non in imputatione peccati actualis Adami, sed in corruptione omnibus insita; & commune factum, non imputatione diuina, sed generatione carnali. Alioqui Diabolus sua tentatione vnicum hominem peccatorem effecisset, Deus (cogitans totus cohorresco) sua illa imputatione reliquos omnes; cuius imputationis demonstra fi potes vel necessitatem, vel iustitiam. Caeterum quantumuis commune fit remedium, tamen non applicatur, non imputatur vlli adulto, nisi consentienti ac per fidem illud apprehendenti, nec nostrum est nisi Christi & Dei dono. Donari autem à Deo nobis peccatum actuale Adami absit vt credam. Vis autem imputationem peccati actualis Adami. antecedeie omnem nostrum fiue habitualem, fiue actualem consensum. Tuam igitur potiùs sententiam commune hoc remedium euertit, quàm firmat.
units.tr: You add: "The same is shown from the promise of the Gospel inserted there in verse 15, concerning the seed of the woman, that is, Christ the deliverer of the human race, who will crush the head of the serpent. Just as from the common punishment it is asserted that the sin was common, so from the common remedy for blotting out that sin it follows that the sin was common to all." But I grant that the first sin is common, yet it lies not in the imputation of Adam's actual sin but in the corruption implanted in all; and it has been made common not by divine imputation but by carnal generation. Otherwise the devil, by his temptation, would have made one man only a sinner, and God (I shudder wholly to think it) would have made all the rest sinners by that imputation of his. Show me, if you can, either the necessity or the justice of that imputation. Moreover, however common the remedy may be, it is nonetheless not applied to, and not imputed to, any adult except one who consents and apprehends it by faith; nor is it ours except by the gift of Christ and God. But that God should give us Adam's actual sin as a gift, far be it from me to believe. You wish, moreover, that the imputation of Adam's actual sin should precede every consent of ours, whether habitual or actual. Therefore your opinion is overturned by this common remedy rather than confirmed by it.

units.la: Quid quod mihi arma ministrat tuæ isti imputationi funesta? Sic enim ratiocinor. Id cui remedium commune opponitur, vel est ipsum commune malum vel causa cur fit malum commune. Opponitur hoc loco remedium commune serpenti; nec est serpens ipsum commune malum, Ergò serpens est causa cur fit malum commune. Non est autem causa mali communis, nisi aut illud ipse omnibus inspirauerit, aut saltem tale malum in vno produxerit, quod sponte, per se, naturali vi sua sese in omnes vt venenum, vt pestis, diffuderit, & propagauerit. Imputatio, inflictio poenae Dei opus est, non serpentis antiqui. Si igitur peccatum actuale non est omnibus commune, nisi imputatione; quia Deus illud omnibus imputat, nec est in nobis peccatum originale seu vitium inhærens, nisi quia nobis in poenam actualis illius imputati à Deo infligitur, mali communitas non est à serpente; Nec ista priuatio iustitiæ originalis & corruptio hæreditaria virus est serpentis, quod nobis afflauit, sed (quod horret animus meus dicere) Dei effectum & opus. Dices fortasse mortem esse opus Diaboli, quæ tamen peccatum sequitur diuinæ imputationis & iudicij interuentu. nempe, quia Diabolus causa est peccati, quod per se & natura sua meretur mortem, nec potest ei in quo, vel à quo est, nisi intercedat satisfactio, non imputari. At peccatum illud primum actuale Adami, cujus ipsi author serpens fuit, natura sua non merebatur omnium hominum corruptionem moralem, nec erat natura sua eiusmodi, vt salua diuina iustitia non posset non imputari omnibus hominibus ad illud vitium ipsis infligendum. Quod si putes tale suisse natura, & discedes à sententia magnorum virorum qui tecum imputationem illam tuentur, & pergratum nobis feceris, si id docueris & probaueris.
units.tr: What about the arguments your own imputation hands me to use against you? I reason as follows. Whatever the remedy opposed to it is either the common evil itself or the cause of the common evil. Here the common remedy is opposed to the serpent, and the serpent is not itself the common evil. Therefore the serpent is the cause of the common evil. But something is the cause of a common evil only if it has either breathed that evil into everyone, or at least produced such an evil in one person that it spreads of its own accord, by its own nature and power, into all, as poison or plague does. Imputation is the work of God's infliction of punishment, not of the ancient serpent. So if actual sin is common to all only through imputation, because God imputes it to all, and if there is no original sin or inherent corruption in us except because it is inflicted on us by God as punishment for the imputed actual sin, then the commonness of evil does not come from the serpent. Nor is that privation of original righteousness and hereditary corruption a poison the serpent breathed upon us. It is (and I shudder to say it) the effect and work of God. You may perhaps say that death is the work of the devil, yet it follows sin through the intervention of divine imputation and judgment. That is because the devil is the cause of a sin which by its own nature deserves death, and unless satisfaction intervenes, death cannot fail to be imputed to the one in whom or by whom the sin is committed. But that first actual sin of Adam, of which the serpent was the author, did not by its own nature deserve the moral corruption of all men. Nor was it by nature such that, with divine justice preserved, it could not fail to be imputed to all men so as to inflict that corruption upon them. If you think it was by nature of that kind, you depart from the opinion of great men who defend that imputation along with you. You would do us a very great favour if you taught and proved this.

units.la: Secundum tuum Argumentum exsculpis ex Pf. 32. 1. 2. Beatus cui dimittitur praevaricatio, cui tegitur peccatum: Beatus homo cui non imputauit Dominus iniquitatem, ea arte, quam mihi mirari magis licet, quàm assequi. Quis enim mentis oculus, vt vt lynceus, videre possit in illis verbis immediatam peccati actualis Adami toti posteritati imputationem? Tu tamen multis verbis efficere conaris, vt eam tecum in illis videam, sed non possum. Vtinam tui argumenti vim adhibita forma syllogistica retexisses, nec magna verborum copia obruisses; ex quibus eam eruere non possum. Testatur Psaltes in genere beatum esse, cui peccatum non imputatur, nempe, quod vel commisit, vel in se habet, quod autem peccatum nobis possit iure imputari, vel non imputari non docet. Probas miserum esse cui peccatum imputatur, Concedo, Addis, si hoc verum est in genere de omni peccato, verum etiam esse de peccato originali, quod in Adamo contraximus, ab Adamo dicendum fuisse videtur. Concedo hoc quoque. Subjicis, vitium illud originis esse poenam primi peccati primorum parentum, id, quoniam poenam proprie dictam intelligis, id ipsum est quod inter nos quaeritur. Ais nomina, quibus Psaltes peccata nuncupauit, posse primam illam Adami rebellionem significare, nempe, haud minus, quam, vel Caini homicidium, vel populi Israelitici rebellionem. Adjicis eam esse ἀνομίαν, qua voce usus est Apostolus in citando hoc loco: Esto; quid inde sequatur nondum intelligo: idem enim de Caini homicidio, de Sodomeorum crimine, de Absalomi incestu & rebellione,&denique de quovis alio cujusvis scelere dicere licet. Sed tu ipse aliquid concludis, te igitur audiamus, Inde, inquis, concludere debemus secundum Apostolum verbis Prophetae ventem, illum esse beatum cui peccata non imputantur, & ex consequenti, illum esse miserum cui peccata imputantur, & cum miseria nostra tota sit a peccato primo Adami, si peccatum illud nobis non imputetur, nos esse miseros, si e contra nobis non imputetur, nos esse beatos. Tu nobis, opinor subsumendum reliquisti, Atqui non sumus beati: Ergo nobis peccatum illud imputatur. Taceo hujus tui argumenti materiam ob terminorum multitudinem formam syllogisticam non admittere. Taceo idem posse de quovis alio peccato dici, si nobis imputetur, nos esse miseros. Aio ut beati simus, non sufficere vnius cujusdam peccati non imputationem, sed requiri omnium. Aio conferre ad meam beatitudinem, non si mihi aliquod peccatum non imputetur, puta incestus Iudæ, sed si mihi illud non imputetur ex gratia, quod mihi posset imputari ex iustitia. Nego autem nobis primum peccatum actuale posse imputari ex iustitia. Aio denique miseriam nostram totam esse à peccato primo Adami, non quia nobis proximè imputetur,sed quia causa est ejus peccati, quod quia nobis inest, ac proinde nostrum est, potest nobis imputari ex iustitia.
units.tr: You draw your second argument from Psalm 32:1–2: Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered: blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute iniquity. You do this by an art that I can admire more than I can attain. For what mental eye, sharp as a lynx's, could see in those words the immediate imputation of Adam's actual sin to his whole posterity? Yet you try hard, with many words, to make me see it with you there, and I cannot. I wish you had set out the force of your argument in syllogistic form, and not buried it under a great abundance of words, from which I cannot extract it. The Psalmist testifies in general that he is blessed to whom sin is not imputed, namely one who has committed it or has it in himself. But he does not teach that sin can rightly be imputed to us, or rightly not imputed. You prove that it is wretched to be the one to whom sin is imputed. I grant it. You add: if this is true in general of every sin, it seems that it must also be said of original sin, which we contracted in Adam, that it is true, and must be said from Adam. I grant this too. You go on to say that the vice of origin is the punishment of the first sin of our first parents. Since you understand punishment in the proper sense, this is exactly what is in question between us. You say that the names by which the Psalmist calls sins can signify that first rebellion of Adam, no less than Cain's murder or the rebellion of the people of Israel. You add that it is lawlessness [ἀνομίαν], the word the Apostle used in quoting this passage. Very well, but I still do not see what follows from that. The same could be said of Cain's murder, the sin of the Sodomites, Absalom's incest and rebellion, and indeed of any crime whatever. But you yourself draw a conclusion, so let us hear you: From this, you say, we must conclude, in the words of the Prophet as the Apostle cites them, that he is blessed whose sins are not imputed, and consequently that he is wretched whose sins are imputed; and since all our misery comes from the first sin of Adam, if that sin is not imputed to us we are wretched, and if on the contrary it is not imputed to us we are blessed. You have left it to me, I suppose, to supply the minor premise: But we are not blessed; therefore that sin is imputed to us. I pass over the fact that the matter of your argument, with its great number of terms, does not admit of syllogistic form. I pass over the fact that the same could be said of any other sin, that if it is imputed to us we are wretched. I say that in order to be blessed it is not enough that some one sin is not imputed, but that all sins must not be imputed. I say that what contributes to my blessedness is not that some sin, say Judas's incest, is not imputed to me, but that the sin which could be imputed to me in justice is not imputed to me in grace. I deny, however, that the first actual sin can be imputed to us in justice. Finally I say that our whole misery comes from the first sin of Adam, not because it is imputed to us immediately, but because it is the cause of that sin which, since it inheres in us and is therefore ours, can be imputed to us in justice.

units.la: Ad firmandam hanc tuam rationem citas ratiocinationem Apostoli probantis Abrahamum fuisse iustificatum, quia credidit Deo, & imputatum est ei ad iustitiam. Quis vnquam sperasset inde posse effici, primum peccatum actuale Adami omnibus hominibus imputari immediatè, & quidem ad hanc poenam, corruptionem scilicet hæreditariam? Nam hæc est nostra quæstio, cujus affirmatio tibi formaliter concludenda fuit. subtilem profectò te esse oportet, ac mirum artificem argumentorum, qui ex huiusmodi locis conficere illam imputationem possis. Sed quid inde concludis? (nam omnia tua verba huc transferre operosum esset, nec necessarium.) Quemadmodum igitur, inquis, homo iustificatur & beatus est, quia credit in eum qui iustificat impium; & fides eius illi imputatur, ad iustitiam sine operibus, quia peccatum non imputatur, sequitur ex regula contrariorum, hominem damnari & miserum esse qui non credit in Deum, quia peccatum illi imputatur ad condemnationem, Concedo. Addis, & in genere omne peccatum quod commisit, Fateor. Subjungis, & in specie hoc peccatum Adami, quod ipsum constituit peccatorem. Hoc jam nego, siquidem, vt par est, per peccatum Adami ejus peccatum actuale intelligis, necnon imputationem immediatam. Id enim (vt habet eruditissimus Chamierus) nos peccatores constituit non formaliter, sed causaliter; quâ de re suo loco.
units.tr: To confirm this reasoning of yours you cite the Apostle's argument proving that Abraham was justified, because he believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness. Who would ever have hoped that from this one could draw the conclusion that the first actual sin of Adam is imputed immediately to all men, and indeed to that punishment, namely hereditary corruption? For this is our question, and you ought to have concluded its affirmation formally. You must surely be a subtle man and a wonderful craftsman of arguments, to be able to build that imputation out of passages of this kind. But what do you conclude from them? (For it would be laborious, and not necessary, to transfer all your words here.) Therefore, you say, just as a man is justified and blessed because he believes in him who justifies the ungodly, and his faith is imputed to him for righteousness without works, because sin is not imputed, it follows by the rule of contraries that a man who does not believe in God is condemned and wretched, because sin is imputed to him for condemnation. I grant it. You add: and in general every sin that he has committed. I confess it. You continue: and in particular this sin of Adam, which itself made him a sinner. This I now deny, since, as is right, by the sin of Adam you mean his actual sin, and also immediate imputation. For that sin (as the most learned Chamier has it) makes us sinners not formally but causally; but of this in its own place.

units.la: Hæc sola inuenisti in vetere Testamento, quibus illam imputationem concludi posse putares. Potuissem & responsiones meas magnorum Theologorum authoritate fulcire, & ijsdem ex locis alia argumenta promere tuis infesta: sed consulo breuitati, & nolo te nimia argumentorum profusione legentem fatigare. Loca in quibus Deus visitare dicitur iniquitatem patrum in filios hic ne commemorasti quidem: vidisti enim ea esse ad tuendam aduersus mea argumenta, quàm ad probandam imputationem peccati actualis Adami, magis accommodata. Reuera enim inde nullum argumentum confici potest, quod non æquè de alijs Adami peccatis ac de primo, deque aliorum parentum nostrorum peccatis, ac de Adami procedat: & limitatio illa in quartam generationem repugnat aperrè imputationi illimitatæ in omnes generationes: & altera illa limitatio in ijs qui me oderunt præsupponit odium Dei in ijs qui visitantur: cùm imputatio primi peccati actualis nullum in infantibus vitium præsupponat, sed, si tibi creditur, faciat. Verùm de his locis alibi.
units.tr: These are the only passages you have found in the Old Testament from which you think that imputation can be concluded. I could have supported my replies with the authority of great theologians, and drawn from the same passages other arguments hostile to your view. But I am sparing of words, and I do not want to weary you, the reader, with too great a profusion of arguments. You have not even mentioned the passages in which God is said to visit the iniquity of the fathers upon the children. You saw, I think, that these are better suited to defending your view against my arguments than to proving the imputation of Adam's actual sin. In truth no argument can be drawn from them which does not proceed equally of the other sins of Adam as of the first, and of the sins of our other parents as of Adam's. Moreover that limitation to the fourth generation plainly contradicts an unlimited imputation to all generations. And that other limitation on those who hate me presupposes hatred of God in those who are visited. Whereas the imputation of the first actual sin presupposes no vice in infants, but, if you are to be believed, makes one. But I will deal with these passages elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc mihi licet ita argumentari. Si dogma de imputatione primi peccati actualis Adami omnibus & singulis hominibus verum est & credendum, vtiq; reuelatum est alicubi in veteri Testamento. Atqui nullibi reuelatum est in veteri Testamento. Non igitur est verum & credendum. Minor patet ex hac nostra disputatione. Majorem probo, quia lex comparata est ad detegendum & patefaciendum peccatum: per legem est cognitio peccati. Non fungitur autem suo hoc munere, vti par est, fi non patefacit illud peccatum quod est omnium hominum commune, quod est omnium aliorum causa, vnde omnium hominum condemnatio pendet. Non patefacit autem fecundum tuam sententiam, qui peccatum ejusmodi vis esse primum peccatum actuale Adami omnibus hominibus imputatum, nisi hæc imputatio ex lege, seu vetere Testamento colligi possit. Deinde, fi peccatum illud actuale omnibus imputatur proximè, idq; tenentur homines credere, nititur imputatio illa lege aliqua, cuius etiam ope cognosci debet, eaque valde antiqua. Cum igitur nulla ejusmodi lex occurrat in veteri Testamento, nullam esse illam imputationem fatendum est. Denique Israëlitæ increduli, qui ante Christi aduentum mortui sunt, iudicati sunt fecundum legem quam à Deo per manum Mosis, acceperunt. Atqui fecundum legem danari non potuerunt immediatè ob peccatum actuale Adami, nec ipsis illud imputari, nisi fecundum legem constare potuerit id peccatum eorum singulorum fuisse peccatum. Idem de omnibus alijs hominibus dicendum. Fit enim omnis iudiciaria imputatio peccati & inflictio pœnæ fecundum aliquam legem. Atqui imputatio immediata peccati actualis omnibus hominibus & vitij inhærentis inflictio, fi, vt tu ais, est, vtique iudiciaria est. Fit igitur fecundum aliquam legem. Eam ergo, fi potes, profer. Nulla certè deprehendi potest in vllo loco scripturæ.
units.tr: Now I may argue thus. If the doctrine that the first actual sin of Adam is imputed to all and each of mankind is true and to be believed, then surely it has been revealed somewhere in the Old Testament. But it is nowhere revealed in the Old Testament. Therefore it is not true and to be believed. The minor premise is plain from this our disputation. I prove the major premise: the law was designed to disclose and make manifest sin; through the law comes the knowledge of sin. But it does not perform this office as it ought, if it does not make manifest that sin which is common to all men, which is the cause of all the others, and on which the condemnation of all men depends. Yet, according to your opinion, which holds that this first actual sin of Adam is imputed to all men, the law does not make it manifest, unless this imputation can be gathered from the law, or from the Old Testament. Next, if that actual sin is imputed to all men immediately, and men are bound to believe this, that imputation rests on some law, by whose help it must also be known, and a very ancient law at that. Since, then, no such law occurs in the Old Testament, we must confess that there is no such imputation. Finally, the unbelieving Israelites who died before the coming of Christ were judged according to the law which they had received from God by the hand of Moses. But they could not have been condemned immediately on account of Adam's actual sin according to that law, nor could that sin have been imputed to them, unless it could be shown from the law that this sin was the sin of each of them. The same must be said of all other men. For every judicial imputation of sin and infliction of punishment is made according to some law. But the immediate imputation of actual sin to all men, and the infliction of inherent sin, if it is as you say, is certainly judicial. It is therefore made according to some law. Produce that law then, if you can. Certainly none can be found in any passage of Scripture.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CAPUT IX.

units.la: Responsio ad Argumenta, quæ pro primi peccati actualis immediata omnibus hominibus imputatione ducuntur è Nouo Testamento.
units.tr: Reply to the arguments which are drawn from the New Testament for the immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin to all men.

units.la: PVGNAS deinceps argumentis è Nouo Testamento petitis, nec aliundè quàm ex Rom. v. 12. & seqq. Reuera si quis est in tota scriptura locus, vnde primi peccati actualis imputatio immediata toti generi humano confici possit, hic profectò vnus est. Ea tamen non video quo pacto elici possit, posita hac hypothesi manasse à primo peccato Adami in omnes homines per generationem carnalem vitium, quod verè peccatum est, damnando generi humano sufficiens. Atque ita sentio, aut argumentis ex eo capite ductis, aut huic hypothesi, quam omnes protestantium Ecclesiæ constantissimè hactenus, tenuerunt, renunciandum esse. Quo autem consilio à te sit factum, nescio, quod cùm in Thesibus obuiam iuerim argumentis quæ ex Rom. v. ducuntur, & meas responsiones omnes tibi percurrendas ac refellendas proposueris, tu tamen eas ad caput vsque ix. tractatus tui relegasti nulla prorsus earum mentione facta hoc loco, quo argumenta illa tractas, interpositis etiam inter eas & hanc tuam tractationem tribus capitibus, quibus meam sententiam humanis testimonijs opprimere conaris. Si conjecturæ locus dandus est, ea ratione animos lectorum occupare voluisti ac praemunire, ne mearum responsionum & rationum aculeis laederentur. In quo, si hoc tuum consilium fuit, videris mihi causae tuae diffidisse ac obfuisse. Veritas enim artem hujusmodi non desiderat, simplex, aperta, ingenua, candida, humilis etiam cum sit, generosum quid spirat, sibi (quae omni re fortior est) & Deo veritatis fidens tum maxime laetatur & splendescit & fulget, cum suo contrario, ut ut fucato comparatur. Id autem, sive illo sive alio consilio a te sit factum, nostram disputationem conturbat, & distrahit, & multa cogit repetere. Huc accedit quod hoc loco commentarium mihi videris scribere potius quam syllogismos nectere: nec habere ob oculos statum controversiae bene constitutum & purgatum; confundis enim saepe quae maxime distingui debent, admisces etiam quaedam quae, ut in se vera sint, huc tamen non spectant, quale illud est quod obseruas, & aliquot exemplis probas, saepe unum apud Hebraeos pro primo sumi. Quominus enim hoc loco sic possit accipi obstat oppositio, quam Apostolus instituit inter unum hominem & unum hominem, illum Adamum hunc Christum. Item inter unum ϖεϱιστεϱϱ & unum δικαιωμα ut taceam scopum Apostoli flagitare, ut unitas hoc loco opponatur pluralitati: sed non iuuat excurrere. Satius igitur ut ego quidem arbitror fuisset, quae tu locis disclusa & disiuncta esse voluisti, ea vitandae vel taediosae repetitionis, vel incommodae distractionis causa, in hunc locum comportare, ac uno contextu sermonis cohaerentia simul oculis legentis subjicere; sed quia tibi aliter visum est, tuae methodo meam accommodabo, teque sequar κ̄ϱ πολιτ, eaque argumenta expendam, quæ tu ex Rom. v. colligere potuisti meis Thesibus in alium locum rejectis.
units.tr: You now attack the arguments taken from the New Testament, and these only from Rom. v. 12 and following. Indeed, if there is any passage in all of Scripture from which the immediate imputation of the first actual sin could be inferred for the whole human race, this certainly is the one. Yet I do not see how that doctrine can be drawn from it, given this hypothesis: that a corruption, which is truly sin and sufficient to condemn the human race, has flowed from the first sin of Adam into all men by carnal generation. And I judge that either the arguments drawn from that passage or this hypothesis, which all the churches of the Protestants have held most firmly until now, must be given up. Why you did this, I do not know. When I met the arguments drawn from Rom. v. in my Theses, and you proposed to run through and refute all my replies, you nevertheless put them off until chapter ix of your treatise, without any mention of them at this point, where you deal with those arguments. You have also interposed three chapters between them and this part of your treatise, in which you try to overwhelm my view with human testimonies. If one may guess, you wanted in this way to occupy and forearm the minds of your readers, so that they would not be wounded by the stings of my replies and reasons. If this was your plan, you seem to me to have distrusted your cause and to have harmed it. For truth does not need such an art. Simple, open, ingenuous, candid, and humble as it is, it breathes something noble; trusting in itself, which is stronger than anything, and in God of truth, it rejoices, shines, and glows most of all when it is set beside its opposite, however painted up. But whether this was done by you with that plan or another, it confuses and scatters our discussion and forces us to repeat much. Moreover, in this place you seem to me to be writing a commentary rather than tying up syllogisms. You do not keep before your eyes a well-established and cleared statement of the controversy. For you often confuse things that ought to be most carefully distinguished, and you also mix in some matters which, however true in themselves, do not bear on this question. Such is your observation, which you prove by several examples, that among the Hebrews one is often taken for first. The opposition which the Apostle sets up between one man and one man, that Adam and this Christ, stands in the way of taking it in this sense here. Likewise between one trespass [παράπτωμα] and one righteousness [δικαίωμα]; I say nothing of the Apostle's aim, which demands that unity be set here against plurality. But I will not digress. It would therefore have been better, as I think, to bring together in this place what you wished to keep separated and divided in different places, to avoid either tedious repetition or awkward dislocation, and to set them side by side before the reader's eyes in one continuous line of argument. But since you have decided otherwise, I will adapt myself to your method and follow you, and I will weigh those arguments which you could gather from Rom. v., my Theses having been referred to another place.

units.la: Ordiris à verf. 12. is sic habet, ὥσπερ δι᾽ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἡ ἁμαρτία εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθε, καὶ διὰ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ὁ θάνατος, καὶ οὕτως εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους ὁ θάνατος διῆλθεν, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον. Sicut per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit, & per peccatum mors, & ita in omnes homines mors pertransfijt, eo quod omnes peccarunt. Sic habet locus: nunc eum excutiamus.
units.tr: You begin from verse 12, which reads: ὥσπερ δι᾽ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἡ ἁμαρτία εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθε, καὶ διὰ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ὁ θάνατος, καὶ οὕτως εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους ὁ θάνατος διῆλθεν, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον. Just as through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death passed upon all men, because all sinned. That is the passage; let us now examine it.

units.la: Si quod in eo latet argumentum illius imputationis, id proculdubio vel ex verbis peccatum in mundum introiit, vel ex sequentibus per peccatum mors, vel ex his ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, vel denique ex verbo ἥμαρτον peccarunt, excidet.
units.tr: If there is any argument for that imputation hidden in it, it will surely come out either from the words sin entered into the world, or from the following words death through sin, or from the phrase ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, or finally from the verb ἥμαρτον, sinned.

units.la: Ex verbis illis, peccatum in mundum introiit, quascunque in partes te vertas, non elicies, nisi istud, Si per peccatum, quod in mundum introiit, intelligendum est peccatum primum actuale Adami, & non potuit peccatum actuale introire in omnes homines aliter quàm per imputationem, consequens est primum peccatum actuale Adami imputariomnibus hominibus. Atqui prius est verum; Ergo & posterius. Nego utrumque antecedentis membrum.
units.tr: From the words sin entered into the world, you will not draw, however you turn them, anything except this: if the sin which entered into the world is to be understood as Adam's first actual sin, and an actual sin could not enter into all men in any way except by imputation, then it follows that Adam's first actual sin is imputed to all men. But the first is true; therefore the second is too. I deny both parts of the antecedent.

units.la: Tu prius probas, nimirum, per peccatum quod in mundum introiit intelligendum esse primum peccatum actuale Adami, sed addis (quod tuam mentem obscurat) id peccatum in nos transfusum originale dici: Et mox, peccatum originale in nobis ex illo esse: Item, Adamum in nos corruptionem genitura transfudisse, quam peccatum originale dicimus. Et paulò post, hoc peccatum ab ipso quidem Adamo commissum esse, sed culpa atque reatu per imputationem in nos trassiisse, Idcoque in ipso actuale & personale fuisse, sed in nobis originale dici. Sic modò peccatum originale cum peccato actuali Adami confundis.modò distinguis,& modò peccatum actuale Adami cum corruptione originaria commisces, modò ab ea separas. Loquere, te rogo & quæso, distinctius & magis enucleatè: nihil enim adeò veritatis indagationi officit, ac vel ambiguitas orationis, vel ejus cui tecum res est inconstantia & lubricitas sermonis. Si, quod nonnulli faciunt, duo credis peccata originalia, vnum imputatum, alterum nobis inhærens, cur nullo loco id dicis aperte? Si non nisi vnum credis, dic constanter, aut cum Pighio id esse peccatum actuale Adami nobis omnibus imputatum, aut cum fidei confessione nostrarum Ecclesiarum corruptionem hæreditariam, seu vitium inhærens: nec duo ista permifce aut confunde, quæ secundum tuam sententiam maximo interuallo inter se distant. Peccatum primum actuale Adami ante quinque millia annorum commissum præteriit, nec permansit in rerum natura: vitium inhærens cum natura humana permansit, estque & viget hodie. Illud vnicum est numero, hujus tot sunt indiuidua quot homines. Illud fuit actio, hoc se habet ad modum habitus. Illud extra nos est, nec possibile est esse in nobis, hoc est intra nos in nobis hærens. Illud tu putas nostrum esse, sed imputatione duntaxat Dei, hoc verè nostrum est, nobis penitus infixum, & inhærens: Illud vis esse culpam, hoc illius pœnam. Hac ambiguitate & confusione sublatâ, videamus quibus rationibus probes, Apostolum per peccatum quod in mundum introiit peccatum actuale Adami intelligere. quæ certè fuit sententia Pighij, quam ipse Bellarminus aliquot argumentis confutauit, sed nolo te præjudiciis vrgere.
units.tr: You first prove that by the sin which entered into the world the first actual sin of Adam must be understood. But you add (which obscures your meaning) that this sin is called original sin transfused into us. And soon after: original sin is in us from that one. Likewise, that Adam transfused into us by generation a corruption, which we call original sin. And a little later, that this sin was committed indeed by Adam himself, but passed over to us by imputation of guilt and liability, and therefore it was actual and personal in him, but in us it is called original. So now you confuse original sin with Adam's actual sin, now you distinguish them, and now you mix Adam's actual sin with the original corruption, and now you separate them. Speak, I beg and ask you, more distinctly and more clearly. For nothing hinders the search for truth so much as either ambiguity of expression or inconsistency and slipperiness of speech on the part of the one with whom one is dealing. If, as some do, you believe there are two original sins, one imputed and the other inherent in us, why do you never say so openly anywhere? If you believe there is only one, say so plainly: either with Pighius that it is the actual sin of Adam imputed to us all, or with the confession of faith of our churches that it is hereditary corruption, or inherent vice. Do not mix or confuse these two, which by your own view are separated by a very great interval. The first actual sin of Adam was committed five thousand years ago and has passed away, and it did not remain in the nature of things. Inherent vice has remained with human nature, and it is alive and thriving today. The former is one in number; the latter is as many individuals as there are men. The former was an act; the latter exists after the manner of a habit. The former is outside us, and it is not possible for it to be in us; the latter is within us, clinging in us. You think the former is ours only by the imputation of God; the latter is truly ours, fixed in us deeply and inherent. You want the former to be guilt; the latter is its punishment. With this ambiguity and confusion removed, let us see by what reasons you prove that the Apostle understands by the sin which entered into the world the actual sin of Adam. This was certainly the opinion of Pighius, which Bellarmine himself refuted by several arguments. But I do not wish to press you with prejudices.

units.la: Vteris, Veteris, quantum colligere possum, quatuor argumentis. 1. Per unum hominem Apostolus intelligit primum hominem scilicet Adamum. Ergo per peccatum quod per unum hominem introiit in Mundum intelligit primum peccatum actuale Adami. Nego sequi. Non enim Apostolus dicit Adami peccatum, sed per Adamum peccatum introiisse in Mundum. Adamum considerat ut huius peccati causam, Mundum, id est, homines ut subiectum: nec docere voluit, quis primus in Mundo peccauerit (nam Adamo prior Eua, & hac prior diabolus peccauit) sed in omnes homines per Adamum introductam esse corruptionem peccati. 2. Apostolus, agit de peccato quod Mundum infecit, & mortem inuexit. Hoc autem conuenit tantum peccato actuali Adami ex quo peccatum originale in nobis. Ergo Apostolus agit tantum de peccato actuali Adami. Distinguo peccatum quod Mundum infecit: nam infecisse dicitur vel formaliter, vel causaliter siue efficienter. Priori modo mundum infecit vitium & corruptio inhaerens, posteriore peccatum actuale Adami. Loquitur autem Apostolus hoc versu de peccato quod infecit mundum priori modo: non enim ait peccatum infecisse mundum, sed introiisse in mundum. Peccatum actuale Adami mundum infecisse dicitur causaliter, quia causa est ejus peccati quod introiit in mundum. Peccatum vero quod introiit in mundum, cum sit intra mundum formaliter eum afficit & inficit in quo est. 3. ἡ ἁμαρτία cum articulo certum peccati indiuiduum designat, adeo quidem ut vix apud Paulum invenias τῆ ἁμαρτίᾳ addito articulo aliud declarare, ut notant doctissimi interpretes. Ergo non designat corruptionem hereditariam, quae non est. vnum peccati indiuiduum, sed peccatum actuale Adami. Nego antecedens. Nullum interpretem me legere memini, qui nomen ἀμάρτημα cum praefixo articulo obseruet certum peccati iudiuiduum seu singulare quoddam peccatum vnum numero apud Paulum significare: contrà obseruant id fere vbique haereditariam illam corruptionem, quae in omnibus hominibus inest ab ortu, designare. Quarta denique tua ratio est petita ex alijs nominibus, quibus tu putas Apostolum hoc peccatum quod in mundum introiit insigniuisse. Quod in sequentibus versibus Apostolus vocat παράβασιν transgressionem, παράπτωμα lapsum seu defectionem, παρακοήν inobedientiam, illud est peccatum actuale Adami. Atqui hoc peccatum quod in mundum introiit, vocat Apostolus παράβασιν, παράπτωμα, & παρακοήν. Ergo hoc peccatum, quod in mundum introiit, est peccatum actuale Adami. Respondeo distinguendum esse nomen παράπτωμα a duobus alijs: Illo enim Apostolus modo peccatum Adami, modo vitium ex peccato Adami in omnibus hominibus ortum designat: His solum peccatum Adami significat, non quidem actuale praecisum ab habituali, sed simul cum habituali. Itaque quantum ad hoc nomen παράπτωμα attinet, nego Maiorem: quantum vero ad alia duo, nego minorem. Deinde nego Apostolum vllo eorum trium nominum peccatum actuale Adami designasse praecisum a corruptione quam in Adamo peperit, cum tamen de peccato actuali ita praecise intelligenda sit haec nostra controuersia. Vis enim peccato illo suo actuali Adamum meruisse cum sibi tum nobis illam corruptionem. Non ergo potes probare per ἁμαρτίαν hoc loco peccatum actuale Adami esse intelligendum. Fac tamen intelligi, negabo peccatum illud introiisse in mundum per imputationem; sed dici introiisse in mundum, quia suum venenum reliquit in Adamo, quod sine eiusmodi imputatione serpsit ab Adamo in Sethum, a Setho in Enosch, ab hoc in Kenanem, & ita paulatim a patre in filios manauit, donec ad nos perueniret propagatione & multiplicatione naturali.
units.tr: You use, as far as I can gather, four arguments. (1) By one man the Apostle understands the first man, namely Adam. Therefore by the sin which entered the world through one man he understands the first actual sin of Adam. I deny the inference. For the Apostle does not say the sin of Adam, but that sin entered into the world through Adam. He considers Adam as the cause of this sin, and the world, that is, men, as its subject. Nor did he wish to teach who first sinned in the world (for Eve sinned before Adam, and the devil before her), but that the corruption of sin was introduced into all men through Adam. (2) The Apostle is speaking of the sin which infected the world and brought in death. But this belongs only to Adam's actual sin, from which original sin is in us. Therefore the Apostle speaks only of Adam's actual sin. I distinguish the sin which infected the world: for it is said to have infected the world either formally or causally, that is, efficiently. In the former way, inherent vice and corruption infected the world; in the latter, Adam's actual sin did. But the Apostle in this verse speaks of the sin which infected the world in the former way. For he does not say that sin infected the world, but that it entered into the world. Adam's actual sin is said to have infected the world causally, because it is the cause of that sin which entered into the world. But the sin which entered into the world, since it is within the world, formally affects and infects that in which it is. (3) ἡ ἁμαρτία [the sin], with the article, designates a definite individual sin; so much so that you will hardly find in Paul τῆ ἁμαρτίᾳ with the article used to mean anything else, as the most learned interpreters note. Therefore it does not designate hereditary corruption, which is not one individual sin, but Adam's actual sin. I deny the antecedent. I do not recall reading any interpreter who notes that the noun ἀμάρτημα [sin], with the prefixed article, signifies in Paul a definite individual sin, or one particular singular sin. On the contrary, they almost everywhere observe that it designates that hereditary corruption which is in all men from birth. (4) Finally, your fourth argument is taken from the other names by which you think the Apostle marked this sin which entered into the world. The Apostle calls the sin in the following verses transgression (παράβασιν), lapse or defection (παράπτωμα), and disobedience (παρακοήν). That is Adam's actual sin. But the Apostle calls this sin which entered into the world transgression (παράβασιν), lapse (παράπτωμα), and disobedience (παρακοήν). Therefore this sin which entered into the world is Adam's actual sin. I reply that the name παράπτωμα must be distinguished from the other two. For in one sense the Apostle designates by it sometimes Adam's sin, sometimes the vice arising from Adam's sin in all men; the other two signify only Adam's sin, not indeed actual sin separated from habitual sin, but together with habitual sin. So, as far as this name παράπτωμα is concerned, I deny the major premise; as far as the other two are concerned, I deny the minor. Next, I deny that the Apostle by any of those three names designated Adam's actual sin separated from the corruption which it brought forth in Adam. Yet this controversy of ours must be understood precisely of actual sin in that sense. For you want Adam to have merited by that actual sin of his both that corruption for himself and for us. Therefore you cannot prove that by ἁμαρτία [sin] in this place Adam's actual sin is to be understood. But grant that it is so understood: I will deny that this sin entered into the world by imputation. Rather, it is said to have entered into the world because it left its poison in Adam, which crept without any such imputation from Adam to Seth, from Seth to Enos, from him to Cainan, and so gradually flowed from father to sons, until it reached us by natural propagation and multiplication.

units.la: Sustinui impetum tuum, vide an possis meum. Hinc enim mihi surgit argumentum tuam euertens sententiam. Dabis mihi profecto dogma illud de imputatione peccati actualis Adami toti generi humano, si verum est, si credendum est, doceri alicubi in Scriptura absolutissimā fidei nostrae normā. Dabis etiam, si cubi docetur, doceri in hoc loco, vbi Apostolus quicquid ab Adamo mali in humanum genus manauit explicat accurate. Dabis tandem quaecunque mala Adamus cum posteris suis communicauit, ea ab Apostolo reuocari ad haec duo, peccatum & mortem. Videamus ergo quodnam peccatum intelligat. Tu vis esse peccatum actuale Adami imputatum omnibus hominibus ad duas poenas, priuationem iustitiae originalis seu vitium originale, & mortem. Ego dico esse vitium originale seu corruptionem haereditariam infingulis hominibus inhaerentem, non autem peccatum actuale Adami singulis hominibus immediate imputatum. Tuam sententiam, quas attulisti, rationes non probant: ijs enim, vt vides, respondi. Ego meam sic probo. Si quod peccatum Apostolus docet Rom. v. fuisse ab Adamo cum omnibus hominibus communicatum, illud profecto est, quod per Adamum docet in mundum introiisse, & per id mortem, ita vt mors in omnes homines pertransiuerit. Atqui peccatum illud, quod docet per Adamum in mundum introiisse, & per id mortem, est corruptio haereditaria, non autem peccatum actuale Adami praecise sumptum. Ergo si aliquod peccatum Apostolus docet, vti revera docet, ab Adamo cum omnibus hominibus communicatum, illud profecto est corruptio haereditaria, non autem peccatum actuale Adami. Maiorem non negabis: est enim manifesta. Certe peccatum per quod ait mortem introiisse in mundum, hoc est, vt ipse exponit,& tu post eum, in omnes homines, est illud cui proxime generis humani mortem & condemnationem adscribit. Minorem probo. Primam rationem mihi ministrat ipsum nomen peccati ἁμαρτία sic enim (vt doctissimus Beza ad hunc versum notauit) vocare solet Apostolus morbum illum haereditarium: adeo quidem vt vix apud Paulum addito articulo aliud declaret. Morbus autem haereditarius non est peccatum actuale Adami, sed corruptio, & vitium ab illo ortum.
units.tr: I have withstood your attack; now see whether you can withstand mine. For from your own position an argument rises up that overturns your view. You will grant me, surely, that the doctrine of the imputation of Adam's actual sin to the whole human race, if it is true and must be believed, is taught somewhere in Scripture, our most absolute norm of faith. You will also grant that, if it is taught anywhere, it is taught in this passage, where the Apostle explains accurately whatever evil flowed from Adam to the human race. And you will grant finally that all the evils Adam communicated to his posterity are traced by the Apostle back to these two, sin and death. Let us see, then, which sin he means. You wish it to be Adam's actual sin, imputed to all men for two penalties: the deprivation of original righteousness, or original vice, and death. I say it is original vice, or hereditary corruption, inhering in each individual man, and not Adam's actual sin imputed immediately to each individual. The reasons you have brought do not prove your view, for, as you see, I have answered them. I prove my own thus. If the sin which the Apostle in Romans 5 teaches was communicated from Adam to all men is the one which he teaches entered the world through Adam, and through it death, so that death passed upon all men, then that sin is certainly the sin through which death came. But the sin which he teaches entered the world through Adam, and through it death, is hereditary corruption, not Adam's actual sin taken strictly by itself. Therefore, if the Apostle teaches any sin, as he really does, communicated from Adam to all men, it is certainly hereditary corruption and not Adam's actual sin. You will not deny the major premise, for it is plain. Surely the sin through which he says death entered the world, that is, as he himself explains, and you after him, into all men, is the one to which he most directly ascribes the death and condemnation of the human race. I prove the minor. The very name of sin, ἁμαρτία [hamartia], supplies my first reason; for, as the most learned Beza noted on this verse, the Apostle is accustomed to call that hereditary disease by this name, so that in Paul it scarcely ever declares anything else when the article is added. But a hereditary disease is not Adam's actual sin; it is a corruption, and a vice arising from him.

units.la: GAR. Etsi sapius peccatum originale, inhaerens in viscenibus hominum, nomine ἁμαρτίας designat Apostolus, non est tamen necessarium, vt vbicumque vocabulum illud vsurpat, intelligatur id peccatum: quod facile agnoscet, qui Paulum legerit de peccato loquentem, Rom. vi. 2. 6. 23: 2. Cor. 15. 56: 2. Thess. 2. 3. Heb. xii. 4.
units.tr: GAR. Although the Apostle more often uses the name sin [hamartia] to designate the original sin inhering in the inner parts of men, it is not necessary that wherever he uses that word, that sin be understood. This will easily be recognized by anyone who has read Paul speaking of sin, Romans 6:2, 6, 23; 2 Corinthians 5:15, 56 [sic]; 2 Thessalonians 2:3; Hebrews 12:4.

units.la: PLAC. Haec prima mea ratio non est mea, sed maximi viri, Bezae, quem Vir doctus per latus meum ferit. Vide sis eius Annot. ad Rom. 5. 12. Per peccatum eo loco id intelligo, quod Calvinus, Beza, Martyr, alijque eiusmodi primae notae Theologi, intellexerunt, à quibus catenus, qui me innouatae doctrinae accusant, discedunt: quod ne pateret, mentionem Bezae, eiusque verba, vnde neruus & robur argumenti pendebat, adeo quidem vt vix apud Paulum addito articulo aliud declaret, alio silentio Vir doctus praeteriit. Non enim ex eo argumentor, quod sepius eo nomine peccatum inhaerens Apostolus designet, sed quod tam sepe, ut vix unquam aliud addito articulo declaret, hic autem additur articulus. Quis vero nescit, vsitatissimam significationem anteponendam esse rationi, nisi forte grauis impediat ratio, quae hic nulla appareat, aut a viro docto affertur. Imo quae exempla affert, ea rationem nostram confirmant potius quam euertunt: in eis enim locis peccati nomine inhaerens vitium vel solum, vel cum fructibus suis intelligitur.
units.tr: PLAC. This first reason of mine is not mine but that of a very great man, Beza, whom the learned man strikes through my side. See his annotations on Romans 5:12. By sin in that place I understand what Calvin, Beza, Martyr, and other theologians of that same first rank have understood, and from whom, in this respect, those who accuse me of novel doctrine depart. So that this would not be exposed, the learned man passed over in silence the mention of Beza and his words, on which the sinew and strength of the argument hang: so that in Paul it scarcely ever declares anything else when the article is added. For I do not argue from the fact that the Apostle designates inhering sin by that name more often, but from the fact that he does so so often that he almost never declares anything else when the article is added, and here the article is added. Who, indeed, does not know that the most common meaning must be preferred to reasoning, unless perhaps a weighty reason stands in the way, which here does not appear, or which the learned man does not bring forward? Indeed, the examples he brings confirm our reasoning rather than overturn it, for in those passages the name sin is understood to mean inhering vice either alone or together with its fruits.

units.la: GAR. 2. Cum imputatio primi peccati, & corruptio hereditaria, sint ἀδιάρετα, etiam hic peccati nomine, ex vi consequentia, intelligi posse corruptionem illam, non inficiamur.
units.tr: GAR. 2. Since the imputation of the first sin and hereditary corruption are inseparable [adiaireta], we do not deny that by the force of the consequence, the name sin here too can be understood to mean that corruption.

units.la: PLAC. Si essent ἀδιάρετα, quandiu manet corruptio, tandiu maneret imputatio: id quod cum omnium Theologorum sententia, quotquot non sunt Pelagiani, pugnat. Tollitur enim imputatio remissione peccati originalis, qua fit, non ut ne fit, sed ut ne imputetur amplius. Quod si peccati quod per unum hominem introiuit in mundum nomine corruptio haereditaria intelligitur, quo argumento probabunt illi, qui nobis in hac causa aduersantur, peccatum actuale intelligi quod nostrum non sit factum nisi per imputationem? Nam intelligendum esse peccatum inhaerens & nomen ἀμάρτια cum articulo, & maximorum theologorum auctoritas, & confessio Aduersariorum satis confirmant.
units.tr: PLAC. If they were inseparable, then as long as the corruption remained, the imputation would remain as well. This is contrary to the opinion of all theologians, as many as are not Pelagians. For imputation is removed by the remission of original sin, which takes place not so that it may not come about, but so that it may not be imputed any longer. But if the name of the sin that entered the world through one man is understood as hereditary corruption, by what argument will those who oppose us in this matter prove that an actual sin is meant, which is not ours except through imputation?
