For that the inhering sin is to be understood, and the name ἁμαρτία [hamartia] with the article, are sufficiently confirmed both by the authority of the greatest theologians and by the admission of our opponents.

units.la: Secundam rationem mihi suppeditant verba sequentia, εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθε in mundum introiit. Per mundum autem omnes homines intelligi cum tu & fere omnes interpretes fateamini, nihil opus est probare. Sic igitur ratiocinor, Peccatum, quod per Adamum in omnes homines introiit, non est peccatum actuale Adami, sed corruptio haereditaria. Atqui Apostolus loquitur de peccato quod per Adamum in omnes homines introiit. Ergo loquitur non de peccato actuali Adami, sed de corruptione haereditaria. Minor est liquida. Maior quomodo negari possit non video. Constat enim & conuenit inter nos per Adamum corruptionem hæreditariam quæ veré peccatum est in omnes homines ingressam esse : quo pofito, quid est quamobrem de ea non accipiamus Apostoli verba ?
units.tr: The second reason is supplied to me by the following words, εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθε [eis ton kosmon eiselthe], entered into the world. That by the world all men are meant, since you and nearly all the interpreters admit it, there is no need to prove. I reason thus: The sin that entered all men through Adam is not Adam's actual sin, but hereditary corruption. But the Apostle speaks of the sin that entered all men through Adam. Therefore he speaks not of Adam's actual sin but of hereditary corruption. The minor is clear. I do not see how the major can be denied. For it is agreed and accepted between us that hereditary corruption, which is truly sin, has entered all men through Adam. Given this, why is there any reason that we should not take the Apostle's words to refer to it?

units.la: G A R. Actuale peccatum Adæ in homines omnes non minus transiit quàm corruptio. Nimirum corruptio inhæfione, peccatum Adæ reatu & imputatione.
units.tr: GAR. Adam's actual sin passed into all men no less than corruption. Corruption, to be sure, by inherence; Adam's sin by guilt and imputation.

units.la: P L A C. Itáne non minus in homines omnes transiit, seu vt loquitur Apostolus, introiuit, quàm corruptio ? Estne igitur peccatum actuale Adami intra nos, non minus quàm corruptio ? aut potestne intra nos esse, & tamen nobis non inesse, non inhærere ? Imputatio illa extra nos est, in Deo, diuque antequam effemus, facta : actuale quoque Adami peccatum desiit esse aliquot annorum millibus antequam esse inciperemus, qui igitur dici potest in nos introiuisse, & quidem illa imputatione ? Deinde conuenit inter nos peccatum habituale per vnum hominem in omnes homines intraffe, idque ipsa experientia confirmat ; sed non conuenit peccatum actuale per vnum hominem in omnes homines intraffe ; hoc enim pernegamus, neque potest probari. Nostra igitur interpretatio negari non potest, cùm fit in confesso. Suam igitur qui nobis aducrfantur, probent interpretationem necesse est, antequam admitti aut possit aut debeat. Denique cùm duo illi introeundi modi, quorum alter fingitur, alter est certus & confessus, prosus sint diuersi, alterque alterius respectu, vel nullus vel figuratus fit, qui potest tam diuersa vnum introeundi verbum semel vsurpatum significare ?
units.tr: PLAC. So then it passed into all men, or, as the Apostle says, entered, no less than corruption? Is Adam's actual sin therefore within us, no less than corruption? Or can it be within us and yet not be in us, not inhere in us? That imputation is outside us, in God, and was made long before we existed; Adam's actual sin too ceased to be some thousands of years before we began to exist. How, then, can it be said to have entered into us, and indeed by that imputation? Furthermore, it is agreed between us that habitual sin entered all men through one man, and experience itself confirms this; but it is not agreed that actual sin entered all men through one man, for this we deny, and it cannot be proved. Our interpretation, therefore, cannot be denied, since it is granted. Those who oppose us must therefore prove their interpretation before it can or ought to be admitted. Finally, since those two modes of entering, of which one is pretended and the other is certain and admitted, are wholly different, and one is either nothing or figurative in relation to the other, how can one verb of entering, used once, signify things so different?

units.la: G A R. Cùm causam iustificationis, non sanctificationis hic tractet Apostolus, nihil mirum est, si exprimaria suâ intentione, hic potius peccatum actuale Adami, quàm corruptionem illam inhærentem spectare voluerit, cùm peccatum ab Adamo patratum, & reatus ex illo consequens, respondeat iustitia Christi, & iustificationi per eam nostra : corruptio vero interna, non illi Christi iustitiæ proprie, sed potiùs inhærenti per Spiritum Sanctum in nobis sanctifitati respondeat. Qna corruptio quanquam hic etiam propter illam quam diximus connexionem comprehendi potest, non tamen Apostolicum scopum directè respicit, sicuti sequentibus de illâ diserte agetur à Paulo.
units.tr: GAR. Since the Apostle here treats the cause of justification, not of sanctification, it is no wonder if, in his principal intention, he meant here to look to Adam's actual sin rather than that inhering corruption: since the sin committed by Adam, and the guilt following from it, correspond to the righteousness of Christ and to our justification through it; but internal corruption corresponds not properly to that righteousness of Christ, but rather to the sanctity inhering in us through the Holy Spirit. Although that corruption can also be comprehended here on account of the connection we have mentioned, it does not directly regard the Apostolic aim, as the Apostle will expressly deal with it in the following passages.

units.la: PLAC. Quid? Nonne corruptio est verè peccatum? Nonne ex illa consequitur reatus? Nonne omnes & singulos homines, ne paruulis quidem exceptis adhuc in utero matrum delitescentibus, æterna mortis reos coram Deo peragit? Nonne ab ea nos imprimis iustificari oportet? Mirum est qui nos innouatæ doctrinæ accusant, tam apertè à recepta ab omnibus Protestantibus doctrina discedere.
units.tr: PLAC. What then? Is corruption not truly sin? Does guilt not follow from it? Does it not make all and each of men, even infants not yet excepted, still hiding in their mothers' wombs, guilty of eternal death before God? Must we not above all be justified by it? It is strange that those who accuse us of novel doctrine should so openly depart from the doctrine received by all Protestants.

units.la: Deinde planum est peccatum actuale Adami, cùm actio fuerit singularis, &, vt tu ipse loqueris, personalis, quæ simul ac fuit præteriit, non potuisse in omnes homines ingredi. Neque potes respondere actionem illam singularem & numero vnicam tantò antequàm nasceremur admissam in omnes homines imputatione introiisse: quis enim vnquam fando audiuit hanc phrasim, in aliquem introire, significare, alicui imputari? Noli, quæso, vt tuam sententiam tuearis vim facere Dei verbo. Actio illa Adami nunquam intra nos fuit, sed neque eius imputatio, quæ si vlla esset, Dei actio esset intra Deum manes, non intra nos. Si dixeris actionem illam Adami quæ peccatum eius actuale fuit, introiisse in nos dici, non quidem ratione sui, sed ratione pœnæ quam est nobis commerita, videlicet corruptionis hæreditariæ, primùm rursus abuteris verbo introeundi: nam aliud est pœnam peccati aliud peccatum in aliquem intrare. Imputata sunt peccata nostra Christo vadi nostro, nemo tamen dixerit per nos peccata in Christum introiisse, quamuis eorum pœnam in se susceperit.
units.tr: Next, it is plain that Adam's actual sin, since it was a single act and, as you yourself put it, personal, could not enter into all men once it had passed. Nor can you answer that this single and unique act entered into all men by imputation long before we were born. For who has ever heard, in any tongue, the phrase to enter into someone meaning to be imputed to someone? I beg you, do not do violence to God's word in order to defend your opinion. That act of Adam was never within us, and neither was its imputation; if there were any such imputation, it would be an act of God remaining within God, not within us. If you say that Adam's act, which was his actual sin, is said to have entered into us, not indeed by reason of itself but by reason of the punishment which we have deserved from it, namely hereditary corruption, then you are again abusing the word enter: for it is one thing for the punishment of a sin to enter into someone, and another for the sin itself to enter. Our sins were imputed to Christ our surety, yet no one would say that through us the sins entered into Christ, even though he took their punishment upon himself.

units.la: GAR. Resp. 1. Eâdem subtilitate ostendi posse, per illud peccatum, non esse intelligendum (quod tamen volunt qui his ratio-
units.tr: GAR. Answer 1. By the same subtlety I can show that by that sin we are not to understand (though those who use these ratio-

units.la: viii. § viii. nibus vtuntur) corruptionem hereditariam, vnicuique nostrum ab origine inhaerentem. Nam ea corruptio non potest dici intrare in nos: cum sit innata & ingenita, & penitissime insita a principio in natura nostra: illud autem intrare aliquo dicitur, quod foris eo delatum est, aut venit aliunde, & antea ibi non erat. Certe nemo nostrum prius fuit, quam fuit corruptus.
units.tr: viii. § viii. nibus. For that corruption cannot be said to enter into us, since it is innate and ingenerate, and most deeply implanted in our nature from the beginning; but that is said to enter somewhere which is brought there from outside, or comes from elsewhere, and was not there before. Certainly none of us existed before he was corrupted.

units.la: PLAC. Eadem quidem esset subtilitas, si posset argumentum meum aeque corruptioni ac peccato actuali accommodari: nunc vero cum haec viri docti subtilitas in argumento a meo valde diuerso sita sit, intelligere non possum, cur eadem subtilitas dicatur, aut quid argumentis meis noceat? Quanquam vim nullam habet. Quis enim non videt per illum peccati introitum non esse intelligendum introitum sitům in motu locali qui proprius est corporum & substantiarum. Quis etiam, nisi sit Pelagianus, non intelligit peccatum intrasse in homines propagatione naturali simul ac gignimur, ac proinde in genitos non fuisse foris delatum? nempe dicitur in nos intrasse, quia revera intra nos est, nec tamen est a creatione, aut ab ipsa humana natura, sed aliunde, a tentatione serpentis & peccato primi hominis actuali. Itaque revera per unum hominem vitium illud in naturam humanam ubi antea non erat, nec esse debebat, intrauit, & una cum natura in nos omnes. id quod de peccato actuali dici non potest. Quod igitur innatum est, id si non est a natura, quominus per parentes in liberos introiisse dicatur, nihil potest prohibere. Sic potest dici per parentem in liberos lepra aut podagra intrasse, quamuis lepra infit liberis ab ortu. Non quidem prius tempore, at prius tamen natura fuimus quam corrupti fuimus. Non potest enim corruptio naturae non esse posterior ipsa natura. Caeterum si prius non fuimus quam corrupti fuimus, & corruptio sequitur imputationem, prius fuimus peccatores quam fuimus, & peccatum imputatum est non existentibus, & falsum est axioma, Non entis nulla sunt accidentia.
units.tr: PLAC. It would indeed be the same subtlety, if my argument could be applied equally to corruption and to actual sin; but since this learned man's subtlety rests on an argument very different from mine, I cannot see why it is called the same subtlety, or how it harms my arguments. Yet it has no force. For who does not see that the entrance of sin in that sense is not to be understood as an entrance by local motion, which belongs to bodies and substances? Who also, unless he is a Pelagian, does not understand that sin entered into men by natural propagation as soon as we are begotten, and therefore was not brought from outside into those who were begotten? It is said to have entered into us because it is in fact within us, yet it is not from creation, or from human nature itself, but from elsewhere: from the temptation of the serpent and the actual sin of the first man. So truly through one man that vice entered into human nature, where it had not been before and where it ought not to be, and with nature it entered into all of us. This cannot be said of actual sin. Therefore, if what is innate is not from nature, nothing can prevent it from being said to enter into children through their parents. In this way one may say that leprosy or gout entered into children through a parent, although leprosy befalls children from birth. Not earlier in time, indeed, but earlier in nature, we existed before we were corrupted. For the corruption of nature cannot be anything other than posterior to nature itself. Moreover, if we did not exist before we were corrupted, and corruption follows imputation, then we were sinners before we existed, and sin was imputed to those not yet existing; and the axiom "non-being has no accidents" is false.

units.la: GAR. 2. Non est absurdum si dicatur peccatum, aut actio singularis Ada introisse, quam si dicatur Christi iustitia intrasse. At ita loquitur Clar. Amyr. in paraphasi huius versus, per unum hominem qui Iesus Christus est, vera iustitia introducta est in mundum, quod de iustitia imputata, non minus quàm de inhærente dicitur. Quibus non displicet si dicatur iustitia imputata introduci vel intrare, quid ni placeat, si dicatur etiam, peccatum imputatum introire?
units.tr: GAR. Answer 2. It is no absurdity to say that sin, or the single act of Adam, entered in, any more than to say that the righteousness of Christ entered in. Yet this is how the famous Amyraut speaks in his paraphrase of this verse: through one man, who is Jesus Christ, true righteousness was brought into the world, which is said of imputed righteousness no less than of inherent righteousness. Since they are not displeased if imputed righteousness is said to be introduced or to enter, why should it not please them if it is also said that imputed sin enters?

units.la: PLAC. Dixitne Clar. Amyr. iustitiam quæ Christo inhæsit, per eum unum in homines intrasse? Non certè: Attamen id ab eo dici oportuit, ut posset eius locutione expositio viri docti defendi. Nempe iustitiæ nomine, quæ per unum hominem in mundum introducta est, aut vehementer fallor, aut cum Calvino remissionem peccatorum intellexit, eamque introductam voluit non in omnes homines, aut in omnes credentes sola imputatione, sed impetratam à Christo & donatam à Patre & prædicatione Evangelij oblatam omnibus & fide acceptam à credentibus, in quibus constans permanet. id quod de actuali Adæ peccato dici similiter non potest.
units.tr: PLAC. Did the famous Amyraut say that the righteousness which inhered in Christ entered into men through that one man? Certainly not; yet he ought to have said it, so that his exposition might be defended by his own wording. Indeed, by the name of righteousness, which was introduced into the world through one man, either I am greatly mistaken or he understood, with Calvin, the remission of sins; and he wished it to be introduced not into all men, or all believers, by imputation alone, but obtained by Christ, bestowed by the Father, offered to all by the preaching of the Gospel and received by faith by believers, in whom it abides constantly. This cannot likewise be said of Adam's actual sin.

units.la: GAR. 3. εἰσελθεῖν sive introduci dicitur sæpius, quod tum demum esse incipit, ut apud Græcos εἰσελθεῖν δίκλω intrare in iudicium, est incipere litem, Et Christus dicitur intrasse, & introductus fuisse in mundum, cum in mundo incepit esse secundum humanitatem suam. Act. 1. 21. Heb. 1. 6. Ergo & cum peccatum incepit esse primum in genere humano, quod fuit per primorum parentum inobedientiam, merito dicitur in mundum intrasse.
units.tr: GAR. Answer 3. To enter in, or to be introduced, is often said of that which then first begins to be; as among the Greeks εἰσελθεῖν δίκλω [to enter into a lawsuit] means to begin a dispute. And Christ is said to have entered and to have been introduced into the world when he began to be in the world according to his humanity: Acts 1. 21; Heb. 1. 6. Therefore, when sin first began to exist in the human race, which happened through the disobedience of our first parents, it is rightly said to have entered into the world.

units.la: PLAC. More eorum qui submerguntur, obuium quodque arripit vir doctus: sed frustra. Significet enim phrasis εἰσελθεῖν δίκλω apud Græcos incipere litem, num sequitur, idem verbum cum quouis alio nomine constructum pro incipere vsurpari? Num ex. g. εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τ' οἶκον, vel εἰς τὴν πόλιν, erit incipere domum vel urbem, aut ita incipere esse in domo vel urbe, ut antea non fueris? Perperam laudatur locus Act. 1. 21. nam ingredi & egredi Hebraismus est, neque nativitatem neque mortem significans, sed conversationem, & vel publicorum vel privatorum officiorum functiones. vide Bez. Ann. in illum locum. Alter quoque Heb 1. 6. virum doctum refellit: intelligendus enim non est de nativitate Christi, sed de secundo eius gloriosissimo adventu, ut patet ex verbis Apostoli, & toto ps. 97. unde sunt desumpta. Cæterum hanc viri docti responsionem refutauit Bellarminus multis rationibus lib. 4. de amiss, Grat. cap. 3. & post eum Chamierus,sed breuiùs, lib r. de hom. corrupt. cap. 5. §. 9.
units.tr: PLAC. Like men who are drowning, the learned man seizes on whatever comes to hand, but in vain. For even if the Greek phrase εἰσελθεῖν δίκλω [to enter into a lawsuit] means to begin a dispute, does it follow that the same verb, when construed with any other noun, is used to mean to begin? For instance, is εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὸν οἶκον [to go into the house], or εἰς τὴν πόλιν [into the city], to begin a house or a city, or so to begin to be in a house or city that you were not there before? The passage Acts 1. 21 is wrongly cited: for to go in and to go out is a Hebraism, signifying neither birth nor death, but a manner of life and the discharge of public or private duties; see Beza's Annotations on that place. The other passage, Heb. 1. 6, also refutes the learned man: for it is not to be understood of the birth of Christ, but of his second and most glorious coming, as is clear from the words of the Apostle and from the whole of Psalm 97, from which they are taken. Moreover, this answer of the learned man has been refuted by Bellarmine with many arguments, in book 4 of De amissione gratiae, chapter 3, and after him by Chamier, but more briefly, in book 1 of De hominis corruptione, chapter 5, §9.

units.la: GAR. 4. Quid est εἰσελθεῖν εἰς κόσμον, nisi ἐλθεῖν εἰς κόσμον, venire in mundum ? Quidni ergo dixerim peccata nostra in Christum εἰσελθεῖν, cum Scriptura dicat, ea venisse in Christum. Dominus fecit venire, vel incurrere in eum iniquitates omnium nostrum. Esai, LIII. 6. Et similiter, peccatum Ada in nos εἰσελθεῖν, in nos venisse, quia eius reatum sustinemus, id est, quia illud imputatum nobis est ? Itaque quanquam introire simpliciter positum, non sit idem quod imputare, tamen peccatum introire, vel venire in aliquem, si res aut locus, vbi phrasis habetur, ita exigit, potest idem esse quod peccatum illud ipsi imputari.
units.tr: GAR. Answer 4. What is "to enter into the world" [εἰσελθεῖν εἰς κόσμον], except "to come into the world" [ἐλθεῖν εἰς κόσμον]? Why, then, should I not say that our sins entered into Christ, since Scripture says that they came into Christ? The Lord made to come upon him, or to fall upon him, the iniquities of us all: Esai. LIII. 6. And similarly, that Adam's sin entered into us, came into us, because we bear its guilt, that is, because it has been imputed to us? Therefore, although to enter simply stated is not the same as to impute, nevertheless to enter into someone, or to come into someone, may be the same as having that sin imputed to him, if the matter or the place where the phrase occurs requires it.

units.la: PLAC. Non potuit diligentius Pighij expositio defendi, quàm fit à viro doćto hoc quidem in loco: nullum enim lapidem non mouet vt extorqueat è manibus orthodoxorum argumentum, quod soliti sunt aduersus Pelagium & Pighium ex verbis Apostoli ducere, per vnum hominem peccatum introiit in mundum. Sed frustra laborat. Expurgnari veritas non potest. Quid est, quare sibi dari Vir doćtus postulet, compositum εἰσελθεῖν, nihil significatione differre à simplici ἐλθεῖν? Aut quis ferat dicentem peccata nostra introiisse in Christum, aut per nos peccatum intrasse in Christum ? Nonne talem locutionem pia refugit conscientia ? Locus Esai. LIII. 6. ad rem non est, tum quia non est idem verbum: יִפְגַּע enim non est fecit ingredi seu introire, sed fecit occurrere, vel incurrere; tum quia iniquitas eo loco non ipsum peccatum, sed pœnam peccati significat. Occurrit enim Christo, incurrit, irruit in eum, &c, si ita vis, intrauit in eum non peccatum, sed sola peccati pœna. Hic autem peccatum à peccati pœna distinguitur: sequitur enim, & per peccatum mors. Itaque probari non potest idem esse posse, peccatum in aliquem ingredi, & peccatum alicui imputari. Quod si peccatum, quatenus à pœna distinguitur, ingressum est in Christum, quid est cur Christus non potuerit dici peccator ? Si hoc est absurdum, illud quoque absurdum esse confitendum est. Sed, vt omnis expugnetur pertinacia, loco introiuit pone imputatum est, vide quàm belle procedet Apostoli oratio, per vnum hominem peccatum imputatum est mundo, & per peccatum mors. Num imputata est mors? num imputata est per peccatum? num peccatum est imputatum per Adamum? Nonne ridiculum, quantum in ipsis est, qui sic contra me disputant, faciunt Apostolum?
units.tr: PLAC. Pighius's exposition could not have been defended more diligently than the learned man has defended it in this passage. He leaves no stone unturned to wrest from the hands of the orthodox the argument they are accustomed to draw against Pelagius and Pighius from the words of the Apostle: by one man sin entered into the world. But he labours in vain. Truth cannot be overthrown. Why does the learned man demand that we grant him that the compound verb [εἰσελθεῖν] differs in meaning not at all from the simple [ἐλθεῖν]? Or who could bear someone saying that our sins have entered into Christ, or that sin has entered into Christ through us? Does not a pious conscience shrink from such an expression? Isaiah 53:6 has nothing to do with the matter, first because the word is not the same: [יִפְגַּע] does not mean "caused to enter" or "went in", but "caused to meet" or "fell upon"; and second because iniquity in that place signifies not sin itself but the punishment of sin. For it meets Christ, falls upon him, rushes at him, and so on; if you like, what entered into him was not sin but only the punishment of sin. Here, however, sin is distinguished from the punishment of sin, for it follows: and death through sin. Therefore it cannot be proved that for sin to enter into someone and for sin to be imputed to someone are the same thing. But if sin, insofar as it is distinguished from punishment, has entered into Christ, why was Christ not able to be called a sinner? If this is absurd, that too must be admitted to be absurd. But, so that all obstinacy may be overcome, put "was imputed" in place of "entered", and see how beautifully the Apostle's speech proceeds: by one man sin was imputed to the world, and death through sin. Was death imputed? Was it imputed through sin? Was sin imputed through Adam? Is it not ridiculous, so far as it lies with them, that those who argue thus against me make the Apostle say such things?

units.la: G A R. 5. Ita quanquam singularis actio, ratione substantiae suae non potest dici introire in alium, tamen ratione reatus introire recte dicitur, quatenus propter actionem illam alius reus habetur, adeoque poenis subiacet.
units.tr: GAR. 5. Thus, although a single action, considered in terms of its substance, cannot be said to enter into another, nevertheless, considered in terms of guilt, it is rightly said to enter, insofar as on account of that action another is held guilty and so is subject to punishments.

units.la: P L A C. Atqui 1. aliud est actio, aliud reatus. Illa est actio, haec relatio, illa transit, hoc manente. Num igitur si reatus recte dicitur introire, recte etiam dicitur introire actio? Num quicquid dicitur de reatu, dici etiam potest de actione? Num actio est relatio? num manet postquam actio transiit? num sequitur actionem? 2. Aliud est propter actionem reum haberi, aliud reatum actionis introire in aliquem: illud externam tantum denominationem significat, hoc aliquid importat amplius. Imo ipse reatus, cum sit relatio, introire dici non potest, nisi aut ratione fundamenti, hoc est, peccati sive sit actio, sive habitus, aut termini, hoc est, poenae, tantum abest ut ratione reatus actio dici possit in alium introire.
units.tr: PLAC. But first, 1. an action is one thing and guilt is another. The one is an action, the other a relation; the one passes away, the other remains. If guilt is rightly said to enter, is an action therefore rightly said to enter too? Whatever is said of guilt can also be said of the action? Is an action a relation? Does it remain after the action has passed? Does it follow the action? 2. To be held guilty on account of an action is one thing; for the guilt of an action to enter into someone is another. The former signifies only an external designation; the latter implies something more. Indeed, guilt itself, since it is a relation, cannot be said to enter except either by reason of its foundation, that is, the sin, whether it is an action or a habit, or by reason of its terminus, that is, the punishment. So far is it from being the case that an action can be said to enter into another by reason of guilt.

units.la: GAR. 6. Denique imputatio peccati, est illa quidem actio Dei, a Deo tanquam iudice profecta, sed in homines tendens, tanquam in terminum, & eo respectu in hominem intrans aut veniens, propter effectus quos in ipso producit, id est, propter poenas quibus eum afficit. Sic maledictio est actio Dei Gen xii. 3. Malach. 2. 2. Et tamen intrare dicitur in homines aliqvos Psal. cix. 18. Maledictio ingredietur, velut aqua, intra eum, & velut oleum in ossa eius. Quod autem imputatio peccati sit actio Dei intra Deum manens Theologi vix concedant, qui cum Dei actiones distinguere soleant in immanentes & transeuntes; immanentes eas vocant, quae in ipso Deo terminantur, ut intellectionem, & volitionem, quae seipsum intelligit & diligit: transeuntes, quae terminantur in creaturas, quales sunt actiones divinae providentiae. Sed hac aliys disceptanda relinquo.
units.tr: GAR. 6. Finally, the imputation of sin is indeed an action of God, proceeding from God as judge, but tending towards men as its terminus, and in that respect entering into or coming to a man on account of the effects it produces in him, that is, on account of the punishments with which it afflicts him. Thus a curse is an action of God, Genesis 12:3; Malachi 2:2. And yet it is said to enter into certain men, Psalm 109:18. The curse will enter, like water, into his inward parts, and like oil into his bones. But that the imputation of sin is an action of God remaining within God, the theologians will scarcely concede; for when they are accustomed to distinguish the actions of God into immanent and transient, they call "immanent" those which terminate in God himself, such as understanding and willing, by which he understands and loves himself; "transient" those which terminate in creatures, such as the actions of divine providence. But I leave these matters to be disputed elsewhere.

units.la: P L A C. Quis vnquam negauit Dei actiones alias esse immanentes, alias transeuntes; illas in Deo, has in creaturis esse? Et quis nescit in hoc posteriore genere ponendam esse maledictionem quæ est actio Dei? Quanquam per maledictionem ps. cix. 18. non significatur actio, sed effectum potius Dei irati, nempe miseria, infortunium, malum pœnæ. Vult Propheta huiusmodi hominem omnibus malis corporalibus & spiritualibus omni ex parte indui & penetrari. Itaque præcessit, optauit vt maledictio obueniret ei, & sequitur, Hoc esto premium aduersantium mihi &c. Quid autem hoc ad rem, qua de agimus, facit? Quæritur quo sensu dixerit Apostolus per vnum hominem peccatum introiuisse in mundum, id est, in homines? Dicis per peccatum intelligendam esse actionem Adami. Quæro, quomodo actio Adami, quæ diu antequam vlli alij homines essent, fuerat præterita ac esse desierat, dici potuit in omnes homines introiuisse? Dicis introiuisse imputatione. Repono, imputationem illam non esse actionem vnius illius hominis, sed solius Dei. Non igitur per vnum hominem, sed per Deum peccatum introiuisse in omnes homines: quo nihil dici potest absurdius. Repono etiam, non fieri imputatione illa vt peccatum actuale, seu actio illa præterita Adami, unquam intra nos fuerit, aut esse possit. Repono denique imputationem, aut esse actionem mentis seu iudicij diuini reputantis nos esse reos actionis illius Adamicæ, aut illius diuini iudicij declarationem lata sententia sermone externo, aut pœnæ inflictionem. Si primum eligis, actio est Dei immanens: non enim alibi est aut esse potest quam in Deo, in Dei mente. Vocant quidem nonnulli Theologi actiones diuinæ mentis & voluntatis, actiones ad extra, quia habent pro obiecto creaturas, sed non vocant actiones transeuntes, nec negant esse actiones immanentes, vt facit hoc loco Vir doctus, admodum inconsiderate. Si secundum, vbi & quando facta est illa declaratio, & num extra nos, an intra nos? Si tertium, repugnat Apostolus qui peccatum hoc loco distinguit à pœna peccati quam mortem vocat. Inflictione pœnæ, hoc est, mortis intrat quidem mors seu pœna, sed non intrat peccatum. Alius est in verbis Apostoli introitus peccati, alius introitus mortis, ille causa est huius.
units.tr: PLAC. Who has ever denied that some of God's actions are immanent and others transient, the former in God, the latter in creatures? And who does not know that a curse, which is an action of God, must be placed in this latter class? Yet in Psalm 109:18 a curse signifies not an action but rather the effect of an angry God, namely misery, calamity, the evil of punishment. The prophet wishes such a man to be clothed and penetrated on every side by all bodily and spiritual evils. Therefore he had first said, may a curse come upon him, and it follows, let this be the reward of those who oppose me, and so on. But what does this have to do with the matter we are discussing? The question is in what sense the Apostle said that by one man sin entered into the world, that is, into men. You say that by "sin" is to be understood the action of Adam. I ask how the action of Adam, which had passed away and ceased to exist long before any other men existed, can be said to have entered into all men. You say it entered by imputation. I reply that this imputation is not an action of that one man but of God alone. Therefore it was not through one man but through God that sin entered into all men, than which nothing more absurd can be said. I reply also that by that imputation the actual sin, or that past action of Adam, never has been or can be within us. I reply finally that imputation is either an action of the mind or judgment of God reckoning us to be guilty of that Adamic action, or a declaration of that divine judgment by an external pronouncement of sentence, or the infliction of punishment. If you choose the first, the action is immanent in God: for it is nowhere else, nor can it be, than in God, in the mind of God. Some theologians do indeed call the actions of the divine mind and will "actions outward", because they have creatures as their object, but they do not call them transient actions, nor do they deny that they are immanent actions, as this learned man does here, quite thoughtlessly. If you choose the second, where and when was that declaration made, and was it outside us or within us? If the third, the Apostle, who in this place distinguishes sin from the punishment of sin, which he calls death, is against you. By the infliction of punishment, that is, death, death or punishment indeed enters, but sin does not enter. The entrance of sin in the Apostle's words is one thing; the entrance of death is another; the former is the cause of the latter.

units.la: Deinde, si peccatum actuale Adami non intrauit in mundum, nisi ratione corruptionis hæreditariæ,
units.tr: Next, if Adam's actual sin entered the world only by reason of hereditary corruption,

units.la: fatendum est hoc attributum intraße in mundum , seu homines , conuenire per se & proprie & proximè corruptioni hæreditariæ,remotè tantùm,& illius corruptionis ratione , peccato actuali Adami· Si igitur corruptio illa est verè & proprie peccatum , etiam post baptismum, vt nostri aduersus Pontificios tuentur , nonne manifestum est, peccatum quòd in mundum intrauit , eius potius descriptionem esse quàm peccati actua lis Adami ? Huc accedit quod Apostolus ait per hoc peccatum mortem introiisse in mundum. Introitus in mundum commune est peccati & mortis attributum. Vtrumque in mundum introiit, sed peccatum per se , mors per peccatum. Mors autem introiit reapse, non imputatione, & mors quæ introiit in mundum non est mors vnius Adami, sed totuplex quot sunt homines. Cùm ergo constet esse peccatum , nempe corruptionem hæreditariam , quod eodem prorsus modo introierit in mundum, quid est, cur id hoc loco non intelligamus potius,quàm id quod neque introitu in mundum , neque numero morti correspondeat ? Denique si per peccatum quod in mundum introyt, peccatum actuale Adami intelligitur, necesse est , vt Apostolus , vel prorsus omiserit corruptionem inhærentem, vel eam mortis nomine comprehenderit. Hoc vtrumque est falsum ; Ergo & illud. Nam, si dixeris eum corruptionem hæreditariam prætermisisse, sequentur duo : Vnum , eam ex hac tota collatione, quam inter primum & secundum Adamum Apostolus instituit, colligi non posse. Non enim alia mala ex Adamo in genus humanum manasse sequentibus versibus docet,quàm quæ hoc ⁊ .12. nominauit. Id autem Pighij causam valdè iuuabit, & quamuis alia extent in sacris literis loca, ex quibus effici possit, nos nasci corruptos peccato, tamen ferè alius nullus est, qui eam corruptionem doceat ab ipso Adamo profectam in omnes homines inuasiffe. Alterum, aut eam corruptionem nullam esse, aut Apostolum aberraffe à suo scopo. Si prius, vicerunt Pelagiani, estque adhuc in integro liberum arbitrium. Posterius patet. Scopus enim Apostoli est docere quæ mala à primo Adamo, quæ contrà bona à fecundo Adamo in genus humanum fluxerint, vt intelligamus mirum non esse, cùm vnus homo ad nos perdendos tam potens fuerit, vnum hominem, Iesum Christum, nos posse feruare. Itaque bona ab hoc in nos profecta malis ab illo profectis accuratè comparat. Quis igitur credat eum voluisse id malum silentio præterire, quod constat & ex Adamo in nos deriuari, & causam omnium nostrorum peccatorum esse? Si verò dixeris, Apostolum mortis nomine corruptionem illam hæreditariam, quæ peccatum est, comprehendisse, primùm discedes ab omnium (quos viderim) interpretum consensu. Deinde causam Pelagianorum aduersus Augustinum iuuabis,mortis nomen de morte animæ accipientium. Tum Apostolum induces cõtrà suum morem nomine mortis absolutè posito, & fine vlla additione, eiusmodi corruptionem significantem, vnumque & idem nomen semel positum, semel intelligendum, simul proprie & figuratè accipientem. Præterea, quis credat mortem cùm à peccato distinguitur, vt fit hoc loco peccatum significare? Adde quod Apostolus probat hoc loco omnes homines esse peccatores, peccatum esse in mundo. id est in hominibus, hoc argumento, quia omnes moriuntur Putasne probare eum peccatum esse in hominibus, quia fit in hominibus peccatum, nimirum corruptio hæreditaria? Num à latente corruptione morali, quæ ipsa erat probanda, ducit argumentum, cùm suppeteret à patente & nota omnium morte? Certè condemnatio & mors sunt apud Apostolum hoc capite ἀπἀτησεως. Condemnamur ad mortem, non ad peccatum. Mors non est condemnationis causa, sed effectum. Contrà peccatum (est autem corruptio hæreditaria, vt iam sæpius dixi, peccatum) condemnationis causa, non effectum. Denique, vt ne sim æquo polixior, cùm ait Apostolus verf. 21. regnasse peccatum in mortem, sitne verisimile alio modo accipi mortem, quàm in antecedenti disputatione Apostoli, cuius versus ille conclusio est? At profectò eo versu id significare non potest, quod sit verè peccatum. Præcessit enim illud verf. 20. lex praeterea introijt, vt peccatum abundaret. vbi autem peccatum abundavit, ibi gratia superabundavit. Illud enim peccati regnum, hæc peccati redundantia id omne in homine complectitur, quod verè peccatum sit, & liquet ex Rom. vi. & vii. id peccatum, quod per legem redundavit & regnauit, esse concupiscentiam, siue corruptionem hæreditariam,
units.tr: it must be granted that this attribute, to have entered into the world, or to enter into men, belongs per se, properly and most immediately to hereditary corruption, and only remotely to Adam's actual sin, by reason of that corruption. So if that corruption is truly and properly sin, even after baptism, as our writers maintain against the Papists, is it not plain that the sin which entered the world is a description of it rather than of Adam's actual sin? Add to this that the Apostle says that death entered the world through this sin. Entering the world is a common attribute of sin and death. Both entered the world, but sin entered in its own right, and death through sin. Death, however, entered in reality, not by imputation, and the death that entered the world is not the death of the one Adam but as many deaths as there are men. Since it is established that there is a sin, namely hereditary corruption, which entered the world in exactly the same way, why should we not understand this in the passage rather than that which corresponds neither to the entrance into the world nor to the number of deaths? Finally, if by the sin which enters the world the actual sin of Adam is meant, the Apostle must either have altogether passed over inherent corruption or included it under the name of death. Both of these are false; therefore so is the other. For if you say he passed over hereditary corruption, two things follow. First, that it cannot be gathered from the whole comparison which the Apostle draws between the first and the second Adam. For in the following verses he teaches that no evils flowed into the human race from Adam other than those he named in Rom. 5.12. This would greatly help the cause of Pighius; and although there are other passages in Holy Scripture from which it can be shown that we are born corrupted by sin, there is almost no one else who teaches that this corruption, derived from Adam himself, has invaded all men. Second, either there is no such corruption, or the Apostle has strayed from his purpose. If the former, the Pelagians have won, and free will is still intact. The latter is clear. For the Apostle's aim is to teach what evils flowed into the human race from the first Adam, and what goods from the second Adam, so that we may understand it is no wonder that one man was powerful enough to ruin us, and one man, Jesus Christ, can save us. Therefore he carefully sets the goods that came to us from the one against the evils that came from the other. Who, then, would believe that he wished to pass over in silence that evil which is known both to derive to us from Adam and to be the cause of all our sins? But if you say that the Apostle comprehended that hereditary corruption, which is sin, under the name of death, you will first depart from the agreement of all the interpreters I have seen. Then you will aid the Pelagian cause against Augustine, who take death to mean the death of the soul. Next, you will make the Apostle, contrary to his custom, use the bare name of death, without any addition, to signify such a corruption, taking one and the same word, used once, to be understood both properly and figuratively. Moreover, who would believe that death, when it is distinguished from sin, here signifies sin? Add that the Apostle proves in this passage that all men are sinners, that sin is in the world, that is, in men, by this argument: because all die. Do you think he proves that sin is in men because sin occurs in men, namely hereditary corruption? Does he draw his argument from a hidden moral corruption, which was itself what had to be proved, when the open and well-known death of all was available? Certainly, in this chapter condemnation and death are correlative [ἀπαρτήσεως]. We are condemned to death, not to sin. Death is not the cause of condemnation but its effect. On the contrary, sin (and hereditary corruption is sin, as I have said many times already) is the cause of condemnation, not its effect. Finally, to avoid being too lengthy: when the Apostle says in verse 21 that sin reigned unto death, is it likely that death is taken in another sense than in the Apostle's preceding argument, of which that verse is the conclusion? But certainly in that verse it cannot mean what is truly sin. For verse 20 comes before it: moreover the law entered, that sin might abound; but where sin abounded, grace did much more abound. For that reign of sin and that overflowing of sin embrace everything in man that is truly sin, and it is clear from Rom. vi and vii that the sin which abounded and reigned through the law is concupiscence, or hereditary corruption,

units.la: Putabis fortasse te horum argumentorum aciem declinare posse, dicendo, per peccatum τὸ ἁμάρτημα intelligi vtrumque & peccatum actuale Adami, & natum ex eo vitium originale; sed id tibi non licet per statum quæstionis, quæ inter nos versatur. Est enim instituta de peccato actuali Adami præcisò à vitio hæreditario. Vis enim primum peccatum actuale Adamo & nobis fuisse imputatum, & quia imputatum, inflictam Adamo & nobis hanc poenam, nimirum vitium seu corruptionem originalem. Itaque secundum tuam sententiam corruptio ista cum peccato actuali Adami non cohaeret, nisi diuinae imputationis interuentu. Quare imputatio naturae ordine corruptionem antecedit. Est igitur peccati actualis Adami praecisi a corruptione haereditaria imputatio tibi probanda, non autem cum ea coniuncti ac confusi. Id quod mihi alia suggerit argumenta, sed, vitandae hoc loco nimiae prolixitatis causa, conferenda in alium locum. Adde quod iam probaui peccatum actuale non introiisse in mundum, hoc est, in homines : unde sequitur hoc attributum in mundum introiit sibi iungere peccatum, non qua significat peccatum, actuale, sed qua significat vitium ex eo mea sententia immediate, tua vero mediante Dei imputatione ortum. Sic opinor meum argumentum firmaui satis.
units.tr: You will perhaps think that you can escape the force of these arguments by saying that by sin [τὸ ἁμάρτημα] both the actual sin of Adam and the vice originating from it is understood. But this is not allowed you by the state of the question which lies between us. For the question has been set up concerning the actual sin of Adam considered apart from hereditary vice. For you hold that Adam's first actual sin was imputed to Adam and to us, and that, because it was imputed, this punishment was inflicted on Adam and on us, namely the vice or original corruption. Accordingly, according to your opinion, that corruption does not cohere with Adam's actual sin except through the intervention of divine imputation. Hence imputation precedes corruption in the order of nature. It is therefore for you to prove the imputation of Adam's actual sin apart from hereditary corruption, not its imputation joined and confused with it. I have other arguments that suggest this, but to avoid excessive length here, I shall postpone them to another place. Add that I have already proved that actual sin did not enter into the world, that is, into men; whence it follows that the phrase entered into the world joins itself to sin not in so far as it signifies actual sin, but in so far as it signifies the vice arising from it, immediately in my opinion, but in yours mediately, through the imputation of God. Thus, I think, I have sufficiently confirmed my argument.

units.la: Vides prima verba Apostoli, quae sequentium sunt fundamentum & materia, mihi, non tibi, fauere. Excutiamus nunc sequentia. Nullum tibi, opinor, argumentum cadet ex his verbis , per peccatum mors : saltem nullius vestigium deprehendo in tuo tractatu. Quid si ego inde aliquid eliciam sententiae tuae aduersum. Dabisne mihi per mortem hoc loco intelligendā esse eam mortem, quam lex Adamo fuerat comminata, poenam scilicet, & stipendium peccati? non video quo iure id negare possis, praesertim cum sententias eam legem ad totum genus humanum spectare, & Adamum, prout Deus minatus fuerat, mortuum esse. Dabis saltem mortem hoc loco significare poenam peccati, quod in mundum introiit : tu autem vis illud peccatum esse peccatum actuale Adami, & illius poenam. esse non tantum mortem corporis & æternam, sed imprimis mortem spiritualem animæ, positam in priuatione iustitiæ originalis, & corruptione hæreditaria: Ex quo sequitur istam corruptionem nomine mortis hoc loco contineri. Atqui iam probaui non contineri. Quod si Apostolus mortis nomine quicquid pœnæ per Adamum in posteros deriuatum est significauit, nec tamen eo nomine corruptionem hæreditariam seu vitium complexus est, vt iam probaui, vides quid sequatur, nempe vitium illud hæreditarium non esse in numero pœnarum quas Adamus mundo intulit, ac proinde peccatum eius actuale non esse mundo imputatum ad illam pœnam, videlicet vitium hæreditarium.
units.tr: You see that the first words of the Apostle, which are the foundation and matter of what follows, favour me, not you. Let us now examine what follows. No argument, I think, will fall to you from these words, through sin, death; at least I can find no trace of one in your treatise. What if I draw from them something against your opinion? Will you grant me that in this passage death must be understood as that death which the law had threatened to Adam, namely the punishment and wages of sin? I do not see by what right you could deny it, especially since the law, as you yourself say, looks to the whole human race, and Adam died as God had threatened. You will grant at least that in this passage death signifies the punishment of the sin which entered into the world. But you want that sin to be Adam's actual sin, and its punishment to be not only bodily and eternal death, but above all the spiritual death of the soul, consisting in the privation of original righteousness and in hereditary corruption. From this it follows that this corruption is contained in this passage under the name of death. But I have already proved that it is not contained. And if the Apostle, under the name of death, signified whatever punishment was derived to posterity through Adam, and yet did not by that name comprehend hereditary corruption or vice, as I have already proved, you see what follows: that this hereditary vice is not among the punishments which Adam brought upon the world, and consequently that his actual sin was not imputed to the world for that punishment, namely hereditary vice.

units.la: Veniamus ad sequêtes voces ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον. Hic magnum scilicet causæ tuæ putas te reperisse præsidium. In verbis ἐφ' ᾧ consistis paulisper, mox ijs desertis ad verbum ἥμαρτον te confers. nempe tu versione, quâ vtuntur Ecclesiæ nostræ, noluisti prorsus reijcere, quamuis satis aperte præ te feras, eam tibi non probari. Itaque, inquis, stabiliatur & maneat uersio nostra gallica, quæ est Iohannis Caluini, eo quod, vel quando omnes peccauerunt. Aduersus eam tamen nonnulla obijcis hoc cap. & cap. ix. quæ cum ad illud caput peruenero, Deo bene iuuante, ad examen reuocabo, & quamuis mea fere nihil interfit quomodo ἐφ' ᾧ reddatur, eo quod, siue in quo, tamen ostendam vertendum esse eo quod, ac tuebor uersionem, quam Ecclesiæ nostræ probant. Interim tu vis explicari hæc verba eo quod vel in quo omnes peccauerunt ex prima parte versiculi. At tibi iam primam illam partem extorsi. Si ergo peccasse omnes dicuntur eo peccato quod in mundum intraiit. Id autem peccatum non probasti esse peccatum actuale Adami, ego vero probaui esse vitium inhærens, quid superest, nisi vt illud peccauerunt interpretemur cum Caluino de vitio nobis singulis innato & insito? Iflud peccare, inquit, est corruptos esse & vitiatos. Gallicè ἐμφατικότερως, Or ce peché, duquel il parle icy, ne signifie autre chose, sinon que nous sommes tous corrompus : illa enim naturalis prauitas quam é matris vtero afferimus, tametsi non ita cito fructus suos edit, peccatum tamen est coram Domino, & eius vltionem meretur. Et paulò post, peccauimus igitur omnes, quia naturali corruptione omnes imbuti sumus : ideoque iniqui ac peruersi,
units.tr: Let us come to the next words, "on which all sinned" [ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον]. Here, no doubt, you think you have found a strong defence for your cause. You pause briefly over the words "on which" [ἐφ' ᾧ], then leave them aside and turn to the verb "sinned" [ἥμαρτον]. You have indeed been unwilling to reject altogether the version our Church uses, though you make it fairly plain that you do not approve of it. So, you say, let our French version stand and remain, the one by John Calvin, which has "because, or inasmuch as, all have sinned". Against it, however, you raise several objections in this chapter and in chapter 9. When I come to that chapter, God helping, I will call them back for examination. Although it matters little to me how ἐφ' ᾧ is rendered, whether "because" or "in which", I will nevertheless show that it must be translated "because", and I will defend the version that our Church approves. Meanwhile you wish these words, "because" or "in which all sinned", to be explained from the first part of the verse. But I have already wrested that first part from you. If then all are said to have sinned by that sin which entered the world, and you have not proved that this sin is Adam's actual sin, whereas I have proved it to be inherent corruption, what remains but to interpret "sinned", with Calvin, of the vice innate and implanted in each of us? To sin, he says, is to be corrupted and vitiated. In French, more emphatically [ἐμφατικότερως]: Now this sin of which he speaks here signifies nothing other than that we are all corrupted. For that natural depravity which we bring from our mother's womb, although it does not bear its fruits so quickly, is nonetheless sin before the Lord, and deserves his vengeance. And a little later: We have all therefore sinned, because we have all been imbued with natural corruption, and therefore are unrighteous and perverse,

units.la: Id tamen negas tibi satisfacere : non enim, inquis, dicit Apostolus quoniam peccatum est in omnibus (immò hoc dicit versu sequente) sed, quoniam omnes peccauerunt ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον, & vtitur verbo actiuo, vt significet peccatum actuale, cuius omnes sint participes. In peccato autem originali non peccauimus actu, nisi quatenus in Adamo peccauimus: nam cum peccauit, pro omnibus suis posteris peccauit, & omnes homines, qui ex illo nati sunt, in illo peccauerunt; quia in illo omnes fuerunt. Vis probandi, si qua est, in tuis istis verbis, in hoc consistit, quòd verbum ἥμαρτον peccauerunt, actiuum cùm sit, significat peccatum actuale. Reliqua petitiones sunt τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ. Atqui verbum illud actiuum, si significat peccatum actuale, profectò peccatum actuale significat ab eo ipso commissum qui peccauit. Profer, si potes, contrarium exemplum. Vide igitur ne hæc tua obseruatio Pelagio faueat. Deinde te non fugit peccatum actuale ab originali omnes Theologos distinguere. Si ergo hoc verbum peccauerunt actuale peccatum significat: igitur non significat originale; quod tu ipse ab actuali hoc loco discernis. Non ergo loquitur Apostolus de peccato originali hoc loco. Sic nobis, quantum in te est, extorques arma, quibus ex hoc loco Pelagium, Pighium, & Socinum conficiamus.
units.tr: You say that this does not satisfy you: satisfacere: non enim, you say, the Apostle does not say that sin is in all (indeed he says this in the following verse), but "because all sinned" [ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον], and he uses an active verb, to signify actual sin, of which all are partakers. But in original sin we did not sin actually, except insofar as we sinned in Adam, for when he sinned, he sinned on behalf of all his posterity, and all men who were born from him sinned in him, because all were in him. If there is any proof in your words, it consists in this: that the verb ἥμαρτον, "sinned", being active, signifies actual sin. The rest are mere petitions of principle [τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ]. Yet that active verb, if it signifies actual sin, certainly signifies sin committed by the very one who sinned. Produce a contrary example, if you can. See, then, that this observation of yours does not favour Pelagius. Further, you are not unaware that all theologians distinguish actual sin from original sin. If, therefore, this verb "sinned" signifies actual sin, it does not signify original sin, which you yourself here distinguish from actual sin. So the Apostle is not speaking here of original sin. Thus, so far as lies in you, you strip from us the weapons with which we might overcome Pelagius, Pighius and Socinus from this passage.

units.la: Sed iuuat te alia via aggredi, quamuis enim nunc quidem meæ sint partes respondere, tuæ argumentari, tamen mihi temperare non possum, quin argumenta, quibus mea causa abundat, vbique disseminem. Dic mihi igitur, quæso, quomodo omnes homines intelligas peccasse peccato actuali Adami? Inculcas passim peccatum illud actuale nostrum esse non posse, nisi per imputationem. Si nostrum non est nisi imputatione, vtique eo non peccauimus nisi imputatione. Quid erit igitur illud omnes peccauerunt? omnibus peccatum actuale imputatum est? Atqui aliud est aliquem peccare, aliud alicui peccatum imputari.
units.tr: But you are glad to attack by another route. For although it is now my part to answer and yours to argue, I cannot refrain from scattering everywhere the arguments in which my cause abounds. Tell me, then, I beg you, how do you understand that all men sinned with Adam's actual sin? You repeatedly insist that this actual sin cannot be ours except by imputation. If it is ours only by imputation, then certainly we did not sin in it except by imputation. What then will "all sinned" [omnes peccauerunt?] mean? Was actual sin imputed to all? But it is one thing for someone to sin, another for sin to be imputed to someone.

units.la: GAR. Respondeo 1. Aliud est si dicas simpliciter aliquem peccare, aliud si, aliquem in alio peccauisse. Nam illud sane prius, ex vi vocis non significat imputationem peccati, sed hoc posterius designat imputationem. Quomodo enim qui multis post saeculis extiterunt, dici possunt iam antea in alio peccasse, nisi quia ille eum actum exercuit, qui posterorum ita reputatur, ac si ipsi illum commisissent? Sic satisfacere aliquem, & alicui satisfactionem imputari, sunt sane longe diuersa, & tamen cum docent Theologi nos in Christo satisfecisse, non aliud sibi volunt, quam Christi satisfactionem nobis imputari, sine Christum eam satisfactionem exhibuisse, qua propter vnionem, quam cum eo habemus tanquam capite nostro spirituali & mystico, nobis imputetur, ita vt apud Deum habeamur, quasi ipsi per nos satisfecissemus.
units.tr: GAR. I answer, first: it is one thing to say simply that someone sins, and another to say that someone has sinned in another. For the former, by the force of the word, does not signify the imputation of sin, but the latter designates imputation. For how could those who came into being many centuries later be said to have sinned in another beforehand, unless because that one performed the act, which is reckoned to his posterity as though they had committed it themselves? Thus to satisfy for someone and to have satisfaction imputed to someone are certainly very different things; and yet when the theologians teach that we have satisfied in Christ, they mean nothing else than that Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us, not that we ourselves exhibited that satisfaction. Because of the union which we have with him as our spiritual and mystical head, it is imputed to us, so that we are regarded before God as though we ourselves had satisfied through ourselves.

units.la: PLAC. Primùm, non dicit Scriptura nos in Adamo peccasse. Deinde, non video cur illa locutio vi sua significet imputationem, qua peccatum alienum, nempe Adami fiat aut factum fit nostrum. Dicimur enim mori in Adamo, nec tamen mors Adami nobis imputatur, dici possumus in Adamo creati fuisse, creati fuisse iusti & beati, ejecti fuisse e paradiso &c, nec tamen eius creatio, aut iustitia originalis, aut eiectio e paradiso nobis imputatur. Potuimus ergo dici in eo peccasse, quomodo dici possumus in eo fuisse, quia ille quàm naturam tam peccatum suum nobiscum communicauit propagatione naturali. Ad satisfactionem Christi quod attinet, cum dicimur in Christo satisfecisse, nihil aliud intelligi mihi videtur, nisi Christum loco nostro pro nobis satisfecisse: num igitur similiter Adamus loco nostro pro nobis peccauit? Tenebamur pro se quisque satisfacere. Id erat nobis impossibile. Christus, qui non tenebatur, vadem nostrum sese constituit, & pro nobis satisfecit. Potestne idem de nobis & Adamo dici? Tenebamurne peccare? num sese Adamus vadem nostrum constituit, vt pro nobis peccaret? Peto etiam, quando in Christo satisfecimus? opinor quando passus est. Num igitur tunc nobis imputata est Christi satisfactio? Tunc igitur fuimus iustificati, nondum existentes, nondum credentes. Non ergo per fidem sumus iustificati, quandoquidem iustificatio nostra tanto nostram & existentiam & fidem antecessit. Adde quod vnionem cum Christo tanquam capite nostro spirituali & mystico non habemus nisi per fidem, sequitur ergo fidem nostram imputatio satisfactionis Christi seu iustificatio nostra. Quid est cur non dicamus similiter nos vnionem non habere cum Adamo tanquam capite peccatorum, nisi per vitium hæreditarium, quo suum nobiscum peccatum communicauit. Itaque posteriorem esse eo vitio peccati Adamici imputationem.
units.tr: PLAC. First, Scripture does not say that we sinned in Adam. Second, I do not see why that expression, by its own force, should signify imputation, by which another's sin, namely Adam's, becomes or is made ours. For we are said to die in Adam, yet Adam's death is not imputed to us. We may be said to have been created in Adam, to have been created righteous and blessed, to have been cast out of paradise, and yet neither his creation, nor his original righteousness, nor his expulsion from paradise is imputed to us. We could therefore be said to have sinned in him in the same way that we can be said to have been in him, because he communicated to us, by natural propagation, both his nature and his sin. As for the satisfaction of Christ, when we are said to have satisfied in Christ, nothing else seems to me to be meant than that Christ satisfied for us in our place. Did Adam then likewise sin for us in our place? We were bound to satisfy each for himself, and this was impossible for us. Christ, who was not bound, set himself up as our surety and satisfied for us. Can the same be said of us and Adam? Were we bound to sin? Did Adam set himself up as our surety, so as to sin for us? I ask also, when did we satisfy in Christ? I suppose when he suffered. Was Christ's satisfaction then imputed to us? Then we were justified while not yet existing and not yet believing. Therefore we were not justified through faith, since our justification preceded both our existence and our faith by so long. Add that we do not have union with Christ as our spiritual and mystical head except through faith; it follows, then, that the imputation of Christ's satisfaction, that is, our justification, is through our faith. Why should we not likewise say that we do not have union with Adam as the head of sinners except through hereditary vice, by which he communicated his sin to us? Thus the imputation of Adam's sin is subsequent to that vice.

units.la: GAR. 2. Neque ignotum est in Scripturis peccandi verbo aliquando significari reatum ex peccato consequentem, secundum illam loquendi rationem, quâ ponitur antecedens pro conse- quente.
units.tr: GAR. 2. Nor is it unknown in Scripture that the word "to sin" sometimes signifies the guilt that follows from sin, according to that manner of speaking in which the antecedent is put for the consequent.

units.la: Vt cùm Iudas secum Beniaminem in Ægyptum abducturus, patrem Iacobum ita alloquitur, Genes. XLIII. 9. Ego spondeo pro eo, de manu mea reposcito eum: Si non reduxero eum ad te, & stitero eum coram te, omnino peccauero tibi omnibus diebus, id est, sim tibi reus, & à te habear profceleratus. Sic Berfabea ad Danidem 1. Regum 1. 21. cùm occubuerit Dominus meus Rex cum patribus suis, ego & filius meus Schelonio erimus peccatores; id est, agetur nobiscum tanquam fontibus & reis, ut exponunt interpretes, & observat Clarissimus Heinsius Exercit. in Ioh. ix. 2. &c. Quid igitur in eo novi erit, si eandem metalepsim Hebrais familiarem hic vsurpari doceamus, ut dicamur in Adamo peccare, id est, pro reis haberi, non minùs quàm si, Adamo peccante, nos ipsi peccavissemus?
units.tr: For example, when Judah, about to take Benjamin with him into Egypt, addresses his father Jacob thus: "I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him. If I bring him not unto thee, and set him before thee, then let me bear the blame for ever" (Gen. 43:9), that is, let me be guilty before you and be held by you as a wicked man. So Bathsheba to David, 1 Kings 1:21: "When my lord the king shall sleep with his fathers, I and my son Solomon shall be counted offenders," that is, we shall be treated as guilty and as culprits, as the interpreters explain, and as the most distinguished Heinsius observes in his Exercitations on John 9:2, etc. What then would be new in this, if we teach that the same metalepsis, familiar to the Hebrews, is used here, so that we are said to sin in Adam, that is, to be held as guilty, no less than if we ourselves had sinned when Adam sinned?

units.la: PLAC. Cùm haec responsio Pighiana fit, ac nostris olim obiecta, eam, me tacente, refellat Martyr, Comm. in Rom. 5. 9. & locor. Comm. Class. 2. cap. 1. §. 8. Postremò, inquit, habemus à Paulo, per inobedientiam unius hominis, multos constitutos esse peccatores; quod indicat, in illis qui nascuntur ex Adamo esse vitium, propter quod peccatores dici possint. Sed hoc Pighius putat se posse eludere, quod peccatores interdum dicantur propter reatum quamuis actio peccandi praeterierit, neque amplius extet. Quamuis hoc ita sit, nunquam tamen ostendere potest e Scripturis, quemquam peccatorem appellari, quin aut in seipso vitium habeat aut certè antea admiserit: nisi dicere velit, Deum homines reos facere, absque ipsorum aliquo peccato. Sed de hac re plura ad N. 19. Fateor igitur, qui puniuntur aut calamitate opprimuntur, peccatores dici, sed non apud Deum, nisi peccatum ipsi aut commiserint, aut in se habuerint: Et verò manifestum est Apostolum in eo esse hoc loco, ut doceat verè peccatum esse in omnes homines propagatum, non autem aliquid quod non sit peccatum, sed peccati tantùm consequens. Si peccati nomen non accipitur proprie hoc loco, sed figuratè, eâ figurâ, quâ ponitur antecedens pro consequente, quomodo ex hoc loco argumentantur adversus Pelagium & Pighium Orthodoxi? Et, si accipitur proprie, quomodo simul accipitur figuratè?
units.tr: PLAC. Since this answer is Pighius's, and was once thrown at our people, Martyr refutes it, though I say nothing, in his Commentary on Romans 5:9, and in the Common Places, Class 2, chapter 1, §8: Finally, he says, we have from Paul that through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners; which shows that in those who are born of Adam there is a vice on account of which they can be called sinners. But Pighius thinks he can escape this by saying that men are sometimes called sinners on account of guilt, although the act of sinning has passed away and no longer exists. Granted that this is so, yet he can never show from the Scriptures that anyone is called a sinner unless he either has the vice in himself or at least committed sin earlier; unless he wishes to say that God makes men guilty without any sin of their own. But more on this matter at no. 19. I grant, then, that those who are punished or overwhelmed by calamity are called sinners, but not before God, unless they have either committed sin or had it in themselves. And it is clear that the Apostle in this place intends to teach that sin has truly been spread to all men, not something which is not sin but only a consequence of sin. If the word "sin" is not taken properly in this place, but figuratively, by that figure in which the antecedent is put for the consequent, how do the Orthodox argue from this passage against Pelagius and Pighius? And if it is taken properly, how is it taken figuratively at the same time?

units.la: Imputant nonnunquam homines vel ignari, vel iniusti, alijs hominibus peccata, qui non peccarunt, & qui peccarunt his nonnunquam Deus peccata non imputat: Et, si cui Deus peccatum imputat, imputat quia peccavit, non facit imputando ut peccauerit. Ordine naturae prius peccatur, quàm peccatum imputatur.
units.tr: Men, sometimes through ignorance or injustice, impute sins to other men who have not sinned, and God sometimes does not impute sins to those who have sinned. And if God imputes sin to anyone, he imputes it because that person has sinned; by imputing, he does not make him to have sinned. In the order of nature, sin is committed before it is imputed.

units.la: GAR. Resp. 1. Deus nemini peccatum imputat, quin ille peccauerit vel in se, vel in alio, id est, quin vel in se peccatum commiserit, vel alius, qui cum arcte coniunctus est; sicut Saulis peccatum filijs eius imputauit, non quia ipsi commisissent, sed quia pater eorum commiserat. Vt sicut Deus testatur in lege, peccata patrum visitare in filijs. 2. Deus imputando peccatum alicui, non facit vt peccauerit, sed supponit eum peccauisse, siue in se, siue in alio. Est enim imputatio peccati, actus Dei iudicialis, quo declarat aliquem esse reum & dignum poena ob peccatum, vt ab initio dictum. 3. Peccatur prius ab aliquo, quam peccatum imputetur; sed non est necessarium, vt ab eo ipso cui peccatum imputatur, prius actu peccatum fuerit; sed necessarium est, vt aliquam habeat coniunctionem cum eo qui peccauit, & cuius peccatum ei imputatur sicut antea docuit Clar. Amyraldus.
units.tr: GAR. Answer 1. God imputes sin to no one unless that person has sinned either in himself or in another; that is, unless he has either committed sin himself or someone closely joined to him has. Thus God imputed the sin of Saul to his sons, not because they had committed it but because their father had. As God testifies in the law, he visits the sins of the fathers upon the children. 2. When God imputes sin to someone, he does not make him to have sinned, but presupposes that he has sinned, either in himself or in another. For the imputation of sin is a judicial act of God, by which he declares someone to be guilty and worthy of punishment on account of sin, as was said at the beginning. 3. Someone sins before sin is imputed; but it is not necessary that the very person to whom sin is imputed should have actually sinned beforehand; it is necessary only that he have some union with the one who sinned, whose sin is imputed to him, as the most distinguished Amyraut taught before.

units.la: PLAC. Idem sonare mihi videntur tres iste Viri docti responsiones, simul igitur omnes refellam. Principio distinguenda est coniunctio cum peccatore: alia enim est coniunctio cum peccatore quatenus est peccator, alia cum peccatore quatenus est homo à quo ducimus originem. Vacare peccato non potest qui cum peccatore coniunctus est quatenus est peccator: particeps enim est eiusdem peccati, vel consensione, vel propagatione, vel imitatione &c. At coniunctio cum alio, quatenus homo est à quo ducimus originem, sola non sufficit, vt peccatum ab alio commissum imputetur; alioqui omnia Adami, omniaque parentum nostrorum peccata, nobis poslent iure imputari, quod, opinor, nemo dixerit: nulla tamen alia coniunctio nos inter & Adamum, ante communicatam ab eo corruptionem hæreditariam esse potuit. Nec iuuat Virum doctum exemplum Saulis: Nam eius filij, cum in se peccatores erant ac digni ob propria peccata illis poenis quas perpessi sunt tum peccati illius paterni participes, vt patet ex verbis ipsius Dei 2. Sam. 21. v. 1. Propter Saulem, & domum eius sanguinariam, eo quod interfecit Gibeonitas. Non igitur solus Saul erat sanguinarius, sed eius domus seu familia. Sic Deus peccata patrum visitat in filijs, nempe cum peccata patrum su[...] in filijs, Non enim vbi non sunt, sed vbi sunt visitantur peccata. Sic olim visitauit in decem tribubus peccatum Ieroboami cuius erant participes & rei, 1. Reg. 14. 16. Deinde non videtur Vir doctus sibi satis constare. Dixerat enim paragrapho praecedente aliquem in alio peccare ex vi vocis designare imputationem, idemque esse in alio peccare ac peccatum alius imputari, Nunc vult esse diuersa; & prius esse peccare in alio, quàm peccatum alius imputari, hocque tanquam posterius, illud supponere, tanquam prius & causam. Deinde passim inculcat peccatum Adami nostrum non esse nisi imputatione: vnde sequitur, nos in Adamo non peccasse nisi imputatione. Attamen nunc vult peccatum Adami nobis imputari, quia nos in Adamo peccauimus. Quomodo autem in Adamo peccauimus, si peccatum Adami nostrum non fuit? Vt igitur prius in Adamo peccauimus, quàm eius peccatum nobis fuit imputatum, sic prius nostrum fuit Adami peccatum, quàm nobis imputaretur. Quomodo ergo passim inculcat nostrum non esse, nisi per imputationem? Denique Deus, inquit, imputando peccatum alicui non facit vt peccauerit. Non facit igitur Deus imputando posteros Adami esse peccatores. Nam peccator non est qui non peccauit. Quomodo ergo dicit Vir doctus peccatum Actuale Adami propagari imputatione, nos inobedientia Adami constitui peccatores imputatione? Vno verbo, si peccatores sumus antequam Deus nobis imputet peccatum Adami, peccatum Adami non introiit in mundum imputatione, sed imputatio introitum illum sequitur. id quod mihi erat probandum.
units.tr: PLAC. These three learned men's answers seem to me to say the same thing, so I will refute them all together. First, a distinction must be made concerning union with a sinner. For there is one union with a sinner insofar as he is a sinner, and another with a sinner insofar as he is a man from whom we derive our origin. One who is united with a sinner insofar as he is a sinner cannot be free from sin, for he is a partaker of the same sin, whether by consent, by propagation, by imitation, or otherwise. But union with another insofar as he is the man from whom we derive our origin is not enough by itself for sin committed by another to be imputed to us; otherwise all the sins of Adam and of all our parents could rightly be imputed to us, which I think no one would say. Yet no other union could exist between us and Adam before the hereditary corruption was communicated by him. Nor does the learned man's example of Saul help him. For his sons, when they were sinners in themselves and worthy of those punishments which they suffered on account of their own sins, were also partakers of that paternal sin, as is clear from God's own words in 2 Samuel 21:1: On account of Saul and his bloody house, because he killed the Gibeonites. So it was not Saul alone who was bloody, but his house or family. So God visits the sins of the fathers upon the children, namely when the sins of the fathers are in the children. For sins are visited not where they are not, but where they are. Thus once he visited upon the ten tribes the sin of Jeroboam, of which they were partakers and guilty (1 Kings 14:16). Next, the learned man does not seem to be consistent with himself. For he had said in the preceding paragraph that to sin in another, by the force of the words, designates imputation, and that to sin in another is the same as another's sin being imputed. Now he wants them to be different, and that to sin in another comes before another's sin is imputed, and that the former, as the later, presupposes the latter as prior and cause. Next, he repeatedly insists that Adam's sin is ours only by imputation; from which it follows that we have sinned in Adam only by imputation. Yet now he wants Adam's sin to be imputed to us because we sinned in Adam. But how did we sin in Adam if Adam's sin was not ours? So if we sinned in Adam before his sin was imputed to us, then Adam's sin was ours before it was imputed to us. How then does he repeatedly insist that it is ours only through imputation? Finally, he says, God, by imputing sin to someone, does not make him to have sinned. Therefore God does not, by imputing, make Adam's posterity sinners. For one who has not sinned is not a sinner. How then does the learned man say that Adam's actual sin is propagated by imputation, and that by Adam's disobedience we are constituted sinners by imputation? In a word, if we are sinners before God imputes Adam's sin to us, then Adam's sin did not enter the world by imputation, but imputation follows that entry. This is what I had to prove.

units.la: Deinde tu vis omnes peccasse in Adamo. Dabis autem fuisse in Adamo quomodo in Adamo peccauerunt: prius enim est esse quàm agere vel peccare. Fuimusne ergo in Adamo imputatione ϖ esse eius? negabis proculdubiò, cur ergo vis nos in eo peccasse imputatione ϖ peccare ipsius?
units.tr: Next, you want all to have sinned in Adam. But you must grant that they were in Adam before they sinned in Adam, for being comes before acting or sinning. Were we then in Adam by imputation or by his being (or by being his)? You will undoubtedly deny that we were in him by imputation. Why then do you want us to have sinned in him by imputation rather than by his doing?

units.la: Dices fortasse istud peccare non significare peccatum imputari. Hinc inferam, igitur peccasse omnes peccato actuali, non quia ipsis imputetur, sed alio modo, quem mihi à te explicari cupio, qui toties negas peccatum actuale Adami nostrum esse alio modo quàm per imputationem. Sed praeterea quaero,
units.tr: You will perhaps say that to sin in this sense does not mean that sin is imputed. Then I will infer that all have sinned with actual sin, not because it is imputed to them, but in some other way, which I want you to explain to me, since you so often deny that Adam's actual sin is ours in any way other than by imputation. But I further ask,

units.la: Quando peccauimus in Adamo eius peccato actuali? an cum illud peccauit, an alio tempore? hauddubie cum illud commisit in paradiso; nullum aliud tempus assignare potes. Audi quid inde sequatur. Qui peccarunt ita vt iustam condemnationem mortis æternæ sibi commeriti sint, illi verè & proprie peccarunt. Qui autem verè & proprie peccarunt, illi tunc cum peccauerunt verè & proprie fuerunt. Qui ergo hodie incipit esse & nascitur infans, ille verè & proprie loquendo fuit iam tum, cum Adamus esset in paradiso, ante aliquot annorum millia: quippe, qui tum verè & proprie peccauit. Itaque quod de se dixit Christus Ioh. 8. 18. Antequam Abraham nasceretur ego sum, nemo fuerit nostrum, qui idem dicere de semetipso non possit.
units.tr: When did we sin in Adam by his actual sin? Was it when he committed it, or at another time? Surely when he committed it in paradise; you cannot assign any other time. Hear what follows from this. Those who sinned so as to have deserved for themselves the just condemnation of eternal death, truly and properly sinned. Those who truly and properly sinned, truly and properly existed at the time when they sinned. So whoever today begins to exist and is born as an infant truly and properly existed already, when Adam was in paradise, many thousands of years ago, since he too truly and properly sinned then. Therefore what Christ said of himself in John 8. 18, Before Abraham was born, I am, none of us could fail to say of himself.

units.la: GAR. Resp. 1. Ex verbis Domini & Dei nostri scommata nectere, vt aliosludibrio exponas, an satis pium sit, aliorum iudicium esto. Malim ego sane perire mihi centum iocos, quàm vt vno sacra Scriptura verbulo abuti velim.
units.tr: GAR. Answer 1. If you twist the words of our Lord and God into jests so as to expose others to mockery, let others judge whether that is pious enough. I would rather lose a hundred jokes of my own than be willing to abuse a single word of Holy Scripture.

units.la: PLAC. Egone hic iocos aut scommata nexui? Imò serio, maximè, inquam, serio argumentatus sum, imputationisque immediatæ absurditatem reuelaui. Quid enim est ioci in hoc argumento? Ex qua opinione sequitur, vnumquemque nostrum posse idem de semetipso dicere quod de se Christus dixit, Antequam Abraham fieret ego sum, illa est falsa & absurda. Id autem sequitur, ex opinione qua dicimur verè & proprie peccasse, atque adeò fuisse tunc cum Adamus esset adhuc in paradiso terrestri. Ergo illa opinio est falsa & absurda. Cum sic argumentor videor ne tibi, Lector, iocari, & ad iocum abuti Scriptura? Non arbitror. Nihil tamen aliud verba quibus sum vsus continent quàm hoc argumentum.
units.tr: PLAC. Have I, then, woven jests or mockery here? Far from it, I argued most seriously, I say, and I laid bare the absurdity of immediate imputation. For what is jesting in this argument? From the opinion that follows, that each of us could say of himself what Christ said of himself, Before Abraham was made, I am, that opinion is false and absurd. But this follows from the opinion by which we are said to have truly and properly sinned, and so to have existed at the time when Adam was still in the earthly paradise. Therefore that opinion is false and absurd. When I argue thus, do I seem to you, reader, to be jesting, and to be abusing Scripture for a joke? I think not. Yet the words I have used contain nothing but this argument.

units.la: GAR. Et qua demum ratio esse potest, vt quis ad infantem vel hominem quemcumque applicet ea verba, quibus teste Calvino, Christus eximit se è vulgo hominum, sibiqué cœlestem ac diuinam virtutem „ virtutem vindicat, cuius sensus ab initio usque mundi in omnia „ saecula diffusus fuerit. Putasne passurum Sanctum Augustinum, ut hic locus vel ioco, vel serio ad creaturam accommodaretur, qui „ cum ea verba diligenter meditatus esset, exclamat, Agnoscite „ Creatorem, discernite creaturam.
units.tr: GAR. And what reason can there possibly be for applying those words, by which, as Calvin testifies, Christ sets himself apart from the common run of men and claims for himself a heavenly and divine power, the sense of which has spread through all ages from the beginning of the world, to an infant or to any man at all? Do you think Saint Augustine would allow this passage to be applied to a creature, whether in jest or in earnest, he who, when he had meditated diligently on those words, cried out: "Acknowledge the Creator, distinguish the creature."

units.la: PLAC. Pro me, contra se, disputare Vir doctus videtur.
