Idem enim cum Calvino & Augustino sentio, idque Disp. xi. lib. 1. pro Divina Domini nostri Iesu Christi natura, satis, opinor, testatum feci; Nunc quoque etiam testor, qui ideo vestram opinionem reicio hoc loco, quia ex ea sequitur maximum absurdum, nempe verba illa Christi cuilibet alii homini convenire posse. Si videtur vobis absurdum hoc consequens, ut est certe, & quidem tam absurdum quam quod maxime, cur non videtur vobis pariter absurdum antecedens unde ducitur?
units.tr: PLAC. The learned man seems to argue for me against himself. For I think the same as Calvin and Augustine, and I have, I believe, sufficiently demonstrated this for the divine nature of our Lord Jesus Christ in Disputation 11, Book 1. I also now bear witness that I reject your opinion in this place because from it there follows a very great absurdity, namely that those words of Christ could apply to any other man. If this consequence seems absurd to you, as it certainly is, and as absurd as anything could be, why does the antecedent from which it is drawn not seem equally absurd to you?

units.la: GAR. 2. Sed ratiocinij vanam subtilitatem consideram in exemplo simili. Ita imputatur nobis Christi satisfactio, ut in Christo satisfecisse dicamur. Accedat e Socinianorum grege quispiam; adversus eam doctrinam arma mutuabitur a Viro docto, & in veritatem subtili argumentatione consurget. Quando vero demum satisfacimus in Christo, satisfactione eius actuali? An cum Christus ipse satisfecit in cruce? An alio tempore? Certe cum satisfecit in cruce. Sed audi. Qui satisfecerunt, ita ut iram Dei placauerint, illi vere satisfecerunt & proprie. Qui vero & proprie satisfecerunt, tunc cum satisfecerunt, vere & proprie fuerunt. Ergone Christianus qui nunc vivit vere fuit, cum Christus penderet in cruce? Quid videtur? Annon valide contortum telum? Dissoluat nodum qui nectere docuit. Nec enim Socinianum refellet, ut non & eadem ratione subtilitatem suam traducat.
units.tr: GAR. 2. But I consider the empty subtlety of this reasoning in a similar example. In the same way Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us, so that we are said to have satisfied in Christ. Let someone from the flock of the Socinians come forward; he will borrow arms against that doctrine from the learned man, and he will rise up against the truth with subtle argument. But when, pray, do we actually satisfy in Christ, by his actual satisfaction? Was it when Christ himself satisfied on the cross? Or at another time? Surely when he satisfied on the cross. But hear the argument. Those who satisfied, so as to appease the wrath of God, truly and properly satisfied. But those who truly and properly satisfied, existed truly and properly at the time when they satisfied. Then does the Christian who now lives truly exist when Christ hung on the cross? What do you think? Is this not a dart cleverly twisted? Let him untie the knot who taught us to tie it. For he will not refute the Socinian unless he too can turn his own subtlety back on himself by the same reasoning.

units.la: PLAC. Hoc exemplum non est simile, nec meam ratiocinationem vllo modo euertit. Imputatur quidem nobis credentibus Christi satisfactio, sed ea imputatio fidem nostram sequitur, non antecedit, nedum ut antecedat nostram existentiam. Iustificamur enim fide, non ante fidem. Cum igitur dicimus satisfecisse in Christo, ut locutio non extat in Scriptura, sic commode accipi debet, nec proprie intelligi potest. Sensus alius esse non debet quam iste, Christus satisfecit pro nobis. Nos non satisfecimus, sed alius, nempe Christus, pro nobis satisfecit. Idemne dici potest de peccato, Nos non peccauimus, sed alius peccauit pro nobis, aut loco nostro? Deinde quæstio, Quando verò demum satisfacimus in Christo, satisfactione eius actuali? parum abest quin sit ridicula: innuit enim duplicem satisfactionem, actualem & habitualem; cùm tamen non vt est peccatum aliud actuale ab Adamo commissum, aliud habituale in nos propagatum ac nobis inhærens, sic vlla sit satisfactio præter eam quæ à Christo loco nostro præstita est. Præterea propositio quando satisfacimus in Christo, cùm propria non sit, eget expositione, & reuocanda est ad propriam: alioqui committitur fallacia plurium interrogationum: continet enim has duas quæstiones 1. Quando Christus satisfecit?
units.tr: PLAC. This example is not similar, and it in no way overturns my reasoning. Christ's satisfaction is indeed imputed to us who believe, but that imputation follows our faith; it does not precede it, much less precede our existence. For we are justified by faith, not before faith. Therefore when we say that we satisfied in Christ, a way of speaking which does not occur in Scripture, it ought to be understood in a sense that is proper and cannot be taken literally. The sense ought to be no other than this: Christ satisfied for us. We did not satisfy, but another, namely Christ, satisfied for us. Can the same be said of sin: "We did not sin, but another sinned for us, or in our place"? Next, the question, When, pray, do we satisfy in Christ, by his actual satisfaction? is almost ridiculous: for it hints at a double satisfaction, actual and habitual; whereas, since there is not one actual sin committed by Adam and another habitual sin propagated into us and inhering in us, so there is no satisfaction except that which was rendered by Christ in our place. Moreover, the proposition "when we satisfy in Christ," since it is not proper, needs explanation and must be traced back to the proper sense; otherwise the fallacy of many questions is committed, for it contains these two questions: 1. When did Christ satisfy?

units.la: 2. Quando nobis Christi satisfactio imputatur? Ad illam respondeo, quando passus est in cruce; Ad hanc, quando credimus in eum. Quod si similiter resoluas quæstionem, Quando peccauimus in Adamo? in has duas, Quando peccauit Adamus? &, Quando imputatur nobis eius peccatum? Facilis erit responsio ad primam, quando manducauit fructum vetitum in paradiso, ad secundam, vt taceam supponi imputationem; cùm tamen, vt dici possimus peccasse in Adamo non sit necessaria imputatio, sufficiat propagatio peccati, respondeo, quando geniti sumus ab Adamo vitiati & corrupti. Quid in eo est absurdi? Nec tamen sic potuit respondere Vir doctus, quippe qui velit peccatum Adami nobis, iam ab eo tempore, quo lapsus est Adam, fuisse imputatum. Cæterum quàm multa sint inter Christi satisfactionem & Adami peccatum discrimina iam aliqnoties obseruauimus, & ad Rom. 5. 19. obseruaturi sumus.
units.tr: 2. When is Christ's satisfaction imputed to us? To the first I answer: when he suffered on the cross; to the second: when we believe in him. But if you resolve the question, "When did we sin in Adam?" similarly into these two, "When did Adam sin?" and "When is his sin imputed to us?" the answer to the first will be easy: when he ate the forbidden fruit in paradise. To the second, not to mention that imputation is assumed, since in order for us to be said to have sinned in Adam, imputation is not necessary, the propagation of sin being sufficient, I answer: when we were born from Adam, corrupted and vitiated. What is absurd in that? Yet the learned man could not answer thus, since he wishes Adam's sin to have been imputed to us from the time when Adam fell. Moreover, how many differences there are between Christ's satisfaction and Adam's sin we have already observed several times, and we shall observe them again on Romans 5. 19.

units.la: 3. Sed & Pelagianus telum arripiet, & in ipsum contorquebit. Nam vbi dicit Apostolus nos in Adamo peccasse, quid intelligit Vir doctus peccati voce? Corruptionem hereditariam, vitium illud originale nostrum, & nobis ingenitum. Itaque in Adamo peccasse, erit in Adamo corruptos & vitiatos esse. Insurget iam Pelagianus, & hac argumentatione fretus queret, Quando corrupti sumus in Adamo peccato eius? An cùm ipse peccauit, & peccando se corrupit, an alio tempore? Certè cùm ipse peccauit, & peccando se corrupit: Etenim non sibi soli peccauit, aut peccato suo nocuit, sed unius illius lapsu multi, imò omnes mortui sunt. Audi iam. Qui ita corrupti fuerunt, ut mortis aeterna rei facti sint, illi verè & proprie corrupti fuerunt. Qui verè & proprie corrupti fuerunt, illi tunc cum corrupti sunt, verè & proprie fuerunt. Ergone infans qui nunc nascitur, verè fuit, cum Adamus peccaret, & peccando seipsum corrumperet? Ita qui laqueos aliis confecerant, in eos se induunt, & quam foveam aliis pararant in eam ipsimet incidunt.
units.tr: 3. But the Pelagian too will seize the dart and turn it against him. For when the Apostle says that we sinned in Adam, what does the learned man understand by the word sin? Hereditary corruption, that original vice of ours, born in us. Therefore to have sinned in Adam will be to have been corrupted and vitiated in Adam. Now the Pelagian will rise up, and relying on this argument he will ask: When were we corrupted by Adam's sin? When he himself sinned, and by sinning corrupted himself, or at another time? Surely when he himself sinned and by sinning corrupted himself. For he did not sin only against himself, nor harm only his own sin, but by the fall of that one man many, indeed all, died. Hear now. Those who were so corrupted that they became liable to eternal death, truly and properly were corrupted. Those who truly and properly were corrupted, truly and properly existed when they were corrupted. Then does the infant who is now born truly exist, when Adam sinned and by sinning corrupted himself? Thus those who had prepared snares for others entangle themselves in them, and the pit they had dug for others they themselves fall into.

units.la: P L A C. Hi laquei nulli sunt, meque facilè expedio. Primùm enim Apostolus non dixit nos in Adamo peccasse, & ut dixisset, propositio nos esse corruptos & vitiatos in Adamo quem sensum habere possit, considerandum est. Sensus est nos deriuata ab Adamo corruptione corruptos esse, vel, quod eòdem redit, corruptionem Adami fuisse fontem unde nostra scaturijt corruptio, vel, corruptum fuisse Adamum, & corruptionem Adami in nos propagatam fuisse. Si ergo quæro, Quando Adamus corruptus fuit? respondebo, cùm primùm peccauit, Quando corrupti fuimus vi communionis quam cum Adamo habemus? Resp. quando geniti sumus. Quid est in ea re difficultatis? Taceo Virum doctum vti fallacia à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter. Aliud enim est esse corruptum secundum quid, seu cum hac limitatione in Adamo, aliud esse corruptum simpliciter seu absque eiusmodi limitatione. Hoc ex illo non sequitur, si temporis illius ratio habeatur, cùm primum Adamus corruptus fuit: significatur enim corruptio radicis seu fontis, non ramorum aut riuorum, quoniam nondum erant: priùs autem est esse quàm esse corruptum. Id quod mihi respondeni non potest, quoniam, ut iam obseruaui, imputationem oppugno quæ diu fuisse creditur, antequam esse inciperemus, & qua factum sit ut verè & propriè peccatores & rei fuerimus.
units.tr: PLAC. These snares are nothing, and I easily escape them. For first, the Apostle did not say that we sinned in Adam. Even if he had said it, we must consider what sense the proposition "we were corrupted and vitiated in Adam" can have. The sense is that we were corrupted by a corruption derived from Adam, or, which comes to the same thing, that Adam's corruption was the fountain from which our corruption flowed, or that Adam was corrupted and his corruption was propagated into us. If I therefore ask, "When was Adam corrupted?", I shall answer, "When he first sinned." If I ask, "When were we corrupted by the force of the communion we have with Adam?", the answer is, "When we were born." What difficulty is there in this? I pass over the learned man's use of the fallacy that argues from a thing said in a certain respect to the same thing said absolutely. For it is one thing to be corrupted in a certain respect, or with this qualification in Adam, and another thing to be corrupted absolutely, without such a qualification. The one does not follow from the other if we take account of the time when Adam was first corrupted. For what is signified is the corruption of the root or fountain, not of the branches or streams, since these did not yet exist. Now being comes before being corrupted. This cannot be answered by my opponent, since, as I have already observed, I am attacking an imputation which is believed to have existed long before we began to be, and by which it came about that we were truly and properly sinners and guilty.

units.la: G A R. 4. Qui sic argumentantur, eos memores esse oportebat eorum, quæ prius dixerunt. Si peccatum Adami accipiatur non pro actione ipsa praecisè sumptâ, sed simul cum corruptione, quam peperit, rectè dici Adami peccatum posteris imputari. Nam ita peccatum erit, & ipsa Adami actio & corruptio consequens. Itaque ut rectè dicimur peccare in Adamo propter corruptionem in nos ab Adamo descendentem : Ita & recte peccare dicemur in eo, propter actionem quae in Adamo praecessit.
units.tr: GAR. 4. Those who argue thus ought to remember what they said before. If the sin of Adam is taken not for the action itself considered precisely, but together with the corruption which it produced, then it is rightly said that Adam's sin is imputed to posterity. For thus the sin will be both Adam's action and the consequent corruption. Therefore, just as we are rightly said to sin in Adam on account of the corruption descending from Adam into us, so we shall rightly be said to sin in him on account of the action which preceded in Adam.

units.la: PLAC. Quomodo id a me fuerit dictum, & quàm non faueat imputationi antecedenti latis patere aibitror ex dictis sup. pag. 161. 162. 163. Quorsum igitur pertineat, & quam vim habeat, hęc Viri docti responsio, non intelligo. Certe corruptio nostra est, quia in nos propagata, intra nos est, actio vero quae corruptione peperit non est nostra nisi quatenus corruptio eius quaedam participatio & in eam consensio est.
units.tr: PLAC. How this was said by me, and how far it is from favouring an imputation prior to our existence, I think is clear from what was said above, pp. 161, 162, 163. What bearing this answer of the learned man has, and what force it carries, I do not understand. Certainly our corruption is within us, because it has been propagated into us. But the action which produced the corruption is not ours, except insofar as the corruption is a certain participation in it and our consent to it.

units.la: GAR. 5. Negatur illud, cui totam suam rationem superstruit Vir doctus, Qui peccarunt, ita ut iustam condemnationem meriti sint, eos vere & proprie peccasse. Quia vere & proprie peccare est in propria & sua persona peccare, & suo non alieno peccato delinquere; Proprium enim alieno opponitur: At etiam qui alieno peccato peccant, id est, quibus alienum peccatum imputatur, ij iustam condemnationem merentur. Nam filij Saulis peccauerunt alieno, nempe patris, peccato, & tamen iustam mortis condemnationem ex Dei mandato perpessi sunt, adeoque meruerunt, quia iusta sunt Dei iudicia. Et peccata, quibus patres actu peccarunt, non sunt proprie peccata filiorum, quia non sunt ab ijs personaliter patrata; & tamen iuxta Decalogi comminationem, propter ea filij in varias poenas & iustam comminationem incurrunt. Ita ergo possumus in Adamo peccasse, ut iustam mortis sententiam meriti simus, & tamen non ideo huc deueniendum est, ut dicamus, nos proprie sine personaliter peccasse, cum Adamus peccauit; sed tantum ita censeri apud Deum, ac si cum ipse peccauit, omnes peccassemus. Nam quicunque ex illo vno multi in seipsis futuri erant, in illo vnus erant; Et in quo erat natura communis, ab illius vitio nemo est immunis, ut loquitur Sanctus Augustin. Epistola centesima sexta.
units.tr: GAR. 5. What he builds his whole argument upon is denied: that those who have sinned, so as to have merited a just condemnation, have truly and properly sinned. For to sin truly and properly is to sin in one's own person and to offend by one's own sin, not by another's; for "proper" is opposed to "another's." But those too who sin by another's sin, that is, to whom another's sin is imputed, deserve a just condemnation. For the sons of Saul sinned by another's sin, namely their father's, and nevertheless suffered the just sentence of death by God's command, and so deserved it, because the judgments of God are just. And the sins by which the fathers actually sinned are not properly the sins of the sons, because they were not committed by them personally; yet according to the threat of the Decalogue, the sons on account of those sins incur various punishments and a just threatening. So we can sin in Adam, so as to have deserved the just sentence of death, and yet it does not follow that we must say we did not sin properly or personally when Adam sinned; rather, we are only so reckoned before God as if we had all sinned when he himself sinned. For all of us who were to be many in ourselves were in that one; and in whom the common nature was, no one is free from the fault of that nature, as Saint Augustine says in Epistle 106.

units.la: PLAC. Putabam vere opponi falso, & proprie τῷ improprie seu figurate, atque ita accipiebam, sed docet me nunc Vir doctus utrumque hoc loco idem valere quod personaliter, vel in propria persona. Quaero igitur, qui ita peccauerunt ut iustam & propriam condemnationem sint commeriti, vtrum vere, an falso peccauerint? Falso, opinor, nemo dixerit. Qui enim dicitur ita peccasse ut iustam condemnationem sit promeritus, si potest probare id falsò dici, fieri non potest vt ob eiusmodi peccatum damnetur ab iudice iusto. Rursus quæro an proprie dici possit peccasse, necne, hoc est, non figurate, aut metaphoricè? Nemo etiam dixerit, peccasse tantùm metaphoricè aut figuratè: cùm enim pœna & peccatum sibi mutuò respondeant, pœna verè & proprie dicta supponit peccatum verè & proprie dictum, alienum quidem cùm pœna infligitur alicui vt vadi peccatoris, suum verò, cùm infligitur vt peccatori pœnam proprie dictam commerito: Nec negari potest quin nascamur ex Adamo verè & proprie peccatores, ab eoque peccatum verè & proprie sic dictum trahamus. Adde quod negat Augustinus, negant theologi alij magni nominis ob alienum peccatum quenquam damnari. Vide si placet verba Martyris à nobis laudata sup. pag. 136. ex loc. Com. Class. 2. cap. I. §. 11. Necnon verba Caluini & Chamieri laudata sup. 95. 96. 97. 98. Addam hæc pauca Martyris, ex eodem loco Com. §. 7. Huic commento, (intelligit commentum Pighij) nos, nec possumus, nec debemus acquiescere: nam ira Dei, nonnisi iustè provocatur. Neque enim ea ciusmodi est, vt temerè, aut fortuitò inflammari possit. Quare oportet in natura nostra aliquid esse prauì, ad quod vlciscendum, ira diuina excitetur. Alioqui, quomodo mereremur veram & proprie dictam condemnationem, si nullum esset nostrum eiusmodi condemnationis meritum? Est nostrum, inquies, imputatione. Facit ergo, inquam, imputatio vt mereamur pœnam æternam, quam alioqui non meremur. Id ne' Dei æquitatem deceat, rogo te, Lector, diligenter considera. Cùm enim scopus nobis propositus debeat esse Dei gloria, vide, quæso, num id fit Deo glorisum, & an eius æquitatem & iustitiam faciat clariorem? Vide etiam an deceat eius veritatem? peccauimus in Adamo, iustam mortis sententiam meriti sumus; idque sine dubio nec falsò nec figuratè dicitur, non tamen proprie siue personaliter peccauimus cùm Adamus peccauit: sed tantùm censemur apud Deù, ac si cùm ipse peccauit, omnes peccassemus. Hoccine iudicium est secundum veritatem? glorisum Deo? At, inquiet aliquis, censemur apud Deum ac si iusti essemus. Nempe reuera iusti sumus, non iustitia legali sed euangelica, non iustitia operum sed fidei, non iustitia a nobis profecta aut acquisita, sed data a Deo & per fidem accepta. Dispar est ratio peccati, non promittitur, non datur a Deo, non accipitur a nondum existente. Verba Augustini causae meae non obsunt: fateor enim ab Adami vitio neminem esse immunem. Ad exemplum filiorum Saulis iam respondimus, eos paterni peccati fuisse participes. Peccata patrum visitantur in filijs, vt dixi, cum reperiuntur in filijs. Dicuntur patrum, quia patres priores illa commenti sunt, commiserunt, filijs vt committerent autores fuerunt, vel exemplo & autoritate, vel educatione & institutione, vel etiam lege.
units.tr: PLAC. I thought that "truly" was rightly opposed to "falsely," and "properly" to "improperly" or "figuratively," and I understood it so. But the learned man now teaches me that both words here mean the same as "personally" or "in one's own person." I ask, therefore: those who so sinned as to have deserved a just and proper condemnation, did they sin truly or falsely? No one, I think, would say falsely. For if someone is said to have sinned so as to have merited a just condemnation, and it could be shown that this is falsely said, it could not be that a just judge would condemn anyone for such a sin. Again I ask whether it can be properly said that they sinned, or not, that is, not figuratively or metaphorically. No one would say they sinned only metaphorically or figuratively. For since punishment and sin correspond to each other, punishment truly and properly so called presupposes sin truly and properly so called: it is another's sin when punishment is inflicted on someone as a surety for the sinner, but one's own when it is inflicted on the sinner as the punishment properly due to him. Nor can it be denied that we are born from Adam truly and properly sinners, and that we draw from him sin truly and properly so called. Add that Augustine denies, and other theologians of great name deny, that anyone is condemned for another's sin. Please see the words of Martyr that we praised above, p. 136, from Loci Communes, Class 2, ch. 1, §11, and also the words of Calvin and Chamier praised above, pp. 95–98. I will add these few words of Martyr from the same locus, §7: We can neither acquiesce in this invention (he means Pighius's invention), nor ought we to: for the wrath of God is not justly provoked except by sin. Nor is it of such a kind that it can be kindled rashly or by chance. Therefore there must be something evil in our nature for which divine wrath is aroused to take vengeance. Otherwise, how would we deserve a true and properly so called condemnation, if we had no such merit of condemnation in ourselves? It is ours, you will say, by imputation. Then imputation, I reply, makes us deserve eternal punishment which otherwise we do not deserve. Reader, I ask you to consider carefully whether this befits the equity of God. For since the aim set before us ought to be the glory of God, see, I beg you, whether this is glorious to God, and whether it makes his equity and justice clearer. See also whether it befits his truth. We sinned in Adam, we have deserved the just sentence of death; and this is undoubtedly said neither falsely nor figuratively, yet we did not sin properly or personally when Adam sinned, but are only reckoned before God as if we had all sinned when he himself sinned. Is this judgment according to the truth? Is it glorious to God? But, someone will say, we are reckoned before God as if we were righteous. Indeed we truly are righteous: not with legal righteousness but with gospel righteousness, not with the righteousness of works but of faith, not with righteousness proceeding from us or acquired by us, but given by God and received through faith. The case of sin is unlike: it is not promised, not given by God, not received by one who does not yet exist. Augustine's words do not harm my cause; for I admit that no one is free from the fault of Adam. As for the example of the sons of Saul, we have already answered that they were partakers of the father's sin. As I said, the sins of the fathers are visited upon the sons when they are found in the sons. They are called the fathers' because the fathers devised and committed those things first, and were authors to the sons of committing them, whether by example and authority, or by upbringing and instruction, or even by law.

units.la: Obijcies, quod etiam hoc loco subiungis Apostolum dixisse Leui fuisse decimatum in Abrahamo, quia adhuc in lumbis patris erat, cum ei occurreret Melchisedecus. Sed Apostolus satis innuit phrasim illam non modo non esse propriam, sed duram, cum eam emolliuit hac praefatione ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν. Deinde ad locum illum respondi in thesibus, & tu meam responsionem tibi sumis refellendam in extremo cap. 9. tui tractatus, quam bene, cum tuis vestigijs insistens ad eum locum peruenero, Deo iuuante, ostendam, eademque opera ratiocinationem Apostoli retegam longe solidissimam, sed ab imputatione, quae inter nos controuertitur, alienam omnino.
units.tr: You will object that in this place you also add that the Apostle said Levi was tithed in Abraham, because he was still in the loins of his father when Melchizedek met him. But the Apostle sufficiently hints that this phrase is not only not proper but harsh, since he softens it with this preface, "as it were" [ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν]. Moreover, I answered that passage in my theses, and you take it upon yourself to refute my answer at the end of chapter 9 of your treatise. How well I will show, God helping, when I come to that place following your footsteps, and by the same work I will uncover the Apostle's reasoning, which is by far the most solid, but altogether foreign to the imputation that is disputed between us.

units.la: Obijcis etiam similem phrasim in re similli eiusdem Apostoli, in Adam omnes moriuntur. Sed ea tuam sententiam euertit. Non vult enim omnes mori in Adamo illa ipsa singulari morte, qua mortuus est Adamus, quae scilicet omnibus imputetur, sed sua quisque propria morte. Sic viuificamur, seu resurgimus in Christo, non per imputationem resurrectionis Christi, sed reali, & quam quisque in se suscipit, resurrectione: Et, cum versu praecedente Apostolus sic loquitur, Quandoquidem per hominem est mors, etiam per hominem est resurrectio mortuorum, non intelligit vnius Adami mortem reliquis hominibus imputatam, nec vnius Christi resurrectionem imputatam, sed mortem & resurrectionem specie vnam, numero multam, qua omnes, quisque sua, moriuntur & resurgunt. Id ita manifestum est vt probatione non egeat. Concludamus igitur, cùm idem Apostolus ait, per vnum hominem peccatum in mundum introiisse, intelligendum esse non singulare illud actuale peccatum quod vnus ille homo commisit, sed peccatum ab illo natum, & in omnes homines sparsum ac propagatum: Et, cùm ait, omnes peccasse in Adamo (quanquam id non dicit) intelligendum esse omnes peccasse, non vno illo singulari peccato actuali Adami illis imputato, sed suo quemque, sibi infito ac proprio peccato, quod ab illo Adami ducit originem. Morimur ergo in Adamo, id est, vi communionis naturalis quae nobis cum Adamo intercedit, non autem in ipsa Adami persona, & viuificamur in Christo, non in ipsa persona Iesu Christi, sed vi communionis nostrae supernaturalis cum ea: sed hac de re rursus cum ad Thesses ventum fuerit.
units.tr: You also object to a similar phrase, in a similar matter, from the same Apostle: "in Adam all die." But that overturns your opinion. For he does not mean that all die in Adam with that singular death by which Adam himself died, which would be imputed to all, but that each dies by his own proper death. So we are made alive, or rise, in Christ, not through the imputation of Christ's resurrection, but by a real resurrection which each one undergoes in himself. And since in the preceding verse the Apostle speaks thus, "For since by man came death, by man also comes the resurrection of the dead," he does not understand the death of one Adam imputed to the rest of men, nor the resurrection of one Christ imputed to them, but a death and a resurrection that are one in kind and many in number, by which all die and rise, each his own. This is so plain that it needs no proof. Let us conclude, then, that when the same Apostle says that through one man sin entered into the world, we must understand not that single actual sin which that one man committed, but the sin born from him and spread and propagated among all men. And when he says that all sinned in Adam (although he does not say this), we must understand that all sinned not by that one singular actual sin of Adam imputed to them, but each by his own sin, implanted in him and proper to him, which derives its origin from Adam. We die therefore in Adam, that is, by virtue of the natural communion which we have with Adam, and not in Adam's own person; and we are made alive in Christ, not in the person of Jesus Christ himself, but by virtue of our supernatural communion with him. But of this matter we shall speak again when we come to the Theses.

units.la: GAR. Resp. 1. Qui negant nos in ipsa Adami persona fuisse morti addictos, illi manifeste deserunt Confessionem Ecclesiarum nostrarum, quae id docet & dicit expresse Art. 10.
units.tr: GAR. Resp. 1. Those who deny that we were given over to death in the person of Adam himself clearly desert the Confession of our Churches, which teaches this and states it expressly in Article 10.

units.la: PLAC. Egóne illam Confessionem defero, quam totam amplector, arctéque teneo, imprimis articulum illum decimum? At nego nos in ipsa Adami persona fuisse morti addictos. Primùm illa verba, fuisse morti addictos, mea non sunt: neque praeterito vsus sum, sed praesenti, neque de addictione locutus sum, sed de ipsa morte. Verba enim Apostoli, Sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita & in Christo omnes viuificabuntur, de præterita eiusmodi addictione intelligi non possunt, vt vel ex futuro, vivificabuntur, perspicuum est. Loquor igitur de morte qua quisque moritur, de resurrectione qua quisque formaliter resurgit. Nec aliud volo, cum nego nos mori in ipsa Adami persona, quàm nos mori ipsa morte Adami nobis imputatâ, cùm nego nos resurgere in ipsa Christi persona, quàm resurgere resurrectione Christi nobis imputatâ, vt patet ex verbis meis antecedentibus. Contrarium ne docet Art. ille Confessionis decimus? Cur igitur cum illo committor? At dicit, nos in ipsius (Adami) persona spoliatos bonis illis omnibus, in omnem hanc miseriam & maledictionem incidisse. Ergo morimur in ipsâ Adami persona, hoc est, morte Adami nobis imputatâ. Nihil tale sequitur ex illis Confessionis verbis. Imò ne imputatio quidem ulla ex ijs colligi potest, vel donorum illorum, vel spoliationis illius, vt plenius declarabitur cap. XII.
units.tr: PLAC. Do I desert that Confession, which I embrace entirely and hold fast, especially that tenth article? But I deny that we were given over to death in the person of Adam. First, the words "were given over to death" are not mine. I have used not the past tense but the present, and I have spoken not of being given over but of death itself. For the words of the Apostle, "As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive," cannot be understood of such a past giving over, as is clear even from the future "shall be made alive." I speak therefore of the death by which each one dies, and of the resurrection by which each one formally rises. Nor do I mean anything else when I deny that we die in the very person of Adam, than that we die by the death of Adam imputed to us; just as, when I deny that we rise in the very person of Christ, I mean only that we rise by the resurrection of Christ imputed to us, as is plain from my preceding words. Does that tenth article of the Confession teach the contrary? Why then am I charged with it? But it says that "we, in his (Adam's) person, having been stripped of all those goods, fell into all this misery and curse." Therefore, you say, we die in the person of Adam himself, that is, by the death of Adam imputed to us. Nothing of the kind follows from those words of the Confession. Indeed, no imputation at all can be gathered from them, either of those gifts or of that stripping, as will be more fully explained in chapter XII.

units.la: GAR. 2. Vnionem cum Adamo naturalem non tantùm agnoscimus, sed etiam imputationis illius, de quâ agitur, fundamentum esse dicimus.
units.tr: GAR. 2. We not only acknowledge the natural union with Adam, but also say that it is the foundation of that imputation which is under discussion.

units.la: PLAC. Si imputatio intelligitur antecedens seu immediata, non est illius fundamentum unio illa. Sed pergat.
units.tr: PLAC. If imputation is understood as antecedent or immediate, that union is not its foundation. But let him go on.

units.la: GAR. Nec minùs certum est vnumquemque nostrum, & mori morte suâ propriâ, & habere corruptionem internam sibi propriam, & personaliter distinctam à corruptione, quam peccatum actuale fecit in Adamo. Habere autem vtrumque ex vi coniunctionis illius, quæ nobis cum Adamo tanquam capite generis intercedit. Illa tamen non impediunt, quominùs ad imputationem ea verba Apostoli pertinere dicantur, cùm testatur, nos in Adamo mori.
units.tr: GAR. Nor is it less certain that each of us both dies his own death and has an internal corruption proper to himself, personally distinct from the corruption which actual sin produced in Adam. We have both by virtue of that conjunction which binds us to Adam as the head of the race. Yet these facts do not prevent the Apostle's words, when he testifies that we die in Adam, from being said to pertain to imputation.

units.la: PLAC. Itáne, ad imputationem mortis Adami? Quis unquam audiuerat, mortem Adami nobis imputari? Manet igitur responsio mea, vel si ita vis, argumentatio, si propositio in Adamo morimur vera est, quamuis mors Adami nobis non imputetur etiam propositio in Adamo peccavimus vera esse potest, quamuis peccatum Adami nobis non imputetur.
units.tr: PLAC. So then, to the imputation of Adam's death? Who ever heard that Adam's death is imputed to us? My answer therefore stands, or, if you prefer, my argument: if the proposition "in Adam we die" is true, although Adam's death is not imputed to us, then the proposition "in Adam we sinned" can be true, although Adam's sin is not imputed to us.

units.la: GAR. Vnde contrario modo concludo, atque collegit Vir doctus. Si dictum Apostoli, in Adamo morimur ad imputationem spectat. spectat: Ergo & quod ait, nos in Adamo peccasse. Atqui prius ad imputationem spectat; ut certa ratione ostendi potest. Nam neque in Noacho, neque in quoquam alio maiorum nostrorum mori dicimur, sed tantum in Adamo; Et tamen sicut dicimur ab Adamo prognati, ita dici possumus prognati a patribus, & omnibus maioribus nostris. Cuius discriminis aliquam prorsus causam esse oportet. Non est autem illa simpliciter quaerenda in coniunctione naturali, aut ea propagatione qua descendimus ab Adamo. Nam non minus a maioribus aliis nostris propagati sumus, neque minus sumus cum eis coniuncti, quam cum Adamo; imo propinquior est cum eis, quam cum Adamo, communio ratione temporis. Neque etiam in eo, quod Adam principium est nostrae originis, sive ille a quo genus humanum incepit. Nam ea quidem legitima causa esse potest, quare in Adamo mori dicamur: sed non est legitima causa quare idem de aliis maioribus dici non possit. &c.
units.tr: GAR. From the opposite side I conclude, as the learned man has concluded, thus. If the saying of the Apostle, "in Adam we die," pertains to imputation, then so does what he says, that we sinned in Adam. But the former pertains to imputation, as can be shown by certain reasoning. For we are not said to die in Noah, nor in any other of our forefathers, but only in Adam; and yet, just as we are said to be descended from Adam, so we can be said to be descended from our fathers and all our forefathers. Some cause of this difference must exist. That cause, however, is not to be sought simply in the natural conjunction, or in that propagation by which we descend from Adam. For we are no less propagated from our other forefathers, nor are we less joined with them than with Adam; indeed, by reason of time, our communion with them is closer than with Adam. Nor is it that Adam is the beginning of our origin, or the one from whom the human race began. For that may indeed be a legitimate cause why we are said to die in Adam, but it is not a legitimate cause why the same cannot be said of the other forefathers. etc.

units.la: PLAC. Quomodo certa ratione ostendi potest, dictum Apostoli in Adamo morimur, ad imputationem spectare, si sine imputatione causa legitima est, quare in Adamo mori dicamur? Agebatur enim de eo quod ab Apostolo dicitur, non de eo quod non dicitur. At quare idem de aliis maioribus non dicitur? Si saepius diceretur ac inculcaretur in Scriptura nos in Adamo mori, merito quaeri posset, quare saepe rem illam repetens Scriptura, perpetuo unius Adami, nunquam aliorum maiorum meminisset: nunc, cum semel id dictum sit, mirum videri non debet, si alij maiores silentio praeteriti sunt, nec locus est silentij illius rationem quaerendi. Si tamen eius ratio reddenda est, ab imputatione arcessi non debet: succresceret enim statim alia quaestio, cur non aeque in aliis maioribus, ac in Adamo, quod imputaretur posteris fuisset? Tandemque ad Dei voluntatem esset confugiendum: quae sine imputatione posset hoc loco pro ratione afferri. Sed non est opus: succurrunt enim aliae rationes, & quidem duae. Prima, a voce omnes. Sicut, inquit Apostolus, omnes in Adamo moriuntur. Iam autem manifestum est omnes in solo Adamo mori. Altera inde peti potest, quod notatur primus fons, prima origo mortis. Reliqui maiores veluti canales fuerunt, per quos peccatum & mors ab illo fonte in nos dimanarunt, suis Adamus primus fuit autor mortis. Sic, communis omnium regum Israelis idolatria peccatum Ieroboami vocatur, non autem alicuius alterius regis, propterea quod primus illius auctor vnus Ieroboamus fuerat.
units.tr: PLAC. How can it be shown by certain reasoning that the Apostle's saying "in Adam we die" pertains to imputation, if without imputation there is a legitimate cause why we are said to die in Adam? For the matter in hand was what the Apostle says, not what he does not say. But why is the same not said of the other forefathers? If it were said more often, and inculcated in Scripture, that we die in Adam, it could rightly be asked why Scripture, repeating the thing so often, always mentioned the one Adam and never the other forefathers. As it is, since it has been said once, it should not seem strange if the other forefathers have been passed over in silence; there is no need to ask the reason for that silence. Yet if its reason must be given, it should not be drawn from imputation. For another question would immediately arise: why was it not equally imputed to posterity from the other forefathers as from Adam? And in the end one would have to flee to the will of God, which could be offered here as the reason without any imputation. But there is no need, for other reasons come to mind, and indeed two. The first is from the word "all." "As," says the Apostle, "in Adam all die." Now it is manifest that all die in Adam alone. The second can be drawn from the fact that the first source is noted, the first origin of death. The other forefathers were, as it were, channels through which sin and death flowed from that source into us; Adam alone was the first author of death. So the idolatry common to all the kings of Israel is called the sin of Jeroboam and not of any other king, because the first author of it had been Jeroboam alone.

units.la: Interim nonne vides omnes homines eodem modo accipi ab Apostolo, cùm in eos mortem transire, & cùm eos peccasse dicit? Mors, inquit, in omnes transiit, quoniam omnes peccarunt. vtrobique vox omnes eosdē homines, eodem modo, significat. Alioqui vitiosus esset Apostoli syllogismus, & ex quatuor terminis componeretur, quem sic struis, Quicunque peccauerunt, in eos mors transiit. Omnes peccauerunt. Igitur in omnes mors transiit. Nam in conclusione vox omnes notat personas omnium hominum inter se & à persona Adami distinctas & separatas. Ergo necesse est vt in minore eadem vox omnium itidem hominum personas distinctas & separatas cum inter se tum ab Adamo significet. Iam autem manifestum est, omnium hominum personas distinctas & separatas à persona Adami non commisisse peccatum illud actuale vnum idemque numero quod Adamus commisit, & tam impossibile esse vt omnium personarum generis humani sit vnicum numero peccatum actuale, quàm vt sit vnica numero mors omnium.
units.tr: Meanwhile, do you not see that the Apostle takes "all men" in the same sense both when he says that death passed upon them and when he says that they sinned? Death, he says, passed upon all men, because all have sinned. In both places the word "all" means the same men in the same way. Otherwise the Apostle's syllogism would be faulty and would have four terms. You may set it out thus: "Whoever have sinned, death has passed upon them. All have sinned. Therefore death has passed upon all." In the conclusion, the word "all" denotes the persons of all men, distinct and separate from one another and from the person of Adam. It must therefore also denote, in the minor premise, the persons of all men, distinct and separate both from one another and from Adam. Now it is plain that the persons of all men, distinct and separate from the person of Adam, did not commit that one and the same numerically single actual sin which Adam committed. And it is as impossible for the persons of the whole human race to have one numerically single actual sin as it is for them to have one numerically single death.

units.la: GAR. Resp. huius rationis quænam sit vis ad impugnandam peccati Adæ imputationem videre difficile est & dicere. Nam aut longè fallor, aut nemo eorum qui pro hac imputatione pugnant, vnquam somniauit personam suam, vel alterius cuiuscunque hominis esse confusam cum persona Adami, aut ita indistantem, vt in vnum ὑφισάμενον cum eâ coaluerit. Hoc ne quidem animo concipi potest. &c.
units.tr: GAR. A reply to this argument is hard to see and hard to state. For unless I am greatly mistaken, none of those who fight for this imputation has ever dreamed that his own person, or that of any other man, was confused with the person of Adam, or so little distinct from it as to have coalesced with it into one ὑφισάμενον. This cannot even be conceived in the mind. etc.

units.la: PLAC. Quandoquidem videre huius rationis vim Vir doctus non potuit, eam explicabo. Meminerit igitur, Lector, si placet, me non impugnare imputationem mediatam seu consequentem quæ cuiusque existentia & corruptione posterior est, sed immediatam & antecedentem, quam Vir doctus communem appellat, & ita describit cap. I. §. xiii. Imputatio, inquit, peccati Adæ communis est, qua peccatum Adæ non ipsum modo reum fecit; sed etiam totum genus, quod in ipso seminaliter & radicaliter continebatur, eodem reatu implicuit, iam ab eo tempore, quo lapsus est Adam. Et paulò post subiungit, Existente autem humana natura in individuo illo principiali, in illo etiam dici possunt homines communiter extitisse. Exiterunt ne igitur à petiona Adami distantes & separati? Non arbitror quenquam hoc dicturum. Et Cap. 2. §. xvii. Communis, inquit, illa sive immediata, quemadmodum posterior fuit prima actuali Adæ transgressione, ita prior fuit personali cuiuscunque hominis ex Adamo prognati existentia, atque adeo etiam corruptione illa, quæ in singulos naturali generatione descendit quatenus ab initio rei fuerunt omnes communiter in Adamo. Facta est igitur ista imputatio cum nondum essemus personæ separatæ & distantes ab Adamo: vel, ut loquitur is quicum mihi res erat, cum considerarem à Deo tanquam unus homo in Adamo. Nunc, opinor, quam vim habeat argumentum, ipse per te, Lector, satis intelligis.
units.tr: PLAC. Since the learned man could not see the force of this argument, I shall explain it. Let the reader remember, if he will, that I am not attacking the mediate or consequent imputation, which comes after each person's existence and corruption, but the immediate and antecedent imputation, which the learned man calls common. He describes it thus in chapter 1, §13: The imputation of Adam's sin is common, by which Adam's sin made not only himself guilty, but also the whole race, which was contained in him seminally and radically, and involved it in the same guilt, from the very time when Adam fell. And shortly after he adds: Since human nature existed in that one principle individual, men can also be said to have existed commonly in him. Did they therefore exist distant from and separate from the person of Adam? I do not think anyone will say so. And in chapter 2, §17: That common or immediate imputation, just as it came after Adam's first actual transgression, so it came before the personal existence of each man descended from Adam, and therefore also before that corruption which descends by natural generation into each individual, inasmuch as from the beginning of the thing all were together in Adam. That imputation therefore took place when we were not yet separate persons distinct from Adam. Or, as the man with whom I have to deal puts it, when I consider men by God as one man in Adam. Now, I think, you yourself, reader, understand well enough what force the argument has.

units.la: Rectius igitur mea sententia fecisses, si Calvini interpretationi acquiescens non contempsisses id quod legere potuisti in Clavi Scripturæ ad nomen peccatum, his verbis, significat quoque crebro verbum נשא peccavit, in prima coniugatione non actionem, sed qualitatem inhærentem, seu sortem ac conditionem hominis, seu esse peccatorem, esse reum, sicut solent verba hebræa sæpissime tantum existentiam rei, non actionem aut passionem aliumve motum indicare. Et paulò post, sic Rom. v. in Adamo omnes peccaverunt: id est, scelerati ac Dei hostes facti sunt. Quæ quasi habitualis significatio verbi & nominis peccati diligenter observanda est. Et rursus, Romanorum quinto, sicut per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introivit, & per peccatum mors, & ita in omnes homines mors pervasit in quo omnes peccaverunt, non actionem sed ipsum habituale, aut potius innatum & essentiale malum significat quod nempe per Adamum omnes facti sint corrupti &c. Eodem sensu Logici notare solent verba in definitionibus posita aptitudinem, non actum designare, ut cum definitur albedo, color qui visum disgregat, id est, qui aptus natus est visum disgregare. Sic cum Dominus dicit omnem arborem malam malos ferre fructus, male colligeret qui infidelium irregenitos infantulos malas arbores esse negaret, quod non ferant malos fructus; haud secus certe ac qui legisset, omnem volucrem volare, male inde concluderet, auiculam recens exclusam, quod nondum volet, volucrem non esse. Itaque Anabaptistis quibusdam idem quod tu obijcientibus peccare esse verbum actiuum & actionem significare, Georgius Sohnius nihil respondit, nisi verba apud hebraeos non tantum significare actualiter, sed etiam habitualiter, hoc est, non tantum actionem, sed etiam desectum & prauitatem inhaerentem.
units.tr: I think you would have done better, if you had acquiesced in Calvin's interpretation rather than despising what you could have read in the Clavis Scripturae under the word sin, in these words: The Hebrew verb [נשא] "sinned" often signifies, in the first conjugation, not an action but an inherent quality, or the state and condition of a man, or being a sinner, being guilty; just as Hebrew verbs very often indicate only the existence of a thing, not an action, a passion or any other motion. And shortly after: So in Romans 5, "in Adam all sinned": that is, they have become wicked and enemies of God. This habitual sense of the verb and noun "sin" must be carefully observed. And again: In Romans 5, "as through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so death spread to all men, in whom all sinned," the word does not signify an action but the habitual, or rather innate and essential evil, which is that all were made corrupt through Adam etc. In the same sense, logicians customarily note that words placed in definitions signify an aptitude and not an act: when whiteness is defined as the colour which disperses sight, that is, which is fitted and born to disperse sight. So when the Lord says that every evil tree bears evil fruit, one would wrongly conclude that unbelievers' unregenerate infants are not evil trees because they do not bear evil fruit. One would reason no differently from someone who read that every bird flies and then wrongly concluded that a newly hatched little bird is not a bird because it cannot yet fly. Thus, when certain Anabaptists objected to you, as you do, that to sin is an active verb and signifies an action, Georgius Sohnius replied only that in Hebrew verbs signify not only actually but also habitually, that is, not only an action but also an inherent defect and depravity.

units.la: Caeterum non satis intelligo tua ista verba, in peccato originali non peccauimus actu, nisi quatenus in Adamo peccauimus. Quid enim? Visne nos actu peccauisse in Adamo tum cum peccauit? Id Zanchius, quem tu pro tua sententia laudas Cap. tui tractatus VII. negat, addita hac ratione, quia nondum eramus actu. Nam qui fieri potuit, ut, quum nondum essemus actu peccaremus actu? Unde sic argumentor, Moriuntur homines actu. Ergo peccauerunt actu. Absurdum enim est ut qui potentia tantum peccauit non autem actu, puniatur actu, & quidem poena grauissima. At qui non peccauerunt actu in Adamo cum peccauit actualiter. Aliud igitur sit oportet peccatum ob quod actu moriantur homines, nempe vitium illud origihale quod omnibus & singulis inest veré, proprie, actu, inhærenter, tam certé actu quàm fuit in ipso Adamo.
units.tr: Moreover, I do not sufficiently understand your words, in original sin we did not sin actually, except insofar as we sinned in Adam. For what? Do you want us to have sinned actually in Adam at the time when he sinned? Zanchius, whom you cite in your chapter 7 in support of your view, denies this, adding the reason that we were not yet actually existing. For how could it happen that, while we did not yet exist actually, we sinned actually? I argue thus: men die actually. Therefore they have sinned actually. For it is absurd that one who sinned only potentially, and not actually, should be punished actually, and that with the most severe punishment. But they did not sin actually in Adam when he sinned actually. Therefore it must be some other sin for which men die actually: namely, that original vice which truly, properly, actually and inherently inheres in all and each, as certainly actually as it was in Adam himself.

units.la: Minus etiam capio quæ subnectis, cum Adamus peccauit, pro omnibus suis posteris peccauit. Si intelligis eum magno omnium posterorum malo peccasse, nihil verius. Hinc enim natum est vitium illud quod genus humanum inuasit & morti addixit: sed si intelligis eum loco nostro peccauisse, nihil dici potuit à te minus considerate. Nam neque id Scriptura dicit vspiam, & valde absurdum est. Satisfecit quidem loco nostro Christus iustitiæ diuinæ, quippe, nos enim tenebamur satisfacere. Moriendum erat omnibus nobis, ipse mortem loco nostro gustauit. Puniendi eramus omnes, ipse omnium loco passus est. Num igitur peccare tenebamur, vt nostro loco Adamus peccaret? Mihi quidem hactenus inauditum fuit peccare aliquem loco alterius tanquam eius vadem posse. Sed fortasse nostræ partes erant legem, tunc Adamo latam, tunc obseruare, atque adeò audire, memoriæ mandare, intelligere, exequi. Adamus autem vt nos hac molestia leuaret se suffecit in locum nostrum qui nostrum officium impleret, nostras partes ageret. Apage tales cogitationes. Profecto, si loco omnium posterorum Adamus legem illam impleuisset, eius posteri ad eandem legem implendam ipsi in proprijs suis personis non fuissent amplius obligati, quemadmodum quia loco nostro Christus iustitiæ diuinæ satisfecit, non tenemur amplius ei satisfacere. Certè quemadmodum tunc temporis nulla erat in mundo persona humana præter Adamum & Euam, sic nulla præter eos duos persona humana aut poterat, aut debebat legi illi pro illo tempore parere. Neque vero Adamus ea mente peccauit vt loco nostro peccaret, neque, si mens ea ipsi fuisset, in cuiusquam potestate est loco alterius non consentientis peccare. Neque id naturæ lex exigebat vt posterorum loco peccaret, neque Dei bonitatem & iustitiam decebat id efficere & constituere. Præterea si loco nostro peccauit & peccatum illud merebatur, poenam quæ esset peccatum videlicet corruptionem, dic mihi, quæso, cur non fit etiam loco nostro illa affectus poena? nam quo tèporis articulo peccauit, eodem corruptus & vitiosus & iniustus factus est. Annon quo nomine peccauit eodem puniri debuit, præsertim eodem momento? nisi velis, quemadmodum sacrificulus pontificius inter celebrandum missam, modò Christi personam induit, modò deponit, atque ita diuersas agit personas eodem penè momento, sic Adamum similiter modò personam nostram repræsentasse, modò suam vnius sustinuisse, atque eodem momento, & peccasse loco nostro, & punitum suo, non nostro. Nam si loco nostro ea poena castigatus fuit quæ est peccatum originale, non conuenit nos eadem poena affici: quàm enim loco nostro peccauit, tam loco nostro punitus est. Sicut enim quamuis ipsi in proprijs nostris personis peccauerimus, tamen quia Christus loco nostro punitus est, non debemus amplius puniri, ita si pro illo peccato actuali punitus est Adamus loco nostro inflictione peccati originalis, non potest amplius pro eodem illo peccato nobis peccatum originale infligi. Vides quo te ducat tua ista assertio pro nobis peccasse Adamum, nimirum ad negandum peccatum nostrum originale. Quod ipsum etiam effici potest hoc argu-
units.tr: I understand even less what you add: when Adam sinned, he sinned for all his posterity. If you mean that he sinned to the great harm of all his posterity, nothing could be truer. For from this came that vice which invaded the human race and doomed it to death. But if you mean that he sinned in our place, nothing could have been said by you less carefully. For Scripture nowhere says this, and it is very absurd. Christ indeed satisfied the divine justice in our place, since we were bound to satisfy it. We all had to die, and he himself tasted death in our place. We were all to be punished, and he suffered for all in their place. Were we then bound to sin, so that Adam might sin in our place? I have certainly never heard before that someone can sin in another's place as his surety. But perhaps our part was to observe that law, given to Adam then, and to hear it, commit it to memory, understand it and carry it out. And Adam, to relieve us of this trouble, was enough for himself to stand in our place, to fulfil our duty and to play our part. Away with such thoughts! Indeed, if Adam had fulfilled that law in the place of all posterity, his descendants would no longer have been bound to fulfil the same law in their own persons, just as, because Christ satisfied divine justice in our place, we are no longer bound to satisfy it. Surely, just as at that time there was no human person in the world except Adam and Eve, so no human person other than those two could either obey or was bound to obey that law for that time. Nor did Adam sin with the intention of sinning in our place; and even if he had had that intention, it is not in anyone's power to sin in the place of another who does not consent. Nor did the law of nature require that he sin in the place of his posterity, nor did the goodness and justice of God fit him to bring this about and to establish it. Furthermore, if he sinned in our place and deserved that punishment, which is sin, namely corruption, tell me, I beg you, why that punishment was not also inflicted on us in his place? For at the very moment when he sinned, he became corrupt, vicious and unjust. Ought he not to be punished at once for the same offence for which he sinned, especially in the same moment? Unless you will say, like the popish little priest who, while celebrating Mass, now puts on the person of Christ and now lays it aside, and so plays different roles at almost the same moment, that Adam likewise sometimes represented our person and sometimes sustained his own alone, and at the same moment both sinned in our place and was punished in his own, not ours. For if he was chastised in our place with that punishment which is original sin, it does not fit that we should be afflicted with the same punishment: for as he sinned in our place, so he was punished in our place. Just as, although we sinned in our own persons, yet because Christ was punished in our place we ought no longer to be punished, so if Adam was punished for that actual sin in our place by the infliction of original sin, original sin cannot any longer be inflicted on us for that same sin. You see where this assertion of yours, that Adam sinned for us, leads you: namely, to deny our original sin. This too can be shown by the following argument, so that you may see more and more how pernicious that opinion is, from which I desire and try to turn you.

units.la: Quod ipsum etiam effici potest hoc argumento, vt videas magis magisque quàm perniciosa sit illa sententia, à qua te dimouere cupio, & conor. Quod Adami peccatum nobis per imputationem conuenit, vel, si ita mauis, nobis proximè & immediatè imputatur, id ex quo sumus reipsa neque à nobis commissum est, neque nobis inhæret. Res manifesta est de peccato actuali Adami: id enim vis nobis imputari, non autem inesse, aut à nobis natis committi. Nam quod per imputationem conuenit, non conuenit per realem inhærentiam siue inexistentiam. Duo isti modi inter se pugnât. Cur enim aut faciam aut patiar quod alius loco meo vel fecit, vel passus est? Atqui si peccatum actuale Adami nobis imputatur, profecto etiam imputatur eius peccatum habituale siue corruptio inhærés. Nam quæ ratio afferri potest pro imputatione peccati actualis Adami, quæ eadem non militet pro imputatione peccati eiusdem habitualis, & quidem validius? Illud enim fuit actio præteriens, hoc vitium permanens: illud iam pridem præterierat cùm anno ætatis 130. Adamus Sethum genuit, à quo nos ducimus originem, hoc verò tum aderat præsens & inhærens penitus facultatibus Adami cùm generationi operam daret: illud vulgò dicitur esse persona, hoc naturæ. Itaque aut æquè aut magis etiam conueniebat Adamo vt capiti nostro & origini, & nostram personam sustinenti, quàm peccatum illud actuale, quod actio fuit singularis. Si ergo peccatum actuale Adami nobis imputatur, imputatur etiam nobis eius vitium siue peccatum habituale & insitum. Si imputatur, non est in nobis. Quod enim nobiscum Adamus communicauit imputatione, id non communicauit nobiscum reali existentia. Quod peccatum peccauimus in persona Adami, id non peccauimus realiter in nostris perfonis postea quàm geniti fumus. Alioqui magis peccatores ex Adamo nasceremur quàm fuit Adam. Nam ei non est imputatum nisi ipsius peccatum actuale & habituale, nobis idem vtrumque, quemadmodum Adamo imputaretur, & præterea imputaretur idem specie peccatum habituale nobis actu insitum ac inhærens : nam, velis nolis, corruptio innata peccatum est, nisi condonetur, imputandum ad mortem. Non modò autem imputatio quam tueris tollit vitium originale, quod tamen nobis, proh dolor, omnibus & singulis medullitus infixum esse, & Scriptura clamat & experientia contestatur, sed ea quoque Dei φιλανθρωπίαν labefactat; quippe qui voluerit Adamum fustinere personam nostram cum peccauit, non voluerit autem nostram personam eundem sustinere cum punitus est : considerauerit eum cum peccauit vt caput nostrum, noluerit eum eodem modo considerare cùm puniretur : voluerit eum peccare loco nostro, noluerit puniri loco nostro : nostras personas ei imposuerit vt peccaret loco nostro, ac eodem momento abstulerit ne puniretur itidem loco nostro; perinde ac fi noftra ipsorum qui nihil ipsi peccaueramus, morte delectatus fuisset, nihilque aliud illa personarum nostrarum impositione Adamo, captaffet quàm occasionem nos omnes efficiendi peccatores. Quod Petrum Martyrem (qui Caluini & Buceri vestigia secutus totus meus est) ac cæteros dicis agnouisse, omnes homines in Adamo peccaffe, mihi non obest, qui clamo omnes homines peccare in Adamo, quomodo in Adamo moriuntur, hoc est, vi communionis quam habent cum Adamo, non autem imputatione singularis eius vel peccati, vel mortis : Peccasse omnes homines in Adamo, quomodo in eo fuerunt. Fuerunt autem in eo non imputatione τῆ esse ipsius, sed quia eius esse est causa τῆ esse omnium: Peccasse igitur in eo omnes, non peccati ipsius imputatione, sed quia peccatum eius est causa peccati omnium; causa, inquam, eo modo quo ipsius esse est causa nostri, non imputationis diuinæ interuentu, sed per generationem & propagationem naturalem.
units.tr: This can be shown by the following argument, so that you may see more and more how pernicious that opinion is, from which I wish and try to draw you away. If the sin of Adam is imputed to us by imputation (or, if you prefer, is imputed to us immediately and directly), then that by which we are, in fact, is neither committed by us nor inheres in us. This is plain about Adam's actual sin. You want it to be imputed to us, not to inhere in us or to be committed by us after we are born. For what belongs to us by imputation does not belong to us by real inherence or existence. These two modes are at odds. Why should I do or suffer what another has done or suffered in my place? But if Adam's actual sin is imputed to us, then surely his habitual sin, or inherent corruption, is imputed to us too. What reason can be given for imputing Adam's actual sin that does not equally, and even more strongly, support imputing his habitual sin? The one was a passing act, the other a lasting vice. The one had long since passed when Adam, at the age of 130, begat Seth, from whom we derive our origin. The other was present and inhered deeply in Adam's faculties while he was engaged in begetting. The one is commonly said to belong to the person, the other to the nature. So Adam, as our head and origin, and as one who bore our person, was equally or even more fittingly the bearer of this habitual vice than of that actual sin, which was a single act. If, then, Adam's actual sin is imputed to us, his vice or habitual and implanted sin is imputed to us as well. If it is imputed, it is not in us. For what Adam shared with us by imputation, he did not share with us by real existence. We sinned in the person of Adam; we did not sin really in our own persons after we were born. Otherwise we would be born greater sinners than Adam was. For only his own actual and habitual sin was imputed to him, whereas for us both the same would be imputed, as they were to Adam, and moreover the same sort of habitual sin would be imputed to us as actually inborn and inhering. For, whether we will it or not, innate corruption is sin, and unless it is pardoned it is imputed to death. Your imputation not only removes original vice, which, alas, is fixed deep within all and each of us, as Scripture cries out and experience bears witness, but it also undermines the philanthropy [φιλανθρωπίαν] of God. For God willed that Adam should bear our person when he sinned, but did not will that he should bear our person when he was punished. He considered him as our head when he sinned, but did not will to consider him in the same way when he was punished. He willed him to sin in our place, but did not will him to be punished in our place. He imposed our persons on him so that he might sin in our place, and in the same moment removed them so that he might not be punished in our place either. It would be as if he had taken pleasure in the death of ourselves, who had done nothing at all, and had gained nothing by this imposition of our persons on Adam except the occasion of making us all sinners. As for your claim that Peter Martyr (who followed the footsteps of Calvin and Bucer and is wholly mine) and the others acknowledged that all men sinned in Adam, this does not harm me, who likewise cry out that all men sin in Adam just as they die in Adam, that is, by the force of the communion they have with Adam, and not by imputation of his singular sin or death. All men sinned in Adam in the way they were in him. But they were in him not by imputation of his being [τῷ εἶναι], but because his being is the cause of the being [τῷ εἶναι] of all. Therefore all sinned in him not by imputation of his sin, but because his sin is the cause of the sin of all: a cause, I say, in the same way that his being is the cause of ours, not through the intervention of divine imputation, but through generation and natural propagation.

units.la: CAPVT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Responsio ad Argumenta, quæ pro immediata imputatione peccati actualis Adami ducuntur ex Rom. 5. verf. 13. & sequentibus.
units.tr: Reply to the arguments drawn for the immediate imputation of Adam's actual sin from Romans 5:13 and following.

units.la: SED pergamus. Ex versu sequente, quo Apostolus id quod dixerat, peccatum introiisse in mundum & omnes homines peccasse, probat, tu nescio quid argumenti colligis, quod & præcedente illo tuo à me iam refutato ac absurdis obruto nititur, & à te ipso continuò destruitur. Nam, inquit Apostolus, usque ad legem peccatum erat in mundo. Peccatum verò non imputatur, quum nulla lex est. Sic, inquis, ex hoc dicto Apostoli argumentor. Peccatum illud, de quo loquitur Apostolus versu immediatè præcedenti; est peccatum illud quod fuit in mundo vsque ad legem, vt patet ex sequela & textura verborum, maximè ex illa particula §, quæ est rationalis. Hoc concedo, & vt memineris rogo, nam & verum est , & ad tuam sententiam euertendam, meam autem firmandam apprime vtile. Subfumis, sed peccatum primum Adami fuit illud peccatum de quo locutus est Apostolus versu immediate precedenti, vt supra probauimus. Nititur igitur hæc tua propositio fuperiori tua argumentatione , quam vides à nobis capite precedente multis telis confossam ac confectam, vt iure meo possim eius loco hanc ponere , Atqui vitium originale omnibus hominibus inhærens est illud peccatum de quo loquutus est Apostolus versu immediate precedenti, vt supra probaui. Ergo peccatum illud quod fuit in mundo vsque ad legem est vitium originale omnibus inhærens , quod vitium omnibus, nisi condonetur per Christum , imputari non fateor modo , sed contendo etiam.
units.tr: But let us proceed. From the following verse, in which the Apostle proves what he had said, that sin entered the world and all men sinned, you draw some kind of argument. It rests on your earlier argument, which I have already refuted and overwhelmed with absurdities, and which you yourself keep undermining. For, says the Apostle, until the law sin was in the world. But sin is not imputed when there is no law. From this saying of the Apostle, you say, I argue as follows: That sin of which the Apostle speaks in the immediately preceding verse is the sin which was in the world until the law, as is clear from the sequence and construction of the words, especially from that particle "for", which is causal. I grant this, and I ask you to remember it, for it is true and very useful for overturning your view and confirming mine. You assume: but Adam's first sin was that sin of which the Apostle spoke in the immediately preceding verse, as we proved above. This proposition of yours therefore rests on your earlier argument, which you see was pierced by many weapons and destroyed by us in the previous chapter. So I may rightly put in its place this one: original sin, inhering in all men, is that sin of which the Apostle spoke in the immediately preceding verse, as I proved above. Therefore the sin which was in the world until the law is original sin, inhering in all, which sin, unless it is pardoned through Christ, I not only admit but also contend is imputed to all.

units.la: Verùm ego alia ratione hoc idem argumentum in te torquebo, quæ non nitetur superiori disputatione, sed eam suo proprio pondere augeat, eoque graui & momentoso. Peccatum illud,de quo loquitur Apoftolus versu immediate precedente, est peccatum illud quod fuit in Mundo vsque ad legem , vt rectè probasti. Atqui peccatum primum actuale Adami non est peccatum illud quod fuit in mundo vsque ad legem. Ergo peccatum primũ actuale Adami non est peccatum illud de quo loquitur Apostolus versu immediate precedenti, ac proinde non est peccatum illud quod in mundum, idest, te interprete in nos introiit, & quo omnes homines peccauerunt. Maiorem propositionem negare non potes ; est enim tua, & , fi negares, facile,vt tu rectè obferuasti, ex particula causali ;&, & textura disputationis Apostolicæ reuinci posses. Minor suapte luce manifesta est. Nonne enim perspicuum est peccatum primum actuale, quod actio fuit singularis, & numero vna, vix horam vnam durans, non fuisse in mundo toto illo tempore, quod ab eo peracto ad legem vsque Mosis fluxit, hoc est, non perdurasse in mundo spatio duorum millium & quingentorum annorum ? hoc certe conuenit vitio originali, quod tamdiu est in mundo, quandiu est genus humanum : sed non conuenit vni actioni indiuiduae & singulari, quae dum fit praeterit cum tempore, & vt non desiisset esse in mundo viuente Adamo cuius accidens quoddam fuit, nimirum actio, tamen eo extincto qui potuit eade mnumero in mundo, id est, in hominibus esse bis mille & quingentos annos? Noli confugere ad imputationem quam iam saepius confutaui: nam aliud est peccatum esse in mundo, aliud imputari mundo: hoc ordine naturae sequitur, illud precedit. Adde quod negare non potes, certe non debes, reuera toto illo tempore peccatum in mundo seu hominibus fuisse, immo regnasse obedientibus eius concupiscentijs hominibus.
units.tr: But I will turn this same argument against you by another line of reasoning, one that does not depend on the earlier dispute but increases its weight by its own force, and with greater and more telling effect. That sin of which the Apostle speaks in the immediately preceding verse is the sin which was in the world until the law, as you rightly proved. But Adam's first actual sin is not the sin which was in the world until the law. Therefore Adam's first actual sin is not that sin of which the Apostle speaks in the immediately preceding verse, and so it is not the sin which entered into the world, that is, by your interpretation into us, and in which all men sinned. You cannot deny the major premise, for it is your own; and if you did deny it, you could easily be refuted, as you rightly observed, from the causal particle and from the structure of the Apostolic argument. The minor premise is manifest in its own light. For is it not plain that the first actual sin, which was a single and singular act, numerically one, lasting scarcely an hour, was not in the world during all the time that flowed from its being committed until the law of Moses, that is, did not persist in the world for two thousand five hundred years? This certainly applies to original sin, which has been in the world as long as the human race exists. But it does not apply to one individual and singular act, which passes away with time as soon as it is done. Although it did not cease to exist while Adam lived, of whom it was a certain accident, namely the act, yet after he died, can it be the same in number in the world, that is, among men, for two thousand five hundred years? Do not take refuge in imputation, which I have already refuted many times, for it is one thing for sin to be in the world, another for it to be imputed to the world; the first comes before the second in the order of nature. Add that you cannot deny, and certainly ought not to deny, that in truth sin was in the world, or among men, during that whole time, and indeed reigned over men who obeyed its lusts.

units.la: GAR. His pedicis facile nos extricabimus. Etenim 1. His verbis Apostolum id confirmare, quod superiori versu dixerat in confesso est, vt iam audiimus. Dixerat autem, omnes in Adamo peccasse, quibus verbis imputationem inobedientia actualis Adae doceri, manifestis rationibus addiximus. Itaque ratio qua id confirmat & elucidat Apostolus hoc Ϗ. 13. non potest non esse imputationi fauorabilis.
units.tr: GAR. We will easily extricate ourselves from these snares. For, first, that the Apostle confirms by these words what he had said in the previous verse is admitted, as we have already heard. He had said that all sinned in Adam, and by clear reasons we have shown that these words teach the imputation of Adam's actual disobedience. Therefore the reason by which the Apostle confirms and clarifies this in verse 13 cannot fail to favour imputation.

units.la: PLAC. Nos vero quàm illae rationes nullae sint, nostris & refponfionibus & rationibus ita clarum fecisse arbitramur, vt nullus fit reliquus dubitandi locus.
units.tr: PLAC. But we think we have made it so clear, by our answers and arguments, how empty those reasons are, that no room for doubt remains.

units.la: GAR. 2. Argumento quod hic vsurpatur aduersus imputationem peccati Adae, non minus vti poterit aliquis aduersus imputationem actualis obedientia Christi. Nam si recte colligitur inobedientiam Adami non fuisse imputatam vsque ad legem, quia non perdurauit vsque ad legem: quidni etiam legitime colligatur, actualem Christi obedientiam, quae fe obedientem praestitit vsque ad mortem, nobis nequaquam imputari posse, quia non duraut vsque ad nostra tempora?
units.tr: GAR. Second, the argument used here against the imputation of Adam's sin could be used just as well by someone against the imputation of Christ's actual obedience. For if it is rightly concluded that Adam's disobedience was not imputed until the law, because it did not last until the law, why should it not likewise be validly concluded that Christ's actual obedience, which He rendered as obedient even unto death, cannot be imputed to us at all, because it does not last until our times?

units.la: P L A C. Non collegi inobedientiam Adami non fuisse imputatam vsque ad legem, quia non perdurauit vsque ad legem. Argumentum meum, quod est inuictum, Vir doctus in aliud transmutat ineptum & absurdum, quod possit facile & traducere, & refellere. Argumentor a verbis Apostoli. Quaeritur quod peccatum fit intelligendum, cum dicit Apostolus, per vnum hominem peccatum introiuit in mundum, & per peccatum mors. Item, eo quod omnes peccauerunt. Aio, illud idem intelligendum esse, quod significatur verbis feqq. Nam vsque ad legem peccatum erat in mundo. Negatne, an concedit Vir doctus? Concedere videtur. Subfumo igitur, Atqui verbis illis significatur peccatum habituale; id enim fuit in mundo hoc est, in hominibus vsque ad legem, nonne? Quid est in hoc meo argumento, quod reprehendi possit. Illud quaeso relege, vt est in manuscripto, & expende, lector aequissime, aut etiam vt recitatum est a Viro docto.
units.tr: PLAC. I did not conclude that Adam's disobedience was not imputed until the law because it did not last until the law. My argument, which is unconquered, my learned opponent turns into another, absurd and foolish one, which he can easily distort and refute. I argue from the words of the Apostle. The question is what sin is to be understood when the Apostle says: through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and again, because all have sinned. I say that the same sin is to be understood as is signified by the following words: For until the law sin was in the world. Does my learned opponent deny this, or concede it? He seems to concede it. I therefore assume: but by those words is signified habitual sin, for that was in the world, that is, among men, until the law, is it not so? What in this argument of mine can be reprehended? I ask you to reread it as it stands in the manuscript, and weigh it, most fair reader, or as it was recited by my learned opponent.

units.la: G.A R. 3. Sed objectio facile vtrinque soluetur, si distinctione vtamur. Nam in obedientia quidem Christi distinguendus est actus a fructu, & existentia ab imputatione. Etsi enim obedientia illa actualis non est amplius ratione actus & existentia; perdurat tamen, & perseuerabit vsque ad finem seculi ratione imputationis & fructus, quatenus vnius obedientia iusti constituuntur multi. Rom. v. 19. Sic in Adami peccato illo primo distingui par est actum a reatu: vt dicamus, actum quidem non duraffe vsque ad legem, cum momento transierit; sed reatum perseueraturum vsque ad mundi finem, quippe cum descendat in vnumquemque naturalium Adae posterorum: Reatus enim ex vno venit in omnes in condemnationem, Rom. v. 16.
units.tr: GAR. Third, the objection can easily be solved on both sides if we use a distinction. In Christ's obedience we must distinguish the act from its fruit, and existence from imputation. For although that actual obedience is no longer in existence as an act, it nevertheless endures, and will continue until the end of the age, in respect of imputation and fruit, inasmuch as by the obedience of one many are made righteous, Romans 5:19. So in Adam's first sin we must likewise distinguish the act from the guilt: we say that the act did not last until the law, since it passed in a moment, but the guilt will continue until the end of the world, since it descends upon each of Adam's natural posterity. For the guilt came from one upon all to condemnation, Romans 5:16.

units.la: P L A C. Cum igitur Apostolus loquatur de peccato quod vsque ad legem fuit in mundo, quid per illud peccatum intelligendum est? Actus? minime; fatetur enim Vir doctus illum non duraffe vsque ad legem, cum momento transierit. Reatus? Igitur per peccatum quod vsque ad legem durauit in mundo, solus reatus intelligendus est. Detur igitur nobis locus aliquis e NouoTestamento in quo ἡ ἁμαρτία pro solo reatu vsurpetur; imò detur saltem aliquis e veteri, vbi sic vsurpetur, cùm de Dei iudicio agitur. Cur enim hoc loco vox illa, tam frequens, acciperetur sensu prorsus inusitato? Hoc primum; Deinde quid fiet de corruptione, quæ verè peccatum est, & reuera fuit in omnibus hominibus vsque ad legem? Quid est cur peccati nomine hoc loco, pro Apostoli more, non debeat intelligi? Potuitne Vir doctus quicquam comminisci, quod magis causam Pighij, imò Pelagij, iuuaret? Quod si dicas, peccatum, quod vsque ad legem in mundo fuit, vna cum reatu corruptionem complecti, quem intelligas reatum quæram; Illum ne qui sequitur corruptionem; (peccatum, enim cùm fit, reatum ex se fundit.) an verò illum qui corruptionem antecedere dicitur, & cuius respectu corruptio non est peccatum, sed pœna peccati? Ille certè excludi non potest: intelligetur igitur corruptio duplici stipata reatu, altero antecedente, altero subsequente, quomodo peccatum accipi aliquando, nullo exemplo probari potest.
units.tr: PLAC. Since the Apostle therefore speaks of the sin which was in the world until the law, what is to be understood by that sin? The act? Not at all; for my learned opponent admits that it did not last until the law, since it passed in a moment. The guilt? Then by the sin which lasted in the world until the law only the guilt is to be understood. Let us therefore be shown some passage from the New Testament in which ἡ ἁμαρτία [the sin] is used of guilt alone; indeed, let at least some passage from the Old Testament be shown where it is so used when the judgment of God is in question. For why should that word, so frequent, be taken here in a sense wholly unusual? This is the first point. Second, what will become of the corruption, which truly is sin and really was in all men until the law? Why should sin not be understood in this place in the Apostle's manner? Could my learned opponent have devised anything that would more help the cause of Pighius, indeed of Pelagius?
