But if you say that the sin which was in the world until the law embraces both guilt and corruption, I ask which guilt you mean: that which follows corruption (for sin, when it exists, pours forth guilt from itself), or that which is said to precede corruption, and with respect to which corruption is not sin but the punishment of sin? The latter certainly cannot be excluded. Therefore corruption will be understood as surrounded by a double guilt, one preceding and one following. How sin can sometimes be taken in this way cannot be proved by any example.

units.la: Huic argumento accedat alterum hinc petitum quod Apostolus non simpliciter dicit peccatum fuisse in mundo, sed addit ἄχρι νόμου vsque ad legem. Intelligit autem procul dubio legem Moisis, quam versu 20. præterea ingressam vt abundaret peccatum docet. Itaque loco ἄχρι νόμου dixit versf. sequente μέχρι μωσέως vsque ad Mosem. Cur autem Apostolus illud vsurpauit vsque ad legem, vsque ad Mosem? Nempe, vt verbis vtar Caluini, dubitari poterat anne ante legem esset peccatum in mundo. Post legem fuisse minimè dubium erat. Tantum hærebat quæstio in tempore legem præcedente. Satis igitur fuit probare peccatum fuisse in mundo ab Adam vsque ad legem. Loquitur ergo Apostolus de peccato quod post legem ita patuit in mundo esse vt probatione non egeret. Atqui primum illud peccatum actuale Adami fuisse omnibus hominibus imputatum immediatè tàm post latam legem Mosis quàm ante obscurum fuit. De eo igitur Apostolus non loquitur. Lata lege vitium innatum sese multò quàm antea clarius prodidit, ac pessimorum fructuum copia redundauit. Sed imputatio primi peccati actualis tam latuit quàm antea, nullo legis præcepto, nulla comminatione. nulla sententia declarata. Immò illa imputatio cum lege Mosaica stare non potest, vt, Deo bene fauente, suo loco planum faciam. Frustrà igitur Apostolus illam temporis circunscriptionem adhibuisset vsque ad legem, si de eiusmodi peccato actuali vnius hominis omnibus imputato quæstio fuisset.
units.tr: To this argument add another, drawn from the fact that the Apostle does not simply say sin was in the world, but adds ἄχρι νόμου, until the law. He undoubtedly means the law of Moses, which in verse 20 he says entered in besides, that sin might abound. So in the following verse, in place of ἄχρι νόμου, he wrote μέχρι Μωϋσέως, until Moses. But why did the Apostle use until the law, until Moses? To put it in Calvin's words, it could be doubted whether sin existed in the world before the law. After the law it was by no means doubtful. The question hung only over the time before the law. It was therefore enough to prove that sin was in the world from Adam until the law. The Apostle speaks, then, of sin which after the law was so plainly in the world that it needed no proof. But that first actual sin of Adam, imputed to all men, was as obscure immediately after the Mosaic law was given as it was before. So the Apostle is not speaking of it. Once the law was given, innate vice revealed itself much more clearly than before, and an abundance of the worst fruits overflowed. But the imputation of the first actual sin remained as hidden as before: there was no precept of the law, no threat, no declared sentence. Indeed, that imputation cannot stand together with the Mosaic law, as I will make plain in its place, God willing. In vain, then, would the Apostle have added that limit of time, until the law, if the question had been about such an actual sin of one man imputed to all.

units.la: GAR. Non est verum peccati illius actualis Adæ imputationem, & ante, & post legem datam, obscuram; corruptionem autem innatam & ex Adamo propagatam, cognitam fuisse. Nam si de Gentibus loquaris extra Ecclesiam, & Dei fœdus agentibus, æquè fuit ignotum vtrumque: Si de fidelibus, & fœderis gratiaque diuinæ consortibus, æque notum vtrumque: Neque enim putandus est Paulus, cùm omnes docuit, in Adamo peccasse, nouum aliquod dogma procudisse, quod sub veteri Testam. fuerit omninò inauditum & incognitum. &c.
units.tr: GAR. It is not true that the imputation of that actual sin of Adam was obscure both before and after the giving of the law, while innate corruption propagated from Adam was known. For if you speak of the Gentiles outside the Church, who had no covenant with God, both were equally unknown; if of the faithful, and partakers of the covenant and of divine grace, both equally known. For Paul, when he taught that all sinned in Adam, is not to be thought to have devised some new dogma, which would have been wholly unheard of and unknown under the Old Testament, etc.

units.la: PLAC. Primùm vnde habet Vir doctus fidelibus veteris Testamenti æquè notum vtrumque fuisse? Ex Scriptura? Cur locum non protulit? Ex traditione non scripta? Non igitur sufficiebat illis Scriptura; Et vbi illa traditio? Ad Paulum fustra confugit, vtrùm enim illam imputationem antecedentem docuerit, nec-ne, nunc quidem inter nos controuertitur: docuisse non probauit Vir doctus; Ego non docuisse jam aliquot argumentis probaui, & in eo sum vt probem. Deinde si æquè ante ac post legem notum fuit, cur Apostolus dixit vsque ad legem? quorsum spectant illa verba? Certè si tam notum fuit ante legem, quàm post legem, peccatum fuisse in mundo, non magis opus fuit probare, peccatum ante quàm post legem in hominibus fuisse. Denique corruptionem innatam post legem, quam ante, notiorem fuisse, ex legis & testimonijs quibus demonstrari potest, & fine qui fuit patefacere peccatum, & experientiâ, ac diserto Apostoli testimonio, peccatum non cognoui nisi per Legem &c, ita clarum est, vt mirum fit cæcutiisse Virum doctum in tanta luce. Subiungit aliquid Augustini ex lib. 16. de Ciuit. Dei cap. 27. quasi ille agnouisset imputationem illam antecedentem, sed frustrà. Nam & malè interpretatus est verba Dei Gen. xvii. 14. peribit anima illius de populo meo, quoniam testamentum meum dissipauit, ea enim de masculo infante accepit nimis duriter, & videtur Vir doctus per testamentum illud non fœdus circuncifionis intelligere, sed lex lata Adamo: cùm tamen nec hæc vnquam fœdus aut testamentum dicatur, & manifestum fit illud debere intelligi. Deinde ideò vult Augustinus perire illum infantem, quia non est regenitus: opponitur autem regeneratio corruptioni inhærenti, quæ habitualis est testamenti Dei dissipatio ab Adamo propagata, non autem imputationi.
units.tr: PLAC. First, where does the learned man get the view that both were equally known to the faithful of the Old Testament? From Scripture? Then why did he not produce a passage? From unwritten tradition? Then Scripture did not suffice for them, and where is that tradition? He flees to Paul in vain. For whether Paul taught that antecedent imputation is now indeed being disputed between us; the learned man has not proved that he taught it, while I have already shown by several arguments that he did not, and I am working to prove it. Next, if it was equally known before and after the law, why did the Apostle say until the law? What do those words refer to? Certainly, if it was as well known before the law as after it that sin was in the world, there was no more need to prove that sin existed in men before the law than after it. Finally, that innate corruption was better known after the law than before can be shown from the law and the testimonies by which it can be demonstrated, from the law's purpose, which was to reveal sin, and from experience, and from the Apostle's plain testimony, I did not know sin except through the Law, etc. It is so clear that it is a wonder the learned man has been blinded in such a light. He adds something from Augustine, City of God book 16, chapter 27, as if Augustine had recognised that antecedent imputation, but in vain. For he also misinterpreted the words of God in Genesis 17:14, that soul shall perish from my people, because he has broken my covenant; he took these too harshly as said of an infant boy, and the learned man seems to understand by that covenant not the covenant of circumcision but the law given to Adam. Yet this is never called a covenant or testament, and it is plain that it must be understood otherwise. Next, Augustine wants that infant to perish because he is not regenerate. But regeneration is opposed to inherent corruption, which is the habitual breaking of God's covenant propagated from Adam, not to imputation.

units.la: Tertium argumentum mihi suppeditant quæ sequuntur apud Apostolum, peccatum non imputatur cum lex non est. Atqui lex non est secundum quam nobis impvtetur peccatum actuale Adami. Ergo non imputatur nobis. Probo minorem: nam maior est Apostoli. Si qua eiusmodi lex esset, ea esset singularis illa de non edendo fructu arboris scientiæ boni & mali. Atqui illa iam ab aliquot annorum millibus non est amplius, sublatâ é rerum natura illa arbore, aut nobis prorsus ignota, &, vt cæteras Dei creaturas, concessâ. Ergo lex non est secundum quam nobis imputetur peccatum actuale Adami: Ac vt lex illa primùm eiecto é paradiso homine, deinde ipso paradiso sublato, esse non desiisset, quemadmodum procul dubiò desiit, tamen eam vt legales cæremonias Dominus suo aduentu abrogasset. Fuit enim interdictum illud ceremonialis quædam lex libertatem arbitrij humani circa rem natura sua indifferentem circunscribens. Quemadmodum igitur non potest nobis imputari violatio legis ceremonialis, quia non sumus sub lege, sic non potest nobis imputari violatio legis olim latæ in paradiso terrestri, quoniam sub ea non sumus, ac iam olim abrogata est. Atque hæc tria argumenta versus 13. mihi dedit, tibi nullum.
units.tr: I have a third argument in what the Apostle says next: sin is not imputed when there is no law. But there is no law by which Adam's actual sin is imputed to us. Therefore it is not imputed to us. I prove the minor premise, since the major is the Apostle's. If there were such a law, it would be that singular one about not eating the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. But that law has not existed for some thousands of years, the tree having been removed from nature, or being utterly unknown to us, and granted, like the other creatures of God. Therefore there is no law by which Adam's actual sin is imputed to us. And even if that law did not cease to exist first when man was cast out of paradise, and then when paradise itself was taken away, as it certainly did cease, the Lord nonetheless abrogated it by his coming, as he abrogated the legal ceremonies. For that prohibition was a kind of ceremonial law, limiting the freedom of human choice about a thing indifferent by its nature. Just as the violation of the ceremonial law cannot be imputed to us because we are not under that law, so the violation of the law once given in the earthly paradise cannot be imputed to us, since we are not under it and it was abrogated long ago. These three arguments he has given me against verse 13; he has given you none.

units.la: GAR. Responsio in promptu est. Imprimis enim quod dicit Apostolus, non imputari peccatum vbi non est lex, omnino genuinum est illi, quod prius dixerat, Roman. iv. 15. Vbi non est lex, ibi nec transgressionem esse, quod Calvinus, ad quem provocat opponens, ita exponit, vt doceat, Apostolum, non loqui de simplici iustitiæ transgressione, à quâ nemo eximitur, sed transgressionem appellare, vbi animus edoctus quid Deo placeat, quidue displiceat, fines voce Dei sibi definitos sciens ac volens perrumpit &c.
units.tr: GAR. The answer is ready. First, what the Apostle says, that sin is not imputed where there is no law, is wholly genuine to him, since he had said earlier, Roman. iv. 15: where there is no law, there is no transgression. Calvin, to whom my opponent appeals, expounds this so as to teach that the Apostle is not speaking of a simple transgression of righteousness, from which no one is exempt, but calls it transgression where a mind, taught what pleases or displeases God, knowing and willing to break through the limits set for it by the voice of God, etc.

units.la: PLAC. Hæc responsio ad rem non est. Propositio enim illa, non imputatur peccatum vbi non est lex accipitur à Calvino cum restrictione ad legem scriptam, & hominum iudicium, Ego verò illam nunc quidem vsurpo absolutè & sine restrictione, quatenus, vniuersaliter accepta, vera est. Quid enim est in genere peccatum, nisi, ἀνομία, aberratio à lege, legis transgressio? & quid est iudiciaria imputatio, nisi actio iudicis iudicantis secundum legem, siue ea naturalis, siue positiua, voce aut scripto, lata fuerit?
units.tr: PLAC. This answer does not meet the point. For that proposition, sin is not imputed where there is no law, is taken by Calvin with a restriction to written law and human judgment. I, however, now use it absolutely and without restriction, insofar as, taken universally, it is true. For what is sin in general, except lawlessness [ἀνομία], a departure from the law, a transgression of the law? And what is judicial imputation, except the action of a judge judging according to law, whether that law was given by nature or by positive enactment, by word of mouth or in writing?

units.la: GAR. Deo non sunt leges externa constituta, secundum quas necessario ipsi agendum sit, præsertim in iudicijs occultis, Deus noster est in cœlo, quodcunque libuerit, facit, Psalmo cxv. ⁊. 3. Atqui imputatio peccati Adæ est actio Dei iudiciaria, vt dictum ab initio, in quâ occultum iudicium & admirabile consilium eius agnoscendum est. Ergo etiam sine lege positâ, potuit illud peccatum imputare. Sic ante legem à Mose traditam, imputatum est Canaani à Deo Chami patris peccatum, & peccati ab Abimelecho commissi poenas dedit familia. Quis legem externam proferat tunc existentem, secundum cuius regulas ea imputatio facta fuerit? PLAC. Primum de lege in genere agebatur, non in specie de lege externa. Aberrat igitur Vir doctus ab argumento cui respondere se profitetur. Deinde, non quaerebatur, an essent positae leges Deo secundum quas ipsi necessario agendum esset. Hoc plane alienum est a propósito. Tantum contendo omnem imputationem peccati judiciariam fieri secundum aliam legem. Quomodo enim actio iudiciaria esse potest, si non fit a iudice, & vt iudicem decet? Iudex autem cum peccatum imputat, cum damnat, cum punit, respectum habet ad legem, vt iustitiae, vt legi satisfiat. Alioqui causam non video, cur eiusmodi actio iudiciaria dicatur. Quod ait imputatum a Deo Canaani peccatum patris Chami fuisse, id si verum est, imputatio illa non fuit actio iudiciaria: itaque non pertinuit ad omnes Chami posteros; aut si iudiciaria fuit, ex omnibus filijs Chami autor vel particeps illius culpae solus Canaam fuit. Certe illius filius, etiam patre Chamo omisso, Noachus, cum maledictionem pronunciaret, nomen, & quidem ter, expressit. Quod §. xxviii. sequente subiungit Vir doctus legem secundum quam illa imputatio iudiciaria fit, esse primordialem illam legem, quo die comederis, morte morieris, mihi mirum videtur. Quo enim argumento ex verbis illis exsculpere manducationem illam omnibus Adami posteris imputari debere? Participes quidem sunt poenarum omnes homines, sed quia sunt participes peccati. Hoc enim propagato, quid est cur illae non propagatae fuissent? Vidit in posteris Adami Deus malitiam omnem inobedientiae Adami, corruptionem haereditariam, hoc est, incredulitatem, inimicitiam habitualem aduersus Deum, legi naturae repugnantiam &c, similiter malos similibus poenis addixit. Flagitat enim naturae lex, vt pariter malis, pariter male fit. Punimur ergo propter peccatum Adami, sed mediante corruptione propagata, a qua immediate sunt illae poenae.
units.tr: GAR. No external laws have been laid down for God, according to which he must necessarily act, especially in hidden judgments. Our God is in heaven; whatever he pleases, he does, Psalm 115:3. But the imputation of Adam's sin is a judicial action of God, as said at the beginning, in which his hidden judgment and wonderful counsel must be acknowledged. Therefore even without a law laid down, he could impute that sin. So before the law was delivered by Moses, the sin of Cham the father was imputed by God to Canaan, and the family paid the penalties of the sin committed by Abimelech. Who can produce an external law existing at that time, according to whose rules that imputation was made? PLAC. First, the discussion was about law in general, not about external law in particular. The learned man therefore strays from the argument he professes to answer. Next, the question was not whether there were laws laid down for God, according to which he must necessarily act. That is quite irrelevant to the point. I contend only that every judicial imputation of sin is made according to some other law. For how can an action be judicial if it is not done by a judge, and as befits a judge? A judge, when he imputes sin, when he condemns, when he punishes, has regard to the law, so that justice is satisfied and the law is satisfied. Otherwise I do not see why such an action should be called judicial. As for his claim that God imputed to Canaan the sin of his father Cham: if that is true, the imputation was not a judicial action, and so it did not extend to all the posterity of Cham; or if it was judicial, Canaan alone, of all the sons of Cham, was the author or sharer of that guilt. Certainly Noah, when he pronounced the curse, named Canaan's father, and indeed did so three times, even though Cham was passed over. That the learned man says in the following section, §. xxviii, that the law according to which that judicial imputation is made is that primordial law, on the day you eat, you shall surely die, seems strange to me. By what argument can it be drawn from those words that the eating must be imputed to all Adam's posterity? All men do indeed share in the punishments, but because they share in the sin. For once that was propagated, why should those punishments not also have been propagated? God saw in Adam's posterity all the malice of Adam's disobedience: hereditary corruption, that is, unbelief, habitual enmity against God, repugnance to the law of nature, and so on. Likewise he consigned the wicked to like punishments. For the law of nature requires that those who are alike in evil be treated alike. We are therefore punished on account of Adam's sin, but through the propagated corruption, from which those punishments come directly.

units.la: GAR. Cum poena proprie dicta, fit vindicatio peccati ex instituto legis a legitimo iudice posita: oportet sane poenas omnes peccati, qua in omnes homines ab Adamo prognatos haftenus incubuerunt, & ad finem vsque saeculorum incubitura sunt, secundum alicuius legis denunciationem esse a Deo inflictas, & porro infligen-
units.tr: GAR. Since punishment properly so called is the vindication of sin, instituted by a law laid down by a lawful judge, it must surely be that all the punishments of sin which have so far lain upon all men born from Adam, and will lie upon them until the end of the ages, have been inflicted by God according to the declaration of some law, and will continue to be inflicted

units.la: Dd d
units.tr: Dd d

units.la: das. Est autem mors, quae omnes iam ab initio mundi homines inuasit, poena peccati ex propria sua natura & conditione. Itaque ab initio omnibus infliftam fuisse consentaneum est, iuxta declarationem alicuius legis antea constitutae. At hac non alia innenietur, quam qua Adamo posita est, & obedientiam ab eo sub diserta mortis comminatione postulauit; cum ab Adamo vsque ad Mosem nulla legatur alia lex vniuersalis, quae poenas transgressoribus minetur ac denunciet.
units.tr: And death, which has seized all men from the beginning of the world, is a punishment of sin from its own nature and condition. It is therefore consistent that it was inflicted on all from the beginning, according to the declaration of some law previously established. But no such law will be found other than the one laid down for Adam, which demanded obedience from him under an explicit threat of death, since from Adam to Moses no other universal law is read that threatens and declares punishments for transgressors.

units.la: PLAC. Praeterquam quod haec ratio est superioris res- ponsionis Viri docti confutatio, laborat triplici falsitate.
units.tr: PLAC. Apart from the fact that this argument is a refutation of the learned man's earlier reply, it suffers from a threefold falsehood.

units.la: Primo falsum est poenas omnes peccati, quae in omnes homines ab Adamo prognatos hactenus incubuerunt, & ad finem vsque seculorum incubiturae sunt, fuisse vindicationem peccati ex instituto legis a legitimo iudice positae. Id patet ex eo quod pleraeque eiusmodi poenae non minus infliguntur pijs, pro quibus Christus plenissime iustitiae & legi satisfecit, quam impijs. Deinde falsum est omnes illas poenas secundum alicuius legis denunciationem esse a Deo inflictas. Quae enim legis denunciatio iubebat infligi Euae multiplicationem dolorum conceptus & partus, & Adamo hanc poenam, ut in sudore vultus sui vesceretur pane, & terra proferret illi spinas & tribulos &c? Tertio falsum est nullam aliam legem vniuersalem generi humano ab Adamo vsque ad Mosem positam fuisse, quae poenas transgressoribus minetur ac denunciet, praeter illam quae obedientiam ab Adamo sub diserta mortis comminatione postulauit. Nam ut omittam legem vniuersalem latam Gen. ix. de homicidio, & de sanguine, nonne ipsi Adamo & toti generi humano lata est lex naturae, quam Apostolus vrget Rom. i. & 2? Denique ut taceam alia vitia, quae in hoc Viri docti argumento deprehendi possunt, aberratio est a statu quaestionis. Non enim nego poenas peccati Adami pertinere ad eius posteros, quia nempe ad eos peccatum Adami pertinet. Communicauit enim nobiscum Adamus per generationem carnalem, peccatum suum, & per peccatum, poenas. Per vnum hominem peccatum ingressum est in mundum, & per peccatum mors. Fateor etiam propagatum in nos peccatum originale dignum esse mortis supplicio, cum sit vere peccatum repugnans legi naturæ, immò omni legi diuinæ. Hæc inter nos controuersa esse non debent. Sed quærebatur de imputatione primi Adæ peccati actualis, antecedente seu immediata, omnibus Adæ posteris, secundum quam legem fiat? Si fit secundum aliquam legem seu legis denunciationem, non potuit non fieri quin lex illa violaretur; cur igitur eam imputationem Vir doctus liberæ Dei voluntati ascribit passim? Si non fit secundum aliquam legem, quomodo est actio iudiciaria, & punitur sic imputatum illud peccatum, vt legi & iustitiæ satisfiat? Nulla enim lex vt sic imputaretur, & imputatum puniretur exigebat.
units.tr: First, it is false that all the punishments of sin which have so far lain upon all men born from Adam, and will lie upon them until the end of the ages, were the vindication of sin by a law instituted and laid down by a lawful judge. This is plain from the fact that most of these punishments are inflicted no less on the godly, for whom Christ has fully satisfied justice and the law, than on the wicked. Second, it is false that all those punishments were inflicted by God according to the declaration of some law. For what declaration of the law commanded that Eve should suffer the multiplication of the pains of conception and childbirth, or that Adam should receive this punishment, that he should eat bread in the sweat of his face, and that the earth should bring forth thorns and thistles for him, and so on? Third, it is false that no other universal law was laid down for the human race from Adam to Moses, one that threatens and declares punishments for transgressors, besides the law which demanded obedience from Adam under an explicit threat of death. For, to pass over the universal law given in Genesis 9 concerning murder and blood, was not the law of nature given to Adam himself and to the whole human race, the law which the Apostle presses in Romans 1 and 2? Finally, to say nothing of the other faults that can be detected in this learned man's argument, it is a departure from the state of the question. For I do not deny that the punishments of Adam's sin pertain to his posterity, because, of course, Adam's sin pertains to them. For Adam has communicated to us by carnal generation his sin, and through sin, its punishments. Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death. I also grant that the original sin propagated into us deserves the punishment of death, since it is truly a sin repugnant to the law of nature, indeed to every divine law. These points ought not to be in dispute between us. But the question was about the imputation of the first Adam's actual sin, antecedent or immediate, to all Adam's posterity: according to what law does this imputation take place? If it takes place according to some law or declaration of a law, it could not but happen that this law was violated; why then does the learned man ascribe that imputation everywhere to the free will of God? If it does not take place according to any law, how is it a judicial act, and how is that sin so imputed punished, so that justice is satisfied? For no law demanded that it be imputed in this way and that the imputed sin be punished.

units.la: GAR. Ad argumentationem, lex illa iam ab aliquot annorum millibus non est amplius &c, Resp. Nec Arborem extare amplius, neque adeo legem illam perdurare, quatenus respiciebat, etionali vsum fructus illius vetiti; sed vt tamen legis perseuerare, quatenus inobedientiæ illi Adami punitionem interminabatur, quæ non Adamo tantum incubitura, verum & in omnes posteros dimanatura esset. Sicut etiam Christus in arbore Crucis directus est, & ibi maledictionem pertulit, ex vi & prascripto legis illius à Deo constitutæ, maledictus qui pendet in ligno, vt docet Paulus Galat. iii. 13. Sublata est Crux, & lex illa non perdurat; & tamen obedientiæ à Christo in maledictione illa Cruce prestita meritum ad nos imputatione gratiosa dimanat, & ad mundi finem dimanaturum est.
units.tr: GAR. To the argument that that law is no longer in force after many thousands of years, the reply is: neither does the tree still stand, nor does that law endure insofar as it regarded the use of the fruit of that forbidden tree. But the law still endures insofar as it threatened punishment for Adam's disobedience, a punishment which was to fall not on Adam alone but to flow down upon all his posterity. Just so, Christ was also hanged on the tree of the cross, and there bore the curse, by the force and prescription of that law established by God: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree," as Paul teaches in Galatians 3:13. The cross has been removed, and that law does not endure; and yet the merit of the obedience rendered by Christ on that accursed cross flows down to us by gracious imputation, and will flow down until the end of the world.

units.la: PLAC. Nec distinctionem illam legis, nec verba, quibus concepta est, exagitabo, tantùm dicam vim legis vel in mandato, vel in comminatione spectari. Illam nec perseuerare, nec ad nos pertinere certum est. Hanc ad nos pertinere nec probat Vir doctus, nec quomodo probari possit intelligo. Nihil enim est in verbis comminationis, ex quo deduci possit, eam ad alios spectare, quàm ad quos spectat mandatum seu interdictum. Quo die comederis ex ea, morte morieris. Quis non videt ad eandem personam vtrumque illud verbum comederis & morieris spectare, non autem hoc ad omnes homines, illud ad solum Adamum? An est sensus, quo die tu & omnes posteri tui comederitis ex ea, tu & posteri tui moriemini? Non certe; Nemo enim posterorum Adami ex ea comedit. Num igitur est sensus, Quo die Tu comederis ex ea, eo die morte morieris tu & omnes posteri tui? Quis non videt verba, & omnes posteri tui, assui textui, nec magis contineri in verbo morieris, quàm in verbo comederis? Quod si eo die mortuus fuisset Adam, vt merebatur eius peccatum, morte corporis & æterna, quàm vnius fuisset peccatum, tam vnius fuisset punitio, & tamen satisfactum fuisset legis comminationi. Exemplum Christi, qui, vt vas noster, loco nostro punitus est, iam aliquoties ostendi nihil iuuare imputationem immediatam primæ Adami actualis inobedientiæ. Miror autem vnde habuerit Vir doctus, Christum in cruce maledictionem pertulisse, ex vi & præscripto legis illius à Deo constitutæ, maledictus qui pendet in ligno. Docet quidem Paulus Gal. 3. 13. Christum pro nobis factum esse maledictionem, idque probat quia pependit in ligno, & scriptum est, maledictus quisquis pendet in ligno. Sed non docet factum fuisse maledictionem ex vi & præscripto illius legis. Nulla enim lex fuit quæ iuberet Christum in crucem agi, nec fit nobis imputatio obedientiæ à Christo in maledictâ illa cruce præstitæ secundam illam legem, aut secundum legem, sed ex mera gratia, secundum promissiones Euangelij.
units.tr: PLAC. I will not attack either that distinction of the law or the words in which it is expressed; I will only say that the force of a law is to be considered either in its command or in its threat. It is certain that the former neither endures nor pertains to us. The learned man neither proves that the latter pertains to us, nor do I understand how it could be proved. For there is nothing in the words of the threat from which it could be deduced that it looks to others than those to whom the command or prohibition looks. On the day you eat of it, you shall surely die. Who does not see that both those words, you eat and you die, look to the same person, and not the one to all men and the other to Adam alone? Or is the sense: on the day that you and all your posterity eat of it, you and your posterity shall die? Certainly not; for none of Adam's posterity ate of it. Is the sense then: on the day that you eat of it, on that day you and all your posterity shall die by death? Who does not see that the words and all your posterity are added to the text, and are no more contained in the word you shall die than in the word you eat? But if Adam had died on that day, as his sin deserved, with death of body and eternal death, the punishment would have been only his, just as the sin was his alone, and the threat of the law would nonetheless have been satisfied. The example of Christ, who was punished in our place as our surety, I have already shown several times to be of no help for the immediate imputation of the first Adam's actual disobedience. But I wonder where the learned man got the idea that Christ bore the curse on the cross by the force and prescription of that law established by God, "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." Paul indeed teaches in Galatians 3:13 that Christ was made a curse for us, and he proves this because he hung on a tree, and it is written, "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." But he does not teach that he was made a curse by the force and prescription of that law. For there was no law which commanded that Christ be brought to the cross; nor is the obedience rendered by Christ on that accursed cross imputed to us according to that law, or by virtue of that law, but out of pure grace, according to the promises of the Gospel.

units.la: GAR. Deinde opponitur, etiamsi lex illa permaneret, tamen abolitam esse respectu nostri, vt legales ceremonias, cum fuerit lex ceremonialis, cuius violatio non potest nobis imputari, quia non sumus sub ea lege; sicut violatio legum ceremonialium non potest nobis imputari, quia sub ijs legibus non agimus. Resp. 1.
units.tr: GAR. Next it is objected that even if that law remained, it has nonetheless been abolished with respect to us, just as the ceremonial laws have been, since it was a ceremonial law, whose violation cannot be imputed to us, because we are not under that law; just as the violation of the ceremonial laws cannot be imputed to us, because we do not act under those laws. Reply 1.

units.la: Qui per Christum redempti sunt, & redemptionis illius participes, ij sane, vt à legibus ceremonialibus, ita etiam ab huius legis primaua rigore liberati sunt, adeoque ad eos non spectant comminationes illi addita. Sed tamen, vt natura prior est gratia (cum gratia naturam superueniat, eamque reformet & instauret) & vnusquisque concipitur prius esse homo, quàm sit fidelis aut Christianus: Ita etiam status naturæ, & lex siue fœdus Naturale prius est fœdere Gratia, adeoque vnusquisque consideratur prius sub fœdere naturali, quàm sub gratuito. Quare non debuit supponi, sed probari nos iam non esse sub ea lege. Nos verò contrario modo concludimus. Sumus naturaliter sub ea lege. Ergo eius violatio merito nobis imputatur.
units.tr: Those who have been redeemed through Christ, and are partakers of that redemption, are indeed freed both from the ceremonial laws and from the stringent rigour of this law, and so the threats added to it do not pertain to them. But nevertheless, just as nature is prior to grace (since grace comes upon nature, and reforms and restores it), and each man is conceived to be first a man before he is a believer or a Christian, so too the state of nature and the law or covenant of nature is prior to the covenant of grace, and so each man is considered first under the natural covenant, before he is considered under the gratuitous one. Therefore it ought not to have been assumed, but proved, that we are no longer under that law. We, on the contrary, conclude in the opposite way: we are naturally under that law; therefore its violation is rightly imputed to us.

units.la: PLAC. Itane fumus naturaliter sub illa lege? Tenemur igitur eam obseruare. Imò ne Adamus quidem naturaliter fuit sub illa lege. Non fuit enim naturaliter in paradiso, nec lex illa naturaliter lata est, sed supernaturaliter per verbum Dei. Sumus quidem sub lege naturæ, quam & habitu, & actu, nimis, proh dolor, violamus. Sed quis non videt legem illam ceremonialem, & positiuam, verbo Dei latam, liberi arbitrij libertatem circa rem natura sua moraliter nec bonam nec malam circumscribentem, hominique non quatenus homo fuit, aut mundi incola, sed tantum quatenus incola fuit paradisi, conuenientem, non fuisse legem naturæ? Putauitne Vir doctus nos naturaliter esse in paradiso terrestri? licere nobis vesci aliis arboribus paradisi? Ad legem autem naturæ quod attinet, obligat omnes & singulos ad obedientiam, sed pro sequemque, & quamdiu est. Ostendi mihi velim aliquid in ea lege, vnde probari possit, primum primi hominis peccatum actuale omnibus illius posteris imputari debere immediate.
units.tr: PLAC. So we are naturally under that law? Then we are bound to keep it. Indeed Adam himself was not naturally under that law. He was not naturally in paradise, and that law was not given by nature but supernaturally, through the word of God. We are indeed under the law of nature, which we violate, alas, both in our disposition and in our acts, far too much. But who does not see that the law of the garden, a ceremonial and positive law given by the word of God, which limited the freedom of the will concerning a thing that is by its nature morally neither good nor bad, belonged not to man as man or as an inhabitant of the world, but only to him as an inhabitant of paradise, and so was not a law of nature? Did the learned man think that we are naturally in the earthly paradise, and that we may eat from the other trees of paradise? As for the law of nature, it binds all and each to obedience, but for as long as, and as far as, we exist. I would like someone to show me anything in that law from which it could be proved that the first sin of the first man, an actual sin, must be imputed immediately to all his posterity.

units.la: GAR. Interim non est quod putemus legitimam esse illam argumentationem; legales ceremonias esse abrogatas; hanc esse legem ceremonialem; itaque abrogatam abolitamque. Nam legales ceremonia cum hic nominantur sine dubitatione intelliguntur statuta illa ritualia siue cerimonialia, quæ sunt à Deo Israeli constituta per manum Mosis, vnde & ceremonia Mosaica vulgò dicuntur. Eas Christi aduentu abrogatas fuisse nihil mirum est, cum vmbræ essent & figuræ, quarum veritas & corpus est in Christo, Coloss. 2. 17. Respiciebant enim omnes ad Christum, tanquam ad complementum suum. At ceremonia, quæ in hac primaua lege inerat, ad Christum non respiciebat, tanquam ad significatum suum. Vnde non consequitur, vt si ceremonia illa Israelitica antiquata sunt, concludendum sit eo ipso, etiam abrogatam esse legem illam primordialem, ita vt nullus sit amplius eius vsus, & ad homines nulla ratione spectet.
units.tr: GAR. Meanwhile there is no reason for us to think that this argument is sound: that the legal ceremonies have been abrogated and abolished; that this is a ceremonial law, and therefore abrogated and abolished. For when legal ceremonies are named here, there is no doubt that those ritual or ceremonial statutes are meant, which were established by God for Israel through the hand of Moses, whence they are commonly called the Mosaic ceremonies. It is no wonder that these were abrogated at the coming of Christ, since they were shadows and figures, whose truth and body is in Christ, Col. 2. 17. For they all looked to Christ as their fulfilment. But the ceremony that was contained in this first law did not look to Christ as its meaning. Hence it does not follow that, because those Israelite ceremonies have been done away with, it must be concluded by that very fact that the first law itself has been abrogated, so that it has no further use and bears on men in no way.

units.la: PLAC. Miseret me Viri docti tantum operæ ponentis, vt probet legem de arbore scientiæ boni & mali, quæ neque alibi fuit quàm in paradiso terrestri, & iam ab aliquot annorum millibus esse desiit in rerum natura, non esse antiquatam. Obseruat autem discrimen inter hanc primam legem ceremonialem, & Mosaicas ceremonias quod nullum est, & ad confirmandum potius quàm euertendum argumentum meum validum esse debet. Nam si ceremoniæ legales erant typi adumbrantes ea quæ Iesu Christi Euangelio reuelata sunt, idem de ceremonia illa antiqua confitendum est. Nonne enim & Adamus, & Eua, & paradisus terrestris, & arbor vitæ, quæ in eius erat medio, vmbræ fuerunt, quarum veritas & corpus est in Christo, aut saltem ad eius doctrinam pertinet? Quid est igitur, cur non idem sentiamus de arbore scientiæ boni & mali?
units.tr: PLAC. I pity the learned man, who takes such pains to prove that the law concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which existed nowhere but in the earthly paradise and has for some thousands of years ceased to exist in the nature of things, has not been abrogated. He notes a difference between this first ceremonial law and the Mosaic ceremonies, which is no difference at all, and it ought to confirm rather than overturn my argument, which is strong. For if the legal ceremonies were types foreshadowing what has been revealed in the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the same must be confessed of that ancient ceremony. For were not Adam, and Eve, and the earthly paradise, and the tree of life that stood in its midst, also shadows, whose truth and body is in Christ, or at least belongs to his teaching? What reason is there, then, why we should not think the same of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil?

units.la: Veniamus ad verf. 14. Sed regnauit mors etiam in eos qui non peccauerunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adam qui est typus futuri. Hic tu recte obseruas Apostolum causam inferre ex effectu, ac probare, omnes peccasse, quia mors regnauit in omnes; ac sic formas argumentum Apostoli, debuisti dicere, tuum. Apostoli enim longe abit a mente. Vbi mors regnat, nec est reatus ex peccato proprio actuali, ibi necessario est imputatio reatus primi peccati. At ante legem mors regnauit, etiam in eos in quibus non fuit reatus ex peccato proprio, nempe in paruulos. Ergo infantibus reatus primi peccati necessario fuit imputatus. Tu ipse vidisti negari posse maiorem: nam praeter reatum ex proprio peccato actuali, & quem frustra probare conaris ex peccato actuali Adæ imputato, est reatus ex proprio peccato innato, & vt ita loquar, habituali. Itaque obuiam is, Nec cauillandum est, inquis, reatum in illis esse a vitio inhærente, & a praua dispositione & corruptione. Nam unde fit, vt rei & corrupti nascantur, nisi quod in Adamo inclusi in illo peccarunt, vt dixit Apostolus, & peccatum illius ipsis imputatum fuit, vt sint rei & corrupti? Nondum enim voluntate propria peccarunt, nec cogitatione, nec verbis, nec actione. Inde sic concludo, Quicunque moriuntur sunt peccatores. Pueri in vtero matrum, aut recens nati moriuntur, vt constat experientia. Ergo pueri in utero matrum & recens nati sunt peccatores. Si sunt peccatores, ideo sunt, vel quod actu peccaverint, vel quod primum peccatum primi parentis ipsis imputetur. Tertium siquidem dari non potest, quod illos constituat peccatores. Nam peccator quis dicitur ob peccatum: nec vllum aliud peccatum potest imputari, nisi illud primum. &c. Quid est negare vitij inhærentis seu corruptionis innatæ reatum, si hoc non est? Putarem tibi ista excidisse imprudenti æstu disputationis abrepto in Pighiani erroris scopulum, nisi te viderem diu hærentem & versantem in hac re probanda, & inculcanda quod à te factum esse, pro eo quo te prosequor amore, vehementer doleo. Dubium autem mihi non est quin admonitus statim pedem ex hoc errore referas, quem tu ipse Cap. 2. huius tui tractatus refutasti, aut saltem refutare præ te tulisti. Ego certe multò pluribus refutarem si mihi, aut cum Pelagio, aut cum Pighio, aut cum Pontificio aliquo (quanquam Pontificij hoc vitium inhærens ante baptismum peccatum esse confitentur, sed post baptismum negant) negotium esset. Nunc cum sit mihi res tecum, fratre, symmista, religionem reformatam profitente & docente, te vel semel monuisse satis esse puto. Pauca tamen quædam respondebo tibi. Quæris unde fit ut rei & corrupti nascamur? Respondeo nos reos nasci, quoniam corrupti nascimur: nullum enim in infante, cum nascitur, reatum agnosco, cuius fundamentum & causa non sit corruptio inhærens. Si rursus quæras unde fiat, ut nascamur corrupti? Respondebo quia nascimur ex corrupto parente. Sic quærenti, cur homo natus sim? Respondeo, quia natus sum ex homine: cur vitiosus? Quia natus sum ex vitioso. Quod natum est ex carne caro est. De natur i peccato viti o tâ nonnisi natura nasci tur vitiosa, id est, peccatrix secundum quod ait Apostolus Paulus, qualis terreus, talis & terreni, & hoc quomodo nisi per feminis ip s inf ectionem ? Sed his ipsis quæstionibus iam supra pluribus satisfeci. Hæc corruptio, quæ & concupiscentia, & peccatum antonomastice, & peccatum peccans dici solet, quæque in irregenitis regnat, in regenitis habitat, primum est peccatum nostrum, scaturigo cæterorum. Ab ea primus noster reatus nascitur imputatâ nobis ad mortem. Moriuntur ergo infantes non ob peccatum alienum, videlicet actuale Adami sibi imputatum, sed ob proprium inhærens, insitum. At, inquis, infantes nondum voluntate propria peccarunt, nec cogitatione, nec verbis, nec actione. Ergo non habent proprium peccatum actuale quidem concedo, habituale vero pernego. Distingue igitur, si placet, inter peccatum quod est actio vel omissio actionis, & peccatum quod est ad ejusmodi actionem vel omissionem propensio, procliuitas, habitus. In peccato actuali, cum sit actio, ratio peccati pendet ex relatione quam habet ad suam causam efficientem, puta voluntatem. In peccato vero habituali, cum sit qualitas, ratio peccati pendet non ex ordine ad causam, sed ex relatione ad subjectum cui inhæret. Nam actio denominat causam, qualitas subjectum. Peccatum igitur infantium non est actio; nihildum enim mali egerunt, sed qualitas voluntati infixa, nimirum obliquitas, prauitas, malitia, cupiditas, ad peccata omnis generis procliuitas. Unde unde venerit illa malitia nihil ad rationem peccati habitualis interest, hoc ipso quod malitia, quod moralis immunditia, quod iniustitia est, ea nos facit formaliter malos, immundos, iniustos, qui cælo recipiamur indignos, qui detrudamur ad inferos dignos. Quod si in vtero materno, vel recens nati nihil mali egimus, id impedimento à natura posito, non autem voluntatis nostræ inclinationi adscribendum, quæ remoto illo naturæ impedimento non prius agit, quàm actione peccat. Vides præter peccatum actuale proprium & peccatum actuale primi parentis imputatum dari tertium, scilicet peccatum habituale ingenitum. Addis paulò pòst, pueros in vtero matrum aut recens natos nondum peccasse actu, idque probas hoc argumento : Qui non habent actum voluntatis non possunt peccare actu proprio. Sed pueri non habent actum voluntatis. Ergo pueri non possunt peccare actu proprio. Respondeo, si peccare actu significat admittere peccatum actuale, totum concedo. Testatur enim Apostolus pueros Esauum & Iacobum nihil boni maliue egisse in vtero materno. Sed id nihil te iuuat, me potius, qui nolo eos commisisse peccatum actuale multis seculis antequam vllam haberent voluntatem, nedum voluntatis actum. At si peccare actu significat habere actu peccatum habituale, aio pueros etiam in vtero materno actu peccare : quamvis enim non habeant malum actum voluntatis, tamen habent malam voluntatem habituali aduersus Dei legem rebellione altissimè imbutam. Addis, pueros legem nescire, & ideo transgredi non posse. Respondeo peccato actuali, Concedo : habituali, nego : vt enim in illis nondum est actualis cognitio legis, sic neque est actualis transgressio, sed hæret tamen lex peccati in membris eorum, immò in ipsa voluntate quoad actum, vt vulgò loquuntur, primum infixa penitus, atque natura sua repugnans legi naturæ. Hæc igitur repugnantia legi Dei & auersio habitualis ab eo quod præcipit, conuersio autem ad id quod vetat, solo Christi sanguine & spiritu medicabilis, est habitualis quædam & permanens transgressio, in pueris & adultis dormientibus: alioqui non æquum esset actu puniri qui actu nullo modo peccassent, nec puniri in propria persona qui in propria persona nullo vnquam modo peccassent.
units.tr: Let us come to verse 14. Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of the transgression of Adam, who is a type of the one to come. Here you rightly observe that the Apostle draws a conclusion from an effect and proves that all have sinned because death reigned over all; yet in setting out the Apostle's argument you should have called it yours, for you have quite missed the Apostle's meaning. Where death reigns, and there is no guilt from one's own actual sin, there the imputation of the guilt of the first sin must necessarily follow. But before the law death reigned, even over those in whom there was no guilt from their own sin, namely over infants. Therefore guilt for the first sin was necessarily imputed to infants. You yourself have seen that the major premise cannot be denied: for besides the guilt from one's own actual sin, and the guilt from Adam's actual sin imputed to us, which you vainly try to prove, there is the guilt from one's own inborn sin, which is, so to speak, habitual. So you object, Nor should it be quibbled, you say, that the guilt in them arises from an inherent vice, from a perverse disposition and corruption. For whence is it that they are born guilty and corrupt, unless because they sinned in Adam, being included in him, as the Apostle said, and his sin was imputed to them, so that they are guilty and corrupt? For they have not yet sinned by their own will, nor in thought, word, or deed. From this I conclude thus: Whoever dies is a sinner. Children in the wombs of their mothers, or newly born, die, as experience shows. Therefore children in the wombs of their mothers and newly born are sinners. If they are sinners, they are so either because they have sinned actually, or because the first sin of the first parent is imputed to them. For a third option cannot be given that would make them sinners. For a sinner is called such on account of sin, and no other sin can be imputed except that first one. And so on. What is it to deny the guilt of inherent vice or innate corruption, if this is not it? I would have thought these things had slipped from you in the heat of disputation, carried onto the reef of Pighius's error, if I did not see you lingering and labouring for a long time over proving and insisting on this point; and I am greatly grieved, out of the affection with which I follow you, that you have done so. Yet I have no doubt that, once warned, you will at once withdraw your foot from this error, which you yourself refuted in chapter 2 of this your treatise, or at least professed to refute. For my part I would refute it at much greater length if I had to deal with Pelagius, or Pighius, or some Papist (although the Papists confess that this inherent vice is sin before baptism, but deny it after baptism). But since my dispute is with you, a brother and fellow communicant professing and teaching the Reformed religion, I think it is enough to have warned you once. Still, I will answer you briefly. You ask, whence is it that we are born guilty and corrupt? I answer that we are born guilty because we are born corrupt, for I acknowledge no guilt in an infant at birth whose foundation and cause is not inherent corruption. If you ask again, whence is it that we are born corrupt? I answer, because we are born of a corrupt parent. So if someone asks, why was I born a man? I answer, because I was born of a man; why am I vicious? Because I was born of a vicious parent. What is born of the flesh is flesh. Thus nature born of sin is only ever born vicious, that is, sinful, according as the Apostle Paul says, as is the earthly, so are they also that are earthly; and how is this, except through the seed itself? But I have already satisfied these very questions above at length. This corruption, which is also called concupiscence, and sin in the strict sense, and sin that sins, which reigns in the unregenerate and dwells in the regenerate, is our first sin, the spring of all the rest. From it our first guilt arises, imputed to us unto death. Infants therefore die not on account of another's sin, namely Adam's actual sin imputed to them, but on account of their own inherent, implanted sin. But, you say, infants have not yet sinned by their own will, nor in thought, word, or deed. Therefore they have no actual sin of their own: I grant that, but deny that they have no habitual sin. Distinguish, then, if you please, between sin which is an act or an omission of an act, and sin which is a propensity, proneness, or habit toward such an act or omission. In actual sin, since it is an act, the nature of the sin depends on its relation to its efficient cause, namely the will. In habitual sin, since it is a quality, the nature of the sin depends not on its relation to a cause but on its relation to the subject in which it inheres. For an act denominates its cause, a quality its subject. So the sin of infants is not an act, for they have done nothing evil yet; it is a quality fixed in the will, namely crookedness, perversity, malice, lust, a proneness to sins of every kind. Whence that malice came makes no difference to the nature of habitual sin, for the very fact that it is malice, moral uncleanness, and injustice makes us formally evil, unclean, and unjust, unworthy to be received into heaven, worthy to be cast down into hell. But if we have done nothing evil in the mother's womb or when newly born, this must be ascribed to an impediment placed by nature, not to the inclination of our will, which, once that impediment of nature is removed, does not act before it sins in act. You see that, besides actual sin of one's own and the actual sin of the first parent imputed to us, there is a third, namely innate habitual sin. You add a little later that children in the wombs of their mothers, or newly born, have not yet sinned in act, and you prove this by this argument: Those who do not have an act of will cannot sin by their own actual act. But children do not have an act of will. Therefore children cannot sin by their own actual act. I answer: if to sin in act means to commit actual sin, I grant the whole. For the Apostle testifies that Esau and Jacob, while in their mother's womb, had done neither good nor evil. But this does nothing for you, and rather helps me, who am unwilling that they committed actual sin many centuries before they had any will at all, let alone an act of will. But if to sin in act means to have habitual sin in act, I say that children sin in act even in the mother's womb: for although they have no evil act of the will, they nevertheless have an evil will, deeply imbued from the outset with rebellion against God's law. You add, children do not know the law, and therefore cannot transgress it. I answer: I grant this as regards actual sin, but deny it as regards habitual sin. For just as there is no actual knowledge of the law in them, so there is no actual transgression; yet the law of sin clings to their members, indeed is fixed deep within the very will as regards its act, as they commonly say, and is by its nature opposed to the law of nature. This opposition to the law of God, and this habitual aversion from what he commands and turning toward what he forbids, which can be healed only by the blood and Spirit of Christ, is a certain habitual and abiding transgression, present in children and in adults while they sleep. Otherwise it would not be just that those should be punished for an act who in no way sinned in act, nor that those should be punished in their own person who never in any way sinned in their own person.

units.la: Hinc aliquot argumenta mihi nascuntur. Primum sic habet. Probat Apostolus omnes homines peccasse siue peccatum esse in mundo, argumento ducto à regno mortis in omnes homines. Atqui eo argumento non potuit probare omnibus hominibus imputari peccatum actuale Adami, nisi negato reatu vitij inhærentis. Hunc autem reatum noluit negare. Noluit igitur eo argumento probare imputationem peccati actualis Adami omnibus hominibus.
units.tr: Several arguments arise for me from this. The first runs as follows. The Apostle proves that all men have sinned, or that sin is in the world, by an argument drawn from the reign of death over all men. But by that argument he could not have proved that Adam's actual sin is imputed immediately to all men, unless he had denied the guilt of inherent vice. Yet he was unwilling to deny that guilt. He was therefore unwilling to prove the imputation of Adam's actual sin to all men by that argument.

units.la: GAR. Resp. 1. non probat Apostolus eo argumento omnes peccasse, sed tantum eos qui ab Adam vsque ad Mosem ante legem datam vixerunt, vt inde concludat, absurdum videri non debere, si iis, qui post legem datam vixerunt, Adæ peccatum imputetur, vt in loci illius analysi diximus superiori cap. n. 18. Quanquam quod ad rem ipsam, non nego eo argumento recte probari posse, omnes omnino homines, nullo quoquam excepto naturalium Adæ posterorum, peccauisse.
units.tr: GAR. Reply 1: the Apostle does not prove by that argument that all have sinned, but only those who lived from Adam to Moses, before the law was given. From this he concludes that it should not seem absurd if Adam's sin is imputed to those who lived after the law was given, as I said in the analysis of that passage above, chapter n. 18. Yet as to the matter itself, I do not deny that by that argument it can rightly be proved that absolutely all men, without any exception among Adam's natural posterity, have sinned.

units.la: PLAC. Quid ad infirmandum argumentum meum facit hæc responsio? Nam siue probet Apostolus eo argumento omnes peccasse, siue probet tantùm eos peccasse, qui ab Adam vsque ad Mosem vixerunt, ad argumenti mei robur nihil prorsus interest. Quanquam manifestum est, hoc non probare Apostolum, nisi ut illud probet: Et vero consilium esse Apoli hoc vniuersè probare, ipse Vir doctus, loco quem citat, affirmauerat. Dixerat nempe, inquit, Apostolus, omnes in Adāmo peccasse, nullo quoquam excepto, eorum qui sunt ab ipso naturaliter prognati. Illud ergo verf. 13. & 14. probat hoc modo. &c.
units.tr: PLAC. What does this reply do to weaken my argument? For whether the Apostle proves by that argument that all have sinned, or only proves that those who lived from Adam to Moses have sinned, makes no difference at all to the strength of my argument. Yet it is clear that the Apostle does not prove this except in order to prove that. And indeed the learned man himself, in the passage he cites, had asserted that this was the Apostle's purpose in general. For he had said, he says, that the Apostle said that all sinned in Adam, with no exception of those who are naturally born of him. Therefore he proves that point in verses 13 and 14 in this way, etc.

units.la: G A R. 2. Nego argumento Apostolico non posse probari imputationem, nisi negata corruptione, vel reatu vitio inhaerentis. Imo cum reatus ex peccato Adae, & ex vitio nobis inhaerente, non sint duo reatus distincti, sed unus idemque reatus ex utroque consurgens, quicunque probat nos reos esse propter peccatum Adae, eadem ratione probat nos esse reos ex vitio inhaerente.
units.tr: GAR. 2. I deny that by the Apostle's argument the imputation cannot be proved unless the corruption or guilt of inherent vice is denied. Indeed, since the guilt arising from Adam's sin and the guilt arising from the vice inherent in us are not two distinct guilts, but one and the same guilt arising from both, whoever proves that we are guilty because of Adam's sin proves by the same reasoning that we are guilty because of inherent vice.

units.la: P L A C. Si imputationem intelligit consequentem seu mediatam, recte negat; sed aberrat a ttatu quaestionis. Agitur enim in argumento de sola imputatione immediata. Itaque cum subjicit ex peccato Adae & ex vitio nobis inhaerente non duos reatus distinctos, sed unum eundemque reatum consurgere, causam meam iuuat: mea enim haec est sententia. Vnus idemque reatus ex utroque consurgit, nimirum ex vitio nobis inhaerente immediate, ex peccato Adae actuali mediate. Haec est imputatio mediata seu consequens corruptionem, quam vrgeo. Nam posita imputatione antecedente seu immediata, necessario sunt duo reatus distincti: nam alter est immediate ex peccato Adae actuali imputato, alter ex vitio nobis inhaerente; ille antecedit corruptionem, hic sequitur, illius respectu corruptio est poena proprie dicta inflicta propter reatum imputati peccati, ut puniatur seu vindicetur, huius vero respectu corruptio nullo modo est poena, sed peccatum tantum; denique corruptio est illius reatus effectum, huius vero fundamentum & causa. Sunt igitur admodum distincti.
units.tr: PLAC. If he understands imputation as consequent or mediate, he rightly denies it, but he strays from the state of the question. For the argument concerns only immediate imputation. Therefore, when he adds that from Adam's sin and from the vice inherent in us there arises not two distinct guilts but one and the same guilt, he helps my cause. For this is my view: one and the same guilt arises from both, namely immediately from the vice inherent in us, and mediately from Adam's actual sin. This is the mediate imputation, or imputation consequent upon corruption, which I press. For once immediate or antecedent imputation is posited, there are necessarily two distinct guilts. For the one arises immediately from Adam's actual sin imputed, the other from the vice inherent in us. The one precedes corruption, the other follows it. With respect to the former, corruption is punishment properly so called, inflicted on account of the guilt of the imputed sin, so that it may be punished or avenged. With respect to the latter, corruption is in no way punishment but only sin. Finally, corruption is the effect of the former guilt but the foundation and cause of the latter. They are therefore quite distinct.

units.la: G A R. 3. In causis sociis, ex vnius positione non est inferenda alterius negatio. At imputatio & corruptio sunt causae sociae & coniunctae reatus illius nostri, quo morti subjicimur. Ergo ex positione reatus prouenientis ab imputatione, non est negandus reatus ex corruptione, neque putandus Apostolus negasse.
units.tr: GAR. 3. In joint causes, the denial of one cannot be inferred from the positing of the other. But imputation and corruption are joint and conjoined causes of that guilt of ours by which we are subjected to death. Therefore, from the positing of the guilt arising from imputation, the guilt arising from corruption is not to be denied, nor is the Apostle to be thought to have denied it.

units.la: P L A C. Quis non videt hanc argumentationem Viri docti, si imputationem intelligit immediatam, nihil nisi petitionem esse πὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ? Sumit enim in minore idipsum quod internos controuertitur. Sin imputationem mediatam intelligit, præterquam quod aberrat à statu quæstionis, falsum est corruptionem & peccatum actuale Adami causas esse socias reatus nostri: hic enim, vt dixi, immediatè est à corruptione, & mediatè, hoc est, mediante corruptione à peccato Adæ actuali. Causarum sociarum altera sine altera non sufficit producendo effectui; sed corruptio sufficit damnando generi humano teste Confessione fidei Art. xi. Peccatum etiam actuale imputatum immediatè, si fides habetur illius imputationis auctoribus, vel defensoribus, meretur corruptionem seu mortem animæ, mortem corporis, & æternam. Non sunt igitur causæ partiales seu sociæ, sed, vt ita loquar, totales. Sed præterea, à positione vnius non inuli negationem alterius, sed tantum affirmaui, eo argumento, quo vtitur Apostolus, ducto à regno mortis, non potuisse probari, omnibus hominibus imputari, nimirum immediatè, peccatum actuale Adami, nisi negato reatu vitij inhærentis. Experiatur qui volet, num ex illo argumento id probari possit, & comperiet verum esse quod dixi. Hoc quia hic Vir doctus non facit, nec facere tentat, à recta & solida disputandi ratione, vt alibi solet, discedit.
units.tr: PLAC. Who does not see that this argument of the learned man, if he understands imputation as immediate, is nothing but a begging of the question (petitio principii)? For in the minor premise he assumes the very thing that is disputed between us. But if he understands mediate imputation, then, besides straying from the state of the question, it is false that corruption and Adam's actual sin are joint causes of our guilt. For this guilt, as I said, comes immediately from corruption, and mediately, that is, through corruption, from Adam's actual sin. Of joint causes, one without the other does not suffice to produce the effect. But corruption suffices to condemn the human race, as the Confession of Faith, Article xi, testifies. Moreover, actual sin imputed immediately, if credence is given to its advocates or defenders, merits corruption or death of the soul, death of the body, and eternal death. They are therefore not partial or joint causes but, so to speak, total ones. But besides, from the positing of one I did not infer the denial of the other. I only affirmed that by that argument which the Apostle uses, drawn from the reign of death, it could not be proved that Adam's actual sin is imputed to all men, namely immediately, unless the guilt of inherent vice is denied. Let whoever wishes try whether this can be proved from that argument, and he will find that what I said is true. Because this learned man does not do so, nor attempts to do so, he departs, as he usually does elsewhere, from sound and right method of disputation.

units.la: Secundum est eiusmodi. Vbi mors regnat, ibi regnat peccatum ad mortem. In omnibus hominibus mors regnat. Ergo in omnibus hominibus regnat peccatum ad mortem. vbi autem peccatum regnat, ibi reuera est, non autem imputatiue tantum. Cum enim secundum Apostolum mors & peccatum reciprocentur: dixit enim versu antecedente, mortem ad omnes pertransiisse, quia omnes peccauerunt, & rursus, peccatum fuisse in mundo, id est, in omnibus hominibus, quia mors regnauit in omnes homines; Certè vbi verè, & reapse, mors est, ibi etiam verè & reapse est peccatum, & vbi est regnum mortis ibi etiam est regnum peccati. Absurdum autem, peccatum vbi verè & reipsa regnat, ibi non esse nisi imputatione. Quod si regnum mortis in omnes homines testatur in omnibus esse & regnare peccatum, Nullum autem sit in omnibus praeter vitium innatum. Fatendum est de eo intelligendam esse ratiocinationem Apostoli, ac proinde ea non doceri imputationem primi peccati actualis immediatam omnibus hominibus.
units.tr: The second argument is of this kind. Where death reigns, there sin reigns unto death. Death reigns over all men. Therefore sin reigns over all men unto death. But where sin reigns, there it truly is, and not merely by imputation. For since, according to the Apostle, death and sin are reciprocal (for he said in the preceding verse that death passed upon all men because all have sinned, and again that sin was in the world, that is, in all men, because death reigned over all men), certainly where death truly and really is, there sin also truly and really is, and where the reign of death is, there also is the reign of sin. But it is absurd that where sin truly and really reigns, it should be there only by imputation. If therefore the reign of death over all men bears witness that sin is in all and reigns in all, and there is nothing in all men except innate vice, it must be admitted that the Apostle's reasoning is to be understood of that, and consequently that it does not teach the immediate imputation of the first actual sin to all men.

units.la: G A R. Ratiocinatio hæc nos ne longâ quidem manu ferit.Vbi peccatum regnat, inquiunt, ibi revera est, non tantùm imputatiuè. Agnosco. Sed quid hoc aduersus me? Argumentabor enim. Vbi peccatum revera est, non tantùm imputatiuè, ibi etiam imputatiuè esse agnoscitur. At vos fatemini & docetis, vbi peccatum regnat, ibi esse revera, & non tantùm imputatiuè. Ergò & ibi esse imputatiuè agnoscitis. Quid igitur vobis ita displicet imputatio peccati?
units.tr: GAR. This reasoning does not even get a hand's breadth from us. Where sin reigns, they say, there it truly is, not merely by imputation. I acknowledge it. But what is this against me? For I will argue thus: where sin truly is, not merely by imputation, there it is also acknowledged to be by imputation. But you confess and teach that where sin reigns, there it truly is and not merely by imputation. Therefore you also acknowledge that there it is by imputation. Why then does the imputation of sin displease you so much?

units.la: P L A C. Hæc responsio & argumentatio nititur voce tantùm, non tantùm imputatiuè: quæ vox neque in Manuscripto extat, neque in verbis meis, vt sunt à Viro dosto recitata. Nempe illam de suo addidit, vt posset sic respondere, & argumentari. Quanquam etiamsi vsus fuissem illa voce tantùm, id nihil mihi officeret. Quod enim in nobis revera est peccatum, id in nobis non est imputatiuè vllo modo: quamuis enim nobis imputari possit, & nisi condonetur, imputetur, tamen non est in nobis per imputationem, sed per veram inhærentiam: & vice versa, peccatum quod dicitur nostrum non esse nisi per imputationem, in nobis revera non est. Si ergo loquitur Apostolus de peccato quod non est in nobis tantùm imputatiuè, sed revera, ceriè non loquitur de peccato actuali Adæ: hoc enim, si dici potest esse in nobis, est in nobis tantùm imputatiuè: sed de peccato propagato, quod imputatur quidem nobis; sed non tantùm nobis imputatur, verùm reuera inhæret in nobis. Nobis porrò non displicet imputatio peccati inhærentis, nec imputatio peccati actualis primi mediata, solam immediatam, seu antecedentem oppugnamus.
units.tr: PLAC. This reply and argument rests on the word merely, not merely by imputation. That word is found neither in my manuscript nor in my words as the learned man has quoted them. He added it on his own, so that he could reply and argue in this way. Yet even if I had used the word merely, it would have done me no harm. For what is truly sin in us is in us not by imputation in any way at all. For although it can be imputed to us, and unless it is pardoned it is imputed, nevertheless it is not in us by imputation but by true inherence. And conversely, sin which is said to be ours only by imputation is not truly in us at all. If therefore the Apostle is speaking of sin which is in us not merely by imputation but truly, he is certainly not speaking of Adam's actual sin. For that, if it can be said to be in us at all, is in us merely by imputation. He is speaking of propagated sin, which is indeed imputed to us, but is not merely imputed to us, rather truly inheres in us. Moreover, the imputation of inherent sin does not displease us, nor the mediate imputation of the first actual sin; we oppose only the immediate or antecedent imputation alone.

units.la: G A R. 2. Quod subiicitur, hunc, nisi fallor, sensum habet. Apostolus loquitur de peccato, quod in omnibus regnat. At non est aliud peccatum, quod in omnibus regnet, prater vitium & corruptionem innatam. Ergo de ea sola loquitur Apostolus. Cujus argumenti partem illam non supponere, sed probare debuerunt, videlicet, non esse aliud peccatum, quod in omnibus regnet, praeter corruptionem hereditariam. Nam potest ea haud immerito negari. Cum enim peccatum regnare dicatur, vbi vim suam exercet, & hominem mortis reum efficit: peccatum autem illud primum & actuale Adami vim suam in omnes homines exerceat, & eos morti addicat, quemadmodum supra fatebantur, cum dicerent Apostolum verbis illis ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον docere, quod mirum videri non debeat in uno unius hominis peccato tantam vim inesse, ut totam hominum multitudinem morti addiceret, cap. 8. n. 17. consequitur, ut recte dici possit, illud actuale peccatum regnare in omnibus.
units.tr: G A R. 2. What follows, unless I am mistaken, has this sense. The Apostle speaks of the sin that reigns in all. But there is no other sin that reigns in all except innate vice and corruption. Therefore the Apostle speaks of that alone. They ought to have proved this part of the argument, not assumed it, namely that there is no other sin that reigns in all besides hereditary corruption. For this can fairly be denied. When sin is said to reign wherever it exercises its power and makes a man liable to death, and that first and actual sin of Adam exercises its power over all men and hands them over to death, as you admitted above when you said that the Apostle teaches this by the words ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον [because all sinned], then it ought not to seem strange that so great a power lies in the one sin of one man, that it hands over the whole multitude of men to death (chap. 8, n. 17). It follows that it can rightly be said that this actual sin reigns in all.

units.la: PLAC. Sic etiam argumentatus sum, Apostolus loquitur de peccato quod in omnibus regnat. Atqui peccatum ubi regnat, ibi revera est. Ergo loquitur de peccato quod est revera in omnibus hominibus. Illud autem est corruptio inhaerens, non autem primum peccatum actuale Adami. Item sic, Apostolus loquitur de peccato in omnibus regnante. Atqui Corruptio est peccatum in omnibus regnans. Loquitur igitur de Corruptione. Iam si loquitur de Corruptione, quo argumento probabitur eum loqui de peccato actuali Adami omnibus immediate imputato? His argumentis nihil respondet. Cui autem respondet, id facile tueor. Primum enim illud constat, in omnibus regnare corruptionem, antequam regenerentur: regnare vero peccatum actuale Adami immediate, seu per imputationem immediatam, id nunc non constat, sed illud ipsum est, quod inter nos controvertitur. Hactenus igitur melior est causa mea quam eorum qui me oppugnant. Supponunt enim, quod probari prius debuit, quam supponi, nec tamen aut probatum ab eis est, aut probari potest. Deinde si peccatum regnare dicitur, vbi vim suam exercet, & hominem mortis reum efficit sola imputatione, quamvis revera non ibi fit, potuit dici peccatum regnare in Domino nostro Iesu Christo mortem ob peccata nostra perpessö. Id quod tamen quominus dici possit pia refugit conscientia. Praeterea cum Deus sit autor imputationis, & imputatio fit causa cur peccatum illud actuale eo modo regnet, Deus erit autor regni peccati: qua à cogitatione etiam conscientia abhorret. Denique cum argumentetur Apostolus à regno mortis ad regnum peccati, & per mortem intelligat, non mortem Adami, sed mortem qua quisque reipsa moritur, consentaneum est, vt peccatum intel-ligat, non peccatum Adami, sed quod reuera in vnoquoque homine est, viuit, regnat, donec per Christum damnetur ac destruatur. Peccatum actuale Adami ex nostra sententia non imputatur, nec totam hominum multitudinem morti addicit, nisi mediante Corruptione. Itaque nobis nullo modo contradicimus.
units.tr: PLAC. I have argued in this way too. The Apostle speaks of sin that reigns in all. But where sin reigns, there it truly is. Therefore he speaks of sin that is truly in all men. That, however, is inherent corruption, not the first actual sin of Adam. Likewise: the Apostle speaks of sin reigning in all. But corruption is the sin reigning in all. Therefore he speaks of corruption. Now if he speaks of corruption, by what argument will it be proved that he speaks of Adam's actual sin imputed immediately to all? My opponents make no reply to these arguments. To the reply that they do make, I can easily hold my ground. For this first point is established, that corruption reigns in all before they are regenerated. But that Adam's actual sin reigns immediately, or through immediate imputation, is not established now; that is precisely what is in dispute between us. So far, then, my cause is better than theirs who oppose me. For they assume what ought to have been proved before it was assumed, and yet it has not been proved by them, nor can it be. Next, if sin is said to reign wherever it exercises its power and makes a man liable to death, by imputation alone, though it is not truly there, then it could be said that sin reigned in our Lord Jesus Christ when he suffered death for our sins. Yet a pious conscience shrinks from saying this. Moreover, since God is the author of imputation, and imputation is the cause why that actual sin reigns in this way, God would be the author of the reign of sin, a thought from which conscience also recoils. Finally, since the Apostle argues from the reign of death to the reign of sin, and by death he means not the death of Adam but the death by which each person actually dies, it follows that by sin he means not the sin of Adam but the sin that is truly in each man, lives, reigns, until it is condemned and destroyed through Christ. On our view, Adam's actual sin is not imputed, nor does it hand the whole multitude of men over to death, except through corruption. Therefore we in no way contradict you.

units.la: Tertium peto ex illis verbis, etiam in eos qui non peccauerunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adam. Quis enim putet Apostolum sic locuturum fuisse, si in eo fuisset vt doceret, omnes homines illud ipsum peccatum actuale, illam ipsammet transgressionem Adami peccasse? Quomodo enim diceret quosdam homines non peccasse quemadmodum ille peccauit, si doceret omnes homines illud ipsum, quod peccauit, peccasse?
units.tr: A third point I seek from those words, even over those who did not sin after the likeness of the transgression of Adam. For who would think the Apostle would have spoken thus if his purpose had been to teach that all men sinned that very sin, that very transgression of Adam? For how could he say that some men did not sin as Adam sinned, if he were teaching that all men sinned the very thing that Adam sinned?

units.la: : G A R. Argumentum ita est. Qui non peccárunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adæ, illi non peccarunt peccatum actuale Adami. At Apostolus dicit esse quosdam homines qui non peccarunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adæ. Ergo significat aliquos esse, qui non peccárunt peccatum actuale Adami. Sed nihil difficile est. Nam qui sunt, qui dicuntur non peccasse ad similitudinem transgressionis Adæ? qui peccatum actuale in propria persona non commiserunt, sicut commisit Adam, quales sunt infantes: qui proinde non possunt dici proprie & personaliter peccatum illud patrasse, quod patrauit Adam. Quod quidem nemo, non dicam de infantibus, sed ne quidem de adultis hactenus somniauit. Sed quibus rationibus probabitur, eos qui personaliter peccatum Adæ non commiserunt, sive infantes, sive adultos, non haberi tamen apud Deum illius actualis peccati reos?
units.tr: G A R. The argument runs thus. Those who did not sin after the likeness of Adam's transgression did not commit Adam's actual sin. But the Apostle says that there are some men who did not sin after the likeness of Adam's transgression. Therefore he means that there are some who did not commit Adam's actual sin. But this is not hard to see. Who are those who are said not to have sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression? Those who did not commit actual sin in their own person, as Adam did, such as infants. Therefore they cannot properly and personally be said to have committed that sin which Adam committed. No one, I will not say about infants, but not even about adults, has hitherto dreamed of this. But by what reasons will it be proved that those who did not personally commit Adam's sin, whether infants or adults, are nonetheless not held before God to be guilty of that actual sin?

units.la: P L A C. Videtur Vir doctus Maiorem argumenti negare. Nam alioqui quo tenderet ista eius responsio, aut quid noceret argumento? Eam igitur sic probo, aut, fi hoc magis placet, argumentum sic formo. Qui peccauerunt, peccatum dissimile transgressioni Adæ, illi non peccaverunt transgressionem Adæ: transgressio enim Adæ non est sibi ipsi dissimilis. Atqui illi qui peccauerunt, nec tamen peccauerunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adæ, peccauerunt peccatum dissimile transgressioni Adæ. Ergo non peccauerunt illam ipsam transgressionem Adæ. Docet enim Apostolus omnes peccaffe, quod peccatum? Peccatum, fi creditur Viro doćto, adeo non dissimile transgressioni Adæ, vt fit ipsa Adæ transgressio? At illud non peccarunt perfonaliter. Imò, inquam, Apostolus tam perfonaliter vult peccaffe, quàm perfonaliter moriuntur. Agitur enim de regno mortis, quod omnibus & singulis perfonaliter conuenit, ex quo infertur regnum peccati omnibus & singulis itidem perfonaliter conuenientes. Omnes enim ita peccauerunt, vt cuiusque propria persona fit peccatrix, fit rea. Quibus perfonaliter peccatum verè, & merito seu iure imputatur, illi perfonaliter peccarunt; alioqui falsò illis perfonaliter imputaretur peccatum, quod perfonaliter illis non conueniret: imputatur enim non vt vadibus peccatorum, sed vt peccatoribus, hoc est, peccati caufisvel subjectis.
units.tr: PLAC. The learned man seems to deny the major premise of the argument. For otherwise, what would his reply aim at, or how would it harm the argument? I therefore prove it thus, or, if you prefer, I frame the argument thus. Those who sinned with a sin unlike Adam's transgression did not sin Adam's transgression, for Adam's transgression is not unlike itself. But those who sinned, and yet did not sin after the likeness of Adam's transgression, sinned with a sin unlike Adam's transgression. Therefore they did not sin that very transgression of Adam. For does the Apostle teach that all sinned, what sin? Is the sin, if the learned man is to be believed, so little unlike Adam's transgression that it is Adam's transgression itself? But they did not sin in person. Rather, I say, the Apostle wants them to have sinned just as personally as they die personally. For he is speaking of the reign of death, which belongs to each and every person personally, and from this it is inferred that the reign of sin belongs to each and every person in the same personal way.
