For all sinned in such a way that each person's own self becomes a sinner and becomes guilty. Those to whom sin is truly and justly, or lawfully, imputed personally, sinned personally. Otherwise sin would be falsely imputed to them personally, which did not personally belong to them. For they are imputed to be not as sureties for sins, but as sinners, that is, as the causes or subjects of sin.

units.la: Pergis, & quia in fine huius versus 14. Apostolus dixit Adamum fuisse typum illius qui venturus erat, videlicet Christi, obseruas inter typum & rem typo adumbratam esse similitudinem oportere: respondere autem hunc typum antitypo in contrario effectu, Et haftenus recte. Explicas autem illam similitudinem sic. Quemadmodum per Adamum peccatum introijt in omnes homines, & per peccatum mors, eo quod in Adamo omnes peccauerunt: sic per Christum iustitia introijt in omnes credentes, & per iustitiam vita, eo quod in Christo omnes credentes pro peccatis satisfecerunt. Hic aliquid defidero. Primum enim duas expositiones verborum simul coniungis, quarum tamen altera te contentum esse oportuit. Deinde dicis omnes homines peccaffe in
units.tr: You go on, and because at the end of this verse 14 the Apostle called Adam a type of him who was to come, namely Christ, you observe that between the type and the thing foreshadowed by the type there must be a likeness, and that this type corresponds to the antitype in an opposite effect. And so far you are right. But you then explain that likeness thus: As through Adam sin entered into all men, and through sin death, because in Adam all sinned, so through Christ righteousness entered into all believers, and through righteousness life, because in Christ all believers made satisfaction for sins. Here I miss something. First, you join two explanations of the words together at once, although you ought to have been content with one of them. Next, you say that all men sinned in

units.la: Adamo eo sensu, quem alienum esse à mente Apostoli docui. Tum in redditione similitudinis mentionem facis modi quo simus compotes iustitiæ Christi, nempe fidei, à qua consultò abstinuit Apostolus in tota hac comparatione. Præterea tu eadem verba in redditione retines, quæ sunt adhibita in protasi, quæ si ipse Apostolus ἀντιθέσεως exprefisset, mea quidem sententia immutasset paululum, atque ad rei naturam accommodasset: non enim quemadmodum peccatum in nos introiit tam verè quàm mors, sic in nos introiit Christi satisfactio tam verè quàm vita. Adhæc tu in ἀντιθέσει vsus es verbis præteriti temporis præter consuetudinem Apostoli in hac collatione. Denique tu vrges illa verba, & ita in omnes homines mors pertransijt, eo quod omnes peccarunt, quæ tamen nihil sunt nisi præcedentium, peccatum introiit in mundum & per peccatum mors, expositio; vt quàm latè vtrumque illud malum pateat intelligamus, ac simul confirmatio: quod enim omnibus hominibus commune est, id à communi omnium hominum origine fluxisse putandum est. Malim igitur hanc comparationem ita simpliciter instituere, Quemadmodum per vnum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit & per peccatum mors, sic per vnum hominem donum iustitiæ indultum est mundo, & per iustitiam vita æterna. Quod si libet etiam illa verba reddere, & ita mors in omnes homines transfijt, quia omnes peccauerunt, sic reddam, & ita vita æterna omnibus communicabitur, quoniam omnes iustificabuntur. Sed hæc verba, vt dixi, non videntur ad iustitiam & vitam accommodanda, & sic accommodata sententiam aut falsam, aut benigna interpretatione molliendam efficiunt. Sed perge. Quemadmodum, addis, satisfactio Christi nostra fit per imputationem, sic peccatum Adami nostrum est per imputationem: & veluti obedientia Christi nobis imputatur, ita transgressio Adami nobis imputatur. Hoc falsum est nec sequitur ullo modo ex collatione quam Apostolus inter primum & secundum Adamum instituit. Christi satisfactio nostra est dono: Itaque vocatur ab Apostolo in hac comparatione χάρισμα, δώρημα, χάρις, δωρεά. Transgressio Adami nostra non est dono. Deum non decuit ea nos donare. Adamus nec voluit nec potuit. Bona dando attribui possunt, non culpae. Est enim peccati imputatio a iustitia, satisfactionis a gratia.
units.tr: Adam, in the sense which I have shown to be foreign to the mind of the Apostle. Then in restating the likeness you mention the manner by which we become partakers of Christ's righteousness, namely faith, which the Apostle deliberately left out of this whole comparison. Moreover, in restating it you keep the same words that were used in the protasis, which, if the Apostle himself had expressed the [ἀντιθέσεως] antithesis, would in my view have been changed a little and fitted to the nature of the matter. For sin did not enter into us as truly as death did, so Christ's satisfaction did not enter into us as truly as life did. Besides, in the antithesis you used verbs in the past tense, contrary to the Apostle's practice in this comparison. Finally, you press those words, and so death passed into all men, because all sinned, which are nothing but an explanation of the preceding words, sin entered into the world, and through sin death, so that we may understand how widely each of those evils extends, and at the same time a confirmation. For what is common to all men must be thought to have flowed from the common origin of all men. I would therefore prefer to set up this comparison simply thus: As through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, so through one man the gift of righteousness has been granted to the world, and through righteousness eternal life. But if you like to render those words also, and so death passed into all men, because all sinned, I will render them thus: and so eternal life will be communicated to all, since all will be justified. But these words, as I said, do not seem to be fitted to righteousness and life, and when so fitted they make the meaning either false or in need of softening by a kindly interpretation. But go on. You add, As Christ's satisfaction becomes ours through imputation, so Adam's sin is ours through imputation; and just as Christ's obedience is imputed to us, so Adam's transgression is imputed to us. This is false, and it does not follow in any way from the comparison which the Apostle draws between the first and the second Adam. Christ's satisfaction is ours by gift. Therefore in this comparison the Apostle calls it χάρισμα, δώρημα, χάρις, δωρεά [free gift, gift, grace, gift]. Adam's transgression is not ours by gift. God was not fitting to give us that. Adam neither wished nor was able to. Good things can be attributed by giving, but not faults. For the imputation of sin comes from justice, the imputation of satisfaction from grace.

units.la: Audi Chamierum, Si nihil habent infantes peccati propriy, cur propria morte pereunt? Nam propter alienam culpam, quae tantum aliena fit, non fit iustitia divina. &c. Quod si excipiat quis seruari fideles propter iustitiam, non suam, sed Christi: Itaque posse etiam damnari propter alienam iniustitiam, is vero non videt comparari valde diuersa: Nam damnatio est a iustitia, salus autem a gratia. Nam si esset etiam ipsa a iustitia, non posset nos aliena iustitia seruare: quare ne aliena quidem culpa damnare.
units.tr: Hear Chamier: "If infants have no sin of their own, why do they perish by their own death? For on account of another's fault, which becomes theirs only by another's guilt, there is no divine justice. And so on." But if anyone should except that the faithful are saved on account of justice, not their own but Christ's, and therefore that one may also be condemned on account of another's injustice, he does not see that the two cases are very different. For condemnation proceeds from justice, but salvation from grace. For if salvation too proceeded from justice, another's justice could not save us; and so neither could another's fault condemn us.

units.la: GAR. Resp. 1. Imputationem peccati ex illa comparatione sequi, si negat disputator; At certe rationes supra demonstrarunt, quae simplici negatione, tanquam oris flatu, dissipari non possunt.
units.tr: GAR. Reply, first: if the disputant denies that imputation of sin follows from that comparison, then the arguments demonstrated above, which cannot be dissolved by a bare denial, as if by a breath of the mouth, certainly stand.

units.la: PLAC. Imputationem primi peccati actualis immediatam nego ex illa comparatione sequi, eaque neque supra demonstrata est, neque ulla ratione demonstrari potest, neque hoc loco vtor simplici negatione, sed rationes & ab Apostolo, & a praestantissimo Chamiero validas mutuatus, sum quibus meam negationem fulcirem.
units.tr: PLAC. I deny that the immediate imputation of the first actual sin follows from that comparison. Nor has it been demonstrated above, nor can it be demonstrated by any argument. Nor do I here use a bare denial; rather, I have borrowed arguments both from the Apostle and from the most distinguished Chamier, sound arguments with which to support my denial.

units.la: GAR. 2. Ratio vero cur Adami transgressio imputari non possit, nullius momenti est, quia scilicet, inquiunt, transgressio est ex iustitia, satisfactio est ex dono, Quasi vero nihil imputari posset, quod est ex iustitia, sed illud tantum quod est ex dono. Atqui fieri potest, vt & quod ex dono est, non imputetur; & quod ex iustitia est, imputetur, &c.
units.tr: GAR. 2. But the reason why Adam's transgression cannot be imputed is of no weight, because, they say, the transgression is from justice, and the satisfaction is from gift. As if indeed nothing could be imputed which is from justice, but only that which is from gift. And yet it can happen that what is from gift is not imputed, and what is from justice is imputed, etc.

units.la: PLAC. Ad id quod mihi obiectum fuerat, Quemadmodum satisfactio Christi nostra fit per imputationem, sic peccatum Adami nostrum est per imputationem, responderam negando, quomodo satisfactio Christi nostra est, eodem modo nostrum esse peccatum Adami: illam enim nostram esse dono, quomodo peccatum Adami nostrum esse non potest. Nonne id verum est? Estne in hac refponfione quod iure queat reprehendi? Quid ergo facit Vir doctus? Perinde disputat ac fi negarem, nihil imputari posse, quod fit ex iustitia; id omne & solum imputari posse, quod fit ex dono: ita fingit sibi monstrum, quod debellet. Hoc mihi satis est hoc loco, nostram esse Christi satisfactionem dono; id quod non negat, nec potest negare Vir doctus; peccatum autem Adami dono nostrum non esse: id quod etiam confiteri mihi videtur. Sed argumentemur ex concessis. Iustitia suum cuique tribuit, non autem alienum. Si ergo nobis tribuit & imputat peccatum actuale primum Adami, nobis id tribuit quia nostrum est. Peto quomodo noftrum est? quomodo Christi satisfactio nostra est? minime; dono enim nostrum nec est, nec esse potest. Propagatione naturali? Non propagatur, nisi quatenus corruptio quae propagatur, illius quaedam communio & habitualis approbatio est; unde nulla exoriri potest imputatio, nisi consequens seu mediata. Imputatione? Facit ergo iustitia, tribuendo seu imputando, nostrum, quod nostrum non erat: id quod non est iuftitiae, praesertim iudicantis secundum legem. Alioqui posset Iudex innocentem quemlibet damnare, imputando nempe ei alterius peccatum, si quidem imputatio sufficeret, ut esse posset ex iustitia peccatum eius cui imputaretur.
units.tr: PLAC. To the objection made to me, "Just as Christ's satisfaction becomes ours by imputation, so Adam's sin is ours by imputation," I answered by denying that Adam's sin is ours in the same way that Christ's satisfaction is ours. For that satisfaction is ours by gift, whereas Adam's sin cannot be ours in that way. Is this not true? Is there anything in this reply that can rightly be found fault with? What, then, does the learned man do? He argues as if I had denied that anything can be imputed which comes from justice, and that only what comes from gift can be imputed. So he invents a monster for himself to overcome. For my present purpose it is enough that Christ's satisfaction is ours by gift, which the learned man does not deny and cannot deny; and that Adam's sin is not ours by gift, which he seems to me also to concede. But let us argue from what is agreed. Justice gives each his due, and not what is another's. If, then, justice assigns and imputes to us Adam's first actual sin, it assigns it to us because it is ours. I ask: how is it ours? In what way is Christ's satisfaction ours? Not at all; for it is not ours by gift, nor can it be. By natural propagation? It is not propagated, except insofar as the corruption that is propagated is a certain participation in that sin and a habitual approval of it; hence no imputation can arise from this except a consequent or mediate one. By imputation? Then justice makes ours, by assigning or imputing, what was not ours; and this is not the office of justice, especially of a judge who judges according to law. Otherwise a judge could condemn any innocent person whatever, by imputing to him another's sin, if imputation were enough to make the sin of the one to whom it is imputed to be from justice.

units.la: GAR. 3. Quid est quod addunt; si satisfactio esset a iustitia, non posset aliena iustitia nos servare? Nam sane quod Christus Patri satisfecit, fuit ex ratione iustitiae divinae, quae nonnisi illa satisfactione praestita poterat abstinere ab universali hominum destructione; quod illi quibuscum agimus multis argumentis alibi astruunt; Et tamen illa satisfactio nobis imputatur. Est ergo a gratia quidem satisfactionis imputatio; sed a iustitia est satisfactionis exactio. Ita ex iniustitia fuit, quod Adam peccavit; ex iustitia, quod eius posteris peccatum illud imputatum est. Sed ex iustitia fuit, quod Christus Patri satisfecit. Ex gratia est, quod illa satisfactio nobis imputatur.
units.tr: GAR. 3. What is the force of what they add: "If satisfaction were from justice, another's justice could not save us"? For surely the fact that Christ satisfied the Father arose from the reason of divine justice, which could not refrain from the universal destruction of mankind except by that satisfaction having been rendered; and those with whom we are dealing assert this elsewhere by many arguments. And yet that satisfaction is imputed to us. So the imputation of satisfaction is indeed from grace; but the exaction of satisfaction is from justice. Thus it was from injustice that Adam sinned; from justice that his sin was imputed to his posterity. But it was from justice that Christ satisfied the Father. It is from grace that this satisfaction is imputed to us.

units.la: PLAC. Nunc Chamierum, cuius verba laudaveram, oppugnat; sed, pro suo more, aliquid in verbis & sensu mutando, ut sibi ipse aptam praebeat aliquid respondendi. Non dixerat Chamierus, si satisfactio esset a iustitia, sed si salus esset a iustitia. Intererat autem discriminis nonnihil inter duas illas voces, salutem & satisfactionem: Certe salus non est ex ratione iustitiae divinae, sed ex mera misericordia & gratia: Nam contraria saluti perditio erat ex ratione iustitiae divinae. Deinde ut maxime salutis nomine satisfactio intelligeretur, spectaretur non respectu iustitiae Patris cui satisfactum est, sed respectu nostri, quorum non est ex iustitia, sed ex dono tantum. Cum igitur illa dono nostra sit, etiam ex gratia est quod nobis imputatur. Ad peccatum autem Adami quod attinet, si nobis imputatur ex iustitia, ideo nobis imputatur, quia vere nostrum est. Non enim nobis tribuit iustitia, nisi quod nostrum est. Prius igitur est nostrum, quam ut nobis imputetur. Falsum ergo est quod toties inculcant, nostrum non esse nisi per imputationem. Iam quaeritur quo iure sit nostrum. Ad coniunctionem naturalem confugere non potes: ita enim nostra essent alia peccata Adami, nec non aliorum parentum nostrorum: Nec ad foedus, cuius neque vestigium vllum apparet in Scriptura, & cum aequitate conciliatio impossibilis.
units.tr: PLAC. Now he attacks Chamier, whose words I had quoted; but, after his custom, he changes something in the words and in the sense, so as to furnish himself with something to answer. Chamier had not said "if satisfaction were from justice," but "if salvation were from justice." There is some difference between the two words, salvation and satisfaction. Certainly salvation is not from the reason of divine justice, but from mere mercy and grace; for the contrary of salvation, destruction, was from the reason of divine justice. Next, even if satisfaction were understood under the name of salvation, it would be viewed not with respect to the justice of the Father to whom satisfaction was made, but with respect to us, for whom it is not from justice but from gift alone. Since, then, that satisfaction is ours by gift, what is imputed to us is also from grace. As for Adam's sin, if it is imputed to us from justice, it is imputed to us because it is truly ours. For justice assigns to us only what is ours. Therefore it is ours before it is imputed to us. It is false, then, what they so often insist: that it is ours only by imputation. Now the question is by what right it is ours. You cannot take refuge in natural conjunction; for then the other sins of Adam, and of our other parents, would also be ours. Nor in covenant, of which no trace appears anywhere in Scripture, and whose reconciliation with equity is impossible.

units.la: Ex versibus sequentibus, in quibus Apostolus summa, ut solet omnia, sapientia hanc Adamum inter & Christum comparationem persequitur, tu observas Apostolum memorare lapsum unius, peccatum unius, reatum ex uno; & inde sic argumentaris, Si lapsus, & culpa, seu reatus unius, qui solus peccavit, est condemnatio omnium hominum, & omnes morti obnoxios reddit, necesse est ut omnes homines sint correi, seu participes eiusdem lapsus & reatus. Atqui verum prius ex Apostolo in textu. Ergo & posterius, scilicet omnes homines esse correos & participes lapsus & reatus Adami, quomodo vero participes, nisi illius vnius lapsus & reatus ipsis imputetur, eo quod in ipso peccauerint? Non obseruabo diligentius tua haec verba: non dicam Apostolum non dixisse lapsum, culpam, reatum vnius, qui solus peccauit, esse condemnationem omnium hominum, cautius locutus est. Non dicam, si Adamus solus peccauerit, nos igitur vna cum eo non peccauisse. Non dicam, si illius vnius lapsus & reatus nobis imputetur, eo quod in ipso peccauimus, nos igitur prius peccasse, ac illud peccatum nostrum esse quàm vt nobis imputetur: Itaque non fieri, vt tu dicere soles, nostrum imputatione. Respondebo tantum illud ipsum quod tu tibi ipse respondes, nos esse participes lapsus Adami ac proinde correos, non quidem illius vnius lapsus & reatus imputatione, sed reali communicatione & propagatione in nos vitiositatis, quam suo illo lapsu contraxit, quae, quia habitualis quaedam inobedientia & rebellio est aduersus Deum ex actuali illa inobedientia nata ac in nos propagata, reos nos facit & condemnatione dignos. Quid reponis? Corruptionem illam revera esse poenam, & effectum illius lapsus. Effectum Concedo. Poenam qualem tu intelligis propriedictam & nostri respectu, Nego. Id affirmasti jam saepius, probare ne semel quidem conatus es. Ego jam refutaui, & Deo dante iterum refutabo suo loco. Addis, sed Apostolus loquitur de reatu, qui est ex vno lapsu. Loquitur sane de reatu, qui ortus quidem est ex vno lapsu Adami, sed mediante corruptione inhaerente. Hoc me docuit Caluinus, vellem te etiam, Quod vnius delicto periisse nos tradit, sic accipe, quia ex ipso in nos corruptio transfusa sit. Neque enim sic perimus eius culpa, quasi extra culpam ipsi simus : sed quia eius peccatum peccati nostri causa est, exitium nostrum illi Paulus adscribit. Peccatum nostrum voco quod nobis ingenitum est, & cum quo nascimur. Idipsum me Martyr quoque, alijque docuerunt Theologi maximi. Sed non libenter humana authoritate diuinam veritatem fulcio, quam suis ipsam viribus satis pollentem semper existimaui. Fateor nos esse participes peccati & reatus Adami, sed nego ideo participes, quia nobis imputetur. Id tibi probandum est, non simpliciter, ut perpetuo facis, affirmandum. Nego corruptionem esse poenam offensae Adami, quemadmodum tu rursus sine vlla probatione inculcas. Transgressio Adami fuit actualis rebellio aduersus Deum, ea reliquit in anima Adami rebellionem habitualem, quam vitium & corruptionem & peccatum originale appellamus, eam sine vlla imputatione tam propagauit, quam ipsam naturam humanam. Hinc quam sumus participes naturae eius humanae, tam sumus participes eius rebellionis. Hanc participationem reatus noster sequitur. Hoc oppugna, si potes.
units.tr: From the following verses, in which the Apostle, with his usual supreme wisdom, pursues this comparison between Adam and Christ, you observe that the Apostle mentions the fall of one, the sin of one, the guilt from one; and from this you argue thus: If the fall, and the fault or guilt, of one who alone sinned is the condemnation of all men, and renders all liable to death, it is necessary that all men be co-guilty, or participants in the same fall and guilt. But the first is true from the Apostle in the text. Therefore the second too: that all men are co-guilty and participants in Adam's fall and guilt. But how are they participants, unless that one fall and guilt is imputed to them, because they sinned in him?" I will not examine your words too closely. I will not say that the Apostle did not speak of the fall, fault, and guilt of one who alone sinned as the condemnation of all men; he spoke more cautiously. I will not say, if Adam alone sinned, then we did not sin together with him. I will not say, if that one fall and guilt is imputed to us because we sinned in him, then we sinned earlier, and that sin was ours before it was imputed to us; and thus it does not happen, as you are accustomed to say, that it becomes ours by imputation. I will answer only what you yourself answer: that we are participants in Adam's fall, and therefore co-guilty; not by imputation of that one fall and guilt, but by the real communication and propagation into us of the vitiosity which he contracted by that fall. Because this is a certain habitual disobedience and rebellion against God, born of that actual disobedience and propagated into us, it makes us guilty and worthy of condemnation. What do you reply? "That corruption is really a punishment, and an effect of that fall." I concede it is an effect. That it is a punishment, in the sense you understand, that is, one inflicted on us, I deny. You have affirmed this many times, and you have not once even tried to prove it. I have already refuted it, and with God's help I will refute it again in its place. You add: "But the Apostle speaks of guilt which arises from one fall." He certainly speaks of guilt which arose indeed from the one fall of Adam, but through the inherent corruption. Calvin taught me this; I wish you would also learn it: "As to what he tells us, that we perished by the offence of one man, take it thus: because corruption was transfused into us from him. For we do not perish by his fault as though we were outside his fault; but because his sin is the cause of our sin, Paul ascribes our destruction to him. I call our sin that which is innate in us and with which we are born." The great theologians Martyr and others have taught me this same thing. But I am not willing to support divine truth by human authority, which I have always considered sufficiently strong by its own powers. I grant that we are participants in Adam's sin and guilt; but I deny that we are participants because it is imputed to us. This you must prove, not simply affirm, as you constantly do. I deny that corruption is the punishment of Adam's offence, as you again insist without any proof. Adam's transgression was an actual rebellion against God; it left in Adam's soul a habitual rebellion, which we call vice, corruption, and original sin; this he propagated, without any imputation, just as he propagated human nature itself. Hence, as we are participants in his human nature, so we are participants in his rebellion. Our guilt follows from this participation. Attack this, if you can.

units.la: GAR. 1. Vt videatur illius responsionis ἐξ ἀντικ renocandi sunt ad scopum Apostoli, qui cum hoc agat, vt ex Adami typo & comparatione illustret doctrinam de iustificatione per imputationem iustitiae Christi, vt diximus; aut parum omnino agit, aut de imputatione primi peccati agit. Neque enim si, non imputatione peccati Adae, sed tantum vitiositatis propagatione, rei sumus, recte & legitime vnquam ex illa comparatione inferri poterit, nos esse iustos imputatione iustitiae Christi. &c.
units.tr: GAR. 1. So that his reply seems to be aimed at the Apostle's purpose, it must be recalled that the Apostle, in setting out the doctrine of justification by the imputation of Christ's righteousness through the type and comparison of Adam, as we have said, either does very little here or else is speaking of the imputation of the first sin. For if we are guilty not through the imputation of Adam's sin, but only through the propagation of his corruption, then no right or lawful inference could ever be drawn from that comparison that we are righteous by the imputation of Christ's righteousness. etc.

units.la: PLAC. Iam aliquoties negauimus comparationem illam inter Christum & Adamum institutam ab Apostolo fuisse. vt illustraret modum per quem iustificamur, seu per quem iuftitia nostra est : is enim modus, cum fit oppositus ei modo quo peccatum est nostrum, dissimilitudinem potius inter vtrumque, quàm similitudinem efficit, eamque dissimilitudinem, vt dixi, Apostolus dissimilibus vtens vocibus fatis aperte insinuauit. Supponit igitur Vir doctus, quod erat probandum, Apoftolum ex illa comparatione inferre velle, nos esse iustos imputatione iustitiæ Christi : hic enim modus nec ab eo exprimitur, nec potest ab illa comparatione deduci, nisi quatenus, vt non damnat in foro peccatum nisi imputetur, sic non iustificat iuftitia nisi ipsa quoque à iudice imputetur. Sed imputatio peccati, quoniam aliunde esse non potest quam à iustitia, quæ suum cuique tribuit, ipsa rei natu à & veritate nititur. Imputatio vero iustitiæ ex gratia cum fit, Dei & Christi donatione nititur: Est enim in nobis reuera peccatum quod nobis imputetur ad condemnationem, sed nulla est in nobis iustitia, quæ possit nobis ad iustificationem imputari, & peccatum Adami nostrum est natura, quia natura propagatum nobis inhæret : Christi vero iustitia nostra est ex gratia; gratuitum enim Dei donum est. Condemnatio est ex merito nostro, iustificatio ex mera Dei gratia.
units.tr: PLAC. We have already more than once denied that the Apostle drew that comparison between Christ and Adam in order to illustrate the manner by which we are justified, or by which our righteousness comes to us. For that manner, since it is the opposite of the manner by which sin came to us, produces a dissimilarity between the two rather than a similarity, and, as I have said, the Apostle clearly hinted at that dissimilarity by using dissimilar words. Therefore the learned man assumes what needed to be proved: that the Apostle means to infer from that comparison that we are righteous by the imputation of Christ's righteousness. For this manner is neither expressed by him nor can it be deduced from that comparison, except in so far as, just as sin does not condemn in the court unless it is imputed, so righteousness does not justify unless it too is imputed by the judge. But the imputation of sin, since it cannot come from anything other than righteousness, which gives each his due, rests upon the very nature of the thing and upon truth. The imputation of righteousness, however, since it comes from grace, rests upon the gift of God and of Christ. For there is truly in us sin which is imputed to us for condemnation, but there is no righteousness in us which can be imputed to us for justification; and Adam's sin is our nature, because, propagated by nature, it inheres in us. But Christ's righteousness is ours by grace, for it is a gift of God freely given. Condemnation is by our merit, justification by the pure grace of God.

units.la: GAR. Si iusti fumus in Christo, quomodo peccatores in Adamo, & in Adamo non imputatione, sed vitiofitatis tantum inhæfione fimus peccatores, rem sibi confessam habent Pontificij, vt ex ista comparatione concludant : Ergo, nos esse iustos in Christo, non aliqua iustitia ipsius imputatione, sed vera iustitia infusione & inhæfione. Ita non possunt nobis doctrinam imputationis peccati excutere, vt non eodem molimine iustitia imputationem concutiant, & iustificationis doctrinam hoc loco ab Apostolo tractatam per latus nostrum confodiant.
units.tr: GAR. If we are righteous in Christ, how are we sinners in Adam? And if in Adam we are sinners not by imputation but only by the inherence of the vice, the Papists have the matter settled for themselves, so that they conclude from this comparison: Therefore we are righteous in Christ not by any imputation of his righteousness, but by the true righteousness infused and inherent. Thus they cannot overthrow for us the doctrine of the imputation of sin without shaking the imputation of righteousness by the same effort, and they pierce through our side the doctrine of justification which the Apostle treats in this place.

units.la: PLAC. Nostræ doctrinæ Vir doctus imputat culpam suæ. Non enim ex nostra, sed ex ipsius falsa hypothesi, nos esse iustos in Christo quomodo peccatores fumus in Adamo, Pontificii illa conclusio sequitur, quæ posita illa hypothesi nulla arte declinari potest. Sic enim illi colligent, Si iusti fumus in Christo, quomodo peccatores fumus in Adamo, & in Adamo non tantùm imputatione ipsius iniustitiæ, sed etiam vera infusitiæ nobis inhærentis communicatione peccatores sumus. Ergo, iusti sumus in Christo non tantum iustitiæ ipsius imputatione, sed etiam veræ iustitiæ nobis inhærentis communicatione ; iu- sti, inquam, sicut peccatores, in foro diuino.
units.tr: PLAC. The learned man lays the blame for his own position on our doctrine. For the Papist conclusion follows not from our teaching but from his own false hypothesis, that we are righteous in Christ as we are sinners in Adam; and given that hypothesis, it cannot be evaded by any skill. For they will argue thus: If we are righteous in Christ as we are sinners in Adam, and in Adam we are sinners not only by the imputation of his unrighteousness but also by the real communication of the inherent corruption, then we are righteous in Christ not only by the imputation of his righteousness but also by the real communication of the inherent righteousness; righteous, I say, just as we are sinners, in the divine court.

units.la: G A R. 2. Quantumuis lapsus primi reatus ad nos non perueniat, nisi mediante Corruptione, quod cum Caluino agnoscimus, & superius expositum est, illud tamen obstare non potest, quominus reatus ille sit non tantum corruptionis nostræ, sed & primi actualis Adæ peccati reatus : Imo contra concludendum est ; quod ad nos peruenit alio mediante, ipsum tamen verè peruenit, vt, lumen solis, quia peruenit ad nos mediante aëre, eo ipso ad nos verè pertingere dicimus. Atqui peccati primi reatus, mediante corruptione ad nos pertingit. Ergo ipse reatus primi peccati verè ad nos peruenit, & ex illo lapsu, & per illum lapsum verè rei sumus.
units.tr: GAR. 2. However much the fall of the first guilt reaches us only through corruption, which we acknowledge with Calvin, and as has been set out above, this does not prevent that guilt from being not only the guilt of our corruption but also the guilt of Adam's first actual sin. Indeed, the conclusion must be the reverse: what reaches us through another means truly does reach us, just as the light of the sun, because it reaches us through the air, we say therefore truly reaches us. But the guilt of the first sin reaches us through corruption. Therefore the guilt of the first sin itself truly reaches us, and by that fall and through that fall we are truly guilty.

units.la: PLAC. Totum concedo. Egregiè hic pro imputatione mediata, contra immediatum loquitur hoc loco Vir doctus. Vtinam sic cum Caluino constanter & ipse sensisset, & omnes sentirent : me certe haberent omni ex parte consentientem. Agnosco enim primi peccati reatum mediante corruptione ad nos pertingere. Nos ex illo lapsu & per illum lapsum, mediatè ; hoc est, mediante corruptione, reos esse : vt sit reatus immediatè à corruptione, & mediatè à primo peccato Adæ. Nec displicet ductum à lumine solis exemplum. Pertingit enim ad nos immediatè lumen solis, non illud quod inhæret in sole, sed illud quod est in aëre à sole.
units.tr: PLAC. I grant the whole. Here the learned man speaks admirably for mediate imputation and against immediate imputation. Would that he had thought so consistently with Calvin, and that all thought so; they would certainly find me in full agreement in every respect. For I acknowledge that the guilt of the first sin reaches us through corruption. We are guilty by that fall and through that fall mediately, that is, through corruption, so that the guilt comes immediately from corruption and mediately from Adam's first sin. Nor do I dislike the example taken from the light of the sun. For the light of the sun reaches us immediately, not that which is in the sun itself, but that which is in the air from the sun.

units.la: G A R. 3. Quomodo rebellio habitualis, quam in ipsius Adami anima transgressio actualis reliquit, sit ipsum vitium & peccatum originale in nobis inhærens : explicet qui poterit. Mihi sane monstro simile videtur, vt quod adhæsit in alterius anima, sine omni imputatione nostrum dicatur, imo nobis inhærere afferatur, cum tamen non amplius sit in mundo : dixisset potius effectum esse & sequelam illius corruptionis in Adami anima hærentis ; sed ipsam illam corruptionem dici nulla ratio patitur, quantum ego quidem cogitatione assequi possum.
units.tr: GAR. 3. How the habitual rebellion which the actual transgression left in Adam's own soul is the very vice and original sin inherent in us, let whoever can explain it. To me it certainly seems a monster, that what cleaved to the soul of another should be called ours without any imputation, and indeed asserted to inhere in us, when it is no longer in the world at all. He should rather have said that it is the effect and consequence of that corruption which clung to Adam's soul; but no reason permits that corruption itself to be so called, as far as I can grasp by thought.

units.la: PLAC. Atqui id explicatum à me satis est in hoc ipso Manuscripti loco, si voluisset Vir doctus attendere. Maluit, vt haberet quod reprehenderet, fingere sibi quiddam monstro simile, quasi illam ipsam rebellionem habitualem, quæ in ipsius Adami anima hæsit, eandem numero nobis inhærere assererem; cum tamen distinctis verbis propagatum una cum natura dixerim: differt autem numero, ut natura, sic rebellio habitualis propagata à propagante. Quid est natura nostra nisi natura Adami propagata? Quid est similiter nostra corruptio, nisi corruptio Adami propagata? Hoc facile intelligit qui vult intelligere.
units.tr: PLAC. Yet this has been explained by me sufficiently in this very passage of the Manuscript, if the learned man had been willing to attend to it. He preferred, so that he would have something to find fault with, to invent for himself something like a monster, as if I asserted that the very same habitual rebellion which clung to Adam's own soul inheres in us in number; whereas I expressly said that it is propagated together with nature. But the habitual rebellion, like nature, differs in number from that which propagates it, once propagated. What is our nature but Adam's nature propagated? What likewise is our corruption but Adam's corruption propagated? He who wishes to understand will easily understand this.

units.la: Repones forte qualem naturam Adamus habuit talem ad nos transmisisse; habuisse autem ream & corruptam; talem igitur ad nos transmisisse. Totum concedo. Tantum observo naturam proprie loquendo nec peccare, nec ream esse. Utrumque personarum est proprium, nec convenit naturæ nisi quatenus certo quodam modo singulari subsistit, hoc est, est persona. Adamus autem primo commisit actionem illam singularem quæ eius est transgressio seu peccatum actuale, deinde hoc ipso corruptus factus est. Itaque eius reatus non modo ex corruptione illa, sed etiam ex eius actione ortus est. Nos autem, quoniam actionem suam propagare non potuit, nullum ab eo trahimus peccatum præter illam corruptionem, neque alium reatum quam eum qui ex illa corruptione nascitur. Quocirca Apostolus observat reatum, qui per unum qui peccavit introiit in mundum, esse ex una offensa tantum, nempe ab Adamo non habemus, nisi unum peccatum habituale sive lapsum habitualem, ex quo vno nostrer reatus. Alioqui poiua inputatione peccati actualis Adami, aut negandus esset reatus qui ex corruptione nascitur, aut fatendum reatum quem ex Adamo habemus esse ex tribus peccatis: primum ex peccato actuali Adami nobis imputato immediate; deinde ex peccato habituali seu corruptione quæ fuit in ipso Adamo : dici enim non potest cur eius peccatum actuale nobis imputetur, non imputetur potius eius corruptio ; hæc enim naturæ peccatum dici solet, illud personæ. Tertiò denique ex corruptione in nos propagata ac nobis inhærente ; vt taceam causam idoneam reddi non posse, quamobrem, si nobis primum peccatum Adami actuale imputatur immediatè, non imputentur etiam reliqua eius peccata actualia : nam si eramus in eius lumbis cùm primùm illud peccatum perpetrauit, eramus pariter in eius lumbis spatio centum & triginta annorum antequam Sethum generaret, cùm eo toto tempore varia peccata admitteret contra legem naturæ. Si dicas solum primum eius peccatum actuale corrupisse naturam, verum quidem dixeris ; sed nihil ad rem, quoniam vis primum illud peccatum actuale præcisè sumptum & Adamo & nobis immediatè imputari, ac quia imputetur, infligi & Adamo & nobis corruptionem in pœnam. Sequitur igitur tuâ sententiâ corruptio imputationem vt pœna, ac proindè causa nullo modo est cur peccatum illud actuale nobis imputetur. Vides igitur illam tuam imputationem verbis illis Apostoli confossam vers.16. πᾶ μὲν γὰρ κρίμα ἐξ ἑνὸς sub. κατάκριμα, Nam reatus quidem est ex vno peccato. Ac ne dicas vnum pro primo vsurpatum, opponit Apostolus vnum multis, non autem secundo ; τὸ δὲ χάρισμα ἐκ πολλῶν παραπτωμάτων εἰς δικαίωμα, donum verò est ex multis peccatis in iustificationem.
units.tr: Perhaps you will reply that Adam transmitted to us a nature such as he had; and he had a nature that was guilty and corrupt; therefore he transmitted such a nature to us. I grant the whole. I only observe that, properly speaking, nature neither sins nor is guilty. Both belong to the person, and they belong to nature only in so far as it subsists in a certain singular way, that is, is a person. But Adam first committed that singular action which is his transgression or actual sin, and then by this very act he was made corrupt. Therefore his guilt arose not only from that corruption but also from his action. But we, since he could not propagate his action, draw from him no sin except that corruption, nor any guilt other than that which arises from that corruption. Wherefore the Apostle observes that the guilt which came into the world through one who sinned arises from one offence only; indeed from Adam we have only one habitual sin or habitual fall, from which one thing our guilt arises. Otherwise, by the imputation of Adam's actual sin, either the guilt which arises from corruption must be denied, or we must confess that the guilt we have from Adam arises from three sins: first, from Adam's actual sin imputed to us immediately; then from the habitual sin or corruption which was in Adam himself, for it cannot be said why his actual sin should be imputed to us and his corruption should not rather be imputed, since the latter is usually called the sin of the nature and the former the sin of the person. Thirdly, finally, from the corruption propagated into us and inhering in us. To say nothing of the fact that no adequate reason can be given why, if Adam's first actual sin is imputed to us immediately, his other actual sins are not imputed as well; for if we were in his loins when he first committed that sin, we were equally in his loins during the one hundred and thirty years before he begot Seth, when he committed various sins against the law of nature throughout all that time. If you say that only his first actual sin corrupted nature, you speak truly; but this is nothing to the point, since you wish that first actual sin, taken precisely, to be imputed immediately both to Adam and to us, and that because it is imputed, corruption is inflicted both on Adam and on us as punishment. It follows therefore, on your opinion, that corruption is imputed as punishment, and so there is in no way a cause why that actual sin should be imputed to us. You see, then, that your imputation is pierced through by those words of the Apostle in verse 16: τὸ μὲν γὰρ κρίμα ἐξ ἑνὸς εἰς κατάκριμα [For the judgment indeed is from one unto condemnation]: For the guilt indeed is from one sin. And lest you say that "one" is used for the first, the Apostle sets one against many, not against a second: τὸ δὲ χάρισμα ἐκ πολλῶν παραπτωμάτων εἰς δικαίωμα [but the free gift is from many offences unto justification].

units.la: Superest vers. 19. ὥσπερ γὰρ διὰ τῆς παρακοῆς τοῦ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἁμαρτωλοὶ κατεστάθησαν οἱ πολλοί, οὕτω καὶ διὰ τῆς ὑπακοῆς τοῦ ἑνὸς δίκαιοι κατασταθήσονται οἱ πολλοί, sicut enim per inobedientiam vnius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita per vnius obedientiam iusti constituentur multi. Hinc sic argumentaris, Si peccatores constituti sumus per inobedientiam ⌣Adami, necesse est ut illius inobedientia nobis imputetur: Nam non potest constituere nos peccatores nisi sit nostra, nec nostra esse potest nisi imputatione. Atqui constituimur peccatores per inobedientiam ⌣Adami. Ergo inobedientia Adami nobis imputatur. Huius tui argumenti solutionem legere potuisti apud eruditissimum Chamierum Pastr. tom. 3. lib. 1. de homine corrupto cap. viii. a me in thesibus laudato §. xvii. eam ab ipso mutuabor, & ad tuum argumentum accommodabo. Per inobedientiam constituimur peccatores vel formaliter, vel causaliter. Formaliter constituimur peccatores per inobedientiam, quae vel a nobis ipsis commissa est, vel in nobis ipsis inest tanquam qualitas peccatrix, ut albus paries formaliter constituitur per albedinem ipsi inhaerentem & podagricus quispiam per habitum podagricum ipsius articulis insitum. Causaliter vero peccatores constituimur per inobedientiam, quae est causa efficiens qualitatis illius peccatricis, quae in nobis haeret. Inobedientia, quae nos constituit formaliter peccatores, nobis imputatur immediate; quae tantum causaliter, ea aut non imputatur, aut si dicitur imputari, id accipiendum est mediate tantum; quia eius causa est quod nobis imputatur. Maior tui argumenti vera esset, si per inobedientiam vnius formaliter constitueremur peccatores, nunc cum id fit impossibile, falsa est.
units.tr: There remains verse 19: "For as by the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one many shall be made righteous" [ὥσπερ γὰρ διὰ τῆς παρακοῆς τοῦ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἁμαρτωλοὶ κατεστάθησαν οἱ πολλοί, οὕτω καὶ διὰ τῆς ὑπακοῆς τοῦ ἑνὸς δίκαιοι κατασταθήσονται οἱ πολλοί]. "For as by the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one many shall be made righteous." From this you argue as follows: "If we have been made sinners through the disobedience of Adam, his disobedience must be imputed to us. For it cannot make us sinners unless it is ours, and it cannot be ours except by imputation. But we are made sinners through the disobedience of Adam. Therefore the disobedience of Adam is imputed to us." You could have read the solution to this argument of yours in the most learned Chamier, Panstratia, vol. 3, bk. 1, On Corrupt Man, ch. 8, which I cited in my theses at §17. I shall borrow it from him and apply it to your argument. We are made sinners through disobedience either formally or causally. We are made sinners formally through disobedience which either was committed by ourselves, or inheres in us as a sinful quality, just as a white wall is made white formally by the whiteness inhering in it, and a gouty man is made gouty by the gouty condition implanted in his joints. We are made sinners causally through disobedience which is the efficient cause of that sinful quality that clings to us. The disobedience that makes us sinners formally is imputed to us immediately. That which makes us sinners only causally is either not imputed, or, if it is said to be imputed, this must be understood only mediately, because its cause is what is imputed to us. The major premise of your argument would be true if we were formally made sinners through the disobedience of one man; but since this is impossible, it is false.

units.la: Vin' probem his ipsis Apostoli verbis non constitui nos formaliter peccatores per vnius hominis, id est, Adami inobedientiam, ac proinde illam nobis non imputari? Id conficio duobus argumentis. Primo sic. Per eam inobedientiam formaliter confliituimur peccatores, quæ formaliter nostra est, vel actio, vel qualitas. Atqui inobedientia vnius hominis non est formaliter inobedientia multorum hominum (opponitur enim hoc loco vnus homo multis) Ergo per inobedientiam vnius hominis multi homines non sunt formaliter constituti peccatores. Rem faciam exemplo claram; Si quis dicat, per suam quisque doctrinam doctus constituitur, id formaliter intelligendum est: est enim doctrina cuiusque forma per quam est doctus. Sed si quis dicat, vnius doctrinâ multi sunt facti vel constituti docti, id erit accipiendum causaliter seu efficienter: nemo enim formaliter doctus est alienâ doctrinâ, sed potest doctrina vnius causa efficiens esse similis doctrinæ in alio. Iam vero sicut nemo alienâ doctrinâ formaliter doctus est aut albedine albus, sic nemo formaliter est peccator alieno peccato. Quare cum dicat Apostolus multos esse constitutos peccatores per inobedientiam vnius, manifestum est id non formaliter, sed causaliter esse accipiendum, nihilque eum aliud velle, nisi vnius inobedientiam causam esse eius vitij & peccati, quo sibi infito multi sunt peccatores.
units.tr: Do you want me to prove from these very words of the Apostle that we are not formally made sinners through the disobedience of one man, that is, of Adam, and that therefore it is not imputed to us? I establish this by two arguments. First, as follows. We are formally made sinners through that disobedience which is formally ours, whether an action or a quality. But the disobedience of one man is not formally the disobedience of many men (for in this place one man is set against many). Therefore many men are not formally made sinners through the disobedience of one man. I shall make the point clear by an example. If someone says that each person is made learned through his own teaching, this must be understood formally: for a person's teaching is the form through which he is learned. But if someone says that many have been made or constituted learned through the teaching of one, this must be understood causally or efficiently: for no one is formally learned by another's teaching, but the teaching of one man may be the efficient cause of a similar teaching in another. Now just as no one is formally learned by another's teaching, or white by another's whiteness, so no one is formally a sinner by another's sin. Therefore, when the Apostle says that many have been made sinners through the disobedience of one, it is clear that this must be understood not formally but causally, and that he means nothing else than that the disobedience of one is the cause of that vice and sin by which many are sinners, when it has been implanted in them.

units.la: GAR. Respondeo 1. Si hoc argumento imputationem peccati Adæ refellere voluit, eodem plane refelli posse imputationem iustitiæ Christi: Nam & plane simili ratione Bellarminus ei refutandæ vtitur lib. 2. de Iustif. cap. 7. Argumento quarto &c. Argumentum ergo Pontificius itâ instituet. Non possumus formaliter constitui iusti, nisi per eam obedientiam quæ est formaliter nostra vel actio, vel qualitas: sicut non possumus constitui formaliter docti, nisi per nostram propriam doctrinam. At obedientia Christi non est formaliter nostra vel actio vel qualitas. Ergo per eam non possumus constitui formaliter iusti. Hoc argumentum est omninò illi geminum, quo hic vtitur Vir doctus &c.
units.tr: GAR. I answer, first: if he wished to refute the imputation of Adam's sin by this argument, the same argument could plainly refute the imputation of Christ's righteousness. For Bellarmine uses the very same reasoning, in a similar way, to refute it, in bk. 2 of On Justification, ch. 7, argument four, etc. The Papist will therefore frame the argument thus: we cannot be formally made righteous except through that obedience which is formally our action or quality, just as we cannot be formally made learned except through our own teaching. But the obedience of Christ is not formally our action or quality. Therefore we cannot be formally made righteous through it. This argument is wholly a twin of the one this learned man uses, etc.

units.la: PLAC. Primùm Vir doctus de me vno refellendo sollicitus Chamierum non deserit modò contra Salmeronem pugnantem, sed per latus meum ferit, Salmeronisque argumentum defendit: Nec mirum; nam si tuetur imputationem immediatam quam impugno, hæc causa illi est cum Pighio & Salmerone communis; nec est vllum discrimen, nisi ratione punitionis illius peccati imputati, quam illi mitiorem statuerunt. Itaque si præstantissimi Chamieri valet responsio aduersus Pighium & Salmeronem, mea certè, quæ eadem prorsus est, repudiari non debet. Non enim, vt obseruare videtur Vir doctus §. xii. Primò argumentatus sum, deinde respondi; sed contrà, primò respondi mutuatâ à Chamiero distinctione, deinde argumentum nexui. Responsionis ne meminit quidem: Argumentum primò absurdo premit, deinde soluere videtur. Absurdum est; eodem plane argumento refelli posse imputationem iustitiæ Christi. Hoc nego, quomodo probat? Plane simili ratione, inquit, Bellarminus ei refutandæ vtitur. Minimè, inquam, gentium. Primum enim non eum sensum, quem primo loco proponit, & concedit, nosque probamus, refellit, sed alium, quem non agnoscimus. Videantur eius verba (recitantur enim à Viro docto memorabili parte mutilata) & Responsio Chamieri Panstr. Tom 3. lib. 21. cap. 20. §. 21. Deinde nihil aliud agit, nisi quod probat nos non esse formaliter iustos per iustitiam Christi; id quod Vir doctus, qui imputationem iustitiæ Christi arctè tenet, concedit. Probat autem argumento quo non sum vsus, nec simili, quia, inquit, cùm in aliquo duæ sunt formæ contrariæ, vna inhærens, altera extrinseca, sine dubio denominatio absoluta sumitur ab inhærente forma potiùs quàm ab extrinseca. Sed Vir doctus ipse argumentum meo simile conficit, quo oppugnat imputationem obedientiæ Christi. Simile quidem est argumentum, sed conclusio, vel ipso Viro docto fatente, concedi potest illibatâ imputatione obedientiæ Christi. Eam igitur non conuello, qui contendo nos alio modo per obedientiam Christi iustos constitui, quàm per inobedientiam Adami constituimur iniusti. Interim tamen argumenti eius nego Minorem, Atqui obedientia Christi non est formaliter nostra vel actio, vel qualitas: est enim nostra, non quidem inhęfiue, sed dono, quo modo, vt iam aliquoties obseruaui, nostra non est Adami inobedientia. Adie quod nobis imputatur Christi satisfactio, non proprie vt est actio, aut qualitas, sed vt est poena, quam loco nostro passus est; quo sensu iustitia dicitur non sensu morali, sed tan ũ forensi. Tantum autem abest vt refellendo imputationem immediatam inobedientiae actualis Adami euertamus imputationem iustitiae Christi, vt contra illam ab hac difsociando, tanquam imparem & malae fidei socium, hanc magis tutam praestare nus.
units.tr: PLAC. First, the learned man, anxious to refute me alone, not only deserts Chamier, who is fighting against Salmeron, but strikes me in the side, and defends the argument of Salmeron. This is not surprising: for if he upholds the immediate imputation that I oppose, this cause is held in common with Pighius and Salmeron, and there is no difference except in the punishment of that imputed sin, which they set as milder. Therefore if the response of the most distinguished Chamier holds good against Pighius and Salmeron, then mine, which is entirely the same, ought not to be rejected. For, as the learned man seems to observe in §12, I did not argue first and respond afterwards; rather, I first responded, using the distinction borrowed from Chamier, and afterwards set out the argument. He does not even mention the response: he presses the argument first as absurd, and then seems to resolve it. It is absurd, he says, that the same argument could refute the imputation of Christ's righteousness. I deny this. How does he prove it? "By exactly the same reasoning," he says, "Bellarmine uses it to refute it." Not at all, I say, by no means. For first, it does not refute the sense that he proposes first and concedes, and that we prove, but another sense that we do not acknowledge. Let his words be looked at (for the learned man quotes them with a memorable part omitted), and Chamier's response in Panstratia, vol. 3, bk. 21, ch. 20, §21. Next, he does nothing except prove that we are not formally righteous through the righteousness of Christ, which the learned man, who holds firmly to the imputation of Christ's righteousness, concedes. Yet he proves it by an argument that I have not used, nor one similar, because, he says, "when in something there are two contrary forms, one inhering and the other extrinsic, the absolute denomination is undoubtedly taken from the inhering form rather than from the extrinsic." But the learned man himself constructs an argument similar to mine, by which he attacks the imputation of Christ's obedience. Indeed the argument is similar, but its conclusion can be granted, as the learned man himself admits, with the imputation of Christ's obedience left unharmed. I therefore do not overthrow that imputation, since I maintain that we are made righteous through the obedience of Christ in a different way from that in which we are made unrighteous through the disobedience of Adam. Meanwhile, I deny the minor premise of his argument: "But the obedience of Christ is not formally our action or quality." For it is ours, not indeed by inherence but by gift; and in the same way, as I have observed several times already, the disobedience of Adam is not ours. Add that what is imputed to us is the satisfaction of Christ, not properly as it is an action or quality, but as it is the punishment that he suffered in our place; in this sense righteousness is called not moral but merely forensic. So far from overthrowing the imputation of Christ's righteousness by refuting the immediate imputation of Adam's actual disobedience, I rather make the imputation of Christ's righteousness safer by dissociating it from that, as from an unequal partner of doubtful good faith.

units.la: G A R. Si qui sic argumentantur, vocem formaliter accipiunt, quomodo fumi solet apud Philosophos, ratione sua nihil efficiunt, quod nos non prolixe largiamur. Quid est enim formalite? Audi Philosophorum primipilos. Formaliter idem est seu ἰσο- δυναμει sequentibus, ἐνυπαρχνη subiecto aliquid quod reipsa inest, vt forma, vel in modum formae, ἐξηκως, habitualiter &c. Haec si ita sunt, agnoscimus nullum esse hominem, qui vel per actualem inobedientiam Adae formaliter peccator sit, vel per actualem obedientiam Christi formaliter iustus. &c. Neque enim dicimus nos imputata iustitiae iustos esse formaliter, sed imputative, non ἐξηκως, sed χηκως; non subiectiue, sed relatiue. Ita nos in hac causa non dicimus, nos imputata Adami inobedientia peccatores esse formaliter, sed imputative, non ἐξηκως, sed χηκως, non subiectiue, sed relatiue.
units.tr: GAR. If those who argue in this way take the word formally as it is commonly used among the Philosophers, they achieve nothing that we do not willingly grant them. For what is formally? Hear the chief of the Philosophers. "Formally" is the same as equivalently [ἰσοδυναμεῖ] in the following senses: inherent in the subject [ἐνυπάρχειν], something which in reality is present, as a form, or in the manner of a form; by habit [ἐξ ἕξεως], habitually, etc. If these things are so, we acknowledge that there is no man who is formally a sinner through the actual disobedience of Adam, or formally righteous through the actual obedience of Christ, etc. For we do not say that we are righteous formally by imputed righteousness, but imputatively, not by habit [ἐξ ἕξεως] but relatively [σχετικῶς]; not subjectively but relatively. So in this matter we do not say that we are formally sinners through the imputed disobedience of Adam, but imputatively, not by habit but relatively, not subjectively but relatively.

units.la: PLAC. Si ita est, Apostolus neque causaliter, neque formaliter voluit multos esse per inobedientiam Adami constitutos peccatores, seu iniustos, sed tantum imputatiue. Hoccine sensit Vir doctus? ita videtur. Atqui constat, nec potest vllo modo negari, multos, seu omnes, esse inobedientia Adami constitutos peccatores causaliter: est enim illa inobedientia causa peccati quo sumus formaliter peccatores. Constat quoque, nec potest negari, omnes esse formaliter peccatores seu iniustos, id quae a prima illa inobedientia Adami profluxisse. Quomodo ergo Apostolus constituit peccatores neque causaliter, neque formaliter intellexit, sed imputatiue tantum, cum verum sit nos esse formaliter peccatores, & huius rei causam esse inobedientiam Adami? Si non fors maliter, sed imputatiuè, non subiectiuè sed relatiuè peccato-res ex Adamo nascimur, vicit Pighius, & originale vitium inhærens aut nullum est, aut non est verè peccatum omnes homines coram Deo reos peragens. Nascimur quidem, inquiet forte aliquis, peccatores formaliter, sed huius peccati inhærentis rationem hoc loco non habet Apostolus, quia non loquitur de sanctificatione, sed de iustificatione. Imò verò, inquam, huius peccati, quia de iustificatione loquitur, habere rationem eum decuit, siquidem est verè peccatum, & omnes homines reos coram Deo peragit, omnibusque damnandis sufficit; eatenus enim maximè iustificationi opponitur, & ab eo iustificandi fuimus. Sed audiamus qua ratione Vir doctus probet nos imputatâ Adami inobedientia non esse formaliter constitutos peccatores.
units.tr: PLAC. If that is so, the Apostle meant that many were constituted sinners, or unrighteous, through Adam's disobedience neither causally nor formally, but only imputatively. Did the learned man really think this? It seems so. But it is certain, and cannot in any way be denied, that all or many were made sinners causally by Adam's disobedience, since that disobedience is the cause of the sin by which we are formally sinners. It is also certain, and cannot be denied, that all are formally sinners or unrighteous, and that this has flowed from that first disobedience of Adam. How then could the Apostle have understood that men are constituted sinners neither causally nor formally, but only imputatively, when it is true that we are formally sinners and that the cause of this is Adam's disobedience? If we are born sinners not formally but imputatively, not subjectively but relatively, then Pighius has won, and inherent original sin either does not exist or is not truly sin, making all men guilty before God. Someone may perhaps reply that we are indeed born formally sinners, but that the Apostle does not take account of this inherent sin here, because he speaks not of sanctification but of justification. On the contrary, I say: since he speaks of justification, he ought to have taken account of this sin, for it is truly sin, it makes all men guilty before God, and it is enough to condemn all; in that respect it is especially opposed to justification, and it is from it that we needed to be justified. But let us hear by what reasoning the learned man proves that we are not constituted formally sinners by the imputed disobedience of Adam.

units.la: GAR. Nam ita peccatores constituimur, quomodo fuimus in Adamo. At in Adamo non fuimus formaliter, sed radicaliter. Ergo neque in eo dici possumus constitui formaliter peccatores; sed quia quod ille fecit, imputatur eis qui in ipso erant radicaliter, id est, ut loquebatur superius Augustinus, qui in seipsis multi sunt, sed in Adamo unus homo erant.
units.tr: GAR. For we are constituted sinners in the same way that we were in Adam. But we were not in Adam formally, but radically. Therefore we cannot be said to be constituted formally sinners in him; rather, what he did is imputed to those who were in him radically, that is, as Augustine said above, they are many in themselves but were one man in Adam.

units.la: PLAC. Quid si subsumam, At in Adamo non fuimus imputatiue. Ergo neque in eo dici possumus constitui imputatiuè peccatores? Quid respondebitur? Negabiturne maior? nullum igitur est hoc argumentum Viri docti. Negabiturne minor? non potest; euidenter vera est: nam neque esse nostrum imputatum est Adamo, neque esse Adami imputatum est nobis. Quomodo ergo fuimus in Adamo? Radicaliter, inquit. Ergo, inquam, constituti sumus peccatores in Adamo radicaliter. Hoc posita maiore necessariò sequitur. Quid porrò est, fuisse in Adamo radicaliter, nisi, Adamum fuisse radicem, unde nos tanquam rami prodijmus? esse Adami fuisse radicem, principium, causam nostri esse? Quid erit ergo constitui radicaliter peccatores in Adamo, nisi Adamum vel Adami peccatum esse radicem, vel principium, vel causam, unde tanquam ramus enatum est peccatum nostrum? Hoc autem ipsum est quod dixi, præeunte Chamiero, nos esse inobedientiâ Adami constitutos peccatores causaliter. Quid enim intereft inter radicaliter & causaliter? Cæterum qui dicit causaliter constitui peccatores, intelligit peccatores constitui pecca-to formaliter inhærente: itaque constitui causaliter, & conftitui formaliter peccatorem fubordinantur, fe'eque mutuò, vt causa & effectum, ponunt & tollunt. Impossibile enim est vt quis constitutus fuerit verè peccator seu iniustus, nec tamen formaliter fuerit peccator seu iniustus. Qui enim iniustum dicit, duo dicit, subiectum vt materiam, & iniustitiam vt formam: Est enim nomen, vt loquuntur, concretum, cujus materiale significatum est persona, formale injustitia. Quod est causa injustitiæ, illud constituit injustum causaliter, ipsa vero injustitia iustum constituit formaliter; est enim ipsa forma & effentia injusti, fine qua nec esse, nec concipi animo potest. Quare fi fumus iniusti imputatâ Adami injustitiâ, constitu̇t nos injustos illa injustitia, non vt causa efficiens nostræ injuftitiæ, sed vt forma, quam justi nomen eo sensu sumptum formaliter significat; id autem mihi est formaliter constituere. Formaliter igitur nos constituit justos imputata Christi justitia, justos, inquam, non sumpto hoc vocabulo sensu morali aut philosophico, sed sensu forensi: est enim satisfactio pro peccatis nostris præstita loco nostro à vade nostro, ac ita nobis donata. Formaliter vero injustos eo modo facere nos non poteft Adami injustitia: non enim loco nostro ab Adamo præstita est, nec vllo modo nobis donata: Iustitia autem Iudicis facit nos peccatores seu injustos imputatione alieni peccati: nihil est enim ejusmodi imputatione alienius à justitia justi judicis. Quamuis igitur dici possit aliquis justus forensi ratione à forma externa, justitia data & imputata, seu remissione, vel abolitione forensi peccatorum, tamen nemo poreft dici peccator veli injustus verè seu in foro diuino ab externâ forma, injustitia alienà imputata. Est enim Dei iudicium secundum veritatem & æquitatem, nec vllo modo causa cur simus peccatores & injusti.
units.tr: PLAC. What if I take the minor premise to be: "But we were not in Adam imputatively"? Then it would follow that we cannot be said to be constituted imputatively sinners in him. What will be replied? Will the major premise be denied? Then this argument of the learned man is nothing. Will the minor be denied? It cannot be; it is plainly true, for neither is our being imputed to Adam, nor Adam's being imputed to us. How then were we in Adam? "Radically," he says. Therefore, I say, we were constituted sinners in Adam radically. This follows necessarily once the major premise is granted. What, moreover, is it to have been in Adam radically, except that Adam was the root from which we came forth as branches? To have Adam's being is to have been the root, the principle, the cause of our being. What then is it to be constituted sinners radically in Adam, except that Adam, or Adam's sin, is the root, or principle, or cause from which our sin has sprung like a branch? This is exactly what I said, following Chamier: that we are constituted sinners causally by Adam's disobedience. For what difference is there between radically and causally? Moreover, whoever says that men are constituted sinners causally understands that they are constituted sinners by sin inhering formally. So being constituted causally and being constituted a sinner formally are subordinate, and they mutually posit and remove each other, as cause and effect do. For it is impossible for someone to be truly constituted a sinner or unrighteous and yet not be formally a sinner or unrighteous. Whoever calls someone unrighteous says two things: the subject, as matter, and unrighteousness, as form. The word, as they say, is concrete: its material signification is the person, its formal signification is unrighteousness. What causes unrighteousness constitutes someone unrighteous causally, but unrighteousness itself constitutes him unrighteous formally, for it is the very form and essence of the unrighteous, without which it can neither exist nor be conceived. Therefore, if we are unrighteous by the imputed unrighteousness of Adam, that unrighteousness makes us unrighteous not as the efficient cause of our unrighteousness but as its form, which the word unrighteous, taken in that sense, signifies formally; and this, for me, is to constitute formally. Therefore the imputed righteousness of Christ constitutes us formally just, just I say, not in a moral or philosophical sense of this word, but in a forensic sense: for it is satisfaction for our sins, offered in our place by our surety, and thus given to us. But Adam's unrighteousness cannot make us formally unrighteous in that way, for it was not offered by Adam in our place, nor was it in any way given to us. The justice of the Judge makes us sinners or unrighteous by the imputation of another's sin, for nothing is more alien to the justice of a just judge than such imputation. Although, therefore, one may be called just in a forensic sense, from an external form (justice given and imputed, that is, forensic remission or abolition of sins), nevertheless no one can truly be called a sinner or unrighteous, in the divine court, from an external form, namely another's unrighteousness imputed. For God's judgment is according to truth and equity, and it is in no way the cause why we are sinners and unrighteous.

units.la: Alterum argumentum duco ex nomine peccatores ἁμάρτωλοί : est enim aduersus Pighium & Socinum obseruatum à magnis Theologis, neminem dici peccatorem in sacris literis coram Deo, qui verè in se peccatum catum non habeat. Id argumentum sic Petrus Martyr proponit aduersus Pighium. Postremo habemus a Paulo per inobedientiam vnius hominis multos constitutos esse peccatores: quod indicat in illis qui nascuntur ex Adamo esse vitium, propter quod peccatores dici pqfint. Scd hoc Pighius putat se posse eludere, quod peccatores interdum dicantur propter reatum, quamuis actio peccandi praeterierit, neque amplius extet. Quamuis hoc ita fit, nunquam tamen ostendere potest ex scripturis quemquam peccatorum appellari, quin, aut in se ipso vitium habeat, aut certe antea admiserit: nisi dicere velit Deum homines reos facere absque ipsorum aliquo peccato. Chamierus vero sic adversus eundem Pighium, vno verbo, nunquam ἀμάρτωλος dicitur de simplici reatu, & absque vllo vitio, aut peccato. Ergo cum dixit Paulus multos esse constitutos peccatores per vnius inobedientiam, nihil aliud intellexit nisi eo Adami peccato effectum esse vt omnes homines revera & in se peccatores essent. Et rursus alio loco, A Paulo autem doceri vnicum esse numero in omnibus peccatum originale: hoc vero insigniter falsum. Nam contra per vnius inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi: eodem capite. Peccator autem est qui ipse habet peccatum suum, non autem cui alienum imputatur. Alibi ἁμάρτωλον nunquam dici, nisi in quo fit peccatum, probat memorabili ratione, alioquin, inquit, Christus dici posset ἁμάρτωλος peccator, quod absit. Enimvero si per vnius hominis peccatum nobis imputatum fumus formaliter peccatores, quid dices de Christo, cui tot aliena sunt imputata?
units.tr: A second argument I derive from the name sinners [ἁμάρτωλοί]. Great theologians have observed against Pighius and Socinus that no one in the Holy Scriptures is called a sinner before God who does not truly have sin in himself. Peter Martyr sets out this argument against Pighius thus: "Lastly, we have from Paul that many were constituted sinners through the disobedience of one man, which indicates that there is a vice in those who are born of Adam, on account of which they can be called sinners." But Pighius thinks he can evade this, because sinners are sometimes called so on account of guilt, although the act of sinning has passed and no longer exists. "Although this is so, he can never show from the Scriptures that anyone is called a sinner unless he either has a vice in himself or has certainly sinned before; unless he wishes to say that God makes men guilty without any sin of their own." Chamier, however, argues against the same Pighius thus: "In a word, [ἁμάρτωλος] is never said of mere guilt, and without any vice or sin. Therefore, when Paul said that many were constituted sinners through the disobedience of one, he understood nothing other than that by that sin of Adam it came about that all men were in truth and in themselves sinners." And again elsewhere: "It is taught by Paul that original sin is one in number in all; but this is notably false. For on the contrary, many are constituted sinners through the disobedience of one, in the same chapter. But a sinner is one who has his own sin, not one to whom another's sin is imputed." Elsewhere, he proves with a memorable argument that [ἁμάρτωλον] is never said except of one in whom sin is present: "otherwise," he says, "Christ could be called a sinner, which God forbid." Indeed, if we are formally sinners through the sin of one man imputed to us, what will you say of Christ, to whom so many alien sins were imputed?

units.la: GAR. Resp. Hoc ita simpliciter dici non posse patet ex i. Reg. 1. 21. Ego & filius meus peccatores, id est, habebimur tanquam peccatores, & nobiscum velut cum peccatoribus agetur. Itaque vanum est argumentum quod hic ex voce peccatores desumitur. Dico enim nihil impedire, quominus hic peccatores vocentur, qui reatum Adæ peccati sustinent.
units.tr: GAR. Reply: that this cannot be said simply in this way is plain from 1 Reg. 1. 21: "I and my son shall be sinners," that is, we shall be reckoned as sinners, and we shall be dealt with as sinners. Therefore the argument drawn here from the word sinners is vain. For I say that nothing prevents those who bear the guilt of Adam's sin from being called sinners here.

units.la: PLAC. Atqui hoc non ita simpliciter dixeram, sed cum hac limitatione quam Vir doctus omisit, coram Deo: ut ad rem non fit vllo modo locus quem laudat ex 1. Reg. 1. 21. Non enim eo loco habita ratione judicij diuini semper veri & iusti, sed judicij humani falsi & iniusti, peccatores Salomon & eius mater dicuntur. Itaque non est vanum argumentum, quod hic ex voce peccatores desumitur, sed solidum & inuictum: Agitur enim hic de constituendis peccatoribus relate ad forum diuinum, non autem ad humanum. Quod subiungit, imputationem primi peccati & corruptionem inhærentem, utrumque unicum reatum efficere, id, ut iam obseruaui, pro imputatione primi peccati mediata militat aduersus immediatam. Pighius sentiebat cum iis, qui mihi in hac causa aduersantur, primum peccatum actuale Adami nobis immediatè imputari. Communis sententia communibus argumentis refellitur. Itaque hoc argumentum, vt alia nonnulla, Theologi aduersus Pighium disputantes mihi suppeditarunt; nihilque potest ei reponi, quod non iuuet causam Pighij. Locus Chamieri, quem hic laudat Vir doctus ex tom. 3. lib. 1. cap. 7. §. 21, egregius est, mihique ita fauorabilis, Viro autem docto repugnans, ut mirari satis non possim qua mente fit ab eo laudatus. Itaque ego quoque illum transcribam; Nec contra est quicquam capite quinto. Nam in eo Paulus de initio tractat humanæ damnationis: quod certum est manasse ab vno illo Adami peccato, per quod constituti sunt peccatores omnes homines; ideoque obnoxij damnationi, & morti. Vides nos esse obnoxios damnationi & morti, quia sumus constituti peccatores. Quid autem per peccatorem intelligit? discere ex eius verbis antecedentibus §. xx. peccator autem est qui ipse habet peccatum suum, NON AVTEM CVI ALIENVM IMPVTATVR. Sed pergat. Itaque illa oppositio in illo, non in nobis, illius obedientia, non sua propria quisque; non est a mente Apostoli; sed a Sophista commento. Non enim subalterna repugnant. In Adamo peccauimus omnes: quia Adamus primus peccauit: & inde initium factum peccati in omnibus hominibus: at in nobis etiam peccamus: quia eius peccato constituti sumus peccatores : id est, ab eo in nos peccatum propagatum. Debebat dicere ex mente Viri docti, id elt, eius peccatum nobis est imputatum. Sed audi quod sequitur; se enim ipse explicat. Et illius inobedientia eodem modo sumus omnes constituti peccatores : quo nostra etiam propria iam vere sumus peccatores: alioqui falsum esset, nos illius inobedientia constitutos esse peccatores. Hæc profecto mea est constitutionis illius, & vocis peccatoris expositio, quam Vir doctus reiecit.
units.tr: PLAC. But I had not said this simply, but with the limitation which the learned man omitted, "before God," so that the passage he cites from 1 Reg. 1. 21 has no bearing on the matter at all. For in that place Solomon and his mother are called sinners not by the judgment of God, which is always true and just, but by a human judgment, which is false and unjust. So the argument drawn here from the word sinners is not vain, but solid and invincible, for what is being dealt with here is the constitution of sinners in relation to the divine court, not the human. As for what he adds, that the imputation of the first sin and inherent corruption together make one guilt, this, as I have already observed, argues for mediate imputation of the first sin against immediate imputation. Pighius agreed with those who oppose me in this cause that Adam's first actual sin is imputed to us immediately. A common opinion is refuted by common arguments. Therefore this argument, like several others, the theologians disputing against Pighius have supplied to me, and nothing can be put in reply to him that does not help Pighius's cause. The passage of Chamier which the learned man quotes here, from vol. 3, book 1, chap. 7, §. 21, is excellent and so favourable to me, yet opposed to the learned man, that I cannot sufficiently wonder with what mind he cited it. So I too will transcribe it: "Nor is there anything contrary in chapter five. For in it Paul treats of the beginning of human condemnation, which is certainly derived from that one sin of Adam, through which all men were constituted sinners, and therefore liable to condemnation and death. You see that we are liable to condemnation and death because we are constituted sinners." But what does he understand by sinner? Learn it from his preceding words, §. 20: "a sinner is one who has his own sin himself, NOT ONE TO WHOM ANOTHER'S SIN IS IMPUTED." But let him go on: "Therefore that opposition, between that one's obedience and not our own, each one's own, is not from the mind of the Apostle but from a sophist's invention. For subordinate things do not conflict. In Adam we all sinned, because Adam sinned first, and thence the beginning of sin was made in all men; but in us also we sin, because we have been constituted sinners by his sin, that is, sin propagated from him into us." He ought to have said, in the mind of the learned man, that his sin was imputed to us. But hear what follows, for he explains himself: "And by his disobedience we are all constituted sinners in the same way that by our own we are now truly sinners; otherwise it would be false that we are constituted sinners by his disobedience." This indeed is my explanation of that constitution and of the word sinner, which the learned man has rejected.

units.la: Sed ex altero huius verf. 19. membro vltimum tuum argumentum educis. Te igitur audiamus. Id vero, inquis, clarius & manifestius patet ex altero membro comparationis quam instituit Apostolus inter primum & secundum Adamum. Nam quemadmodum a primo vno est peccatum, reatus, & mors, sic ab uno Iesu Christo est gratia, iustitia, & vita. In illo malum, in hoc remedium. Hinc conclusio est facilis & manifesta; velut omnia hæc bona habemus in Christo per imputationem obedientiæ & iustitiæ illius, sic omnia illa mala habemus in Adamo per imputationem inobedientiæ & peccati ipsius. Facilis quidem tibi fuit hæc conclusio, sed mihi non est manifesta: Immo falsum apparet eius posterius membrum. In priore illud etiam observo, gratiam, quâ nobis datus est Christus, quâ data & imputata est eius obedientia, non haberi per imputationem obedientiæ Christi; id enim contradictionem implicaret. Sed tu sic argumentaris, Obedientia illa Christi nos constituit iustos coram Deo, & dat vitam, quia nobis imputatur. Ergo ex oppositione sequitur, inobedientiam Adami nos constituere peccatores & morti obnoxios reddere, quia nobis imputatur. Nego id sequi; cur non sequatur, rationem reddidi & probaui in Thesibus: Si sic similiter colligam, quid respondebis? Obedientia illa Christi nos constituit iustos coram Deo,
units.tr: But you draw your last argument from the other part of this verse 19. So let us hear you. That, you say, is clearer and more manifest from the other member of the comparison that the Apostle draws between the first and the second Adam. For as from the one first man comes sin, guilt and death, so from the one Jesus Christ comes grace, righteousness and life. In the one is the evil, in the other the remedy. From this the conclusion is easy and plain: just as we have all these good things in Christ through the imputation of his obedience and righteousness, so we have all those evils in Adam through the imputation of his disobedience and sin. That conclusion was easy for you, but it is not plain to me. Indeed, its latter part looks false. In the former part I also observe that the grace by which Christ was given to us, by which his obedience was given and imputed, is not had through the imputation of Christ's obedience; for that would involve a contradiction. But you argue thus: Christ's obedience makes us righteous before God and gives life, because it is imputed to us.
