Therefore, by parity, it follows that Adam's disobedience makes us sinners and renders us liable to death, because it is imputed to us. I deny that this follows. Why it does not follow I have given my reasons and proved in my Theses. If I draw the same inference in a similar way, what will you answer? Christ's obedience makes us righteous before God,

units.la: & dat vitam, quoniam illa nobis Dei summa gratia data est. Ergo ex oppositione sequitur inobedientiam Adami nos constituere peccatores, quoniam illa nobis ex gratia data est: vel sic, Obedientia Christi nos constituit iustos coram Deo, quoniam Christus fuit vas noster & nostro loco satisfecit. Ergo ex oppositione sequitur inobedientiam Adami nos constituere peccatores, quia Adamus fuit vas noster, & nostro loco rebellis Deo fuit: vel sic, Obedientia Christi nos constituit iustos coram Deo, quia ei per fidem consentimus. Ergo ex oppositione sequitur inobedientiam Adami nos constituere peccatores, quia ei consentimus. Item, obedientia Christi nos constituit iustos sensu forensi tantum per imputationem, non autem per infusionem iustitiæ, quæ mereatur vitam æternam. Ergo ex oppositione sequitur inobedientiam Adami nos constituere peccatores sensu forensi tantum per imputationem, non autem per propagationem iniustitiæ seu vitij, quod mereatur mortem æternam. Denique (nam infinitum esset talia omnia enumerare) obedientia Christi nos constituit iustos ex vere iniustis, idque supernaturaliter, non per carnalem generationem, sic ut tota nostra iustificatio, quanta quanta est, posita sit in illius imputatione. Ergo ex oppositione sequitur, inobedientiam Adami nos ex vere iustis constituere peccatores eodem modo. Si tibi non probantur hæ consequentiæ, causam non video, cur tua mihi probetur. Ceterum huius tui argumenti solutionem potuisti legere apud Calvinum in Rom. v. xvii. & Clarissimum D. Rivetum in summa Controversi. Tract. iv. q. 2. §. 8. de eodem plura habebis in Apologia pro thesibus meis.
units.tr: and gives life, because that obedience was given to us by the highest grace of God. Therefore, by parity, it follows that Adam's disobedience makes us sinners, because it was given to us out of grace. Or thus: Christ's obedience makes us righteous before God, because Christ was our surety and satisfied in our place. Therefore, by parity, it follows that Adam's disobedience makes us sinners, because Adam was our surety and rebelled against God in our place. Or thus: Christ's obedience makes us righteous before God, because we consent to it by faith. Therefore, by parity, it follows that Adam's disobedience makes us sinners, because we consent to it. Again: Christ's obedience makes us righteous only in a forensic sense, through imputation, and not through the infusion of a righteousness that merits eternal life. Therefore, by parity, it follows that Adam's disobedience makes us sinners only in a forensic sense, through imputation, and not through the propagation of unrighteousness or vice that merits eternal death. Finally (for it would be endless to list all such inferences), Christ's obedience makes us righteous out of those who are truly unrighteous, and this supernaturally, not by carnal generation, so that our whole justification, however great it is, rests on the imputation of his obedience. Therefore, by parity, it follows that Adam's disobedience makes us, out of those who are truly righteous, sinners in the same way. If these inferences do not seem to you valid, I do not see why yours should seem valid to me. Moreover, you could have read the solution of this argument of yours in Calvin on Romans 5, verse 17, and in the most distinguished Dr. Rivet's Summa of Controversies, tract 4, question 2, section 8. You will find more on the same point in my Apology for my Theses.

units.la: GAR. Resp. eius ratiocinationis consequentiam cum ratione negari non posse. Demus enim integrum Syllogismum. Ille eiusmodi erit. Sicut obedientia Christi nos constituit iustos, ita & inobedientia Adami peccatores. Atqui obedientia Christi nos iustos constituit, quia imputatur. Ergo & inobedientia Adae nos peccatores constituit, quia imputatur. Argumentum est legitime constitutum ratione formae. Itaque consequentia negari non debuit.
units.tr: GAR. I reply that the consequence of this reasoning cannot be denied with reason. Let us grant the full syllogism. It would be of this kind: Just as Christ's obedience makes us righteous, so Adam's disobedience makes us sinners. But Christ's obedience makes us righteous because it is imputed. Therefore Adam's disobedience also makes us sinners because it is imputed. The argument is lawfully constructed in respect of its form. Therefore the consequence ought not to have been denied.

units.la: PLAC. Negaui consequentiam; quia Syllogismus mihi obiectus, non erat integer, sed enthymema; quod cum constet ex duabus propositionibus, vna praemissa, & conclusione, quarum illa antecedens, haec consequens vocatur, nihil prohibet, idque fieri consueuit, vt negetur consequentia; id quod perinde valet ac si negaretur omissa propositio. Nunc cum suae integritati restituatur Syllogismus a Viro docto, respondeo ad Maiorem; eam aut universaliter intelligi, aut particulariter; si illud, falsam esse, si hoc, nullam esse consequentiam Syllogismi in prima figura ex maiore particulari constantis. vel sic, voces Sicut, ita, notant similitudinem, vel in ipsa rei veritate sitam, vel in modo illius veritatis: Si prius, negatur consequentia: fallacia enim est. Nam cum maior intelligenda sit de ipsa re, non autem de rei illius modo, subiungitur ei minor in qua agitur de rei modo: itaque sunt quatuor termini. Si posterius, negatur propositio: quam enim egregia est in ipsa re similitudo, tam est conspicua dissimilitudo in modo, vt exemplis feci manifestum.
units.tr: PLAC. I denied the consequence because the syllogism put to me was not complete but an enthymeme; which, since it consists of two propositions, one premise and a conclusion, of which the first is called the antecedent and the second the consequent, may well have a consequence denied, as is customary; and this comes to the same thing as denying the omitted proposition. Now that the syllogism has been restored to completeness by the learned author, I reply to the major premise: it must be understood either universally or particularly. If the former, it is false; if the latter, there is no valid consequence in a first-figure syllogism with a particular major premise. Or again: the words just as and so signal a likeness either in the very truth of the thing or in the mode of that truth. If the former, the consequence is denied, for it is a fallacy. For since the major premise must be understood of the thing itself and not of the mode of that thing, a minor premise dealing with the mode of the thing is subjoined to it; and so there are four terms. If the latter, the proposition is denied; for just as striking as the likeness is in the thing itself, so conspicuous is the dissimilarity in the mode, as I have made clear by examples.

units.la: At subiungit Vir doctus, Maior est ex Apostolo, nisi quod comparationis partes transponuntur, vt ex protasi fiat apodosis, & contra. Maior certe est ex Apostolo, sed non est urgenda similitudo praeter Apostoli mentem. Extensio similitudinis ad modum rei non est de mente Apostoli, eiusque propositionem ex verissima falsam facit. Haec propositio maior nititur differentis Christi verbis, debemus esse misericordes sicut Pater noster est misericors. Luc. 6. 36. Transponantur similiter partes similitudinis. Sicut Deus est misericors, ita debemus esse misericordes; & subsumatur minor vera, Atqui Deus est misericors ellentialiter, sequitur falsa conclusio, Ergo debemus esse misericordes essentialiter: Nimirum quia similitudo praeter Christi mentem ad modum rei vniuersaliter extenditur, & ita vel falsa fit propositio, vel committitur fallacia à figura dictionis.
units.tr: But the learned author adds: The major premise is from the Apostle, except that the parts of the comparison are transposed, so that the protasis becomes the apodosis and vice versa. The major premise is certainly from the Apostle, but the likeness must not be pressed beyond the mind of the Apostle. To extend the likeness to the mode of the thing is not the mind of the Apostle, and it makes his proposition false out of one that is most true. This major premise rests on the words of Christ: Be merciful, as your Father also is merciful. Luke 6:36. Let the parts of the likeness be similarly transposed: As God is merciful, so ought we to be merciful; and let a true minor premise be subsumed: But God is merciful essentially. There follows a false conclusion: Therefore we ought to be merciful essentially. Clearly this is because the likeness, beyond Christ's mind, is universally extended to the mode of the thing, and so either the proposition becomes false or a fallacy of the figure of speech is committed.

units.la: GAR. 2, Non ij sumus qui ex illis comparationis Apostolicæ verbis exististimemus quemlibet comparationis modum colligi posse; Esset enim hoc absurdissimum. &c.
units.tr: GAR. 2. We are not of those who, from those words of the Apostolic comparison, think that any mode of comparison whatever may be inferred; for this would be most absurd, etc.

units.la: PLAC. Ergo, inquam, propositio Argumenti cui respondeo, de modo comparationis accepta, non est vniuersaliter vera, sed particulariter duntaxat; quo posito sequitur non bene concludere argumentum, quippe, in prima figura ex maiore particulari.
units.tr: PLAC. Therefore, I say, the proposition of the argument to which I reply, taken with respect to the mode of the comparison, is not universally true but only particularly true; and given this, it follows that the argument does not conclude well, being in the first figure with a particular major premise.

units.la: GAR. Sed titulum respicimus, id est, scopum & seriem Paulinæ disputationis attendimus. Voluit enim, vt diximus, & saepius monere oportet, ostendere rationem iustificationis nostræ coram Deo per imputatam iustitiam ex nobili typo Adæ. At certè non potuit illam imputationem iustitiæ, Adami typo confirmare, si non in Adamo præcessit aliquid, quod ad imputationem pertineat. Sicut ergo Paulus in negotio, quod habebat præ manibus, iustificationem ex imputatâ iustitiâ ostendit per exemplum condemnationis ex imputato Adæ peccato: Ita nos Pauli vestigiis inhærentes, ex iustitiâ Christi imputatione colligimus imputationem inobedientiæ Adæ.
units.tr: GAR. But we look to the title, that is, we attend to the scope and sequence of Paul's argument. For he wished, as we have said, and it must be often pointed out, to show from the noble type of Adam the ground of our justification before God through imputed righteousness. Indeed he could not have confirmed that imputation of righteousness by the type of Adam, unless something had preceded in Adam that pertains to imputation. Therefore, just as Paul, in the matter he had in hand, showed justification through imputed righteousness by the example of condemnation through the imputed sin of Adam, so we, adhering to the footsteps of Paul, infer from the imputation of Christ's righteousness the imputation of Adam's disobedience.

units.la: PLAC. Id nec dicendum erat, nec saepius monendum, sed probandum, saltem semel, quod cum à Viro docto factum non sit, conferre nihil poterit ad firmandum argumentum. Rem ipsam confirmare voluit Apostolus nobili illa comparatione, non rei modum, quem dissimilem esse non obscurè innuit, vt à nobis iam saepius est obseruatum, cum illud quod est à Christo vocauit χάρισμα, χάριν, ἀπρῆμα &c, illud vero quod ab Adamo ἁμαρτία &c. Cæterum quoniam de iustificatione agitur, non constituimur iusti in foro diuino nisi imputata iustitia, nec peccatores seu iniusti nisi imputato peccato seu iniustitia: Quoniam autem nulla est in nobis iustitia, quæ possit nobis imputari ad iustificationem nostram, aliena nobis opus est, quæ dono nostra fit, & quia nostra, nobis possit iure imputari: Peccatores vero fumus peccato inhærente, vt nihil opus fit ad nos damnandos peccato alieno, nec peccatum alienum poteft nostrum esse dono; itaque imputari non potest, nisi mediante peccato inhærente quod peccati Adæ participatio est.
units.tr: PLAC. This should neither have been said nor often repeated, but proved, at least once; since the learned author has not done so, it can contribute nothing to strengthening his argument. The Apostle wished to confirm the thing itself by that noble comparison, not the mode of the thing, which he clearly hints is dissimilar, as we have often observed already, when he called what comes from Christ the gift [χάρισμα], the grace [χάρις], the free gift [...], and what comes from Adam sin [ἁμαρτία], etc. Moreover, since the question is about justification, we are not constituted righteous in the divine court except by imputed righteousness, nor sinners or unrighteous except by imputed sin or unrighteousness. Since there is no righteousness in us that could be imputed to us for our justification, we need an alien righteousness, which is made ours by gift, and which can rightly be imputed to us because it is made ours. But we are sinners by indwelling sin, so that there is no need for another's sin to condemn us, nor can another's sin become ours by gift; so it cannot be imputed, except through indwelling sin, which is the participation in Adam's sin.

units.la: Interim quia versum 21. citas, nec tamen quicquam argumenti ex eo exsculpis. Ego ex eo & præcedente argumentum colligam. Peccatum, quod ut abundaret lex Mosis præterea introijt, quodque abundauit, & regnauit ad mortem, est illud peccatum, quod per vnum hominem introiit in mundum, & per ipsum mors, vt manifestum est ex connexione versuum 20. & 21. cum antecedentibus. Sed peccatum, quod vt abundaret lex Mosis præterea introiit, & quod reuera abundauit, & quod regnauit ad mortem, non est peccatum actuale Adami imputatum, sed vitium inhærens, vt patet ex Rom. vi. 12. & 7. 8. 11. 13. 17.. Ergo peccatum, quod in mundum introiit, & per ipsum mors, non est peccatum actuale Adami nobis imputatum, sed vitium nobis inhabitans & inhærens.
units.tr: Meanwhile, since you cite verse 21 but draw no argument from it, I will draw one from that verse and the one before it. The sin that "entered in besides, that the offence might abound" under the law of Moses, that "abounded" and "reigned unto death," is the same sin that "entered into the world by one man, and death by sin," as is clear from the connection of verses 20 and 21 with what precedes. But the sin that entered in besides under the law of Moses, that really abounded, and that reigned unto death, is not Adam's actual sin imputed to us but the inhering vice, as appears from Rom. vi. 12. & 7. 8. 11. 13. 17. Therefore the sin that entered the world, and death through it, is not Adam's actual sin imputed to us but a vice dwelling and inhering in us.

units.la: Denique laudas 1. Cor. 15. verf. 21. 22. Per hominem mors, per hominem quoque resurrectio mortuorum; sicut enim in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita & in Christo omnes viuificabuntur. Sed quid habet iste locus, quod faueat imputationi peccati actualis Adami? Per hominem est mors, non vna numero reliquis hominibus imputata, sed hominum sua quisque morte moritur. In Adamo omnes moriuntur, sed sua quisque morte, non illa singulari vnius imputata omnibus. Idem de resurrectione statuendum; sua enim quisque resurrectione resurgit, sed vi Christi. At, inquis, Apostolus considerat omnes homines in Adamo mortuos. Visne igitur hoc quoque, ipsam illam mortem, quá Adamus mortuus est, omnibus imputari. Si igitur potuerunt considerari omnes homines in Adamo mortui, nec tamen omnibus imputari mors Adami, cur non potuerunt in Adamo omnes homines peccatores, nec tamen eius peccatum actuale omnibus imputari ? Quanquam falsum est consideratos fuisse ab Apostolo omnes homines in Adamo mortuos : loquitur enim de morte, qua quotidie & moriuntur & morientur homines, quæque adeò singularis, sua cuique, in propria persona reapse tàm conuenit, quàm olim Adamo sua ipsius vnius mors singularis. Sed, inquis, quemadmodum hi qui viuificantur considerantur in Christo cui vniuersi per fidem, & iustitia eius illis im-putatur ad iustificationem ; Cur non & cæteri considerabuntur in Adamo tanquam ipsi vniti, & peccatum ipsius illis imputari ad condemnationem? qui hoc negat, vereor ne alterutrum negare velit. Noli quæso de tuis fratribus, de seruis alienis, ita iudicare, qui imputationem illam peccati actualis non negant, nisi quia eam nec in Scriptura reperiunt, & Scripturæ repugnare vident, & Deo valdè iniuriosam credunt : itaque ab ea ex animo abhorrent. Cæterum errorem Socini negantis satisfactionem Domini nostri Iesu Christi nobis ad iustificationem imputari ex animo etiam detestor : inque illa imputatione totius meæ salutis spem constituo. Itaque eam sedulò ab improbabili illa vestrâ peccati actualis Adami imputatione separo, ne, si copulentur ac connectantur, disturbatâ aduersariorum machinis illa peccati primi imputatione, imputatio lunitiæ Christi iliius ruinis implicata, aliquid detrimenti capere videatur, quæ alioqui suis proprijs innixa fundamentis, totius religionis Christianæ bafis est ipsa terra solidior. Caeterum qui viuificantur considerantur in Christo id est communione Christi, & qui moriuntur, considerantur in communione Adami. Illa communio est spiritualis, haec carnalis. Illa ex gratia, haec ex natura: itaque nihil prohibet illam niti imputatione gratuita: huius dispar est ratio. Rursus imputatio iustitiae est ex gratia, peccati ex iustitia. Potest autem gratia tribuere alicui id quod ei non debetur, iustitia non potest. Dat gratia beneficium immerenti, iustitia poenam nisi merenti non irrogat, si meritum praemij imputatur non habenti, gratia est: at si poenae meritum non habenti imputetur nec iustitia est, nec gratia, nec quo nomine, nisi iniustitiae, appellari possit intelligo.
units.tr: Lastly you cite 1 Cor. 15. verses 21, 22: By man came death, by man also came the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive. But what does this passage have to do with the imputation of Adam's actual sin? By man comes death, but not one death imputed to all the rest of mankind; each man dies his own death. In Adam all die, but each dies his own death, not that single death of one man imputed to all. The same must be said of the resurrection: each rises by his own resurrection, but by the power of Christ. But, you say, the Apostle regards all men as dead in Adam. Do you then want that very death by which Adam died to be imputed to all? If all men could be regarded as dead in Adam without Adam's death being imputed to all, why could not all men be regarded as sinners in Adam without his actual sin being imputed to all? Yet it is false that the Apostle regarded all men as dead in Adam: he speaks of the death by which men die every day and will die, a death so individual and so truly belonging to each person in his own person as Adam's own single death once was to him. But, you say, just as those who are made alive are regarded as in Christ, with whom all are united through faith, and his righteousness is imputed to them for justification, why should not the rest also be regarded as in Adam, as united to him, and his sin be imputed to them for condemnation? Whoever denies this, I fear, is willing to deny the one or the other. Please, do not judge in this way about your brothers, about servants not your own, who do not deny that imputation of actual sin except because they find it nowhere in Scripture, see that it conflicts with Scripture, and believe it to be grossly injurious to God; therefore they shrink from it with all their heart. Moreover, I heartily detest the error of Socinus, who denies that the satisfaction of our Lord Jesus Christ is imputed to us for justification, and in that imputation I place the whole hope of my salvation. Therefore I carefully separate it from that unlikely imputation of Adam's actual sin of yours, lest, if they were joined and connected, the imputation of the first sin being overthrown by the engines of the adversaries, the imputation of Christ's righteousness should seem to suffer some loss, entangled in the ruins of that other; whereas it, resting on its own proper foundations, is firmer than the earth itself, the basis of the whole Christian religion. Moreover, those who are made alive are regarded as in Christ, that is, in communion with Christ, and those who die are regarded as in communion with Adam. That communion is spiritual, this one carnal; that one is from grace, this one from nature. Therefore nothing prevents the former from resting on gratuitous imputation; the reason for the latter is different. Again, the imputation of righteousness is from grace, the imputation of sin from justice. But grace can bestow on someone what is not owed to him; justice cannot. Grace gives a benefit to the undeserving; justice does not inflict punishment except on the deserving. If the merit of a reward is imputed to one who has no such merit, that is grace; but if the merit of punishment is imputed to one who has none, I do not understand what it can be called, except injustice, and not justice or grace.

units.la: GAR. Resp. 1. Festinasse videtur aliquantulum Vir doctus cum dixit communionem nostram spiritualem cum Christo niti imputatione gratuita iustitiae. Quia communionem cum Christo oportet esse priorem omnibus beneficijs, quae in Christo Deus nobis impertitur. Christus enim nobis primum datur, deinde per Christum, & in Christo, beneficia omnia conceduntur, Roman. viii. 32. Cum igitur inter ea beneficia numerari debeat iustitia imputatio, non ea niti dicenda est communio quam habemus cum Christo, sed potius illa communio fundamentum esse, cui & imputatio iustitia, & alia beneficia inaedificentur.
units.tr: GAR. Reply 1. The learned man seems to have hurried a little when he said that our spiritual communion with Christ rests on the gratuitous imputation of righteousness. For communion with Christ must come before all the benefits that God bestows upon us in Christ. For Christ is first given to us, and then all things are given through Christ and in Christ, Rom. viii. 32. Since, therefore, the imputation of righteousness must be counted among those benefits, the communion we have with Christ should not be said to rest on it; rather that communion is the foundation on which both the imputation of righteousness and the other benefits are built.

units.la: PLAC. Festinasse aliquantulum vitiosum non est, modo ne nimium. Loquebar de communione nostra cum Christo cuius vi viuificamur, seu resurgimus: cum dixi niti imputatione gratuita Christi. Id vir doctus reprehendit; quare? quia communionem cum Christo oportet esse priorem omnibus beneficijs, quae in Christo Deus nobis impertitur. Nimirum communio cum Christo suos habet gradus. Eius si spectes initium in fide, cum primum credimus in Christum, facile assentior viro docto, sed si progressum spectes, secus res habet. Loquebar autem non de ipso primo communionis illius initio, sed de eius progressu, de communione quam habemus cum Christi resurrectione, quæ niti ut iustificatione seu remissione peccatorum, atque adeò communione quam habemus cum eius morte. Rom. 6. 4. Vita enim iustificationem sequitur, ut mors condemnationem.
units.tr: PLAC. To have hurried a little is not a fault, provided it is not too much. I was speaking of our communion with Christ, by whose power we are made alive, or rise again, when I said that it rests on the gratuitous imputation of Christ. The learned man finds fault with this; why? Because communion with Christ must come before all the benefits that God bestows upon us in Christ. Of course communion with Christ has its degrees. If you look at its beginning in faith, when we first believe in Christ, I readily agree with the learned man; but if you look at its progress, the matter is otherwise. Now I was speaking not of the very first beginning of that communion but of its progress, of the communion we have with the resurrection of Christ, which rests on justification, or the remission of sins, and thus on the communion we have with his death (Rom. 6:4). For life follows justification as death follows condemnation.

units.la: GAR. 2. Sicut ea communio est idonea causa, quare nobis impertitur Christi iustitia: sic & coniunctio carnalis cum Adamo idonea causa esse potest, quare nobis imputetur Adami peccatum.
units.tr: GAR. 2. Just as that communion is a suitable cause why Christ's righteousness is bestowed on us, so also the carnal union with Adam can be a suitable cause why Adam's sin is imputed to us.

units.la: PLAC. Communio cum Christo fit per fidem. Fides est donatæ & oblatæ in Christo iustitiæ acceptio. Iustitia autem data à Deo & accepta à nobis nostra est; itaque nobis imputatur. Coniunctio carnalis cum Adamo, vel simpliciter est cum Adamo homine, vel cum Adamo peccatore: illa sita est in communione naturæ humanæ ab Adamo propagatæ, hæc in communione vitij naturæ inhærentis ab Adamo propagati. Illa sola non est idonea causa, quare nobis imputetur Adami peccatum; hæc idonea quidem causa est cur nobis peccatum Adami imputetur; sed ea imputatio non est immediata illa quam reijcio, sed mediata quam admitto.
units.tr: PLAC. Communion with Christ comes about through faith. Faith is the acceptance of the righteousness offered and given in Christ. But righteousness given by God and accepted by us is ours; therefore it is imputed to us. The carnal union with Adam is either simply union with Adam as a man, or union with Adam as a sinner. The former lies in the communion of human nature propagated from Adam; the latter in the communion of the vice of inhering nature propagated from Adam. The former alone is not a suitable cause why Adam's sin should be imputed to us; the latter is indeed a suitable cause why Adam's sin is imputed to us; but that imputation is not the immediate one that I reject, but the mediate one that I admit.

units.la: GAR. 3. In imputatione peccati Adæ, iustitia Dei non irrogat pœnam immerenti, sed aliqua ratione merenti. Itaque distinctione opus est. Nam quemadmodum iustitia est vel personalis & propria, vel aliena imputata. Ita meritum pœnæ aliud est proprium & personale, aliud participatum & commune, quod scilicet ex imputatione est, sive illa naturalis aut politica coniunctionis vinculo nittura, sive fœdere aliquo speciali; sive etiam utroque, ut fit in imputatione peccati Adæ, de quo sæpius dictum.
units.tr: GAR. 3. In the imputation of Adam's sin, the justice of God does not inflict punishment on one who has not deserved it, but on one who in some way has deserved it. Therefore a distinction is needed. For just as righteousness is either personal and one's own, or imputed and another's, so the merit of punishment is one thing that is one's own and personal, and another that is shared and common, which arises from imputation, whether that rests on the bond of natural or political union, or on some special covenant, or on both, as happens in the imputation of Adam's sin, about which I have spoken often.

units.la: PLAC. Volui ostendere discrimen inter gratiam & iustitiam, nec id Vir doctus conuellit, vtitur enim rationis loco distinctione. Quo iustitiæ alienæ imputatio nitatur, fatis, ut arbitror, expositum est. Quo nitatur imputatio peccati alieni, nempe Adami exponit secundum mentem suam Vir doctus. Id enim ait esse coniunctionem naturalem: hanc vero, si naturæ intelligatur coniunctio, non peccati, non sufficere ex eo patet, quod neque alia Adami, peccata, neque aliorum maiorum, dicuntur imputari; cum tamen non minor fit coniunctio naturæ: adiungit quidem coniunctioni naturali fœdus speciale; sed huius fœderis specialis probationem ex Scriptura petimus. Vides iam, opinor, quàm faciles solutu tuæ fuerint rationes : iacent non dissolutæ modo & dissipatæ, sed contrarijs argumentis multò & pluribus & graiuioribus prorsus obrutæ. Plures non attulisti nulla ingenij culpa, sed quia sententiam quam tueris omnis Scriptura, omnis ratio deficit; obtinuit duntaxat his postremis sæcnlis quorundam magnorum virorum incogitantiâ, quorum nomen plurimi re non attentè consideratâ secuti sunt : quod vt Deus tibi, & alijs omnibus, condonet ex toto corde supplex à Domino nostro Iesu Christo peto.
units.tr: PLAC. I wanted to show the difference between grace and righteousness, and the learned man does not overturn this; he uses a distinction in place of an argument. On what the imputation of another's righteousness rests, I think enough has been set out. On what the imputation of another's sin, namely Adam's, rests, the learned man explains according to his own mind: he says it is natural union. But that this natural union, if it is understood as union of nature and not of sin, is not sufficient, is clear from the fact that neither Adam's other sins nor those of his ancestors are said to be imputed, although the union of nature is no less. He does indeed add a special covenant to the natural union; but for proof of this special covenant we seek Scripture. I think you now see how easily your arguments could be solved: they lie not merely unsolved and scattered, but are utterly overwhelmed by many more and weightier contrary arguments. You have brought forward no more not from any lack of ingenuity, but because all Scripture and all reason fail the opinion you defend; it has prevailed only in these last centuries through the thoughtlessness of certain great men, whom many have followed without considering the matter carefully. May God pardon you and all others for this; I earnestly ask it of our Lord Jesus Christ with my whole heart.

units.la: CAPVT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Respondetur ad Patrum loca, quæ pro imputatione primi peccati Actualis adducuntur Cap. VI.
units.tr: A reply to the passages of the Fathers which are adduced for the imputation of the first actual sin, Chapter VI.

units.la: CVM tam paucas, tamque imbecillas rationes pro imputatione immediata primi peccati actualis omnibus hominibus, inuenire potueris, mirum non est, si suppetias petis à Patribus; quos tamen præfaris te citare, non vt fidei fundamentum, aut normam, (hunc honorem habes foli Scripturæ) sed vt testes fidei suorum temporum. Possem eos facile submouere ab hac quæstione. Nam dogma illud de imputatione primi peccati actualis, vel habetur in sacris literis, vel non habetur. Si non habetur, aut Scriptura fidei nostræ perfecta norma non est, aut non est credendum, vt vt illud docuissent Patres. Si habetur, age illud in ea quæramus : pauca continet volumina : perspicuè docet quicquid est nobis cognitu necessarium ad salutem. Eam igitur scrutemur. Multò id cùm facilius erit, tum tutius. Si Patres illud dogma in Scriptura non viderunt, quid est cur eos sequamur errantes extra Scripturam ? Si viderunt, quid est, cur idem & videre non possis, & mihi offendere ? quod si dogma illud pugnat cum sacris literis, audiendi non sunt qui id docent, etiamsi Patres sint, aut, vt loquitur Apostolus, Angeli de Cœlo. Clamo autem pugnare. Audi igitur primùm Scripturam, tum, si opus est, aduoca Patres. At tu maluisti imitari Pontificios, quos iuuat etiam Patres, vt fidei Ecclesiæ fui temporis testes proferre. Qui tamen non vt testes, sed vt doctores, nec vt aliorum omnium, sed vt suam quisque sententiam proferentes scripserunt. Eos tamen, quando ita tibi visum est, audiamus, eóque libentius quòd tibi profecto potius quàm mihi aduersentur: stant omnes à partibus meis. Quicquid pronunciant id, vel æquè ad meam ac tuam sententiam accommodatum est, vel tuæ repugnat, meæ fauet. Testes appello illa ipsa loca, quæ tu citasti ex sex tantum Patribus, Origene, Cypriano, Ambrosio, Augustino, Theophylacto, Bernardo; quorum primi & postremi quàm exigua sit authoritas, te fugere non potest. Quid enim isti Patres dicunt, quod putes obesse sententiæ meæ ? Num dicunt (quæ tua est sententia, meæ opposita) peccatum primum actuale Adami omnibus hominibus necessario & immediate imputari ad has poenas proprie dictas, mortè animæ quæ est vitium originale, Mortem corporis, & mortem æternam? Minimè. Nullus Patrum id dixit. Num saltem aliquid dicunt, unde talis imputatio bonâ consequentiâ colligi possit? nihil prorsus. Quid ergo dicunt?
units.tr: Since you could find so few and such feeble arguments for the immediate imputation of the first actual sin to all men, it is no wonder that you seek help from the Fathers. You say beforehand that you cite them not as the foundation or rule of faith (that honour you reserve for Scripture alone) but as witnesses to the faith of their own times. I could easily remove them from this question. That doctrine of the imputation of the first actual sin is either found in the sacred writings or it is not. If it is not, then either Scripture is not a complete rule of our faith, or the Fathers taught it without being credible. If it is found there, let us look for it in Scripture itself. It is a small collection of books, and it teaches clearly whatever we need to know for salvation. Let us therefore examine it, which will be much easier and safer. If the Fathers did not see this doctrine in Scripture, why should we follow them when they err outside Scripture? If they did see it, why can you not see it too, and why does it offend me? And if this doctrine contradicts the sacred writings, then those who teach it must not be heard, even if they are Fathers, or, as the Apostle puts it, angels from heaven. I say, however, that it does contradict them. Hear Scripture first, then, and if need be call the Fathers as well. But you preferred to imitate the Papists, who like to bring forward the Fathers as witnesses of the faith of the Church in their time. Yet the Fathers did not write as witnesses but as teachers, and not for everyone but each stating his own opinion. Still, since it has pleased you, let us hear them, and all the more willingly because they are clearly more opposed to you than to me. All of them stand on my side. Whatever they pronounce either agrees equally with my opinion and yours, or it contradicts yours and favours mine. I summon as witnesses those very passages which you cited from only six Fathers: Origen, Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, Theophylact and Bernard. You cannot overlook how slight the authority of the first and last of these is. For what do these Fathers say that you could think damages my view? Do they say (which is your view and opposed to mine) that the first actual sin of Adam is necessarily and immediately imputed to all men for those punishments properly so called: the death of the soul, which is original sin, the death of the body, and eternal death? Not at all. None of the Fathers said that. Do they at least say anything from which such an imputation could be rightly inferred? Nothing at all. What then do they say?

units.la: Dicunt, omnes homines fuisse in lumbis Adam, cùm adhuc esset in paradiso: Fuisse Adam, & in illo fuisse omnes: Fuisse omnes in primo homine, quando ille peccauit. Agnosco communes tibi & mihi locutiones. Sed amabo te, fuimusne in lumbis Adam duntaxat, cùm in paradiso primum suum peccatum actuale committeret. Nonne fuimus etiam in eius lumbis, cum eiectus e paradiso multa alia peccaret? Hinc igitur, si conficitur imputatio primi peccati actualis, conficietur eadem operâ imputatio reliquorum peccatorum Adami, saltem eorum, quae centum & triginta annorum spatio, antequam Sethum gigneret, admisit. Fuimusne in lumbis solius Adami, & non etiam aut aequè, aut magis aliorum parentum nostrorum intermediorum & proximorum? Non assentior Origeni sic colligenti, Si Leui qui generatione quarta post Abraham nascitur in lumbis Abrahae fuisse perhibetur, multò magis omnes homines qui in hoc mundo nascuntur, & nati sunt, in lumbis erant Adae, cùm adhuc esset in paradiso. Nam certè Leui non fuit in Adam, nisi quia fuit in Abraham; itaque si magis & minus hic locum habent, magis fuit in Abraham quàm in Adam, iuxta illud tritum in scholis, Propter quod vnumquodque est tale, illud est magis tale. Non fuimus in Adam, nisi vt effectum in causa. Porrò effectum magis est in causa sua proxima, quàm in remotissima. Nihil ab Adamo accepi immediatè, sed per longam seriem parentum, qui singuli genuerunt, non vt instrumenta aut membra Adami, sed vt causæ, æquè ac Adamus, principales : Et quicquid fui, cùm nascerer, id totum secundùm Deum proximis meis parentibus debeo proximè, avis meis remotè, proavis remotius, abavis & atavis adhuc remotius, Adamo omnium remotissimè. Si igitur fuimus in alijs nostris parentibus æquè, aut etiam magis, quàm in Adamo, hinc si efficitur imputatio peccati actualis Adami, efficitur eâdem operâ, ut debeant posteris etiam reliquorum parentum peccata imputari; quod tu ipse agnoscis Apostolo repugnare, unum hominem, unum peccatum inculcanti. Cur ergo Patres dicunt nos in Adamo fuisse? nempe ut intelligamus mirum non esse, si, cum ab eo traxerimus naturam, traxerimus cum natura etiam vitium. Traximus autem ab eo vitium & vitij subiectum naturam, non immediatè, sed alijs nostris parentibus mediantibus. Hinc mihi nascitur contra tuam sententiam novum argumentum. Nam qui non fuimus in Adamo immediatè & proximè non potuimus in eo immediatè & proximè peccare, sed mediantibus duntaxat omnibus alijs nostris parentibus. Attamen, si vera tua est sententia, in eo peccavimus immediatè. Tam enim proximè nobis eius peccatum primum actuale imputatur, quàm ipsi imputatum est, tam saltem, quàm nostris parentibus intermedijs.
units.tr: They say: all men were in the loins of Adam while he was still in paradise; Adam was, and in him all were; all were in the first man when he sinned. I recognise that these phrases are common to you and to me. But tell me, please: were we in the loins of Adam only when he committed his first actual sin in paradise? Were we not also in his loins when, driven out of paradise, he committed many other sins? So if the imputation of the first actual sin of Adam follows from this, the imputation of his other sins will follow at the same time, at least those which he committed in the span of one hundred and thirty years before he begot Seth. Were we in the loins of Adam alone, and not equally, or even more, in those of our other intermediate and nearer parents? I do not agree with Origen when he reasons thus: If Levi, who was born in the fourth generation after Abraham, is said to have been in the loins of Abraham, much more are all men who are born in this world, and have been born, in the loins of Adam, while he was still in paradise. For Levi was surely not in Adam except because he was in Abraham; so if there is a more and a less here, he was more in Abraham than in Adam, according to the common saying in the schools: whatever is the cause of something is more so than that thing itself. We were in Adam only as an effect in its cause. Now an effect is more in its nearest cause than in its most remote. I received nothing from Adam immediately, but through a long series of parents, each of whom begot me, not as instruments or members of Adam, but as principal causes, just as Adam was. Whatever I am, when I was born, I owe, under God, to my immediate parents most immediately, to my grandparents remotely, to my great-grandparents more remotely, to my great-great-grandparents and their ancestors still more remotely, and to Adam most remotely of all. So if we were in our other parents equally, or even more, than in Adam, then if the imputation of Adam's actual sin follows, it follows at the same time that the sins of all our other parents must be imputed to their posterity as well. You yourself admit that this contradicts the Apostle, who insists on one man and one sin. Why then do the Fathers say that we were in Adam? Surely so that we understand it is no wonder that, since we drew our nature from him, we drew sin along with that nature. But we drew from him the sinful nature and its subject, not immediately, but with our other parents as intermediaries. Hence a new argument arises for me against your view. For we who were not in Adam immediately and nearest could not have sinned in him immediately and nearest, but only through all our other parents as intermediaries. Yet if your view is true, we sinned in him immediately. For his first actual sin is imputed to us as closely as it was imputed to him, at least as closely as to our intermediate parents.

units.la: Deinde quæro, cùm dicimur fuisse in Adamo, qualis ea locutio fit, propria, an impropria? Propria esse non potest, nisi velis falsum esse primum illud omnis ratiocinationis principium, impossibile est simul esse & non esse. Proprie enim loquendo tunc, cùm Adamus peccauit, fuisemus, & non fuisemus; quæ aperta est contradictionis implicatio. Fuisemus proprie ex hypothesi, non fuissemus proprie loquendo, vt pater. Nulla enim tunc pars nostri fuit, immo ne femen quidem, aut pars feminis ex quo sumus procreati. Generatio est mutatio a non esse ad esse. Quod gignitur, aut fit, ante non erat: attamen praestrata est generationi materia, quae in genito permanet, & non esse geniti, cum incipit generari, priuatio est, non negatio. Sed cum peccaret Adamus, nondum erat quicquam materiae, vnde geniti sumus, ne remotissime quidem. Nam cum anno demum centesimo & trigesimo vitae Adami natus sit Seth secundus parens noster, non fit verisimile iam tum cum Adamus peccaret, in eo femen fuisse quo Sethum genuit: quod, si vllum fuisset in Cainum & Abelem esset insumptum. Itaque tunc non fuimus, non iam priuatiue, sed prorsus negatiue. Sed quid opus est probare nos proprie loquendo non fuisse aliquot annorum millibus antequam esse inciperemus? Iam si ista locutio fuimus in Adamo, propria non est, reuocanda est ad propriam, κυριολεκτικον τῆς μεταφορᾶς. Quid ergo significat proprie? nihil nisi nos ducere ab Adamo originem: esse Adami esse causam nostri esse. Qualis autem est causa? non essentialis, sed accidentalis, non proxima, sed remota, non propria, sed communis, & quae ad nos gignendos non magis per se contulit, quam ad multos gignendos, qui gigni quidem potuerunt, sed tamen defectu causae proxime geniti non sunt; quibus libenter quaesiuerim, an non etiam imputari debeat Adae peccatum. Potuit enim Adam eos mediate & remote, vt nos, gignere: Et vix poteft intelligi, quomodo vt quis ante quinque annorum millia fuerit, vel non fuerit, id pendere ab hodierna vel crastina actione possit. Sed pergamus? Quid adhuc dicunt illi Patres?
units.tr: Next I ask: when we are said to have been in Adam, is that way of speaking proper or improper? It cannot be proper, unless you wish to deny the first principle of all reasoning, it is impossible for a thing to be and not to be at the same time. For speaking properly, at the time when Adam sinned we both were and were not, which is an obvious contradiction. We would have been properly speaking only on a hypothesis; properly speaking we were not, as is clear. For then no part of us existed, not even the seed, nor any part of the seed from which we were produced. Generation is a change from not being to being. What is begotten or made did not exist before; yet matter is provided for the generation, which remains in what is begotten, and the non-being of the begotten, when it begins to be generated, is a privation, not a negation. But when Adam sinned, there was as yet no matter from which we were born, not even in the most remote sense. For since our second parent Seth was born only in the hundred and thirtieth year of Adam's life, it is not likely that at the time when Adam sinned there was in him the seed by which he begot Seth; and if there had been any, it would have been used up in Cain and Abel. So at that time we were not, not merely privatively but altogether negatively. But why is it necessary to prove that we did not properly exist for some thousands of years before we began to be? Now if the expression "we were in Adam" is not proper, it must be traced back to the proper sense, [κυριολεκτικον τῆς μεταφορᾶς], the literal sense of the metaphor. What then does "properly" mean? Nothing except that we derive our origin from Adam: that Adam's being is the cause of our being. But what sort of cause is it? Not essential but accidental, not proximate but remote, not peculiar but common, and one which contributed to begetting us no more directly than to begetting many others who could indeed have been begotten but, for lack of a proximate cause, were not. On these I would gladly ask whether the sin of Adam ought not also to be imputed to them. For Adam could have begotten them mediately and remotely, as he did us. And it can hardly be understood how whether someone existed or did not exist five thousand years ago could depend on today's or tomorrow's action. But shall we go on? What else do those Fathers say?

units.la: Dicunt nos in Adam peccasse, & quidem quasi in massa; & verba Apostoli, ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον, reddunt in quo omnes peccaverunt. Quid inde sequitur? Peccatum actuale Adami nobis omnibus imputari? non magis recte, quàm quia in eo fuimus, sequitur nobis eius esse imputari, aut, quia in eo creati sumus, nobis eius creationem imputari, aut, quia in eo mortui sumus, nobis mortem eius imputari. Dicunt nos in eo peccasse, quoniam in eo fuimus. Atqui non fuimus in eo proprie. Non peccavimus igitur in eo proprie. Cur ergo vis eius peccatum nobis imputari proprie, & quia imputetur, nos proprie, immo proprissime, puniri, & quidem ea poena, quae sit peccatum? Argumentum invictum. Qui proprie loquendo non fuerunt in Adamo, illi proprie loquendo non peccarunt in Adamo. Atqui proprie loquendo non fuimus in Adamo. Ergo proprie loquendo non peccavimus in Adamo. Iam subsumo. Qui proprie loquendo non peccarunt, & his proprie loquendo peccatum imputari & poena infligi non potest. Atqui proprie loquendo non peccavimus in Adamo. Ergo proprie loquendo peccatum illud Adami nobis imputari, & poena irrogari non debet.
units.tr: They say that we sinned in Adam, and indeed as if in a lump; and they render the Apostle's words ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον [ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον] as in whom all have sinned. What follows from this? That Adam's actual sin is imputed to all of us? That does not follow any more than it follows that we are liable for his act because we were in him, or that his creation is imputed to us because we were created in him, or that his death is imputed to us because we died in him. They say we sinned in him because we were in him. But we were not in him properly. Therefore we did not sin in him properly. Why then do you want his sin imputed to us properly, and, because it is imputed, want us to be punished properly, and indeed most properly, with that penalty which is sin itself? This is an unanswerable argument. Those who, properly speaking, were not in Adam did not, properly speaking, sin in Adam. But we, properly speaking, were not in Adam. Therefore we, properly speaking, did not sin in Adam. Now I assume the minor. Those who properly speaking did not sin cannot properly have sin imputed to them, nor be properly punished. But we, properly speaking, did not sin in Adam. Therefore that sin of Adam ought not to be imputed to us properly, nor punishment inflicted on us.

units.la: Adde quod ex eo quod in Adamo fuisse & peccasse dicimur, non potes inde inferre, simpliciter nos aut fuisse tunc temporis, aut peccasse, nisi fallaciam committendo à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter: tamen simpliciter peccasse nos oportet id peccatum, quod nobis vere & proprie imputatur ad poenas proprie dictas ac grauissimas. Abstine ne igitur, quæso, ab hac fallacia, neque puta phrasin illam, nos in Adam peccasse, meæ sententiæ obesse, quam (si ex figurata reuocetur ad propriam) continet: reuocatur enim sic, peccatum nostrum ducit originem à peccato Adami, vel sic, peccatum est causa peccati nostri. Hoc significauit Ambrosius, cùm dixit, in Adam omnes peccasse quasi in massa, subiecit enim hanc rationem, ipse enim per peccatum corruptus, quos genuit omnes nati sunt sub peccato. Nempe corruptus corruptos genuit. Quod ex Adam sub peccato nascimur, id corruptioni Adami tribuit, non autem peccato eius actuali, nisi mediante corruptione Adami. Illud autem, quasi in Massa, dicitur valdè improprie & figuratè; Massa enim causam materialem potius quàm efficientem designat. Nos autem in Adamo, vt in causa efficiente fuimus potius, quàm vt in materia, aut massa; Et quod in Massa est, actu est. Nos autem in Adamo non fuimus actu, sed potestate, eaque remotissimâ, ac nonnisi mediantibus omnibus aliis nostris parentibus. Interim peccauimus in Adamo, vt in Massa, quoniam, quemadmodum natura Adami fuit quasi Massa naturæ nostræ, sic vitium inhærens Adamo fuit quasi Massa vitij nostri, quod verè peccatum est, vt ita loquar, habituale.
units.tr: Add that from the fact that we are said to have been in Adam and to have sinned in him, you cannot infer that we simply were at that time, or simply sinned, unless you commit the fallacy of moving from a statement qualified in some respect to an unqualified one. Yet we must simply have sinned in the sin that is truly and properly imputed to us for punishments properly so called and most grievous. Please, therefore, refrain from this fallacy, and do not think that the phrase we sinned in Adam stands in the way of my view, which it contains when it is restored from the figurative to the proper sense. For it is restored thus: our sin derives its origin from the sin of Adam; or thus: the sin of Adam is the cause of our sin. This is what Ambrose meant when he said all sinned in Adam as if in a lump; for he added this reason, for he himself, corrupted through sin, begot all those who are born under sin. Clearly one who was corrupted begot corrupted offspring. That we are born under sin from Adam, he ascribes to the corruption of Adam, not to his actual sin, except through the corruption of Adam. But as if in a lump is said very improperly and figuratively; for lump designates the material cause rather than the efficient cause. We, however, were in Adam as in an efficient cause rather than as in matter or a lump; and what is in a lump is actually present. But we were not actually in Adam, only potentially, and that in a very remote way, and only through all our other parents. Meanwhile we sinned in Adam as in a lump, because just as Adam's nature was, as it were, a lump of our nature, so the vice inherent in Adam was, as it were, a lump of our vice, which is truly sin, so to speak, habitual.

units.la: Dicunt, in Adam omnes peccauisse, quando omnes ille unus homo fuerunt, & explicatiùs, in Adam omnes tunc peccasse, quando in eius natura, illa vi insita quâ hos gignere poterat, adhuc omnes ille unus fuerunt; Item, omnem hominem terrenum nihil esse origine nisi Adam: Sed hæc omnia meæ sententiæ sunt consentanea. Quàm enim omnes homines vnus ille homo fuerunt, nimirum Adam, tam omnia peccata originalia, quæ singulis hominibus inhærent, fuerunt vnum illud peccatum, quod Adamo inhæsit ex peccato ipsius actuali enatum. Sed tuæ aduersantur: nam vt peccatum actuale Adami nobis vere & proprie imputaretur, oporteret nos omnes vere & proprie fuisse illum vnum hominem, qui illud commisit; quod affirmare non iam ratiocinari, sed insanire foret. Fuimus ergo omnes vnus ille homo improprie, quia non modo eiusdem cum eo speciei sumus, sed etiam ab eo oriundi; sic nostra peccata originalia fuerunt vnius illius hominis peccatum, quia non modo eiusdem sunt speciei cum illius peccato, vt ita loquar, habituali, sed etiam ab eo sunt oriunda; ac omnino quam rationem homines habent ad primum hominem, eandem habent corruptiones nostræ naturales ad primi hominis corruptionem.
units.tr: They say all sinned in Adam, when all were that one man, and more fully, all sinned then in Adam, when in his nature, by that inborn power by which he could beget these, they were still all that one man; likewise, every earthly man is nothing in origin but Adam. But all these things agree with my view. For just as all men were that one man, namely Adam, so all original sins, which inhere in individual men, were that one sin which inhered in Adam, derived from his actual sin. But your view conflicts with these statements; for in order for Adam's actual sin to be truly and properly imputed to us, we would all have to have truly and properly been that one man who committed it. To affirm this would be not reasoning but madness. We were therefore all that one man improperly, because we are not only of the same species as he, but also descended from him. Thus our original sins were the sin of that one man, because they are not only of the same species as his sin, so to speak habitual, but also descended from it. And altogether, the relation that men have to the first man, our natural corruptions have to the corruption of the first man.

units.la: Dicunt etiam, omnes in illo vno Testamentum Dei dissipauisse, in quo omnes peccauerunt. Testamentum autem illud primum, quod factum est ad hominem primum, illud esse, qua die ederitis morte moriemini: Item, prævaricatores legis illius, qua in paradiso data est, agnosci. Hoc quoque meæ, non tuæ conuenit sententiæ. Quo modo enim vis nos primum illud testamentum diffipasse? nullo modo nisi imputatione. Vis ergo nos Testamentum illud diffipasse tantum imputatiue. Atqui ego volo nos illud vere & reipsa diffipasse, nempe corruptio illa quam ab Adamo trahimus, nihil aliud est, quam legis illius prævaricatio, quam Testamenti illius diffiqatio habitualis, plane talis, qualis illa Adami fuit vnde orta est. In Adamo igitur Testamentum illud dissipauimus, legem illam transgressi sumus, quoniam eius transgressio, prævaricatio, Testamenti diuini dissipatio habitualis in nos transiit, non imputatione, sed, plane quomodo ipsius natura, generatione & propagatione carnali. Neque nos verba illa dissipandi & prævaricandi turbare debent, quæ imputationem haud quaquam significant: Alioqui de Christo, cui, vt vadi nostro, peccata nostra imputata sunt, vsurpari possent; quod tamen dicere pius animus horret. Nam solemne est omnibus hominibus propensiones & habitus verbis describere actiones significantibus, vt supra obseruaui. Porrò corruptio ista, quam ab Adami peccato naturali propagatione traximus, imago est Adami corrupti ac vetus Adam, cum suis actibus & operibus mortificandus, deponendus, exuendus, crucifigendus. Habet autem ista corruptio, cùm sit verè peccatum, suum reatum non antecedentem, cuius sit pœna, sed consequentem, cuius sit fundamentum vel causa. Itaque.
units.tr: They also say all in that one broke the covenant of God, in whom all sinned. That first covenant, which was made with the first man, was that on the day you eat, you shall surely die. Likewise, the transgressors of that law, which was given in paradise, are acknowledged. This also agrees with my view, not yours. For how do you want us to have broken that first covenant? In no way except by imputation. You want us therefore to have broken that covenant only imputatively. But I maintain that we really and in fact broke it; namely, that corruption which we draw from Adam is nothing other than the transgression of that law, a habitual breach of that covenant, just like that of Adam from which it arose. In Adam, then, we broke that covenant, we transgressed that law, since his transgression, his prevarication, his habitual breach of the divine covenant passed over into us, not by imputation, but just as his very nature did, by generation and carnal propagation. Nor should those words breaking and transgressing disturb us, which by no means signify imputation. Otherwise they could be applied to Christ, to whom our sins were imputed as to our surety, which yet a pious mind shrinks from saying. For it is customary for all men to describe propensities and habits by words that signify actions, as I observed above. Moreover, that corruption which we drew from Adam's sin by natural propagation is the image of corrupt Adam, the old Adam, to be mortified, put off, put away, and crucified with his acts and works. This corruption, since it is truly sin, has its guilt not preceding it, of which it would be the punishment, but following it, of which it is the foundation or cause. And so.

units.la: Dicunt Patres, nos ab Adamo traxisse reatum, nempe quia causam reatus traximus, nimirrum peccatum seu vitium originale. Item, peccato primi hominis nasci obnoxios: eius crimine factos esse mortales; Et si qua alia sunt eiusmodi, quæ profecto vera sunt, siue per peccatum primi bominis ipsum eius vitium nobis carnali generatione infusum intelligas, cuius reatu nascentes inuoluntur, seu peccatum eius actuale, quod nos, mediante corruptione quam peperit, reatu implicat, & mortis pœnā. Quid enim, putasne nos ab Adamo trahere solum reatum, & non causam ipsam reatus? Poenam, & non meritum poenae? Si ita sentis, cadit in te fulmen Concilij Arausicani secundi, Si quis solli Adae prævaricationem suam, non & eius propagini, asserit nocuisse: aut certe mortem tantum corporis, quæ poena peccati est, non autem & peccatum, quod mors est animæ, per unum hominem in omne genus humanum transfiffe, iniustitiam Deo dabit, contradicens Apostolo. Verba huius Concilij pondera: sunt enim valde notanda; meamque causam in primis iuuant. Asserit duo mala per unum hominem in omne genus humanum transijsse, mortem quae est poena, & peccatum: quod autem peccatum? Num illud actuale præcise sumptum, de quo nostra hæc disputatio instituta est? Minimè: id enim primum describit ita, ut dicat esse mortem animæ. Est autem mors animæ posita, non in actione illa Adami, quæ tot sæculis antequam inciperet esse anima nostra præterijt, sed in corruptione & iniustitia quæ animæ inhæret, & quam tu ipse aliquoties mortem animæ esse dixisti. Deinde, vult peccatum non minus quam mortem transijsse in omne genus humanum. Mors autem non transijt imputatione. Ergo nec peccatum. Adde quod ponere in nobis vere & proprie & reipsa mortem seu poenam peccati, & non ponere in nobis vere, & proprie, & reipsa peccatum, causam meritoriam poenae, non congruit cum Concilij illius verbis. Nam qui poenam peccati in Adami propagine agnoscunt, non autem peccatum, illi non facile negauerint imputari propagini stirpis peccatum ad illam poenam: Vides autem Concilium duas afferre rationes quae tuam caycam iugulant: primam his verbis iniustitiam Deo dabit, alteram illis, contradicens Apostolo. Prior præsupponit non posse sine iniustitia propaginem puniri ob peccatum stirpis, si non sit in eâ peccatum, quod pœnam mereatur. Altera docet peccatum, quod mors est animæ, illud ipsum peccatum esse quod Apostolus affirmauit per vnum hominem introïsse in mundum, ac mortem per ipsum: quibus duobus tu tota ista disputatione contradixisti. Sed quid præterea dicunt Patres.
units.tr: The Fathers say that we drew guilt from Adam, namely because we drew the cause of guilt, that is, sin or original vice. Likewise, that we are born liable to the sin of the first man; by his crime we were made mortal; and whatever other statements of this kind there are, which are certainly true, whether you understand by the sin of the first man his own vice infused into us by carnal generation, by whose guilt we are involved at birth, or his actual sin, which entangles us in guilt through the corruption it brought forth, and in the punishment of death. For do you suppose that we draw from Adam only guilt, and not the cause of guilt itself? Punishment, and not the merit of punishment? If you think so, the thunderbolt of the Second Council of Orange falls on you: If anyone asserts that the prevarication of Adam harmed himself only, and not also his offspring; or certainly that only the death of the body, which is the punishment of sin, and not also sin, which is the death of the soul, passed through one man into the whole human race, he will be doing injustice to God, contradicting the Apostle. The words of this Council carry weight; for they are to be carefully noted, and they especially help my case. It asserts that two evils passed through one man into the whole human race: death, which is punishment, and sin. But what sin? Is it the actual sin taken precisely, which is the subject of this disputation? Not at all: for it first describes it in such a way as to say that it is the death of the soul. But the death of the soul is placed not in that action of Adam, which passed away many centuries before our soul began to exist, but in the corruption and injustice that inheres in the soul, which you yourself have several times called the death of the soul. Next, it wills that sin no less than death passed into the whole human race. But death did not pass by imputation. Therefore neither did sin. Add that to place in us truly, properly and really death or the punishment of sin, and not to place in us truly, properly and really sin, the meritorious cause of the punishment, does not agree with the words of that Council. For those who acknowledge the punishment of sin in the offspring of Adam, but not sin, would not easily deny that the sin of the stock is imputed to the offspring for that punishment. You see, moreover, that the Council brings two reasons that cut the throat of your cause: the first in these words, he will be doing injustice to God, the second in those, contradicting the Apostle. The first presupposes that the offspring cannot be punished for the sin of the stock without injustice, unless there is in it sin deserving punishment. The second teaches that the sin which is the death of the soul is that very sin which the Apostle affirmed entered the world through one man, and death through it; in this whole disputation you have contradicted both of these. But what else the Fathers say.

units.la: Dicunt, omnes homines in Adamo expulsos esse de paradiso, cum ipse inde pulsus est: hanc eius delicti condemnationem in omnes homines peruenisse. Nempe eiectus ex paradiso non potuit liberis intra paradisum operam dare: ibi enim quisque gignit, vbi est, non autem vbi non est; ibi familiam habet, vbi habitat, non autem vbi sibi esse non licet. Porrò quos genuit Adamus, eos ad imaginem & similitudinem suam genuit, corruptus corruptos, vitiosus vitiosos, immundus immundos, ac propterea indignos quibus Paradisus redderetur.
units.tr: They say that all men were driven out of paradise in Adam when he himself was expelled from it, and this condemnation of his offence has come upon all men. Certainly, one who has been cast out of paradise could not beget children within paradise. For a man begets where he is, not where he is not; he has his family where he lives, not where he is not permitted to be. Moreover, Adam begot those whom he begot in his own image and likeness: corrupt, he begot the corrupt; vicious, he begot the vicious; unclean, he begot the unclean, and so unworthy to have paradise restored to them.

units.la: Item dicunt, perisse Adamum, & nos omnes in eo, ob vnius delictum nos esse mortuos: mortis vinculum nos tenuisse in eo; Et si qua alia sunt eiusmodi, ex quibus nullis fidiculis immediata primi peceati actualis imputatio omnibus hominibus elici potest: sed contrà potius non imputatio. An enim quia in eo eiecti fuimus e paradiso, nobis eius eiectio & expulsio imputatur? An quia periit & mortui sumus in eo, nobis eius perditio & mors imputatur? An quia condemnati sumus in eo, nobis eius condemnatio & punitio imputatur? An quia spoliati sumus in eo iustitia originali, nobis illa spoliatio imputatur? An quia corrupti sumus in eo, nobis eius corruptio imputatur?
units.tr: They also say that Adam perished, and all of us perished in him, dying on account of the one offence; we were held in the bond of death in him. And whatever other sayings of this kind there are, from none of which can an immediate imputation of the first actual sin be drawn to all men by any thread. Rather, on the contrary, they point to a non-imputation. Is it because we were driven out of paradise in him that his expulsion and banishment are imputed to us? Is it because he perished and died in him that his ruin and death are imputed to us? Is it because we were condemned in him that his condemnation and punishment are imputed to us? Is it because we were stripped of original righteousness in him that that deprivation is imputed to us? Is it because we were corrupted in him that his corruption is imputed to us?

units.la: Periimus igitur in Adam, quia nobiscum non per imputationem, sed per carnalem generationem perditionem suam communicauit, corruptionem scilicet suam, & vitium inhærens, & per corruptionem illam, quia vere peccatum est, reatum mortis. Itaque ob illius delictum morimur, quia illius delictum causa est nostri delicti, & nostrum delictum causa est mortis nostræ. Nosti autem illud tritum quod est causa causæ, est etiam causa causati. Quia, inquit Calvinus, eius peccatum peccati nostri causa est, exitium noftrum illi Paulus adscribit. Quem locum iam plenius citaui.
units.tr: We perished in Adam, then, because he communicated his ruin to us not by imputation but by carnal generation, namely his corruption and the indwelling vice, and through that corruption, since it is truly sin, the guilt of death. Thus we die on account of his offence, because his offence is the cause of our offence, and our offence is the cause of our death. You know the common saying: what is the cause of a cause is also the cause of what is caused. Because, says Calvin, his sin is the cause of our sin, Paul ascribes our ruin to him. I have already cited that passage more fully.

units.la: Locum é Cypriano, quia tu eius verba maximè notanda dixisti, totum adscribam. Quanto magis prohiberi non debet à Baptismo infans, qui recens natus nihil peccauit, nisi quod secundum Adam carnaliter natus, contagium mortis antiquæ prima natiuitate contraxit? qui ad remissam peccatorum accipiendam hoc ipso facilius accedit, quod illi remittuntur non propria, sed aliena peccata. Putas hunc locum tibi valde fauere. Quid si ostendero, tuam illam sententiam euertere, meam firmare? Non ponderasti illa verba, qui recens natus NIHIL PECCAVIT, NISI quod secundum Adam carnaliter natus CONTAGIVM mortis antiquæ primâ natiuitate contraxit. Quid est illud contagium, nisi corruptio inhærens? & quomodo illam corruptionem contraxit? non imputatione peccati actualis Adami (peccasset enim etiam illud peccatum, ) sed carnali natiuitate. Dic mihi etiam peccata aliena plurali numero dixit si solum primum peccatum actuale, numero vnicum & singulare intellexit? Annon respexit ad illud pf. 51. 8. in iniquitatibus conceptus sum.: Et in peccatis concepit me mater mea ; ex quibus peccati quidem inhærentis contagium , actualis vero imputatio nequaquam colligi potest. Quæro etiam , per peccata illa aliena quid intelligas ? solum ne primum peccatum actuale imputatum ? negauit igitur Cyprianus peccatum inhærens originale, quæ fuit Pelagij hæresis : peccatum enim proculdubio intelligit illud de quo dixerat, nihil peccauit, nisi &c. An vtrumque & actuale imputatum , & habituale inhærens ? Potest igitur & debet peccatum seu vitium inhærens alienorum peccatorum nomine intelligi ? Quare nihil suppetit, quo probes ijs vocibus actuale imputatum fignificari.
units.tr: I shall set out the whole passage from Cyprian, since you said his words were especially to be noted. How much more ought an infant not to be kept from baptism, who, newly born, has sinned in nothing, except that, being born carnally according to Adam, he has contracted by his first birth the contagion of the ancient death? He comes all the more easily to the receiving of the remission of sins, because what is forgiven him is not his own sins but those of another. You think this passage greatly favours you. What if I show that it overturns your opinion and confirms mine? Have you not weighed those words: who, newly born, has sinned in NOTHING, EXCEPT that, being born carnally according to Adam, he has contracted the CONTAGION of the ancient death by his first birth? What is that contagion, if not inherent corruption? And how did he contract that corruption? Not by imputation of Adam's actual sin (for even if he had sinned, that sin too would have been his), but by carnal birth. Tell me also: when he said other people's sins in the plural, did he mean only the first actual sin, which is one and singular in number? Did he not have in view that verse of the Psalm, Ps. 51. 8, I was conceived in iniquities; and in sins did my mother conceive me? From which words the contagion of inherent sin can certainly be gathered, but by no means actual imputation. I ask further: by those other people's sins, what do you understand? Only the first actual sin imputed? Then Cyprian denied inherent original sin, which was the heresy of Pelagius; for he undoubtedly means by sin that of which he had said he has sinned in nothing, except, and so on. Or does he mean both the actual sin imputed and the habitual sin inherent? Can sin or vice that inheres, then, be understood under the name of other people's sins? Therefore you have nothing by which you could prove that actual imputation is signified by those words.

units.la: Sed audiamus Augustinum hæc ipsa Ambrosij verba interpretantem. Nulla, obijciebant Pelagiani, ratione concedi tur, vt Deus qui propria peccata remittit imputet aliena, Quid respondet Augustinus? remittit, sed spiritu regeneratis, non carne generatis. Imputat vero, NON IAM ALIENA, SED PROPRIA: aliena quippe erant, quando ij qui propagata ea portarent nondum erant. Nunc vero carnali generatione iam eorum sunt, quibus nondum spirituali regeneratione dimissa sunt. Hæc Augustini verba tu quoque laudasti, sed contra te. Nam, si in tua fuisset sententia , debuisset respondere, Deum quidem nobis imputare aliena peccata , sed quæ illa ipsa imputatione fiunt nostra : quæ responsio difficultatem auxisset, non sustulisset. Quærebatur enim, quomodo cum Dei iustitia & bonitate congruere posset, vt nobis imputaret peccata aliena ? Iam si dicas , vt facis , imputatione fieri nostra , sequitur prius ordine naturæ nobis imputari , quàm nostra esse, quippe, cùm quod nostra sint, imputationis sit effectum. Quod igitur imputatione nostra fiunt, non facit vt illa imputatio iusta fit; immo si non est iusta, auget eius iniustitiam; siquidem ea fit, vt non modo puniamur, sed etiam fiamus peccatores: sic enim duas iniurias accipimus, peccatum, & poenam. Quia igitur in tua sententia non fuit Augustinus, sed in ea quam tueor, respondit, id quod res est, quodque obiectioni satisfacit, imputare Deum non iam aliena, sed propria: quibus verbis notat conditionem illorum peccatorum cum imputantur, non autem postquam imputata sunt, ut manifestum est. Atqui te ipso confitente, & vero ipsa ratione clamante, primum peccatum actuale Adami, si nobis, vt tu sentis, immediate imputatur, non potest naturae ordine prius nostrum esse, nobis proprium, quam nobis imputetur. De eo igitur imputato nec obiectio Pelagianorum, nec responsio Augustini loquitur. Huc accedit quod peccatum actuale Adami praecise sumptum ita alienum est, vt non possit esse proprium cuiusque nostrum. Quicquid enim mihi proprium est, id si qualitas est, mihi inhaeret, si actio, a me, quatenus ab aliis hominibus distinguor, aliquo modo producta est. Simili argumento visus est Chamierus, Dico inquit, nullum peccatum unum numero posse esse commune omnibus hominibus. Nam peccatum vel qualitas est, vel actio. Qualitas vt peccatum originale, actio vt peccatum quodlibet actuale. At nulla qualitas, una eademque numero potest pluribus subiectis communicari. Vt candor qui est in nive, idem numero non potest esse in Cygno, aut lana. Actiones autem sunt suppositorum. Quare idem homicidium a Caino patratum non potest esse a Lamecho. Itaque nego peccatum illud Adami esse peccatum originale: non. non enim potest omnibus esse commune, sive numero, quia est actio; sive specie, quia est individuum actus. Si igitur peccatum illud actuale Adami non est commune omnium, quomodo singulorum est idem numero proprium? Hoc igitur utrumque simul convenire non potest actuali primo peccato, sed egregie convenit corruptioni singulis inhæreti, quæ aliena est respectu causæ, propria respectu subiecti: aliena est, quia venit aliunde quam à nobis, propria est, quia nobis ipsis inhæret, ut propria qualitas: sic lepra a parente in sobolem propagata dici potest & aliena, & propria: aliena, quia venit à parente; propria, quia hæret in sobole. Atque hanc esse mentem Augustini, ipse sequentibus verbis exponit. Aliena quippe erant, quando qui propagata ea portarent, nondum erant. Tunc enim nonnili in alijs erant. Nunc vero carnali generatione iam eorum sunt, quibus nondum spirituali regeneratione dimissa sunt. Hic notanda sunt primum illa verba, qui propagata ea portarent; deinde ista, carnali generatione iam eorum sunt. Observuo autem primo loco vocem propagata, quæ non convenit peccato actuali Adami: singulare enim cum sit ac numero unicum, nullo modo multiplicabile, propagari certè non potest: nam omne propagatum differt numero ab eo à quo propagatum est. Natura humana in Adamo propagata non fuit, sed, ut ita loquar, propagans, in nobis autem propagata est ab eo: sic peccatum idem numero, quod in Adamo fuit, propagans quidem fortasse, propagatum certè dici non potuit. Necesse est igitur ut ista peccata propagata numero differant ab Adami peccato. Deinde observuo verbum illud portarent, quod non accipitur ab Augustino quo sensu solet in Scriptura pro puniri. ob peccata, sed pro illa sustinere propagata ac sibi inhærentia; quo certè modo non potest à nobis portari peccatum actuale Adami. Denique non dixit, nunc vero diuina imputatione iam eorum sunt, quibus nondum spirituali regeneratione dimissa sunt, quæ tua est sententia; sed nunc vero carnali generatione &c; si carnali generatione nostra sunt, non igitur nostra sunt imputatione. Nam quod generatione carnali nostrum est, Id, siue nobis imputetur, siue non imputetur, nostrum est. Cæterum hæc eadem Augustini verba Petrus Martyr & Bullingerus, præ nobis duobus heroes, interpretati sunt, non vt tu de peccato actuali imputato, sed, vt ego, de vitio inhærente. Obijciebantur, inquit Martyr, illi à Pelagianis duo argumenta satis arguta & difficilia. Vnum: Qui fieri possit, vt Deus qui pro sua bonitate nostra ipsorum peccata remittit, velit imputare aliena. &c. Ad primum respondet, Deum summe bonum esse, neque quod isti assumunt, in culpa Originis imputare nobis alienum peccatum, sed nostram ipsorum iniquitatem, quæ nostræ naturæ adhæret iam inde ab ipsi origine. Hæc Martyr, sequuntur verba Bullingeri. Concludimus igitur secum infantes damnationem ab vtero materno afferre in mundum: naturam enim corruptam afferunt, ac propterea sua culpa & vitio, non autem aliena à peream. Quamvis enim alicubi Sanctus Augustinus vt deatur hoc peccatum alienum, vel ab alio traducitum, vt propagari clarius ostenderet, appellare; tamen ipse hoc peccatum vere nostrum esse, ac suum cuique proprium, confitetur. Superest Bernardi Abbatis Clareuallensis testimonium, quod facile contemnissem, nisi tu maximè notandum dixisses. Cùm enim iste Monachus ixculo, vt tu notasti, vndecimo, hoc est, corruptissimo floruerit, non debet mirum videri, si non fuit expers erroris: cuius rei vel illa ipsa verba, quae tu laudasti, testes esse possunt. vt, &c, si nesciens in Adam peristi, nesciens vivificeris in Christo. Nesciisti quando ad lignum vetitum vetus Adam tetendit manus noxias: nesciisti nihilominus quando in ligno salutifero innoxias manus Christus extendit. Nam nescientes quidem per Adamum facti sumus peccatores, sed nescientes non fimus iusti per Christum: est enim fides, qua iustificamur seu viuificamur in Christo, cognitio quaedam. Carnalis vero generatio, qua fimus peccatores in Adam, nec cognitio est, nec ab eo qui gignitur, mente cognoscitur. Sed fortasse de solis infantibus loquitur, quamuis hominem in genere & uniuersim compellet. vtvt fit, nihil dicit quod meae sententiae incommodet. Nam si culpam vocat alienam, aliena lauit aqua quos culpa inquinauerat aliena, corrigit se continuo, Nec tamen sic alienam dixerim vt negem nostram; alioqui nec inquinaret. Est igitur ita aliena vt sit nostra: nec nos aliena inquinat, sed nostra: quare nobis imputatur, vt nostra est, non vt est aliena: imputatur enim qua nos inquinat. Non igitur nostra est, vt tu putas, imputatione; alioqui non inquinatos Deus sua illa imputatione seu actione inquinaret, quod absit. Haec igitur prima verba, vt tu vides, mihi potius faucent quam tibi; siquid igitur mihi aduersatur, id in his sequentibus consistat necesse est, Sed aliena est, quia in Adam omnes nescientes peccauimus: nostra, quia etsi in alios tamen peccauimus. Et nobis iusto Dei iudicio imputabatur, licet occulto. Non vrgebis quod ait nos in Adamo peccauisse, iam enim quam haec locutio mihi non obstit, satis me ostendisse arbitror; sed vrgebis proculdubio postrema verba, & nobis iusto Dei iudicio imputabatur licet occulto. Ea igitur expendamus. Primum non ait simpliciter culpam nostram esse, quia nobis imputabatur, quæ tua est sententia, sed culpam nostram esse, quia etsi in alio, nos tamen peccauimus & nobis imputabatur. Nostrum, vt ita loquar, peccasse imputatio sequebatur, non præcedebat. Deinde, Vel nobis iam genitis & existentibus imputatam fuisse illam culpam, quodam sensu alienam, alio nostram, & nobis propriam, intelligit; vel nobis nondum existentibus quando Adamus peccavit. Prius si eligis; aio culpam illam, quæ erat in mundo, sed, cum nondum essemus, aliena à nobis, simul ac fuimus nostra fuit, nobis propria, sitam esse in vitiositate innata & inhærente nobis, eamque, quia proprie peccatum sit, nobis iusto Dei iudicio, nisi remissa fuerit, & condonata in Christo, imputatam fuisse: atque sic Bernardum interpretor. Si vero posterius eligis; primo id mihi videtur alienum à nostra quæstione, qui de imputatione disputamus, qua nobis, cum sumus, peccatum imputatur; deinde absurdum mihi videtur ei, qui nondum sit, iam imputari peccatum, tam certe absurdum quam eum puniri, qui nondum esse coeperit. Si tamen culpa illa nobis imputabatur nondum genitis, fiebat ista imputatio in sola Dei præscientia, cui futura sunt præsentia; quam autem nos præuidebat futuros, tam præuidebat etiam futuros corruptos, ac ob hanc corruptionem deriuatam in nos ab Adamo damnabiles. Quandocunque igitur Deus nobis peccatum originis imputare dicatur, sive cum sumus, sive antequam simus, sive in tempore, sive ab æterno, id peccatum aliud nihil est quàm inhærens illud à natiuitate nobis vitium, quod à primo nostro parente non per imputationem, sed per carnalem generationem traximus. Vides, vt confido, Frater obseruande, nihil te reperiffe in tota antiquitate quod non fit consentaneum meæ sententiæ, neque verò, nisi me animus fallit, reperiri à quoquam potest. Quod si mihi liberet, tuo exemplo, Patrum scrinia compilare, possem ex eorum monumentis, multo & plura, & certiora, & quæ nulla arte eludi possent testimonia, & pro mea sententia, & contra tuam excitare, ac proferre: sed mihi tempero, partim ne quod in Pontificijs iure reprehensum est à nostris, committere videar, partim quia veritas, quam tueor, diuinis abundè munita præsidijs, humana non desiderat, partim quia, nunc quidem, mihi satis est impetum tuum sustinere, ac respondentis partes tueri.
units.tr: But let us hear Augustine himself interpreting these very words of Ambrose. "No reason can be granted," the Pelagians objected, "why God, who forgives our own sins, should impute the sins of others." What does Augustine reply? "He forgives, but to those regenerated by the Spirit, not to those born of the flesh. He imputes, however, NOT NOW OTHER MEN'S SINS BUT THEIR OWN: for they were other men's while those who were to carry them on had not yet existed.
