Now, however, by carnal generation they already belong to those to whom they have not yet been remitted by spiritual regeneration." You too have praised these words of Augustine, but against yourself. For if your opinion had been his, he ought to have answered that God indeed imputes other men's sins to us, but that they become ours by that very imputation. That answer would have increased the difficulty, not removed it. The question was how it could agree with God's justice and goodness that he should impute to us the sins of others. Now if you say, as you do, that they become ours by imputation, it follows that in the order of nature we are imputed sins before they are ours, since their being ours is the effect of the imputation. What becomes ours by imputation therefore does not make that imputation just; on the contrary, if it is not just, it adds to its injustice. For the result is that we are not only punished but also made sinners, and so we suffer two wrongs, the sin and the punishment. Since, then, Augustine was not on your side but on the side I defend, he answered what is the case and what satisfies the objection: God imputes not now other men's, but their own. By these words he marks the condition of those sins when they are imputed, not after they have been imputed, as is plain. And yet, as you yourself confess and reason itself cries out, if the first actual sin of Adam is imputed to us immediately, as you think, it cannot be ours and our own in the order of nature before it is imputed to us. Neither the Pelagians' objection nor Augustine's answer therefore speaks of that imputed sin. Add to this that the actual sin of Adam, taken precisely, is so foreign to us that it cannot be the proper possession of any one of us. For whatever is properly mine, if it is a quality, inheres in me; if it is an action, it has been produced by me in some way, insofar as I am distinguished from other men. Chamier seems to have used a similar argument: "I say," he says, "that no single sin numerically one can be common to all men. For a sin is either a quality or an action. As original sin it is a quality, and as any actual sin it is an action. But no quality, numerically one and the same, can be communicated to several subjects. As the whiteness that is in snow cannot be numerically the same in a swan or in wool. Actions, however, belong to persons. Hence the same murder committed by Cain cannot be committed by Lamech. Therefore I deny that that sin of Adam is original sin: not. For it cannot be common to all, whether numerically, because it is an action, or specifically, because it is the individual act." If, then, that actual sin of Adam is not common to all, how can it be the same numerically and the proper possession of each? These two things cannot both agree with the first actual sin. They agree admirably, however, with the corruption that inheres in each person, which is foreign with respect to its cause and proper with respect to its subject. It is foreign because it comes from elsewhere than from ourselves; it is proper because it inheres in ourselves, like a proper quality. Thus leprosy passed from a parent into offspring can be called both foreign and proper: foreign, because it comes from the parent; proper, because it adheres in the offspring. And that this is Augustine's meaning he himself explains in the words that follow: "For they were other men's while those who were to carry them on had not yet existed." For then they existed only in others. "Now, however, by carnal generation they already belong to those to whom they have not yet been remitted by spiritual regeneration." Here two phrases must be noted: first, "who were to carry them on," and then, "by carnal generation they already belong to them." I observe, in the first place, the word propagata ("handed on"), which does not fit Adam's actual sin. For since that sin is singular and unique in number, it cannot be multiplied and certainly cannot be propagated, for everything propagated differs in number from that from which it is propagated. Human nature was not propagated in Adam but, so to speak, was propagating; in us, however, it has been propagated from him. So sin, the same in number as it was in Adam, may perhaps be propagating, but it could not be called propagated. It is necessary, therefore, that those propagated sins differ in number from the sin of Adam. Next I observe the word portarent ("carry"), which Augustine does not use in the sense it usually has in Scripture, of being punished for sins, but in the sense of bearing those propagated sins that cling to them; and in that sense the actual sin of Adam certainly cannot be carried by us. Finally, he did not say "now, however, by divine imputation they already belong to those to whom they have not yet been remitted by spiritual regeneration," which is your opinion; he said "now, however, by carnal generation," and so on. If they are ours by carnal generation, then they are not ours by imputation. For what is ours by carnal generation is ours whether or not it is imputed to us. Moreover, Peter Martyr and Bullinger, two heroes before us both, interpreted these same words of Augustine, not as you do of imputed actual sin, but as I do of inherent vice. "There were objected," says Martyr, "to him by the Pelagians two rather subtle and difficult arguments. One: How can it be that God, who by his goodness forgives our own sins, should wish to impute those of others? etc. To the first he answers that God is supremely good, and that he does not impute to us in original guilt another's sin, as they assume, but our own iniquity, which has adhered to our nature from its very origin." So far Martyr; now follow the words of Bullinger. "We conclude, then, with him that infants bring damnation into the world from their mother's womb: for they bring a corrupted nature, and therefore they are damned by their own guilt and vice, not by another's. For although St. Augustine somewhere calls this sin 'another's' or 'derived from another,' in order to show more clearly that it is propagated, nevertheless he himself confesses that this sin is truly ours and proper to each person." There remains the testimony of Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, which I could easily have disregarded, had you not said "especially to be noted." For since this monk flourished in the eleventh century, as you noted, that is, in the most corrupt age, it should not seem surprising if he was not free from error. Of this the very words you praised may be witnesses: "Just as, if, not knowing, you perished in Adam, so, not knowing, you are made alive in Christ. You did not know when the old Adam stretched out his harmful hands to the forbidden tree; you did not know, nonetheless, when Christ stretched out his harmless hands on the tree of salvation." For indeed we were made sinners through Adam without knowing it, but we are not made righteous through Christ without knowing it: for faith, by which we are justified or made alive in Christ, is a certain knowledge. But carnal generation, by which we are made sinners in Adam, is neither knowledge nor is it perceived in mind by the one who is begotten. Perhaps, however, he speaks only of infants, although he addresses man in general and universally. Whatever the case, he says nothing that is inconvenient to my opinion. For if he calls the guilt "another's," "the water washed away those whom another's guilt had defiled," he immediately corrects himself: "Nor, however, would I call it so foreign as to deny that it is ours; otherwise it would not defile." It is therefore so foreign that it is ours: it does not defile us as foreign, but as ours; therefore it is imputed to us as ours, not as foreign, for it is imputed insofar as it defiles us. It is not, therefore, ours by imputation, as you think; otherwise God by that very imputation or action would defile those who were not defiled, which is far from the truth. These first words, then, as you see, favour me rather than you; if anything is opposed to me, it must lie in the following words: "But it is foreign, because in Adam we all sinned without knowing it; it is ours, because although we sinned in another, nevertheless we sinned," and "it was imputed to us by the just judgment of God, though hidden." You will not press the phrase that we sinned in Adam, for I think I have sufficiently shown that this expression is no obstacle to me. But you will no doubt press the final words: "it was imputed to us by the just judgment of God, though hidden." Let us weigh them, then. First, he does not say simply that the guilt is ours because it was imputed to us, which is your opinion; he says the guilt is ours "because, although in another, we nevertheless sinned and it was imputed to us." The imputation of our having sinned, so to speak, followed it; it did not precede it. Next, he means either that the guilt, which was in some sense foreign and in another sense ours and proper to us, was imputed to us after we were born and existed, or that it was imputed to us when we did not yet exist, when Adam sinned. If you choose the former, I say that the guilt which was in the world, but was foreign to us while we did not yet exist, became proper to us as soon as we existed. It lies in the innate and inherent vice that adheres to us, and because it is properly sin, it was imputed to us by the just judgment of God, unless it is remitted and pardoned in Christ. This is how I interpret Bernard. If, however, you choose the latter, then first this seems to me foreign to our question, since we are debating the imputation by which sin is imputed to us when we exist; and second, it seems absurd to me that sin should be imputed to one who does not yet exist, as absurd as that one should be punished who has not yet begun to be. Yet if that guilt was imputed to us before we were born, that imputation took place only in God's foreknowledge, to whom future things are present; and as he foresaw us as future, so he also foresaw us as future corrupted, and on account of this corruption derived into us from Adam, deserving damnation. Therefore, whenever God is said to impute original sin to us, whether when we exist or before we exist, whether in time or from eternity, that sin is nothing other than the inherent vice which we have drawn from birth, not by imputation but by carnal generation from our first parent. You see, I trust, honoured brother, that you have found nothing in all antiquity that does not agree with my opinion, and indeed, unless my mind deceives me, nothing can be found by anyone. If it pleased me to plunder the archives of the Fathers after your example, I could bring forth from their records many more, and more certain, testimonies, which no art could evade, both for my opinion and against yours. But I restrain myself, partly lest I seem to commit what our people have rightly censured in the Papists, partly because the truth I defend, being abundantly fortified by divine aids, does not need human ones, and partly because, for now, it is enough for me to withstand your attack and to play the part of the respondent.

units.la: CAPVT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Non posse ex Confessionibus Ecclesiarum Reformatarum imputationem illam primi peccati Actualis elici.
units.tr: That the imputation of Adam's first actual sin cannot be drawn from the Confessions of the Reformed Churches.

units.la: PATRIBVS subjungis Ecclesias reformatas, Earumque & Confessiones profers, & quorundam doctorum suffragia, possem te hinc pellere, & ad Scripturam reuocare facillimè. Constans enim est omnium Ecclesiarum Reformatarum sententia, Scripturam esse fidei nostræ regulam perfectissimam, cui nihil addi, nihil detrahi possit. Itaque nihil extra Scripturam credendum esse. Ex quo manifestum est, dogma illud tuum de imputatione peccati Adami actualis, cum ex Scriptura probari non possit, alienum à doctrina Ecclesiarum Reformatarum esse. Constans etiam est omnium Ecclesiarum Reformatarum doctrina, quicquid adversatur sacris literis, id non modo non credendum esse, sed toto etiam pectore detestandum. Contendo autem tuum illud dogma sacris literis repugnare, ac peto & flagito, ut me id demonstrantem fratres mei patienter audire fustineant. Meas demonstrationes habebis Deo bene favente in Apologia Thesium mearum.
units.tr: You append the Reformed Churches to the Fathers and cite their Confessions and the support of certain teachers. I could easily drive you from this position and recall you to Scripture. For it is the settled view of all the Reformed Churches that Scripture is the most perfect rule of our faith, to which nothing may be added and from which nothing may be taken. Therefore nothing is to be believed beyond Scripture. It follows clearly that your doctrine of the imputation of Adam's actual sin, since it cannot be proved from Scripture, is foreign to the teaching of the Reformed Churches. It is also the settled doctrine of all the Reformed Churches that whatever contradicts the sacred writings must not only not be believed but abhorred with the whole heart. I contend, however, that your doctrine contradicts the sacred writings, and I ask and demand that my brethren patiently bear with me while I demonstrate this. With God's favour you will have my demonstrations in the Apology for my Theses.

units.la: Constans quoque est sententia Ecclesiarum Reformatarum, Deum esse iustissimum, æquissimum, optimum, nec ei imputandam esse peccatorum nostrorum causam. Cum igitur eo pertineat tuum illud dogma de imputatione primi peccati actualis, ut causa peccati, & condemnationis posterorum Adami Deo imputetur, ut iam aliquoties probaui, profecto fatendum est tuum illud dogma alienissimum esse à doctrina Ecclesiarum nostrarum. Denique constans est Ecclesiarum Reformatarum sententia Dominum Nostrum Iesum Christum natura sua peccatorem non fuisse : nam si peccator fuisset natura ac propterea filius irae, proculdubio hominum redemptor & servator esse non potuisset. Atqui ego contendo & demonstraturum me confido, idque sequi ex tuo illo dogmate. Quibus igitur argumentis hoc & superiora euinco, iisdem eademque opera planum facio tuum illud dogma pro Ecclesiarum reformatarum dogmate nequaquam habendum esse.
units.tr: It is also the settled view of the Reformed Churches that God is most just, most equitable and best, and that the cause of our sins is not to be imputed to him. Since your doctrine of the imputation of Adam's first actual sin tends to this, namely that the cause of sin and of the condemnation of Adam's posterity is imputed to God, as I have already shown several times, it must surely be admitted that your doctrine is most alien to the teaching of our Churches. Finally, it is the settled view of the Reformed Churches that our Lord Jesus Christ was not a sinner by nature; for if he had been a sinner by nature, and therefore a child of wrath, he could undoubtedly not have been the redeemer and saviour of men. But I contend, and I am confident I shall demonstrate, that this follows from your doctrine. Therefore, by the same arguments by which I overturn this and the preceding point, I make it plain at the same time that your doctrine cannot be held as the doctrine of the Reformed Churches.

units.la: Id quod ipsum ex illis ipsis Confessionibus fidei, quas citas, colligere potuisti. Explicant enim humanæ miseriæ causam, peccatum originale accuratè describunt, nullam tamen faciunt mentionem imputationis peccati actualis Adami. Vnde sic argumentor. Si eam imputationem Ecclesiæ Reformatæ, omnes vnanimi consensu, credidissent, vt traditam in scripturis & creditu necessariam, vt cuius negatio olim sit damnata in Pelagianis, debuerunt eius mentionem aliquam facere vel in omnibus suis consessionibus fidei, vel saltem in earum aliqua. At nullam prorsus in vlla Confessione fecerunt. Non igitur eam crediderunt. Item sic, si peccatum originale est duplex, imputatum & inhærens, illud præcipuum ac huius causa, profectò male descripserunt peccatum originale in suis fidei confessionibus omnes Ecclesiæ reformatæ. Hoc autem qua, ducor erga Ecclesias reformatas reuerentia, mihi videtur valdè absurdum ergo & illud. Mala enim est definitio seu descriptio, quæ descripto angustior est, quæ non conuenit toti definito, sed eius duntaxat vni parti, & quidem minus præcipuæ. Attamen omnes peccati originalis, quæ habentur in fidei confessionibus, descriptiones foli vitio inhærenti conueniunt, peccato actuali imputato nullo modo. Itaque necesse est fateri malas esse, quæ suis procul dubio authoribus sunt visæ optimæ, nec immeritò. Sed quando ita visum est tibi, excutiamus singulas.
units.tr: This you could have gathered from the very Confessions of faith that you cite. For they explain the cause of human misery and describe original sin accurately, yet they make no mention at all of the imputation of Adam's actual sin. Hence I argue thus: if the Reformed Churches had all believed with one consent that imputation, as taught in the Scriptures and necessary to be believed (its denial having once been condemned in the Pelagians), they ought to have made some mention of it either in all their Confessions of faith or at least in some one of them. But they made no mention of it whatever in any Confession. Therefore they did not believe it. Likewise: if original sin is twofold, imputed and inherent, and the imputed is the chief part and its cause, then all the Reformed Churches have certainly described original sin badly in their Confessions of faith. Yet out of the reverence I feel for the Reformed Churches, this seems to me very absurd. A definition or description is faulty when it is narrower than what is described, when it does not fit the whole thing defined but only one part of it, and that a less important one. But all the descriptions of original sin found in the Confessions of faith apply to inherent vice only, and in no way to imputed actual sin. It must therefore be admitted that they are faulty, though to their authors they doubtless seemed excellent, and not without reason. But since it has seemed so to you, let us examine them one by one.

units.la: GAR Si simplex Confessionum silentium ita vrgendum est in omni Religionis capite, vt ex eo colligatur aliquid non esse habendum pro articulo doctrinæ, quam Protestantes Ecclesiæ communiter amplectantur, verecor vt eliminanda sint multa, quæ, qui doctrinæ imputationis sunt iniquiores, pro veritatibus Christianis obtrudunt, de quibus tamen altum in Confessionibus nostris silentium. Deinde, non est quod omnia quae pertinent ad doctrinam Christianam putemus intra finem Confessionum aut posse aut debere concludi. Non posse certum est, quia Confessiones succinctae ac breves sunt, ut ne nimia mole excrescentes, iam in iustos libros & tractatus evadant, quod necessarium esset, si in singulis doctrinae apicibus esset immorandum. Sed nec debere liquet, quia in Confessionibus summa tantum & praecipua capita exponuntur, quae omnes scire inter est, & in quorum fide praesertim constituitur Religionis Christianae ratio. Catera doctoribus explicanda relinquuntur, non quod non recipiantur ab Ecclesia, ut vel inde patet, quod libri eas doctrinas complexi plerumque publicis approbationibus muniuntur; sed quia ea satis est Confessionibus exprimi, quorum cognitio maiorem habet necessitatem, & quae propius salutem contingunt, & quae fundamenti instar habent, cui reliqua innituntur, vel certe a quo non abscedunt.
units.tr: GAR. If the mere silence of the Confessions is to be pressed in every head of religion, so that it is inferred that something is not to be held as an article of doctrine commonly embraced by the Protestant Churches, I fear that many things which the more unfair teachers of the doctrine of imputation put forward as Christian truths, and about which there is nonetheless deep silence in our Confessions, would have to be struck out. Further, we need not suppose that everything pertaining to Christian doctrine can or should be comprised within the bounds of the Confessions. That it cannot is certain, since the Confessions are brief and succinct, lest by excessive bulk they grow into large books and treatises, which would be necessary if one had to linger over every fine point of doctrine. Nor is it clear that they should, since the Confessions set out only the sum and principal heads, which everyone ought to know and on whose faith the reasoning of the Christian religion chiefly rests. The rest is left to teachers to explain, not because it is not received by the Church (as is evident from the fact that books embracing these doctrines are generally supported by public approval), but because it suffices that the Confessions express those things whose knowledge is more necessary, which touch salvation more closely, and which serve as the foundation on which the rest rests, or at least from which the rest does not depart.

units.la: PLAC. Non sum a simplici silentio Confessionum argumentatus, ut patet legenti. Stat igitur duplicis robur integrum argumenti. Addo etiam, nec futuram longiorem Consessionem, si imputationis meminisset, nisi forte verbo uno, aut linea, & illam imputationem, si eius propugnatoribus credendum est, fundamentum & causam esse omnium Adae posterorum miseriae. Illa peccatores constituti sunt omnes & rei mortis aeternae: Illa quicquid est in omnibus originalis peccati nititur: Illi imprimis iustificatio, quam per Christum habemus, opponitur. De numero igitur earum doctrinarum censenda est, quae omitti non debuerunt, siquidem eius defensores non errant.
units.tr: PLAC. I did not argue from the mere silence of the Confessions, as is clear to the reader. The full force of my double argument therefore stands. I add also that the imputation, if its defenders are to be believed, is the foundation and cause of all the misery of Adam's posterity; if it had been mentioned, the Confession would not be any longer, unless perhaps in a single word or a line. By it all men are made sinners and liable to eternal death; on it rests whatever is in all men of original sin; and above all it is opposed to the justification we have through Christ. It must therefore be counted among those doctrines which ought not to have been omitted, provided its defenders are not mistaken.

units.la: GAR. Tertio nimium audax est illa asseueratio, nullam prorsus in vlla Confessione mentionem factam fuisse huius imputationis. Neque vocabulum moror, quia de re ipsa non de voce agitur; & quanquam imputandi verbum in Confessionibus hic non occurrat, rem tamen eo verbo significatam Confessionibus saltem nonnullis contineri & manifeste satis comprehendi, non potest abque obfirmato contradicendi proposito negari. Quid est enim imputari nobis peccatum Adae, aliud, quam nos propter illud reos esse, nos illius poenam sustinere, propter illud mortem & varias poenas nobis incumbere. Atqui eiusmodi reatum, & poenam in nos descendere Confessiones agnoscunt.
units.tr: GAR. Thirdly, that assertion is too bold, namely that no mention whatever of this imputation was made in any Confession. I do not dwell on the word, since the matter itself is in question and not the term; and although the verb to impute does not occur here in the Confessions, the thing signified by that word is contained in at least some of the Confessions and is sufficiently plainly comprehended, which cannot be denied except by one obstinately set on contradicting. For what is it for Adam's sin to be imputed to us, other than that we are guilty on account of it, that we bear its punishment, and that death and various penalties fall upon us on account of it? Yet the Confessions acknowledge that such guilt and punishment descend upon us.

units.la: P L A C. Primum quod dat accipio, non occurrere in Consessionibus imputandi verbum de peccato Adae usurpatum; quod certe mirum, si imputationem illam omnes Ecclesiae protestantes unanimi consensu tenuerunt. Rem significatam contineri ait, saltem in nonnullis. Illud saltem in nonnullis, tacita confessio est in quibusdam, ne dicam plerisque, non contineri. Sed quaenam est illa res significata? Nos, inquit, propter peccatum Adae reos esse. Quis nostrum hoc negat, aut negavit unquam? Sed distinguere oportet, ut iam aliquoties feci, cum peccatum Adae, tum vocem propter. Nam, si per peccatum Adae intelligitur corruptio in nos ab Adamo deriuata, id nobis proxime seu immediate imputatur antequam condonetur, Hanc imputationem constanter agnosco. Si per peccatum Adae intelligitur eius primum peccatum actuale; distinguo illud propter; nam vel sensus est nos propter illud peccatum proxime & immediate reos esse, qui sensus est a Confessionibus alienus; vel sensus est nos esse reos propter illud mediate tantum, hoc est, mediante corruptione illa haereditaria; atque is sensus nobis nihil obest. Neglecta distinctione imputationis oberrat perpetuo Vir doctus eadem Chorda, seseque in eo probando fatigat quod minime controuertitur. Propter peccatum Adae mors & variae poenae nobis incumbunt, nempe propter peccatum Adae quod intra nos est, proxime; propter peccatum Adae quod extra nos in Adamo fuit, remote. Quod enim est causa corruptionis nostrae, id causa est reatus corruptionis nostrae, nimirum mediate seu remote. Quam igitur abest a Confessionibus imputandi verbum, tam etiam abest res significata quam nego.
units.tr: PLAC. First, I accept what you grant: that the word imputing, applied to Adam's sin, does not occur in the Confessions; which is certainly remarkable, if all the Protestant Churches held that imputation with one consent. You say the thing signified is contained in them, at least in some. That at least in some is a tacit admission that it is not contained in some, not to say most. But what is this thing signified? "We," he says, "are guilty because of Adam's sin." Which of us denies this, or has ever denied it? But, as I have done several times already, one must distinguish both the phrase Adam's sin and the word because of. For if by Adam's sin is meant the corruption derived to us from Adam, then this is imputed to us immediately or directly before it is forgiven; this imputation I constantly acknowledge. If by Adam's sin is meant his first actual sin, I distinguish the phrase because of: either the sense is that we are guilty immediately and directly because of that sin, which sense is alien to the Confessions; or the sense is that we are guilty because of it only mediately, that is, through that hereditary corruption; and this sense does us no harm. By neglecting this distinction of imputation, the learned man wanders perpetually on the same string, and wearies himself in proving what is in no way disputed. Because of Adam's sin death and various penalties fall upon us: namely, because of the sin that is within us, immediately; because of the sin that was in Adam outside us, remotely. For what is the cause of our corruption is the cause of the guilt of our corruption, that is, mediately or remotely. Therefore, as far as the word imputing is absent from the Confessions, so far is the thing signified, which I deny, absent too.

units.la: Gallica nostra, inquis, assensum praebent satis manifestum. ( Non certe tuae sententiae, sed meae potius. ) Nam Art. 9. ita habetur, Credimus hominem creatum purum, & integrum, & imagini Dei conformem, sua ipsius culpa excidisse a gratia quam acceperat, proinde seipsum a Deo omnis iustitia, & bonorum omnium fonte abalienasse. Nunquid, addis, ille homo est Adam primus homo? Ergo quod homo excidit a gratia Dei & abalienatus est a Deo, nonne culpa primi illius hominis? Equidem quid tibi velis his duabus interrogationibus non assequor. quid enim per hominem illum qui excidit a gratia & abalieniatus est a Deo intelligis? Num ipsum Adamum? sensus est igitur sua ipsius culpa Adamum excidisse, quo nihil est verius. Num genus humanum? fateor illud quoque abalienatum esse a Deo culpa Adami: sed de modo quaeritur inter nos, vtrum per imputationem illius culpae, an vero per vitiositatis illius culpae propagationem & multiplicationem? Tu prius asseris; Ego posterius. Tu vis culpam Adami nostram esse imputatione, ego reali communicatione & propagatione illius vitiositatis, quam in Adamo culpa illa reliquerat. Nihil habes in illis Confessionis verbis, vnde tua magis quam mea sententia probari possit. Quanquam nihil necesse est per hominem eo loco Adami sobolem intelligere, de qua sequens articulus loquitur; sed describit Confessio in quantam depravationem & corruptionem primus homo ex statu integritatis ceciderit, vt sequenti articulo doceat eius sobolem totam contagione corruptionis illius infectam esse. Caeterum cum homo dicitur creatus purus, & integer, & imagini Dei conformis, vtrum id de solo Adamo, an de reliquis etiam hominibus intelligendum est? Si de solo Adam, de eodem vtique solo sequentia in eodem Articulo verba intelligenda sunt. Si de reliquis hominibus, quaero, quomodo fuerint creati puri & integri? Dices in Adamo. Vtrum igitur per imputationem creationis, puritatis, integritatis Adami? Non arbitror. Quomodo igitur? quia nempe si perstitisset in integritate, eos genuisset puros, integros, imagini Dei conformes. Cur ergo non eodem modo intelligis nos in eo peccasse, quia nos genuit sui similes, peccatores, corruptos, imagini Dei dissentaneos? Sed, inquis, quod sequitur art. 10. id clarius explicat. Credimus totam Adami sobolem hac contagione infectam esse, quam peccatum originale vocamus, vitium videlicet ex propagatione manans,&c. Certè explicari mea sententia clarius non potuit; tuæ quod faueat ne quidem. Laudas etiam sequentia, Nec putamus necessarium esse inquirere, quinam posset hoc peccatum ab uno ad alterum propagari, sufficit enim quæ Deus Adamo largitus erat non ipsi soli, sed etiam toti ipsius posteritati fuisse data, ac proinde nos in ipsius persona omnibus illis bonis spoliatos, in omnem hanc miseriam & maledictionem incidisse. Hæc omnia mihi rectissime dicta videntur, & meæ sententiæ congruenter. Tu tamen singula ponderas, ac nescio quid mihi repugnans elicere satagis, Hæc, inquis, sonant peccatum originis, & contagionem illam, quæ nos maledictioni submittit, esse ab eo quod sumus Adami soboles. Recte sane: sonant igitur id quod te aduersus defendo, reatum nostrum ex contagione illa seu vitio originis nasci, eamque sequi, non autem, quemadmodum tu putas, antecedere ut causam. Subijcis notandum esse quod dicimur, in ipsius persona omnibus bonis spoliati in miseriam & maledictionem incidisse. Id aduersus tuam sententiam noto libenter, ac primum obseruo spoliationem illam antecedere, miseriam & maledictionem subsequi; nempe illa peccatum sonat, hæc poenam. Deinde quæro, quo sensu dicamur spoliati fuisse omnibus illis bonis in persona Adami ? an per imputationem illius ipsius priuationis illorum bonorum, quæ fuit in Adamo ? Bis igitur nobis priuatio illorum bonorum imputatur, quæ semel tantum Adamo fuit imputata : nam & illa quæ in Adamo fuit nobis imputatur, & illa etiam quæ nobis ipsis inest : cur non enim hæc ipsa quoque nobis imputaretur, cum fit intra nos, nobis inhærens ? Profecto eodem sensu spoliati fuimus illis bonis in persona Adami; quo illis donati fueramus in eius persona. Fueramus autem illis donati in eius persona, non per imputationem, sed quia bona illa, si conseruasset, nobiscum reapse, vna cum sua natura, per generationem communicasset, ac propagasset. Eodem modo fuimus in eo bonis illis spoliati, non per imputationem, sed per propagationem spoliatæ illis bonis naturæ. Tu tamen inde nescio quid argumenti colligis, quod sic habet. Si priuatio boni & casus in malum est effectum peccati, peccauimus in persona illius in quo priuati fuimus bono, & in malum incidimus. Atqui priuati fuimus bono & in malum lapsi fumus in persona Adami ex confessione nostra. Ergo in persona Adami peccauimus. Etsi maioris necessitatem nullam video, tamen non grauate concedo conclusionem. Subsumis, sed nondum eramus, nec quisquam posterorum cum peccauit: unde sequitur peccatum quod personaliter commisit, non esse peccatum sibi, nisi quatenus illi tribuitur & imputatur, quia est ab eo, & in eo consideratur. Hoc vero nego sequi: perinde est ac si, quia in eius persona fuimus, & tamen nondum eramus quamdiu fuit, colligeres, igitur eius esse personale nobis imputari, quia sumus ab eo. In eo fuimus, quia eius esse propagatum est in nos; in eo peccauimus, quia eius peccatum in nos similiter propagatum est.
units.tr: Our Gallican Confession, you say, gives sufficiently clear assent. (Certainly not to your view, but rather to mine.) For Article 9 reads thus: "We believe that man, created pure and whole and conformed to the image of God, fell from the grace he had received through his own fault, and therefore separated himself from God, the fount of all righteousness and of all good things." Is that man, you add, the first man Adam? Therefore, that man fell from grace and was alienated from God, was that not through the fault of that first man? Indeed, I do not grasp what you wish to achieve with these two questions. For by the man who fell from grace and was alienated from God, what do you understand? Adam himself? Then the sense is that Adam fell through his own fault, which is nothing truer. The human race? I admit that it too was alienated from God through Adam's fault. But the question between us is about the manner: is that fault imputed to us, or rather is its vitiosity propagated and multiplied in us? You assert the former; I the latter. You want Adam's fault to be ours by imputation; I by the real communication and propagation of that vitiosity which that fault had left in Adam. In those words of the Confession there is nothing by which your view can be proved rather than mine. Yet there is no need to understand by "man" in that place Adam's offspring, of whom the following article speaks; the Confession describes to what depth and corruption the first man fell from the state of integrity, so that in the following article it may teach that his whole offspring is infected by the contagion of that corruption. Moreover, when man is said to have been created pure, whole and conformed to the image of God, is this to be understood of Adam alone, or of the rest of mankind too? If of Adam alone, then the words that follow in the same article must be understood of him alone too. If of the rest of mankind, I ask, how were they created pure and whole? You will say, in Adam. By imputation, then, of Adam's creation, purity and integrity? I do not think so. In what way, then? Namely, because if he had persisted in integrity, he would have begotten them pure, whole and conformed to the image of God. Why, then, do you not understand in the same way that we sinned in him, since he begot us like himself, sinners, corrupt, and unlike the image of God? But, you say, what follows in Article 10 explains this more clearly: "We believe that the whole offspring of Adam is infected by this contagion, which we call original sin, namely a vice flowing from propagation," etc. Certainly it could not have been explained more clearly according to my view; nor does it favour yours in the least. You also praise what follows: "Nor do we think it necessary to inquire how this sin could be propagated from one to another; for it is enough that the gifts which God bestowed on Adam were given not to him alone but to his whole posterity, and therefore that we, in his person, were stripped of all those good things and fell into all this misery and curse." All these things seem to me most rightly said and congruent with my view. Yet you weigh each word and strive to draw out something that I think contradicts me. "These words," you say, "sound that original sin, and that contagion which subjects us to the curse, is from the fact that we are Adam's offspring." Rightly so indeed: they therefore sound what I defend against you, that our guilt arises from that contagion or vice of origin, and follows it, and not, as you suppose, that it precedes as its cause. You add that we ought to note that we are said to have been stripped of all good things in Adam's person and to have fallen into misery and curse. I gladly note this against your view, and first I observe that the stripping precedes and the misery and curse follow; namely, the former sounds of sin, the latter of punishment. Next I ask in what sense we are said to have been stripped of all those good things in Adam's person: by the imputation of that very privation of those good things which was in Adam? Thus the privation of those good things is imputed to us twice, though it was imputed to Adam only once: for both that which was in Adam is imputed to us, and that which inheres in us ourselves. For why should not this very thing also be imputed to us, since it is within us and cleaves to us? Surely we were stripped of those good things in Adam's person in the same sense in which we had been endowed with them in his person. Now we had been endowed with them in his person not by imputation, but because, had he kept them, he would have communicated and propagated them to us in reality, together with his nature, by generation. In the same way we were stripped of them in him not by imputation, but by the propagation of a nature stripped of those good things. Yet you gather from this some argument, I know not what, which runs thus: "If the privation of good and the fall into evil is the effect of sin, we sinned in the person of him in whom we were deprived of the good and fell into evil. But we were deprived of the good and fell into evil in Adam's person, by our own confession. Therefore we sinned in Adam's person." Although I see no need for the major premise, I nonetheless readily grant the conclusion. You subjoin: "But we did not yet exist, nor did any of the posterity when he sinned; whence it follows that the sin which he committed personally is not a sin to us, except insofar as it is attributed and imputed to us, because it is from him and is considered in him." This I deny follows. It is just as if you were to infer, because we were in his person and yet did not yet exist while he did, that therefore his personal act is imputed to us because we are from him. We were in him because his being has been propagated into us; we sinned in him because his sin has likewise been propagated into us.

units.la: G A R. Quanquam hæc ad corruptionem illam pertinent, quæ lapsu Adæ labefecit totum genus humanum, & propagatione naturali in omnes & singulos diffunditur; tamen non esse hinc excludendam, sed potius comprehendendam imputationem peccati Adæ, patet ex eo, quod in Adami, non in aliorum maiorum persona (poliati dicimur & in miseriam lapsi; nimirum quia in Adamo aliquid præcessit, quod in aliis non præcessit; &c.
units.tr: GAR. Although these things pertain to that corruption which by Adam's fall weakened the whole human race and is diffused by natural propagation into all and each; nevertheless, that the imputation of Adam's sin is not to be excluded from this here, but rather to be comprehended, is evident from the fact that we are said to have been stripped and to have fallen into misery in Adam's, and not in the person of other forefathers; namely, because something preceded in Adam which did not precede in others; etc.

units.la: P L A C. Hactenus bene. Præcessit enim in Adamo peccatum actuale quod Corruptionem illam produxit: in aliis maioribus nostris corruptionem nullum peccatum actuale antecessit. In eo igitur tanquam fonte, ac causa illius spoliationis dicimur bonis illis spoliati: illa enim solus accepit, habuit, possedit, actuali sua inobedientia amisit, & quia amisit, non habuit, nec ad nos transmittere potuit. Id de aliis dici non potest, qui huius spoliationis non magis, quàm nos, autores, nec minus participes fuerunt. Sic quamuis peccatum Ieroboham commune fuerit omnium Regum Israelis, tamen vnius Ieroboami peccatum vocari solet, non aliorum Regum; quoniam ille primus autor fuit illius peccati, alij Reges non item. Id autem nullam imputationem importat, quæ Corruptionem, vt causa, antecesserit. Nam & sine tali imputatione propagari Corruptio potuit, & nulla iusta causa fuit, cur actio Adami propria & personalis per imputationem fieret actio omnium.
units.tr: PLAC. So far, well. For actual sin preceded in Adam, and this produced that corruption; in our other forefathers no actual sin preceded the corruption. In him, therefore, as in the fount and cause of that privation, we are said to have been stripped of those good things; for he alone received them, had them, possessed them, and by his actual disobedience lost them, and because he lost them, he did not have them, nor could he transmit them to us. This cannot be said of the others, who were no more the authors of this privation than we were, nor any less partakers in it. Thus, although the sin of Jeroboam was common to all the kings of Israel, it is nevertheless usually called the sin of Jeroboam alone and not of the other kings, because he was the first author of that sin, and the others were not. But this brings with it no imputation which preceded the corruption as its cause. For corruption could have been propagated even without such an imputation, and there was no just reason why the action of Adam, which was his own and personal, should become by imputation the action of all.

units.la: Quod in alia Confessione fidei nomine Ecclesiarum Gallicarum scripta, vt coram Imperatore & Principibus Germaniæ ederetur, explicatur in hæc verba, omnes natura exitio & damnationi obnoxij, sumus, non tantum quia Adamus peccauit, sed quoniam peccatores & ipsi fumus ab vtero, Id mihi nequaquam nocet. Fateor enim ad damnationem nostram pertinere, & peccatum Adami, & peccatum nostrum natiuum; illud vt causam remotam seu mediatam, hoc vt causam proximam seu mediatam.
units.tr: In another confession of faith, written in the name of the Gallican Churches so that it might be published before the Emperor and the princes of Germany, it is explained in these words: "We are all by nature liable to destruction and damnation, not only because Adam sinned, but because we ourselves are sinners from the womb." This does me no harm at all. For I admit that both the sin of Adam and our own innate sin contribute to our condemnation: the former as the remote or mediate cause, the latter as the proximate or immediate cause.

units.la: Sed tu speras lumen à sequenti articulo; eum ergo recitemus, Credimus hoc vitium esse vere peccatum, quod omnes & singulos homines, ne parvulis quidem exceptis adhuc in utero matrum delitescentibus, aeterna mortis reos coram Deo peragit. Affirmamus quoque hoc vitium, etiam post baptismum, esse vere peccatum quod ad culpam attinet, quamvis qui filij Dei sunt minime idcirco condemnentur, quoniam videlicet Deus pro gratuita sua bonitate & misericordia illud ipsis non imputat. Quis sperasset te pro tua sententia haec verba citaturum fuisse? Tu tamen, qua es ἀγχιστεία, in ijs medium deprehendisti quo eam probares. Cum, inquis, dicimus vitium illud, peccatum illud originis, esse vere peccatum, etiam in parvulis, in utero matrum delitescentibus, & satis esse ad condemnationem, agnoscimus illos eo esse infectos, quia peccaverunt in persona Adami: nondum enim quicquam fecerunt boni vel mali, ut loquitur Apostolus. Non capio mentem tuam. Visne hoc vitio infici infantes, quia illis peccatum actuale Adami imputetur? nihil est in verbis illis confessionis unde id possit excul pi ullo modo. Visne vitium illud dici vere peccatum ac homines reos peragere non ratione sui, sed antecedentis & conjunctae imputationis peccati actualis Adami, ex qua sola reatus exsurgat? Si ita sentis, longe abis a mente huius Confessionis. Primum definit hoc vitium esse vere peccatum; Atqui non est vere peccatum, si non dicitur peccatum, nisi quia aut est effectum peccati, aut est coniunctum cum imputatione alicuius peccati: sic ipsa mors corporis vere peccatum dici posset, quod tamen nemo dixerit. Deinde affirmat hoc vitium omnes homines reos peragere coram Deo: sequitur igitur vitium reatus, non antecedit. Tertio asserit hoc vitium, etiam post baptismum, esse vere peccatum, quamvis non imputetur, nec fit cum villa antecedentis peccati imputatione coniunctum. Denique nota tibi est controuersia quæ nobis intercedit cum Ecclesia Romana de concupiscentia, seu vitio illo originis, sitne post baptismum adhuc veré peccatum. Nostri summo omnium Protestantium consensu probant esse veré peccatum, non ducto ab imputatione peccati actualis Adami argumento, sed variis argumentis, quæ probant ipsam concupiscentiam per se se peccatum esse formaliter & proprie, non quomodo actio; nam revera infantes in vtero materno nihildum boni vel mali fecerunt, sed quomodo qualitas voluntati penitus infixa peccatum dici potest. Addis, Et cum dicimus illam culpam & reatum aboleri in ijs qui filij Dei sunt, quia eis Deus non imputat, numquid fatemur alijs imputari qui damnantur ob illud peccatum? Certè fatemur ijs qui pereunt imputari vitium illud, quandoquidem veré peccatum est, ac eos coram Deo reos peragit. Cæterùm si vitium illud veré peccatum est, & omnes ac singulos homines coram Deo reos peragit, quid opus est ad condemnationem hominum vt illis peccatum actuale Adami, quod tu ipse personale fuisse fateris, imputetur? Cur vitio illo non contentus vis tibi alijsque singularem illam actionem Adami imputari, qua legem transgressus est? Potuitne fidei Confessio difertius, clarius, significantius docere, generis humani reatum ac condemnationem esse proximè & immediatè à vitio illo omnibus & singulis ingenito, ac proinde non esse à peccato actuali Adami, nisi mediatè & remotè? Porrò hæc tua verba, cum dicimus illam culpam & reatum aboleri in ijs qui filij Dei sunt, repugnant phrasi Confessionis: Illa enim culpam distinguit à reatu, & hunc in baptismo aboleri, illam post baptismum remanere testatur. Gallicam confessionem sequitur Helvetica. Artic. 8: cuius tu verba non transcripsisti; tantum tria in illo Articulo observasti; vnum, quod dictum Apostoli ad Rom, v. producitur, Sicut per vnum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit, ac per peccatum Mors, &c. Nam, inquis, dictum Apostoli sententiam nostram continet & firmat. Quàm id abest à vero, liquet ex cap. 9. & 10. huius meæ responsionis, immo ex hac ipsa Confessione: declarat enim initio articuli 8. quod peccatum introierit in Mundum, & deinde quæ mors, verba adscribam, non enim possum melius meam fidem exprimere. Fuit homo ab initio à Deo conditus ad imaginem Dei in justitia & sanctitate veritatis bonus & rectus, sed insticti sirpentis & suâ culpâ à bonitate & rectitudine deficiens peccato morti variisque calamitatibus factus est obnoxius. Et qualis factus est à lapsu, tales sunt omnes qui ex ipsô prognati sunt, peccato, inquam, morti variisque obnoxij calamitatibus. Audis, ut in illo Apostoli dicto, peccatum primo loco nominatum, deinde mortem; quod ergo peccatum intelligunt? non certè primum illud actuale Adami, quæ tua est sententia, sed, quæ mea est sententia, natiuam corruptionem: sic enim ipsi verbis sequentibus sese Heluetij explicant, Peccatum intelligimus esse natiuam illam hominis corruptionem ex primis illis nostris parentibus in nos omnes deriuatam vel propagatam, qua concupiscentiis prauis immersi, &c. quo nomine merito nostro irae Dei obnoxij poenis subjicimur iustis. Deinde subijciunt se per mortem intelligere non tantum corpoream mortem, sed etiam supplicia sempiterna peccatis & corruptioni nostrae debita. In cujus doctrinæ confirmationem laudant Eph. 2. eramus mortui delictis & peccatis, &c. & Rom. v. Sicut per vnum hominem peccatum in mundum intröiit, &c. & addunt agnoscimus ergo in omnibus esse originale peccatum. Docet igitur hæc Confessio, & quidem aperte, peccatum cui nascimur ex Adamo obnoxij, & per illud mortì, esse natiuam corruptionem; itaque locum illum Apostoli tibi adimit, mihi vendicat: ac non modò silentio suo tuam sententiam tacitè improbat, sed meam etiam disertè affirmat.
units.tr: But you hope for light from the following article. Let us quote it, then: "We believe that this vice is truly sin, which, even in infants not excepted, still hidden in their mothers' wombs, makes all and each of mankind guilty of eternal death before God. We affirm also that this vice, even after baptism, is truly sin as far as guilt is concerned, although those who are children of God are by no means condemned on that account, since God, out of his free goodness and mercy, does not impute it to them." Who would have expected you to cite these words in support of your opinion? Yet you, the kinsman-redeemer [ἀγχιστεία], have found in them a middle term by which to prove it. "When we say," you write, "that this vice, that sin of origin, is truly sin, even in infants still hidden in their mothers' wombs, and that it is enough for condemnation, we acknowledge that they are infected with it because they sinned in the person of Adam: for they have not yet done anything good or evil, as the Apostle says." I do not grasp your meaning. Do you want infants to be infected with this vice because Adam's actual sin is imputed to them? There is nothing in those words of the confession from which that could be drawn in any way. Do you want that vice to be called truly sin, and men to be made guilty not by reason of themselves but by the imputation, antecedent and conjoined, of Adam's actual sin, from which alone guilt arises? If that is your view, you are far from the mind of this Confession. First, it defines this vice to be truly sin. But it is not truly sin unless it is called sin only because it is either the effect of sin or is joined with the imputation of some sin: thus bodily death itself could be called truly sin, which nobody has ever said. Next, it affirms that this vice makes all men guilty before God: so guilt follows the vice; it does not precede it. Third, it asserts that this vice, even after baptism, is truly sin, although it is not imputed, and is not joined with any imputation of a preceding sin. Finally, the controversy that lies between us and the Roman Church about concupiscence, or that vice of origin, is known to you: whether it is still truly sin after baptism. All our people, with the consent of practically all Protestants, hold that it is truly sin, not by an argument drawn from the imputation of Adam's actual sin, but by various arguments which show that concupiscence itself is sin formally and properly, not in the way that an action is; for indeed infants in their mothers' wombs have not yet done anything good or evil, but it is sin in the way that a quality deeply implanted in the will can be called sin. You add: "And when we say that this guilt and liability is abolished in those who are children of God, because God does not impute it to them, do we not admit that it is imputed to others who are condemned on account of that sin?" Certainly we admit that this vice is imputed to those who perish, since it is truly sin and makes them guilty before God. But if this vice is truly sin, and makes all and each of men guilty before God, what need is there, for the condemnation of men, that Adam's actual sin, which you yourself admit was personal, should also be imputed to them? Why, not content with that vice, do you wish Adam's singular action to be imputed to you and others, the action by which he transgressed the law? Could the Confession of faith have taught more plainly, more clearly, more pointedly, that the guilt and condemnation of the human race come immediately and directly from that vice innate in all and each, and therefore come from Adam's actual sin only mediately and remotely? Moreover, your words, "when we say that this guilt and liability is abolished in those who are children of God," contradict the wording of the Confession. For it distinguishes guilt from liability, and testifies that the latter is abolished in baptism, while the former remains after baptism. The Helvetic Confession follows the Gallican Confession. Article 8: you did not transcribe its words, but noted only three things in that article. One is that the saying of the Apostle in Romans 5 is adduced: "As by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin," etc. "For," you say, "the saying of the Apostle contains and confirms our opinion." How far that is from the truth is clear from chapters 9 and 10 of this my reply, and indeed from this very Confession: for at the beginning of Article 8 it declares that sin entered into the world, and then what death is. I shall quote the words, for I could not express my faith better. "Man was at the beginning created by God in the image of God, good and upright in righteousness and holiness of truth; but by the instigation of the serpent and by his own fault, falling away from goodness and uprightness, he was made liable to sin, death, and various calamities. And such as he became by the fall, such are all who are descended from him: liable, I say, to sin, to death, and to various calamities." You hear how, in that saying of the Apostle, sin is named first, and then death. What, then, do they understand by sin? Certainly not Adam's first actual sin, as you hold, but, as I hold, native corruption. For the Helvetians themselves explain themselves in the following words: "By sin we understand that native corruption of man, derived or propagated to all of us from our first parents, by which, immersed in wicked desires, etc., we are rightly subjected, by this name, to the wrath of God and to just punishments." Then they add that by death they understand "not only bodily death, but also the eternal punishments owed to our sins and corruption." In confirmation of this doctrine they cite Ephesians 2, "we were dead in trespasses and sins," etc., and Romans 5, "As by one man sin entered into the world," etc., and they add: "we acknowledge therefore that original sin is in all." This Confession therefore teaches, and indeed plainly, that the sin into which we are born from Adam makes us liable, and through it to death, and that it is native corruption. Thus it takes that passage of the Apostle from you and claims it for me; and not only does it tacitly reject your opinion by its silence, but it also explicitly affirms mine.

units.la: Alterum quod obseruas est, quod paulò post additur, sentimus per omnia in hac causa cum Augustino, quisua ex scripturis sacris protulit atque defendit. Augustinus autem, inquis, sententiam nostram manifestò tuetur. Qui factum est igitur vt eam ex libris ejus probare non potueris? Hoc igitur quicquid est in te retorqueo. Heluetij sentiunt per omnia in hac causa cum Augustino. Atqui Augustinus non credidit, non docuit imputationem immediatam peccati actualis Adami omnibus hominibus: immò multa docuit ejusmodi imputationi repugnantia. Non igitur eam imputationem Heluetij crediderunt. Possem minorem huius argumenti multis rebus necessariis demonstrare, nisi me quodammodo puderet reformatum niti Patrum authoritate in re præsertim per Scripturam certâ & perspicuâ.
units.tr: The second point you note is what is added shortly after: "We agree in all things in this matter with Augustine, who drew and defended his view from the holy Scriptures." Augustine, you say, clearly supports our opinion. How then is it that you could not prove it from his books? So I turn back upon you whatever this is. The Helvetians agree in all things in this matter with Augustine. But Augustine did not believe or teach the immediate imputation of Adam's actual sin to all men; indeed he taught many things repugnant to such an imputation. Therefore the Helvetians did not believe that imputation. I could demonstrate the minor premise of this argument by many necessary points, were I not in some measure ashamed for a Reformed writer to rest on the authority of the Fathers, especially in a matter which is certain and clear through Scripture.

units.la: Tertiò denique obseruas in Art. 15. de Iustificatione asseri Deum propter solum Christum propitium esse peccatis nostris, nec illa nobis imputare, imputare autem justitiam Christi pro nostra. Vnde elicis, Si peccatum non imputatur fidelibus propter Christum; igitur imputari infidelibus. Quod cum dicatur de omni peccato, dicitur etiam de peccato originis. Et ex consequenti de peccato illo primo Adami cuius rei sumus, & consideratur tanquam nostrum peccatum, quatenus nobis imputatur. Hoc postremum nego sequi ex Antecedente: sufficit enim imputari peccatum originis, quod suum cuique inest. Repetis, sic accipiendam semper esse oppositionem inter Adamum & Christum, peccatum Adami & iustitiam Christi, vt quemadmodum, cum in Christo consideramur, justitia ejus nobis imputatur, ita cum in Adamo consideramur, peccatum ipsius nobis imputetur. Augustinus longe aliter hanc oppositionem explicat. Sicut ille, inquit, in quo omnes vivificabuntur, præterquam quod se ad iustitiam exemplum imitantibus præbuit, dat etiam sui spiritus occultisimam fidelibus gratiam, quam latenter infundit & paruulis, sic & ille, in quo omnes moriuntur, præterquam quod eis, qui præceptum domini voluntate transgrediuntur, imitationis exemplum est, occulta etiam tabe carnalis concupiscentia sua tabificauit in se omnes de sua stirpe venientes. Et paulò post, Legimus, inquit, iustificari in Christo qui credunt in eum propter occultam communicationem & inspirationem gratiæ spiritualis, qua quisquis hæret domino, vnus spiritus est, innuens damnari in Adamo qui ex eo nascuntur propter occultam communicationem & propagationem carnalis concupiscentiæ, in qua constanter peccatum Originale situm esse docet & passim inculcat. Eandem oppositionem ijsdem Augustini verbis Bucerus ipse quoque exponit. A Confessione Helvetica transis ad Scoticanam, prætermissis aliis duabus Helveticis, necnon Anglicana, tuæ sententiæ haudquaquam fauentibus. Adscribis autem ex eius art. 3. hæc verba, Qua transgressione, quæ vulgò dicitur originale peccatum, prorsus deformata est illa Dei in homine imago, ipseque eius posteri natura facti sunt inimici Dei, mancipia sathanæ, & serui peccati. adeo vt mors aterna habuerit potentiam & dominium in omnes. Et exclamas, quid manifestius? Nam transgressionem Adami vocant originale peccatum. Agnoscunt igitur omnes homines, qui peccato originis infecti sunt, etiam illius transgressionis reos. Non autem sunt rei, nisi quatenus illis imputatur. Nempe tu verba illa, quæ vulgo dicitur originale peccatum, refers ad antecedentem tranfgressionem ; in quo mihi videris autoribus huius confessionis αὐτοσχεδιασμῶν tribuere : reuera enim non ipsa transgressio Adami, sed ab illa natum vitium seu corruptio vulgo dicebatur peccatum originale. Id liquere potest ex omnibus aliis confessionibus, quæ peccatum originis constanter in illo vitio collocant, necnon ex Scotorum Catechismo à Ioh. Gragio Regis Concionatore composito & paulo post illam confessionem edito. Nam quæstioni quid est peccatum originale ? respondetur, Corruptio totius naturæ nostræ, nulla facta mentione imputationis peccati Adami. Itaque Dauid Parœus, qui tibi in hac causa suspectus esse non potest, fatetur vsum & consuetudinem loquendi in Ecclesia & scholis obtinuisse hæc duo; vnum ne peccatum originis cum peccato primo confundatur, sed vt effectus à causa, fluuius à scaturigine discernatur: alterum, vt nomine originalis peccati sola prauitas habitualis seu deformatio naturæ censeatur. Isque vsus etiam in scholis pontificijs obtinuit. Id quod, si opus esset, posset multis exemplis facere liquidum. Puto igitur in illa confessione relatiuum quæ positum esse pro quod vel quæ res, ac erratum esse vel Typographi vel corrector qui illud construendum putauit cum antecedente nomine fœminini generis, cùm pertineat potius ad id quod sequitur explicandum; sic enim & cum aliis confessionibus & cum rei veritate consentiet. Sed fac nullum esse mendum, quid dicit illa confessio? Transgressionem primorum parentum esse peccatum originale? Non, sed vulgo dici peccatum originale. Recte, an secus, non pronunciat. Sed fac affirmasse transgressionem Adami esse peccatum originale. Primum distinguo Originale, vt ar Parei verbis, dicitur enim ambigue, actiue quod originat (vt sic loquar) seu originem dat rei, & passiue quod originatur, seu originem trahit aliunde. Ita peccatum originale dicitur ambigue, tam peccatum originans, hoc est, peccatum primum Adami qua fuit personalis transgressio, quam peccatum originatum. Ergo igitur transgressio Adami peccatum originale priore sensu, hoc est, actiue, quia origo fuit & causa peccati quod nobis omnibus ab origine inest, sed causa per propagationem naturalem, non autem per diuinam imputationem. Inde non sequitur nobis illam transgressionem imputari. Deinde distinguo transgressionem Adami: nam vel praecise significat actionem illam singularem qua Dei legem violauit, vel habitualem corruptionem ex illa actione natam & in omnes homines propagatam, quo sensu omnes dicunt, & tu ipse aliquoties, peccatum Adami in nos transire, propagari, transfundi, trajici, deriuari; quo sensu verum est transgressionem eius peccatum esse originale, etiam passiue, sed non quatenus eius fuit vt subiecti. Propagata enim in nos & reipsa traiecta illa transgressio nostrum est peccatum originale. Ea autem deformata est Dei imago formaliter quidem in eo in quo est, causaliter vero in eius prole. Hanc autem corruptionem, quatenus intra nos est, nobis nisi condonetur propter Christum, imputari iam saepius dixi. GAR. Hic videmus transgressionem illam primam, quae peccatum Adami actuale fuit, ad peccatum nostrum originale pertinere. Non potest autem pertinere nisi nostra sit, quorum scilicet est originale peccatum; & nostra esse non potest, nisi vel imputatione, vel inhaesione: inhaesione porro nostram esse impossibile est, tum quia iam a multis faculis transiit, tum quia non in alio haesit, quam in ipso Adamo. Itaque eo deueniendum est, ut nostra dicatur imputatione, quatenus eius reatus & poena ad nos pertingit.
units.tr: Thirdly, you note that in Article 15 on justification it is affirmed that God is propitious to our sins for Christ alone, and does not impute them to us, but imputes the righteousness of Christ as ours. From this you infer: If sin is not imputed to believers on account of Christ, then it is imputed to unbelievers. Since this is said of every sin, it is also said of original sin. And consequently of that first sin of Adam, of which we are guilty, and it is regarded as our sin, inasmuch as it is imputed to us. I deny that this last follows from the antecedent: it is enough that the sin of origin is imputed, which inheres in each person. You repeat that the opposition between Adam and Christ, Adam's sin and Christ's righteousness, must always be understood in such a way that, just as when we are considered in Christ his righteousness is imputed to us, so when we are considered in Adam his sin is imputed to us. Augustine explains this opposition in a very different way. As he, in whom all shall be made alive, besides offering himself as an example for those who imitate his righteousness, also gives to the faithful the most hidden grace of his Spirit, which he secretly infuses even into infants, so also he, in whom all die, besides being an example of imitation to those who transgress the Lord's command by their will, has also by his own hidden corruption of carnal concupiscence infected all who come from his stock. And a little later: We read, he says, that those who believe in Christ are justified in him, on account of the hidden communication and inspiration of spiritual grace, by which whoever cleaves to the Lord is one spirit; implying that those who are born of Adam are condemned in him, on account of the hidden communication and propagation of carnal concupiscence, in which he teaches that original sin is constantly situated and everywhere inculcates. Bucer himself also explains this same opposition in the same words of Augustine. From the Helvetic Confession you pass to the Scottish, passing over the other two Helvetic confessions and the English, which by no means favour your opinion. You quote from article 3 of the Scottish one these words: By that transgression, which is commonly called original sin, that image of God in man was utterly defaced, and his posterity itself became enemies of God, slaves of Satan, and servants of sin, so that eternal death has had power and dominion over all. And you exclaim: What could be plainer? For they call the transgression of Adam original sin. All men, therefore, who are infected with original sin acknowledge that they are also guilty of that transgression. But they are not guilty except inasmuch as it is imputed to them. Indeed, you refer the words which is commonly called original sin to the preceding transgression; in this I think you attribute to the authors of this confession improvisations [αὐτοσχεδιασμῶν]. For in truth it was not Adam's transgression itself, but the vice or corruption born from it, that was commonly called original sin. This can be made clear from all the other confessions, which consistently locate original sin in that vice, and also from the Scottish Catechism composed by John Craig, the King's preacher, and published shortly after that confession. For to the question What is original sin? the answer is given: The corruption of our whole nature, with no mention made of the imputation of Adam's sin. Accordingly David Pareus, who cannot be suspect to you in this matter, admits that usage and custom in the Church and the schools has established two things: first, that original sin should not be confused with the first sin, but that effect should be distinguished from cause, as a stream from its spring; second, that under the name of original sin only the habitual depravity or deformity of nature is understood. And this usage also prevailed in the Papist schools. This, if it were necessary, could be made plain by many examples. I think, therefore, that in that confession the relative quae is put for quod or quae res, and that either the printer or the corrector, who thought it should be construed with the preceding feminine noun, has erred, since it belongs rather to explaining what follows; for so it will agree both with the other confessions and with the truth of the matter. But suppose there is no error: what does that confession say? That the transgression of our first parents is original sin? No, but that it is commonly called original sin. Whether rightly or not, it does not pronounce. But suppose it had affirmed that Adam's transgression is original sin. First I distinguish "original": as in Pareus's words, it is said in fact ambiguously, actively, in that it originates (so to speak) or gives origin to a thing, and passively, in that it is originated, or draws its origin from elsewhere. Thus original sin is said ambiguously, both the sin which originates, that is, Adam's first sin as it was a personal transgression, and the sin which is originated. Therefore Adam's transgression is original sin in the former sense, that is, actively, because it was the origin and cause of the sin which is inherent in all of us from our origin; but it was the cause through natural propagation, not through divine imputation. From this it does not follow that this transgression is imputed to us. Next I distinguish "Adam's transgression": for it either signifies precisely that single act by which he violated God's law, or the habitual corruption born from that act and propagated into all men. In the latter sense all say, and you yourself have said several times, that Adam's sin passes into us, is propagated, poured in, transmitted, derived. In this sense it is true that his transgression is original sin, even passively, but not as it was his as the subject. For that transgression, propagated into us and in fact transmitted, is our original sin. And this is the image of God defaced, formally indeed in the one in whom it is, but causally in his offspring. Moreover, I have said more than once that this corruption, as far as it is within us, is imputed to us unless it is pardoned on account of Christ. GAR. Here we see that the first transgression, which was Adam's actual sin, pertains to our original sin. But it cannot pertain to us unless it is ours, namely those whose original sin it is; and it cannot be ours unless by imputation or by inherence. Now it is impossible for it to be ours by inherence, both because it passed away many ages ago, and because it did not inhere in anyone but Adam himself. Therefore we must come to this, that it is called ours by imputation, inasmuch as his guilt and punishment reach us.

units.la: PLAC. Prima Adae transgressio actualis ad peccatum nostrum originale pertinet; ac propterea ab eo distingui debet: alioqui stabiliret haec Confessio errorem Pighii. Pertinet autem ut illius causa. Quod igitur subiungitur, Non potest autem pertinere nisi nostra sit, negari facile, probari vero non potest. Quod additur, nostra esse non potest, nisi vel imputatione, vel inhaesione, falsum est; potest enim nostra esse consensione: nam qui consentit in peccatum alterius, eo ipso sese peccati illius facit participem, & reum. Potest etiam fieri nostra propagatione, quatenus Corruptionem ut semen suum produxit in Adamo, quo propagato in Adami posteros, propagari ipsa quoque dici potuit. Porro si nostra esse non potuit inhaesione, etiam nostra esse non potuit imputatione. Pugnat enim talis imputatio cum Dei iudicis iustitia, ut iam saepius inculcaui.
units.tr: PLAC. Adam's first actual transgression pertains to our original sin, and therefore must be distinguished from it; otherwise this Confession would establish the error of Pighius. It pertains, however, as its cause. Therefore what is added, it cannot pertain unless it is ours, is easily denied, but cannot be proved. What is added, it cannot be ours unless by imputation or by inherence, is false; for it can be ours by consent: for whoever consents to another's sin, by that very fact makes himself a sharer in it and guilty of it. It can also become ours by propagation, inasmuch as Adam, as its seed, produced corruption, and when this was propagated into Adam's posterity it could also be said to be propagated itself. Further, if it could not be ours by inherence, neither could it be ours by imputation. For such an imputation is inconsistent with the justice of God as judge, as I have often insisted.

units.la: Sequitur Confessio Belgica Art. xv. Credimus Adami inobedientia peccatum quod vocant originis in totum genus humanum sparsum & effusum fuisse. Est autem peccatum originis corruptio totius naturae & vitium hereditarium, quo & ipsi infantes in matris vtero polluti sunt: quodque, velut noxia quaedam radix, genus omne peccatorum in homine progerminat, estque tam turpe & execrabile coram Deo, ut ad vniuersi generis humani condemnationem sufficiat. Hoc ipsum credo. Tu praeterea vis me credere imputationem peccati actualis Adami vniuersalem ac immediatam omnibus hominibus: eius neque vola neque vestigium vllum mihi apparet in
units.tr: The Belgic Confession follows, Article 15. We believe that the disobedience of Adam is the sin which they call original, and that it has been spread and poured out over the whole human race. Original sin is the corruption of the whole nature and a hereditary vice, by which even infants themselves are polluted in their mother's womb; and which, like some noxious root, sprouts every kind of sin in man, and is so foul and detestable before God that it is sufficient for the condemnation of the whole human race. This very thing I believe. Besides this, you want me to believe that the imputation of Adam's actual sin is universal and immediate to all men: no hint or trace of it appears to me in this confession.

units.la: hac confessione, Sed, inquis, inobedientiam illam Adami constituunt causam illius corruptionis, adstruunt etiam peccatum illud originis non esse sine illa inobedientia, & utrumque in illo peccato considerari, tum imputationem illius inobedientiæ, tum vitium inhærens. Hoc nullis fidiculis ex verbis illis elici potest. Inobedientia actualis causa fuit vitij inhærentis in Adamo; hoc vitium a b Adamo propagatum est simul cum natura humana in Seth, à Setho in Enofch, & ita deinceps à patre in filium, sine illa inobedientia actuali, quæ iam pridem præterierat ac esse desierat. Cæterum tu reatum vis esse peccati actualis imputati, & antecedere corruptionem seu vitium hæreditarium: quippe, cum hoc putes illius pœnam esse proprie dictam. Illa vero Confessio, sicut & cæteræ, reatum vitio tribuit, Esque, inquit, tam turpe & execrabile coram Deo, ut adversi generis humani condemnationem sufficiat. Laudas etiam hæc verba sequentis articuli, Postea quam tota Adami soboles sic in perditionem & exitium primi hominis culpa præcipitata fuit; in quibus nihil video quod non valde congruat cum mea sententia. Adiungis & vrges quod sequitur in eodem Art. Alios in illo suo lapsu & perditione relinquendo, in quem sese ipsi præcipites dederunt. Ego vero contrà illa verba sese ipsi adversus te vrgeo; & quæro, ex tua sententia quomodo reprobi sese ipsi præcipites dederint in illum lapsum? nam si per illum lapsum intelligis ipsum lapsum Adami, cum is eorum non fit nisi Dei imputatione, profecto non ipsi se se, sed ipsos potius Deus sua illa imputatione in lapsum illum præcipitauit: nam quo factum est vt lapsus ille eorum factus fuerit, qui alioqui eorum lapsus non fuisset, eo proculdubio præcipitati sunt in illum lapsum. Si vero per illum lapsum intelligis vitium insitum, quandoquidem illis inflictum est à Deo in poenam peccati actualis Adami, quod eorum non est nisi imputatione diuina, eodem res recidit, in vitium illud à Deo praecipites dati sunt, non autem à seipsis ipsi, qui seu inflictionis seu imputationis diuinae respectu habent se merè passiue. Itaque secundum tuam sententiam verba illa Confessionis sunt falsa. Ego verò illa ad meam sententiam facilè accommodo. Nam per lapsum illum & perditionem, intelligo non peccatum, sed condemnationem & exitium, in quod dicuntur sese ipsi praecipites dedisse, quia illud suo illo sibi inhaerente ac proprio vitio promeriti sunt: nempe causa illorum exitij haeret in ipsis, non autem extra eos in Adamo, vel in Deo. Vtrumque ergo eodem articulo docet illa Confessio, & culpâ Adami homines in exitium fuisse praecipitatos, & in exitium sese ipsos dedisse praecipites; vt simul huius exitij & causam remotam in culpa Adami, & proximam in vniuscuiusque prauitate & culpa innatâ significaret, quam prauitatem immediatè & proximè Adamus Setho, hic Enoscho, iste Kenani, & ita deinceps proximus quisque parens proximè & immediatè filiis suis, Adamus autem remotè tantum, contagione quadam & propagatione naturali communicauit, ita vt ad eius vitij propagationem tot homines concurrerint, quot fuere patres. Huc accedit quòd Confessio illa lapsus illius & perditionis nomine, non eam modò intelligit, quae ex peccato originali nascitur proximè, sed illam quoque comprehendit, quam propriis peccatis actualibus reprobi, sibi quisque, accersunt: nam quemadmodum electos suos Deus seruat ab omni damnatione originali & acquisita, sic in vtraque reprobos relinquit.
units.tr: in this confession: "But," you say, "they hold that disobedience to be the cause of that corruption, and they also maintain that original sin is not without that disobedience, and that in that sin two things are to be considered: the imputation of that disobedience and the inherent vice." Nothing of this can be squeezed out of those words, however hard one tries. The actual disobedience was the cause of the inherent vice in Adam. This vice was passed on from Adam to Seth together with human nature, from Seth to Enoch, and so from father to son in turn, without that actual disobedience, which had long since passed and ceased to exist. But you want the guilt to belong to the actual sin that is imputed, and to precede the corruption or hereditary vice, since you think the corruption is properly its punishment. That Confession, however, like the others, ascribes guilt to the vice: and it is so vile and detestable before God that it is enough for the condemnation of the whole human race. You also praise these words of the following article: After the whole offspring of Adam had thus been hurled into perdition and destruction by the fault of the first man; in these words I see nothing that does not agree well with my opinion. You add, and press, what follows in the same article: leaving them in that fall and perdition, into which they threw themselves headlong. But I press against you precisely the words they threw themselves, and I ask: according to your view, how did the reprobate throw themselves headlong into that fall? For if by that fall you understand the fall of Adam itself, since it belongs to them only by the imputation of God, then surely it was not they who threw themselves, but rather God who by that imputation hurled them into that fall. For by the very act by which that fall became theirs, which otherwise would not have been theirs, they were undoubtedly hurled into it. If on the other hand you understand by that fall the inherent vice, since it was inflicted on them by God as the punishment of Adam's actual sin, which belongs to them only by divine imputation, the matter comes to the same thing: they were hurled by God into that vice, not hurled themselves, since in respect of both the infliction and the divine imputation they are merely passive. Therefore, according to your opinion, those words of the Confession are false. But I easily fit them to my own opinion. For by that fall and perdition I understand not sin but condemnation and destruction, into which they are said to have thrown themselves headlong, because they deserved it by their own vice, which clings to them and is their own: the cause of that destruction lies in them, not outside them, in Adam or in God. That Confession therefore teaches both things in the same article: that men were hurled into destruction by the fault of Adam, and that they threw themselves headlong into destruction; so that it might signify at once the remote cause of this destruction in the fault of Adam and the proximate cause in the depravity and innate fault of each person. This depravity Adam communicated immediately and proximately to Seth, Seth to Enos, Enos to Kenan, and so on, each nearest parent immediately and proximately to his own sons, while Adam communicated it only remotely, by a certain contagion and natural propagation; so that as many men concurred in the propagation of that vice as there were fathers. To this is added that the Confession, under the name of that fall and perdition, understands not only that which is born proximately from original sin, but also that which the reprobate draw down upon themselves by their own actual sins; for just as God preserves his elect from all condemnation, both original and acquired, so in both respects he leaves the reprobate.

units.la: Hinc transfis ad Augustanam Confessionem, quam tuæ sententiæ ais euidentissime subscribere Art. 2. Item docent, quod post lapsum Adæ omnes homines naturali modo propagati nascentes habeant peccatum originis. Intelligimus autem peccatum originis quod sic vocant sancti Patres, & omnes Orthodoxi, & piè eruditi in Ecclesia, videlicet reatum quo nascentes propter Adæ lapsum rei sunt iræ Dei & mortis æternæ, & ipsam corruptionem humanæ naturæ propagatam ab Adamo. Quibus verbis, inquis, aperte distinguunt reatum propter lapsum à corruptione naturæ, & considerant in peccato originis primò reatum, deinde corruptionem. Reatus autem quid aliud est, nisi obligatio ad pœnam propter Adæ lapsum, in quo lapsi sumus, & propter primum illud primi hominis peccatum, quod nobis imputatur? Unde sequitur reatum non subsequi, sed antecedere corruptionem ex confessione illa Augustana.
