Respondeat pro me Sohnius Theologiæ Doctor & Professor Heidelbergæ, secundò, inquit, docetur (in secunda editione Confessionis Augustanæ ex qua tu verba illa citasti: nam prima editio nullam faciebat mentionem reatus, sed sic erat concepta, Item docent quod post lapsum Adæ omnes homines secundum naturam propagati nascantur cum peccato, hoc est, sine metu Dei, sine fidecia erga Deum, & cum concupiscentia) quid sit peccatum originis, quod sic vocant sancti patres, omnes Orthodoxi, & piè eruditi. Vbi definitio iterum est partialis. Nam partes duæ sunt ex quibus peccatum definitur: nempe reatus & ipsa corruptio humanæ naturæ propagata ab Adamo, ex quibus tamen ordine prior est corruptio, posterior reatus, hoc est, quia corrupti fumus ideo rei fumus irae Dei & aeternae damnationis. Et paulo post, Reatus hic primum definitur quo nascentes propter Adae lapsum rei sunt irae Dei & mortis aeternae. Quae definitio dextre intelligenda est. Neque enim propter Adae lapsum tanquam alienum peccatum tantum, sed (vt in repetitione Augustanae Consessionis, & in locis communibus Melanchthonis diserte dicitur) propter subsecutam & in nos propagatam naturae corruptionem, atque adeo propter culpam propriam rei sumus. Posui in principio hujus examinis, dum statutum quaestionis constituerem, verba Ægidij Huntij celebris Augustanae Confessionis Theologi affirmantis peccatum Adami posteris imputari tantum mediate, nimirum mediante corruptione hereditaria. Ex quo manifestum est eum quoque reatum post corruptionem posuisse, ac censuisse, nascentes reos esse irae divinae propter lapsum Adae mediate & remote, propter corruptionem vero proxime & immediate. Itaque in illa Confessione duas causas reatus exprimi, proximam & remotam. Atque haec est nunc quidem mea responsio ad verba prorsus gemina, quae tu citasti, ex Confessione Saxonica. Itaque non est illius Confessionis religione impeditus Iohannes Gerardus Professor Theologiae Ienae, quin Bellarmino distinguenti peccatum originale in actuale illud Adami & peruersitatem ex eo natam, diserte contradiceret. De vtriusque Confessionis scriptore Melanchthone bene admones. Id enim, vt paulo post videbimus, cap. seq. causam meam iuuabit. Nunc obseruasi placet, in priore editione Confessionis Augustanae haec verba haberi, damnant Pelagianos & alios qui vitium originis negant esse peccatum. Nullibi autem reperies damnari qui negant peccatum actuale Adami posteris imputari: quanquam id non nego, nisi addita hac limitatione proximi vel immediate.
units.tr: Next you pass to the Augsburg Confession, which you say most evidently subscribes to your opinion, Article 2: Likewise they teach that after the fall of Adam all men born by natural generation have original sin. We understand original sin, as the holy Fathers and all Orthodox and piously learned men in the Church call it, to be the guilt by which those born, on account of Adam's fall, are liable to the wrath of God and eternal death, and the corruption of human nature itself propagated from Adam. In these words, you say, they clearly distinguish the guilt on account of the fall from the corruption of nature, and they consider in original sin first the guilt and then the corruption. But what else is guilt than the obligation to punishment on account of Adam's fall, in which we have fallen, and on account of that first sin of the first man, which is imputed to us? Hence it follows, from that Augsburg Confession, that guilt does not follow but precedes corruption. Let Sohnius, Doctor of Theology and Professor at Heidelberg, answer for me. Secondly, he says, it is taught (in the second edition of the Augsburg Confession, from which you cited those words; for the first edition made no mention of guilt, but was worded thus: Likewise they teach that after the fall of Adam all men born according to nature are born with sin, that is, without fear of God, without trust in God, and with concupiscence) what original sin is, which the holy Fathers, all Orthodox and piously learned men call such. Here the definition is again partial. For there are two parts from which sin is defined: namely guilt and the corruption of human nature itself propagated from Adam. Of these, corruption is prior in order, and guilt posterior, that is, because we are corrupted, therefore we are guilty of the wrath of God and eternal damnation. And a little later: This guilt is first defined as that by which those born are, on account of Adam's fall, liable to the wrath of God and eternal death. This definition must be understood rightly. For it is not on account of Adam's fall as a sin merely foreign to us, but (as is plainly said in the repetition of the Augsburg Confession and in Melanchthon's Loci communes) on account of the corruption of nature that followed and was propagated into us, and so on account of our own fault we are guilty. At the beginning of this examination, when I set out the state of the question, I put the words of Giles Hunnius, the famous theologian of the Augsburg Confession, affirming that Adam's sin is imputed to posterity only mediately, namely through hereditary corruption. From this it is clear that he too placed guilt after corruption, and judged that those born are guilty of the wrath of God because of Adam's fall mediately and remotely, but because of corruption proximately and immediately. Thus two causes of guilt are expressed in that Confession, the proximate and the remote. And this is my present answer to the two entirely similar passages that you cited from the Saxon Confession. Accordingly John Gerhard, Professor of Theology at Jena, was not hindered by the scruple of that Confession from plainly contradicting Bellarmine, who distinguished original sin into that actual sin of Adam and the perversity born from it. You rightly remind us of the writer of both Confessions, Melanchthon. For, as we shall see a little later in the following chapter, this will help my cause. Now I am pleased to have observed that in the earlier edition of the Augsburg Confession these words are found: They condemn the Pelagians and others who deny that the vice of origin is sin. Nowhere, however, will you find that those are condemned who deny that Adam's actual sin is imputed to posterity; although I do not deny this, except with the added limitation proximately or immediately.

units.la: In Confessione Vvitembergica sic laudatur Apostoli ad Rom. v. 12. verba, Ad Rom. 5. per vnius delictum propagatum est malum in omnes homines ad condemnationem. Vide an id congruat cum tua verborum Apostoli expositione. In confessione Bohemica leguntur haec verba, Deinde docent ex scripturis, quod homines agnoscere debeant propter peccata ab hac radice nascentia, dignam sibi imminere perditionem formidabilem Dei vindictam impendere, & dignam suis factis gehennae poenam propositam esse. Peccati actualis Adami imputati, aut reatus inde nati, nullam, vt vides, mentionem faciunt, quo tamen loco fieri debuisset, siquidem in tua fuissent sententia. Percurrimus omnes Confessiones Fidei Ecclesiarum Reformatarum. Mirum est eas summo consensu conspirasse ad tuam illam imputationem non docendam.
units.tr: In the Confession of Wittenberg the words of the Apostle in Romans 5:12 are cited thus: Rom. 5. Through the offence of one, evil has spread to all men unto condemnation. See whether this agrees with your exposition of the Apostle's words. In the Bohemian Confession these words are read: Then they teach from Scripture that men ought to recognise that, on account of sins springing from this root, a deserved perdition hangs over them, the dreadful vengeance of God is impending, and the punishment of hell, deserved by their own deeds, is set before them. As you see, they make no mention of the imputed actual sin of Adam, or of the guilt arising from it; yet they ought to have done so in that place, if it had been your opinion. We have gone through all the Confessions of Faith of the Reformed Churches. It is remarkable that they have agreed with the greatest unanimity in not teaching that imputation of yours.

units.la: Sed tu illis addis scriptum recentius, Canones Synodi Dordrechtanae, quos ego, vt par est, maximi facio; Fateris non dici canonibus illis peccatum illud primum primi hominis omnibus imputari disertis verbis. Ratio est, inquis, quia non fuit de ea re controversia inter remonstrates & Orthodoxos. Itaque noluit nec debuit Synodus tam precise decidere, quomodo illud peccatum Adami nostrum sit peccatum, & nos faciat reos. Putasne igitur eam voluisse quaestionem illam decidere oblique & per consequentiam absque ulla deliberatione, ullo examine? Mihi quidem id non fit verisimile. Itaque nihil deprehendo in Canonibus eius non consentaneum meae sententiae. Nam quod in primo canone dicuntur omnes homines in Adamo peccasse, id æque meæ ac tuæ sententiæ congruit, vt iam aliquoties liquidum feci. Vrges verba Art.2.de 3.& 4.capp. Qualis autem post lapsum fuit homo tales & liberos procreauit, nempe, corruptus corruptos; corruptione ab Adamo in omnes posteros (solo Christo excepto) per vitiosa naturæ propagationem iusto Dei iudicio deriuata. At quid opus fuit imputatione, vt qualis homo fuit post lapsum, tales & liberos procrearet? Cur non æque absque imputatione propagari contagiosa vitiositas potuit, ac ipsa natura, cui inseparabiliter inhæret? Sed te mouent verba illa, iusto Dei iudicio. Quid enim, inquis, hoc sibi vult, nisi Deum iusto suo iudicio habuisse omnes homines pro peccatoribus post lapsum primi hominis, quia omnes in illo peccarunt, & peccatum eius omnibus imputatur, unde illa corruptio in omnes diffusa est. Verum debuisti etiam obseruare, Synodum non dicere corruptionem ab Adamo in omnes posteros per imputationem peccati eius actualis omnibus posteris, quæ tua est sententia, sed, quæ mea est, per vitiosa naturæ propagationem deriuari.
units.tr: But you add a more recent document, the Canons of the Synod of Dort, which I rightly hold in the highest regard. You admit that those canons do not say in express words that this first sin of the first man is imputed to all. The reason, you say, is that there was no controversy about this matter between the Remonstrants and the Orthodox. So the Synod neither wished nor needed to decide so precisely how that sin of Adam is our sin and makes us guilty. But do you think it wished to settle that question obliquely and by inference, without any deliberation or examination? For my part, that does not seem likely. Therefore I find nothing in its Canons inconsistent with my view. For the statement in the first canon that all men sinned in Adam agrees as well with my view as with yours, as I have already made clear several times. You press the words of Article 2 of chapters 3 and 4: But as man was after the fall, so he begot children: corrupt children from a corrupt father, the corruption derived from Adam to all his posterity (Christ alone excepted) by the sinful propagation of nature, through the just judgment of God. But what need was there for imputation for man, being what he became after the fall, to beget such children? Why could contagious vitiosity not be propagated just as well without imputation, as nature itself, to which it adheres inseparably? But those words, by the just judgment of God, move you. For what, you say, does this mean, unless that God by his just judgment held all men to be sinners after the fall of the first man, because all sinned in him and his sin is imputed to all, whence that corruption has spread to all? But you should also have observed that the Synod does not say that corruption is derived from Adam to all posterity by the imputation of his actual sin to all posterity, which is your view; it says, as mine does, that it is derived by the sinful propagation of nature.

units.la: Quod autem addidit iusto Dei iudicio, id non potest accipi de iudicio Dei peccatum actuale Adami eius posteris imputantis: imputatur enim posteris Adami eius peccatum vel ante, vel post vitiosæ naturæ propagationem. Si post, propagatio illa effectum non est illius imputationis, quippe, quam antecessit. Si prius, imputatur igitur posteris Adami antequam sint posteri Adami. Non enim sunt posteri Adami, nisi quia profectam ab Adamo generationem & propagationem terminant. Filius non antecedit, sed sequitur generationem. Confugies haud dubie ad præscientiam Dei, sed frustra: nam si fuerunt in Dei præscientia... cientia futuri Adæ posteri , fuerunt etiam in Dei præscientia generationes , per quas futuri erant posteri Adami. Præsciuit enim Deus singulos futuros quomodo sunt futuri. Vt igitur in ipso euentu , sic etiam in Dei præscientia, naturæ ordine , generatio & propagatio posteros Adami antecessit: imputatio autem sequuta est. Imputatur enim posteris Adami peccatum Adami , quia sunt posteri Adami ; quare imputatio peccati Adami, si qua fuit, ea propagationem sequuta est, non antecessit. Hoc argumentum mihi inuictum apparet. Noli igitur putare propagationem vitiosæ naturæ profectam esse ab imputatione peccati actualis Adami toti eius posteritati : id enim profecto contradictione se implicat. Tam absurdam sententiam equidem non ausim tam venerandæ Synodo tribuere. Cur ergo meminit iusti iudicij Dei ? nempe , cum Deus & omnisciusfit & omnipotens , non potuit ea propagatio, quæ vniuersum genus humanum peccato & per peccatum morti subiecit, fieri, nisi Deo sapienter permittente. Permissio autem illa , siue potius non impeditio , profecta est a Dei consilio , Decreto, iudicio. Id iudicium Synodus vt impiis & profanis hominibus os obthuret, monet iustum esse. Est autem iustum primo sensu negatiuo , quia non est iniustum. Deus enim non tenebatur aut ab Adamo vitiositatem illam auferre prorsus , aut vitiositatis illius contagionem ac propagationem impedire. Deinde iustum est, quoniam, vt dicit alicubi Augustinus , quid æquius est quam non impedire naturæ cursum ? Denique æquum etiam fuit non impedire quominus pateret omnibus creaturis quanta sit contagio peccati : dici enim non potest quantum peccati odium & horrorem pijs vel Angelis, vel hominibus tristis hæc experientia incutit. Adde hanc propagationem cessisse in pœnam & castigationem Adamo, nec Adamo foli, sed reliquis etiā parentibus,qui suæ in liberos vitiofitatis propagatæ solent amaros frudus gustare. Sic satius est iustum illud iudicium explicare, quàm fingere Deum imputaffe peccatum Adami ei qui non erat filius Adami, vt tali modo fieret filius Adami. Quasi meriti essemus, vt tali modo generaremur ac peccatores nafceremur. Sed de eodem illo Dei iudicio quid nobis sentiendum videretur, iam exposueramus in extremo Capitis v i.
units.tr: But as to what it adds, by the just judgment of God, this cannot be taken to mean God's judgment imputing Adam's actual sin to his posterity. For Adam's sin is imputed to his posterity either before or after the sinful propagation of nature. If after, that propagation is not the effect of the imputation, since it came before it. If before, then Adam's sin is imputed to Adam's posterity before they are Adam's posterity. For they are not Adam's posterity except in so far as they terminate the generation and propagation proceeding from Adam. A son does not precede his generation but follows it. You will doubtless flee to God's foreknowledge, but in vain: for if the future posterity of Adam was in God's foreknowledge, so too were the generations by which they were to be Adam's posterity. For God foreknew each one as he would be. So, both in the event itself and in God's foreknowledge, generation and propagation came before Adam's posterity in the order of nature, and imputation followed. For Adam's sin is imputed to Adam's posterity because they are his posterity; so any imputation of Adam's sin followed the propagation and did not precede it. This argument seems to me unanswerable. Do not therefore think that the propagation of sinful nature proceeded from the imputation of Adam's actual sin to his whole posterity: that certainly involves a contradiction. I would not dare to attribute so absurd a view to so venerable a Synod. Why then does it mention the just judgment of God? Because God is both all-knowing and almighty, that propagation, which subjected the whole human race to sin and through sin to death, could not have taken place unless God wisely permitted it. That permission, or rather non-hindrance, proceeded from God's counsel, decree and judgment. The Synod says this judgment is just, so as to stop the mouths of impious and profane men. It is just first in a negative sense, because it is not unjust. For God was not bound either to remove that vitiosity from Adam altogether, or to prevent the contagion and propagation of that vitiosity. Next, it is just because, as Augustine says somewhere, what is fairer than not to hinder the course of nature? Lastly, it was also fitting not to prevent all creatures from seeing how great the contagion of sin is: for no one can say how great a hatred and horror of sin this sad experience strikes into the godly, whether angels or men. Add that this propagation was a punishment and chastisement to Adam, and not to Adam alone but also to the other parents, who are wont to taste the bitter fruits of the vitiosity they have passed on to their children. Thus it is better to explain that just judgment in this way than to imagine that God imputed Adam's sin to one who was not a son of Adam, so that in this way he might become a son of Adam. As if we deserved to be generated in such a manner and to be born sinners. But what we should think about that same judgment of God, we had already set out at the end of chapter 6.

units.la: G A R. Addo & Canones Dordracenos cap, 1. th. 1. Omnes homines in Adamo peccauerunt, & reifaeti fiunt maledictionis & mortis æterna. Aliud fine dubio est in sese, aliud in Adamo peccare; aliud esse in fe reum, aliud esse reum in Adamo: nempe illud inhaefionem peccati in nobis fpeēat, hoc peccati, quod olim in Adamo inhaesit, imputationem.
units.tr: G A R. I add also the Canons of Dort, chapter 1, article 1: All men sinned in Adam, and have become liable to the curse and to eternal death. Doubtless it is one thing to sin in oneself and another to sin in Adam; one thing to be guilty in oneself and another to be guilty in Adam. The former refers to the inherence of sin in us; the latter to the imputation of the sin which once inhered in Adam.

units.la: P L A C. Pro imputatione dic propagationem, & totum concedo. Sed illa phrasis, nos in Adamo peccasse, quid importet, & quàm sententiæ meæ non repugnet, tam lepius, eftendi. Subiungi Vir doctus Catechismi Tigurini hæc verba, Quomodo peccatum primorum nostrorum parentum in nos derivatum est? Resp. Ita vt omnes nos in ipsis peccaverimus, Rom. 5. 12. & peccatum per carnalem generationem acceperimus. In quibus nihil video mea quod pugnet cum sententia. Addit explicationem è Commentario manuscripto, qua dicitur peccatum Protoplastorum fieri nostrum duobus modis 1. per imputationem &c. 2. per generationem ab Adamo &c. Sed neque Commentarij manuscripti, quem nunquam vidi, magna esse debet apud me auctoritas, & quid opus est vt peccatum Adami fiat nostrum duobus modis, cum vnus abundè sufficiat? Si nostrum fit per generationem ab Adamo, quid opus est, vt fiat nostrum per alium modum, nempe per imputationem? Ita enim idem peccatum bis fieret nostrum, nosque faceret bis reos, semel per actionem naturalem, nimirum generationem, aciterum per actionem supernaturalem, nempe Dei iudiciariam imputationem.
units.tr: P L A C. For "imputation," say "propagation," and I concede everything. But what the phrase we sinned in Adam means, and how it does not conflict with my view, I have shown so often. You add the words of the learned man from the Tigurine Catechism: How has the sin of our first parents been derived to us? Answer: so that we all sinned in them, Rom. 5.12, and received sin through carnal generation. In these words I see nothing that conflicts with my view. He adds an explanation from a manuscript commentary, which says that the sin of the first parents becomes ours in two ways: 1. by imputation, etc.; 2. by generation from Adam, etc. But a manuscript commentary, which I have never seen, should not carry great authority with me, nor is there any need for Adam's sin to become ours in two ways when one is quite sufficient. If it becomes ours through generation from Adam, what need is there for it to become ours in another way, namely by imputation? For in that case the same sin would become ours twice and make us guilty twice: once by a natural action, namely generation, and again by a supernatural action, namely God's judicial imputation.

units.la: G A R. In ordine Scholæ Geneuensis, qui subiunctus est statutis Ecclesiasticis Ecclesiæ Geneuensis extat Confessionis formula omnibus Scholæ auditoribus præscripta cuius Art. 4. ita habet.
units.tr: G A R. In the order of the School of Geneva, which is appended to the ecclesiastical statutes of the Church of Geneva, there is a formula of confession prescribed to all the students of the School, whose Article 4 reads thus:

units.la: ,, Confiteor omnem nostram corruptionem & vitia, quibus labora-,, mus, ex eo profluxisse, quod Adam omnium pater sua rebellione ,, sese à Deo alienauit. Quo fit vt singuli nascamur peccato originis ,, infecti, & ab ipso matris vtero, à Deo maledicti ac damnati, ,, non propter alienum delictum duntaxat, sed & propter improbi-,, tatem quæ intra nos est, tum quoque cum non apparet. Audisduo delictum alienum, & improbitatem propriam.
units.tr: I confess that all our corruption and the vices by which we labour have flowed from this: that Adam, the father of all, by his rebellion estranged himself from God. Hence it is that each of us is born infected with original sin, and from the very womb of his mother is cursed and condemned by God, not only on account of another's offence, but also on account of the wickedness which is within us, even when it does not appear. You hear "another's offence" and "your own wickedness."

units.la: P L A C. Audio, nempe illud vt maledictionis & damnationis nostræ causam mediatam, hanc vt mediatam. Alioqui difceffiflet Ecclesia Geneuensis à doctrina Caluini, cuius hæc sunt verba Inst. lib. 2. Cap. 1. §. viii. Sic omnibus natura noftra partibus vitiati peruersique (fumus autem ab ipso matris utero sic vitiati) iam ob talem DVNTAXAT corruptionem damnati merito connixiique coram Deo tenemur, Intellige, proxime seu immediate.
units.tr: PLAC. I hear it, namely that the former is the mediate cause of our curse and damnation, and the latter likewise mediate. Otherwise the Church of Geneva would have departed from the teaching of Calvin, whose words are these (Inst. 2.1.8): Thus our whole nature, vitiated and perverted in all its parts (and we are so vitiated from the mother's womb itself), we are justly held condemned and liable before God on account of such corruption alone. Understand: proximately, or immediately.

units.la: CAPVT XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: Imputationem Immediatam seu Antecedentem alie- nam fuisse ab eorum doctrina, quorum opera Deus potissimum usus est ad Ecclesiam Reformandam.
units.tr: The immediate or antecedent imputation was foreign to the doctrine of those by whose work God chiefly reformed the Church.

units.la: PVBLICIS suffragijs, inquis, jungamus & priuata. Quid? putasne me aut iurasse, aut debuisse iurare in verba priuati cuiuslibet doctoris? Non ita iniquus es vt velis ab eorum opinionibus fidem nostram pendere. An si hic aut ille rectam viam hac in re non tenuit, si se coeno sententiae, quam refello, inquinauit, si à Dei verbi puritate desciuit, eius me decet exemplum imitari? Nonne mei potius officij est, quoad eius possum & licet, errantes reuocare in viam, ac cauere ne aliorum vestigijs insistentes fratres & conserui mei in hanc pedicam imprudentes incurrant? Itaque non erat quamobrem te fatigares in conquirendis vndique recentium Theologorum testimonijs. Nam si qui hac in re tecum errarunt, in eo sum vt te dilectissimum in Christo fratrem moneam, ne in illo errore admonitus perseueres, quem pro indulta mihi à Domino nostro Iesu Christo gratia tibi monstro & detego. Tamen ne hujusmodi nominum splendor perstringat oculos tuos, aio tuam illam sententiam quam oppugno initio Reformationis à multis fuisse negatam, satis fuerit duos protulisse testes minime suspectos. Audiuisti
units.tr: "Let us join private suffrages with public ones," you say. What? Do you think I have sworn, or ought to have sworn, to the words of any private teacher whatever? You are not so unfair as to want our faith to hang on their opinions. Or if this or that man did not keep to the right path in this matter, if he has defiled himself with the mire of the opinion I refute, if he has departed from the purity of God's Word, is it fitting that I imitate his example? Is it not rather my duty, as far as I can and am permitted, to call back those who err onto the road, and to take care that my brothers and fellow-servants who follow in others' footsteps do not unwittingly fall into this snare? So there was no reason for you to tire yourself by searching everywhere for the testimonies of recent theologians. For if some have erred with you in this matter, I am here to warn you, my most beloved brother in Christ, not to persist in that error, which I show and expose to you by the grace given me by our Lord Jesus Christ. Yet, lest the splendour of such names dazzle your eyes, I say that the opinion you hold, which I oppose, was denied by many at the beginning of the Reformation. It will be enough to have produced two witnesses who are by no means suspect. You have already heard Pareus admit that the usage and custom of speaking has prevailed in the Church and the schools, so that by the name of original sin only habitual depravity is understood. Now hear Zanchius.

units.la: Note: the top line "Resp. ad Loca Calvini" is the running head; the printed letters "B" and similar are not present. iam Pareum fatentem vsum & consuetudinem loquendi obtinuisse iu Ecclesia & Scholis,vt peccati originalis nomine sola prauitas habitualis censeatur. Audi nunc Zanchium. Hac, inquit, de causa (quoniam non transijt in nos actu) multi negant inobedientiam illam Adæ simpliciter in nos transire : sed tantum vitium naturæ & concupiscentiam cum priuatione iustitiæ originalis: quam eorum sententiam suæ opponit affirmantis per imputationem transire.. vides multos fuisse qui id negarent. Obiter obseruo Zanchium verbo tranfeundi abuti: aliud enim est peccatum in nos transire, aliud nobis imputari fiue attribui; &, fi transit per imputationem, non igitur transit per propagationem & contagionem. Item, fi per imputationem transit, hæc transitio Deo imputanti ascribenda est, illa igitur Dei actio, hoc est, imputatio, cuius tu neque necefsitatem, neque iustitiam demonstrare potes, causa est adæquata & reciproca cur in nos transeat. Sed his miffis de quibus & iam dictum est, & dicendum erit alio loco, idem Zanchius intelligens suam illam doctrinam de imputatione primi peccati nouam posse videri, conatur eam authoritate fulcire: Eadem vero, inquit, est doctrina multorum, qui nostro tempore scripserunt, doctorum virorum. Cur non dixit omnium, fi omnium fuit? aut cur id monuit, fi fuit illa doctrina tum temporis in Ecclesijs & Scholis recepta? Certè, addit Vvolfgangus Musculus vir doctissimus, & excellentissimus sacrarum literarum examinator mecum sentit. Cur non potius nominauit Lutherum, Caluinum, Zuinglium, Bucerum, &c. fi eos fecu sentire putauit? Quorsum illa Musculi elogia non præmissa modo eius testimonio, sed subjuncta etiam, hæc, inquit, doctissimus Musculus, cuius iudicium ego magni facio ? Præter Musculum neminem nominauit, nisi Philippum, cuius tamen verba non adscripsit.
units.tr: "For this reason," he says, "(since it did not pass into us in act) many deny that Adam's disobedience simply passes into us, but only the vice of nature and concupiscence with privation of original righteousness." He sets this opinion of theirs against his own, that the sin passes into us by imputation. You see that there were many who denied it. I observe in passing that Zanchius abuses the word "to pass". It is one thing for sin to pass into us, another for it to be imputed or ascribed to us. If it passes by imputation, then it does not pass by propagation and contagion. Likewise, if it passes by imputation, this transition must be ascribed to God who imputes. So God's action, that is, imputation, whose necessity and justice you cannot demonstrate, is the adequate and reciprocal cause of its passing into us. But setting these aside, which have already been mentioned and will be discussed elsewhere, the same Zanchius, aware that his doctrine of the imputation of the first sin may seem new, tries to support it by authority: "Yet the same," he says, "is the doctrine of many learned men who have written in our time." Why did he not say "of all", if it was the doctrine of all? Or why did he issue this warning, if that doctrine was then received in the Churches and schools? "Certainly," he adds, "Wolfgang Musculus, a most learned man and most excellent examiner of the sacred letters, agrees with me." Why did he not rather name Luther, Calvin, Zwingli, Bucer, and the rest, if he thought they held the same view? Why are those eulogies of Musculus given not only before his testimony but also after it: "This, says the most learned Musculus, whose judgment I hold in high regard?" Apart from Musculus he named no one, except Philip, whose words however he did not cite.

units.la: Sed ad te redeamus, tu Caluinum, Lutherum, Melanchtonem, & nonnullos alios in tuam sententiam citas. Fateor multos Zanchium esse absque ferio examine secutos, ac tecum errasse. Sed cur in eo numero Lutherum ponas causam non habes, nisi quia Consessionibus Augustanæ & Saxonicæ subscripsit, quas ostendi neque tuæ causæ fauere, neque meæ aduersari. Itaque ijs subscripserunt Ægidius Hunnius, Iohannes Gerardus & alij qui nihilominus imputationem illam immediatam peccati actualis Adami, non iam per consequentiam, sed distinctis verbis, negarunt: & quamuis illæ confessiones notæ essent Bellarmino, is tamen non dubitauit illius imputationis negationem Lutheranis tribuere. Philippus autem Melanchton imputationem illam non tam docuit vt suam, quàm, quominus ab alijs doceretur, non impediuit. Traditis enim peccati originis definitionibus meæ sententiæ consentaneis subiunxit, Si quis vult addere natos etiam propter lapsum Adæ reos esse, NON IMPEDIO. Et paulo ante tradita peccati in genere definitione addit. Si quis imaginatur peccatum Originis de peccato tantum esse reatum propter lapsum Adæ, sine prauitate in nobis errat, Si quis autem contendit, nascentes esse reos & propter Adæ lapsum & propter prauitatem nobisçum nascentem, non impedio; quominus addat eam particulam definitioni, quod peccatum sit tum reatus propter Adæ lapsum tum defectus, &c. Itaque totus fuit in probanda & explicanda prauitate illa naturali; dogma illud de reatu propter Adæ lapsum, tanquam alienum nec
units.tr: But let us return to you. You cite Calvin, Luther, Melanchthon, and some others in favour of your opinion. I grant that many followed Zanchius without a thorough examination, and erred with you. But you have no reason to count Luther among them, except that he subscribed the Augsburg and Saxon Confessions, which I have shown favour neither your cause nor oppose mine. Indeed, Aegidius Hunnius, Johann Gerhard and others subscribed to them, and yet they denied that immediate imputation of Adam's actual sin, not merely by inference but in plain words. And although those confessions were well known to Bellarmine, he did not hesitate to attribute the denial of that imputation to the Lutherans. Philip Melanchthon did not so much teach that imputation as his own view, but he did not prevent others from teaching it. For after setting out definitions of original sin consistent with my opinion, he added: "If anyone wishes to add that children are also guilty because of Adam's fall, I DO NOT PREVENT IT." And a little before, after giving his definition of sin in general, he adds: "If anyone imagines that original sin is only guilt because of Adam's fall, without depravity in us, he errs. If anyone, however, contends that those who are born are guilty both because of Adam's fall and because of the depravity born with us, I do not prevent him from adding that particle to the definition, that sin is both guilt because of Adam's fall and defect, etc." So he was wholly concerned with proving and explaining that natural depravity; that dogma of guilt because of Adam's fall, as something foreign, he neither approved nor disapproved, and

units.la: Ppp probauit nec improbauit. Si vt suum, vt verum, vt creditu necessarium sibi docendum putaffet, an dixifset si quis contendat, si quis vult addere, Item non impedi o? Et tamen Zanchius adeo Theologorum suffragijs deflituebatur, vt alium non haberet quem pro sua sententia potius laudaret, patronum, vt vides, admodum indifferentem, ex cuius scriptis possem contra te multa proferre. Sed eum mittamus praestantissimum quidem virum, sed qui tamen suos naevos habuit, cujus vnicum proferam ex ijsdem locis communibus loco de peccatis actualibus, Manifestum est, inquit, elec- tos & renatos posse amittere gratiam.
units.tr: if he had thought it to be taught as his own, as true, and as necessary to believe, would he have said "if anyone contends, if anyone wishes to add," and likewise "I do not prevent it?" And yet Zanchius was so lacking in the support of theologians that he had no other man he could praise for his opinion as a patron, one, as you see, quite indifferent, from whose writings I could bring forward much against you. But let us pass him over, a most excellent man indeed, yet one who had his own blemishes. I will quote from him just one remark from the same common places, in the place on actual sins: "It is evident," he says, "that the elect and the regenerate can lose grace."

units.la: Venio ad Caluinum, virum incomparabilem. Eum nego in tua illa sententia fuisse; idemque de Zuinglio, de Bucero, de Petro Martyre, de Bulingero, de Gualtero, de Aretio, de Thoffano, de Szegedino, de Camerone & alijs dico. Ex his omnibus duos pertrahere in tuas partes conatus es, Caluinum & Martyrem, sed frustra.
units.tr: I come to Calvin, an incomparable man. I deny that he was in your opinion; and I say the same of Zwingli, Bucer, Peter Martyr, Bullinger, Walter, Aretius, Tossanus, Szegedin, Cameron and others. Of all these you have tried to draw two into your party, Calvin and Martyr, but in vain.

units.la: Ad Caluinum quod attinet, Tu fateris in toto cap. 1. lib. 2. eum nullibi quod notaueris loqui de illa imputatione. Sed, inquis, nullibi etiam negat hanc imputationem. Itaque sensus illius eliciendus est ex consequentis ver- borum ipsius. At, inquam, si non loquitur de illa imputatione, eo ipso tacite negat illam imputationē: tractat enim ex professo de peccato originis eo in loco. Si illam imputationem credidit, si putauit dogma esse & traditum in sacris literis & credendum fidelibus, idque peccatum actuale imputatum, esse aut ipsum peccatum originale, aut illius partem primariam ac praecipuam, nonne debuit eam docere & probare? Quid erat quamobrem suum de peccato originali tractatum hac parte mutilaret? aut Ecclesiæ dogma necessarium inuideret? Adde quod eo capite versatur in definiendo peccato originali diligenter & accurate, & profitetur eam se tradere illius definitionem, quæ veritati sibi videatur optimè consentanea. Videtur ergo, inquit, peccatum originale hereditaria naturæ nostræ prauitas & corruptio in omnes animæ partes diffusa, quæ primum facit reos iræ Dei, tum etiam opera in nobis profert quæ Scriptura vocat opera carnis. Habuissetne Calvinus hanc definitionem pro optima, si iudicasset eam peccati originis vnam duntaxat partem, eamque minùs præcipuam explicare? Conscientiam tuam appello testem, num tu, qua es in sententia, sic peccatum originale cùm definiuisses tum tractasses, prætermisso prorsus peccato actuali Adæ imputato? Agnosce igitur Caluinum in tua illa sententia minimè fuisse.
units.tr: As for Calvin: you admit that in the whole first chapter of the second book he nowhere, as you have noticed, speaks of that imputation. But, you say, he nowhere denies this imputation either. Therefore his meaning must be drawn from the sequence of his own words. But I say: if he does not speak of that imputation, he thereby tacitly denies it, for he treats of original sin on purpose in that place. If he believed in that imputation, if he thought it a doctrine both taught in the sacred letters and to be believed by the faithful, and that the imputed actual sin is either original sin itself or its primary and chief part, ought he not to have taught and proved it? Why would he have mutilated his own treatment of original sin in this part? Or why would he have grudged the Church a necessary dogma? Add that in that chapter he deals carefully and accurately in defining original sin, and professes that he is giving that definition which seems to him most consistent with the truth. It seems, then, he says, that original sin is the hereditary depravity and corruption of our nature, diffused through all parts of the soul, which first makes us liable to the wrath of God, and then also produces in us those works which Scripture calls the works of the flesh. Would Calvin have held this definition to be the best if he had judged it to explain only one part, and that less principal, of original sin? I call your conscience as witness: whether you, in the opinion you hold, when you defined and treated original sin, did so while entirely passing over the imputed actual sin of Adam? Acknowledge, therefore, that Calvin was by no means in your opinion.

units.la: Tu idem laudatis ex Inst. lib. 3 v. cap. 15. §10. vbi agitur de Beneficijs Baptismi his verbis, Dominus hoc signo nobis pollicetur plenam solidamque remissionem satiam esse, & culpæ quæ imputanda nobis erat, & pœnæ quæ ob culpam luenda, fateris eum de imputatione loqui, non antecedente, sed subsequente corruptionem & prauitatem, quæ est in quouis homine nascente, addisque facile esse id colligere ex ipsius verbis. Cur igitur verba illa laudasti? At, inquis, nullibi antecedentem negat. Immo eo ipso quod hoc loco eam non intelligit, negat tacitè: per culpam enim quæ nobis imputanda erat omnem culpam completi debuit, quæ baptismo remittitur. Atqui manifestum est, te ipso fatente, per culpam illam quæ nobis imputanda erat, eum actualem Adami inobedientiam non intellexisse. Non putauit igitur eam nobis baptismo remitti. Remittitur autem si imputatur: Non putauit igitur eam nobis ante baptismum imputari.
units.tr: You also cite Institutes book 3, chapter 15, section 10, where he treats of the benefits of baptism in these words: "The Lord promises us by this sign that the full and solid remission both of the guilt which was to be imputed to us and of the punishment which was to be paid for that guilt is sure." You admit that he speaks of an imputation that follows, not precedes, the corruption and depravity present in every human being at birth, and you add that this is easy to gather from his own words. Why then did you cite those words? "But," you say, "he nowhere denies an antecedent imputation." On the contrary, by the very fact that he does not understand it in this place, he denies it tacitly. For the guilt which was to be imputed to us must have meant all the guilt that baptism remits. But it is manifest, as you yourself grant, that by that guilt which was to be imputed to us he did not mean Adam's actual disobedience. He therefore did not think that this is remitted to us by baptism. Yet it is remitted only if it is imputed. He therefore did not think it was imputed to us before baptism.

units.la: Verum tu ex alijs locis existimas imputationem illam antecedentem colligi posse per consequentiam. Quid ergo alibi dixit Caluinus ? Adæ lapsu & defictione totum genus humanum maledictioni fuisse addictum. Ob vnius culpam fieri omnes reos. Intellige, mediante corruptione in omnes propagata. id cum ex eius vniuersa disputatione de peccato Originali apparet, tum ex his verbis quæ iam semel adscripsi, quod vnius delicto periisse nos tradit, sic accipe: quia ex ipso in nos corruptio transfusa sit. Neque enim sic perimus eius culpa quasi extra culpam ipsi simus: sed quia eius peccatum peccati nostri causa est, exitium nostrum illi. Paulus adscribit peccatum nostrum voco quod nobis ingenitum est, & cum quo nascimur.
units.tr: But you think that this antecedent imputation can be inferred by consequence from other passages. What, then, did Calvin say elsewhere? "By the fall and defection of Adam the whole human race was given over to the curse. Through the guilt of one, all are made guilty." Understand this as through corruption spread into all. This appears both from his whole discussion of original sin and from the words I have already quoted once: "What he tells us we perished by the sin of one, take thus: because corruption was transfused into us from him. For we do not perish by his guilt as if we were outside that guilt ourselves; but because his sin is the cause of our sin, our ruin is his. Paul ascribes to it our sin, which I call what is innate in us and with which we are born."

units.la: Quid adhuc dixit? Ibidem, inquis, damnat Pelagij profanum Commentum Adam suo tantum damno peccasse, nihil nocuisse posteris; vnde sequitur ipsum approbare contrarium, scilicet Adamum peccando nocuisse posteris. Nonne hoc ipsum & probo, & doceo, & inculco? At, inquis, hoc peccasse nos ducit ad primum peccatum, nempe vt ad fontem & causam mali illius, quod inde ad posteros defluxit. Sic qui pestem contrahit, & post aliis affricat, non suo tantum, sed aliorum etiam damno eam contraxisse dicitur. At, inquis, statuit suisse Adamum humanæ naturæ non progenitorem modo, sed quasi radicem, atque ideo in illius corruptione merito vitiatum fuisse hominum genus. Quid tum postea? Idem & statuo, & clamo. Nempe, vt ipse ait, à radice putrefacta rami putridi prodierunt, qui suam putredinem transfmiserunt ad alios cxse nascentes surculos.
units.tr: What else did he say? "In the same place," you say, "he condemns the profane invention of Pelagius that Adam sinned only to his own loss and harmed no posterity; whence it follows that he approves the contrary, namely that Adam by sinning harmed his posterity." Do I not myself prove this, teach it, and insist on it? But, you say, "this leads us to hold that we sinned in the first sin," namely as to the source and cause of that evil which flowed from it to posterity. So too one who contracts a plague and afterwards passes it on to others is said to have contracted it not only to his own loss but to the loss of others also. "But," you say, "he holds that Adam was the progenitor not only of human nature but, as it were, its root, and therefore the human race was rightly corrupted in his corruption." What follows from that? I too both hold and proclaim the same. Indeed, as he himself says, "from the putrefied root came putrid branches, which passed their putrefaction on to the shoots born from them."

units.la: Sed tu imprimis vrges hæc eius verba, Extra controuersiam est Christi iustitiam communicatione nostram esse, & ex ea vitam: simul consicitur vtramque ita in Adam fuisse perditam, vt in Christo recuperetur; peccatum vero & mortem ita per Adam obrepsisse, vt per Christum aboleantur. Non sunt obscura verba, iustificari multos per Christi obedientiam, quemadmodū, per Adæ inobedientiam peccatores fuerant constituti: Ideoque inter eos duos hanc esse relationem, quod hic nos suo exitio inuolutos secum perdidit, ille nos sua gratia in salutem restituit. Quid in his verbis est quod meæ sententiæ repugnet? Hinc, inquis, infero, si iustitia nostra fit communicatione, tum iniustitia Adami nostra est etiam communicatione. Esto; quid inde? nostra autem, subjungis, fit iustitia Christi communicatione cum imputatur per fidem, Aio illud cum imputatur, quamuis verum sit, tamen alienum esse ab illa comparatione inter Christum & Adamum, vt instituitur ab Apostolo & Caluino. Sed quid concludis? Igitur & iniustitia Adami nostra est communicatione, cum imputatur propter generationem. Dic propter ingenitam prauitatem; vt quàm imputatio iustitiæ Christi sequitur fidem, tam imputatio iniustitiæ Adami sequatur deriuatam ab eo prauitatem: nam vt communicatur iustitia Christi per fidem quæ est Dei donum, sic communicatur nobis iniustitia Adami per defluxam ab eo vitiofitatem. Per generationem naturalem simus filij Adami quatenus Adam fuit homo: similes enim ei sumus in natura; at per vitiositatis & prauitatis propagationem simus filij Adami quatenus fuit peccator: similes enim ei sumus in prauitate seu peccato. Iterum, inquis, iustificamur per Christi obedientiam, quemadmodum per Adæ inobed entiam peccatores constituimur. Atqui iustificamur per Christi obedientiam imputatam. Ergo & peccatores constituimur per inobedientiam Adae nobis imputatam. Nec, (Addis) est Cauillandum, non agi de Modo. Caluinus enim infert quemadmodum, vt designet vtrobique eundem modum. At quis negabit Caluinum affirmare nos iustificari per Christi obedientiam imputatam? Equidem id non nego: tantum nego illam imputationem pertinere ad illam comparationem. Nam alioqui, velis nolis fatendum est esse aliquam in Modo dissimilitudinem. Audi ipsum met Caluinum. Porro, inquit, duas hic differentias inter Christum & Adamum adnotare operae pretium est: quas non ideo subticuit Apostolus, quia negligendas censeret, sed quia praesentis argumenti nihil referebat eas enumerare. Prior est, quod peccato Adae non per solam imputationem damnamur, ac si alienipeccati exigeretur a nobis poenam, sed ideo poenam eius sustinemus quia & culpa sumus rei, quatenus scilicet natura nostra in ipso vitiata iniquitatis reatu obstringitur apud Deum. At per Christi iustitiam ALIO MODO in salutem restituimur: neque enim ideo nobis accepta fertur. QVIA INTRA NOS sit: sed quod Christum ipsum cum bonis suis omnibus Patris largitate nobis donatum possidemus. Itaque donum iustitiae non qualitatem, qua nos Deus imbuat, ut perperam quidam interpretantur, sed gratuitam iustitiae imputationem significat. Vides ab ipso Caluino modi dissimilitudinem obseruari, & quidem hanc ipsam quam oppugnas; atque adeo actualis peccati Adami imputationem negari. Cur ergo vrget aduersus Pelagianos illud quemadmodum? quia Pelagiana imitatio non iam modum communicationis, sed ipsam communicationem tollit. Negabant enim Pelagiani vere nobis ab Adamo iniustitiam communicari. Itaque ipsam rei veritatem negabant, in qua positam esse similitudinem, non autem in veritatis modo, & iam probaui, & iterum probaturus sum Deo bene fauente in Apologia Thesium.
units.tr: But you chiefly press these words of his: "It is beyond controversy that the righteousness of Christ becomes ours by communication, and life from it; at the same time it is made clear that both were lost in Adam so that they might be recovered in Christ; but sin and death crept in through Adam so that they might be abolished through Christ. The words are not obscure: many are justified through the obedience of Christ, just as through the disobedience of Adam they were made sinners. Hence the relation between those two is this: the one involved us in his ruin and destroyed us along with himself; the other restored us to salvation by his grace." What in these words opposes my view? "From this," you say, "I infer that if our righteousness comes by communication, then the unrighteousness of Adam is ours also by communication." Granted; what follows? "But our righteousness," you add, "comes by communication of the righteousness of Christ when it is imputed through faith." I say "when it is imputed": although this is true, it is nonetheless foreign to that comparison between Christ and Adam as the Apostle and Calvin set it up. But what do you conclude? "Therefore the unrighteousness of Adam is also ours by communication, when it is imputed on account of generation." Say rather: on account of innate depravity. Just as the imputation of Christ's righteousness follows faith, so the imputation of Adam's unrighteousness should follow the depravity derived from him. For as the righteousness of Christ is communicated through faith, which is the gift of God, so the unrighteousness of Adam is communicated to us through the vitiated nature that flows from him. By natural generation we are sons of Adam as far as Adam was a man, for we are like him in nature; but by the propagation of vitiation and depravity we are sons of Adam as far as he was a sinner, for we are like him in depravity or sin. "Again," you say, "we are justified through the obedience of Christ, just as we are made sinners through the disobedience of Adam. But we are justified through the imputed obedience of Christ. Therefore we are also made sinners through the disobedience of Adam imputed to us. Nor," you add, "is it to be cavilled that the question is not about the manner. For Calvin writes 'just as' to mark the same manner in both cases." But who will deny that Calvin affirms that we are justified through the imputed obedience of Christ? I do not deny that; I only deny that this imputation belongs to that comparison. For otherwise, whether we like it or not, we must admit some dissimilarity in the manner. Hear Calvin himself: "Moreover, it is worth noting two differences here between Christ and Adam, which the Apostle did not pass over because he thought them to be neglected, but because it did not matter to the present argument to enumerate them. The first is that we are condemned for Adam's sin not by imputation alone, as if we were made to pay the penalty of another's sin, but we also undergo his punishment because we are guilty of the fault itself, insofar as our nature, vitiated in him, is bound over to guilt before God. But through the righteousness of Christ we are restored to salvation in another way: for it is not reckoned to us because it is inside us, but because we possess Christ himself with all his goods, given to us by the bounty of the Father. Thus the gift of righteousness signifies not a quality with which God imbues us, as some wrongly interpret, but the gratuitous imputation of righteousness." You see that the dissimilarity of manner is observed by Calvin himself, and indeed this very dissimilarity that you attack; and so the imputation of Adam's actual sin is denied. Why then does he press that "just as" against the Pelagians? Because the Pelagian imitation removes not the manner of communication but communication itself. For the Pelagians denied that unrighteousness is truly communicated to us from Adam. They therefore denied the very truth of the matter, in which the likeness consists, not merely the manner of the truth. I have already proved this, and by God's favour I shall prove it again in the Apology for the Theses.

units.la: Quid adhuc dixit Caluinus quod illi imputationi fauere videatur? Laudas ex Institut. lib. iii. cap. 23. § 7. haec verba, Neque enim factum est naturaliter ut a salute exciderent omnes vnius parentis culpa. Cunctos mortales in vnius hominis persona morti aeternae mancipatos fuisse Scriptura clamat. Hoc cum naturae adscribi nequeat ab admirabili Dei consilio profectum esse minime obscurum est. Iterum quaero, unde factum est vt tot gentes vna cum liberis aeternae morti inuoluerent lapsus Adae, nisi quia Deo ita visum est? Subjungis hanc interrogationem, Cum negat naturaliter factum, neque naturae adscribi posse, nunquid affirmit non tantum, neque simpliciter esse a generatione, quae natura est, sed praecipue a decreto Dei ita volentis & imputantis lapsum & peccatum Adae? Miror te hunc locum citasse: nam & verba quae proxime antecedunt, & illa quae interiecta sunt clamant loqui Caluinum non de iudicio Dei imputantis peccatum hominibus, sed de praedestinatione & praeordinatione peccati: sic enim exorditur hanc sectionem, disertis verbis hoc extare negant, decretum fuisse a Deo vt sua defectione periret Adam. Et paulo post, Atqui praedestinatio velint, nolint in posteris se proferri: Neque enim factum est naturaliter vt a salute exciderent omnes vnius parentis culpa. Quid eos prohibet fateri de vno homine, quod inuiti de toto humano genere concedunt, &c. Cur verba illa neque enim factum est, &c, a praecedentibus & sequentibus separasti, quae, vt vides, vociferantur de prædestinatione agi, non autem de imputatione iudiciaria peccati actualis Adami toti posteritati, quam Caluinus nunquam docuit? Nonne manifestum est eum ducere argumentum à peccato & ruina totius generis humani ad peccatum ipsius Adami, vt quàm illud est ab ordinatione diuina, tam euincat etiam istud ab ordinatione diuina esse? Constat autem peccatum Adami non esse profectum ab antecedente imputatione. Loquitur igitur, non de Dei imputantis peccatum iudicio, sed de Dei peccatum permittentis & ordinantis decreto. Hinc autem tantùm abest vt tua illa imputatio confici possit, vt necessario argumento euerti queat. vult enim Caluinus parem esse rationem ruinæ totius generis humani & lapsus Adami. Quid eos, inquit, prohibet fateri de uno homine, & quod inuiti de toto genere humano concedunt? Et paulò post, Nec absurdum videri debet quod dico Deum non modo primi hominis casum, & in eo posterorum ruinam præuidisse: sed arbitrio quoque suo dispensasse. Atqui posita tua illa imputatione admodum dispar est vtriusque ratio, vt hæc nulla sit consequentia, si ab ordinatione diuina est quod poteri Adæ pereunt, itidem ab ordinatione diuina est quod Adam lapsus est: Non enim huic imputari potuit peccatum vt laberetur, quemadmodum illis imputatum est peccatum Adæ vt perirent. Posita igitur illa tua imputatione ruit argumentatio Caluini: non enim si Dei nobis imputantis peccatum Adami iudicio cecidimus, consequens est vt Adamus caderet Deum decreuisse, id quod concludere Caluinus instituerat.
units.tr: What else did Calvin say that seems to favour that imputation? You cite from Institutes book 3, chapter 23, section 7, these words: "For it did not happen naturally that all were excluded from salvation through the fault of one parent. Scripture proclaims that all mortals were delivered over to eternal death in the person of one man. Since this cannot be ascribed to nature, it is quite clear that it proceeded from the admirable counsel of God. Again I ask, whence did it come about that the fall of Adam involved so many nations along with their children in eternal death, unless because it seemed good to God?" You add this question: "When he denies that it happened naturally, and that it can be ascribed to nature, does he not also affirm that it is not merely, nor simply, from generation, which is nature, but chiefly from the decree of God, who willed and imputed Adam's fall and sin?" I am surprised that you cited this passage. For both the words immediately before and those inserted after it proclaim that Calvin is speaking not of God's judgement imputing sin to men, but of the predestination and foreordination of sin. For he begins this section thus: "They deny in plain words that it was decreed by God that Adam should perish by his own defection." And shortly after: "But predestination, whether they like it or not, is brought forth in posterity. For it did not happen naturally that all were excluded from salvation through the fault of one parent. Why does what they unwillingly concede about the whole human race prevent them from confessing it about one man, etc.?" Why did you separate the words "for it did not happen, etc." from what precedes and follows them, which, as you see, cry out that the subject is predestination, and not the judicial imputation of Adam's actual sin to all posterity, which Calvin never taught? Is it not manifest that he draws an argument from the sin and ruin of the whole human race to the sin of Adam himself, so that just as the former comes from divine ordination, so the latter is shown to come from divine ordination too? It is certain, however, that the sin of Adam did not proceed from an antecedent imputation. He therefore speaks not of God's judgement imputing sin, but of God's decree permitting and ordaining sin. Yet your imputation is so far from being established by this that it can be overturned by a necessary argument. For Calvin wishes the reason for the ruin of the whole human race and for Adam's fall to be the same. "Why," he says, "does it prevent them from confessing about one man what they unwillingly concede about the whole human race? And shortly after: Nor should it seem absurd when I say that God not only foresaw the fall of the first man and the ruin of his posterity in him, but also disposed it by his own will." But on your imputation the two reasons are very unlike, so that this inference fails: if our perishing through Adam's sin comes from divine ordination, it does not follow that Adam's falling does too. For sin could not be imputed to Adam so that he should fall, in the way that Adam's sin was imputed to them so that they should perish. Therefore, with your imputation posited, Calvin's argument collapses: for if we fell through God's judgement imputing Adam's sin to us, it does not follow that Adam fell because God decreed it, which is what Calvin had set out to conclude.

units.la: Similem locum profers ex Comment. in Gen. cap. 3. verf. 6. 3. verf. 6. his verbis, Nunc si quis obiciat iniquum esse vt poenam alieni peccati luant infantes, Respondeo, quicquid donorum nobis in Adæ persona contulerat Deus potuisse iure optima auferre, cum ille impie defecit. Neque opus est confugere ad vetus illud quorundam figmentum, quod animæ ex traduce oriantur. Neque enim naturaliter ex Adæ progenie corruptionem traxerunt posteri: sed id potius ex Dei ordinatione pendet; qui sicuti totam humani generis naturam in uno homine ornauerat præstantissimis dotibus, ita in eodem ipsam nudauit. Iam vero ex quo in Adam corrupti sumus non sustinemus alieni delicti poenam, sed propria culpa rei sumus. Magnam tibi habeo gratiam quod me huius loci admonueris: attente enim inspectus meam sententiam egregie confirmat. Sed antequam id ostendo, quid inde inferas audiamus. Hic, inquis, iterum negat Caluinus nos naturaliter ex Adæ progenie corruptionem trahere, & affirmit id esse ex Dei ordinatione. Non ergo vult id simpliciter esse a natura propter genituram: sed maxime ex Dei ordinatione. Quid autem est, quasi illa Dei ordinatio, nisi decretum illud Dei iuste imputantis peccatum ab Adamo commissum omnibus & singulis illius posteris? Illa est imputatio antecedens, scilicet statim a lapsu Adami: de subsequente ita loquitur Caluinus, ex quo in Adam corrupti sumus propria culpa rei sumus. Duo vrges, vnum quod neget naturaliter, alterum quod affirmet ex Dei ordinatione nos ex Adæ progenie corruptionem trahere. Prius ita hic negat, vt alibi affirmet; & vero constat per naturalem generationem corruptionem propagari: id docet Scriptura, id clamat Antiquitas, id Ecclesia omnium sæculorum credidit. Audi igitur sese explicantem ipsum Caluinum, natura, inquit, vitiositatem fluxisse negat. niffe negamus, vt significemus aduentitiam magis esse qualitatem, qua homini acciderit, quam substantialem proprietatem, qua ab initio indita fuerit. Vocamus tamen naturalem, ne quis ab vnoquoque prava consuetudine comparari putet, quum hereditario iure vniuersos comprehensos teneat. Negat igitur esse à natura, hoc est, esse substantialem proprietatem: Negat esse à natura qualis ab initio creata fuit: Negat esse à Natura quo sensu Natura à nonnullis vt independens à Deo concipitur. Intelligit autem per ordinationem Dei non imputationem culpae Adami, sed praedestinationem. Vnde ergo, inquit alibi, illa hominii prauitas vt à Deo sio deficiat? ne ex creatione esse putetur, Elogio suo approbauerat Deus quod profectum erat à seipso. Propria ergo malitia quam acceperat à Domino puram naturam corrupit, sui ruina totam posteritatem in exitium secum attraxit. Quare in corrupta potius humani generis natura euidentem damnationis causam, quae nobis propinquior est, contemplemur, quam abscónditam ac penitus incomprehensibilem inquiramus in Dei praedestinatione. Praedestinationem audis, imputationem non audis. Annon si tecum sensisset, iussisset nos etiam in illa tua imputatione generis humani damnationis causam contemplari, & quidem vel solum, vel praecipue? Sed verba à te laudata propius inspiciamus, Obijciebatur iniquum esse vt poenam alieni peccati, hoc est, peccati Adami luant insontes. Respondet Caluinus negando insontes alieni peccati poenam luere, ex quo, inquit, in Adam corrupti sumus non sustinemus alieni delicti poenam, sed propria culpa rei sumus. Nempe, corruptio & sua cuique propria inest, & vere peccatum est. Verum quia recurrebat quaestio de illa corruptione, quam ab inobedientia Adæ fluxisse dicebat, Caluinus it obuiam; ac ne putaretur vel à natura esse qualis fuit primum creata, vel à natura independente à Deo, eam non à natura, sed à Dei ordinatione pendere ait. Hujus autem ordinationis & rationem,& iustitiam explicat: Rationem quidem,nam eam collocat in præstantissimorum donorum ablatione, quibus naturam in vno homine ornauerat: iustitiam vero; Deum enim affirmat dona, quæ nobis in Adæ persona contulerat, potuisse iure auferre. Quæro quo sensu dicatur Deus dona nobis in Adæ persona contulisse? Num sensu, vt ita loquar, imputatiuo? Num ita vt possis inde vel donorum illorum, vel alterius cuiusdam rei imputationem antecedentem inferre? Non certè. Quo sensu igitur ea nobis contulisse dicitur? quia sic illa indiderat Adamo vt essent naturalia, propaganda,multiplicanda, communicanda cum natura per generationem naturalem. Quid ergo vetat quominus eodem modo ea nobis abstulisse in Adamo dicatur, quia sic abstulit, vt eorum priuatio facta sit naturalis, hoc est, propaganda cum natura. Cæterum quod ait Caluinus, Deum nobis dona illa abstulisse, id commodè est accipiendum, ne Deum faciamus peccati authorem: est enim iustitiæ priuatio siue in Adamo, siue in nobis sit, formaliter peccatum, vides iam opinor hunc Caluini locum tibi non fauere. Nunc obesse ostendo, & quidem duobus modis. Primum enim obiectioni iniquum esse vt pœnam alieni peccati luant infantes, nulla potuit afferri responsio consentanea sententiæ tuæ, nisi, aut id iniquum non esse, aut peccatum Adami fieri nostrum imputatione: neutrum tamen respondet Caluinus; non fuit igitur Caluinus in tua sententia. Deinde eius verba, ex quo in Adam corrupti sumus non sustinemus alieni delicti poenam, sed propria culpa rei sumus, posita tua sententia sunt falsa. Nam illa ipsa corruptio, si tibi creditur, poena est proprie dicta peccati Adae, quod hoc loco per peccatum alienum intelligitur. Itaque, si tibi creditur, ex quo corrupti sumus, & quandiu corrupti sumus, sustinemus alieni delicti poenam. Huc accedit quod tu mortem & corporis, & aeternam ascribis peccato actuali Adami nobis imputato vel soli, vel saltem praecipue; eam autem ex quo corrupti sumus patimur: quare ex quo corrupti sumus sustinemus poenam delicti Adami, reclamante Calvino. Adde quod, aut nunquam sustinemus poenam peccati Adae, aut eam sustinemus ex quo corrupti sumus. Ex quo enim homines sumus corrupti sumus. Antequam autem essemus, poenam sustinere non potuimus.
units.tr: A similar passage you cite from the Commentary on Genesis, chapter 3, verse 6, in these words: 3. verse 6. Now if anyone objects that it is unjust for infants to pay the penalty of another's sin, I answer: whatever gifts God had bestowed on us in the person of Adam, he could justly take away, since Adam impiously fell away. Nor is there any need to take refuge in that old fiction of certain men, that souls come by traduction. For posterity did not contract corruption naturally from the offspring of Adam; it depends rather on the ordinance of God, who, just as he had adorned the whole nature of the human race in one man with the most excellent gifts, so in the same man he stripped it bare. Indeed, from the time we were corrupted in Adam, we do not suffer the penalty of another's crime, but are guilty of our own fault. I am greatly obliged to you for reminding me of this passage, for when it is carefully examined it strongly confirms my view. But before I show this, let us hear what you infer from it. Here, you say, Calvin again denies that we contract corruption naturally from the offspring of Adam, and he affirms that it comes from the ordinance of God. He therefore does not want it to be simply from nature by generation, but chiefly from the ordinance of God. But what is this so-called ordinance of God, except that decree of God by which he justly imputes the sin committed by Adam to all and each of his posterity? That is the antecedent imputation, namely immediately from the fall of Adam; of the subsequent one Calvin speaks thus: from the time we were corrupted in Adam, we are guilty of our own fault. You press two points: one, that he denies it is naturally, the other, that he affirms it comes from the ordinance of God, that we contract corruption from the offspring of Adam. As for the first, he denies it here in such a way that elsewhere he affirms it; and indeed it is established that corruption is propagated by natural generation. Scripture teaches this, Antiquity proclaims it, and the Church of all ages has believed it. Hear, then, Calvin himself explaining himself: he says that vitiosity does not flow from nature. We deny that it does so, to signify that it is rather an accidental quality which has befallen man than a substantial property which was implanted from the beginning. Yet we call it natural, lest anyone think it is acquired by each person through bad custom, since by hereditary right it holds all men in its grip. He therefore denies that it is from nature, that is, that it is a substantial property; he denies that it is from nature as it was created at the beginning; he denies that it is from Nature in the sense in which some conceive Nature as independent of God. But by the ordinance of God he understands not the imputation of Adam's guilt but predestination. Whence then, he says elsewhere, does that depravity of man come, that it so falls away from God? Lest it be thought to arise from creation, God had approved by his own praise what proceeded from himself. Therefore the proper malice which man had received from the Lord corrupted his pure nature, and by his own ruin drew the whole posterity with him to destruction. Wherefore, let us rather contemplate, in the corrupted nature of the human race, the evident cause of damnation, which is nearer to us, than seek the hidden and wholly incomprehensible cause in the predestination of God. You hear of predestination; you do not hear of imputation. Would he not, if he had agreed with you, have bidden us also to contemplate in that imputation of yours the cause of the damnation of the human race, and indeed either alone or chiefly? But let us look more closely at the words you have praised. The objection was: it is unjust that the innocent should pay the penalty of another's sin, that is, of the sin of Adam. Calvin answers by denying that the innocent pay the penalty of another's sin: from the time we were corrupted in Adam, we do not suffer the penalty of another's crime, but are guilty of our own fault. Clearly, corruption is present in each person as his own and is truly sin. But because the question about that corruption, which he said flowed from the disobedience of Adam, kept recurring, Calvin meets it head on; and so that it might not be thought either to be from nature as it was first created, or from a nature independent of God, he says it depends not on nature but on the ordinance of God. He explains both the reason for this ordinance and its justice: the reason, indeed, since he places it in the taking away of the most excellent gifts with which he had adorned nature in one man; the justice, since he affirms that God could justly take away the gifts which he had bestowed on us in the person of Adam. I ask in what sense it is said that God bestowed gifts on us in the person of Adam. Is it in an imputative sense, so to speak? Is it so that you could from this infer an antecedent imputation of those gifts or of some other thing? Certainly not. In what sense, then, is it said that he bestowed them on us? Because he had so implanted them in Adam that they were natural, to be propagated, multiplied, and communicated with nature by natural generation. What then prevents it from being said in the same way that he took them away from us in Adam, because he took them away in such a manner that their privation became natural, that is, propagated with nature? Moreover, when Calvin says that God took those gifts from us, it is to be understood properly, lest we make God the author of sin; for the privation of righteousness, whether it is in Adam or in us, is formally sin. I think you now see that this passage of Calvin does not favour you. Now I show that it is harmful to you, and in two ways. First, to the objection that it is unjust for infants to pay the penalty of another's sin, no answer could be given consistent with your view, unless either that it is not unjust, or that Adam's sin becomes ours by imputation. Yet Calvin answers neither; therefore Calvin was not on your side. Second, his words, from the time we were corrupted in Adam we do not suffer the penalty of another's crime, but are guilty of our own fault, are false on your view. For that very corruption, if I may believe you, is properly the penalty of Adam's sin, which in this passage is understood by another's sin. Therefore, if I may believe you, from the time we were corrupted, and as long as we are corrupted, we do suffer the penalty of another's crime. To this is added that you ascribe both bodily death and eternal death to the actual sin of Adam imputed to us, either alone or at least chiefly; but we suffer that from the time we were corrupted. Therefore, from the time we were corrupted, we suffer the penalty of Adam's offence, Calvin protesting. Add that either we never suffer the penalty of Adam's sin, or we suffer it from the time we were corrupted. For from the time we are men, we are corrupted. But before we existed, we could not suffer a penalty.

units.la: Quid adhuc profers ex Calvino? Duo loca idem innuentia, Alterum ex breui formula Confessionis Fidei: Alterum ex Confessione Fidei nomine Ecclesiarum Gallicarum, ut coram S. C. M. ederetur. Prior habet, Singuli nascimur originis peccato infecti, & ab ipso matris utero maledicti ac damnati, non propter alienum delictum duntaxat, sed propter improbitatem, quae intra nos est tum quoque cum non apparet. Posterior vero sic, De homine ita praeunte Scriptura sentimus, nempe quod humanum genus per Adami lapsum corruptum sit, quod omnes natura exitio & damnationi obnoxii simus, non tantum quia Adamus ipse peccavit, sed quoniam peccatores & ipsi sumus ab utero. Vrges illa verba, non propter alienum delictum duntaxat, non tantum quia Adamus ipse peccavit. Ergo, inquis, fatetur Calvinus nos esse maledictos propter alienum delictum. Quidni, inquam, id enim ipse quoque ego fateor, sed remote, sed mediate: nisi ita accipis, concilia, sipotes, Calvinum cum Calvino. Iam negauit ex quo corrupti sumus nos sustinere alieni delicti poenam, Nisi id sufficit, accipe alia eiusdem Calvini verba difertissima, Haec itaque duo distincte observanda: nempe, quod sic omnibus naturae nostrae partibus vitiati perversique, iam OB TALEM DVNTAXAT CORRVPTIONEM damnati merito conuictique coram Deo tenemur. Audis nos esse damnatos duntaxat ob talem corruptionem. Nihil potuit dici clarius aut pro illa limitatione quam attuli, aut contra immediatam imputationem peccati Adae. Dicam aliquid amplius, Tu, Tu, inquam, vis nos esse maledictos & damnatos propter delictum Adae duntaxat. itaque illis ipsis verbis quae laudasti contradicis. Vis enim nos ob solum peccatum Adae nobis imputatum nos esse maledictos & damnatos ad has tres poenas corruptionem, mortem corporis, & mortem aeternam. Hanc profecto maledictionem & condemnationem atrociissimam non partiris inter peccatum Adae & improbitatem quae intra nos est, sed totam, quanta quanta est, foli peccato alieno Adae adscribis.
units.tr: What else do you bring forward from Calvin? Two passages pointing to the same thing. The first from the brief formula of the Confession of Faith; the second from the Confession of Faith in the name of the French Churches, to be put forth before His Sacred Imperial Majesty. The first reads: Each of us is born infected with original sin, and cursed and condemned from the very womb of our mother, not only on account of another's offence, but on account of the wickedness which is within us, even when it does not appear. The second reads thus: Concerning man, we think as Scripture teaches before us, namely that the human race has been corrupted through the fall of Adam, and that all of us by nature are liable to destruction and damnation, not only because Adam himself sinned, but because we ourselves are sinners from the womb. You press those words, not on account of another's offence alone, not only because Adam himself sinned. Therefore, you say, Calvin confesses that we are cursed on account of another's offence. Why not, I reply; for I myself also confess this, but remotely and mediately. Unless you take it so, reconcile, if you can, Calvin with Calvin. Now he denied that from the time we were corrupted we suffer the penalty of another's offence. If that is not enough, take another most express passage from the same Calvin: These two things must be carefully observed: namely, that we, being thus corrupted and perverted in all parts of our nature, are rightly held guilty and convicted before God on account of such corruption alone. You hear that we are condemned alone on account of such corruption. Nothing could be said more clearly, either in favour of the limitation I quoted, or against the immediate imputation of Adam's sin. I will say something more. You, you, I say, want us to be cursed and condemned on account of Adam's offence alone. Thus you contradict the very words you have praised. For you want us to be cursed and condemned, on account of Adam's sin alone imputed to us, to these three penalties: corruption, bodily death, and eternal death. Indeed, you do not divide this most atrocious curse and condemnation between Adam's sin and the wickedness which is within us, but you ascribe the whole of it, however great it is, to Adam's offence alone.

units.la: Temperare mihi non possum, quin huc transferam quae ibidem sequuntur Calvini verba, tuae, vt quod maxime, opinioni oppolita, Neque, inquit, ista est alieni delicti obligatio. Quod enim dicitur nos per Adae peccatum obnoxios esse factos Dei iudicio: non ita est accipiendum, ac si insuntes ipsi & immerentes culpam delicti eius sustineremus: sed quia per eius transgressionem maledictione induti sumus omnes, dicitur ille nos obstrictos esse. Ab illo tamen non sola in nos poena grassata est, sed infillata ab ipso lues in nobis resident, cui jure poena debetur. Quare Augustinus utcunque alienum peccatum saepe vocet, quo clarius ostendat propagine in nos deriuari, simul tamen & proprium unicuique asserit; Et Apostolus ipse difertissime testatur ideo mortem in omnes peruagatam, quod omnes peccarint, id est, involuti sint originali peccato, & eius maculis inquinati. Itaque ideo infantes quoque ipsi, dum suam secum damnationem a matris utero afferunt, non alieno, sed suo ipsorum vitio sunt obstricti. Nam tametsi sua iniquitatis fructus nondum protulerint, habent tamen in se inclusum semen: imo tota eorum natura quoddam est peccati semen: ideo non odiosa & abominabilis Deo esse non potest. Unde sequitur proprie coram Deo censeri peccatum, quia non effet reatus absque culpa. Nihil, opinor, dici potuit difertius aduersus illam imputationem quam tueris; &, quod notandum est, citat Caluinus Augustinum & Apostolum. His adde, si placet, quae idem Caluinus habet Comment in Rom. v. 12. Observua, inquit, quem hic (Apostolus) ponat ordinem. Peccatum enim praecessisse dicit: ex eo sequutam esse mortem: sunt enim qui contendunt nos ita peccato Adae esse perditos, ac si nulla nostra culpa periremus, ideo tantum, quasi ille nobis peccasset. Atqui diserte affirmat Paulus in omnes propagatum esse peccatum qui eius poenam luunt. Atque id deinde propius urget, cum rationem assignat paulo post cur omnis Adae posteritas subiaceat mortis imperio; nempe, inquit, quoniam omnes peccauimus. Porro istud peccare est corruptos esse & vitiatos. Noli putare te ista tela, quibus tua sententia conficitur, vlla vel corporis declinatione, vel arte posse vitare. A Caluino ad Petrum Martyrem veniamus. Eum fateris tuam hypothefin non ita clare tenere ; tamen quædam eius laudas, quæ mihi posita iam in tam aperta luce veritate non videntur egere respon-sione. Satis erit prolatis aliquot eius locis docere eum meam hypothesin aperte & clare tenuisse ; quanquam ad hoc vnus iste posset sufficere. Dico, inquit, in vnoquoque nostrum, quoties puniimur, causam esse cur puniri debeamus : itaque in omnibus non alienam, sed propriam cuiusque culpam damnari. Quod si legimus, Deum in nobis vlcisci peccatum Adami, id ita intelligendum est, quod vitium nostrum ab illo habuit originem. Vt si quis peste laborans alios inficiat & illi moriantur: dicetur illorum quisque non aliena, sed propria, & sua peste esse mortuus. At si quis eos dicat ex eius peste vnde centagium contraxerunt perisse : id ita intelligendum est, quod is primus pestem inuexit, & illis affricuit. Huic addi potest locus quem iam citaui cap. xi. Ad primum (Augustinus) respondet Deum summè bonum esse, neque, quod isti assumunt, in culpa originis imputare nobis alienum peccatum, sed nostram ipsorum iniquitatem, quæ nostræ natura adhæret iam inde ab ipsa origine.
units.tr: I cannot refrain from quoting the words of Calvin that follow there, which oppose your view as strongly as possible: Nor, he says, is that an obligation for another's offence. For when it is said that we were made liable to God's judgment through Adam's sin, this is not to be understood as if we, though not involved and undeserving, bore the guilt of his offence; but because through his transgression we were all clothed with a curse, he is said to have bound us. Yet the punishment that fell on us from him was not the only thing; the plague infused by him also remains in us, and by right the punishment is owed to it. Therefore Augustine, though he often calls it another's sin, so that he may show more clearly that it is derived to us by propagation, at the same time also asserts that it belongs to each one. And the Apostle himself most plainly testifies that death spread over all because all have sinned, that is, they were involved in original sin and polluted by its stains. Therefore even infants, while they bring their own condemnation with them from the mother's womb, are bound not by another's fault but by their own vice. For although they have not yet produced the fruit of their iniquity, they have the seed enclosed within them; indeed their whole nature is a certain seed of sin, and therefore cannot be other than odious and abominable to God. Whence it follows that sin is properly reckoned before God, because there would be no guilt without fault. Nothing, I think, could have been said more plainly against that imputation which you defend; and, what must be noted, Calvin cites Augustine and the Apostle. To these add, if you please, what the same Calvin says in his commentary on Romans 5:12: Observe, he says, the order which the Apostle here sets down. For he says that sin came first, and from it death followed.
