For there are some who contend that we have been so ruined by the sin of Adam as if we perished through no fault of our own, only because he had sinned as it were on our behalf. Yet Paul plainly affirms that sin has been spread to all who bear its punishment. And he presses this more closely afterwards, when he gives the reason why all Adam's posterity lies under the dominion of death; namely, he says, because all have sinned. Moreover, to sin in this way is to be corrupted and vitiated. Do not think that you can avoid those weapons by which your opinion is overthrown, by any bodily dodge or artifice. Let us come from Calvin to Peter Martyr. You confess that he does not hold your hypothesis so clearly; yet you praise some of his statements, which, to me, since the truth now lies in such open light, do not seem to need an answer. It will be enough, by citing some of his passages, to show that he held my hypothesis openly and clearly, although this one place could suffice for the purpose. I say, he says, that in each one of us, whenever we are punished, there is a cause why we ought to be punished; so that in all, it is not another's but each one's own fault that is condemned. But if we read that God avenges the sin of Adam in us, this must be understood to mean that our vice took its origin from him. As if someone, suffering from plague, infects others and they die: each of them will be said to have died not by another's plague but by his own, and by his own plague. But if someone says that they perished from his plague, from which they contracted contagion, this must be understood to mean that he first brought in the plague and communicated it to them. To this may be added the passage which I have already cited in chapter 11: To the first objection, Augustine answers that God is supremely good, and that he does not impute to us, as those men assume, another's sin in the guilt of origin, but our own iniquity, which has clung to our nature from its very origin.

units.la: Histertium adiungo. Pighij sententiam his verbis exposuerat, culpam igitur originis, vnicam statuit transgressionem Adami. Cui vni nos omnes vult nasci obnoxios non propter aliquod vitium, aut culpam, aut depranationem, quam in nobis habeamus. In quo descriptionem tuæ sententiæ agnoscere debes : vis enim nos omnes culpæ Adami nasci obnoxios non propter aliquod vitium, aut culpam, aut depravationem quam in nobis habeamus : hanc enim statuis pœnam esse culpæ Adami nobis imputatæ. Audi igitur tuam sententiam æque ac Pighij refutantem Martyrem.
units.tr: I add a third. Pighius had set out his opinion in these words: He therefore establishes the guilt of origin as the one transgression of Adam. To this one he wills that we all be born liable, not on account of any vice, fault or depravity that we have in ourselves. In this you ought to recognise a description of your own opinion: for you want us all to be born liable to Adam's guilt not on account of any vice, fault or depravity that we have in ourselves; for you hold that this is the punishment of Adam's guilt imputed to us. Hear, then, Martyr refuting your opinion just as much as that of Pighius.

units.la: Verum, inquit, contra sententiam in primis illud facit, quod iam bis diximus, videlicet infantes mori. Mors enim nihil iuris habet vbi non est peccatum, nisi dicere velimus Deum punire innocentem. Confirmatur autem hac ratio ex argumento Pauli quo probauit peccatum fuisse ante legem: quia Mors, inquit, regnauit ab Adamo vsque ad Mosem. Atqui iuxta Pighij sententiam, hec ratio hebetissima videri potest. Diceret enim quisquam: Etsi illi mortui fuerint, tamen ex eo non sequitur illos habuisse peccatum. Mors, enim illis contingit propter Adamum, ob cuius peccatum redditi sumus mortales. Ille, vt vides, totum ius mortis fundat in peccato inhærente, tu cum Pighio vel solum, vel præcipue in imputato: ille si qui punitur peccatum in se non habeat, clamat puniri innocentem; idque detestatur: Tu cum Pighio vel innocentem esse negas cui peccatum Adami imputetur, vel absurdum esse talem innocentem puniri. Denique posita imputatione peccati actualis Adami hebetissima est contra Pighium hæc Apostoli & Martyris argumentatio, quam tamen Martyr validissimam iudicauit.
units.tr: But, he says, against that opinion, in the first place, there is what we have already said twice, namely that infants die. For death has no right where there is no sin, unless we are willing to say that God punishes the innocent. And this reasoning is confirmed by the argument of Paul by which he proved that sin existed before the law: because death, he says, reigned from Adam to Moses. Yet according to the opinion of Pighius, this reasoning may seem very dull. For someone might say: Even if those infants died, it does not follow from this that they had sin. For death befell them on account of Adam, through whose sin we were made mortal. He, as you see, grounds the whole right of death in inherent sin; you, with Pighius, grounds it solely or chiefly in imputed sin. He, if someone who is punished has no sin in himself, cries out that the innocent is being punished, and he detests this; you, with Pighius, either deny that someone is innocent to whom Adam's sin is imputed, or you say it is absurd for such an innocent person to be punished. In short, on the supposition of the imputation of Adam's actual sin, this argument of the Apostle and of Martyr is very dull against Pighius, although Martyr judged it most valid.

units.la: Vis aliud Martyris argumentum? Quid aliud, inquit, fecit Apostolus cum scriberet ad Ephesios nos esse natura filios irae, nisi peccatum inesse in vnoquoque nostrum &c. Nam ira Dei nonnisi iuste provocatur: neque enim ea eiusmodi est, vt temere aut fortuito inflammari possit. quare oportet in natura nostra aliquid esse prauum, ad quod vt eiscendum ira diuina excitetur. Nititur, vt vides, haec argumentatio hypothesi tuae contraria non sufficere peccatum Adae actuale ad iram Dei in nos iuste prouocandam.
units.tr: Do you want another argument of Martyr's? What else, he says, did the Apostle do when he wrote to the Ephesians that we are by nature children of wrath, except to show that sin is present in each one of us? For the wrath of God is not justly provoked except by sin: nor is it of such a kind that it can be kindled rashly or by chance. Therefore there must be something depraved in our nature, by which the divine wrath is aroused to be cast out. This argument, as you see, rests on the claim that Adam's actual sin, which is contrary to your hypothesis, does not suffice to provoke God's wrath justly against us.

units.la: Addatur: & tertium, Postremo inquit, habemus ā Paulo per inobedientiam vnius hominis multos constitutos esse. esse vitium, propter quod peccatores dici possint. Sed hoc Pighius putat se posse eludere, quod peccatores interdum dicantur propter reatum, quamuis actio peccandi praeterierit, neque amplius extet. Quamuis hoc ita sit, Nunquam tamen ostendere potest e Scripturis, quemquam peccatorem appellari quin aut in seipso vitium habeat, aut certe antea admiserit: nisi dicere velit, Deum homines reos facere absque ipsorum aliquo peccato. Hoc idem docet ad verf.19.cap.v. Epist.ad Rom. Hic, inquit, annotabimus, cum Apostolus dicit per unius obedientiam peccatores multos esse constitutos, ex his verbis argumentum haberi adversus eos qui putant peccatum originis non esse cuique proprium, sed unum tantum extitisse, illudque fuisse in Adamo, quo nos nexi & obligati simus ad mortem & damnationem. Quum enim dicantur peccatores constituti, oportet ut ipsi aut peccatum habeant, aut saltem habuerint: nam alieno vitio nemo dicitur peccator. Nihil potuit contra tuam sententiam vel differtius, vel clarius dici. neque ex huiusmodi argumentationum nexibus expedire te potes, quin eadem opera expedias & Pighium. Quemadmodum autem vocem peccatores Martyr, non ut tu & Pighius, sed ut ego, interpretatur, sic comparationem quam inter Christum & Adamum Apostolus instituit, ille, non ut tu de imputatione, sed ut Augustinus, Caluinus, Bucerus, &c. sine vlla mentione imputationis exponit, Deinde, inquit, haec opinio (Pelagianorum) confutatur ex eo quod Paulus antithesin facit inter Christum & Adamum. At Christi iustitia non tantum proponitur nobis imitanda: sed etiam ut qui credunt in eum, animo mutentur, spiritu corrigantur, & omnibus viribus emendentur. Quamobrem vicissim requiritur ad rationem ἀντιθέσεως, ut prater malum exemplum, quod Adamus exhibuit posteris, naturam etiam illorum depravaverit, utque Augustinus depeccatorum meritis & remissione loquitur, tabe quadam tabificaverit.
units.tr: Add a third: Lastly, he says, we have from Paul that many were constituted sinners through the disobedience of one man. There must be a vice on account of which they can be called sinners. But Pighius thinks he can evade this, because men are sometimes called sinners on account of guilt, although the act of sinning has passed away and no longer exists. Even granting this, he can never show from the Scriptures that anyone is called a sinner unless he either has vice in himself or at least committed it before. Unless he is willing to say that God makes men guilty without any sin of their own. Martyr teaches the same thing on verse 19 of Romans 5: Here, he says, we shall note that when the Apostle says that many were constituted sinners through the obedience of one, from these words an argument is to be had against those who think that original sin is not proper to each person, but that only one existed, and that it was in Adam, by which we were bound and obligated to death and condemnation. For since they are said to have been constituted sinners, it is necessary that they themselves have sin, or at least had it; for no one is called a sinner through another's vice. Nothing could have been said more pointedly or more clearly against your opinion. Nor can you extricate yourself from the knots of such arguments without at the same time extricating Pighius. But just as Martyr interprets the word sinners not as you and Pighius do, but as I do, so the comparison which the Apostle draws between Christ and Adam he sets out not as you do concerning imputation, but as Augustine, Calvin, Bucer, and others do, without any mention of imputation. Then, he says, this opinion (of the Pelagians) is refuted by the fact that Paul makes an antithesis between Christ and Adam. But the righteousness of Christ is not only set before us to be imitated; it is also so that those who believe in him are changed in mind, corrected in spirit, and amended with all their powers. Wherefore, conversely, the rule of antithesis [ἀντιθέσεως] requires that, besides the bad example which Adam set before his posterity, he also depraved their nature, and, as Augustine speaks of sins by their merits and remission, stained it with a certain taint.

units.la: His accedat & quartum eiusdem Martyris argumentum, Scribitur, inquit, in Propheta: filius non portabit iniquitatem patris; & anima quae peccaverit ipsa morietur: quod certe, si Pighio credimus, falsum erit, cum pueri moriantur & rei sint aeternae damnationis, quamvis nihil peccaverint. Ad quam absurditatem nos non cogimur, qui ponimus in unoquoque homine nascente vitium & causam, quare moriatur & condemnetur. Et iterum alio loco, Alterum illorum argumentum sumitur ex Propheta Ezech. filius non portabit iniquitatem patris. Ad hoc uno verbo possemus respondere, ut modo diximus, videlicet, filios non patrum iniquitatem portare, sed propriam ac suam, quae a nativitate cuique inhaeret. Posteaquam autem varias illius loci expositiones expendit, tandem sic concludit, Dicimus itaque sententiam Prophetae generaliter veram esse, & omnes vel pueros, vel adultos, tam veteris, quam Novi Testamenti portare quemque iniquitatem suam. Omnes enim qui nascuntur, in ipsis habent peccatum & corruptionem propter quam puniri debeant. Quare haec sententia nostram opinionem confirmat, tantum abest ut contra nos adduci possit. Sed ea maxime facit contra Pighium, &c. Haec argumenta a Martyre mutuata Thesibus meis inserueram breviter verbis, nec ea sunt a te soluta, quod ut spero planum faciam in Apologia Thesium. His omnibus addendum, Martyrem peccati originalis definitionem, quam potuit, accuratam attulisse, & per partes diligentissime explicasse, & adversus Pighium & Pelagianos disputasse copiose, & in verba Apostoli quibus imputationem peccati actualis Adami vis contineri, magna accuratione commentarium elaborasse, nec tamen vel expresse, vel per consequentiam vllo modo illam imputationem docuisse, quam si credidisset, dubitabile non est, quin eam aperte docuisset alicubi. Quis enim, nisi insaniat, rem ita ex professo tractare, & definire, ac explicare velit, vt eius partem praecipuam & maxime memorabilem prorsus praetermittat? Iam, vt vides, à partibus meis stant duo illi magni viri, Caluinus & Martyr; idem puta de Bucero, de Zuinglio, de Bulingero, de Vireto, de Aretio, de Zgedino, de Thoffano, de Gualtero, de Camerone, & alijs quibusdam, quorum, quia tu nullam fecisti mentionem, & in nimiam molem video hanc meam responsionem excrescere, non adscribam testimonia. De Chamiero qui tuam sententiam aliquot argumentis refutauit, alius erit dicendi locus, videlicet in secunda parte huius examinis. De Zanchio & alijs quos citas, nihil dicam. Si qui, loco auri, argenti, & lapidum pretiosorum, hanc stipulam aedificarunt, vides quàm facile admoto igne sacrarum literarum id flammam concipiat, & comburatur. Noli admonitus eadem stipula tuum aedificium de honestare. Vtinam illi non degeneraffent hac in re à magnis illis viris Caluino, Bucero, Zuinglio, Martyre, &c. quorum in vestigijs si pedem pono, si Consessionibus Ecclesiarum Reformatarum mordicus adhaerefco, si Augustini aliorumque Patrum orthodoxorum ductum sequor, si inuictis nitor rationibus, si ad Scripturae normam doctrinam exigo meam, quid est quamobrem huius aut illius authoritate ab hac recta & regia via seduci me sinam? De postrema Synodo Carentonensi cuius mentione hoc tuum caput: vii: claudis nihil opus est quicquam dicere : agetur, vt spero, hæc res in proxima Synodo accuratius, & veritas in apertam protrahetur lucem ; mihi certè nihil optabilius est quàm, vt si erro, meus mihi error monstretur, eum libentissimè agnituro & deposituro: si non erro, ne contra Dei veritatem omni re fortiorem militent ministri Dei. Hoc à Deo Optimo Maximo & Domino nostro Iesu Christo Dei filio supplex ex animo dies noctesque peto, & vt mecum certes in tuis apud Deum precibus, te etiam atque etiam rogo.
units.tr: To this may be added the fourth argument of the same Martyr: "It is written, he says, in the Prophet: 'The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the soul that sinneth, it shall die.' This is certainly false, if we believe Pighius, since children die and are liable to eternal damnation although they have sinned nothing. We are not forced into this absurdity, since we hold that in every man at birth there is a defect and a cause why he should die and be condemned." And again in another place: "The other of their arguments is taken from the Prophet Ezekiel: 'The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.'" To this one word could be answered, as we have just said, namely that sons do not bear the iniquity of their fathers but their own, which clings to each one from birth. After he has weighed the various interpretations of that passage, he at last concludes: "We say, therefore, that the saying of the Prophet is generally true, and that all, both children and adults, of the Old and New Testament alike, bear each his own iniquity. For all who are born have in themselves sin and corruption on account of which they ought to be punished. Hence this saying confirms our opinion; so far is it from being able to be brought against us." But it works most strongly against Pighius, etc. I had briefly inserted these arguments, borrowed from the Martyr, into my Theses, and they have not been answered by you; as I hope to make plain in the Apology for the Theses. To all this must be added that the Martyr brought forward as accurate a definition of original sin as he could, explained it part by part most diligently, disputed copiously against Pighius and the Pelagians, and laboured with great care on a commentary on the words of the Apostle in which the force of the imputation of Adam's actual sin is said to be contained; and yet he nowhere, either expressly or by any consequence, taught that imputation in any way. If he had believed it, there is no doubt that he would have taught it openly somewhere. For who, unless he were mad, would wish to treat, define and explain a matter so professedly and yet altogether pass over its chief and most noteworthy part? Now, as you see, on my side stand those two great men, Calvin and Martyr; think the same of Bucer, Zwingli, Bullinger, Viret, Aretius, Zanchius [Zgedinus], Thoffanus, Gualtherus, Camerarius, and certain others, whose testimonies I will not cite, since you have made no mention of them and I see this reply of mine swelling to an excessive bulk. Concerning Chamier, who refuted your opinion with several arguments, there will be another place to speak, namely in the second part of this examination. Of Zanchius and the others whom you cite I will say nothing. If some men built this straw instead of gold, silver and precious stones, you see how easily it catches fire when the flame of Holy Scripture is applied and is burned. Do not, warned by this, try to adorn your building with the same straw. Would that those men had not degenerated in this matter from those great men, Calvin, Bucer, Zwingli, Martyr, and the rest! If I set my foot in their footsteps, if I cling tenaciously to the Confessions of the Reformed Churches, if I follow the lead of Augustine and the other orthodox Fathers, if I rest on unconquered arguments, if I bring my doctrine to the rule of Scripture, why should I allow myself to be led away from this straight and royal road by the authority of this man or that? As for the last Synod of Charenton, which you close this seventh chapter of yours by mentioning, there is no need to say anything about it. This matter will, I hope, be treated more exactly at the next Synod, and the truth will be drawn out into open light. For my part, nothing is more to be wished than that, if I am in error, my error be shown to me, and I will most willingly acknowledge and abandon it; if I am not in error, that the ministers of God not fight against the truth of God, which is stronger than everything. This I ask earnestly, day and night, of God Most Good and Greatest, and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God; and I earnestly ask you too, that you contend with me in your prayers to God.

units.la: G A R. Si Caluinus, Martyr, & pauci quidam alij in eam denenissent sententiam, vt nullam esse Adamici peccati imputationem pertenderent, æquius tamen videri poterat ac tutius, vt auditores suos Doƈti viri per tritum à reliquis omnibus Doƈtoribus tramitem deducerent, qaàm vt paucorum, quantumuis cætera eximiorum virorum, ϰωεiας δόξας vnanimi reliquorum consensui anteferendas putarent. Nam quanta sit in hoc capite Confessionum publicarum & Theologorum per Europam Reformatorum veterum & Recentiorum concordia, nemo, post eum quem confecimus indicem, in dubium revocare potest. &c.
units.tr: GAR. If Calvin, Martyr and a few others had fallen into that opinion, so as to maintain that there is no imputation of Adam's sin, it could nevertheless have seemed more fair and safer for learned men to lead their hearers by the beaten path followed by all the other teachers, than to think that the empty opinions of a few men, however otherwise eminent, were to be preferred to the unanimous agreement of the rest. For how great the agreement is on this point among the public Confessions and the Reformed theologians of Europe, both old and recent, no one, after the index which I have compiled, can call in doubt. etc.

units.la: PLAC. Primùm nunquam dixi aut scripsi Caluinum, Martyrem, &c, nullam esse Adamici peccati imputationem pertendisse. Distinxi enim constanter imputationem immediatam à mediata : illam ab eorum doctrina alienam esse contendo, hanc non item; habeoque ea in reipsum D. Garissolium confitentem, vti iam est obseruatum sup. pag.21. Deinde miror mihi vitio verti, quod sequor Caluinum & Martyrem, & alios celeberrimos Theologos, à quorum vestigijs doleo eos, qui me accusant, cursum deflexisse: sequuti enim mihi videntur tritam à Christo, à Prophetis, ab Apostolis, & antiquis Doƈtoribus, viam, quam, vt patuit, omnes Ecclesiæ Protestantes mirabili consensu publicis suis Confessionibus descripserunt. Ab hac via si alij quidam exerrarunt, vt vt multi, num mihi quoque siit cum illis errandum? Videntur in hac causa viri doćti eorum obliti, quæ solent aduersus Pontificios tam solidè & animosè disputare, ac imprimis Art. V. Confessionis Fidei; qui articulus fundamentum mihi videtur Ecclesiæ Reformatæ, sicut oppositum dogma, sequendum esse tritum à plerisque omnibus Doctoribus tramitem, ut ut verbo Dei minus congruere videatur, fundamentum est Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ.
units.tr: PLAC. First, I never said or wrote that Calvin, Martyr, etc. had maintained that there is no imputation of Adam's sin. For I have consistently distinguished immediate imputation from mediate; I contend that the former is alien to their teaching, but the latter is not; and I have their statements on this point, including those of the same Garissolius himself, as has already been noted above on page 21. Next, I am surprised that it is held against me that I follow Calvin and Martyr and the other most celebrated theologians, from whose footsteps I regret that those who accuse me have turned aside. For they seem to me to have followed the path trodden by Christ, the Prophets, the Apostles and the ancient teachers, which, as is clear, all the Protestant Churches have with remarkable agreement described in their public Confessions. If some others have strayed from this path, however many they are, must I too go astray with them? In this matter learned men seem to have forgotten what they are accustomed to argue so solidly and spiritedly against the Papists, and especially Article V of the Confession of Faith; which article seems to me the foundation of the Reformed Church, just as the opposing dogma, that one must follow the path trodden by most of the teachers, even if it seems less agreeable to the Word of God, is the foundation of the Papist Church.

units.la: GAR. Verum, quod secundo loco adjiciendum est, Si Calvinus, Martyr, &c, de imputatione vel omnino siluisse, vel plane pauca scripsisse dicantur, non id inde fuit, quod nullam imputationem agnoscerent, aut quod eam plenam ad peccati originalis rationem omnino pertinere inficiarentur.
units.tr: GAR. But, which must be added in the second place: if Calvin, Martyr, etc. are said to have either wholly kept silence about imputation, or to have written very little plainly, the reason for this was not that they acknowledged no imputation, or that they denied that it wholly pertains to the account of original sin.

units.la: PLAC. Quis dicit eos nullam imputationem agnouisse? Ego enim contendo eos agnouisse imputationem mediatam. De sola immediata quæstio est, num eam agnouerint, necne? Vides, Lector, perpetuâ fere elenchi ignorantiâ viri docti disputationem laborare. Loquitur autem perinde ac si eorum cogitationes dum scriberent, haberet perspectas. Sed pergit.
units.tr: PLAC. Who says that they acknowledged no imputation? For I contend that they acknowledged mediate imputation. The question concerns only immediate imputation, whether they acknowledged that or not. You see, Reader, how this learned man labours under an almost constant ignorance of the point in dispute. He speaks as though he had their thoughts clearly before him while they were writing. But he goes on.

units.la: GAR. Alia igitur illius sive silentij, sive parcæ declarationis causæ inquirendæ sunt, quæ duæ sine dubio esse potuerunt. Nam primum eo tempore scribebant, cum nondum in controversiam distinctè vocabatur, an peccatum Adami posteris imputaretur. Scilicet nondum Socini hæresis, aut Arminianorum setta caput exeruerat. Et Anabaptistæ peccatum originale simpliciter negabant, non autem hanc doctrinæ partem speciatim exagitabant. Cum omnia ex hac parte in tuto essent, minus accurarunt huius doctrinæ fundamenta latius exponere, qui in aliis capitibus molestos experiebantur Adversarios.
units.tr: GAR. Other causes, then, must be sought for their silence or their sparing explanation, and there could undoubtedly be two. For, first, they were writing at a time when it was not yet being clearly brought into controversy whether Adam's sin is imputed to his posterity. Certainly the heresy of Socinus had not yet raised its head, nor the sect of the Arminians. And the Anabaptists simply denied original sin, but did not particularly assail this part of doctrine. Since everything on this side was secure, they took less care to set out the foundations of this doctrine more fully, since they were dealing with troublesome opponents on other chapters.

units.la: PLAC. Clamat Vir doctus negasse Pelagianos Adæ peccatum imputari posteritati, in quâ negatione hæresis eorum partem fuisse contendit. Atqui iam pridem exortî fuerant Pelagiani, eorumque errores maximi illi Viri secuti Augustinum aliosque Patres diligenter confutant. Est igitur prorsus nulla hæc prima causa.
units.tr: PLAC. The learned man cries out that the Pelagians denied that Adam's sin is imputed to posterity, and he contends that this denial was part of their heresy. But the Pelagians had arisen long before, and those great men, following Augustine and the other Fathers, diligently refute their errors. This first cause, therefore, is altogether nothing.

units.la: GAR. Et verò simile quid in aliâ causâ respondere solitos, qui in hac nobis aduersantur, non est ignotum. Disputantes enim aduersus Socinum pro necessitate Satisfactionis Christi, non modò necessitatem eam ex suppositione decreti divini astruunt, sed absolulute necessariam fuisse docent eam satisfactionem, vt velint non fuisse alium modum possibilem, quo saluaremur a Deo, alius tamen serfus Calvino. &c.
units.tr: GAR. And it is not unknown that those who oppose us in this matter are accustomed to answer something similar in another cause. For those who dispute against Socinus for the necessity of Christ's satisfaction not only assert that necessity on the supposition of the divine decree, but teach that that satisfaction was absolutely necessary, so that they would have there to be no other possible way by which we might be saved by God, though another [may be] less pleasing to Calvin, etc.

units.la: PLAC. Satisfactionis necessitatem quidem credimur, sed tamen cum hac limitatione, quantum animus noster capere potest. Nam alioqui infinitas esse scimus Diuinae scientiae abyssos, eiusque vias inscrutabiles. Fateor etiam cum Martyrie salutem humanam multis aliis rationibus & viis, modo Deus voluisset, parari potuisse. Quid enim quominus quicquid voluisset daret effectum potuisset impedire? Sed tamen reuera talem satisfactionem putamus eius virtutes flagitasse; itaque necessariam affirmamus. Quid hoc causae nostrae nocet? Dicimusne haeresim quandam extitisse ante Caluini & Martyris tempora, in negatione illius necessitatis consistentem, vt vult Vir doctus Pelagianam haeresim in negatione imputationis immediatae, saltem ex parte, positam fuisse? Si qui simul & negarunt absolutam satisfactionis necessitatem, & crediderunt satisfactionem, num propterea minus totam & integram satisfactionem habuerunt? Nimirum necessitas satisfactionis necessarius pars est satisfactionis, & in satisfactione includitur. At peccatum imputatum putatur ab ijs, qui nos oppugnant, plane necessarium, ac peccati originalis primariam & praecipuam partem; ex quo sequitur, eam, cum definitur, cum tractatur peccatum originale, omitti non debere: alioqui pro toto pars tantum describeretur, & pro integro peccato originali non haberetur peccatum originale nisi mutilum & praecipua ac prima fui parte truncatum. Non est igitur simile id quod Vir doctus nobis obijcit tanquam simile.
units.tr: PLAC. We do believe in the necessity of satisfaction, but with this limitation: so far as our mind can grasp it. For we know that the depths of divine wisdom are otherwise infinite, and its ways unsearchable. I also grant with Martyr that human salvation could have been brought about by many other means and ways, provided God had willed it. For what could have prevented God from bringing about whatever he willed? Yet we truly think that his attributes demanded precisely this kind of satisfaction, and so we affirm it to be necessary. How does this harm our cause? Do we say that some heresy arose before the times of Calvin and Martyr, consisting in the denial of that necessity, just as the learned man wants the Pelagian heresy to have consisted, at least in part, in the denial of immediate imputation? If some both denied the absolute necessity of satisfaction and believed in satisfaction, have they on that account had less than the whole and entire satisfaction? Surely the necessity of satisfaction is a necessary part of satisfaction and is included in it. But those who oppose us consider the imputed sin to be plainly necessary, and the primary and chief part of original sin. It follows that when original sin is defined and treated, this part must not be omitted. Otherwise a part would be described in place of the whole, and original sin would not be regarded as complete unless it were mutilated and truncated of its first and principal part. Therefore what the learned man throws at us as a parallel is no parallel at all.

units.la: GAR. Adiungamus etiam alteram causam. Nimirum aduersus recentem & πολυσπνλλος Pontificiorum quorundam ac nominatim Alberti Pighij & Ambrosij Catharini sententiam in illis renascentis Euangelij principijs feriam opera collocari consentaneum erat, ne nouis phaleris & fucis ornatus Pelagianissimus obtruderetur. Illi enim ne quid Pelagianum sapere viderentur, peccati Originalis doctrinam se ambabus vlnis amplecti profitebantur: sed vbi in rem praesentem ventum erat, totam illius peccati naturam sola imputatione, siue reatu primi Adae peccati definiebant: internam nullam & innatam atque inhaerentem a conceptione corruptionem agnoscebant. Itaque disceptantes aduersus eiusmodi sententiâ Calui-um, Martyrem, & alios nihil erat opus in iis explicandis aut probandis accuratius immorari, de quibus nulla tum agitabatur controuersia, & quæ Aduersarij non modo prolixè largiebantur, sed & quibuscunque poterant rationibus firmabant, &c.
units.tr: GAR. Let us also add a second consideration. Namely, it was fitting that we set our work against the recent and verbose opinion of certain Papists, and especially of Albert Pighius and Ambrose Catharinus, in those principles of the renewed Gospel, lest a thoroughly Pelagian doctrine, dressed up in new trappings and disguises, be foisted upon us. For those men, lest they seem to savour of anything Pelagian, professed that they embraced the doctrine of original sin with both arms. But when they came to the matter itself, they defined the whole nature of that sin by imputation alone, that is, by the guilt of the first Adam's sin. They acknowledged no internal, innate corruption inhering from conception. Therefore, in disputing against this opinion, Calvin, Martyr and the others had no need to dwell more carefully on explaining or proving those points about which there was then no controversy, and which the adversaries not only freely conceded but also confirmed by whatever reasons they could, etc.

units.la: PLAC. Hoc quicquid est caulæ retorqueo. Erat enim opus, quandoquidem Aduersarij imputationem affirmabant, corruptionem negabant, vt illam Caluinus, Martyr, &c, concederent, hanc probarent, eâque ratione quod non esset controuersum à statu quæstionis separarent. Deinde, non aduersus solos illos Pontificios disputabant, sed aduersus Pelagianos, aliosque in negotio religionis errantes. Tum, an propterea tradenda erat doctrina de peccato originis imperfecta? an propterea definitiones conficiendæ definito angustiores & quæ illius partem tantummodo minùs præcipuam explicarent? Denique, an propterea ea argumenta contra Pighium erant afferenda, quæ imputationem refellerent? De manibus enim maximorum illorum virorum omnia fere illa argumenta accepi, quibus imputationem immediatam primi Adæ peccati actualis impugnaui.
units.tr: PLAC. I turn this back upon the cause, whatever it is. For it was necessary, since our adversaries affirmed imputation and denied corruption, that Calvin, Martyr and the rest should concede the former and prove the latter, and by that method separate what was not in dispute from the state of the question. Next, they were not disputing against those Papists alone, but against Pelagians and others who erred in matters of religion. Then, was the doctrine of original sin therefore to be delivered in an incomplete form? Were definitions therefore to be drawn up narrower than what they defined, explaining only a less principal part of it? Finally, were those arguments therefore to be brought against Pighius which refute imputation? For I received from the hands of those greatest men almost all the arguments with which I assailed the immediate imputation of Adam's actual sin.

units.la: GAR. Enimuerò illud tertio loco adiycimus, non esse quod existimemus incomparabiles illos viros imputationem primi peccati, reatum propter Adæ inobedientiam, defectionem in lumbis Adæ, irrogationem pœnarum propter Adæ delictum, aut ignorâsse, aut negâsse, aut pro derelicto habuisse. &c.
units.tr: GAR. Moreover, we add thirdly that we should not think those incomparable men were either ignorant of, or denied, or regarded as abandoned, the imputation of the first sin: guilt on account of Adam's disobedience, the defection in the loins of Adam, the infliction of punishments on account of Adam's offence, etc.

units.la: PLAC. Hic quoque vides, pie Lector, id quod passim obseruari potuit, Virum doctum peccare ignorantia elenchi. Do enim libenter incomparabiles illos Viros agnouisse imputationem primi peccati, immediatam, si per primum peccatum intelligitur propagata corruptio; mediatam, si primum Adami peccatum actuale intelligitur; reatum propter Adæ inobedientiam quæ intra nos est, proximè, & reatum propter Adæ inobedientiam quæ extra nos in Adam fuit, remotè seu mediante corruptione: defectionem in lumbis Adæ, quatenus ex eius lumbis quàm naturam tam naturæ defectionem seu vitiositatem per carnalem generationem traximus: irrogationem pœnarum propter Adæ delictum, nempe mediante corruptione quæ pœnas illas meretur immediatè. Quid opus fuit id probare quod vltro concedimus? Si verum est quod supra dixit c. ix. §.pag. 29.& nos iam notauimus p. 21. Lapsus primi reatus ad nos non peruenit nisi mediante corruptione, quod cum Calvino agnoscimus, cùm sibi constiterit Caluinus, tiustrà in eius libris quæruntur loca, quibus impugner. Vt sit finis, Caluinus in causa̅n & originem corruptionis diligenter inquirit Inst. lib. 2. c. 1. §.6. Eamque Dei actioni seu imputationi iudiciariæ plurimum abest vt tribuat. Itaque quæcunque ex Caluino vndique corrasit, ea cum mea sententia vel iam facis conciliata sunt, vel facilè conciliari posse videntur; vt ijs expendendis nihil opus sit hunc librum longiorem facere. Vnum tamen prætermitti non debet, conatur probare corruptionem dici pœnam à Caluino proprie, non autem ob eas causas quas commemorauì supra pag. 185. Nam, inquit, cùm ea sit proprie distapœna, quæ à iudice infligitur in vindistam criminis: Caluinus autem hanc pœnam in nos deriuari doceat à Deo iudice, & eam vocet vindistam & seueram vltionem, ex iudicio & iustitia Dei procedentem, dubium nemini esse potest, quin de pœna proprie distà locutus fuerit, ac proinde imputationem agnouerit. Sed sallitur: Non enim eiusmodi pœnæ nomine intelligenda est Corruptio, sed quæ Corruptioni debetur maledictio, seu pœna. Videtur enim respexisse ad illa Caluini verba Inst. lib.2.cap.1. §.4. Quia verò non leue delictum, sed detestabile fuisse scelus oportet quod tam seuerè vltus est Deus, species ipsa peccati in lapsu Adæ consideranda nobis est, quæ horribilem Dei vindistam accendit in totum humanum genus. Cur enim id non accipiamus eodem modo, quo illud Rom. 5. 15. Vnius delicto multi mortui sunt, accipi vult idem Caluinus? Quod, inquit, vnius delicto perisse non tradit, sic accipe: quia ex ipso in nos corruptio transfusa sit. Neque enim sic perimus eius culpa, quasi extra culpam ipsi simus: sed quia eius peccatum, peccati nostri causa est, exitium nostrum illi Paulus adscribit. Delictum igitur Adami horribilem Dei vindictam accendit in totum humanum genus, quia sese diffudit & propagauit in totum humanum genus. Vniuersum enim suum semen Adamus ea in quam lapsus est vitiositate infecit. Atque ita instillata ab ipso lues in nobis residet, cuiure: iurepœna debetur, & ob talem duntaxat corruptionem damnati merito conuictique coram Deo tenemur. Alioqui, cùm poena, quæ vindicta est, sit satisfactoria, pœnam satisfactoriam aliquam in hoc sæculo sustineremus; id quod an sit Caluini & Ecclesiæ Reformatæ doctrinæ consentaneum, tibi, Lector æquissime, iudicandum relinquo. Plura non addam, neque reliquam testimoniorum farraginem, quam vndecunque potuerunt Viri docti conquisiuerunt atque congesserunt velut in aceruum, excutiam & singillatim expendam; quædam à meis stant partibus, quædam neutris fauent, non pauca mihi aduersantur: quæ tamen, si omnia à me dissentirent, non putarem anteponenda esse testimonijs Scripturæ, argumentisque quibus nitor, quantum quidem capere possum, plane necessarijs.
units.tr: PLAC. Here too you see, kind reader, what could be observed everywhere: the learned man errs through ignorance of the point at issue. For I gladly grant that those incomparable men acknowledged the imputation of the first sin: immediate, if by the first sin is understood the propagated corruption; mediate, if the first actual sin of Adam is meant; guilt on account of Adam's disobedience, which is within us, proximately; and guilt on account of Adam's disobedience, which was in Adam outside us, remotely or through the mediation of corruption; defection in the loins of Adam, insofar as through carnal generation we drew from his loins not only nature but also the defection or vitiosity of nature; infliction of punishments on account of Adam's offence, namely through the mediation of corruption, which immediately deserves those punishments. Why was it necessary to prove what we concede of our own accord? If what he said above in chapter 9, §, p. 29, is true, and what we already noted at p. 21, namely that "the fall's guilt does not reach us except through the mediation of corruption, which we acknowledge with Calvin," and if Calvin has been consistent with himself, then it is in vain that passages are sought in his books by which I might be attacked. To make an end: Calvin inquires diligently into the cause and origin of corruption, Inst. 2.1.6, and is far from attributing it to God's action or judicial imputation. Therefore, whatever you have gathered from Calvin on all sides, either it is already reconciled with my opinion or it seems easily reconcilable with it, so there is no need to make this book longer by weighing it. One thing, however, must not be passed over. He tries to prove that corruption is called punishment by Calvin in the proper sense, and not for those reasons I mentioned above at p. 185. "For," he says, "since that is properly punishment which a judge inflicts to avenge a crime, and Calvin teaches that this punishment is derived to us from God the judge, and calls it vengeance and severe retribution proceeding from the judgment and justice of God, there can be no doubt that he spoke of punishment properly so called, and therefore acknowledged imputation." But he is mistaken. For by the name of such punishment is to be understood not corruption, but the curse or punishment owed to corruption. For he seems to have had regard to those words of Calvin, Inst. 2.1.4: "But since it must have been not a light offence but a detestable crime that God avenged so severely, we must consider the very nature of the sin in Adam's fall, which kindled the horrible vengeance of God against the whole human race." For why should we not take it in the same way as that passage Rom. 5. 15, "By the offence of one many died," which Calvin also wishes to be taken thus? "What Paul does not say perished by the offence of one, understand thus: because corruption was poured into us from him. For we do not perish by his fault as if we ourselves were outside the fault; but because his sin is the cause of our sin, Paul ascribes our ruin to him." Therefore Adam's offence kindled the horrible vengeance of God against the whole human race, because it spread and propagated itself through the whole human race. "For Adam infected his whole seed with that vitiosity into which he fell." And so "the plague instilled by him remains in us, and it is by this that punishment is due, and on account of such corruption alone we are held guilty and convicted before God." Otherwise, since punishment, which is vengeance, is satisfactory, we would be undergoing some satisfactory punishment in this age. Whether this agrees with the doctrine of Calvin and of the Reformed Church, I leave for you, most fair reader, to judge. I will add no more, nor will I examine and weigh one by one the rest of the heap of testimonies, which learned men have gathered from wherever they could and piled up like a heap. Some stand on my side, some favour neither party, and not a few oppose me. Yet even if all of them dissented from me, I would not think they should be preferred to the testimonies of Scripture and to the arguments on which I rest, which are, so far as I can grasp, plainly necessary.

units.la: CAPVT XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Respondetur ad Cap. viii. & ostenditur Ecclesiam Romanam non consensisse in illam imputationem.
units.tr: It is answered to chapter 8, and it is shown that the Roman Church has not agreed to that imputation.

units.la: PARVM abest quin hic exclamem, o tempora o mores! vbinam gentium sumus? Reformati, Euangelij Ministri, qui solam Scripturam audiendam clamant, qui ne Patrum quidem testimonijs agi causas Pontificias volunt, hi apud Reformatos, Euangelij Ministros, Theologiæ Professores, non modo Patrum antiquorum, sed priuatorum huius & præcedentis sæculi Doctorum, sed Pontificiorum etiam ipsorum authoritate pugnant! sed nolo hoc tuum consilium exagitare: obest enim causæ tuæ, quam Scripturæ & testimonijs, & argumentis destitui oportet confugientem ad confractam arundinem Pontificij consensus. Fateor ex quorundam Pontificiorum affrictu quosdam ex nostris istum errorem contraxisse : sed factum est, nescio quomodo, vt magis in nostros grassaretur, quàm in Pontificios. Non est enim quod de Pontificiæ Ecclesiæ consensu glorieris, non modò quia nulla est eius apud nos authoritas; sed quia non sentit tecum. Non certè Concilium Tridentinum, vt vel legenti manifestum est; Nec satis mirari possum, quo consilio fuerit à te, & quidem cum elogio, laudatum. Non Magister sententiarum, cuius hæc verba contra te citas distinct. 32. Quærit, inquis, qua justitia animæ munda ex creatione peccatum imputetur, & respondet, Ideo recte potest dici imputari animæ illud peccatum quod ex corruptione corporis ineuitabiliter trahit. Non enim ait animæ imputari peccatum actuale Adami, sed illud peccatum quod ex corruptione corporis ineuitabiliter trahit ? Quod autem illud est peccatum, nisi originale, quod perpetuo Lombardus à peccato actuali Adami distinguit, & negat esse actuale, & in concupiscentia cum Augustino collocat, & de eo intelligit Apostoli verba peccatum intrauit in mundum, item, peccatores sunt constituti multi; & refellit eos, qui putabant peccatum originale esse reatum pœnæ propeccato primi hominis, & qui verba Apostoli, per vnum hominem peccatum intrauit in mundum, de peccato actuali Adæ acceperunt, hos ait, fuisse Pelagianos. Legefi placet eius distinct. 30. Non etiam Thomas. Nam quæ citas ex 1. 2. q. 81. a. 1. iam expendi, & quàm tibi non foueant ostendi. Quæ autem allegas ex summa contra gentiles, eodem spectant, vt nimirum imputationem iuuuant corruptione posteriorem. Concilio Tridentino, Lombardo, &
units.tr: I can scarcely keep from exclaiming, "O the times, O the manners! Where in the world are we?" Reformed men, ministers of the Gospel, who cry out that only Scripture is to be heard, who do not want the causes of the Papists pleaded even by the testimonies of the Fathers: these men, among the Reformed, ministers of the Gospel and professors of theology, fight not only by the authority of the ancient Fathers but also by that of private teachers of this and the previous century, and even by that of the Papists themselves! But I do not want to attack your plan, for it harms your cause. A cause that must lack Scripture, testimonies and arguments has to take refuge in the broken reed of Papist consensus. I admit that some of ours have caught this error from the contact of certain Papists. But it happened, I know not how, that it raged more among our own people than among the Papists. There is no reason for you to boast of the consent of the Papist Church, not only because it has no authority among us, but because it does not agree with you. Certainly the Council of Trent does not, as is plain even to one who reads it. Nor can I sufficiently wonder with what purpose you praised it, and indeed with an encomium. Nor does the Master of Sentences, whose words you cite against yourself, distinction 32. He asks, you say, by what justice the soul, pure from creation, is imputed sin, and he answers, "Therefore it can rightly be said that the sin is imputed to the soul which it inevitably draws from the corruption of the body." For he does not say that the actual sin of Adam is imputed to the soul, but that sin which it inevitably draws from the corruption of the body. What sin is that, however, except original sin? Lombard constantly distinguishes this from the actual sin of Adam, denies that it is actual, places it in concupiscence with Augustine, and understands of it the Apostle's words, sin entered into the world, and likewise many were made sinners. He refutes those who thought original sin is the guilt of punishment for the sin of the first man, and who took the Apostle's words, through one man sin entered into the world, of the actual sin of Adam; these, he says, were Pelagians. I am pleased to have read his distinction 30. Nor does Thomas either. For what you cite from 1.2, q. 81, a. 1, I have already weighed, and I have shown how little it favours you. What you cite from the Summa against the Gentiles bears on the same point, namely that it supports imputation by a corruption posterior to it. You add to the Council of Trent, Lombard, and

units.la: Thomæ addis, non sine elogio, Bellarmirum tibi in speciem magis quàm re ipsa fauentem, præterea neminem. Ego verò, ut intelligas quàm non sit tibi gloriandum de consensu Ecclesiæ Romanæ, proferam contra te duos aut tres testes. Prodeat primus Anselmus Abbas, Archiepiscopus, Abbate Bernardo, quem tu sanctum appellasti & inter Patres numerasti, aliquot annis antiquior, Negauerat Deum filijs imputare peccata parentum, atque vrserat verba Dei apud Ezechielem, Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris, Hinc nascebatur obiectio de peccato originali, cui sic occurrit. At si obijcitur, inquit, quia omnes qui non saluantur per fidem, quæ est in Christo, portant iniquitatem & onus Adæ, ut per hoc velit probare infantes, aut aliorum quoque parentum iniquitatem similiter debere portare, aut illius non debere, consideret diligenter, quia non portant peccatum Adæ, sed suum. Nam aliud fuit peccatum Adæ, aliud infantum; quia differunt, ut dictum est: illud enim fuit causa, istud est effectus: Adam caruit debita iustitia, non quam alius, sed quam ipse deseruit. Infantes carent ea, non quam ipsi, sed alius dereliquit. Non est ergo idem peccatum Adæ & infantum; Et cum dicit Apostolus, quod supra posui, quia mors regnauit ab Adam vsque ad Mosem, etiam in eos qui non peccauerunt in similitudinem prævaricationis Adæ, sicut significat infantum minus esse quàm Adæ peccatum, ita aperte monstratur aliud esse. Quapropter cum damnatur infans propeccato originali, damnatur non propeccato Adæ, sed pro suo. Nam si ipse non haberet suum peccatum, non damnaretur. Ita ergo non portat iniquitatem Adæ, sed suam, quamuis ideo dicatur portare, quia iniquitas illius peccati istius causa fuit. Huic qui Patribus accensuri potuit, subjungam Ie- lib de Concc. ptu Virtg & peccato origin. cap. 2 fuitam Iustinianum de Chryfostomi, & Concilij Tridentini, & sua ipsius sententia testimonium perhibentem. Chrysostomus, inquit, id solum contendit non esse nos reos ob illud ipsum Adæ peccatum, quod ab illo patratum est, quod verissimum censeri debet; quandoquidem originale peccatum, ut tridentinum Concilium definit, origine quidem unum, sed propagatione transfusum in omnes inest unicuique proprium, ac suum. Isti comitem dabo Estium primarium in Academia Duacena Theologiae Professorem, Comment. in Rom. cap. v. verf. 12. Peccatum, inquit, accipitur generaliter; sed proprie tamen, ut significet id omne quod veram culpæ rationem habet, sive quid aliud: sed hic verificatio fit de peccato quod propagatur, id est, de peccato originali. Hoc autem non est ipsa actualis Adæ transgressio, quæ nonnisi in illo esse potuit, & in eo deleta fuit per pœnitentiam, sed peccatum in quo, & cum quo singuli eius posteri nascuntur: quod etsi Adæ peccatum sit, id est, eius voluntate factum, ideoque & origine unum: propagatione tamen transfusum omnibus inest, unicuique proprium, quemadmodum loquitur ac definit tridentina Synodus Canone tertio. His, si opus esset, Stapletonum, aliosque subjungerem: sed piget me in eiusmodi hominum testimonijs vel conquirendis, vel describendis bonas horas inutiliter collocare. Tu, si mihi credes, in posterum missis humanis præsidijs ad divina oracula te convertes, ijsque contentus eris, quæ quicquid nobis est ad salutem credendum & plenè, & perspicuè reuelant.
units.tr: Thomas, not without praise, Bellarmine, who favours you in appearance more than in reality, and no one else. But I, so that you may understand how little you have to boast of the consent of the Roman Church, will bring forward two or three witnesses against you. Let the first come forward: Anselm, abbot and archbishop, some years older than Abbot Bernard, whom you called holy and numbered among the Fathers. He had denied that God imputes the sins of parents to their children, and had urged the words of God in Ezekiel, "The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father." From this an objection about original sin arose, to which he replies thus: "But if it is objected that all who are not saved through the faith which is in Christ bear the iniquity and burden of Adam, so that by this one wishes to prove that infants, or the iniquity of other parents also, ought similarly to bear it, or ought not to bear it, let him consider carefully, because they do not bear the sin of Adam but their own. For the sin of Adam was one thing, that of infants another, because they differ, as has been said. For the former was the cause, the latter is the effect. Adam lacked the due righteousness, not which another, but which he himself abandoned. Infants lack it, not which they themselves, but which another abandoned. The sin of Adam and of infants is therefore not the same." And when the Apostle says, "which I have placed above, that death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of the transgression of Adam," he clearly shows, as he signifies that the sin of infants is less than that of Adam, that the one is other than the other. Therefore when an infant is condemned for original sin, he is condemned not for the sin of Adam but for his own. For if he did not have his own sin, he would not be condemned. So he does not bear the iniquity of Adam but his own, although he is said to bear it because that iniquity of Adam was the cause of this one." To this man, who could be numbered among the Fathers, I will add Justinian, who bears witness to Chrysostom, to the Council of Trent, and to his own opinion. Chrysostom, he says, "contends only that we are not guilty on account of that very sin of Adam which was committed by him, which ought to be judged most true; since original sin, as the Council of Trent defines, is one in origin but transmitted by propagation, and it is present in each one as his own and proper." As companion to these I will give Estius, the foremost professor of theology in the Academy of Douai, in his commentary on Romans 5:12: "Sin, he says, is taken generally; but properly, nonetheless, so as to signify all that has the true character of guilt, or something else. But here the statement is made about sin that is propagated, that is, about original sin. This is not the actual transgression of Adam itself, which could exist only in him, and was blotted out in him through repentance; but it is the sin in which and with which each of his posterity is born. Although this is the sin of Adam, that is, done by his will, and therefore one in origin, nonetheless, transmitted by propagation, it is present in all, each one's own, just as the Synod of Trent speaks and defines in its third canon." If it were necessary I would add Stapleton and others to these. But I am vexed to spend good hours uselessly, either in seeking out or in copying out the testimonies of such men. You, if you believe me, will in future, having put aside human aids, turn to the divine oracles, and be content with those which fully and plainly reveal whatever we must believe for salvation.
